profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-06T13:40:47.72+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial command
Later Student Tiāntāi
Tang,
an ancient state name.
Lù Démíng said: King Chéng of Zhōu’s younger maternal uncle Shū Yú was enfeoffed in Táng,
its territory being the ruins where Emperor Yáo and Xià Yǔ had their capitals.
In Hàn times it was called Tàiyuán Commandery,
located west of the ancient Jìzhōu’s Tàiháng and Héng Mountains,
in the region of Tàiyuán and Tàiyuè.
The ancestors of the Lǐ Táng,
Lǐ Hǔ and Lǐ Bì, along with six others, assisted Zhōu in attacking Wèi and achieved merit,
all becoming Pillars of the State,
known as the Eight Pillar State families.
When Emperor Mǐn of Zhōu received the abdication from Wèi,
Hǔ had already died,
so his achievements were posthumously recorded,
and he was enfeoffed as Duke of Táng.
He gave birth to Bǐng,
who inherited the enfeoffment.
Bǐng gave birth to Yuān,
who inherited the enfeoffment,
raised troops and captured Cháng’ān,
was promoted to King of Táng,
and subsequently received the abdication from Suí,
thus the state was named Táng.
Emperor Gāozǔ, Divine Yáo, Great Sage, Luminous and Filial Emperor, First Part, First Scroll
His personal name was Yuān,
courtesy name Shūdé,
originally from Chéngjǐ in Lǒngxī.
His seventh-generation ancestor Hǎo was king of Xīliáng,
known as King Wǔzhāo of Liáng.
Down to his great-grandson Xī, the family settled in Wǔchuān;
Xī’s grandson Hǔ,
following Emperor Wén of Zhōu,
first made his home in Cháng’ān.
First year of Wǔdé
(Wùyín, 618)
In this year, in the fifth month, he received the abdication from Suí,
and first changed the era name.
1 Spring,
first month,
first day, Dīngwèi.
The Suí Emperor Gōng issued an edict that the King of Táng could wear his sword and shoes when ascending the hall,
and be announced without his personal name.
Suí Records: According to Hàn customs, from the Son of Heaven down to all officials, none failed to wear a sword.
Cài Mó’s discussion states: Great ministers granted special courtesies all wore swords and shoes when ascending the hall;
it was not that attendants removed them,
but rather to guard against blades.
In recent times, wooden ones were used,
the origin of which is unclear;
Dōng Qí established regulations,
calling them “image swords,”
meaning they resembled swords.
During Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu’s time,
when all officials gathered for banquets,
they also wore swords when ascending their seats.
By the beginning of Kāihuáng,
following the old practice,
when wearing court attire and ascending the hall,
they still did not remove them.
In the twelfth year,
due to Cài Zhēng’s memorial,
it was first decreed that all who attended court assemblies and should ascend to sit in the hall,
must remove both sword and shoes;
those who did not sit,
if summoned by edict to report matters,
and needed to ascend the hall,
also removed their swords at their mats before ascending.
The Nàyán, Huángmén, Nèishǐ Lìng, Shìláng, and Shèrén, being officials serving in close attendance, did not remove them,
and their swords were real blades, not imitations.
Also,
according to the fixed decree of the first year of Xiánkāng of Jìn,
by precedent, from the Son of Heaven downward, all wore robes, caps, and swords;
now the Son of Heaven had jade-adorned, fire-pearl-pommeled swords,
only attendants wore swords when ascending the hall;
from princes and dukes downward,
unless granted special courtesy,
when summoned to ascend the hall,
all went to their mats,
removed them and then ascended.
Double-soled shoes are called xì,
single-soled shoes are called lǚ.
All who were not attendants,
removed their shoes when ascending the hall.
Xì were worn only with ceremonial caps and full attire;
lǚ were used with all other attire.
In all court assemblies, when announcing and bowing,
it was said, “So-and-so, official of such-and-such”;
not using the personal name,
was also a special courtesy.
Shàng,
read as shǎng at that time.
Biāo,
read as pīzhāo.
After the King of Táng captured Cháng’ān,
he sent letters instructing the various commanderies and counties,
and so from the east, starting from Shāngluò,
Suí Records: Shāngluò County belonged to Shàngluò Commandery,
taking its name from Shāng Mountain and Luò River.
the chief officials of commanderies and counties, leaders of bandits, and chieftains of Dí and Qiāng tribes,
vied in sending their sons and younger brothers for audience to request surrender,
the responsible office replied with letters,
numbering a hundred daily.
2 After Wáng Shìchōng obtained the troops of the Eastern Capital,
he advanced to attack Lǐ Mì north of the Luò River,
defeated him,
and subsequently stationed his army north of Gǒng.
(North of Gǒng County.)
On Xīnyǒu day
Shìchōng ordered each army to construct pontoon bridges to cross the Luò River and attack Mì.
The army whose bridge was completed first would advance first,
resulting in an uncoordinated advance.
The Tiger Guard General Wáng Biàn breached the outer palisades of Mì's camp.
Panic and disturbance arose within Mì's camp,
and it was on the verge of collapse.
Shìchōng, unaware of this,
sounded the horn to recall his troops.
Mì then led his dare-to-die warriors to take advantage of the situation and attack.
Shìchōng suffered a major defeat,
with over ten thousand men drowning while scrambling for the bridges.
Wáng Biàn died,
and Shìchōng barely escaped with his life.
All the armies north of the Luò River collapsed.
Shìchōng did not dare enter the Eastern Capital,
but headed north towards Héyáng.
That night,
a fierce wind brought cold rain.
The soldiers waded through water and became soaked.
Several tens of thousands more froze to death on the roads.
Shìchōng alone reached Héyáng with several thousand men.
Textual Analysis: The Suí Shū and Běi Shǐ biographies of Lǐ Mì state:
"Shìchōng again moved his camp north of the Luò River,
facing Gǒng County to the south.
Afterwards, he built pontoon bridges on the Luò River
and attacked Mì with his entire force.
Mì launched a counterattack.
The government troops retreated slightly,
and tens of thousands of them trampled and drowned each other.
Shìchōng barely escaped.
He did not dare return to the Eastern Capital,
but fled to Héyáng.
That night,
over a foot of snow fell.
Nearly all the troops following him perished."
The biography of Wáng Shìchōng states:
"Chōng was utterly defeated.
Over ten thousand men drowned in the water.
At that time, the weather was cold with heavy snow.
After the soldiers crossed the water,
their clothes were all soaked.
Several tens of thousands more froze to death on the roads."
The Biography of the Duke of Púshān states:
"Shìchōng moved his camp to the north bank of the Luò River,
facing Mì across the river.
Mì then built a long wall,
dug deep moats,
surrounding an area of seventy lǐ to fortify himself.
On the 15th,
Shìchōng fought Mì east of the Shíkū Temple.
Mì's army retreated and was defeated.
Shìchōng crossed the Luò River to press the advantage,
advancing close to the Cāngchéng to establish his camp and trenches.
Mì unleashed his troops in a fierce battle.
Shìchōng's soldiers and horses abandoned their weapons and fled.
Countless numbers drowned.
Mì also issued a public proclamation to his headquarters, stating: 'Shìchōng stationed his troops north of the Luò River at dawn on the 11th of this month,
and stealthily entered Yuèchéng.
On the 15th of the same month,
Shìchōng and Wáng Biàncái and others again stealthily crossed the river south of Cāngchéng,
daring to press close to the city walls.'"
The Hé Luò Jì states: On the 16th,
"Chōng fought Mì east of the Shíkū Temple."
It also states:
"That night,
they encountered fierce winds and cold, driving rain.
The soldiers froze to death,
with scarcely one in ten surviving.
Chōng escaped and fled under cover of night,
heading straight for Héyáng."
The rest is as in the Biography of the Duke of Púshān.
The Lüè Jì states:
"On Xīnyǒu day,
Wáng Shìchōng and others moved their troops north of the Luò River.
He then ordered the armies to deploy troops along the bank.
Each army separately built pontoon bridges.
The army whose bridge was completed first would cross immediately.
As the advance was uncoordinated,
Lǐ Mì sprung an ambush.
Our army was utterly defeated.
Fifty or sixty percent of the troops drowned while scrambling for the bridges."
The Zá Jì states:
"In the twelfth month,
the Prince of Yuè sent the Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, Wéi Jì, and others to lead thirty thousand garrison troops, all placed under Shìchōng's command."
It also states:
"After Wáng Biànzòng and others were defeated,
the various armies also collapsed.
They scrambled for the bridges and plunged into the water.
The majority died.
Wáng Biànzòng and others all perished.
Only Shìchōng, having been defeated, escaped.
He fled with several hundred cavalry to Dàtōng City.
The defeated soldiers who managed to return
encountered heavy rain on the road.
Six or seven thousand froze to death.
Shìchōng stayed in Dàtōng for over ten days,
fearing punishment and not daring to return.
In the 14th year,
first month,
the Prince of Yuè sent Shìchōng's elder brother, Shìyùn, to Dàtōng to console and instruct him,
pardoning Shìchōng's crime of losing the army."
According to Lǐ Dàoxuán's memorial urging Lǐ Mì to assume the throne, it states:
"At that time, the month of Tàicòu had just begun,
when drizzle is not yet appropriate,
yet a sudden downpour fell,
and the frozen dead were nearly all gone."
Now, synthesizing information from various texts,
the date follows the Biography of the Duke of Púshān,
and the rain follows the Hé Luò Jì.
The Prince of Yuè, Tóng, sent an envoy to pardon him,
summoning him back to the Eastern Capital,
and bestowed gold, silk, and beautiful women to appease him.
Shìchōng gathered the scattered survivors,
obtaining over ten thousand men,
and stationed them at Hánjiā City.
(Hánjiā City
was likely located north of the capital city.
According to the Old Táng Shū biography of Wáng Shìchōng,
Hánjiā
was a granary city.)
Mì, riding the momentum of victory, advanced and occupied Jīnyōng City.
He repaired its gates, walls, and buildings and resided there.
The sounds of gongs and drums
could be heard in the Eastern Capital.
Before long,
he commanded a force of three hundred thousand,
arrayed them at Běimáng,
and pressed south towards the Shàngchūn Gate.
On Yǐchǒu day,
the Grand Master of the Palace with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon, Duàn Dá, and the Minister of Revenue, Wéi Jīn, led troops to resist him.
Dá, seeing the size of Mì's forces,
became frightened and retreated first.
Mì unleashed his troops to take advantage,
and the army subsequently collapsed.
Wéi Jīn died.
Textual Analysis: The Suí Shū biographies do not mention the date of this battle.
The Biography of the Duke of Púshān places this battle on the ninth day of the fourth month.
The Lüè Jì also states:
"In the fourth month,
on Yǐwèi day,
Lǐ Mì led his forces north to occupy Mángshān,
connecting south to the Shàngchūn Gate.
Duàn Dá, Wéi Jīn, and others led troops to resist him.
Before the armies engaged, Dá became frightened,
retreated first into the city,
and the army subsequently collapsed into chaos."
Yǐwèi day
was the 21st.
Now, according to the Hé Luò Jì,
"On the 19th day of the first month,
Shìchōng again fought Mì outside the Shàngchūn Gate,
and Wéi Jīn perished there."
Also,
in the second month,
Fáng Yànzǎo's letter to Dòu Jiàndé also stated
"The command headquarters, on the 19th of last month, personally led fierce troops
west to capture Luòyì."
The dates from the fourth month onward in the Biography of the Duke of Púshān
often conflict and do not match events.
The date now follows the Hé Luò Jì,
and the events follow the Lüè Jì and the Suí Shū biography of Duàn Dá.
According to Suí dynasty regulations: the Director of the Bureau of Operations,
was subordinate to the Minister of War.
Dòu Jiàndé, Zhū Càn, Mèng Hǎigōng, Xú Yuánlǎng, and others all sent envoys presenting memorials urging Mì to assume the throne.
Mì's officials, Péi Rénjī and others, also submitted memorials requesting he assume the imperial title.
Mì said:
"The Eastern Capital is not yet pacified.
This matter cannot be discussed."
3 On Wùchén day,
the Prince of Táng appointed his heir, Jiànchéng, as Left Marshal,
and the Duke of Qín, Shìmín, as Right Marshal,
to supervise an army of over one hundred thousand men to rescue the Eastern Capital.
4 The Eastern Capital was short of food.

The Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury, Yuán Wéndū, and others recruited those willing to defend the city without consuming government rations by offering them honorary second-rank positions.
Consequently, merchants holding ivory tablets and attending court
were too numerous to count.
(The "xiàng" refers to the ivory tablet.
It is the ivory tablet.
Since the Western Wèi,
officials of the fifth rank and above commonly used ivory.
Merchant,
pronounced gǔ.
Court/attend court,
pronounced zhí yáo fān.
Count/surpass,
pronounced shēng.)
5 In the second month,
on the day Jǐmǎo,
the Prince of Táng dispatched Tàicháng Qīng Zhèng Yuánshí to lead troops out through Shāng and Luò,
to pacify Nányáng.
Emperor Yáng had changed Dèng Prefecture to Nányáng Commandery.
Shí,
pronounced like "shū" and "yù".
Jiàng (to lead),
pronounced jí liàng.
The Sui dynasty's twelve Wèi Prefectures each had a Chief Clerk and an Adjutant.
Emperor Yáng changed Ān Prefecture to Ānlù Commandery;
Jīng Prefecture,
to Nán Commandery;
Xiāng Prefecture,
to Xiāngyáng Commandery.
6 Lǐ Mì sent Fáng Yànzǎo, Zhèng Tǐng, and others
east out of Líyáng,
to travel by separate routes to summon and pacify the prefectures and counties.
He appointed Liáng Commandery Grand Administrator Yáng Wāng as Shàngzhùguó and Sòng Prefecture Commander-in-Chief.
Emperor Yáng had changed Sòng Prefecture to Liáng Commandery.
Shǒu (to administer),
pronounced shì yòu.
"In the past at Yōngqiū,
you once pursued and captured me,
the event is recorded in the 183rd scroll, the 12th year of the Dàyè era.
I dare not presume."
Guǎn Zhòng shot Duke Huán of Qí, hitting his belt hook,
yet Duke Huán employed him as his chancellor.
In Jìn, the eunuch Pī attacked Prince Chóng'ěr,
cutting off his sleeve,
yet Duke Wén bore no grudge.
Here, "qū" (sleeve cuff) is used for "mèi" (sleeve).
Shè (to shoot),
pronounced ér yì.
Jī (to presume),
pronounced jū xī.
Mì also treated him with restraint and control.
Yànzǎo sent a letter summoning Dòu Jiàndé,
urging him to come and see Mì.
Jiàndé replied in writing,
with humble words and generous gifts,
using the excuse of Luó Yì's southern invasion,
requesting to defend the northern frontier.
Yànzǎo returned,
reaching Wèi Prefecture,
where the bandit leader Wáng Dérén ambushed and killed him.
Dérén had tens of thousands of followers,
occupying Línlǜ Mountain.
Wèi Prefecture,
under the Sui, was Jí Commandery.
Línlǜ Mountain,
is in Línlǜ County of Wèi Commandery.
Lǜ,
pronounced lú.
He was a scourge to several prefectures.
7 In the third month,
on the day Jǐyǒu,
Qí Duke Lǐ Yuánjí was appointed as Zhènběi General.
Textual analysis notes: The Chuàngyè Zhù states,
"The Tàiyuán Liúshǒu was changed to the Zhènběi Prefecture,"
on the day Jǐsì of the twelfth month last year.
This was likely mentioned in connection with Yuánjí's advancement to the title of Qí Duke.
We now follow the Shílù.
He was permitted to act according to circumstances.
8 Sui Emperor Yáng arrived at Jiāngdū.
In the 12th year of the Dàyè era,
Emperor Yáng reached Jiāngdū.
Within the palace, there were over a hundred chambers,
each richly furnished and supplied,
filled with beauties.
Each day, one chamber was designated as host.
Jiāngdū Commandery Deputy Zhào Yuánkǎng was in charge of providing wine and food.
The Emperor, Empress Xiāo, and his favored consorts would go from one feast to another,
wine cups never leaving their lips,
and the over one thousand accompanying consorts were also often drunk.
However, seeing the peril and disorder in the realm,
the Emperor's mind was also troubled and unsettled.
After court, he would wear a headscarf and short robe,
lean on a staff and stroll,
traversing all the terraces and pavilions,
not stopping until night,
anxiously gazing at the scenery,
fearing only that it was not enough.
The Emperor himself was skilled in divination, astrology, and physiognomy,
and enjoyed speaking the Wú dialect.
He often set out wine at night,
looked up at the celestial phenomena,
and said to Empress Xiāo:
"Out there, many people are plotting against me (nóng),
People of Wú generally refer to themselves as 'nóng'.
but you will not fail to become Empress Shěn,
to Chángchéng Gōng,
Chén Shūbǎo.
Shūbǎo's empress was Lady Shěn.
Thereupon, he drained his cup and became deeply intoxicated.
He also once held up a mirror to look at himself,
turned and said to Empress Xiāo:
"What a fine head and neck,
who will be the one to chop it off!"
The Empress, alarmed, asked the reason,
the Emperor laughed and said:
"Nobility and baseness, suffering and joy,
take turns replacing each other,
what harm is there in that!"
The Emperor, seeing the Central Plains already in chaos,
had no intention of returning north.
He wished to make Dānyáng his capital.
The Emperor had changed Jiǎng Prefecture to Dānyáng Commandery,
intending to make Jiànkāng his capital.
Textual analysis notes: The Dàyè Jì states:
"The Emperor wished to make a southern tour to Kuàijī."
We now follow the Suī Shū.
He ordered his assembled ministers to deliberate in court.
Nèishǐ Shìláng Yú Shìjī and others all considered it good;
Right Guard General-in-Chief Lǐ Cái strenuously argued it was not feasible,
requesting the imperial carriage to return to Cháng'ān,
and left after a heated dispute with Shìjī.
Menxià Lùshì Héngshuǐ Lǐ Tóngkè said:
According to Sui regulations,
the Menxià Department had six each of Lùshì, Tōngshì, and Lìngshǐ.
Héngshuǐ County belonged to Xìndū Commandery,
established in the 16th year of the Kāihuáng era from the northern border of Xìndū, the western border of Wǔyì, and the southern border of Xiàbó.
Sòng Bái said: Héngshuǐ County,
was originally the Hàn dynasty's Táo County.
"Jiāngdōng is low and damp,
the land is treacherous and narrow.
Internally, it must support the imperial household,
externally, it must supply the three armies.
The people cannot bear the burden,
and I fear it will ultimately lead to dispersal and disorder."
The Censor impeached Tóngkè for slandering and undermining court governance.
Thereupon, the dukes and ministers all flattered, saying:
"The people of Jiāngdōng have long hoped for Your Majesty's presence,
if Your Majesty crosses the river,
to pacify and rule over them,
this would be the work of the Great Yǔ."
Yǔ made a southern inspection tour,
and assembled the feudal lords at Kuàijī.
He planned to move the capital there.
At that time, the provisions in Jiāngdū were exhausted,
and many of the elite troops accompanying the imperial carriage were from Guānzhōng.
Having been away from home for a long time, they longed for their hometowns.
Seeing that the Emperor had no intention of heading west,
many plotted to defect and return home.
The Commandant Dòu Xián then led his troops westward in flight.
The Emperor dispatched cavalry to pursue and execute him,
but those fleeing still did not stop.
The Emperor was troubled by this.
The Tiger-Ben Commandant Sīmǎ Dékān, a native of Fúfēng, had long been favored by the Emperor.
The Emperor put him in charge of the elite troops, stationing them in the eastern part of the city.
Dékān conspired with his close associates, Tiger-Ben Commandant Yuán Lǐ and Attendant of the Direct Access to the Palace Péi Qiántōng, saying:
Emperor Yang established the Left and Right Gatekeeper Offices, each with six Attendants of the Direct Access to the Palace,
of the fifth rank.
"Now, every one of the elite troops wants to flee.
If I report this,
I fear I will be executed before anything happens.
If I do not report it,
and the matter comes to light later,
I will still not escape the extermination of my clan.
What should we do?
Moreover, I have heard that Guānzhōng has fallen,
and Lǐ Xiàocháng has rebelled from Huàyīn.
This matter is recorded in the previous volume, last year.
Huà,
read as 'hù huà'.
He wants to kill them.
Our families are all in the west.
How can we not worry about this!"
Both of them were frightened
and said:
"Then what plan should we adopt?"
Dékān said:
"If the elite troops are going to flee,
it would be better to go with them."
Both of them said:
"Good!"
Consequently, they began to recruit others.
The Palace Secretariat Scribe Yuán Mǐn, Tiger-Tooth Commandant Zhào Xíngshū, Eagle-Soaring Commandant Mèng Bǐng, Seal and Tally Attendant Niú
Fāngyù, Chief Attendant Xǔ Hóngrén, Xuē Shìliáng, City Gate Attendant Táng Fèngyì, Chief Physician Zhāng Kǎi, and Meritorious Attendant Yáng Shìlǎn, among others,
at the beginning of the Suí dynasty,
the Chancellery oversaw six bureaus: City Gates, Imperial Meals, Imperial Medicine, Seals and Tallies, Imperial Storehouse, and Palace Interior,
each with its own Chief Attendant.
Emperor Yang placed the City Gates, Imperial Meals, Imperial Medicine, and Imperial Storehouse bureaus under the Palace Administration;
changed the Seal and Tally Supervisor to Attendant;
established a Commandant for the City Gates,
later changing the Commandant to City Gate Attendant;
and also established the positions of Director of Medicine and Assistant Physician, among others.
It is likely that the Chief Physician is the Director of Medicine.
Meritorious Attendant,
is one of the three types of Attendants.
Seal,
read as 'sī shì'.
Chief,
read as 'zhī liǎng'.
day and night formed alliances and made agreements,
openly discussing plans for rebellion in public gatherings,
without any fear or avoidance.
A palace maid reported to Empress Xiāo, saying:
"Everyone outside wants to rebel."
The Empress said:
"Go ahead and report it."
The palace maid spoke to the Emperor,
who became furious,
considering it inappropriate for her to speak of such matters,
and had her executed.
Afterwards, palace maids again reported to the Empress,
who said:
"The affairs of the empire have reached this point in a single day.
There is no way to save it.
What is the use of speaking about it?
It only worries the Emperor!"
From then on, no one spoke of it again.
Zhào Xíngshū had long been close with the Assistant Director of the Palace Buildings Yǔwén Zhìjí.
Yáng Shìlǎn
was Zhìjí's nephew.
The two informed Zhìjí of their plot;
Zhìjí was greatly pleased.
Dékān and the others planned to form their faction and flee west on the full moon day of the third month.
Zhìjí said:
"Although the sovereign is without virtue,
his authority and commands still hold sway.
If you gentlemen flee,
you will merely be following Dòu Xián to your deaths.
Now Heaven truly intends to destroy Suí.
Heroes are rising everywhere.
Tens of thousands are already united in their intent to rebel.
Seizing this opportunity to undertake a great enterprise
is the work of founding an imperial dynasty."
Dékān and the others agreed.
Xíngshū and Xuē Shìliáng requested that Zhìjí's elder brother, General of the Right Garrison Guard and Duke of Xǔ, Yǔwén Huàjí, be made their leader.
After the agreement was settled,
they informed Huàjí.
Huàjí was by nature timid and cowardly.
Upon hearing this,
his countenance changed and he broke into a sweat.
However, he eventually went along with it.
An examination of discrepancies: The Biography of the Duke of Púshān says:
"Zhào Xíngshū and Yáng Shìlǎn informed Yǔwén Huàjí of Sīmǎ Dékān's plot.
Huàjí and his brothers were overjoyed upon hearing it
and consequently summoned Dékān and the others for a meeting.
Yǔwén Shìjí persuaded Dékān and the others, saying: 'You gentlemen, acting on the hearts of the common people,
are planning an extraordinary undertaking.
Merely intending to flee
is certainly not a long-term strategy.'
Dékān said: 'What should we do then?'
Shìjí said: 'Although the sovereign is said to be without virtue,
his officials still fear and obey him.
If they hear of your rebellion and flight,
they will certainly pursue and capture you urgently.
The case of Dòu Xián
is a clear warning from the recent past.
It would be better to strictly command your troops and horses,
attack his palace,
follow the people's desires,
proclaim the deposition of the benighted and cruel ruler,
and the undertaking is sure to succeed.
Afterwards, carefully establish a wise and enlightened ruler.
The empire can then be pacified,
and we will have no worries.
Once merit and achievement are gathered,
you gentlemen will sit and enjoy glory and emolument.
Even if the undertaking does not succeed,
your prestige and reputation will be greatly enhanced,

If they come to challenge us to battle,
be careful not to respond.
Wait until my illness improves,
and I will defeat them for you."
Kāishān withdrew
and said to Wénjìng:
"The Prince is worried that you cannot handle this,
hence these words.
Moreover, if the enemy hears the Prince is ill,
they will surely look down on us.
We should display our military might to intimidate them."
So they deployed their forces southwest of Gāozhǐ,
relying on their numbers and not setting up defenses.
Jǔ secretly moved his army to attack their rear.
On the Rénzǐ day,
they fought at Qiǎnshuǐyuán.
(The *New Annals*: Yílù County in Bīn Province had Qiǎnshuǐyuán.)
Five or six out of ten soldiers died.
The great generals Mùróng Luóhóu, Lǐ Ānyuǎn, and Liú Hóngjī were all lost.
Shìmín led his troops back to Cháng'ān.
Jǔ then captured Gāozhǐ,
and collected the dead Táng soldiers to build a victory mound;
Wénjìng and others were all dismissed from their posts.
On the 47th day, Yǐmǎo,
the rebel leader of Yúlín, Guō Zǐhé, sent an envoy to surrender,
and was appointed Area Commander of Líng Province.
48. Whenever Lǐ Mì achieved a victory in battle,
he would invariably send a messenger to report the success to the Lord of Huángtài.
The people of Suí were all delighted,
but Wáng Shìchōng alone said to his subordinates:
"Yuán Wéndū and his ilk
are nothing more than petty clerks.
Observing the situation,
I believe they will certainly be captured by Lǐ Mì.
Moreover, our soldiers have repeatedly fought against Mì,
losing their fathers, brothers, and sons.
The casualties, both past and present, are already numerous.
If one day we become subordinate to him,
our kind will be wiped out!"
He intended to incite anger among his troops.
Wéndū, hearing of this,
became greatly afraid.
Together with Lú Chǔ and others, he plotted to take advantage of Shìchōng's attendance at court
to ambush and kill him with hidden soldiers.
Duàn Dá was by nature mediocre and cowardly.
Fearing their plan would not succeed,
he sent his son-in-law Zhāng Zhì to inform Shìchōng of Chǔ and the others' plot.
On the night of the Wùwǔ day, during the third watch,
Shìchōng led his troops to attack Hánjiā Gate.
Hánjiā Gate
was likely named for its connection to Hánjiā City.
Examination of Discrepancies says: The Héluò Jì records:
"Initially,

Lú Chǔ privately said to Wéndū: 'Wáng Shìchōng is merely a general of the external army,

and have been lenient, overlooking faults.
Yet he, in turn, presumes to control personnel matters,
acting arrogantly and arbitrarily.
If he is not eliminated,
I fear he will become a calamity for the state.'
Wéndū said: 'He cannot be killed immediately.

Chǔ said: 'Good.'
Wéndū, holding the memorial, entered the palace hall,

Zhào Jìqīng privately informed Shìchōng,

because of the imperial aunt.
Initially,
Shìchōng's wife, Xiāo shì, died early.
Later, there was a woman named Hú shì,
who was also in Jiāngdū.

At this point, contending for power,
he raised troops."
Wéndū and others ordered Zhào Fānghǎi to pursue Shìchōng back and forth,
but Shìchōng feigned illness and did not accept the summons."
According to this, Shìchōng's conflict with Wéndū was precisely over the matter of contending with Lǐ Mì, leading to mutual attempts to kill each other.
I fear the events did not stem from this cause.
Therefore, I do not adopt this account.
(Shìchōng) entered and served the Lord of Huángtài, who held court in the Qiányáng Hall.

Duàn Dá then ordered General Huáng Táoshù to seize and deliver Wéndū.
Wéndū, looking back at the Lord of Huángtài, said:

The Lord of Huángtài, weeping bitterly, sent him away.

The Lord of Huángtài said to Shìchōng:
"You arbitrarily killed each other,
without even reporting it.
Is this the way of a minister?
If you wish to exercise your brute force,
how dare you involve me!"
Shìchōng prostrated himself, weeping, and apologized:
"I was selected and promoted by the late emperor.
Even grinding my bones to powder would not repay his kindness.
Wéndū and others harbored treacherous intentions,
wishing to summon Lǐ Mì to endanger the state.
Resenting my opposition,
they deeply accumulated suspicion and hatred towards me.
I was forced to save my own life,
and had no time to report.
If within my heart I harbor evil intentions,
and betray Your Majesty,
may Heaven, Earth, the Sun, and the Moon,
which truly shine upon all,
cause my entire family to be exterminated,

His words and tears flowed together.
The Lord of Huángtài believed him to be sincere,
led him and ordered him to ascend the hall,
spoke with him for a long time,
and then went with him to see the Empress Dowager;
(she was) the mother of the Lord of Huángtài, Liú Liángdì.
(Shìchōng) claimed he dared not have disloyal thoughts.
He was then appointed Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs and Commander-in-Chief of All Internal and External Military Affairs.
By noon,
they captured Zhào Chángwén and Guō Wényì,
and killed them.

is pronounced zhǎng.

Shìchōng moved from Hánjiā City to reside in the Department of State Affairs,
gradually building a faction of supporters,
and arbitrarily exercised authority.
He appointed his elder brother Shìyūn as Head of the Palace Secretariat,
who entered and resided within the palace precincts.
His sons and nephews all commanded troops.
He divided government affairs into ten categories,
placing all of them under the control of his partisans.
His power shook both inside and outside the court.

49. Lǐ Mì was about to proceed to court.
Upon reaching Wēn,
(Note: According to the Suí Records,

he then returned to Jīnyōng.
The Eastern Capital suffered a great famine.
Private coinage was rampant and debased.
More than half were adulterated with tin rings.
At the beginning of the Suí Kāihuáng reign,
coins in circulation
all had to be alloyed with tin solder.
Since tin solder was cheap,
many sought profit,
and privately minted coins
could not be prohibited or regulated.
An edict was then issued forbidding private mining in places where tin solder was produced,
standards were posted with sample coins,
and those not matching the samples were not allowed into the market.
By the end of the Dàyè reign,
the imperial laws and order were lax and disordered,
private minting increased further,
and coins became increasingly thin and inferior.
Initially, each thousand still weighed two catties,
gradually lightening to one catty.
Some cut iron sheets,
or trimmed leather and pasted paper to make coins,
using them mixed together.
Huán
is pronounced huán.
One hú of rice cost eighty to ninety thousand coins.
In the early years of the Wǔdé era (618-626 AD),
Lǐ Mì had once studied under the Confucian scholar Xú Wényuǎn.
Wényuǎn served as the Chancellor of the National University (Guózǐ Jìjiǔ) for the Huángtài Emperor (Yáng Tóng),
and once went out himself to gather firewood,
where he was captured by Lǐ Mì's army.
Lǐ Mì ordered Wényuǎn to sit facing south,
prepared the rites appropriate for a disciple,
and bowed to him facing north.
Wényuǎn said:
"Since this old man has received such generous courtesy,
how dare I not speak my mind fully!
I wonder if the General's ambition is to become like Yǐ Yǐn and Huò Guāng, to restore a broken lineage and support a tottering state?
If so, then although this old man is in his declining years,
I am still willing to exert my utmost effort;
but if you aim to be like Wáng Mǎng or Dǒng Zhuó,
taking advantage of peril to seek profit,
then there is no use for this old man!"
Lǐ Mì kowtowed and said:
"Recently, having received the court's command,
I have been appointed to a high ducal position.
I hope to exhaust my mediocre and shallow abilities
to rescue and aid the nation in its distress.
This is my fundamental ambition."
Wényuǎn said:
"General, you are the son of a famous minister.
Lǐ Mì,
was the son of Lǐ Kuān;
Kuān was a general of the Northern Zhōu dynasty,
renowned for his bravery and prowess.
If you can correct your course before going too far astray,
you can still be counted as a loyal and righteous minister!"
Later, when Wáng Shìchōng killed Yuán Wéndū and others,
Lǐ Mì again sought advice from Wényuǎn.
Wényuǎn said:
"Shìchōng was also a student of my school.
His character is cruel, narrow-minded, and intolerant.
Now that he has seized this power,
he is certain to harbor treacherous designs.
Your previous plan, General, will not succeed.
Unless you defeat Shìchōng,
you cannot enter the court."
Lǐ Mì said:
"I initially thought you, Sir, were merely a Confucian scholar,
not conversant with current affairs.
But now you sit and decide grand strategies—
how profoundly insightful you are!"
Wényuǎn
was the great-great-grandson of Xú Xiàosì.
Xú Xiàosì
served as Chancellor under the Southern Qí dynasty.
On the gēngshēn day,
an edict was issued ordering that all the detached palaces and pleasure resorts of the Suí dynasty be abolished.
On the wùchén day,

The Suí Commandery Administrator of Héjiān, Wáng Cóng, defended the commandery city against the bandit rebels.
Dòu Jiàndé attacked him,
but for over a year could not take the city.
Upon hearing the news of Emperor Yáng's death,
Wáng Cóng led his officials and soldiers in holding mourning ceremonies,
and all those on the city walls wept.
Dòu Jiàndé sent an envoy to offer condolences.
Cóng, through the envoy, requested to surrender.
Jiàndé withdrew his troops and prepared a feast to receive him.
When Cóng spoke of the Suí's fall,
he prostrated himself and wept bitterly.
Jiàndé also wept for him.
His generals said:
"Cóng resisted our army for a long time,
causing many casualties.
He only surrendered when his strength was exhausted.
We request that he be boiled alive."
Jiàndé said:
"Cóng
is a loyal minister.
I intend to reward him to encourage service to one's sovereign.
How can we kill him!
In the past, when we were bandits at Gāojībó,
we might have killed indiscriminately;
but now we wish to pacify the people
and stabilize the realm.
How can we harm loyal and good men!"
He then proclaimed to the army:
"Whoever had previous grievances with Wáng Cóng and dares to act recklessly
will have his three clans exterminated!"
He appointed Cóng as Prefect of Yíngzhōu.
He also re-established Héjiān Commandery as Yíngzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Yíngzhōu,
was the Hàn dynasty's Héjiān Kingdom,
the Later Hàn's Lèchéng Kingdom;

Even among bandits, there is a code of honor—

when Jiàndé captured Jǐngchéng,

Cáo Zhēn and others all said:

Xiè Tǒngshī and others were all former Sui officials,

Xiè Tǒngshī and others were captured by Li Gui,
see Volume 184, the seventh month of the first year of Yìníng.

and does not plan for the state's interests.

Li Gui considered this correct,
and from then on, the officials and people became estranged and resentful.
This laid the groundwork for Li Gui's defeat and downfall.

It would be best if you, Illustrious Duke, exhaust your loyalty and sacrifice yourself for the state,

Shìchōng deceitfully praised his words and sent him away.
When Shìchōng discussed receiving the Nine Distinctions,

Duàn Dá said:

The Emperor Huángtài looked intently at Dá and said:
"As you wish!"
Xīnsì day [May 2, 619],
Dá and others, using an edict of the Emperor Huángtài, appointed Shìchōng as Chancellor of State,
granted him the Yellow Axe of authority,
placed him in charge of all administration,

The State of Zhèng established officials from Chancellor down.
33. Earlier,
Yǔwén Huàjí had appointed the Suí Chief Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, Zhèng Shànguǒ, as Minister of Revenue.
He followed Huàjí to Liáochéng,
and supervised the fighting for Huàjí,
where he was hit by a stray arrow.
When Dòu Jiàndé captured Liáochéng,
Wáng Cóng captured Shànguǒ

"You come from a family of famous ministers.
(Zhèng Shànguǒ's father, Zhèng Chéng,
fought against Yùchí Jiǒng
and died fighting bravely,
thus making them a famous minister's family of the Suí.)
How could you exert yourself for a regicidal traitor,
fighting bitterly and being wounded to this extent!"
Shànguǒ was greatly ashamed
and wanted to kill himself.
Sòng Zhèngběn rushed to save and stop him.
Jiàndé again did not treat him with courtesy,
so he fled to Xiàngzhōu.
The Prince of Huái'ān, Lǐ Shéntōng, sent him to Cháng'ān.
On the gēngwǔ day [April 21, 619],
Shànguǒ arrived.
The Emperor treated him with great courtesy,
appointing him as Left Assistant of the Heir Apparent and Acting Vice Director of the Secretariat.
How could ministers of the Suì house like Yǔwén Shìjí and Zhèng Shànguǒ
be employed again!
34. The Prince of Qí, Lǐ Yuánjí, hinted to the elders of Bìngzhōu to go to the capital and request that he remain.
On the jiǎshēn day [May 5, 619],

the five prefectures of Huáinán all sent envoys to surrender.

On the 38th day, Jiǎwǔ,
Wáng Shìchōng sent his general Gāo Pí to raid Yìzhōu.
According to the New Records: In the first year of Wǔdé,

still using the old name of the state from the Northern Qí.
General,

39. A Dōngdū Daoist priest, Huán Fǎsì, presented the "Confucius’s Closed Room Record" to Wáng Shìchōng,

Shìchōng was greatly pleased,

Shìchōng also captured various birds,

Thereupon, Duàn Dá, on the order of the Huángtài Emperor,

The officials urged him to ascend,

The Grand Councilor Sū Wēi was old,
and unable to attend court audiences,

wanted to dazzle the officials and people,
so each time he urged ascension,
he would always include Wēi’s name.
On the day he received the special honors,
he supported Wēi and placed him above all the officials,

40. In summer,
the fourth month,
Liú Wǔzhōu led Turkic troops,
and stationed them at Huángshé Ridge,
the ridge is north of Yúcì County.
Prince of Qí, Yuánjí, sent General of Chariots and Cavalry Zhāng Dá with infantry

test,
means to try.
Cavalry,
read as qí jì fān.
Yuánjí forced him to go,

Dá was resentful,
on Gēngzǐ,
he led Wǔzhōu to attack Yúcì,

Yúcì County belongs to Bìngzhōu,
an ancient county from the Hàn.
41. Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Duàn Què,
had a fondness for alcohol,
was ordered to console and reward Zhū Càn at Jútán.
In February of this year,

now recorded as Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,

Cavalier,
read as xī dǎn fān.
Attendant,

Reward,
read as lì dào fān.
On Xīnchǒu,
drunk, he insulted Càn, saying:
"I hear you like to eat people,

Like,
read as hū dào fān.
Eat,
read as tú làn fān,

same below.
"Eating a drunk person is just like eating pickled pork."
Què was angry,
and cursed:
"A mad bandit entering court,

Càn then seized Què and several dozen of his followers at the seat,

42. Wáng Shìchōng ordered his Chief Clerk Wéi Jié, Yáng Xù, and others, along with the Erudite of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices from Héngshuǐ, Kǒng Yǐngdá,

The Huángtài Emperor drew his knees together and leaned on the table,

"The empire,
is the empire of Gāozǔ,
if the Suí’s fortune has not ended,
such words should not be spoken;
if Heaven’s Mandate has indeed changed,
why bother with abdication!
You all are either old ministers of my ancestors,
or hold high positions in the court,
since you have such words,
what more can I hope for!"
His expression was stern,
his words cold and severe.
After retiring from court,
he wept before the Empress Dowager.
Shìchōng again sent someone to tell him:
"Now the realm is not yet peaceful,
we must establish an elder ruler,
when the four directions are pacified,
we will restore the throne to you,
as previously sworn."
Referring to the oath made in the palace in the seventh month of last year.
On Guǐmǎo,
Shìchōng claimed the Huángtài Emperor’s order,
abdicating the throne to Zhèng,
and sent his elder brother Shìyùn to imprison the Huángtài Emperor in the Hánliáng Hall.
Although there were three memorials declining and edicts urging,
the Huángtài Emperor knew nothing of them.
He sent generals to lead troops into the palace city to clear it,

an edict appointed Wáng Bó as Commander of Qízhōu,

44. On Jiǎchén,
sent the Minister of Justice from Xīnlè, Láng Chǔzhī, to pacify Shāndōng,

Xīnlè,

Lè,

Wáng Shìchōng prepared the imperial carriage and entered the palace,

Yángzhōu,
the area of Guǎnglíng and Jiāngdū from the Hàn,
since the Hàn,

should have

Yùn,

Shìyùn
was Wáng Shìchōng's elder brother.
He also appointed the National University Assistant Instructor, the man from Wú, Lù Démíng, as Preceptor to the Prince of Hàn.

Later generations followed this.
The Analects record Confucius saying:

Master Zhū said: Xiū,
means dried meat.
Ten strips make a bundle.

Later generations, based on the Master's words,

He took the bādòu powder,

Bādòu is poisonous,

Sàn,

Facing him, he excreted,
and ultimately did not speak with him.
Démíng's given name was Lǎng,

Lù Démíng surpassed Kǒng Yǐngdá by far.
Wáng Shìchōng set up couches in several places such as below the palace gate and the Xuánwǔ Gate,
sitting without a fixed location,
personally receiving memorials and petitions;
sometimes he rode lightly through the streets and markets,
also without clearing the way,
as the Son of Heaven clears the way before proceeding.
Qí,
is pronounced jì.
Wáng Shìchōng held the reins and proceeded slowly,

"In the past, the Son of Heaven resided deep within the ninefold palace,

Now, I, Shìchōng, do not covet the heavenly throne,

just like a provincial governor,
personally overseeing all affairs,
I should discuss court governance together with the officials and commoners.
I still fear the gates have restrictions and limits,
so now I set up a seat outside the gate to hold court and listen,
you should each speak your mind fully."
He also ordered the West Court Hall to receive grievances and injustices,
and the East Court Hall to receive forthright remonstrance.
Consequently, those presenting strategies and submitting letters numbered several hundred daily,
the flow of items was already excessive,
making it difficult to review them all.
After a few days,
he no longer came out again.
On the 48th day, Dòu Jiàndé heard that Wáng Shìchōng
had proclaimed himself emperor,
so he severed relations with him,
and for the first time erected the Son of Heaven's banners and flags,

and posthumously honored Emperor Yáng of Suí as Emperor Mǐn.
When Prince Qí Yáng Jiǎn died,
he left a posthumous son Zhèngdào.
Jiàndé established him as the Duke of Yún,
but still relied on the Türks to strengthen his military power.
The Suí Yìchéng Princess sent an envoy to welcome Empress Xiāo and Princess Nányáng.

and also sent Yǔwén Huàjí's head to present to the Yìchéng Princess.
On the 49th day, the bǐngchén day,

On the wùwǔ day,
an edict ordered the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, Lǐ Zhòngwén, to lead troops to rescue Bìngzhōu.
On the 50th day, Wáng Shìchōng's general Qiū Huáiyì, residing at the Menxià Nèishěng,
summoned Prince Yuè Lǐ Jùndù, Prince Hàn Wáng Xuánshù, and general Guō Shìhéng to drink, gamble, and mingle with singing girls and concubines.
The Investigating Censor Zhāng Yùngǔ impeached him.
Shìchōng was greatly angered,
and ordered the Sànshǒu guards to seize Jùndù and Xuánshù,
slapping their ears several dozen times;
Sànshǒu refers to
the Sànshǒu guard.
For all court assembly guards,
the Three Guards took turns on duty,
divided into five guards: First, the Gòngfèng Guard,
composed of the Left and Right Guards;
second, the Qīn Guard,
composed of the Personal Guard;
third, the Xūn Guard,

fourth, the Yì Guard,
composed of the Flanking Guard;
all wore pheasant-feather caps and crimson lined robes.
Fifth, the Sànshǒu Guard,
composed of members from the Personal, Meritorious, and Flanking Guards,
wearing crimson silk vests,
embroidered with wild horses,
seated in rows under the eastern and western corridors.
In Táng, these were called the Five Guards of the Yá.
Táng likely followed the Suì system,
and Shìchōng also followed the Suì system.
Jì,
is pronounced jì.
Tán,
is pronounced tán.
Sàn,
is pronounced sàn.
Pī,
is pronounced piē,
also pī.
He caned each of them several dozen times.
The main hall of the Luòyáng imperial palace was called the Qiányáng Hall,
to the left of the hall was the Eastern Upper Pavilion,
to the right was the Western Upper Pavilion,
each pavilion had its own gate.
He rewarded Yùngǔ with one hundred bolts of silk,
and promoted him to Gentleman of the Household of the Heir Apparent.
Jùndù
was the son of Shìchōng's elder brother.
Whenever Shìchōng held court,
he earnestly instructed and admonished,
his words repetitive,
covering myriad topics and details,
until the attendants and guards could not bear the fatigue,
and the various offices reporting affairs
grew weary of listening and receiving.
The Censor-in-chief Sū Liáng remonstrated, saying:
"Your Majesty speaks too much without getting to the main point.
The main point
is like what the Hàn people called the 'essentials'.
Why trouble with so many words!"
Shìchōng remained silent for a long while,
but did not punish Liáng.
However, his nature being such,
he ultimately could not change.
On the 51st day, Wáng Shìchōng attacked Yīzhōu several times,
but the Area Commander-in-chief Zhāng Shànxiàng resisted him;
when provisions were exhausted,
and reinforcements did not arrive,
on the guǐhài day,
the city fell.
Shànxiàng cursed Shìchōng vehemently until his death.
The Emperor heard of it,
and sighed, saying:
"I have failed Shànxiàng,
Shànxiàng did not fail me!"
He granted his son the title of Duke of Xiāngchéng Commandery.
In the fifth month,
Wáng Shìchōng captured Yìzhōu,
and again invaded Xī Jìzhōu.
The New History records: Jìyuán County,
in the second year of Wǔdé,
Wáng Shìchōng's general Dīng Bódé surrendered the county,

Fù,
is pronounced fù.
Jì,
is pronounced jǐ.
53. Lǐ Guǐ's general Ān Xiūrén's elder brother Ān Xìngguì,
served in Cháng'ān.
He submitted a memorial requesting to persuade Guǐ,
to explain to him the consequences of fortune and disaster.
The Emperor said:
"Guǐ relies on his troops and the perilous terrain,
and has allied with the Tǔyùhún and Tūjué.
Tǔ,
follows the entering tone of 'tūn'.
Yù,
pronounced 'yù'.
Jué,
Jiǔwù fān.
I still fear we cannot overcome him;
how could mere words bring him to submission!"
Xìngguì said:
"Your servant's family is in Liángzhōu,
for generations a prominent and influential clan,
trusted and followed by both the common people and the tribes;
my younger brother Xiūrén is trusted by Guǐ,
and our sons and younger brothers in key positions number in the tens.
If I go to persuade him,
if Guǐ listens to me, that is of course good.
If he does not listen,
plotting against him from within his inner circle,

The Emperor then sent him.
Xìngguì arrived in Wǔwēi,
and Guǐ appointed him as General of the Left and Right Guards.
Xìngguì seized an opportunity to persuade Guǐ, saying:
"The territory of Liáng is no more than a thousand lǐ,

Now Táng has risen from Tàiyuán,
taken Hán and Qín,
and rules the Central Plains.
In battle they are sure to win,
in attack they are sure to take;
this is likely Heaven's will,
not merely human effort.
It would be better to surrender Héxī and submit to them;
then the achievement of Dòu Róng will be seen again today!"
The matter of Dòu Róng is seen in the Annals of Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn.
Fù,
Fúyòu fān.
Guǐ said: "I rely on the strength of mountains and rivers;
though they are powerful,
what can they do to me!
You came from Táng,

Xìngguì apologized and said:
"Your servant has heard that 'to be wealthy and noble and not return to one's hometown is like wearing embroidered robes at night' —
these are Xiàng Yǔ's words.
Yī,
Yújì fān.
How could I be willing to submit to Táng!
I merely wish to offer my foolish thoughts;
whether to accept them or not lies with Your Majesty."
Thereupon he withdrew and secretly joined with Xiūrén to rally the various Hú tribes to raise troops and attack Guǐ.
Guǐ went out to battle but was defeated,

Xìngguì proclaimed to the people:

The people in the city vied to come out and join Xìngguì.
Guǐ, with his plans exhausted,
ascended the Jade Maiden Terrace with his wife and children.
Guǐ built the Jade Maiden Terrace;
see the previous year in the previous scroll.
On the gēngchén day,

Dèng Xiǎo was in Cháng'ān,

The Emperor said:
"You were a minister serving another;
upon hearing of your state's destruction,

You were not loyal to Lǐ Guǐ;

He then dismissed him from office for life.
In the second month of this year,

Guǐ was brought to Cháng'ān,

the Hú of Líshí, Liú Lóng'ér

80 The Western Turkic Kèsuōnà Khān had a feud with the Northern Turks.
Kèsuōnà was in Cháng'ān.
The Northern Turks sent an envoy requesting his execution.
The Emperor did not consent.
His ministers all said:
"To protect one man and lose a state's goodwill,
will surely bring trouble later!"
The Prince of Qín, Lǐ Shìmín, said:
"A man in dire straits came to us for refuge.
Killing him would be unjust."
The Emperor hesitated for a long time,
but having no alternative,
on Bǐngxū day,
he invited Kèsuōnà to a banquet in the inner palace.
Afterwards, he sent him to the Secretariat,
and allowed the Northern Turkic envoy to kill him.
81. Lǐ Bù Shàngshū Lǐ Gāng was appointed as Tàizǐ Zhānshì.
According to the "Hànshū Bǎiguān Biǎo," the position of Zhānshì
originated as an official title during the Qín dynasty,
responsible for managing the households of the empress and the crown prince.
Yìng Shào explained: "Zhān" means
to oversee,
to provide for,
indicating the duty of serving in the crown prince's household.
During the Jìn, Sòng, and later Northern Wèi dynasties, the position gradually became more important.
In Northern Qí, the Zhānshì oversaw all affairs within and outside the Eastern Palace,
with no matter too large or small escaping his jurisdiction.
In the later Northern Zhōu, the positions of Tàizǐ Gōngzhèng and Gōngyǐn were established;
Suí reinstated the Zhānshì;
Táng placed the Zhānshì in charge of the administration of the three temples and ten guard commands of the Eastern Palace.
After some time,
the crown prince gradually grew close to petty individuals,
resenting Qínwáng Lǐ Shìmín for his high achievements,
and harbored considerable suspicion and jealousy toward him.
Lǐ Gāng repeatedly remonstrated, but the crown prince would not listen,
so Lǐ Gāng requested to retire due to old age.
The emperor scolded him, saying:
"You served as Chief Clerk to Hé Pānrén,
yet you consider it shameful to serve as my Shàngshū!
Moreover, I have just appointed you to guide and assist Jiànchéng,
yet you stubbornly seek to leave.
Why is this?"
Lǐ Gāng kowtowed and said:
"Pānrén
was a bandit.
Whenever he intended to kill people recklessly,
I would remonstrate, and he would stop.
Serving as his Chief Clerk,
I could do so without shame.
The account of serving as Chief Clerk is found in the 184th volume, under the first year of Yìníng.
I am untalented.
My words are like water thrown against stone—
that is, when water is thrown against stone,
although the stone may get wet, it cannot absorb the water.
How dare I long defile the Heavenly Terrace and disgrace the Eastern Court!"
"Heavenly Terrace"
refers to the Shàngshū Shěng.
"Eastern Court"
refers to the Eastern Palace.
"Defile"
is pronounced wù.
"Court"
is pronounced zhāo.
"I know you are an upright man.
Please stay and diligently assist my son."
On the Wùzǐ day,
Lǐ Gāng was appointed as Tàizǐ Shǎobǎo,
retaining his positions as Shàngshū and Zhānshì.
Lǐ Gāng again submitted a memorial admonishing the crown prince for his excessive drinking,
his belief in slander and evil,
and his alienation from his own flesh and blood.
The crown prince was displeased,
yet his behavior remained unchanged.
Lǐ Gāng, depressed and unable to fulfill his ambitions,
that year,
firmly claimed old age and illness as reasons to resign.
An edict relieved him of his duties as Shàngshū,
but he remained as Shǎobǎo.
82. Huái'ānwáng Lǐ Shéntōng sent the Pacification Commissioner Zhāng Dàoyuán to garrison Zhàozhōu.
On the Gēngyín day,
Dòu Jiàndé captured Zhàozhōu,
seizing Commander Zhāng Zhì'áng and Dàoyuán.
Dòu Jiàndé, because these two men and Xíngzhōu Cìshǐ Chén Jūnbīn had not surrendered earlier,
intended to execute them.
Guózǐ Jìjiǔ Líng Jìng remonstrated, saying:
"A subject serves his own lord.
Their steadfast defense and refusal to surrender
demonstrates their loyalty.
If Your Highness kills them now,
how will you encourage your own subordinates?"
Dòu Jiàndé angrily said:
"When I arrived at the city walls,
they still would not surrender.
They were captured only after their strength was exhausted.
How can they be spared!"
Líng Jìng said:
"Now Your Highness has sent the general Gāo Shìxīng to resist Luó Yì at Yìshuǐ.
As soon as Yì arrived,
Shìxīng surrendered.
What does Your Highness think of that?"
Dòu Jiàndé then realized his error,
and immediately ordered their release.
83. On the Yǐwèi day,
Liáng Shīdū again invaded Yánzhōu.
Duàn Décāo attacked and defeated him,
beheading over two thousand,
and Shīdū fled with over a hundred cavalry.
Décāo, for his merit, was appointed Zhùguó,
and granted the title of Píngyuán Jùngōng.
Fūzhōu Cìshǐ, Fūchéng Zhuànggōng Liáng Lǐ, died in battle.
According to the Suí records: Shàngjùn
was established by Later Wèi as Dōng Qínzhōu.
Later it was changed to Běi Huázhōu,
and in Western Wèi to Fūzhōu.
In the second year of Dàyè, it was changed to Fūchéng Jùn,
later changed to Shàngjùn,
and in Táng times became Fūzhōu.
"Fū"
is pronounced fū.
84. In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Jǐhài day,
Liángzhōu Zǒngguǎn Yáng Gōngrén was additionally appointed as Nàyán;
Yōuzhōu Zǒngguǎn, Yāngōng Luó Yì, was granted the imperial surname Lǐ,
and enfeoffed as Yānjùnwáng.
He was promoted from Guógōng to Jùnwáng.
According to Táng regulations,
a Guógōng's stipendiary fief comprised three thousand households,
a Jùnwáng's comprised five thousand households,
both ranking as First Grade.
"Yān"
is pronounced yīn jiān.
On the Xīnchǒu day,
Lǐ Yì defeated Dòu Jiàndé at Héngshuǐ.
Héngshuǐ Xiàn
belonged to Jìzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Héngshuǐ Xiàn was originally the Hàn dynasty's Táo Xiàn.
In the sixteenth year of the Suí dynasty's Kāihuáng era,
Héngshuǐ Xiàn was established.
85. On the Guǐmǎo day,
Zuǒ Wǔhòu Dàjiāngjūn Páng Yù was appointed as Liángzhōu Zǒngguǎn.
At that time, the Lǎo people in Jízhōu rebelled.
According to the New Records: In the first year of Wǔdé,
Nánjiāng from Liángzhōu, and Fúyáng, Chángchí, Báishí from Bāzhōu were separated
to establish Jízhōu.
According to the Old Records,
this was the area of Hàn Dàngqú
and Fúyáng.
Sòng Bái said: Later Wèi's Emperor Gōng changed the Eastern Bāzhōu of Liáng to Jízhōu,
named after the Jíchuān River to its northeast.
"Lǎo"
is pronounced lǎo.
The Lǎo people occupied strategic positions and defended themselves,
preventing the army from advancing,
and supplies were running low.
The assimilated Lǎo and the rebels were neighbors, relatives, and allies;
those near the borders were assimilated Lǎo,
those farther away were unassimilated Lǎo.
They requested Páng Yù to withdraw.
Páng Yù publicly declared:
"The autumn grain is about to ripen.
The common people must not harvest it.
All of it is to be supplied to the army.
I will not return until the rebels are pacified."
Those who heard this were greatly afraid, saying:
"If the great army does not leave,
we will all starve to death."
Some brave men among them then entered the rebel camps,
secretly plotted with their relatives there,
beheaded their chieftains and surrendered.
The remaining rebels scattered.
Páng Yù pursued and suppressed them,
pacifying the area completely.
86 Liú Wǔzhōu's general Sòng Jīngāng advanced and attacked Huìzhōu,
capturing it.
(New History: In the first year of Yìníng, Huìzhōu was established with Yìchéng and Jiàngxiàn from Jiàngjùn,
named after the Huì River.)
(General,
read as jí liàng fān;
same below.)
(Huì,
read as gǔ wài fān.)
Péi Jì was timid by nature,
lacking the strategies of a commander.
He only dispatched messengers in succession,
urging the residents of Yú and Tài prefectures to enter walled fortresses,
and burning their accumulated stores.
(Luòyì,
means continuous and unbroken.)
(New History: In the first year of Yìníng,
Ānyìjùn was established with Ānyì, Yúxiāng, and Xià from Púzhōu,
renamed Yúzhōu in the first year of Wǔdé.
Also in the first year of Yìníng,
Fényīnjùn was established with Fényīn and Lóngmén from Púzhōu,
renamed Tàizhōu in the first year of Wǔdé.)
(Messenger,
read as shū lì fān.)
(Urge,
read as cù.)
(Accumulated stores,
the first character read as zǐ cì fān,
the second as cí yù fān;
nowadays many people read them as usual,
which is incorrect.)
All thought of becoming bandits.
Lǚ Chóngmào of Xiàxiàn gathered a crowd and proclaimed himself King of Wèi,
to respond to Wǔzhōu.
(Xiàxiàn,
the ancient land of Duke Yú,
with Jìshān and Yúbǎn both within the county's boundaries.
Under Suí, it belonged to Hédōngjùn,
at this time it belonged to Yúzhōu.
Dù Yòu said: Xiàxiàn,
was the territory of Hàn's Ānyìxiàn;
the Xià capital was at Ānyì,
the city was fifteen lǐ north of the county,
hence the county was named after it.
Xià,
read as hù yǎ fān.)
(They were defeated by him.)
An edict ordered Yǒng'ānwáng Lǐ Xiàojī,
Dúgū Huái'ēn, Shǎnzhōu Zǒngguǎn Yú Jūn, Nèishǐ Shìláng Táng Jiǎn, and others to lead troops to suppress them.
At that time, Wáng Xíngběn still held Púfǎn,
which had not fallen,
and he also responded to Wǔzhōu.
(Last year in December,
the Suí general Yáo Jūnsù died,
and Wáng Xíngběn held Púfǎn,
as seen in the previous volume.)
The Emperor issued a handwritten edict saying:
"The enemy's situation is like this,
it is difficult to contend with them head-on.
We should abandon the lands east of the Great River,
and carefully guard only Guānxī."
(This refers to west of Pújīn Pass.)
(West of the pass.)
"Tàiyuán,
is the foundation of the royal enterprise,
the root of the state;
Hédōng is wealthy and substantial,
providing resources for the capital.
If we abandon it entirely,
I secretly feel indignation and regret.
I wish to borrow thirty thousand elite troops from Your Majesty,
and I am confident I can pacify and exterminate Wǔzhōu,
and recover Fén and Jìn."
The Emperor then mobilized all the Guānzhōng troops to reinforce those under Lǐ Shìmín's command,
and sent him to attack Wǔzhōu.
On Yǐmǎo,
the Emperor went to Huàyīn,
arriving at Chángchūn Palace to see him off.
87 Dòu Jiàndé led troops towards Wèizhōu.
(Wèizhōu,
was the territory of Hàn's Jíxiàn.
Eastern Wèi established Yìzhōu,
later Zhōu changed it to Wèizhōu,
governing Jí.
Sòng Bái said: Its prefectural city,
before Suí, was called Zhènchéng.
According to Jùnguó Xiàndào Jì: King Wǔ attacked King Zhòu,
arrayed his troops here,
hence the name.
He often marched in three columns,
with baggage and the weak in the center,
infantry and cavalry flanking left and right,
about three lǐ apart.
Jiàndé advanced with a thousand cavalry,
passing thirty lǐ beyond Líyáng.
(Líyángxiàn,
was one hundred twenty lǐ northeast of Wèizhōu.)
Xiàogāng was brave and fierce,
skilled with horse and lance.
He encountered Jiàndé,
and attacked him.
Jiàndé was defeated and fled;
the troops on the right came to his rescue.
(Right side,
using Hànshū terminology.
This refers to Jiàndé's troops on the right.)
Jiàndé was enraged,
turned back and attacked Líyáng,
capturing it.
(Examination of discrepancies: According to Shílù,
Líyáng fell on Bǐngzǐ in November,
likely the date the report arrived.
Now following Gémìng Jì.)
Lǐ Shìjì's father Lǐ Gài, Wèi Zhēng, and the Emperor's sister Tóng'ān Gōngzhǔ.
Only Lǐ Shìjì escaped with several hundred cavalry across the river.
After a few days,
for the sake of his father,
he returned and surrendered to Jiàndé.
Wèizhōu, hearing of Líyáng's fall,
also surrendered.
Jiàndé appointed Lǐ Shìjì as Left Xiāowèi General,
and had him guard Líyáng,
often keeping his father Lǐ Gài with him as a hostage.
He appointed Wèi Zhēng as Jǐqū Shèrén.
The slave of Huázhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Guǐ killed Guǐ,
and brought his head to surrender to Jiàndé.
Jiàndé said:
"A slave killing his master is a great treasonous act,
why should I accept this!"
He immediately ordered the slave executed,
and returned the head to Huázhōu.
The officials and people were moved and pleased,
and that same day requested to surrender.
Thereupon, the neighboring prefectures and counties, as well as Xú Yuánlǎng and others, all submitted upon hearing the news.
On Jǐwèi,
Jiàndé returned to Míngzhōu,
built Wànchūn Palace,
and moved his capital there.
He placed Huái'ānwáng Lǐ Shéntōng at Xiàbó.
(Xiàbóxiàn at that time belonged to Jìzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Xiàbó,
is an old Hàn county.
Yìng Shào said: Tàishān has Bóxiàn,
hence this is called Xià [Lower].
The old county was twenty lǐ south of the present county.
The present county was moved north of Héngshuǐ by Later Wèi,
commonly called the old county town.
In the sixth year of Zhōu Jiàndé,
the county was moved again to its present location.
The present location,
is the Later Hàn Jì Zūn's fortress,
resting north against Héngshuǐ.)
88 Xíngjūn Zǒngguǎn Luó Shìxìn led brave warriors into the outer walls of Luòyáng at night,
set fire to Qīnghuà Lǐ, and returned.
On Rénxū,
Shìxìn captured Qīngchéng Fort.
(Likely a fort built at Qīngchéng Palace.)
89 Wáng Shìchōng personally led troops on a campaign to Huátái,
approaching Líyáng.
Wèishì city commander Shí Déruì, Biànzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Yàohàn, and Bózhōu Cìshǐ Dīng Shūzé sent messengers to surrender to him.
(Biànzhōu,
the ancient territory of Dàliáng.
During the Warring States period, it was the capital of Wèi.
Under Hàn, it was Chénliújùn.
Under Eastern Wèi, it was Liángzhōu.
Later Zhōu changed it to Biànzhōu,
because the city was near the Biàn River,
hence the name.
Sòng Bái said: Bózhōu,
during the Spring and Autumn period was the Jiāo settlement of the Eastern State.
Under Hàn, it was Qiáoxiàn.
Under Wèi, it was Qiáojùn.
Later, Zhōu Wǔdì established Bózhōu,
distantly taking the name of the ancient Nánbó to name the prefecture.)
(Lead troops,
read as jí liàng fān.)
(Messenger,
read as shū lì fān.)
(Yàohàn,
was the elder brother of Bódāng.)
Xiàhóu Duān arrived at Líyáng.
In the fourth month of this year,
Xiàhóu Duān was dispatched to pacify the region east of the Huái River.
Summer,
Hù Yǎ fān.
He crossed the Yellow River from Chányuān.
In the sixteenth year of the Suí dynasty's Kāihuáng era,
Chányuān County was established,
at that time belonging to Lí Prefecture.
Chán,
shì lián fān.
Eastward to the sea,
southward to the Huái River,
over twenty prefectures
all sent envoys to surrender.
When he reached Qiáo Prefecture,
Old records: Línyú County of Bó Prefecture,
the Suí established Qiáo Prefecture.
The return route was then cut off.
Duān had always won the hearts of the people,
the two thousand men following him,
though their provisions were exhausted, could not bear to abandon him.
Duān sat in the marshes,
killed horses to feed the troops,
and then sighed and said to them:
"Your hometowns have all already submitted to the rebels,
only because of our shared experiences and feelings,
you have not yet abandoned me.
Wěi,
means to abandon.
You cannot follow me;
you have wives and children,
you should not emulate me.
You can cut off my head and return to the rebels,
you will surely gain wealth and honor."
The men all wept and said:
"You, sir, have no kinship with the Táng imperial house,
only out of loyalty and righteousness,
are determined not to seek survival.
Though we are lowly,
our hearts are also human,
how could we harm you, sir, to seek profit!"
Duān said:
"If you cannot bear to see me killed,
I will cut my own throat."
The men held him back,
and then they advanced together again.
Traveling stealthily for five days,
those who starved to death or were attacked by rebels and scattered or lost amounted to more than half,
only fifty-two men remained walking together.
They picked wild beans and ate them raw.
Duān held the imperial tally and never let it leave his person.
He repeatedly sent his followers to disperse
and seek survival on their own,
but the men again refused.
At that time, all the lands south of the Yellow River had entered Wáng Shìchōng's control,
only the prefectural governor Lǐ Gōngyì held firm for the Táng,
he sent troops to welcome Duān,
and provided him lodging and supplies.
Wáng Shìchōng sent an envoy to summon Duān,
took off his own clothes and gave them to him,
and also sent a letter of appointment,
appointing Duān as Duke of Huáinán Commandery and Junior Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel;
Duān, facing the envoy, burned the letter and destroyed the clothes,
saying:
"Xiàhóu Duān is the Son of Heaven's great envoy,
how could he accept an office from Wáng Shìchōng!
If you want me to go,
you can only take my head."
Then he untied the yak-tail banner from the tally and kept it close,
placed a blade on the pole,
and headed west from the mountains.
There were no more paths,
they braved and trampled through thorns,
traveling day and night,
and reached Yíyáng.
Yíyáng,
Táng's Xióng Prefecture.
They were eaten by tigers and wolves,
and lost another half;
those who survived had their hair and beards falling out,
no longer looking human.
Duān went to the court to see the Emperor,
only apologizing for having achieved no merit,
initially not speaking of the hardships at all,
the Emperor again appointed him as Director of the Palace Library.
Láng Chǔzhī reached Shāndōng,
and was also captured by Dòu Jiàndé,
Chǔzhī did not yield,
and eventually managed to return.
Láng Chǔzhī and Xiàhóu Duān were sent as envoys at the same time.
The history states that at the rise of the Táng,
those sent as envoys to the four directions,
were all able to not disgrace their sovereign's command.
Huán,
cóng xuān fān.
Wáng Shìchōng sent his cousin Shìbiàn with troops from Xú and Bó to attack Yōngqiū.
Lǐ Gōngyì sent an envoy to seek aid,
the Emperor, because it was separated by rebel territory,

Gōngyì then left his subordinate Lǐ Shànxíng to guard Yōngqiū,

When he reached Xiāngchéng,

Gōngyì said:

Shìchōng was angry,

Shànxíng also perished.
The Emperor enfeoffed Gōngyì's son as Duke of Xiāngyì.
On the jiǎzǐ day,
the Emperor sacrificed at Huà Mountain.

and has a mountain temple.
Huà,
hù huà fān.
