bestowed upon him the title of Duke of Hàndōng,
and often sent him to lead surprise troops to raid east and west,
or to infiltrate enemy territory to spy on their strengths and weaknesses.
Hēità often seized opportunities to attack fiercely,
achieving victories and returning.
4 In the twelfth month,
on Gēngshēn,
the Emperor hunted at Huà Shān.
5 Yú Jūn advised Prince Yǒng'ān, Xiàojī, to urgently attack Lǚ Chóngmào.
Dúgū Huái'ēn requested to first complete the siege equipment,
and then advance.
Xiàojī agreed.
Chóngmào sought help from Sòng Jīngāng.
Jīngāng sent his commanders, Shànyáng Commandant Yùchí Jìngdé and Xún Xiàng, to lead troops and suddenly arrive at Xià County.
Xiàojī was attacked from both inside and outside,
and his army was severely defeated.
Xiàojī, Huái'ēn, Jūn, Táng Jiǎn, and the marching commander Liú Shìràng were all captured.
Jìngdé's given name was Gōng,
but he was known by his courtesy name.
The Emperor summoned Péi Jì to court,
reprimanded him for the army's defeat,
and handed him over to the officials.
Soon after, he was released,
and his favor and treatment grew even more generous.
Yùchí Jìngdé and Xún Xiàng were about to return to Huì Prefecture.
Prince Qín, Shìmín, sent the Minister of War Yīn Kāishān, Commander Qín Shūbǎo, and others to intercept them at Měiliángchuān.
They heavily defeated them,
beheading over two thousand.
Shortly after,
Jìngdé and Xún Xiàng secretly led elite cavalry to aid Wáng Xíngběn at Púfǎn.
Shìmín personally led three thousand infantry and cavalry, taking a shortcut at night to hurry to Ānyì.
Ānyì,
an ancient county,
at that time belonged to Yú Prefecture.
Jiàng,
read as jiàng.
Jiàn,
read as jiàn.
Qū,
read as qū.
He heavily defeated them.
Jìngdé and Xiàng barely escaped with their lives,
and all their troops were captured.
They returned to Bǎibì.
All the commanders requested to engage Sòng Jīngāng in battle.
Shìmín said:
"Jīngāng has advanced deep into enemy territory with his army,
his elite troops and fierce commanders
are all gathered here.
Wǔzhōu holds Tàiyuán,
relying on Jīngāng as his shield.
His army
has no stored provisions,
relying on plunder for supplies.
His advantage lies in a quick battle.
We will fortify our camp and nurture our strength to blunt his edge,
dispatch troops to Fén and Xí,
and strike at his heart and belly.
Fén and Xí
were the territories of the Sui's Lóngquán and Xīhé commanderies.
Sǔn Miǎn said: Fén Prefecture
was originally the territory of Zīshì County in the Hàn's Xīhé Commandery.
The Wei established Xīhé Commandery at Zīshì,
which is the present prefectural city.
The Zuǒzhuàn says: Chóng'ěr resided at Pú,
which is the old Pú city of Xíchuān County.
In the Hàn, it was Púzǐ County.
Between the Later Wei, Qí, and Zhōu, it was Fén Prefecture.
In the Sui, it became Xí Prefecture.
The Ěryǎ says: Low and damp land is called xí.
Because the prefecture is near marshes and low-lying damp land,
it was named Xí.
He will surely flee.
We should wait for this opportunity,
and not rush into battle."
Prince Yǒng'ān Zhuàng, Xiàojī, plotted to escape and return,
but Liú Wǔzhōu killed him.
6 Li Shìjì again sent someone to persuade Dòu Jiàndé, saying:
"The two prefectures of Cáo and Dài,
have complete and substantial households.
The Sui established Cáo Prefecture at Jìyīn,
and Dài Prefecture at Chéngwǔ.
At the beginning of the Dàyè era,
the two prefectures were abolished,
and merged into Jìyīn Commandery.
During the Dàyè turmoil,
they became prefectures again.
Fù,
read as fù.
Shuì,
read as shuì.
They are outwardly aligned with the Zhèng people but inwardly divided;
Wáng Shìchōng's state was named Zhèng.
They can be captured on schedule.
Once we have Lord Hǎi,
and approach Xú and Yǎn,
(Wáng Shìchōng at that time sent Wáng Shìbiàn to occupy Xú Prefecture,
and Xú Yuánlǎng occupied Yǎn Prefecture.)
Jiàndé considered this reasonable,
and intended to personally campaign in Hénán.
He first sent his branch secretariat official Cáo Dàn and others to lead fifty thousand troops across the river.
Examination of discrepancies: The Veritable Records places this in the first month of the following year.
Now following the Gémìng Jì.
1 Spring,
first month,
General Qín Wǔtōng attacked Wáng Xíngběn at Púfǎn.
Xíngběn came out to fight but was defeated.
His provisions were exhausted and aid was cut off.
He wanted to break through the siege and flee,
but no one followed him.
On Wùyín,
he opened the gates and surrendered.
On Xīnsì,
the Emperor went to Pú Prefecture,
and executed Xíngběn.
Pú Prefecture administered Púfǎn.
Sòng Bái said: Pú Prefecture
was the Hàn's Hédōng Commandery Púfǎn County.
It was originally Shùn's capital.
During the Zhōu, it was the territory of Yú, Guó, Gěng, Yáng, and Ruì.
During the Warring States period, it was Wèi territory.
The Hàn established Hédōng Commandery.
The early Later Wei established Yōng Prefecture.
In the first year of Yánhé,
it was changed to Tài Prefecture.
The Later Zhōu changed it to Pú Prefecture.
Sòng Jīngāng besieged Jiàng Prefecture.
Jiàng Prefecture administered Zhèngpíng.
On Guǐsì,
the Emperor returned to Cháng'ān.
2 Li Shìjì plotted to wait until Dòu Jiàndé reached Hénán,
then launch a surprise attack on his camp,
kill him,
hoping to obtain his father, along with Jiàndé's land, and defect to the Táng.
It happened that Jiàndé's wife was giving birth,
and he did not arrive for a long time.
Cáo Dàn was the brother-in-law of Jiàndé.
In Hénán,
he committed many acts of aggression and harassment,
causing resentment among all the bandit leaders who were nominally subordinate to him.
The bandit leader Lǐ Wénxiāng of Wèijùn,
also known as Lǐ Shānghú,
gathered over five thousand men
and occupied the central sandbar at Mèngjīn;
this was the central sandbar fortress at Héyáng.
Sòng Bái said: The central sandbar fortress
was built by Eastern Wèi,
and the Héyáng Pass was established there.
Tǎn is pronounced tǎn.
He was also skilled in horsemanship and archery
and called himself Commander-in-Chief Huò.
Examination of discrepancies: According to the *Record of the Revolution*,
Shānghú’s mother, née Zhāng,
was called
“Lady General.”
Here we follow the *Record of Héluò*.
He went in to pay respects to Shānghú’s mother.
The mother tearfully said to Shìjī:
“The Dòu clan is unprincipled—
how can you serve them!”
Shìjī replied:
“Do not worry, mother.
In no more than a month,
I will kill him
and together we will return to Táng!”
Shìjī took his leave.
The mother said to Shānghú:
“Lord Dōnghǎi has promised to join me in plotting against this traitor.
Delays breed complications—
why wait for him to come?
It is better to act swiftly.”
That night,
Shānghú invited twenty-three of Cáo Dàn’s subordinate officers
to drink wine
and killed them all.
Cáo Dàn’s other generals Gāo Yǎxián and Ruǎn Jūnmíng were still north of the river and had not yet crossed.
Shānghú used four large boats to ferry three hundred soldiers from north of the river.
When they reached midstream,
he killed them all.
A veterinarian who swam away escaped.
Veterinarians were those who could treat oxen and horses and followed the army.
Jiàng is pronounced jiàng.
Sōu is pronounced sōu.
He reported to Cáo Dàn,
who tightened security and prepared defenses.
After Shānghú had launched his action,
he then sent someone to inform Lǐ Shìjī.
Shìjī’s camp was connected to Cáo Dàn’s.
Guō Xiàokè urged Shìjī to attack Dàn,
but Shìjī hesitated.
Hearing that Dàn was already prepared,
he then, along with Xiàokè, led several dozen cavalrymen and fled to join [the Táng].
Shānghú further led two thousand elite troops
north to attack Ruǎn Jūnmíng
and defeated him.
Gāo Yǎxián gathered his troops and withdrew.
Shānghú pursued him
but, failing to catch up, returned.
Jiàndé’s ministers requested the execution of Lǐ Gài.
Jiàndé said:
“Shìjī is a Táng minister
who was captured by us.
Not forgetting his original court
makes him a loyal minister.
What crime has his father committed!”
He then pardoned him.
On the jiǎwǔ day,
Shìjī and Xiàokè reached Cháng’ān.
Cáo Dàn then captured Jìzhōu.
At the beginning of the Wǔdé era,
Zhāng Qīngtè occupied Jìběi.
The Jìběi commandery was Jìzhōu.
Later, when Jiàndé and Táng were locked in stalemate at Hǔláo,
Zhāng Qīngtè’s grain transport was captured by Táng.
It seems he had earlier surrendered Jìzhōu to Cáo Dàn.
Jì is pronounced jǐ.
In the second month,
on the gēngzǐ day,
the Emperor went to Huàyīn.
Liú Wǔzhōu sent troops to raid Lùzhōu,
capturing Zhǎngzǐ and Húguān.
Both counties belonged to Lùzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Lùzhōu
was the state of the Lùzǐ in the Spring and Autumn period;
during Qín and Hàn it was the Shàngdǎng commandery;
Later Zhōu established Lùzhōu,
named after the rivers Fén and Lù that flowed through it.
The Emperor sent General Wáng Xíngmǐn of Hédōng to assist.
Hédōng County was attached to Púzhōu,
which was Púfǎn.
In the sixteenth year of the Suí Kāihuáng era,
Púfǎn was divided to establish the county.
At the beginning of the Dàyè era,
Púfǎn was merged into it.
Someone said that Zǐwǔ would rebel,
so Xíngmǐn beheaded Zǐwǔ to warn the troops.
On the yǐsì day,
Wǔzhōu again sent troops to raid Lùzhōu,
but Xíngmǐn repelled them.
On the rénzǐ day,
the Kāizhōu barbarian Rǎn Zhàozé captured Tōngzhōu.
Old records: Kāizhōu
was Shèngshān County of the Suí Bādōng commandery;
Shèngshān
was the Qúrǔn County of the Hàn Bā commandery.
In the first year of Yìníng,
Shèngshān and Xīnpǔ of Bādōng,
and Wànshì and Xīliú of Tōngchuān,
were separated to establish Wànzhōu.
In the first year of Wǔdé,
it was renamed Kāizhōu.
Tōngzhōu
was the territory of Dàngqú County in Hàn times;
Liáng established Wànzhōu,
Northern Wèi renamed it Tōngzhōu,
Suí made it the Tōngchuān commandery,
and in the first year of Wǔdé it was restored as Tōngzhōu.
Sūn Miǎn said: Tōngzhōu was originally Dàngqú County of Hàn times;
within it were over ten thousand qǐng of land,
hence it was named Wànzhōu;
Later Wèi, because Wànzhōu was situated at a crossroads of four routes,
renamed it Tōngzhōu;
in Sòng times it was Dázhōu.
On the jiǎyín day,
General Sāng Xiǎnhé and others were sent to attack Lǚ Chóngmào at Xiàxiàn.
Earlier, Minister of Works Dúgū Huái’ēn attacked Púfǎn
but could not capture it for a long time,
suffering many losses.
The Emperor repeatedly reproached him in edicts,
and Huái’ēn thus became resentful.
The Emperor once jokingly said to Huái’ēn:
“The sons of your paternal aunts have all become emperors”—
referring to Suí Yángdì and the current Emperor.
Huái’ēn also rather prided himself on this,
sometimes clenching his wrist and saying:
“Is it only the women in our family who become noble?”
The empresses of Zhōu Míngdì, Suí Wéndì, and the Emperor’s mother were all from the Dúgū clan.
Wàn is pronounced wàn.
It happened that Huái’ēn, Jūnbǎo, and Táng Jiǎn were all captured by Yùchí Jìngdé.
Jūnbǎo said to Jiǎn:
“Minister Dúgū was recently planning a great undertaking.
If he had decided earlier,
would we have suffered this humiliation!”
When Prince of Qín Lǐ Shìmín defeated Jìngdé at Měiliángchuān,
Huái’ēn escaped and returned.
The Emperor again sent him to lead troops and attack Púfǎn.
Jūnbǎo again said to Jiǎn:
“Minister Dúgū has managed to escape and return,
and is again at Púfǎn—
truly, a king does not die!”
Jiǎn, fearing that Huái’ēn would succeed in his plot,
then persuaded Yùchí Jìngdé
to send Liú Shìràng back to make peace with Táng.
Jìngdé agreed,
and thus reported Huái’ēn’s rebellious intentions.
At that time, Wáng Xíngběn had already surrendered,
and Huái’ēn entered and occupied his city.
The Emperor was about to cross the river to visit Huái’ēn’s camp
and had already boarded the boat
when Shìràng arrived.
The Emperor was greatly startled and said:
“That I escaped disaster—
is it not Heaven’s will!”
He then sent for Huái’ēn.
Huái’ēn, unaware that his plot was exposed,
came lightly by boat.
He was immediately seized and handed over to the officials,
and his accomplices were separately arrested.
On the jiǎyín day,
Huái’ēn and his accomplices were executed.
Dòu Jiàndé attacked Lǐ Shānghú
and killed him.
Jiàndé
encouraged agriculture and sericulture in Míngzhōu,
so that within his territory there were no bandits,
and merchants and travelers could lodge in the open countryside.
9. The Tujue (Turkic) Chùluó Kèhán welcomed Yáng Zhèngdào,
establishing him as King of Suí.
Yáng Zhèngdào was
the posthumous son of Prince Qí, Yáng Jiǎn.
Jué,
read as *jiǔ wù*.
Chù,
read as *chāng lǚ*.
Kè,
read with the entering tone from the *kān* initial.
Hán,
read as *hán*.
Chùluó gave him all the remaining Suí people to command,
and he had a following of ten thousand men.
He established the hundred officials,
all following the Suí system,
and resided in Dìngxiāng.
This was likely the Dìngxiāng Commandery of the Suí,
governing the Dàlì City.
10. In the third month,
on the Yǐchǒu day,
Liú Wǔzhōu sent his general Zhāng Wànsuì to raid Hào Prefecture,
but Lǐ Zhòngwén attacked and drove him off,
capturing and beheading several thousand men.
11. The title Nàyán was changed to Shìzhōng,
Nèishǐ Lìng was changed to Zhōngshū Lìng,
and Jǐshì Láng was changed to Jǐshì Zhōng.
These were restorations of old official titles.
Dù Yòu said: According to the Hàn system,
the Jǐshì Zhōng
attended court audiences daily and reviewed memorials submitted to the Imperial Secretariat,
and because they served within the palace halls,
they were called Jǐshì Zhōng (Servicemen Within).
The Eastern Hàn abolished the post,
the Wèi restored it,
and the Northern and Southern Dynasties followed suit.
Under the Later Zhōu, the Tiānguān department had a Jǐshì Zhōng,
responsible for managing the Six Classics
and serving at the emperor's side;
later, a separate Jǐshì Zhōng was established,
outside the Six Ministries system.
At the beginning of the Suí,
the Ministry of Personnel established the Jǐshì Láng,
and by Emperor Yáng's time,
it was moved to the Menxià (Chancellery) bureau,
with four officials appointed,
responsible for reviewing memorials.
At this time,
it was changed to Jǐshì Zhōng.
In the second year of the Lóngshuò era,
it was changed to Dōngtái Shèrén;
in the first year of the Xiánhēng era,
it was restored to the old title.
Its duties were to attend the emperor, read and endorse memorial drafts,
correct errors and omissions,
and handle various matters of the bureau.
The title Jǐshì Zhōng essentially used the Hàn name
to perform the duties of the Zhōu and Suí.
12. On the Jiǎxū day,
Fēng Déyí, the Vice Director of the Secretariat, was appointed as Zhōngshū Lìng.
13. Generals, commanders, prefectures, and counties under Wáng Shìchōng surrendered,
continuously month after month.
Shìchōng thus tightened his laws:
if one person fled or rebelled,
the entire family, regardless of age, would be executed;
but if father and son, brothers, or husband and wife reported on each other, they could be spared.
He also organized households into groups of five for mutual security.
If an entire family fled,
and the four neighboring families failed to detect it,
they would all be executed.
The more people he killed, the more fled,
to the point where even woodcutters
had limits on their comings and goings;
both public and private sectors were distressed and hard-pressed,
and people found life unbearable.
He also turned the palace city into a great prison.
Those he suspected,
along with their families, were detained in the palace;
when generals went out on campaigns,
their families were also held hostage in the palace.
The number of those imprisoned often did not fall below ten thousand,
and dozens died of starvation daily.
Shìchōng also appointed officials from the central ministries as Camp Field Commissioners for the twelve prefectures of Sī, Zhèng, Guǎn, Yuán, Yī, Yīn, Liáng, Còu, Sōng, Gǔ, Huái, and Dé.
Shìchōng made Luò Prefecture into Sī Prefecture,
Sìshuǐ into Zhèng Prefecture,
Guǎnchéng into Guǎn Prefecture,
Qìnshuǐ into Yuán Prefecture,
Xiāngchéng into Yī Prefecture,
Huòjiā into Yīn Prefecture,
and Suīyáng into Liáng Prefecture.
As for Còu Prefecture,
it is missing from records;
the *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Among the ancient sites of Zhèng Prefecture is Còu River,
so Còu Prefecture was likely established there.
Sōngyáng was made Sōng Prefecture,
Dàgǔ into Gǔ Prefecture,
Hénèi into Huái Prefecture,
and Wǔdé into Dé Prefecture.
The officials were overjoyed, as if ascending to immortality.
Chéng and Láng
refer to the Left and Right Directors of the Imperial Secretariat and the various Bureau Directors.
The historian records this to show that Wáng Shìchōng was heading toward defeat.
14. On the Jiǎshēn day,
Deputy Commander Zhāng Lún defeated Liú Wǔzhōu at Hào Prefecture,
capturing and beheading over a thousand men.
15. The Duke of Xīhé, Zhāng Lún,
this Zhāng Lún is the same as the Zhāng Lún above;
above his official title is recorded,
here his noble rank is recorded.
Shí Prefecture
was the Líshí Commandery of the Suí.
On the Yǐyǒu day,
Lǐ Zhēn was appointed as Commander-in-Chief of Shí Prefecture,
granted the imperial surname Lǐ,
and enfeoffed as Prince of Péngshān Commandery.
16. The Mán chieftain Rǎn Zhàozé raided Xìn Prefecture.
According to the *New Annals*: Xìn Prefecture
was the Bādōng Commandery of the Suí,
changed to Kuí Prefecture in the second year of the Wǔdé era;
the historian records it using the old prefectural name.
Dù Yòu said: Kuí Prefecture
was the State of Yú during the Spring and Autumn period.
The Liáng established Xìn Prefecture.
In the second year of the Táng Wǔdé era,
to avoid the taboo of the emperor's maternal grandfather Dúgū Xìn's name,
it was changed to Kuí Prefecture,
governing Fèngjié County.
Chieftain,
read as *cí yóu*.
The raid was unsuccessful.
Lǐ Jìng led eight hundred troops,
launched a surprise attack,
and beheaded him,
capturing over five thousand men;
on the Jǐchǒu day,
he recaptured the two prefectures of Kāi and Tōng.
Lǐ Xiàogōng also attacked Xiāo Xiǎn's Eastern Peace Prince Yántí,
and beheaded him.
17. In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Bǐngshēn day,
the emperor sacrificed at Huà Mountain;
on the Rényín day,
he returned to Cháng'ān.
18. The Yìzhōu Circuit Branch Secretariat was established,
with the six Commanderies of Yì, Lì, Kuài, Fū,
Jīng, and Suì placed under its jurisdiction.
Yì Prefecture
was the Shǔ Commandery of the Suí.
Lì Prefecture
was the Yìchéng Commandery of the Suí,
the Lí Prefecture of the Liáng,
the Jìnshòu of the Jìn,
the Hànshòu of the Shǔ,
and the Jiāméng of the Hàn.
Kuài Prefecture
was the Kuàiníng Garrison of the Suí's Liángchuān County,
and the Kuài Prefecture of the Western Wèi.
Fū Prefecture
was the Shàng Commandery of the Suí,
the Fū Prefecture of the Western Wèi,
and the Zhōngbù Fūchéng Commandery of the Northern Huà Prefecture under the Later Wèi,
which during the Tàihé era was the Eastern Qín Prefecture.
Jīng Prefecture
was the Āndìng Commandery of the Suí.
Suì Prefecture
was the Suìníng Commandery of the Suí,
and the Guǎnghàn County of the Hàn.
At this time, the territory under the Yìzhōu Branch Secretariat
stretched from Shǔ
across Lǒng and northeastward.
19. Liú Wǔzhōu repeatedly attacked Hào Prefecture,
but was defeated by Lǐ Zhòngwén.
Sòng Jīngāng's army ran out of food;
on the Dīngwèi day,
Jīngāng fled northward,
and Prince of Qín Lǐ Shìmín pursued him.
20. Luó Shìxìn besieged Cíjiàn.
The *Suí Annals* note: Shòu'ān County in Hénán Commandery had Cíjiàn.
The *Commentary on the Waterways Classic* states: Xīn'ān has the Xiào River,
and ten *li* east of the Xiào River is a stream
that people call Cíjiàn.
Shìxìn stabbed Wáng Xuányìng, knocking him off his horse,
but someone rescued him,
and he escaped.
21. On the Rénzǐ day,
Yáng Shìlín, the Commissioner of the Xiǎnzhōu Circuit Branch Secretariat, was appointed as its Director.
Last year in the first month,
Yáng Shìlín had surrendered.
22. On the Jiǎyín day,
Prince of Qín Lǐ Shìmín was additionally appointed as Director of the Yìzhōu Circuit Branch Secretariat.
23 Prince of Qin, Lǐ Shìmín, pursued Xún Xiàng at Lǚzhōu.
New Records: In the first year of Yìníng,
Huòyì, Zhàochéng, and Fénxī of Jìnzhōu,
Língshí of Fénzhōu,
were established as Huòshān Commandery.
In the first year of Wǔdé,
it was called Lǚzhōu.
Lǚzhōu likely administered Huòyì.
Xiàng,
read as Xī Liàng.
Riding the momentum of victory, he pursued the fleeing enemy,
covering over 200 li in one day and night,
engaging in dozens of battles.
Upon reaching Gāobì Ridge,
Commander Liú Hóngjī seized the reins and remonstrated:
"Your Highness has defeated the bandits,
pursued them this far,
your achievements are already sufficient.
To advance deep without cease,
do you not value your own life?
Moreover, the soldiers are hungry and weary.
It would be appropriate to encamp here,
await the full assembly of troops and provisions,
and then advance again.
It would not be too late."
Shìmín said:
"Sòng Jīngāng, having exhausted his schemes, flees;
the morale of his troops is disheartened and collapsing.
Success is difficult to achieve yet easy to lose,
opportunity is hard to come by yet easy to miss.
We must seize him by exploiting this momentum.
If we linger further,
allowing him to establish plans and complete preparations,
he will become impossible to attack again.
I exhaust my loyalty in service to the state,
how could I spare a thought for my own person!"
He then spurred his horse forward,
and the officers and soldiers dared not speak of hunger again.
He caught up with Sòng Jīngāng at Quèshǔ Valley,
fought eight battles in one day,
and defeated him in all,
capturing and beheading tens of thousands.
At night,
they camped on the western plain of Quèshǔ Valley.
Shìmín had not eaten for two days,
and had not removed his armor for three days.
The army had only one sheep,
which Shìmín shared with his officers and soldiers to eat.
On Bǐngchén,
Yú Jūn, Commander of Shǎnzhōu, escaped from Sòng Jīngāng's side and came.
Shìmín led his troops towards Jièxiū.
Jièxiū
was the seat of Jièzhōu administration.
Qù,
read as Qī Yù,
also read as Qūnxū.
They exited
the west gate,
deployed their battle formation with their backs to the city,
stretching seven li from north to south.
Shìmín sent Commander Lǐ Shìjì to engage them in battle.
He retreated slightly,
and the enemy took advantage of this.
Shìmín led elite cavalry to attack them,
emerging behind their formation.
Sòng Jīngāng suffered a major defeat,
with three thousand heads taken.
Sòng Jīngāng fled on light cavalry,
and Shìmín pursued him for several tens of li,
reaching Zhāngnán Fort.
Zhāngnán
was likely a person's name,

He said to the Emperor:

ultimately killing Fǎmíng and departing.
On the jiǎshēn day,
commanders Zhāng Zhènzhōu of Shūzhōu and others attacked Chén Dāngshì, general of Fǔ Gōngzǐ, at Huángshā of Yóuzhōu,
inflicting a major defeat.
In the third year of Wǔdé, Nán Xúzhōu was established at Jīngxìan of Xuānzhōu,
then renamed Yóuzhōu.
On the 59th dīnghài day,
the emperor hunted in Huáyīn.
On the jǐchǒu day,
he awaited and honored Qín Wáng Shìmín at Zhōngwù camp,
as the Qín Wáng returned from Bìngzhōu.
Laó,
pronounced lìdào.
In the twelfth month of the 60th year,
on the Guǐmǎo day,
Pacification Commissioner Lǐ Dàliàng lured Zhāng Shàn'ān,
and captured him.
Dàliàng attacked Shàn'ān at Hóngzhōu,
forming ranks across the water from Shàn'ān,
speaking to each other from a distance.
Dàliàng explained the consequences of fortune and misfortune,
and Shàn'ān said:
"Shàn'ān initially had no rebellious intent,
but was misled by his generals and soldiers;
I wish to surrender, but fear I may not be spared."
Dàliàng said:
"If Commander Zhāng has the heart to surrender,
then we are of one family."
Thereupon, he rode alone across the water into Shàn'ān's ranks,
clasped hands with Shàn'ān and spoke together,
showing there was no suspicion or estrangement.
Shàn'ān was greatly pleased,
and thus agreed to surrender.
Shortly after, Shàn'ān led several dozen cavalry to Dàliàng's camp,
Dàliàng stopped his cavalry outside the gate,
led Shàn'ān inside,
and spoke with him.
After a long while,
Shàn'ān took his leave to depart,
Dàliàng ordered warriors to seize him,
and his accompanying cavalry all fled.
When Shàn'ān's camp heard of this,
they were enraged,
and came forth with all their troops,
intending to attack Dàliàng.
Dàliàng sent someone to explain to them, saying:
"I am not detaining the Commander.
The Commander wholeheartedly wishes to return to the state,
and said to me: 'If I return to camp,
I fear the generals and soldiers may have differing opinions,
and I will be controlled by them.'
Therefore, he stayed of his own accord and did not leave,
why are you gentlemen angry with me!"
His partisans again cursed loudly, saying:
"Commander Zhāng has betrayed us to ingratiate himself with others."
Thereupon, they all dispersed and fled.
Dàliàng pursued and attacked them,
capturing many.
He sent Shàn'ān to Cháng'ān,
Shàn'ān claimed he had no contact with Fǔ Gōngshí,
the Emperor pardoned his crime,
and treated him well;
when Gōngshí was defeated,
correspondence between them was discovered,
and he was then executed.
61 On the Jiǎyín day,
the imperial carriage arrived at Cháng'ān.
62 On the Jǐsì day,
the Tūjué raided Dìngzhōu,
the provincial troops attacked and drove them away.

the Báijiǎn and Báigǒu Qiāng both sent envoys to present tribute.
"Báijiǎn",
likely should be
"Báilán".
The Suīshū states the Fùguó had tribes such as Báilán and Báigǒu,
their customs roughly similar to the Dǎngxiàng,
some were subjects of the Tǔyùhún,
others attached to the Fùguó.
The Xīnshū: The Báilán Qiāng,
the Tǔbō call them Dīnglíng,
to the left bordering the Dǎngxiàng,
to the right connecting with Duōmí,
capable soldiers ten thousand strong,
brave in battle,
skilled at making weapons.
In the sixth year of Wǔdé,
envoys came to court,
the following year their territory was made into Wéi and Gōng provinces.
The Báigǒu Qiāng bordered Dōnghuìzhōu,
capable soldiers only a thousand strong.
Shǐ,
read as shǐ.

first month,

provinces establishing Grand Impartial and Just,

Evaluating prestige and rank,

Wéichuān Commandery,

the old territory of Zhūtí Commandery,
not this one.

Its southern border reaches Jiāngyáng,
the Mín Mountains stretch westward in continuous ridges,

The land connects to Shíniǔ Mountain,

On the 12th day, Jǐwèi,
Gāo Kāidào's general Zhāng Jīnshù killed Kāidào and came to surrender.
Kāidào saw that all under heaven was settled,
and wished to surrender,

Gāo Kāidào had surrendered and then rebelled again,
and he knew himself to be guilty of such reversals.
Shù,
suǒ jiǎo fān.
Thus he had no intention of surrendering.
His officers and soldiers were all men from Shāndōng,
who longed for their hometowns,
and all had thoughts of leaving.
Kāidào selected several hundred brave warriors,
calling them his adopted sons,
and often had them guard within the inner chambers,
putting Jīnshù in charge of them.
The former general of Liú Hēità, Zhāng Jūnlì, who had fled and was with Kāidào,
secretly plotted with Jīnshù to capture Kāidào.
Jīnshù sent several of his confederates into the inner chambers,
to play games with the adopted sons.
Towards evening,
they secretly cut their bowstrings,
and hid knives and lances under the beds.
At nightfall,
they grabbed them and rushed out.
When people sleep, their eyes close and it becomes dark.
Shuò,
sè jiǎo fān.
Míng,
mò dìng fān.
They attacked Kāidào's chambers.
The adopted sons were about to defend themselves,
but their bowstrings were all severed,
and their knives and lances were already missing,
so they scrambled out to surrender;
Jūnlì also lit a fire outside to coordinate with them,
causing panic and confusion inside and out.
Kāidào knew he could not escape,
so he donned his armor, took up his weapons, and sat in the hall,
making music and drinking heartily with his wives and concubines.
The crowd feared his bravery,
and did not dare to press him.
As dawn approached,
Kāidào hanged himself,
and his wives, concubines, and sons then committed suicide.
Jīnshù arrayed his troops,
rounded up all the adopted sons and executed them,
and also killed Jūnlì,

Commentary on the Water Classic: The lake water originates from Dōnglíng Township in Lújiāng Commandery,
which is what the Tribute of Yǔ refers to as
"passing Jiǔjiāng and reaching Dōnglíng".
Flowing southwest,
the water accumulates to form a lake,
west of the lake is Qīnglín Mountain.
Also, southeast of present-day Dāngtú County is Qīngshān.
They built a crescent-shaped city wall,
extending over ten li in length,
and also established fortifications west of the river to resist the imperial army.
Lǐ Xiàogōng and Lǐ Jìng led the fleet to station at Shū Prefecture.
Lǐ Shìjì led ten thousand infantry across the Huái River,
captured Shòuyáng,
and stationed at Xiáshí.
Huìliàng and others held their fortifications and did not engage in battle.
Lǐ Xiàogōng sent surprise troops to cut off their supply routes.
Huìliàng's troops ran short of food.
At night,
they sent troops to approach Lǐ Xiàogōng's camp,
but Lǐ Xiàogōng held firm and did not move.
Lǐ Xiàogōng gathered his generals to discuss military affairs.
All said:
"Huìliàng and others possess strong troops
and occupy dangerous positions on water and land.
Attacking them cannot be done quickly.
It would be better to head directly for Dānyáng,
strike their lair.
Once Dānyáng collapses,
Huìliàng and others will surrender on their own!"
Lǐ Xiàogōng was about to follow this suggestion,
but Lǐ Jìng said:
"Although Gōngshí's elite troops are here in these two armies on water and land,
the troops he personally commands are also not few.
Now, if we cannot even capture the various stockades at Bówàng,
and Gōngshí holds Shítóu firmly,
how could it be easy to take?
If we attack Dānyáng,
and cannot capture it within ten days or a month,
with Huìliàng following behind us,
we would be attacked from both front and rear.
This is a dangerous path.
Lǐ Jìng's argument here is roughly similar to Chángsūn Wújì's argument at Ānshì.
However, Lǐ Jìng achieved decisive victory, while Tàizōng achieved no merit.
When the army withdrew from Ānshì,
Lǐ Jìng blamed him for not being able to adopt Lǐ Dàozōng's strategy.
This is why employing troops is so difficult.
Their hearts are not unwilling to fight,
but precisely because Gōngshí established a plan to make them cautious,
wanting to wear out our troops.
If we now attack their city to provoke them,
we can defeat them in one move!"
Lǐ Xiàogōng agreed.
He sent weak troops to attack the enemy camp first, while deploying elite troops in formation to await them.
The attackers of the fortifications were defeated and fled.
The enemy troops pursued them.
After traveling several li,
they encountered the main army.
Engaging in battle,
they were greatly defeated.
This is the old stratagem from the Zuǒ Zhuàn where the five great officers of Chǔ defeated the Wú army to destroy Shūjiū.
"Do you not recognize me?
How dare you come to fight me!"
Many of the enemy troops were former subordinates of Kàn Léng,
and all lacked the will to fight.
Some even bowed in respect.
Because of this, they were defeated.
Lǐ Xiàogōng and Lǐ Jìng took advantage of the victory to pursue the fleeing enemy.
Fighting over a hundred li,
both the Bóshān and Qīnglín garrisons collapsed.
Huìliàng, Zhèngtōng, and others fled back.
Over ten thousand were killed, wounded, or drowned.
Lǐ Jìng's troops arrived at Dānyáng first.
Gōngshí was greatly frightened.
With tens of thousands of troops,
he abandoned the city and fled east,
intending to join Zuǒ Yóuxiān at Kuàijī.
Lǐ Shìjì pursued him.
Gōngshí reached Jùróng.
Jùróng County belonged to Dānyáng Commandery in Hàn times.
At that time, it belonged to Jiǎng Prefecture,
located ninety li east of Jiànkāng City.
At night,
he stayed at Cháng Prefecture.
His general Wú Sāo and others plotted to seize him.
Gōngshí became aware of it.
Abandoning his wife and children,
he alone led several dozen close confidants,
broke through the gate, and fled.
He reached Wǔkāng.
Wú divided Wūchéng and Yúháng to establish Yǒng'ān County.
Jìn changed it to Yǒngkāng,
then changed it again to Wǔkāng.
It belonged to Hú Prefecture,
located one hundred and seven li southwest of the prefecture.
Xīmén Jūnyí died in battle.
They captured Gōngshí,
sent him to Dānyáng to be beheaded and his head displayed,
hunted down the remaining partisans,
executed them all,
and the region south of the Yangtze was pacified.
On Jǐhài,
Lǐ Xiàogōng was appointed Right Vice Director of the Eastern Branch Department of the Imperial Secretariat,
and Lǐ Jìng was appointed Minister of War.
Shortly after,
the Branch Department was abolished.
Lǐ Xiàogōng was appointed Grand Governor of Yáng Prefecture,
and Lǐ Jìng was appointed Chief Administrator of the headquarters.
The Emperor deeply praised Lǐ Jìng's achievements,
saying:
"Jìng
is the fatal illness of Xiāo and Fǔ."
Meaning that both Xiāo Xiǎn and Fǔ Gōngshí were killed by Lǐ Jìng.
Huāng,
pronounced "huāng".
Kàn Léng had many achievements,
and was quite boastful about them.
Gōngshí falsely accused Léng of conspiring with him.
When Zhào Jùn Wáng Lǐ Xiàogōng confiscated the lands and residences of the rebel partisans,
confiscation means
recording all the lands and residences owned by the rebel partisans,
seizing them and bringing them into official possession.
Lǐ Xiàogōng also confiscated his;
Léng appealed for justice,
offending Lǐ Xiàogōng.
Lǐ Xiàogōng became angry
and executed him for plotting rebellion.
On the 19th day, summer,
fourth month,
Gēngzǐ, the first day,
a general amnesty was declared in the empire.
On this day,
new laws and ordinances were promulgated,
adding fifty-three new articles compared to the old regulations of the Kāihuáng era.
In the 20th year, the Jūntián (Equal-field), Zū (Grain Tax), Yōng (Corvée Commutation), and Diào (Household Textile Tax) systems were initially established:
For able-bodied adult males (dīng) and semi-adult males (zhōng),
one qǐng of land was granted.
For those with severe disabilities, the grant was reduced by six-tenths;
for widows and concubines, it was reduced by seven-tenths.
In all cases, two-tenths of the land was designated as hereditary property (shìyè),
and eight-tenths as life-term allotment (kǒufēn).
Each adult male (dīng) annually paid a grain tax (zū),
amounting to two dàn of millet.
The household textile tax (diào) varied according to local production,
consisting of patterned silk (líng), plain silk (juàn), a coarse silk fabric (shī), or cloth (bù).
Annual corvée service was set at twenty days;
if service was not performed, a commutation fee (yōng) was collected,
at the rate of three chǐ of silk per day.
The New Treatise states: In general, for granted land,
an adult male (dīng) annually delivered two hú of millet,
which was called the grain tax (zū).
For an adult male (dīng),
according to the local products of his district,
he annually delivered two pǐ of plain silk (juàn),
two zhàng of patterned silk (líng) or coarse silk (shī),
for cloth (bù) the amount was increased by one-fifth,
along with three liǎng of silk floss,
and three jīn of hemp.
In non-sericulture districts, fourteen liǎng of silver were delivered instead,
which was called the household textile tax (diào).
The annual labor service obligation was twenty days,
with an additional two days in leap years;
if service was not performed,
the commutation fee (yōng) was collected,
at the rate of three chǐ [of silk] per day.
Shī (coarse silk fabric),
is pronounced shìzhī.
Zēng (silk fabric),
resembles cloth.
For service of fifteen days,
the household textile tax (diào) was exempted;
for thirty days,
both the grain tax (zū) and household textile tax (diào) were exempted.
In cases of disaster from flood, drought, insects, or frost,
if the damage reached four-tenths or more, the grain tax (zū) was exempted;
if damage reached six-tenths or more, the household textile tax (diào) was exempted;
if damage reached seven-tenths or more, all taxes and corvée service were exempted.
The wealth and property of the common people were divided into nine grades.
Upper, middle, and lower, each having three sub-grades.
Five lǐ constituted a xiāng (district),
four households constituted a lín (neighborhood),
and four lín constituted a bǎo (ward).
Textual Analysis states: The Táng Lì (Tang Calendar) says:
"Four households constitute a lín,
five households constitute a bǎo."
According to the Tōngdiǎn (Comprehensive Statutes),
four lín constitute a bǎo.
The Táng Lì is mistaken.
Rural settlements were called cūn (villages).
Families receiving official salaries
were not permitted to compete for profit with the common people;
artisans, merchants, and miscellaneous categories
were not allowed to enter the ranks of scholar-officials.
At birth, males and females were classified as huáng (infant),
at four years as xiǎo (child),
at sixteen as zhōng (semi-adult),
at twenty as dīng (adult),
and at sixty as lǎo (elder).
Annual population registers (jìzhàng) were compiled,
and household registers (hùjí) were compiled every three years.
21st day, Dīngwèi:
The Dǎngxiàng (Tangut) raided Sōngzhōu.
22nd day, Gēngshēn:
The Court Receptionist (tōngshì shèrén) Lǐ Fèngqǐ attacked the rebellious Lǎo people in Wànzhōu,
and pacified them.
Later Wèi divided Qú Rǔ,
and established Yúquán County.
Later Zhōu changed it to Wànchuān,
Suí changed it to Nánpǔ,
placing it under Xìnzhōu.
In the first year of the Wǔdé era, Wànzhōu (Nánpǔ Commandery) was separately established.
Lǎo (tribal people),
is pronounced lǔ hào;
the same below.
23rd, fifth month:
Xīnwèi day:
The Tūjué (Turks) raided Shuòzhōu.
24th, Jiǎxū day:
The Qiāng and the Tǔyùhún jointly raided Sōngzhōu.
Tǔ (in Tǔyùhún),
follows the entering tone of tūn.
Yù (in Tǔyùhún),
is pronounced yù.
The Governor of Fúzhōu, Jiǎng Shànhé, attacked them via the Fāngzhōu route.
Western Wèi expelled the Tǔyùhún,
and established Dèngzhōu.
In the seventh year of the Suí Kāihuáng era,
it was renamed Fúzhōu,
Tóngchāng Commandery.
In the first year of the Wǔdé era,
Zuǒfēng and Yìxié of Huìzhōu were separated,
to establish Yìzhōu,
Línyì Commandery.
Under the Táng system,
a Prefect of an Upper Prefecture (shàngzhōu cìshǐ),
held rank of Cong Sānpǐn;
of a Middle Prefecture (zhōngzhōu),
Zhèng Sìpǐn Shàng;
of a Lower Prefecture (xiàzhōu),
Zhèng Sìpǐn Xià.
25th, Bǐngxū day:
The Rénzhì Palace was constructed at Yíjūn.
Yíjūn County was established at the site of the ancient Duì Xǔ city.
Under Suí, it belonged to the Jīngzhào Commandery;
at this time it belonged to Yízhōu.
26th, Dīnghài day:
Dòu Guǐ defeated the rebellious Lǎo people at Fāngshān,
capturing over twenty thousand people.

Later Student from Tiāntái
Seventh Year of the Wǔdé Era
(Jiǎshēn, 624)
1 Sixth month:
Xīnchǒu day:
The Emperor went to the Rénzhì Palace to escape the heat.
The Emperor had built the Rénzhì Palace in Yíjūn County of Yízhōu.
2 Xīnhài day:
The Lǎo people in Shuāngzhōu and Fúzhōu rebelled.
The Governor of Nányīnzhōu, Lǐ Guāngdù, and others were sent to attack and pacify them.
Shuāngzhōu,
Yǒngxī Commandery,
was the territory of the Hàn Duānxī County.
Also, Xìnyì County of Shuāngzhōu,
in the first year of Wǔdé, was divided to establish Huáidé County,
and Nánfúzhōu was concurrently established.
Nányīnzhōu,
Yùlín Commandery,
was the territory of the Hàn Guǎngyù County.
Later, Hàn's Gǔ Yǒng served as Governor of Yùlín,
causing over a hundred thousand Wū Xǔ people to submit,
opening up and establishing seven counties,
which is this area.
Shuāng (in Shuāngzhōu),
is pronounced lǚ jiāng.
Lǎo (tribal people),
is pronounced lǔ hào.
3 Bǐngchén day:
The Tǔyùhún raided Fúzhōu.
This Fúzhōu was established on the lands of the Shēng Qiāng (raw Qiang),
as noted above.
Tǔ (in Tǔyùhún),
follows the entering tone of tūn.
Yù (in Tǔyùhún),
is pronounced yù.
4 Rénxū day:
The Governor of Qìngzhōu, Yáng Wéngàn, rebelled.
Qìngzhōu, Hónghuà Commandery,
was the territory of the Hàn Běidì's Mǎlǐng and Fāngqú counties.
According to Sòng Bái's Xù Tōngdiǎn: Three lǐ southeast of Qìngzhōu Hónghuà Commandery was the Bù Zhú city.
In the eleventh year of the Later Wèi Dàtǒng era, Shuòzhōu was established.
Suí Wéndì changed it to establish the Héchuān Garrison.
In the sixteenth year,
Qìngzhōu was established,
taking the auspicious name Qìng (celebration) for its excellence.
The present commandery city is named Wèilǐchéng,
at the confluence of the Báimǎ two rivers,
also called Bù Zhú city.
The attached Guō'ānhuà County,
was established by Suí as Héshuǐ County,
changed by Wǔdé to Héchuān County,
changed by Zhēnguān to Hónghuà County,
and soon the county name was changed following the commandery.
The subordinate Huáchí County,
was the territory of the Hàn Guīdé County;
Lèpán County,
was the territory of the Hàn Fùpíng County;
Mǎlǐng and Fāngqú
then became the territory of the Tōngyuǎn Army.
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì states: The Hàn Yùzhì County
is present-day Qìngzhōu Hónghuà County.
Previously,
Prince of Qí, Lǐ Yuánjí, urged the Crown Prince Lǐ Jiànchéng to eliminate the Prince of Qín, Lǐ Shìmín,
saying:
"I will personally kill him for my elder brother!"
When Shìmín accompanied the Emperor on a visit to Yuánjí's residence,
Yuánjí had his guard commander Yǔwén Bǎo lie in ambush within the bedchamber,
intending to assassinate Shìmín.
Jiànchéng's nature was rather kind and tolerant,
and he hastily stopped it.
Yuánjí said angrily:
"I was planning this for my elder brother's sake,
what is it to me!"
Jiànchéng recruited over two thousand brave warriors from Cháng'ān and the surrounding regions to serve as guards for the Eastern Palace,
stationing them in the Left and Right Chánglín,
where they were called the Chánglín troops.
The Eastern Palace had Left and Right Chánglín gates.
Examination of discrepancies: The Old Biography states:
"Jiànchéng privately summoned brave warriors from all directions,
and also recruited over two thousand ruffians from Cháng'ān,
keeping them as palace troops,
stationing them in the Left and Right Chánglín,
calling them the Chánglín troops."
The Veritable Records state:
"Yuánjí, seeing that the Prince of Qín had achieved great merits,
often harbored jealousy and malice,
his words were vile,
and his slanders grew increasingly severe.
He often said to Jiànchéng: 'I should kill him with my own hands for you, elder brother.'
Jiànchéng's nature was rather benevolent and tolerant,
and initially he stopped him;
but as Yuánjí repeatedly urged,
Jiànchéng later agreed.
Yuánjí then urged swift action,
and together with Jiànchéng, they each recruited strong men,
often hiding criminals among them,
rewarding them,
plotting to carry out treason.
Their secretary, Róng Jiǔsī, wrote a poem to satirize them, saying:
'Adorned with paints like Chéngqìng,
lavished with silks like Zhuānzhū.'
Yet they did not realize it.
The registrar Péi Xuānyǎn, after being dismissed from office, switched to serving in the Prince of Qín's residence,
and fearing he would leak their affairs,
they poisoned him.
After this man's death,
everyone was terrified,
knowing of the matter,
but none dared speak of it.
Later, they formed connections within the palace,
and together with Jiànchéng, they both had relations with the Virtuous Consort Yǐn,
using her as internal support."
The Old Biography also states:
"They heavily bribed the Secretariat Director Féng Déyí to serve as their ally.
As a result, Gāozǔ grew somewhat distant from Tàizōng and showed increased favor to Yuánjí."
Now, we only select and record the credible parts.
They stationed them in various wards east of the palace,
intending to supplement the Eastern Palace's permanent guards.
Kědá,
a non-Han surname.
Qí,
pronounced as jì.
Yān,
pronounced as yīnjiān.
According to the Tang Six Codes: All officials assigned to palace guard duty,
take turns based on their rotation order.
Generals, vice generals, and colonels of the various guards, as well as the commanders, deputy commanders, Qiānniú bodyguards, personal guards, and the Crown Prince's Qiānniú, all serve on duty;
Zhéchōng and Guǒyì officers assigned to guard duty
serve one day on duty,
two days off;
various types of permanent guards, such as Sījiē, Zhōnghòu, and Sīgē, serve five days on duty,
ten days off.
Shàng,
pronounced as shízhǎng;
the following "shàng" in the context of reporting a rebellion is the same.
The Emperor summoned Jiànchéng and reprimanded him,
exiling Kědázhì to Xīzhōu.
Yáng Wéngàn had once served as a guard in the Eastern Palace,
and Jiànchéng was close to him,
privately ordering him to recruit strong men and send them to Cháng'ān.
The Emperor was about to visit the Rénzhì Palace,
ordering Jiànchéng to remain in the capital,
while Shìmín and Yuánjí both accompanied him.
Jiànchéng sent Yuánjí to plot against Shìmín,
saying:
"The plan for our safety or peril
will be decided this year."
He also sent the colonel Ěrzhū Huàn and the captain Qiáo Gōngshān to deliver armor to Wéngàn.
The two men reached Bīnzhōu,
and reported the rebellion.
Bīnzhōu was the location of the Hàn dynasty's Qī County;
at the end of the Hàn dynasty, the Xīnpíng Commandery was established,
with the ancient Bīn Pavilion to the northeast,
and the Later Wèi established Bīnzhōu.
When Ěrzhū Huàn and others reached Bīnzhōu,
they claimed there was an urgent rebellion,
and Bīnzhōu reported it,
allowing them to reach the Rénzhì Palace.
Yí,
pronounced as yújì.
Jiàng,
pronounced as jíliàng.
Xiào,
pronounced as hùjiào.
So that
they could coordinate from inside and outside;
Examination of discrepancies: The Comprehensive Record states:
"Jiànchéng sent the colonel Ěrzhū Huàn and the captain Qiáo Gōngshān to deliver armor to Wéngàn,
ordering him to raise troops;
Huàn and others, upon reaching Bīnzhōu,
feared punishment,
and reported it."
Liú Sù's Minor Stories states:
"Someone falsely accused the Eastern Palace."
Now, we follow the Veritable Records.
The Emperor was furious,
and under the pretext of other matters,
issued a handwritten edict summoning Jiànchéng,
ordering him to come to the imperial encampment.
Jiànchéng was afraid
and dared not go.
The Crown Prince's secretary Xú Shīmó urged him to seize the city and raise troops;
Examination of discrepancies: The Comprehensive Record writes
"Shīyù."
Now, we follow the Veritable Records.
Dismissing his attendants,
he went to apologize to the Emperor,
and Jiànchéng then went to the Rénzhì Palace.
Before reaching sixty lǐ,
he left all his officials at the Máo Hóngbīn Fort,
which was built by the Later Wèi general Máo Hóngbīn,
hence the name.
Sòng Bái said: Sānyuán County had the Hóngbīn Stockade;
during the Xiàochāng era of the Later Wèi,
when Xiāo Bǎoyín rebelled,
Máo Hóngbīn built a stockade to defend against him,
its old city located fifteen lǐ north of the county.
He kowtowed to apologize for his crime,
throwing himself forcefully,
nearly to the point of collapse.
The Emperor's anger did not subside,
and that night,
he placed him under a tent,
Zhèng Kāngchéng said: A tent is above,
or a tent spread out on the ground.
He ordered the Palace Supervisor Chén Fú to guard him,
and sent the Minister of Agriculture Yǔwén Yǐng to swiftly summon Wéngàn.
In the early Hàn, the Office of Grain Intendant was established;
Emperor Jǐng changed it to Grand Minister of Agriculture,
and Emperor Wǔ added the character "Sī";
the Liáng dynasty established the Twelve Ministers, including the Minister of Agriculture,
responsible for state granaries and storage.
Yǔwén Yǐng informed him of the situation,
and Wéngàn then raised troops in rebellion.
The Emperor sent the Left Martial Guard General Qián Jiǔlǒng and the Língzhōu Commander Yáng Shīdào to attack him.
On the jiǎzǐ day,
the Emperor summoned the Prince of Qín, Shìmín, to discuss the matter.
Shìmín said:
"Wéngàn is a petty man,
daring to commit such madness and rebellion;
I estimate that the officials in his prefecture have already captured and executed him;
if not,
we should simply send one general to suppress him."
The Emperor said:
"Not so.
Wéngàn's affair involves Jiànchéng,
and I fear many may respond to him.
You should go yourself.
When you return,
I will establish you as Crown Prince.
I cannot imitate Emperor Wén of Suí by killing his own son,
so I will enfeoff Jiànchéng as the Prince of Shǔ.
Shǔ's troops are weak,
and if in the future he can serve you,
you should spare him;
if he cannot serve you,
it will be easy for you to take him!"
The Emperor, considering that Rénzhì Palace was located in the mountains,
feared that rebel troops might suddenly rise up.
At night,
he led the palace guards southward out of the mountains.
After traveling several dozen lǐ,
the officials of the Eastern Palace
arrived one after another.
He ordered them to form groups of thirty men each,
and dispatched troops to surround and guard them.
The next day,
he returned to Rénzhì Palace.
Examination of Discrepancies states: The Veritable Records say:
"When Gāozǔ left the mountains,
Jiànchéng was anxious and resentful,
lying inside his tent.
Dù Yān, the Military Officer of the Tiāncè Army, requested to take advantage of the chaos to attack him,

The Táng Tǒngjì says:

he passed by Jiànchéng's tent at night.
He estimated that Jiànchéng had only about ten attendants around him,

saying: 'Regarding today's matter,
we will all follow Your Highness's command.
If you order us to eliminate him,
now is the time.'
Tàizōng rebuked them and stopped them.
Later, when he returned and told his staff about the incident,
all the civil and military officials urged him: 'Wéngàn is committing treason for the Crown Prince,
and this is known throughout the empire.
If we use the hands of palace officials to deal with him,
it would align perfectly with Heaven's will.'
Tàizōng said: 'I have just received His Majesty's gracious decree.
How could I bear to turn against it so quickly!
Even if there were grounds to oppose it,
for you to speak of such things,
it is absolutely unreasonable.'
His staff urged him again,
but he ultimately refused and would not listen."
According to this, at that time, Gāozǔ had no intention of executing Jiànchéng,
so how would his attendants dare to kill him arbitrarily!
This account is not adopted here.
After Shìmín departed,
Yuánjí and the imperial concubines took turns pleading for Jiànchéng,

The Emperor's mind then changed,
and he sent Jiànchéng back to the capital to remain in charge there.
He only reproached him for the discord among brothers,
blaming it on the Crown Prince's Advisor Wáng Guī, Left Guard Commander Wéi Tǐng,
(The Left and Right Guard Commanders were in charge of the administration and orders for the Eastern Palace's feather guard troops and weapons.

Shuài,
is pronounced suǒ lǜ fān.)
and exiled them to Xīzhōu.
Tǐng
was the son of Wéi Chōng.
Wéi Chōng served Emperor Wén of Suí,

After Luòyáng was pacified,

Fáng Xuánlíng considered Dù Yān to be cunning and scheming,

the seventh month,
on Jǐsì,

His followers all scattered.

On Xīnsì,
the Tǔyùhún and Dǎngxiàng invaded Sōngzhōu.
(Tǔ,

Yù,

11. On Guǐwèi,
the Turks invaded Yīnpán.
(Yīnpán County,
belonged to Āndìng in the Hàn Dynasty,

12. On Jiǎshēn,
Jiǎng Shànhé, the Prefect of Fúzhōu, attacked the Tǔyùhún at Chìmó Town in Sōngzhōu
and defeated them.
13. On Jǐchǒu,
the Turkic Tùlì Shè and Yuǎn Jūnzhāng invaded Bìngzhōu.
14. On Jiǎzǐ,
the imperial carriage returned to the capital.
15. Someone advised the Emperor, saying:
"The reason the Turks repeatedly invade Guānzhōng
is because the women, children, jade, and silk are all in Cháng'ān.
If we burn Cháng'ān and do not make it the capital,
then the barbarian invasions will cease of their own accord."
The Emperor thought this reasonable,
and sent the Vice Director of the Secretariat Yǔwén Shìjí to cross the Southern Mountains to Fán and Dèng,
to survey habitable lands.
(Crossing the Southern Mountains of Cháng'ān and exiting through Shāngzhōu,
one reaches Fán and Dèng.
Xíng,
is pronounced xià mèng fān.)
Crown Prince Jiànchéng, Prince of Qí Yuánjí, and Péi Jì all supported this plan.
Although Xiāo Yǔ and others knew it was unfeasible, they did not dare to remonstrate.
The Prince of Qín, Shìmín, remonstrated, saying:
"The troubles caused by the Róng and Dí barbarians
have existed since ancient times.
Your Majesty, with your divine martial prowess, rose like a dragon,
illuminating and settling the Central Plains.
You have a million elite troops,
invincible in every campaign.
How can you, because of the barbarian invasions disturbing the borders,
hastily move the capital to avoid them,
bringing shame upon the empire,
and becoming a laughingstock for a hundred generations!
That Huò Qùbìng was merely a general of the Hàn court,
yet he was determined to exterminate the Xiōngnú.
How much more so I, who unworthily hold a frontier post?
I beg for a period of several years,
and request to bind Xiélì by the neck,
and bring him before the palace gates.
If I fail to achieve this,
then moving the capital will not be too late."
The Emperor said:
"Excellent."
Jiànchéng said:
"In the past, Fán Kuài wanted to lead a hundred thousand troops to rampage through the land of the Xiōngnú.
(The event is recorded in the twelfth scroll, third year of Emperor Huì of Hàn.)"
Shìmín said:
"The circumstances are different,
and the use of troops varies.
Fán Kuài was a petty fellow—
what is there to speak of him!
Within ten years,
I will surely pacify the northern deserts.
This is not
an empty boast!"
(This sets the stage for Tàizōng's later destruction of the Turks.)
Jiànchéng and the imperial concubines then jointly slandered Shìmín, saying:
"Although the Turks have repeatedly caused trouble on the borders,
they retreat once they receive bribes.
The Prince of Qín outwardly uses the pretext of resisting the invaders,
but inwardly he desires to monopolize military authority,
to fulfill his plot of usurpation!"
The Emperor went hunting south of the city,
with the Crown Prince and the Princes of Qín and Qí accompanying him.
The Emperor ordered the three sons to gallop and shoot in a competition.
Jiànchéng had a steppe horse,
stout and strong but prone to stumbling.
He gave it to Shìmín, saying:
"This horse is very swift,
capable of leaping across ravines several zhàng wide.
You, brother, are skilled at riding;
try mounting it."
Shìmín rode it in pursuit of deer.
The horse stumbled,
but Shìmín leaped off and landed several paces away.
When the horse rose,
he mounted it again.
This happened three times.
Turning to Yǔwén Shìjí, he said:
"He intended to kill me with this,
but life and death are fated—
what harm could it possibly do!"
When Jiànchéng heard of this,
he had a concubine slander Shìmín to the Emperor,
saying:
"The Prince of Qín claims,
'I possess the Mandate of Heaven,
and am destined to be the ruler of the realm—
how could I die a meaningless death!'"
The Emperor was greatly enraged.
He first summoned Jiànchéng and Yuánjí,
then called Shìmín in
and rebuked him:
"The Son of Heaven possesses the Mandate of Heaven by nature;
it cannot be sought through intellect or force.
Why are you so eager to seek it?"
Shìmín removed his cap and kowtowed,
requesting to be handed over to the judicial authorities for investigation.
The Emperor's anger did not subside.
Just then, an official reported that the Turks had invaded.
The Emperor then changed his expression, consoled and encouraged Shìmín,
ordered him to put on his cap and belt,
and consulted with him on the Turkic matter.
In the intercalary month,
on Jǐwèi day,
an edict was issued for Shìmín and Yuánjí to lead troops out of Bīnzhōu to defend against the Turks,
and the Emperor bid them farewell at Lánchí.
Lánchí
was the place where Qín Shǐhuáng encountered bandits.
The Commentary to the Records of the Grand Historian states: According to the Treatise on Geography,
Wèichéng County had Lánchí Palace.
The Correct Meaning states: According to the Comprehensive Gazetteer,
Lánchí Pond was the ancient Lánchí,
located within the boundaries of Xiányáng County.
The Records of Qín states: The First Emperor channeled the Wèi River to form a pond,
constructed Penglai and Yingzhou islets,
carved a stone whale,
two hundred zhàng long;
this was the place where he encountered bandits.
He then ordered Shìmín to suppress them.
After the matter was pacified,
suspicion and resentment grew even deeper.
16. Earlier, during the Suí dynasty's end, Wéi Rénshòu of Jīngzhào served as Judicial Assistant in Shǔ Commandery.
According to the New Book's Treatise on Officials: The Judicial Officer of each prefecture's Legal Section
was responsible for adjudicating cases according to law,
overseeing bandits and thieves,
and managing the confiscation of illicit goods.
There was also the position of Adjutant,
with a note stating: In the early Wǔdé period, the title 'Administrative Assistant' was changed to 'Administrative Adjutant,'
and soon after to 'Adjutant.'
Thus, the Assistant was equivalent to the Adjutant position.
They still faced west to pay respects to Rénshòu before worshiping the Buddha and then dying.
The history states that regarding Wéi Rénshòu's judgments,
people themselves felt no injustice.
For,
read as yú wèi fān.
Cuàn Hóngdá led the southwestern barbarians to submit to the interior.
The court sent envoys to pacify them,
but most were greedy and corrupt,
causing suffering among the distant people,
and some rebelled.
Rénshòu was then the Chief Clerk of the Governor of Xīzhōu.
The Emperor, hearing of his reputation,
appointed him Acting Governor of Nánníngzhōu,
with his administration temporarily based in Yuèxī.
Xīzhōu
was Yuèxī Commandery.
Xī,
pronounced suǐ.
Chief,
pronounced zhī liǎng fān.
Rénshòu was by nature tolerant and generous,
with insight and judgment.
After receiving his appointment,
he led five hundred soldiers to the Xī'ěr River,
traversing several thousand lǐ.
The tribal chiefs of the Mán and Yí peoples all submitted upon hearing of his approach,
coming to see Rénshòu.
Rénshòu, acting under imperial authority, established seven prefectures and fifteen counties,
appointing their respective chiefs as prefects and magistrates.
According to the Old Book's Treatise on Geography,
in that year, Xīníng, Yù, Xīpíng, Lì, Nányún, Mó, and Nánníng prefectures were established.
The Treatise also mentions Xīpíng Prefecture,
also established that year.
Chief,
pronounced suǒ lèi fān.
The Mán and Yí peoples were pleased and submitted.
As he was about to return,
the chiefs all said:
"The Son of Heaven sent you, sir, to govern Nánníng;
why are you leaving so hastily?"
Rénshòu used the excuse that the city walls were not yet built.
The Mán and Yí peoples then joined together to build a city for Rénshòu,
constructing government offices,
completing them within ten days.
Rénshòu then said:
"I received an edict only to inspect and pacify;
I dare not presume to stay."
The Mán and Yí peoples wept as they saw him off,
and each sent their sons or younger brothers to present tribute.
On Rénxū day,
Rénshòu returned to court.
The Emperor was greatly pleased
and ordered Rénshòu to relocate his garrison to Nánníng,
stationing troops there.
17. Yuàn Jūnzhāng led the Turks to raid Shuòzhōu.
18. In the eighth month,
on Wùchén day,
the Turks raided Yuánzhōu.
19. On Jǐsì day,
the Tǔyùhún raided Shànzhōu.
Shànzhōu was Xīpíng Commandery,
the former capital of the Tūfà clan.
Shàn,
pronounced shí zhàn fān.
20. On Rénshēn day,
the Turks raided Xīnzhōu.
On Bǐngzǐ day,
they raided Bìngzhōu;
the capital was placed under martial law.
On Wùyín day,
they raided Suízhōu.
Suízhōu
was Diāoyīn Commandery.
Diāoyīn was an ancient county,
belonging to Shàng Commandery in Hàn times,
now the area north of Yánzhōu in the Héngshān region.
Sǔn Miǎn stated: Suízhōu
was inhabited by the Báidí during the Spring and Autumn period,
became Shàng Commandery under Qín,
was established as Shàngzhōu under the Later Wèi,
then renamed Suízhōu,
taking its name from Suídé County.
At this time,
the two khans, Xiélì and Tūlì, invaded with their entire nation,
forming a continuous line of camps advancing southward.
The Prince of Qin, Lǐ Shìmín, led troops to resist them.
It happened that Guānzhōng had experienced prolonged rain,
causing grain transport to be cut off.
The soldiers were exhausted from campaigning,
and their weapons and equipment were worn out.
Both the court and the army were deeply concerned.
Shìmín encountered the enemy at Bīnzhōu,
marshaled his troops, and prepared for battle.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
the khans suddenly arrived west of the city with over ten thousand cavalry,
deploying at Wǔlǒng Bǎn.
The officers and soldiers were terrified.
Shìmín said to Yuánjí:
"Now the enemy cavalry is pressing upon us.
We cannot show them weakness.
We must fight them in battle.
Can you go with me?"
Yuánjí, frightened, said:
"The enemy's situation is like this.
How can we rashly go out?
If by any chance we are defeated,
would regret be of any use!"
Shìmín said:
"If you dare not go out,
I will go alone.
You stay here and watch."
Shìmín's going out alone served outwardly to display his might to the Tūjué,
and inwardly to subdue Yuánjí's heart.
He announced to them:
"Our state has established peaceful relations with the khans through marriage alliance.
Why have you broken the treaty,
penetrating deep into our territory?
I am the Prince of Qin.
If the khan is capable of fighting,
come out alone and fight me.
If you bring your multitude,
I will simply oppose them with these hundred horsemen."
Xiélì could not fathom his intentions,
and laughed without responding.
Xiélì had always admired the Prince of Qin's divine martial prowess,
fearing that he was challenging with a hundred horsemen
while concealing a large army to surround and attack from all sides,
therefore he did not dare respond.
He sent a horseman to tell Tūlì:
"You formerly made an alliance with me,
pledging mutual aid in times of crisis.
Now you lead troops to attack me.
How can you be without the sentiment of shared incense and fire!"
In ancient times, alliances and oaths were pledged before Heaven, Earth, mountains, rivers, spirits, and deities,
involving only the smearing of blood.
In later ages, there were those who swore oaths facing deities,
and those who swore oaths revering the Buddha,
whence began the matter of incense and fire.
The Prince of Qin used this to sow suspicion in Xiélì's heart.
Tūlì, fearing he would be suspected by Xiélì because of this,
therefore also did not dare respond.
As they were about to cross the ditch stream,
Xiélì, seeing Shìmín coming out lightly,
and hearing the words about incense and fire,
suspected that Tūlì had a plot with Shìmín.
He then sent to stop Shìmín, saying:
"Your Highness need not cross.
I have no other intention.
I merely wish to reaffirm and solidify our alliance treaty with Your Highness."
He then led his troops to withdraw slightly.
After this, the continuous rain became even heavier.
Shìmín said to his generals:
"What the enemy relies on is bows and arrows.
Now the accumulated rain has lasted a long time.
Both sinew and glue have dissolved.
Their bows cannot be used.
They are like birds with broken wings.
We dwell in houses and eat cooked food,
our sabers and lances are sharp.
'Xī' means
'sharp' or 'hard'.
If we do not seize this opportunity,
what else are we waiting for!"
He then secretly led his troops out at night,
advancing through the rain.
The Tūjué were greatly alarmed.
Shìmín also sent someone to explain the advantages and disadvantages to Tūlì.
Tūlì was pleased,
and obeyed his command.
Xiélì wanted to fight,
but Tūlì would not agree.
He then sent Tūlì and his subordinate commander, Āshǐnà Sīmó, to see Shìmín,
requesting peace and marriage alliance.
Shìmín agreed.
Sīmó was
Xiélì's paternal uncle.
Tūlì then entrusted himself to Shìmín,
requesting to become sworn brothers.
Shìmín also comforted him with kindness and goodwill,
made an alliance with him, and they departed.
This sets the stage for Tūlì's later surrender.
On the day Gēngyín,
the Prefect of Qízhōu, Chái Shào, defeated the Tūjué at Dùyáng Gǔ.
Dùyáng Mountain is in Fúfēng County, Qízhōu.
Kǒng Yǐngdá's "Shī Pǔ" says: The Zhōuyuán refers to
the southern land of Qí Mountain,
belonging to Dùyáng.
The terrain is perilous and obstructed,
yet the fields of the plain are fertile and beautiful.
Dùyáng was
a Hàn dynasty county,
belonging to Fúfēng.
There is Dùyáng Mountain,
north of the mountain is Dùyáng Gǔ.
On the day Rénshēn,
the Tūjué Āshǐnà Sīmó came for an audience.
The Emperor had him ascend the imperial couch,
and consoled and rewarded him.
Sīmó's appearance resembled that of the Hú people,
not like the Tūjué.
Therefore, Chǔluó suspected he was not of the Āshǐnà lineage.
Through the reigns of Chǔluó and Xiélì,
he always served as a subordinate commander,
and never attained command of troops or held a high military post.
After entering the court,
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Héshùn.
On the day Dīngyǒu,
the Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, Péi Jì, was sent as envoy to the Tūjué.
On the 21st day of the ninth month,
on the day Guǐmǎo,

later renamed Huānzhōu.
On the 22nd day,

the tenth month,
on the day Jǐsì,
the Tūjué invaded Gānzhōu.

Hù County belongs to Jīngzhào,

Hù
is pronounced 'hù'.
On the day Guǐyǒu,
he visited Zhōngnán.

is also written as

Diézhōu is
Héchuān Commandery,

Upon arriving at the prefecture,

summoned his relatives and old friends,
and feasted and drank merrily with them.
With his hair loose and sitting informally with legs spread,

Afterwards, he distributed gold and silk among them,
wept,
and bid them farewell,

"Today, Zhāng Zhènzhōu can still drink joyfully with old friends,

I will be the Governor of Shūzhōu, governing the people.
The rites separate ruler and subject,

From then on, when relatives or old friends violated the law,

Examination of discrepancies: The old basic annals,
"On the 6th day of the 8th month,
the Tūjué invaded Dìngzhōu,
the Crown Prince was ordered to go to Yōuzhōu,

Táng system: For length, based on northern black millet of medium size,
the width of one grain is a fēn,

one chǐ two cùn is a large chǐ,

For capacity, based on black millet of medium size,

two yuè are a gě,

ten shēng are a dǒu,
three dǒu are a large dǒu,
ten dǒu are a hú.
For weight, based on black millet of medium size,

twenty-four zhū are a liǎng,

Buddhist scriptures say that Buddha left home as a crown prince,
hence the statement that as the legitimate heir he rebelled against his father.
The Buddhist law does not require bowing to rulers or parents,

In the past, a woman of the Yǒushēn clan was picking mulberry leaves by the Yī River,

The mother awoke and looked,
and water was indeed flowing from the mortar.
She warned her neighbors and fled,
looking back to see the entire settlement submerged by water.
His mother turned into a hollow mulberry tree,
and the child was inside it.
The woman of the Yǒushēn clan took him and presented him,

He was taught and made a minister,

‘One who is unfilial has no parents’—

The “Treatise on Astronomy” of the Hàn dynasty states: When Venus crosses the sky,

Mèng Kāng’s commentary says: This means it rises in the east and sets in the west,

if it rises in the east, it should set in the east;
if it rises in the west, it should set in the west.
If it passes the meridian, it crosses the sky.

is yang,

Liú Xiàng’s “Discourse on the Five Cycles” states: Venus is lesser yīn,
weak and unable to move freely.
Therefore, it takes sì and wèi as boundaries;
it cannot cross the sky and move.
If it crosses the sky, it appears in the daytime,
and its omen indicates military conflict and mourning,
disloyalty,

Shìmín summoned Zhēng and said to him:
"Why did you sow discord between me and my brothers?"
The crowd felt fear and anxiety for him,
but Zhēng’s demeanor remained composed.
He replied:
"Had the former Crown Prince followed Zhēng’s advice earlier,
he would certainly not have met today’s disaster."
Shìmín had always valued his talent,
so he changed his expression and treated him with courtesy,
appointing him as Registrar of the Heir Apparent's Household.
The Registrar of the Heir Apparent's Household
holds a rank of 7b, upper grade,
and is in charge of seals, inspections, and auditing affairs of the office.
In the sixth month of last year,
Wáng Guī and others were exiled to Xīzhōu.
Xī
is pronounced "suǐ."
Shìmín ordered the release of the hawks and hounds from the imperial parks,
halted tributes from the four quarters,
allowed all officials to present their proposals on governance,
and simplified and sternly enforced government decrees.
Both the court and the populace were greatly pleased.
Qūtū Tōng was appointed as Left Vice Director of the Shǎndōng Circuit Branch Department of State Affairs,
to garrison Luòyáng.
Dòu Guǐ, Vice Director of the Yìzhōu Branch Department of State Affairs, was at odds with the Branch Department Secretaries Wéi Yúnqǐ and Guō Xíngfāng.
Yúnqǐ’s younger brother Qìng Jiǎn and many of his clan had served the Crown Prince Jiànchéng.
After Jiànchéng’s death,
Guǐ falsely accused Yúnqǐ of conspiring with Jiànchéng in rebellion,
arrested him, and executed him.
Xíngfāng, fearing for his life,
fled to the capital.
Guǐ pursued him,
but failed to catch him.
The Tǔyùhún invaded Mínzhōu.
Tǔ
is pronounced in the entering tone, like "tūn."
Yù
is pronounced "yù."
The Tūjué invaded Lǒngzhōu;
on the xīnwèi day,
they invaded Wèizhōu;
Right Guard General-in-Chief Chái Shào was sent to attack them.
The Yìzhōu Grand Branch Department of State Affairs was abolished,
and a Grand Military Governor Office was established.
On the rénshēn day,
the Emperor issued a handwritten edict to Péi Jì and others, saying:
"We shall add the revered title of Retired Emperor."
On the xīnsì day,
Lújiāng Prince Yuàn, Grand Military Governor of Yōuzhōu, rebelled.
Right Guard General Wáng Jūnkuò killed him
and sent his head to the capital.
Initially,
the Emperor considered Lǐ Yuàn to be timid and cowardly, lacking the talent of a commander,
so he sent Wáng Jūnkuò to assist him.
Jūnkuò was originally a bandit,
brave, fierce, treacherous, and cunning.
Yuàn trusted him wholeheartedly and relied on him,
even promising him a marriage alliance.
Crown Prince Lǐ Jiànchéng plotted to harm the Prince of Qín,
and secretly formed an alliance with Yuàn.
After Jiànchéng’s death,
an edict was issued dispatching the Court Receptionist Cuī Dūnlǐ to summon Yuàn via post-horse relay.
The Court Receptionist
was an official equivalent to the Yèzhě of the Qín dynasty.
During the Jìn dynasty, the positions of Shèrén and Tōngshì were established, one each,
subordinate to the Zhōngshū Secretariat.
In the Eastern Jìn, they were called Tōngshì Shèrén.
In the Táng dynasty, it was a position of the sixth rank, upper grade.
They were responsible for guiding and admitting officials for court audiences and managing those taking leave or expressing gratitude in the palace courtyard.
Whenever close ministers entered to attend,
or civil and military officials took their positions,
they were guided in advancing or withdrawing.
All memorials from the four quarters,
and tribute from barbarian tribes,
were received and presented.
Yuàn consulted Jūnkuò.
Jūnkuò wanted to capture Yuàn to claim merit,
so he persuaded him, saying:
"If Your Highness enters the capital,
you will certainly not be spared.
Now you command tens of thousands of troops—
why submit to the summons of a single envoy
and throw yourself into the net?"
They wept together.
Yuàn said:
"I now entrust my life to you,
and the decision to act is made."
They then seized Dūnlǐ
and interrogated him about affairs in the capital.
Dūnlǐ remained unyielding,
so Yuàn imprisoned him.
He dispatched post-horse relays to conscript troops
and summoned Wáng Shēn, the Governor of Yān Prefecture, to Jì
to discuss matters with him.
During the Suí dynasty, the Liáoxī Commandery was established at the old city of Rǔluó within the territory of Yíng Prefecture.
In the first year of Wǔdé, it was renamed Yān Prefecture.
In the sixth year,
it was moved from Yíng Prefecture to within the walls of Yōu Prefecture,
and Běiyān Prefecture was established at Huáiróng.
In the sixth year of Wǔdé,
Lǐ Yì came from Yōu Prefecture to the court.
Wáng Shēn served as Chief Clerk,
effectively administering the prefecture’s affairs.
The people of Yōu Prefecture had long trusted and obeyed him.
Yuàn intended to rebel,
so he summoned him to discuss matters.
Yān:
pronounced as yīn jiān.
Shēn:
pronounced as shū zhēn.
"Wáng Jūnkuò is treacherous and untrustworthy;
he should not be entrusted with authority.
He ought to be removed early,
and replaced by Wáng Shēn."
Yuàn could not decide.
Jūnkuò learned of this,
went to see Shēn,
who was bathing at the time.
Shēn came out holding his hair,
and Jūnkuò beheaded him with his own hands.
Holding Shēn’s head, he announced to the crowd:
"Lǐ Yuàn and Wáng Shēn conspired to rebel together,
imprisoned the imperial envoy,
and arbitrarily conscripted troops.
Now Shēn has been executed;
only Lǐ Yuàn remains,
and he can do nothing.
Would you rather follow Yuàn and be exterminated along with your clans,
or follow me to attain wealth and honor?"
The crowd all said:
"We wish to follow you in punishing the traitor."
Jūnkuò then led over a thousand of his subordinates,
scaled the western wall and entered.
Yuàn was unaware of this.
Jūnkuò entered the prison and freed Dūnlǐ.
Only then did Yuàn realize what had happened.
He hastily led several hundred of his attendants, donned armor, and went out,
encountering Jūnkuò outside the gate.
Jūnkuò said to Yuàn’s followers:
"Lǐ Yuàn is a rebel—
why follow him into boiling water and fire?"
They all discarded their weapons and scattered.
Only Yuàn remained.
He cursed Jūnkuò, saying:
"You villain betrayed me—
retribution will come to you!"
Jūnkuò then seized Yuàn
and strangled him.
On Rénwǔ,
Wáng Jūnkuò was appointed Left Guard General-in-Chief and concurrently Military Governor of Yōu Prefecture,
and Yuàn’s household and property were bestowed upon him.
Dūnlǐ
was the grandson of Cuī Zhòngfāng.
Cuī Zhòngfāng served under the Zhōu dynasty
and presented strategies for conquering Qí.
During the Suí dynasty,
he presented strategies for conquering Chén.
He was the grandson of Cuī Xiàofēn.

When Wèi Zhēng reached Cízhōu,

"On the day I received my orders,

Kǎi,

43. On the day Bǐngzǐ,

Suǒ,

Khan Xiélì advanced to the north of the Biàn Bridge over the Wèi River,

To observe the actual situation.
Sīlì boasted,

The Emperor reprimanded him, saying:

Meaning the number cannot be calculated.
Yí,

Though you are barbarians,

I should execute you now!"
Sīlì feared and begged for mercy.
Asking to be spared from death.
The Emperor said:

the barbarians will think I fear them,

So he imprisoned Sīlì in the Department of Affairs Under the Imperial Secretariat.
The Emperor personally exited the Xuánwǔ Gate,
and with six horsemen including Gāo Shìlián and Fáng Xuánlíng, went directly to the shore of the Wèi River,
where he spoke with Jiélì across the water,
reproaching him for breaking the treaty.
The Turks were greatly astonished,
and all dismounted and bowed in a circle.
Soon after, the various armies arrived in succession,
their banners and armor covering the fields.
Jiélì, seeing that Zhíshīsīlì had not returned,
and that the Emperor had ventured out lightly with only a few,
yet with a very imposing military display,
showed a fearful expression.
The Emperor signaled his armies to withdraw and deploy in formation,
remaining alone to speak with Jiélì.
Xiāo Yǔ, thinking the Emperor was underestimating the enemy,
grasped the horse's bridle and firmly remonstrated.
The Emperor said:
"I have already considered this thoroughly,
it is not something you understand.
The reason the Turks dared to come with their entire nation,
advancing directly to the outskirts of the capital,
is because they believe there is internal trouble in our country,
referring to the recent trouble of killing Jiànchéng and Yuánjí.
Trouble,
is read as dàn.
They think I cannot resist and defend.
If I show them weakness,
closing the gates and defending from within,
the barbarians will surely unleash their troops to plunder widely,

Therefore, I rode out lightly with a few horsemen,
to show as if I take them lightly;
and also to display and awe them with our military might,
making them
certain to fight;
taking the barbarians by surprise,
causing them to lose their plans.
Since the barbarians have penetrated deep into our territory,
they are bound to have fear in their hearts,
so if we fight them we will win,
and if we make peace it will be firm.
Subduing the Turks
depends on this one move.
You just watch!"
That day,
Jiélì came to request peace,

The Emperor returned to the palace that same day.
On the yǐyǒu day,
he again went to the west of the city,

The Turks led their troops away.
Xiāo Yǔ asked the Emperor:

We, your subjects, were also doubtful.
Then the barbarians retreated on their own.
What was the strategy behind this?"
The Emperor said:
"I observed that although the Turks' multitude was large, it was not orderly.
The intent of their ruler and ministers was solely to seek bribes.
At the time they requested peace,
the khan was alone on the west side of the water,
meaning west of the Wèi River.
Kě,

Hán,
is pronounced hán.

If we had attacked their multitude then,

Once they got what they desired,

Then we can nurture our might and watch for an opening,

If you want to take something,

Lǎozǐ said: If you want to snatch it away,

Do you understand this?"
Xiāo Yǔ bowed twice and said:
"It is beyond my reach."
Meaning his own wisdom and consideration could not attain this.

The Emperor once said:
"Since my youth, I have campaigned in all directions,

Whenever I observe an enemy's battle formation,

I often use my weak forces to engage their strong ones,

When they exploit my weakness and pursue,

When I exploit their weakness,
