"I raised troops in Guānxī,
and was the first to respond to the righteous banner.
The event is recorded in the 184th scroll, the first year of Yìníng of Suí Gōngdì.
Yet those whose merit is ranked above mine—
I privately find this unacceptable."
The Emperor said:
"When the righteous banner first rose,
although you, Imperial Uncle, were the first to initiate raising troops,
it was likely also to manage your own escape from disaster.
Later, when Dòu Jiàndé devoured Shāndōng,
your entire army was annihilated;
the event is recorded in the 188th scroll, the second year of Wǔdé.
You, Imperial Uncle, fled north at the mere sight of the enemy's approach.
The event is recorded in the 189th scroll, the fourth year.
As for securing the altars of state,
when discussing merit and bestowing rewards,
they certainly should precede you, Imperial Uncle.
You, Imperial Uncle,
are the state's closest kin.
I truly have nothing I begrudge you,
but I cannot indiscriminately grant you the same rewards as the meritorious officials based on personal favor alone!"
The various generals then said to each other:
"His Majesty is supremely just.
Even towards Huái'ān Prince, he shows no partiality.
How dare we, his subjects, not be content with our lot?"
Thus, they were all pleased and submitted.
Fáng Xuánlíng once said:
"Those old retainers of the Qín Prince's residence who have not been promoted in office
all lament and complain, saying: 'We have served by your side,
for how many years now?
Yet now, when official appointments are made,
we are placed behind those from the former Crown Prince's and Qí Prince's residences.'"
The Emperor said:
"A true ruler is supremely just and without selfishness,
therefore he can win the hearts of all under heaven.
The food and clothing I and you gentlemen consume daily
are all taken from the people.
Therefore, establishing offices and dividing duties
is for the sake of the people.
We should select the worthy and talented to employ them.
How can we prioritize based on whether they are new or old?
If the new are worthy
and the old are unworthy,
how can we discard the new and choose the old?
Now, without considering their worthiness or unworthiness, they simply voice complaints.
Is this the proper way of governance?"
3 An edict stated:
"The common people may not arbitrarily establish temples to evil spirits.
Apart from the orthodox arts of divination,
all other miscellaneous forms of prognostication
are to be completely prohibited."
4 The Emperor gathered over 200,000 scrolls of books from the four categories in the Hóngwén Hall.
Ōuyáng Xiū said: The rise and fall of successive dynasties,
and the level of literary writings changing with the times,
yet their transformations are myriad,
impossible to exhaust fully—
how numerous they are!
Since the Hàn dynasty,
historians have listed their names, authors, and sequence,
categorizing them as the Six Arts, Seven Summaries.
By the Táng dynasty, they began to be divided into four categories:
Classics, Histories, Masters, and Collections,
arranged in the order of Jiǎ, Yǐ, Bǐng, Dīng,
called the Four Treasuries books,
also known as the Four Categories books.
Táng Huìyào: In the fourth year of Wǔdé,
the Xiūwén Institute was established under the Chancellery.
In the third month of the ninth year,
it was renamed the Hóngwén Institute.
In the ninth month of that year,
Tàizōng ascended the throne in the Hóngwén Hall,
gathered over 200,000 scrolls of books from the four categories,
and established the Hóngwén Institute beside the hall.
In the third year of Zhēnguàn, it was moved west of the Nàyì Gate.
According to the Tàijí Palace diagram from the Gé edition: The Hóngwén Institute was east of the Chancellery,
but the Hóngwén Hall is not recorded.
The Nàyì Gate was west of the Jiādé Gate.
This is our dynasty's Chóngwén Institute.
To avoid the taboo of the Xuānzǔ Emperor's name,
the character
"Hóng"
was changed to
"Chóng".
Officials holding substantive posts concurrently served as Academicians,
ordered to take turns staying on duty overnight.
During intervals in court sessions,
they were led into the inner halls,
to discuss past words and deeds,
and deliberate on government affairs,
sometimes continuing until midnight before concluding.
Táng Tàizōng used military force to quell disasters and chaos,
moving among the ranks,
those who accompanied him
were all brave and martial warriors from the northwest.
Once the realm was settled,
he meticulously selected students for the Hóngwén Institute.
Those with whom he discussed and deliberated day and night
were all Confucian scholars from the southeast.
Thus, for those wishing to preserve achievements,
apart from Confucians, what else can they rely on?
Gēng,
pronounced gōng héng fān.
Cháo,
pronounced zhí yáo fān.
Xíng,
pronounced xià mèng fān.
Què,
pronounced qì yuè fān.
5 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the first day Bǐngchén,
there was a solar eclipse.
6 An edict was issued posthumously enfeoffing the former Crown Prince Jiànchéng as Prince of Xī,
with the posthumous title Yǐn;
and Qí Prince Yuánjí as Prince of
Cì,
Xī,
an ancient state name.
Rules for Posthumous Titles: Concealing faults and not achieving completion is called Yǐn.
Not thinking of forgetting affection is called Cì;
cruel, tyrannical, and without kin is called Cì.
Shì,
pronounced shén zhì fān.
Cì,
pronounced lú dá fān.
On the burial day,
the Emperor wept for them at the Yíqiū Gate,
with great sorrow.
Tàijí Palace diagram: The Yíqiū Gate was west of the Qiānqiū Hall,
and east of the Bǎifú Gate.
Examination of discrepancies: The Gāozǔ Shílù and the biographies of Jiànchéng and Yuánjí state:
"When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
they were reburied and granted posthumous titles."
Tàizōng Shílù and the basic annals do not record the burial month and day,
only Táng Lì places it in the tenth month of this year.
Zhēnguàn Zhèngyào places this memorial in the second year.
According to this year, in the seventh month, Wèi Zhēng was appointed Remonstrance Counselor,
sent to pacify Shāndōng,
and Wáng Guī had not yet become Vice Director of the Chancellery.
The burial of Jiànchéng and Yuánjí was likely later,
but there is no other specific year, month, or day to attach it to,
so for now, we follow Táng Lì.
He ordered all former officials of the Crown Prince's and Prince's residences to attend the funeral.
7 On the day Guǐhài,
the Emperor's son, Zhōngshān Prince Chéngqián, was established as Crown Prince.
He was eight years old.
He was born in the Chéngqián Hall,
hence he was named accordingly.
8 On the Gēngchén day,
the initial determination of meritorious officials' actual fiefs was made with distinctions.
The Táng dynasty's noble ranks had nine grades: the first was Wáng (Prince),
with a fief of ten thousand households,
and a principal first rank;
the second was Sìwáng (Hereditary Prince) and Jùnwáng (Commandery Prince),
with a fief of five thousand households,
and an auxiliary first rank;
the third was Guógōng (Duke of a State),
with a fief of three thousand households,
and an auxiliary first rank;
the fourth was Kāiguó Jùngōng (Founding Duke of a Commandery),
with a fief of two thousand households,
and a principal second rank;
the fifth was Kāiguó Xiàngōng (Founding Duke of a County),
with a fief of one thousand five hundred households,
and an auxiliary second rank;
the sixth was Kāiguó Xiànhóu (Founding Marquis of a County),
with a fief of one thousand households,
and an auxiliary third rank;
the seventh was Kāiguó Xiànbó (Founding Earl of a County),
with a fief of seven hundred households,
and a principal fourth rank, upper grade;
the eighth was Kāiguó Xiànzǐ (Founding Viscount of a County),
with a fief of five hundred households,
and a principal fifth rank, upper grade;
the ninth was Kāiguó Xiànnán (Founding Baron of a County),
with a fief of three hundred households,
and an auxiliary fifth rank, upper grade.
For all fief households,
the standard was set at three adult males or more,
with one-third of the annual tax revenue going to the imperial court;
those who received actual fiefs
obtained genuine households distributed across various prefectures.
9 Earlier,
Xiāo Yǔ recommended Féng Déyí to the Retired Emperor,
and the Retired Emperor appointed him as Zhōngshū Lìng (Head of the Secretariat).
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
Xiāo Yǔ became Zuǒ Púyè (Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs),
and Féng Déyí became Yòu Púyè (Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs).
After matters were decided upon,
Féng Déyí repeatedly reversed his stance
in front of the Emperor,
leading to a rift between them.
At that time, Fáng Xuánlíng and Dù Rúhuì were newly in power,
and both distanced themselves from Xiāo Yǔ while drawing close to Féng Déyí.
During the early years of Tàizōng's reign,
despite the virtue of Fáng and Dù,
and the forthrightness of Xiāo Yǔ,
they did not become close.
Instead, he drew close to Féng Déyí,
likely because Xiāo Yǔ's aloofness and directness
made it difficult to collaborate with him during times of crisis and uncertainty,
while Féng Déyí's cunning and calculations
meant that without establishing closeness,
one could not discern his true intentions.
Later ministers
lacked the ability to weigh such considerations in their hearts,
merely saying "draw close to gentlemen,
keep away from petty men,"
but none were able to achieve success.
Subsequently, Xiāo Yǔ submitted a sealed memorial discussing this,
but its arguments were sparse and disjointed,
and thus it offended the Emperor's wishes.
It happened that Xiāo Yǔ and Chén Shūdá had an angry dispute in front of the Emperor.
On the Gēngchén day,
Xiāo Yǔ and Chén Shūdá were both convicted of disrespect,
and were dismissed from office.
Textual Analysis: The Old Biography states,
"Tàizōng, because Fáng Xuánlíng and others had high merit,
(Xiāo Yǔ) thus offended the Emperor's wishes,
and was dismissed to his home.
Shortly after, he was appointed Shàoshī (Junior Mentor),
and again became Zuǒ Púyè,
but was dismissed due to his angry dispute with Chén Shūdá."
According to the Veritable Records, the dispute occurred before his appointment as Shàoshī,
and we follow that here.
10 On the Jiǎshēn day,
the Minister of Revenue Péi Jǔ memorialized,
"For the people who suffered from the Tūjué's violent trampling,
I request that each household be granted one bolt of silk."
The Emperor said:
"I govern my subjects with sincerity and trust,
and do not wish to have an empty name for relief and compassion without the substance.
Households vary in size;
how can we grant rewards uniformly!"
Thereupon, the distribution was calculated based on the number of individuals.
11 Earlier,
the Retired Emperor wished to strengthen the imperial clan to pacify the realm,
so even second and third cousins of the emperor
(those sharing the same great-grandfather are second cousins,
those sharing the same high ancestor are third cousins.
Cóng (cousin),
pronunciation note: cái yòng fān.)
even if they were mere children, were all enfeoffed as princes,
resulting in several tens of princes.
(The enfeoffment of imperial clan members as commandery princes
is seen in scroll 190, year 5.)
"Enfeoffing imperial sons everywhere—
is it beneficial for the realm?"
Féng Déyí replied:
"In previous eras, only the emperor's sons and brothers were made princes;
apart from them, unless one had great merit,
none were made princes.
The Retired Emperor promoted harmony among the nine clans,
and generously enfeoffed the imperial clan.
Since the two Hàn dynasties, there has never been as many as there are now.
Since the noble titles are already lofty,
they are provided with many laborers.
(Laborers
refer to categories like fáng gé shù pú, bái zhí, etc.)"
The Emperor said:
"Indeed.
I, as the Son of Heaven,
am here to nurture the people;
how can I burden the people to nurture my own clan!"
In the eleventh month,
on the Gēngyín day,
the imperial clan commandery princes were all demoted to county dukes,
with only a few who had merit not being demoted.
12 On the Bǐngwǔ day,
the Emperor discussed with his close ministers about stopping theft.
Some requested using severe laws to prohibit it.
The Emperor smiled at them
(a smile that does not break the countenance is called shěn).
Shěn,
pronunciation: shì rěn fān.
"The reason why the people become thieves
is because taxes are numerous and corvée labor is heavy,
officials are greedy and demanding,
and hunger and cold press upon their persons,
so they have no leisure to care about integrity and shame.
I should eliminate extravagance and reduce expenses,
lighten corvée labor and reduce taxes,
select and employ honest officials,
so that the people have ample clothing and food.
Then they naturally will not become thieves;
what need is there for severe laws!"
From then on, after several years,
the realm was peaceful and prosperous,
lost items were not picked up on the roads,
outer doors were not closed at night,
and merchants and travelers lodged in the open countryside.
The Emperor also once said to his attending ministers:
"The ruler relies on the state,
and the state relies on the people.
To exploit the people to serve the ruler
is like cutting flesh to fill the belly.
When the belly is full, the body perishes;
when the ruler is rich, the state falls.
Therefore, the troubles of a ruler
do not come from outside,
but often arise from himself.
If desires are extravagant, then expenses are broad;
if expenses are broad, then taxes are heavy;
if taxes are heavy, then the people are distressed;
if the people are distressed, then the state is endangered;
if the state is endangered, then the ruler is lost.
I often reflect on this,
and therefore dare not indulge my desires."
13 In the twelfth month,
on the Jǐsì day,
the Grand Governor of Yìzhōu, Dòu Guǐ, memorialized that the Lǎo people had rebelled.
(In the sixth month of this year,
the Grand Executive Bureau was abolished,
and the Grand Governor's Office was established.
Afterwards, the various prefectural governor's offices were divided into upper, middle, and lower grades: the governor of a major prefecture held auxiliary second rank,
the Chief Administrator held auxiliary third rank,
the Military Administrator held auxiliary fourth rank;
the governor of a middle prefecture held principal third rank,
the Deputy Governor held principal fourth rank,
the Chief Administrator held principal fifth rank, upper grade,
the Military Administrator held principal fifth rank, lower grade;
the governor of a lower prefecture held auxiliary third rank,
and the Deputy Governor, Chief Administrator, and Military Administrator were all demoted by one rank accordingly.)
Lǎo,
pronunciation: lǔ hào fān.
The Emperor said:
"The Lǎo people rely on the barriers of mountains and forests,
occasionally emerging to pilfer like rats;
this is their common custom.
If the governors and prefects can pacify them with kindness and trust,
they will naturally submit and follow.
How can we lightly mobilize armed forces,
plunder their people like fishing and hunting,
treating them like birds and beasts?
Is this the intention of being parents to the people!"
In the end, he did not grant permission.
14 The Emperor said to Péi Jì:
"Recently, there have been many submitting written statements on affairs.
I have pasted them all on the walls of my chamber,
so I can go in and out and review them.
Whenever I ponder the way of governance,
sometimes it is deep into the night before I sleep.
You, gentlemen, should also diligently attend to your duties,
to match my intent in this."
The Emperor diligently sought good governance,
frequently summoning Wèi Zhēng into his private chambers,
to consult on successes and failures;
Wèi Zhēng spoke everything he knew without reserve,
and the Emperor gladly accepted and praised his advice.
The Emperor dispatched an envoy to conscript soldiers,
and Féng Déyí memorialized:
"Even though middle-aged males are not yet eighteen,
those with robust physiques
may also be conscripted together."
According to the Táng system: commoners at sixteen were considered middle-aged males,
at eighteen they began to be considered adult males,
at twenty-one they became full adult males,
and were liable for corvée labor.
When the edict was issued,
Wèi Zhēng firmly insisted it was unacceptable,
and refused to endorse the edict.
According to the Táng system,
the Secretariat Drafter (Zhōngshū Shèrén) would endorse edicts.
Wèi Zhēng was then a Remonstrance Official (Jiànyì Dàfū);
or did Tàizōng also have him jointly endorse it?
The Emperor grew angry,
summoned him, and reproached him, saying:
"Those middle-aged males who are robust
are crafty commoners deceitfully evading military service;
what harm is there in conscripting them,
that you are so stubbornly opposed!"
He replied:
"The key to military strength lies in commanding it with the right principles,
not in numbers.
If Your Majesty selects the strong and healthy,
and commands them with principle,
it will be enough to be invincible under heaven.
Why must you conscript many of the young and weak merely to inflate empty numbers!
Moreover, Your Majesty often says: 'I govern the realm with sincerity and trustworthiness,
wishing to ensure that none among the officials and people practice deception.'
Now, not long after ascending the throne,
you have broken trust several times!"
The Emperor, startled, said:
"In what have I broken trust?"
He replied:
"When Your Majesty first ascended the throne,
you issued an edict stating: 'All debts owed to the government
are to be entirely remitted.'
The relevant officials considered that debts owed to the Prince of Qín's household administration
were not government property,
and continued to press for their collection as before.
Your Majesty, having been promoted from Prince of Qín to Son of Heaven,
if the property of the princely household administration
is not government property, then what is it!
Furthermore, it was said: 'Those within the Guānzhōng region are exempted from two years of land tax and household levies,
and those outside Guānzhōng are granted one year of exemption from corvée.'
Subsequently, there was another edict stating: 'For those who have already performed corvée or already paid taxes,
the exemption will begin from the following year.'
After they were dispersed and returned home,
taxes were levied again,
so the common people certainly could not help but find it strange.
Now, having already collected the taxes,
you are again conscripting them as soldiers;
how can this be called starting from the following year!
Moreover, those with whom Your Majesty shares the governance of the realm are the prefects and county magistrates;
in ordinary times, when reviewing documents,
you fully entrust matters to them;
yet when it comes to conscripting soldiers,
you alone suspect them of deceit—
is this what is called governing with sincerity and trustworthiness!"
The Emperor, pleased, said:
"Previously, I thought your stubbornness meant you did not understand governance,
but now your discourse on the fundamental principles of the state
truly captures their essence.
If commands and decrees are not trustworthy,
then the people will not know what to follow,
and how can the realm be governed!
My fault is profound!"
He then did not conscript the middle-aged males,
and bestowed upon Wèi Zhēng a golden jar.
The Emperor heard of the reputation of Jǐngzhōu Registrar's Assistant (Lùshì Cānjūn) Zhāng Xuánsù.
Jǐngzhōu:
the territory of Gé County in the Hàn dynasty's Píngyuán Commandery,
the Suí established Gōnggāo County,
belonging to Guànzhōu.
The Táng pacified Héběi,
and divided Gōnggāo to establish Jǐngzhōu.
The Registrar's Assistant of an Upper Prefecture,
rank 7b upper,
was in charge of checking documents, provincial offices, and copying summaries;
the Registrar was in charge of receiving matters and noting the time,
and also checking for errors.
The Emperor asked him about the way of governance,
and he replied:
"The Suí sovereign liked to personally manage all affairs,
not entrusting them to his ministers;
the ministers, fearful,
only knew to receive orders and carry them out,
none daring to disobey.
Using the intelligence of one man to decide the affairs of the realm,
even if successes and failures were half and half,
the errors would already be many;
with subordinates flattering and the sovereign being misled,
how could it not perish!
If Your Majesty can carefully select ministers and delegate responsibilities to them,
sitting loftily in serene majesty and examining their successes and failures to apply rewards and punishments,
why worry about not achieving good governance!
Furthermore,
I observe that during the chaos at the end of the Suí,
those who wished to contend for the realm were no more than ten-odd individuals;
the rest all sought to protect their villages and families,
waiting to submit to a ruler who possessed the Way.
Thus, I know that those among the common people who delight in chaos are also few;
it is merely that the ruler cannot bring them peace."
The Emperor approved of his words,
and promoted him to Investigating Censor (Shì Yùshǐ).
Former Yōuzhōu Secretary (Jìshì) serving directly in the Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shěng), Zhāng Yùngǔ, presented the "Admonition on the Great Treasure" (Dà Bǎo Zhēn).
In the Táng, the various prefectures did not have the post of Secretary;
only princely domains had a Secretary's Assistant (Jìshì Cānjūn),
rank 6b upper.
Yùngǔ was likely Secretary when Prince of Lújiāng, Lǐ Yuàn, supervised Yōuzhōu.
According to the Táng system,
if one's official seniority was insufficient,
one could serve directly in a ministry under another official title.
Presented;
Shí Zhǎng fān.
"The sage receives the mandate,
rescuing the drowning and relieving distress;
therefore, he uses the one to govern the realm,
not using the realm to serve the one."
It also said:
"Though the ninefold palace is majestic within,
where one dwells is but knee-space;
those benighted, unknowing,
build their terraces of jade and chambers of jasper.
Though eight delicacies are spread before,
what one eats is but to suit the taste;
Zhōu Lǐ: the Provisioner,
used eight delicacies.
The commentary states: Delicacies,
refer to chún'áo, chúnwú, pàotún, pàozāng, dǎozhēn, zì, áo, gānliáo.
Chún,
zhī chún fān.
Wú,
mò hú fān,
also pronounced wǔ yóu fān.
Zāng,
zuò láng fān.
Liáo,
lì diāo fān.
They pile up dregs like hills and make ponds of wine."
It also said:
"Do not be muddled and dim,
nor overly scrutinizing and sharp;
though the crown's tassels obscure the eyes, see the formless;
though the yellow silk plugs the ears, hear the soundless."
The crown with front tassels
was to obscure clear sight.
The yellow silk filling the ears
was to block acute hearing.
Shī Gǔ said: Using yellow silk to make a circle,
attached with two cords to the crown,
hanging beside the two ears,
signifying not listening to outside matters.
Tǒu,
tā kǒu fān.
Sāi,
xī zé fān.
He bestowed upon him a bundle of silk.
According to the Táng system: For a bestowal of ten lengths,
the standard was three bolts of silk,
three ends of cloth,
and four bundles of floss silk;
if it was ten lengths of assorted silks,
then two bolts of silk cloth,
two bolts of coarse silk,
two bolts of damask,
and four bolts of plain silk;
if bestowing brocade and silks to foreign guests,
the standard for ten lengths
was one piece of brocade,
two bolts of damask,
four bolts of plain silk,
and four bundles of floss silk;
for seasonal clothing, if called a full set, it was given completely;
if called a partial set, it was given reduced.
For the gatherings at the winter solstice,
when it is said 'bestow bundles of silk in varying amounts,'
for those of the fifth rank and above, five bolts;
for those of the sixth rank and below, two bolts;
titled ladies received according to their husbands or sons.
The Assistant of the Court of Judicial Review (Dàlǐ Chéng),
rank 6a,
was in charge of dividing and judging the affairs of the court.
In the 15th year, the emperor summoned Fù Yì,
granted him food,
and said:
"The petition you presented before,
nearly brought disaster upon me.
The matter was recorded in the previous volume in the sixth month of that year.
Nearly,
explained as grief and reliance.
Minister, you should speak your mind completely in such matters,
do not be deterred by past experiences."
The emperor once said to Yì:
"Buddhism as a teaching,
is profoundly mysterious and worthy of emulation.
Why do you alone fail to comprehend its principles?"
Yì replied:
"Buddha is but a cunning person from the Western regions,
deceiving and dazzling those lands.
People of China who are inclined to deviance,
take the esoteric discussions of Zhuāng and Lǎo,
embellish them with beguiling words,
to deceive the ignorant populace,
bringing no benefit to the people,
and harm to the nation.
I do not fail to understand,
I simply disdain learning it."
The emperor somewhat agreed with this.
In the 16th year, the emperor was troubled by officials frequently accepting bribes,
flouting the law for personal gain is called bribery.
Bribery,
pronounced qiú.
An official at the Department of Gate Affairs accepted a piece of silk,
the Department of Gate Affairs,
under the Ministry of Justice,
was responsible for managing nationwide entrances and exits, and scrutinized their administration,
with six clerks.
According to the Tang dynasty protocol,
a piece of cloth or silk measured 1 foot 8 inches wide and 40 feet long.
Péi Jù, Minister of Civil Affairs, remonstrated:
"For officials accepting bribes,
the crime truly deserves death;
however, if Your Majesty causes someone to send a bribe, which is then accepted,
it is entrapping someone into breaking the law,
which I fear is not what is meant by 'lead by virtue,
and regulate by ritual.'
Quoting Confucius' Analects.
Lead,
read as dǎo.
Summoning civil and military officials of the fifth rank and above, he informed them saying:
"Péi Jù can fulfill his official duties and contest with vigor,
not yielding for appearance's sake,
if in all matters this is so,
what worry is there for governance not being good!"
Minister Guāng remarked: In the words of the ancients: When the ruler is wise, the minister is upright.
Péi Jù was obsequious under the Suí but loyal under the Táng,
not because his nature changed;
when a ruler detests hearing criticisms,
then loyalty transforms into flattery,
when a ruler delights in hearing straightforward words,
then flattery transforms into loyalty.
This signifies that the ruler is the standard,
the minister is the shadow;
when the standard moves, the shadow follows.
In the 17th year,
Emperor promoted his son, the Prince of Chángshā, Khè, to Duke of Hàn, and the Prince of Yíyáng, Yòu, to Duke of Chǔ.
In the 18th year, the three states of Silla, Baekje, and Goguryeo had longstanding enmities.
The Northern History states: Silla originally belonged to the Jinhan people,
located southeast of Goguryeo,
also known as the Qínhán.
It is said that during the Qin dynasty, people fled conscription,
came to Mǎhán,
took a piece of its eastern territory to settle,
hence named Qínhán.
Initially, it comprised six states,
later divided into twelve,
Silla being one of them.
Some claim when Wèi's Guǎn Qiūjiàn defeated Goguryeo,
they fled to Wòzhā,
later restored their state,
those who remained became Silla,
encompassing the territories of Wòzhā, Bùnài, Hán, and Huì.
Its king was originally a Baekje person,
fled by sea to Silla,
subsequently ruled its state,
and became a vassal of Baekje;
later strengthened,
thus, turned against Baekje.
Baekje attacked Goguryeo,
seeking help,
mobilized troops to defeat it.
Henceforth they attacked each other relentlessly,
later capturing the Baekje king,
and killed him,
intensifying their enmity.
Goryeo,
pronounced lìzhī.
The emperor dispatched Zhū Zǐshē, an assistant tutor from the School of the Son of Heaven, to convey the imperial intentions.
During the Jin Dynasty, in the fourth year of Xiánníng, a state academy was established,
appointing a Libationer and a Doctor each,
fifteen assistant tutors,
to educate students.
In the tenth year of the Xiaowu era,
the number of assistant tutors was reduced to ten.
During the Tang dynasty, there were five assistant tutors,
from the sixth rank superior,
responsible for assisting Doctors in teaching classics.
Emperor Tàizōng, the Literary and Martial Sacred, Vastly Filial Emperor,
surname Shìmín,
was the second son of Emperor Gāozǔ.
The emperor was posthumously titled Emperor Wén,
temple name Tàizōng;
in the fifth year of the Xiánhéŋg era,
posthumously honored as Emperor Wénwǔshèng;
in the eighth year of the Tiānbǎo period,
further honored as Emperor Wénwǔdàshèng;
in the thirteenth year,
additionally titled Emperor Wénwǔdàshèngdàguāngxiào.
In the first year of the Zhēnguān era
(Dīnghài, 627)
Spring,
the first month,
Yǐyǒu,
the era name was changed.
On Dīnghài,
the emperor hosted a banquet for loyal ministers,
and played the music of Prince Qín's victory over Chén.
The emperor said:
"When I was entrusted to campaign,
among the people, this tune arose,
although it does not convey the civil virtues of grace and composure,
nevertheless, achievements arose from this,
and I dare not forget the foundation."
Fēng Déyí said:
"Your Majesty, with divine martial force you pacified the realm,
how could civil virtues compare?"
The emperor said:
"To quell chaos requires martial strength,
to maintain achievements requires civil governance,
the use of civil and martial strategies,
is based on the season and time.
To say civil virtues do not compare to martial might,
that statement goes too far!"
Déyí bowed and apologized.
On Jǐhài,
a decree was issued:
"From now on, when the Secretariat, Chancellery, and those above the third rank enter the court to discuss matters,
admonishing officials are to be assigned to accompany them,
to immediately remonstrate any errors."
Chéng Dàchāng said: During the Tang dynasty, the Western Inner Tai Chi Hall,
was the site for receiving audiences at new and full moons,
being the main hall.
North of the Tai Chi Hall are the Liang Yi Halls,
the usual place for daily audiences.
The East and West side chambers by the Tai Chi Hall both have doors for entry,
and then one can proceed north to the Liang Yi.
This was the system during Emperor Tàizōng's time for entering chambers.
From Emperor Gāozōng onward,
they mostly resided in the Eastern Inner courts,
with ceremonies at the Xuanzheng Hall,
called the court,
the court holding masses;
if held at the private Purple Palace Hall,
it was called entering the chamber.
If not held at the Xuanzheng Hall, but at the Purple Palace,
they would summon the guards from the court,
enter through the chamber gate,
officials waiting at court,
could then enter with them,
called entering the chamber.
The emperor commanded Chángsūn Wújì, Minister of Personnel, and others, with scholars and legal officials, to discuss and establish laws and decrees again,
reducing fifty strangulation sentences to amputation of the right toe;
the emperor still found this too harsh,
and said:
"Corporal punishment has been abolished for a long time,
a suitable replacement should be found."
Péi Hóngxiàn, law clerk to the Prince of Shǔ,
it was the Tang system,
that princes had officials responsible for achievements, granaries, households, troops, cavalry, law, and scholar affairs,
ranked seventh superior.
Exiled three thousand miles,
subject to labor for three years;
and a decree followed this.
According to the examination of historical discrepancies: Both the New and Old Records of Punishments state
"subject to labor for two years."
However, it follows Wáng Pǔ's general guidelines.
5 The Emperor considered the Minister of War, Dài Zhòu, to be loyal, incorruptible, fair, and upright.
The Minister of War
was responsible for managing military registers and the ranks and grades of all military officers in the empire, as well as the numbers of the various guard and commandery units.
The Emperor, because many candidates for official selection were fraudulently claiming qualifications and hereditary privileges,
issued an edict ordering them to confess voluntarily.
Those who did not confess would be executed.
Not long after,
a case of fraudulent claims was discovered.
The Emperor wanted to execute the person.
Dài Zhòu memorialized:
"According to the law, he should be exiled."
The Emperor angrily said:
"Do you wish to uphold the law and cause Us to break Our promise?"
Dài Zhòu replied:
"Edicts are issued based on momentary feelings of joy or anger.
Laws are what the state uses to establish great trust throughout the empire.
Your Majesty was angered by the prevalence of fraud among the candidates,
and therefore wished to execute him.
However, having realized this is not permissible,
and then judging the case according to the law,
this is precisely enduring a minor anger to preserve great trust."
The Emperor said:
"If you are able to uphold the law,
what worries do We have!"
Dài Zhòu repeatedly risked offending the Emperor's countenance to uphold the law,
his words flowing like a spring.
The Emperor followed his advice in all cases,
and there were no unjust imprisonments in the empire.
6 The Emperor ordered Féng Déyí to recommend worthy men.
For a long time, he recommended no one.
The Emperor questioned him about it.
He replied:
"It is not that I am not doing my utmost,
but it is simply that there are no extraordinary talents at present!"
The Emperor said:
"A gentleman employs men as he uses tools,
each according to his strengths.
Those who achieved good governance in ancient times,
did they perhaps borrow talents from other eras?
The real problem is that one fails to recognize them.
How can one slander all the men of an age!"
Féng Déyí withdrew in shame.
The Censor-in-Chief Dù Yān memorialized:
"I fear there may be delays or errors in the documents of the various government offices.
I request that censors be sent to the offices to inspect and verify them."
The Emperor asked Féng Déyí about this.
He replied:
"Offices are established and duties divided,
each having its own responsibilities.
If there truly are faults or violations,
the censors should naturally investigate and report them.
But if they were to go around to all the offices,
searching for flaws and faults,
it would be excessively troublesome and trivial."
Dù Yān fell silent.
The Emperor asked Dù Yān:
"Why do you not argue further?"
He replied:
"In the affairs of the empire,
one must act with utmost impartiality.
If something is good, one should follow it.
What Déyí said
truly grasps the main principle.
I am sincerely convinced,
and dare not persist in error."
The Emperor, pleased, said:
"If you gentlemen can all be like this,
what worries do We have!"
7 The Grand General of the Right Flank Guards, Zhǎngsūn Shùndé, accepted a bribe of silk.
When the matter was discovered,
the Emperor said:
"If Shùndé could truly benefit the state,
We would share the state treasury with him.
Why must he be so greedy and corrupt!"
Still, valuing his past achievements,
the Emperor did not punish him for the crime,
but instead bestowed several dozen bolts of silk upon him in the palace courtyard.
The Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, Hú Yǎn, said:
"Shùndé perverted the law by accepting property.
His crime cannot be pardoned.
Why bestow silk upon him again?"
The Emperor said:
"If he possesses human feeling,
the shame of receiving this silk
will be worse than suffering punishment.
If he feels no shame,
he is merely a beast.
What good would killing him do!"
8 On the Xīnchǒu day,
the Tiānjié General, the Prince of Yàn Commandery Lǐ Yì, rebelled, holding Jīngzhōu.
The Yízhōu Circuit was made the Tiānjié Army,
with one general appointed.
Yàn,
pronounced with the initial yīn and the rhyme jiān.
When Yì first came to court,
in the fifth year of the Wǔdé era,
Yì led troops to join the Crown Prince Jiànchéng in a campaign against Liú Hēità,
and subsequently came to court.
Cháo (court),
pronounced zhí yáo fān.
When attendants of the Prince of Qín went to his camp,
Yì assaulted them without reason.
The Retired Emperor was furious,
had Yì arrested and imprisoned,
but later released him.
When the present Emperor ascended the throne,
Yì felt inwardly uneasy.
The sorcerer Lǐ Wǔjiè from Cáozhōu
said to Yì:
"The noble aura of a king has already manifested on you!"
He urged him to rebel.
Yì then falsely claimed to have received a secret edict,
and mobilized troops to march on the court.
He then led his troops to Bīnzhōu.
The Assistant Administrator of Bīnzhōu, Zhào Cíhào, galloped out to meet him.
The Assistant Administrators of the various prefectures
were the same as Deputy Administrators.
An edict appointed the Minister of Personnel Zhǎngsūn Wújì and others as Campaign Commanders to lead troops against him.
When Zhào Cíhào heard the government troops were approaching,
he secretly plotted with the Commander Yáng Jí to deal with Yì.
The plot was discovered,
and Yì imprisoned Cíhào.
Yáng Jí, stationed outside the city, realized a change had occurred,
mobilized his troops and attacked.
Yì's forces collapsed,
and he abandoned his wife and children,
intending to flee to the Türks.
When he reached Wūshì,
his attendants beheaded him,
and sent his head to Cháng'ān.
His younger brother, Shòu,
who was the Military Governor of Lìzhōu,
was also executed for his involvement.
9 Initially, during the turmoil at the end of the Sui dynasty,
when chaos and disorder prevailed at the end of the Sui,
heroes arose together,
gathering followers and seizing territory,
each striving to be the strongest.
When the Táng arose,
they led their followers in submitting,
and the Retired Emperor, to honor and reward them, carved out and established prefectures and counties for them.
Consequently, the number of prefectures and counties
doubled compared to the periods of Kāihuáng and Dàyè.
The Emperor, considering the population small and the officials numerous,
thought about reforming this malady.
In the second month,
he ordered a major consolidation and reduction,
and, following the convenience of mountains and rivers,
divided the empire into ten circuits: The first was called Guānnèi,
the second Hénán,
the third Hédōng,
the fourth Héběi,
the fifth Shānnán,
the sixth Lǒngyòu,
the seventh Huáinán,
the eighth Jiāngnán,
the ninth Jiànnán,
and the tenth Lǐngnán.
Jīngzhào, Tóng, Huá, Shāng, Qí, Bīn, Lǒng, Jīng, Yuán, Níng, Qìng, Fū, Fáng, Dān, Yán, Líng, Huì, Yán, Xià, Suí, Yín, Fēng, and Shèng constituted the Guānnèi Circuit.
Luò, Rǔ, Shǎn, Guó, Zhèng, Huá, Xǔ, Yǐng, Chén, Cài, Biàn, Sòng, Bó, Xú, Háo, Sù, Yùn, Qí, Cáo, Pú, Qīng, Zī, Dēng, Lái, Dì, Yǎn, Hǎi, and Yí constituted the Hénán Circuit.
Pú, Jìn, Jiàng, Fén, Xí, Bìng, Nánfén, Liáo, Qìn, Lán, Shí, Xīn, Dài, Shuò, Yù, Zé, and Lù constituted the Hédōng Circuit.
Huái, Mèng, Wèi, Bó, Xiàng, Wèi, Dàn, Bèi, Xíng, Míng, Cí, Héng, Jì, Shēn, Zhào, Cāng, Jǐng, Dé, Yì, Dìng, Yōu, Zhuō, Yíng, Mò, Yàn, Tán, Yíng, and Píng constituted the Héběi Circuit.

Jīng, Xiá, Guī, Kuí, Lǐ, Lǎng, Zhōng, Fú, Wàn, Xiāng, Táng, Suí, Dèng, Jūn, Fáng, Yǐng, Fù, Jīn, Liáng, Yáng, Lì, Fèng, Xīng, Chéng, Fú, Wén, Bì, Bā, Péng, Tōng, Kāi, Lóng, Guǒ, and Qú constituted the Shānnán Circuit.
Qín, Wèi, Hé, Shàn, Lán, Jiē, Táo, Mín, Kuò, Dié, Dàng, Liáng, Guā, Shā, Gān, and Sù constituted the Lǒngyòu Circuit.
Yáng, Chǔ, Chú, Hé, Shòu, Lú, Shū, Guāng, Qí, Huáng, Ān, and Shēn constituted the Huáinán Circuit.

Rùn, Cháng, Sū, Hú, Háng, Mù, Yuè, Qú, Wù, Kuò, Tāi, Fú, Jiàn, Quán, Xuān, Shè, Chí, Hóng, Jiāng, È, Yuè, Ráo, Xìn, Qián, Jí, Yuán, Fǔ, Tán, Héng, Yǒng, Dào, Chēn, Shào, Qián, Chén, Yí, Sī, and Bó constituted the Jiāngnán Circuit.
Yì, Jiā, Méi, Qióng, Jiǎn, Zī, Xī, Yǎ, Nánhuì, Yì, Wéi, Sōng, Yáo, Gōng, Róng, Zǐ, Suì, Mián, Jiàn, Hé, Lóng, Pǔ, Yú, Líng, Róng, and Lú constituted the Jiànnán Circuit.

Guǎng, Pān, Xún, Cháo, Nánkāng, Shuāng, Duān, Xīn, Fēng, Nándàng, Chūn, Luó, Nánshí, Gāo, Nánhé, Yá, Zhèn, Yōng, Nánfāng, Nánjiǎn, Chún, Qīn, Nányǐn, Xiàng, Téng, Guì, Wú, Hè, Lián, Nánkūn, Jìng, Lè, Nángōng, Róng, Róng, Láo, Nánlín, Nánfú, Nányuè, Nányì, Jiāo, Lù, Fēng, Ài, and Nándé constituted the Lǐngnán Circuit.
10 In the third month,
on the Guǐsì day,
the Empress led the inner and outer titled ladies in personally tending silkworms.
Inner titled ladies
were female officials within the palace,
from Noble Consorts down to Attendants for Hand Towels,
also divided into nine ranks.
Outer titled ladies had six categories: The mothers and wives of Princes, Inheriting Princes, and Commandery Princes were designated,
the mothers and wives of Dukes of the State of the first rank were designated State Ladies,
the mothers and wives of officials of the third rank and above were designated Commandery Ladies,
the mothers and wives of officials of the fourth rank were designated Commandery Mistresses,
the mothers and wives of officials of the fifth rank were designated County Mistresses,
and the mothers and wives of holders of merit titles of the fourth rank who had been enfeoffed
were designated Township Mistresses.
For all outer titled ladies attending court audiences,
their status was determined by the rank of their husbands or sons.
According to Táng regulations,
the Empress, on an auspicious sì day in late spring, made offerings to the First Sericulturalist,
and then proceeded to personally gather mulberry leaves.
The Treatise on Carriages and Dress states: When the Empress personally tends silkworms,
she wears a chrysanthemum-colored robe,
made of yellow gauze.
Shuài (to lead),
is pronounced shuài.
11 In the intercalary month,
on the Guǐchǒu day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the 12th day, Renshēn,
the Emperor said to the Crown Prince's Junior Tutor, Xiāo Yǔ:
"Since my youth, I have been fond of bows and arrows.
I obtained over ten fine bows,
and considered them unsurpassable.
Recently, I showed them to a bow-maker,
who said, 'None are made of truly fine material.'
I asked him the reason.
The craftsman said:
'If the heartwood of the wood is not straight,
then its grain will all be askew.
Although the bow may be powerful, the arrows it shoots will not fly straight.'
Only then did I realize that my earlier discernment was not precise.
I pacified the realm with bows and arrows,
yet my understanding of them is still incomplete.
How much less can I possibly know all the affairs under heaven!"
He then ordered capital officials of the fifth rank and above
(Capital officials refer to those holding substantive posts in the capital)
to be frequently summoned for audiences,
to inquire about the hardships of the common people
and the successes and failures of governance.
13. The Governor of Liángzhōu, Prince Chánglè, Yòuliáng,
was by nature violent and crude.
Over a hundred of his attendants
were all scoundrels and ne'er-do-wells
who oppressed and brutalized the common people.
He also engaged in trade with the Qiāng and Hú peoples.
Someone reported that Yòuliáng harbored rebellious intentions.
The Emperor dispatched the Secretariat Director, Yǔwén Shìjí, post-haste to replace him
and also to investigate the matter.
Yòuliáng's attendants grew fearful
and plotted to abduct him and flee north to the barbarians;
they also wanted to kill Shìjí and seize Héxī.
Someone again reported their plot.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on Guǐsì,
Yòuliáng was ordered to commit suicide.
14. In the fifth month,
Yuàn Jūnzhāng led his followers in surrender.
Earlier,
Jūnzhāng had led the Turks in capturing Mǎyì
and killing Gāo Mǎnzhèng.
(This event is recorded in the 190th scroll, the sixth year of Emperor Gāozǔ's Wǔdé reign.)
(Jué, pronounced jiǔ wù fān.)
The Héng'ān Garrison of Suínèi County in Suìzhōu
was the Píngchéng which served as the capital of the Later Wèi.
Later, the Táng established Yúnzhōu and Yúnzhōng County there.
(Héng, pronounced hù dēng fān.)
Many abandoned Jūnzhāng and came to surrender.
Jūnzhāng, fearful,
also surrendered,
requesting to guard the northern frontier to atone for his crimes.
The Retired Emperor permitted this.
Jūnzhāng requested a sworn covenant.
The Retired Emperor sent Yuán Pǔ, a man from Yànmén, to bestow upon him a golden tally.
(Yànmén County was attached to Dàizhōu; it was the territory of the Hàn's Guǎngwǔ County.)
Jūnzhāng hesitated and could not decide.
Guō Zǐwēi of Héng'ān advised Jūnzhāng,
"Héng'ān's terrain is perilous and its walls strong.
The Turks are currently powerful;
we should rely on them and observe the changes.
We must not submit ourselves to others."
Jūnzhāng then seized Yuán Pǔ and sent him to the Turks,
realigning with them
and repeatedly joining the Turks in raids.
By now,
seeing that Xiélì's administration was in disorder,
he knew they were not reliable,
and so led his followers in surrender.
(Yuàn Jūnzhāng rose up together with Liú Wǔzhōu and only surrendered at this time.)
(Ruì was the name of an ancient state.)
15. Someone submitted a memorial requesting the removal of sycophantic ministers.
The Emperor asked:
"Who are the sycophantic ministers?"
The reply was:
"Your subject lives in obscurity among the marshes and cannot precisely know who they are.
I hope Your Majesty, when speaking with your ministers,
might feign anger to test them.
Those who uphold principle and do not yield are upright ministers;
those who fear authority and comply with your wishes are sycophants."
The Emperor said:
"The ruler is the source;
the ministers are the stream.
If the source is muddied, one cannot expect the stream to be clear.
If the ruler himself practices deceit,
how can he demand uprightness from his ministers!
I intend to govern the realm with utmost sincerity.
Seeing that former emperors enjoyed using petty tricks and cunning to deal with their ministers,
I have always secretly felt ashamed for them.
Your strategy, though good,
is not one I will adopt."
16. In the sixth month,
on Xīnsì,
the Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, the Duke Mì of Míng, Fēng Déyí, passed away.
(Regarding the posthumous title 'Míng': The canon says, 'Deliberating with far-reaching decisiveness is called Míng.' Commentary states: Self-reliance approaches arbitrariness.)
17. On Rénchén,
the Crown Prince's Junior Tutor, Xiāo Yǔ, was again appointed Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.
(Xiāo Yǔ was dismissed from office last year.)
(Fù, pronounced fú yòu fān; the following fù is the same.)
(Shào, pronounced shǐ zhào fān.)
(Yǔ, pronounced yǔ.)
18. On Wùshēn,
the Emperor discussed with his attending ministers the long and short reigns of the Zhōu and Qín.
Xiāo Yǔ replied:
"King Zhòu acted without principle, so King Wǔ campaigned against him.
The Zhōu and the six states were without crime, yet the First Emperor of Qín destroyed them.
Although both gained the realm, the hearts of the people differed."
The Emperor said:
"You know one aspect but not the other.
After the Zhōu gained the realm, they further cultivated benevolence and righteousness.
After the Qín gained the realm, they increasingly esteemed deceit and force.
This is the reason for the difference in the length of their reigns.
For one may perhaps gain it by contrary means,
but one cannot maintain it without accord."
Yǔ apologized, acknowledging he had not considered this.
19. There was a great drought in Shāndōng.
An edict was issued ordering relief and aid locally,
and exempting this year's land taxes.
20. In autumn,
the seventh month,
on Rénzǐ,
the Minister of Personnel, Zhǎngsūn Wújì, was appointed Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.
Wújì and the Emperor had been friends since their commoner days.
Added to this was his status as a relative of the imperial consort
and his merit in assisting the founding of the dynasty.
(Wújì was the Empress's elder brother; his merit lay in assisting in the execution of Jiànchéng and Yuánjí.)
(Zhǎng, pronounced zhī liǎng fān.)
The favor and treatment he received surpassed that of all other ministers.
The Emperor had wished to make him Chancellor several times.

(Ōuyáng Xiū said: The Táng followed the Suì system, whereby the heads of the Three Departments—the Department of State Affairs, the Chancellery, and the Secretariat—jointly deliberated on state affairs. This was the duty of the Chancellor. Later, because Tàizōng had been the Head of the Department of State Affairs, subjects avoided daring to hold that post. From then on, the Vice Directors became the heads of the Department of State Affairs and, together with the Heads of the Chancellery and Secretariat, were called Chancellors. Their rank being already exalted, the Emperor was reluctant to confer it lightly. Therefore, officials often held the duties of Chancellor under other titles, such as Dù Yān serving as Minister of Personnel while participating in deliberations on court affairs, or Wèi Zhēng serving as Director of the Palace Library while participating in court affairs. Other titles included participating in deliberations on successes and failures, or participating in the administration of affairs, etc. The names varied, but all referred to the duties of Chancellor.)
(Shuò, pronounced suǒ jiǎo fān.)
"I occupy a position in the inner palace;
the honor and favor bestowed upon my family have reached their peak.
I sincerely do not wish for my brothers to again hold the reins of state power.
The examples of the Lǚ, Huò, and Shàngguān families can serve as a bone-deep warning.
I beg Your Majesty to consider this with compassion!"
The Emperor did not heed her
and ultimately appointed him.
21. Initially,
the Tūjué people were simple and honest,
and their governance and decrees were straightforward and uncomplicated.
The Khagan Xiélì obtained a Chinese man named Zhào Déyán,
whom he entrusted and employed.
Déyán monopolized authority and power,
frequently altering old customs,
making governance and decrees burdensome and harsh,
so the people of the state began to be displeased.
Xiélì also favored and trusted various Hú people while distancing himself from the Tūjué,
and the Hú people were greedy and avaricious,
often duplicitous,
leading to military conflicts every year;
he repeatedly raised armies to suppress those who were duplicitous,
so there was no year of peace.
Gēng,
gōng héng fān.
Hào,
hū dào fān.
Mào,
mò běi fān.
Snow fell several feet deep,
many mixed livestock died,
and there were successive years of famine,
so the people all suffered from cold and hunger.
Xiélì’s expenditures were insufficient,
and he heavily taxed the various tribes,
causing internal and external resentment and alienation,
with many tribes rebelling,
and his military power gradually weakened.
Many who discussed affairs requested to attack him,
and the Emperor asked Xiāo Yǔ and Zhǎngsūn Wújì,
saying:
"Xiélì and his ministers are deluded and tyrannical,
and their peril and downfall are certain.
If we attack them now,
we have just recently made an alliance with them;
if we do not attack,
I fear we will miss the opportunity;
what should we do?"
Yǔ requested to attack them.
Wújì replied:
"If the barbarians do not violate the frontier, to break faith and weary the people by attacking them
is not the way of a true king’s army."
The Emperor then desisted.
22. The Emperor asked the dukes and ministers about strategies for long-lasting rule,
and Xiāo Yǔ said:
"The Three Dynasties practiced enfeeffment and endured long,
while Qín stood isolated and perished quickly."
The Emperor considered this correct,
and thus began discussions about enfeeffment.
23. The Vice Director of the Chancellery, Wáng Guī, had a secret memorial,
which he attached to the Palace Attendant Gāo Shìlián,
but it was suppressed and not reported.
When the Emperor heard of this,
in the eighth month,
on the Wùxū day,
he sent Shìlián out to be the Grand Governor of Ān Prefecture.
24. In the ninth month,
on the Gēngxū day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
25. On the Xīnyǒu day,
the Secretariat Director Yǔwén Shìjí was dismissed to be the Palace Attendant,
and the Censor-in-Chief Dù Yān participated in court governance.
Participation in governance by other officials began from this.
Yān recommended the Vice Director of the Ministry of Justice, Dǐ Huáidào,
(The Vice Director of the Ministry of Justice
assists the Minister and Vice Ministers,
upholding the statutes and regulations,
and distinguishing the severity of penalties.)
Dǐ,
dīng lǐ fān,
is a surname;
in the Later Wèi there was Dǐ Zhēn.
[Yán:
"Dǐ"
changed to
"Zhì."
He replied:
"When Emperor Yáng was about to go to Jiāngdū,
he summoned the hundred officials to ask about plans for travel or staying,
and Huáidào was a Secretary in the Ministry of Personnel.
Táng inherited the Sui system,
and each bureau of the ministries had Secretaries,
rank 9b.
I personally witnessed this."
The Emperor said:
"You praise Huáidào as being right,
why did you not remonstrate properly yourself?"
He replied:
"At that time, I did not hold an important position,
and I also knew that remonstrance would not be heeded,
so dying in vain would have been of no benefit."
The Emperor said:
"You knew that Emperor Yáng could not be remonstrated with,
why did you serve in his court?
Since you served in his court,
how could you not remonstrate?
When you served under Sui,
it might be said that your position was lowly;
later, when you served under Wáng Shìchōng,
you were honored and prominent,
why did you also not remonstrate?"
He replied:
"I did not fail to remonstrate with Shìchōng,
but he simply did not heed it."
The Emperor said:
"If Shìchōng was virtuous and accepted remonstrance,
he should not have lost the state;
if he was tyrannical and rejected remonstrance,
how did you avoid disaster?"
Yān could not reply.
The Emperor said:

Jūnkuò, while in the prefecture,

The Chief Clerk Lǐ Xuándào,
a maternal cousin of Fáng Xuánlíng,
entrusted Jūnkuò with a letter.
Jūnkuò privately opened it,

when he reached Wèinán,
(the Later Wèi established Wèinán Commandery between Xīnfēng and Zhèng counties,
Sui abolished the commandery and made it a county,
under the jurisdiction of the Metropolitan Governor,

he was about to flee to the Tūjué,
but was killed by local people.

(Tán is a surname;

Chieftain,
cí yóu fān.

Various prefectures reported that Àng was rebelling,

The Emperor said:

30 Someone accused Right Assistant Wèi Zhēng of favoring his relatives,

"Zhēng did not maintain formalities,

The Emperor ordered Yànbó to reprimand Zhēng,

"Your servant has heard that ruler and minister are of one body,

The Emperor, startled, said:

Zhēng bowed twice and said:

ruler and ministers worked together in harmony,

Lóngpáng and Bǐgān,
remonstrated directly at court and argued,
were personally executed and their states perished,
these are called loyal ministers."
The Emperor was pleased,
and bestowed five hundred bolts of silk.
The Emperor's spirit and bearing were heroic and resolute,
and when ministers came for an audience,
they all lost their composure;
the Emperor knew this,
and whenever he saw someone presenting a matter,
he would certainly give them kind words and a pleasant expression,
hoping to hear admonitions and remonstrances.
He once said to the dukes and ministers:
"If a person wants to see his own form,
he must rely on a bright mirror;
if a ruler wants to know his own faults,
he must await loyal ministers.
If a ruler stubbornly rejects remonstrance and considers himself wise,
and his ministers flatter and follow his wishes,
once the ruler loses the state,
how can the ministers alone be preserved!
Like Yú Shìjī and others who fawned upon Emperor Yáng to preserve their wealth and rank,
when Emperor Yáng was assassinated,
Shìjī and others were also executed.
(The event is recorded in the 185th scroll, the first year of Emperor Gāozǔ's Wǔdé reign.)
In matters of gain and loss,
do not hesitate to speak fully!"

32 The Emperor said to the dukes and ministers:

Extravagance, beauty, and rare treasures,

then danger and ruin will arrive immediately.
I wanted to build a hall,

Thus, for twenty years,

According to the Táng system,
all imperial edicts, decrees, and commands,

once issued,

(To correct;
Běi jiǎo fān.)
If there are differences,
and debates and discussions go back and forth,
striving for utmost appropriateness,
abandoning one's own view to follow others,
what harm is there!
Lately, some protect their own shortcomings,
thus creating grievances and rifts;
some avoid private grudges,
knowing it is not right,
(meaning knowing it is wrong but not correcting it.)
becoming a deep affliction for the myriad people,
this is the governance of a perishing state.
In Emperor Yáng's time,
all officials, inside and outside,

at that time,

thus the wickedness of the Yǒumiáo (有苗) was able to reach his ears;

the widowers and widows had complaints against the Miáo (苗).
Shàng (上),

Reaching out with his four keen senses,

Shùn (舜) had clear vision and keen hearing,
and was wary of appointing men,
thus the Four Villains could not escape his punishment.
Gòng (共),
