Then the high ministers cannot block information,
and the sentiments of those below can reach the ruler."
The Emperor said:
"Well said!"
The Emperor said to Huángmén Shìláng (黃門侍郎) Wáng Guī (王珪):
"In the fourteenth year of Kāihuáng (開皇) there was a great drought,
Suí Wéndì (隋文帝) did not permit relief distribution,
but ordered the people to go to Shāndōng (山東) for food,
by the end of his reign,
the empire's stored reserves could supply fifty years.
Yángdì (煬帝), relying on this wealth and abundance,
had an extravagant heart that knew no satiety,
and ultimately lost the empire.
As long as the granary stores are sufficient to prepare for lean years,
what use is the rest!"
6 In the second month,
the Emperor said to his attending ministers:
"People say the Son of Heaven is supremely noble,
and has nothing to fear or dread.
But I am not so,
above I fear the surveillance of August Heaven,
below I dread the gaze of my ministers,
diligent and cautious,
still fearing I may not accord with Heaven's will,
and not meet people's expectations."
Wèi Zhēng (魏徵) said:
"This is truly essential for achieving good governance,
I hope Your Majesty remains as careful at the end as at the beginning,
then all will be well."
7 The Emperor said to Fáng Xuánlíng (房玄齡) and others:
"In governance, nothing is more important than utmost impartiality.
In the past, Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮) banished Liào Lì (廖立) and Lǐ Yán (李嚴) to the southern barbarian lands,
when Liàng died, both Lì and Yán wept in sorrow,
some even died of grief,
(see the seventy-second volume, Wèi Míngdì (魏明帝) Qīnglóng (青龍) second year.)
Liào (廖),
pronounced like lì jiù (力救),
also like lì diào (力弔).
Zú (卒),
pronounced like zǐ xù (子恤).
Also, Gāo Jiǒng (高熲) as Suí (隋) Chancellor,
was fair and understood the principles of governance,
the rise and fall of Suí (隋)
was tied to Jiǒng's survival or demise.
(See the records of Suí (隋).)
You all must take the worthy chancellors of former times as your models!"
8 In the third month, on the wùyín day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
9 On the rénzǐ day,
Hú Yǎn, the Junior Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, presented the monthly prisoner register.
The Emperor ordered that from now on, all death penalty cases must be reviewed by officials of the fourth rank and above from the Secretariat and the Chancellery,
including the heads and deputies of the two departments down to the Remonstrance Officials.
This was to prevent wrongful convictions and excessive punishments.
Subsequently, when the prisoners were brought forward, among them was Zhèng Shànguǒ, the Prefect of Qízhōu.
The Emperor said to Hú Yǎn:
"Although Shànguǒ has committed a crime, his official rank is not low. How can he be placed among the other prisoners?
From now on, officials of the third rank and above who commit crimes need not be brought forward in this manner. They may await further instructions at the court assembly hall."
The Tàijí Palace's Chéngtiān Gate had east and west court assembly halls on its left and right.
10 Guānzhōng suffered from drought and famine, and many people sold their children to obtain food and clothing.
On the jǐsì day, an edict was issued ordering the imperial treasury to provide gold and silk to redeem these children and return them to their parents.
On the gēngwǔ day, an edict was issued pardoning the empire due to last year's continuous rain and this year's drought and locusts.
The edict stated in part:
"If the harvests could be abundant and the empire peaceful, I would willingly bear the disasters myself to preserve the myriad states. This is my wish, and I would accept it without regret."
It happened that rain fell in the affected areas, and the people were greatly pleased.
11 In summer, the fourth month, on the jǐmǎo day, an edict was issued stating:
"During the chaos and separation at the end of the Suí dynasty, famine ensued, and exposed bones filled the wilderness, distressing to see.
It is appropriate to order the local officials to collect and bury them."
12 Earlier, Tūlì Kèhán of the Tūjué had established his headquarters directly north of Yōuzhōu, ruling the eastern region.
Dozens of tribes, such as the Xī and Xí, rebelled against the Tūjué and came to surrender.
Jiélì Kèhán blamed Tūlì for losing his followers.
When Xuēyántuó, Huíhé, and others defeated Yùgǔshè, Jiélì sent Tūlì to attack them, but Tūlì's troops were also defeated, and he fled back with light cavalry.
Jiélì was angry, detained him for over ten days, and had him flogged.
From then on, Tūlì resented Jiélì and secretly planned to rebel against him.
Jiélì repeatedly demanded troops from Tūlì, but Tūlì refused and submitted a request to come to court.
The Emperor said to his attending officials:
"In the past, the Tūjué were strong, with a million archers, and they encroached upon Zhōngxià, becoming arrogant and oppressive, thus losing their people.
Now they voluntarily request to come to court. Unless they are in dire straits, would they do so?
I have heard this, and I am both pleased and fearful. Why?
If the Tūjué decline, our borders will be peaceful, hence my pleasure.
However, if I lose the Way, someday I may also end up like the Tūjué. Can I not fear?
You, my ministers, should not hesitate to offer earnest remonstrance to assist me where I fall short."
Jiélì launched troops to attack Tūlì. On the dīnghài day, Tūlì sent an envoy to seek help.
The Emperor consulted with his senior ministers:
"I am sworn brothers with Tūlì. When he is in crisis, I cannot fail to rescue him."
(They became sworn brothers; see the seventh year of Wǔdé in the previous volume. This refers to the oath at the Wèi Bridge; see the ninth year of Wǔdé in the previous volume.)
Dù Rúhuì, the Minister of War, said:
"The Róng and Dí have no integrity and will ultimately break their promises. If we do not take advantage of their turmoil to seize them now, we will regret it later.
To subdue the chaotic and attack the perishing is a saying from Zhònghuǐ's Admonition in the Book of Documents."
On the bǐngshēn day, the chieftain of the Qìdān led his tribe to surrender.
Jiélì sent an envoy to request exchanging Liáng Shīdū for the Qìdān.
The Emperor said to the envoy:
"The Qìdān and the Tūjué are different peoples. Now that they have come to submit, why demand them back?
Shīdū is a man of Zhōngguó, yet he stole our land and oppressed our people. The Tūjué accepted and sheltered him.
When I raised troops to attack him, they repeatedly came to his rescue. He is like a fish swimming in a cauldron; why worry that he will not be ours?
Even if we cannot capture him, I would never exchange surrendered people for him."
Previously, the Emperor knew that the Tūjué government was in chaos and could not protect Liáng Shīdū, so he sent a letter to advise him, but Shīdū refused to comply.
The Emperor sent Liú Mín, the Chief Clerk of the Xiàzhōu Military Command, and Sīmǎ Liú Lánchéng to plan against him.

Liú Mín and others repeatedly sent light cavalry to trample his crops, spread discord, and sow division among his officials, causing his state to gradually weaken, with surrenders following one after another.
His famous general Lǐ Zhèngbǎo and others plotted to capture Shīdū, but the plan was exposed, and they fled to our side. From then on, suspicion grew between superiors and subordinates.
Liú Mín and others, knowing he could be taken, submitted a memorial requesting troops.

The Emperor sent Chái Shào, the Great General of the Right Guard, and Xuē Wànjūn, the Junior Supervisor of the Palace Administration, to attack him, and also sent Liú Mín and others to occupy the eastern city of Shuòfāng to pressure him.
(The capture of the eastern city is recorded in the fifth year of Wǔdé in volume 190.)
Liú Lánchéng lowered his flags and silenced his drums, not going out.
Shīdū fled under cover of darkness, and Liú Lánchéng pursued and defeated him.

The Tūjué sent a large force to rescue Shīdū. Before Chái Shào and others reached Shuòfāng, they encountered the Tūjué several tens of lǐ away, attacked fiercely, and routed them, then besieged Shuòfāng.
The Tūjué did not dare to rescue further, and the city's food ran out.
On the rényín day, Shīdū's cousin Luòrén killed Shīdū and surrendered the city.
(Liáng Shīdū raised troops at the end of the Suí dynasty's Dàyè era and was destroyed at this time.)
13 The Minister of Ceremonies, Zǔ Xiàosūn,
considered that the music of the Liáng and Chén dynasties was largely from Wú and Chǔ,
while that of the Zhōu and Qí dynasties was largely from the Hú and Yí peoples.
Therefore, he carefully blended the northern and southern styles,
examined them against ancient tones,
and composed the Táng dynasty's refined music,
comprising a total of eighty-four modes, thirty-one pieces, and twelve harmonies.
The pitch standards have seven tones,
and the twelve pitch standards yield eighty-four modes in total.
The Suí dynasty had fourteen pieces of Huángxià music;
Xiàosūn established twelve harmonies,
modeling them after the perfect numbers of heaven,
making a total of thirty-one pieces.
The twelve harmonies are:
first, Yùhé;
second, Shùnhé;
third, Yǒnghé;
fourth, Sùhé;
fifth, Yōnghé;
sixth, Shòuhé;
seventh, Shūhé;
eighth, Tàihé;
ninth, Zhāohé;
tenth, Xiūhé;
eleventh, Zhènghé;
twelfth, Chénghé.
The character "diào" (mode)
is pronounced "tiáo."
The character "hé" (harmony) is pronounced as usual.
The Hàn dynasty's Commandant of Harmonious Pitch
wore a seal and ribbon of the two-thousand-bushel rank.
The Táng dynasty's Gentleman of Harmonious Pitch
held the eighth rank, upper grade,
and was subordinate to the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
On the yǐyǒu day,
Xiàosūn and others presented the new music.
The Emperor said:
"Rites and music
are merely teachings established by sages based on human sentiments.
The rise and fall of governance—
how could it depend on these?"
The Grand Master of Remonstrance, Dù Yān, said:
"When Qí was about to perish,
they composed the 'Companion' melody.
During the Northern Qí period,
Yáng Jùnzhī often wrote six-character song lyrics,
which were licentious and clumsy,
yet circulated among the common people,
known as 'Yáng Wǔ Companion.'
They also composed 'Jade Tree Backyard Flowers.'
Dù Yòu said: 'Jade Tree Backyard Flowers,'
'Magnificent Yellow Oriole Lingers,'
'Golden Hairpins Hanging at Both Temples,'
were all created by the last ruler of Chén.
He constantly composed poems in response with the palace ladies and court officials.
The Director of the Grand Music Bureau, Hé Xū, selected the most frivolous and ornate among them to set to this melody.
Travelers on the road who heard it all wept in sorrow.
How can one say that the rise and fall of governance is not reflected in music!"
The Emperor said:
"That is not so.
Music can move people,
so joyful people hearing it become happy,
while sorrowful people hearing it become sad.
Joy and sorrow lie in people's hearts,
not in the music itself.
In a government on the verge of collapse,
the people are inevitably distressed and suffering,
so they feel sorrow upon hearing music.
Now both melodies still exist;
if I were to play them for you,
would you feel sorrow?"
The Right Director of the Department of State Affairs, Wèi Zhēng, said:
"The ancients said, 'When we speak of rites,
are we merely speaking of jades and silks?
When we speak of music,
are we merely speaking of bells and drums?'
The Analects record Confucius's words.
It is not about the sounds themselves."
Your servant Guāng remarks: I have heard that Chuí could determine squares and circles with his eyes,
and measure curves and straight lines with his mind.
Chuí
was a skilled artisan of antiquity.
The character "duó" (measure)
is pronounced "tuò."
What he used to teach others
was surely only the compass and square.
Sages achieve without striving and attain without thinking,
yet they cannot impart this directly to others.
What they impart to others
is surely only rites and music.
Rites
are what the sages practiced;
music
is what the sages delighted in.
Sages practiced uprightness and delighted in harmony,
and further wished to share this with all under heaven,
to pass it down for a hundred generations.
Thus they created rites and music.
Therefore, when craftsmen apply Chuí's compass and square to make vessels,
this too is the achievement of Chuí.
When rulers apply the rites and music of the Five Emperors and Three Kings to govern the world,
this too is the governance of the Five Emperors and Three Kings.
The Five Emperors and Three Kings
have long departed from this world,
yet later generations, seeing their rites, know what they practiced;
hearing their music, know what they delighted in—
as if they were still vividly present in the world.
Is this not the achievement of rites and music?
Now, rites and music have essence and form:
Harmony and balance
are the essence;
appearance and sound
are the form.
Neither can be neglected.
The former kings upheld the essence of rites and music,
never letting it leave their hearts for a moment;
they practiced the form of rites and music,
never letting it stray far from their persons.
Arising within the household,
manifesting in the court,
spreading to villages, suburbs, and neighborhoods,
reaching the feudal lords,
flowing throughout the four seas—
from sacrifices and military campaigns to eating, drinking, rising, and resting,
they were never outside the realm of rites and music.
After several decades or a century of this,
then governance and transformation became pervasive,
and phoenixes came to pay homage.
If one lacks the essence and merely possesses the form,
practicing it for one day and abandoning it for a hundred,
seeking to transform customs and morals—
truly, that is difficult indeed.
Therefore, when Emperor Wǔ of Hàn established the Harmonious Pitch office
and sang of heavenly auspices,
it was not without beauty,
yet he could not avoid issuing edicts of mourning.
See the Basic Annals.
When they examined the pitch standards and pipes,
it was not without precision,
yet they could not avert the disaster at the Jiàntái.
Wáng Mǎng ordered Liú Xīn to examine and fix the pitch standards and pipes,
with the Director of Music in charge.
Bān Gù adopted this for his Treatise on Harmonics and the Calendar.
The events at Jiàntái are recorded in the Annals of Huáiyáng of Hàn.
The character "jiàn"
is pronounced "ziān."
When they tuned metal and stone instruments,
it was not without thoroughness,
yet they could not prevent the calamity at Píngyáng.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn had Xún Xù fix the bell pitches.
The calamity at Píngyáng
refers to the captivity of Emperors Huái and Mǐn.
When they made the four instruments,
it was not without discernment,
yet they could not escape the humiliation at Táichéng.
The four instruments
refer to the making of the four pitch pipes.
The event is recorded in the 145th scroll, under the first year of Tiānjiān.
The humiliation at Táichéng is recorded in the 162nd scroll, under the third year of Tàiqīng.
Even if Shùn's music, called Sháo,
Yǔ's music, called Xià,
Tāng's music, called Huò,
and King Wǔ of Zhōu's music, called Wǔ,
were all preserved in the world,
the character "xià"
is pronounced "hù yǎ."
The character "huò"
is pronounced "hù gù."
they would not suffice to match them,
and could not even transform a single person,
let alone all under heaven!
This is like holding Chuí's compass and square without craftsmen or materials,
sitting and waiting for vessels to be completed—
in the end, it is impossible.
Moreover, the licentious and deluded rulers of Qí and Chén,
with their music of perishing states,
briefly played in the court—
how could they transform the sorrows and joys of an entire age!
The character "zàn" (briefly)
is the same as "temporary."
The character "lè" (joy)
is pronounced "luò."
How could one speak so easily
and so decisively condemn the sages in this manner!
Ritual is not merely about dignified demeanor,
yet without dignified demeanor, ritual cannot be carried out.
Music is not merely about sounds,
yet without sounds, music cannot be perceived.
Take a mountain as an example:
picking up a single clod of earth or stone and calling it a mountain is impossible,
yet if all the earth and stones are removed,
where would the mountain be?
Therefore, it is said:
“Without substance, nothing is established;
without form, nothing can be carried out.”
This is recorded in the *Lǐqì*.
How is this different from looking at a fist-sized stone and belittling Mount Tài?
If what you say is true,
then the creation of music by the Five Emperors and Three Kings would all be false.
“A gentleman, regarding what he does not know,
should leave it unspoken,”
as recorded in the *Analects*, the words of Confucius.
On the 14th day of the Wùzǐ year,
the Emperor said to his attending ministers:
“I have read the collected works of Emperor Yáng of Suí,
and his writing is profound and extensive.
He also recognized Yáo and Shùn as virtuous and Jié and Zhòu as tyrannical,
yet why were his actions so contrary to this?”
Wèi Zhēng replied:
“Even if a ruler is sagacious and wise,
he should still humble himself to accept others’ counsel.
Thus, the wise offer their strategies,
and the brave exert their strength.
Emperor Yáng relied on his exceptional talent,
becoming arrogant and self-indulgent.
Therefore, while his mouth recited the words of Yáo and Shùn, his actions were those of Jié and Zhòu,
and he remained unaware of this until his downfall.”
The Emperor said:
“The past is not far away;
it serves as a lesson for us!”
15. Locusts appeared within the capital region.
On the Xīnmǎo day,
the Emperor entered the imperial garden,
exiting through the Xuánwǔ Gate and heading north into the forbidden park.
He picked up several locusts,
and prayed to them:
“The people rely on grain for their lives,
yet you consume it.
Better to eat my lungs and intestines.”
He raised his hand to swallow them,
but his attendants admonished him:
“Such vile creatures may cause illness.”
The Emperor said:
“I suffer disaster on behalf of the people;
why should I avoid illness?”
He then swallowed them.
That year,
the locusts did not cause disaster.
16. The Emperor said:
“Whenever I hold court,
before uttering a single word,
I always reflect three times,
fearing it may harm the people.
That is why I do not speak much.”
Dù Zhènglún, the Supervising Secretary in charge of recording daily affairs, said:
“My duty is to record words.
In ancient times, there were left and right historians:
the left historian recorded the Son of Heaven’s words,
and the right historian recorded his actions.
The Suí dynasty first established the position of Jìqī Shèrén.
In the second year of Zhēnguān,
the Jìqī Shèrén was abolished,
and its duties were transferred to the Chancellery,
with two Jìqī Láng appointed.
Those who held this duty concurrently with other offices
were called Zhī Jìqī Zhù or Zhī Jìqī Shì.
I must record everything,
not only because it may cause harm today,
but also because it may invite criticism in the future.”
The Emperor was pleased,
and rewarded him with two hundred bolts of silk.
17. The Emperor said:
“Emperor Wǔ of Liáng and his ministers only discussed suffering and emptiness,
meaning their discussions focused solely on ascetic practices and emptiness.
The officials could not even ride horses.
When Emperor Yuán of Liáng was besieged by the Zhōu army,
he was still lecturing on the *Lǎozǐ*,
while the officials listened in military attire.
This event is recorded in the 165th scroll, in the third year of Chéngshèng of Emperor Yuán of Liáng.
What I admire
are only the ways of Yáo, Shùn, the Zhōu dynasty, and Confucius.
I consider them as wings are to a bird,
as water is to a fish.
To lose them is to die;
they cannot be absent even for a moment.”
18. Regarding Péi Qiántōng, the Governor of Chénzhōu,
who was an old acquaintance of Emperor Yáng of Suí,
and had received special favor and appointment,
yet participated in regicide and rebellion,
as recorded in the 185th scroll, in the first year of Wǔdé of Emperor Gāozǔ.
According to the *Zīzhì Tōngjiàn*, events are divided into sections.
Wherever a section changes,
a space is usually left,
marking a new section.
Since this section begins with a space,
before the word “regarding,”
there should be
“the Emperor”
to make the text clear.
After repeated amnesties,
he fortunately avoided the extermination of his clan,
but he could not be allowed to govern the people.
Thus, an edict was issued to strip him of his official status
and exile him to Huānzhōu.
In the first year of Zhēnguān,
Dénán Prefecture of Dézhōu was renamed Huānzhōu.
“He helped overthrow the Suí dynasty to pave the way for the Great Táng,”
and he considered himself meritorious,
often showing signs of dissatisfaction.
After being convicted,
he died resentful and angry.
19. In autumn,
the seventh month,

an edict was issued: the followers of Yǔwén Huàjí—Niú Fāngyù, Governor of Láizhōu; Xuē Shìliáng, Governor of Jiàngzhōu; Táng Fèngyì, Chief Secretary of the Governor-General of Guǎngzhōu; and Yuán Lǐ, former Suí dynasty Military General—were all stripped of their official status and exiled to the frontier.
20. The Emperor said to his attending ministers:
“There is an old saying: ‘Amnesty is the fortune of petty men,
the misfortune of gentlemen.’
‘If amnesty is granted twice a year,
good people fall silent.’
Nurturing weeds harms good grain;
pardoning the guilty harms the innocent.
Therefore, since I ascended the throne,
I have not wished to grant amnesty frequently,
fearing that petty men would rely on it and lightly violate the laws!”
Punctuated by Wáng Chóngwǔ, reviewed by Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí.
Compiled by Sīmǎ Guāng by imperial order.
Later student from Tiāntái.
Second year of Zhēnguān
(Wùzǐ year, 628)
1. In the ninth month,
on the Bǐngwǔ day,
it was first ordered that retired officials
rank above their original grade.
According to the *Táng Huìyào*,
at that time, an edict stated that civil and military officials who retired due to old age
should, when attending court,
rank above officials of the same grade currently in office.
Guān,
read as gǔ wán.
2. The Emperor said:
“Recently, I have seen ministers repeatedly submitting memorials congratulating auspicious signs.
If households are well-supplied and people are content, even without auspicious signs,
it does not hinder being like Yáo and Shùn.
If the people are filled with sorrow and resentment, even with many auspicious signs,
it does not hinder being like Jié and Zhòu.
During the Northern Wèi dynasty,
officials burned the intertwined trees
and cooked the white pheasant to eat it.
How could that be considered perfect governance?”
On the Dīngwèi day,
an edict was issued:
“From now on, only major auspicious signs may be reported in memorials.
According to the *Yízhì Lìng*,
stars of virtue and auspicious clouds are considered major auspicious signs,
with sixty-four such items;
white wolves and red rabbits are upper auspicious signs,
with thirty-eight such items;
black crows and red wild geese are middle auspicious signs,
with thirty-two such items;
abundant grain, auspicious grass, and intertwined trees are lower auspicious signs,
with fourteen such items.
They should only be reported to the relevant authorities.”
The *Táng Liùdiǎn* states: the Director of the Ministry of Rites
is responsible for identifying all auspicious signs that appear.
The magpies’ nest was shaped like a waist drum,
and the left and right ministers offered congratulations.
The Emperor said:
“I have often laughed at Emperor Yáng of Suí for his fondness for auspicious signs.
True auspiciousness lies in obtaining worthy men.
What is there to congratulate?”
He ordered the nest destroyed
and the magpies released into the wild.
3. There had been little rain for days.
The Secretariat Drafter Lǐ Bǎiyào submitted a memorial, saying:
"Although palace women were released in previous years,
I have privately heard that in the Taishanghuang Palace and the Ye Ting,
there are still many useless women.
Not only do they waste food and clothing in vain,
but the accumulation of yin energy
is also sufficient to cause drought."
The Emperor said:
"Women confined deep within the palace
are truly pitiable.
Beyond sweeping and cleaning,
what use are they?
They should all be released,
allowed to seek husbands."
Thereupon, he dispatched the Left Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs Dài Zhòu and the Supervising Secretary of Huánshuǐ, Dù Zhènglún
(Huánshuǐ County
was established in the sixth year of the Jiàndé era of the Zhou dynasty by dividing the northeastern boundary of Línzhāng,
belonging to Wèi Prefecture.
Huán
is pronounced 'yuán'.) to carry this out. Over 3,000 women were released in total.
4. On the Jǐwèi day,
the Tūjué raided the border.
Some court ministers requested the repair of the ancient Great Wall.
(The ancient Great Wall
was the one built by Méng Tián of Qin.
From the Han to the Sui dynasties,
various walls and fortifications were built along the border,
but none matched the Qin Great Wall in length and extent.
Cháo
is pronounced 'zhí yáo fān'.) The Emperor said:
"The Tūjué have suffered successive disasters and anomalies.
Xiélì does not fear them and cultivate virtue;
instead, his tyranny grows ever more severe.
Kin attack each other;
their downfall is imminent.
I am about to clear the desert for you all;
why should we trouble the people to repair distant barriers!"
5. On the Rénshēn day,
the former Minister of the Court of the Imperial Granaries, Dòu Jìng, was appointed as the Military Governor of Xià Prefecture.
While at the Court of the Imperial Granaries,
the Vice Minister Zhào Yuánkǎi was skilled at amassing wealth through exactions.
Jìng despised him,
and said loudly to his subordinates:
(The subordinates of the Court of the Imperial Granaries

18. Fáng Xuánlíng and Wáng Guī were in charge of evaluating both capital and provincial officials.
The Táng evaluation method: All heads of government offices
annually assessed the merits and faults of their subordinates,
ranking them into nine grades.
For officials within the regular bureaucratic system,
they were appraised based on four virtues: first, being known for virtue and righteousness;
second, being clearly distinguished for integrity and caution;
third, being commendable for fairness and impartiality;
fourth, being diligent and never remiss.
In addition to these virtuous qualities,
there were twenty-seven highest achievements: first, presenting sound advice and correcting faults,
rectifying omissions and making up for deficiencies,
was the highest achievement for close attendants;
second, evaluating and selecting people,
promoting all the talented and worthy,
was the highest achievement for selection officials;
third, promoting the pure and discouraging the corrupt,
with praise and criticism always appropriate,
was the highest achievement for examination officials;
fourth, rituals and ceremonies,
always conforming to the classics,
was the highest achievement for ritual officials;
fifth, musical tones in perfect harmony,
never losing the rhythm,
was the highest achievement for music officials;
sixth, decisive and without delay,
judgments and decisions reasonable,
was the highest achievement for adjudicating officials;
seventh, commanding with method,
guarding without fail,
was the highest achievement for palace guards;
eighth, soldiers well-trained,
military equipment fully prepared,
was the highest achievement for commanding officers;
ninth, investigations uncovering the truth,
judgments fair and equitable,
was the highest achievement for judicial officials;
tenth, collation meticulous and thorough,
skilled in editing and finalizing,
was the highest achievement for proofreading officials;
eleventh, receiving edicts and presenting memorials,
articulating clearly and promptly,
was the highest achievement for transmission officials;
twelfth, instructing and guiding with method,
students fully engaged in their studies,
was the highest achievement for educational officials;
thirteenth, rewards and punishments strict and clear,
always victorious in attack and battle,
was the highest achievement for military generals;
fourteenth, promoting ritual and righteousness,
bringing order to their jurisdiction,
was the highest achievement for administrative and instructional officials;
fifteenth, recording in detail and correctly,
both wording and reasoning excellent,
was the highest achievement for literary and historical officials;
sixteenth, investigations thorough and meticulous,
impeachments and recommendations always appropriate,
was the highest achievement for censorial officials;
seventeenth, skilled in verification and review,
exposing errors without concealment,
was the highest achievement for inspection officials;
eighteenth, official duties well managed,
provisions and support strongly maintained,
was the highest achievement for supervisory officials;
nineteenth, all tasks fully accomplished,
laborers and craftsmen without complaints,
was the highest achievement for labor management officials;
twentieth, plowing and weeding timely,
harvests meeting targets,
was the highest achievement for agricultural colony officials;
twenty-first, careful in storage,
clear in disbursements and receipts,
was the highest achievement for granary and treasury officials;
twenty-second, calculating waxing and waning,
investigating principles with precision,
was the highest achievement for calendar officials;
twenty-third, divination, prognostication, medicine, and fortune-telling,
with many notable efficacies,
was the highest achievement for technical specialists;
twenty-fourth, inspections methodical,
travelers unimpeded,
was the highest achievement for checkpoint and ferry officials;
twenty-fifth, markets undisturbed,
fraud and excess prevented,
was the highest achievement for market officials;
twenty-sixth, livestock well-fed and thriving,
breeding and multiplying abundantly,
was the highest achievement for pastoral officials;
twenty-seventh, borders peaceful and orderly,
city walls and moats well-maintained,
was the highest achievement for garrison and defense officials.
One highest achievement and four virtues
was rated as Upper Upper;
one highest achievement and three virtues
was rated as Upper Middle;
one highest achievement and two virtues
was rated as Upper Lower;
no highest achievement but having two virtues
was rated as Middle Upper;
no highest achievement but having one virtue
was rated as Middle Middle;
official duties roughly managed,
no reputation for virtue or highest achievement,
was rated as Middle Lower;
likes and dislikes based on personal feelings,
judgments and decisions contrary to reason,
was rated as Lower Upper;
turning one's back on public duty for private interests,
official duties neglected and deficient,
was rated as Lower Middle;
holding office with flattery and deceit,
with evidence of greed and corruption,
was rated as Lower Lower.
All finalized evaluations were gathered at the Department of State Affairs,
and the grades were announced before being memorialized.
The Emperor ordered Hóu Jūnjí to investigate the matter.
Wèi Zhēng remonstrated, saying:
"Xuánlíng and Guī are both veteran court ministers,
long trusted by Your Majesty for their loyalty and integrity.
Since they have evaluated many people,
is it possible that not one or two were inappropriate!
Examining the circumstances,
they ultimately were not acting out of favoritism.
If an investigation uncovers such instances,
then they can no longer be trusted,
how could they continue to hold important positions!
Moreover, Wàn Jǐ has recently been constantly present in the evaluation hall,
yet he never raised any objections;
only when he himself did not receive a favorable evaluation,
did he begin to present arguments.
This is precisely intended to provoke Your Majesty's anger,
not out of sincere devotion to the state.
Even if the investigation finds it true,
it would not benefit the court;
if it is fundamentally false,
it would only cause Your Majesty to lose trust in your appointed ministers.
What I cherish is the principle of governance,
not daring to blindly favor these two ministers."
The Emperor then released the matter and did not inquire further.

The Emperor pitied him,

now I occupy the highest position,
and am master of the entire realm.

how dare I violate it!"
He bestowed silk upon him and sent him away.

now Dàtóng City's Yǒngjì Barrier.
North passing the Great Marsh,
seventeen lǐ to Jīnhé.
Rèn,
pronounced rén.
Jiélì fled at night with several horsemen,
hiding in a desolate valley.
Sūníshī, fearful,
galloped in pursuit and captured him.
On Gēngchén,
Deputy Commander Zhāng Bǎoxiāng led troops to suddenly arrive at Shābōluó's camp,
capturing Jiélì and sending him to the capital.
Sūníshī led all his followers to surrender,
and the lands south of the desert were thus emptied.
8 The Duke of Chéng of Cài, Dù Rúhuì, was critically ill.
Dù Rúhuì was first enfeoffed as Duke of Cài,
after his death he was posthumously enfeoffed as Duke of Lái.
Hè Chēn's posthumous naming rules: Assisting the ruler to achieve success is called chéng;
harmony among the people and blessings for the ministers is called chéng.
The Emperor personally went to visit him.
On Jiǎshēn,
he passed away.
Whenever the Emperor obtained something excellent,
he would think of Rúhuì,
and send envoys to bestow it upon his family.
After a long time,
when speaking of Rúhuì,
he would inevitably shed tears,
and said to Fáng Xuánlíng:
"You and Rúhuì together assisted me,
now I only see you,
and no longer see Rúhuì!"
9 The Tujue Khan, Jiélì Kèhán, arrived at Cháng'ān.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day Wùxū,
the Emperor ascended the Shùntiān Tower.
The Old Book's Annals of Emperors states:
He ascended the Shùntiān Gate.
The Tang Liudian records: Among the southern gates of the imperial city,
the central one was called Chéngtiān Gate.
It was built in the second year of the Sui dynasty's Kāihuáng era.
Initially named Guǎngyáng Gate,
in the first year of the Rénshòu era,
it was renamed Zhāoyáng Gate.
In the first year of the Wǔdé era,
it was renamed Shùntiān Gate.
In the first year of the Shénlóng era,
it was renamed Chéngtiān Gate.
For occasions such as the New Year's Day or the Winter Solstice,
when grand banquets were held,
pardons were granted and crimes forgiven,
the old was discarded and the new established,
and when receiving tribute from all states
and guests from the Four Barbarians,
the Emperor would conduct governance from the Chéngtiān Gate,
which corresponds to the ancient outer court.
The Shùntiān Tower
refers to the tower of the Shùntiān Gate.
Jiélì was summoned for an audience,
and the Emperor enumerated his offenses, saying:
"You relied on the achievements of your father and elder brother,
indulged in debauchery and tyranny, leading to your downfall—this is your first crime.
You repeatedly formed alliances with us and then betrayed them—this is the second.
Arrogant in your strength and fond of war,
leaving bones exposed like wild grass—this is the third.
Trampling our crops,
plundering our sons and daughters—this is the fourth.
I pardoned your crimes,
preserved your state,
yet you delayed and did not come—this is the fifth.
However, since the incident at Biàn Bridge,
you have not launched any major invasions.
(Regarding Biàn Bridge,
the event is recorded in the 191st volume, under the ninth year of Gāozǔ's Wǔdé era.)
(The pronunciation of 'see' [jiàn] is xiàn,
read as xián biàn.)
(The pronunciation of 'enumerate' [shǔ] is suǒ jù,
also suǒ zhǔ.)
(The pronunciation of 'repeatedly' [shuò] is suǒ jiǎo.)
(The pronunciation of 'betray' [bèi] is pú mèi.)
(The pronunciation of 'fond' [hào] is hū bào.)
(The pronunciation of 'exposed' [pù] is bù bǔ.)
(The pronunciation of 'again' [fù] is fú yòu;
the following 'again' [fù] is the same.)
(The pronunciation of 'trample' [róu] is rén jiǔ.)
Jiélì wept, apologized, and withdrew.
An edict ordered him to be housed in the Tàipú [Court],
and provided with generous provisions.
When the Retired Emperor heard of Jiélì's capture,
he sighed and said:
"Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn was trapped at Báidēng
and could not achieve vengeance;
now my son is able to annihilate the Tujue.
I entrusted the right person,
so what more is there to worry about!"
The Retired Emperor summoned the Emperor, over ten high-ranking ministers, various princes, and princesses to a drinking feast at the Língyān Pavilion.
(According to the palace map in the Pavilion edition: North of the Liǎngyí Hall is the Yánjiā Hall,
east of the Yánjiā Hall is the Gōngchén Pavilion,
and east of the Gōngchén Pavilion is the Língyān Pavilion.)
The Retired Emperor played the pipa himself,
the Emperor danced,
the dukes and ministers rose in turn to offer toasts,
and the event lasted until night before concluding.
After the Turks were destroyed,
some of their tribes submitted to the north and attached themselves to the Xueyantuo,
while others fled west to the Western Regions.
Those who surrendered to the Tang still numbered over a hundred thousand people.
An edict was issued ordering the ministers to discuss the appropriate measures for dealing with them.
Most court officials said:
"The northern barbarians have been a threat to China since ancient times.
Now, fortunately, they have been defeated and destroyed.
They should all be relocated to the region between Yǎn and Yù in Hénán.
This Yǎn and Yù
refers to the broad boundaries of the Nine Provinces traced by Yǔ.
Cháo,
pronounced zhí yáo fān.
Scatter them among the prefectures and counties,
teach them farming and weaving,
so that the barbarians can be transformed into farmers,
and the lands north of the frontier will be permanently emptied."
Zhōngshū Shìláng Yán Shīgǔ believed:
"Both the Turks and the Tiělè were peoples whom even the ancients could not subjugate.
Since Your Majesty has obtained and subjugated them,
I request that they all be settled north of the Hé.
Héběi,
meaning north of the Northern River.
Let them govern their own tribes,
and there will never be trouble again."
Lǐbù Shìláng Lǐ Bǎiyào believed:
"Although the Turks are called one nation,
their tribes are divided,
each with their own chieftains.
Now, taking advantage of their dispersal,
each should be established as rulers according to their original tribal divisions,
without being subordinate to one another;
even if we wish to preserve the Āshǐnà clan,
they should only be allowed to maintain their own clan.
When the state is divided, it becomes weak and easy to control;
when forces are balanced, it is difficult for them to annex each other.
Each preserving themselves,
they will certainly be unable to rival China.
I also request that a Protectorate be established in Dìngxiāng,
to oversee and regulate them.
This is a long-term strategy for pacifying the frontier."
Xiàzhōu Dūdū Dòu Jìng
believed:
"The nature of the Róng and Dí
is like that of beasts.
They cannot be intimidated by laws and punishments,
nor can they be taught benevolence and righteousness.
Moreover, their attachment to their homeland
is not easily forgotten.
Placing them within China
brings harm without benefit.
I fear that once trouble arises,
they will violate our royal domain.
It would be better to take advantage of their defeated and remnant state,
bestow upon them unexpected grace,
confer upon them titles of princes and marquises,
marry them to women of the imperial clan,
divide their lands,
split their tribes,
so that their power is weakened and their forces divided,
making them easy to control.
This will ensure they remain vassals forever,
and the frontier will be permanently secure."
Wēn Yànbó believed:
"Relocating them to the region between Yǎn and Yù
goes against their nature,
and is not a way to preserve and nurture them.
I request to follow the precedent of Hàn Emperor Jiànwǔ,
settling the surrendered Xiongnu near the frontier,
preserving their tribes intact,
respecting their customs,
to populate the empty lands,
so that they can serve as a protective barrier for China.
This is an excellent strategy."
Wèi Zhēng believed:
"The Turks have been bandits and invaders for generations,
enemies of the people.
Now, fortunately, they have been defeated and destroyed.
Since Your Majesty, due to their surrender,
cannot bear to kill them all,
they should be allowed to return to their homeland.
They must not be kept within China.
These Róng and Dí have human faces but the hearts of beasts.
When weak, they beg for submission;
when strong, they rebel.
This is their constant nature.
Now, the surrendered number nearly a hundred thousand.
In a few years,
their numbers will multiply,
and they will surely become a disease close to the heart.
Do not regret it later.
At the beginning of the Jìn dynasty, various Hú peoples lived mixed with the people within China.
Guō Qīn and Jiāng Tǒng
both advised Emperor Wǔ to drive them beyond the frontier to prevent disorder.
Guō Qīn's discussion is found in scroll 81, year Tàikāng 1 of Jìn Emperor Wǔ.
Jiāng Tǒng's discussion is found in scroll 83, year Yǒngxī 9 of Emperor Huì.
More than twenty years later,
the region between Yī and Luò
became a land of felt and fur,
a clear lesson from past events!"
Yànbó said:
"The king's relation to all things
is like heaven covering and earth supporting,
leaving nothing out.
Now the Turks, in dire straits, have come to submit to us.
How can we abandon and not accept them!
Confucius said: 'In teaching, there should be no distinction of classes.'
If we save them from death,
provide them with livelihoods,
teach them ritual and righteousness,
in a few years,
they will all become our people.
Select their chieftains
to serve in the palace guard.
Awed by authority and grateful for virtue,
what future trouble could there be!"
The Emperor ultimately adopted Yànbó's strategy,
settling the surrendered Turks
from Yōuzhōu in the east
to Língzhōu in the west.
The lands formerly ruled by Tūlì were divided,
establishing the four prefectural protectorates of Shùn, Yòu, Huà, and Cháng.
The lands of Jiélì were also divided into six prefectures,
with the Dìngxiāng Protectorate established on the left,
and the Yúnzhōng Protectorate on the right,
to govern their people.
The Dìngxiāng Protectorate was temporarily administered from Níngshuò,
and the Yúnzhōng Protectorate was temporarily administered from within the territory of Shuòfāng.
According to this, Níngshuò County also belonged to Shuòfāng Commandery.
The Old Book biography of Wēn Yànbó says: The Emperor followed Yànbó's proposal,
settling the surrendered people in the Shuòfāng region.
Thus, it is clear that the two protectorates were temporarily administered from Shuòfāng.
In the fifth month,
on Xīnwèi,
Tūlì was appointed as Shùnzhōu Dūdū,
to lead the officials of his tribe.
Shùnzhōu
was temporarily administered from Wǔliǔ Shù, south of Yíngzhōu.
Shuài,
pronounced shuài.
"Your ancestor Qǐmín fled to the Suí alone,
and the Suí established him as the Great Kèhán,
who possessed the northern wilderness.
This event is recorded in scroll 178, year Kāihuáng 19 of Suí Emperor Wén.
Kě,
pronounced cóng kān rù shēng.
Hán,
pronounced hán.
This event is recorded in scroll 182, year Dàyè 11 of Emperor Yáng.
That is why you are in such ruin and chaos today.
The reason I do not establish you as Kèhán
is to learn from the previous incident involving Qǐmín.
Now I appoint you as Dūdū.
You should diligently uphold the laws of China,
and not invade or plunder.
This is not only for the long-term peace of China,
but also to ensure the perpetual preservation of your clan!"
On Rénshēn,
Āshǐnà Sūníshī was appointed as Huáidé Commandery Prince,
and Āshǐnà Sīmó as Huáihuà Commandery Prince.
When Jiélì was defeated,
the chieftains of the various tribes all abandoned Jiélì and surrendered.
Only Sīmó followed him,
and was eventually captured along with Jiélì.
The Emperor praised his loyalty,
appointed him as Right Wǔhòu Dàjiāngjūn,
and soon made him Běikāizhōu Dūdū,
to govern Jiélì's former people.
Textual analysis says: The Old Biography says he was Huàzhōu Dūdū.
But Huàzhōu was originally Tūlì's territory,
so how could he govern Jiélì's tribes?
On Dīngchǒu,
Right Wǔwèi Dàjiāngjūn Shǐ Dànài was appointed as Fēngzhōu Dūdū.
The Suí established Fēngzhōu from Wǔyuán Commandery,
abolished it early in the Dàyè era,
at the beginning of the Táng,
Zhāng Chángxùn surrendered,
and Fēngzhōu was re-established,
but soon abolished again.
This year,
using surrendered Turk households,
Fēngzhōu Jiǔyuán Commandery was established.
All were appointed as generals and colonels,
stationed throughout the court.
Over a hundred held positions of the fifth rank or above,
nearly half the number of court officials.
Consequently, nearly ten thousand households came to reside in Cháng'ān.
On the 10th, Xīnsì,
an edict was issued:
"From now on, in lawsuits,
if a party is dissatisfied after a judgment by the Shàngshū Shěng,
they may present their case to the Eastern Palace,
and entrust the Crown Prince to adjudicate.
If they still do not accept the judgment,
then it may be reported to the Emperor."
On the 11th day, Dīnghài,
the Censor-in-Chief, Xiāo Yǔ, impeached and memorialized that Lǐ Jìng, upon breaking the headquarters of the Xiéli Khagan,
had no discipline in commanding his army,
and the precious goods of the Turks
were all plundered and exhausted.
He requested that Jìng be handed over to the judicial authorities for investigation and punishment.
The Emperor specially issued an edict not to impeach him.
When Jìng entered for an audience,
the Emperor severely reprimanded and reproached him,
and Jìng kowtowed in apology.
After a long while,
the Emperor then said:
"Sui's Shǐ Wànsuì defeated the Dátóu Khagan,
received no reward for his merit,
and was executed due to an offense.
Kè,
follow the reading of the sound 'kè'.
Hán,
pronounced as 'hán'.
The event is recorded in the 179th volume, the 20th year of the Kāihuáng era of Sui Wéndì.
I record your merit,
and pardon your offense."
He promoted Jìng to Left Guanglù Grand Master,
bestowed upon him a thousand bolts of silk,
and increased his actual food-producing households, bringing the total to five hundred households.
Not long after,
the Emperor said to Jìng:
"Previously, someone slandered you.
Now, my mind is already awakened.
Do not hold it in your heart."
He further bestowed two thousand bolts of silk.
On the 12th day, Línyì presented fire pearls.
The Tángshū states: East of Pólì is the country of Luóchà.
Its people are extremely ugly,
with red hair and black bodies,
beast-like teeth and eagle-like claws.
They trade with the people of Línyì,
coming at night,
covering their own faces.
Their country produces fire pearls,
shaped like crystal.
At noon,
if one holds the pearl to catch the sun's shadow,
and places mugwort beneath it,
then fire emerges.
They requested permission to attack it.
The Emperor said:
"Those who love war perish.
Sui Yángdì and the Xiéli Khagan
are both examples I have personally witnessed.
Defeating a small state is not martial,
moreover, victory is not certain!
Mere words and language,
why should they be taken to heart!"
On the 13th day, in the sixth month,
Dīngyǒu,
Āshǐnà Sūníshī was appointed as Governor of Běiníng Prefecture,
and the Central Guard General Shǐ Shànyìng was appointed as Governor of Běifǔ Prefecture.
Rényín,
the Right Xiāowèi General Kāng Sū was appointed as Governor of Běi'ān Prefecture.
These three prefectures, along with the later four prefectures of Yòu, Huà, Cháng, and Běikāi, were all eventually abolished.
Shǐ Shànyìng was also of the Āshǐnà clan;
the history merely records his surname.
Xiāo,
pronounced as 'jiān yáo fān'.
On the 14th day, Yǐmǎo,
laborers were conscripted to repair the Luòyáng Palace in preparation for an imperial tour.
The Jǐshìzhōng Zhāng Xuánsù submitted a memorial remonstrating,
believing that:
"There is no scheduled date for an imperial tour to Luòyáng, yet the palace buildings are being repaired in advance;
this is not an urgent matter for today.
In the past, Hàn Gāozǔ accepted Lóu Jìng's advice
and moved the capital from Luòyáng to Cháng'ān.
The event is recorded in the 11th volume, the fifth year of Hàn Gāozǔ.
Jǐngdì employed Cháo Cuò's counsel, and the Seven States brought about disaster.
The event is recorded in the 16th volume, the third year of Hàn Jǐngdì.
Cháo,
pronounced as 'zhí yáo fān'.
Cuò,
pronounced as 'qī gù fān'.
How does the closeness of the Turks
compare to the Seven States?
How can we not be concerned about this first,
while palaces can be hastily built,
and the imperial carriage can be lightly moved!
I observe that when the Sui initially constructed palaces,
as there were no large trees near the mountains,
they all had to be transported from distant places.
Two thousand men pulled a single pillar,
using wood for wheels.
Then, from the friction and rubbing, fire emerged,
so they cast iron for the hubs.
After traveling one or two lǐ,
the iron hubs would break,
and they had to dispatch several hundred men carrying spare iron hubs to follow and replace them.
In a full day, they could only travel twenty or thirty lǐ.
Calculating the cost of a single pillar,
several hundred thousand man-days of labor had already been used.
The rest can be imagined.
When Your Majesty first pacified Luòyáng,
all the grand and extravagant Sui palaces were ordered destroyed.
See the 189th volume, the fourth year of the Wǔdé era of Gāozǔ.
Lìng,
pronounced as 'lì dīng fān'.
Now to undertake construction again,
why despise it in the past and emulate it today!
Moreover, considering the financial resources and strength of today,
how do they compare to the Sui era?
Your Majesty employs people who are wounded and scarred,
inheriting the malpractices of the fallen Sui.
I fear it may be even worse than Yángdì!"
The Emperor said to Xuánsù:
"You say I am not as good as Yángdì;
how do I compare to Jié and Zhòu?"
He replied:
"If this labor service does not cease,
it will likewise lead to chaos!"
The Emperor sighed and said:
"I did not think it through thoroughly,
and thus came to this!"
Turning to Fáng Xuánlíng, he said:
"I considered Luòyáng central to the land,
with equal distances for tribute from all directions,
intending to benefit the people,
therefore I ordered its construction.
Now, what Xuánsù said is truly reasonable.
We should immediately cease the labor service.
If someday I have business in Luòyáng,
even dwelling in the open would not be harmful."
He then bestowed upon Xuánsù two hundred bolts of patterned silk.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the first day, Jiǎzǐ,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the 16th day, Yǐchǒu,
the Emperor asked Fáng Xuánlíng and Xiāo Yǔ:
"What kind of ruler was Sui Wéndì?"
They replied:
"Wéndì was diligent in governance.
Whenever he held court,
it sometimes lasted until the sun declined.
For officials of the fifth rank and above,
he would have them sit and discuss affairs.
Guards passed meals for them to eat;
the guards and attendants could not leave their posts,
and had no leisure to sit and eat,
so they stood and had meals passed to them.
Zhì,
pronounced as 'zhí lì fān';
the same below.
Cháo,
pronounced as 'zhí yáo fān'.
Cān,
pronounced as 'qiān ān fān'.
He was also a ruler who exerted himself to the utmost."
The Emperor said:
"You have grasped one aspect,
but do not know the other.
Wéndì was not enlightened yet fond of scrutinizing;
not being enlightened meant his illumination was not comprehensive,
fond of scrutinizing meant he was overly suspicious of things.
He decided all matters himself,
not entrusting them to his ministers.
The world is vast,
with myriad affairs daily.
Although he again toiled his spirit and strained his body,
how could he manage everything correctly!
The ministers, knowing the ruler's intentions,
merely accepted decisions and followed orders.
Even if there were errors and faults,
none dared to remonstrate or dispute.
This is why it perished in the second generation.
I am not like this.
I select worthy and talented men from the world,
place them in the hundred offices,
and have them consider the affairs of the world.
Matters pass through the prime minister,
who examines them thoroughly for convenience and security,
and then memorializes for my attention.
Those with merit are rewarded,
those with offenses are punished.
Who would dare not exhaust their heart and strength to fulfill their duties?
Why worry about the world not being well-governed!"
Thereupon, he commanded all offices:
"From now on, if any imperial edict or decree issued for implementation is inconvenient,
all should firmly memorialize about it.
Do not flatter and comply,
failing to express your own views fully."
On the 17th day, Guǐyǒu,
the former Tàizǐ Shǎobǎo, Lǐ Gāng, was appointed as Tàizǐ Shǎoshī,
and the concurrent Yùshǐ Dàfū, Xiāo Yǔ, was appointed as Tàizǐ Shǎofù.
The three Junior Mentors of the Táng Eastern Palace
were all of the second rank,
in charge of instructing the Crown Prince.
Shǎo,
pronounced as 'shǐ zhào fān'.
Yǔ,
pronounced as 'yǔ'.
Li Gāng had a foot ailment.
The Emperor bestowed upon him a sedan chair,
a sedan chair,
that is, a hand-carried sedan chair.
He was frequently summoned into the inner palace,
to be consulted on governmental affairs.
Whenever he arrived at the Eastern Palace,
the Crown Prince personally paid him respects.
Whenever the Crown Prince attended to official duties,
the Emperor ordered Li Gāng and Fáng Xuánlíng to
attend and sit with him.
Previously,
Xiāo Yǔ participated in deliberations on court affairs with the chief ministers.
Yǔ was of a stern disposition and eloquent in debate,
Fáng Xuánlíng and others were all unable to oppose him,
but the Emperor mostly did not adopt his proposals.
Examination of discrepancies states: The Old Biography says:
"Xuánlíng and others knew in their hearts that he was right,
but did not adopt his words."
According to this, if Xuánlíng's intentions were thus,
how could he be considered a worthy minister!
Moreover, the adoption or rejection of matters lay with Tàizōng,
not with Xuánlíng.
This is not adopted here.
Yǔ impeached and memorialized against them,
but the Emperor ultimately did not inquire into it.
Yǔ, because of this, became discontented and lost his bearings,
and was subsequently dismissed from the post of Censor-in-Chief,
being made Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince,
and no longer participated in or was informed of court administration.
18 The tribes of the Western Türks were scattered in Yīwú.
Yīwú,
that is, the location of the Hàn dynasty's Yīwúlú,
lies beyond the great desert,
2,730 lǐ east to Yángguān.
In this year, Yīwú County and Yī Prefecture, Yīwú Commandery were established in that territory.
Jué,
jiǔ wù fān.
Zhǒng,
zhāng yǒng fān.
They stored grain at the desert pass,
this desert,
is the desert east of Yīwú.
Shǐ,
shū lì fān.
Qì,
qī jì fān.
Zhù,
dīng lǚ fān.
Envoys were sent to summon and pacify them,
they were seen constantly on the roads.
Dàliàng submitted a memorial stating:
"Those who wish to win over distant regions must first pacify those nearby.
The Central Plains are like the root and trunk,
the Four Barbarians are like the branches and leaves.
To exhaust the Central Plains in order to serve the Four Barbarians
is like uprooting the trunk to benefit the branches and leaves.
I have examined the distant examples of Qín and Hàn,
and observed the recent case of the Suí court.
Their external engagements with the Róng and Dí
all led to exhaustion and ruin.
Now summoning the Western Türks,
we only see toil and expense,
and do not see its benefit.
Moreover, the prefectures and counties of Héxī are desolate,
Gān, Liáng, Guā, Shā, Sù and other prefectures,
all belong to Héxī.
They have only just begun to be cultivated and harvested;
now they are again burdened with supplying this undertaking,
the people will be unable to bear it.
It would be better to temporarily cease the summons and pacification as expedient.
The territory of Yīwú
is mostly sandy desert.
If its people either establish their own rulers and chiefs,
or seek to declare themselves subjects and submit to the interior,
loosely control and accept them,
let them dwell outside the frontier,
to serve as a protective screen for the Central Plains.
This would be bestowing nominal favor while reaping actual benefit."
The Emperor followed this advice.
19 In the eighth month,
on the bǐngwǔ day,
an edict was issued stating:
"There has been no distinction in rank for ordinary court dress.
From now on, those of the third rank and above shall wear purple,
the fourth and fifth ranks shall wear crimson,
the sixth and seventh ranks shall wear green,
the eighth rank shall wear blue;
women shall follow the color of their husbands."
From the fourth rank downwards,
crimson, green, and blue had variations in shade,
the ninth rank then wore light blue.
20 On the jiǎyín day,
an edict appointed the Minister of War Lǐ Jìng as Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.
Jìng's nature was deep and steady,
whenever he participated in deliberations with the chief ministers of the time,
he was respectful and cautious as if unable to speak.
21 After the Türks were destroyed,
the Military Governor of Yíng Prefecture, Xuē Wànshū, sent the Qìdān chieftain Tānmòzhé to persuade and advise the various tribes of the northeast,
the Xī, Xí, Shìwéi and more than ten other tribes all submitted to the interior.
Wànshū
was the elder brother of Wànjūn.
22 On the wùwǔ day,
the Türk Yùgǔshè came to surrender.
Yùgǔshè,
was the younger brother of Tūlì.
After Jiélì was defeated,
Yùgǔshè fled to Gāochāng.
Hearing that Tūlì was being treated with courtesy by Táng,
he then came to surrender.
23 In the ninth month,
on the wùchén day,
the lord of the Yīwú city came to court.
At the end of the Suí,
Yīwú submitted to the interior,
and Yīwú Commandery was established.
When the Suí fell into disorder,
it became subject to the Türks.
After Jiélì was destroyed,
he led his subordinate seven cities to surrender,
and accordingly, Western Yī Prefecture was established in that territory.
Western Yī Prefecture,
was renamed Yī Prefecture in the sixth year.
24 The Sījié tribe was suffering from famine and poverty.
The Prefect of Shuò Prefecture, Xīnfēng's Zhāng Jiǎn, gathered and settled them.
Those who did not come,
still resided north of the desert.
Qì,
qī jì fān.
Jiǎn also did not prohibit this.
When Jiǎn was transferred to be Military Governor of Shèng Prefecture,
the prefectural officials reported that the Sījié were about to rebel.
An edict ordered Jiǎn to go and investigate.
Jiǎn rode alone into their tribe to persuade and advise them,
and relocated them to Dài Prefecture.
He was then appointed Acting Military Governor of Dài Prefecture,
and the Sījié ultimately did not rebel.
Jiǎn thereupon encouraged them to cultivate military farms,
and the year saw a great harvest.
Jiǎn feared that if the barbarians accumulated much wealth,
they might harbor disloyal intentions,
so he memorialized requesting government grain purchases to fill the frontier stores.
The tribe was pleased,
cultivated the farms with even greater effort,
and the frontier defenses were thus strengthened.
25 On the bǐngzǐ day,
the lands of the southern Man were opened up and Fèi Prefecture and Yí Prefecture were established.
Both prefectures were located in the territory of the Hàn dynasty's Zāngkē Commandery.
In the fourth year of Wǔdé,
Yí Prefecture was established with Níngyí County of Sī Prefecture,
and was abolished in the first year of Zhēnguān.
In this year, again using Dūshàng County of Sī Prefecture, the southern Man were opened up,
and Yí Prefecture, Yìquán Commandery was established,
which was the territory of the Suí dynasty's Míngyáng Commandery.
Fèi Prefecture, Fúchuān Commandery,
was the territory of Fúchuān County of the Suí dynasty's Qián'ān Commandery.
In this year, it was established by separating Fúchuān and Fúyáng from Sī Prefecture and opening up the southern Man.
Sòng Bái said: Fèi Prefecture derived its name from the Fèi River within the prefectural boundaries.
26 On the jǐmǎo day,
the Emperor visited Lǒng Prefecture.
The Later Wèi divided the territories of Jīng and Qí Prefectures to establish Eastern Qín Prefecture.
In the seventeenth year of Dàtǒng,
it was renamed Lǒng Prefecture, governing Yuán County,
located 496 lǐ west of Cháng'ān.
27 In winter,
the eleventh month,
on the rénchén day,
the Right Guard General-in-Chief Hóu Jūnjí was appointed Minister of War,
and participated in deliberations on court administration.
28 On the jiǎzǐ day,
the imperial carriage returned to the capital.
29 The Emperor read a book on acupuncture and moxibustion from the Bright Hall,
which said
"the connecting vessels of a person's five viscera
all attach to the back."
The Táng Catalogue of Books lists the Huángdì Bright Hall Classic, Bright Hall Reclining and Sideways Human Diagrams, Bright Hall Human Form Diagrams, Bright Hall Acupuncture Point Diagrams,
all being books on acupuncture and moxibustion.
Zàng,
cú làng fān.
Zhēn,
zhū shēn fān.
Jiǔ,
jū yòu fān.
On the wùyín day
an edict was issued that from now on, prisoners must not be flogged on the back.
30 In the twelfth month,
on the jiǎchén day,
the Emperor hunted at the Deer Park;
In the first year of Wǔdé,
Lùyuàn County was established by separating Gāolíng from Jīngzhào.
On the yǐsì day
he returned to the palace.
On the 31st day, the jiǎyín day,
King Qū Wéntài of Gāochāng came to court.
All the states of the Western Regions wished to send envoys to present tribute through Wéntài,
and the Emperor dispatched Wéntài's minister, Yàndáhégàn, to go and welcome them.
Wèi Zhēng remonstrated, saying:
"In the past, Emperor Guāngwǔ did not allow the Western Regions to send hostages,
nor did he establish a Protector-General,
believing that China should not be burdened by the barbarians.
This matter is recorded in the 43rd year of the Jiànwǔ era of Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn.
Previously, when Wéntài came,
the labor and expense were already excessive,
referring to when Wéntài entered Táng territory.
His retinue numbered no less than a thousand people.
The border people were impoverished and exhausted,
and could not bear the burden.
If merchants are allowed to come and go,
trading with the border people,
that would be acceptable.
But if they are treated as honored guests,
it is not beneficial for China."
At that time, Yàndáhégàn had already departed,
but the Emperor immediately ordered him to stop.
32. The various chancellors were attending a banquet,
and the Emperor said to Wáng Guī:
"Your discernment is profound,
and you are also skilled in discussion.
From Fáng Xuánlíng downwards,
you should evaluate them all,
and also say how you compare with these gentlemen."
He replied:
"Diligently serving the state,
knowing what must be done and doing it without fail,
I am not as good as Xuánlíng.
Talented in both civil and military affairs,
capable as a general and as a minister,
I am not as good as Lǐ Jìng.
Presenting memorials in detail and clarity,
handling affairs with fairness and accuracy,
I am not as good as Wēn Yànbó.
Managing complex and difficult matters,
ensuring all tasks are accomplished,
I am not as good as Dài Zhòu.
Feeling ashamed if the ruler does not equal Yáo and Shùn,
taking remonstrance as his personal responsibility,
I am not as good as Wèi Zhēng.
As for encouraging the good and suppressing the evil,
hating wickedness and loving virtue,
compared to these gentlemen,
I have some small strength."
The Emperor deeply agreed,
and all admired his accurate assessment.
33. When the Emperor first ascended the throne,
he once spoke with his close ministers about moral transformation.
The Emperor said:
"Now, following a great disorder,
I fear the people will not be easily transformed."
Wèi Zhēng replied:
"Not so.
People long at peace become arrogant and indolent;
arrogance and indolence make them difficult to instruct.
People who have experienced disorder are sorrowful and bitter;
sorrow and bitterness make them easy to transform.
It is like how the hungry are easily fed,
and the thirsty are easily given drink."
These are the words of Mèngzǐ.
Yì (易),
read with the tone of yǐ (以豉翻).
Féng Déyí objected, saying:
"Since the Three Dynasties,
people have gradually become deceitful and cunning.
Therefore, Qín employed laws and punishments,
and Hàn mixed in hegemonic methods.
They wished to transform but could not;
how could they have been able but unwilling!
Wèi Zhēng is a bookish scholar,
unaware of current affairs.
If we believe his empty theories,
it will surely ruin the state."
Zhēng said:
"The Five Emperors and Three Kings transformed the people without changing them.
In the past, the Yellow Emperor campaigned against Chīyóu,
Zhuānxū executed the Jiǔlí,
Tāng exiled Jié,
King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
and all were able to personally bring about great peace.
When the age of Shénnóng declined,
Chīyóu became tyrannical,
and the Yellow Emperor campaigned against him,
capturing and killing Chīyóu.
When the age of Shàohào declined,
the Jiǔlí disrupted virtue,
and Zhuānxū executed them.
Chéng Tāng exiled Jié to Náncháo.
King Wǔ killed Zhòu at Mùyě.
If you say the ancients were pure and simple,
and gradually became deceitful and cunning,
then by today,
they should have all turned into ghosts and demons!
How could a ruler govern them then!"
The Emperor ultimately followed Zhēng's advice.
In the first year,
Guānzhōng suffered famine,
and a dǒu of rice cost a bolt of silk.
In the second year,
there were locusts across the land.
In the third year,
there was great flooding.
The Emperor worked diligently to comfort the people,
and though the people went east and west seeking food,
they never complained.
That year,
there was a great harvest across the land.
Those who had scattered all returned to their villages.
A dǒu of rice cost only three or four coins.
Throughout the year, only twenty-nine people were sentenced to death.
From the east reaching the sea,
to the south reaching the Wǔlǐng mountains,
outer doors were left unbolted,
travelers did not need to carry provisions,
for they could obtain what they needed along the roads.
The Emperor said to Zhǎngsūn Wújì:
"At the beginning of the Zhēnguàn era,
those who submitted memorials all said: 'The ruler should wield authority alone,
and not delegate it to his ministers.'
They also said: 'You should display military might,
and campaign against the barbarians of the four directions.'
Only Wèi Zhēng advised me to 'lay down arms and cultivate culture,
for when China is at peace,
the barbarians of the four directions will submit of themselves.'
I followed his advice.
Now, Xiélì has been captured,
his chieftains all serve as guards with swords at their belts,
and their tribes all wear Chinese dress.
This is due to Zhēng's efforts.
I only regret that Féng Déyí cannot see this!"
Féng Déyí died in the first year.
"The defeat of the Turks,
and the peace and prosperity within the seas,
are all due to Your Majesty's might and virtue.
What strength have I contributed!"
The Emperor said:
"I was able to employ you,
and you were able to fulfill your duties.
So how could the achievement be mine alone!"
34. Fáng Xuánlíng reported,
"Inspecting the armory and weapons in the storehouses,
they far surpass those of the Suí era."
The Emperor said:
"Weapons and military preparedness
are indeed indispensable;
but did Emperor Yáng of Suí lack weapons!
Yet he ultimately lost the empire.
If you gentlemen exert your efforts
to bring peace and stability to the people,
that is my armor and weapons."
35. The Emperor said to the Director of the Palace Library, Xiāo Jǐng:
"In the Suí era, did you often see the Empress?"
The Empress Xiāo of Emperor Yáng of Suí
was Jǐng's sister,
hence the Emperor asked about this.
Shù (數),
read as suǒ jiǎo fān (所角翻).
"Her own children could not even see her;
who am I,
that I could see her!"
Wèi Zhēng said:
"I have heard that Emperor Yáng did not trust Prince Qí,
and constantly had palace envoys observe him.
Emperor Yáng's suspicion and guarding against Prince Qí Jiǎn is briefly recorded in the Suí annals.
Héng (恆),
read as hù dēng fān (戶登翻).
Shǐ (使),
read as shū lì fān (疏吏翻).
If he heard he was happy about something accomplished,
he would say, 'What affair is he plotting that he succeeds and is happy!'
If he heard he was worried and distressed,
he would say, 'He has other intentions, that is why.'
Even between father and son it was like this,
let alone with others!"
The Emperor laughed and said:
"Now, my regard for Yáng Zhèngdào
is far better than Emperor Yáng's regard for Prince Qí."
Jǐng
was the elder brother of Xiāo Yǔ.
36. Sìyèhù Kèhán of the Western Turks, being the son of the former Kèhán,
was supported by the masses,
and many chieftains from Mòhèduō Kèhán's tribe defected to him.
Sìyèhù led troops to attack Mòhèduō.
Mòhèduō's troops were defeated,
and he fled to the Jīnshān mountains,

The various tribes together recommended Sìyèhù as the Great Kèhán.
The conflict between Sìyèhù and Mòhèduō
began in the second year of the previous reign.
1. In spring,

The Táng system: All tribute envoys from the realm
arrived at the capital on the 25th day of the tenth month.

Cháo,
read as zhí yáo fān.
Shǐ,

Earlier,

"Hàodé's illness is evident;
zhēng,
means clear,
evidence,
verification.
Bèi,
read as pí yì fān;
same below.
The Investigating Censor Quán Wànjì impeached and memorialized:

guàn,

Zhì,
read as zhí zhī fān.
Hé,

Xiàng,

Quán Wànjì and the Attendant Censor Lǐ Rénfā,

causing many senior ministers to be repeatedly reprimanded and angered.
Wèi Zhēng remonstrated, saying:
"Wànjì and others are petty men,
who do not understand the greater principles.
They consider exposure as uprightness,
and slander as loyalty.
Your Majesty is not unaware of their incompetence,
but you employ them because they are without fear or taboo,
wishing to use them to caution and spur the various ministers.
However, Wànjì and others, relying on favor and wielding power,
carry out their treacherous schemes.
All those they impeach and attack
are not guilty.
Even if Your Majesty cannot promote the good to encourage proper customs,
how can you be intimate with the treacherous to harm yourself!"
The Emperor was silent,
and bestowed five hundred bolts of silk.
After some time,
the treacherous conduct of Wànjì and others was exposed by itself,

This sets the background for the Emperor's distancing from Quán Wànjì.
13 In the ninth month,
the Emperor renovated the Rénshòu Palace,
and renamed it the Jiǔchéng Palace.
He also planned to renovate the Luòyáng Palace.
The Minister of Revenue Dài Zhòu submitted a memorial remonstrating,
stating that
"the chaos and separation have just subsided,

If construction projects continue without cease,
the public and private labor and expense
will likely be unbearable!"
The Emperor praised him, saying:
"Dài Zhòu is not a relative of mine,

and speaks without reservation what he knows,
I therefore reward him with office and rank."
After some time,

Jìn dug ponds and built hills,
with extravagant carvings and decorations.
The Emperor
immediately ordered them destroyed,
and dismissed Jìn from his post.
In the winter of the 14th year,
in the tenth month,
on the day Bǐngwǔ,
the Emperor was chasing rabbits in the rear garden.
The garden walls of Táng Dynasty Cháng'ān were vast and extensive,
encompassing the old city of Hàn Dynasty Cháng'ān within them.
Chéng Dàchāng said: North of the Táng Dynasty's Tàijí Palace was the inner garden,
and beyond that was the forbidden garden;
the Tàijí Palace was located in the northern part of the capital city,
the inner garden was further north of the palace,
and the forbidden garden was even north of the inner garden.
The forbidden garden was extensive,
its western side completely enclosing the capital city of the Hàn Dynasty,
reaching east to the Bà River,
while its southwestern sides
extended out in front of the Tàijí Palace,
aligning with the Chéngtiān Gate;
west of the Chéngtiān Gate,
three gates stood in a row,
all belonging to the forbidden garden:
they were called Guānghuà,
Fānglín,
and Jǐngyào.
The "Six Codes" states: The forbidden garden is north of the imperial palace's inner city,
bordering the Wèi River to the north,
reaching the Chǎn River to the east,
and extending to the capital city to the west,
with a circumference of 120 lǐ.
"Heaven has ordained Your Majesty as the parent of the Huáxià and foreign peoples,
how can you take yourself lightly!"
The Emperor was about to chase deer,
when Sīlì removed his headscarf and untied his belt,
knelt down and firmly remonstrated,
causing the Emperor to stop.
At the beginning of the 15th year,
the Emperor ordered his ministers to discuss the feudal system.
Wèi Zhēng argued:
"If feudal lords are established,
then the ministers and officials will all rely on salaries and emoluments,
inevitably leading to heavy taxation.
Moreover,
the tax revenue from the capital region is not abundant,
and it relies on areas outside the capital;
if all these are allocated as feudal territories,
state expenditures will suddenly fall short.
Furthermore,
Yān, Qín, Zhào, and Dài all border foreign tribes;
if an emergency arises,
calling troops from the interior,
it would be difficult for them to rush to the front."
The Vice Minister of Rites, Lǐ Bǎiyào, argued:
"The length of a dynasty's fortune,
is determined by Heaven's decree.
Yáo and Shùn were great sages,
yet they could not secure it forever;
Hàn and Wèi were of humble origins,
yet they could not repel it.
Now, if the descendants of meritorious officials and relatives all have people and territories,
after a change of generations,
they will become arrogant, indulgent, and unrestrained,
engaging in warfare and mutual destruction,
causing even greater harm to the people.
It would be better to have prefects and magistrates take turns governing."
The Vice Minister of the Secretariat, Yán Shīgǔ, argued:
"It would be better to enfeoff the
sons as kings,
not allowing them to become too powerful,
interspersed with prefectures and counties,
living in a mixed and staggered arrangement,
mutually supporting each other,
each guarding their own borders,
cooperating with one heart,
sufficient to support the capital;
appoint officials for them,
all selected by the central departments,
beyond the laws and decrees,
they must not abuse authority or impose punishments arbitrarily,
and the rituals of court tribute,
should be clearly regulated.
Once this system is established,
it will be secure for ten thousand generations."
In the eleventh month,
an edict was issued:
"The imperial clan and meritorious officials,
should be appointed to guard the frontier regions,
bequeathing this to their descendants.
Unless there is a major offense,
they shall not be deposed or dismissed.
The relevant departments shall clearly formulate regulations,
determine the ranks, and report them."
On the day Dīngsì,
Línyì presented a multicolored parrot.
Parrots,
are birds that can speak.
Wàn Zhèn's "Nánzhōu Zhì" says: There are three types of parrots: one white,
one green,
and one multicolored.
South of Jiāozhōu,
all countries have them.
The white and multicolored ones,
are especially intelligent.
Lù Diàn's "Píyǎ": Parrots have human-like tongues and can speak,
with green feathers and red beaks.
The green ones are the common variety.
According to old accounts,
most birds have toes,
three in front and one behind,
and their lower eyelids blink upward;
only parrots have four toes evenly divided,
with both eyelids moving,
like human eyes.
Eyelid,
pronounced lì jiǎn fān,
refers to the eyelid.
Blink,
pronounced cè qià fān,
means the movement of the eyes.
On the day Dīngmǎo,
Xīnluó presented two beautiful women;

The Emperor happily said:
"Even the parrot from Línyì could speak of suffering from the cold,
longing to return to its country,
how much more these two women, far from their relatives!"
Both the parrot
and the women were entrusted to the envoys and sent back.
The state of Wō sent an envoy to present tribute,
and the Emperor dispatched Gāo Biǎorén, the prefect of Xīnzhōu, bearing the imperial insignia to pacify them;
Biǎorén disputed etiquette with their king,

On the day Bǐngzǐ,
the Emperor sacrificed at the Yuánqiū altar.
In the twelfth month,
Lǐ Shìnán, a secretary of the Court of Imperial Stud, opened up sixteen prefectures and forty-seven counties in the territory of the Dǎngxiàng.
The Emperor said to his attending ministers:
"I consider the death penalty to be extremely grave,
therefore I ordered three reviews of petitions,
hoping to consider the matter thoroughly.
Yet the officials completed the three reviews
in a short moment.
Moreover,
in ancient times when people were executed,
the ruler would cease music and reduce meals.
Although I do not have regularly scheduled music in my court,
I often refrain from drinking wine and eating meat on such occasions,
but there is no established decree.
Also,
when various departments decide on legal cases,
they only rely on the letter of the law;
even if the circumstances are pitiable,
they dare not violate the law.
How can there be no injustices among them!"
On the day Dīnghài,
a decree was issued:
"For those deciding on death sentences,
within two days, five reviews of petitions shall be conducted;
for those in the various prefectures, three reviews shall be conducted.
On the day of execution,
the imperial kitchen shall not serve wine or meat,
and the Inner Music Academy and the Court of Imperial Sacrifices shall not perform music.
During the Wǔdé era,
the Inner Music Academy was established within the palace,
with inner music doctors.
The Court of Imperial Sacrifices had the Office of Music and the Office of Drums and Winds.
For those who, according to the law, deserve death but whose circumstances are pitiable,
a record of the case shall be submitted for review."
As a result, many lives were spared.
For the five reviews of petitions,
one or two days before the decision,
and on the day of the decision, three more reviews were conducted;
only for those guilty of 'è nì' was one review conducted.
The Suí Dynasty established the ten abominations,
the fourth being 'è nì',
referring to beating or plotting to kill grandparents or parents,
or killing uncles, aunts, brothers, children, maternal grandparents, husbands, or the grandparents or parents of the husband;
the Táng Dynasty followed this.
On the day Jǐhài,
the assembly envoy, Lìzhōu Commander Wǔ Shìyuè, and others again submitted a memorial requesting the fēngshàn ceremony,
but it was not permitted.
On the day Rényín,

on the day Wùshēn,
he returned to the palace.
The Emperor said to his ministers:
"I often fear that I might arbitrarily bestow rewards or punishments due to joy or anger,
therefore I wish for you to remonstrate to the utmost.
You should also accept others' remonstrance,
and not dislike others for opposing
what you desire.
If you cannot accept remonstrance yourselves,
how can you remonstrate with others?"
24. The state of Kāng sought to submit and become an internal dependency.
The state of Kāng,
was the state of Kāngjū of the Hàn dynasty,
also called Sàmòjiān,
or Sàmòjiān,
and during the Northern Wèi dynasty it was called Xīwànjīn.

see the previous scroll, fourth year.
Duōlù Kèhán and his brothers contended for the state.
This event is recorded in the same place.
He led troops in a surprise attack and defeated the Western Tujue,
seizing nearly half of their territory,

He proclaimed himself
Dábù Kèhán.
Shè'ěr then said to the various tribes:
"The ones who first caused chaos and destroyed our state

I should avenge the former Kèhán and attack and annihilate them."
The various tribes all advised against it, saying:

Shè'ěr did not listen.
He attacked the Xuēyántuó north of the desert,
