At that time, Diélìshī Kèhán ascended to power;
see the previous scroll, eighth year.
Many abandoned Shè'ěr and fled back.
They fled back to Diélìshī.
Shè'ěr suffered a major defeat,
fled and sought protection in Gāochāng.
Of his original troops, only a little over ten thousand households remained.
Fearing further pressure from the Western Tujue,
he then led his followers to surrender.
An imperial decree settled his tribe north of Língzhōu,

He married the Emperor's younger sister, Princess Nányáng Zhǎng.
Both the New and Old Histories record it as
"Princess Héngyáng Zhǎng".
Yáng zhǎng,

According to Táng regulations,

if the rank was low but the assigned position was high, it was called "shǒu";
if the rank was high but the assigned position was low, it was called "xíng".
Here, Zhāng Liàng acted as Dūdū,

Sons can still be had again,

Thereupon, he wept and sobbed uncontrollably.
The Emperor's weeping and sobbing—
was it perhaps thinking of the matters concerning Jiànchéng and Yuánjí?

Tèjìn

8 Empress Zhǎngsūn was by nature benevolent, filial, frugal, and simple.
She loved reading,
and often calmly discussed ancient matters with the Emperor,
thereby offering criticism and suggestions,
which provided great benefit.
Sometimes the Emperor would reprimand or become angry with palace women without just cause,
and the Empress would also feign anger,
requesting to personally interrogate them,
then ordering them imprisoned.
She would wait until the Emperor's anger subsided,
and then slowly plead their case.
Because of this, within the palace,
punishments were never unjust or excessive.
Princess Yùzhāng lost her mother early,
and the Empress took her in and raised her,
showing her more maternal love than to her own children.
Princess Yùzhāng
was the Emperor's daughter,
and later married down to Táng Yìshí.

read yú wèi.
Kǔn,
read kǔ běn.
Sàng,
read xī làng.
The Empress personally cared for and attended to her,
even giving up her own medicine and meals to provide for her.

In instructing her sons,
she always prioritized humility and frugality.
The Crown Prince's wet nurse, Lady Suì'ān
According to Táng regulations,

Mùzhōu

The Emperor fell ill,

The Empress attended upon him,

She often carried poison tied to her sash,

"If the worst should happen,

The Empress had long suffered from a respiratory ailment.
The previous year, when she accompanied the Emperor on a visit to the Jiǔchéng Palace,
Chái Shào and others reported a rebellion in the middle of the night.
The Emperor donned his armor and went out of the hall to inquire about the situation.
The Empress, despite her illness, followed him.
Those around her tried to stop her,
but the Empress said:
"Since His Majesty is alarmed,
how could I remain at ease in my heart!"
From then on, her illness grew much worse.
The Crown Prince said to the Empress:
"Medicine has been exhausted, yet your illness does not heal.
I request to petition for a pardon of criminals and for allowing people to enter the monastic life,
hoping perhaps to obtain blessings from the unseen realm."
The Empress said:
"Life and death are matters of fate,
not something that wisdom or strength can alter.
If doing good brings fortune,
then I have done no evil;
if it is not so,
what benefit is there in vainly seeking it!
Granting amnesty is a major affair of state,
and cannot be done frequently.
The teachings of Daoism and Buddhism are heterodox doctrines,
which erode the state and harm the people.
These are things His Majesty has never done,
so how could I, a mere woman, cause him to do what he does not do!
If you must carry out your words,
I would rather die quickly!"
The Crown Prince did not dare to submit the petition,
but privately spoke of it to Fáng Xuánlíng.
Xuánlíng reported it to the Emperor,
who was grieved,
and wished to issue an amnesty for her sake.
The Empress firmly stopped him.
When her illness became critical,
she took leave of the Emperor.
At that time, Fáng Xuánlíng had been dismissed and returned to his residence.
The Empress said to the Emperor:
"Xuánlíng has served Your Majesty for a long time,
cautious and discreet,
never divulging
extraordinary plans or secret strategies.
If there is no major fault,
I hope you will not cast him aside.
As for my own clan,
they have attained rank and emolument through distant kinship ties.
The Hànshū says: Not having the closeness of jiāfú.

They are prone to perilous downfall.

Zhāolíng

Shìjí wanted to open the camp gate to admit them;

The messenger said:

Zhìxuán said:
"In the middle of the night, it is impossible to distinguish authenticity."
He detained the messenger until dawn.
The Emperor heard of it and sighed, saying:
"A true general!"
The Emperor again composed a text and had it engraved on stone,
stating:
"The Empress was frugal and thrifty,
and left instructions for a simple burial,
believing that 'the hearts of thieves and robbers
only seek treasures and valuables.
Since there are no treasures or valuables,
what else could they seek?'
My original intention
is also the same.
A ruler regards the world as his home;
why must possessions be placed in the tomb
to be considered his own?
Now, using Jiǔzōng Mountain as the tomb,
the labor of quarrying stone involved only a little over a hundred workers,
and was completed in a few dozen days.
No gold or jade is stored,
and the figures of people, horses, and utensils
are all made of clay and wood,
merely taking their forms.
This should hopefully make treacherous thieves lose interest,
so that both the living and the dead are free from burdens.
It should serve as a model for generations of descendants to follow."
The Emperor, unable to stop thinking of the Empress,
built a multi-story tower in the imperial garden
to gaze toward Zhāolíng.
Once, he invited Wèi Zhēng to ascend it with him
and asked him to look.
Wèi Zhēng stared intently and said:
"Your servant is dim-sighted
and cannot see it."
The Emperor pointed it out to him,
and Wèi Zhēng said:
"Your servant thought Your Majesty was looking toward Xiànlíng.
As for Zhāolíng,
your servant indeed sees it."
The Emperor wept

Shǐ,

"Since the Central Kingdom is at peace,

12 Wèi Wáng Tài was favored by the Emperor,
and someone said that many officials of the third rank and above looked down on Wèi Wáng.
The Emperor was angry,
summoned those of the third rank and above,
and with a stern face reproached them, saying:
"During the time of Suí Wéndì,
officials of the first rank and below were all trampled upon by the various princes.
Were they not the sons of the Son of Heaven?
I merely do not allow my sons to act recklessly,
but I hear that those of the third rank and above all look down on them.
If I were to indulge them,
could they not humiliate you all?"
Fáng Xuánlíng and the others were all terrified, sweating, and bowed in apology.
Only Wèi Zhēng maintained a solemn expression and said:
"Your servant privately believes that among the current ministers,
none would dare to look down on Wèi Wáng.
In terms of propriety,
ministers and sons are one.
In the Spring and Autumn period,
even low-ranking royal envoys,
were ranked above the feudal lords.
Spring and Autumn Annals: In the seventh year of Duke Xī,

the Duke met with the royal envoy, the Marquis of Qí, the Duke of Sòng, the Marquis of Wèi, the Baron of Xǔ, the Earl of Cáo, the heir of Chén, Guǎn, and the heir of Zhèng, Huá, to form an alliance at Táo.
The Gōngyáng Commentary says: What is a royal envoy?
A person of low rank.
Why is he ranked above the feudal lords?
Because of the former king's command.
Your Majesty honors and treats them with propriety.
If the laws and order were greatly corrupted,
that would be a different matter;
but with a sage and enlightened ruler above,
Wèi Wáng certainly has no reason to humiliate the ministers.
Suí Wéndì indulged his sons,
allowing them to frequently act without propriety,
and in the end, they were all exterminated.
Is that worthy of emulation?"
The Emperor, pleased, said:
"Words that reach the heart of reason
are impossible not to accept.
I, due to private affection, forgot public righteousness.
In my earlier anger,
I thought I was unquestionably right,
but upon hearing Wèi Zhēng's words,
I now realize I was in the wrong.
How can a ruler speak so easily!"
13 The Emperor said:
"Laws and decrees must not be changed frequently.
Frequent changes lead to confusion,
and officials cannot remember them all;
moreover, discrepancies between earlier and later versions
allow clerks to engage in malpractice.
From now on, when changing laws,
all should be carried out with thorough consideration and caution."
14 Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ Quán Wànjì submitted a memorial, saying:
"In Xuān and Ráo prefectures, silver is abundantly produced.
If mined,
it could yield several million strings of coins annually."
The Emperor said:
"I am honored to be the Son of Heaven,
and what I lack is not wealth,
but regret that I have not heard good advice to benefit the people.
Rather than gaining several million strings of coins,
how much better to obtain one worthy talent!
You have never recommended a single worthy person or dismissed a single incompetent one,
yet you focus solely on the profits from silver taxation.
In ancient times, Yáo and Shùn cast jade discs into the mountains
and threw pearls into the valleys.
Lù Jiǎ's New Discourses says: Sages do not value pearls and jade but treasure their own virtue.
Therefore, Shùn discarded gold on the rugged mountains
and cast away pearls and jade into the rivers of the Five Lakes,
to curb licentious and evil desires.
This matter is recorded in the fifty-seventh volume, under the first year of the Guānghé era of Hàn Língdì.
Cáng,
read as cú làng fān.

According to the Tang system: the Zhéchōng Dūwèi of an Upper Prefecture held a rank of Zhèng Sì Pǐn Shàng,
of a Middle Prefecture Zhèng Sì Pǐn Xià,

The Guǒyì Dūwèi of an Upper Prefecture held a rank of Cóng Wǔ Pǐn Xià,
of a Middle Prefecture Zhèng Liù Pǐn Shàng,

Gēng,
pronounced gōng héng fān.
Jiàng,

Six hundred and thirty-four prefectural military offices were established,
with two hundred and sixty-one within the Guān Nèi region,
all subordinate to the various Imperial Guards and the Six Guards of the Eastern Palace.
The Six Guards of the Eastern Palace were: the Left and Right Guard Commandants,
analogous to the Left and Right Guard Generals of the Imperial Court;
the Left and Right Zōng Guard Commandants,
analogous to the Left and Right Lǐngjūn Generals;
the Left and Right Jiānmén Commandants,
analogous to the Left and Right Jiānmén Generals.
Later, the Left and Right Yúhòu Commandants were also established,
analogous to the Left and Right Jīnyú Generals;
and the Left and Right Nèi Commandants,
analogous to the Left and Right Qiānniú Generals.
Collectively, they were called the Ten Commandants.
A Middle Prefecture had one thousand men,
a Lower Prefecture eight hundred men.
Three hundred men formed a Tuán,
with a Xiàowèi in command;
fifty men formed a Duì,
with a Zhèng in command;
ten men formed a Huǒ,
with a Zhǎng in command.
Each man's weapons, armor, provisions, and equipment were of specified quantities,
all prepared by himself,
stored in the armory,
and issued when on campaign.
Men became soldiers at age twenty,
and were exempted at sixty.
Those skilled in riding and archery became Yuèqí,
meaning Yuèqí,
refers to their strength and bravery enabling them to surpass others.
Qí,
pronounced qí jì fān.
Every year in the last month of winter,
the Zhéchōng Dūwèi led his subordinates in military training,
and for those entitled to horses, the government provided funds for their purchase.
Those eligible for guard duty served in rotations,
with the Ministry of War assigning rotations based on distance,
distant areas having fewer rotations, nearby areas more frequent,
each rotation lasting one month.
According to the regulations of the time,
five hundred lǐ entailed five rotations,
one thousand lǐ seven rotations,
one thousand five hundred lǐ eight rotations,
two thousand lǐ ten rotations,
and beyond two thousand lǐ twelve rotations.
If selected for extended guard duty,
five hundred lǐ entailed seven rotations,
one thousand lǐ eight rotations,
two thousand lǐ ten rotations,
and beyond two thousand lǐ twelve rotations.
Shàng,
pronounced shí zhǎng fān.
Shù,
pronounced suǒ jiǎo fān.
Gēng,
pronounced gōng héng fān.
1 In spring,
the first month,
Kuài Prince Lǐ Yuányù was transferred to become Dèng Prince,
and Qiáo Prince Lǐ Yuánmíng became Shū Prince.
2 On Xīnmǎo day,
Wú Prince Lǐ Kè was appointed Governor of Ānzhōu,
Jìn Prince Lǐ Zhì Governor of Bìngzhōu,
and Jì Prince Lǐ Shèn Governor of Qínzhōu.
As they were about to depart for their posts,
the Emperor bestowed upon them a written admonition, saying:
"I wished to give you precious playthings,
but feared it would only increase your arrogance and extravagance.
It is better that you receive these words."
3 The Emperor constructed the Fēishān Palace.
Observing that the following year the Míngdé Palace and the Xuánpǔ Garden of the Fēishān Palace were dismantled to provide for the Luòyáng people whose homes were destroyed by flood,
we know the Fēishān Palace was also in Luòyáng.
On Gēngzǐ day,
the Tèjìn Wèi Zhēng submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Emperor Yáng relied on his wealth and power,
gave no thought to future calamities,
indulged in extreme luxury and desires,
reduced the common people to destitution,
until he himself perished at the hands of others,
and the state became ruins.
Your Majesty, having restored order from chaos,
should reflect on why Suí was lost,
and why we were gained,
dismantle the lofty halls,
and be content with humble palaces;
if you expand upon the existing foundations,
follow the old ways and add ornamentation,
this would be replacing chaos with chaos,
disaster and misfortune are sure to follow,
hard to gain, easy to lose —
can you not bear this in mind!"
4 Fáng Xuánlíng and others, having previously received the imperial decree to establish laws and statutes,
proposed:
"Under the old law,
if brothers lived separately,
the protection of rank did not extend to each other,
yet in cases of plotting rebellion, all were executed by association;
while grandfathers and grandsons enjoyed such protection,
and were only sentenced to exile.
Considering ritual and sentiment,
this is deeply inappropriate.
Now, in establishing the law,
grandfathers, grandsons, and brothers implicated by association shall all be sentenced to penal servitude."
The Emperor approved.
From then on, compared to ancient times, capital punishment
was reduced by more than half,
and the empire praised and relied on this.
Fáng Xuánlíng and others established five hundred articles of law,
setting twenty grades of punishment,
with five grades of flogging,
from ten to fifty strokes.
Five grades of caning,
from sixty to one hundred strokes.
Five grades of penal servitude,
from one to three years.
Three grades of exile,
from one thousand to three thousand lǐ.
Two grades of capital punishment,
strangulation and decapitation.
Seventy-one articles reduced exile to penal servitude,
and in general, eliminating complexities and removing harmful provisions,
changing severe punishments to lighter ones,
were too numerous to record.
They also established over one thousand five hundred and ninety articles of statutes.
Under the old Wǔdé system,
the Sacrificial Ceremony at the Imperial Academy
honored Zhōu Gōng as the First Sage,
with Confucius receiving secondary sacrifice;
Fáng Xuánlíng and others proposed to cease sacrificing to Zhōu Gōng,
making Confucius the First Sage,
with Yán Huí receiving secondary sacrifice.
They also edited the decrees and regulations since Wǔdé,
retaining seven hundred articles,
and at this time promulgated them.
They also standardized the cangue, fetters, iron collar, chain, cane, and flogging rod,
all with prescribed lengths and widths.
The device for restraining the neck was called the cangue,
for restraining the hands, fetters.
The iron collar,
was an iron band for confinement.
The chain,
was an iron chain for shackling.
The cane,
was three chǐ five cùn long,
with knots shaved off.
The interrogation cane,
had a large end diameter of three fēn two lí,
small end two fēn two lí.
The ordinary cane,
large end two fēn seven lí,
small end one fēn seven lí.
The flogging rod,
large end two fēn,
small end one fēn and a half.
Niǔ,
pronounced nǚ jiǔ fān.
Since the death of Zhāng Yùngǔ,
see the fifth year of the previous scroll.
there were instances of wrongful convictions,
yet no punishment was imposed.
The Emperor once asked the Chief Minister of the Court of Judicial Review Liú Déwēi:
"Recently, the net of punishment has become somewhat tighter,
why is that?"
He replied:
"This lies with the sovereign,
not with his subjects.
If the ruler favors leniency, then it is lenient;
if he favors severity, then it is severe.
The legal text states: wrongful conviction reduces punishment by three grades,
wrongful acquittal reduces punishment by five grades.
Now, wrongful conviction of the innocent goes unpunished,
while wrongful acquittal incurs severe penalty,
therefore officials each seek to protect themselves,
vying to apply the law harshly,
not because they are instructed to do so,
but out of fear of punishment.
If Your Majesty would judge all cases strictly according to the law,
this trend would immediately change."
The Emperor was pleased,
and followed his advice.
From then on, judicial decisions were fair and just.
5 The Emperor, considering that in the Han dynasty imperial tombs were prepared in advance,
thus sparing later generations hasty labor and expense,
and also being intent on frugal burial,
feared his descendants might follow contemporary customs in extravagance and waste.
In the second month,
on the day Dīngsì,
he personally established his final instructions:
to use the mountain as the tomb mound,
with space only for the coffin.
6 On the day Jiǎzǐ,

judging their abundance or frugality to decide rewards or punishments,
(see the twelfth year of the Dàyè era, scroll 183.)

The Emperor, startled, said:

now such provisions are supplied.

8 In the third month,
on the first day, Bǐngxū,

9 On the day Gēngzǐ,
the Emperor held a banquet at the Western Park of the Luòyáng Palace,
boating on the Jīcuì Pond.
(The Luòyáng Western Park
extended north to Běimáng,

"Emperor Yáng of Suí built this palace and park,

"Shù"
likely should be
"Kǎi".)

on the day Bǐngwǔ,
an edict was issued to implement them.
11 The Emperor appointed Wáng Guī, Minister of Rites, as the Preceptor to Prince Tài of Wèi.
(In the early Táng, following the systems of Wèi and Jìn,

"You should serve Guī as you would serve me."
Whenever Tài saw Guī,
he would bow first,

Guī's son, Jìngzhí, married Nánpíng Princess.
The Princess

When princesses married down,

12 Ministers again requested the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices.
(In the fifth year,
the assembled envoys from various prefectures requested the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices;
in the sixth year,
civil and military officials requested them;
now the multitude of ministers again requested them.
Again,
fú yòu fān.)
Fáng Xuánlíng deliberated and decided on the matter.
13 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day Jǐmǎo,
Wèi Zhēng submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Many rulers are good at beginnings,
but few can bring things to a successful conclusion.
Is it because gaining power is easy but maintaining it is difficult?
It is because in times of deep concern, they exert sincerity and defer to those below,
but in comfort and ease, they become arrogant and self-indulgent, looking down on others.
Deferring to those below unites even the Hú and Yuè;
looking down on others alienates even the six closest relatives.
Even if one intimidates them with威严 and anger,
they will only obey in appearance while their hearts remain unconvinced.
If a ruler, upon seeing something desirable, can think of knowing contentment;
when about to undertake construction, can think of knowing when to stop;
when in a high and perilous position, can think of humility and lowering oneself;
when facing fullness and abundance, can think of restraint and reduction;
when encountering pleasure and enjoyment, can think of moderation;
when in peace and comfort, can think of future calamity;
to prevent obstruction and blindness, can think of broadening acceptance;
to hate slander and evil, can think of rectifying oneself;
when bestowing ranks and rewards, can think of excess due to favor;
when applying punishments and penalties, can think of abuse due to anger;
(Excess,
exceeding proper measure;
abuse,
inappropriate increase.)
and moreover selects the worthy and employs the capable,
then indeed one can govern through non-action,
so why must one toil spirit and weary body to take on the responsibilities of all the offices!"

1 In the fifth month,

Wèi Zhēng submitted a memorial,

"Your Majesty's desire for goodness is not as strong as in former times,
and your readiness to correct faults upon hearing them is somewhat less than in days past.
Reprimands and punishments have accumulated,
and威严 and anger have grown slightly harsher.
Thus I know that 'nobility does not anticipate arrogance,
wealth does not anticipate extravagance'
are not empty words.
(The Shū, Zhōuguān says: 'Position does not anticipate arrogance,
emolument does not anticipate extravagance.'
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary says: 'Nobility does not arrange with arrogance, yet arrogance arrives of itself;
wealth does not arrange with extravagance, yet extravagance arrives of itself.'
Wèi Zhēng quotes this.)
Considering the present situation,
how can it be compared!
Yet Suí, with its wealth and strength, acted and faced danger,
while we, with our scantiness and weakness, remained still and achieved security.
The principle of security and danger
is clearly before our eyes.
In the past, when Suí was not yet in chaos,
it assumed it certainly would not fall into chaos;
when it was not yet destroyed,
it assumed it certainly would not be destroyed.
Therefore, taxes and corvée were endless,
campaigns and expeditions did not cease,
until disaster was about to befall them, and they still were not awake to it.
For reflecting on form, nothing is better than still water;
for reflecting on failure, nothing is better than a perished state.
I sincerely hope you will take Suí as a mirror,
abandon extravagance and follow frugality,
draw close to the loyal and distance the crafty,
and in the present time of peace,
practice the reverence and frugality of former days.
Then you will achieve perfection and utmost excellence,
truly beyond praise.
Gaining power is truly difficult,
but maintaining it is very easy.
Since Your Majesty was able to achieve what is difficult,
how could you be unable to preserve what is easy!"

According to the Tang Liù Diǎn,

The Emperor then followed Wáng Guī's memorial.

2. The Minister of Personnel Gāo Shìlián, the Vice Director of the Chancellery Wéi Tǐng, the Vice Minister of Rites Línghú Défēn, and the Vice Director of the Secretariat Cén Wénběn completed the compilation of the Record of Clans and Families,
and presented it to the Emperor.
Previously,
prominent families from east of the mountains, the Cuī, Lú, Lǐ, and Zhèng clans,
were fond of boasting about their regional prestige.
Although their status had declined over generations,
if other clans wished to form marriage alliances with them,
the Báihǔ Tōng says: Hūn (marriage),
is because the ceremony is performed at dusk (hūn),
hence called hūn.
Yīn (姻),
is because the woman follows (yīn) the husband,
hence called yīn.
A worthy explanation says: The wife's father is called hūn,
the husband's father is called yīn.
some would abandon their own local origins and falsely claim affiliation with famous clans,
or brothers of equal rank would further oppress each other using their wives' clans.
The Emperor detested this,
and ordered Gāo Shìlián and others to extensively collect genealogical records from across the realm,
verify them against historical texts,
examine their authenticity,
distinguish their generational order,
rank them in order,
commend and promote the loyal and worthy,
demote and remove the treacherous and rebellious,
dividing them into nine grades.
Gāo Shìlián and others ranked Vice Director of the Chancellery Cuī Míngàn as first.
The Emperor said:
"Hàn Gāozǔ, along with Xiāo Hé, Cáo Shēn, Fán Kuài, and Guàn Yīng, all rose from commoners of the alleys and lanes,
yet you gentlemen still revere and admire them today,
considering them heroes and worthies.
How could it be because of hereditary emoluments!
The Gāo clan only held power in the region east of the mountains,
the Liáng and Chén dynasties were secluded south of the Yangtze,
although they had notable figures,
what is there worth mentioning!
Moreover, their descendants' talent and conduct have declined and become shallow,
their offices and ranks have fallen,
yet they still arrogantly pride themselves on their family background,
peddling their lineage like pine and catalpa trees,
relying on connections with the rich and powerful,
abandoning integrity and forgetting shame.
I do not understand why people in the world value them!
Now, those of the third rank and above,
some through virtuous conduct,
some through meritorious service,
some through literary accomplishment,
have attained positions of honor and prominence.
Those old families of a declining age,
what is truly admirable about them!
And when seeking marriage with them,
even if one pays much gold and silk,
one is still looked down upon by them.
I do not understand the reasoning for this!
Jiě (解),
means explanation.
Abandoning reputation and seeking substance,
yet you gentlemen still rank Cuī Míngàn as first,
this is belittling my court's official ranks and yielding to vulgar sentiment."
He then ordered a revision,
basing the ranking solely on the current dynasty's official grades and salaries,
thereupon placing the imperial clan first,
the imperial relatives by marriage second,
and demoting Cuī Míngàn to third.
The order of the nine grades was:
the imperial clan as Upper-Upper,
the imperial relatives by marriage as Upper-Middle,
and Cuī Míngàn as Upper-Lower.
[The record included] one thousand six hundred and fifty-one families,
and was promulgated throughout the realm.

Lǎo (獠),

As no one remonstrated,
he was rewarded.'
This was guiding them to speak out.
Sīhù Liǔ Xióng falsely claimed Suí dynasty official seniority,

refers to official ranks granted by the Suí court.
You accepted Dài Zhòu's remonstrance and stopped.

The matter of Huángfǔ Déshēn is seen in the eighth year of the previous volume.
Shàng,

Lǎo,

the Emperor sent the envoy Féng Déxiá to pacify and console Tǔbō.
Tǔ,
cóng tūn rù shēng.

the Emperor did not grant it.

Lòngzàn then sent troops to attack Tǔyùhún.
Tǔyùhún could not withstand,

On the 16th, Jiǎyín,

Wèi Zhēng said:

The Emperor said:
"Xuánlíng and I together seized the empire,

However, the difficulty of founding an enterprise

Xuánlíng and the others bowed and said:

1. In spring,

The Táng dynasty's ritual for visiting imperial tombs: A temporary palace is set up
ten lǐ from the tomb,
a seat is arranged in the fasting chamber,
a minor station is set up southwest of the path to the tomb,
and a major station is set up southwest of the burial chamber.
The ministers' station is southwest of the major station,
and the station for those in attendance is further southwest,
all facing east.
Civil officials are to the north,
military officials to the south,
and the assembly envoys further south,
all according to the suitability of the land.
When the emperor arrives at the temporary palace,
he proceeds to the fasting chamber,
the tomb overseer presents the jade register for endorsement,
the imperial position is set at the southeastern corner of the tomb,
facing west;
if there are hills or slopes obstructing,
then adjust according to the terrain.
Another position is set southeast of the eastern steps of the burial chamber's hall,
facing west,
with a wine stand placed southeast of the hall's entrance.
Officials, accompanying imperial clan members, and guest envoys take their positions on the left and right of the spirit path.
At the burial chamber, they stand in ordered rows according to direction in front of the major station.
On that day, five kè before dawn,
yellow banners and guards are arrayed at the tomb,
three kè later,
the officials in charge, imperial clan members of the fifth rank and above, relatives of the third rank and above, and guest envoys who should attend take their positions.
The emperor, in plain clothes, rides a horse with a canopy and parasols,
accompanied by mounted attendants,
and proceeds to the minor station.
Exiting the station to his position,
he bows twice,
then bows twice again,
all present also bow twice,
and bow twice again.
After a short while,
the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices requests leave,
the emperor bows twice,
and bows twice again.
The Master of Ceremonies says:
"We take our leave."
All present bow twice.
The emperor returns to the minor station,
mounts his horse and proceeds to the major station,
the guards stand in formation awaiting the procession,
officials, imperial clan members, relatives, and guest envoys line up in order in front of the station.
The emperor walks to the southern gate of the burial chamber,
the guards halt,
and he enters,
via the eastern corridor,
advances to the position southeast of the hall steps,
bows twice,
ascends via the eastern steps,
faces north and bows twice,
bows twice again,
enters to inspect the clothing and artifacts,
wipes the curtains and mats,
presents the offerings of the grand sacrifice,
adding delicacies.
The emperor goes to the wine stand, pours wine,
enters and makes three libations,
then stands facing north.
Two Grand Invocators hold the jade register and stand outside the door,
facing east, kneel and read,
the emperor bows twice,
bows twice again,
then exits the door,
stands facing north directly ahead.
The Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices requests leave,
the emperor bows twice,
exits the eastern gate,
returns to the major station,
and stays overnight at the temporary palace.
On the dīngwèi day
he returned to the palace.

Xuánlíng considered that he had held the position of chief minister for fifteen years,
Left and Right Vice Directors,

Fáng Xuánlíng was appointed as Head of the Secretariat,

he became Left Vice Director,

Shào,

Prince Hán Yuánjiā,

Xuánlíng persistently requested without cease,

and he then assumed his post.
The Crown Prince wished to pay respects to Xuánlíng,

Xuánlíng considered that the Ministry of Revenue was crucial to the interests of the empire,

The Táng system: The Director of the Ministry of Revenue,
was in charge of the empire's taxes and levies,
the appropriateness of the abundance or scarcity of goods,
the advantages of land and water routes,
calculating annual expenditures and allocating resources,
from near to far,

it was related to the major plans of the state.
Xuánlíng examined officials and sought worthy men,

From the mid-Táng period onward,

3. The Minister of Rites, the Duke of Yǒngníng, Wáng Guī, passed away.
Yǒngníng County
belonged to Luòzhōu.
He had been extremely frugal in his personal upkeep.
According to the regulations,
officials of the third rank and above were all to establish family temples.
The Táng system stipulated: Officials of the third rank and above could establish temples,
and offer sacrifices to three generations of ancestors.
He alone performed sacrifices in his private chamber.
He was impeached by the judicial authorities.
The Emperor did not pursue the matter,

4. In the second month,
on the gēngchén day,
Yùchí Jìngdé was appointed as the Military Governor of Fūzhōu.
The Emperor once said to Jìngdé:
"Some people say you are plotting rebellion,
why is that?"
He replied:
"It is true that your subject rebelled!
I followed Your Majesty in campaigns across the land,
personally experienced a hundred battles.
That I survive today
is only due to the remnants of blades and arrows.
Now that the realm is settled,
do you now suspect me of rebellion?"
Thereupon, he removed his garments and threw them to the ground,
revealing his scars and wounds.
The Emperor wept for him,
and said:
"Put your clothes back on.
I do not suspect you.
It is precisely because I do not suspect you that I spoke to you about it.
Why should you harbor resentment?"
The Emperor also once said to Jìngdé:
"I wish to give my daughter to you in marriage,
what do you think?"
Jìngdé kowtowed and declined, saying:
"Although my wife is humble and plain,
we have shared poverty and lowly status for a long time.
Although I am unlearned,
I have heard that the ancients did not abandon their wives upon gaining wealth.
This is not what your subject desires."
The Emperor then desisted.

Grief and resentment accumulate.
This refers to those who were confiscated into the harem due to family members being implicated in crimes.

those who are confiscated government slaves or are originally from lowly and humble backgrounds,

saying, "I endured hardships to serve Your Majesty,

Previously,

Fearing dawn would break,
