was an archery hall.
According to the palace layout of the Tàijí Palace,
the archery hall was located north of the Yìchūn Gate.
A great feast was held for three days.
Subsequently, Zhìshèng was appointed General of the Left Martial Guard and Duke of Jīnchéng Commandery.
The Emperor obtained musicians from Gāochāng,
and assigned them to the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
increasing the nine types of music to ten.
The Tang Liudian states: For grand banquets,
ten types of musical performances are set up in the courtyard,
to represent both Huáxià and foreign traditions.
The first is the banquet music performance,
including dances such as the Jǐngyún Music,
the Qìngshàn Music,
the Pòchén Music,
and the Chéngtiān Music;
the second is the Qīngyuè performance,
the third is the Xīliáng performance,
the fourth is the Tiānzhú performance,
the fifth is the Gāolì performance,
the sixth is the Qiūcí performance,
the seventh is the Ānguó performance,
the eighth is the Shūlè performance,
the ninth is the Gāochāng performance,
and the tenth is the Kāngguó performance.
When Jūnjí conquered Gāochāng,
he privately took its treasures;
the soldiers knew about it,
and competed in looting,
which Jūnjí could not prevent.
He was impeached by the relevant officials,
and an edict ordered Jūnjí and others imprisoned.
The Vice Director of the Secretariat, Cén Wénběn, submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Gāochāng was in chaos,
and Your Majesty ordered Jūnjí and others to campaign and conquer it.
Within less than ten days,
they were all handed over to the Court of Judicial Review.
Although Jūnjí and others brought this upon themselves,
I fear that people throughout the land may suspect that Your Majesty only records their faults and overlooks their merits.
I have heard that when appointing generals and sending out armies,
the primary goal is to defeat the enemy.
If they can defeat the enemy,
even if they are greedy, they should be rewarded;
if they are defeated,
even if they are honest, they should be punished.
Thus, Li Guǎnglì and Chén Tāng of the Han,
Wáng Jùn of the Jin,
and Hán Qínhǔ of the Sui,
all bore guilt and censure,
but their rulers, considering their merits,
all granted them titles and rewards.
For Li Guǎnglì's affair, see Volume 20, the fourth year of the Tàichū era of Emperor Wu of Han.
For Chén Tāng's affair, see Volume 29, the first year of the Jìngníng era of Emperor Yuan of Han.
For Wáng Jùn's affair, see Volume 81, the first year of the Tàikāng era of Emperor Wu of Jin.
For Hán Qínhǔ's affair, see Volume 177, the ninth year of the Kāihuáng era of Emperor Wen of Sui.
Among generals and commanders,
few are honest and cautious,
while many are greedy and seeking.
Therefore, the Military Strategies of Huángshígōng says: 'Employ the wise,
employ the brave,
employ the greedy,
employ the foolish.
Thus, the wise delight in establishing their achievements,
the brave are fond of carrying out their ambitions,
the greedy eagerly pursue their gains,
and the foolish do not consider death.'
I humbly hope that you will record their small contributions,
and forget their major faults,
allowing Jūnjí to return to the ranks of the court,
and be available for service again.
Although he may not be a pure and upright minister,
he can still serve as a greedy and foolish general.
In this way, although Your Majesty bends the law, your virtue will be even more manifest,
and although Jūnjí and others receive pardon, their faults will be even more exposed."
The Emperor then released him.
There was also an accusation that Xuē Wànjūn had engaged in illicit relations with a woman from Gāochāng.
Xuē Wànjūn did not admit to it.
The woman from Gāochāng was brought out from the inner palace and handed over to the Dàlǐ Temple,
to be confronted and cross-examined with Xuē Wànjūn.
Wèi Zhēng remonstrated, saying:
"Your servant has heard, 'A ruler employs his ministers with propriety,
and ministers serve their ruler with loyalty.'
This is recorded in the Analects as Confucius's reply to Duke Dìng of Lǔ.
If the accusation is true, the gain is slight;
if it is false, the loss is grave.
In the past, Duke Mù of Qín gave wine to the men who had stolen his horse.
Duke Mù of Qín lost his horse,
and three hundred men from the wilds of Qíxià found it and ate it together.
The officials pursued and captured them,
intending to punish them according to the law.
The Duke said:
'A gentleman does not harm people because of livestock.
I have heard that eating horse meat without drinking wine
injures a person.'
He then gave them wine to drink.
Later, when Duke Mù attacked Jìn,
those three hundred men, hearing that Duke Mù was besieged by Jìn,
charged with their weapons, vying to die,
to repay the kindness of having been given horse meat.
Thereupon, Duke Mù captured the Marquis of Jìn and returned.
'Drink' [yǐn] is pronounced yìn.
(Annotation on pronunciation).
The Shuōyuàn records: King Zhuāng of Chǔ was bestowing wine upon his assembled ministers.
As dusk fell,
and they were thoroughly intoxicated,
the candles went out.
Someone tugged at the robe of a beautiful woman.
The beautiful woman grasped and broke off the tassel of his cap,
and informed the king, urging him to bring a light to see
who had the broken tassel.
The king said:
'I bestowed wine upon others,
causing them to become drunk and lose propriety.
How can I wish to display a woman's chastity and disgrace a gentleman?'
He then commanded his attendants:
'Today, all who drink with me
must break off their cap tassels to show their joy.'
The assembled ministers all broke off their tassels, and then the lights were brought,
and they enjoyed themselves to the fullest before dispersing.
Later, when Chǔ fought with Jìn,
there was one minister who was always at the forefront,
engaging in five encounters, each time taking heads and repelling the enemy,
ultimately securing victory.
King Zhuāng, finding it strange, inquired,
and it turned out to be the man who had broken his tassel that night, repaying the king.
How can you fail to match these two rulers?"
The emperor immediately released him.
Hóu Jūnjí's horse had a sore on its forehead caused by worms.
The marching commander Zhào Yuánkǎi personally used his finger to touch the pus and smell it.
'Sore' [chuāng] is pronounced zhòng.
(Annotation on pronunciation).
Worms eating [flesh] is called a sore.
'Smell' [xiù]
is pronounced xù.
He was demoted to Prefect of Kuòzhōu.
Yǒngjiā Commandery:
In the ninth year of the Suí dynasty's Kāihuáng era, Chùzhōu was established.
In the thirteenth year, it was renamed Kuòzhōu.
'Impeach' [hé]
is pronounced hài,
also pronounced hé.
After the pacification of Gāochāng,
all the generals immediately received rewards.
The marching commander Āshǐnà Shè'ěr, because there was no imperial decree,
alone did not accept any reward.
Only after a separate decree was issued
did he accept it,
and what he took was only the old, weak, worn-out, and damaged items.
The emperor praised his integrity and caution,
and bestowed upon him a treasured sword obtained from Gāochāng and a thousand bolts of assorted silks.
20 On the Guǐmǎo day,
the emperor hunted at Fánchuān.
Lì Dàoyuán said: Fánchuān was located in the Hàn dynasty's Dù County,
also called Fánxiāng.
When Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn arrived at Yuèyáng,
because Fán Kuài's merit in flooding Fèiqiū was greatest,
he bestowed upon him a fief in this district,
hence the name Fánchuān.
Chéng Dàchāng said: Fánchuān,
also called Yùsù Chuān,
is located thirty-five lǐ south of Wànnián County.
On the Yǐsì day
he returned to the palace.
21 Wèi Zhēng submitted a memorial,
believing that:
"The assembled ministers at court,
those entrusted with pivotal responsibilities,
though their duties are weighty,
the trust in them is not yet profound.
Therefore, some people harbor self-doubt,
and their minds are filled with opportunism.
Your Majesty is lenient in major matters,
but severe regarding minor offenses.
When reproaching in anger on the spot,
it is hard to avoid favoritism and prejudice.
Entrusting great ministers with the overall situation,
and holding minor officials accountable for small matters—
this is the way of governance.
Now, when assigning duties,
you value the great ministers and belittle the minor officials;
but when issues arise,
you trust the minor officials and suspect the great ministers.
Trusting those you belittle,
and suspecting those you value—
if you seek to achieve orderly governance,
how can it be possible!
If you appoint someone to a high office,
yet seek out their minor faults,
then the clerks with their writing brushes,
complying with the imperial will, will make it a common practice,
manipulating the law and playing with statutes,
twisting circumstances to establish their guilt.
If they speak in their own defense,
you will think their hearts are not submitting to the charge;
if they remain silent,
you will think all their alleged offenses are true.
Advancing or retreating, they are in a dilemma,
unable to clarify themselves.
The poem 'Sāng Róu' says: 'Advancing or retreating, they are in a dire strait.'
The commentary states: 'Gǔ' means
exhausted, at an impasse.
Thus, hypocrisy and deceit become the custom!"
The emperor accepted his advice.
22 The emperor said to his attending ministers:
"Although I have pacified the realm,
maintaining it is very difficult."
Wèi Zhēng replied:
"Your servant has heard that winning in battle is easy,
but preserving victory is difficult.
That Your Majesty has spoken these words
is a blessing for the ancestral temple and the altars of state!"
23 The emperor heard that the Right Supervisor of the Heir Apparent, Zhāng Xuánsù, had repeatedly remonstrated and disputed in the Eastern Palace.
He promoted him to Silver青光祿大夫,
and appointed him as Acting Left Supervisor of the Heir Apparent.
The heir apparent once beat a drum in the palace,
and Zhāng Xuánsù knocked on the gate, earnestly remonstrating.
The heir apparent brought out the drum
and smashed it in front of Zhāng Xuánsù.
The heir apparent had not appeared to meet with his officials for a long time.
Zhāng Xuánsù remonstrated, saying:
"The court selects outstanding and worthy men to assist your supreme virtue.
Now, months often pass with movement,
yet you do not see your palace officials.
How can this contribute even the slightest benefit!
Moreover, within the palace there are only women.
I wonder if there is anyone capable like Fán Jī?"
Fán Jī
was a consort of King Zhuāng of Chǔ.
King Zhuāng was fond of hunting.
Fán Jī, for his sake, refused to eat the meat of birds and beasts.
She scorned and laughed at Yúqiūzǐ.
Yúqiūzǐ felt ashamed because of her,
and recommended Sūnshū Áo to become chancellor.
King Zhuāng thereby achieved hegemony.
Xuánsù served as a minor clerk in the Ministry of Justice in his youth.
The Emperor once asked him in front of the court officials:
"What official position did you hold under the Suí dynasty?"
He replied:
"County Lieutenant."
The Emperor asked further:
"What position did you hold before becoming a Lieutenant?"
He replied:
"A position outside the regular ranks."
According to the Suí dynasty's system of viewing ranks,
it was equivalent to the Táng dynasty's selection for positions outside the regular ranks.
Sòng Bái said: Under the Táng system,
one of the Directors of the Bureau of Appointments in the Ministry of Personnel
was in charge of evaluating the ranks, grades, and classes of all civilian officials in the empire.
Another was in charge of minor selections,
also divided into nine grades,
commonly referred to as provisional appointments.
Because they were outside the nine regular streams,
it was called selection for positions outside the regular ranks,
also known as minor selection.
Dù Yòu said: During the Sòng and Qí dynasties, positions outside the regular ranks
began with the record-keepers of the various guards and the clerks of the five departments.
"Which bureau?"
Xuánsù felt ashamed,
and upon leaving the chamber could barely walk,
his face ashen like ashes.
The Remonstrance Official Chǔ Suìliáng submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Only when a ruler treats his ministers with propriety
can they exert their full efforts.
Although Xuánsù comes from a humble background,
Your Majesty values his talent,
promoted him to the third rank,
and entrusted him with assisting the Crown Prince.
How can you then question him in front of the assembled ministers about his humble origins!
To discard past kindness,
and create a moment of shame,
causing him distress in his heart,
how then can you expect him to uphold integrity and die for righteousness!"
The Emperor said:
"I also regret asking that question,
your memorial deeply resonates with my thoughts."
Suìliáng
was the son of Liàng.
Chǔ Liàng
initially served Xuē Jǔ,
during the Wǔdé era,
he was an Academician of the Literary Institute.
Fújiā sometimes recounted his past experiences in public gatherings,
concealing nothing.
The historian remarks that Sūn Fújiā's understanding and magnanimity surpassed Zhāng Xuánsù.
Jiā,
is pronounced like qiú jiā.
Zuò,
is pronounced like cuó wò.
24 The Prefect of Dài Prefecture, Jiǎ Chóng, because someone under his jurisdiction committed one of the Ten Abominations,
The articles of the Ten Abominations are: first, plotting rebellion;
second, plotting great sedition;
third, plotting treason;
fourth, plotting wicked sedition;
fifth, depravity;
sixth, great irreverence;
seventh, unfilial conduct;
eighth, discord;
ninth, unrighteousness;
tenth, incest.
The Emperor said:
"In the past, even the great sages Yáo and Shùn,
noble as Sons of Heaven,
could not transform their own sons;
how much less can Chóng, as a prefect,
alone make all the people under his jurisdiction virtuous!
If he is demoted or dismissed for this,
then prefectures and counties will cover up for each other,
and release criminals.
From now on, if any prefecture has someone committing one of the Ten Abominations,
do not impeach the prefect,
but only order them to clearly investigate and correct,
and punish according to the law,
so as to hopefully eradicate wickedness and evil."
25 The Emperor personally oversaw military training,
and because the troop formations were not orderly,
ordered General Zhāng Shìguì to cane the Colonels and others;
angry that the caning was too light,
he had Shìguì handed over to the officials.
Wèi Zhēng remonstrated, saying:
"The duty of a general,
is to serve as the claws and teeth of the state;
to have them carry out canings,
is already not in accordance with later laws,
how much more to hand them over to officials for light caning!"
The Emperor immediately released him.
26 Those who presented matters often requested the Emperor to personally review memorials and reports,
to prevent obstruction and concealment.
The Emperor asked Wèi Zhēng about this,
who replied:
"These people do not understand the greater principle;
if they must have Your Majesty personally attend to each one,
not only would it be for court affairs,
but also for the affairs of prefectures and counties."
Wáng Chóngwǔ punctuated; Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí proofread.
Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial command.
Later student from Tiāntāi.
The fifteenth year of Zhēnguàn
(Xīnchǒu, 641)
1 Spring,
first month,
on Jiǎxū,
appointed the Tibetan Lù Dōngzàn as General of the Right Guard.
The Emperor praised Lù Dōngzàn for his adept responses,
and gave him the daughter of Duchess Lángyé's granddaughter, Duàn, as his wife;
he declined, saying:
"In my country, I already have a wife,
chosen by my parents,
whom I cannot abandon.
Moreover, the Tsanpo has not yet been granted an audience with the Princess,
how dare a vassal marry first!"
The Emperor esteemed him even more for this,
but wishing to bestow generous favor to win him over,
ultimately did not comply with his wish.
The historian remarks that even barbarians can conduct themselves with propriety,
while the Central Kingdom cannot treat them with propriety.
On Dīngchǒu,
ordered the Minister of Rites, Jiāngxià Prince Dàozōng, to bear the credentials and escort Princess Wénchéng to Tibet.
The Tsanpo was greatly pleased,
and upon meeting Dàozōng,
performed all the rites of a son-in-law.
Admiring the beauty of Chinese clothing and ceremonial guards,
he built a separate city wall and palace for the Princess to reside in,
and wore fine silks himself to meet the Princess.
His people all painted their faces with red ochre,
which the Princess disliked,
so the Tsanpo ordered it prohibited;
he also gradually reformed his suspicious and violent nature,
sending his sons and younger brothers to the Imperial Academy,
to study the Book of Songs and the Book of Documents.
2 On Yǐhài,
the Türk Qaghan Hóulìbì
finally led his tribe across the river.
He received the edict the previous year,
and now finally crossed the river.
Jué,
is pronounced like jiǔ wù.
Bì,
is pronounced like pí bì.
Kě,
follows the entering tone of cóng kān.
Hán,
is pronounced like hán.
Shuài,
is read as shuài.
Dù Yòu said: The old Dìngxiāng City,
is located about three hundred li north of Shuò Prefecture's Mǎyì Commandery.
He had forty thousand able-bodied soldiers,
and ninety thousand horses.
He still submitted a memorial saying:
"I have undeservedly received great favor,
as the leader of the tribe,
I wish for my sons and grandsons to serve as a single watchdog for the state,
guarding and barking at the northern gate.
If the Xueyantuo invade and press upon us,
I request to move
my family inside the Great Wall."
An edict granted his request.
3 The Emperor was about to visit Luòyáng,
and ordered the Crown Prince to oversee state affairs,
leaving the Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, Gāo Shìlián, to assist him.
On Xīnsì,
he traveled as far as the hot springs.
Xīnfēng had the hot springs at Lí Mountain,
and Huá Prefecture had the Hot Springs Garrison.
Hoping the Emperor would be alarmed and stop,
they shot at the traveling palace at night,
with five arrows reaching the sleeping quarters;
all were judged as great sedition.
Of the Ten Abominations,
the second is plotting great sedition.
The commentary states: plotting to destroy the imperial ancestral temples, mountain tombs, and palaces.
The Discussion on the Penal Code says: Those under this article,
violate discipline and oppose order,
act contrary to the Way and rebel against virtue,
their sedition is of the greatest magnitude,
hence it is called great sedition.
To judge as great sedition means,
it is not exactly committing the exact article of great sedition,
but because they violate discipline and oppose order,
they are judged guilty as great sedition.
9 On the Jǐyǒu day,
a comet appeared in the Tàiwēi constellation.
The Grand Astrologer Xuē Yǐ submitted a memorial,
advising against the eastern fēng sacrifice.
On the Xīnhài day,
the Court Diarist Chǔ Suìliáng also spoke against it;
on the Bǐngchén day,
an edict was issued to cancel the fēng and shàn sacrifices.
10 The Crown Prince's Household Manager Yú Zhìníng was mourning the death of his mother,
but he was soon recalled to resume his duties.
According to the Essentials of Government,
during the Wǔdé reign period, a regulation was established
that civil officials mourning the death of a parent
were permitted to leave their posts.
"Recall to office" (qǐfù)
refers to summoning someone from the mourning hut (amidst the rush mat and clods of earth) to resume their official duties.
It is also called "overriding natural affection" (duóqíng).
(The Crown Prince) hindered agricultural work;
he was also fond of the music of Zhèng and Wèi;
Yú Zhìníng remonstrated,
but (the Crown Prince) did not listen.
He further doted on and was intimate with eunuchs,
keeping them constantly by his side.
Yú Zhìníng submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Since the time of Yìyá,
eunuchs who have caused the downfall of states are not few.
Now Your Highness personally favors this group,
allowing them to bully and insult the officials and gentry.
This cannot be allowed to continue."
The Crown Prince conscripted the Stable Attendants and others,
not allowing them to rotate shifts for half a year.
The Imperial Stables Bureau of the Court of the Imperial Stud had a Stables Office;
it had one hundred groom-drivers.
Previously, they took turns serving the two palaces.
According to the Six Statutes,
the Crown Prince's Stables Bureau had a Stables and Pastures Office,
with fifteen wing-drivers,
and thirty carriage drivers.
The New Book records
"Dágēzhī".
The Crown Prince was greatly enraged,
and sent assassins Zhāng Sīzhèng and Hégàn Chéngjī to kill him.
The two men entered his residence,
and saw Yú Zhìníng sleeping on a rush mat with a clod of earth for a pillow.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: Sleeping on a rush mat and using a clod of earth for a pillow
refers to a filial son residing in a mourning hut,
sleeping on a rush mat,
with his head resting on a clod of earth.
"Chǔ" (to reside)
is pronounced chāng lǚ fān.
11 The Shābōluó Yèhù Kèhán of the Western Turks repeatedly sent envoys to present tribute.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Jiǎxū day,
the Emperor ordered the Left Guard General Zhāng Dàshī, bearing the imperial insignia, to proceed to his territory and formally invest him as Kèhán,
bestowing upon him drums and banners.
The Emperor also ordered the envoy to take a large amount of gold and silk,
traveling through various states to purchase fine horses.
Wèi Zhēng remonstrated, saying:
"The Kèhán's position is not yet settled, yet you first purchase horses.
He will certainly think that Your Majesty's true intention is to buy horses,
and that establishing the Kèhán is merely a pretext.
If the Kèhán is established,
his gratitude will surely be shallow;
if he is not established,
his resentment will be profound indeed.
The various states hearing of this
will also look down upon the Central Kingdom.
You may not even obtain the horses through purchase,
and even if you do, it is not honorable.
If you can merely bring peace and stability to them,
then the horses of the various states
will come of their own accord without seeking them."
The Emperor happily desisted.
The Yǐpí Duōlù Kèhán and the Shābōluó Yèhù attacked each other.
Yǐpí Duōlù gradually grew powerful,
and many states of the Western Regions submitted to him.
Not long after,
Yǐpí Duōlù sent the Tǔtún of Shíguó to attack the Shābōluó Yèhù,
captured him,
and killed him.
Tǔtún
is a Turkic official title,
appointed to oversee various states.
The establishment of the Shābōluó Yèhù is recorded in the thirteenth year of the previous scroll.
"Jǐ" (almost)
is pronounced jū qǐ fān.
12 On the Bǐngzǐ day,
the Emperor pointed to the palace hall and said to his attending ministers:
"Governing the empire is like building this hall.
Once the construction is complete,
do not frequently alter or move it.
If you change a single rafter,
or adjust a single tile,
stepping on it will cause it to shake,
and there will surely be damage.
If one admires extraordinary achievements,
changes laws and regulations,
and does not maintain constancy in virtue,
the toil and disturbance will indeed be great."
13 The Emperor sent the Director of the Bureau of Operations, Chén Dàdé, as an envoy to Gāolì.
The Bureau of Operations
is in charge of the maps of the empire and the numbers of city walls, moats, garrison posts, and beacon towers,
distinguishes the distances of the various states and the submission of the Four Barbarians,
and concerning all regions of the five directions,
the establishment and abolition of capitals and cities,
and border disputes,
it investigates and corrects them.
"Shǐ" (to send)
is pronounced shū lì fān.
"Lì" (Gāolì)
is pronounced lì zhī fān.
On the Jǐhài day,
he returned from Gāolì.
When Chén Dàdé first entered their territory,
wishing to know the mountains, rivers, and customs,
wherever he went to a city or town,
he would give patterned silks to the local officials,
saying:
"I have a refined love for mountains and rivers.
If there are scenic spots here,
I wish to view them."
The officials were pleased,
and guided him on tours,
so that he went everywhere.
He often saw people from the Central Kingdom,
who said of themselves:
"My family is in such-and-such commandery.
At the end of the Suí, I joined the army,
was captured in Gāolì.
Gāolì gave me a wandering woman as a wife.
I live intermingled with the Gāolì people,
and it has been nearly half a lifetime."
They then asked about the survival or death of their relatives.
Chén Dàdé deceived them, saying:
"They are all well."
They all wept as they told each other.
Several days later,
people of Suí who saw him and wept
were everywhere in the suburbs and countryside.
Chén Dàdé reported to the Emperor, saying:
"That country, hearing of Gāochāng's destruction,
is greatly afraid.
The diligence of their lodging and reception
exceeded the usual standard."
The Emperor said:
"Gāolì was originally the territory of the Four Commanderies.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn established the four commanderies of Líntún, Zhēnpān, Lèlàng, and Xuāntú.
Gāolì possesses that land.
They will certainly mobilize the entire country to rescue it.
(We would) separately dispatch a naval force from Dōnglái,
proceeding by sea route towards Píngrǎng.
Combining land and naval forces,
capturing it would not be difficult.
However, the prefectures and counties of Shāndōng are still devastated and not yet recovered.
I do not wish to burden them!"
Observing the Emperor's words,
he already had the intention to take Gāolì.
"Zhài" (devastation)
is pronounced zé jiè fān.
14 On the Yǐsì day,
the Emperor said to his attending ministers:
"I have two joys and one fear.
In recent years, the harvests have been abundant,
a peck of grain in Cháng'ān costs only three or four coins—
this is one joy.
The northern barbarians have long been submissive,
and the border regions are without concern—
this is the second joy.
When there is peace and order, arrogance and extravagance easily arise.
Arrogance and extravagance lead immediately to danger and ruin—
this is the one fear."
15 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Xīnmǎo day,
the Emperor held a hunting inspection at Yīquē;
on the Rénchén day,
he proceeded to Sōngyáng.
Yīquē County
was formerly called Xīnchéng.
In the eighteenth year of the Suí Kāihuáng reign, it was renamed;
it has the Yīquē pass.
Sōngyáng County
was formerly called Yǐngyáng.
In the sixth year of the Suí Kāihuáng reign,
it was changed to Wǔlín.
In the eighteenth year,
it was changed to Lúnshì.
In the first year of the Dàyè reign,
it was changed to Sōngyáng;
it has Mount Sōnggāo.
Both belonged to Luò Prefecture.
On the Xīnchǒu day,
he returned to the palace.
16 Li Shìjì, the Chief Administrator of Bīngzhōu, served in the province for sixteen years,
where his orders were carried out and prohibitions observed,
and both the common people and the barbarians were content and submitted to his rule.
The Emperor said:
"Emperor Yáng of Suí exhausted the people,
building the Great Wall to defend against the Turks,
yet in the end it was of no benefit.
I have merely placed Li Shìjì at Jìnyáng, and the border dust remains undisturbed.
He serves as the Great Wall;
is that not magnificent!"
In the eleventh month,
on Gēngshēn,
Shìjì was appointed Minister of War.
17 On Rénshēn,
the imperial carriage returned west to Cháng'ān.
18 Zhēnzhū Kèhán of the Xuēyántuó, hearing that the Emperor was going east to perform the Fēng sacrifice,
said to his subordinates:
"When the Son of Heaven performs the Fēng sacrifice at Mount Tài,
all his troops and horses will accompany him,
and the border regions will certainly be empty.
If we seize Sīmó at this time,
it will be like breaking rotten wood."
He then ordered his son Dàdùshè to mobilize troops from the Tóngluó, Púgǔ, Huíhé, Mòhé, and Xí tribes,
totaling two hundred thousand men,
to cross south of the desert,
encamp at Báidào Chuān,
and occupy Shànyáng Ridge to attack the Turks.
Shànyáng Ridge
is located north of Shànyáng County in Shuòzhōu.
Sīmó led his tribes into the Great Wall,
defended Shuòzhōu,
and sent messengers to report the emergency.
On Guǐyǒu,
the Emperor ordered Zhāng Jiǎn, the Military Governor of Yíngzhōu, to lead his cavalry and troops from the Xī, Xí, and Qìdān tribes to pressure their eastern border;
appointed Li Shìjì, the Minister of War, as Commander of the Shuòzhōu Circuit Expeditionary Army,
leading sixty thousand troops,
with twelve hundred cavalry,
to encamp at Yǔfāng;
appointed Lǐ Dàliàng, the Great General of the Right Guard, as Commander of the Língzhōu Circuit Expeditionary Army,
leading forty thousand troops,
with five thousand cavalry,
to encamp at Língwǔ;
Língwǔ County belongs to Língwǔ Commandery in Língzhōu.
"Leading troops"
is interpreted as Liàng.
He was appointed Commander of the Qìngzhōu Circuit Expeditionary Army,
and advanced from Yúnzhōng;
Lǐ Xíyù, the Military Governor of Liángzhōu, was appointed Commander of the Liángzhōu Circuit Expeditionary Army,
advancing from the west.
When the various generals took their leave,
the Emperor admonished them, saying:
"The Xuēyántuó, relying on their strength and prosperity,
crossed the desert and came south,
traveling several thousand lǐ,
and their horses are already exhausted and thin.
In general, the principle of employing troops is
to advance swiftly when seeing advantage,
and retreat swiftly when facing disadvantage.
The Xuēyántuó failed to catch Sīmó unprepared,
and attack him urgently;
Sīmó entered the Great Wall,
and they still did not retreat swiftly.
I have already ordered Sīmó to burn the autumn grass,
so their provisions are daily exhausted,
and they find nothing in the wilds.
Recently, scouts have come,
reporting that their horses have nearly finished gnawing the branches and bark of the trees.
You should coordinate with Sīmó to form pincers,
and need not engage in swift battle.
Wait until they are about to retreat,
then strike fiercely together,
and you will surely defeat them."
19 In the twelfth month,
on Wùzǐ,
the imperial carriage arrived at the capital.
20 On Jǐhài,
the Xuēyántuó sent an envoy for an audience,
requesting peace and marriage with the Turks.
On Jiǎchén,
Li Shìjì defeated the Xuēyántuó at Nuòzhēn Shuǐ.
Leaving the ancient city of Yúnzhōng,
and traveling northwest about four hundred lǐ,
one reaches Nuòzhēn Shuǐ.
"See"
is interpreted as Xiàn.
"Defeat"
is interpreted as Bàimài.
When the Xuēyántuó attacked Shābōluó of the Western Turks and Āshǐnà Shè'ěr,
they both achieved victory through infantry combat;
and when they were about to invade,
they extensively trained in infantry combat,
forming groups of five men,
with one holding the horses,
and the other four fighting in front.
When victorious, they were given horses to pursue the fleeing enemy.
At this time, Dàdùshè led thirty thousand cavalry to press against the Great Wall,
intending to attack the Turks,
but Sīmó had already fled,
and realizing he could not succeed,
he sent men to climb the wall and curse them.
Just then, Li Shìjì led the Táng troops to arrive,
raising dust that filled the sky.
Dàdùshè became afraid,
and led his forces north from Chìkē Luò in retreat.
Shìjì selected six thousand elite cavalry from his command and the Turks to intercept them via a direct route,
crossed Báidào Chuān,
and caught up with them at Qīngshān.
Dàdùshè retreated for several days,
reaching Nuòzhēn Shuǐ,
where he marshaled his troops to turn and fight,
forming a battle line ten lǐ long.
The Turks first engaged them in battle,
but were unsuccessful,
and retreated.
Dàdùshè pursued them in victory,
encountered the Táng troops,
and the Xuēyántuó shot ten thousand arrows together,
causing many Táng horses to die.
Shìjì ordered his soldiers to all dismount,
grasp long spears,
and charge straight forward.
The Xuēyántuó forces collapsed,
and Deputy Commander Xuē Wànchè led several thousand cavalry to capture those holding the horses.
The Xuēyántuó lost their horses,
and did not know what to do.
The Táng troops attacked fiercely,
beheading over three thousand,
and capturing over fifty thousand.
Dàdùshè escaped with his life,
and Wànchè pursued but could not catch him.
His forces reached north of the desert,
where they encountered heavy snow,
and eight or nine out of ten people and livestock froze to death.
Li Shìjì returned with his army to Dìngxiāng,
and the Sījié tribe of Turks living in Wǔtái rebelled and fled.
Wǔtái
was originally Lǘsī County of Tàiyuán in the Hàn dynasty,
long abandoned,
renamed Lǘyí in the Later Wèi,
and in the early Dàyè era,
renamed Wǔtái,
with Wǔtái Mountain;
it belongs to Dàizhōu.
Just as Shìjì's army was returning,
they attacked from both sides,
and exterminated them all.
On Bǐngzǐ,
the Xuēyántuó envoy took leave to return,
and the Emperor said to him:
"I agreed with you and the Turks to take the great desert as the boundary.
If there are any who invade each other,
I will punish them.
You, relying on your own strength,
crossed the desert to attack the Turks.
Li Shìjì led only several thousand cavalry,
and you were already in such a wretched state!
Go back and tell the Kèhán:
In all actions, weighing advantages and disadvantages,
he should carefully choose what is appropriate."
21 The Emperor asked Wèi Zhēng:
"Why have the court officials lately been particularly silent on matters?"
He replied:
"If Your Majesty humbly accepts and adopts advice,
there will certainly be those who speak.
In general, among ministers, those who sacrifice themselves for the state are few,
while those who love themselves are many.
They fear punishment,
and therefore do not speak."
The Emperor said:
"Indeed.
When ministers remonstrate and offend the imperial will,
they often face punishment and execution,
how is this different from stepping into boiling water or fire, or braving naked blades!
Therefore, Yǔ bowed to good words,
as seen in the 'Three Counsels' of the Book of Documents."
Fáng Xuánlíng and Gāo Shìlián encountered Shàofǔ Shǎojiàn Dòu Désù on the road.
The Qín dynasty established the Shàofǔ,
which was in charge of taxes from mountains and marshes.
The Hàn dynasty had it manage treasures and goods of the inner treasury.
The Liáng dynasty first made it a ministry headed by a Qīng,
the Suí dynasty changed it to a Jiān;
in the Táng dynasty, its head was of the third rank,
and the Shǎojiàn was of the fourth rank.
They were in charge of supplying the work of various artisans and craftsmen.
All the clothing and equipment of the Son of Heaven,
the ceremonial regulations for the hundred officials,
the display of colors and preparation of items—
all were to be supplied by them leading their subordinates.
"What construction is recently underway near the North Gate?"
Désù reported this.
The Emperor was angry
and reprimanded Xuánlíng and the others, saying:
"You gentlemen only need to know about the administrative affairs of the Southern Yá;
what does minor construction at the North Gate
have to do with you!"
The Táng dynasty's main Yá was in the south,
hence it was called the Southern Yá;
the Xuánwǔ Gate was in the north,
and was called the North Gate.
Liú Féng's Shì Shǐ states: Military texts say: The Yá banner
is the essence of the general.
Whenever a Yá is first established,
it must be on a Zhì day.
A Zhì day
is one where the celestial stem's element in the Five Phases
overcomes the earthly branch's element from above.
Also, the Shàngshū states: There are two Mén banners, eight panels each,
colored red.
They are the banners of the general's Yá gate,
carried out ahead to lead the general's procession.
Also, the Huángdì Chūjūn Jué says: The Yá banner
is the essence of the general;
the metal drums and bells
are the spirit of the general.
The Zhōulǐ Sīcháng zhí states: For military campaigns and assemblies, a Jīng gate is set up.
Using Jīng banners to make a gate
is the Qí gate.
Later generations in the military then established the Yámén Jiàng,
and also had Yá troops;
the official in charge of these troops
was named Yāyá.
As for the morning and evening assemblies at government offices,
where military officials paid their respects twice,
these were also called Yá.
Once this term became familiar,
even the Son of Heaven receiving court audiences in the main hall
was called the Zhèngyá.
Wèi Zhēng came forward and said:
"I do not know why Your Majesty is reprimanding Xuánlíng and the others,
nor for what Xuánlíng and the others should apologize!
Xuánlíng and the others are Your Majesty's limbs, ears, and eyes;
how could there be matters, both internal and external, that they should not know about!
If the construction is proper,
they should assist Your Majesty in completing it;
if it is improper,
they should request Your Majesty to stop it.
Inquiring of the responsible office
is perfectly reasonable.
I do not know for what crime they are being reprimanded,
nor for what crime they should apologize!"
The Emperor felt deeply ashamed.
22 The Emperor once said to his attending ministers during court:
"I, as the ruler of men,
often handle both the duties of general and minister."
Jǐshìzhōng Zhāng Xíngchéng withdrew and submitted a memorial,
believing that:
"Yǔ did not boast or claim credit, yet no one in the world could contend with him.
The Shū: Shùn said to Yǔ: Because you do not boast,
no one in the world contends with you over ability;
because you do not claim credit,
no one in the world contends with you over achievement.
Cháo,
pronounced zhí yáo fān;
same below.
Jiàng,
pronounced jí liàng fān.
Xiàng,
pronounced xī liàng fān.
Ér shàng,
pronounced shí zhǎng fān.
We ministers are truly unworthy to gaze upon your brilliant light;
yet it is unnecessary to speak of this during court.
With the dignity of the Ten Thousand Chariots,
to compete for achievement and contend over ability with your ministers,
I privately believe it is not befitting for Your Majesty."
The Emperor greatly approved of this.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on Yǐchǒu,
Prince of Wèi Lǐ Tài presented the Kuòdìzhì.
Tài loved learning;
Sīmǎ Sū Xù persuaded Tài,
saying that the worthy kings of antiquity all recruited scholars and compiled books,
so Tài petitioned to undertake this compilation.
At that time, Tài petitioned to have Xiāo Déyán, Yán Yìn, Jiǎng Yàqīng, Xǔ Yǎn, and others come to his residence to compile it.
Hǎo,
pronounced hū dào fān.
Shuō,
pronounced shū ruì fān.
He broadly gathered talented men of the time;
people gathered like spokes to a hub,
and his gate and courtyard were like a market.
Tài's monthly allowance exceeded that of the Crown Prince.
Jiànyì Dàfū Chǔ Suíliáng submitted a memorial,
believing that:
"The sages established rituals,
honoring the legitimate heir and keeping the lesser sons humble.
The heir apparent's use of goods is not accounted for,
and he shares them with the king.
Zhōulǐ: The king and the heir apparent only have their meals not accounted for;
for other clothing and goods,
the heir apparent's are still all accounted for.
Huì,
pronounced gǔ wài fān.
They must not exceed the legitimate heir,
in order to block the gradual rise of suspicion,
and eliminate the source of calamity and disorder.
If those who should be close are kept distant,
and those who should be honored are kept humble,
then the cunning and deceitful
will seize the opportunity to act.
In the past, the Hàn Empress Dowager Dòu doted on Prince Xiàowáng of Liáng,
who ultimately died of grief;
see the Annals of Hàn Jǐngdì.
Sāi,
pronounced xī zé fān.
Zú,
pronounced zǐ xù fān.
It also nearly led to ruin.
See the Annals of Xuāndì and Yuándì.
Jī,
pronounced jū xī fān;
same below.
He should be shown the rules of ritual,
instructed in humility and frugality,
to become a fine vessel.
This is what is called 'the sages' teaching succeeds without severity.'"
The Xiàojīng records Confucius's words.
The Emperor also ordered Tài to move to reside in the Wǔdé Hall;
Wèi Zhēng submitted a memorial,
believing that:
"Your Majesty loves the Prince of Wèi,
and always wishes to keep him safe and secure.
You should constantly restrain his arrogance and extravagance,
and not place him in a position of suspicion.
Now moving him to reside in this hall,
which is to the west of the Eastern Palace,
where Hǎilíng once resided—
Lǐ Yuánjí was posthumously enfeoffed as Prince Cì of Hǎilíng.
Although the times and circumstances are different,
I fear the Prince of Wèi's heart may not be at ease."
The Emperor said:
"I nearly made this mistake."
He immediately sent Tài back to his own residence.
2 On Xīnwèi,
those sentenced to death were transferred to populate Xīzhōu,
while those sentenced to exile or penal servitude were sent to garrison duty,
each according to the severity of their crime determining the length of their term.
3 An edict ordered the empire to register vagrants without household registration,
with a deadline by the end of next year to complete the registration.
Fù means
to be registered.
4 Cén Wénběn, who concurrently held the position of Zhōngshū Shìláng, was appointed as Zhōngshū Shìláng,
solely in charge of confidential matters.
There were two Zhōngshū Shìláng.
At that time, Wénběn alone was used,
so he exclusively handled confidential matters.
14. After the Western Turkic Yabghu Qaghan Yǐpídūlù killed the Shābōluó Yèhù,
he annexed his forces,
and then attacked Tǔhuǒluó,
destroying it.
Dù Yòu said: Tǔhuǒluó is also called Tǔhǎoyí.
During the Later Wèi period, Tǔhūluó was located five hundred li west of the Cōnglǐng Mountains,
south of the Wūhǔ River,
which is the Guīshuǐ River.
Yǐpídūlù then became arrogant and domineering,
detained Táng envoys,
invaded and ravaged the Western Regions,
and sent troops to attack Yīzhōu.
Guō Xiàokè led two thousand light cavalry from Wūgǔ to intercept them,
and defeated them.
Yǐpídūlù also sent the Chùyuè and Chùmì tribes to besiege Tiānshān.
To the southwest of Xīzhōu were the Nánpíng and Ānchāng cities,
and another one hundred twenty li further was the Tiānshān Army garrison.
Guō Xiàokè took advantage of the victory to capture the city where the Chùyuè Yìjīn resided,
pursued the fleeing enemy to the Èsuǒ Mountain,
and accepted the surrender of the Chùmì people before returning.
Previously,
after Gāochāng was pacified,
over a thousand soldiers were sent annually to garrison the area.
Chǔ Suìliáng submitted a memorial,
stating:
"When a sage king governs,
he prioritizes Huáxià (the Central Plains) and only then deals with the Yí-Dí (barbarian tribes).
Your Majesty raised troops to capture Gāochāng,
causing several commanderies to become desolate,
and for years they have not recovered;
not recovered,
meaning they cannot return to their former state of peace.
People are taken far from their hometowns,
bankrupting themselves to prepare equipment.
Moreover, exiled convicts,
who are all unscrupulous youths,
only serve to disturb the border regions,
how could they be of any benefit to the military campaigns!
Many of those sent repeatedly flee,
merely causing trouble with pursuits and arrests.
Additionally, the routes they travel,
pass through a thousand li of desert,
where the winter wind cuts like a knife,
and the summer wind burns like fire.
Travelers coming and going
often die encountering these conditions.
Even if there were beacon alerts from Zhāngyè or Jiǔquán,
desert,
qī jì fān.
Yè,
pronounced yì.
we would ultimately have to dispatch troops and provisions from the various prefectures of Lǒngyòu to deal with them.
Thus, Héxī is
the heart and core of the Middle Kingdom;
Gāochāng is merely
the limbs of others;
why should we exhaust our fundamental strength to serve a useless land!
Moreover, when Your Majesty obtained the lands of the Tūjué and Tǔyùhún,
you did not keep their territories,
but established rulers for them to govern.
Should Gāochāng alone not be treated similarly!
If they rebel, capture them;
if they submit, enfeoff them.
No punishment is more awe-inspiring,
no virtue is more profound.
I hope you will instead select a suitable descendant of Gāochāng,
and let him rule his country.
Generation after generation,
bearing the great grace,
they will forever be a protective vassal of the Táng house,
bringing internal peace and external tranquility.
Would that not be good!"
The Emperor did not listen.
When the Western Turks invaded,
the Emperor regretted it,
saying:
"Wèi Zhēng and Chǔ Suìliáng advised me to re-establish Gāochāng,
but I did not heed their words.
Now I blame myself."
Yǐpídūlù attacked Kāngjū to the west,
passing through Mǐguó on the way,
and conquered it.
Mǐguó,
also called Mímò,
or Mǐmòhè,
governed from the Mòxīdé city,
one hundred li north from the state of Kāngjū.
Yǐpídūlù did not share the spoils with his subordinates,
and his general Níshúchuò seized them.
Yǐpídūlù was enraged,
and beheaded Níshúchuò to make an example,
causing widespread anger and resentment.
Níshúchuò's subordinate general Húlùwū attacked him,
and Yǐpídūlù's forces scattered and fled,
taking refuge in the Báishuǐ Hú city.
Thereupon, the various tribes of Nǔshībì and Wūlìchuò, who were under Yǐpídūlù's command, sent envoys to the imperial court,
requesting the deposition of Yǐpídūlù,
and the installation of a new Qaghan.
The Emperor sent an envoy bearing the imperial seal and edict,
to install the son of Mòhèduō
(Mòhèduō appears in the second year of the 193rd volume).
Seal,
sī shì fān.
After Yǐpíshèkuì was installed,
he courteously sent back all the Táng envoys detained by Yǐpídūlù,
and led his troops to attack Yǐpídūlù at Báishuǐ Hú city.
Yǐpídūlù sent troops to attack him,
and Yǐpíshèkuì was badly defeated.
Yǐpídūlù sent envoys to summon his former tribes,
but the former tribes all said:
"Even if a thousand of us died in battle,
and only one remained,
we would still not follow you!"
Yǐpídūlù realized he no longer had the support of the masses,
and fled west to Tǔhuǒluó.
Examination of discrepancies: The Old Tūjué Biography states:
"Protector-General Guō Xiàokè defeated Dūlù.
In the fifteenth year,
Wūlìchuò and others requested the installation of a Qaghan."
According to the above, it already says
"In the fifteenth year, Shābōluó Yèhù Qaghan was officially appointed."
Below it should not again say
"fifteenth year",
suspecting
the character "six"
was mistakenly written as
"five"
In the twentieth year,
the Veritable Records narrate the dispersal of Dūlù's troops,
and his staying at Báishuǐ Hú city,
also stating
"This was in the fifteenth year of Zhēnguān."
According to the Veritable Records of the sixteenth year,
"On the Guǐyǒu day of the ninth month,
Guō Xiàokè, Governor of Liángzhōu, was appointed Protector-General of Ānxī."
Then Dūlù's invasion of Yīzhōu should have occurred after this,
how could he have already been defeated and dispersed in the fifteenth year!
The error in the Tūjué Biography,
likely stems from this.
Now, because Guō Xiàokè became Protector-General,
it is mentioned together.
The events of Yǐpídūlù's installation are seen in the twelfth year of the previous volume.
15. In winter,
tenth month,
on Bǐngshēn,
the Palace Chamberlain, Duke Yǔn of Yǐng, Yǔwén Shìjí, died.
Hè Chēn's rules for posthumous titles: "Bringing ruin and disorder to all laws is called 'Yǔn' (profligate);
neglecting virtue and ruining propriety is called 'Yǔn'."
Died,
zǐ xù fān.
The Emperor once saw a beautiful tree,
and Shìjí followed, praising it incessantly.
The Emperor sternly said:
"Wèi Zhēng often advised me to stay away from flatterers,
I didn't know who the flatterers were,
and suspected it might be you.
Now it turns out I was not wrong!"
Shìjí kowtowed and apologized.
16. The Emperor said to his attending officials:
"Xuēyántuó is powerful and unyielding north of the desert.
Now there are only two strategies to deal with them:
either send troops to exterminate them,
or give them a marriage alliance to pacify them.
Which of the two should we choose?"
Fáng Xuánlíng replied:
"The Middle Kingdom has only recently been stabilized,
warfare is inauspicious and dangerous.
I believe a marriage alliance is advisable."
The Emperor said:
"Right.
I am the parent of the people.
If it can benefit them,
why begrudge a single daughter!"
Previously, the mother of the Left Guard General Qìbì Hélì, Lady Gūzāng, and his younger brother, the Governor of Hèlánzhōu, Shāmén, were both in Liángzhōu.
The Emperor sent Hélì to return for a visit,
and also to pacify his tribe.
At that time, Xuēyántuó was strong,
and the Qìbì tribe all wanted to submit to them.
Hélì was greatly alarmed and said:
"The sovereign's grace is so profound,
how can you suddenly rebel!"
His followers said:
"Your mother and the Governor have already gone to them,
how can you not go!"
Hélì said:
"Shāmén is filial to his parents,
I am loyal to my sovereign.
I will certainly not follow you."
His followers seized him and took him to Xuēyántuó,
placing him before Zhēnzhū's tent.
Hélì sat with legs apart defiantly,
drew his sword, faced east and shouted loudly:
"How could a Táng man of principle suffer humiliation in a barbarian court!
Heaven, Earth, sun, and moon,
bear witness to my heart!"
He then cut off his left ear as an oath.
Zhēnzhū wanted to kill him,
but his wife advised against it and he stopped.
The Emperor heard that the Qibi tribe had rebelled,
and said:
"This certainly is not Hé Lì's intention."
Those around him said:
"The Rong and Di peoples are naturally close to their own kind.
Hé Lì entering the Xueyántuó
is like a fish returning to water."
The Emperor said:
"That is not so.
Hé Lì's heart is like iron and stone;
he certainly will not betray me."
It so happened that an envoy arrived from the Xueyántuó,
who gave a full account of the situation.
The Emperor wept for him,
and said to those around him:
"How is Hé Lì truly?"
He immediately ordered the Vice-Minister of War, Cuī Dūnlǐ, to take his credentials and instruct the Xueyántuó,
offering the Princess Xīnxīng in marriage
in order to seek Hé Lì's return.
The Princess Xīnxīng
was an imperial daughter.
He was appointed Right Guard General of the Rapid as Tigers.
17 In the eleventh month,
on the bǐngchén day,
the Emperor held a military hunt at Wǔgōng.
18 On the dīngsì day,
Zhāng Jiǎn, the Military Governor of Yíng Prefecture, reported that Quán Gàisūwén, the great man of the eastern region of Gāolì, had assassinated his king, Wǔ.
Quán
is a surname.

surname Quán;
he claimed to have been born in water,

Lì,

Textual analysis says: The Old Biography states

Now we follow the Veritable Records.
The king and his high officials planned to execute him.
Gàisūwén secretly learned of this,
gathered all his tribal troops as if for a military inspection,

cut him into several pieces,

He established the king's younger brother's son, Zàng, as king;

Gàisūwén's appearance was imposing and majestic,
his spirit bold and unrestrained.
He wore five swords on his person,
and those around him dared not look up at him.
Every time he mounted or dismounted his horse,
he often ordered nobles and military officers to lie on the ground for him to tread upon.
When traveling, he always arranged his procession in orderly ranks.
Those leading the way would give a long shout,
and then people would all flee and scatter,
not avoiding pits or valleys.
The roads were cleared of travelers,
and the people of the country suffered greatly from this.
19 On the rénxū day,
the Emperor held a military hunt at Qíyáng.
In the seventh year of the Zhēnguàn era,
Qíyáng County was established by dividing Qíshān County of Qí Prefecture and Shàngyí County of Yōng Prefecture,
belonging to Qí Prefecture.
He summoned the elderly former residents of Wǔgōng for a feast and bestowal of gifts,

20 On the rénshēn day,
the Emperor said:
"I am the ruler of the myriad people,
and I wish to make them all prosperous and honored.
If I instruct them in ritual and righteousness,
so that the young respect their elders and wives respect their husbands,
then they will all be honorable.
If I lighten corvée duties and reduce taxes,
so that each manages his own livelihood and occupation,
then they will all be prosperous.
If every household is provided for and every person has enough,
even if I do not listen to music,
joy will be within me."
21 Péi Xíngzhuāng, the Prefect of Bó Prefecture, submitted a memorial requesting an attack on Gāolì.
The Emperor said:
"King Wǔ of Gāolì fulfilled his tribute duties without fail.
He was assassinated by a treacherous minister,
and I deeply grieve for him;
I certainly have not forgotten.
However, to take advantage of mourning and chaos to seize it,
even if successful, would not be honorable.
Moreover, the Shāndōng region is devastated and impoverished;
I cannot bear to speak of using military force."
22 When Emperor Gāozǔ entered the passes,
the Sui dynasty Brave and Martial General of Féngyì, Dǎng Rénhóng, led over two thousand troops to join Emperor Gāozǔ at Púbǎn.
He followed in pacifying the capital.
These were all events of the first year of the Yìníng era of the Sui Emperor Gōng.
Jiàng,
read with the sound of jiàng.
Dǎng,
read with the sound of dǎng.
When the great army campaigned eastward,
Rénhóng continuously transported supplies without interruption.
This refers to the campaign against Wáng Shìchōng.
Shǎn,
read with the sound of shǎn.
The Liáng established Qiánwéi Commandery,
and set up Róng Prefecture.
The Sui abolished the prefecture and made it a commandery.
The Táng again changed the commandery back to a prefecture.
Wherever he went, he left a notable reputation and record,
and the Emperor held him in high esteem.
However, his nature was greedy.
After leaving Guǎngzhōu,
he was accused by others,
with embezzlement exceeding a million,
a crime deserving death.
The Emperor said to his attending ministers:
"Yesterday I saw the Court of Judicial Review submit five memorials requesting Rénhóng's execution.
By the regulations of the fifth year,
for prisoners sentenced to death,
there should be five memorials of review over three days.
It was just time for the afternoon meal,
so I ordered the table cleared;
yet I sought a way to spare his life for him,
but ultimately could not find one.
Now I wish to bend the law and beg you all for him."
In the twelfth month,
on the first day, rénwǔ,
the Emperor again summoned officials of the fifth rank and above to assemble in front of the Tàijí Hall,
and said:
"The law
is what the ruler receives from Heaven;
one cannot use personal feelings and break trust.
Now I, for personal reasons regarding Dǎng Rénhóng, wish to pardon him.
This is to bring disorder to the law,
and to betray Heaven above.
I wish to spread straw mats in the southern suburbs,
and daily partake only of vegetarian food,
to confess my fault to Heaven for three days."
Fáng Xuánlíng and others all said:
"The power of life and death
is what the ruler alone possesses.
Why must you humble and blame yourself to such an extent!"
The Emperor did not agree.
The assembled ministers kowtowed in the courtyard, firmly pleading,
from morning until the sun declined in the west.
The Emperor then issued a handwritten edict,
declaring himself:
"I have three faults: failing to understand people clearly,
first;
using personal feelings to disorder the law,
second;
failing to reward the good,
and failing to punish the evil,
third.
Since you all firmly remonstrate,
I shall temporarily comply with your request."
Thereupon he demoted Rénhóng to commoner status,
and exiled him to Qīn Prefecture.
23 On the guǐmǎo day,
the Emperor went to the hot springs at Líshān;
on the jiǎchén day,
he hunted at Líshān.
The Emperor ascended the mountain,
and saw a break in the hunting enclosure.
Turning to those around him, he said:
"If I see it is not in order and do not punish,
then I let military law fall into disuse;
if I punish,
then it is I, from a high position looking down, seeking out people's faults."
So he used the pretext of the dangerous path,
and guided his reins into a valley to avoid it.
On the yǐsì day,
he returned to the palace.
The Ministry of Justice proposed that
"the law on implicating relatives in cases of rebellion, which currently only confiscates brothers as government property, is too lenient;
we request changing it to the death penalty."
An imperial edict ordered the eight high ministers to deliberate on it.
The deliberators all believed that
"according to the laws of the Qin, Han, Wei, and Jin dynasties,
rebels were all exterminated along with their three clans.
Now it is appropriate to follow the Ministry of Justice's request."
The Supervising Secretary Cuī Rénshī驳斥 said:
"In ancient times, the crimes of fathers and sons, brothers did not implicate each other.
How can we use the cruel laws of the fallen Qin to alter the moderate statutes of the flourishing Zhou!
The Rites of Zhou, Office of Autumn: For punishing a peaceful state,
use moderate statutes.
Fathers and sons, brothers, crimes not implicating each other,
is Zhou law.
驳,
bó, northern horn turning.
If this burdens their hearts,
and this is disregarded,
then what love is there for brothers!"
The Emperor followed his advice.
25 The Emperor asked his attending officials:
"Throughout history, sometimes the ruler is chaotic while the ministers are orderly,
sometimes the ruler is orderly while the ministers are chaotic.
Which of these two is better?"
Wèi Zhēng replied:
"If the ruler is orderly, then rewards and punishments for good and evil are appropriate,
how could the ministers then create chaos!
If he is not orderly,
indulging in tyranny and stubbornly rejecting advice,
even if there are good ministers,
what could they possibly implement!"
The Emperor said:
"Did not Qí Wénxuān, with Yáng Zūnyàn,
represent a case of a chaotic ruler with orderly ministers?"
He replied:

the event is seen in the 166th scroll, Liáng Jìngdì Tàipíng First Year.

7 On the dīngwèi day,
the Emperor said:
"A ruler has but one mind,
yet those who assail it are many.
Some use valor and strength,
some use eloquent speech,
some use flattery,
some use treachery and deceit,
some use base desires.
They converge like spokes to attack it,
each seeking to promote themselves,
to gain favor and emolument.
If the ruler shows the slightest laxity,
and accepts even one of them,
then danger and ruin follow,
which is why it is difficult."
8 On the wùshēn day,
the Emperor ordered portraits of meritorious officials—Duke Zhào Chángsūn Wújì, Yuánwáng of Zhàojùn Lǐ Xiàogōng,
(Explanation of posthumous titles: 'Yuán' means having great achievements and abundant virtue;
'Yuán' also means upholding goodness and practicing virtue.)
Dù Rúhuì was initially enfeoffed as Duke of Cài,
after his death,
his title was transferred to Duke of Lái.
(Explanation of posthumous titles: 'Jié' means being honest and self-restrained.)
Yún,
pronounced yún;
same below.
Chái Shào,
should be Xǔ Shào.
Duke Xiāng Liú Zhènghuì, Duke Jǔ Táng Jiǎn, Duke Yīng Lǐ Shìjì, Duke Húzhuàng Qín Shūbǎo, and others—to be painted in the Língyān Pavilion.
Those whose noble rank is recorded without their posthumous title
were still alive;
those whose noble rank and posthumous title are both recorded
had already died.
The Nánbù Xīnshū states: The Língyān Pavilion is located beside the Sānqīng Hall in the Western Palace,
and the portraits of the meritorious officials all face north.
Inside the pavilion, there is a central partition;
on the inner side facing north are painted the marquises and kings of highest merit,
while outside the partition are the meritorious officials in order of precedence.
Chéng Dàchāng said: Inside the pavilion, there are three partitions in total.
The innermost layer depicts the chief ministers of highest merit,
the outer layer depicts the marquises and kings of highest merit,
and the outermost layer depicts the meritorious officials in order of precedence.
Although these three partitions are divided into inner and outer layers,
the portraits of the meritorious officials all face north,
perhaps because it is beside the Sānqīng Hall,
and facing north is considered respectful!
I believe that facing north
is the ritual of a subject,
not because it is beside the Sānqīng Hall.
9 The Governor of Qízhōu, Prince Qí Lǐ Yòu,
was frivolous and impetuous by nature.
His maternal uncle, the Assistant Director of the Imperial Stables, Yīn Hóngzhì, advised him, saying:
(The Imperial Stables Bureau,

Chùnà Chuò was likely also a tribal chieftain of the Western Turks.

Shú,

questioned him.

The Emperor heard that the Governor of Míng Prefecture, Chéng Míngzhèn, was skilled in using troops.

How dare you, beside the Son of Heaven,

Míngzhèn apologized, saying:
"I, a crude and rustic minister,

Just now, my mind was entirely focused on formulating a response,

His demeanor remained composed,
and his responses became even clearer and more articulate.
The Emperor then sighed and said:
"Fáng Xuánlíng has been by my side for over twenty years,
and every time he sees me reprimand others,

This is why Xuánlíng is considered loyal and cautious.
Chǔ,
read as Chǔ.
Yet when I once reprimanded him,

His reasoning and speech remained flawless—

second, using the righteous to punish the rebellious;
third, using order to take advantage of disorder;

I announce this to the common people,

Tàizōng believed Gāolì was certainly conquerable, yet ultimately did not conquer it.

on Xīnchǒu day,

Settle,
chǔ, pronunciation chānglǚ.
Xià,

jiàng, pronunciation jíliàng.
Xià,
