a muddy swamp over two hundred lǐ in extent,
impassable for men and horses.
The Grand Architect Yán Lìdé laid earth to build a bridge,
and the army proceeded without delay.
On Rénshēn,
they crossed eastward over the marsh.
On Yǐhài,
forty thousand Gāolì infantry and cavalry came to relieve Liáodōng.
Dàozōng, Prince of Jiāngxià, led four thousand cavalry to meet and attack them.
Everyone in the army believed the disparity in numbers was too great,
and that it would be better to dig deep trenches and build high ramparts to await the arrival of the imperial carriage.
Dàozōng said:
"The enemy, relying on their numbers,
underestimates us.
Having come from afar, they are weary and exhausted;
attacking them will certainly lead to their defeat.
Moreover, we are the vanguard,
and should clear the way to await the imperial carriage.
How can we leave the enemy for our sovereign and father!"
"Not leaving the enemy for the sovereign and father" —
these were the words of Hàn's Gěng Yǎn.
Chéng,
read as shèng.
Yí,
read as wèi.
Guǒyì Commandant Mǎ Wénjǔ said:
"Without encountering a formidable enemy,
how can a warrior prove his valor!"
He spurred his horse toward the enemy,
and wherever he went, they crumbled.
The troops' hearts were somewhat steadied.
Once the battle was joined,
the Campaign Commander Zhāng Jūnyì retreated and fled,
and the Táng troops fared poorly.
Dàozōng gathered the scattered soldiers,
climbed a height to survey the situation,
and saw that the Gāolì formation was in disarray.
With several dozen brave cavalry, he charged into them,
cutting left and right through their ranks.
Li Shìjì led troops to assist him,
and the Gāolì were utterly defeated,
with over a thousand heads taken.
On Dīngchǒu,
the imperial carriage crossed the Liáo River.
The bridge was dismantled
to strengthen the soldiers' resolve.
They encamped at Mǎshǒu Mountain.
The Emperor rewarded and bestowed gifts upon Dàozōng, Prince of Jiāngxià,
promoted Mǎ Wénjǔ to the rank of General of the Household,
and executed Zhāng Jūnyì.
Rewarding merit without fail
and punishing cowardice without fail
ensures that officers and soldiers understand what to emulate and what to avoid.
Láo,
read as lào.
Seeing soldiers carrying earth to fill the moat,
the Emperor took the heaviest loads from them
and carried them on his horse.
Attending officials vied to carry earth to the foot of the city wall.
Li Shìjì attacked Liáodōng City
day and night without rest.
After twelve days,
the Emperor led elite troops to join him,
surrounding the city with hundreds of layers of troops.
The sound of war drums and shouts shook heaven and earth.
On Jiǎshēn,
a strong south wind blew.
The Emperor sent crack troops to climb to the top of scaling poles
and set fire to the southwestern tower of the city.
The flames spread into the city,
whereupon he signaled the officers and soldiers to scale the walls.
The Gāolì fought fiercely but could not withstand the assault,
and the city was thus captured.
Over ten thousand people were killed,
and more than ten thousand able-bodied soldiers were captured,
along with forty thousand men and women.
The city was made Liáo Prefecture.
Present-day Liáoyáng Prefecture of the Great Yuán.
On Yǐwèi,
they advanced to Báiyán City.
On Bǐngshēn,
the Great General of the Right Guard, Lǐ Sīmó, was struck by a crossbow bolt.
The Emperor personally sucked the blood from his wound;
when the officers and soldiers heard of this,
they were deeply moved.
Wūgǔ City sent over ten thousand troops as reinforcements for Báiyán.
Sailing northeast from Dēng Prefecture to Wūhú Island,
then traveling five hundred lǐ east along the coastal flats,
passing Qīngní Pǔ, Táohuā Pǔ, Xìngrén Pǔ, Shírén Wāng, and Tuótuó Wān,
one reaches the Wūgǔ River.
Hé Lì threw himself into the enemy formation,
and a lance struck him in the waist.
Xuē Wànbèi, the Chief of the Imperial Carriages, rode alone to rescue him,
pulling Hé Lì out from amidst the myriad enemy troops and returning with him.
Hé Lì's spirit grew even fiercer;
he bound his wound and fought on.
His accompanying cavalry fought valiantly,
and they defeated the Gāolì troops,
pursuing them for several tens of lǐ,
taking over a thousand heads,
and ceasing only when darkness fell.
Wànbèi
was the younger brother of Wànchè.
Punctuated by Wáng Chóngwǔ, proofread by Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí.
Compiled by
Sīmǎ Guāng
by imperial command.
Later student from Tiāntāi.
The nineteenth year of the Zhēnguàn era
1 In the sixth month,
on Dīngyǒu,
Li Shìjì attacked the southwestern side of Báiyán City,
while the Emperor oversaw the attack from the northwest.
The city commander, Sūn Dàiyīn, secretly sent a trusted aide to request surrender.
Approaching the city wall,
he threw down a knife and an axe as tokens of good faith,
and said:
"Your servant wishes to surrender,
but there are those in the city who will not comply."
The Emperor gave a Táng banner to his envoy,
saying:
"If you are determined to surrender,
you should raise this on the city wall."
Dàiyīn raised the banner,
and the people in the city, thinking Táng troops had already scaled the walls,
all followed suit.
When the Emperor captured Liáodōng,
Báiyán City had requested to surrender,
but later reneged.
Angered by their duplicity,
the Emperor ordered the army:
"When the city is taken, all its people and goods shall be given as rewards to the soldiers."
This meant using the men, women, and wealth as rewards.
Leading several dozen armored soldiers, he requested:
"The reason soldiers brave arrows and stones,
disregarding their own lives,
is their desire for plunder and captives.
Now that the city is on the verge of falling,
why accept their surrender again,
disappointing the hearts of the fighting men!"
From Shìjì's words,
it seems the habits of his youthful bandit days were not yet eradicated.
"What you say, General, is correct.
However, to unleash the troops to kill and seize their wives and children
is something I cannot bear.
For those under your command who have merit,
I will reward them from the treasury stores,
hoping thereby to redeem this city through you, General."
Shìjì then withdrew.
They obtained over ten thousand men and women from the city.
The Emperor set up a tent by the water to accept their surrender,
and moreover bestowed food upon them.
Those over eighty years old were given silk in varying amounts.
Soldiers from other cities who were in Báiyán were all consoled and instructed,
provided with provisions and weapons,
and allowed to go wherever they wished.
Previously,
the Chief Clerk of Liáodōng City had been killed by his subordinates,
and his assistant fled with his
wife and children to Báiyán.
The assistant
was an official position;
it had existed since the Later Wèi dynasty.
When Hèbá Yuè attacked Yùchí Púsà,
Púsà sent an assistant to convey a message.
Xiān,
read as xiàn.
Shěng,
read as xǐng.
He was bestowed five bolts of silk;
a hearse was made for the Chief Clerk,
and his remains were returned to Píngrǎng.
Báiyán City was made Yán Prefecture,
with Sūn Dàiyīn appointed as its Governor.
Qìbì Hé Lì's wound was severe.
The Emperor personally applied medicine for him.
They tracked down and captured Gāo Tūbó, the man who had stabbed Hé Lì,
and handed him over to Hé Lì to execute himself.
Hé Lì memorialized, saying:
"He braved the blade for his lord to stab your servant;
he is a loyal and brave warrior.
I had never met him before,
and there was no enmity between us."
He then released him.
Initially,
the Mòlízhī dispatched seven hundred men from Jiāshī City to garrison Gàimóu City.
Lǐ Shìjì captured them all,
and these men requested to join the army and serve.
The Emperor said:
"Your families are all in Jiāshī.
If you fight for me,
the Mòlízhī will certainly kill your wives and children.
To gain the service of one man and destroy a whole family—
I cannot bear it."
On the Wùxū day,
they were all provided with provisions and gifts and sent back.
On the Jǐhài day,
Gàimóu City was made into Gài Prefecture.
On the Dīngwèi day,
the imperial carriage departed from Liáodōng.
On the Bǐngchén day,
it arrived at Ānshì City.
Ānshì
was an ancient county of the Hàn,
belonging to Liáodōng Commandery;
the old book's biography of Xuē Rénguì writes it as
"Āndì City."
On the Dīngsì day,
Yánshòu and Huìzhēn, the Nòusà of the northern part of Gāolì, led a force of 150,000 Gāolì and Mòhé troops to relieve Ānshì.
The "Account of the Eastern Barbarians" in the *History of the Later Hàn* states: Gāogōulí had five clans: the Xiāonú, Juénú, Shùnnú, Guànnú, and Guìlóu.
Xián's commentary says: According to the current Gāolì five divisions: the first is the Internal Division,
also called the Yellow Division,
which is the Guìlóu Division;
the second is the Northern Division,
also called the Rear Division,
which is the Juénú Division;
the third is the Eastern Division,
also called the Left Division,
which is the Shùnnú Division;
the fourth is the Southern Division,
also called the Front Division,
which is the Guànnú Division;
the fifth is the Western Division,
also called the Right Division,
which is the Xiāonú Division.
According to the *History of the Northern Dynasties*,
each of the five divisions of Gāolì had a Nòusà,
which was the title of their chieftains.
Nòu
is pronounced as nú wū.
The *New Book* states: In large cities of Gāolì, one Nòusà was appointed,
equivalent to a Dūdū.
Lì
is pronounced as lì zhī.
Mòhé
is pronounced as mò hé.
"Now, Yánshòu has three strategies: to lead his troops straight forward,
link up with Ānshì City to form a fortified camp,
occupy the perilous heights of the mountains,
consume the grain within the city,
and let the Mòhé plunder our oxen and horses.
Attacking them would not yield quick success,
and if they wish to retreat, the muddy roads would hinder them,
thus trapping our army—
this is the superior strategy.
If Gāo Yánshòu adopts this superior strategy,
I wonder how Tàizōng would have responded!
Only the strategy of Dàozōng, Prince of Jiāngxià, would suffice.
To flee under cover of night—
this is the middling strategy.
Without assessing his own wisdom and ability,
to come and engage us in battle—
this is the inferior strategy.
You gentlemen observe him—
he will certainly adopt the inferior strategy,
and his capture is already within my sight!"
Gāolì had the position of Duìlú,
an old and experienced official.
The "Account of the Eastern Barbarians" states: Gāogōulí established offices,
including Xiāngjiā, Duìlú, and Pèizhě.
Chén Shòu said: If they established the office of Duìlú, they did not establish Pèizhě;
if they established Pèizhě, they did not establish Duìlú.
Xuē Jūzhèng said: Among Gāolì officials,
the highest-ranking is called the Great Duìlú,
equivalent to the first rank,
who oversees all state affairs.
Below the Duìlú,
there are a total of eleven ranks of officials.
They established over sixty prefectures and counties,
with large cities appointing a Nòusà,
equivalent to a Dūdū;
small cities appointing a Yùnshǐ,
equivalent to a Cìshǐ.
"The King of Qín internally eliminated powerful heroes,
externally subjugated the Róng and Dí barbarians,
and independently became emperor—
this is a talent that commands the age.
Now he has brought the forces of the entire realm here—
we cannot oppose him.
For our strategy,
it is best to halt our troops and not engage in battle,
prolonging the conflict over time,
and dispatch separate surprise forces to cut off their supply routes.
Once their provisions are exhausted,
they will be unable to seek battle,
and with no road to retreat—
only then can we be victorious."
This is precisely the superior strategy that the Emperor spoke of.
They led their army straight forward,
stopping forty *lǐ* from Ānshì City.
The Emperor, still fearing they might hesitate and not advance,
ordered the Great General of the Left Guard, Āshǐnà Shè'ěr, to lead a thousand Tūjué cavalry to lure them.
As soon as the armies engaged, he feigned retreat.
The Gāolì troops said to each other:
"They are easy to deal with!"
They all rushed forward to pursue them,
reaching a point eight *lǐ* southeast of Ānshì City,
where they arrayed themselves along the mountain.
The Emperor summoned all his generals to discuss strategy.
Zhǎngsūn Wújì replied:
"I have heard that when facing the enemy before battle,
one must first observe the morale of the soldiers.
I have just passed through the various camps,
and I saw that when the soldiers heard the Gāolì had arrived,
they all drew their swords and tied their banners,
with joy visible on their faces.
This is an army certain of victory.
Your Majesty, before you came of age,
personally took part in battle formations.
All the ingenious strategies and victories
were devised by Your Majesty's sagely planning,
and the generals merely carried out the plans.
For today's matter,
I beg Your Majesty to point the way!"
Using hunting as a metaphor,
indicating the tracks of the beast,
so the hounds can pursue and kill it.
"Since you gentlemen defer to me in this manner,
I shall deliberate for you."
Then he, along with Wújì and others, rode with several hundred cavalry to a high point to observe,
surveying the terrain and features,
to identify places suitable for ambushes and for advancing and retreating.
The Gāolì and Mòhé combined their forces into a formation
forty *lǐ* long.
Dàozōng, Prince of Jiāngxià, said:
"Gāolì has mobilized the entire country to resist the imperial army,
so the defense of Píngrǎng must be weak.
I wish to borrow five thousand elite troops from you,
to overturn their very foundation.
Then their several hundred thousand troops will surrender without a fight."
The Emperor did not respond.
This sets the stage for the Emperor's later regret at not using Dàozōng's strategy.
Xià
is pronounced as hù yǎ.
"I came because your country's powerful minister assassinated his sovereign,
and thus I came to punish the crime.
As for engaging in battle,
it is not my original intent.
Upon entering your territory,
we did not receive fodder and grain,
so we took a few of your cities.
Once your country resumes the rituals of a subject state,
then what was lost will certainly be restored."
Yánshòu believed this,
and made no further preparations.
The Emperor summoned civil and military officials at night to plan the operation.
He ordered Lǐ Shìjì to deploy fifteen thousand infantry and cavalry on the western ridge.
Chángsūn Wújì led eleven thousand elite troops as a surprise force,
emerging from a narrow valley north of the mountain to strike the enemy from behind.
The Emperor personally commanded four thousand infantry and cavalry,
carrying drums and horns,
with banners lowered,
and ascended the northern mountain.
He commanded all armies to charge and attack fiercely upon hearing the drums and horns.
He then ordered officials to set up a surrender tent beside the court hall.
On the Wǔwǔ day,
Yánshòu and others only saw Lǐ Shìjì’s formation,
and marshaled their troops to engage.
The Emperor saw dust rising from Chángsūn Wújì’s army,
ordered the drums and horns to sound,
and raised the banners.
All armies roared and advanced together.
Yánshòu and others were greatly frightened,
wanting to divide their forces to resist,
but their formation was already in chaos.
At that moment, there was thunder and lightning,
and just as the battle commenced, thunder and lightning arrived.
Lóngmén
was the location of the Hàn dynasty’s Píshì County.
In the Later Wèi, it was called Lóngmén County,
and Lóngmén Commandery was also established.
The Suí dynasty abolished the commandery,
placing the county under Púzhōu.
In the early Wǔdé era of the Táng,
it served as the seat of Tàizhōu.
In the seventeenth year of the Zhēnguàn era, the prefecture was abolished,
and it was placed under Jiàngzhōu.
Xuē Rénguì enlisted as a recruit from the commoner registers.
Shouting loudly, he broke through enemy formations,
invincible wherever he went.
The Gāolì troops were routed,
and the main army pressed the advantage,
causing the Gāolì troops to collapse completely,
with over twenty thousand heads taken.
The Emperor saw Xuē Rénguì,
summoned him, and appointed him as a Yóujī Jiāngjūn.
According to Táng regulations,
the military honorary ranks,
Yóujī Jiāngjūn,
was of the lower fifth rank.
He was the sixth-generation descendant of Āndū.
Xuē Āndū was a general
renowned for his bravery between the Sòng and Wèi dynasties.
He was known by his courtesy name.
Yánshòu and others led their remaining troops to fortify themselves by the mountain.
The Emperor ordered all armies to surround them,
and Chángsūn Wújì dismantled all bridges,
cutting off their retreat.
On the Jǐwèi day,
Yánshòu and Huìzhēn led their thirty-six thousand eight hundred troops to request surrender.
Examination of discrepancies: The Veritable Records state:
“Lǐ Jì memorialized: ‘Had Your Majesty not personally come,
I and Dàozōng would have led tens of thousands to attack Ānshì City without success.
Yánshòu and others would have arrived with over a hundred thousand troops,
and soldiers inside the city would have opened the gates to sally forth.
I would have been caught between head and tail,
turning on my heels to defeat,
and would certainly have been bound by Yánshòu and others and sent to Píngrǎng,
laughed at by Mòlízhī and others.
Today, I dare thank Your Majesty for the grace of sparing my life.’
The Emperor, always familiar with Jì,
smiled and nodded.”
However, Jì later led troops alone to conquer Gāolì.
How could it necessarily require Tàizōng’s personal presence?
This is not the historian’s empty praise,
but Jì’s flattering words.
It is not adopted here.
They advanced on their knees,
bowing and prostrating to plead for their lives.
The Emperor said to them:
“Youngsters of the Eastern Barbarians,
leaping about by the sea,
when it comes to crushing fortifications and deciding victory,
you are certainly no match for the old men.
From now on, dare you still battle the Son of Heaven?”
All prostrated on the ground, unable to reply.
The Emperor selected thirty-five hundred chieftains, from the Nòusà rank downward,
conferred military ranks upon them,
and relocated them inland.
The rest were released,
sent back to Píngrǎng.
All raised both hands and knocked their foreheads on the ground,
cheering so loudly it was heard for tens of lǐ.
Three thousand three hundred Mòhé people were captured,
and all were buried alive,
because the Mòhé had attacked the formation.
Fifty thousand oxen,
ten thousand suits of iron armor,
and other equipment in similar quantities were seized.
The entire state of Gāolì was greatly alarmed.
Later, Huángchéng and Yínchéng both abandoned their positions and fled,
leaving hundreds of lǐ without a trace of human activity.
The Emperor sent a dispatch by post horse to report to the Crown Prince,
and also wrote to Gāo Shìlián and others, saying:
“As a general, am I not like this?
What do you think?”
The historian notes that Tàizōng had a heart that boasted of his achievements.
Jiàng (general)
is pronounced with the falling-rising tone.
According to the Old History,
the mountain was originally named Liù Shān.
Gēng (to change)
is pronounced with the level tone.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Xīnwèi day,
the Emperor moved camp to the eastern ridge of Ānshì City.
On the Jǐmǎo day,
an edict was issued to mark the corpses of those who died in battle,
to be brought back with the army upon its return.
On the Wùzǐ day,
Gāo Yánshòu was appointed as Hónglú Qīng,
and Gāo Huìzhēn as Sīnóng Qīng.
Zhāng Liàng’s army passed by Jiàn’ān City,
with fortifications not yet secured,
and many soldiers went out to gather firewood or herd.
Gāolì troops suddenly arrived,
causing panic and disturbance in the army.
Liàng, always timid,
sat on a folding chair,
staring straight ahead without speaking.
The officers and soldiers saw this,
and instead thought him courageous.
Commander Zhāng Jīnshù and others beat drums, marshaled troops, and attacked Gāolì,
defeating them.
In the eighth month,
on the Jiǎchén day,
scouts captured Mòlízhī’s spy, Gāo Zhúlí,
and brought him bound with hands behind his back to the army gate.
Bound with hands behind the back means tying both hands behind.
Qí (cavalry)
is pronounced with the falling-rising tone.
Dié (spy)
is pronounced with the falling-rising tone;
similarly below.
They untied him and asked:
“Why are you so thin?”
He replied:
“I secretly traveled by hidden paths,
and have not eaten for several days.”
They ordered food given to him,
and said:
“You are a spy,
you should quickly return with your report.
Take a message for me to Mòlízhī:
If you want to know military news,
you can send someone directly to my place.
Why travel secretly and endure such hardship!”
Zhúlí was barefoot,
so the Emperor gave him straw sandals and sent him off.
On the Bǐngwǔ day,
camp was moved to the south of Ānshì City.
While the Emperor was beyond Liáo,
whenever setting up camp,
he only established clear sentries and scouts,
without digging trenches or building ramparts.
Even when close to the city,
the Gāolì troops never dared to come out to raid or plunder.
Soldiers traveled alone and camped in the open as if within the Central Plains.
The historian notes that the Emperor’s awe extended to distant lands,
exemplifying the saying that a good commander needs no formation.
When the Emperor
campaigned against Gāolì,
the Xuēyántuó sent an envoy with tribute.
The Emperor said to him:
“Tell your Khan:
Kě (can)
is pronounced with the entering tone.
Hán (Khan)
is pronounced with the level tone.
If you can raid,
you should come quickly!”
Zhēnzhū Khan was terrified,
sent an envoy to apologize,
and offered to send troops to assist the army.
The Emperor refused.
After Gāolì was defeated at Zhùbì Shān,
Mòlízhī sent Mòhé to persuade Zhēnzhū,
tempting him with great profit.
Zhēnzhū, intimidated, did not dare to move.
In the ninth month,
on the Rénshēn day,
Zhēnzhū died.
The Emperor observed mourning for him.
Initially,
Zhēnzhū requested that his eldest son by a concubine, Yè Mǎng, be made the Tūlìshī Khagan,
residing in the east,
to rule over the various tribes;
and his legitimate son, Bá Zhuó, be made the Sìyèhù Khagan,
residing in the west,
to rule over the Xuēyántuó.
An imperial edict granted this,
and both were formally appointed with due ceremony.
Yè Mǎng was by nature rash and restless,
quick to use military force,
and was at odds with Bá Zhuó.
When Zhēnzhū died,
they came to attend the funeral.
After the burial,
Yè Mǎng, fearing Bá Zhuó would plot against him,
first returned to his own territory.
Bá Zhuó pursued and attacked, killing him,
and proclaimed himself the Jiélì Jùlì Xuēshā Duōmí Khagan.
This laid the groundwork for the disorder and downfall of the Xuēyántuó.
2 When the Emperor conquered Báiyán,
he said to Lǐ Shìjì:
"I have heard that Ānshì City is well-fortified and its troops are elite,
its city commander is talented and brave.
During Mòlízhī's rebellion,
the city held out and did not submit.
Mòlízhī attacked but could not take it,
and therefore made peace with them.
Jiàn'ān's troops are weak and its provisions are scarce.
If we take them by surprise,
we are sure to capture it.
You should first attack Jiàn'ān.
Once Jiàn'ān falls,
then Ānshì will be within our grasp.
This is what military strategy calls 'there are cities one does not attack'
A saying from Sunzi's Art of War.
"Jiàn'ān is to the south,
Ānshì is to the north,
and all our army's provisions are in Liáodōng.
Now, if we bypass Ānshì to attack Jiàn'ān,
what if the enemy cuts off our supply route?
What shall we do then?
It would be better to first attack Ānshì.
Once Ānshì falls,
we can then advance with drums beating and take Jiàn'ān."
The Emperor said:
"Since I have appointed you as commander,
how can I not follow your strategy?
Do not delay my affairs!"
Shìjì then attacked Ānshì.
When the people of Ānshì saw the Emperor's banners and canopy,
they would climb the walls and shout defiantly.
The Emperor was angered,
and Shìjì requested that on the day the city was taken,
all the men and women be buried alive.
When the people of Ānshì heard this,
they defended even more resolutely,
and the attack dragged on without success.
Gāo Yánshòu and Gāo Huìzhēn petitioned the Emperor, saying:
"We, your servants, having pledged ourselves to the great state,
dare not withhold our sincere advice.
We wish for Your Majesty to achieve great success early,
so that we, your servants, may be reunited with our wives and children.
The people of Ānshì are devoted to their homes,
each fighting for himself,
and are not easily overcome quickly.
Now, we, your servants, with over a hundred thousand troops from Gāolì,
saw the banners and fled in defeat.
The people of the state are terrified.
The Nòusà of Wūgǔ City is old and feeble,
and cannot hold firm.
If we shift our troops to attack it,
it will fall by evening if we arrive in the morning.
The other small cities along the way
will surely flee at the mere rumor of our approach.
Then we can gather their supplies and provisions,
advance with drums beating,
and Píngrǎng will certainly not hold."
Some ministers also said:
"Zhāng Liàng's army is at Shāchéng,
Shāchéng is Bēishāchéng.
Taking advantage of Gāolì's fear and panic,
we should combine our forces to capture Wūgǔ City,
cross the Yālù River,
and directly seize Píngrǎng.
The opportunity lies in this move."
The Emperor was about to follow this advice,
but only Chángsūn Wújì thought:
"The Son of Heaven personally leading a campaign
is different from other generals.
We cannot take risks and rely on luck.
Now, the enemy forces in Jiàn'ān and Xīnchéng
still number a hundred thousand.
If we head towards Wūgǔ,
they will all be at our rear.
It would be better to first defeat Ānshì,
take Jiàn'ān,
and then advance unimpeded.
This is the perfectly safe strategy."
The Emperor then stopped.
When Tàizōng pacified the realm,
he often achieved victory through surprise tactics.
Only in the Liáodōng campaign,
he wished to defeat the enemy with absolute safety,
which is why he achieved no success.
The various armies urgently attacked Ānshì.
The Emperor heard the sounds of chickens and pigs from within the city,
and said to Lǐ Shìjì:

People's conduct and abilities

when I see the unworthy, I pity them,

Rulers often detest the upright,

These five things

For if one takes the highest as a model,

if one takes the middling as a model,
one will inevitably become inferior.
Since I have occupied the throne,
my failings have been many:
brocades, embroideries, pearls, and jade have never ceased before me;

hounds, horses, hawks, and falcons have been obtained from afar without exception;
traveling and touring the four directions,
the provisions and accommodations have caused toil and trouble.
These are all my grave faults;
do not consider them right and emulate them.

With benefits many and harms few,

with merit great and faults slight,
therefore the enterprise does not fall.

if you exert yourself to do good,
then the state will only be secure;
if you are arrogant, indolent, extravagant, and unrestrained,
then you yourself will not be preserved.
Moreover, what is achieved slowly but lost quickly—
is the state;
what is lost easily but gained with difficulty—
is the position.

The Tang Huiyao states: According to the old system,

When [the emperor] campaigned westward against Qiūcí,
with Cuìwēi [Palace] and Yùhuá [Palace],
construction projects followed one after another,
and furthermore, clothing and playthings were rather extravagant and wasteful.
She submitted a memorial remonstrating,
its gist stating:
"Using the finite fruits of agricultural labor,
to fill the boundless, huge waves;
scheming to obtain the multitudes of others not yet captured,
while losing our own army already formed.
In the past, Qín Shǐhuáng annexed the Six States,
but instead hastened the foundation of peril and ruin.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn possessed the three regions,
yet ended up creating the enterprise of overthrow and defeat;
Wèi, Shǔ, and Wú stood like the three legs of a tripod,
until Jìn unified them.
Was it not because they abandoned virtue, treated their states lightly,
schemed for profit, forgot peril,
and indulged their feelings and gave free rein to their desires?
From this we know that a vast territory is not the method for lasting peace,
and people's toil is the source of easy disorder."
She also said:
"Although again thatched huts are displayed to show frugality,
still the fatigue of timber and stone [construction] arises;
employing hired labor,
is not without the flaw of causing annoyance and disturbance."

"Precious playthings and clever crafts,
are indeed the axe and adze that destroy a state;
pearls, jade, brocades, and embroideries,
are truly the poisoned wine that confuses the mind."
She also said:

one still fears they will become extravagant;
if one establishes laws based on extravagance,
how can one restrain what comes after!"
The emperor approved of her words,
and treated her with great courtesy and respect.

Initially,
the king of Central India, Shīluóyìduō, had the strongest army,
and all four Indias submitted to him.
The country of India,
known in Han times as Shendu,
is also called Magadha,
or Brahman.
It is 9,600 li from the capital,
located south of the Congling Mountains,
with a territory of 30,000 li,
divided into five Indias: East, West, South, North, and Central.
South India borders the sea,
North India reaches the Snow Mountains,
East India meets the sea,
and connects with Fúnán and Línyì,
West India borders Jìbīn and Persia,
and Central India lies at the confluence of the four Indias.
Its capital is called Chábóhéluó City.
Dù Yòu said: India
is of the Saka people.
Yán Shīgǔ said: Saka
means "explained."
All the states sent envoys to present tribute.
When Shīluóyìduō died,
the country fell into great turmoil,
and his minister Āluónàshùn seized power for himself,
mobilizing Hu troops to attack Xuáncè.
Xuáncè led thirty followers into battle,
but his strength was no match,
and they were all captured.
Āluónàshùn plundered all the tribute goods from the various states.
Xuáncè escaped under cover of night,
reaching the western border of Tibet,
where he sent letters to summon troops from neighboring countries.
Tibet dispatched 1,200 elite soldiers,
and Nípó sent over 7,000 cavalry to join him.
The country of Nípóluó lies directly west of Tibet in Lèlíng Plain,
and is subject to Tibet.
Tǔ,
pronounced from tūn entering tone.
Qí,
pronounced qí jì fān.
After three consecutive days of battle,
they achieved a great victory,
beheading over 3,000,
with nearly 10,000 drowning in the water.
Āluónàshùn abandoned the city and fled,
later gathering his remaining forces,
and returned to fight Shīrén;
they were defeated again,
and Āluónàshùn was captured.
The remaining forces supported him and the prince,
blocking the Gāntuówèi River.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù says: Mount Kunlun,
called Mount Anòudá by Buddhists,
has the Yellow River emerging from its northeastern corner,
bending and flowing southeast into Púchāng Sea,
then flowing underground from Púchāng Sea,
emerging south at Jīshí to become China's Yellow River.
West of Kunlun,
a great river emerges,
called the Xīntóu River,
flowing southwest past Wūchángguó,
then southeast past Central India,
also called the Ganges,
then west past the north of the Four Great Stupas,
and west past the north of Tuówèiguó.
The so-called Gāntuówèi River likely refers to this.
The forces scattered,
and he and the prince were captured,
with 12,000 men and women taken prisoner.
Thus, India was shaken,
and over 580 cities, towns, and settlements surrendered,
capturing Āluónàshùn and returning.
Xuáncè was appointed as Cháosàn Dàfū.
The Tang system: the civil rank of Cháosàn Dàfū,
is from the fifth rank, lower grade.
Cháo,
pronounced zhí yáo fān.
Sàn,
pronounced xī dǎn fān.
6 In the sixth month,
on Yǐchǒu,
the Báixí tribe was made Jūyán Prefecture.
7 On Guǐyǒu,
Tèjìn Sòng Gōng Xiāo Yǔ died.
The Tàicháng proposed the posthumous title
"Dé,"
while the Shàngshū proposed
"Sù."
The Duke of Zhou's posthumous title system: "Sù" means firm virtue achieving completion.
Shì,
pronounced shí lì fān.
"A posthumous title
reflects one's conduct,
and should be accurate;
he may be posthumously titled Zhēngbiǎn Gōng."
Hè Chēn's posthumous title system: "Zhēng" means upright and unbending;
"Biǎn" means frugal and stingy without virtue;
narrow-minded and hasty governance is called "biǎn."
The emperor's daughter, Princess Xiāngchéng.
The emperor wanted to build a mansion for her,
but the princess firmly declined,
saying:
"A wife serving her parents-in-law
should be by their side morning and night.
If living in a separate mansion,
much would be lacking."
The emperor then ordered the mansion to be built at Yǔ's residence.
8 The emperor, considering Gāolì exhausted and weakened,
planned to mobilize 300,000 troops the following year,
to destroy it in one strike.
Some argued that for a large eastern campaign,
provisions for a year must be prepared,
which pack animals could not carry,
so ships should be readied for water transport.
During the Sui's end, Jiànnán alone had no bandits,
and during the recent Liáodōng campaign,
Jiànnán was again not involved,
its people being prosperous,
so they should be made to build ships.
The emperor agreed.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
he sent Right Commandant's Office Chief Clerk Qiáng Wěi
(the Commandant's Office
was also divided into Left and Right,
each with a Chief Clerk;
this refers to the Left and Right Qiānniú Offices).
Qiáng,
pronounced qí liǎng fān,
is a surname.
The largest ships were up to 100 chi long,
half as wide.
Separate envoys were sent by waterway,
from Wū Gorge to Jiāng and Yáng,
heading to Láizhōu.
9 On Gēngyín,
the Western Turkic minister Qūlìchuò requested to lead his troops to attack Qiūcí.
10 Initially,
Left Martial Guard General, Duke of Wǔlián County, Wǔ'ān Lǐ Jūnxiàn was stationed at Xuánwǔ Gate.
Wǔlián County at that time belonged to Shǐzhōu,
later changed to Jiànzhōu.
Wǔ'ān County,
in Han times belonged to Wèi Commandery,
in Jin times to Guǎngpíng Commandery,
in Later Zhou and Sui times to Míngzhōu.
Left and Right Martial Guard Generals were Southern Guard generals;
stationed at Xuánwǔ Gate,
they commanded the Northern Gate guard.
The court astronomer divined:
"A female ruler will flourish."
There was also a secret prophecy circulating among the people:
"After three generations of Tang,
a female ruler of the Wǔ clan will replace and possess the empire."
The emperor detested this.
Once, feasting with military officials in the palace,
they played a drinking game,
where
one person acted as the game master,
and the others took turns.
Later, each was asked to tell their childhood name,
which was part of the game.
Jūnxiàn said his name was Wǔniáng,
startling the emperor,
who laughed and said:
"What kind of woman
is so brave and strong!"
Moreover, Jūnxiàn's official title and fief both contained
the character "Wǔ,"
which the emperor deeply disliked.
Later, he was sent out as Huàzhōu Governor.
A commoner named Yuán Dàoxìn,
claimed he could abstain from food,
and understood Buddhist teachings,
whom Jūnxiàn deeply revered and trusted,
often meeting with him,
dismissing others to speak privately.
The censor reported Jūnxiàn associating with sorcerers,
plotting rebellion.
On Rénchén,
Jūnxiàn was executed,
and his family property confiscated.
The Emperor secretly asked the Grand Astrologer Lǐ Chúnfēng:
"The prophecy recorded in the secret texts—
is it truly credible?"
He replied:
"Your servant, looking up, has examined the celestial signs;
looking down, has scrutinized the calculations of fate.
That person is already within Your Majesty's palace,
among your close relatives.
From now on, within no more than thirty years,
she will rule the world,
and nearly exterminate the descendants of the Táng.
The omen is already formed."
The Emperor said:
"What if we kill all those who are suspected?"
He replied:
"What is ordained by Heaven,
man cannot oppose.
The one destined to rule will not die;
it would only result in many innocent deaths.
Moreover, from now on, thirty years hence,
that person will already be old,
and perhaps will have a somewhat compassionate heart,
so the calamity might be less severe.
Now, even if we could find and kill her,
Heaven might then produce a vigorous one to unleash her resentment and venom,
and I fear that Your Majesty's descendants
would be left with none to survive!"
The Emperor then desisted.
11 The Minister of Works, Duke Wénzhāo of Liáng, Fáng Xuánlíng, was left in charge of the capital.
His illness became critical.
The Emperor summoned him to the Yùhuá Palace.
He was carried in a sedan chair into the hall,
and only alighted beside the imperial throne.
They faced each other, shedding tears.
He was thus kept at the palace.
When the Emperor heard he had slightly improved, joy showed on his face;
when he worsened, the Emperor became anxious and haggard.
Xuánlíng said to his sons:
"I have received great kindness from my sovereign.
Now, under heaven all is at peace,
only the eastern campaign remains unfinished.
All the ministers dare not remonstrate.
If I know [the danger] and do not speak,
even in death I would bear unabsolved blame."
He then submitted a memorial of remonstrance,
stating:
"Lǎozǐ said: 'Knowing contentment avoids disgrace;
knowing when to stop avoids danger.'
Your Majesty's achievements, fame, authority, and virtue are already sufficient.
Expanding territory and opening frontiers should also cease.
Moreover, whenever Your Majesty decides the fate of a serious prisoner,
you invariably order triple review and quintuple petition,
reduce to plain meals,
and stop music—
see scroll 193, the fifth year.
Now you drive innocent soldiers,
consigning them beneath blades and points,
causing their livers and brains to smear the ground.
Is this alone not pitiable enough?
To be scrupulous in applying punishments
is to value human life.
To be eager in employing troops
is to forget that human life should be valued.
Comparing that with this,
Xuánlíng's words can be called profound, keen, clear, and evident.
If they deserve execution, execute them;
if they harass the common people,
destroy them;
if in future they can become a threat to the Central Kingdom,
eliminate them.
Now, lacking these three justifications, you trouble the Central Kingdom for no reason,
internally to avenge the disgrace of former dynasties,
externally to exact revenge for Xīnluó.
Is this not preserving the small
while damaging the great?
Speaking to this point,
it is clearly seen that Gāolì need not be campaigned against.
Among the court ministers at that time who remonstrated against the eastern campaign,
none could reach this level.
This flowed from loyal sincerity and earnestness.
For 'wèi,'
read yú wèi fān.
Burn the ships that brave the waves,
dismiss the recruited multitudes,
and naturally Huá and Yí will celebrate and rely [on you],
the distant will be awed, the near will be at peace.
Your servant will soon enter the earth.
If I am fortunate enough to have these mournful cries recorded—
The Analects: When Zēngzǐ was ill,
Mèng Jìngzǐ inquired of him.
Zēngzǐ said:
'When a bird is about to die,
its song is mournful;
when a man is about to die,
his words are good.'"
Xuánlíng's son, Fáng Yí'ài, was married to the Emperor's daughter, Princess Gāoyáng.
The Emperor said to the princess:
"He is so critically ill,
yet he still worries for my state and family."
The Emperor personally went to see him,
clasped his hand to bid farewell,
and could not control his grief.
On the guǐmǎo day,
he died.
Liǔ Fāng said: Xuánlíng assisted Tàizōng in pacifying the world.
Until the end of his term as chancellor,
altogether thirty-two years,
the world hailed him as a worthy minister.
Yet his deeds left no trace to follow,
such was the perfection of his virtue.
Therefore, while Tàizōng settled disasters and rebellions, Fáng and Dù did not speak of merit;
while Wáng and Wèi excelled at remonstrance, Fáng and Dù yielded the credit for worthiness;
while Lǐ Jìng and Lǐ Shìjì excelled at commanding troops, Fáng and Dù implemented their strategies.
The new commentary states:
"Fáng and Dù assisted with civil governance."
For 'jiàng,'
read jí liàng fān.
They skillfully attributed goodness to the sovereign.
To be a revered minister of the Táng,
how fitting!
12 In the eighth month,
on the jǐyǒu day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
13 On the dīngchǒu day,
an edict ordered the Yuèzhōu都督府 and the prefectures of Wù, Hóng, etc., to build 1,100 seagoing ships and double-hulled vessels.
Dōngyáng Commandery:
after Suí pacified Chén,
Wùzhōu was established.
For 'fǎng,'
read fǔ wàng fān.
For 'sōu,'
read sū zāo fān.
14 On the xīnwèi day,
the Left Guard General-in-Chief Zhíshīsīlì was dispatched via the Jīnshān route to attack the remaining bandits of Xuēyántuó.
15 In the ninth month,
on the gēngchén day,
the Commander-in-Chief of the Kūnqiū route expedition, Āshǐnà Shè'ěr, attacked the Chùyuè and Chùmì tribes,
defeated them,
and the remaining multitude all surrendered.
16 On the guǐwèi day,
Xuē Wànchè and others returned from campaigning against Gāolì.
Wànchè, while with the army,
was overbearing and insulting to others.
Péi Xíngfāng reported his discontent and resentment.
He was convicted, removed from his post,
and exiled to Xiàngzhōu.
Péi Xíngfāng was deputy to Wànchè on the eastern campaign;
see the previous scroll, last year.
Xiàngzhōu:
the territory of the former Hàn Tánzhōng Zhōngliū county.
In Suí times, it was Guìlín county of Shǐ'ān commandery.
In the fourth year of Táng Wǔdé,
Xiàngzhōu Guìlín commandery was established,
named for Mount Xiàng.
17 On the jǐchǒu day,
Xīnluó reported being attacked by Bǎijì,
which had captured thirteen of its cities.
18 On the jǐhài day,
Chǔ Suíliáng, Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, was appointed Zhōngshū Lìng.
19 Qiáng Wěi and others conscripted people to build ships.
The corvée extended to the mountain Lǎo people.
The Lǎo in the three prefectures of Yǎ, Qióng, and Méi rebelled.
On the rényín day,
Zhāng Shìguì, Governor of Màozhōu, and Liáng Jiànfāng, General of the Right Guard, were dispatched with over 20,000 troops from Lǒngyòu and Xiázhōng to attack them.
The people of Shǔ suffered under the shipbuilding corvée.
Some requested to pay a fee to hire people from Tánzhōu to build the ships;
the Emperor permitted it.
The prefectures and counties enforced the demands harshly and urgently.
People had to sell their fields, houses, and even their children, yet still could not meet the demands.
Grain prices soared,
and the region beyond Jiàn[mén] was in turmoil.
The area south of Jiànmén Pass was called 'Beyond Jiàn,'
meaning inside the capital, outside the various Huá regions.
The Vice Minister of the Court of the Imperial Granaries, Zhǎngsūn Zhīrén, was sent post-haste to inspect.
Zhīrén reported:
"The people of Shǔ are frail
and cannot endure severe labor.
For one large ship,
the hired service payment is 2,236 bolts of silk.
Timber has already been felled in the mountains and valleys,
but hauling is not yet finished.
Yet the ship service payment is levied again.
These two burdens come together,
and the people cannot bear it.
They should be nurtured and preserved."
The Emperor then decreed that the ship service payments for Tánzhōu would all be provided by the government.
20 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the guǐchǒu day,
the imperial carriage returned to the capital.
In the 21st year, Huíhé Tǔmídù's nephew Wūhé had an illicit relationship with his uncle's wife.
Wūhé and Jùlù Mòhè Dáguān Jùluóbó,
both of whom were sons-in-law of the Tūjué Chēbí Kèhán,
conspired together to kill Tǔmídù and defect to Chēbí.
Wūhé led a dozen or so cavalry in a night raid against Tǔmídù,
killing him.
The Deputy Protector-General of Yānrán, Yuán Lǐchén, sent someone to lure Wūhé,
promising to memorialize the emperor to appoint him as Governor of Hànhǎi.
Wūhé rode lightly to Lǐchén to give thanks,
whereupon Lǐchén arrested and beheaded him,
and reported the matter.
The Emperor, fearing the Huíhé tribes would scatter,
sent the Minister of War Cuī Dūnlǐ to go and pacify them.
After some time,
Jùluóbó came for an audience,
and the Emperor detained him and did not let him return.
From this, the Huíhé again declined.
See,
Xián, biàn fān.
In the 22nd year, Āshǐnà Shè'ěr, having already defeated the Chùyuè and Chùmì tribes,
led his troops from west of Yānqí towards the northern borders of Qiūcí.
He divided his forces into five routes,
launching a surprise attack.
The King of Yānqí, Xuēpó Ānàzhī, abandoned his city and fled to Qiūcí,
seeking refuge in its eastern territory.
Shè'ěr sent troops in pursuit,
capturing and beheading him.
In the 16th year,
Guō Xiàokè had defeated Yānqí,
establishing Lìpó Zhǔn as king,
but Ānàzhī killed him.
Now, the guilty party has been apprehended.
The New Book states: He established Tūqízhī's younger brother Pójiālì as king.
This follows the Old Book.
Follow,
cái yòng fān.
Qiūcí was greatly shaken,
and many of its defending generals abandoned their cities and fled.
Shè'ěr advanced and stationed his troops at Qìkǒu,
three hundred *li* from its capital city.
"Qìkǒu",
in the New and Old Books, is written as
"Qìshí".
The capital of Qiūcí was Yīluólú City,
backed by the White Mountain to the north,
also called Ājiétián Mountain.
General,
jí liàng fān.
Desert,
qī jì fān.
The Right Guard General Cáo Jìshū followed behind.
Arriving at Duōhè City,
the King of Qiūcí, Hēlìbùshībì, his Chancellor Nàlì, and Jiélièdiān led a force of fifty thousand to resist.
As soon as the battle lines clashed,
Shè'ěr feigned retreat with his troops,
and Qiūcí pursued with its entire force.
After traveling thirty *li*,
they joined with Jìshū's army.
Qiūcí, now fearful,
was about to retreat,
when Jìshū pressed the attack,
inflicting a major defeat on Qiūcí,
pursuing them for eighty *li* in their flight.
On the 23rd, Jiǎxū day,
the son of the late Huíhé Tǔmídù, former Left Garrison Guard Senior General Pólùn, was appointed Left Valiant Guard Senior General, Great Xílìfā, and Governor of Hànhǎi.
In the 11th month,
on the Gēngzǐ day,
the Qìdān leader Kūgē and the Xī leader Kědùzhě both led their tribes to submit to the interior.
The Qìdān tribe was made into the Sōngmò Prefecture.
Dù Yòu said: The land of Sōngmò
lies north of Liǔchéng Commandery.
Furthermore, their separate leaders such as Dájī and others were made into nine prefectures including Qiàoluò,
each with their Rǔhé leaders appointed as Prefects.
The prefectures were Qiàoluò, Wúféng, Yǔlíng, Báilián, Túhé, Wàndān, Pǐlí, Chìshān, and together with Sōngmò Prefecture, they made nine.
Qiào,
qī xiào fān.
Kědùzhě was made Governor;
furthermore, their separate leaders such as Āhuì and others were made into five prefectures including Ruòshuǐ,
also each with their Rǔhé leaders appointed as Prefects.
The prefectures were Ruòshuǐ, Qílí, Luòhuái, Tàilǔ, and Kěyě.
On the Xīnchǒu day,
the Eastern Barbarian Commandant office was established in Yíng Prefecture.
In the 12th month,
on the Gēngwǔ day,
the Crown Prince completed the construction of the Dàcí'ēn Temple for Empress Wéndé.
*Xījīng Zájì*: In the outer city of the Western Capital,
on the third bridge east of the Zhūquè Street,
the first street east of the Imperial City, Jìnyè Ward,
the former site of the Suí dynasty's Wúlòu Temple,
the Crown Prince built the temple on this land,
to pray for blessings for Empress Wéndé.
Bamboos and trees were dense and deep,
making it the foremost scenic spot in the capital.
*Yōng Lù* says: The Cí'ēn Temple is on the third street east of Zhūquè Street,
the fifteenth ward from north to south,
named Jìnchāng Ward.
The temple faces the Huángqú Canal to the south,
with dense bamboos and trees.
For,
yú wèi fān.
The King of Qiūcí, Bùshībì, having been defeated,
fled and held the capital city.
Āshǐnà Shè'ěr advanced his army and pressed him,
and Bùshībì fled west with light cavalry.
Shè'ěr captured his city,
and had the Protector-General of Ānxī, Guō Xiàokè, guard it.
The Prefect of Shā Prefecture Sū Hǎizhèng and the Imperial Equipage Attendant Xuē Wànbèi led elite cavalry in pursuit of Bùshībì.
After traveling six hundred *li*,
Bùshībì, in dire straits,
held out in Bōhuàn City.
From the Ānxī headquarters, going west out of Zhèjué Pass,
crossing the Báimǎ River for over four hundred *li* leads to Bōhuàn City.
Cavalry,
qí jì fān.
Lead,
read as shuài;
same below.
In the intercalary month,
on the Dīngchǒu day,
they captured it,
seizing Bùshībì and Jiélièdiān.
Nàlì escaped alone,
secretly leading troops from the Western Tūjué along with over ten thousand of his own country's soldiers,
to launch a surprise attack on Xiàokè.
Xiàokè was encamped outside the city.
Some people of Qiūcí warned him,
but Xiàokè paid no heed.
Nàlì arrived suddenly,
and Xiàokè led his troops, over a thousand men, intending to enter the city,
but Nàlì's men had already scaled the walls.
Surrendered Hú within the city responded in concert with them,
together attacking Xiàokè.
Arrows and blades fell like rain,
and Xiàokè could not withstand them.
As he was about to go back out,
he died at the western gate.
Great turmoil erupted in the city.
The Director of the Granaries Section, Cuī Yìchāo,
The Granaries Section Director,
is in charge of managing the empire's granaries and storage,
receiving tax grain,
and disbursing salaries and provisions.
It belongs to the Ministry of Revenue.
Yìchāo accompanied the army in this official capacity.
He guarded the military supplies and materiel,
and fought the Qiūcí forces within the city.
Cáo Jìshū and Hán Wēi were also encamped outside the city,
and attacked from the northwest corner of the city.
Nàlì retreated only after a night,
leaving over three thousand heads severed.
The city then began to settle.
Over ten days later,
Nàlì again led over ten thousand Qiūcí people from north of the mountains towards the capital.
North of the mountains,
likely refers to the area north of the White Mountain.
Towards,
qī yù fān.
They were soundly defeated,
with eight thousand heads taken.
Nàlì fled alone on horseback,
but the people of Qiūcí captured him,
and delivered him to the army headquarters.
Āshǐnà Shè'ěr had, before and after, captured five of their major cities.
He sent the Left Guard Commandant Quán Zhīfǔ to the various cities,
explaining the consequences of resistance and submission.
All came forward in succession to request surrender,
totaling over seven hundred cities captured,
and tens of thousands of men and women taken captive.
Shè'ěr then summoned their elders,
proclaimed the imperial majesty and authority,
and explained the purpose of the punitive expedition.
He established the king's younger brother, the Yèhù, as king;
the people of Qiūcí were greatly pleased.
The Western Regions were shaken with fear.
The Western Tūjué, Yútián, and Ān states vied to present camels, horses, and army provisions.
Shè'ěr erected a stone to record his achievements and then returned.
On the 27th, Wùyín day,
the Qūnqiū Circuit Campaign Commander, Left Valiant Guard General Āshǐnà Hèlǔ, was appointed Nífú Shābōluó Yèhù,
and bestowed with drums and banners,
to summon and subdue the Western Tūjué who had not submitted.
Giving Hèlǔ these trappings of authority
only hastened his rebellion.
Valiant,
jiān yáo fān.
Banner,
tú dào fān.
On the 28th, Guǐwèi day,
the Sīnlú Chancellor Jīn Chūnqiū and his son Wénwáng came for an audience.
Chūnqiū
was the younger brother of Zhēndé.
The Emperor appointed Chūnqiū as a Special Advanced Attendant,
and Wénwáng as Left Martial Guard General.
Chūnqiū requested to change his ceremonial dress to follow that of the Central Kingdom,
and winter garments from the palace were bestowed upon him.
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the Xīnhài day,
the King of Qiūcí, Bùshībì, along with his chancellor Nàlì and others, arrived at the capital.
The Emperor reprimanded them but then released them,
appointing Bùshībì as General of the Left Martial Guard.
2. The Túmòzhī and other southwestern barbarians submitted to the interior,
and their territory was made into the four prefectures of Bàng, Wàng, Lǎn, and Qiū,
placed under the jurisdiction of the Lǎngzhōu Military Governor's Office.
The Túmòzhī barbarians were located west of the Cuàn barbarians.
"Lǎngzhōu"
should be
"Lángzhōu."
In the first year of the Wǔdé era,
the southern region was opened up,
and the old Nánníngzhōu was re-established.
In the eighth year of the Zhēnguān era,
it was renamed Lángzhōu,
because the area originally belonged to the Yèláng Kingdom.
3. The Emperor, because the Tūjué Chēbí Kèhán had not come to court,
dispatched Right Valiant Guard General Gāo Kǎn to mobilize troops from the Huíhé, Púgǔ, and others to attack him.
When the troops entered his territory,
various tribes surrendered one after another.
Báxīmì Tútún Féiluóchá surrendered,
and his territory was made into Xīnlízhōu.
The Old Book states: Chēbí's eldest son, Jiémàntuó,
originally governed the Báxīmì tribe,
and sent his son Ānshuò to court.
The Emperor praised him,
and established Xīnlízhōu for him.
Court,
pronounced as zhí yáo fān.
Surrender,
pronounced as hù jiāng fān.
Examination of discrepancies says: The Gāozōng Shílù states:
"Initially,
the Tūjué Chēbí Kèhán sent his son Chēbōluó to present tribute,
Tàizōng dispatched an envoy to summon him,
but he did not come.
Tàizōng was greatly angered,
and dispatched Right Valiant Guard General Gāo Kǎn to lead Huíhé, Púgǔ, and other troops to attack him.
His subordinate tribes surrendered one after another.
His son Jiémàntuó, who originally governed the Báxīmì tribe,
tearfully advised his father,
requesting to return to the state;
Chēbí did not listen.
Jiémàntuó then turned against his father and came to surrender,
and his territory was made into Xīnlízhōu."
The Old Biography states:
"In the twenty-third year,
Right Valiant Guard General Gāo Kǎn was secretly dispatched to lead Huíhé, Púgǔ, and other troops to attack him.
His chieftains, Gēluólùnízhíquè Xìlìfā, Nǎibásèfú, Chùmùkūn, Mòhèduō Xìjīn, and others,
led their tribes,
turned against Chēbí,
and surrendered one after another.
Chēbí's eldest son Jiémàntuó originally governed the Báxīmì tribe.
Before Chēbí was defeated,
he sent his son Ānshuò to court.
Tàizōng praised him,
appointed him General of the Left Garrison Guard,
and further established Xīnlízhōu to govern his people."
Now follow the Tàizōng Shílù.
4. In the second month,
on the Bǐngxū day,
the Yáochí Military Governor's Office was established.
This name was derived from the "Mùtiānzǐ Zhuàn," where the Queen Mother of the West feasted the Son of Heaven at Yáochí.
On the Wùzǐ day,
Left Guard General Āshǐnà Hèlǔ was appointed as Military Governor of Yáochí.
5. In the third month,
on the Bǐngchén day,
the Fēngzhōu Military Governor's Office was established,
with Yānrán Protector Lǐ Sùlì concurrently serving as Military Governor.
6. Last winter there was a drought,
and only now did rain come.
On the Xīnyǒu day,
the Emperor, despite his illness, went to the Xiǎndào Gate,
and issued a general pardon.
On the Dīngmǎo day,
he ordered the Crown Prince to handle government affairs at the Jīnyè Gate.
According to the Táng Liù Diǎn: The Gatekeeper is in charge of the capital city gates, imperial city gates, palace gates, and various other gates.
Gates like Míngdé are capital city gates,
gates like Zhūquè are imperial city gates,
gates like Chéngtiān are palace city gates,
gates like Jiādé are palace gates,
and gates like Tàijí are hall gates.
The various gates leading to the interior,
together with the Shànggé Gate,
Xiǎndào and Jīnyè,
are these also gates leading to the interior?
Maps and records cannot fully document them.
7. In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Yǐhài day,
the Emperor traveled to Cuìwēi Palace.
8. The Emperor said to the Crown Prince:
"Lǐ Shìjì has abundant talent and wisdom,
but you have no favor with him,
and I fear he will not be loyal.
I will now demote him.
If he departs immediately,
after I die,
you can later appoint him as Chief Minister,
and trust him closely;
if he hesitates and looks back,
you should kill him."
In the fifth month,
on the Wùwǔ day,
Lǐ Shìjì, who held the title of Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn, was appointed as Military Governor of Diézhōu.
Shìjì received the edict,
and left without returning home.
History records that Tàizōng used strategy to control Lǐ Shìjì,
and Shìjì also used strategy to serve his lord.
Dù Yòu said: Diézhōu is 1,340 lǐ from the capital.
Sūn Miǎn said: From the Qín to the Wèi,
Diézhōu was occupied by various Qiāng tribes.
Emperor Wǔ of the Zhōu expelled the Qiāng,
and then established Diézhōu,
named after the overlapping mountains.
9. On the Xīnyǒu day,
the Grand Preceptor of the Three Excellencies, Duke Jǐngwǔ of Wèi, Lǐ Jìng, passed away.
10. The Emperor's dysentery worsened severely,
and the Crown Prince stayed by his side day and night,
sometimes not eating for several days,
and his hair even turned white in places.
The Emperor wept and said:
"You are so filial and loving,
what regret do I have in dying!"
On the Dīngmǎo day,
his condition became critical,
and he summoned Zhǎngsūn Wújì into the Hánfēng Hall.
Hánfēng Hall
is in Cuìwēi Palace.
He reached out and touched Wújì's chin,
and Wújì wept,
overcome with grief;
the Emperor ultimately could not speak,
and thus ordered Wújì to leave.
On the Jǐsì day,
he again summoned Wújì and Chǔ Suìliáng into his bedchamber,
and said to them:
"I now entrust all future affairs to you gentlemen.
The Crown Prince is benevolent and filial,
as you know,
guide him well!"
He said to the Crown Prince:
"With Wújì and Suìliáng here,
you need not worry about the empire!"
He also said to Suìliáng:
"Wújì has been utterly loyal to me,
and I owe much of my possession of the empire
to his efforts.
After I die,
do not let slanderers come between you."
He then ordered Suìliáng to draft his final edict.
After a while,
the Emperor passed away.
He was fifty-three years old.
The Crown Prince embraced Wújì's neck,
wailing until he nearly fainted.
Wújì wiped away his tears,
and requested to handle various affairs to stabilize both inside and outside.
The Crown Prince continued to mourn bitterly,
and Wújì said:
"The late Emperor entrusted the ancestral temple and the state to Your Highness.
How can you act like a commoner and only weep!"
They then kept the death secret and did not announce the mourning.
On the Gēngwǔ day,
Wújì and others requested the Crown Prince to return first,
with flying cavalry, elite troops, and veteran generals following.
On the Xīnwèi day,
the Crown Prince entered the capital city.
The late Emperor's horse-drawn carriage,
with guards as usual,
followed the Crown Prince and arrived,
halting at the Liǎngyí Hall.
Yú Zhìníng, Left Tutor of the Crown Prince, was appointed as Palace Attendant,
and Junior Supervisor of the Household of the Crown Prince Zhāng Xíngchéng concurrently served as Palace Attendant.
Gāo Jìfǔ, Acting Minister of Justice, Right Tutor of the Crown Prince, and concurrently Vice Minister of Personnel, was appointed concurrently as Secretariat Director.
On the Rénshēn day,
mourning was announced at the Tàijí Hall,
the final edict was proclaimed,
and the Crown Prince ascended the throne.
Tàijí Hall
is the main audience hall of the Western Palace.
Mourning was announced here,
and the Crown Prince ascended the throne before the coffin.
The state cannot be left without a ruler;
ordinary minor affairs
are entrusted to the relevant officials.
Princes serving as military governors or prefects
are all permitted to come for mourning,
except for Prince Pú, Lǐ Tài.
The Liáodōng campaign and various construction projects were halted.
Several hundred foreigners serving at court or who had come to present tribute,
upon hearing of the mourning, all wailed in grief,
cutting their hair, slashing their faces, and slicing their ears,
so that blood flowed and stained the ground.
In the sixth month,
on the first day, jiaxu,
Emperor Gāozōng ascended the throne,
and granted amnesty to the empire.
On the 11th day, dingchou,
Lǐ Jì, the military governor of Diézhōu, was appointed as Tejin, concurrent Inspector of Luòzhōu Prefecture, and Guardian of the Luòyáng Palace.
Lǐ Shìjì removed
the character "shì"
from his name,
to avoid the taboo of Tàizōng's two-character name.
Shǒu (guardian)
is pronounced shǒu.
Previously,
regarding Tàizōng's two-character name,
an order was issued that the empire need not avoid using the characters separately;
by this time,
official titles that violated the late emperor's taboo began to be changed.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: According to the Qūlǐ,
mourning ends and taboos begin.
The commentary states: This is to revere the names of spirits and deities.
Huì (taboo)
means to avoid.
The living do not avoid each other's names.
The Marquis of Wèi was named È,
and there was a senior official also named È;
ruler and subject having the same name
was not criticized in the Spring and Autumn Annals.
According to the seventh year of Zhāogōng,
Marquis È of Wèi died.
The Gǔliáng Commentary states: In the first year of Zhāogōng, there was a Qí È of Wèi.
Now, why is there a Marquis È of Wèi?
It is said that ruler and subject had the same name,
and a gentleman does not deprive others of the names given by their parents.
On the 13th day, guǐwèi,
Zhǎngsūn Wújì was appointed as Grand Commandant,
concurrently serving as Inspector of the Secretariat,
and overseeing the affairs of the Departments of State Affairs and the Chancellery.
Wújì firmly declined to oversee the Department of State Affairs,
and the emperor permitted it,
still ordering him to serve as Grand Commandant with the rank of Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn.
According to the Táng system: the Three Dukes held the first rank.
Wújì, having become Grand Commandant,
was ordered to hold the rank of Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn;
this was a lapse in the court's deliberations at the time.
On guǐsì,
Lǐ Jì was appointed as Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn.
After Āshǐnà Shè'ěr conquered Qiūcí,
the Chief Clerk of the Campaign, Xuē Wànbèi, requested to use military might to persuade Fúshéxìn, the king of Yútián, to come to court,
and Shè'ěr agreed.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on jǐyǒu,
Fúshéxìn followed Wànbèi to court,
and an edict ordered him to pay respects before the imperial coffin.
In the eighth month,
on guǐyǒu,
at night,
an earthquake occurred,
with Jìnzhōu suffering the most severely,
crushing over five thousand people to death.
On gēngyín,
Emperor Wén was buried at the Zhāolíng Mausoleum.
The Zhāolíng Mausoleum is located sixty li northwest of Lǐquán County, Jīngzhào, on Jiǔzōng Mountain.
After Táng Tàizōng,
subjects and officials generally referred to their ruler by his temple name;
was it not because descendants, subjects, and the people also found fault with the excessive and often inaccurate posthumous titles,
and the ancient principle of honoring ancestors for their merits and virtue had faded!
The emperor sent someone to convey that the previous decree did not permit it.
Fourteen chieftains of barbarian tribes who had been captured and subdued by the late emperor, such as Xiélì,
all had stone statues carved in their likeness,
with their names inscribed and placed inside the Northern Sima Gate.
On dīngyǒu,
Xǔ Jìngzōng, the Minister of Rites, memorialized that the temple of the Hóngnóng Prefecture Lord should be dismantled.
The Hóngnóng Prefecture Lord
was Zhòng'ěr, the Grand Administrator of Hóngnóng in Wèi,
who was Gāozōng's seventh-generation ancestor;
as the kinship had expired, the temple should be dismantled.
This was approved.
The Grand Temple has eastern and western side chambers,
flanking the main chamber on both sides,
hence called side chambers.
In the ninth month,
on yǐmǎo,
Lǐ Jì was appointed as Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.
This was in accordance with the late emperor's final decree.
In winter,
the tenth month,
the various tribes of the Tūjué were organized into five prefectures, including Shèlì, subordinate to the Yúnzhōng Area Command.
The five prefectures: Shèlì Prefecture, Sīpì Prefecture, Āshǐnà Prefecture, Chuò Prefecture, and Báidēng Prefecture.
History only records Sūnóng Prefecture, Ādé Prefecture, Zhíshī Prefecture, and Báyán Prefecture;
the other two prefectures are missing.
On yǐhài,
the emperor asked Táng Lín, the Chief Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, about the number of prisoners,
and he replied:
"There are currently over fifty prisoners,
only two of whom deserve death."
The emperor was pleased.
The emperor once reviewed the prisoners,
and many of those sentenced by the former minister cried out claiming injustice,
while those sentenced by Lín alone remained silent.
The emperor, puzzled, asked the reason.
The prisoners said:
"Under Minister Táng's judgment,
there was originally no injustice."
The emperor sighed for a long time,
and said:
"Should not those who administer justice be like this!"
The emperor appointed Nòngzàn, the Tsanpo of Tǔbō, as Commandant of the Imperial Carriage.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn established three commandants: Commandant of the Imperial Carriage,
Commandant of the Imperial Cavalry,
and Commandant of the Cavalry.
The Táng used Commandant of the Cavalry as an honorary title,
Commandant of the Imperial Carriage was conferred on those who married princesses,
and Commandant of the Imperial Carriage was no longer awarded.
The Tsanpo sent a letter to Zhǎngsūn Wújì and others, saying:
"The Son of Heaven has just ascended the throne;
if there are disloyal subjects,
I shall lead troops to the state to suppress and eliminate them."
The Tǔbō, upon Tàizōng's passing,
naturally developed a contemptuous attitude toward the Central Kingdom.
In the twelfth month,
an edict was issued for Prince Pú, Tài, to establish a household with officials,
with carriages, attire, precious delicacies,
specially granted exceptional treatment.
Emperor Gāozōng, the Celestial Emperor, Great Sage, Greatly Filial and Venerable, First Part, First Section
His taboo name was Zhì,
courtesy name Wéishàn,
childhood name Zhìnú,
the ninth son of Tàizōng.
In the first year of Wénmíng,
he was posthumously titled Celestial Emperor,
temple name Gāozōng;
in the eighth year of Tiānbǎo,
the honorific title Gāozōng, Celestial Emperor, Great Sage Emperor was added;
in the thirteenth year,
the honorific title Gāozōng, Celestial Emperor, Great Sage, Greatly Filial and Venerable Emperor was added.
First year of Yǒnghuī
(gēngxū, 650)
In spring,
the first month,
on the first day, xīnchǒu,
the era name was changed.
On bǐngwǔ,
Lady Wáng was established as empress.
The empress
was the granddaughter of Sīzhèng.
Wáng Sīzhèng defended Yǐngchuān for Western Wèi,
and perished under Eastern Wèi.
On jǐwèi,
Zhāng Xíngchéng was appointed as Palace Attendant.
On xīnyǒu,
the emperor summoned the assembly envoys,
and said to them:
"We have just ascended the throne;
if there are matters inconvenient for the people, you should fully state them,
and if not exhaustive, submit sealed memorials."
From then on, ten prefectural governors were daily brought into the inner court,
to inquire about the people's hardships,
and their governance.
A man from Luòyáng, Lǐ Hóngtài, falsely accused Zhǎngsūn Wújì of plotting rebellion,
and the emperor ordered his immediate execution.
Wújì and Chǔ Suìliáng worked together in assisting governance,
and the emperor also respected and treated the two with courtesy,
humbly listening to them.
With the emperor's high regard for the two as such,
Empress Wǔ slandered and removed them,
even pushing them into the abyss without regret.
The harm caused by cunning women has long been known.
The people were prosperous and peaceful,
with the lingering legacy of the Zhēnguàn era.
Tàizōng's daughter, Princess Héngshān, was to marry into the Zhǎngsūn family,
and the officials considered that the mourning period had been publicly concluded,
wishing to have the wedding this autumn.
Yú Zhìníng submitted a memorial stating:
"Emperor Wén of Hàn established the system,
originally for the sake of the empire's people.
The princess's mourning attire was originally the most severe;
even if the attire is removed according to precedent,
how can emotions change according to precedent?
I request to wait until the three-year mourning is completed for the wedding."
The emperor followed this.
In the second month,
on xīnmǎo,
the imperial son Xiào was enfeoffed as Prince of Xǔ,
Shàngjīn as Prince,
and Sùjié as Prince of Yōng.
The emperor's consort, Lady Zhèng, bore Xiào,
Lady Yáng bore Shàngjīn,
and Lady Xiāo Shū bore Sùjié.
Yōng
is pronounced yōng.
7. In summer,
in the fifth month,
on the Rénxū day,
the Tǔbō (Tibetan) Tsanpo (king), Nòngzàn, died.
His legitimate son had died early,
so his grandson was established as Tsanpo.
The Tsanpo was young and weak,
and all government affairs were decided by the Chief Minister, Lù Dōngzàn.
Lù Dōngzàn was intelligent, perceptive, and sternly dignified.
In conducting military campaigns, he had methods.
The reason Tǔbō became powerful and strong,
awing and subjugating the Dī and Qiāng peoples,
was all due to his strategies.
8. In the sixth month,
Gāo Kǎn attacked the Tūjué (Turks),
reaching the Āxī Mountains.
The Qèbí Kèhán summoned the troops of the various tribes, but none came.
He fled with several hundred cavalry.
Gāo Kǎn led elite cavalry in pursuit to the Jīnshān (Altai Mountains),
captured him, and brought him back.
His followers all surrendered.
9. Earlier,
Āshǐnà Shè'ěr had captured the Qiūcí (Kucha) king Bùshībì,
and established his younger brother as king.
(This event is recorded in the 26th year of Tàizōng's Zhēnguàn reign.)
Their chieftains contended for the throne,
attacking each other in turn.
In autumn,
in the eighth month,
on the Rénwǔ day,
an imperial edict ordered that Bùshībì be restored as king of Qiūcí,
sent him back to his country,
to pacify his people.
10. In the ninth month,
on the Gēngzǐ day,
Gāo Kǎn brought the captured Qèbí Kèhán to the capital.
He was pardoned,
appointed General of the Left Martial Guard,
and his remaining followers were settled at the Yùdūjūn Mountains.
(The character 處 [chǔ] is pronounced chǔ, according to Chānglǚ's gloss.)
Gāo Kǎn was made a Wèi General.
The Táng did not have a "Wèi General" position;
there must be a missing character before the character "Wèi"
Two Protectorates were established: the Dānyú and the Hànhǎi.
The Dānyú Protectorate administered the three Commanderies of Lángshān, Yúnzhōng, and Sānggān,
and fourteen prefectures including Sūnóng;
the Hànhǎi Protectorate administered the seven Commanderies of Hànhǎi, Jīnwēi, Xīnlí, etc.,
and eight prefectures including Xiān'è;
each had their chieftains appointed as Prefects or Commanders.
The New History records
"twenty-four Sūnóng prefectures",
while the Old History records
"fourteen prefectures".
Furthermore, examining later events, in the first year of the Tiāolù reign,
the two tribes of Wēnfù and Fèngzhí rebelled,
and twenty-four prefectures all rebelled in response,
thus
the character "two"
(i.e., twenty) is correct.
However, the Dānyú Protectorate's recorded jurisdictions in history
include four prefectures such as Sūnóng,
five prefectures such as Shělì, and the four prefectures of Yùshè, Yìshī, Bēishī, and Chìlüè under the Sānggān Commandery,
and the three prefectures of Hèlǔ, Géluó, and Diē under the Hūyán Commandery,
amounting to only nineteen prefectures.
The other five prefectures are lost,
with no record.
There were also the Dìngxiāng and Hūyán Commanderies but no Lángshān Commandery,
indicating that their establishment, abolition, division, and merger
cannot be detailed.
The Lángshān Commandery
was abolished and made a prefecture in the third year of the Xiǎnqìng reign.
"Jīnwēi"
should be
"Jīnwēi".
The Hànhǎi Protectorate administered the six Commanderies of Hànhǎi, Jīnwēi, Xīnlí, Yōulíng, Guīlín, and Jiānkūn,
with one lost;
and the eight prefectures of Xiān'è, Jùnjī, Yúwú, Jīluò, Jūyán, Tiányán, Yúxī, Húnhé, and Zhúlóng.
Sòng Bái said: The Zhènwǔ Army was formerly the Dānyú Protectorate,
located at the Shènglè County of the Hàn Dynasty's Dìngxiāng Commandery,
south of the Yīn Mountains,
north of the Yellow River,
120 lǐ southwest to the East Shòuxiáng City.
The Hànhǎi Protectorate was later moved to the homeland of the Huíhé.
(The character 乾 [gān] is pronounced gān.)
11. On the Guǐhài day,
the Emperor went hunting,
encountered rain,
and asked the Remonstrance Official, Chānglè Gǔ Nàlǜ:
"How can an oiled garment be made not to leak?"
(The Zhìgǔzi says: Only the method of oiling silk and oiled hats began in the Chén Dynasty.)
(The character 樂 [lè] is pronounced lè.)
"If made with tiles,
it certainly will not leak."
The Emperor was pleased,
and because of this, he stopped the hunt.
12. Lǐ Jì firmly requested to be relieved of his duties.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the Wùchén day,
Lǐ Jì was relieved of his post as Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs,
and made Kaifu Yitong Sansi and Tong Zhongshu Menxia Sanpin.
13. On the Jǐwèi day,
the Investigating Censor, Yángwǔ Wéi Sīqiān
(Yángwǔ County
belonged to Hénán Commandery in the Hàn Dynasty,
and since the Jìn Dynasty, it has belonged to Xíngyáng Commandery.)
(The character 監 [jiān] is pronounced jiān, according to the gloss.)
The Secretariat was responsible for receiving tribute from all quarters and handling memorials and communications,
hence there were interpreters.
(The character 劾 [hé] is pronounced hé, according to the gloss,
also pronounced hé.)
Wéi Sīqiān memorialized:
"The establishment of official price assessments
is for meeting state needs.
For transactions among officials,
how can they be fixed according to the official assessment!
Ruì Cè manipulated the law through documents,
pandering to subordinates and deceiving superiors,
a crime deserving execution."
On that day,
Chǔ Suìliáng was demoted to Prefect of Tóngzhōu,
and Ruì Cè to Prefect of Xúnzhōu.
Sīqiān's given name was Rényuē,
but he was known by his courtesy name.
14. In the twelfth month,
on the Gēngwǔ day,
the Commander of Zǐzhōu, Xiè Wànsuì, the Commander of Yǎnzhōu, Xiè Fǎxīng, and the Commander of Qiánzhōu, Lǐ Mèngcháng, campaigned against the rebellious Lǎo people of Yǎnzhōu.
("Zǐzhōu"
should be
"Zāngzhōu".
In the third year of the Wǔdé reign,
the chieftain of the Zāngkē barbarians, Xiè Lóngyǔ, surrendered,
and his territory was made into Zāngzhōu.
"Yǎnzhōu"
should be
"Chōngzhōu",
established in the third year of the Wǔdé reign,
from a separate branch of the Zāngkē barbarians.
Yǎnzhōu
was also a barbarian prefecture,
established in the fourth year of the Zhēnguàn reign.
All belonged to the Qiánzhōu Commander's jurisdiction.
(The character 黔 [qián] is pronounced qián.)
(The character 獠 [lǎo] is pronounced lǎo, according to the gloss.)
They were killed by the Lǎo people.
1. In spring,
in the first month,
on the Yǐsì day,
the Vice Director of the Chancellery, Yǔwén Jié, and the Vice Director of the Secretariat, Liǔ Shì, were both made Tong Zhongshu Menxia Sanpin.
(Liǔ Shì
was the son of Liǔ Hēng's elder brother.
Liǔ Hēng
was the grandson of Liǔ Qìng, Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs of the Western Wèi,
and the son-in-law of Dòu Dàn.
Liǔ Hēng's wife was the daughter of the Princess of Xiāngyáng.)
2. The General of the Left Rapid as Tigers Guard and Commander of Yáochí, Āshǐnà Hèlǔ,
gathered the scattered and dispersed,
and his tents and followers gradually increased.
Hearing of Tàizōng's death,
he plotted to attack and seize the two prefectures of Xī and Tíng.
The Prefect of Tíngzhōu, Luò Hóngyì, learned of his plot,
memorialized about it,
and the Emperor sent the Interpreter, Qiáo Bǎomíng, to gallop there and console and pacify him.
Qiáo Bǎomíng persuaded Hèlǔ
to send his eldest son, Diéyùn, to serve in the palace guard.
He was appointed Central General of the Right Rapid as Tigers Guard,
but was soon sent back.
Diéyùn then persuaded his father to lead his followers west,
where they defeated the Yǐpí Shèkuì Kèhán,
annexed his followers,
and established their headquarters at Shuānghé and Qiānquán.
From Shuānghé southwest to Hèlǔ's headquarters was 200 lǐ.
Qiānquán was within the territory of the Shíguó,
and was also southwest of Hèlǔ's headquarters.
The New History says: West from Sùyè City 400 lǐ to Qiānquán,
a land extending over 200 lǐ,
with the Snowy Mountains to the south,
flat land on three sides,
with many springs and pools,
hence the name.
The five Chuò of the Duōlù tribe and the five Èjīn of the Nǔshībì tribe all submitted to him.
He had several hundred thousand victorious troops,
allied with the Yǐpí Duōlù Kèhán,
and the Chùyuè, Chùmì, and many states of the Western Regions submitted to him.
He appointed Diéyùn as Mòhèduō Yèhù.
3. The king of Yānqí, Póqiélì, died.
The people petitioned to re-establish the former king, Tūqízhī.
In summer,
in the fourth month,
an edict appointed Tūqízhī as General of the Right Martial Guard,
and sent him back to his country.
4. Jīnzhōu Cìshǐ, Téngwáng Lǐ Yuányīng, was arrogant, extravagant, and unrestrained.
While residing in mourning,
he hunted and roamed without restraint.
He repeatedly opened the city gates at night,
troubling and harassing the common people.
Sometimes he would shoot people with pellets from a slingshot,
or bury people in the snow for amusement and laughter.
The Emperor sent him a letter sternly reprimanding him,
and said:
"The ways to seek pleasure
are also many and varied.
Jìnlínggōng was a depraved ruler—
how is he worthy of being taken as a model!
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
'Jìnlínggōng did not act as a ruler should;
he shot pellets at people from a tower to watch them dodge the pellets.'
I cannot
bring you to justice according to the law,
so now I am writing to give you a 'lower-upper' evaluation to shame your heart."
Lǐ Yuányīng and Jiǎngwáng Lǐ Yùn both were fond of amassing wealth.
The Emperor once bestowed five hundred bolts of silk each upon the various princes,
but only these two princes were excluded.
He issued an edict saying:
"Uncle Téng and Elder Brother Jiǎng can manage their own affairs;

Give them two cartloads of hemp to use as strings for coins."
The two princes were greatly ashamed.

cú làng fān.)

Wújì, as the Emperor's maternal uncle assisting in governance,

I wish to make them submit.
West of that Bónòng connects with Huángguā, Yèyú, and the Xī'ěr River.

with Lake Yèyú,

They are more numerous than in the Shǔ region,

Now, taking advantage of the defeat of the Báishuǐ troops,

The Minister of Justice Lǐ Dàorù memorialized:

The imperial stables
means the inner stables.
"Dàorù is a judicial official;

I am blaming myself,

As soon as I ascended the tower yesterday,

The actions of an emperor

I have already burned this jū,

The rest all gathered and held strategic strongholds,

Màozhōu:
Checking the new and old records, it is not found;

Empress Wáng had no sons.

How many

The present

people of the Táng often used this phrase.
He was the son of Shìlián.

Prince Pú

Fángzhōu

the monk Zhìxù and several others privately served the princess,

held a rank of 7b,

He was responsible for managing women's work within the palace,
overseeing the registration of palace women,
and handling their additions and removals.
The character "禨"

and also "jì."
Previously,
the Commandant-escort Xuē Wànchè

The character "先"

He was transferred to the post of Prefect of Níngzhōu,

Yuánjǐng's daughter was married to Yì'ài's younger brother, Yìzé,

Yuánjǐng once said himself

The Commandant-escort Chái Lìngwǔ,
son of Chái Shào,

Princess Bālíng
was Emperor Tàizōng's daughter.

Princess Gāoyáng plotted to depose Yìzhí,

Yìzhí also reported the crimes of Yì'ài and the princess,

"Their crimes are full and their wickedness ripe,

The emperor ordered Zhǎngsūn Wújì to investigate the matter,

The mother of the Minister of Works and Commander of Ānzhōu, Prince Wú, Kè,

Kè had both civil and military talents,

Kè had long enjoyed high prestige,
