Yì'ài, aware of this,
claimed to have conspired with Kè,

This matter is recorded in Volumes 196 and 197, the 17th year of the Zhēnguàn era.
In the 1st year of spring,
on the 2nd month,
on the Jiǎshēn day,

The emperor tearfully said to his attending ministers:

Wànchè loudly exclaimed before his execution:

Before Prince Wú Kè died,

On the Yǐyǒu day,
the Palace Attendant and concurrently Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent, Yǔwén Jié,

The character "夏"

The character "骁"

were exiled to Lǐngbiǎo.

During the early Táng dynasty, it belonged to Chūnzhōu.
The practice of offering sacrifices to Fáng Xuánlíng alongside the imperial ancestors was abolished.
Zhèng Qiáo said: Pángēng stated: "Now I make a great offering to the former kings,

all those who had rendered meritorious service were sacrificed to in the Great Winter Sacrifice.
According to Hàn dynasty regulations,
meritorious officials were sacrificed to in the courtyard.

In the 2nd year, the Kaifu Yitong Sansi Lǐ Jì was appointed as Minister of Works.
3. Initially,
the king of Línyì, Fàn Tóulì, died.
His son Zhēnlóng succeeded him,

Jiā Dú then seized the throne for himself,

The queen was unable to govern the state effectively.
There was a man named Zhūgě Dì,

so he fled south to Zhēnlà.
Zhēnlà,
also known as Jímò,

It was 27,000 lǐ from the capital.
To the east, it bordered Chēqú;
to the west, it adjoined Piào;
to the south, it was bounded by the sea;
to the north, it connected with Dàomíng;

In the early Zhēnguàn period,
it annexed Fúnán
and took possession of its territory.
He married the queen,
and only then did the populace become settled.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on Wùzǐ,

4. In autumn,
the ninth month,
on Rénxū,
the Right Deputy Director, the Duke of Dìng of Běipíng, Zhāng Xíngchéng, passed away.

Chǔ Suìliáng was appointed Right Deputy Director,

5. In winter,
the tenth month,
on Gēngzǐ,
the Emperor traveled to the hot springs at Líshān;
on Yǐsì,

6. Initially,
a woman from Mùzhōu named Chén Shuòzhēn
(Wú Sūnquán divided Dānyáng to establish Xīn'ān Commandery,

early Dàyè period,

together with her brother-in-law Zhāng Shūyìn raised troops in rebellion,

Jiǔyù Zhì: The county is 105 lǐ east of the prefecture.
Xiàng Ānshì said: Tónglú County,
in the fourth year of Wèi Huángchū,
Wú established it,
because beside the Tóng Stream there was a large yǐ tree,
its hanging branches forming a canopy,

looking from afar like a hut,

Shuài,
read as shuài.)
Leading two thousand troops, she captured Mùzhōu and Yúqián.
(Yúqián County,
Hàn era belonged to Dānyáng Commandery,
Jìn and Sòng eras belonged to Wúxīng Commandery,
Liáng and Chén eras belonged to Qiántáng Commandery,
Suí and Táng eras belonged to Hángzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Wúyuè Chūnqiū records,
Qín relocated the great Yuè people who spoke bird language and placed them in Qián.
Kàn Yīn's Shísānzhōu Zhì:
"Qián",
read as
"qián".
Wú Lù and Dìlǐ Zhì: West of the county is Qián Mountain.
Originally,
the character "Qián"
did not have
the "water" radical,
until the Suí dynasty added
the "water" radical.
Yú,
pronounced as its usual reading.)
They were unsuccessful,
and an edict ordered the Governor of Yángzhōu, Fáng Rényù, to dispatch troops to suppress them.
Shuòzhēn sent her associate Tóng Wénbǎo with four thousand men to raid Wùzhōu.
The Prefect of Wùzhōu, Cuī Yìxuán, mobilized troops to resist them.
Among the common people, rumors spread that Shuòzhēn possessed divine powers,
and that anyone who opposed her troops would have their clan exterminated,
causing the soldiers to be terrified.
The Registrar of the Bureau of Merit, Cuī Xuánjí, said:
(The Bureaus of Merit, Granaries, Households, Military, Justice, and Works are the so-called prefectural administrative offices.)
"Raising troops with righteous cause may still fail to succeed;
how much more so relying on sorcery and deceit—
how could that last long!"
Yìxuán appointed Xuánjí as the vanguard,
and personally led the prefectural troops to follow,
reaching the Xiàhuái garrison,
where they encountered the rebels
and engaged them in battle.
His attendants used shields to protect Yìxuán,
but Yìxuán said:
"If the Prefect avoids arrows,
who among the men will fight to the death!"
He ordered them removed.
Thereupon, the soldiers fought with unified fervor,
and the rebel forces were utterly routed,
with several thousand heads taken.
He allowed the remaining rebels to surrender and confess;
advancing to the borders of Mùzhōu,
those who surrendered numbered in the tens of thousands.
In the eleventh month,
on Gēngxū,
Fáng Rényù's army joined forces,
and they captured Shuòzhēn and Shūyìn,
executing them.
The remaining rebels were all pacified.
Yìxuán was promoted to Censor-in-Chief for his merit.
(The Censor-in-Chief
is the Emperor's eyes and ears;
it is not a position for rewarding merit.
Later, Cuī Yìxuán, following the Empress's directive, prosecuted Chángsūn Wújì and others—
was this not disgracing his office!)
7. On Guǐchǒu,
the Minister of War, Cuī Dūnlǐ, was appointed as Shìzhōng.
8. In the twelfth month,
on Gēngzǐ,
the Shìzhōng, Duke Xiàn of Tiáo, Gāo Jìfǔ, passed away.
According to the rules for posthumous titles: "Extensive knowledge and many abilities is called Xiàn."
Tiáo,
pronounced tiáo.
9. This year,
the Western Turkic Yǐpí Duōlù Kèhán died.

defeated him,
and took over a thousand heads.
1. In spring,
the first month,
on Rénxū,
the Qiang chieftain Dòngjiù submitted to the court,

was the great chieftain of the Tèlàng Shēngqiāng Bǔlóu tribe.)
Jiànzhōu was a jīmí prefecture,
subordinate to the Sōngzhōu Military Governor's Office.
2. In the third month,
on Wùwǔ,
the Emperor traveled to Wànnián Palace.
(Examination of discrepancies: The Shílù records events from Wùwǔ onward
as occurring in the second month.
According to the perpetual calendar,
the second month began on Dīngchǒu,
so there was no Wùwǔ.
Wùwǔ
is the twelfth day of the third month.)
3. On Gēngshēn,
posthumous honors were added to thirteen martial and virtuous meritorious officials, including Qūtū Tōng.
Initially,
Empress Wáng had no sons,
while Xiāo Shū enjoyed favor.
Examination of discrepancies states: The New and Old Books of Táng sometimes write
"Xiāo Shū,"
sometimes
"Xiāo Liángdì."
The Veritable Records all write
"Liángdì,"
and the edict deposing Empress Wáng also says
"Lady Xiāo the Liángdì."
According to the ranks and titles of the inner palace at that time, there was no title Liángdì,
only the crown prince's palace in the Hàn dynasty had Liángdì.
It is suspected that when Emperor Gāozōng was crown prince,
Lady Xiāo was a Liángdì,
and upon his accession,
she was appointed Shū.
When the Emperor was crown prince,
he entered to attend upon Tàizōng,
saw the Talented Lady Wǔ and was pleased with her.
Talented Lady,
a rank instituted by Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
equivalent to officials receiving a thousand shí or less;
during the Sòng and Qí periods,
it was considered a sinecure;
Liáng, below the Nine Concubines,
established Five Duties and Three Duties,
the Talented Lady ranked among the Three Duties,
equivalent to Commandant-Escort;
Táng followed the Suì system,
with five Talented Ladies,
of the fifth rank proper.
Lady Wǔ followed the crowd to Ganyè Temple to become a nun.
The Cháng'ān Records state: In the fifth month of the twenty-third year of the Zhēnguàn era,
Tàizōng passed away,
that same year, the Jìdù Nunnery in Ānyè Ward was converted into Língbǎo Temple,
and all of Tàizōng's consorts were tonsured as nuns to reside there.
Chéng Dàchāng said: Comparing the Comprehensive Mirror, the Cháng'ān Records, and Lǚ Dàfáng's Map of Cháng'ān,
the Comprehensive Mirror states Lady Wǔ was at Ganyè Temple,
the Cháng'ān Records states at Ānyè Temple,
only this differs.
However, the Records can describe the temple's location and its history,
so Ānyè is correct.
The Emperor went to the temple to offer incense,
saw her,
Lady Wǔ wept,
the Emperor also wept.
Empress Wáng heard of this,
secretly ordered Lady Wǔ to grow her hair long,
and urged the Emperor to take her into the inner palace,
intending to use her to undermine Lady Xiāo's favor.
Lady Wǔ was clever and intelligent,
skilled in stratagems,
upon first entering the palace,
she used humble words and submissive demeanor to serve the Empress;
the Empress favored her,
and often praised her beauty to the Emperor.
Before long, she gained great favor,
and was appointed as Zhaoyí.
The Empress and Lady Xiāo's favor both declined,
and they joined together to slander her,
but the Emperor did not accept any of it.
The Zhaoyí wished to posthumously honor her father but had no pretext,
so she used the commendation of meritorious officials as a cover,
and Wǔ Shìhuò was included among them.
This sets the stage for the deposition of the Empress and Lady Xiāo.
Huò,
pronounced yī guó fān.
4 On the yǐchǒu day,
the Emperor went to Fèngquán Hot Springs;
Fèngquán Hot Springs are in Méi County, Qí Prefecture.
On the sì day,
he returned to Wànnián Palace.
5 In summer,
the fourth month,
Dàshí dispatched troops to attack Persia.
The state of Persia was situated west of the Dá'è River,
over fifteen thousand lǐ from the capital,
bordering Tǔhuǒluó and Kāng to the east,
adjacent to the Kěsà tribe of the Turks to the north,
and facing the sea to the southwest.
Their ancestor was King Pòsīsēnì,
a descendant branch of the Great Yuèzhī,
the king took this as his surname,
and also as the state's name.
Dù Yòu said: The state of Persia is the former territory of Tiáozhī,
a separate branch of the Great Yuèzhī,
their ancestor was King Pòsīsēnì,
hence the name.
Dàshí was originally Persian territory.
During the Dàyè era of Suì,
a Persian man herded at Jùfēnmó place,
a mountain had a beast,
which said:
"West of the mountain, three caves contain sharp weapons,
black in substance with white patterns,
he who obtains them will be king."
He went to look,
and it was as said.
The stone inscription said there would be rebellion,
so he deceived the masses, gathering desperadoes at the Héng Hé River,
plundering merchants and travelers,
fortified the western border and declared himself king,
moved the black stone and treasured it.
The people of the state went to attack,
but all were greatly defeated and returned,
thus he became strong.
The son of Yīsìhóu, Bēilùsī, fled to Tǔhuǒluó.
The Dàshí troops withdrew,
Tǔhuǒluó dispatched troops to establish Bēilùsī as King of Persia and then returned.

at night,
heavy rain fell,

this is the Xuánwǔ Gate of Wànnián Palace.
The gates of the Táng detached palaces,
generally imitated the system of the palace city.
Right Guard Commandant-Langjiàng Xuē Rénguì said:
Táng system: From the Left and Right Guards to the Left and Right Jīnwú Guards,
their subordinates each have Left and Right Zhōnglángjiàng Offices,
with Zhōnglángjiàng and Left Lángjiàng, Right Lángjiàng.
Jiàng,
pronounced jí liàng fān.
"How can there be guards on duty,
when the Son of Heaven is in danger, dare to fear death!"
He then climbed the gate beam and shouted loudly to alert those inside the palace.
The Emperor hastily went out and ascended a high place,
soon water entered the sleeping hall,

Emperor Wén of Suì established Rénshòu Palace north of Qí Prefecture.
Early in the Dàyè era,
Pǔrùn County was established.
In the second year of Yìníng,
a white qílín was captured at the palace,
thus Línyóu County was established from the palace, dividing Pǔrùn.
Rénshòu Palace,
Táng changed to Jiǔchéng Palace,
and later changed to Wànnián Palace.
Drowned,
pronounced nú dí fān.

11 In autumn,
the seventh
month,
on the dīngyǒu day,

12 On the wùxū day,
the Emperor said to officials of the fifth rank and above:
"Recently, while attending the late Emperor,
I saw officials of the fifth rank and above discussing affairs,
some would present their cases in person after the guards retired,
Táng system: During regular court sessions, all guards stand in formation,
after they retire, chief ministers and remonstrance officials present matters.
it went on all day without cease;
is it that today there are no matters,
why do you all remain silent?"
In the thirteenth year, winter,
tenth month,
41,000 people from Yōngzhōu were hired to build the outer walls of Cháng'ān,
completing the work in thirty days.
"Hired" means
compensating their labor with money or goods,
not merely conscripting their labor.
Yōng,
pronounced Yòng.
On the Guǐchǒu day,

stating:
"When Emperor Huì of Hàn walled Cháng'ān,
he soon passed away;
see the events in the twelfth scroll, third and fifth years of Emperor Huì of Hàn.
Submitted,
pronounced Shízhǎng;
same below.
There will surely be great calamity."
Yú Zhìníng and others considered Jǐngxuān's words bordering on sedition,

The Emperor said:

14. Gāolì sent its general Āngù to lead Gāolì and Mòhé troops to attack the Qìdān;

15. This year saw a great harvest,
with millet in Luòzhōu costing two and a half coins per dǒu,
and polished rice eleven coins per dǒu.
16. Empress Wáng, Xiāo Shūfēi, and Consort Wǔ Zhaoyí accused each other in turn,
but the Emperor did not believe the words of the Empress and Shūfēi,
trusting only Zhaoyí.
The Empress could not ingratiate herself with those around the Emperor;
her mother, Lady Liǔ of the State of Wèi, and her maternal uncle, Secretariat Director Liǔ Shì, when visiting the Six Palaces,
also did not observe proper etiquette.
Consort Wǔ Zhaoyí watched for those whom the Empress did not respect,
and would wholeheartedly befriend them,
sharing the rewards she received with them.
Thus, the movements of the Empress and Shūfēi
were always known to Zhaoyí,
who reported everything to the Emperor.
Although the Empress's favor had declined,
the Emperor had not yet considered deposing her.
It happened that Zhaoyí gave birth to a daughter;
the Empress, pitying the child, played with her.
After the Empress left,
Zhaoyí secretly strangled the infant,
covering her with a quilt.
When the Emperor arrived,
Zhaoyí pretended to be cheerful,
uncovering the quilt to look at the child,
and finding the girl already dead,
she immediately cried out in shock.
Asked her attendants,
they all said:
"The Empress was just here."
The Emperor angrily said:
"The Empress killed my daughter!"
Zhaoyí then wept, enumerating the Empress's crimes.
The Empress had no way to clear herself,
and from then on, the Emperor intended to depose her.
Yet he feared the senior officials would not comply,
so he went with Zhaoyí to visit Grand Commandant Zhǎngsūn Wújì at his residence,
drinking merrily and enjoying themselves greatly.
During the feast, he appointed three sons of Wújì's favorite concubine to the posts of Court Gentleman for Consultation,
and also bestowed upon Wújì ten cartloads of gold, treasures, silks, and brocades.
The Emperor then casually remarked that the Empress had no sons, hinting to Wújì,
but Wújì responded with other topics,
ultimately not complying with the Emperor's wish.
The Emperor and Zhaoyí left displeased.
Zhaoyí also had her mother, Lady Yáng, visit Wújì's residence,
repeatedly making requests,
but Wújì never agreed.
Minister of Rites Xǔ Jìngzōng also repeatedly urged Wújì,
but Wújì sternly rebuked him.
The Emperor further bestowed extraordinary gifts upon Wújì's sons, both legitimate and illegitimate,
his intent being clear.
If Wújì wished to correct his improper thoughts,
he could have declined and not accepted.
This sets the stage for Wújì's offense.
Repeatedly,
pronounced Suǒjiǎo.
Rebuked,
pronounced Zhīshé.
1. Spring,
first month,
on the Rénshēn day, the first day of the month,
the Emperor paid homage at the Zhāolíng;
on the Jiǎxū day,
he returned to the palace.
2. On the Jǐchǒu day,
Xīzhōu Circuit Campaign Commander Cáo Jìshū defeated the Húcóng, Xiǎnyǎng, and Chēlǔ tribes among others at Xiéshān,
capturing over ten cities.
Húcóng
was one of the five tribes under the jurisdiction of the Jiànshān Pacification Commissioner;
Xiǎnyǎng and Chēlǔ were also separate barbarian tribes.
"Chēlǔ"
is written as
"Dōnglǔ" in the New Book.
Xī,
pronounced Suǐ.
3. On the Gēngyín day,
the Emperor's son Lǐ Hóng was enfeoffed as Prince of Dài,
and Lǐ Xián as Prince of Lù.
4. Gāolì allied with Bǎijì and Mòhé,
invading the northern border of Xīnluó,
capturing thirty-three cities;
King Chūnqiū of Xīnluó sent an envoy seeking aid.
Second month,
on the Yǐchǒu day,
Yíngzhōu Governor Chéng Míngzhèn and Left Guard General-in-Chief Sū Dìngfāng were dispatched with troops to attack Gāolì.
5. Summer,
fifth month,
on the Rénwǔ day,
Míngzhèn and others crossed the Liáo River.
Seeing their forces were few, the Gāolì
opened their gates and crossed the Guìduān River to engage them,
according to the Old Book biography of Chéng Míngzhèn,
the Guìduān River should be southwest of Xīnchéng.
Few,
pronounced Shīzhǎo.
They were heavily defeated,
with over a thousand killed or captured,

6. On the Guǐwèi day,
Right Guard Grand General Chéng Zhījié was appointed as Commander-in-Chief of the Cōngshān Circuit Campaign.
Cōngshān is the Cōnglíng Mountains.
7. On the Rénchén day,
Hán Yuàn was appointed as Palace Attendant,
and Lái Jì as Secretariat Director.
8. Sixth month,
Consort Wǔ Zhaoyí falsely accused Empress Wáng and her mother, Lady Liǔ of the State of Wèi, of practicing witchcraft,
and an edict was issued forbidding the Empress's mother, Lady Liǔ, from entering the palace.
Autumn,
seventh month,
on the Wùyín day,
Minister of Personnel Liǔ Shì was demoted to Prefect of Suìzhōu.
As Shì traveled to Fúfēng,
in the first year of the Wǔdé era,
Qíshān was divided to establish Wéichuān County,
named after the Wéi River;
in the eighth year of the Zhēnguàn era,
it was renamed Fúfēng,
under Qízhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: the county is eighty lǐ east of the prefecture.
He was further demoted to Prefect of Róngzhōu.
Róngzhōu
was located in the lands of Nán'ān and Jiāngyáng of Hàn,
in Suí times it was Dàláo County,
under Zīzhōu.
In the first year of the Wǔdé era,
it was separated to establish Róngzhōu.
Further,
pronounced Fúyòu.
The Táng followed the Suí system,
where the rear palace had the ranks of Guì, Shū, Dé, and Xián, all equivalent to the first rank.
The Emperor wished to specially establish the rank of Chén,
appointing Consort Wǔ Zhaoyí to it.
Hán Yuàn and Lái Jì remonstrated,
stating there was no precedent for it,
and the idea was abandoned.
Examination of discrepancies: The Táng Calendar places this in the fourth month of this year,
but I follow the Veritable Records.
In the fourth month,
Hán Yuàn and Lái Jì were not yet Palace Attendant and Secretariat Director.
The Táng Calendar also states:
"Yuàn and Jì remonstrated,
but the Emperor did not listen."
According to the edict establishing Empress Wǔ,
she is still referred to as Consort Wǔ.
Thus, she was never made Chén.
I follow the Institutional History.
The Secretariat Drafter Lǐ Yìfǔ of Ráoyáng, who was disliked by Zhǎngsūn Wújì,
was demoted to the position of Sima of Bì Prefecture.
In the eighth year of the Wǔdé era,
Bì Prefecture was established by partitioning land from Shǐníng County of Bā Prefecture.
Yìfǔ secretly learned of this,
and sought advice from the Secretariat Drafter Wáng Déjiǎn of Yōuzhōu.
Déjiǎn said:
"The Emperor wishes to establish Consort Wǔ as Empress,
but hesitates and has not yet decided,
solely because he fears objections from the chief ministers.
If you can propose and establish her,
then you will turn disaster into fortune."
Yìfǔ agreed with this.
That day,
he took Déjiǎn's place on duty,
knocked on the palace gate to submit a memorial,
requesting the deposition of Empress Wáng,
and the establishment of Consort Wǔ,
to satisfy the hearts of the myriad people.
The Emperor was pleased,
summoned him for an audience,
spoke with him,
bestowed a peck of pearls,
and retained him in his former post.
Consort Wǔ also secretly sent an envoy to reward and encourage him,
and soon he was exceptionally promoted to Vice Director of the Secretariat.
Textual Analysis: The Old Biography states:
"When Emperor Gāozōng was about to establish Empress Wǔ,
Yìfǔ secretly supported and assisted,
and was promoted to Vice Director of the Secretariat, participating in the affairs of the Secretariat-Chancellery, overseeing the compilation of the national history,
and was enfeoffed as Baron of Guǎngpíng County."
The New Book's Basic Annals and Chronological Tables both state
"In the seventh month of this year,
Yìfǔ became Vice Director of the Secretariat and participated in the administration of state affairs."
The Veritable Records only states
"exceptionally promoted to Vice Director of the Secretariat."
The Chart of Chief Ministers states:
"In the eleventh month,
he became Vice Director of the Secretariat and participated in the administration of state affairs."
I now follow this.
9 On the yǐyǒu day,
the Palace Attendant Cuī Dūnlǐ was appointed as Director of the Secretariat.

The Court Physician,
with two positions,
was in charge of compounding the imperial medicines and diagnosing illnesses and prescribing treatments.
11 The Magistrate of Cháng'ān, Péi Xíngjiǎn, heard that Consort Wǔ was to be established as Empress,
and believed that the nation's disasters would certainly begin from this.
He privately discussed the matter with Zhǎngsūn Wújì and Chǔ Suìliáng.
Yuán Gōngyú heard of this,
and reported it to Consort Wǔ's mother, Lady Yáng.
Xíngjiǎn was consequently demoted to the position of Chief Clerk of the Xīzhōu Governor's Office.
According to the Táng system: The six counties of Cháng'ān, Wànnián, Hénán, Luòyáng, Tàiyuán, and Jìnyáng,
were called the Capital Counties.
The Magistrate of a Capital County,
was of the fifth rank, upper grade.
Xīzhōu,
was a Middle Governor's Office;
the Chief Clerk of a Middle Governor's Office was also of the fifth rank, upper grade.
However, being transferred from under the imperial chariot to assist in a border prefecture,
was considered a demotion.
He was the son of Péi Rénjī.
Péi Rénjī,
a Suì general,
defected to Lǐ Mì,
and was killed by Wáng Shìchōng.
12 In the ninth month,
on the wùchén day,
Xǔ Jìngzōng was appointed as Minister of Rites.
One day, the Emperor retired from court,
and summoned Zhǎngsūn Wújì, Lǐ Jì, Yú Zhìníng, and Chǔ Suìliáng into the inner palace.
Suìliáng said:
"Today's summons
is mostly about the Empress.
Since the Emperor's mind is already made up,
opposing him will certainly lead to death.
The Grand Commandant is the Emperor's maternal uncle,
the Minister of Works is a meritorious official;
we must not allow the Emperor to bear the name of killing his maternal uncle and a meritorious official.
I, Suìliáng, rose from humble origins,
without the merit of battlefield service,
yet reached this position,
and moreover received the late Emperor's trust and commission.
If I do not dispute this to the death,
how will I face the late Emperor below!"
Jì claimed illness and did not enter.
Wújì and the others arrived at the inner palace,
and the Emperor, looking at Wújì, said:
"The Empress has no sons,
while Consort Wǔ has a son.
Now I wish to establish Consort Wǔ as Empress,
what do you think?"
Suìliáng replied:
"The Empress is from a distinguished family,
and was married to Your Majesty by the late Emperor.
On his deathbed,
the late Emperor took Your Majesty's hand and said to me: 'My fine son and fine daughter-in-law,
I now entrust them to you.'
This Your Majesty heard,
the words still ring in my ears.
The Empress has not been heard to have any faults,
how can she be lightly deposed!
I dare not wrongly obey Your Majesty,
and transgress the late Emperor's command!"
The Emperor was displeased and ended the audience.
The next day, he spoke of it again.
Suìliáng said:
"If Your Majesty must change the Empress,
I humbly request that you carefully select from the noble families of the realm,
why must it be Lady Wǔ?
Lady Wǔ served the late Emperor,
as everyone knows.
The eyes and ears of the realm,
how can they be deceived?
For ten thousand generations to come,
what will they say of Your Majesty!
I beg you to reconsider carefully!
I have now offended Your Majesty,
my crime deserves death."
Thereupon, he placed his official tablet on the palace steps,
removed his headscarf, and kowtowed until his head bled, saying:
"I return Your Majesty's tablet,
I beg to be sent back to my fields and village."
The Emperor was greatly angered,
and ordered him taken out.
Consort Wǔ, from behind the curtain, loudly said:
"Why not beat this southern barbarian to death!"
Wújì said:
"Suìliáng received the late Emperor's dying command,
even if he has committed a crime, he cannot be punished."
Yú Zhìníng did not dare to speak.
Hán Yuàn took advantage of an opportunity to present a memorial,
weeping bitterly and remonstrating with utmost sincerity.
The Emperor did not accept it.
The next day, he remonstrated again,
overcome with grief,
and the Emperor ordered him to be led out.
Hán Yuàn then submitted another written memorial of remonstrance, saying:
"Even common men and women
still choose each other carefully,
how much more should the Son of Heaven!
The Empress is the motherly model for all states;
good and evil stem from her.
Therefore, Mó Mǔ assisted Huángdì,
Hàn Shū, Biǎo of Ancient and Modern People: Mó Mǔ,
Huángdì,
gave birth to Cāng Lín.
Shī Gǔ said: Mó,
pronounced 'mó';
that is Mó Mǔ.
Hé Chéngtiān's Zuǎn Wén said: Mó Mǔ
was an ugly woman,
yet Huángdì loved and favored her.
Mó,
pronounced 'mó'.
Dá Jǐ,
a beautiful woman of the Yǒusū clan,
was loved by Zhòu,
who obeyed only Dá Jǐ's words,
and ultimately lost the Yīn dynasty because of it.
Dá,
should be pronounced 'dá'.
Bāo Sì destroyed it."
These are the words from the Xiǎoyǎ poem Zhēngyuè.
Hán Yuàn's meaning was
that Mó Mǔ, though ugly, assisted Huángdì in possessing the empire,
while Dá Jǐ and Bāo Sì, with their beauty, caused the downfall of Yīn and Zhōu.
For a woman, virtue lies not in appearance.
I have often sighed in lament,
never thinking that today such defilement would tarnish our sage era.
If actions are not according to law,
what will future generations see!
Zuǒzhuàn,
these are the words of Cáo Guì remonstrating with Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ.
Do not become a laughingstock for posterity!
If your servant
can benefit the state,
even the punishment of being minced into pickled meat,
is your servant's duty!
In the past, the King of Wú did not heed Zǐxū's advice, and deer roamed in Gūsū.
Hàn Wǔ Bèi said: In the past, Zǐxū remonstrated with the King of Wú,
but the King of Wú did not listen.
Then he said,
"I now see deer roaming on the Gūsū Terrace."
Shī Gǔ said: Gūsū,
a terrace named after the mountain,
was located twenty-five lǐ southwest of the state of Wú.
Fàn Chéngdà's Wújùn Zhì said: The Gūsū Terrace was on Gūsū Mountain.
The old Tújīng says: Thirty lǐ west of Wú County.
The continued Tújīng says: Thirty-five lǐ.
Shǐjì Zhèngyì says: Thirty lǐ southwest of Wú County,
on Gūsū Mountain at the northwestern foot of Héng Mountain.
Thorns and brambles will grow in the palace courtyards,
and the ancestral temples will cease to receive blood sacrifices—
the day is not far off!"
Lái Jì submitted a memorial of remonstrance, saying:
"When a king establishes an empress,
he follows the models of Heaven and Earth,
and must choose from a renowned family of propriety and education,
one who is virtuous, gentle, and refined,
to fulfill the hopes of the realm,
and satisfy the will of the spirits.
Therefore, King Wén of Zhōu built boats to welcome Tàisì,
and thus flourished the transformation of the Guānjū,
and the common people received blessings.
Tàisì
was King Wén's [wife].
The Shī says: He fixed the auspicious day,
and personally welcomed her at the Wèi River,
building boats to form a bridge,
displaying his glory.
Tàisì assisted King Wén in establishing the royal enterprise,
therefore the Guānjū praises her virtue.
Chēng,
pronounced 'chēng'.
Zào,
pronounced 'zào'.
To make a servant girl empress
would cause the imperial line to be cut off,
and the altars of state to collapse.
This matter is seen in the Annals of Emperor Chéng of Hàn.
The disaster of the great Hàn was like this,
I beg Your Majesty to examine this carefully!"
The Emperor did not accept any of these remonstrances.
The words of Chǔ Suìliáng, Hán Yuàn, and Lái Jì were all deeply earnest and poignant.
At this time, it was not long after the Zhēnguàn era,
and the spirit of scholar-officials daring to speak out had not yet waned.
But after these three were punished,
the ministers at court merely followed Empress Wǔ's will,
how could they speak what was difficult to say!
On another day,
Lǐ Jì entered for an audience.
The Emperor asked him:
"I wish to establish Wǔ Zhāoyí as empress,
but Suìliáng stubbornly insists it cannot be done.
Since Suìliáng is a minister entrusted with the late emperor's will,
should the matter be dropped for now?"
He replied:
"This is Your Majesty's family matter,
why must you ask outsiders!"
Ever since Lǐ Jì spoke these words,
Lǐ Línfǔ adopted them to bring about Emperor Míng's disaster of killing his three sons.
The discussion about Dézōng's Shū Prince also followed this reasoning.
If not for Lǐ Bì,
the Crown Prince would have been in peril!
Xǔ Jìngzōng declared publicly at court:
"If a country bumpkin harvests an extra ten hú of wheat,
he still wants to change his wife;
how much more should the Son of Heaven, wishing to establish an empress,
have others meddling and recklessly raising objections!"
Zhāoyí ordered her attendants to report this.
On Gēngwǔ,
Suìliáng was demoted to Military Governor of Tánzhōu.
Tánzhōu
was 2,445 lǐ south of the capital.
Wáng Chóngwǔ punctuated; Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí proofread.
Sīmǎ Guāng
respectfully compiled by imperial order.
Later student from Tiāntāi.
Sixth year of Yǒnghuī
(yǐmǎo, 655)
1. Winter,
tenth month,
on Jǐyǒu,
an edict was issued stating:
"Empress Wáng and Xiāo Shūfēi plotted to administer poison,
they are deposed as commoners.
Their mothers and brothers,
are all stripped of titles,
and exiled to Lǐngnán."
Xǔ Jìngzōng memorialized:
"The official appointment document of the late Tèjìn, posthumously awarded Sikōng, Wáng Rényòu, still exists,
allowing the remaining evil of rebellion to still receive hereditary privilege.
Táng system: All who receive office are given a tally,
called an appointment document.
Sikōng,
rank Zheng Yīpǐn.
For all officials of rank three and above,
the privilege extends to great-grandsons."
This was approved.
On Yǐmǎo,
all officials submitted a petition requesting the establishment of a central palace (empress).
Then an edict was issued stating:
"The Wǔ clan is distinguished for its merits,
its status is illustrious with honors and official robes.
Previously, Wǔ was selected for the rear palace due to her talent and virtue,
her reputation was esteemed in the pepper chambers,
her virtue illuminated the orchid side chambers.
When I was formerly Crown Prince,
I specially received the late emperor's kindness,
often having her attend and accompany me,
never leaving morning or evening.
Within the palace confines,
she constantly disciplined herself,
among the consorts and concubines,
she never caused conflict or drew attention,
the sage emperor observed and understood this,
often bestowing praise and admiration,
and thus bestowed Wǔ upon me,
the matter is like that of Zhèngjūn."
Zhèngjūn,
the matter is seen in scroll 27, third year of Gānlù of Emperor Xuān of Hàn.
On Dīngsì,
a general amnesty was declared.
On this day,
the Empress submitted a memorial stating:
"Previously, when Your Majesty made your servant Chényí,
Hán Yuàn and Lái Jì opposed it face-to-face and argued at court,
the matter is seen in the previous scroll, last year.
Yuàn,
pronounced 'yuàn'.
Zhé,
pronounced 'zhé'.
Zhēng,
read as 'zhèng'.
Was this not out of deep loyalty for the state?
I beg to reward and honor them."
The Emperor showed the memorial to Yuàn and others.
Yuàn and others became even more worried and fearful,
repeatedly requesting to leave their posts,
but the Emperor did not permit it.
Eleventh month,
on Dīngmǎo, the first day,
from the palace hall, the Emperor ordered Sikōng Lǐ Jì to bestow the imperial seal and ribbons to establish Empress Wǔ.
On this day,
all officials paid respects to the Empress at the Sùyì Gate.
The former Empress Wáng shì and
the former Shūfū Xiāo shì
were both imprisoned in a separate courtyard.
The Emperor once thought of them,
and went incognito to their place.
Seeing their chambers were sealed extremely tightly,
with only a hole in the wall to pass food vessels through,
he was moved with pity and saddened.
He called out:
"Where are the Empress and the Shūfū?"
Wáng shì replied weeping:
"We convicts have become palace maids;
how can we still bear such honorable titles!"
She added:
"If Your Majesty remembers past times,
and allows us to see the sun and moon again,
we beg to name this courtyard 'Huíxīn Yuàn' (Courtyard of Repentance/Change of Heart)."
The Emperor said:
"We shall make arrangements."
When Empress Wǔ heard of this,
she was greatly enraged.
She sent people to cane Wáng shì and Xiāo shì one hundred strokes each,
cut off their hands and feet,
and threw them
into wine jars,
saying:
"Let these two hags get drunk to the bone!"
They died after several days,
and were then beheaded.
When Wáng shì first heard the edict proclaimed,
she bowed twice and said:
"May the Emperor live ten thousand years!
Since the Zhaoyí (Consort Wǔ) receives favor,
death is my lot."
The Shūfū cursed:
"That sorceress Wǔ,
to have gone this far!
May I be reborn as a cat,
and Wǔ as a rat,
and in every life seize her by the throat."
From then on, no cats were kept in the palace.
Soon after, Wáng shì's surname was changed to Mǎng shì (Serpent),
and Xiāo shì's to Xiāo shì (Owl).
Empress Wǔ repeatedly saw Wáng and Xiāo haunting her as vengeful spirits,
with disheveled hair and dripping blood as they were at death.
Later, when she moved to reside in Pénglái Palace,
she saw them again.
Therefore, she mostly stayed in Luòyáng,
and never returned to Cháng'ān for the rest of her life.
On the Jǐsì day,
Xǔ Jìngzōng memorialized:
"Since the beginning of the Yǒnghuī reign,
the state's foundation (the heir) had not been born,
so temporarily a comet was borrowed,
to exceptionally elevate the 'bright pair'.
The Dàxiàng (Great Image) of the Lí hexagram in the Yìjīng says: 'Brightness doubled constitutes Lí;
the great man in accordance with this continues the brightness and illuminates the four quarters.'
'Suì' (comet)
is pronounced xiáng suì.
The true heir descended with divine favor,
meaning Dàiwáng Lǐ Hóng,
son of Empress Wǔ,
should be established.
The torchlight should be extinguished.
Cuī Bào's Gǔjīn Zhù says: When Emperor Wén of Hàn (?)
was Crown Prince,
musicians sang four stanzas praising the Crown Prince's virtue: the first was 'The Sun's Double Radiance',
the second 'The Moon's Double Halo',
the third 'The Stars' Double Brilliance',
the fourth 'The Sea's Double Moisture'.
Zhuāngzǐ says: 'When the sun and moon have come forth, if the torch-fire is not extinguished,
is it not difficult for it to give light?'
'Chóng' (double)
is pronounced zhí lóng.
'Jué' (torch)
is pronounced jí lüè.
For a long time, the position has been wrongly occupied in the heavenly court;
the upper and lower garments have been inverted,
causing deviation from the proper position of Zhèn!
Zhèn,
is the eldest son,
who guards the altars of soil and grain and the ancestral temple,
and serves as the chief sacrificer.
Matters between father and son
are difficult for others to speak of,
as per Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's words to Tián Qiānqiū.
I would certainly incur severe punishment;
beneath the Black Dragon's chin there are contrary scales a foot across,
to touch them is death;
this illustrates that the sovereign's majesty cannot be offended.
Yet your subject is willing."
The Emperor summoned him for an audience,
questioned him,
and he replied:
"The Crown Prince
is the foundation of the state.
If the foundation is not yet correct,
the myriad states have nothing to fix their hearts upon.
Moreover, he who is now in the Eastern Palace
was born of lowly origin.
Now knowing the state already has a legitimate嫡 son,
he will certainly be uneasy.
Occupying a position while harboring self-doubt
is probably not a blessing for the ancestral temple.
I hope Your Majesty will consider this carefully."
The Emperor said:
"Lǐ Zhōng has already offered to yield."
Xǔ Jìngzōng replied:
"If he can be like Tàibó,
I hope he will quickly follow through."
2. The Western Turkic Jié Bì Dá Dù Shè repeatedly sent envoys requesting troops to attack Shābōluó Kèhán.
On the Jiǎxū day,
the Emperor sent Yuán Lǐchén, Governor of Fēng Prefecture, to confer by imperial edict the title of Kèhán upon Jié Bì Dá Dù Shè.
Lǐchén reached Suìyè City.
From Gōngyuè City he passed Sīhún Chuān,
crossed the Yīlí River to the Suìyè border,
then traveled west another thousand lǐ to Suìyè City,
which was within the jurisdiction of the Yānqí Governor's Office.
He could not proceed further.
Most of Jié Bì Dá Dù Shè's tribes had been annexed by Shābōluó,
and the remaining people were few and weak,
not supported by the other clans.
Lǐchén ultimately did not confer the title and returned.
3. Lǐ Yìfǔ, Vice Director of the Secretariat, participated in administration (as a chancellor).
Yìfǔ's appearance was gentle and respectful.
When speaking with people,
he would always smile pleasantly,
but he was cunning, sinister, jealous, and ruthless.
Therefore, contemporaries said Yìfǔ had a knife within his smile;
also, because he was soft yet harmed others,
they called him 'Lǐ the Cat'.
First year of Xiǎnqìng
(Bǐngchén, 656)
1. Spring,
first month,
on the Xīnwèi day,
Crown Prince Lǐ Zhōng was made Prince of Liáng and Governor of Liáng Prefecture;
Dàiwáng Lǐ Hóng, son of the Empress, was established as Crown Prince.
He was four years old.
After Zhōng was deposed,
his officials all feared punishment and fled into hiding;
none dared see him.
Only Lǐ Ānrén, the Right Assistant of the Heir Apparent, visited Zhōng,
weeping, bowing, and taking his leave before departing.
Ānrén
was the grandson of Lǐ Gāng.
Lǐ Gāng was renowned for his integrity between the Suí and Táng dynasties.
2. On the Rénshēn day,
a general amnesty was declared in the empire,
and the era name was changed.
3. Second month,
on the Xīnhài day,
Wǔ Shìyuè was posthumously awarded the title of Minister over the Masses (Sītú),
and granted the title of Duke of Zhōu.
4. Third month,
Dù Zhènglún, Vice Minister of Revenue, was appointed as Vice Director of the Chancellery and given the designation Tóng Sānpǐn (Participant in Deliberations on Important Affairs of State).
In the first year of Xiǎnqìng,
the Ministry of Revenue was renamed the Ministry of Finance (Dùzhī).
'Dù'
is pronounced tuó luò.
5. Summer,
fourth month,
on the Rénzǐ day,
Xiè Wúlíng of Jǔ Prefecture raised troops in rebellion.
The various Mán of Jǔ Prefecture were also tribes of the Eastern Xiè Mán.
Jǔ Prefecture was established in the fourth year of Wǔdé.
6. On the Jǐwèi day,
the Emperor said to his attending ministers:
"We ponder the way of nurturing the people,
but have not grasped its essentials.
You, gentlemen, expound them for Us!"
Lái Jì replied:
"Formerly, Duke Huán of Qí was traveling,
and saw an old man suffering from hunger and cold.
He ordered food to be bestowed upon him.
The old man said: 'I wish it could be bestowed upon all the hungry of the state.'
When bestowed clothing,
he said: 'I wish it could be bestowed upon all the cold of the state.'
The Duke said: 'How can Our storehouses suffice to relieve the hunger and cold of the whole state?'
The old man said: 'If you, my lord, do not encroach upon the farming seasons,
then all the people of the state will have surplus food.
If you do not encroach upon the silkworm's crucial time,
then all the people of the state will have surplus clothing!'
Therefore, the way for a ruler to nurture the people
lies solely in reducing their taxes and corvée.
Now, the corvée laborers from Shāndōng
number tens of thousands each year.
Conscripting them makes the people excessively toil;
commuting the service makes the people incur great expense.
I hope Your Majesty, apart from what the state truly requires,
will remit all the rest."
The Emperor followed his advice.
7 In the sixth month,
on the Xīnhài day,
the ritual officials submitted a memorial requesting the cessation of the sacrificial pairing of Tàizǔ and Shìzǔ.
When Gāozǔ received the abdication,
he posthumously honored his grandfather Hǔ as Emperor Jǐng,
with the temple name Tàizǔ;
his father Bǐng as Emperor Yuán,
with the temple name Shìzǔ.
Tàizōng was paired with the Five Emperors in the Bright Hall.
In the early years of the Wǔdé era,
a circular mound altar was established two lǐ east of the road outside the Míngdé Gate.
The altar system had four tiers,
each eight chǐ and one cùn wide.
The bottom tier was twenty zhàng wide,
the second tier fifteen zhàng wide,
the third tier ten zhàng wide,
and the fourth tier five zhàng wide.
During each sacrifice,
the seats for the August Heaven God and the paired emperor were set on the flat platform,
using straw mats,
and earthenware vessels.
The Five Directional Gods, the sun and moon, the inner officials, middle officials, outer officials, and all the stars
were all included in the sacrifices.
The seats for the Five Directional Gods and the sun and moon, totaling seven,
were placed on the second level of the altar;
the seats for the five planets and below, totaling fifty-five,
were on the third level of the altar;
the seats for the twenty-eight mansions and below, totaling one hundred thirty-five,
were on the fourth level of the altar;
the seats for the outer officials, totaling one hundred twenty-two,
were inside the outer wall at the base of the altar;
the seats for all the stars, totaling three hundred sixty,
were outside the outer wall.
Emperor Jǐng was paired with the circular mound,
and Emperor Yuán was paired with the Bright Hall.
8 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Yǐchǒu day,
the chieftain of the Xī'ěr barbarians, Yáng Dòngfù, the chieftain of the Xiǎnhé barbarians, Wáng Lángqí, and the chieftains of Láng,
Kūn, Lí, and Pán prefectures, Wáng Jiāchōng and others, led their people to submit to the court.
Lí Prefecture was originally Xīníng Prefecture.
In the seventh year of the Wǔdé era,
it was established by dividing two counties from Nánníng Prefecture.
In the eighth year of the Zhēnguān era,
it was renamed Lí Prefecture.
Its territory bordered Kūn Prefecture to the north,
which was the land of the Jìn dynasty's Liángshuǐ Commandery.
Pán Prefecture was originally Xīpíng Prefecture,
established in the fourth year of the Wǔdé era.
In the eighth year of the Zhēnguān era,
it was renamed.
It was the land of the Jìn dynasty's Xīnggǔ Commandery.
ěr,
pronounced as lì.
Chieftain,
pronounced as cí yóu.
To lead,
read as shuài.
9 On the Guǐwèi day,
Zhōngshū Lìng Cuī Dūnlǐ was appointed as Tàizǐ Shǎoshī and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sān Pǐn.
In the eighth month,
on the Bǐngshēn day,
Gù'ān Zhāo Gōng Cuī Dūnlǐ passed away.
According to the rules of posthumous titles: "Having a dignified and respectful appearance is called Zhāo";
"Having illustrious virtue and being diligent is called Zhāo."
10 On the Xīnchǒu day,
the military commander of the Cōngshān Circuit, Chéng Zhījié, attacked the Western Turks,
engaging the Geluó
and Chùyuè tribes at Yúmù Valley.
The people of the five tribes—Chùyuè, Chùmì, Gūsū, Geluólù, and Nǔshībì—
were those ruled by Hèlǔ when he was Yèhù.
According to the New Book,
Geluólù is Geluólù.
"Yúmù Valley,"
the Old Book's Basic Annals records as
"Yúmù Valley."
Over a thousand heads were taken.
Deputy Commander Zhōu Zhìdù attacked the Tūqíshī and Chùmùkūn tribes at Yān City,
capturing it.
The five tribes of the Western Turks' Duōlù,
Chùmùkūn and Tūqíshī were both one tribe.
According to the New Book,
Yān City was where the Chùmùkūn resided.
Chù,
pronounced as chāng lǚ.
11 On the Yǐsì day,
the king of Qiūcí, Bùshībì, came to court.
12 Lǐ Yìfǔ, relying on the emperor's favor, wielded power.
A woman from Luò Prefecture, Chúnyú Shì,
was beautiful,
and was imprisoned in the Dàlǐ Prison.
Yìfǔ instructed Dàlǐ Sìchéng Bì Zhèngyì to unlawfully release her,
intending to take her as a concubine.
Dàlǐ Qīng Duàn Bǎoxuán became suspicious and reported it.
The emperor ordered Jǐshìzhōng Liú Rénguǐ and others to investigate.
Yìfǔ, fearing the matter would be exposed,
forced Zhèngyì to hang himself in prison.
The emperor knew of this,
but pardoned Yìfǔ and did not question him.
Shìyùshǐ Liánshuǐ's Wáng Yìfāng wanted to submit a memorial impeaching him.
Liánshuǐ,
formerly called Xiāngbēn,
was part of Dōnghǎi Commandery.
During the Eastern Wèi, it was renamed Hǎi'ān Commandery.
In the early years of the Suí dynasty's Kāihuáng era,
the commandery was abolished,
and Xiāngbēn was renamed Liánshuǐ,
belonging to Hǎi Prefecture.
During the Táng, it belonged to Sìshuǐ.
Lián,
pronounced as lián.
"Yìfāng, as a Yùshǐ,
if he does not expose treacherous ministers, he is disloyal;
if he exposes them, he endangers himself and brings worry to his parents, which is unfilial.
Unable to decide between these two,
what should he do?"
His mother said:
"In the past, Wáng Líng's mother
gave her life to establish her son's reputation.
The event is recorded in the ninth volume, the first year of Hàn Gāozǔ.
I would die without regret!"
Yìfāng then submitted a memorial:
"Yìfǔ, under the imperial carriage,
dared to kill a sixth-rank Sìchéng;
according to the Táng Liù Diǎn: Dàlǐ Sìchéng
holds the rank of Cóng Liù Pǐn Shàng.
It was also because he feared Yìfǔ's power
that he took his own life to silence the matter.
If this is allowed,
then the power of life and death
will not come from the emperor,
and this trend must not be allowed to grow.
I request a further investigation!"
Thus, during the court audience,
he shouted at Yìfǔ, ordering him to step down;
Yìfǔ looked around and did not retreat.
Yìfāng shouted three times,
and as the emperor remained silent,
Yìfǔ finally hurried out.
Yìfāng then read the impeachment memorial.
The emperor pardoned Yìfǔ and did not question him,
but instead accused Yìfāng of slandering and insulting a high minister,
using disrespectful language,
and demoted him to Lái Prefecture Sīhù.
13 In the ninth month,
a violent storm struck Kuò Prefecture,
causing the sea to overflow,
drowning over four thousand households.
According to the New Annals: Chù Prefecture was originally Kuò Prefecture's Yǒngjiā Commandery.
At that time, it also included the territory of Yǒngjiā.
In the first year of the Shàngyuán era,
Wēn Prefecture was established by division.
14 In winter,
the eleventh month,
on the Bǐngyín day,
the chieftain of the Shēng Qiāng, Làng Wǒlìbō, and others led their people to submit to the court.
Their territory was used to establish Zhè and Gǒng prefectures.
Zhè Prefecture,
Péngshān Commandery.
Gǒng Prefecture,
established with the Bónán Fúlángkǒng tribe,
both belonged to the Sōng Prefecture Dūdū Fǔ.
Sòng Bái said: Zhè Prefecture was named for its expansion,
pronounced as dá gè.
On the 15th day of the twelfth month,
Chéng Zhījié led his army to Yīngsuōchuān,
where they encountered twenty thousand cavalry of the Western Turkic Khaganate.
An additional twenty thousand cavalry from a separate tribe, the Shǔníshī and others, subsequently arrived.
The Shǔníshī
were one of the five Duōlù Chù.
They resided in Yīngsuōchuān,
and later the Yīngsuō Chief Command was established there.
Suō,
pronunciation: sù hé fān.
The Western Turks were heavily defeated,
and were pursued for twenty *li*,
with over fifteen hundred killed or captured.
The horses and equipment captured,
stretching across the mountains and plains,
were beyond count.
Deputy Commander-in-Chief Wáng Wéndù, jealous of his success,
said to Zhījié:
"Although we are said to have defeated the enemy this time,
our own army also suffered casualties.
Taking risks and acting rashly
is a method that determines success or failure;
why be so hasty as to do this!
From now on, we should always form square formations,
placing the baggage train inside,
and fight only when we encounter the enemy.
This is the perfectly safe strategy."
He also falsely claimed to have received a separate edict,
stating that because Zhījié relied on courage and underestimated the enemy,

plotted to kill Míshè,

The New Book's biography is roughly the same.

doubts cannot be clarified,

Liú Shànyīn conferred Níshú as Xīlìbì Duōlù Kèhán,
the next year Níshú died,
his younger brother Tóng'é Shè was established,

after another three years Xìlìshī was not supported by the masses,
the western tribes again established Yùgǔ Shè as Yǐpí Duōlù Kèhán.
The two Kèhán fought militarily,
Xìlìshī and Yǐpí successively fled and died in other countries,
and Shèkuì actually succeeded them.
Emperor Tàizōng passed away,
Hèlǔ rebelled,
and Shèkuì was annexed by Hèlǔ.
The generational sequence of the Western Türk,
is clearly examinable.

Liú Shànyīn was sent to establish Míshè as Xīlìbì Duōlù Kèhán.
Looking at the Biography of Níshú,
then the one Shànyīn established,
was Níshú.
Looking at the Biography of Míshè,
then the one Shànyīn established,
was Míshè.
The doubts in the Textual Examination,
should be regarding this.

Commentary: The Veritable Records state:

The Emperor exclaimed in alarm: ‘How could there be such a thing?

giving rise to minor suspicions,
but as for immediate rebellion,

Jìngzōng reported: ‘From beginning to end of my investigation,
since Fèngjié mentioned the name Zhào Shī,
and we obtained a forged letter
that was written by Jìfāng,
I suspected that Wújì intended to rebel.
If he were to secretly carry out schemes to sow discord,
and remove loyal ministers and close relatives,
and if this plan were to succeed,
power would naturally revert to Wújì.
The traces have already been revealed,
yet Your Majesty still has doubts;
I fear it will not be a blessing for the state.’”
The Old Book biography of Wújì states:

claiming that the Investigating Censor Lǐ Cháo was associating with Wújì to plot rebellion.
An edict ordered Jìngzōng and Màojiàng to interrogate them.”
The Táng Calendar and the Comprehensive Record are roughly the same as the Veritable Records.
Now, Fèngjié was the one who made the accusation;
how could those conducting the interrogation instead search Fèngjié’s home?
Moreover, whose private letter was it that was addressed to Zhào Shī?
If it was Jìfāng’s letter,
how could it be in Fèngjié’s home?
If it was in Fèngjié’s home,
Fèngjié should have produced it to initiate the lawsuit;
why wait until after a search to obtain it?
Furthermore, if it is said that Zhào Shī is Wújì,
then it was actually a letter to Wújì;
how could it be called a forged letter?
The Veritable Records’ account of this matter is extremely careless,
with discrepancies from beginning to end,
making it impossible to know the detailed truth.
Therefore, I have only taken the general meaning.
What is stated in the Old Book biography,
though concise and direct,
yet Emperor Gāozōng initially had no suspicions about Wújì’s heart;
thus, when Lǐ Hóngtài accused Wújì of rebellion,

Why, in the case of Fèngjié, would he specifically order Jìngzōng to interrogate him?
Moreover, the Veritable Records came earlier and are detailed,
while the biographies came later and are brief,
so they cannot be relied upon either.
“My family is unfortunate;

"Accompanying door wealth" refers to when the bride's family status is not high enough,

The next southwestern star is called Qīngxīng (Minister Star),
presiding over Yínghuò (Mars),

prognostications are made based on them.

Ōuyáng Xiū said: The Dì and Xiá
are grand sacrifices.
The Xiá involves the joint offering of food to ancestors according to their Zhao-Mu order at the temple of the Great Ancestor,
while the Dì is for carefully distinguishing their seniority and rank.
This is the meaning of the Dì and Xiá sacrifices.
However, those who formulated the rites erred in this regard,
leading to discrepancies in the number of years between them,
misplacement of ancestral positions,
leaving those who debated the rites unsure of what to follow.
The Rites state: Hold the Xiá sacrifice every three years,
and the Dì sacrifice every five years.
The Commentary says: Perform the grand sacrifice twice in five years.
In the tenth month of the third year of the Shàngyuán era of Emperor Gāozōng, the Xiá sacrifice was due,
and officials debated the number of years.
Shǐ Càn and others proposed
that after the mourning period for a new ruler ends, the Xiá sacrifice should be held,
followed by the Dì sacrifice the next year.
Thereafter,
the grand sacrifices should be held twice every five years.
Thus, the interval between two Dì sacrifices is five years,
with the Xiá always occurring three years after a Dì,
and the Dì always occurring two years after a Xiá.
In the eighth year of Duke Xuān of Lǔ,
the Dì sacrifice was held for Duke Xī.
This was likely because the three-year mourning period had ended, followed by the Xiá,
and the Dì was held the next year,
leading to another Dì in the eighth year.
In the twentieth year of Duke Zhāo, a Dì was held,
and another was held in the twenty-fifth year,
which illustrates this point.
At the time, because their arguments were supported by classical sources,
the proposal was adopted.

During the Southern Qí dynasty, the Sīzhōu was established.

During the Later Zhōu dynasty, it was renamed Shēnzhōu.
During the Suí dynasty, it was renamed Yìzhōu,

The Left Aide to the Heir Apparent and concurrent Third-Rank Official of the Secretariat-Chancellery, Zhāng Dà'ān, was implicated for flattering and attaching himself to the Crown Prince,

Upon reaching Héngshuǐ,
which is about one hundred and forty lǐ from Jīnhé.

Fú Niàn headed north,

yet you receive salary for your kin,

Bīnwáng drowned himself,

over two chǐ wide,

The old system: all officials of the ninth rank and above holding substantive posts
also held nominal ranks,
called their base rank.
Substantive posts were assigned according to ability,
sometimes moving from idle to busy positions,
or from high to low,
with transfers and changes
being irregular.
Nominal ranks were entirely determined by family background and hereditary privilege,
then advanced based on merit and seniority.
The Wǔdé statutes stipulated that substantive posts were separated from nominal offices,
if one rank short it was called concurrent,
if the substantive post was lower, the nominal office was not separated.
The Zhēnguàn statutes designated those with higher substantive posts as "acting,"
those with lower substantive posts as "executing,"
still holding nominal ranks,
and if one rank short, still called concurrent,
sometimes holding nominal offices,
sometimes acting,
used interchangeably.
Holding two substantive posts was also called concurrent,
causing considerable confusion.
In the second year of Xiánhēng,
it was uniformly changed to "acting."
The concurrent when one rank short,
(pronounced as in the original text);
the concurrent when holding two substantive posts,
(pronounced as in the original text);
