Jìngyè, Yóu, Zhīqí, Qiúrén, and Bīnwáng fled back to Jiāngdū,
burned the account books,
took their wives and children and hid at Suàn Mountain,
and sent a handwritten letter summoning Zōng Chén.
Initially, Jìngyè and Zōng Chén had a wooden tally as an agreement.
At that time, the tally was lost,
Zōng Chén was suspicious and did not go,
some said Zōng Chén had already submitted.
Jìngyè went to sea,
wishing to flee to the Eastern Barbarians.
When he reached the border of Hǎilíng,
he was impeded by winds.
The rebel general Wáng Nàxiāng beheaded him and came to surrender.
The remaining followers threw themselves into the water and died."
Now we follow the Shílù and Táng Tǒngjì.
(Jìngyè's) head was sent to Shéndū,
and Yáng, Rùn, and Chǔ prefectures were pacified.
Chén Yuè comments: If Jìngyè could have employed Wèi Sīwēn's strategy,
heading straight for Hé and Luò,
focusing solely on the task of restoring (the dynasty),
even if his army were defeated and he himself executed,
there would still be loyalty and righteousness in it.
Yet he delusionally hoped for the royal aura of Jīnlíng,
this was truly rebellion,
how could he not be defeated!
When Jìngyè rose up,
he sent Jìngyóu to lead five thousand troops,
to advance westward along the river,
capturing territory in Hézhōu.
The former Bachelor of the Hóngwén Academy, Gāo Zǐgòng from Lìyáng, led several hundred men from his hometown to resist him,
and Jìngyóu could not advance westward.
For this achievement, (Zǐgòng) was appointed Gentleman for Court Discussion and Assistant Instructor of the National University.
Lìyáng County,
in the Hàn dynasty belonged to Jiǔjiāng Commandery,
in the Jìn dynasty, Lìyáng Commandery was established.
When it came to the Northern Qí having peaceful relations with Liáng,
Hézhōu was established,
the Suí and Táng dynasties followed this.
Later, the Directorate of Education was renamed the Directorate of the National University.
According to the Táng Liù Diǎn: The Hóngwén Academy,
had Academicians of the fifth rank and above.
The Assistant Instructor of the National University was Cong Liù Pǐn Shàng,
responsible for assisting the Erudites in dividing up the classics for teaching.
Gentleman for Court Discussion,
was Cong Wǔ Pǐn Xià.
Shuài (to lead),
is read as shuài.
Cháo (court),
is pronounced cháo, tone rising.
Sàn (discussion),
is pronounced sàn, tone falling.
On the Dīngmǎo day,
Guō Dàijǔ was dismissed and made Left Tutor of the Heir Apparent;
Luángtái Shìláng Wéi Fāngzhì was appointed Fènggé Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
Fāngzhì
was the grandson of Yúnqǐ.
Wéi Yúnqǐ served between the Suí and Táng dynasties.
In the twelfth month,
Liú Jǐngxiān was further demoted to Assistant Chief Clerk of Jízhōu,
and Guō Dàijǔ was demoted to Prefect of Yuèzhōu.
Yuèzhōu,
was 2,237 lǐ southeast of the capital,
and 1,816 lǐ to the eastern capital.
At the beginning,
when Pei Yán was imprisoned,
the Pacification Commissioner of the Chányú Circuit and General of the Left Martial Guard, Chéng Wùtǐng, secretly submitted a memorial pleading for him,
thereby offending the imperial will.
Wùtǐng had always been on good terms with Táng Zhīqí and Dù Qiúrén,
and someone slandered him, saying,
"Wùtǐng conspired with Pei Yán and Xú Jìngyè."
On the guǐmǎo day,
the Left Eagle Yang General Pei Shàoyè was dispatched to execute him in the army.
The Examination of Discrepancies says: The Táng Tǒngjì states:
"Afterward, the Empress Dowager was furious,
summoned the assembled ministers, and said: 'I have done nothing to wrong the empire,
do all of you ministers know this?'
The ministers replied: 'Yes.'
The Empress Dowager said: 'I served the late emperor for over twenty years,
and was deeply concerned for the empire!
The wealth and honor of the dukes and ministers
were all bestowed by me;
the peace and happiness of the empire,
I nurtured and cultivated.
When the late emperor left his ministers,
he entrusted the empire to my care,
not loving his own person but loving the common people.
Now, those who lead rebellions
all come from among the generals, ministers, and officials.
How deeply have they wronged me!
Moreover, among you, are there any veteran ministers who received the late emperor's bequest,
more stubborn and difficult to control than Pei Yán?
Are there any scions of noble military families,
more capable of rallying desperadoes than Xú Jìngyè?
Are there any seasoned generals holding troops,
more victorious in battle than Chéng Wùtǐng?
These three men,
were men of renown,
yet they were detrimental to me,
and I could execute them.
If any of you can surpass these three,
then act immediately;
if not,
you must reform your hearts and serve me,
and do not become the laughingstock of the empire.'
The ministers kowtowed,
not daring to look up,
and said: 'We will do as the Empress Dowager commands.'
I fear that Empress Wǔ would not have been so frivolous."
Now, I do not adopt this.
When the Turks heard of Wùtǐng's death,
they held feasts everywhere in celebration;
they also built a shrine for Wùtǐng,
and whenever they went on a campaign,
they would pray to him.
The Empress Dowager, because the Governor of Xiàzhōu, Wáng Fāngyì, had served jointly with Wùtǐng,
and they had always been close and friendly,
and also because he was a relative of the deposed empress,
summoned him and imprisoned him,
then exiled him to Yázhōu, where he died.
Old records: Yázhōu is 7,460 lǐ from the capital,
and 6,300 lǐ from the Eastern Capital.
First year of Chuígōng
(yǐyǒu, 685)
1 Spring,
first month,
dīngwèi, first day,
amnesty was granted to the empire,
and the era name was changed.
2 The Empress Dowager, considering Xú Sīwén loyal,
specially exempted him from being implicated,
and appointed him as Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Stud.
Implication means
being implicated and punished due to one's relatives or associates.
In the Guāngzhái era, the Court of Imperial Stud was renamed the Court of Imperial Equipages.
"Jìngyè changed your surname to Wǔ,
I will not take it away now."
3 On the gēngxū day,
Qiān Wèidào was appointed as Acting Imperial Secretary.
Imperial Secretary
is the Secretariat Director.
4 On the wùchén day,
the Left Grand Councilor of Wénchāng, Third Rank with the Secretariat-Chancellery, Duke Wénxiàn of Lèchéng, Liú Rénguǐ, passed away.
Left Grand Councilor of Wénchāng
is the Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.
5 Second month,
guǐwèi day,
an edict was issued:
"The petition drum and the lung stone placed at the court,
the petition drum is at the western court hall,
the lung stone is at the eastern court hall.
Court,
read as cháo.
If there are those who beat the drum or stand on the stone,
order the censors to receive their petitions and report them."
6 On the yǐsì day,
Wǔ Chéngsì, Minister of the Ministry of Rites, and Péi Jūdào, Minister of the Ministry of Justice, were appointed.
In the Guāngzhái era, the Ministry of Rites was renamed the Ministry of Spring,
and the Ministry of Justice was renamed the Ministry of Autumn.
Minister,
read as shàng.
Sì,
read as sì.
Right Grand Master of Thorough Governance,
is the Right Grand Censor.
7 The Turks, Ashina Qutlugh and others, repeatedly raided the borders.
Chúnyú Chǔpíng, General of the Left Jade Seal Guard, was appointed as Commander of the Yángqǔ Circuit Campaign Army,
to attack them.
8 Shěn Jūnliàng, Grand Master of Remonstrance and Third Rank with the Secretariat-Chancellery, was dismissed.
9 Third month,
Cuī Chá, Grand Master of Remonstrance and Third Rank with the Secretariat-Chancellery, was dismissed.
10 On the bǐngchén day,
the Prince of Lúlíng was moved to Fángzhōu.
Old records: Fángzhōu
is 1,195 lǐ south of the capital,
and 1,185 lǐ from the Eastern Capital.
Dù Yòu said: Fángzhōu
is the land of the ancient states of Mí and Yōng.
In the Spring and Autumn period, the Chu ruler defeated the Mí army at Fángzhǔ,
which is here.
In the Cáo Wèi period, it was Zhúshān County of Xīnchéng Commandery.
Then it was the ancient state of Yōng,
the Shàngyōng County of the Qín and Hàn periods.
11 On the xīnyǒu day,
Wǔ Chéngsì was dismissed.
12 On the xīnwèi day,
the Chuígōng Code was promulgated.
13 There were court officials who had been demoted and went to complain to the chief ministers.
Imperial Secretary Qiān Wèidào said:
"This is the Empress Dowager's decision."
Liú Yīzhī, Third Rank with the Secretariat-Chancellery, said:
"Being implicated and having one's position changed
is due to the memorials and requests of us ministers."
When the Empress Dowager heard of this,
in summer,
fourth month,
on the bǐngzǐ day,
she demoted Wèidào to Governor of Qīngzhōu,
and promoted Yīzhī to Grand Master of the Palace.
Grand Master of the Palace
is Upper Fourth Rank.
Liú Yīzhī's original position was Administrator of the Household of the Prince of Yù.
Administrator of the Household of a Prince
is Lower Fourth Rank.
"The ruler and ministers are one body;
how can one shift the blame to the ruler
and claim the good for oneself!"
14 On the guǐwèi day,
the Turks raided Dàizhōu;
Chúnyú Chǔpíng led troops to rescue it;
when they reached Xīnzhōu,
they were defeated by the Turks,
with over 5,000 dead.
15 On the bǐng
wǔ day,
Péi Jūdào was appointed as Imperial Secretary.
Wang Dézhēn, the Director of the Chancellery, was exiled to Xiàngzhōu.
Xiàngzhōu is 4,989 lǐ from the capital.
16 On the jǐyǒu day,
Sū Liángsì, Minister of the Ministry of Works, was appointed as Director of the Chancellery.
In the Guāngzhái era, the Ministry of Works was renamed the Ministry of Winter.
17 On the rénxū day,
an edict was issued that all officials of the ninth rank and above, as well as commoners,
were to recommend themselves.
This allowed all those with talent to speak up and seek advancement and employment.
Order,
read as lìng.
18 On the rénshēn day,
Wéi Fāngzhì was appointed Third Rank with the Secretariat-Chancellery.
19 Sixth month,
Wéi Dàijià, Minister of the Ministry of Personnel, was appointed Third Rank with the Secretariat-Chancellery.
In the Guāngzhái era, the Ministry of Personnel was renamed the Ministry of Heaven.
He was the elder brother of Wànshí.
20 The Tóngluó, Púgù, and other tribes rebelled.
Zuǒ Bàotāo Guard General Liú Jìngtóng was dispatched to mobilize cavalry from Héxī to set out from Jūyán Sea to attack them.
In Gānzhōu, from Shāndān County, cross the Zhāngyē River to the north,
proceed northwest,
exit the Hé Lí Mountain gorge,
follow the east bank of the river,
wind northeast for a thousand lǐ,
and there is the Níngkòu Army.
Northeast of the army is the Jūyán Sea.
Cavalry,
read as jì.
An edict was issued to temporarily establish the Protectorate General to Pacify the North at Tóngchéng to accept surrendering tribes.
Tóngchéng
is the Tóngchéng garrison of Shāndān,
renamed the Níngkòu Army in the second year of Tiānbǎo.
Surrender,
read as xiáng.
21 Autumn,
seventh month,
on the jǐyǒu day,
Wèi Xuántóng, Left Vice Director of Wénchāng, was appointed as Vice Director of the Chancellery and Third Rank with the Secretariat-Chancellery.
Left Vice Director of Wénchāng
is the Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.
22 An edict was issued that from now on, when sacrificing to Heaven and Earth,
Gāozǔ, Tàizōng, and Gāozōng would all be seated as companions;
this followed the proposal of Yuán Wànqǐng, Drafter of the Secretariat, and others.
23 Ninth month,
on the dīngmǎo day,
Wáng Guǒ, Governor of Guǎngzhōu, attacked the rebellious Lǎo people
and pacified them.
In the winter of the 24th year,
in the eleventh month,
on the Guǐmǎo day,
the Heavenly Official Minister Wéi Dàijià was appointed as the Commander-in-Chief of the Yānrán Circuit Expeditionary Force to campaign against Tibet.
Previously,
after the deaths of the Western Turkic Khagans Xīngxīwáng and Jìwǎngjué,
the ten tribes were left without a leader,
and many of the tribes scattered and dispersed.
The Empress Dowager then promoted Xīngxīwáng's son, Yuán Qìng, who held the position of Central Commandant of the Left Leopard Guard's Yì Mansion,
(All the guards of the Táng dynasty had Central Commandants and Commandants in their Yì Mansions.)
(Jiàng,
pronounced as liàng.)
and concurrently appointed him as Protector of Kūnlíng,
to succeed Xīngxīwáng Khagan and oversee the five Dūlù tribes.
25. Chén Zǐ'áng, a Proofreader at the Lín Tái from Shèhóng,
(In the Guāngzhái era, the Secretariat was renamed Lín Tái; Proofreaders,
of the ninth rank, lower grade,
were responsible for correcting texts.)
(Shèhóng County,
belonged to Zǐ Prefecture;
it was the territory of the Hàn dynasty's Qī County;
during the Later Wèi, Shèjiāng County was established separately,
because six lǐ east of Lóulǚ Beach there was a Shè River;
during the Western Wèi, it was mistakenly written as Shèhóng.)
believed:
"When the court dispatches envoys to inspect the four directions,
they must not appoint unsuitable individuals,
and the same applies to Prefects and County Magistrates—
they must be chosen carefully.
In recent years, the people have been exhausted by military campaigns,
and they must be pacified."
The summary of his statement reads:
"If envoys are not chosen carefully,
then promotions and demotions will not be clear,
punishments will not be just,
factions will advance,
and the loyal and upright will be pushed aside;
it will only cause the people to repair roads,
seeing off and welcoming guests,
with no benefit at all.
As the proverb says:
'To know a person,
observe those they employ.'
This must be done with caution."
He also said:
"The Grand Councilors are Your Majesty's heart and mind;
the Prefects and County Magistrates are Your Majesty's hands and feet;
how can one govern alone without a heart, mind, hands, or feet!"
He further said:
"The world has critical junctures,
from which fortune and disaster arise.
When the juncture is calm, there is fortune;
when it is agitated, there is disaster.
The people are such a juncture.
When the people are at peace, they enjoy their lives;
when they are not at peace, they treat death lightly.
When they treat death lightly, there is nothing they will not do;
rebellion and disorder seize the opportunity,
and the world falls into chaos!"
He also said:
"Emperor Suí Yáng did not know that the world had critical junctures,
and he trusted greedy and deceitful ministers,
hoping to profit from the barbarians,
but in the end, he perished.
This serves as a stark warning—
is it not profound!"
26. The Empress Dowager restored the old White Horse Temple
and appointed the monk Huáiyì as its abbot.
(Yáo Sīlián said: During the reign of Emperor Hàn Míng,
the Western Regions sent a white horse carrying Buddhist scriptures to Luòyáng,
and thus the White Horse Temple was established.
Wèi Shōu said: The Hàn dynasty established the White Horse Temple west of Yōng Gate in Luò City.
This refers to the old Luò City;
the Táng dynasty's Luò City
was relocated during the Suí dynasty.)
He was a native of Hù,
originally surnamed Féng,
named Xiǎobǎo,
and sold medicine in the markets of Luòyáng.
He was introduced through Princess Qiānjīn,
(Princess Qiānjīn
was the daughter of Emperor Gāozǔ.)
The Empress Dowager wanted him to enter and leave the palace,
so he was ordained as a monk
and given the name Huáiyì.
Because his family was humble and poor,
she ordered him to join the clan of the Commandant of the Imperial Guards, Xuē Shào,
and commanded Xuē Shào to treat him as an uncle.
(Xuē Shào married the Empress Dowager's daughter, Princess Tàipíng.)
More than ten eunuchs attended to him;
when officials or commoners encountered him, they fled and avoided him.
Those who approached him
were often beaten until their heads bled,
and he would leave them behind,
regardless of whether they lived or died.
When he saw Daoist priests, he would beat them mercilessly
and shave their heads before leaving.
High-ranking officials prostrated themselves to pay respects to him;
Wǔ Chéngsì and Wǔ Sānsī both served him with the etiquette of servants,
holding the reins for him,
but Huáiyì treated them as if they were nobody.
He gathered many unruly youths,
ordained them as monks,
and they rampantly broke the law,
with no one daring to speak out.
The Right Censor Féng Sīxù repeatedly tried to restrain them according to the law,
(Right Censorate
refers to the Right Surveillance Bureau.)
but Huáiyì ordered his followers to beat him,
nearly to death.
1. In spring,
in the first month,
the Empress Dowager issued an edict to return governance to the emperor.
Emperor Ruìzōng knew that the Empress Dowager was not sincere,
so he submitted a memorial firmly declining;
the Empress Dowager resumed governance and issued decrees in her own name.
On the Xīnyǒu day,
a general amnesty was declared.
2. In the second month,
on the Xīnwèi day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
3. After Lǐ Xiàoyì, the Grand General of the Right Guard, suppressed Xú Jìngyè,
his reputation grew significantly.
Wǔ Chéngsì and others despised him
and repeatedly slandered him to the Empress Dowager,
leading to his demotion to Prefect of Shī Prefecture.
4. In the third month,
on the Wùshēn day,
the Empress Dowager ordered the casting of bronze boxes:
the eastern one was called
"Yán'ēn" (Extending Kindness),
for those submitting literary works or seeking official positions;
the southern one was called
"Zhāojiàn" (Soliciting Admonitions),
for those commenting on the successes and failures of court policies;
the western one was called
"Shēnyuān" (Redressing Injustices),
for those with grievances or injustices;
the northern one was called
"Tōngxuán" (Communicating the Mysterious),
for those reporting celestial phenomena, disasters, or military secrets.
The four boxes
were each painted in the color corresponding to their direction.
(Zhèngjiàn
refers to the Remonstrance Officials.
In the first year of the Chuígōng era,
Left and Right Supplements were established, one each,
of the seventh rank, upper grade;
Left and Right Omissions were established, two each,
of the eighth rank, upper grade;
they were responsible for offering remonstrance and advice,
standing in rank below the Left and Right Historians;
the Left belonged to the Chancellery,
the Right to the Secretariat.
Shíguān
is similar to today's guarantors.)
When Xú Jìngyè rebelled,
Yú Bǎojiā, the son of the Attendant Censor Yú Chéngyè, taught Jìngyè how to make blade chariots and crossbows.
After Jìngyè's defeat,
Bǎojiā barely escaped punishment.
The Empress Dowager wanted to know everything happening among the people,
so Bǎojiā submitted a memorial
requesting the casting of bronze boxes to receive secret memorials from the world.
The device consisted of a single chamber
with four compartments inside,
each with an opening on top
to receive memorials,
allowing them to be inserted but not retrieved.
The Empress Dowager approved of this.
(Commentary: The Tǒng Jì and Táng Lì both state that the bronze boxes were made in the eighth month.
Here, the Shí Lù and the old annals are followed.
Also, the Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi records the name as
"Yú Sīxuān,"
stating:
"The Emperor wanted to make boxes,
summoned craftsmen,
but no one could make them.
Sīxuān responded to the imperial order and made them,
which perfectly met the specifications,
so they were used."
Here, the Yùshǐ Tái Jì is followed.)
His enemies submitted a memorial through the box
accusing Bǎojiā of making weapons for Jìngyè,
causing heavy casualties among the government troops,
and he was subsequently executed.
After the rebellion of Xǔ Jìngyè, the Empress Dowager
suspected that many people in the empire were plotting against her.
Moreover, she had long monopolized state affairs,
and her personal conduct was improper.
Knowing that the imperial clan and high officials resented and
were discontented in their hearts,
she wished to carry out large-scale executions to intimidate them.
Therefore, she widely opened the door to secret denunciations.
For those who made secret denunciations,
officials were not allowed to question them.
All were provided with post horses.
Under the Táng system: traveling by relay carriage allowed four stages per day,
while traveling by post horse allowed six stages per day.
Generally, for those provided with horses,
officials of the first rank received eight horses,
the second rank six horses,
the third rank five horses,
the fourth and fifth ranks four horses,
the sixth rank three horses,
and the seventh rank and below two horses.
For those provided with relay carriages,
the first rank received ten horses,
the second rank nine horses,
the third rank eight horses,
the fourth and fifth ranks four horses,
the sixth and seventh ranks two horses,
and the eighth and ninth ranks one horse.
For those of the third rank and above summoned by imperial decree,
four horses were provided;
for the fifth rank, three horses;
and for the sixth rank and below, varying amounts.
One stage
was thirty lǐ.
According to the Táng Liù Diǎn: for the fourth and fifth ranks,
the regular food allowance consisted of seven dishes.
Daily provisions included two shēng of fine rice,
two shēng and three gě of wheat flour,
one and a half shēng of wine,
three portions of mutton,
two melons,
and varying amounts of salt, fermented beans, scallions, ginger, mallow, leeks, and the like.
According to the Xīn Táng Shū: for the fifth rank’s food allowance,
miscellaneous expenses amounted to six hundred coins per month.
Even farmers and woodcutters
could be summoned for an audience.
They were lodged at guesthouses,
which
were under the supervision of the Director of Receptions of the Court of State Ceremonial.
“Lodged”
means provided with accommodations.
“See”
is pronounced xiàn.
They were then promoted to office without regard to seniority,
and those whose accusations were unfounded were not questioned.
As a result, secret informants from all directions swarmed like bees,
and people all stood with overlapping feet and held their breath in fear.
There was a foreigner named Suǒ Yuánlǐ
who understood the Empress Dowager’s intentions.
He was summoned for an audience due to a secret denunciation
and was promoted to the rank of Yóujī General,
then ordered to investigate cases involving imperial decrees.
Yuánlǐ was by nature cruel and ruthless.
When interrogating one person, he would invariably force them to implicate dozens or even hundreds of others.
The Empress Dowager repeatedly summoned him for audiences and rewarded him to enhance his authority.
Subsequently, Zhōu Xìng of Cháng’ān, a Secretary in the Department of State Affairs,
(Under the Táng system, the Department of State Affairs had Secretaries
who managed the Directors and Clerks of various offices.)
“Shàng”
is pronounced cháng.
and others rose one after another.
Xìng was repeatedly promoted to Vice Minister of the Ministry of Justice,
while Jùnchén was repeatedly promoted to Vice Censor-in-Chief.
Together, they privately kept hundreds of ruffians,
focusing solely on the business of secret denunciations.
If they wanted to frame someone,
they would order accusations to be made simultaneously from several places,
with the details of the allegations identical.
Jùnchén and Wàn Guójùn of Luòyáng, an Evaluator in the Ministry of Punishments
(During the Guāngzhái era, the Dàlǐ Temple was renamed the Ministry of Punishments. Evaluators
held the eighth rank,
responsible for conducting investigations on missions.)
taught their followers to ensnare the innocent,
weaving tales of rebellion,
fabricating and arranging
evidence with supporting details.
Whenever the Empress Dowager received a secret informant,
she would order Yuánlǐ and others to interrogate them.
They competed to devise cruel methods of interrogation,
with names such as
“Stabilize All Pulses,”
“Sudden Earth Roar,”
“Death-Pig Sorrow,”
“Seek Family Ruin,”
and “Admit Rebellion Is True.”
Some would bind the hands and feet with a rafter and twist it,
calling it
“Phoenix Drying Its Wings.”
Others would tie an object around the waist,
pulling the cangue forward,
calling it
“Donkey Colt Pulling a Stake.”
Some would make the prisoner kneel and hold up the cangue,
piling bricks on top,
calling it
“Immortal Presenting Fruit.”
Others would make the prisoner stand on a tall wooden pole,
pulling the end of the cangue backward,
calling it
“Jade Maiden Ascending the Ladder.”
Some would hang the prisoner upside down, suspending a stone from the head,
or pour vinegar into the nose,
or place an iron ring around the head and drive in wedges,
sometimes until the skull split and brains oozed out.
Whenever they obtained a prisoner,
they would first display the torture instruments to them,
causing all to tremble and sweat profusely,
and falsely confess at the mere sight.
Whenever there was an amnesty decree,
Jùnchén would order the jailers to first kill the important prisoners,
and only then announce the decree.
The Empress Dowager considered him loyal,
and favored and trusted him even more.
Both inside and outside the court, people feared these few individuals
more than tigers or wolves.
The Proofreader of the Lin Terrace, Chén Zǐ'áng, submitted a memorial:
He believed:
"The officials, resenting Xú Jìngyè for initiating rebellion and inciting disaster,
sought to eradicate the source of treachery,
and exhaustively pursued his accomplices.
Consequently, they caused Your Majesty to widely establish prisons for interrogation by imperial decree,
and to institute severe punishments.
Those whose conduct involved suspicion,
or whose words implicated others,
were all exhaustively arrested, interrogated, and investigated.
There were even treacherous men who,
taking advantage of the perilous situation, falsely accused others,
denouncing and reporting on those who seemed suspicious,
hoping to obtain noble titles and rewards.
I fear this is not in accordance with the principle of punishing the guilty and comforting the people.
I humbly observe that in the empire today,
the common people have longed for peace for a long time.
Thus, although rebellion was instigated in Yángzhōu,
lasting nearly fifty days,
the realm remained tranquil,
without the slightest disturbance.
Your Majesty does not devote yourself to profound silence to rescue the weary people,
but instead relies on awe and punishment, thereby losing their hopes.
I, in my foolish ignorance,
am secretly greatly perplexed.
I observe that from all quarters, secret accusations are made,
imprisoning hundreds and thousands of people.
Yet when these cases are thoroughly investigated,
not one in a hundred proves true.
Your Majesty, in your benevolence and forbearance,
again bends the law to tolerate them.
Consequently, you have allowed factions of the wicked and evil to gratify themselves by settling scores with each other.
The slightest grudge leads to claims of having secret information.
When one person is accused,
a hundred fill the prisons.
Envoys pursue and arrest,
their carriages and caps crowding the markets like a marketplace.
Some say that Your Majesty loves one person but harms a hundred,
causing the empire to murmur anxiously,
not knowing where to find peace.
I have heard that in the final years of the Suí dynasty,
the empire was still peaceful.
When Yáng Xuángǎn rebelled,
he was defeated in less than a month.
The decay of the empire
had not yet reached the point of total collapse.
The hearts of the people,
still hoped for prosperous livelihoods.
'Zhēng rén'
means the same as 'zhēng mín' (the people).
To avoid the taboo of Tàizōng's name,
the character
'mín'
was changed to
'rén'.
'Lè'
is pronounced luò.
Yet they allowed the Minister of War, Fán Zǐgài, to exclusively carry out slaughter,
exhaustively pursuing accomplices.
The heroic men of the realm
all met with calamity.
This led to killing people like hemp,
with blood flowing to form marshes.
The event is recorded in the 182nd volume, in the ninth year of the Dàyè era.
Only then did people begin to think of rebellion,
and thus heroes and leaders arose together, and the Suí clan perished.
Once a major inquisition begins,
it cannot avoid excesses.
The wronged sigh and lament,
disturbing and injuring the harmonious ether.
This gives rise to pestilence and epidemics,
followed by floods and droughts.
Once people lose their livelihoods,
then minds inclined towards disaster and rebellion are fearfully born.
The wise kings of antiquity valued and were cautious in applying punishments and laws,
precisely because they feared this.
In the past, during the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn, when the witchcraft inquisition arose,
it caused the Crown Prince to flee,
with troops clashing at the palace gates.
The number of innocent people killed reached tens of millions,
and the ancestral temple nearly toppled.
Fortunately, Emperor Wǔ obtained the letter from the Three Elders of Húguān,
and, with sudden clarity, was awakened to understanding.
He exterminated Jiāng Chōng and his three clans.
The event is recorded in the 22nd volume, in the second and third years of the Zhēnghé era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
'Jī'
is pronounced jī.
Only then did the empire find peace.
The ancients said:
'Do not forget the affairs of the past,
for they are teachers for the future.'
These are the words of the Grand Historian in the Records of the Grand Historian.
The Empress Dowager did not listen.
5 In summer,
in the fourth month,
the Empress Dowager cast a great instrument,
and placed it at the Northern Tower.
The Northern Tower was likely outside the Xuánwǔ Gate.
6 Cén Chángqiàn was appointed as Nèishǐ.
In the sixth month,
on the xīnwèi day,
Sū Liángsì was appointed as Left Minister, and Wéi Dàijià, concurrently Tóng Fènggé Luántái Sānpǐn, was appointed as Right Minister.
On the jǐmǎo day,
Wéi Sīqiān was appointed as Nàyán.
Sū Liángsì encountered the monk Huáiyì in the court hall.
Huáiyì was arrogant and did not show proper respect.
Liángsì was greatly angered,
and ordered his attendants to seize and drag him,
slapping his face several dozen times.
Huáiyì complained to the Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager said:
"Master should enter and exit by the North Gate.
The Southern Offices are where the ministers come and go;
do not offend them."
The Empress Dowager claimed that Huáiyì had ingenious skill,
and therefore had him enter the forbidden palace to undertake construction.
The Reminder, Wáng Qiúlǐ of Chángshè, submitted a memorial.
Chángshè
was a Hàn county.
In Suí, it was renamed Yǐngchuān.
In the fourth year of the Wǔdé era, it reverted to its old name,
and was attached to Xǔ Prefecture.
'Shàng'
is pronounced shàng.
"During Tàizōng's time,
there was Luó Hēihēi, who was skilled at playing the pipa.
Tàizōng had him castrated to serve as a palace attendant,
and had him teach the palace ladies.
If Your Majesty believes Huáiyì has ingenious talent,
and wishes to employ him in the palace,
I request that he be castrated,
so as not to bring disorder to the palace quarters."
The memorial was suppressed and not issued.
7 In autumn,
in the ninth month,
on the dīngwèi day,
Húsèluó, son of the Western Türk Jìwǎngjué Kèhán, was appointed as General of the Right Yùqián Guard,
succeeding as Jìwǎngjué Kèhán to oversee the Five Nǔshībì tribes.
8 On the jǐsì day,
Yōng Prefecture reported that a mountain had surged forth southeast of Xīnfēng County.
Xīnfēng was renamed Qìngshān County.
Xīnfēng had belonged to Jīngzhào since Hàn times.
Yú Wénjùn of Jiānglíng submitted a letter:
Jiānglíng County was attached to Jīng Prefecture.
"When the celestial ether is not harmonious, cold and heat occur together;
when the human ether is not harmonious, warts and growths appear;
when the terrestrial ether is not harmonious, mounds and hills emerge.
Now, Your Majesty, as a female ruler, occupies the yang position,
reversing the hard and the soft.
Therefore, the terrestrial ether is blocked and obstructed,
and mountains transform into disasters.
Your Majesty calls it 'Qìngshān' (Auspicious Mountain),
but I do not consider it auspicious.
In my foolish opinion, you should humble yourself and cultivate virtue to respond to Heaven's reproach.
Otherwise,
calamity will arrive!"
The Empress Dowager was angered
and exiled him to beyond the mountains.
Later, he was killed by the envoys of the six circuits.
The envoys of the six circuits are mentioned later in the 205th volume, in the second year of the Chángshòu era.
'Shǐ'
is pronounced shǐ.
9 The Türks invaded.
The Grand General of the Left Yīngyáng Guard, Hēichǐ Chángzhī, resisted them.
Reaching Liǎngjǐng,
he encountered over three thousand Türks.
Seeing the Táng troops,
they all dismounted and donned armor.
Chángzhī charged them with over two hundred cavalry,
and they all abandoned their armor and fled.
At dusk,
a large force of Türks arrived.
Chángzhī ordered fires to be lit in the camp.
To the southeast, more fires also arose.
The enemy suspected there were troops responding to each other,
and thus fled during the night.
10 Dí Rénjié served as Prefect of Níng Prefecture.
The Investigating Censor of the Right Terrace, Guō Hàn of Jìnlíng, was touring and inspecting Lǒngyòu.
Wherever he went, he conducted many investigations and impeachments.
Entering the territory of Níng Prefecture,
elders singing praises of the Prefect's virtue filled the roads.
Hàn recommended him to the court,
and he was summoned to serve as Vice-Minister of the Winter Offices.
Punctuated by Wáng Chóngwǔ; proofread by Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí.
Compiled by
Sīmǎ Guāng
by imperial command.
Later
student from Tiāntāi.
Third year of the Chuígōng era (Dīnghài, 687).
1. In spring,
in the intercalary first month,
on the day Dīngmǎo,
the imperial son Chéng Měi was enfeoffed as the Prince of Héng.
(At this time, Ruìzōng was emperor,
hence Chéng Měi and others were all considered imperial sons.)
Héng:
pronunciation is hù dēng.
Textual analysis notes: The Tang Calendar, the old Basic Annals, and the new biographies all record it as
"Chéng Yì".
The present text follows the Veritable Records.
Lóng Fàn was made the Prince of Wèi,
and Lóng Yè was made the Prince of Zhào.
2. In the second month,
on the day Bǐngchén,
the Eastern Turks' Gǔdǔlù and others raided Chāngpíng.
Chāngpíng:
a county from the Later Hàn,
belonging to the Kingdom of Guǎngyáng.
During Suí, it belonged to Zhuō Commandery.
During Táng, it belonged to Yōu Prefecture.
3. In the third month,
on the day Yǐchǒu,
the Nàyán Wéi Sīqiān retired from his post as Grand Master of the Palace.
4. In summer,
in the fourth month,
Sū Liángsì was ordered to remain in charge of the Western Capital.
At that time, the Director of the Palace Administration, Péi Fěigōng, was concurrently in charge of the Capital Parks.
(In the Guāngzhái period, the Directorate for the Palace Buildings was renamed the Directorate of the Palace Administration.)
The Capital Parks:
the parks of the Western Capital.
Liángsì said:
"In the past, Gōngyí Xiū served as Prime Minister of Lǔ,
yet he could still uproot the sunflowers and dismiss the weaving women.
(Dǒng Zhòngshū said: Gōngyí Xiū served as Prime Minister of Lǔ.
He went to his home,
saw silk being woven,
became angry and left.
His wife was eating at home and had eaten some sunflower greens,
he became displeased and uprooted the sunflowers.
He said:
'I already receive an official salary,
how can I also take the profit of the gardeners and weavers!'
Prime Minister:
pronunciation xiàng.
Dismiss:
pronunciation qù.)
And so it stopped.
5. On the day Rénxū,
Péi Jūdào was made Nàyán.
In the fifth month,
on the day Bǐngyín,
the Vice Minister of the Ministry of War, Zhāng Guāngfǔ of Jīngzhào, was made Vice Director of the Phoenix Pavilion and participated in the administration of state affairs.

6. The Vice Director of the Phoenix Pavilion and participant in the administration of state affairs of the Phoenix Pavilion and Luan Terrace, Liú Yīzhī, privately said to the Secretary of the Phoenix Pavilion, Jiǎ Dàyǐn of Yǒngnián:
Yǒngnián:
originally the Hàn county of Qūliáng.
During Wèi, it was the seat of Guǎngpíng Commandery.
During Suí, the commandery was abolished and it became Guǎngpíng County.
Later it was changed to Jīzé;
in the first year of the Rénshòu era, it was changed to Yǒngyuán
[year]
to avoid the taboo of the Crown Prince Guǎng's name.
During Táng, it was attached to Míng Prefecture.
"Since the Empress Dowager has deposed the incompetent and established the wise,
what need is there for her to hold court and exercise imperial power?
It would be better to return governance to the emperor
to put the hearts of the people at ease."
Dàyǐn secretly reported this.
The Empress Dowager was displeased.
She said to her attendants:
"Yīzhī was promoted by me."
(Liú Yīzhī rose from being a Scholar of the North Gate to become a minister,
hence this statement.)
Someone accused Yīzhī of accepting gold from Sūn Wànróng, the Governor of Guīchéng Prefecture.
(In the 22nd year of the Zhēnguàn era,
a separate tribe of the Khitan was used to establish Guīchéng Prefecture,
subordinate to the Sōngmò Governorate.)
Again:
pronunciation fú yòu.
The Empress Dowager ordered Wáng Běnlì, the Prefect of Sù Prefecture, to investigate him.
Běnlì announced the imperial decree and showed it to him.
Yīzhī said:
"If it has not passed through the Phoenix Pavilion and Luan Terrace,
how can it be called an imperial decree!"
The Empress Dowager was greatly angered,
considering this to be resistance against an imperial envoy.
On the day Gēngwǔ,
he was ordered to commit suicide at home.
When Yīzhī was first imprisoned,
Ruìzōng submitted a petition on his behalf pleading his case.
His relatives and friends all congratulated him.
Yīzhī said:
"This is precisely what will hasten my death."
Before his execution,
he bathed,
his expression calm and composed.
He personally drafted a memorial of thanks,
completing several pages immediately.
The Lang Official of the Unicorn Terrace, Guō Hàn,
(In the Guāngzhái period, the Palace Library Lang Official was renamed Unicorn Terrace Lang Official.)
and the Literary Scholar of the Crown Prince's Palace Library Bureau,
rank 6a,
in charge of attending to literary matters,
praised his literary talent. The Empress Dowager heard of this,
demoted Hàn to be a Judicial Officer of Wū Prefecture,
and Sījūn to be a Granary Officer of Bō Prefecture.
(In the 8th year of the Zhēnguàn era,
Wū Prefecture was established from the Lóngbiāo County of Chén Prefecture;
in the 9th year,
Bō Prefecture was established from the Zāngkē County of the Suí-era Zāngkē Commandery.)
Old Records: Wū Prefecture,
4,197 lǐ south of the capital,
3,900 lǐ from the Eastern Capital.
Bō Prefecture,
4,450 lǐ south of the capital,
4,960 lǐ from the Eastern Capital.
7. In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day Rénchén,
Wèi Xuántóng was made concurrent Nàyán.
8. The Lǐ households of Lǐngnán had previously paid half the tax.
The Protector-General of Jiāozhǐ, Liú Yányòu, made them pay the full amount.
The Lǐ households did not comply.
Yányòu executed their leaders.
Their partisans, Lǐ Sīshèn and others, rebelled,
capturing the city of the Protectorate of Ānnán.
(In the first year of the Tiáolù era of Gāozōng,
the Jiāo Prefecture Governorate was changed to the Protectorate of Ānnán.)
Lǐ:
pronunciation lǐ.
Cáo Xuánjìng, the Military Administrator of Guì Prefecture, led troops to attack Sīshèn and others,
and beheaded them.
9. The Eastern Turks' Gǔdǔlù and Yuánzhēn raided Shuò Prefecture.
Hēichǐ Chángzhī, the Grand Commander of the Yānrán Circuit, was sent to attack them,
with the Left General of the Imperial Insignia Guard, Lǐ Duōzuò, as his deputy.
They heavily defeated the Turks at Huánghuāduī.
(This is likely Huángguāduī.)
According to records, Shuò Prefecture had Huánghuāduī,
located in Shénwǔchuān.
The Turks all scattered and fled north of the desert.
Duōzuò's family for generations had been chieftains of the Mòhé.
He gained entry into the palace guard due to military achievements.
Hēichǐ Chángzhī, whenever he received rewards,
would distribute them among his officers and soldiers.
He had a fine horse that was injured by a soldier.
His subordinates requested that the soldier be flogged.
Chángzhī said:
"How can I have a soldier flogged over my private horse!"
In the end, he did not pursue the matter.
10. In the ninth month,
on the day Jǐmǎo,
a man named Yáng Chūchéng from Guó Prefecture falsely claimed to be a General of the Gentlemen of the Guards,
and forged an imperial decree to recruit people in the marketplace to welcome the Prince of Lúlíng back from Fáng Prefecture.
The affair was discovered,
and he was executed.
11. In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day Gēngzǐ,
the Central General of the Right Gate Guard, Cuàn Bǎobì, engaged the Eastern Turks' Gǔdǔlù and Yuánzhēn in battle.
His entire army was lost,
and Bǎobì fled back alone on a light horse.
Bǎobì, seeing that Hēichǐ Chángzhī had achieved merit,
submitted a request to pursue and destroy the remaining enemy.
An edict ordered him to consult with Chángzhī,
and to provide distant support.
Bǎobì, wishing to claim the entire credit for himself,
did not wait for Chángzhī.
He led 13,000 elite troops ahead,
advancing over 2,000 lǐ beyond the frontier,
launching a surprise attack on their tribes.
Upon arrival,
he first sent men to announce his coming,
allowing them to prepare thoroughly.
When they engaged in battle,
he was consequently defeated.
The Empress Dowager executed Bǎobì;
she changed Gǔdǔlù's name to Bùzúlù.
12. Wèi Xuántóng was ordered to remain in charge of the Western Capital.
13. Wǔ Chéngsì again had someone falsely accuse Lǐ Xiàoyì of saying of himself,
“My name contains the character ‘tù’ (rabbit);
the rabbit
is a creature of the moon,
so I am destined to have heavenly fortune.”
This meant he had the destiny to become the Son of Heaven.
[Note on pronunciation for] ‘fèn’ (fortune):
fú wèn fān.
In the eleventh month,
on the day Wùyín,
his death sentence was reduced, he was stripped of his official status,
exiled to Dānzhōu, where he died.
Dānzhōu
was formerly Dān’ěr County;
Dānzhōu was established in the fifth year of the Wǔdé era.
According to old records: Dānzhōu was 7,442 lǐ from the capital.
[Note on pronunciation for] Dān:
tú gān fān.
[Note on pronunciation for] zú (died):
zǐ xù fān.
Textual analysis notes: The New Annals state:
“In the fifth month of the first year of the Tiānshòu era, on the day Jǐhài,
Liáng Duke Lǐ Xiàoyì was executed.
Xiàoyì was initially enfeoffed as Duke of Liáng Commandery;
for his merit in suppressing Xú Jìngyè’s rebellion,
he was re-enfeoffed as Duke of Wú;
in the third year of the Chuígōng era,
his death sentence was reduced and he was stripped of his official status,
exiled to Dānzhōu.
At that time, his noble rank should have been revoked.”
The New Biography states:
“He was exiled to Dānzhōu and died there.”
The Annals and Biography contradict each other.
The Táng Lì states:
“On the eleventh day of the fourth month, Yìzhōu Chief Clerk Lǐ Xiàoyì was executed.
This was also a former position he held.”
The Tǒng Jì states,
“Lǐ Xiàoyì and his associates Cuī Yuánfǎng and Péi Ānqī were executed.”
The Táng Lì states,
“and his associates Cuī Zhīxián, Dǒng Yuánfǎng, Péi Ānqī, etc.”
Now, we follow the Veritable Records and the Old Biography.
14. The Empress Dowager intended to send Wéi Dàijià to lead troops to attack Tǔbō.
Textual analysis notes: The Veritable Records state,
“In the twelfth month, on the day Rénchén,
Dàijià was appointed as Grand Commander of the Ānxī Circuit,
overseeing thirty-six commanders to attack Tǔbō.”
It does not mention the outcome of the campaign.
By the first year of the Yǒngchāng era, in the fifth month,
it again states
“Dàijià was ordered to attack Tǔbō,
and in the seventh month, he was defeated at the Yínshíjiā River.”
According to his main biography, it does not mention he led troops twice;
therefore, we delete this event.
It was requested that, following the old system, a Censor be sent to supervise the army.
The Empress Dowager said:
“In ancient times, when enlightened rulers dispatched generals,
all matters outside the capital gates were entrusted to them.
Recently, I have heard that when Censors supervise the army,
every matter in the army, great or small, must be reported to and receive approval from them.
For subordinates to control superiors
is not in accordance with proper regulations;
moreover, how can they then be held accountable for achieving merit!”
Thus, the practice was abolished.
15. This year,
there was a great famine across the land,
particularly severe in Shāndōng and Guānnèi.
1. In spring,
in the first month,
on the day Jiǎzǐ,
temples for Gāozǔ, Tàizōng, and Gāozōng were established in Shéndū,
with seasonal sacrifices conducted according to the rituals of the Western Temples.
The Western Temples
refer to the ancestral temples in the Western Capital.
The Empress Dowager ordered officials to deliberate on the number of chambers for the Chóngxiān Temple (Temple of Honored Ancestors).
Sīlǐ Doctor Zhōu Cóng requested it be made with seven chambers.
[Note:] During the Guāngzhái era, the Tàicháng was renamed Sīlǐ.
The historian notes that Zhōu Cóng’s request
was currying favor and迎合ing the ruler’s wishes.
Chūnguān Vice-Minister Jiǎ Dàyǐn memorialized:
“According to ritual,
the Son of Heaven has seven temples,
feudal lords have five temples.
This is an unchanging principle for all kings.
Now, Zhōu Cóng cites baseless discussions,
extensively relates unusual hearsay,
directly advocates elevating the ritual status of the one holding court authority,
and does not adhere to the constant standards of the state.
The Empress Dowager personally received the late emperor’s entrustment,
glorifying the great plan.
The number of chambers for her Chóngxiān Temple should correspond to that of feudal lords.
The state’s ancestral temples should not be arbitrarily altered.”
The Empress Dowager then desisted.
2. During the reigns of Tàizōng and Gāozōng,
there were repeated desires to establish a Míngtáng (Hall of Enlightenment),
and various Confucian scholars debated its system,
but no decision was reached and the matter was dropped.
When the Empress Dowager assumed power,
she alone discussed its design with the Northern Gate Scholars,
not consulting the various Confucian scholars.
The Confucian scholars believed the Míngtáng should be located in the bǐng-sì direction south of the capital,
beyond three lǐ,
and within seven lǐ.
The Empress Dowager considered this too far from the palace.
In the second month,
on the day Gēngwǔ,
the Qiányuán Hall was demolished,
and on its site, the Míngtáng was constructed,
with the monk Huáiyì appointed as overseer,
employing tens of thousands of laborers.
3. In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day Wùxū,
the Crown Prince’s Communications Secretary Hǎo Xiàngxián was executed.
[Note on] Táng system:
The Crown Prince’s Communications Secretary was rank 7b lower,
responsible for guiding palace officials during audiences, farewells, and inquiries.
He was the grandson of Hǎo Chǔjùn.
Initially,
the Empress Dowager bore a grudge against Chǔjùn,
referring to his remonstrance to Gāozōng in the second year of the Shàngyuán era.
The Empress Dowager ordered Zhōu Xìng to interrogate him,
resulting in a conviction for Xiàngxián’s entire clan.
Xiàngxián’s family members went to the court hall,
to plead their grievance to Investigating Censor Lè’ān Rèn Xuánzhí.
Lè’ān Commandery
was Dìzhōu.
[Note on pronunciation for] cháo (court):
zhí yáo fān.
[Note on pronunciation for] jiān (supervise):
gǔ xián fān.
Xuánzhí was dismissed from his post for this.
As Xiàngxián faced execution,
he vehemently cursed the Empress Dowager,
exposing hidden misconduct within the palace,
seized firewood from market people to strike the executioners;
the Jīnwū guards together fought and killed him.
The Empress Dowager ordered his corpse dismembered,
his father’s and grandfather’s graves dug up,
and their coffins destroyed and bodies burned.
From then on, for the remainder of the Empress Dowager’s lifetime,
whenever judges executed someone,
they would first stuff a wooden ball into the person’s mouth.
4. Wǔ Chéngsì had white stone carved with the text:
“The Holy Mother oversees the people,
the imperial enterprise flourishes forever.”
The carved characters were filled in with purple stone mixed with medicinal substances.
On the day Gēngwǔ,
he had a man from Yōngzhōu, Táng Tóngtài, present a memorial offering it.
[Note:] Suí’s Jīngzhào Commandery was renamed Yōngzhōu in the first year of the Wǔdé era.
[Note on pronunciation for] Yōng:
yú yòng fān.
The Empress Dowager was pleased,
named the stone
the “Precious Diagram”.
And promoted Tóngtài to the rank of Yóujī General.
In the fifth month,
on the day Wùchén,
an edict was issued that she would personally worship at the Luò River,
to receive the
“Precious Diagram”;
perform ceremonies at the southern suburb altar,
offering thanks to the Vast Heaven;
after the rituals concluded,
proceed to the Míngtáng,
to receive assembled officials.
Commanded all regional governors, prefects, imperial clan members, and maternal relatives to gather at Shéndū ten days before the worship at the Luò.
On the day Yǐhài,
the Empress Dowager added the honorific title “Holy Mother Divine Sovereign”.
5. In the sixth month,
on the first day, Dīnghài,
there was a solar eclipse.
6. On the day Rényín,
three seals for the Divine Sovereign were made.
7. The Grand Princess of Dōngyáng had her fief reduced,
and along with her two sons, was relocated to Wūzhōu.
The princess
was a daughter of Tàizōng.
[Note on pronunciation for] zhǎng (grand):
zhī liǎng fān.
The Empress Dowager, because the Gāo family was the maternal clan of Zhǎngsūn Wújì,
thus detested them.
8. The Grand Commissioner for Inspection of the Jiāngnán Circuit and Vice-Minister of the Winter Ministry, Dí Rénjié, because the Wú and Chǔ regions had many illicit shrines,
memorialized to burn over 1,700 of them,
retaining only the four shrines for Xià Yǔ, Wú Tàibó, Jì Zhá, and Wǔ Yuán.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the day Dīngsì,
a general amnesty was proclaimed across the empire.
The
"Bǎo Tú"
was renamed
"Tiānshòu Shèng Tú" (Heaven-Bestowed Sacred Chart).
The Luòshuǐ River was renamed the Yǒngchāng Luòshuǐ,
its river god was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Xiǎnshèng,
granted the special advancement (tèjìn) rank,
fishing was prohibited on it,
and sacrifices to it were made equal to those for the Four Great Rivers.
According to Táng dynasty regulations,
sacrifices to the Sacred Mountains and Great Rivers were considered middle-grade sacrifices.
The "Shèng Tú Quán" (Sacred Chart Spring),
had the county of Yǒngchāng established beside it.
Furthermore, Mount Sōngshān was renamed Shén Yuè (Sacred Mountain),
its mountain god was enfeoffed as the Prince of Tiānzhōng,
appointed Grand Preceptor (Tàishī), Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers (Shǐchíjié), and Grand Governor of the Sacred Mountain (Shén Yuè Dà Dūdū),
and grazing was prohibited there.
Also, because an auspicious stone had been previously obtained at the Sìshuǐ River,
the Sìshuǐ was renamed Guǎngwǔ.
The Sìshuǐ area
was the Chénggāo County of the Hàn dynasty,
belonging to the Hénán Commandery.
In the Later Wèi dynasty it became Chénggāo Commandery,
where the Dōngzhōng Prefecture was established.
In the 18th year of the Suí dynasty's Kāihuáng era, Chénggāo was renamed Sìshuǐ,

Dù Yù said: The wives of brothers call each other sì.
Generally, sisters-in-law address each other

(In ancient times when establishing a state, there were guests and revered ones. The successors of the two previous dynasties were guests, treated with guest rites. Yán Shīgǔ said: "Kè" means respect; treating them with added respect is also like treating them as guests. Zhèng Xuán considered the Two Kings and the Three Revered Ones together as the Five Dynasties, and later scholars mostly followed his theory. The Táng originally had the Later Zhōu and Suí successors as the Two Kingly Successors; now this was changed. This "Zhōu" refers to the Later Zhōu.)

so Chángqiàn was dismissed and ordered to campaign westward against Tǔbō.
Before he arrived,
he was recalled,
and imprisoned.
Wǔ Chéngsì also slandered Gé Fǔyuán.
Lái Jùnchén further coerced Chángqiàn's son, Língyuán,
forcing him to implicate Sīlǐ Qīng and concurrently acting Nàyán Ōuyáng Tōng and several dozen others,
all claiming they were conspiring to rebel.
Ōuyáng Tōng was interrogated by Lái Jùnchén,
subjected to all five tortures,
yet he never uttered any differing words.
Lái Jùnchén then forged a confession from Ōuyáng Tōng.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Jǐyǒu,
Chángqiàn, Fǔyuán, Tōng, and others were all executed for their alleged crimes.
Wáng Qìngzhī had an audience with the Empress Dowager,
who said:
"The imperial heir is my son,
how can I depose him?"
Qìngzhī replied:
"'The spirits do not enjoy offerings from those not of their kind,
and the people do not sacrifice to those not of their clan.'
These are the words of Hú Tū, a senior official of Jìn from the Zuǒzhuàn.
How can we make the Lǐ clan the heirs!"
The Empress Dowager instructed him to leave.
Qìngzhī prostrated himself on the ground,
weeping and pleading as if ready to die,
refusing to leave.
The Empress Dowager then gave him a stamped paper pass, saying:
"If you wish to see me,
show this to the gatekeepers."
From then on, Qìngzhī repeatedly sought audiences,
which greatly angered the Empress Dowager.
She ordered Fènggé Shìláng Lǐ Zhāodé to administer a caning to Qìngzhī.
Zhāodé led him outside the Guāngzhèng Gate.
The southern wall of Luòyáng Palace had three gates:
the central one was called Yìngtiān,
the left one Xīngjiào,
and the right one Guāngzhèng.
"This villain wants to depose our imperial heir
and establish Wǔ Chéngsì,"
he ordered him to be beaten,
until blood flowed from his eyes and ears,
and then he was caned to death.
Examination of discrepancies: The Old Biography states:
"At the beginning of Yánzǎi,
Fènggé Shèrén Zhāng Jiāfú ordered several hundred frivolous and wicked youths from Luòyáng, led by Wáng Qìngzhī, to go to the palace gate,
submitting a memorial requesting that Wǔ Chéngsì be established as Crown Prince,
but Wǔ Zétiān did not permit it."
The Tánglì records,
regarding Zhāodé,
that in the first year of Yǒngchāng, he was demoted from Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng to Língshuǐ Wèi of Zhènzhōu.
According to the Veritable Records,
he first became Chancellor in the first year of Chángshòu.
The Old Biography states
that the caning to death of Qìngzhī occurred after he became Chancellor.
According to the Yùshǐ Tái Jì,
Zhāodé was transferred from Zhōngchéng to Fènggé Shìláng.
It seems he was temporarily demoted to Língshuǐ,
but was soon recalled and appointed Fènggé Shìláng.
The caning to death of Qìngzhī,
according to the Yùshǐ Tái Jì,
occurred when he was Fènggé Shìláng,
not after he became Chancellor.
The Old Biography may have mistakenly recorded Zàichū as Yánzǎi.
Qìngzhī's submission of the memorial might have been in the year Zàichū.
The Veritable Records mentions it in connection with the deaths of Cén Chángqiàn and Gé Fǔyuán.
Now, we synthesize the accounts from the Veritable Records, Yùshǐ Tái Jì, and the Old Biography.
Zhāodé then said to the Empress Dowager:
"The Heavenly Emperor,
is Your Majesty's husband;
the imperial heir,
is Your Majesty's son.
Your Majesty possesses the empire,
and should pass it on to your sons and grandsons for ten thousand generations.
How can you make a nephew your heir!
Since ancient times, there has never been a case where a nephew became Son of Heaven and established a temple for his aunt!
Moreover, Your Majesty received the entrustment from the Heavenly Emperor.
If you give the empire to Chéngsì,
then the Heavenly Emperor will receive no sacrifices."
The Empress Dowager also considered this reasonable.
Zhāodé
was the son of Lǐ Qiányòu.
Lǐ Qiányòu
was the one who saved Péi Rénguǐ at the beginning of the Zhēnguàn era.
29 On the day Rénchén,
Luántái Shìláng, Tóng Píngzhāng Shì Yuè Sīhuì, and Right Guard General Lǐ Ānjìng were executed.
Ānjìng
was the grandson of Lǐ Gāng.
Lǐ Gāng was renowned for his integrity and principles during the Suí and Táng transition;
Ānjìng can be said to have not disgraced his ancestor.
All the dukes, ministers, and officials submitted memorials urging the Empress Dowager to ascend the throne,
but Ānjìng alone sternly refused.
When he was imprisoned,
Lái Jùnchén interrogated him about his rebellion,
and Ānjìng said:
"As an old minister of the Táng house,
if you must kill me, then kill me!
If you ask about rebellion,
I truly have nothing to say."
Jùnchén ultimately executed him.
30 Tàixuéshēng Wáng Xúnzhī submitted a memorial,
requesting leave to return to his hometown;
the Empress Dowager granted it.
Dí Rénjié said:
"I have heard that the ruler alone holds the power over life and death and does not delegate it,
while all other matters are left to the relevant officials.
Therefore, the Left and Right Chéng
do not handle cases involving punishments less than tú;
the Left and Right Xiàng
only adjudicate cases involving liú or above,
because they are of gradually higher rank.
As for a student requesting leave,
it is a matter for the Chéng or Zhǔbù.
The Guózǐjiàn Chéng of the Táng,
rank Cong Liùpǐn Xià,
is in charge of supervising the Guózǐjiàn;
the Zhǔbù is rank Cong Qīpǐn Xià.
If such matters all require imperial approval, how can all affairs under heaven be handled!
If you truly wish not to contravene their wishes,
I request that a general regulation be established."
The Empress Dowager approved of this.

First Year of Chángshòu
(Rénchén, 692)
In the fourth month of this year,
the era name was changed to Rúyì;
in the ninth month,
it was changed to Chángshòu.
Before the fourth month, it was still the third year of Tiānshòu.
1 In the first month,
on the first day, Wùchén,
the Empress Dowager performed sacrifices at the Wànxiàng Shéngōng.
2 In the twelfth month,
Yùchí Fúshéxióng, son of the former King of Yútián, was established as King of Yútián.
3 In spring,
the first month,
on the day Dīngmǎo,
the Empress Dowager summoned the men recommended by the Pacification Commissioners for an audience.
For the Pacification Commissioners, see the previous scroll, the first year of the Tiānshòu era.
To summon for an audience is pronounced xiàn.
Xiàn is pronounced with the xián tone.
Commissioner is pronounced shǐ.
Shǐ is pronounced with the shūlì tone.
She promoted and employed them all.
Those of higher rank were tested for positions such as Fènggé Sheren and Jǐshìzhōng,
while those of lower rank were tested for positions like Yuánwàiláng, Shìyùshǐ, Bǔquē, Shíyí, and Jiàoshūláng.
In the Táng dynasty, the Jiàoshūláng
was a position of the ninth rank, upper grade.
The Textual Analysis states: According to the Tǒngjì:

It is suspected that this is the same event.

A recommended man, Shěn Quánjiāo, added to it:

"Eyes clouded by chaff"

"Blinded"

He was impeached for slandering the court's governance,

The Empress Dowager smiled and said:
"If only you all were not excessive,
why worry about what others say!
His crime should be pardoned."
The censor was greatly ashamed.
Although the Empress Dowager indiscriminately used official positions and salaries to win over the hearts of the people,
those who were incompetent
were soon dismissed,
or even punished and executed.
Wielding the power of punishment and reward to control the realm,
governance issued from herself,
she was perceptive and decisive,
so the talented and virtuous of the time also competed to serve her.
4 Guō Bà, the Assistant Magistrate of Nínglíng from Lújiāng, curried favor with the Empress Dowager through flattery.

belonged to Sòngzhōu.

belonging to Lúzhōu.
The Textual Analysis states: The New History biography

The Old History biography and the Yùshǐ Tái Jì both give only Bà,

The Qiǎnzǎi says he responded to the call for revolutionary recommendations,

We now follow the Tái Jì.
When Vice Censor-in-Chief Wèi Yuánzhōng fell ill,

He then tasted his feces

when Emperor Yáng of Suí built the Eastern Capital,

there were only low walls.

Cuī

Judge Wáng Déshòu said to Dí Rénjié:
Judge

Dí Rénjié said:

Hóu Sīzhǐ interrogated Wèi Yuánzhōng.

Since Dí Rénjié had confessed to rebellion,

Dí Rénjié tore a piece of his quilt and wrote a statement of injustice on it,
placed it inside a padded garment,

Dí Rénjié's son, Dí Guāngyuǎn, obtained the letter

The son of Yuè Sīhuì was not yet ten years old when he was confiscated into the Ministry of Agriculture.

The Empress Dowager's mind became slightly awakened.
She summoned Dí Rénjié and others for an audience and asked:

She produced the petition and showed it to them,

Jiāngxià: originally the land of Shāyí County in the Hàn Dynasty,

Fúlíng County: in the Hàn Dynasty, it belonged to Bā Commandery.

Shǔ established Xīxiāng County.

Fú: pronunciation fú.

spoke to the Empress Dowager, saying:

was the Hàn dynasty's Āndìng Marquisate,
located at the old city seven li west of the county seat at that time.
During the Zhōu and Qí dynasties, it was Āndìng County,
and during the Sui dynasty, it was renamed Lùchéng County,
belonging to Jìzhōu in the Táng dynasty.
According to Táng regulations,
the Zhǔbù of an upper county held the rank of Zhèng Jiǔpǐn Xià,
while that of a middle or lower county held the rank of Cóng Jiǔpǐn Shàng.
Hǎo,
is pronounced with the tone "hào."
He praised Yǒugōng for adhering to the Way and benevolence,
firmly upholding integrity and moral principles,
never changing his conduct whether in high or low status, life or death.
He posed a guest's question:
"Who in the present day can be compared to Lord Xú?"
The host replied:
"The world is vast,
and people are numerous.
Some may hide their traces and conceal their brilliance,
so I dare not make false claims.
But based on what I have seen and heard,
there is only one such person,
and he must be sought among the ancients."
The guest asked:
"How does he compare to Zhāng Shìzhī?"
The host replied:
"What Shìzhī practiced was very easy,
but what Lord Xú practiced was very difficult.
Between difficulty and ease,
superiority and inferiority become apparent.
Lord Zhāng lived during the time of Hàn Wéndì,
when the world was at peace.
As for cases like stealing the jade ring from the Gāomiào Temple or startling a horse on the Wèi Bridge,
it was merely a matter of upholding the law.
The events are recorded in the fourteenth volume, third year of Hàn Wéndì.
Lord Xú lived in an era of revolution,
amid a time of renewal.
Old retainers of the Táng dynasty
harbored treacherous intentions,
causing the ruler to be suspicious.
Figures like Zhōu Xīng and Lái Jùnchén
were like the Four Fiends of Yáo's time,
who embellished evil words to slander virtuous men.
Yet Lord Xú remained steadfast in the good Way even unto death,
deeply understanding and clarifying matters,
nearly falling into prison,
and repeatedly entangled in legal nets.
This is what you have heard—
is it not difficult indeed!"
Examination of discrepancies: The Cháoyě Qiānzǎi states:
"At that time, Lái Jùnchén fabricated charges against people,
always first submitting a memorial,
and upon receiving imperial approval,
he would then memorialize for confiscation of property.
Xú Yǒugōng released death row prisoners,
also first submitting a memorial,
stating that someone's crime deserved exemption,
and upon receiving imperial approval,
he would then overturn the verdict.
Yǒugōng was fond of exonerating crimes,
but he always acted upon imperial instruction first,
and did not act on his own authority."
This likely reflects how people at the time saw that those whom Jùnchén executed
and those whom Yǒugōng exonerated
often achieved their desired outcomes,
leading to suspicion that they first submitted memorials.
If Yǒugōng had always acted upon imperial instruction first,
how could he have faced the death penalty three times?
This account is not adopted here.
"If he were appointed Sīxíng Qīng,
he could fully display his talents."
The host replied:
"You only see that Lord Xú applied the law impartially,
and think he is suitable for the position of Sīxíng.
But I observe this man—
within his heart,
what cannot be contained?
If he were employed,
what task could he not accomplish?
How could he be limited to just Sīxíng!"

3 Jīzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Sīlǐ studied physiognomy with the occultist Zhāng Jǐngcáng,
and Jǐngcáng told Sīlǐ that he would pass through Jīzhōu
and rise to the position of Tàishī.
Sīlǐ thought that Tàishī was the highest position for a subject,
and that it could not be achieved without aiding in the establishment of a new dynasty.
So he conspired with Luòzhōu Lùshì Cānjūn Qílián Yào to rebel,
secretly associating with court officials,
using physiognomy as a pretext,
promising them wealth and honor.
Once they were pleased,

"Qílián Yào has the Mandate of Heaven,

Fènggé Shèrén Wáng Jù concurrently handled affairs as Tiānguān Shìláng,
and appointed Sīlǐ as Jīzhōu Cìshǐ.
Míngtáng Wèi Jí
Xū learned of the plot

In the first year of the Zǒngzhāng era of Gāozōng,

The Empress Dowager ordered Hé'nèi Prince Wǔ Yìzōng to investigate the matter.
Yìzōng instructed Sīlǐ to implicate many court officials,

As a result, anyone who slightly displeased him was implicated.
Thus, Sīlǐ implicated Fènggé Shìláng Tóng Píngzhāngshì Lǐ Yuánsù, Xiàguān Shìláng Tóng Píngzhāngshì Sūn Yuánhēng, Zhī Tiānguān Shìláng Shì Shí Bàozhōng, Liú Qí, Jǐshìzhōng Zhōu Pàn,
and Wáng Jù's elder brother, Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Miǎn, and younger brother, Jiānchá Yùshǐ Zhù, among others,

They were subjected to extreme torture to secure convictions.
On the Rénxū day,

Initially,
Yìzōng treated Sīlǐ leniently in public,
