The memorial was submitted for three days,
but she did not issue a response.
Wáng Jíshàn said:
"Jùnchén is cruel, cunning, greedy, and violent,
the arch-villain of the state.
If he is not removed,
he will surely shake the court."
When the Empress Dowager was touring the gardens,
Jí Xū held the reins.
The Empress Dowager asked him about outside affairs.
He replied:
"People outside only wonder why Lái Jùnchén's memorial has not been approved."
The Empress Dowager said:
"Jùnchén has rendered service to the state;
I am still considering it."
Xū said:
"Yú Ānyuǎn reported that Huī Zhēn was rebelling,
and indeed he later rebelled. (The matter of Zhēn is seen in the fourth year of the Chuígōng era in the previous scroll.)
Jùnchén gathered disaffected individuals,
falsely accused and framed good people,
amassed bribes like a mountain,
and filled the roads with wronged souls.
He is a traitor to the state;
why should he be pitied!"
The Empress Dowager then approved the memorial.
On the dīngmǎo day,
Zhāodé and Jùnchén were both executed in the marketplace.
People of the time all mourned Zhāodé and rejoiced at Jùnchén's death.
His enemies fought to eat Jùnchén's flesh;
it was gone in a moment.
They gouged out his eyes, peeled off his face,
ripped open his belly and pulled out his heart,
trampling it into mud.
Knowing that the world hated him,
the Empress Dowager issued an edict enumerating his crimes,
stating:
"He should be punished with the extermination of his clan to vent the anger of the common people.
His family may be confiscated according to the law."
Officials and commoners all congratulated each other on the roads, saying:
"From now on, those who sleep can finally rest their backs on the mat."
Jùnchén was rewarded with ten male and female slaves for his merit in reporting Qílián Yào.
When Jùnchén inspected the female slaves of the Court of the Imperial Granaries,

he found none suitable. (According to the *Táng Liùdiǎn*, the Assistant of the Court of the Imperial Granaries was in charge of all government household male and female slaves. When they reached adulthood, they were first matched according to their status. If granted as rewards, their wives and children were allowed to accompany them. If their households were confiscated due to crimes, they were assigned to various offices according to their abilities, with skilled women entering the Inner Palace.)
Hearing that the Tūjué general Húsèluó had a female slave who was good at singing and dancing,
he wanted to obtain her as a reward,
so he had someone falsely accuse Húsèluó of rebellion.
Several thousand tribal chieftains went to the palace, cutting their ears and slashing their faces to plead his innocence.
It was only when Jùnchén was executed that he was spared.
While Jùnchén was in power,
the Ministry of Personnel, accepting his recommendations, would appoint hundreds of people at a time, bypassing regular procedures.
After Jùnchén's downfall,
the vice ministers all confessed.
The Empress Dowager reprimanded them.
They replied:
"We have betrayed Your Majesty;
we deserve death!
If we disrupted the laws of the state,
the crime would only affect ourselves;
but if we disobeyed Jùnchén's words,
our clans would be immediately exterminated."
The Empress Dowager then pardoned them.

The Director of the Imperial Parks, Hóu Mǐn (the Táng Court of the Imperial Granaries had a Director of the Imperial Parks, rank 7b, in charge of matters related to imperial gardens and parklands. He oversaw the planting of fruit trees and vegetables for court assemblies and sacrifices, and was responsible for storing ice in the last month of winter.)
was advised by his wife, Dǒng shì:
"Jùnchén is a traitor to the state;
his downfall is imminent.
You should distance yourself from him."
Mǐn followed her advice.
Jùnchén became angry

and had him appointed as the Magistrate of Wǔlóng. (Wǔlóng County belonged to Tiánzhōu, established by opening barbarian territories. The *Old History* writes it as 'Wǔlóng,' stating that the date of its establishment and abolition is unknown. Also, Fúzhōu had a Wǔlóng County, established in the second year of the Wǔdé era by dividing Fúlíng.)
His wife said:
"Leave quickly; do not stay!"
After Jùnchén's downfall,
his followers were all exiled to Lǐngnán,
but Mǐn alone was spared.
The Empress Dowager summoned Yú Ānyuǎn to serve as the Provisioner of the Palace and promoted Jí Xū to Right Censor-in-Chief.
14. Appointed the Acting Vice Minister of the Ministry of War, Zōng Chǔkè, as Tongpingzhangshi.
15. Wǔ Yìzōng's army reached Zhàozhōu.
Hearing that the Qìdān general Luò Wùzhěng was leading several thousand cavalry to Jìzhōu,
Yìzōng became afraid
and wanted to flee south.
Someone said:
"The enemy has no supply train
and relies on plunder for provisions.
If we hold our position and defend,
they will surely disperse due to the situation.
Attacking them then
could achieve great merit."
Yìzōng did not listen
and retreated to Xiàngzhōu,
abandoning a great amount of military supplies and equipment.
The Qìdān then massacred Zhàozhōu.
On the jiǎwǔ day,
Sūn Wànróng was killed by his slave.
After Wànróng defeated Wáng Xiàojié,
he built a city in a strategic location four hundred lǐ northwest of Liǔchéng,
leaving behind the elderly, weak, women, and children,
along with the captured equipment and supplies,
under the guard of his brother-in-law Yǐ Yuānyǔ.
He then led elite troops to attack Yōuzhōu.
Fearing that the Tūjué Mòchuò would attack his rear,
he sent five men to Hēishā (Hēishā was the Tūjué court. 'Yǔ' is pronounced with a falling-rising tone.)
to tell Mòchuò:
"I have already defeated Wáng Xiàojié's million-strong army;
the Táng people are terrified.
I request to join with the Khan to take Yōuzhōu while we have the advantage."
Three men arrived first;
Mòchuò was pleased
and rewarded them with crimson robes.
The two who arrived later;
Mòchuò was angry at their delay
and intended to kill them.
The two said:
"Please allow us one word before we die."
Mòchuò asked the reason.
The two reported the situation of the Qìdān.
Mòchuò then killed the first three and rewarded the two with crimson robes,
making them guides.
He sent troops to capture the Qìdān's new city,
killing the captured Liángzhōu Governor Xǔ Qīnmíng to sacrifice to heaven.
He besieged the new city for three days
and captured it. (The new city was the one previously built by the Qìdān, located northwest of Liǔchéng.)
He sent Yǐ Yuānyǔ to swiftly report to Wànróng.
At that time, Wàn Róng was locked in a stalemate with the Táng forces.
When the army heard the news,
they were terrified.
The Xī people rebelled against Wàn Róng.
The Divine Troops Route Commander-in-Chief Yáng Xuánjī attacked from the front,
and the Xī troops attacked from the rear,
capturing his general Hé Āxiǎo.
Wàn Róng's army suffered a major collapse,
and he led several thousand light cavalry eastward in flight.
The Vanguard Commander-in-Chief Zhāng Jiǔjié dispatched troops to intercept him along the road.
Wàn Róng, in desperate straits,
fled with his slave to the east of the Lù River.
The Bàoqiū River flows from beyond the frontier,
passes south through Lù County of Yōuzhōu,
and is called the Lù River.
He sighed and said:
"Now, if I wish to return to the Táng,
my crime is already great.
If I return to the Tūjué, I will also die.
If I return to Xīnlúo, I will also die.
Where shall I go!"
His slave beheaded him and surrendered,
and his head was displayed on the gate of the Sìfāng Guǎn.
The Hàn dynasty had a Mán Yí Dǐ on Gǎo Street.
The Later Wèi established residences for envoys from various states.
Later, four guesthouses were built to accommodate those who came from all directions to surrender,
as recorded in the 149th year of the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng, in the first year of the Pǔtōng era.
By the time of Emperor Yáng of Suí, the Sìfāng Guǎn was established outside the Jiànguó Gate,
to receive envoys and guests from all directions,
each managing affairs related to their respective regions and border trade,
under the jurisdiction of the Hónglú Temple.
In the Táng dynasty, the Sìfāng Guǎn was placed under the Zhōngshū Shěng,
managed by the Tōngshì Shèrén.
Xiāo (to display a severed head),
pronounced Jiānyáo.
16 On the Wùzǐ day,
Tèjìn Wǔ Chéngsì and Chūnguān Shàngshū Wǔ Sānsī were both appointed Tóng Fènggé Luántái Sānpǐn.
17 On the Xīnmǎo day,
an edict was issued: as the Qìdān had just been pacified,
Héneì Wáng Wǔ Yìzōng, Lóu Shīdé, and Wèizhōu Cìshǐ Dí Rénjié were ordered to separately lead routes to pacify Héběi.
Wherever Yìzōng went, he was cruel and brutal.
Among the people were those who had been coerced by the Qìdān and had now returned.
Yìzōng considered them all rebels,
and had their gallbladders cut out while they were still alive.
Previously,
Hé Āxiǎo was fond of killing people.
The people of Héběi said of them:
"Only these two Hés,
kill the most people."
Wǔ Yìzōng was enfeoffed as Héneì Wáng,
and together with Hé Āxiǎo, they were called
"the two Hés."
18 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Dīngyǒu day,
Kūnmíng submitted and became attached,
and Dòu Zhōu was established.
19 Wǔ Chéngsì and Wǔ Sānsī were both dismissed from government affairs.
20 On the Gēngwǔ day,
Wǔ Yōuyí returned in triumph from Yōuzhōu.
Wǔ Yìzōng memorialized that the Héběi commoners who had followed the rebels should all have their clans exterminated.
Zuǒ Shíyí Wáng Qiúlǐ refuted him in court, saying:
"These people originally had no military preparations,
their strength could not overcome the rebels,
and they reluctantly followed them to seek survival.
How could they have had rebellious intentions against the state!
Yìzōng commanded a powerful army of several hundred thousand,
yet he retreated at the mere rumor of the enemy,
allowing the rebel forces to spread.
Now he wishes to shift the blame onto the confused people in the countryside,
showing disloyalty as a minister.
I request that Yìzōng be beheaded first to apologize to Héběi!"
Yìzōng was unable to reply.
Sīxíng Qīng Dù Jǐngjiǎn also memorialized:
"These are all people who were coerced,
I request that they all be pardoned."
The Empress Dowager complied.
21 In the eighth month,
on the Bǐngxū day,
Nàyán Yáo Shú was demoted to Yìzhōu Zhǎngshǐ due to an offense,
and Tàizǐ Gōng Yǐn Dòulú Qīnwàng was appointed Wénchāng Yòuxiàng, Fènggé Luántái Sānpǐn.
During the Tiānshòu era, the Tàizǐ Zhānshì was changed to Tàizǐ Gōng Yǐn.
Above "Fènggé"
there should be
the character "tóng"
Kǎoyì says: The Xīn Biǎo records,
"On the Gēngzǐ day,
Dí Rénjié was concurrently appointed Nàyán,
Wǔ Sānsī was appointed Jiàoxiào Nèishǐ,
and Qīnwàng was appointed Wénchāng Yòuxiàng, Tóng Sānpǐn."
The Jiù Jì and Zhuàn, and the Xīn Jì, do not mention this.
There is no Gēngzǐ day this month.
The appointments of Dí Rénjié and Wǔ Sānsī occurred the following year.
The Xīn Biǎo mistakenly duplicates this.
22 In the ninth month,
on the Rénchén day,
a grand sacrifice was held at the Tōngtiān Palace,
a general amnesty was proclaimed,
and the era name was changed.
The era name was changed to Shéngōng.
23 On the Gēngxū day,
Lóu Shīdé was appointed Acting Nàyán.
24 On the Jiǎyín day,
the Empress Dowager said to her attending ministers:
"Recently, Zhōu Xìng and Lái Jùnchén investigated cases,
often implicating court ministers,
saying they plotted rebellion;
the state has constant laws,
how dare I violate them!
In between, I suspected it might not be true,
so I sent close ministers to the prisons to interrogate them,
obtained their handwritten confessions,
and they all admitted guilt themselves,
so I did not doubt it.
Since Xìng and Jùnchén died,
I have not heard of any more rebels.
Does this mean those who died before were not wronged?"
Xiàguān Shìláng Yáo Yuánchóng replied:
"Since the Chuígǒng era, those who died for plotting rebellion,
were mostly framed by Xìng and others,
who considered it their achievement.
When Your Majesty sent close ministers to interrogate them,
the close ministers themselves could not ensure their own safety,
how could they dare to change anything!
If those interrogated retracted their statements,
they feared suffering cruel torture,
so they preferred to die quickly.
Fortunately, Heaven enlightened Your Majesty's heart,
and Xìng and others were executed.
I pledge with my hundred family members to guarantee for Your Majesty,
that from now on, among the ministers inside and outside the court, there will be no more rebels;
if there is the slightest concrete evidence,
I request to be punished for the crime of knowing but not reporting."
The Empress Dowager was pleased and said:
"In the past, the chief ministers all went along with these matters,
making me appear as a ruler who indulged in cruel punishments;
hearing your words,
deeply accords with my heart."
She bestowed upon Yuánchóng a thousand strings of cash.
At that time, many people appealed for Wèi Yuánzhōng's wrongs,
and the Empress Dowager summoned him again and appointed him Sùzhèng Zhōngchéng.
Yuánzhōng had previously been sentenced to execution and exile four times.
Kǎoyì says: The Jiù Zhuàn says he was exiled three times,
but now we follow the Yùshǐ Tái Jì.
According to the Xīn Shū: Yuánzhōng was Luòyáng Lìng,
was implicated in Zhōu Xìng's case and sentenced to death,
but due to his achievements in pacifying Yáng and Chǔ,
he was exiled instead.
Over a year later,
he was framed by Lái Jùnchén,
and as he was about to be executed,
the Empress Dowager sent Wáng Yǐnkè to proclaim an edict pardoning him.
This is the second incident.
The Zīzhì Tōngjiàn records Wáng Yǐnkè proclaiming the pardon in the first year of the Yǒngchāng era,
and by the first year of the Chángshòu era, he was again imprisoned and demoted.
This is the third incident.
Later, in the third year of the Cháng'ān era, he was again demoted to Gāoyào Wèi.
This is the fourth incident.
It is unknown how the Yùshǐ Tái Jì records this.
The Empress Dowager asked:
"In the past, you were slandered several times,
why was that?"
He replied:
"I am like a deer,
and those who weave nets wanted to get my flesh to make soup,
how could I avoid it!"
25 In winter,
the intercalary tenth month,
on the Jiǎyín day,
Yōuzhōu Dūdū Dí Rénjié was appointed Luántái Shìláng,
and Sīxíng Qīng Dù Jǐngjiǎn was appointed Fènggé Shìláng,
both concurrently appointed Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
Rénjié submitted a memorial,
stating:
"The Four Barbarians were born by Heaven,
all beyond the territories of the ancient kings.
Thus, to the east they are blocked by the vast sea,
to the west hindered by the shifting sands,
to the north obstructed by the great desert,
and to the south impeded by the Five Ridges.
This is how Heaven has set boundaries for the barbarians and separated the inner lands from the outer.
Since the records in the classics,
and the reach of sound teachings,
what the Three Dynasties could not achieve,
our state has now entirely encompassed.
The poet boasted of the campaign against the Tàiyuán,
and praised the spread of virtuous transformation to the Jiāng and Hàn rivers.
The poem 'June'
describes King Xuān's northern expedition.
The poem says:
'We attacked the Xiǎnyǔn,
and reached Tàiyuán.'
Also, the poem 'Hàn Guǎng'
praises King Wén's way spreading to the southern states,
and the virtuous transformation reaching the regions of the Jiāng and Hàn rivers.
All these are within the territory of our state.
As for using military force beyond the borders,
seeking merit in distant lands,
exhausting the treasury's wealth to contend for barren land,
gaining their people does not increase our taxes,
acquiring their land cannot be farmed or woven,
merely pursuing the reputation of civilizing distant barbarians,
without focusing on the methods of strengthening the foundation and pacifying the people—
this is what Qín Shǐhuáng and Hàn Wǔdì did,
not the enterprise of the Five Emperors and Three Kings.
Shǐhuáng exhausted military force and pursued warfare to the extreme,
striving to expand territory,
with the dead lying like hemp,
leading to the collapse and rebellion of the realm.
The event is recorded in the Annals of Qín.
The people were impoverished and destitute,
bandits rose like swarms;
in his later years, he repented and realized,
ceased warfare and halted corvée labor,
thus he could be blessed by Heaven.
The event is recorded in the Annals of Hàn Wǔdì.
The expenses grew ever wider,
with garrisons in the west at the Four Garrisons,
and in the east at Āndōng,
conscription and levies increased daily,
leaving the people empty and exhausted.
Now, east of the pass there is famine,
in Shǔ and Hàn people flee,
south of the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
exactions and demands do not cease,
people cannot return to their livelihoods,
and join together to become bandits.
Once the root is shaken,
troubles and calamities will not be shallow.
The reason for this
is all due to contending for the barren lands of the barbarians,
violating the way of nurturing the common people.
In the past, Hàn Yuándì adopted Jiǎ Juānzhī's advice and abolished the Zhūyá Commandery.
The event is recorded in the twenty-eighth year, the second year of the Chūyuán era.
The event is recorded in the twenty-fifth year, the second year of the Yuánkāng era.
This was because he feared exhausting the people's strength.
Recently, in the Zhēnguàn era, the Nine Surnames were pacified,
and Lǐ Sīmó was established as Khan,
to rule over the various tribes.
See the one hundred and ninetieth year, the thirteenth year of the Zhēnguàn era.
When they submit, pacify them,
achieving the principle of 'pushing aside the perishing and securing the surviving.'
The 'Announcement of Zhònghuǐ' in the Book of Documents says: 'Push aside the perishing and secure the surviving,
then the state will flourish.'
'Push'
is pronounced tuī.
This is the recent exemplary model,
the established precedent for managing the borders.
I humbly suggest that Āshǐnà Húsèluó should be established as Khan,
entrusted with the Four Garrisons,
to continue the extinguished state of the Gāo clan,
meaning Gāolì.
Save military expenses in distant regions,
and concentrate armor and troops at the frontier,
so that the barbarians have no opportunity for invasion or insult—this is sufficient.
Why must we exhaust their dens and lairs,
contending with ants over length and shortness!
We should only order the border troops,
to guard carefully and prepare defenses,
send scouts far out,
gather supplies and grain,
wait for them to come on their own,
and then attack them.
With rest awaiting labor, the soldiers' strength doubles;
with the host defending against guests, we gain the advantage;
with strong walls and cleared fields, the bandits gain nothing;
naturally, if the two enemies advance deep, they face the risk of stumbling,
if they advance shallowly, they surely gain no plunder.
After several years like this,
we can make the two foes submit without attack."
The two enemies, the two foes,
both refer to the Turks and Tibetans.
Those with insight agreed with this.
26 The Secretariat Drafter Lǐ Qiáo, in charge of the Ministry of Personnel selection affairs,
began establishing several thousand supernumerary officials.
27 Previously, the calendar officials took this month as the first month,
and the twelfth month as the intercalary month.
The Empress Dowager wanted the first day of the first month, jiǎzǐ, to coincide with the winter solstice,
so she issued an edict stating:
"The last day of the previous month still sees the moon,
which violates the heavenly order.
The last day,
refers to the last day of the previous month.
The coming month is the first month."
First year of Shènglì
(Wùxū, 698)
1 First month,
first day jiǎzǐ,
winter solstice,
the Empress Dowager offered sacrifices at the Tōngtiān Palace;

second month,
yǐwèi,

4 Wǔ Chéngsì and Sānsī sought to become heir apparent,
repeatedly sending people to persuade the Empress Dowager, saying:
"Since ancient times, no Son of Heaven has made someone of a different surname his heir."
The Empress Dowager was undecided.
Dí Rénjié often spoke leisurely to the Empress Dowager, saying:
"Emperor Wén combed the wind and bathed in the rain,
personally braved the spearpoints,
to pacify the realm,
and passed it to his sons and grandsons.
The Great Emperor entrusted his two sons to Your Majesty.
Gāozōng's posthumous title is Celestial Emperor Great.
The two sons,
refer to the Prince of Lúlíng and the Heir Apparent.
Is this not perhaps against Heaven's will!
Moreover, which is closer, aunt-nephew or mother-son?
Your Majesty's relation to Chéngsì and Sānsī
is aunt-nephew.
To the Prince of Lúlíng and the Heir Apparent,
it is mother-son.
Then after ten thousand years,
when accompanying in the Grand Temple,
the succession will be endless;
if a nephew is established,
I have never heard of a nephew becoming Son of Heaven and placing his aunt in the temple."
The Empress Dowager said:
"This is my family matter,
you should not interfere."
Rénjié said:
"The ruler takes the four seas as his home,
within the four seas,
who is not his subject,
what is not Your Majesty's family matter!
The ruler is the head,
the ministers are the limbs,
in principle they form one body,
moreover, I occupy the position of chancellor,
how can I not interfere!"
He also urged the Empress Dowager to recall the Prince of Lúlíng.
The Prince of Lúlíng,
in the first year of Guāngzhái was moved to Jūnzhōu,
in the first year of Chuígōng was moved to Fángzhōu.
The Empress Dowager gradually became aware.
Another day,
she said to Rénjié:
"I dreamed of a large parrot with both wings broken,
what does it mean?"
He replied:
"Wǔ is Your Majesty's surname,
the two wings,
are the two sons.
If Your Majesty raises the two sons,
then the two wings will flutter."
From then on, the Empress Dowager had no intention of establishing Chéngsì or Sānsī.
When Sūn Wànróng besieged Yōuzhōu,
he sent a proclamation to the court saying:
"Why not return Lúlíng Wáng to us?"
Jí Xū, Zhāng Yìzhī, and Zhāng Chāngzōng all served as attendants in the Kònghè Jiān.
That year, the Kònghè Jiān was established to accommodate those favored by the emperor.
Jí Xū calmly advised the two brothers:
"You brothers enjoy such high favor and prestige,
yet it is not due to your virtue or achievements.
Many in the empire look askance and gnash their teeth at you.
If you do not perform great deeds for the empire,
how can you preserve yourselves?
I privately worry for you!"
The two brothers grew fearful,
and with tears asked for a plan.
Jí Xū said:
"The scholars and commoners of the empire have not forgotten the virtue of the Táng,
and all long for the return of Lúlíng Wáng.
The Sovereign is advanced in years,
and the great enterprise must be entrusted to someone;
the various Wǔ princes are not in her favor.
Why not calmly advise the Sovereign to establish Lúlíng Wáng as heir to fulfill the hopes of the people!
In this way,
not only will you avoid disaster,
but you can also preserve your wealth and status for a long time."
The two brothers agreed,
and seized opportunities to repeatedly speak of this to the Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager knew the plan came from Jí Xū,
so she summoned and questioned him.
Jí Xū again explained the advantages and disadvantages to the Empress Dowager in detail,
and only then did the Empress Dowager's mind become settled.
Examination of Discrepancies says: There exists a Biography of Lord Dí of Liáng,
said to be compiled by Lǐ Yōng,
but its language is vulgar and absurd,
likely not by Lǐ Yōng.
It states:
"The Empress accepted the proposals of the various Wǔ,
intending to transfer the ancestral altars,
planning to establish Wǔ Sānsī as heir apparent,
and moved Lúlíng Wáng to Fánglíng.
The various Wǔ secretly schemed,
day and night offering counsel: 'Your Majesty's surname is Wǔ,
you should establish a Wǔ,
for there has never been an emperor who took someone of a different surname as heir.'
After the Empress Dowager had already agreed,
she ceremoniously asked her ministers: 'My years are declining,
the state lacks a designated heir,
now I wish to choose a worthy,
who is fit for it?
Though I may find someone,
it ultimately rests on your deliberations.'
Most of the chief ministers had heard the decision was made,
and their words all followed her intent;
Dí Rénjié alone stepped back and stood,
silent without a word.
The Empress Dowager asked: 'You alone are silent,
you must have a different view.'
Lord Dí said: 'I do.
I observe the celestial signs above,
and see no indication of a change of ruler;
examining the hearts of the people,
they have not truly tired of Táng virtue.'
The Empress Dowager said: 'How do you know this?'
Lord Dí said: 'Recently, the Xiongnu invaded the border,
Your Majesty sent Prince Liáng Sānsī to recruit in the capital markets,
but after over a month,
he had not gathered a thousand men.
Later, Lúlíng Wáng followed,
and before twenty days had passed,
the number exceeded fifty thousand.
From this, it is clear
the people's hearts have not turned away.
If Your Majesty wishes to continue the line,
if not Lúlíng Wáng,
I truly know of no other.'

Cháoyǐn offered himself as a sacrificial animal,
bathed, and lay on the sacrificial altar,
requesting to take the Empress Dowager's place in fate.
The Empress Dowager's illness slightly improved,
and she rewarded him generously.
On the Dīngyǒu day,
she returned from Gōushì.
11 Previously,
the Tibetan Tsanpu, Qínǔxīnòng, was still young,
and Lùn Qīnlíng and his brothers held power.
They were all brave and strategic,
and the various tribes feared them.
Qīnlíng remained in the center to govern,
while his younger brothers held military power and controlled various regions.
Zànpó often resided in the eastern region,
and was a threat to the Central Kingdom for over thirty years.
As Qínǔxīnòng gradually grew older,
he secretly plotted with the minister Lùn Yán to eliminate them.
When Qīnlíng was away,
the Tsanpu pretended to go hunting,
gathered troops, and arrested over two thousand of Qīnlíng's relatives and associates,
executing them.
He then sent envoys to summon Qīnlíng and his brothers.
Qīnlíng and others raised troops and refused the order.
The Tsanpu led troops to attack them,
Qīnlíng's forces collapsed,
and he committed suicide.
In summer, the fourth month,
Zànpó led over a thousand of his troops to surrender.
The Empress Dowager ordered Guō Yuánzhèn, the Military Equipment Officer of the Left Martial Guard, and Fūméng Lìngqīng, the Grand Commissioner of the Héyuán Army, to lead cavalry to welcome them.
Fūméng,
is a surname.
According to the Genealogy of Surnames,
Fūméng,
is a Qiang double surname.
During the Later Qin dynasty, there was General Jiànwēi, Fūméng Dàqiāng.
Qīnlíng's son, Gōngrén,
surrendered with the seven thousand tents of Tǔyùhún under his command,
and was appointed General of the Left Jade Bell Guard and Duke of Jiǔquán Commandery.
12 On the Rénchén day,
Wèi Yuánzhōng was appointed Acting Governor of Bīng Prefecture,
and concurrently served as Grand Commander of the Tiānbīng Army,
to guard against the Turks.
Lóu Shīdé was appointed Deputy Grand Commander of the Tiānbīng Army,
and concurrently served as Grand Commissioner of the Lǒngyòu Armies,
specifically in charge of pacifying and comforting the surrendered Tibetans.
13 The Empress Dowager was advanced in age,
and worried that after her death, the Crown Prince and the various Wǔ clan members would not get along.
On the Rényín day,
she ordered the Crown Prince, the Prince of Xiāng, Princess Tàipíng, and Wǔ Yōujì, among others, to write an oath,
which was announced to heaven and earth in the Bright Hall,
inscribed on an iron certificate,
and stored in the Historiography Institute.
14 In autumn,
the seventh month,
Wǔ Yōuyí, the Prince of Jiàn'ān, was ordered to remain in the Western Capital,
replacing Wǔ Yōuwàng, the Prince of Kuàijī.
15 On the Bǐngchén day,
1,400 tents of the Tǔyùhún tribe submitted to the court.
Tǔ,
pronounced as tǔ, entering tone.
Yù,
pronounced as yù.
16 In the eighth month,
on the Guǐsì day,
Tūqíshī Wūzhìlè sent his son Zhēnǔ to pay a visit.
After the Western Turks were defeated,
the Tūqíshī began to rise.
Tūqíshī Wūzhìlè,
was a separate tribe of the Western Turks.
Initially subordinate to Húsèluó,
he held the title Mòhè Dágān.
Later, when Húsèluó came to court,
his territory was annexed by Wūzhìlè.
Qí,
pronounced as qí jì fān.
Jiàn,
pronounced as xián biàn fān.
17 An edict stated:
"Local officials of prefectures and counties,
unless they have received an imperial decree,
must not erect steles without authorization."
18 Wáng Jíshàn, the Palace Secretary, although lacking scholarly knowledge,
was upright and unwavering,
possessing the integrity of a great minister.
Whenever Zhāng Yìzhī and his brothers attended inner court banquets,
they no longer observed the etiquette of subjects;
Jíshàn repeatedly memorialized that this was unacceptable.
The Empress Dowager was displeased,
and said to Jíshàn:
"Since you are advanced in age,
it is not suitable for you to continue attending recreational banquets.
You may simply oversee matters within the palace."
Gé,
refers to the palace halls.
He requested leave for over a month;
the Empress Dowager did not inquire about him.
Jíshàn sighed and said:
"How can there be a Secretariat Director whom the Son of Heaven does not see for a single day?
The situation is clear!"
He then submitted a memorial requesting retirement,
but the Empress Dowager did not permit it.
On the Gēngzǐ day,
Jíshàn was appointed Left Chancellor of Wenchang,
and Dòulú Qīnwàng, the Palace Steward of the Crown Prince, was appointed Right Chancellor of Wenchang,
both still concurrently serving as Tongfenggèluántái Sānpǐn.
Yáng Zàisī, the Vice Minister of the Luán Pavilion and Tongpingzhangshi, was dismissed and appointed Grand Master of the Left Censorate.
That is, the Left Grand Master of Censors.
On the Dīngwèi day,
the Prince of Xiāng was concurrently appointed Acting Grand Protector of Ānběi.
Lù Yuánfāng, the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel, was appointed Vice Minister of the Luán Pavilion and Tongpingzhangshi.
19 Lóu Shīdé, the Palace Attendant and Grand Commissioner of the Lǒngyòu Armies, passed away.
Lóu Shīdé served in Hézhōu and Lǒngyòu,
for more than forty years in total,
remaining reverent, diligent, and never negligent,
bringing peace to both the common people and the barbarians.
His nature was deep, steady, broad-minded, and forgiving.
When Dí Rénjié entered the office of chancellor,
it was actually Shīdé who recommended him;
but Rénjié did not know this,
and in his mind rather looked down upon Shīdé,
repeatedly pushing him out to provincial posts.
The Empress Dowager became aware of this,
and once asked Rénjié:
"Is Shīdé worthy?"
He replied:
"As a general, he is capable of carefully guarding the frontiers,
but as for being worthy, your subject does not know."
She asked again:
"Does Shīdé understand men?"
He replied:
"Your subject once served as his colleague,
but never heard that he understood men."
The Empress Dowager said:
"That I, the emperor, came to know you,
was due to Shīdé's recommendation.
He can indeed be said to understand men."
After Rénjié left,
he sighed and said:
"Lord Lóu's great virtue
has encompassed me for a long time,
yet I could not perceive its bounds."
At that time, false accusations and entanglements were rampant,
yet Shīdé, having long served as general and chancellor,
alone was able to preserve his merit and reputation till the end,
and people respected him for this.
On the 20th day, Wùshēn,
Wǔ Sānsī was appointed as Nèishǐ.
On the 21st day, in the ninth month,
on Yǐhài,
the Empress Dowager visited Fúchāng;
Fúchāng County belonged to the Eastern Capital,
originally called Yíyáng County,
renamed in the second year of the Wǔdé era,
taking its name from the Suí dynasty Fúchāng Palace.
On Wùyín,
she returned to Shéndū.
On the 22nd day, Gēngzǐ,
the Duke of Xíngzhēn, Wáng Jíshàn, passed away.
On the 23rd day, the Yellow River overflowed,
sweeping away over a thousand households of commoners' homes in Jìyuán.
Jìyuán was originally the town of Yuán in the Spring and Autumn period,
during the Hàn, it was within the boundaries of Yuán County in Hédōng,
in the sixteenth year of the Suí dynasty's Kāihuáng era, Jìyuán County was established,
belonging to Huáizhōu.
Jì,
is pronounced zǐ lǐ.
In the 24th month, winter,
tenth month,
on Dīnghài,
Lùn Zànpó arrived at the capital,
the Empress Dowager treated him with great favor and bestowed lavish rewards,
appointing him as Right Guard Grand General,
and ordering him to lead his troops to guard Hóngyuán Valley.
Hóngyuán Valley lies within the boundaries of Chāngsōng County in Liángzhōu.
To order to lead,
is pronounced jí liàng.
On the 25th day, the sons of the Crown Prince and Prince Xiàng once again left their residences.
The sons of Prince Xiàng had been confined within the palace,
see the second year of the Tiānshòu era, scroll 204.
Again,
is pronounced fú yòu;
below, 'again' is not the same.
Since the Empress Dowager assumed regency,
she often appointed various princes of the Wǔ clan and Commandants of the Imperial Sons-in-Law as Jìujūn Jìjiǔ,
and many of the Bóshì and Zhùjiào were also not Confucian scholars.
Moreover, due to the suburban altars,
the Bright Hall,
the worship at Luò,
and the feng sacrifice at Sōng,
the suburban altars,
refer to the sacrifice at the circular mound in the southern suburbs.
The sacrifices at the Wànxiàng Shén Palace and the Tōngtiān Palace,
were both held at the Bright Hall.
In the fourth year of Chuígǒng, the worship at Luò was performed,
in the first year of Wànsuì Tōngtiān, the feng sacrifice at Mount Sōng was held.
The Zhāiláng,
were those who held the dòu and biān vessels, and presented the zūn, yí, léi, and xǐ vessels for sacrificial ceremonies.
As a result, students no longer pursued their studies,
and over twenty years,
schools were nearly abandoned.
Moreover, those who had been falsely accused by the cruel officials of the past,
their relatives and friends were displaced and scattered,
and had not yet received pardon and forgiveness.
Wéi Sìlì, a Shèrén of the Fènggé Pavilion, submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Current customs increasingly belittle Confucian learning,
and the Way of the former kings
is neglected and no longer discussed.
It would be appropriate to order the sons and younger brothers of princes and dukes and below
all to enter the National Academy,
and not allow them to advance in official careers through other paths.
Furthermore,
since the incidents in Yáng and Yù,
referring to Xú Jìngyè raising troops in Yángzhōu,
and Prince Yuè Zhēn raising troops in Yùzhōu.
cruel officials seized the opportunity,
solely intent on killing people to seek advancement.
Thanks to Your Majesty's sagely discernment,
Zhōu, Qiū, Wáng, and Lái were successively executed,
in the second year of Tiānshòu,
Zhōu Xīng was exiled to death,
and Qiū Shénjì was executed.
In the first year of Yánzǎi, Wáng Hóngyì was executed,
in the first year of Shéngōng, Lái Jùnchén was executed.
It was as if seeing the warmth of spring again.
As for men like Dí Rénjié and Wèi Yuánzhōng,
who in the past underwent interrogation,
they also both falsely confessed,
had it not been for Your Majesty's clear investigation,
they would have been made into mincemeat;
now Your Majesty has elevated and employed them,
and they have all become good ministers.
Why were they wrong before and are right now?
It is truly due to having been wrongly accused and then clearly distinguished.
Your subject fears that those who in the past bore grievances and were punished are very numerous,
and they are all like this.
I humbly hope Your Majesty will expand the benevolence of Heaven and Earth,
broaden the application of thunder and rain,
and since the Chuígǒng era,
regardless of the severity of the crimes,
all be clearly cleansed,
the deceased be posthumously restored to their official ranks and titles,
and the living be allowed to return to their hometowns.
If this is done,
then all under heaven will know that the past injustices and excesses
were not Your Majesty's intention,
but all the fault of the prison officials,
and both the living and the dead will rejoice,
influencing and harmonizing the vital energy."
The Empress Dowager could not follow this advice.
Sìlì
was the half-brother of Chéngqìng.
Their mother, née Wáng,
treated Chéngqìng very harshly,
whenever she caned Chéngqìng,
Sìlì would certainly remove his clothes and request to take his place;
if his mother did not allow it,
he would then cane himself in private,
and his mother would therefore gradually become more lenient.
Chéngqìng served as a Shèrén of the Fènggé Pavilion,
but left his post due to illness.
At that time, Sìlì was the magistrate of Láiwú County,
Láiwú County,
belonged to the Tàishān Commandery in the Hàn,
was abolished in the Jìn,
later, the Northern Wèi established Yíng County at the old city site,
in the early Zhēnguàn era of the Táng, it was abolished and merged into Bóchéng County,
later, Láiwú County was re-established at the abolished Yíng County site,
belonging to Yǎnzhōu.
"Your father once said,
'I have two sons,
fit to serve Your Majesty.'
You brothers in office,
are indeed as your father said.
I now appoint you to replace your elder brother,
and will not use anyone else."
That same day, he was appointed Shèrén of the Fènggé Pavilion.
In this year,
the Türks' Mòchuò appointed his younger brother Duōxīfú as Left Wing Chà,
and Gǔdǔlù's son Mòjǔ as Right Wing Chà,
each commanding over twenty thousand troops;
his son Fújù was made Lesser Kèhán,
positioned above the two Chà,
ruling over the Shíxìng such as Chùmùkūn,
with over forty thousand troops,
and also titled Tuòxī Kèhán.
The Chùmùkūn Shíxìng,
were tribes under the Western Türks,
hence the title Tuòxī.
First year of Jiǔshì
(Gēngzǐ, 700)
This year, the era name was changed starting in the fifth month.
In the first month,
on Wùyín,
Nèishǐ Wǔ Sānsī was dismissed and made Tèjìn and Tàizǐ Shǎobǎo.
Textual Analysis says: The New Annals and Tables both state,
"On Wùwǔ, Jí Xū was demoted to magistrate of Yǎnchuān,
on Rénshēn,
Sānsī was dismissed,"
and in between he never returned to the chancellorship.
In the eleventh month of the next year, on Rénshēn,
it again states Sānsī was dismissed.
The day and official title are the same,
likely an erroneous duplication.
Now follow the Veritable Records.
Textual Analysis says: The Veritable Records only states he was demoted and exiled due to an incident.
The Qiǎn Zǎi and New History both state he was demoted to magistrate of Yǎnchuān.
Now follow the Records of the Censorate.
The Empress Dowager, considering Wěi Xū to have capability and strategic acumen,
entrusted him with matters close to her heart.
Xū once disputed with Wǔ Yìzōng before the Empress Dowager over credit for the Zhào Prefecture campaign.
Xū was tall and imposing with a silver tongue,
while Yìzōng was short, stooped, and hunchbacked.
Xū looked at Yìzōng,
his voice and demeanor arrogant and overbearing.
The Empress Dowager was displeased by this,
and said:
"Xū, in my very presence,
still belittles my Wǔ family members.
How could he be relied upon in the future!"
Another day,
when Xū was presenting a matter,
just as he was citing ancient and modern precedents,
the Empress Dowager angrily said:
"What you, Minister, are saying,
I have heard to the point of surfeit.
Say no more!
Emperor Tàizōng had a horse named Lion Steed,
robust and swift, but none could tame or control it.
I, as a palace maid attending at his side,
said to Emperor Tàizōng: 'This humble maid can subdue it,
but three things are required:
first, an iron whip;
second, an iron mace;
third, a dagger.
If striking it with the iron whip does not make it submit,
then use the mace to strike its head.
If it still does not submit,
then use the dagger to cut its throat.'
Emperor Tàizōng admired my resolve.
Today, are you, Minister, worthy of soiling my dagger?"
Xū, terrified and sweating,
prostrated himself begging for his life,
and only then did she stop.
The various Wǔ family members resented him for siding with the Crown Prince.
Together they exposed the matter of his younger brother fraudulently obtaining an official post,
and because of this, he was convicted and demoted.
On the day of his farewell audience,
he was granted an audience.
Weeping, he said:
"Your servant now departs far from the imperial court,
never to have the chance to see you again.
I wish to state one thing."
The Empress Dowager ordered him to sit,
and asked him.
Xū said:
"Mixing earth and water to make clay,
is there contention?"
The Empress Dowager said:
"There is not."
He continued:
"Dividing it in half to make a Buddha statue,
and half to make a Celestial Venerable statue,
is there contention?"
She said:
"There is contention."
Xū kowtowed and said:
"If the imperial clan and the maternal relatives each keep to their proper stations,
then the realm will be at peace.
Now the Crown Prince is already established, yet the maternal relatives are still made kings.
This is Your Majesty driving them to inevitable future contention,
leaving neither side at peace."
The Empress Dowager said:
"I am also aware of this.
But matters have already reached this state,
there is nothing to be done."
Observing how the Empress Dowager made her two sons and the various Wǔ family members swear oaths,
shows she truly knew the situation was bound to lead to this and resorted to this inferior strategy.
2 In the twelfth month,
on Xīnsì day,
the late Grandson Lǐ Chóngrùn was posthumously enfeoffed as Prince of Shào,
and his younger brother Chóngmào as Prince of Běihǎi.
3 The Empress Dowager asked Luán Tái Shìláng
Lù Yuánfāng about external affairs.
He replied:
"Your servant occupies the position of Chancellor;
on major matters, I dare not fail to inform you.
Trivial matters among the people,
are not worth troubling Your Sagely Ears."
Because of this, he offended her will.
On Gēngyín day,
he was dismissed to become Sīlǐ Qīng.
During the Guāngzhái era, the Tàicháng Qīng was renamed Sīlǐ Qīng.
Yuánfāng was a man of integrity and caution.
Twice serving as Chancellor,
whenever the Empress Dowager had promotions or appointments to make,
she often consulted him.
Yuánfāng would seal his responses and present them,
never leaking information.
On his deathbed,
he took all his memorial drafts and burned them,
saying:
"I have performed many hidden acts of virtue for others;
surely my descendants will not decline!"
4 The Western Turkic 'Utmost Loyalty Serving the Sovereign' Khagan, Húsèluó, was appointed as Grand Commander of the Píngxī Army,
to garrison Suìyè.
5 On Dīngyǒu day,
Dí Rénjié was appointed as Nèishǐ.
6 On Gēngzǐ day,
Wénchāng Zuǒ Chéng Wéi Jùyuán was appointed as Nàyán.
Textual Analysis says: The New Annals and Tables state:
"On Gēngzǐ day,
Wénchāng Zuǒ Xiàng Wéi Jùyuán became Nàyán;
in the tenth month,
on Dīngsì day,
he was dismissed."
Previously, it was not stated that Jùyuán was Zuǒ Xiàng.
The Old Annals and Biographies do not mention it.
This is likely an error of Zuǒ Chéng for Zuǒ Xiàng.
On Yǐsì day,
the Empress Dowager visited Sōng Mountain.
In spring,
the first month,
on Dīngmǎo day,
she visited the hot springs in Rǔ Prefecture.
On Wùyín day,
she returned to Shéndū.
She had the Sānyáng Palace built at Shícóng in Gàochéng.
Sānyáng Palace was 160 lǐ from Luò City.
In the first year of the Wànsuì Dēngfēng era,
the name of Yángchéng County in the Eastern Capital was changed to Gàochéng,
to mark the successful completion of sacrifices to the sacred mountain.
Cóng:
pronounced zāngzōng,
also shìjiāng.
7 In the second month,
on Yǐwèi day,
Tóng Fènggé Luántái Sānpǐn Dòulú Qīnwàng was dismissed to become Tàizǐ Bīnkè.
8 In the third month,
the Tǔyùhún 'Qīnghǎi King' Xuānchāo was appointed as 'Wūdì Yě Bá Qín Zhōng' Khagan.
Xuānchāo
was the grandson of Nuòhébō.
9 In summer,
the fourth month,
on Wùshēn day,
the Empress Dowager went to Sānyáng Palace to escape the heat.
A foreign monk invited the imperial carriage to observe a śarīra burial.
The Empress Dowager agreed.
Dí Rénjié knelt before her horse and said:
"Buddha is a deity of the barbarians,
not worthy of causing the ruler of All-under-Heaven to bend.
That foreign monk is deceitful;
he merely wishes to lure the imperial carriage to delude people near and far.
The mountain path is perilous and narrow,
unable to accommodate the imperial guards.
It is not a place for the imperial carriage to approach."
The Empress Dowager turned back midway and said:
"To fulfill the righteous spirit of my loyal minister."
10 In the fifth month,
on Jǐyǒu, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
11 The Empress Dowager ordered the Hóng Prefecture monk Hú Chāo to compound an elixir of longevity.
It took three years to complete,
costing an immense sum.
The Empress Dowager took it,
and her illness slightly improved.
On Guǐchǒu day,
she granted a general amnesty to the realm,
and changed the era name to Jiǔshì;
removing the title 'Heavenly Tablet Golden Wheel Great Sage'.
12 In the sixth month,
the Kòng Hè (Control Cranes) establishment was renamed the Fèngchén (Serve the Imperial) Office,
with Zhāng Yìzhī appointed as Fèngchén Lìng.
Whenever the Empress Dowager held private banquets in the inner palace,
she would invariably summon the various Wǔ members, Yìzhī, and his younger brother, Mìshū Jiān Zhāng Chāngzōng, to drink, gamble, jest, and banter.
The Empress Dowager, wishing to conceal these activities,
ordered Yìzhī, Chāngzōng, and literary scholars like Lǐ Qiáo to compile the Sānjiào Zhūyīng in the inner palace.
The Three Teachings are
Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism.
The Empress Dowager ordered Chāngzōng to don feathered robes,
play the shēng,
and ride a wooden crane in the courtyard;
the literary scholars all composed poems praising him.
The Empress Dowager also selected many handsome youths to serve as Fèngchén Inner Attendants.
Right Bǔquē Zhū Jìngzé remonstrated:
"Your Majesty's inner favorites already include Yìzhī and Chāngzōng,
which is sufficient.
Recently, I have heard that Right Jiānmén Wèi Zhǎngshǐ Hóu Xiáng and others,
(Note: Each guard and prefecture office of the Táng had a Zhǎngshǐ,
rank 6b,
each in charge of managing the affairs of their respective offices.
Jiān:
pronounced gǔxián.)
act shamelessly and without propriety,
seeking to become Fèngchén Inner Attendants.
Their lack of ritual and decorum
overflows into court hearings.
My duty lies in remonstrance,
I dare not fail to report this."
The Empress Dowager consoled him, saying:
"Were it not for your forthright words,
I would not have known of this."
She awarded him one hundred bolts of patterned silk.
Yìzhī and Chāngzōng vied to outdo each other in extravagance and luxury.
Their younger brother Chāngyí served as the magistrate of Luòyáng,
and he never refused any request for favor.
Once, during an early morning court session,
a candidate for official appointment named Xuē,
offered fifty taels of gold along with his application form, intercepting Chāngyí's horse to bribe him.
Chāngyí accepted the gold,
and upon reaching the court hall,
handed the application to the Vice Minister of Personnel, Zhāng Xī.
A few days later,
Zhāng Xī lost the application form,
and went to ask Chāngyí about it.
Chāngyí scolded him, saying:
"You incompetent man!
I don't remember either,
but just give the position to anyone surnamed Xuē."
Zhāng Xī, frightened,
withdrew,
searched the roster and found over sixty candidates surnamed Xuē,
and had all of them appointed to official posts.
Zhāng Xī
was the nephew of Zhāng Wénguàn.
(Zhāng Wénguàn appears in the second year of the Qiánfēng era of Emperor Gāozōng, in volume 201.)
13 Earlier,
the Khitan general Lǐ Kǎigù
was skilled in using lassos, mounted archery, and wielding the lance.
Whenever he broke through enemy formations,
it was like a falcon diving into a flock of crows,
and wherever he went, he swept all before him.
At the Battle of Huángzhāng,
Zhāng Xuányù and Má Rénjié were both captured by him.
(This event is recorded in the first year of the Wànsuì Tōngtiān era, in the previous volume.)
He was also a Khitan general,
and repeatedly defeated Táng forces.
After Sūn Wànróng died,
both he and his comrade surrendered.
The officials in charge, blaming them for their late surrender,
petitioned to have their clans exterminated.
Dí Rénjié said:
"Kǎigù and his comrade are both exceptionally brave and fierce,
and they served their former masters with all their strength.
They will surely serve us with all their strength as well.
If we treat them with virtue and kindness,
they will all be of use to us."
He petitioned to pardon them.
His close associates all tried to dissuade him,
but Dí Rénjié said:
"If it benefits the state,
how can I consider my own safety!"
The Empress Dowager followed his advice,
and pardoned them.
He further requested official posts for them.
The Empress Dowager appointed Lǐ Kǎigù as General of the Left Guard of the Jade Seal,
and his comrade as General of the Right Guard of Martial Might,
and sent them to lead troops to attack the remaining Khitan rebels,
pacifying them completely.

First Year of Jiǔshì
(Gēngzǐ, 700 AD)
1 Autumn,
seventh month,
captives were presented at the Hánshū Hall.
(Lǐ Kǎigù presented the Khitan captives.)
(The Hánshū Hall was likely located in the Sānyáng Palace.)
He was granted the imperial surname Wǔ.
The Duke of Zhào and the high ministers were summoned for a joint banquet.
(Summoning the Duke of Zhào and the high ministers refers to a joint banquet for generals and ministers.)
"This is your achievement."
She was about to reward him,
but he replied:
"This is due to Your Majesty's majestic might,
and the efforts of the generals.
What achievement have I contributed!"
He firmly declined and did not accept.
2 Intercalary month,
Wùyín day,

Textual Analysis says: The Biography of Lord Liáng states:
"Zhāng Jiànzhī, Huán Yànfàn, Jìng Huī, Cuī Xuánwěi, and Yuán Shùjǐ were all recommended by the Lord.
The Lord once, after retiring from a meal,
said to these five lords: 'My regret is that I am aged and frail,
my body may perish like the morning dew,
and I will not live to see the great achievements of you five lords.
I hope you each preserve and cherish yourselves,
and I wish you to exhaust your fundamental loyalty.'
The five lords understood in their hearts and witnessed with their eyes,
and silently comprehended the Lord's meaning.
When the Lord was bedridden with illness,
the five lords came to inquire after him,
and they sat facing each other all day,
yet he did not utter a single word.
After a short while,
tears flowed onto his pillow,
and they merely looked at each other.
When the five lords withdrew,
they could not fathom the reason in turn.
Yuán Shùjǐ said: 'Could it be that his strength is failing further,
and we need to ask about his family affairs?'
Zhāng Jiànzhī said: 'I have never heard of a great worthy neglecting state affairs for family matters.'
Shortly after,
he summoned Lords Zhāng Jiànzhī, Yuán Shùjǐ, and Huán Yànfàn to enter,
while the other two lords stood outside the door.
He said: 'My silence earlier
was because of those two lords.
These two lords are capable of decisive action but cannot keep secrets.
If I had first discussed it with them,
the matter would certainly have leaked out.
Once it leaked,
then the state would be altered and our families would perish.
If, when the time comes, they are not included in the plan,
the affair will also not succeed.
Prince Liáng Sīsī holds power;
he must be seized first and then we act.
Otherwise,
it will certainly instead give rise to
great calamity.'
After Lord Dí passed away,
over a year later,
the five lords secretly met in a secluded place,
recounted the Lord's words at that time,
and reaffirmed their covenant.
After the meal was cleared,
they looked at each other wishing to speak,
but the time had not yet come.
Fearing to break their previous promise,
they wished to speak but stopped,
repeating this several times.
Huán Yànfàn then recounted his words.
Before his words were finished,
they heard outside the windows,
a sound like thunder,
and in a moment wind and rain arose,
making it impossible to see even at close range.
The mats and bedding they were sitting on were all thrown onto the steps below.
The five lords trembled with fear,
not knowing what to rely on.
They then said to each other: 'This is because Lord Dí's loyalty and fervor reached the extreme,
borrowing this spiritual transformation to startle our hearts.
He did not wish us to discuss this matter beforehand.
The time has not yet come,
we must not speak of it again.'
Shortly after,
the sky cleared and the sun shone,
no different from before.
After Yìzhī and others were executed,
Yuán said to Lord Zhāng: 'There were words left behind,
telling us to first seize Sīsī.
How can we let him go?'
Lord Zhāng said: 'Once the great affair is accomplished,
he is like an object on a mat,
how could he escape!'
Later, Prince Liáng communicated with those inside the palace,
and the five lords were indeed slandered by him,
all suffering exile.
The anticipated years and months for the restoration,
and the bequeathed plan and model, were not the least bit different."
According to this analysis: Jiànzhī and the other five men happened to be in office at the same time,
cooperating to achieve merit.
How could Rénjié have foreknown their affair,
recommending precisely these five men,
solely intending for them to assist in establishing the Crown Prince?
Moreover, if Yìzhī and others had grounds to be executed,
and the Crown Prince had a situation allowing his establishment,
Rénjié, being the minister himself,
why would he wait for five years later,
needing Jiànzhī and others to then act?
This is probably because the writer of the biography, due to the five men's merit in restoring the dynasty,
attached the affair to them,
saying they were all recommended by Rénjié,
and received instruction from Rénjié.
Its words are deceitful, strange, and unsubstantiated,
and are not adopted here.
The Old Biography only records the names of the three men Jiànzhī, Yànfàn, and Huī being recommended,
and we follow that here.
Someone said to Rénjié:
"All the peaches and plums under heaven,
are at your gate."
Chéng Dàchāng's Yǎnfánlù: Zhào Jiǎnzǐ said to Yáng Hǔ:
"Only the worthy are able to repay kindness,
the unworthy cannot.
He who plants peach and plum trees,
rests in their shade in summer,
and eats their fruit in autumn;
he who plants thistles and thorns,
finds no rest in their shade in summer,
and gets their thorns in autumn.
What you have gained now,
are thistles and thorns."
The present world universally refers to recommended scholars as peaches and plums,
the explanation all originates from this.
"Recommending the worthy is for the state,
not for private gain."
Initially,
when Rénjié was Prefect of Wèizhōu,
see scroll 205, Wànsuì Tōngtiān first year.
The common people established a living shrine for him.
Later, his son Jǐnghuī served as Registrar of Wèizhōu,
and his greed and cruelty became a plague upon the people.
The people then destroyed his statue.
The history states that Dí Rénjié's utmost loyalty,
serves to encourage all under heaven who serve as ministers;
stating that his shrine was destroyed due to Jǐnghuī's greed and cruelty,
serves to warn all under heaven who serve as sons.

bestowed food upon him,
comforted and instructed him, then sent him away.
The Empress Dowager was advanced in years,
and often delegated government affairs to the brothers Zhāng Yìzhī and Zhāng Chāngzōng.
Shào Prince Lǐ Zhòngrùn, his younger sister Princess Yǒngtài, and her husband, Wèi Prince Wǔ Yánjī, privately discussed this matter.
Yìzhī reported it to the Empress Dowager.
In the 9th month, on the rénshēn day (the 3rd),
the Empress Dowager forced them all to commit suicide.

(Textual analysis note: The biography of Zhòngrùn states: "Zhòngrùn was framed by someone, and together with his sister Princess Yǒngtài's husband, Wèi Prince Wǔ Yánjī, they privately discussed how the Zhāng Yìzhī brothers could wantonly enter the palace; Wǔ Zétiān ordered them beaten to death."
We now follow the Shílù.)
(Yánjī was the son of Wǔ Chéngsì.
Chéngsì was the Empress Dowager's nephew.)
On the bǐngshēn day (the 27th),
the Prince of Xiāng was appointed to oversee the affairs of the Left and Right Yulin Guard Grand Generals.
In winter, the 10th month, on the rényín day (the 3rd),
the Empress Dowager traveled west and entered the pass.
On the xīnyǒu day (the 22nd),

A general amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed.
(The era name was changed to Cháng'ān.)
In the 11th month, on the wùyín day (the 9th),
the Hányuán Palace was renamed Dàmíng Palace.

(The Eastern Palace of Cháng'ān was originally called Dàmíng Palace. In the 3rd year of the Lóngshuò era of Emperor Gāozōng, it was renamed Pénglái Palace. In the 1st year of the Xiánhēng era, it was renamed Hányuán Palace. Now its old name was restored.)
The Vice Minister of Personnel, Cuī Xuánwěi of Ānpíng,

(The Táng Ministry of Personnel had eighty clerks for its four bureaus.)

He was thus reappointed Vice Minister of Personnel,
and additionally bestowed seventy bolts of patterned silk.

(Táng regulation: For a bestowal of ten bolts, the standard was three bolts of plain silk, three lengths of cloth, and four bundles of silk floss. For ten bolts of assorted patterned silks, it was two bolts of damask silk, two bolts of twill silk, two bolts of figured silk, and four bolts of plain silk.)
The Director of the Bureau of Receptions, Guō Yuánzhèn, was appointed Military Commissioner of Liáng Prefecture and Grand Commissioner of the Armies of Lǒngyòu.

(The Táng Director of Receptions was in charge of affairs concerning the descendants of the two former dynasties and the visits and tributes of various foreign tribes; it belonged to the Ministry of Rites.
'Commissioner' is pronounced with the shūlì fān.)
Previously,
the territory of Liáng Prefecture from north to south was no more than over four hundred lǐ.
The Tūjué and Tǔbō frequently reached the city walls within the year,
and the people suffered from it.
Yuánzhèn first established the Hérong Fort at the Xiákǒu in the southern territory,
and the Báitíng Army in the desert of the northern territory.
(Dù Yòu states: The Báitíng Garrison is five hundred lǐ northwest of Liáng Prefecture city.
'Desert' is pronounced with the qījì fān.)
He expanded the prefectural territory by fifteen hundred lǐ.
From then on, invaders no longer reached the city walls.
Yuánzhèn also ordered the Prefect of Gān Prefecture, Lǐ Hàntōng, to open up and establish military agricultural colonies,
making full use of the advantages of water and land.
Previously, a hú of millet or wheat in Liáng Prefecture cost several thousand coins.
After Hàntōng implemented collection and management,
(Collection and management means gathering the people and directing their farming.)
military grain stores accumulated enough to last for decades.
Yuánzhèn was skilled at pacifying and governing.
During his five years in Liáng Prefecture,
both foreigners and Chinese feared and admired him.
His orders were carried out and prohibitions observed.
Cattle and sheep covered the wilderness,
and lost articles were not picked up on the road.
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the day Yǐyǒu,
the military examination was first established.
The system of the military examination
included selections for long-range target shooting, mounted archery, foot archery, flat shooting, tube shooting, mounted lance, lifting the bar, weight carrying, and physical stature.
The *Tang Liu Dian* states: The military examination assessed candidates in seven categories: First, shooting at long-range targets,
testing by shooting thirty arrows at long-range targets without missing beyond the third courtyard being considered passing,
hitting the central courtyard was superior,
hitting the next courtyard was next to superior,
hitting the outer courtyard was secondary.
Second, mounted archery,
shooting and hitting both targets was superior,
hitting one or missing one was next to superior,
missing both was secondary.
Third, mounted lance,
hitting three or four boards was superior,
hitting two boards was next to superior,
hitting one board or missing was secondary.
Fourth, foot archery,
hitting a straw man was considered next to superior,
even if hit but not according to the method,
or according to the method but missing was secondary.
Fifth, appearance and stature,
those with a height of six chǐ or more were considered next to superior,
those below were secondary.
Sixth, speech,
those with impressive demeanor and capable of leadership were considered next to superior,
those without were secondary.
Seventh, weightlifting,
referred to as lifting the bar,
generally achieving five lifts or more was considered passing.
All were tested, and those with high rankings were reported by name.

on the day Gēngyín,

He spoke without regard for his own life in submitting the memorial,

Chariot,

In the first year of Guāngzhái,

internal and external government offices shall not handle them."

From Jiéshí westward beyond the Four Garrisons,

the strategic points of mountains and rivers,

the strategic points of mountains and rivers,

*Kǎo Yì* says: *Sōng Chuāng Zá Lù* records:
"Zhōngzōng once summoned the sons of Chancellors Sū Guī and Lǐ Qiáo for an audience,

they were welcomed and patted before the vermilion robe,

He then said to the two boys: 'You should state the meaning of the books you have studied,

Tǐng responded: 'Wood follows the ink line to become straight,

According to this, Tǐng was already a Yùshǐ this year,
when Guī was Chancellor, Tǐng was a Zhōngshū Shèrén,
father and son jointly held the Privy Council,
not in childhood.
Now not adopted.

An attendant said that the former Píngxiāng Commandant of Yīshì, Zhāng Jiāzhēn, possessed extraordinary talent.

is pronounced yú wèi fān.)

The Zhūquè Gate

When Yìzhī and others saw this memorial,

Jùn,

Dāntú,

Jiān,

"These matters are all true,

Moreover, Your Majesty holds the power of life and death,

The Empress Dowager said:

He replied:

The Empress Dowager's anger subsided.

The Empress Dowager once ordered court nobles to gather for a banquet,

Yìzhī had always feared Jǐng,

The Vice Minister of Personnel Zhèng Gǎo said to Jǐng:

"Speaking in terms of official protocol,

Disciples and household slaves address their master as 'Láng',

The Palace Supervisor Cuī Shénqìng submitted a memorial:

Shǐ'ān Commandery,

According to the Old Book of Táng, the biographies of Xuē Jìchǎng and Jìng Huī, the Táng Tǒngjì, the Táng Lì, and the Biography of Lord Di Liáng, all state

Only the Records of the Censorate states
"Jiànzhī argued firmly,

The New Book of Táng, Yànfàn's biography, also states:

let him remain for the Son of Heaven to deal with.'
Jìchǎng sighed and said: 'I have no place to die.'"
