Zhāng Jiànzhī from Vice Minister of Justice participated in government affairs,
in the eleventh month,
he served as Vice Minister of the Secretariat.
When Yìzhī was executed,
only these two were chief ministers.
In the first year of Shénlóng era,
in the first month,
Yuán Shùjǐ from Vice Minister of Justice became Vice Minister of the Secretariat and participated in government affairs;
on the Gēngxū day,
Zhāng Jiànzhī became Minister of War,
Xuánwěi served as Palace Secretary,
Jìng Huī and Huán Yànfàn both became Chancellors;
in the third month,
Shùjǐ served as Head of the Secretariat;
in the fourth month,
Jiànzhī became Head of the Secretariat,
Jìng Huī became Palace Attendant.
This is the order of promotions and transfers of the Five Princes.
It is suspected that the Veritable Records only lists Jiànzhī first because he was the chief planner in executing Yìzhī.
Therefore, Jiànzhī is listed first.
Huī and Yànfàn were both Palace Attendants,
it is suspected that the Palace Attendant ranked above the Head of the Secretariat,
so in the memorials to reduce the Wǔ clan and relieve them of governmental duties, Huī is listed first.
When iron certificates were granted,
Xuánwěi had already been given the title Specially Advanced,
while Huī and others were given Specially Advanced only after being relieved of governmental duties,
and Xuánwěi remained as before,
it is suspected that although Specially Advanced was a sinecure rank, its grade was the highest,
so Xuánwěi was listed first.
Yànfàn and Huī were both Palace Attendants,
but Yànfàn suffered the most cruel fate,
it is suspected that the Kāiyuán edict and the historians specially listed him first,
not necessarily according to the order of positions at that time.
During the times of Empress Wǔ and Emperor Zhōngzōng,
it is suspected that the Palace Attendant ranked above the Head of the Secretariat.
They were granted gold, silk, saddles, and horses,
and ordered to attend court only on the first and fifteenth days of the month;
additionally, Yànfàn was granted the surname Wéi,
making him share the same lineage register as the Empress.
Soon after, Xuánwěi was appointed Concurrent Inspector and Chief Administrator of Yì Prefecture, in charge of the Governor's duties,
and later changed to Governor of Liáng Prefecture.
Yì Prefecture,
is 2,379 lǐ southwest of the capital,
and 3,216 lǐ from the Eastern Capital.
Liáng Prefecture is 1,223 lǐ from the capital,
and 2,078 lǐ from the Eastern Capital.
Those who did not attach themselves to the Wǔ clan were dismissed,
those who had been expelled by the Five Princes were reinstated,
and great power entirely returned to Sānsī.
When the Five Princes requested the reduction of the Wu clan's various princes,
they sought someone to draft the memorial,
but no one was willing to do it.
The Secretariat Drafter Cén Xī composed it,
with extremely vehement language;
the Secretariat Drafter Bì Gǒu of Yǎnshī was next in line to read the memorial,
and his words and expression were stern and severe.
After Wǔ Sānsī gained power,
Xī was transferred to the post of Junior Supervisor of the Palace Library,
and Gǒu was sent out to serve as Prefect of Rùnzhōu.
Rùnzhōu
is located 2,821 lǐ southeast of the capital,
and 1,797 lǐ from the Eastern Capital.
The Prefect of Yìzhōu, Zhào Lǚwēn,
was the elder brother of Huán Yànfàn's wife.
When Yànfàn executed the two Zhāngs,
he claimed that Lǚwēn had participated in the plot,
and summoned him to serve as Junior Minister of the Court of the Imperial Granaries.
Lǚwēn presented Yànfàn with two maidservants;
when Yànfàn was removed from political office,
Lǚwēn took back the maidservants.
The Emperor praised Sòng Jǐng for his loyalty and integrity,
and repeatedly promoted him to the post of Vice Director of the Chancellery.
Wǔ Sānsī once tried to entrust a matter to Jǐng,
but Jǐng sternly refused, saying:
"Now that the Empress Dowager has restored the throne to her son,
you, Prince, should retire to your mansion as a marquis.
How can you still interfere in court politics?
Have you not seen what happened to Lǚ Chǎn and Lǚ Lù?"
On the 27th, Wéi Ānshí was concurrently appointed as Acting Director of the Secretariat,
Wèi Yuánzhōng as Acting Director of the Chancellery,
Lǐ Zhàn as Senior Adviser of the Right,
Zhào Chéng'ēn as Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments,
and Yáng Yuányǎn as Minister of the Court of the Imperial Guard.
Previously,
Yuányǎn knew that Sānsī was gradually gaining influence,
and requested to resign and become a monk.
The Emperor did not permit it.
Jìng Huī heard of this,
laughed, and said:
"If I had known earlier,
I would have urged the Emperor to allow it.
Shaving off that barbarian head
would have been wonderful!"
Yuányǎn had a thick beard resembling that of a barbarian,
so Huī teased him.
Yuányǎn said:
"When merit is achieved and fame attained,
not retreating will bring danger.
This is a sincere request from the heart."
Zhōng
means sincerity;
yóuzhōng
means speaking from genuine sincerity.
Huī understood his meaning,
and was startled and displeased.
When Huī and others were implicated,
Yuányǎn alone was spared.
On the 28th, Imperial Consort Shàngguān advised Empress Wéi to follow the precedent of Zétiān,
submitting a memorial requesting that all scholars and commoners observe three years of mourning for their divorced mothers,
and also requesting that commoners be considered adults at age twenty-three,
and exempted from corvée at age fifty-nine.
Under the Táng system,
adulthood began at twenty-one,
and old age at sixty.
The Emperor approved both proposals.
On the 29th, Guǐmǎo,
an edict
demoted the various Wǔ clan members:
Prince of Liáng, Wǔ Sānsī, became Prince of Déjìng,
and Prince of Dìng, Wǔ Yōujì, became Prince of Lèshòu.
Both were demoted to county princes.
Déjìng County belonged to Xiàzhōu;
Lèshòu County belonged to Shēnzhōu.
This was done to appease public sentiment.
On the 30th, Jiǎchén,
Táng Xiùjǐng was appointed as Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs,
remaining as Joint Manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery as before;
Dòulú Qīnwàng was appointed as Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.
On the 31st, in the sixth month,
on Rénzǐ,
Left Guard General-in-Chief Péi Sīshuō was appointed as Grand Commander of the Língwǔ Army,
to guard against the Turks.
On the 32nd, Guǐhài,
Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs Dòulú Qīnwàng was ordered
that for important military and state affairs,
the Secretariat-Chancellery should jointly deliberate.
Previously,
the Vice Directors of the Department of State Affairs were the chief ministers,
but later most concurrently held positions in the Secretariat-Chancellery,
deciding court affairs in the morning
and departmental matters in the afternoon.
Departmental matters
referred to affairs of the Department of State Affairs.
Qīnwàng served solely as Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs,
not daring to participate in political affairs,
hence this order.
Thereafter, those solely appointed as Vice Directors of the Department of State Affairs
no longer served as ministers.
Additionally, Wéi Ānshí was appointed as Director of the Secretariat,
Wèi Yuánzhōng as Director of the Chancellery,
and Yáng Zàisī as Acting Director of the Secretariat.
On the 33rd, Dīngmǎo,
the Filial and Reverent Emperor was enshrined in the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
with the temple name Yìzōng.
The late Crown Prince Hóng was posthumously titled Filial and Reverent Emperor,
the Emperor's elder brother.
On the 34th, Wùchén,
the Luò River overflowed,
flooding over two thousand households.
On the 35th, in autumn,
the seventh month,
on Xīnsì,
the Crown Prince's Advisor Wéi Jùyuán was appointed as Joint Manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery,
remaining as Commander of the Western Capital as before.
On the 36th, the Specially Advanced Han Yáng Prince Zhāng Jiànzhī submitted a memorial requesting to return to Xiāngzhōu to recuperate from illness;
on Yǐwèi,
Jiànzhī was appointed as Prefect of Xiāngzhōu,
not handling prefectural affairs,
and receiving his full salary.
Under the Táng system,
Specially Advanced was rank 2a,
and Commandery Prince was rank 1b;
from the higher rank, he received rank 1a salary,
with a monthly stipend of 8,000 [coins],
food allowance of 1,800,
and miscellaneous expenses of 1,200.
Upper Prefecture Prefect was rank 3b,
with a monthly stipend of 5,100,
and miscellaneous expenses of 900.
On the 37th, seventeen prefectures north and south of the Yellow River suffered major floods.
In the eighth month,
on Wùshēn,
due to the flood disaster, the Emperor sought frank advice.
Right Guard Cavalry Section Adjutant Sòng Wùguāng of Xīhé submitted a memorial,

(Note: The various guard offices of the Táng had four section adjutants: stores, infantry, cavalry, and armor. The Cavalry Section Adjutant was in charge of registers and care of miscellaneous livestock inside and outside, and all guard horses on duty were divided into seven shifts based on distance, changing monthly, and horses were provided for those leaving the palace city by imperial order. Xīhé County belonged to Fénzhōu. Cavalry is pronounced qí jì fān. Submitted is pronounced shí zhǎng fān. Memorial is pronounced suǒ qù fān.) stating:
"Water is a yin element,
symbolizing subjects and concubines.
I fear there may be those in the inner court interfering with outer court politics.
This should be stopped at its萌芽.
Now, continuous rain persists,
and the ward gates are closed to pray for relief,
to the extent that people in the alleys call the ward gates 'the ministers,'
saying the court uses them to harmonize yin and yang.
(Sòng Bái said: Under the Táng system,
during prolonged rain, the north gates of wards and markets were closed to pray for clear weather.)
The Crown Prince is the foundation of the state;
a virtuous and capable person should be selected and established early.
Also,
the influence of maternal relatives is too great,
such as Wǔ Sānsī and others.
They should be relieved of key positions,
and generously provided with salaries and rewards.
Also,
Zhèng Pǔsī and Yè Jìngnéng used minor skills to usurp high positions,
which is also a detriment to court politics."
The memorial was submitted,
but no response was given.
On the 38th, Rénxū,
Lady Zhào was posthumously established as Empress Gōng.
(Zhào's death is recorded in the second year of Gāozōng's Shàngyuán era, in the 202nd scroll.)
(Textual analysis note: The old basic annals say
"on Jiǎzǐ,"
but now follow the Veritable Records.)
On the 39th, in the ninth month,
on Rénwǔ,
the Emperor sacrificed to the Supreme Deity of Heaven and the Sovereign Earth in the Bright Hall,
with Gāozōng as associate.
In the early years of the Shenlóng era (around 705 AD),
the Emperor (Zhōngzōng) was in Fánglíng,
where the provincial authorities imposed very strict restrictions;
the prefectural governors, Hézhāng Zhījiǎn from Hédōng and Cuī Jìngsì from Língchāng,
Hédōng,
was formerly Púbǎn;
it was attached to Hédōng Commandery.
The Suí dynasty abolished the commandery,
and changed Púbǎn to Hédōng County.
The Táng dynasty followed this,
and attached it to Pú Prefecture.
The Suí dynasty divided Suānzǎo County,
and established Língchāng County,
named after the river crossing;
in the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Huá Prefecture.
Jiǎn,
is pronounced with the ninth tone.
They provided ample supplies.
The Emperor was grateful to them,
and promoted Zhījiǎn from Governor of Bèi Prefecture to General of the Left Guard,
bestowing upon him the title of Duke of Fànyáng.
Jìngsì had already died,
so his son Wāng was sought out.
He was fond of drinking,
and was unfit for official duties,
so he was given a fifth-rank sinecure position.
According to the *Táng Liù Diǎn*,
Emperor Yáng of Suí established the Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary as a regular fifth-rank sinecure.
Emperor Wén of Suí established the Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary as a regular fourth-rank sinecure,
which Emperor Yáng changed to lower fifth-rank.
41. Shàngluò Prince Wéi Xuánzhēn was reburied,
with all ceremonies following the precedent of the Prince of Tàiyuán.
Wǔ Shìyuē was enfeoffed as Prince of Tàiyuán.
42. On Guǐsì,
the Crown Prince's Guest and Joint Manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery, Wéi Jùyuán, was dismissed and made Minister of Rites,
because his paternal uncle, Wéi Ānshí, had been appointed as Head of the Secretariat.
43. General of the Left Guard Jì Chǔnè from Shàngguī was concurrently appointed as Acting Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury,
because Chǔnè had married the elder sister of Wǔ Sānsī's wife.
44. In winter,
the tenth month,
Táng Xiūjǐng was ordered to remain in the capital to guard it.
45. On Guǐhài,
the Emperor went to Lóngmén;
on Yǐchǒu,
he hunted at Xīn'ān and then returned.
46. On Xīnwèi,
Wèi Yuánzhōng was appointed as Head of the Secretariat,
and Yáng Zàisī as Head of the Chancellery.
47. In the eleventh month,
on Wùyín,
the officials presented the Emperor with the honorific title "Emperor Responding to Heaven,"
and the Empress as "Empress Obeying Heaven."
On Rénwǔ,
the Emperor and the Empress
went to the Imperial Ancestral Temple to give thanks,
and a general amnesty was declared;
the Prince of Xiāng and Princess Tàipíng had their actual fiefs increased,
both reaching ten thousand households.
48. On Jǐchǒu,
the Emperor ascended the southern tower of Luòchéng,
the southwestern gate of the imperial city in Luòyáng was called the Luòchéng Gate,
inside the gate was the Luòchéng Hall.
The "Pōhán Húxì" was the same as the "Qǐhán Húxì,"
originating from the Western Regions, from the state of Kāng among the Hú people.
In the eleventh month, they drummed and danced to beg for cold,
splashing water on each other for amusement.
In the later years of Empress Wǔ, it began to be performed in the last month of winter.
Considering it
"to plan for the cold season appropriately,
Qīngyuán County belonged to Bìng Prefecture,
established by the Suí dynasty at the ancient Gěngyáng City,
named after the water.
The *Book of Documents*, *Hóngfàn* says: To plan for the cold season appropriately.
The commentary says: If the ruler can plan, then the cold season will be favorable.
Ruò,
means favorable.
Shàng,
is pronounced with the rising tone.
Shū,
is pronounced with the departing tone.
They drummed and danced on the roads to seek it!"
The memorial was submitted,
but not accepted.
49. On Rényín,
Zétiān (Empress Wǔ) passed away in the Shàngyáng Palace,
at the age of eighty-two.
Her final decree stated:
"Remove the imperial title,
and be called Zétiān Dàshèng Empress.
The families of Wáng and Xiāo, as well as the relatives of Chǔ Suìliáng, Hán Yuàn, and Liǔ Shì, are all to be pardoned."
When Empress Wǔ was established,
Empress Wáng and Consort Xiāo Shū were imprisoned and deposed,
and did not die a good death.
Chǔ Suìliáng and Hán Yuàn died remonstrating,
Liǔ Shì died because he was a relative of Empress Wáng,
and their relatives were all exiled.
The Emperor was in mourning,
and Wèi Yuánzhōng acted as Chief Minister for three days.
Yuánzhōng had long been known for his loyalty and integrity,
and both inside and outside the court relied on him;
Wǔ Sānsī feared him,
and forged the Empress Dowager's final decree,
to comfort and instruct Yuánzhōng,
bestowing upon him an actual fief of one hundred households.
Yuánzhōng received the decree,
and was moved to tears,
those who saw it said:
"The matter is over!"
Knowing that he would not dare to discuss matters related to the Wǔ family again.
In the twelfth month,
on Dīngmǎo,
the Emperor began to receive officials in the Tóngmíng Hall.
50. The Empress Dowager was to be buried together with Emperor Gāozōng in the Qiánlíng Mausoleum.
The Supervising Secretary Yán Shànsī submitted a memorial,
believing that:
"The underground palace of Qiánlíng has stone doors,
sealed with iron,
now to open the doors,
chiseling and carving will be necessary.
The way of the spirits,
values secrecy and profundity,
mobilizing the masses and adding labor,
may cause much disturbance and disrespect.
Moreover, joint burial is not an ancient practice;
among the Han dynasty mausoleums,
most empresses were not buried together.
From the Wèi and Jìn dynasties onward,
joint burials began to occur.
I hope that a more auspicious site beside Qiánlíng can be chosen for a mausoleum.
If the spirits are aware,
the paths of the underworld will naturally connect;
if they are unaware,
what benefit is there in joint burial!"
This was not followed.
51. This year,
the Ministry of Revenue reported that the empire had six million one hundred and fifty thousand households,
and thirty-seven million one hundred and forty thousand and some odd individuals.
1. In spring,
the first month,
on Wùxū,
Lǐ Qiáo, the Minister of Personnel, was made Joint Manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery,
and the Vice Director of the Secretariat, Yú Wéiqiān, was made Joint Manager of Affairs.
2. In the intercalary month,
on Bǐngwǔ,
an edict was issued:
"Princesses Tàipíng, Chángníng, Ānlè, Yíchéng, Xīndū, Dìng'ān, and Jīnchéng are all to establish their own administrations,
and set up official staff."
From Chángníng onward, all were the Emperor's daughters.
Lè,
is pronounced with the falling tone.
3. Wǔ Sānsī, because Jìng Huī, Huán Yànfàn, and Yuán Shùjǐ were still in the capital,
was wary of them.
On Yǐmǎo,
he sent them out to be prefects of Huá, Míng, and Yù Prefectures.
According to old records,
Huá Prefecture was 1,440 lǐ from the capital,
and 530 lǐ from the eastern capital.
Míng Prefecture,
was 1,585 lǐ northeast of the capital,
and 857 lǐ from the eastern capital.
Yù Prefecture,
was 1,540 lǐ from the capital,
and 670 lǐ from the eastern capital.
*Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù*, *Xīn Jì*, and the new and old biographies do not record the month and year when Cuī Xuánwěi and Huī and others were sent out as prefects,
only the *Jiù Jì* and the *Tǒng Jì*, *Táng Lì* mention these three.
Probably Xuánwěi had already been sent out earlier,
but it is not known when.
However, when Huī and others were demoted to Sima,
they were prefects of Lǎng, Bó, Yǐng, and Jūn Prefectures,
so they must have been transferred again later.
The *Táng Lì* and *Tǒng Jì* place this after the execution of Wáng Tóngjiǎo,
now we follow this.
4. The monk Wànhuí from Wénxiāng was bestowed the title Duke of Fǎyún.
Wànhuí's surname was Zhāng.
Initially,
his mother prayed to a statue of Guānyīn and became pregnant with Huí.
Huí was born foolish,
and only began to speak at eight or nine years old.
Even his parents treated him like a pig or dog.
His elder brother was serving in Ānxī,
and news was cut off.
His parents sent him to inquire,
one day,
he left in the morning with prepared provisions,
and returned home in the evening,
astonishing his parents.
Hóngnóng was ten thousand lǐ from Ānxī,
because he returned from ten thousand lǐ away,
he was called Wànhuí (Ten Thousand Returns).
Empress Wǔ bestowed upon him brocade robes and a golden belt.
5. On Jiǎxū,
the tribal chief of the Tūqíshī, Wūzhìlè, was made Prince of Huáidé Commandery.
6. In the second month,
on Yǐwèi,
Wéi Jùyuán, the Minister of Justice, was made Joint Manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery,
and still acknowledged kinship with the Empress.
7 On the bǐngshēn day,
the monk Huìfàn and eight others were all promoted to the fifth-rank grade,
and were granted the titles of commandery and county dukes;
the Daoist priest Shǐ Chóng'ēn and others were promoted to the
fifth-rank grade,
and appointed as Chancellor of the National University,
with the same status as regular officials;
the Táng Huìyào states: In the fifth year of the Yǒnghuī era,
Jiǎng Xiàozhāng was appointed as Imperial Physician,
an extra post specially created,
yet with the same status as a regular official.
This marked the beginning of extra officials.
8 Twenty officials from the Left and Right Censorates, as well as those of the fifth rank and above both inside and outside the court, were selected as Circuit Inspectors for the ten circuits,
entrusted with overseeing officials and comforting the people,
recommending the worthy and rectifying judicial cases,
with replacements every two years,
and their promotions or demotions determined based on their merits and faults.

The Governor of Yìzhōu, Jiāng Shīdù of Wèi County; the Vice Director of the Ministry of Rites, Mǎ Huáisù; the Palace Censor, Yuán Qiányào of Línzhāng; the Investigating Censor, Lú Huáishèn of Língchāng; and the Vice Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud, Lǐ Jié of Fǔyáng, were all among them.
Wèi County,
belonged to Wèi Commandery during the Hàn dynasty,
and at that time belonged to Wèizhōu.
Due to the taboo name of Emperor Mǐn of Jìn, Yè,
Yè was renamed Línzhāng,
though by that time, Yè City had already fallen.
Later, the Later Zhào restored it as Yè County.
The Eastern Wèi divided Yè, Nèihuáng, Chìqiū, and Féixiāng,
establishing Línzhāng County,
which belonged to Wèi Commandery.
During the Zhōu, Suí, and Táng dynasties, it belonged to Xiàngzhōu.
Fǔyáng,
was originally part of Wǔ'ān County during the Hàn dynasty,
and later, during the Northern Zhōu, Fǔyáng County was established,
belonging to Xiàngzhōu.
Fǔ,
is pronounced as "fǔ."
9 In the third month,
on the jiǎchén day,
the Secretariat Director Wéi Ānshí was dismissed and made Minister of Revenue;
the Minister of Revenue Sū Guī was appointed as Palace Attendant and left in charge of the Western Capital.
Guī,
was the father of Sū Tǐng.
Táng Xiùjǐng retired from office.
10. Initially,
the Junior Court of Imperial Entertainments Assistant, Sòng Zhīwèn of Hóngnóng, and his younger brother, the Cāngzhōu Granary Administrator Sòng Zhīxùn
(Hóngnóng County was attached to Guó Prefecture,
its seat located on the Hóngnóng River.)
Under the Táng system,
the Granary Section Administrator (Sīcāng Cānjūn Shì) was in charge of land taxes, cloth levies, government offices, kitchens, granaries, warehouses, and markets.
They fled back to the Eastern Capital,
hiding in the home of their friend, the Minister of Imperial Banquets and Commandant of Imperial Consorts, Wáng Tóngjiǎo.
Tóngjiǎo detested the actions of Wǔ Sānsī and Empress Wéi,
and whenever he spoke of it with those close to him,
he would gnash his teeth in anger.
Zhīxùn overheard this from behind a curtain,
and secretly sent his son Sòng Tán and his nephew, the Collator of the Palace Library Lǐ Quān, to inform Sānsī,
hoping to redeem himself.
Sānsī sent Tán, Quān, and the Fǔzhōu Granary Administrator Rǎn Zǔyōng
(Fǔzhōu:
in Hàn times, this was the territory of Nánchāng and Nánchéng counties.
During the Wú under Sūn Liàng, the Línchuān commandery was established here.
After Suí pacified Chén,
Fǔ Prefecture was established.)
(Tán:
pronunciation: tú hán.)
(Quān:
pronunciation: chǒu yuán.)
(Shòuchūn County:
under the Hàn, it belonged to Huáinán commandery.
During Jìn, to avoid the taboo of Empress Dowager Zhèng's name,
it was changed to Shòuyáng.
Under Suí, it was restored to Shòuchūn County,
attached to Shòu Prefecture.)
(Jǐng:
pronunciation: jù yǒng.)
plotted to murder Sānsī,
then lead troops to the palace gates,
and depose the Empress.
The Emperor ordered the Censor-in-Chief Lǐ Chéngjiā and Investigating Censor Yáo Shàozhī to investigate the matter,
and also ordered Yáng Zàisī, Lǐ Qiáo, and Wéi Jùyuán to assist in the verification.
Zhòngzhī detailed Sānsī's crimes,
implicating the inner palace.
Zàisī and Jùyuán pretended to be asleep and did not listen;
Qiáo and Shàozhī ordered him taken away and sent to prison.
Zhòngzhī looked back,
continuing to speak without cease,
so Shàozhī ordered him beaten,
breaking his arm.
Zhòngzhī cried out loudly:
"I have already lost to you in death,
but I will accuse you before Heaven!"
On the gēngxū day,
Tóngjiǎo and others were all sentenced to execution.
(Textual analysis notes: The Records of the Censorate state:
"Tóngjiǎo and Zhāng Zhòngzhī plotted to kill Sānsī,
but were exposed by Sòng Tán.
Censor-in-Chief Lǐ Chéngjiā and Censor Yáo Shàozhī conducted the interrogation,
and the matter implicated the inner palace.
An internal decree ordered the chief ministers to question them.
The various chief ministers pretended to be asleep and heard nothing,
only Qiáo and Chéngjiā secretly discussed it,
and Tóngjiǎo, Zhòngzhī, and others met with clan extermination.")
It also states:
"Zhāng Zhòngzhī plotted to kill Wǔ Sānsī,
Sòng Zhīxùn's son Tán learned of the plot,
and was about to expose it,
but had not yet done so.
It happened that Rǎn Zǔyōng and Lǐ Quān reported it on the road,
and Zǔyōng and Quān informed him.")
It also states:
"Zhāng Zhòngzhī, Sòng Zhīxùn, and Zǔ Yánqìng plotted to fire a bronze crossbow hidden in their sleeves at Sānsī,
but waited for an opportunity that never came.
Zhīxùn's son Tán secretly exposed it,
and an edict ordered Lǐ Chéngjiā and Shàozhī to interrogate them inside the Xīnkāi Gate.
Initially,
Shàozhī intended to handle the matter justly,
but before it was settled,
an edict ordered the chief ministers to jointly question them.
The various ministers feared Sānsī,
and merely forced themselves to pretend not to hear.
Zhòngzhī and Yánqìng said that among the ministers were those who curried favor with Sānsī,
and repeatedly whispered in Chéngjiā's ear,
also persuading and enticing Shàozhī,
so the situation changed.
They then secretly stationed over ten strong men,
ordered them to bring Zhòngzhī for questioning,
and upon arrival, gagged him, bound his hands behind his back,
and sent him to be imprisoned.
Shàozhī returned and said to Zhòngzhī: 'Third Brother Zhāng,
the matter has failed!'
Zhòngzhī firmly stated Sānsī's treasonous acts,
so Shàozhī ordered him beaten until his arm broke.
Zhòngzhī cried out to Heaven six or seven times,
saying, 'Shàozhī, you rebel!
My arm is broken,
I have lost to you,
but I will accuse you before the Heavenly Court!'
Then he was forced to confess to treason and met with clan extermination.")
The Comprehensive Records of Court and Country states:
"Initially,
Zhīxùn fawned upon and attached himself to the Zhāng Yìzhī brothers,
and was sent out to serve as Cāngzhōu Granary Administrator.
He then fled back,
and Wáng Tóngjiǎo hid him in a small room.
Tóngjiǎo
was a man of passionate spirit,
and was indignant at the rebellious Wéi and Wǔ Sānsī for throwing the state into disorder.
When he discussed it with one or two close associates,
he would often gnash his teeth.
Zhīxùn eavesdropped from behind a curtain,
and sent his nephew Tán to submit a written accusation,
hoping to gain the favor of the rebellious Wéi.
Wǔ Sānsī and others were indeed greatly angered,
and memorialized for the execution of Tóngjiǎo's faction.")
The Veritable Records state:
"Tóngjiǎo and Zhōu Jǐng secretly plotted to kill Sānsī,
and so gathered officers and soldiers,
planning to seize the opportunity when Empress Zétiān's funeral procession set out to ambush and kill Sānsī.
Lǐ Quān and others learned of it and informed Sānsī,
so Sānsī accused Tóngjiǎo and others of plotting rebellion,
and they were ultimately sentenced to execution.")
The Táng Calendar and Comprehensive Annals are also roughly the same as the Veritable Records,
but state
"Zhòngzhī accidentally leaked the plot to his friend Sòng Zhīwèn,
and Zhīwèn pretended to agree.
Zǔyōng and Zhīxùn also participated in the plot,
but later betrayed it.
Lǐ Quān was Zhīwèn's nephew,
and was ordered to inform Sānsī,
thus accusing Tóngjiǎo of plotting rebellion.")
The Old Biography states:
"Zhīwèn was demoted to Assistant of Shuāng Prefecture,
and not long after fled back,
hiding in Zhāng Zhòngzhī's home.
Zhòngzhī and Tóngjiǎo plotted to kill Wǔ Sānsī,
and Zhīwèn ordered his elder brother's son to expose the matter to redeem himself.
After Tóngjiǎo and others were convicted,
Zhīwèn was appointed as a Registrar of the Court of State Ceremonial.")
(Analysis: Sānsī enjoyed favor with Emperor Zhōngzōng and Empress Wéi,
and his power overshadowed the realm.
If Tóngjiǎo and others had rashly killed him,
how could they have remained peacefully unharmed?
If they did not have the ambition to coerce the sovereign,
how could they have lightly undertaken such a plot?
Also, the statement
'firing a bronze crossbow from their sleeves'
is almost like child's play.
It is likely that out of hatred for Sānsī,
they may have spoken with Zhòngzhī, Jǐng, and others about wanting to kill him,
and Zhīxùn and others informed Sānsī.
Sānsī then instructed Tán and others to falsely accuse Tóngjiǎo,
saying they plotted to ambush and kill Sānsī on the day the funeral procession set out,
and then depose the Empress and rebel.
I now follow the Comprehensive Records.)
Zhōu Jǐng fled into the temple of Bǐgān,
and declared loudly:
"Bǐgān was a loyal minister of antiquity,
he knows my heart.
Sānsī and the Empress engage in licentiousness,
endangering the state.
They will soon have their heads displayed in the marketplace,
I only regret I will not live to see it!"
He then slit his own throat.
Zhīwèn, Zhīxùn, Tán, Quān, and Zǔyōng were all appointed to capital offices.
(Capital offices
refer to official posts in the capital,
also called capital bureau officials.)
11. Wǔ Sānsī and Empress Wéi day and night slandered Jǐng Huī and others without cease,
and further demoted Huī to Prefect of Lǎng Prefecture,
Cuī Xuánwěi to Prefect of Jūn Prefecture,
Huán Yànfàn to Prefect of Bó Prefecture,
and Yuán Shùjǐ to Prefect of Yǐng Prefecture.
(Yǐng Prefecture:
in Hàn times, this was the territory of Jìnglíng County.
During the Eastern Jìn, the Jìnglíng commandery was established.
Under Western Wèi, Wēn Prefecture was established.
Under Northern Zhōu, Yǐng Prefecture was established.)
(Fù:
pronunciation: fú yòu.)
They were considered faction members and were demoted.
12. A great number of supernumerary officials were appointed,
totaling over two thousand from the capital bureaus and various prefectures,
and eunuchs promoted above the seventh rank to supernumerary positions numbered nearly a thousand more.
Wèi Yuánzhōng returned from Duānzhōu
and served as chancellor.
Wèi Yuánzhōng had previously been demoted to the post of county defender of Gāoyào.
Gāoyào County was attached to Duānzhōu.
Xiàng,
pronounced xī liàng fān.
He merely went along with the times;
both inside and outside the court, people were disappointed.
Suānzǎo County Defender Yuán Chǔkè
Suānzǎo County,
during the Hàn and Jìn dynasties belonged to Chénliú Commandery,
was abolished during the Later Qí,
re-established in the sixth year of the Kāihuáng era of Suí,
belonged to Zhèngzhōu,
and during Táng belonged to Huázhōu.
believed:
"Our sovereign has newly accepted the Mandate,
and should renew his virtue,
quoting the text from the 'Xián Yǒu Yī Dé' chapter of the Shū.
He should dismiss petty men,
to promote great transformation.
How can you be content with your glory and favor,
and remain silent and compliant!
Now, not establishing a Crown Prince early,
selecting tutors and mentors to assist him,
is the first fault.
Princesses establishing their own administrations and appointing staff,
is the second fault.
Honoring and promoting Buddhist monks,
allowing them to frequent the gates of the powerful,
leveraging influence to accept bribes,
is the third fault.
Actors and petty men,
improperly obtaining official ranks,
is the fourth fault.
When officials select and recommend worthy talents,
all are obtained through bribery and influence-seeking,
is the fifth fault.
Favoring and promoting eunuchs,
nearly a thousand of them,
creating steps toward prolonged disorder,
is the sixth fault.
Princes, dukes, and noble relatives,
receiving rewards and gifts without limit,
competing in extravagance and waste,
is the seventh fault.
Widely appointing supernumerary officials,
wasting resources and harming the people,
is the eighth fault.
Palace ladies from previous reigns,
being allowed to reside outside the palace at their convenience,
entering and exiting without restriction,
engaging in connections and soliciting favors,
is the ninth fault.
These nine faults,
specifically refer to types like Shàngguān Jiéyú and Hèlóu Shànggōng.
Cháo,
pronounced zhí yáo fān.
Confusing the sovereign's judgment,
improperly obtaining salaries and positions,
is the tenth fault.
The tenth fault specifically refers to types like Yè Jìngnéng and Zhèng Pǔsī.
If you, my lord, do not correct them,
who will correct them!"
Yuánzhōng received the letter,
and could only feel ashamed and offer apologies.
13 In summer,
the fourth month,
the posthumous title of the Empress's father Wéi Xuánzhēn was changed to Fēng Prince,
and the Empress's four younger brothers were all posthumously granted commandery prince titles.
The four brothers are
Xún, Hào, Dòng, and Cǐ.
14 On Jǐchǒu,
Left Sanqí Chángshì and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn Lǐ Huáiyuǎn retired.
15 Recluse Wéi
Yuèjiāng submitted a memorial accusing Wǔ Sānsī of secretly communicating with the inner palace,
and that he would certainly rebel;
the Emperor was greatly enraged,
and ordered him executed.
Huángmén Shìláng Sòng Jǐng memorialized requesting an investigation,
the Emperor became even angrier,
without time to adjust his headscarf,
slipped on his shoes and went out through a side gate.
Side gate,
not the main exit gate.
Chéng Dàchāng said: At the Táng Dàmíng Palace audience hall, outside the Left and Right Jīnyǔ guards,
there were what were called side gates,
because they were beside the Duānmén.
Inferring from the side gates of the Cháng'ān Dàmíng Palace,
then the side gates of the Luòyáng Palace can be known accordingly.
Xǐ,
pronounced suǒ xǐ fān,
means shoes worn without heels.
"I thought he had already been executed,
is he still not yet!"
Ordered to hasten the execution.
Jǐng said:
"People say there are private relations in the palace with Sānsī,
Your Majesty does not investigate but executes him,
I fear there will certainly be secret discussions throughout the land."
He firmly requested an investigation,
the Emperor did not permit it,
Jǐng said:
"If you must execute Yuèjiāng,
please execute me first!
Otherwise,
I dare not ultimately obey the decree."
The Emperor's anger slightly subsided.
Left Yùshǐ Dàfū Sū Xiàng,
Jǐshìzhōng Xú Jiān, and Dàlǐ Qīng Cháng'ān Yǐn Sīzhēn all believed that executing in the height of summer
violated the seasonal ordinances.
The Emperor then ordered him to be caned,
and exiled to Lǐngnán.
One day after the autumn equinox,
at dawn,
Guǎngzhōu Dūdū Zhōu Rénguǐ executed him.
Textual analysis note: The Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi states:
"Zhōu Rénguǐ executed him one day after the autumn equinox at dawn,
there was an amnesty decree but it did not reach in time."
The Tǒng Jì,
records Yuèjiāng's death attached to the end of this year,
the Táng Jì places it in the second month,
the Old Biography and Táng Lì both place it after the deaths of the Five Princes.
Considering that Jìng Huī and others were killed in the seventh month of this year,
if it were later,
Xú Jiān's memorial could not say
"Zhūxià is in Chén,"
and Sīzhēn could not say
"the month of growth and development."
Now, summarizing the event, it is attached to this month.
16 Yùshǐ Dàfū Lǐ Chéngjiā attached himself to Wǔ Sānsī,
and slandered Yǐn Sīzhēn at court.
Sīzhēn said:
"You attach yourself to treacherous ministers,
plotting disloyalty,
first eliminating loyal ministers!"
Chéngjiā was angry,
impeached and memorialized against Sīzhēn,
who was sent out as Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Old Records:
Qīngzhōu,
2,520 lǐ northeast of the capital,
1,507 lǐ to the Eastern Capital.
"You are usually reticent in speech,
yet when refuting Chéngjiā at court,
how were you so quick-witted?"
Sīzhēn said:
"Things that cannot make a sound,
when agitated, will sound.
Chéngjiā relied on his authority to bully,
I, in righteousness, could not accept humiliation,
and also do not know where the words came from."
17 Wǔ Sānsī disliked Sòng Jǐng,
and sent him out as Jiǎnjiào Bèizhōu Cìshǐ.
Old Records: Bèizhōu,
1,782 lǐ northeast of the capital,
993 lǐ to the Eastern Capital.
18 In the fifth month,
on Gēngshēn,
Zétiān Dàshèng Huánghòu was buried at Qiánlíng.
19 Wǔ Sānsī had Zhèng Yīn accuse Lángzhōu Cìshǐ Jìng Huī, Bózhōu Cìshǐ Wéi Yànfàn,
Huán Yànfàn was at that time granted the surname Wéi,
and thus referred to as such.
Yīn,
pronounced yú jīn fān.
Bó,
pronounced páng gè fān.
In the sixth month,
on Wùyín,
Huī was demoted to Yázhōu Sīmǎ,
Yànfàn to Shuāngzhōu Sīmǎ,
Jiǎnzhī to Xīnzhōu Sīmǎ,
Shùjǐ to Dòuzhōu Sīmǎ,
Xuánwěi to Báizhōu Sīmǎ,
all appointed as supernumerary officials,
still in permanent posts,
their merit titles were revoked;
Yànfàn's surname was restored to Huán.
After Wǔ Sānsī had killed the Five Princes,
his power overshadowed that of the sovereign.
He often said:
"I do not know who in this world are called good men,
and who are called evil men;
but those who are good to me are good men,
and those who are evil to me are evil men."

At that time, Minister of War Zōng Chǔkè, Director of the Palace Buildings Zōng Jìnqīng, Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury Jì Chǔnè, and Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial Gān Yuánjiǎn were all wings and feathers for Wǔ Sānsī.

Vice Censor-in-Chief Zhōu Lìyòng, Investigating Censor Rǎn Zǔyōng, Assistant Minister of the Imperial Stud Lǐ Jùn, Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments Sòng Zhīxùn, and Investigating Censor Yáo Shàozhī were all eyes and ears for Wǔ Sānsī.
People at the time called them the Five Dogs.
25 In the ninth month,
on the Wùwǔ day,
Left Adviser to the Heir Apparent and Co-Manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery Lǐ Huáiyuǎn died.
26 Earlier,
when Lǐ Qiáo was Vice Minister of Personnel,
wishing to build up personal favors,
and seeking to become a chief minister again,
he memorialized to greatly increase the number of supernumerary officials,
widely recruiting relatives and acquaintances of the powerful and noble.
After he became chief minister,
the selection and appointment of officials became disordered,
and the state treasury was depleted.
He then submitted another memorial speaking of the evils of excessive officials,
and requested to resign;
the Emperor consoled him and did not permit it.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Jǐmǎo day,
the imperial carriage departed from the Eastern Capital.
The former Acting Inspector and Prefect of Bīngzhōu, Zhāng Rényuàn, was appointed Acting Inspector, General of the Left Guard of the Palace Gates, and concurrently Prefect of Luòzhōu.
On the Wùxū day,
the imperial carriage arrived at the Western Capital.
In the eleventh month,
on the Yǐsì day,
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
27 On the Bǐngchén day,
Dòu Cóngyī, Prefect of Púzhōu, was appointed Prefect of Yōngzhōu.
Cóngyī
was the son of Dòu Déxuán.
Dòu Déxuán appears in the first year of the Líndé era of Emperor Gāozōng, in the 201st scroll.
Avoiding the taboo name of the Empress's father,
he changed his name to Cóngyī.
He often flattered and attached himself to the powerful and noble.
Princess Tàipíng and a Buddhist temple disputed over a watermill.
Lǐ Yuánhóng, the Registrar of Yōngzhōu, adjudicated it to the temple.

According to the Táng system: The Registrar of the Bureau of Households manages household registers, tax accounts, travel permits, exemption certificates, miscellaneous corvée labor, tax arrears, distinctions between commoners and base people, fodder and straw, inns, marriages, land disputes, and commending filial piety and fraternal duty.
Dòu Cóngyī repeatedly ordered Yuánhóng to change the judgment.
Yuánhóng wrote boldly on the back of the judgment:
"The Southern Mountain may be moved,
but this judgment shall not be changed!"
Cóngyī could not force him to alter it.
Yuánhóng
was the son of Lǐ Dàoguǎng.
Lǐ Dàoguǎng appears in the first year of the Wànsuì Tōngtiān era of Empress Wǔ, in the 205th scroll.
28 Earlier,
the Director of the Palace Library, Zhèng Pǔsī, had his daughter entered into the rear palace.
Investigating Censor Cuī Rìyòng of Língchāng submitted an impeachment memorial against him,
but the Emperor did not listen.
Pǔsī gathered a faction in Yōngzhōu and Qízhōu,
plotting to rebel.
The affair was discovered,
and Sū Guī, the Commandant of the Western Capital, arrested and imprisoned him,
thoroughly investigating the matter.
Pǔsī's wife, the fifth Madame, through sorcery, had gained favor with the Empress.
The Emperor issued an edict ordering Guī not to prosecute.
When the imperial carriage returned to the Western Capital,
Guī argued vehemently at court.
The Emperor suppressed Guī and protected Pǔsī.
Attendant Censor Fàn Xiànzhōng stepped forward and said:
"I request that Sū Guī be beheaded!"
The Emperor said:
"Why?"
He replied:
"Guī, as a high minister left in charge of the capital,
was unable to first behead Pǔsī,
and then report it,
allowing him to confuse Your Majesty's hearing.
His crime is great.
Moreover, Pǔsī's evidence of rebellion is clear,
yet Your Majesty perversely argues on his behalf.
I have heard that a king does not die;
is this not what is meant?
I wish to be granted death first,
rather than serve Pǔsī facing north."
Wèi Yuánzhōng said:
"Sū Guī is a man of integrity;
he does not apply punishments unjustly.
Pǔsī, by law, deserves death."
The Emperor, having no alternative,
on the Wùwǔ day,
exiled Pǔsī to Dānzhōu.
The rest of his faction were all executed.
29 In the twelfth month,
on the Jǐmǎo day,
the Türk Mòchuò invaded Míngshā.
Língzhōu had a Míngshā Prefecture.
In the second year of the Wǔdé era,
Míngshā County was established as Huìzhōu.
In the sixth year of the Zhēnguān era,
the prefecture was abolished,
and Huánzhōu was established instead,
named because the great river curved around it.
In the ninth year, the prefecture was abolished,
and the county was returned to Língzhōu.
In this year, it was invaded by Mòchuò,
and the administration was moved to the old Fēng'ān City.
Sòng Bái said: Míngshā was originally the territory of Fùpíng County in the Hàn dynasty.
Later, the Zhōu dynasty established Huìzhōu here,
soon establishing Míngshā Garrison.
The Suí dynasty established Huánzhōu,
named because the great mountains curved around it.
In this place, when people and horses walk on the sand, it makes a sound,
different from other sands,
hence it is called Míngshā (Sounding Sand).
The army was defeated,
with over six thousand dead.
On the Dīng
sì day,
the Türks advanced to invade Yuánzhōu, Huìzhōu, and other prefectures.
In the second year of the Wǔdé era, Xīhuìzhōu was established with Huìníng Garrison of Píngliáng Commandery.
In the eighth year of the Zhēnguān era, it was renamed Huìzhōu.
Zhōngyì was dismissed from office.
30 Guō Yuánzhèn, Grand Protector-General of Ānxī, went to the headquarters of the Türgesh leader Wūzhìlè to discuss military affairs.
The weather was stormy with wind and snow.
Yuánzhèn stood in front of the tent,
speaking with Wūzhìlè.
After a long time,
the snow was deep,
but Yuánzhèn did not move his feet.
Wūzhìlè was old,
and could not bear the cold.
When the meeting ended, he died.
His son, Suōgē, marshaled troops intending to attack Yuánzhèn.
The Deputy Commissioner, Vice Censor-in-Chief Xiè Wǎn, learned of this,
and urged Yuánzhèn to flee at night.
Yuánzhèn said:
"I treat people with a sincere heart;
what is there to suspect or fear!
Moreover, we are deep in enemy territory;
where would I flee to!"
He lay down calmly and did not move.
The next morning,
he entered and mourned,
very sorrowfully.
Suōgē was moved by his righteousness,
and treated Yuánzhèn as before.
On the Wùxū day,
Suōgē was made to inherit the titles of Governor of Wàlùzhōu and Prince Huáidé.
In the first year of the Xiǎnqìng era of Emperor Gāozōng, the Wàlùzhōu Governor's Office was established with the Suōgē Mòhè tribe of the Türgesh.
Wà
is pronounced wū mò.
31 Princess Ānlè, relying on imperial favor, was arrogant and willful.
She sold offices and adjudicated cases for bribes,
her influence pervading the court and the countryside.
Sometimes she herself drafted imperial edicts,
covered the text,
and had the Emperor sign them.
The Emperor would laugh and comply,
never even looking at them.
She personally requested to be made Crown Princess.
Although the Emperor did not consent,
he also did not reprimand her.
Examination of discrepancies: The Tǒngjì says:
"Princess Ānlè privately requested to depose the Crown Prince and establish herself as Crown Princess.
The Emperor asked Wèi Yuánzhōng about it.
Yuánzhōng said: 'The Crown Prince is the heir of the state,
the foundation of the people.
Now that he is without fault,
how can he be lightly moved,
to make the Princess Crown Princess!
What title would the Princess's Consort then have?
The world would certainly find it very strange and shocking.
I fear this is not the way for the Princess to secure herself.'
The Princess learned of this,
and memorialized: 'Yuánzhōng
is a stubborn Shāndōng country bumpkin.
How is he worthy of discussing the expedient great affairs of the state, or the merits and faults of ceremonial regulations!
Āmǔzǐ (Empress Wǔ) herself still became Son of Heaven.
Moreover, I am a princess.
To become Crown Princess,
what is there that cannot be done!'"
Considering that Emperor Zhōngzōng, though foolish,
surely knew that establishing a Crown Princess was unacceptable.
Why would he need to wait for Yuánzhōng's words?
Now we follow the Old Biography.
First year of the Jǐnglóng era
(Dīngwèi, 707)
The era name was changed in the ninth month of this year.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the Gēngxū day,
an edict was issued because the Tūjué (Turk) Mòchuò had invaded the border,
ordering officials both inside and outside the court to each submit strategies for pacifying the Tūjué.
Right Rectifier of Omissions Lú Fǔ submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Xì Hú delighted in ritual and music,
was devoted to the Book of Songs and Book of Documents,
and became the Marshal of Jìn;
Zuǒzhuàn: Duke Wén of Jìn held a military review at Bèilú,
established three armies,
and sought a marshal.
Zhào Cuī said:
'Xì Hú is suitable.
I have frequently heard his words,
he delights in ritual and music and is devoted to the Book of Songs and Book of Documents.
The Book of Songs and Book of Documents
are the storehouses of righteousness;
ritual and music
are the standards of virtue;
virtue and righteousness
are the roots of benefit.
Your Lordship should try him.'
Thereupon, he made Xì Hú command the central army.
Shuài,
read as suǒ lèi fān.
He established the merit of pacifying Wú.
See the first year of the Tàikāng era of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn, scroll 81.
He did not select a man merely for his courage.
Zuǒzhuàn says: The central army plans strategy, the rear is strong.
The commentary says: The central army devises plans.
The talent of a brave general
is fundamentally insufficient to shoulder great responsibilities.
Furthermore,
in the battle of Míngshā,
the commanding general fled first;
the defeat at Míngshā
also specifically refers to Shāzhā Zhōngyì.
Xiāo,
read as jiān yáo fān.
Jiàng,
read as jí liàng fān.
If rewards and punishments are clear,
no enemy will fail to submit.
Also,
the border prefecture governors
should be carefully selected,
so that they can train soldiers and chariots,
accumulate supplies and grain,
defending when [the enemy] comes,
and preparing when they leave.
Last year there were droughts in all directions,
it is not easy to raise an army.
We should govern the interior to affect the exterior,
pacify the near to attract the distant,
wait until the granaries are full,
and the soldiers well-trained,
then launch a major campaign to attack them.'
The Emperor approved of it.
2 In the second month,
on the Bǐngxū day,
the Emperor sent Wǔ Yōujì and Wǔ Sānsī to Qiánlíng to pray for rain.
Soon after, rain fell,
the Emperor was pleased,
and issued an edict restoring the Wǔ clan's Chóng'ēn Temple as well as Hàolíng and Shùnlíng.
After the Emperor was restored to the throne,
he changed the Wǔ clan's Chóngzūn Temple to Chóng'ēn Temple;
after the Empress Dowager passed away,
the Chóng'ēn Temple was abolished.
Hàolíng and Shùnlíng,
see the second year of the Tiānshòu era, scroll 204.
Textual analysis says: The old basic annals,
'On the Jǐsì day of the first month,
sent Wǔ Yōujì and Wǔ Sānsī to Qiánlíng to pray for rain to Empress Zétiān.'
The new basic annals,
'On the Jiǎwǔ day,
established officials for the Róngxiān Mausoleum to honor virtue and ancestors.'
According to the perpetual calendar,
the first month began on the Gēngzǐ day,
there is no Jǐsì day;
the second month began on the Gēngwǔ day,
there is no Jiǎwǔ day.
Now follow the Veritable Records.
The mausoleum was called Róngxiān;
last year, the Empress's father Wéi Xuánzhēn was posthumously enfeoffed as the Prince of Fēng.
Court Gentleman for Ceremonial Yáng Fú said:
'The Imperial Ancestral Temple all selects sons of officials of the seventh rank and below to serve as fasting attendants,
now the Chóng'ēn Temple selects sons of the fifth rank,
I do not know what the Imperial Ancestral Temple should do?'
The Emperor ordered that the Imperial Ancestral Temple also follow the standard of the Chóng'ēn Temple.
Fú said:
'Using a minister as the standard for a ruler
is still considered overstepping and rebellious,
how much more so using a ruler as the standard for a minister!'

19. On the Rénxū day,
the Left and Right Imperial Forest Army's "Thousand Cavalry" was renamed "Ten Thousand Cavalry".
20. In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Dīngchǒu day,
General of the Left Garrison Guard Zhāng Rényuàn was appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Shuòfāng Circuit,
to attack the Turks.
The character "大" (great)
is missing below
"左屯衞" (Left Garrison Guard)
The barbarians had already retreated.
He pursued and attacked them,
inflicting a major defeat.
21. Sū Ānhéng, an Instructor of the Inner Training Institute.
The Training Institute,
originally named the Inner Literary Institute,
selected one palace woman with literary talent to be an Academician,
to teach and train the palace women.
Empress Wǔ changed it to the Training Institute,
and later changed it to the Hanlin Inner Instruction Bureau,
because its location was within the palace precincts.
The *New History* says: It was in charge of teaching palace women writing, calculation, and various arts.
The character "恒"
is pronounced "héng".
When Crown Prince Chóngjùn executed Wǔ Sānsī,
Ānhéng himself claimed
"this was my plan".
After the Crown Prince's defeat,
someone reported him;
on the Wùyín day,
he was executed.
22. In the twelfth month,
on the Yǐchǒu day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
23. This year,
the Emperor sent envoys along various routes to the Jiāng and Huái regions to redeem captured creatures.
The Emperor, considering that the people of Jiāng and Huái catching fish and turtles harmed life,
dispatched envoys along routes to redeem them with money and goods.
The character "使" (envoy)
is pronounced "shǐ".
Fángzǐ County
belonged to the Chángshān Commandery in the Hàn,
to the Zhào Commandery in the Jìn and Later Wèi,
and to Zhào Prefecture in the Suí and Táng.
"The villagers of Jiāngnán
'villagers'
means local people.

they changed
'民' (people)
to
'人' (persons)."
The character "上"
is pronounced "shàng".
The character "疏"
is pronounced "shū".
The profits from fish and turtles
are resources for the common people.
Although the private intent of clouds and rain may bestow some small benefit;
the grace of nurturing life has not yet reached the ordinary people.
Why is this?
The abundance of rivers and lakes
allows for limitless propagation;
but the resources of the state treasury
are easily exhausted when disbursed.
If the expenditure is small,
what success can the relief achieve!
If the expenditure is large,
then regular disbursements will be lacking.
In saving creatures,
how can it compare to caring for the people!
Moreover, those who trade in live creatures
look only to profit.
When coins arrive daily,
(ancient times had metal knives, coins, and cloth used as currency,
hence the term 'coin-knife'),
[AS-8DB8]
if you bestow it for one morning,
they will multiply their efforts a hundredfold.
It would be better to redirect the money and goods used for redemption,

Reviving the state and loving the people—

Second Year of the Jǐnglóng Era
(Wùshēn, 708 CE) 1. In spring,
the second month,
on the Gēngyín day,
it was reported from the palace that a five-colored cloud had risen from the skirt in the Empress's clothes hamper. The Emperor ordered it to be depicted and shown to all officials.
Wéi Jùyuán requested that it be proclaimed throughout the land.
The Emperor agreed,
and furthermore granted a general amnesty.
2. Jiāyè Zhìzhōng memorialized:
"In the past, before the Divine Yáo Emperor (i.e., Táng Gāozǔ) received the Mandate,
the people of the world sang the 'Táo Lǐ Zǐ' song;
(Regarding) 'Táo Lǐ Zǐ', see volume 180, the thirteenth year of the Dàyè era of Suí Yángdì.
Jiā,
pronounced as jū jiā.
The people of the world sang the 'Qínwáng Pòzhèn Yuè';
(Regarding) 'Pòzhèn Yuè', see volume 192, the first year of the Zhēnguàn era of Tàizōng.
The people of the world sang the 'Tángtáng' song;
At the beginning of the Tiáolù era,
there was a folk ballad in the capital that said
'Cè tángtáng,
náo tángtáng'.
(Regarding these) words,
Tàicháng Chéng Lǐ Sìzhēn said:
"'Cè' means not upright,
'náo' means not peaceful.
Since the Suí dynasty,
the Music Bureau has had the 'Tángtáng' melody.
Repeating the word 'táng' twice
is an omen that the Táng will receive the Mandate a second time."
Zhèng Qiáo said: 'Tángtáng',
was composed by Chén Hòuzhǔ,
and Táng Gāozōng often sang it.
The people of the world sang the 'Wǔmèi Niáng' song;
After the Yǒnghuī era,
the people sang the 'Wǔmèi Niáng' melody,
but it seems this melody already existed during the Suí dynasty.
Wǔ,
pronounced wǔ.
The people of the world sang the 'Yīngwáng Shízhōu' song;
This song is not seen in the historical records.
Zhìzhōng, because His Majesty was initially enfeoffed as the Prince of Yīng,
thus interpreted it as a sign of receiving the Mandate.
The people of the world sang the 'Sāng Tiáo Wéi' song;
At the end of the Yǒnghuī era,
there was a village song: 'Sāng tiáo wéi yě, nǚ shí wéi yě'.
(According to) the Treatise on Music: Zhìzhōng thus interpreted it as praising the Empress's virtue,
her dedication to sericulture,
and providing for the ancestral temple affairs.
He presented twelve pieces of 'Sāng Wéi' songs.
(Saying) she presided over sericulture matters,
he respectfully presented twelve pieces of 'Sāng Wéi' songs,
requesting they be compiled into the Music Bureau repertoire,
to be performed when the Empress sacrifices to the First Sericulturalist."
Tàicháng Qīng Zhèng Yīn further elaborated on this.
The Emperor was pleased,
and all received generous rewards.
3. Right Supplements Omission Official Zhào Yánxǐ submitted a statement:
"Zhōu and Táng are unified,
their prophetic mandates converge,
therefore Gāozōng enfeoffed Your Majesty as the Prince of Zhōu;
In the second year of Xiǎnqìng,
the Emperor was enfeoffed as Prince of Zhōu,
in the second year of Yífèng,
he was transferred and enfeoffed as Prince of Yīng.
Táng Tóngtài presented the Luòshuǐ Chart.
See volume 204, the third year of the Chuígǒng era of Empress Wǔ.
Even a hundred generations hence can be known.
Your Majesty succeeded Zétiān,
your descendants shall rule the world for a hundred generations."
The Emperor was pleased,
and promoted Yánxǐ to Remonstrance Official.
4. On Dīnghài,
Xiāo Zhìzhōng submitted a memorial,
believing that:
"Those favored by grace may only be enriched with gold and silk,
fed with fine grain and meat,
but public office should not be used for private purposes.
Now official positions are already numerous,
the number of officials has doubled,
yet their demands are insatiable,
increasing daily.
Your Majesty bestows immeasurable grace,
yet close relatives make boundless requests,
selling offices for personal gain,
peddling justice to serve private interests.
Within the ministries and courts,
high-ranking officials fill the halls,
neglecting affairs and not attending to their duties,
relying on power to openly violate laws and regulations,
merely bringing disgrace to their offices,
with no benefit to the governance of the time."
Although the Emperor praised his sentiment,
he ultimately could not employ it.
5. In the third month,
on Bǐngchén,
Shuòfāng Circuit Grand Commander Zhāng Rényuàn built the Three Shòuxiáng Fortresses on the river.
The Central Shòuxiáng Fortress was on the north bank of the Yellow River,
over 1,300 lǐ south of Shuòfāng,
where the Ānběi Protectorate was administered.
The Eastern Shòuxiáng Fortress was 200 lǐ northeast of Shèng Prefecture,
over 1,600 lǐ southwest of Shuòfāng.
The Western Shòuxiáng Fortress was 80 lǐ north of Fēng Prefecture, outside the Yellow River,
over 1,000 lǐ southeast of Shuòfāng.
Sòng Qí said: The central fortress was directly south of Shuòfāng,
the western fortress was directly south of Língwǔ,
the eastern fortress was directly south of Yúguān.
Sòng Bái said: The Eastern Shòuxiáng Fortress was 120 lǐ northeast to the Shànyú Protectorate,
400 lǐ southeast to Shuò Prefecture,
8 lǐ southwest across the river to Shèng Prefecture,
300 lǐ west to the Central Shòuxiáng Fortress,
originally the territory of the Hàn Yúnzhōng Commandery.
The Central Shòuxiáng Fortress was 200 lǐ northwest to Tiāndé Army,
400 lǐ south to Lín Prefecture,
500 lǐ north to the Qìkǒu,
originally the territory of the Qín Jiǔyuán Commandery,
in Yúlín,
renamed Wǔyuán by the Hàn,
in the tenth year of Kāiyuán, the Ānběi Grand Protectorate was established here.
The Western Shòuxiáng Fortress was 80 lǐ southeast across the river to Fēng Prefecture,
700 lǐ southwest to Dìngyuǎn Fortress,
300 lǐ northeast to the Qìkǒu.
Xiáng,
pronounced hù jiāng.
Initially,
the Shuòfāng army and the Tūjué used the river as their border,
north of the river was the Fúyún Shrine,
the shrine was on Fúyún Duī,
hence the name.
Jué,
pronounced jiǔ wù.
They would always first go to the shrine to pray,
then graze their horses, gather troops, and cross the river.
At that time, Mòchuò led all his forces west to attack the Tūqíshī,
Rényuàn requested to take advantage of the emptiness to seize the land south of the desert,
and build the Three Shòuxiáng Fortresses north of the river,
with the ends responding to each other,
to cut off their path for southern raids.
Crown Prince Junior Tutor Táng Xiùjǐng believed
"Since the two Hàn dynasties, all have used the great river as a northern barrier,
now building fortresses in enemy territory,
I fear it will toil the people and waste effort,
and ultimately be captured by the enemy."
Rényuàn persistently pleaded without cease,
and the Emperor ultimately followed his plan.
Rényuàn petitioned to retain garrison troops whose annual tour of duty was complete to assist in the project,
(those) border garrison soldiers whose annual tour was complete and should return home,
were retained to assist in the fortress construction work.
Rényuàn captured them all,
and beheaded them beneath the fortress walls,
the army trembled with fear,
and the work was completed in sixty days.
Using the Fúyún Shrine as the central fortress,
it was over 400 lǐ from both the eastern and western fortresses,
all occupying strategic crossings and key points.
Sòng Bái said: The Eastern Shòuxiáng Fortress was originally Hàn Yúnzhōng Commandery territory,
the Central Shòuxiáng Fortress was originally Qín Jiǔyuán Commandery territory,
the Western Shòuxiáng Fortress was roughly the old administrative site of the Hàn Línhé County.
North of Niútóu Cháonà Mountain,
Cháonà Mountain,

garrisoning Nuòzhēn Shuǐ to act as patrol guard.
The Patrol Commander,
led patrol troops to conduct reconnaissance.
From the Central Shòuxiáng Fortress, 200 lǐ west to Dàtóng Chuān,
240-odd lǐ north to Bùyuèduō Mountain,
then 300-odd lǐ northeast to Dìgēdá Fortress,

selected from the army those brave and familiar with mountains, rivers, springs, and wells to fill,
day and night patrolling and watching beyond the watchtowers and barriers,

their deputy commanders and junior officers,

Shǐ,
pronounced shū lì.
Shuòfāng no longer suffered from enemy raids and plunder,

Rényuàn built the three fortresses,
without setting up barbicans or defensive equipment.
Barbican gates,
are the ancient hanging gates.
Some say: building a wall outside the gate to screen and protect the city gate,

Outside the barbican,

Rényuàn said:
"In warfare, the emphasis is on taking the offensive,

When the enemy arrives,

Anyone who looks back towards the fortress,

Later, Cháng Yuánkǎi became Shuòfāng Army Commander,

Therefore, people esteemed Rényuàn and looked down upon Yuánkǎi.
6 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the Guǐwèi day,
four Grand Academicians of the Xiūwén Institute were established,
eight Direct Academicians,
and twelve Academicians,
selecting those skilled in literary composition among the dukes, ministers, and below, such as Lǐ Qiáo, to fill these positions.
In the fourth year of the Wǔdé era,
the Xiūwén Institute was established under the Chancellery,
and in the ninth year,
it was renamed the Hóngwén Institute.
Those of the fifth rank and above were called Academicians,
those of the sixth rank and above were called Direct Academicians,
and there were also Literary Scholars directly attached to the Institute,
all of whom were concurrently held by other officials.
After Empress Wǔ's Chuígōng era,
the chief ministers concurrently took charge of the Institute's affairs,
and were called Institute Masters.
In the first year of the Shénlóng era,
to avoid the taboo of the Filial and Reverent Emperor,
it was renamed the Zhāowén Institute,
and in the second year, it was renamed the Xiūwén Institute.
Shàngguān Zhāoróng advised the emperor to establish four Grand Academicians to symbolize the four seasons,
eight Direct Academicians to symbolize the eight solar terms,
and twelve Academicians to symbolize the twelve two-hour periods.
Whenever the imperial clan or relatives held banquets,
the Academicians were all in attendance,
composing poems and responding in kind,
with Shàngguān Zhāoróng ranking their works.
The Northern Qí Héqīng new regulations included the position of Zhāoróng,
one of the eighty-one imperial consorts.
In the Táng dynasty, the Zhāoróng ranked below the Zhāoyí,
second among the nine ranks.
In the winter of that year,
Shàngguān Jiéyú was promoted to Zhāoróng.
Those who participated in the banquets
were only a few from the Secretariat, Chancellery, long-serving princes and dukes, and close relatives of the nobility.
For grand banquets,
the eight senior officials, nine ministers, and officials of the fifth rank and above from various departments were summoned to attend.
As a result, the whole empire competed in pursuing literary elegance,
while scholars of Confucian learning and loyal admonishers had no chance of advancement.
7 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the Guǐsì day,
Zhāng Rényuàn, Left Guard General of the Garrison and Grand Commander of Shuòfāng Circuit, was appointed as a co-chief minister of the Secretariat-Chancellery.
8 On the Jiǎwǔ day,
Lǚ Yuántài, the Commandant of Qīngyuán, submitted a memorial,
stating:
"The borders are not yet peaceful,
garrison duties do not cease,
the soldiers are exhausted and suffering,
transport and supply are worn out,
yet Buddhist monasteries are being built,
expanding daily and monthly,
exhausting the people and squandering wealth,
with no end in sight.
In the past, Huángdì, Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ established their virtue and left their names through frugality and righteousness.
Since the Jìn and Sòng dynasties,
pagodas and temples have competed in construction,
yet chaos and turmoil have followed one after another,
because their preferences were misguided,
they vied in extravagance and luxury,
and the people could not bear the burden.
I humbly hope that the funds for construction
be redirected to cover border defense expenses,
so that beacon fires may forever cease,
and the people may become prosperous,
then the compassionate charity of Tathāgata,
and his heart of equality,

The memorial was submitted,
but it was ignored.

with thirty thousand coins, one could become a monk or nun.

Shàngguān Jiéyú and other palace women established many private residences outside the palace,
coming and going without restraint,

Princess Ānlè was especially arrogant and domineering,

imitating the palace,

Water was channeled to resemble the Tiānjīn,

separated by mountains to the east,

Moreover, you can take revenge,
compared to entering the court,
how can it be spoken of in the same breath!"
Guō Qiánguàn,
a native of Lìchéng,
Lìchéng County,
belonged to Jǐnán Commandery during the Hàn and Jìn dynasties,
and since the Later Wèi, it has been attached to Qí Prefecture.
Zhōngjié agreed with his words,
and sent a secret envoy to bribe Chǔkè and Chǔnè,

Yuánzhèn heard of their plot,
and submitted a memorial,
stating:
"In previous years, the reason why Tibet invaded our borders
was precisely because they failed to obtain the lands of the Ten Clans and the Four Garrisons.
The matter of seeking the Ten Clans and the Four Garrisons
begins in the first year of Wàn Suì Tōng Tiān under Empress Wǔ, in the 205th volume.
Wèi,
read as yú wěi.
The following néng wéi is the same.
This refers to their paying tribute and the marriage of Princess Jīnchéng.
Bǐ,
read as pí zhì.
It was simply because the country was beset by internal troubles,
meaning the Tsanpo died on a southern campaign,
and the country fell into great chaos,
with legitimate and illegitimate sons contending for the throne,

slaughtering and destroying each other.
Nàn,
read as nǎi dàn.
Fearing that China would take advantage of their weakness,
they temporarily humbled themselves and sought to ingratiate themselves.
Once their country is somewhat stable,
how could they forget to seize the lands of the Ten Clans and the Four Garrisons!
Now, Zhōngjié does not consider the grand strategy of the state,
but simply wishes to act as a guide for Tibet.
I fear that the crisis of the Four Garrisons
will begin from this.
Recently, due to Mòchuò's aggression,
there were many who responded,
and coupled with the exhaustion of the Four Garrisons' troops,
the situation did not allow for Zhōngjié to manage affairs,
not out of pity for the Türgesh.
Zhōngjié does not understand the intentions of the state, both internal and external, and instead seeks help from Tibet;
if Tibet achieves its aims,
then Zhōngjié will be in their grasp,
how could he still serve the Tang!
In previous years, Tibet had no gratitude towards China,
yet still sought the lands of the Ten Clans and the Four Garrisons;
this refers to the events of the first year of Wàn Suì Tōng Tiān.
They requested the division of Yútián and Shūlè,
I do not know on what grounds to refuse them!
Moreover,
the various barbarian tribes under their jurisdiction and the Brahmins are currently not submitting.
If they borrow Tang troops to assist in suppressing them,
I also do not know with what words to refuse them!
Therefore, wise men of ancient times were all unwilling to accept favors from the barbarians,
because they foresaw that their requests would be insatiable,
and ultimately become a future calamity.
Furthermore,
their request for Āshǐnà Xiàn—
is it not because Xiàn is a descendant of the Khan,
and they wish to rely on him to win over the Ten Clans?
According to records, Xiàn's father Yuánqìng,
his uncle Púluó,
his elder brother Tuǐzǐ, as well as Húsèluó, Huáidào, etc.,
are all descendants of the Khan.
In the past, both the Tang and Tibet had extensively established them as Khans,
hoping to pacify the Ten Clans.
In the first year of Chuí Gōng under Empress Wǔ, Yuánqìng was enfeoffed as Khan,
see the 203rd volume.
The enfeoffment of Húsèluó,
according to the Old Book, is also in the second year of that volume.
Tuǐzǐ appears in the first year of Yán Zài, in the 205th volume.
In the fourth year of Cháng'ān, Huáidào was enfeoffed as Khan,
see the 207th volume.
Púluó and Tuǐzǐ
were likely both established by Tibet.
Tuǐ,
read as tuǐ wěi.
Soon they were destroyed.
Why?
These individuals did not possess extraordinary talent,
their grace and authority were insufficient to move the masses.
Although they were descendants of the old Khans,
the people's hearts never truly attached to them.
Moreover, Xiàn is even more distant than his father and brothers.
If Zhōngjié's own military strength could induce or coerce the Ten Clans,
then there would be no need to seek the establishment of a Khan's descendant.
Also,
they wish to have Guō Qiánguàn enter Bá Hán Nà,
to mobilize its troops.
Previously, Qiánguàn had already once, together with Zhōngjié, entered Bá Hán Nà to mobilize troops,
but could not obtain a single piece of armor or horse,
and Bá Hán Nà, unable to bear the invasion and harassment,
turned south to seek Tibet,
supported Tuǐzǐ,
and returned to invade the Four Garrisons.
At that time, Bá Hán Nà had no powerful enemies around to aid it,
Qiánguàn and others wantonly plundered,
as if walking through unguarded territory,
yet still brought about trouble with Tuǐzǐ.
Now, to the north there is Suōgé,
who in times of crisis will join forces with them.
Internally, the various Hu tribes will fortify their walls and resist,
externally, the Turks will watch for opportunities to intercept.
I estimate that Qiánguàn and others on this expedition
will certainly not achieve their aims as in previous years;
facing enemies both internal and external,
they will plunge themselves into danger and destruction,
merely creating enmity with the barbarians,
causing unrest in the Four Garrisons.
In my humble estimation,
this is truly not a good plan."
Chǔkè and others did not listen,
and proposed
"to send Féng Jiābīn as an envoy to pacify Zhōngjié,
with Attendant Censor Lǚ Shǒusù to manage the Four Garrisons,
appoint General Niú Shījiǎng as Deputy Protector-General of Ānxī,
mobilize troops from Gānzhōu, Liángzhōu and westwards,
and also summon Tibet,
to attack Suōgé."
Suōgé had sent an envoy, Suōlà, to present horses in the capital.
Hearing of the plot,
he rushed back to report to Suōgé.
Thereupon, Suōgé dispatched five thousand cavalry from Ānxī,
five thousand from Bōhuàn,
five thousand from Yānqí,
and five thousand from Shūlè,
to invade.
Yuánzhèn was in Shūlè,
fortifying at the river mouth,
and did not dare to come out.
Zhōngjié welcomed Jiābīn at the Jìshū River mouth,
Suōgé sent troops to attack them,
captured Zhōngjié alive,
killed Jiābīn,
captured Lǚ Shǒusù at Pìchéng,
tied him to a post at the relay station,
and killed him.
12. The Emperor, because Princess Ānlè was about to marry Left Guard Central General Wǔ Yánxiù,

Shǐ,
read as shū lì.
When Yōuxù was about to arrive,

intending to perform the ritual of inquiring about the Way,

When the guards entered,

and stood in front of the Liǎngyí Hall.
He was led to the position for inquiring about the Way.
He bowed twice according to the usual ritual.
Generally, when officials leaving the central court for provincial posts come to take leave,
or when provincial officials enter the court for an audience, they are led in for an audience.
Those taking leave or having an audience do not join the ranks of the hundred officials,
but form their own separate line,
called the leave-and-audience line.
Dù Yòu said: According to Tang regulations: Attending officials (Left and Right Sanqi Regular Attendants,
Menxia and Zhongshu Vice Directors,
Remonstrance Counselors,
Jishizhong,
Zhongshu Sheren,
Left and Right Supplements and Omissions,
Tongshi Sheren are in the horizontal line),

According to the regulations on ranks and forms,
former officials summoned for an audience,
and those coming to court for an audience,

those who left office for a reason are placed below officials of the same rank.
In the end, the intended ritual was not completed.

Initially,

Yánxiù was handsome in appearance,

According to the "Tang Liudian,"
among the six palace offices,

who were in charge of ceremonial regalia and guard matters.
Furthermore, according to Tang regulations,

However, princesses rode in subdued pheasant carriages,

13 On the Guǐwèi day,
Niú Shījiǎng fought against Tuqishi Suōgě at Huǒshāo City,

Suōgě then captured Ānxī,
the Ānxī Protectorate,
which was at that time in Qiūcí.
He sent an envoy to present a memorial,

Chǔkè again memorialized to have Zhōu Yǐtì replace Guō Yuánzhèn in commanding the troops,
and to summon Yuánzhèn to court.
He also proposed making Āshǐnà Xiàn the Qaghan of the Ten Tribes,

Suōgě sent a letter to Yuánzhèn,

"I initially had no enmity with the Tang,
but only hatred for Quēchuò.
Minister Zōng accepted gold from Quēchuò,
intending to unjustly destroy my tribe.
Vice Censor-in-Chief Féng and Protector-General Niú came one after another.
Minister Zōng refers to Chǔkè,
Vice Censor-in-Chief Féng refers to Jiābīn,
Protector-General Niú refers to Shījiǎng,

Shǐ Xiàn is Āshǐnà Xiàn,

Yuánzhèn presented Suōgě's letter.
Chǔkè was enraged,

He was summoned,
and was about to be punished.
Yuánzhèn had his son Hóng secretly submit a memorial detailing the situation,
begging to remain and pacify the western territories,
and not daring to return.
Zhōu Yǐtì was eventually sentenced to exile to Báizhōu,
and Yuánzhèn was reinstated to replace Yǐtì.
Suōgě's crimes were pardoned,
and he was enfeoffed as the Qaghan of the Fourteen Tribes.
The Western Turks originally had ten tribes;
now, Yànmài, Géluólù, Mòhè Dágàn, and Dūmózhī were added to make fourteen tribes.
14 The Lady of Handsome Fairness Shàngguān was made a Lady of Bright Countenance.
15 In the twelfth month,
Vice Censor-in-Chief Yáo Tíngjūn memorialized, stating:
"Recently, I have observed that various offices do not follow the statutes, ordinances, regulations, and precedents.
Matters, whether great or small, are all reported.
I have heard that the ruler appoints ministers,
and ministers uphold the law.
With myriad affairs piling up,
it is impossible to review them all.
How can repairing a water channel
or cutting down a withered tree
all require the emperor's personal decision!
From now on, if it is a major military or state matter or something not covered by the regulations,
allow them to memorialize for a decision.
For all other matters, let them be handled according to the law.
If there are those who deliberately create doubts and delays,

16 On the last day of the month, Dīngsì,
an edict was issued for the Secretariat, the Chancellery, the academicians, the princes, and the imperial sons-in-law to enter the inner palace to keep watch on New Year's Eve.
Torches were set up in the courtyard,
