and music was played.
The inner palace
refers to the inner halls.
The banquet to keep watch on New Year's Eve
did not exist in ancient times.
Liáng poet Yǔ Jiānyú's poem on New Year's Eve says:
"Let us pour cypress leaf wine,
and try to offer the plate of five pungents."
It seems this already existed south of the Yangtze,
but it had not yet reached the point where ruler and ministers reveled together.
Emperor Suí Yáng's extravagance and licentiousness
meant that every New Year's Eve,
dozens of fire mountains were set up in the courtyards in front of the halls,
all made of agarwood roots.
For each mountain, several cartloads of agarwood were burned.
When the flames dimmed, they were doused with jiǎjiān oil,
causing flames to rise several zhang high,
and the fragrance could be smelled for dozens of lǐ.
In one night,
over two hundred cartloads of agarwood were used,
and over two hundred shí of jiǎjiān oil.
Ōuyáng Xiū's poem says:
"The Suí palace kept watch with agarwood fires,"
referring to this.
The emperor's doing this
is merely following in the footsteps of the fallen Suí.
The emperor said to the Censor-in-Chief Dòu Cóngyī:
"I have heard that you have long been without a spouse,
and I am very concerned.
Tonight is New Year's Eve,
and I shall arrange a wedding for you."
Cóngyī merely assented and bowed in thanks.
Shortly after, palace attendants led the way with lanterns, screens, and gold-threaded silk fans from the western corridor.
The palace attendants
under the Tang held rank 4a,
and were in charge of serving within the palace, announcing matters, and entering and exiting the palace precincts.
In the Later Wèi, they were called the Chamberlain of the Long Autumn;
in the Northern Qí, they were called the Palace Attendant;
in the Later Zhōu, they were called the Senior Gentleman of the Inner Administration;
in the Suí, they were called the Palace Attendant;
the Tang followed this.
The highest status of eunuchs
reached this point.
If there were exceptional achievements and merits,
some were appointed as Grand Generals,
while still concurrently holding the position of Palace Attendant.
Shàng
is pronounced shǎng.
Flower hairpins:
according to Tang regulations, the ceremonial dress of titled women included pheasant robes.

For inner titled women, these were worn when receiving enfeoffment, participating in sericulture, attending court assemblies; for outer titled women, they were worn at weddings, when receiving enfeoffment, participating in sericulture, and at grand court assemblies.
The base color was blue,
embroidered with pheasants,
arranged in rows on the upper and lower garments,
with nine ranks in total.
First rank: nine ranks of pheasants,
nine clusters of flower hairpins;
second rank: eight ranks of pheasants,
eight clusters of flower hairpins;
from the third to the fifth rank, each was reduced by one.
Ceremonial dress
was worn by inner titled women for regular audiences, and by outer titled women for court audiences, farewells, and ceremonial gatherings.
The design was the same as the pheasant robe,
with the addition of a double pendant and a small ribbon,
and shoes instead of formal slippers.
Rén yī
is pronounced yì.
The emperor ordered Cóngyī to recite several "fan-removing" poems.
On the wedding night in the Tang,
there were "hastening the bride" poems and "fan-removing" poems.
Lǐ Shāngyǐn's "Fan-Removing Poem for Scholar Dǒng" says:
"Do not bring the painted fan out from behind the curtain,
obscuring the spring mountains and hindering the superior talent.
If you say the full moon is round,
here you must let the osmanthus bloom."
She removed the flowers, changed her clothes, and came out.
Upon looking carefully,
it turned out to be the empress's old wet nurse, Wáng shì,
originally a southern barbarian slave girl.
The emperor and the attending ministers laughed heartily.
An edict was issued enfeoffing her as the Lady of Jǔ,
and she was married to Cóngyī as his wife.
It was customary to call the husband of a wet nurse
"Āzhē."
Whenever Cóngyī had an audience or submitted a memorial,
he referred to himself as
"the Āzhē of Empress Yìshèng."
People of the time called him
"the Āzhē of the State,"
and Cóngyī was pleased and wore a self-satisfied expression.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the Dīngmǎo day,
an order was issued to expand the Shèngshàn Temple in the eastern capital.
According to records, there was already a Shèngshàn Temple in the western capital,
and there was also a Shèngshàn Temple in the eastern capital.
Both were built by the emperor
to seek posthumous blessings for Empress Wǔ.
2 Princesses Chángníng, Ānlè, and others often allowed their servants to seize commoners' sons and daughters to make them slaves.
Investigating Censor Yuán Cóngzhī arrested and imprisoned them,
and prosecuted them.
The princesses complained to the emperor,
and the emperor personally issued an order to release them.
Cóngzhī memorialized, stating:
"If Your Majesty allows slaves to seize good people,
how will you govern the empire!"
The emperor ultimately released them.
3 In the second month, on
Jǐchǒu (the 26th day),
the Emperor visited the Xuánwǔ Gate,
and with his close ministers, watched the palace ladies play tug-of-war.
They used a large hemp rope and a giant bamboo, dividing into teams to pull against each other,
which was called "tug-of-war",
to determine victory or defeat.
Textual Analysis says: The Táng Jì states:
"Watched the palace ladies hold a great feast."
We now follow the Veritable Records.
High ministers and nobles acted as merchants,
trading with them,
which led to angry disputes,
with vulgar and disrespectful language.
The Emperor and Empress attended to watch for amusement.
4 On Bǐngshēn (the 3rd day),
Investigating Censor Cuī Wǎn, facing the ceremonial guard, impeached Zōng Chǔkè and Jì Chǔnè for secretly communicating with the Róng and Dí tribes,
accepting their bribes,

This refers to accepting bribes from Quēchuò Zhōngjié,
leading to Suōgé's rebellion.
Textual Analysis says: The Jǐnglóng Wénguǎn Jì states:
"Investigating Censor Cuī Wǎn, in full official attire,
faced the ceremonial guard and impeached the Grand Academician, Minister of War, and Duke Yǐng of the State Zōng Chǔkè, as well as Palace Attendant-in-ordinary Jì Chǔnè.

and memorialized: 'Your servant, though mediocre and foolish,

The Emperor nodded,
and said to Wǎn: 'I know about Chǔkè's matter.
Leave for now,
and wait until after the ceremonial guard is dismissed.'
After the guard was dismissed,
Wǎn then continued his memorial;
an imperial order commanded him to be questioned at the Western Bureau.
The Secretariat-Chancellery memorialized that there was no evidence of wrongdoing;
an imperial directive was issued ordering him to return to his post.
Initially,
Suōgé and his father and Āshǐnà Zhōngjié were mortal enemies for generations,
Suōgé repeatedly begged the state to eliminate Zhōngjié,
and the Protector-General of Ānxī Guō Yuánzhèn submitted a memorial requesting to grant his petition.
Zōng Chǔkè stubbornly insisted,
saying 'Zhōngjié served the state with utmost loyalty,
defending the Jade Gate.
If we allow Suōgé to eliminate him,
I fear it would not accord with the principle of using authority to aid the weak.'
Because of this, the Emperor did not grant the request.
Not long after,
Suōgé killed Investigating Secretary Féng Jiābīn and Palace Censor Lǚ Shǒusù,
destroyed Zhōngjié,
and invaded and harassed the Four Garrisons.
At that time, the Vice-Commander of the Suìyè Garrison Defense Commissioner, Zhōu Yǐtí, led several hundred garrison troops and routed him heavily,
recapturing the tens of thousands of people from Zhōngjié and the Yútián tribe that he had seized.
When the report arrived,
the Emperor was greatly pleased,
appointed Yǐtí as General of the Left Guard of the Barracks,
and also transferred Yuánzhèn's position as Commissioner of the Four Garrisons to him;
an imperial edict reprimanded Yuánzhèn in writing.
Zōng proposed dispatching elite troops,
ordering Yǐtí and Guō Qiánguàn to campaign north,
and also inviting Tǔbō and various tribes of the Western Regions to join forces in attacking Suōgé;
Right Censor-in-chief Xiè Wǎn argued that this was not permissible.
In the end, they made peace with him.
Suōgé, hearing of the earlier proposal,
was greatly resentful,
and then submitted a statement to Yuánzhèn,
claiming that Zōng had previously taken gold from Zhōngjié.
The Emperor questioned him about it,
and Zōng fully reported the previous events.
At that time, the two princesses Tàipíng and Ānlè, due to their imperial kinship, power, and favor,
each established factions,
secretly vying to overthrow each other,
so that from important officials down to chief ministers, all were divided into two groups.
At that time, Tàipíng especially was on bad terms with Zōng,
therefore she prompted Wǎn to impeach him;
the external rumor that he took Suōgé's gold
is incorrect."
We now follow the Veritable Records and the Jì.
When a high minister was impeached,
he would bow and hasten out,
lowering his head is called 'fǔ';
bending the back is called 'lǚ'.
Lǚ,
is pronounced lì zhǔ fān.
At this point,
Chǔkè became even more furious and changed countenance,
declaring his own loyalty and outspokenness,
and that he was falsely accused by Wǎn.
The Emperor ultimately did not pursue a thorough investigation,
but ordered Wǎn and Chǔkè to become sworn brothers to reconcile them.
People of the time called him
"the Peacemaking Son of Heaven".
5 On Rényín (the 9th day),
Wéi Jùyuán was appointed Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs,
Yáng Zàisī was appointed Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs,
both concurrently participated in the administration of state affairs as Tong Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn.
6 The Emperor frequently held banquets and gatherings with his close ministers and academicians,
ordering each to perform their skills for amusement.
Minister of Works Zhāng Xī danced the "Tán Róngniáng",
Director of the Palace Buildings Zōng Jìnqīng danced the "Húntuō",
(Note: Zhǎngsūn Wújì used black sheep wool to make Húntuō felt hats,
many people imitated him,
calling them the "Duke Zhào Húntuō",
and subsequently developed it into a dance.)
In the early Rúyì era,
a folk song said:
"Yellow roe deer, yellow roe deer, hiding in the grass,
I bend my bow and shoot you wounded."
This was also developed into a dance.
This is what is now called the "Heavenly India Divine Incantation".
The Director of Studies of the National University, Hé Dōng Guō Shānyùn, alone said:
"Your servant has no particular skill,
I request to sing ancient poems."
The Emperor permitted it.
Shānyùn then sang "The Deer Cry" and "The Cricket".
"The Deer Cry",
is for feasting ministers and honored guests;
"The Cricket",
takes the meaning of enjoying pleasure without excess.
However, Shānyùn merely wished to display his own learning,
and attach himself to Confucian scholarship,
not that he was capable of guiding the ruler towards goodness.
The Emperor bestowed an edict upon Shānyùn,
praising his intention,
and granted him a set of seasonal clothing.
The Emperor also once feasted with his attending ministers,
having each compose "Huíbō" lyrics.
At that time, during an inner palace banquet when the wine was flowing freely,
the attending ministers all rose to perform the Huíbō dance,
therefore he ordered them to compose Huíbō lyrics.
Some used it to seek glory and emolument for themselves.
Remonstrance Official Lǐ Jǐngbó said:
"Huíbō at this time with the wine cup.
This humble official's duty lies in admonition and correction.
Attending the feast, already past three cups,
(The Zuǒzhuàn says: A minister attending his ruler
at a feast should not exceed three cups;
exceeding three cups
is contrary to ritual.)"
The Emperor was displeased.
Xiāo Zhìzhōng said:
"This is a true Remonstrance Official."
7 In the third month, on
Wùwǔ (the 25th day),
Zōng Chǔkè was appointed Secretariat Director,
Xiāo Zhìzhōng was appointed Palace Attendant-in-ordinary,
and the Chief Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury, Wéi Sìlì, was appointed Vice Director of the Secretariat and Tong Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn.
Textual Analysis says: The New Tables state:
"Sìlì served as Minister of War."
We now follow the Veritable Records.
Cuī Shí had an affair with Shàngguān Zhāoróng,
therefore Zhāoróng recommended him to become chancellor.
(Note: Yànzhāo
was from Zhāngyè.)
Zhāngyè,
was originally the land of the Húnxié King of the Xiōngnú.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn established Zhāngyè Commandery and Lùdé County.
Yìng Shào said: To extend the state's arm and provide support,
therefore it was called Zhāngyè (Extending the Arm).
Lùdé,
was the commandery seat,
and was a Xiōngnú royal title.
Jìn changed Lùdé to Yǒngpíng.
Later Wèi established the Zhāngyè Army.
In the 17th year of the Suí Kāihuáng era,
Yǒngpíng was changed to Jiǔquán,
and in the early Dàyè era it was changed to Zhāngyè County.
Since the Western Wèi, its location

On Dīngyǒu,

The Erudites of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, Táng Shào and Jiǎng Qīnxù, refuted this,
believing:
"Zhèng Xuán's commentary on the 'Inner Offices of Service' section of the Rites of Zhōu

The Rites of Zhōu states in the 'Inner Steward' section: For great sacrifices,
when the empress performs the libation offering, he assists;
it is the same for the jade cup.
The commentary states: This refers to sacrifices in the ancestral temple.
After the king performs the libation and goes out to receive the sacrificial animal,
the empress then follows from behind to perform the libation.
'Offering'
refers to presenting the raw and cooked meats;
the empress also follows from behind to make the offering.
The 'jade cup'
refers to when the impersonator of the deceased finishes eating,
after the king offers wine to the impersonator,
the empress makes the second offering,
and the cup is adorned with jade.
Also, the 'Inner Offices of Service' section: They are in charge of the six ceremonial robes of the queen: the huīyī, yúdí, quēdí, júyī, zhǎnyī, and tuànyī, all with plain silk lining.
The commentary states: The huīyī, yúdí, and quēdí
are all sacrificial robes.
When accompanying the king to sacrifice to former kings, she wears the huīyī;
when sacrificing to former lords, she wears the yúdí;
when sacrificing to minor spirits, she wears the quēdí.
Nowadays, there is the guīyī,
which is probably a surviving custom from these three dì robes.
According to the Rites of Zhōu,
the 'great sacrifices' mentioned by the Inner Steward
specifically refer to sacrifices in the ancestral temple.
Zhù Qīnmíng and others, based on the Táng system which considered sacrifices to Heaven and Earth and the ancestral temple both as great sacrifices,
thus used the 'great sacrifices' of the Rites of Zhōu to force an interpretation to flatter Empress Wéi.
Furthermore, the libation, the offering, and the jade cup mentioned in Zhèng Xuán's interpretation of the Rites of Zhōu
were three sequential rituals during the sacrifice;
now Qīnmíng says the empress performs the libation offering using the jade cup,
which also contradicts Zhèng's interpretation,
being his own theory.

Emperor Ruìzōng, the Mystically True, Great Sage, Great Prosperity, and Filial Emperor
His personal name was Dàn,

First year of Jǐngyún
(Gēngxū, 710)
In this year, the era name was changed to Tánglóng in June,
and in July it was changed to Jǐngyún.
1 In spring,
first month,

Chéng Dàchāng said: The Pear Garden is north of Guānghuà Gate.
Guānghuà Gate
is the first gate on the western end of the southern side of the imperial park,

Both Pénglái Palace and Yíchūn Court
are not within the Pear Garden.
Wéi Jùyuán and Táng Xiūjǐng, being old and frail,

fourth month,

Entering the imperial park through Fānglín Gate,
the area was referred to as Fānglín Garden.
Cherries,
according to the Ěryǎ, are called xiē jīng táo.
The trees are shady,
and the fruit ripens before other fruits,
as large as a thumb,
round and red in color,
with a sweet taste.
Each cluster typically has ten to twenty fruits,
with pits as large as beans.
Because orioles eat them,
they are also called “hán táo” (orioles’ fruit).
5 Earlier, during Empress Wǔ Zétiān’s reign,
a well at the home of a commoner named Wáng Chún in the eastern corner of Cháng’ān overflowed,
forming a large pond of several tens of qǐng,
named Lóngqìng Pond.
The pond was south of Lóngqìng Ward.
Chéng Dàchāng said: The rise of emperors
often involves signs and auspicious omens,
which may have some basis in principle,
but many are fabricated.
According to the Liù Diǎn,
there was a well in Lóngqìng Ward
that suddenly surged into a small pond,
with a circumference of over ten zhàng,
often shrouded in mist,
and occasionally a yellow dragon appeared within.
By the Jǐngyún era,
it secretly overflowed again,
the pond gradually expanded,
and the residents all moved away,
eventually forming a vast dragon pond.
However, upon careful examination,
the Cháng’ān Zhì states: Lóng Pond is south of Yuèlóng Gate,
originally flat land.
After the early years of Chuígōng,
rainwater accumulated into a small stream;
later, water from the Lóngshǒu Canal was diverted to irrigate it,
and it gradually expanded.
By the Jǐnglóng era,
it spanned several qǐng,
with a depth of several zhàng,
and there were often tales of clouds and dragons,
leading to its name, Dragon Pond.
The record also states: southeast of the Suí outer city was the Lóngshǒu Dam,
from which Chǎn River water was divided and flowed north to Chánglè Slope,
splitting into two channels.
The western channel flowed southwest from Yǒngjiā Ward past Xīngqìng Palace.
Thus, the reason Xīngqìng could transform flat land into a dragon pond
was actually due to the diversion of Chǎn River water.
However, the Liù Diǎn account
completely omits the fact of the Chǎn River diversion,
instead claiming the well first overflowed,
then a spring emerged,
and the two waters combined to form the pond,
attributing it solely to supernatural transformation.
Shòuchūn Prince Chéngqì,
Línzī Prince Lóngjī,
Héngyáng Prince Chéngyì,
Bālíng Prince Lóngfàn,
Péngchéng Prince Lóngyè.

“There has long been an aura of imperial majesty,

the emperor visited Lóngqìng Pond.
Examination of discrepancies: The Jǐnglóng Wénguǎn Jì records it as the twelfth day of the month.
According to the perpetual calendar,

Here, we follow the Veritable Records and Basic Annals.
He feasted with his attendants,

gate restrictions and keys,

Yàn,
pronounced yīn jiān.
Fù,
pronounced fú yòu.
Shàng,

Zhù Qīnmíng, the Director of the National University, volunteered to perform the "Eight Winds Dance."

The "Eight Winds Dance" referred to by Zhù Qīnmíng
was not the dance mentioned by Zhòng Zhòng, a senior official of the State of Lǔ during the Spring and Autumn period, which was said to regulate the eight musical tones and circulate the eight winds.
Rather, it merely borrowed the name "Eight Winds" to exhibit all manner of lewd and ugly postures.
Nowadays, people refer to unrestrained and unbridled behavior as "fēng" (wind),
and this is what Qīnmíng meant by the "Eight Winds."
Qīnmíng had always been renowned for his Confucian scholarship.

the Park Director, Zhōng Shàojīng from Gàn County,

Gàn County,

Yōng Prefecture under the Táng had 131 garrisons,

Wéi Bō and Gāo Sōng frequently flogged and beat the Ten Thousand Cavalry,

History records that Lóngjī had great strategic vision,

bài,

On the Gēngzǐ day,
during the late afternoon,
Lǐ Lóngjī, dressed in plain clothes, entered the imperial park with Liú Yōuqiú and others.
The Táng imperial park was located north of the imperial city.
The park walls stretched twenty-seven lǐ from east to west,
and thirty lǐ from north to south.
To the east, it reached the Bà River,
to the west, it connected to the old Cháng'ān city,
to the south, it bordered the capital city,
and to the north, it rested against the Wèi River.
Within the park, there were twenty-four detached palaces, pavilions, and viewing towers.
The old Hàn dynasty Cháng'ān city walls spanned thirteen lǐ from east to west,
and all were incorporated into the park.
Zhōng Shàojīng regretted his involvement and

Shàojīng then hurried out to bow and receive them.
Lóngjī took his hand and sat with him.
Zhōng Shàojīng hurrying out to bow and receive them
showed his respect and allegiance to Lóngjī;

When night fell,

Stars scattered across the sky like snow.

Fúshùn drew his sword and charged straight into the Yǔlín barracks,

"Whoever dares to harbor divided loyalties and aid the rebel faction,

"The Wǔ clan

At that time, the young emperor was in the Tàijí Hall.
Liú Yōuqiú said:

Why not settle it early?"
Lóngjī hastily stopped him.
They searched for and arrested all members of the Wéi clan within the palace and those guarding the various gates,
along with all those who had been trusted confidants of Empress Wéi, and beheaded them all.
By dawn,
order was restored both inside and outside the palace.
On the Xīnsì day,
Lóngjī went out to see the Prince of Xiàng,

The Prince of Xiàng embraced him and wept, saying:
"That the altars of state and the ancestral temples did not fall to the ground
is due to your strength."
They then welcomed the Prince of Xiàng in to assist the young emperor.
They closed the palace gates and the capital city gates,
and dispatched the Ten-Thousand Cavalry in different directions to arrest the relatives and associates of the Wéis.
They beheaded Wéi Wēn, the Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent and Concurrently Vice Director of the Secretariat-Chancellery with the Third Rank, north of the Eastern Market.
Zhōngshū Lìng Zōng Chǔkè, wearing mourning clothes of coarse hemp, escaped riding a black donkey.
When he reached the Tōnghuà Gate,
the gatekeeper said:
"You, sir,

The Textual Analysis notes: The Tàishàng Shílù states:

We now follow the Qiánzǎi.

therefore, we do not adopt this.

They comforted and instructed the common people.
The Táng Liùdiǎn states: The western wall of the imperial city has two gates:
the northern one is called Ānfú,
the southern one is called Shùnyì.
The Ānfú Gate faces directly west to the Kāiyuǎn Gate.
Zhào Lǚwēn had exhausted the state's resources to serve Princess Ānlè,
building mansions for her,
constructing towers and digging ponds without end.
He tucked in his purple robe,
and used his neck to pull the princess's ox-cart.
When the princess died,
Lǚwēn rushed to beneath the Ānfú Tower, performed a dance, and shouted "Long live the Emperor!";
before his voice had faded,
the Prince of Xiàng ordered the Ten-Thousand Cavalry to behead him.
The common people, resentful of the forced labor he had imposed,
vied to cut flesh from his body until it was completely gone.
The Director of the Palace Library, Prince of Biàn Lǐ Yōng, had married Empress Wéi's younger sister, the Lady of the State of Chóng.
"Chóng"
is the name of an ancient state.
Yōng
was the grandson of Lǐ Fèng.
Fèng
was a son of Emperor Gāozǔ.
His family urged him to flee and hide,
but Jùyuán said:

How can I hear of trouble and not go to face it?"
He went out to the main street of the capital,

Then they displayed the heads of Mǎ Qínkè, Yáng Jūn, and Yè Jìngnéng on poles,
and exposed Empress Wéi's corpse in the market.
Cuī Rìyòng led troops to exterminate the various Wéis at Dùqū.
South of the Táng capital city,
the Wéi and Dù clans resided,
hence the areas were called Wéiqū and Dùqū.
A saying goes:
"South of the city, Wéi and Dù,
a mere foot and a half from Heaven."

encroaching upon and residing in Dùqū.

is pronounced "jiàng",

On this day,
a general amnesty was declared throughout the land,
stating:

Línzī Wáng Lǐ Lóngjī was appointed as Píng Wáng,
concurrently overseeing the inner and outer stables.
While Píng Wáng was nominally titled after the state of Píngzhōu,

According to the Six Codes: the Director of the Imperial Stables

The Wǔ clan relatives
were almost entirely executed, exiled, or banished.

because Wǔ Yōuxù and Wǔ Píngyī were able to avoid power and stay away from influence,
while Wǔ Huìfēi was still capable of causing the calamity that led to the deaths of three sons.
The Minister of Personnel and concurrent Chief Minister Zhāng Jiāfú was captured and executed while traveling to Huáizhōu.

Huázhōu

Huáizhōu

Liú Yōuqiú was in the Tàijí Hall,

The nine courts of the Táng dynasty all had clerks,

which was considered outside the regular official hierarchy.
Shào
is pronounced as "shào."
He acted arbitrarily in rewards and punishments,

Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices Xuē Jǐ urged him to submit a memorial politely declining the appointment,

The Book of Songs says: "Illustrious is the Grand-Master Yin,

9 The Emperor intended to establish a crown prince.
Since Sòngwáng Lǐ Chéngqì was the eldest son by the principal wife,
while Píngwáng Lǐ Lóngjī had rendered great service,
he hesitated and could not decide.
Chéngqì declined, saying:
"When the state is at peace, precedence is given to the eldest son by the principal wife;
when the state is in peril, precedence is given to the one with merit.
If this principle is violated,
the entire realm will be disappointed.
I would rather die than presume to be above Píngwáng."
He tearfully and persistently pleaded for days.
Many high officials also said that Píngwáng, having great merit, should be established.
Liú Yōuqiú said:
"Your subject has heard that he who removes calamity from the realm
should enjoy the blessings of the realm.
Píngwáng saved the altars of state from peril,
rescued his sovereign and father from distress.
In terms of merit, none is greater;
in terms of virtue, none is more worthy.
There should be no doubt."
The Emperor followed this advice.
On Dīngwèi day,
Píngwáng Lǐ Lóngjī was established as Crown Prince.
Textual analysis notes: Liú Zǐxuán first compiled the Veritable Records of the Tàishàng Huáng,

We now follow the Tàishàng Huáng Records.
Not permitted.

Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ was deep, astute, and full of strategic acumen.

Empress Wéi and Ānlè Gōngzhǔ both feared her,

Having repeatedly achieved great merit,

The Emperor often consulted with her on major policies.

Sānláng,

From the chief ministers down,

The number of scholars she recommended who rapidly rose to high and prestigious positions was beyond count.
Her power overshadowed that of the sovereign.
Those rushing to attach themselves to her gate were like a marketplace crowd.
Her sons Xuē Chóngxíng, Chóngmǐn, and Chóngjiǎn were all enfeoffed as princes.
Her fields and gardens spread throughout the near suburbs.

1 In the eighth month,
on Gēngyín,

The county officials galloped out,

the conspirators all fled and hid,

The Attendant Censor of the Vicegerent's Office, Lǐ Yōng, encountered Zhòng Fú at the Tiānjīn Bridge,

Zhòng Fú first rushed towards the Left and Right Garrison Camps,
the camps shot at him,

(Cuī Rìzhī was the paternal cousin of Cuī Rìyòng.) He was appointed Vicegerent of the Eastern Capital for his merit.
Zheng Yin was ugly in appearance and had a thick beard.

put on women's clothing,

he was captured,
subjected to interrogation,

Zhāng Língjūn's spirit and expression were composed as usual,

Earlier,
Zheng Yin had attached himself to Lái Jùnchén and thereby advanced;
after Jùnchén was executed,
he attached himself to Zhāng Yìzhī;
after Yìzhī was executed,

The history states: Although Zhāng Língjūn was a man who delighted in calamity and loved disorder,

As for Zheng Yin,
he shifted back and forth among treacherous factions,
coveting profit without regard for consequence,
yet his fear of death was such as this—
how could he be sufficient to manage great affairs!
Yán Shànsī was exiled to Jìngzhōu.

10 Princess Tàipíng, because the Crown Prince was young,

19. The eunuch Yán Xìngguì attempted to use his influence to pressure Cháng'ān County Magistrate Lǐ Cháoyǐn regarding a matter.

Yōngnú County,
since the Hàn dynasty, had belonged to Yúyáng Commandery.

and in the Táng, to Yōu Prefecture.
Lúlóng was the Hàn dynasty's Féirú County,
belonging to Liáoxī Commandery.

its name was changed to Lúlóng,
and it was placed under Běipíng Commandery.

Xí,
pronounced as 'xí'.
They were not defeated.
21. According to the old system,
officials of the third rank and above were appointed by cèshū (imperial patent),
those of the fifth rank and above by zhìshū (imperial decree),
and those of the sixth rank and below by chìshū (imperial order).

The Táng system of imperial pronouncements had seven types: first, cèshū (patent); second, zhìshū (decree); third, wèiláo zhìshū (decree of commendation); fourth, fāchì (issuance of an order); fifth, chìzhǐ (imperial rescript); sixth, lùnshì chìshū (order discussing affairs); seventh, chìdié (order document).
Civil appointments were under the Ministry of Personnel,
military appointments under the Ministry of War.
The Minister was called the Central Evaluator,
the Vice Ministers the Eastern and Western Evaluators.
These were the so-called Three Evaluations.
When favorites held power,
the selection process became confused,
and all order was lost.
At this time,
Sòng Jǐng was appointed as Minister of Personnel,
with Lǐ Yì and Lú Cóngyuàn as Vice Ministers.
None of them feared the powerful,
and the path of personal solicitation was cut off.
Over ten thousand candidates gathered,
but after the three evaluations, fewer than two thousand remained.
People admired their fairness.
Yáo Yuánzhī was appointed as Minister of War,
with Lù Xiàngxiān and Lú Huáishèn as Vice Ministers.
The military selection process was also well-ordered.
Cóngyuàn was
a clansman of Lú Chéngqìng.
Lú Chéngqìng appears in the 200th scroll, in the fourth year of Emperor Gāozōng's Xiǎnqìng era.
He was the son of Yuánfāng.
Lù Yuánfāng appears in the 205th scroll, in the first year of Empress Zétiān's Zhèngshèng era.
22. The Attendant Censor Nièchéng County's Ní Ruòshuǐ,
Nièchéng County belonged to the Zhēndìng Principality in the Former Hàn,
and from the Later Hàn onward to Jùlù Commandery.
In the Táng, it belonged to Héng Prefecture.
He curried favor by criticizing the sovereign;
this refers to his suggestion during the suburban sacrifices that Empress Wéi should perform the secondary offering.
Shān Yùn was appointed Prefect of Kuò Prefecture.
According to old records: Ráo Prefecture was
3,263 lǐ southeast of the capital.
Kuò Prefecture was later renamed Chù Prefecture,
4,278 lǐ southeast of the capital.
23. Attendant Censor Yáng Fú
impeached and investigated without avoiding the powerful and noble.
The powerful and noble slandered him.
The Emperor said:
"When a hawk seizes a cunning hare,
one must quickly aid it,
otherwise it will surely be bitten in return.
A censor restraining the wicked is the same.
If the ruler does not protect him,
then he too will be bitten by the wicked."
Fú was
the grandnephew of Suí Emperor Wéndì.
24. The positions of Héxī Military Commissioner, Fiscal Commissioner, and Camp Fields Commissioner, among others, were established.
They oversaw Liáng, Gān, Sù, Yī, Guā, Shā, and Xī, seven prefectures in total,
with headquarters in Liáng Prefecture.
According to Táng regulations,
all frontier armies had Fiscal Commissioners
to manage military supplies, provisions, and equipment.
If the Military Commissioner did not concurrently hold the Fiscal Commissioner post,
then the Fiscal Commissioner operated as a separate office.
If he did hold it concurrently,
then the Military Commissioner handled fiscal matters himself.
Whenever frontier defense, garrisoning, or transport proved insufficient,
military agricultural colonies were established to increase army reserves,
hence the Camp Fields Commissioner.
Shǐ,
pronounced 'shǐ'.
Dù,
pronounced 'duó'.
25. The Zhì barbarians of Yáo Prefecture
had previously submitted to Tibet.
Acting Investigating Censor Lǐ Zhīgǔ requested troops to attack them.
After they surrendered,
he further requested to build a city,
establish prefectures and counties,
and heavily tax them.
The Vice Minister of the Imperial Secretariat Xú Jiān considered this inadvisable.
Sentence break.
Zhīgǔ mobilized Jiànnán troops to build the city
and then intended to execute their chieftains,
seizing their women and children as slaves.
The Zhì barbarians became enraged.
The barbarian chieftain Pángmíng led Tibetan troops to attack Zhīgǔ,
killed him,

Yān,
pronounced yīnjiān.
Jìn,

the Xī chieftain Kědùzhě submitted,

Chieftain,

Pú,

At this time,
Quán, commanding General of the Left Xiaowei Guard Lǐ Kǎiluò
and General of the Left Weiwei Guard Zhōu Yǐtì, mobilized 20,000 troops and 8,000 cavalry,
dividing them into three armies,
to launch a surprise attack on the Xī and Qìdān.
General Wū Kělì remonstrated, saying:
"The roads are treacherous and the weather is hot;
sending an isolated army on a distant raid,
you are certain to be defeated."
Quán said:
"Xuē Nè has been on the border for years,
yet he has ultimately failed to recover Yíng Prefecture for the state.
(The fall of Yíng Prefecture is recorded in Volume 205, in the first year of the Wànsuì Tōngtiān era of Empress Wǔ.)
(Wéi,
pronounced yúwèi.)
If we go, we are certain to achieve merit."
He sent Kǎiluò to lead 4,000 cavalry as the vanguard.
They encountered 8,000 Xī cavalry,
and Kǎiluò's battle went unfavorably.
Quán was timid and cowardly,
not daring to go to the rescue.
He led his troops, intending to withdraw.
The enemy pressed the attack,
and the Táng forces suffered a great defeat.
Quán took up a defensive position against a mountain, forming a square formation to fortify himself.
Dà Pú sent a message to Quán, saying:
"Since the court has already established peaceful relations with us,
why has this great army now come?"

Kǎiluò did not obey orders;
he rashly engaged you in battle.

Dà Pú said:
"If that is so,
where is the token of state trust?"
Quán gathered all the silk fabrics in the army,
obtaining over ten thousand bolts,
and together with purple robes, gold belts, and fish pouches, presented them as gifts.
(In the second year of the Yǒnghuī era of Emperor Gāozōng,
civil and military officials of the fifth rank and above serving in the capital

In the second year of the Chuígǒng era of Empress Tiānhòu,

The Táng Liùdiǎn states: The portable fish tally

The Crown Prince used jade,
imperial princes used gold,

The pouches for those of the third rank and above were adorned with gold,

"I request that you, General, return south,

The officers and soldiers were terrified,

The enemy pursued and attacked them,

Mòchuò executed them both.

17 Tàipíng Princess had a diviner speak to the Emperor, saying:

the position of the Son of Heaven.

(Huì,
pronounced xiángsuì,
also pronounced suì,
also pronounced suì.)
The Emperor said:
"To transmit virtue and avoid disaster—
my resolve is firm."
Tàipíng Princess and her faction all strenuously remonstrated,
considering it unacceptable.
The Emperor said:
"During the time of Emperor Zhōngzōng,
treacherous individuals held power,
and celestial anomalies occurred repeatedly.
I then urged Zhōngzōng to select a worthy son to establish as heir in response to the portents,
but Zhōngzōng was displeased,
and I was so worried and fearful that I could not eat for several days.
How can it be that I could urge it in his case,

The Crown Prince heard of this,
rushed in to see the Emperor,
threw himself to the ground,

I fear I am not capable of bearing the responsibility.
I do not understand why Your Majesty would suddenly transmit the great position to me.
Why is this?"
The Emperor said:
"The reason the altars of state were again secured,
the reason I obtained the empire,
was all due to your efforts.
Now there is a portent concerning the Imperial Seat,
therefore I transmit it to you,
to turn calamity into fortune.
Why do you doubt it!"
The Crown Prince firmly declined.
The Emperor said:
"If you wish to be a filial son,
why must you wait until before the coffin to then ascend the throne!"
The Crown Prince left in tears.
On Rénchén,
an edict was issued to transmit the throne to the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince submitted a memorial firmly declining.
Tàipíng Princess advised the Emperor that even after transmitting the throne,
he should still personally oversee the important affairs of government.
The Emperor then said to the Crown Prince:
"Do you consider the affairs of the empire so weighty
that you wish for me to continue managing them?
In antiquity, when Shùn abdicated to Yǔ,
he still personally undertook inspection tours.
(After Shùn abdicated to Yǔ,
he went on a southern inspection tour and died at Cāngwú;
this is cited as a precedent.)
How could he forget his family and state!
As for military and state affairs of great importance,
I should concurrently oversee them."
In the eighth month,
on Gēngzǐ,
Emperor Xuánzōng ascended the throne.
Emperor Ruìzōng was honored as Retired Emperor.
The Retired Emperor referred to himself as zhèn,

The Emperor referred to himself as yǔ,
and his commands were termed zhì and chì.
He held court daily at the Wǔdé Hall.
Appointments and dismissals of officials of the third rank and above, and decisions on major punishments and government affairs, were decided by the Retired Emperor.
All other matters were decided by the Emperor.

Héng,

23. Initially,
a man from Hénèi named Wáng Jū was involved in the plot of Wáng Tóngjiǎo.
This refers to the first year of the Shénlóng era of Emperor Zhōngzōng, when Wáng Tóngjiǎo plotted to assassinate Wǔ Sānsī.
He worked as a copyist in Jiāngdū.
When the Emperor was still the Crown Prince,

and was selected to fill the position of Zhūjì Assistant Magistrate.
Zhūjì
was the former capital of King Yúncháng of Yuè.
From the Hàn dynasty onward, it became a county,
belonging to Kuàijī.
When Wáng Jū arrived at the court,
he deliberately walked slowly and looked around haughtily.
A eunuch said:
"His Highness is behind the curtain."
Wáng Jū replied:
"What do you mean by 'His Highness'?
Nowadays, there is only Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ!"
Employing the old stratagem of Fàn Jū,
he said this to provoke the Crown Prince.
When they spoke,
Wáng Jū said:
"Wéi Shùrén committed regicide and rebellion,
but the people's hearts were not with her,
so executing her was easy.
Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ,
the daughter of Empress Wǔ,
is incomparably vicious and cunning.
Many high officials are at her service,
and I secretly worry about this."
The Crown Prince invited him to sit on the same couch,
and said tearfully:
"The Sovereign shares a bond of flesh and blood
only with Tàipíng.
Speaking of this might hurt the Sovereign's feelings,
but not speaking allows the danger to deepen daily.
What should be done about this?"
Wáng Jū said:
"The filial piety of a Son of Heaven
differs from that of a common man.
He should devote himself to securing the ancestral temple and the altars of soil and grain.
Princess Gài,
the elder sister of Emperor Zhāo of Hàn,
was raised by him from childhood,
yet when she committed a crime, she was still executed.
The matter is recorded in the Hàn Annals.
Gài,
is pronounced as in ancient times, Gě.
Gòng,
is pronounced jūyòng.
Yǎng,
is pronounced yángshàng.
How can one be concerned with minor proprieties!"
The Crown Prince was pleased and said:
"What talents do you possess,
that you might accompany me?"
Wáng Jū said:
"I can perform alchemy and jesting satire."
Fēiliàn (flying alchemy),
refers to flying cinnabar to refine elixirs.
The Old Táng History records Wáng Jū's words as:
"Flying cinnabar and refining sand,
jesting and satirical recitation,
I can stand shoulder to shoulder with entertainers."
The Táng Liù Diǎn states: The Sīzhí of the Household Administration of the Heir Apparent is in charge of impeaching officials,
and investigating and reporting on official duties.
He was promoted several times to become a Zhōngshèrén of the Heir Apparent;

originally were the Shèrén of the Heir Apparent in the Hàn and Wèi dynasties.
When Emperor Huì of Jìn was the Crown Prince,
he selected four Shèrén who were talented in literature and of fine character,
to handle documents together with the Zhōngshùzǐ.
In the third year of the Xiánníng era,
when Prince Yōu of Qí became Grand Tutor,
the name was then changed to Zhōngshèrén.
Together with the Zhōngshùzǐ, they were in charge of prohibitions and orders,
rectifying violations and deficiencies,
attending to the left and right,
acting as masters of ceremony and overseeing decorum,
offering full admonitions and accepting advice.
He was appointed as a Vice Director of the Secretariat.
Textual analysis says: Zhèng Qǐ's Kāitiān Chuánxìn Jì states:
"When the Emperor was still a prince,
he often amused himself in the southern suburbs between the Wéi and Dù families,
chasing after cunning hares,
so delighted he forgot to return.
Once, with a dozen or so of his companions,
extremely weary,
they rested under a large tree in the Fēngbù area.
It happened that a scholar invited the Emperor to his home.
He was very poor,
having only a village wife and a donkey.
The Emperor had not sat long
when the scholar slaughtered the donkey, pulled garlic, and prepared a feast,
with wine and meat in abundance.
The Emperor looked at him and found him remarkable.
When they conversed,
he was open and extraordinary.
Asked his name,
it was Wáng Jū.
From then on, whenever the Emperor traveled in the Wéi-Dù area,
he would always visit Wáng Jū's home.
Wáng Jū's counsel suited the Emperor's intentions,
and the Emperor grew increasingly close and favorable towards him.
When the Wéi clan monopolized power,
the Emperor was deeply worried,
and secretly confided only in Wáng Jū.
Wáng Jū said: 'If they rebel, then kill them,
what is there to doubt!'
The Emperor then adopted Wáng Jū's plan,
quelled the calamity,
and repeatedly promoted him to Vice Director of the Secretariat,
and he truly shared in the sacrifices at the imperial temple."
Now we follow the Old Biography.
At that time,
many of the chief ministers were partisans of Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ.
Liú Yōuqiú plotted with the Right Yǔlín General Zhāng Wěi to use Yǔlín troops to execute them.
He had Zhāng Wěi secretly say to the Emperor:
"Dòu Huáizhēn, Cuī Shí, and Cén Xī all advanced through the Princess's influence,
and day and night they plot without cease.
If we do not plan early,
once trouble arises,
how will the Tàishàng Huáng be able to rest in peace!
I request that they be swiftly executed.
Textual analysis says: The Old Biography states,
"Liú Yōuqiú considered his merit greater than that of any other court official,
and aspired to the posts of Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs and concurrently Director of the Secretariat.
Soon, Dòu Huáizhēn became Left Vice Director,
and Cuī Shí became Director of the Secretariat.
Yōuqiú was very discontent,
which showed in his words and expression,
and so he and Zhāng Wěi requested their execution."
However, Yōuqiú had always been utterly devoted to Xuánzōng;
Shí and others attached themselves to Tàipíng,
it was not that Yōuqiú harmed them out of personal resentment.
This version is not adopted here.
We only await Your Majesty's command."
The Emperor deeply agreed.
Zhāng Wěi leaked the plot to the Investigating Censor Dèng Guāngbīn.
The Emperor was greatly alarmed,
and hastily submitted a memorial detailing the situation.
On the bǐngchén day,
Liú Yōuqiú was imprisoned.
The officials in charge memorialized:
"Yōuqiú and others have sown discord among flesh and blood,
their crime deserves death."
The Emperor spoke on Yōuqiú's behalf, saying he had great merit,
and should not be killed.
On the guǐhài day,
Yōuqiú was exiled to Fēngzhōu.
Fēngzhōu,
was the location of the Fēngyáng county of Hàn's Guǎngxìn commandery.
Liáng established it as Chéngzhōu,
Suí changed it to Fēngzhōu,
Táng placed it under the Guǎngzhōu military governor's jurisdiction.
The Old Geography records: Fēngzhōu was 4,510 lǐ from the capital by land and water.
Guāngbīn was exiled to Xiùzhōu.
The Old Geography records: Fēngzhōu,
was the Jiāníng county of Suí's Jiāozhǐ commandery,
established in the fourth year of the Wǔdé era.
Fēngzhōu was 7,710 lǐ from the capital;
Xiùzhōu was 6,090 lǐ from the capital.
Initially,
when Cuī Shí was the governor of Xiāngzhōu,
he secretly corresponded with Prince Qiáo, Lǐ Chóngfú,
and Chóngfú sent him a gold belt.
After Chóngfú's defeat,
Shí deserved death,
but Zhāng Yuè and Liú Yōuqiú intervened and protected him, so he was spared.
Later, Shí attached himself to Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ,
and plotted with the Princess to remove Yuè from his post,
making him a Left Aide in the Eastern Capital administration.
When Yōuqiú was exiled to Fēngzhōu,
Shí hinted to the military governor of Guǎngzhōu, Zhōu Lìzhēn,
to have him killed.
Fēngzhōu
was under the jurisdiction of the Guǎngzhōu military governor.
Jié became aware of the plot,
and detained Yōuqiú, not sending him on.
Lìzhēn repeatedly sent official documents demanding him,
but Jié did not comply,
so Lìzhēn reported it.
Shí repeatedly pressured Jié,
to make him send Yōuqiú.
Yōuqiú said to Jié:
"Sir, by defying the chief minister to protect an exile,
you cannot possibly preserve yourself,
and will only bring trouble upon yourself."
He firmly requested to proceed to Guǎngzhōu.
Jié said:
"The offense for which you, Sir, are punished is not one that severs friendship.
If I, Jié, incur punishment because of you, Sir,
I will have no regrets."
In the end, he delayed and did not send him.
Thus, Yōuqiú escaped harm.
24. In the ninth month,
on the dīngmǎo day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the 25th day, Xīnmǎo,
the Emperor established his son Lǐ Sìshēng as Prince of Shǎn.
Sìshēng's mother was a woman of the Yáng clan,
the great-granddaughter of Yáng Shìdá.
Yáng Shìdá served under the Suí,

26. In winter,
the tenth month,
on Gēngzǐ,

27. On Guǐmǎo,

from Hé and Lǒng in the west,

31. In the twelfth month,
Lǐ Rìzhī, Minister of Justice, requested to retire.
While in office,
Rìzhī never resorted to flogging, yet affairs were accomplished.
In the Ministry of Justice, there was a clerk
who, three days after receiving an imperial order,
forgot to carry it out.
Rìzhī was angry,
called for a cane,
assembled the subordinate officials and was about to beat him,
but then said:
"If I beat you,
people in the world will certainly say you provoked Lǐ Rìzhī's anger,
received Lǐ Rìzhī's cane,
and cannot be considered a proper man.
Your wife and children will also abandon you."
He then released him.
The clerks were all moved and pleased,
and none dared to offend again.
If there was any delay or error,
the group would collectively reprimand the offender.
First Year of the Kāiyuán Era
(Guǐchǒu, 713)
The era name was changed only in the twelfth month of this year.
1. In spring,
the first month,
on Yǐhài,
an edict stated:
"Imperial Guardsmen shall henceforth enter service at twenty-five,
and be discharged at fifty.
Yǔlín Flying Cavalry shall also be selected and supplemented from the Imperial Guardsmen."
2. Xiāo Zhìzhōng, Minister of Personnel, was appointed Zhōngshū Lìng.
3. The Emperor's frontier inspection tour was rescheduled;
the recruited soldiers were each dispersed and sent back,
with an agreement to reassemble in the eighth month,
but ultimately the tour did not take place.
4. In the second month,
on the night of Gēngzǐ,
the palace gates were opened and lanterns were lit.
According to the biography of Yán Tǐngzhī in the Old Book: On the full moon of the first month of the second year of the Xiāntiān era,
the foreign monk Pótuó requested to open the gates at night and light thousands of lanterns.
In the first year,
having received the abdication,
there was no time to grant a nationwide feast,
so it was done retroactively.
Feast (pú),
pronounced pú.
The Retired Emperor and the Emperor ascended the gate tower to watch,
sometimes continuing from night into day,
for over a month in total.
The Emperor's propensity for extravagance was already revealed here.
Performers (jì),
pronounced qǐ.
He considered:
"Feasts are for benefiting the people,
gathering contributions for joy.
Now, expending the labor of ten thousand people,
to fund a hundred entertainments,
is not the way to glorify the imperial virtue and beautify customs."
He then stopped it.
5. Initially,
after Gāolì was destroyed,
(The destruction of Gāolì is recorded in the first year of the Zǒngzhāng era of Emperor Gāozōng, in scroll 201.)
and after Lǐ Jìnzhōng rebelled,
(Lǐ Jìnzhōng's rebellion is recorded in the first year of the Wànsuì Tōngtiān era of Empress Wǔ, in scroll 205.)
According to the Fēngsú Tōng: The surname Dà,
descended from Dàtíngshì;
Dàkuǎn was the teacher of Emperor Zhuān.
According to the Lǐjì: Dàlián was good at observing mourning,
he was a son of the Eastern Barbarians.
Thus, the surname Dà among the Eastern Barbarians has existed since ancient times.
Tribe (zhǒng),
pronounced zhǎng.
They relied on dangerous terrain to fortify themselves.
After Jìnzhōng died,
Empress Wǔ sent General Lǐ Kǎigù to attack the remaining partisans.
Kǎigù attacked Qǐsìběiyǔ,
beheaded him,
led his troops across Tiānmén Ridge,
and pressured Dà Zuòróng.
The New Book: Tiānmén Ridge is three hundred lǐ north of the Tǔhùzhēn River.
Kǎigù was badly defeated,
barely escaping with his life.
Zuòróng then led his followers east to occupy Dōngmóu Mountain,
built a city, and settled there.
Dōngmóu Mountain is within the territory of the Yìlóu state,
situated two thousand lǐ east of Yíngzhōu,
bordering Xīnlúo to the south (and north?) with the Ní River as the boundary,
reaching the sea to the east,
and Qìdān to the west.
Lead (shuài),
pronounced shuài.
People of Gāolì and Mòhé gradually joined him,
his territory extended two thousand lǐ,
with over a hundred thousand households,
and several tens of thousands of effective troops.
He proclaimed himself King of Zhènguó,
and submitted to the Türks.
At that time, both the Xī and Qìdān had rebelled,
the roads were blocked,
and Empress Wǔ could not launch a campaign.
When Emperor Zhōngzōng ascended the throne,
he sent the Investigating Censor Zhāng Xíngjí to summon and pacify him,
and Zuòróng sent his son to serve at court.
At this time,
Zuòróng was appointed Grand General of the Left Flank Guards and Prince of Bóhǎi Commandery;
his territory was made the Hūhàn Prefecture,
and Zuòróng was made its concurrent Governor.
The Mòhé grew powerful from this time;
they began to drop the name Mòhé,

It is truly because the loyal and upright often oppose the ruler's wishes,
while the flattering and wicked often comply with his inclinations.
Accumulated opposition breeds hatred,
accumulated compliance breeds affection.

The emperor had always been affectionate and fraternal,

Upon first ascending the throne,

The various princes would pay their respects each morning at a side gate,

When the emperor finished holding court,

Within the palace,

He set up five tents within the palace hall,

Sometimes they would discuss literature and compose poems,

Chéngqì was skilled at the flute,

Once, when Yè was ill,

The emperor said:
"If only the Prince drinks this medicine and recovers,
what does a beard matter?"
Chéngqì was especially respectful and cautious,

In the 42nd year of the sexagenary cycle,
Xuē Nà engaged the Tibetans in battle at Wǔjiē.
The Commentary on the Waterways Classic states: Wǔjiē City is located east of the Han Dynasty's Dídào County, northwest of Báishí Mountain.
During the Tang, it was the Wǔjiē postal station,
and both it and Dàlái Valley fell within the boundaries of Líntáo Wèiyuán County.
Liú Xù said: The Wǔjiē postal station was on the western border of Wèi Prefecture.
At that time, the Minister of the Imperial Stud and Commissioner of Pastures of Lǒngyòu, Wáng Jùn, led his two thousand troops to join Xuē Nà in attacking the Tibetans.
Bèndáyán commanded a Tibetan army of one hundred thousand, encamped at Dàlái Valley.
Wáng Jùn selected seven hundred brave warriors,
dressed them in Hu clothing,
and launched a night attack.
He placed numerous drums and horns five li behind them.
When the vanguard encountered the enemy and gave a great shout,
the men behind sounded the drums and horns in response.
The barbarians thought a large army had arrived,
were frightened,
and killed and wounded each other,
with casualties numbering in the tens of thousands.
Xuē Nà was then at Wǔjiē,
twenty li from Dàlái Valley,
with the barbarian army blocking the area between them.
Wáng Jùn again went out at night to attack them,
and the barbarians suffered a great rout,
finally allowing him to join forces with Xuē Nà's army.
They pursued the fleeing enemy to the Táo River,
and fought again at Chángchéng Fort.
The Qin built the Great Wall,
starting from Líntáo,
hence the fort was named accordingly.
Fù,
read as fú yòu fān.
The total number of enemy killed and captured in these engagements reached tens of thousands.
The commander of the Fēng'ān Army, Wáng Hǎibīn, died in battle.
On the Wùchén day,
Yáo Chóng, Lú Huáishèn, and others memorialized:
"Previously, the Tibetans used the river as their border.
During the Shénlóng period, when a princess was given in marriage,
they crossed the river and built a city,
establishing the Dúshān and Jiǔqǔ armies.
This was the Jiǔqǔ territory given by Yáng Jǔ.
They also built a bridge over the river.
Now that the Tibetans have rebelled,
we should destroy the bridge and raze the city."
The Emperor agreed.
He appointed Wáng Hǎibīn's son, Zhōngsì, as a Gentleman of Courtiers of Scattered Rank and Chief Steward of the Imperial Carriages,
and raised him within the palace.
On the Jǐsì day of the 43rd year,
the Turkic Qaghan Mòchuò again sent an envoy to request a marriage alliance.
The Emperor promised to welcome the princess the following year.
In the 44th year, tribes of the Western Turks, such as the Húlùwū, came to Běitíng to request to surrender.
These were Western Turks.
Jiàng,
read as hù jiāng fān;
same below.
On the Yǐyǒu day,
he ordered the Left Rapid as Valiant Guard Commandant Yùchí Huái to go as envoy to Tibet,

The Tibetans sent their minister Zōng'é Yīnmáo
to the Táo River to request peace,
using the etiquette between equal states.
The Emperor refused.
From then on, they invaded the border year after year.
An examination of discrepancies: The Táng Lì states:
"On the Dīngchǒu day of the seventh month in the fourth year,
because of their defeat the previous year, the Tibetans
sent their minister Sòng'é Yīnmáo to the frontier to request peace.
Relying on their military strength,
they sought the etiquette of an equal state;
the Son of Heaven was angered."
According to this, from then until the fourth year,
it was not the previous year.
Since it says they requested peace due to defeat,
how could it also say they relied on their military strength?
Since it says the Son of Heaven was angered,
how could he have agreed to their peace in the eighth month of that same year?
Now we follow the Old Biography.
In the eleventh month,
on the Xīnmǎo day,
Emperor Shāng was buried.
On the Bǐngshēn day,
he dispatched the Left Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Xiè Wǎn to go to Běitíng to convey his regards to the surrendered Turks,
and to handle matters as he saw fit.
In the twelfth month,
on the Rénxū day,
Shātuó Jīnshān came to court.
On the Jiǎzǐ day,
the office of Military Commissioner-in-Chief of Lǒngyòu was established,
to oversee the twelve prefectures of Shàn, Fèng, Hé, Wèi, Lán, Lín, Wǔ, Táo, Mín, Guō, Dié, and Dàng.
"Xū"
should be

The character "sì"
is extraneous.

should be

should be

Lín Prefecture was originally the land of Dídào in the Han Dynasty's Lǒngxī Commandery.
The Jin established Wǔshǐ Commandery there.
The Sui abolished the commandery and restored it as Dídào County,
belonging to Lán Prefecture.
In the third year of the Tiānbǎo era, Lín Prefecture was finally established by division.
Both the New and Old Histories state this.
According to this,
then Lín Prefecture had already been established for a long time.
Wǔ Prefecture
was the ancient land of Báimǎ.
Emperor Wu of Han opened it up and established Wǔdū Commandery.
The Western Wei changed it to Shímén County,
and established Wǔ Prefecture.
Dàng Prefecture
was the land of the Dàngchāng Qiang during the Later Wei.
The Later Zhou established Dàngchāng Commandery,
and in the first year of the Tiānhé era, established Dàng Prefecture.
Shàn,
read as shí zhàn fān,
also pronounced shàn.
Dàng,
read as tú làng fān.
On the Yǐchǒu day,
the Emperor's son Sìzhēn was enfeoffed as Prince of Zēng.
An examination of discrepancies: The Veritable Records here writes
"Prince of Zēng",
but later writes

Now we follow the Old Biography.
Upon detailed examination of the two histories, New and Old,
Sìzhēn was enfeoffed in this year together with Sìchū and Sìxuán.
However, Sìzhēn was actually the Emperor's fourth son,
not the eldest.
The eldest son was Sìzhí,
and the second son was Sìqiān.
In the first year of the Xiāntiān era,
Sìzhí was enfeoffed as Prince of Tán,
and Sìqiān as Prince of Yǐng.
Sìzhǔ was enfeoffed as Prince of Juàn.
"Sìzhǔ"
should be

] On the Xīnsì day,
Prince Yǐng Sìqiān was established as Crown Prince.
Sìzhēn
was the Emperor's eldest son,
his mother being Liú Huá.
Liú Huá
was the mother of Prince Tán Sìzhí.
If the mother of Prince Zēng Sìzhēn was Qián.
This is also an error.
He was the second son,
his mother being Zhào Lì.
The Emperor established the consorts Huì, Lì, and Huá,
to replace the Three Ladies.
She was favored by the Emperor,
hence he was established.
Establishing a son because of the mother's favor;
when the mother's favor wanes, the son's affection will slacken.
This sets the stage for the later deposing of the Crown Prince.
Chàng,
pronounced chāng.
In this year,
the office of Military Commissioner, Strategic Commander, and Garrison Commander-in-Chief of Yōuzhōu was established,
overseeing the six prefectures of Yōu, Yì, Píng, Tán, Guī, and Yān.
The younger brother of the Turkic Shǐ Qaghan Shǒuzhōng, Zhēnǔ, resented that the tribe allotted to him was fewer than his elder brother's,
so he rebelled and went over to the Turks,
requesting to serve as a guide
to attack Shǒuzhōng.
Mòchuò sent twenty thousand troops to attack Shǒuzhōng,
captured him, and returned.
He said to Zhēnǔ:
"You betrayed your elder brother,
what loyalty would you have for me?"
And then killed him as well.
This is recorded
to warn those brothers who daily pursue warfare and borrow the hand of others to achieve their ambitions.
In the spring,
first month,
on the Guǐmǎo day,
Lú Huáishèn was appointed Acting Minister of Personnel and concurrently Gatekeeper of the Yellow Gate.
Huáishèn was pure, cautious, frugal, and simple.
He did not accumulate property or assets.
Although honored as a minister and chancellor,
the salaries and gifts he received
he immediately distributed among relatives and old friends.
His wife and children could not avoid hunger and cold,
and his dwelling did not shelter them from wind and rain.
Yáo Chóng once had a son who passed away,
and he requested leave for over ten days.
Government affairs piled up,
and Huái Shèn was unable to make decisions.
Anxious and fearful,
he entered the palace to apologize to the Emperor.
The Emperor said:
"I have entrusted the affairs of the empire to Yáo Chóng,
and you, my minister, are here to maintain peace and order."
After Chóng returned,
in a short while,
he resolved all pending matters,
looking rather pleased with himself.
He turned to the Imperial Secretary Qí Huàn and asked:
"As a chancellor,
to whom can I be compared?"
Huàn did not reply.
Chóng said:
"How do I compare to Guǎn Zhòng and Yàn Yīng?"
Huàn said:
"Although the laws of Guǎn and Yàn could not be perpetuated after their deaths,
they at least endured throughout their lifetimes.
The laws you establish
are often altered soon after,
so it seems you do not quite match them."
Chóng said:
"Then what am I, after all?"
Huàn said:
"You, sir, may be called a chancellor who rescues the times."
Chóng was delighted,
threw down his brush, and said:
"A chancellor who rescues the times—
is that easily achieved!"
Huái Shèn served as chancellor alongside Chóng,
but knowing his own ability was inferior to Chóng's,
he deferred to him in all matters.
Contemporaries called him
"the dining companion chancellor."
Your subject Guāng remarks: In ancient times, Bào Shū towards Guǎn Zhòng,
and Zǐ Pí towards Zǐ Chǎn,
both held higher positions,
yet recognized their worth and yielded to them,
entrusting them with state governance;
Confucius praised them.
When Guǎn Zhòng requested to be imprisoned in Lǔ,
Bào Shū brought him back,
and said to Duke Huán:
"Guǎn Yíwú's governance surpasses even Gāo Xī;
he may be made chancellor."
Duke Huán employed him,
and thus became hegemon over the feudal lords.
When Zhèng's Zǐ Pí was in charge of the state,
he handed governance to Zǐ Chǎn,
but Zǐ Chǎn declined.
Zǐ Pí said:
"If I, Hǔ, lead and obey,
who would dare not obey!"
So he entrusted him with governance,
and the state of Zhèng was greatly well-ordered.
To yield,
xiá jià fān.
They fully adhered to his laws,
making no changes;
thus the Hàn dynasty's enterprise was accomplished.
This matter is recorded in the twelfth volume, second year of Emperor Huì of Hàn.
To change,
gōng héng fān.
Those who serve as subordinates,
caring only for their own safety and emoluments while following along,
disregarding the safety or peril of the state,
are truly offenders.
When the worthy and wise are in power,
those who serve as subordinates,
using folly and confusion to disrupt their governance,
stubbornness to divide their authority,
jealousy to ruin their achievements,
obstinacy to steal their fame,
these too are offenders.
Chóng,
a worthy chancellor of Táng,
and Huái Shèn, joining hearts and efforts with him,
to assist in the peaceful governance of Emperor Míng—
how could they be offenders!
The "Qín Oath" says:
"If there be one minister,
sincere and single-minded,
with no other skill;
his heart is at ease,
as if capable of tolerance;
when others have skill,
it is as if he himself possessed it;
when others are wise and sage,
his heart delights in them,
not merely as if spoken from his own mouth;
such a one can tolerate them,
to protect my descendants and the black-haired people,
and indeed it is beneficial."
This describes Huái Shèn.

5. In Shāndōng, there was a great plague of locusts.
Some people, by the fields, burned incense, prostrated themselves, and made offerings, not daring to kill them.
Yáo Chóng memorialized, requesting to send censors to supervise the prefectures and counties in capturing and burying them.
Some argued that the locusts were too numerous,
and it would be impossible to eliminate them all.
The Emperor also doubted it.
Chóng said:
"Now the locusts fill Shāndōng,
and the people of Hénán and Héběi
have almost all fled into exile.
How can we sit by and watch them devour the seedlings,
and not even attempt to save them?
Even if we cannot eliminate them all,

The Emperor then followed his advice.
Lú Huáishèn believed that killing too many locusts
might harm the harmonious qi.
Chóng said:
"In the past, King Zhuāng of Chǔ swallowed a leech and his illness was cured.
Jiǎ Yì's writings say: The King of Chǔ ate cold pickles and found a leech.
He then swallowed it,
and developed an abdominal illness so he could not eat.
The Prime Minister entered to inquire about his illness.
The King said:
'I ate pickles and found a leech.
If I do not punish the offense,
it means the law is abandoned and authority is not established.
If I reprimand and execute them,
I fear all the food supervisors would die.
So I swallowed it.'
The Prime Minister said:
'The Way of Heaven shows no partiality;
it assists only the virtuous.
The King has benevolent virtue,
so the illness will not harm you.'
The King's illness indeed got better.
'Leech'
is pronounced 'zhì'.
The Shuōyuàn records: When Sūnshū Áo was a child,
he went out and saw a two-headed snake.
He killed it and buried it,
then returned home crying.
His mother asked the reason.
He said:
'I saw a two-headed snake,
and I fear I will die.'
His mother said:
'Where is the snake?'
He said:
'I heard that whoever sees a two-headed snake dies.
Fearing others might see it again,
I have already killed and buried it.'
His mother said:
'Do not worry.
You will not die.
I have heard that Heaven always repays hidden virtue with good fortune.'
If killing locusts brings disaster,

The Director of the Palace Buildings Wéi Còu submitted a memorial,
believing that:
"Now the Western Regions are submissive.

Emperor Yáo of Táng harmonized the myriad states.

Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's affairs are seen in the Hàn records.
'Xià'
is pronounced 'xià'.
All praise belongs to Emperor Yáo of Táng,

Báhánnà was
