Sūlù was quite adept at pacifying and comforting the people.
The tribes of the Ten Clans gradually submitted to him.
He amassed a force of two hundred thousand men,
and thus came to control the western regions.
Soon, he sent an envoy to have an audience.
That year,
Sūlù was appointed General of the Left Imperial Guard and Grand Commissioner for Pacification of the Jīnfāng Circuit.
The west is associated with the element metal,
hence the name Jīnfāng (Metal Direction) Circuit.
19. The younger sister's husband of the Empress, the Director of the Palace Clothing Service, Zhǎngsūn Xīn, had a minor grievance and was at odds with the Censor-in-Chief Lǐ Jié.
The Palace Administration had six bureaus: Food, Medicine, Clothing, Quarters, Steeds, and Carriages,
each with two Directors.
The Director of the Palace Clothing Service was in charge of supplying the Son of Heaven's clothing,
examining its regulations,
distinguishing its types and quantities, and presenting it for imperial use.
1. In spring,
the first month,
Xīn and his brother-in-law Yáng Xiānyù lay in wait for Jié in an alleyway and beat him.
Jié submitted a memorial stating his grievance:
"My hair and skin were injured;
though this pains my person,
my official cap and robes were violated;
this truly brings disgrace upon the state."
The Emperor was furious.
He ordered Xīn to be caned to death at the court hall,
to apologize to the hundred officials.
He also sent an edict to console Jié, saying:
"Xīn and the others were my close relatives.
I failed to instruct and guide them,
allowing them to violate an official.
Even imposing the extreme penalty
is insufficient to atone for the crime.
You, sir, should maintain a resolute heart in hating evil,
and not take such wicked men to heart."
2. On Dīnghài,
Prince Chéngqì of Sòng changed his name to Xiàn,
and Prince Chéngyì of Shēn changed his name to Huī.
The two princes changed their names because the character 'chéng' violated the posthumous title of Empress Zhāochéng.
Gēng
is pronounced gēng.
3. On Yǐyǒu,
the Military Commissioner of Lǒngyòu, Guō Qiánguì, memorialized that
his slaves Shí Liángcái and seven others had all performed military service,
and requested that they be appointed as Guerrilla Generals.
According to Táng regulations: Guerrilla General is a rank of the lower fifth grade.
Lú Huáishèn and others memorialized:
"Guō Qiánguì, relying on his minor achievements,
presumptuously disrespected established regulations,
requesting the fifth rank for his slaves.
This truly disrupts order and discipline;
it should not be permitted."
The Emperor followed their advice.
4. On Bǐngwǔ,
Prince Sìzhēn of Zēng was appointed Grand Protector-General of Ānběi and Grand Commissioner for Pacifying the Various Tribes of Hédōng, Guānnèi, and Lǒngyòu.
According to the New and Old Histories, this should also be Prince Sìzhí of Tán.
Recording him as Prince Sìzhēn of Zēng
is an error.
And the New and Old Histories record Ānběi as Ānxī,
which is also an error.
Shǐ
is pronounced shǐ.
The rest follow this.
Prince Sìshēng of Shǎn was appointed Grand Protector-General of Ānxī and Grand Commissioner for Pacifying the Various Tribes of Héxī and the Four Garrisons,
with the Ānxī Protector-General Guō Qiánguì as his deputy.
Neither prince left the palace.
The practice of princes holding military commissioner titles in absentia began from this.
5. In the second month,
on Bǐngchén,
the Emperor visited the hot springs at Líshān.
6. Tǔbō besieged Sōngzhōu.
7. On Dīngmǎo,
the Emperor returned to the palace.
8. On Xīnwèi,
the Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs, Ní Ruòshuǐ, was appointed Prefect of Biànzhōu and concurrently Investigating Commissioner of Hénán.
*Táng Huìyào*: On the nineteenth day of the second month of the twenty-second year of Kāiyuán,
the ten circuit Investigating and Pacifying Commissioners were first established.
According to this,
Investigating Commissioners were first established,
and the Investigating and Pacifying Commissioners were established in the twenty-second year.
*Old Geography*: Biànzhōu
is 1,350 *lǐ* east of the capital.
Capital officials of talent and reputation were selected for these posts,
but scholars and officials of the time still looked down on provincial appointments.
The Investigating Commissioner of Yángzhōu, Bān Jǐngqiàn, was recalled to the capital to serve as Junior Minister of the Court of Judicial Review.
Passing through Dàliáng,
the Táng Biànzhōu administered Jùnyí County,
which was ancient Dàliáng.
The Prefect stood gazing at the dust raised by his carriage,
and only returned after a long while.
He said to his subordinates:
"For Master Bān to make this journey,
how is it different from ascending to immortality!"
9. On Guǐyǒu,
the Military Governor of Sōngzhōu, Sūn Rénxiàn, launched a surprise attack on Tǔbō forces beneath the city walls,
and inflicted a major defeat upon them.
The Emperor once sent eunuchs to the Jiangnán region to fetch jīaojīng and xīchì birds,
intending to place them in the imperial gardens.
The envoys caused disturbances wherever they went.
Passing through Biànzhōu,
Ní Ruòshuǐ submitted a memorial stating:
"At present, farming and sericulture are at a critical juncture,
yet we are netting and capturing birds to provide amusement for the imperial gardens and ponds.
Transporting them from as far as the Jiāng and Lǐng regions,
via water and land routes,
and feeding them with fine grain and meat.
Those who witness this along the roads,
would they not think Your Majesty values birds over people?
Your Majesty should regard the phoenix as a common bird,
and the qílín as a common beast;
how much less then should jīaojīng and xīchì birds
be considered precious!"
The Emperor personally wrote an edict thanking Ruòshuǐ,
bestowed upon him forty bolts of silk,
and released all the birds.
11 Locusts again swarmed in great numbers in Shāndōng,
and Yáo Chóng again ordered their capture.
Ní Ruòshuǐ argued:
"Locusts are a calamity from Heaven,
not something human effort can manage.
We should cultivate virtue to avert them.
During Liú Cōng's time,
they often captured and buried them,
but the harm only grew worse."
He resisted the imperial censor,
refusing to follow the order.
Chóng sent a dispatch to Ruòshuǐ saying:
"Liú Cōng was a false ruler,
whose virtue could not overcome the ominous;
today's sage court,
the ominous cannot overcome virtue.
In ancient times, under good administrators,
locusts did not enter their territories.
If cultivating virtue could avert them,
would those places have lacked virtue to cause it otherwise?"
Ruòshuǐ then dared not disobey.
In summer,
the fifth month,
on the jiǎchén day,
an edict commissioned envoys to thoroughly investigate which prefectures and counties were diligent or negligent in catching locusts,
and report their names accordingly.
Consequently, although locust disasters occurred for successive years,
there was no great famine.
12 Someone said to the Emperor:
"This year's selection and appointment process is excessively lax,
the county magistrates are incompetent."
When they came to express gratitude for their appointments,
the Emperor summoned all the county magistrates to the courtyard of the Xuānzhèng Hall.
The main hall of the Dàmíng Palace is called the Hányuán Hall,
to its north is the Xuānzhèng Hall.
Only Wéi Jì, the magistrate of Juànchéng County, ranked first in the reasoning and expression of his response.
Juànchéng is an ancient county,
under the Hàn, it belonged to Jìyīn Commandery,
under the Later Hàn, it was the seat of Yǎnzhōu,
under the Jìn, it belonged to Púyáng Commandery,
under the Táng, it was attached to Púzhōu.
Juàn,
pronounced as in 'juàn' (吉掾翻).
He was promoted from a magistrate of a 'jǐn' county to one of a 'cìchì' county.
And he was ordered to take up his post;
"Bǎi"
should be
"shí".
The Vice Minister of Personnel Lú Cóngyuàn was demoted to Prefect of Yùzhōu,
and Lǐ Cháoyǐn was demoted to Prefect of Huázhōu.
Old records state: Huázhōu is 1,440 lǐ from the capital.
Cháo,
pronounced as in 'zhí yáo fān'.
Textual analysis notes: Wéi Jì's biography says
"he was asked one policy question on pacifying the people."
Here we follow the Táng Calendar.
Lú Cóngyuàn's biography states:
"The Emperor summoned all the newly appointed county magistrates,
and simultaneously tested them with policy questions in the palace courtyard.
Those who scored in the lowest grade
were all sent back to study."
The Táng Calendar places the test in the fourth month,
and the demotions of Cóngyuàn and Cháoyǐn in the fifth month.
Cháoyǐn's biography says:
"In spring of the fourth year,
because the county magistrates appointed were not suitable,
he was demoted."
Here we follow the Táng Calendar.
Also, Wéi Jì's biography says:
"At that time, someone secretly memorialized the Emperor saying: 'This year, the Ministry of Personnel's selection and appointment process is excessively lax,
the county magistrates are incompetent,
with no proper screening at all.'
On the day the magistrates came to express gratitude,
they were led into the palace courtyard and asked policy questions on pacifying the people.
Over a hundred people were tested,
only Jì's policy response ranked first,
some did not even write on paper.
Jì was promoted to magistrate of Lǐquán,
over twenty people were returned to their former posts,
and forty-five were sent back to study."
Here we also follow the Táng Calendar.
Both he and Cháoyǐn were reputed to be competent.
The history records Cóngyuàn and Cháoyǐn as competent,
thus the earlier criticism was incorrect.
Chēng,
pronounced as in 'chǐ zhèng fān'.
During Gāozōng's reign,
Mǎ Zǎi and Péi Xíngjiǎn in the Ministry of Personnel were most renowned,
contemporaries said the Ministry of Personnel had Mǎ and Péi earlier,
and later had Lú and Lǐ.
Jì
was the son of Sìlì.
Wéi Sìlì,
son of Sīqiān,
served as chancellor during the Cháng'ān period.
13 A foreigner submitted a memorial stating that the lands south of the sea had many pearls, kingfisher feathers, and rare treasures.
"South of the sea" refers to countries like Línyì, Fúnán, Zhēnlà, etc.
Shàng,
pronounced as in 'shí zhǎng fān'.
He also spoke of the profits from maritime trade;
and further wished to go to the Lion Country
The Lion Country,
is a country near Tiānzhú,
located in the southwestern seas.
Originally it had no people,
only ghosts, spirits, and dragons dwelled there.
Merchants from various countries came to trade,
the ghosts and spirits were not seen in form,
but would bring out precious treasures,
display the acceptable price,
and the merchants would take them according to the price.
The land is mild and pleasant,
with no distinction between winter and summer.
People from various countries, hearing the land was pleasant,
therefore vied to go there,
some who stayed and settled
eventually formed a large country;
they were able to tame lions,
hence the country was named accordingly.
He also suggested placing them in the palace women's quarters.
The Emperor ordered the Investigating Censor Yáng Fànchén to go with the foreigner to seek these things.
Fànchén calmly memorialized:
"Your Majesty two years ago burned pearls, jade, brocades, and embroideries,
to show they would no longer be used.
How do the things sought now differ from those burned?
Competing for profit with merchants in maritime trade
is hardly fitting for a sovereign's dignity.
The properties of foreign medicines,
are often unknown in the Central Kingdom;
how much less then should foreign women
be placed in the palace women's quarters!
The Censor,
is an official serving as the Emperor's eyes and ears;
if there are major military or state affairs,
although your subject would brave miasmic fevers,
he would not dare decline even unto death.
This is merely a foreigner's attempt to dazzle and curry favor,
it does not benefit Your Majesty's sage virtue.
I privately fear this is not Your Majesty's original intent,
I beg you to consider this carefully."
The Emperor immediately acknowledged his own fault,
consoled and instructed him, and abandoned the matter.
14 In the sixth month,
on the guǐhài day,
the Retired Emperor passed away in the Bǎifú Hall.
He was fifty-five years old.
Textual analysis notes: The Veritable Records of Ruìzōng and Xuánzōng both say the jiǎzǐ day.
According to the text below,
"On the jǐsì day,
the first seventh-day memorial service for Ruìzōng,
Wàn'ān Princess was ordained as a Daoist nun."
Here we follow the Old Basic Annals and the Táng Calendar.
On the jǐsì day
the Emperor's daughter Wàn'ān Princess became a female Daoist priestess,
wishing to accumulate blessings for the deceased.
On the Guǐyǒu day (the 15th),
the Báyègù tribe beheaded the Turkic Khagan Mòchuò and presented his head.
At that time, Mòchuò was attacking the Báyègù in the north,
and had heavily defeated them at the Dúlè River.
Relying on his victory, he returned carelessly,
without making any defensive preparations.
He encountered a fleeing soldier of the Báyègù named Jiézhìluè,
who suddenly emerged from the willow grove
and beheaded him.
His army was defeated and scattered,
his soldiers fled in disarray,
hence the term "fleeing soldier."
復 (fù),
pronounced fú yòu fān.
迸 (bèng),
pronounced běi mèng fān.
A "zǐjiàng"
is a minor officer.
According to Tang regulations,
each army had one senior general,
eight special aides,
and sixteen attendants.
There were two deputy generals,
who shared the management of military affairs.
Their aides and attendants were half the number of the senior general's.
There were two administrative assistants,
and four clerks.
There were four commanders-in-chief,
two in charge of the left and right patrols,
and two in charge of the left and right guard commanders.
Each had five attendants.
There were eight minor officers,
responsible for deploying battle formations,
distinguishing signals from gongs and drums, and making dispositions.
Each had two attendants.
Textual analysis notes: The Táng Lì records it as
"Bóyègù,"
but here we follow the Veritable Records.
The Táng Lì also says
"Líng Quán led the Tèlè and Huíhé tribes and beheaded Mòchuò at the Dúlè River,"
but here we follow the Old Biography.
The Old Biography says
"envoy to the foreign tribes Hǎo Língjiǎn,"
but here we follow the Táng Lì.
Furthermore, both the Old and New Annals record that Mòchuò was beheaded on the Guǐyǒu day of the sixth month,
and the Táng Lì also places it in the sixth month.
The Xuánzōng Veritable Records
contain an imperial edict dated the Wùyín day of the seventh month addressed to the surrendered Turks, stating:
"Taking advantage of their weakness,
we have long sought to eliminate them.
For anyone who can capture Mòchuò,
a reward has already been established."
This was likely before the report of his death had arrived.
His head was displayed on the main street.
The five tribes of Báyègù, Huíhé, Tóngluó, Xí, and Púgù all came to surrender,
and were settled north of the Dàwǔ Army.
Mòchuò's son, the Lesser Khagan, was installed,
but Gǔduōlù's son Quètèlè attacked and killed him.
Gǔduōlù is Gǔdǔlù,
the elder brother of Mòchuò.
He rebelled in the second year of Yǒngchún,
and died in the second year of Tiānshòu,
after which Mòchuò succeeded him.
They installed his elder brother, the Left Virtuous King Mòjílián,
who became the Bìjiā Khagan.
The people of the nation called him
"Xiǎoshā."
Bìjiā firmly offered the state to Quètèlè,
but Quètèlè declined to accept it.
He was then made Left Virtuous King,
exclusively in charge of military affairs.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Rénchén day,
the Court of Imperial Sacrifices doctors Chén Zhēnjié and Sū Xiàn, on the grounds that the seven chambers of the Grand Temple were full,
requested that the spirit tablet of Emperor Zhōngzōng be moved to a separate temple,
and that the spirit tablet of Emperor Ruìzōng be enshrined in the Grand Temple;
this was approved.
They also petitioned to move Empress Zhāochéng to be enshrined with Emperor Ruìzōng,
while Empress Sùmíng remained to be worshipped at the Yíkūn Temple.
Empress Sùmíng
was the principal wife of Emperor Ruìzōng.
Empress Zhāochéng
was the secondary wife,
but because she gave birth to the emperor, she was elevated to be enshrined with Emperor Ruìzōng,
while Empress Sùmíng was worshipped in a separate temple,
which was contrary to ritual.
The Yíkūn Temple
is mentioned in the second year of Jǐngyún in the previous scroll.
On the Yǐsì day,
a temple for Emperor Zhōngzōng was established west of the Grand Temple.
On the Xīnwèi day,
the Qìdān leader Lǐ Shīhuó and the Xī leader Lǐ Dàpú led their tribes to surrender.
During the Wànsuì Tōngtiān era of Empress Wǔ,
the Xī and Qìdān rebelled.
After the emperor ascended the throne,
Sūn Quán and Xuē Nè successively suffered military defeats,
yet these two foreign tribes did not dare to take advantage of their victories to encroach upon China.
Instead, they came to surrender together,
which was due to China's stable and strong position,
which had won over their hearts.
酺 (pú),
pronounced pú.
帥 (shuài),
read as shuài.
降 (xiáng),
pronounced hù jiāng fān;
same below.
Based on their eight tribal chieftains,
they were appointed as prefects.
At the end of the Zhēnguàn era,
the Dájī tribe of the Qìdān was made the Qiàoluò Prefecture,
the Hébiàn tribe the Tánhàn Prefecture,
the Dúhuó tribe the Wúféng Prefecture,
the Fēnwèn tribe the Yǔlíng Prefecture,
the Tūbiàn tribe the Rìlián Prefecture,
the Ruìxī tribe the Túhé Prefecture,
the Zhuìjīn tribe the Wàndān Prefecture,
and the Fú tribe the Pǐlí and Chìshān Prefectures,
totaling, together with the Sōngmò Commandery, six tribes and ten prefectures.
Now, their chieftains were again each made prefects.
Lǐ Dàpú was made Prince of Ráolè Commandery, Acting General of the Right Golden Bird Guard, and concurrently Governor of Ráolè.
Lǐ Shīhuó
was a paternal cousin of Lǐ Jìnzhōng.
Lǐ Jìnzhōng was the rebel leader during the Wànsuì Tōngtiān era.
樂 (lè),
pronounced luò.
從 (cóng),
pronounced cái yòng fān.
The Tǔbō again requested peace;
the emperor granted it.
After the Turkic Khagan Mòchuò died,
the Xī, Qìdān, Báyègù, and other tribes all submitted to the interior.
The Tūqíshī leader Sūlù again proclaimed himself Khagan.
The Turkic tribes were largely scattered and dispersed,
which troubled the Bìjiā Khagan.
He therefore summoned Tūnyùgǔ, who had been an officer under Mòchuò,
to serve as his chief strategist.
Tūnyùgǔ was over seventy years old,
highly intelligent and resourceful,
and trusted and respected by the people.
The surrendered Turkic households settled in the Héqū region,
(the bend of the northern river).
處 (chǔ),
pronounced chāng lǚ fān.
Many of them again rebelled and returned to him.
The Chief Administrator of Bīngzhōu, Wáng Jùn, submitted a memorial stating:
"These people only came to surrender in groups because their own state was in turmoil;
if that land becomes peaceful,
they will certainly rebel and leave again.
Now, placing them in the Héqū region,
these individuals are cunning and fierce,
truly difficult to control and govern.
They often do not obey the constraints of the military and prefectural authorities,
raising troops to plunder and raid.
It is heard that many of those who have fled already have communications and interactions with the barbarians,
transmitting detailed information.
This is essentially nurturing these people to become spies.
As days and months accumulate,
their deceit and treachery will deepen further,
watching for gaps along the border,
which will become a major calamity.
When the barbarian cavalry come south to pasture,
they will certainly serve as internal collaborators,
pressing upon our military prefectures,
leaving us attacked from both inside and outside.
Even if we had Hán Xìn and Péng Yuè,
we could not achieve victory.
I hope that at the turn of autumn and winter,
we can assemble a large force of troops,
explain to them the advantages and disadvantages,
provide them with supplies and grain,
and relocate them to the interior.
After twenty years,
gradually changing their old customs,
they will all become strong soldiers.
Although it will be temporarily laborious for a time,
it will bring eternal peace and stability.
Recently, border defense generals and officials, as well as envoys who go beyond the border,
often speak with flattering words,
none of which reflect the actual situation.
Some say the northern barbarians are destroyed,
others say the surrendered households are settled and peaceful,
all wishing to boast of their own achievements,
not truly able to be loyal and serve the state.
I hope you will examine these glib tongues.
Confucius said:
'I detest those whose glib tongues overturn states and families.'
Critics will certainly say: 'The state previously placed surrendered households in Héqū,
and all obtained peace and stability,'
referring to the Zhēnguàn period.
This is a case where the matter is the same but the times are different,
which must not be overlooked.
In the past,
after Jiélì perished,
the surrendered people no longer had divided loyalties,
hence long-term peace without change was achieved.
Now the northern barbarians still exist,"
referring to Mòchuò being dead,
but Píjiā having risen.
Some cherish their kindness,
or have relatives among them,
how could they be willing to come south!
Compared to that time,
it is certainly not the same.
That time,
refers to the Zhēnguàn period.
Willing,
pronounced luò.
Relocating them to the interior,
is the best policy;
stationing many troops and horses,
making extensive preparations,
with Huá and Yí intermixed,
causing people labor and great expense,
is the second-best policy;
maintaining the present situation,
is the worst policy.
I hope you will carefully consider these three strategies,
choose the beneficial one and act.
Even if due to relocation some flee,
those captured will all belong to Táng;
if left until the river freezes,
I fear changes will certainly occur."
The memorial was submitted,
but no reply was received;
the surrendered households Diēsītài, Āxīlàn, and others indeed rebelled.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the jiǎchén day,
Xuē Nà, the Grand Commander of Shuòfāng, was ordered to dispatch troops to pursue and suppress them.
Wáng Jùn led Bīngzhōu troops westward across the river,
marching day and night,
pursued the rebels,
defeated them,
beheading and capturing three thousand.
Previously,
the Deputy Protector-General of Chányú, Zhāng Zhīyùn, had collected all the weapons of the surrendered households,
ordering them to cross the river southward,
which angered the surrendered households.
The Imperial Censor Zhōngchéng Jiāng Huì served as Border Inspector,
the surrendered households complained about having no bows and arrows,
unable to hunt,
so Huì returned all to them;
the surrendered households obtained them,
and then rebelled.
Zhāng Zhīyùn made no preparations,
fought them at Qīnggāng Ridge,
Qīnggāng Ridge is north of Fāngqú County in Qìngzhōu,
south of Língzhōu.
They intended to send them to the Tūjué;
reaching the territory of Suízhōu,
General Guō Zhīyùn with Shuòfāng troops intercepted and attacked them,
greatly defeating their forces at Hēishān Hūyán Valley,
the barbarians released Zhāng Zhīyùn and left.
The Emperor, because Zhāng Zhīyùn lost his army,
beheaded him as a public warning.
After Píjiā Kèhán obtained Sītài and others,
he wished to invade southward.
Tūnyùgǔ said:
"The Táng ruler is heroic and martial,
the people harmonious and the year abundant,
there is no gap,
we cannot act.
Our people are newly gathered,
strength still weary and weak,
we should rest and recuperate for several years,
then observe changes and act."
Píjiā also wanted to build a city,
and establish Buddhist and Daoist temples,
Tūnyùgǔ said:
"It cannot be done.
The Tūjué population is sparse,
not one percent of the Táng family's,
the reason we can be their enemy,
is precisely because we follow water and grass,
dwelling without fixed abode,
hunting as our livelihood,
everyone practices martial skills,
when strong we advance to raid and plunder,
when weak we hide in mountains and forests.
Though Táng troops are many,
they have no means to apply them.
If we build cities and dwell,
changing old customs,
once we suffer defeat,
we will certainly be destroyed.
The teachings of Buddhism and Daoism,
instruct people in benevolence and weakness,
not techniques for contending and winning through force,
they must not be exalted."
Píjiā then stopped.
On the gēngwǔ day,
the Great Sage Emperor was buried at Qiáolíng,
Qiáolíng is thirty lǐ from Púchéng County in Tóngzhōu.
That year, Púchéng County was renamed Fèngxiān County,
under the jurisdiction of Jīngzhào Yǐn.
The Grand Censor Dàfū Lǐ Jié supervised the construction at Qiáolíng,
his assistant official Wáng Xù committed corruption,
Jié investigated him,
but was instead framed by him,
demoted to Prefect of Qúzhōu.
Qúzhōu,
the land of Xīn'ān and Tàimò in Hàn times,
in Jìn, Xīn'ān was changed to Xìn'ān,
Tàimò changed to Lóngqiū,
under Dōngyáng Commandery,
in the fourth year of Táng Wǔdé, Qúzhōu was separately established.
Qúzhōu,
is 4,712 lǐ southeast of the capital.
In the eleventh month,
on the jǐmǎo day,
the Gatekeeper Supervisor Lú Huáishèn was critically ill,
submitted a memorial recommending Sòng Jǐng, Lǐ Jié, Lǐ Cháoyǐn, and Lú Cóngyuàn as important talents for an enlightened age,
their offenses minor,
what is discarded major,
hoping for compassionate consideration;
the Emperor deeply accepted it.
On the yǐwèi day,
he passed away.
Examination of discrepancies: Zhèng Chùhuī's "Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Mínghuáng" states:
"Huáishèn served as Gatekeeper Supervisor and Minister of Personnel,
having been bedridden ill for a long time,
Sòng Jǐng and Lú Cóngyuàn visited him together.
Huáishèn always esteemed these two men,
holding their hands said: 'You gentlemen serve as frontier ministers,
the ruler seeks governance very urgently,
but having enjoyed the state for many years,
recently has grown somewhat weary of diligence,
certainly someone will take advantage to advance,
you must remember this.'"

Shān (痁),

This is likely

We now follow the Old Biography.
Chóng repeatedly requested to relinquish his ministerial position,

Nèishì
was the head official of the Nèishìshěng,

Nèishì
was rank 4b lower;
Nèichángshì,
rank 5a upper.
No one could fathom Jǐng's thoughts,

Sīxù, accustomed to prestige and favor,

The Emperor sighed for a long time,

On the 23rd, Bǐngchén day,

on the Yǐchǒu day,
he returned to the palace.
In the intercalary month,
on the Jǐhài day,
Yáo Chóng was dismissed and made Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Yuán Qiányào was dismissed and made Governor of Jīngzhào and Imperial Guard of the Western Capital.
Sòng Jǐng, Minister of Justice, was appointed Acting Minister of Personnel and concurrently Huángmén Jiān,
and Zǐwēi Shìláng Sū Tǐng was made Tóngpíngzhāngshì.
As Chancellor,
Jǐng focused on selecting personnel,
assigning posts according to ability,
so that all officials were suited to their positions;
impartial in punishments and rewards,
he dared to remonstrate frankly even at the risk of offending.
The Emperor deeply respected and stood in awe of him,
and even when disagreeing,
would yield to him.
Since Empress Zétiān's time, the Turkic Mòchuò had been a menace to China,
keeping the court anxious even at mealtimes,
and exhausting the empire's strength without subduing him.
Hǎo Língquán obtained his head,
considering it an unparalleled achievement.
Jǐng, fearing that the Emperor's fondness for military exploits

severely curtailed the reward,
and only after over a year appointed him a Langjiàng;
Língquán died weeping in anguish.
Hǎo Língquán achieved merit through others' efforts;
appointing him Langjiàng
was not suppression.
Jiàng (將),
pronounced jí liàng fān.
Jǐng and Sū Tǐng worked together in great harmony.
Tǐng often yielded to Jǐng in matters,
and whenever Jǐng discussed affairs, Tǐng supported him.
Jǐng once said to someone:
"I have served with both father and son Sū in the ministerial office.

(Púyè
refers to Sū Guī.)
"In administrative skill and acuity,

According to the Old Book biography of Sū Tǐng,
Tǐng, as Zǐwēi Shìláng, was made Tóng Zǐwēi Huángmén Píngzhāngshì.
Yáo and Sòng served as Chancellors successively.
Chóng excelled at adapting to change and managing affairs,
while Jǐng excelled at upholding laws and maintaining integrity.
Their temperaments differed,
yet they cooperated in assisting the ruler,
making taxes and corvée equitable,
punishments clear and sparing,
and the people prosperous.
Among Táng's worthy chancellors,
earlier ones were called Fáng, Dù,
later ones Yáo, Sòng;
others could not compare.
Whenever the two had an audience,
the Emperor would rise for them,
and upon their departure, see them off from the palace hall.
When Lǐ Línfǔ became Chancellor,
though his favor and authority surpassed Yáo and Sòng's,
the ceremonial treatment was far inferior.
The historian concludes by mentioning this.
Qí Huǎn was well-versed in contemporary affairs.
Yáo and Sòng often seated two individuals to consult on their doubts,
and later sighed, saying:
"To understand antiquity,
ask Lord Gāo;
to understand the present,
ask Lord Qí;
then governance will lack nothing."
On the 25th, Xīnchǒu day,
the Ten Circuit Surveillance Commissioners were abolished.
(They were re-established in the second year of Kāiyuán.)
According to the old system,
officials of rank 6b and below were all delegated to the Shàngshūshěng for recommendation and appointment.
This year,
it was first decreed that Yuánwàiláng, Imperial Censors, Qǐjūláng, Yíguān, and Bǔquē officials would not be subject to this process.
Yuánwàiláng, Imperial Censors, Qǐjūláng, Yíguān, and Bǔquē
were all important officials of the central departments,
to be personally appointed by the sovereign,
not recommended by the Shàngshūshěng.
According to the Táng system,
Yuánwàiláng were rank 6b,
Shìyùshǐ and Qǐjūláng were also rank 6b,
Bǔquē were rank 7,

1. In spring,
the first month,
on Guǐmǎo,
the four chambers of the Grand Ancestral Temple collapsed.
The Emperor wore plain garments and avoided the main hall.
At that time, the Emperor was about to travel to the Eastern Capital.
Old records state: The distance from the Eastern Capital to the Western Capital is 850 li.
He replied:
"Your Majesty's three-year mourning period has not yet concluded.
Last year in the sixth month, Emperor Ruìzōng passed away,
hence this statement.
I fear it may not align with the will of Heaven,

He also asked Yáo Chóng,
who replied:

Over the years, they have decayed and rotted, leading to the collapse.

what is there to find strange about it!
This means it is insufficient to be considered a calamitous omen.
Your Majesty is traveling to the Eastern Capital due to poor harvests in Guānzhōng.

"Enter the inner chambers to serve" means

Cháo (court/audience),
is pronounced zhāo.

Chǔ Wúliàng's words
were forthright and honest.
Shàng (submit),

Yuǎn (distance),

On Xīnhài,

"Your Majesty is currently on an inspection tour.

Examination of discrepancies: According to the Shílù:

The two accounts contradict each other.
Probably the Governor of Hénán at that time was someone else,

Also, the Mínghuáng Zálù states:
"The Emperor traveled to the Eastern Capital.

Someone said: 'The Six Armies are crowded within it,

Lìshì returned and reported: 'Yáo Chóng is wearing coarse hemp clothes, riding a small horse, and holding the reins under the shade of trees.'
The Emperor happily said: 'I understand.'

sacrifice,

上 (shàng),

3 Xīnyǒu,
an edict prohibited debased coins.
In the fourth year of the Wǔdé era, Kāiyuán Tōngbǎo coins were minted.
Thereafter, illicit minting gradually arose.
In the fifth year of the Xiǎnqìng era, due to the abundance of debased coins,
the government purchased them,
exchanging one good coin for five debased ones.
The people hoarded debased coins, awaiting a relaxation of the ban.
After the Qiánfēng era,
private coins violating the law daily multiplied,
some even minted on boats and rafts upon rivers.
An edict ordered the collection of debased coins at various locations,
yet the malpractice did not cease.
During Empress Wǔ's time,
coins, unless pierced or made of iron, tin, or copper dross,
were all permitted for use;
even coins of refined copper, stamped, or gritty were circulated.
From then on, illicit minting swarmed like bees,
and officials were unable to capture [the offenders].
During the Xiāntiān period,
coins in the two capitals became increasingly adulterated;
some melted tin to mold coins,
producing hundreds in a short time,
hence the prohibition.
Debased coins from among the people were collected and melted down,
to be recast into standard coins.
Consequently, the capital was thrown into chaos,
and trade nearly ceased.
Sòng Jǐng and Sū Tǐng requested to release twenty thousand strings of coins from the Tàifǔ treasury to establish markets in the northern and southern [parts of the city],

Examination of discrepancies: According to the Veritable Records:
"Rénchén,

totaling three hundred thousand,
all under the command of the Shòufāng circuit marching commander Wáng Jùn;"
yet subsequently, no mention of the campaign's outcome is seen.
Considering that in the first month of this year,
the Tūjué requested peace,
and the Emperor issued a reply edict;
then launching a campaign against them in the second month
seems unlikely.
The Old Annals and the biographies of Wáng Jùn and the Tūjué contain no record of a military campaign this month.
The New Tūjué Biography states:
"Mòjílián sent an envoy to request peace.
The Emperor, considering it insincere,
replied but did not grant it.
Soon after, he issued an edict to attack them,
placing Wáng Jùn in command,
scheduling a rendezvous in the eighth year at the Jīluò River."
Military operations value secrecy;
it is improbable that an edict would be issued two years in advance.
This likely attaches the Veritable Records to the Old Biography.
Assemble [troops] as appropriate;
if no action is required, each shall return to their tribe to pursue livelihood,

The Tang dynasty's Xiāngyǐnjiǔ ceremony:
the Cìshǐ served as the host,
first summoning retired local elders of virtue to plan it,
with the worthiest as the honored guest,
the next as the secondary guest,
and the next as the general guests,
and performing the rites with them.
In the counties, the Magistrate served as the host,
with one elderly person from the locality aged sixty or above who had virtue and prestige as the honored guest,
the next as the secondary guest,
the next as the three guests,
and the next as the general guests.
Those aged sixty had three dòu of food,
those aged seventy had four dòu,
those aged eighty had five dòu,
those aged ninety and the host all had six dòu.
After the host, honored guest, secondary guest, three guests, and general guests had ascended,
and taken their seats,
the musicians holding the sè ascended the steps to their positions,
and performed "Lù Míng".
When the song ended,
the shēng players entered and stood north-facing below the hall,
performing "Nán Gāi".
Then there was alternating singing,
singing "Nán Yǒu Jiā Yú",
the shēng playing "Chóng Qiū",
then combined music of "Zhōu Nán Guān Jū" and "Shào Nán Què Cháo".
The Master of Ceremonies ascended from the western steps,
praised the rites,
raised the zhì cup,
and admonished them with the fundamentals of loyalty and filial piety,
the host, honored guest, secondary guest, and below all bowed twice.
After the ceremonial toasts were completed,
then unlimited drinking was performed,
with unlimited music.

The Emperor thought this reasonable.
At the time, Sòng Jǐng and Zhōngshū Shìláng, Tóng Píngzhāngshì Sū Tǐng proposed strictly prohibiting bad coins.
The problem of bad coins was especially severe in the Jiāng and Huái regions.
Sòng Jǐng appointed Investigating Censor Xiāo Yǐnzhī as commissioner to confiscate bad coins.
Yǐnzhī was harsh, urgent, and caused much disturbance,
filling the roads with complaints and sighs.
The Emperor then demoted Yǐnzhī from his post.
On Xīnsì,
Sòng Jǐng was removed from his post and made Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
and Sū Tǐng was made Minister of Rites.
Examination of discrepancies: The Tang Calendar states
“the 28th day, Xīnmǎo,”
while the Old Annals state
“Jǐmǎo.”
According to the calendar, there was no Xīnmǎo in this month.
Now, we follow the Veritable Records.
Bìngzhōu Chángshǐ Zhāng Jiāzhēn was made Zhōngshū Shìláng,
and concurrently Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Thereafter, the ban on coins was relaxed,
and bad coins circulated again.
3 In the second month,
on Wùxū,
the imperial prince Mǐn died.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Prince Huái.
This Prince Huái took a prefecture as his state name.
4 On Rénzǐ,
an edict was issued stating that no corvée duty was heavier than military service.
Once one became a guardsman,
they served until sixty before being exempted.
The age limit should be shortened,
so that the common people could take turns serving.
5 In summer,
the fourth month,
on Bǐngwǔ,
envoys were sent to confer official patents upon King Wūzhǎng, King Gǔduō, and King Jùwèi.
These three states were all west of Dàshí.
Wūzhǎng is Wūcháng,
also called Wūtú.
Gǔduō is east of Huòshā,
also called Āduōluó.
Its administrative seat was at Sīzhùjiàn City.
Jùwèi,
also called Shāngmí,
had its administrative seat at Āshēyù Shīduō City,
north of the Bólù River in the Great Snowy Mountains.
The land was cold,
and people lived in cave dwellings in winter.
Duō
should be pronounced as mò.
These three states did not submit [to Dàshí],
so they were rewarded.
6 In the fifth month,
on Xīnyǒu,
the Ten Circuit Surveillance Commissioners were re-established.
The abolition of the Surveillance Commissioners is mentioned in the fifth year of the previous scroll.
7 On Dīngmǎo,
Yuán Qiányào was made Shìzhōng,
and Zhāng Jiāzhēn was made Zhōngshū Lìng.
Qiányào memorialized:
“Families in influential positions often hold capital posts,
causing talented and virtuous men to languish in obscurity outside the capital.
I have three sons, all in the capital.
I request that two of them be sent out.”
The Emperor agreed.
Consequently, an edict was issued praising Qiányào’s fairness,
ordering civil and military officials to emulate him.
As a result, over a hundred officials were sent out from the capital.
Zhāng Jiāzhēn was capable and efficient in administrative affairs,
but he was also arrogant, impatient, and self-willed.
Zhōngshū Shèrén Miáo Yánsì, Lǚ Tàiyī, Examination Officer Yuán Jiājìng, and Palace Censor Cuī Xùn were all recommended by Jiāzhēn.
He often discussed government affairs with them.
These four wielded considerable power,
and people of the time said:
“The Duke’s four talents:
Miáo, Lǚ, Cuī, and Yuán.”
8 In the sixth month,
the Chán and Gǔ Rivers overflowed,
drowning nearly two thousand people.
9 The surrendered Tūjué households, including Púgù Dudū Sháomó and the Diē tribe, were scattered near Shòuxiáng City.
Shuòfāng Grand Commissioner Wáng Jùn reported that they were secretly colluding with the Tūjué,
plotting to capture the military city,
and secretly requested permission to execute them.
He lured Sháomó and others to a banquet at Shòuxiáng City,
where hidden soldiers killed them all.
The surrendered households in the Héqū region were almost entirely wiped out.
The Báyègù and Tóngluó tribes near the Dàtóng and Héngyě armies,
hearing of this, were all terrified.
The Dàtóng Army is the Dàwǔ Army,
renamed in the first year of Dàzú of Empress Wǔ.
Dù Yòu said: It is three hundred lǐ north of Dàizhōu,
and eight hundred lǐ from Bìngzhōu.
Jùn
is pronounced as jùn.
Lure
is pronounced as yòu.
Terrified
is pronounced as xiōng.
Bìngzhōu Chángshǐ, Tiānbīng Military Commissioner Grand Commissioner Zhāng Yuè led twenty cavalry,
holding his credentials, went to their tribes to pacify and comfort them,
and even spent the night in their tents.
Deputy Commissioner Lǐ Xiàn, believing the barbarians’ intentions were untrustworthy,
sent a swift letter to stop him.
Zhāng Yuè replied in a letter:
“My flesh is not that of a yellow sheep,
so I certainly do not fear being eaten;
northerners call river deer ‘yellow sheep.’
I certainly do not fear being stabbed.
Horses not raised by households or in pastures but born wild in the wilderness
are called wild horses.
The Analects records Zǐzhāng’s words.
Thus, the Báyègù and Tóngluó tribes were pacified.
10 In winter,
the tenth month,
on Xīnsì,
the Emperor traveled to Chángchūn Palace;
on Rénwǔ,
he hunted at Xiàguī.
11 The Emperor prohibited the princes,
not allowing them to associate with powerful ministers.
The Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments and Commandant-escort Péi Xūjǐ feasted and traveled with Prince Fàn of Qí,
and also privately harbored books of prophecies;
on the wùzǐ day,
Xūjǐ was exiled to Xīnzhōu,
and separated from his princess.
Princess Huòguó, daughter of Emperor Ruìzōng,
had married Xūjǐ.
Old records: Xīnzhōu was 5,052 lǐ from the capital.
The Táng Court of Imperial Sacrifices had six Grand Supplicators,
rank 9a.
Tíngqí was demoted to Registrar of Yǎzhōu,
and È to Assistant Magistrate of Shānchí.
Shānchí County,
during the Hàn and Jìn dynasties belonged to Tàishān Commandery,
during the Sòng dynasty belonged to the Eastern Tàiyuán Commandery,
during the Suí dynasty was abolished and merged into Chángqīng County of Jìzhōu;
in the first year of the Wǔdé era it was separately established as Shānchí County,
belonging to Qízhōu.
shuò,
pronounced suǒ jiǎo fān.
He said to his attendants:
"There is naturally no rift between us brothers,
it is merely those who pursue advancement and competition who forcibly attach themselves.
I will never blame my brothers for this."
The Emperor once fell ill,
Wéi Bīn, the Inner Duty Officer and younger brother of Prince Yè of Xuē
Táng Liù Diǎn: The Eastern Palace had an Inner Duty Bureau,
with two Inner Duty Officers,
in charge of seals, parasols and fans, tables, and clothing matters,
their duties analogous to the Chief of the Imperial Carriages.
When the matter was discovered,
Bīn was beaten to death,
and Xún was demoted to Prefect of Jǐnzhōu.
In the second year of the Chuígōng era of Empress Wǔ, Jǐnzhōu was established from the lands of Máyáng County of Chénzhōu and the opened mountain caves.
The Emperor descended the steps, took Prince Yè's hand and said:
"If I ever had the intention to suspect my brothers,
may Heaven and Earth truly strike me down."
He then feasted and drank with him,
and comforted and instructed him,
ordering him to resume his position.
12 In the eleventh month,
on the yǐmǎo day,
the Emperor returned to the capital.
13 On the xīnwèi day,
the Turks invaded Gān, Liáng and other prefectures,
Liángzhōu was five hundred lǐ west to Gānzhōu.
Textual analysis says: According to Táng Lì,
the Turks invaded Liángzhōu in the ninth month.
The Old Book of Turks says:
"In the winter of the eighth year,
the Censor-in-chief Wáng Jùn was the Grand Commander of Shuòfāng,
and memorialized requesting a western campaign against the Báxīmì,
and to mobilize the two tribes of Xī and Qìdān in the east,
planning for the beginning of autumn the next year,
to lead the Shuòfāng troops in several routes to advance together,
and surprise the Turkic headquarters on the Jīluò River."
According to this, Wáng Jùn was the Military Governor of Yōuzhōu this month,
now follow the Veritable Records and the Old Annals.
They plundered the Qìbì tribe and left.
During the Zhēnguàn era,
the Qìbì surrendered,
and their tribe was settled in Liángzhōu.
Qì,
pronounced qī qì fān.
Bì,
pronounced pí bì fān.
Previously,
the Grand Commander of Shuòfāng Wáng Jùn memorialized requesting to mobilize the Báxīmì from the west,
the chieftain of the Báxīmì had the surname Āshǐnà,
likely also of Turkic stock,
residing in Běitíng.
xiān,
pronounced xī jiàn fān.
Planning to surprise Píqié's headquarters on the Jīluò River this autumn;
the Jīluò River likely originates from the Jīluò Mountains.
He was greatly afraid.
Tūnyùgǔ said:
"There is nothing to fear.
The Báxīmì are at Běitíng,
and are extremely far from the Xī and Qìdān,
their situations cannot support each other;
the Shuòfāng troops likely also cannot come here.
If they must be able to come,
wait until they are about to arrive,
move the headquarters north for three days,
and the Táng troops' provisions will be exhausted and they will leave on their own.
Moreover, the Báxīmì are frivolous and fond of profit,
having received Wáng Jùn's agreement,
they will certainly be pleased and arrive first.
Jùn and Zhāng Jiāzhēn do not get along,
their memorials and requests often do not correspond,
he certainly will not dare to send out troops.
History says that the plans of those at court and on the frontier were not in harmony,
and were spied upon by the barbarians.
If the Báxīmì come alone,
attack and capture them,
the situation is very easy."
Subsequently, the Báxīmì indeed dispatched troops to approach the Turkic headquarters,
but the Shuòfāng and the Xī and Qìdān troops did not arrive,
the Báxīmì became afraid,
and retreated.
Píqié wanted to attack them,
Tūnyùgǔ said:
"These people are a thousand lǐ from home,
they will fight to the death,
they cannot be attacked.
It is better to follow them with troops."
Two hundred lǐ from Běitíng,
Tūnyùgǔ divided his troops to take a side path and first surround Běitíng,
then released his troops to attack the Báxīmì,
defeating them greatly.
The Báxīmì forces scattered and fled,
heading towards Běitíng,
but could not enter,
and were all captured by the Turks.
Tūnyùgǔ led his troops back,
exited at Chìtíng,
and plundered the sheep and horses of Liángzhōu,
Yáng Jìngshù dispatched Vice General Lú Gōnglì and Administrative Official Yuán Chéng to lead troops to intercept them.
Tūnyùgǔ said to his troops:
"We have come riding on victory,
Jìngshù has sent out troops,
we will certainly defeat them."
Gōnglì and others arrived at Shāndān,
Shāndān County,
during the Hàn dynasty belonged to Zhāngyè Commandery,
during the Later Hàn and Jìn dynasties belonged to the Western Commandery,
during the Later Wèi was called Shāndān,
during the Suí dynasty again called Shāndān,
belonging to Gānzhōu.
The Táng troops were greatly defeated,
Gōnglì and Chéng escaped with their lives.
Píqié from then on greatly rose in power,
possessing all of Mòchuò's people.
14 The Qìdān officer Kětūgān was brave and won the hearts of the people,
Lǐ Suōgù was suspicious and fearful,
and wanted to remove him.
This year,
Kětūgān raised troops to attack Suōgù,
Suōgù was defeated and fled to Yíngzhōu.
The Military Governor of Yíngzhōu Xǔ Qīndàn dispatched the Protector-General of Āndōng Xuē Tài to lead five hundred brave troops along with the Xī King Lǐ Dàpú to support Suōgù in attacking him,
but were defeated in battle,
Suōgù and Lǐ Dàpú were both killed by Kětūgān,
Xuē Tài was captured alive,
and Yíngzhōu was shaken with fear.
Xǔ Qīndàn moved his army into Yúguān,
Kětūgān established Suōgù's paternal cousin Yùgān as leader,
and sent an envoy to request punishment.
The Emperor pardoned Kětūgān's crime,
appointed Yùgān as Military Governor of Sōngmò,
and appointed Lǐ Dàpú's younger brother Lǔsū as Military Governor of Ráolè.
1 In spring,
the first month,
an edict stripped Yáng Jìngshù of his official titles and ranks,
because of the defeat at Shāndān.
He still filled the various commissioner positions.
The various commissioners,
refer to the Military, Supply, and Military Colony Commissioners, etc.
2 On the bǐngchén day,
Púzhōu was changed to Hézhōng Prefecture,
establishing the central capital's bureaucracy,
exactly following the standards of Jīngzhào and Hénán.
3 On the bǐngyín day,
the Emperor went to the hot springs at Líshān;
on the yǐhài day,
he returned to the palace.
4 The Investigating Censor Yǔwén Róng submitted a memorial saying,
that throughout the empire households and population were fleeing and moving,
and deceit and fraud were very prevalent,
and requested to conduct an investigation and registration.
Róng,
was the great-great-grandson of Bì.
Yǔwén Bì,
see scroll 172, seventh year of the Tàijiàn era of Emperor Xuān of Chén.
jiān,
pronounced gǔ xián fān.
shàng,
pronounced shí zhǎng fān.
Bì,
the ancient character for bì.
He approved it.
In the second month,
on the yǐyǒu day,
an edict ordered the relevant officials to discuss methods for gathering the drifting and displaced people, and investigating and interrogating deceit and fraud, and report them.
5 On the bǐngxū day,
the Tūjué (Turks) under Bìjiā (毗伽) again sent envoys to seek peace.
The Emperor sent a letter,
instructing them that
"In the past, our state and the Tūjué made peace through marriage alliances,
both Chinese and barbarians lived in ease and comfort,
and weapons of war were laid to rest;
our state purchased sheep and horses from the Tūjué,
and the Tūjué received silk and cloth from our state,
both sides were amply supplied.
For several decades now,
this has no longer been as of old,
precisely because Mòchuò (默啜) was faithless,
speaking peace while harboring rebellion in his heart,
repeatedly launching predatory troops,
raiding and plundering our border regions,
incurring the wrath of men and gods,
until he lost his life and head—
the verification of fortune and misfortune
is something the Khagan himself has witnessed.
Now you tread the same path,
launching a surprise attack on Gānzhōu and Liángzhōu,
and then hastily dispatch envoys,
coming again to seek good relations.
Our state is like heaven in its sheltering,
like the sea in its capacity,
we only consider your present intentions,
and do not pursue past faults.
If the Khagan truly has sincere intentions,
then let us together preserve lasting fortune;
if not,
there is no need to trouble your envoys to travel back and forth in vain.
If you invade our borders,
we are also prepared to respond.
May the Khagan carefully consider this!"
6 On the dīnghài day,
an edict was issued:
"Households that have fled from prefectures and counties are permitted to voluntarily report themselves within one hundred days;
they may either register where they currently reside,
or be documented to return to their native places,
each according to their wish.
Those who do not report themselves after the deadline
will be investigated and registered by force,
and exiled to border prefectures;
any official or private party who dares to conceal or shelter them will be punished."
Yǔwén Róng was appointed as commissioner,
to investigate and register fleeing households and land outside the registers,
uncovering many fraudulent cases.
He was promoted to Vice Director of the Ministry of War and concurrently Palace Censor.
Róng petitioned to establish ten Encouragement of Agriculture Investigating Commissioners,
(the Tōngdiǎn and New History both say twenty-nine persons,
and the Tōngdiǎn even lists their names.)
who were dispatched throughout the empire.
For newly registered client households,
taxes and corvée were exempted for six years.
The commissioners competed in being harsh and exacting,
prefectures and counties, following their lead, caused labor and disturbance,
and the common people suffered from it.
Deputy Magistrate Huángfǔ Jǐng of Yángzhái submitted a memorial describing the situation;
(Yángzhái County,
belonged to Yǐngchuān Commandery in the Hàn,
to Hénán Commandery in the Jìn,
the Later Wèi established Yángzhái Commandery,
the Suí abolished the commandery and made it a county,
belonging to Xiāngchéng Commandery,
in the early Táng it belonged to Sōngzhōu,
in the first year of Zhēnguàn it belonged to Xǔzhōu,
in the second year of Lóngshuò it was transferred to belong to Luòzhōu as a metropolitan county.)
Jǐng,
(pronounced jūyǒng.)
Jǐng was demoted to Deputy Magistrate of Yíngchuān.
Prefectures and counties, currying favor with the imperial will,
strove to achieve high numbers,
falsely inflating their counts,
sometimes even registering actual households as clients,
altogether obtaining over 800,000 households,
and land corresponding to that amount.
7 Kāng Dàibīn of the Lánchízhōu Hú (tribes) incited the various surrendered tribes to rebel together,

the fourth month,
they captured the Six Hú Prefectures,
having a force of 70,000,

the Emperor ordered Wáng Jùn, Grand Commander of Shuòfāng, and Guō Zhīyùn, Military Commissioner of Lǒngyòu, to jointly suppress them.
8 On the wùxū day,
an imperial order:
"For capital officials of the fifth rank and above,
and local officials of prefectural governors and senior assistants of the Four Prefectures,
(the Four Prefectures
refer to Jīngzhào Prefecture, Hénán Prefecture, Hézhōng Prefecture, and Tàiyuán Prefecture.)
based on the quality of their governance, good or bad,
those who recommended them shall be rewarded or punished."

to coordinate with Wáng Jùn and Zhāng Yuè, Grand Commissioner of the Tiānbīng Army, in suppressing Kāng Dàibīn.
10 In the sixth month,
on the jǐmǎo day,
Zhōngdū (the Central Capital) was abolished,

The Governor of Púzhōu, Lù Xiàngxiān, governed with leniency and simplicity;

The Registrar of the prefecture said to Xiàngxiān:

rank 9a,

Chuí,
(pronounced zhǐchuí.)
"Human feelings are not far apart;

If flogging must be used to demonstrate authority,

The Registrar retreated in shame.
Xiàngxiān once said to someone:
"Under heaven, there are originally no troubles;
it is only mediocre people who stir them up.
If one can clarify the source,
why worry about disorder not being governed!"

the seventh month,

Xiān,
(pronounced xījiàn.)
Dǎng,

Jiàng,
(pronounced jíliàng.)
Qí,

The Dǎngxiàng then turned to fight the Hú,

Yuè pacified and settled the Dǎngxiàng,

12 In the ninth month,
on the yǐsì day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
13 When Kāng Dàibīn rebelled,
an edict ordered Guō Zhīyùn to coordinate with Wáng Jùn in suppressing him;
Jùn submitted a memorial saying,
the Shuòfāng troops themselves had sufficient strength,
and requested an order for Zhīyùn to return to his own army.
Before a reply arrived,
Zhīyùn had already come,

Those whom Jùn had persuaded to surrender,
Zhīyùn again allowed his troops to attack them;

(Wáng Jùn's demotion in office,

On the 14th day (dingwei),
the Duke of Wénxiàn of Liáng, Yáo Chóng, passed away.
In his final instructions, he said:
"Buddhism takes purity and compassion as its foundation.
Yet foolish people copy scriptures and build statues,
hoping to seek blessings.
In the past, when the Northern Zhōu and Northern Qí divided the realm,
Zhōu destroyed scriptures and statues while strengthening its military,
while Qí revered pagodas and temples but neglected penal administration.
When they clashed in battle one day,
Qí perished and Zhōu prevailed.
More recently, the various Wǔ and Wéi clans
built monasteries and ordained people
beyond count,
yet it did not save them from clan extermination.
Do not imitate those childish people who remain unenlightened their whole lives,
performing posthumous rites to seek blessings in the afterlife!
Daoist priests, seeing monks gain benefits,
imitate their practices;
especially do not invite them into your homes.
This should forever serve as a model for later generations!"
On the 15th day (guǐhài),
Zhāng Yuè was appointed as Minister of War and given the additional title of Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn.
Commentary: The Cháoyě Qiānzǎi states:
"When Yuè was the Prefect of Bìngzhōu,
he flattered Wáng Máozhòng.
When Máozhòng inspected the border,
Yuè prepared a lavish feast at the Tiānbīng Army camp.
Suddenly an imperial edict arrived,
appointing him Minister of War and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Sānpǐn.
After expressing gratitude,
he embraced Máozhòng and danced,
kissing the tip of his boot."
This account is not adopted here.
In the winter,
the tenth month,
Guō Zhīyùn, the Military Commissioner-in-Chief of Héxī and Lǒngyòu, passed away.
Zhīyùn and
Wáng Jùnchuò, the Deputy Commander of the Right Guard from the same county,

and were feared by the barbarians.
Contemporaries referred to them as Wáng and Guō.
Jùnchuò then succeeded Zhīyùn as the Military Commissioner of Héxī and Lǒngyòu,
concurrently serving as the Governor of Liángzhōu.
In the eleventh month,
on the bǐngchén day,
Yuán Xíngchōng, the Director of the National University, presented the "Four Catalogs" of books:
the first part being the catalog of classics,
the second part the catalog of histories,
the third part the catalog of philosophical works,
and the fourth part the catalog of literary collections.
Commentary: The Jíxián Zhùjì places this in the spring of the ninth year.
Here, the Táng Lì, Tǒngjì, and Old Annals are followed.
On the gēngwǔ day,
a general amnesty was declared throughout the realm.
In the twelfth month,
on the yǐyǒu day,
the Emperor traveled to the hot springs at Líshān;
on the rénchén day,
he returned to the palace.
That year,
all the princes serving as military governors or prefects
