He was posthumously granted the title Crown Prince Huìwén.
The Emperor reduced his meals for several decades in mourning.
The officials submitted memorials urging him persistently,
and only then did he resume normalcy.
7 On the *dīnghài* day,
the Governor of Tàiyuán, Zhāng Xiàosōng, reported,
"There is a man named Lǐ Zǐqiáo,
who claims to be a royal prince,
saying he was born in Lùzhōu,
and his mother is named Zhào."
The Emperor ordered him beaten to death.
8 On the *xīnchǒu* day,
armies were established in Dìng, Héng, Mò, Yì, and Cāng prefectures to guard against the Turks.
The Běipíng Army was established in Dìngzhōu,
the Héngyáng Army in Héngzhōu,
the Tángxīng Army in Mòzhōu,
the Gāoyáng Army in Yìzhōu,
and the Hénghǎi Army in Cāngzhōu.
(Héng
is pronounced *hù dēng fān*.)
9 The Emperor wished to make Wǔ Huìguì his Empress.
Someone submitted a statement:
"The Wǔ clan are sworn enemies with whom one cannot share the same sky.
How can one of them be made the mother of the state!
People widely say that Zhāng Yuè seeks the merit of establishing an Empress,
to further his plan of returning to the Chancellorship.
Moreover, the Crown Prince is not born of Huìguì,
and she has her own sons.
If she ascends to the imperial position,
the Crown Prince will certainly be in danger."
The Emperor then desisted.
However, within the palace, her ceremonial rank
was entirely that of an Empress.
10 Fifth month,
on the *guǐmǎo* day,
the Ministry of Revenue reported that this year's households numbered 7,069,565,
and the population 41,419,712.
11 Autumn,
seventh month,
great floods occurred north and south of the Yellow River,
drowning thousands.
12 Eighth month,
on the *bǐngwǔ* day, the first day of the month,
Wèizhōu reported that the Yellow River had overflowed.
On the thirteenth day of the ninth month,
the day Jǐchǒu,
Dù Xiān, the Vice Grand Protector of Anxi and Military Commissioner of Qìxī, was appointed as a Tongpingzhangshi.
Qì
is pronounced qījì.
Xiān
is pronounced xīlián.
Since Wáng Xiàojié recaptured the Four Garrisons,
(The recapture of the Four Garrisons is recorded in the 205th scroll, in the first year of the Chángshòu era of Empress Wǔ.)
thirty thousand Táng troops were stationed there,
and the common people suffered from the burden of this service.
Among those who served as Protectors-General,
only Tián Yángmíng, Guō Yuánzhèn, Zhāng Sōng, and Dù Xiān implemented good governance,
and were praised by the people.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Gēngshēn,
the Emperor traveled to the Guǎngchéng Hot Springs in Rǔzhōu.
Examination of discrepancies: Lìnghú Huàn's "Veritable Records of Dàizōng" states:
"The Emperor was born on the thirteenth day of the tenth month in the fourteenth year of the Kāiyuán era.
At that time, Emperor Xuánzōng was at the hot springs in Rǔzhōu.
Someone who observed auras said
there was an imperial aura in the palace.
Emperor Xuánzōng returned to the palace that very day,
and that night Dàizōng was born."
According to the "Veritable Records of Xuánzōng,"
on the sixteenth day of this month, Gēngshēn, he first went to the hot springs,
and returned to the palace on Jǐsì,
which differs from the "Veritable Records of Dàizōng."
The old annals state
"he was born on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month."
The old biography of the Empress states:
"Empress Zhāngjìng, née Wú, was implicated in her father's case and entered the palace service.
In the twenty-third year of the Kāiyuán era,
Emperor Xuánzōng visited the residence of the Prince of Zhōng.
Seeing the prince's simple attire and surroundings,
with no attendants by his side,
he ordered General Gāo Lìshì to select women from the palace service to bestow upon him,
and Empress Wú was among those registered.
The following year,
she gave birth to Emperor Dàizōng,
and died in the eighteenth year."
According to this, Dàizōng was born this year,
yet it says Empress Wú was bestowed upon the Prince of Zhōng in the twenty-third year,
and died in the eighteenth year.
This is likely an error, taking the thirteenth year for the twenty-third.
"Old Stories from the Liǔ Family" states:
"While Sùzōng was Crown Prince, he was framed by Lǐ Línfǔ,
and his situation was precarious on several occasions.
Not long after,
his beard and temples turned grey.
Once, during an early morning audience,
the Emperor saw him
and said sadly: 'You return to your residence,
I will visit you.'
When the Emperor arrived,
he saw that the palace courtyards and halls were not swept clean,
musical instruments were covered in dust,
and there were no female entertainers among the attendants.
The Emperor was moved by this sight.
He ordered Gāo Lìshì to have the palace service check the registers and select three women,
whom he then bestowed upon the Crown Prince.
Empress Zhāngjìng, née Wú, was among those chosen,
and she gave birth to Dàizōng."
According to the records, in the twenty-third year of Kāiyuán,
Lǐ Línfǔ first became chancellor.
In the twenty-fifth year, Crown Prince Yīng was deposed.
In the twenty-sixth year, Sùzōng was established as Crown Prince.
In the fifth year of the Tiānbǎo era, Lǐ Línfǔ first instigated the case against Wéi Jiān.
The stories recorded in "Old Stories"
are all fictitious and exaggerated,
and the dates do not match.
The new history's biography of the Empress adopts them entirely,
but I do not adopt them here.
According to records, the Hàn dynasty Guǎngchéng Park was located within the boundaries of Liáng County, Rǔzhōu in the Táng,
and there were hot springs in that area.
On the day Jǐyǒu,
he returned to the palace.
In the twelfth month,
on the day Dīngsì,
the Emperor traveled to Shòu'ān
and hunted at Fāngxiù Chuān.
On the day Rénxū,
he returned to the palace.
Yáng Sīxù campaigned against rebellious Lǎo tribesmen,
capturing alive over three thousand people including Liáng Dàhǎi,
and beheading twenty thousand before returning.
This year,
the Hēishuǐ Mòhé sent an envoy for an audience.
(The Hēishuǐ Mòhé were southwest of the Liúguǐ state. The Nǚzhēn are their descendants.)
Mòhé
is pronounced mòhé.
Audience (jiàn)
is pronounced xiánbiàn.
A Chief Clerk was still appointed to govern them.
("Chief Clerk" (chángshǐ)
is probably an error for
"Chief Official" (chánglì).)
"Still appointed" (réng wèi)
is pronounced yú wèi fān.
Wǔyì, king of the Bóhǎi Mòhé, said:
"The Hēishuǐ route to the Táng passes through our territory.
Previously, we requested a Tudun from the Turks. (The Turks appointed Tuduns to lead the states that submitted to them.)
Tūjué
is pronounced jiǔ wù fān.
Now, without informing us, they requested officials from the Táng.
This must mean they have conspired with the Táng,
intending to attack us from both front and rear."
He sent his younger brother by the same mother, Ményì, and his maternal uncle Rèn Yǎ to lead troops to attack Hēishuǐ.
Ményì had once been a hostage in the Táng.
He remonstrated, saying:
"Hēishuǐ requested officials from the Táng,
and if we attack them for this reason,
it is rebellion against the Táng.
The Táng is a great power.
In the past, at the height of Gāolì's power,
with over three hundred thousand strong soldiers,
they defied Táng orders,
and were utterly wiped out. (Utterly wiped out means the state perished with no survivors. This is recorded in the annals of Tàizōng and Gāozōng.)
Lì
is pronounced lìzhī fān.
Once they became enemies with the Táng,
that was the situation leading to the destruction of their state."
Wǔyì did not listen
and forcibly sent him.
When Ményì reached the border,
he again sent a letter strenuously remonstrating.
Wǔyì became angry.
He sent his elder cousin Dàyīxià to replace him in commanding the army,
and summoned him, intending to kill him.
Ményì abandoned his troops
and fled by a side road to seek refuge.
An imperial decree appointed him as General of the Left Flank Guard.
Wǔyì sent an envoy presenting a memorial accusing Ményì of crimes,
requesting his execution.
The Emperor secretly sent Ményì to Ānxī.
He detained the envoy
and separately sent a reply stating
that Ményì had already been exiled to Lǐngnán.
When Wǔyì found out,
he submitted a memorial stating,
"A great power should demonstrate trustworthiness to others. How can it engage in such deception?"
He firmly requested Ményì's execution.
The Emperor, because Hónglú Junior Minister Lǐ Dàosuì and Yuán Fù failed to supervise their subordinates effectively,
resulting in a leak,
demoted them both. (The Táng had nine courts, each with two Junior Ministers. The Hónglú Court was in charge of guests from the four barbarians, hence leaking information was considered a crime.)
Lú
is pronounced língrú fān.
Junior Minister (shǎoqīng)
is pronounced shǐzhào fān.
Your servant Guāng remarks: What allows a sovereign to subdue the four barbarians
is nothing but prestige and trustworthiness.
Ményì, having been loyal, incurred a crime
and sought refuge with the Son of Heaven.
The Son of Heaven should have investigated the right and wrong of the matter,
rewarding Ményì and punishing Wǔyì. That is the proper way of governance.
Even if he could not launch a punitive expedition,
he should still have righteously informed Wǔyì that Ményì was not guilty.
Now, Emperor Mínghuáng's might could not subdue Wǔyì,
and his grace could not protect Ményì.
Instead, he imitated petty men, using deceptive words and thus becoming embarrassed by a small state.
Then he punished the Hónglú officials for the leak.
Is this not shameful indeed!
18. Dù Xiān served as Protector-General of Ānxī.
The Tūqíshī's Jiāohé Princess dispatched a Yá official with a thousand horses to Ānxī for trade.
The envoy conveyed the princess's instruction.
Dù Xiān angrily said:
"The daughter of Āshǐnà,
the Jiāohé Princess,
is the daughter of Āshǐnà Huáidào.
He caned her envoy,
detained him and did not send him back;
the horses all died from exposure in the snow.
The Tūqíshī Khagan Sūlù was greatly enraged,
and sent troops to raid the Four Garrisons.
At that time, Dù Xiān had entered the court,
(Note: shǐ,
read as shū lì fān.)
(Note: cháo,
read as zhí yáo fān;
same below.)
They defended the city walls and held their ground;
the people, livestock, and stored provisions of the Four Garrisons
were all plundered by Sūlù,
and only Ānxī remained.
Later, when Sūlù heard that Dù Xiān had entered the government as chancellor,
he gradually withdrew his troops,
and soon sent an envoy to present tribute.
1. In spring,
the first month,
on Xīnchǒu,
Liángzhōu Commander Wáng Jūn'ào defeated Tǔbō west of Qīnghǎi.
Initially,
Tǔbō, relying on its strength,
sent letters using the etiquette of an equal state,
(see events in the second year of the 211th scroll).
The Emperor was often angered by this.
Upon returning from the eastern fēng sacrifice,
Zhāng Yuè said to the Emperor:
"Tǔbō is disrespectful,
they truly deserve to be punished and eliminated,
but we have been at war for over ten years,
Gān, Liáng, Hé, and Shàn
cannot bear the hardship,
although our armies have repeatedly been victorious,
what we gain does not compensate for what we lose.
I hear they regret their faults and seek peace,
I wish you would allow them to submit sincerely,
to relieve the border people."
The Emperor said:
"Wait until I discuss it with Wáng Jūn'ào."
After Zhāng Yuè withdrew,
he said to Yuán Qiányào:
"Jūn'ào is brave but lacks strategy,
he often thinks of achieving success by luck,
if the two states make peace through marriage alliance,
how can he achieve merit!
My words will certainly not be heeded."
When Jūn'ào entered the court,
he indeed requested to launch a deep campaign against them.
Last winter,
the Tǔbō general Xīnuòluó raided Dàdǒu Valley,
attacked Gānzhōu,
burned and plundered before leaving.
Jūn'ào estimated that their troops were weary,
led troops to follow them closely,
there was heavy snow,
many of the enemy froze to death,
and they returned west from the Jīshí Army.
West of Dáhuà County in Kuòzhōu was the Jīshí Army,
originally the Jìngbiān Garrison,
established as an army in the second year of Yífèng,
east of it was the Huángshā Garrison.
'Ào'
burned the grass along the road.
When Xīnuòluó reached Dàfēi River,
wanting to rest the soldiers and horses,
but the wild grass was all gone,
over half of the horses died.
Jūn'ào and Qínzhōu Commander Zhāng Jǐngshùn pursued them,
caught up with them west of Qīnghǎi,
and crossed over the ice.
Xīnuòluó had already left,
they defeated his rear army,
capturing his baggage train, sheep, and horses by the tens of thousands before returning.
Jūn'ào was promoted to Left Yǔlín Grand General for his merit,
and his father Shòu was appointed as Junior Supervisor of the Imperial Workshops and retired.
The Emperor from then on increasingly pursued military achievements on the borders.
2. Initially,
a man from Luòyáng named Liú Zōngqì submitted a memorial,
requesting to block the old Biàn estuary at Sìshuǐ,
and instead divert the Huáng River into the Biàn at Yíngzé;
(In the fourth year of Suí Kāihuáng, Guǎngwǔ County was established from part of Xíngyáng,
renamed Yíngzé in the first year of Rénshòu,
belonging to Zhèngzhōu.)
(Note: shàng,
read as shí zhǎng fān.)
(Note: sāi,
read as xī zé fān;
same below.)
(Note: sì,
read as sì.)
(Note: biàn,
read as pí biàn fān.)
By this time,
the new canal was silted up and impassable,
Liú Zōngqì was demoted to commander of the Ānhuái garrison in Xúnzhōu.
The Emperor ordered the Grand Artisan Fàn Ānjí to mobilize thirty thousand people from Hénán, Huái, Zhèng, Biàn, Huá, and Wèi to dredge the old canal,
which was completed in ten days.
3. The Censor-in-chief Cuī Yǐnfǔ and Vice Censor-in-chief Yǔwén Róng,
fearing that Right Chancellor Zhāng Yuè would be reappointed,
repeatedly submitted memorials slandering him,
each forming factions.
The Emperor disliked this,
in the second month,
on Yǐsì,
he issued an edict ordering Yuè to retire,
Yǐnfǔ was dismissed from office to serve his mother,
and Róng was sent out to serve as Prefect of Wèizhōu.
4. On Yǐmǎo,
an edict was issued:
"For households that flee from various prefectures,
after having been registered and assessed by the Encouragement of Agriculture Commissioner, if there are further fugitives,
upon arrival they shall pay the annual taxes and corvée according to the standard for commoners,
and those liable for military service shall be conscripted first."
5. In summer,
the fifth month,
on Guǐyǒu,

the Emperor appointed all his sons, such as Prince Qìng Lǐ Tán, to concurrently hold the titles of Regional Governor, Prefect, Commander, Military Commissioner, Grand Protector, and Pacification Commissioner,
but they did not actually leave the capital.
Initially,
Tàizōng favored Prince Jìn,
Prince Jìn Lǐ Zhì,
who later became Gāozōng.
Prince Yù also, as Wǔ Hòu's youngest son, did not leave the palace,
and only after being demoted from Crown Prince to Prince Xiàng did he leave the palace.
(Note: chū gé.)
During Zhōngzōng's reign,
Prince Qiáo lost favor,
and was exiled to an outer prefecture;
Prince Wēn was seventeen years old,
yet still resided within the palace.
(Prince Qiáo,
was Lǐ Chóngfú.
Prince Wēn,
was Lǐ Chóngmào.)
Attached to the palace garden wall was the Ten Princes Residence,
on the fifth street east of Zhūquè Street was Ānguó Temple,
east of the temple, attached to the palace garden wall was a large residence,
divided to accommodate ten princes.
(The ten princes
refer to Qìng, Zhōng, Dì, È, Róng, Yí, Tái, Yǐng, Yǒng, and Jì.)
Later, Princes Shèng, Shòu, Chén, Fēng, Cháng, and Liáng, upon receiving their fiefs, also moved into this inner residence,
making it the Sixteen Princes Residence.
Eunuchs supervised them,
they went through the double walls to pay respects,
and from then on they did not leave the palace again;
although they established princely establishments with officials and held regional military commands,
only the Lecturers entered at times to teach,
the other princely establishment officials
only exchanged greetings and paid respects during festivals;
the officials of their regional commands
did not even exchange greetings.
As the grandsons gradually increased in number,
the Hundred Grandsons Compound was also established.
The Crown Prince also did not reside in the Eastern Palace,
but often stayed in a separate courtyard where the imperial carriage happened to be.
6. The Emperor ordered palace ladies and below to raise silkworms in the palace,
wanting them to understand women's work.
On Dīngyǒu,
the summer solstice,
he bestowed silk upon the noble and close officials,
each person one bundle.
(Dù Yòu said: According to Táng regulations,
six liǎng of silk constituted a bundle,
five liǎng of silk constituted a skein,
three jīn of hemp constituted a bundle.
It is unknown how heavy a silk bundle was.)
(Note: lì,
read as láng jì fān.)
7. In autumn,
the seventh month,
on Wùyín,
the Huáng River overflowed in Jìzhōu.
8. On Jǐmǎo,
the Minister of Rites, Duke Wénxiàn of Xǔ, Sū Tǐng, passed away.
9 In the ninth month,
on the day Bǐngzǐ,
the Tibetan general Xìnuóluó Gōnglù and Zhúlóng Mǎngbùzhī captured Guāzhōu,
seizing Prefect Tián Yuánxiàn and the father of Héxī Jédùshǐ Wáng Jūnchuò,
and advanced to attack the Yùmén Army.
Note: Wáng Jūnchuò's father, Shòu, had retired as a Junior Palace Steward and was living in his hometown.
The Yùmén Army was located two hundred lǐ west of Sùzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Xīmén County in Sùzhōu
was where the Hàn dynasty abolished the garrison at Yùmén Pass
and relocated its people here,
hence it was called Yùmén County.
The stone gate was surrounded by mountains,
spanning twenty lǐ,
with numerous streams flowing north into Yánxīng Sea.
They sent him back to Liángzhōu,
saying to Wáng Jūnchuò:
"General, you have always pledged loyalty and courage to the state,
why not fight a battle!"
Wáng Jūnchuò ascended the city wall, looked west, and wept,
but ultimately did not dare to send out troops.
Meanwhile, Mǎngbùzhī separately attacked Chánglè County.
Sòng Bái said: Chánglè County belonged to Guāzhōu,
originally the Wèi dynasty's Yíhé Commandery,
and the territory of the Former Liáng's Liángxīng County.
Liáng Wǔzhāowáng established the Chánglè Garrison east of Sānwēi Mountain,
and in the fifth year of the Táng dynasty's Wǔdé era, it was changed to Chánglè County.
After Guāzhōu fell,
Xìnuóluó gathered all his troops to join the attack.
After more than ten days,
the Tibetans exhausted their strength,
unable to capture it,
they sent someone to persuade them to surrender;
they refused.
The Tibetans said:
"Since the magistrate will not surrender,
you should gather the wealth in the city as a gift to us,
and we will withdraw."
Jiǎ Shīshùn asked to strip the soldiers of their clothes;
Xìnuóluó realized there was no wealth,
so he led his troops away,
destroying the walls of Guāzhōu.
Jiǎ Shīshùn quickly opened the gates,
collected weapons,
and repaired the defenses;
the barbarians indeed sent elite cavalry back,
observed the city,
saw there were preparations,
and then left.
Tián Yuánxiàn could not hold Guāzhōu, but Jiǎ Shīshùn could hold Chánglè,
truly, the security of a region depends on the person in charge.
Fù,
pronounced fú yòu fān.
Chān,
pronounced chǒu lián fān,
also chǒu yàn fān.
He was from Qízhōu.
10 Earlier,
when the Türk Mòchuò was powerful,
he seized the lands of the Tiělè,
so the four tribes of Huíhé, Qìbì, Sījié, and Hún crossed the desert and moved to live between Gānzhōu and Liángzhōu to avoid him.
When Wáng Jūnchuò was still obscure,
he traveled among the four tribes,
and was looked down upon by them;
after becoming Héxī Jédùshǐ,
he disciplined them with the law.
The four tribes felt humiliated and resentful,
and secretly sent envoys to the Eastern Capital to plead their case.
Wáng Jūnchuò hastily sent a courier to report
"the four tribes are difficult to control,
and secretly plan to rebel."
The emperor sent a palace envoy to investigate,
but the tribes ultimately did not receive justice.
As a result, the Grand Governor of Hànhǎi, Huíhé Chéngzōng, was exiled to Rángzhōu,
Hún Dàdé was exiled to Jízhōu,
and Hèlán Dūdū Qìbì Chéngmíng was exiled to Téngzhōu.
Téngzhōu
was the territory of the Hàn dynasty's Cāngwú and Měnglíng Counties,
the Jìn dynasty established Yǒngpíng Commandery,
and the Suí dynasty established Téngzhōu.
Huíhé Fúdìnán was appointed as Grand Governor of Hànhǎi.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
Right Sanqí Chángshì Lǐ Lìngwèn was demoted to Fǔzhōu Biéjià.
Old records: Fǔzhōu
was 3,312 lǐ southeast of the capital.
11 On the day Bǐngxū,
the Türk Bìjiā Kèhán sent his minister Méilù Chuò to present tribute.
When the Tibetans invaded Guāzhōu,
they sent a letter to Bìjiā,
wanting to join him in the invasion,
but Bìjiā presented the letter to the court.
The emperor praised him,
allowing trade at the Western Shòuxiáng City,
each year bringing several hundred thousand bolts of silk to trade for warhorses,
to aid the military,
and also to serve as breeding stock for the imperial pastures,
from then on the state's horses became even stronger.
12 In the intercalary month,
on the day Gēngzǐ,
the Tibetan Tsanpo and the Türgesh Sūlù besieged Ānxī City,
but Ānxī Deputy Grand Protector Zhào Yízhēn repelled them.
13 Huíhé Chéngzōng's clansman, Hànhǎi Sima Hùshū,
gathered a group to avenge Chéngzōng.
At that time, the Tibetans sent envoys via a side route to the Türks,
and Wáng Jūnchuò led elite cavalry to intercept them at Sùzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: In the first year of the Suí dynasty's Rénshòu era, Sùzhōu was established by dividing Fúlù County of Gānzhōu.
It was two hundred lǐ southeast to Chìliǔjiān in Gānzhōu,
and three hundred forty lǐ southwest to the Ānlè Beacon at the border of Guāzhōu.
At Gǒngbǐ Station south of Gānzhōu,
Hùshū's ambush suddenly emerged,
seized Wáng Jūnchuò's insignia and tally,
first killed his administrative assistant Sòng Zhēn,
cut out his heart and said:
"You were the one who started the plot."
Wáng Jūnchuò led several dozen of his men in fierce combat,
from morning until late afternoon,
until all his men were dead.
Hùshū killed Wáng Jūnchuò,
loaded his corpse and fled toward Tibet;
Liángzhōu troops caught up with them,
and Hùshū abandoned the corpse and escaped.
Examination of discrepancies: The Old Biography says:
"After the Huíhé killed Wáng Jūnchuò,
the emperor ordered Guō Zhīyùn to pursue and expel them."
But note: Guō Zhīyùn had already died in the ninth year,
and Wáng Jūnchuò succeeded him as commander of Liángzhōu;
the Old Biography is mistaken.
14 On the day Gēngshēn,
the imperial carriage departed from the Eastern Capital,
in winter,
on the day Jǐmǎo,
arrived at the Western Capital.
The character "winter"
below is missing
the two characters "tenth month"
15 On the day Xīnsì,
Left Jīnyùwèi Dàjiāngjūn Xìn'ānwáng Lǐ Wěi was appointed as Deputy Grand Envoy of Shuòfāng Jédùshǐ.
Lǐ Wěi
was the grandson of Lǐ Kè.
Wúwáng Lǐ Kè
was the son of Tàizōng.
Wěi,
pronounced xū wéi fān.
At that time, Wáng Jūnchuò had just been defeated,
and Hézhōu and Lǒng were in shock and fear.
Xiāo Sōng appointed Xíngbù Yuánwàiláng Péi Kuān as administrative assistant,
and together with Wáng Jūnchuò's former assistant Niú Xiānkè, they managed military affairs,
and people's hearts gradually calmed.
Péi Kuān
was the younger cousin of Péi Cuǐ.
Niú Xiānkè was originally a minor clerk from Chúngū.
Chúngū County
belonged to the Hàn dynasty's Běidì Commandery,
and to the Later Hàn and Jìn dynasties' Āndìng Commandery.
The Later Wèi established Zhàopíng Commandery,
the Later Zhōu abolished the commandery,
and the county was placed under Jīngzhōu.
Liú Xù said: The Jédùshǐ had two administrative assistants,
but their rank was not specified.
Chún,
pronounced rú lún fān.
Gū,
pronounced gōng hū fān.
He was Wáng Jūnchuò's trusted confidant.
Xiāo Sōng also recommended Jiànkāng Army Commander Héběi's Zhāng Shǒuguī as Guāzhōu Prefect.
Northwest of Gānzhōu, one hundred ninety lǐ at Qílián Mountain, was the Jiànkāng Army.
Héběi County belonged to Shǎnzhōu.
The wooden frames for the walls had just been erected,
as the poem says: "They bound the frames to carry earth."
The frames were placed on both sides,
with earth packed between them and tamped down.
Gàn,
also refers to planks.
Kǒng Ānguó said: The sides are called gàn.
Shuài,
pronounced shuài.
The people in the city looked at each other, pale-faced,
with no will to fight.
Zhāng Shǒuguī said:
"They are many, we are few,
and we are still recovering from wounds,
we cannot engage them with weapons,
we must use a clever plan to win."
So he set up wine and music on the city walls.
The barbarians suspected there were preparations,
and did not dare to attack but withdrew.
Zhāng Shǒuguī then sent out troops to attack them,
and the barbarians fled in defeat.
Zhāng Shǒuguī then repaired the city walls and markets,
gathered the scattered people,
and all returned to their former occupations.
The court praised his achievements,
made Guāzhōu a Dūdūfǔ,
and appointed Zhāng Shǒuguī as Dūdū.
Xìnuóluó's prestige was very high,
so Xiāo Sōng spread disinformation among the Tibetans,
saying he had secretly communicated with the Central Kingdom,
and the Tsanpo summoned and executed him;
from then on, Tibet declined somewhat.
On the 16th day of the 12th month,
the day Wùyín,
an edict was issued, considering Tǔbō as a border threat.
It ordered the Lǒngyòu Circuit and various armies to muster 56,000 troops,
and the Héxī Circuit and various armies to muster 40,000 troops.
The Fǔbīng system was abolished,
and a comprehensive law was implemented to organize local militia,
which was called
"Tuánbīng" (organized militia).
Ten thousand troops from Shuòfāng assembled at Huìzhōu for autumn defense.
By early winter,
as there was no invasion, they were disbanded.
They would wait for the enemy to invade,
then coordinate attacks from both front and rear.
On the 17th day, the day Yǐhài,
the Emperor visited the hot springs at Líshān;
on the day Bǐngxū,
he returned to the palace.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day Rényín,
the Deputy Grand Protector-General of Ānxī, Zhào Yízhēn, defeated Tǔbō at Qǔzǐchéng.
2 On the day Jiǎyín,
Yǔwén Róng, the Prefect of Wèizhōu, was appointed as Vice Minister of Revenue and concurrently Prefect of Wèizhōu,
serving as the Pacification Commissioner of the Héběi Circuit.
The position of Pacification Commissioner began here.
Commissioner,
read as shǐ;
the same below.
3 On the day Yǐmǎo,
the Lǎo people of Chūn, Shuāng, and other prefectures, Chén Xíngfàn, Féng Lín of Guǎngzhōu, and Hé Yóulǔ rebelled,
capturing over forty cities.
Xíngfàn proclaimed himself Emperor,
Yóulǔ proclaimed himself Grand General Who Stabilizes the State,
and Lín proclaimed himself King of Nányuè,
intending to occupy the region south of the Five Ridges.
The Emperor ordered the Palace Attendant Yáng Sīxù to mobilize troops from Guìzhōu and nearby areas north of the ridges to suppress them.
4 On the day Bǐngyín,
Yǔwén Róng, Prefect of Wèizhōu, was appointed as Acting Prefect of Biànzhōu,
serving as the Commissioner for Canals, Dikes, and Breaches of the Nine Rivers in the Hénán and Héběi regions.
Róng proposed using the old courses of the Nine Rivers from the Yǔ Gòng to open paddy fields,
and to exchange funds for land transport,
with the government collecting the profits.
However, construction projects were incessant,
and most endeavors were unsuccessful.
5 In the second month,
on the day Rénshēn,
the retired Right Chancellor of the Department of State Affairs, Zhāng Yuè, was appointed concurrently as Academician of the Jíxián Hall.
Although Yuè had retired from political affairs,
he devoted himself to literary and historical duties.
Whenever the court faced major issues,
the Emperor often sent palace eunuchs to consult him.
The history records that Zhāng Yuè's favor and regard never waned.
Shàng,
read as chángyáng.
Xiàng,
read as xīliàng.
Yuè,
read as yuè.
Shǐ,
read as shǐ.
6 On the day Rénchén,
the Guōqí were renamed the Left and Right Yǔlín Army Flying Cavalry.
The Guōqí are mentioned in the 13th year of the previous scroll.
Guō,
read as xūguō,
also as gǔguō.
Qí,
read as qíjì.
7 In autumn,
the seventh month,
the Tǔbō general Xīmòlǎng invaded Guāzhōu.
Tǔ,
read as tǔ.
Jiàng,
read as jíliàng.
On the day Yǐsì,
the Héxī Military Commissioner Xiāo Sōng and the Lǒngyòu Military Commissioner Zhāng Zhōngliàng heavily defeated Tǔbō at Kěbō Gǔ.
According to the New Book's Tǔbō Biography,
Kěbō Gǔ should be west of Qīnghǎi.
An examination of discrepancies: The Veritable Records, Táng Calendar, and Xiāo Sōng's biography record
"Zhāng Zhìliàng."
Here, the Old Basic Annals and Tǔbō Biography are followed.
They captured the Dà Mòmén Fortress,
located in the Jiǔqū region.
They burned the Luòtuó Bridge and returned.
8 In the eighth month,
on the day Yǐsì,
the Specially Advanced official Zhāng Yuè presented the Kāiyuán Dàyǎn Calendar,
which was put into use.
The monk Yīxíng deduced the Dàyǎn numbers to establish the method,
responding to solar terms, lunar phases, and solar eclipses to create the new calendar,
hence it was called the Dàyǎn Calendar.
Shàng,
read as shízhǎng.
9 On the day Xīnmǎo,
the Left Jīnyú General Dù Bīnkè defeated Tǔbō at the foot of Qílián Fortress.
Qílián Fortress is at Qílián Mountain in Zhāngyè County, Gānzhōu.
Xiāo Sōng sent Bīnkè with four thousand crossbowmen to attack.
The battle lasted from morning until dusk,
and Tǔbō suffered a major rout,
with one of their generals captured.
The enemy scattered and fled into the mountains,
their cries echoing from all directions.
10 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Jǐmǎo,
the Emperor visited the hot springs at Líshān;
on the day Jǐchǒu,
he returned to the palace.
An examination of discrepancies: The Veritable Records state
"the 12th month, day Dīngmǎo."
It also says
"visited the hot springs palace."
It does not mention his return.
The Táng Calendar records,
"On Dīngmǎo, visited the hot springs;
on Dīngchǒu, returned to the palace."
Considering that he had already visited the hot springs this month,
it is likely a repetition,
and is not adopted here.
11 In the 11th month,
on the day Guǐsì,
the Deputy Grand Envoy of the Héxī Military Commission, Xiāo Sōng, was appointed as Minister of War and Participant in Determining Government Matters.
12 In the 12th month,
on the day Bǐngyín,
an edict was issued:
"Long-term conscripts have no fixed return date,
which is hard for people to bear.
They should be divided into five rotations,
with one rotation sent home each year to rest and bathe,
and after five years, they will be rewarded with five promotions."
13 This year,
a regulation was issued that household registrations be fixed every three years,
divided into nine grades.
14 Yáng Sīxù campaigned against Chén Xíngfàn.
Upon reaching Shuāngzhōu,
he defeated them,
capturing Hé Yóulǔ and Féng Lín.
Xíngfàn fled to the Yúnjì and Pánliáo caves.
Sīxù pursued and captured him,
eventually taking him alive,
and executed him.
In total, sixty thousand heads were taken.
Sīxù was a strict person;
his subordinate officers reporting to him dared not look up,
so his military campaigns were always successful.
However, he was cruel and ruthless.
The prisoners he captured
sometimes had their faces skinned alive,
or their scalps torn off by cutting along the hairline with a knife.
He would rip off their scalps;
the barbarians feared him.
1 In spring,
the second month,
on the day Dīngmǎo,
the Military Commissioner of Xīzhōu, Zhāng Shǒusù,
defeated the southwestern barbarians,
capturing Kūnmíng and Yánchéng.
Kūnmíng County belonged to Xīzhōu.
It was the territory of the Hàn Dynasty's Dìngzuò County.
In the Later Zhōu, the Dìngzuò Garrison was established.
In the second year of the Wǔdé era, it was renamed Kūnmíng County,
because its location connected to Kūnmíng.
The county had salt and iron resources,
and a city was built to protect them,
hence there was also Yánchéng.
Xī,
read as suǐ.
2 In the third month,
the Military Commissioner of Guāzhōu, Zhāng Shǒuguī, and the Prefect of Shāzhōu, Jiǎ Shīshùn, attacked the Tǔbō army at Dàtóng,
and heavily defeated them.
3 On the day Jiǎyín,
Xìn'ān Wáng Lǐ Tí, the military governor of Shuòfāng, attacked the Tibetan fortress of Shíbǎo Chéng,
and captured it.
Earlier,
the Tibetans had captured Shíbǎo Chéng,
left troops to hold it,
and used it to raid and harass the region west of the Yellow River.
The Emperor ordered Lǐ Tí to consult with the commanders of Héxī and Lǒngyòu on plans to attack and seize it.
All the generals believed that Shíbǎo Chéng was situated in a perilous location with a long and difficult approach,
and that if the attack failed,
they would have no way to return safely.
They suggested it was better to hold their troops and watch for an opportunity.
Lǐ Tí did not listen.
He led his troops deep into enemy territory,
launched a fierce assault and captured it.
He then
deployed troops to hold the strategic points,
preventing the enemy from advancing.
From then on, the armies of Hé-Lǒng conducted patrols,
expanding the frontier by over a thousand *li*.
When the Emperor heard this,
he was greatly pleased,
and renamed Shíbǎo Chéng as Zhènwǔ Jūn.
From Héyuán Jūn in Shànchéng County of Shànzhōu, traveling 120 *li* west leads to Báishuǐ Jūn,
another 60 *li* southwest to Dìngróng Chéng,
and another 7 *li* south across a stream is Shíbǎo Chéng,
originally the Tibetan fortress of Tiě Rèn Chéng.
Sòng Bái said: Shíbǎo Chéng lies west of Lóngzhī County,
with cliffs thousands of *ren* high on all sides,
a winding stone path,
three or four *li* long,
and thirty *li* west to Chì Lǐng.
Gēng,
pronounced as *gēng*, *héng*.
4 On the day Bǐngchén,
the Director of the Imperial Academy, Yáng Yáng, submitted a memorial stating,
believing that:
"The relevant ministry proposes to limit the number of successful candidates in the *míngjīng* and *jìnshì* examinations nationwide,
to no more than one hundred per year.
I have observed that those entering official service through the 'flowing out' (*liúwài*) channel [non-examination recruitment]
number over two thousand each year,
while the *míngjīng* and *jìnshì* candidates do not constitute even one-tenth of that.
This means that scholars who diligently pursue the Way and its studies are not as successful in obtaining office as clerks and minor officials.
I fear that Confucian customs will gradually decline,
and a sense of integrity and shame will daily diminish.
If it is considered that too many people are entering official service,
then reductions should be made across all categories,
and not solely suppressing the *míngjīng* and *jìnshì* paths."
He also memorialized
that "the various
departments, when testing *míngjīng* candidates by 'filling in the blanks' (*tiě*),
do not focus on seeking the main ideas of the classics and their commentaries,
but instead specialize in selecting obscure and difficult points,
asking about isolated passages, disconnected sentences, or specific years, months, and days;
I request that from now on, only straightforward passages be used for the *tiě* test."
The Táng dynasty's categories for selecting scholars
included the *jìnshì*
and the *míngjīng*.
For the *míngjīng* examination,
first came the *tiěwén* (fill-in-the-blanks test on the classics),
then an oral examination on the general meaning of ten passages from the classics,
and answering three policy questions on contemporary affairs;
candidates were graded on the thoroughness and coarseness of their literary reasoning into the categories of top superior, superior middle, superior inferior, and middle superior,
with these four grades considered as having passed (*jídì*).
For the *jìnshì* examination,
candidates answered five policy questions on contemporary affairs,
and took one *tiě* test on a major classic;
complete mastery of both the classic and the policy questions resulted in a first-class (*jiǎ*) pass,
while passing four policy questions and correctly filling four or more blanks in the *tiě* test resulted in a second-class (*yǐ*) pass.
The *Tōngdiǎn* states: Under the Táng system,
for the *tiějīng* (fill-in-the-blanks on classics) test,
the examined classic was covered at both ends,
leaving only a single line exposed in the middle,
a piece of paper was cut to cover three characters,
generally three characters were covered,
the number could vary,
the pass/fail standard was not uniform,
sometimes getting four, five, or six correct was considered a pass.
5 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day Gēngwǔ,
the Dì sacrifice was performed at the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
In the early Táng,
during the Xiá sacrifice, ancestors were arranged in order of generations (Zhāo-Mù),
while during the Dì sacrifice, each was worshipped separately in their own chamber.
At this time,
the Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, Wéi Tāo, and others memorialized,
"If this is the case,
the Dì sacrifice is no different from a regular offering;
we request that for both the Dì and Xiá sacrifices, ancestors be arranged in Zhāo-Mù order."
This was approved.
Tāo
was the son of Wéi Ānshí's elder brother.
6 In the fifth month,
on the day Rénchén,
the ten circuits and the two metropolitan area surveillance commissioners for the capital and eastern capital were re-established.
Yōng, Tóng, Huá, Shāng, Qí, and Bīn constituted the capital metropolitan area,
Luò and Rǔ constituted the eastern capital metropolitan area.
In the 12th year [of the Kāiyuán era],
the surveillance commissioners for the various circuits were abolished,
now they were re-established.
Fù (復),
pronounced *fù*, *yòu fān*,
or as the character's usual reading.
7 Earlier,
Zhāng Yuè, Zhāng Jiāzhēn, Lǐ Yuánhóng, and Dù Xiān successively served as chief ministers wielding power,
while Yuán Qiányào maintained himself with purity and caution,
often deferring matters to Yuè and the others,
merely assenting and adding his signature.
Yuánhóng and Xiān often disagreed in their deliberations,
leading to a rift between them,
and they submitted mutual accusations.
The Emperor was displeased.
In the sixth month,
on the day Jiǎxū,
he demoted the Vice Director of the Chancellery and concurrent *Tóng Píngzhāng Shì* Dù Xiān to be the Senior Administrator of Jīngzhōu,
and the Vice Director of the Secretariat and concurrent *Tóng Píngzhāng Shì* Lǐ Yuánhóng to be the Prefect of Cáozhōu.
According to old records,
Cáozhōu
was 1,453 *li* northeast of the capital.
[Yuán Qiányào] was made only Left Chief Minister;
in the early Kāiyuán era,
the Left and Right Vice Directors of the Department of State Affairs were renamed Left and Right Chief Ministers.
In the early Táng,
the Vice Directors of the Department of State Affairs oversaw all matters without exception,
they were the true chief ministers.
By the first year of the Shénlóng era of Emperor Zhōngzōng, when Dòulú Qīnwàng solely held the post of Vice Director,
he did not dare participate in government affairs,
thereafter, those solely appointed as Vice Directors no longer participated in policy-making,
although they bore the title of Chief Minister,
it was no longer the function of the early Táng chief minister.
Now Yuán Qiányào was made only Left Chief Minister,
meaning he was only the Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs,
and no longer participated in policy-making.
The Vice Minister of War Péi Guāngtíng was made Vice Director of the Secretariat,
and concurrently *Tóng Píngzhāng Shì*;
Xiāo Sōng was made concurrent Director of the Secretariat,
and held the remote command of Héxī.
He held the remote command of the military governor of Héxī.
8 The Palace Attendant-in-ordinary Wáng Máozhòng became related by marriage to the Longwu General Gé Fúshùn.
Máozhòng was trusted by the Emperor,
and his advice was always followed,
therefore many of the generals of the Northern Gate (imperial guards) attached themselves to him,
their promotions and demotions were solely at his direction.
The Vice Minister of Personnel, Qí Huàn, seized an opportunity to speak to the Emperor, saying:
"Fúshùn commands the imperial guards,
what Gé Fúshùn commands
is the Wànqí (Ten Thousand Cavalry),
hence this statement.
Máozhòng is a petty man,
excessive favor will breed treachery;
if you do not deal with this early,
I fear it will become a future calamity."
The Emperor, pleased, said:
"I know you are loyal and sincere,
I will gradually consider what is appropriate."
Huàn said:
"If the ruler is not discreet, he will lose his ministers,"
a saying from the Great Commentary of the *Yì* (Book of Changes).
It happened that the Assistant Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, Má Chá, was demoted for an offense to be the Vice Prefect of Xīngzhōu.
According to old records,
Xīngzhōu was 948 *li* from the capital.
[Qí Huàn] went outside the city to see him off,
and during this, recounted the admonishing words he had spoken in the palace;
Chá was by nature frivolous and treacherous,
and promptly reported it.
The Emperor was angry,
summoned Huàn and reprimanded him, saying:
"You doubted my discretion,
yet you spoke of it to Má Chá,
how could that be considered discreet?
Moreover, Chá has always been without virtue,
how could you not know this?"
Huàn kowtowed in apology.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the day Dīngsì,
an edict was issued:
"Huàn and Chá colluded to sow discord among generals and ministers,
and alienated ruler and subject.
Huàn is to be made Assistant Magistrate of Liángdé in Gāozhōu,
Chá is to be made Defender of Huánghuà in Xúnzhōu."
Liángdé was also located in the territory of the Hàn dynasty's Hépǔ County,
the Wú established the Gāoliáng Commandery there,
the Chén dynasty partitioned it and established Wùdé County,
later changed to Liángdé.
Xúnzhōu,
was in the territory of the Hàn dynasty's Bùshān and Ēlín counties.
The Liáng dynasty established the Guìpíng Commandery at Bùshān,
the Suì abolished the commandery and made it a county,
and also established Huánghuà County at Ēlín,
the Suì abolished it and merged it into Guìpíng.
In the 7th year of the Zhēnguàn era, Xúnzhōu was established,
with its seat at Guìpíng,
and Huánghuà County was re-established and placed under its jurisdiction.
9 In the eighth month,
on Guǐhài day,
the Emperor held a banquet for all officials at the Huā'è Pavilion to celebrate his birthday.
Examination of Discrepancies states: The Veritable Records say,
"Guǐhài was the first day of the month."
According to the perpetual calendar,
the first day of this month was Jǐwèi;
Guǐhài
was the fifth day.
Gù Kuàng's song says:
"On the fifth night of the eighth month, auspicious airs are fresh,
Zhāochéng Empress Dowager gave birth to a sage."
The Veritable Records are in error.
It was requested that the fifth day of the eighth month each year be designated as the Qiānqiū Festival,
proclaimed throughout the land,
and all were ordered to feast and make merry.
The practice of bestowing banquets on the imperial birthday began from this.
Later, the Qiānqiū Festival was changed to the Tiāncháng Festival.
Emperors Dézōng, Shùnzōng, Xiànzōng, and Mùzōng did not establish festival names.
Order,
read as lìng, with the initial "l" and the final "ing".
Music/joy,
read as luò.
Since ancient times,
the Shè sacrifice has been performed on Wù days.
10 On Gēngchén day,
the Minister of Works Zhāng Jiāzhēn passed away.
Jiāzhēn did not accumulate family property.
When someone urged him to purchase fields and residences,
Jiāzhēn said:
"I am honored to be a general and minister,
why should I worry about cold and hunger!
If I were to incur guilt,
even if I had fields and residences,
they would be of no use.
Recently I have seen court officials extensively occupying good fields;
upon their death,
these merely become resources for their unworthy sons and brothers to indulge in wine and women.
I do not adopt such a practice."
Those who heard this considered him right.
11 On Xīnsì day,
an edict was issued because many among the people were illicitly minting coins,
beginning the prohibition of private sales of copper, lead, tin, and the use of copper for utensils;
those who mined copper, lead, and tin
must sell them to the government.
12 Yǔwén Róng was by nature astute and quick-witted,
adept in response and debate.
He gained the Emperor's favor through his management of finances and taxes,
and began extensively establishing various commissioners,
competing to amass wealth,
causing the hundred officials to gradually lose their proper duties and the Emperor's mind to become increasingly extravagant.
The history states that during Táng Xuánzōng's time,
opening the floodgates of profit began with Yǔwén Róng.
He was careless, impetuous, and talkative,
fond of boasting and self-promotion.
While serving as chancellor,
he said to people:
"If I remain in this position for a few months,
then all under heaven will be without troubles."
Xìn'ān Prince Lǐ Yī,
due to military achievements, enjoyed the Emperor's favor,
for his merit in pacifying Shíbǎo Fortress.
When Yī came to court,
Róng had the censor Lǐ Yín impeach him,
but this was leaked to an acquaintance.
Yī heard of it,
and first reported it to the Emperor.
The next day,
when Yín's memorial was indeed presented,
the Emperor was angry.
In the ninth month,
on Rénzǐ day,
Róng was consequently demoted to Prefect of Rǔzhōu.
Examination of Discrepancies states: The Old Biography says:
"Palace Censor Lǐ Zhòu summoned Yī via post horse to imprison him;
after Yī pleaded his case and was vindicated,
Róng was demoted for favoring and forming a clique with Lǐ Zhòu."
Now we follow the Táng Calendar.
From Jiǎxū day in the sixth month
to Rénzǐ day in the ninth month,
is ninety-nine days.
All originated from Róng.
13 In winter,
the tenth month,
on Wùwǔ day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse,
not complete, like a hook.
14 After Yǔwén Róng had been punished,
state funds became insufficient.
The Emperor again thought of him,
and said to Péi Guāngtíng:
"You all spoke of Róng's faults,
and I have already dismissed him.
Now state funds are insufficient,
what is to be done!
How will you all assist me?"
Guāngtíng and others were afraid and could not reply.
It happened that there was an anonymous accusation reporting Róng's bribery and corruption,
and he was further demoted to Pínglè County Lieutenant.
Pínglè County
was located in the area of Lìpǔ in the Cāngwú Commandery of Hàn,
Jìn established Pínglè County,
belonging to Shǐ'ān Commandery.
Táng divided and established Zhāozhōu;
there is the Pínglè River.
Lè,
read as luò.
Examination of Discrepancies states: The Táng Calendar says:
"Péi Guāngtíng and others prompted the officials to impeach him,
accumulating his embezzlement to a huge amount."
The Old Biography says:
"Péi Guāngtíng, then concurrently Censor-in-chief,
again impeached Róng for forming cliques through associations and his son accepting bribes, etc."
Now we follow the Veritable Records and the Comprehensive Annals.
Also, the Táng Calendar says
"on Yǐwèi day of the tenth month".
According to the perpetual calendar,
the tenth month began on Wùwǔ day,
there is no Yǐwèi.
Now we follow the Comprehensive Annals.
Vice Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury Jiǎng Cén memorialized that Róng, while in Biànzhōu, had embezzled government funds amounting to a huge sum.
An order was issued to thoroughly investigate the matter.
Róng was consequently exiled to Yánzhōu.
In the second year of the Diàolù era of Gāozōng,
Yánzhōu was established by dividing Héngzhōu and Guìzhōu,
named because it was north of Yángāng.
Investigate/thoroughly,
read as zhí.
15 In the eleventh month,
on Xīnmǎo day,
the Emperor made a tour to pay respects at the five mausoleums: Qiáo, Dìng, Xiàn, Zhāo, and Qián;
the order of visiting the five mausoleums
was based on the distance and sequence of the imperial procession's route.
On Wùshēn day
he returned to the palace;
a general amnesty was declared,
and the common people's land tax for this year was entirely halved.
16 In the twelfth month,
on Xīnyǒu day,
the Emperor went to the hot springs at Xīnfēng;
on Rénshēn day,
he returned to the palace.
The Xīnfēng hot springs are the Líshān hot springs,
Lí Mountain is in Xīnfēng County.
1 In spring,
the first month,
Examination of Discrepancies states: The Veritable Records say:
"On Guǐyǒu day,
the Emperor held court at the Hányuán Hall to receive New Year's congratulations."
According to the perpetual calendar,
the first day of this month was Bǐngxū,
there is no Guǐyǒu.
The events of this year in the Veritable Records differ from the Basic Annals, the Táng Calendar, and the Comprehensive Annals;
the Jiǎzǐ day in the first month is completely erroneous;
it is suspected that the original text was lost,
and later people supplemented it.
The New Annals only rely on the Old Annals,
and do not adopt the Veritable Records of this year at all.
It also says:
"On Dīngsì day,
he personally welcomed the ethers in the eastern suburbs,
and issued an edict,

Previously,

only considered the individual's capability,
sometimes promoting them exceptionally out of order,
sometimes leaving them in low positions until old age;
there were those with official status for over twenty years who never received a salary.
Furthermore,

sometimes transferring from a large to a small one,
sometimes initially near
then later distant,
all without established regulations.
Guāngtíng first memorialized to implement the system of seniority-based qualifications.
Officials were to be assembled based on the number of selection cycles since leaving office,
meaning after leaving an official post,
how many selection cycles had passed,
each was ranked and assembled at the Ministry of Personnel according to the number.
Those of lower rank had more selection cycles;
regardless of capability,
once the selection quota was full, they were appointed,
limiting advancement by years and steps,
not allowing overstepping.
Those not under reprimand
only rose, never fell.
This was the "Tenure-based Grading" of Cuī Liàng of the Later Wei,
followed and implemented,
persisting to this day.
Talented and outstanding individuals

It was called
the "Sacred Book,"

Sòng Jǐng disputed it but could not change it.
Guāngtíng also ordered that appointments for non-official stream personnel also pass review by the Chancellery.

During the Northern Wei dynasty, Xiè County was divided to establish Yúxiāng County.
In the seventeenth year of the Zhēnguàn era, Xiè County was abolished and merged into Yúxiāng County.
In the twentieth year, Xiè County was re-established and Yúxiāng County was abolished.
In the second year of the Tiānshòu era,
Xiè County was again divided to establish Yúxiāng County,
definitively making them two separate counties.

is pronounced with the reading hù mǎi fān.

10 In Guānzhōng, prolonged rains had caused grain prices to rise.
The emperor planned to travel to the Eastern Capital,
and summoned the capital prefect, Péi Yàoqīng, to discuss the matter.
Péi replied:
"Guānzhōng is where the imperial enterprise originated,
and should remain unchanged for a hundred generations;
however, due to its narrow land and scarce grain,
the imperial carriage occasionally travels to the Eastern Capital to alleviate the pressure.
I have heard that during the Zhēnguàn and Yǒnghuī eras,
official salaries and grain rations were not excessive,
and transporting one to two hundred thousand shí of grain annually from east of the passes was sufficient to meet needs,
allowing the imperial carriage to remain peacefully in place.
Now expenditures have gradually increased,
and transport volumes are several times greater than before,
yet they still cannot meet demand,
forcing Your Majesty to repeatedly brave cold and heat to relieve the people of the west.
If now the tax rice collected by the Ministry of Revenue were all sent to the Eastern Capital,
and from there transported by water,
gradually replenishing Guānzhōng,
then if Guānzhōng had several years'储备,
there would be no worry about floods or droughts.
Moreover, people from Wú are unaccustomed to river transport,
and delays occur along the way;
as time passes,
hidden theft arises.
I propose establishing granaries at the river mouth,
the river mouth being where the Biàn River meets the Huáng Hé.
The granary at the river mouth is called the Wǔláo Granary.
Officials should hire transport to divide the grain into the Huáng Hé and Luò River routes.
Additionally, establish one granary each east and west of Sānmén.
Yǔ cut through Dǐzhù,
where two rocks appear in the water like pillars,
hence the name Dǐzhù.
Here, the river divides into three channels flowing between them,
thus it is also called Sānmén.
At that time, the Jíjīn Granary was established east of Sānmén,
and the Yán Granary to the west.
When the water is dangerous, halt transport;
when the water is clear, proceed downstream.
Alternatively, open mountain roads
for cart transport to pass through.
At that time, an eighteen-lǐ mountain road was cut beside Sānmén for land transport,
to avoid the dangers of Dǐzhù.
This would save enormous expenses.
Along the banks of the Huáng Hé and Wèi River,
there are old granaries from the Hàn and Suí dynasties,
which could be repaired without difficulty."
The emperor deeply agreed with his words.

13 Hán Xiū frequently argued with Xiāo Sōng before the emperor,
bluntly pointing out Xiāo's faults,
which displeased the emperor.
Xiāo then requested to retire due to old age.
The emperor said:
"I have not grown weary of you;

He replied:
"I have received great favor,

While Your Majesty has not yet grown weary of me,
I can still retire gracefully;
if you had grown weary of me,
my head would not be safe,

With that, he shed tears.
Xiāo Sōng adopted a pitiable demeanor,
both to preserve his own favor and position,
and also to undermine Hán Xiū.
The emperor said:
"You may return for now;
I will consider this carefully."

In this year,

the empire was divided into the Capital Region, Eastern Capital Region, Guannei, Hénán, Hédōng, Héběi, Lǒngyòu, Shānnán Eastern Circuit, Shānnán Western Circuit, Jiànnán, Huáinán, Jiāngnán Eastern Circuit, Jiāngnán Western Circuit, Qiánzhōng, and Lǐngnán,
making fifteen circuits in total.
An Investigating Commissioner was established for each,
who would inspect for illegal activities according to six regulations.
The two Capital Regions were overseen by the Vice Censor-in-Chief,
while the rest all selected virtuous Regional Inspectors to oversee them.
The Capital Region Investigating Commissioner's office was located within the Western Capital city.
The Eastern Capital Region's office was in the Eastern Capital.
The Guannei Investigating Commissioner was overseen by a capital official.
The Hénán Investigating Commissioner's office was in Biànzhōu,
Hédōng's in Púzhōu,
Héběi's in Wèizhōu,
Lǒngyòu's in Shànzhōu,
Shānnán Eastern Circuit's in Xiāngzhōu,
the Western Circuit's in Liángzhōu,
Huáinán's in Yángzhōu,
Jiāngnán Eastern Circuit's in Sūzhōu,
the Western Circuit's in Hóngzhōu,
Qiánzhōng's in Qiánzhōu,
Jiànnán's in Yìzhōu,
Lǐngnán's in Guǎngzhōu.
Later, there were cases where a Frontier Military Governor concurrently held the post of Investigating Commissioner,
so the Guānzhōng Circuit was certainly not restricted to capital officials,
and the locations of the various circuit Investigating Commissioners' offices were also difficult to uniformly fix.
Thus, the commissioners were not abolished or changed.
Only when altering old regulations
was it necessary to report for approval;
for all other matters, they were permitted to act according to what was expedient,
acting first and reporting afterwards.
15. The Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury, Yáng Chónglǐ,
was the son of Yáng Zhèngdào.
Yáng Zhèngdào
was the grandson of Emperor Yáng of Suí,
and the son of Prince Qí, Jiǎn.
None of those who had served as Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury before or after could match him.
At that time, peace had lasted for a long while,
and goods and wealth were piled up like mountains.
Anything that had passed through Minister Yáng's hands
was without exception exquisite;
each year, through auditing and economizing,
he saved several million strings of cash.
In this year,
he retired from the post of Minister of Revenue,
being over ninety years old.
The Emperor asked his ministers:
"Among Chónglǐ's sons,
who can succeed his father?"
They replied:
"Chónglǐ has three sons,
Shènyú, Shènjīn, and Shènmíng.
All are honest, diligent, and talented,
but Shènjīn is the best."
The Emperor then promoted Shènjīn from Magistrate of Rǔyáng to Investigating Censor,
put in charge of disbursements and receipts for the Court of the Imperial Treasury.
Shènmíng was appointed Acting Investigating Censor,
put in charge of disbursements from the Hánjiā Granary,
the Hánjiā Granary being in the Eastern Capital.
To oversee;
read as 'jiān', with the pronunciation 'gōng xián fān'.
The Emperor was very pleased with them.
Shènjīn memorialized that for the cloth and silk delivered by the various prefectures, any that were stained, soiled, torn, or damaged
were all sent back to their original prefectures to levy compensation money,
which was then used to purchase light goods.
Levies and requisitions thus began to increase.

The 22nd year of the Kāiyuán era
(Jiǎxū year, 734 AD)
1. In spring,
the first month,
on Jǐsì,
the Emperor departed from the Western Capital;
on Jǐchǒu,
he arrived at the Eastern Capital.
Zhāng Jiǔlíng came from Sháozhōu for an audience,
requesting to complete the mourning period;
this was not permitted.
2. In the second month,
on Rényín,
Qínzhōu experienced successive earthquakes,
destroying nearly all public and private buildings.
Over four thousand officials and commoners were crushed to death;
the Left Chancellor, Xiāo Sōng, was ordered to provide relief.
3. The alchemist Zhāng Guǒ claimed to possess the arts of immortality,
deceiving people by saying he had been a Palace Attendant in the time of Emperor Yáo,
and was now several thousand years old.
He often traveled to and from Héngshān,
Héngshān at that time being within the boundaries of Héngyáng County, Dìngzhōu.
To deceive;
read as 'kuàng', with the pronunciation 'jū kuàng fān'.
Héng;
read as 'héng', with the pronunciation 'hù dēng fān'.
He was summoned several times but did not come.
The Regional Inspector of Xiàngzhōu, Wéi Jì, recommended him.
The Emperor dispatched the Secretariat Drafter, Xú Qiáo, bearing an imperial seal letter to welcome him.
On Gēngyín,
he arrived at the Eastern Capital,
entering the palace in a sedan chair,
and was treated with great favor and courtesy.
4. Zhāng Jiǔlíng requested that the minting of coin not be prohibited.
In the third month,
on Gēngchén,
an edict ordered the百官 officials to discuss it.
Péi Yàoqīng and others all said:
"Once this door is opened,
I fear petty people will abandon farming to chase profit,
and inferior and counterfeit coin will become even worse."
Since the time of Empress Wǔ,
there had been much inferior coin among the people,
which the government could not prohibit.
"If we tax copper and commute corvée labor,
then government mints can be established.
Calculating the cost and estimating the labor,
then private minting would be unprofitable.
It is easy and can last,
simple and difficult to falsify.
Moreover, the nature of coin
is to be valued for facilitating trade.
The benefit does not lie in having much;
why must we wait for private minting before we have enough for use!"
The Right Gate Guard's Record Keeper Adjutant, Liú Zhì, said:
(The Táng dynasty's sixteen guard headquarters all had Record Keeper Adjuncts,
rank 8b lower,
in charge of receiving matters from the various bureaus and from the five headquarters' outer offices,
checking accounts and copying summaries,
sealing and issuing paper and brushes.)
To oversee;
read as 'jiān', with the pronunciation 'gǔ xián fān'.
"When people are rich, they cannot be encouraged by rewards;
when poor, they cannot be restrained by authority.
If private minting is permitted,
the poor certainly will not be able to do it.
I fear the poor will become poorer and become servants to the rich,
while the rich become richer and indulge their desires.
In the time of Emperor Wén of Hàn,
the Prince of Wú, Liú Pì, was as wealthy as the Son of Heaven,
which was due to his minting coin."
(The event is seen in scroll 14, the fifth year of Emperor Wén of Hàn.)
Pì;
read as 'pì', with the pronunciation 'pǐ bèi fān'.
To equal;
read as 'liè', with the pronunciation 'lì chuò fān'.
Zhì
was the son of Liú Zǐxuán.
Liú Zǐxuán
is Liú Zhījǐ.
To avoid the Emperor's personal name taboo,
he went by his courtesy name.
5. In summer,
the fourth month,
on Rénchén,
the Military Commissioner of Shuòfāng, Prince Xìn'ān Lǐ Wěi, was concurrently appointed Investigating and Administrative Commissioner of the Guānnei Circuit,
with his jurisdiction increased to include twelve prefectures such as Jīng and Yuán.
6 The Vice Minister of Personnel, Lǐ Línfǔ,
was gentle, flattering, and full of cunning schemes.
He deeply ingratiated himself with the eunuchs and the families of imperial consorts,
spying on the emperor's movements and activities.
There was nothing he did not know.
Because of this, whenever he responded to the emperor's inquiries,
he often spoke in accordance with the imperial will,
which pleased the emperor.
At that time, Consort Wǔ was favored and her influence overshadowed the entire rear palace.
She gave birth to Shòu Prince Lǐ Qīng,
and none of the other princes could compare to him.
The Crown Prince gradually became estranged and neglected.
Línfǔ then spoke to Consort Wǔ through the eunuchs,
expressing his wish to spare no effort in protecting Shòu Prince.
Consort Wǔ was grateful to him
and secretly assisted him from within the palace.
Because of this, he was promoted to Vice Minister of the Imperial Secretariat.
Textual Analysis says: The Old Biography states:
"Initially,
the wife of the Palace Attendant Péi Guāngtíng was the daughter of Wǔ Sānsī.
She was crafty and resourceful
and had an illicit affair with Línfǔ.
The eunuch Gāo Lìshì originally came from the household of Wǔ Sānsī.
When Guāngtíng died,
Lady Wǔ, in her grief, pleaded with Lìshì,
asking that Línfǔ replace her husband's position;
Lìshì did not dare to speak of it.
Emperor Xuánzōng ordered the Secretariat Director Xiāo Sōng to select a chief minister;
after a long time,
he recommended the Right Assistant Director Hán Xiū.
Emperor Xuánzōng agreed
and ordered the drafting of the edict.
Lìshì immediately leaked this to Lady Wǔ,
who then had Línfǔ inform Xiū.
After Xiū became chief minister,
he was very grateful to Línfǔ.
He became at odds with Sōng
and recommended that Línfǔ was fit to be chief minister.
Consort Wǔ secretly assisted him,
and he was thus appointed Vice Minister of the Imperial Secretariat.
Emperor Xuánzōng's favor and treatment of him grew even deeper."
According to this, Guāngtíng's wife
was merely a widow.
How would she dare to hastily recommend her illicit lover to replace her husband as chief minister!
Hán Xiū was upright and honest.
Even if he had received advance notice from Línfǔ,
he certainly would not have recommended him to be chief minister.
This account is not adopted here.
On the Wùzǐ day,
Péi Yàogīng was appointed as Palace Attendant,
Zhāng Jiǔlíng as Secretariat Director,
and Línfǔ as Minister of Rites and Co-Chief Minister of the Secretariat-Chancellery.
This laid the groundwork for Lǐ Línfǔ's rise to power and the Crown Prince's eventual deposition.
Yán Zhēnqīng's memorial stated:
"After the Tiānbǎo era,
the eunuch Yuán Sīyì daily proclaimed imperial edicts to the Secretariat.
He would invariably inform Línfǔ of Emperor Xuánzōng's every movement and activity.
Línfǔ would anticipate the emperor's wishes and submit proposals accordingly.
Emperor Xuánzōng was pleasantly surprised as if by divine intervention.
Through this,
his authority and imperial favor grew daily."
7 The emperor planted wheat in the imperial park.
Leading the Crown Prince and others, he personally went to harvest it,
saying to them:
"This is for offering to the ancestral temple,
therefore I dare not fail to participate personally.
Moreover, I want you all to understand the hardships of farming."
He also distributed it widely among his attending officials, saying:
"Recently, I sent people to inspect the crops in the fields,
but they often did not report the truth.
Therefore, I planted this myself to observe it."
In matters of planting and cultivation,
the heavens may not provide timely rain or sunshine,
the land may vary in fertility or barrenness,
and human effort may be diligent or lacking.
Therefore, the harvest may vary in abundance or scarcity.
If the ruler does not encroach upon the farming seasons,
and the people can exert their full strength,
then the land will yield its full potential.
Is it really necessary to plant oneself to observe the results?
8 In the sixth month,
on the Rénchén day,
the Yōuzhōu Military Governor Zhāng Shǒuguī achieved a great victory over the Qìdān,
and sent an envoy to present the news of victory.
9 Prince Xuè, Lǐ Yè, fell seriously ill.
The emperor was deeply concerned,
and his appearance and hair changed from worry.
In the seventh month,
on the Jǐsì day,
he passed away.
He was posthumously honored as Crown Prince Huìxuān.
10 The emperor appointed Péi Yàogīng as Transport Commissioner for Jiānghuái and Hénán.
Textual Analysis says: The Old Annals states:
"He was appointed as Commissioner for Procurement south of the Jiāng and Huái."
Here, we follow the Old Treatise on Food and Money.
In the eighth month,
on the Rényín day,
the Héyīn Granary was established east of the transport depot,
and the Bǎiyá Granary to the west.
In the second year of the Xiánhēng era of Emperor Gāozōng,
a granary was established at Bǎiyá in Héyáng County, Luò Prefecture.
It was abolished in the tenth year of the Kāiyuán era,
and now it was re-established on the old foundation.
A salt granary was established to the west;
an eighteen-li canal was dug to avoid the dangers of the Sānmén area.
Consulting the New and Old Treatises,
it was actually an eighteen-li cart road cut through the mountains,
not a canal.
Grain from Jiāng and Huái was transported by boat to the Hánjiā Granary in the Eastern Capital.
It was then hired out for land transport by cart
for three hundred lǐ to Shǎn Prefecture,
at a rate of ten
coins per two hú.
Yàogīng ordered that all grain transported by boat from Jiāng and Huái be delivered to the Héyīn Granary.
Then, using boats on the Yellow River, it was transported to the Hánjiā Granary and the Tàiyuán Granary.
From the Tàiyuán Granary, it entered the Wèi River and was transported to Guānzhōng.
Over a period of three years,
seven million hú of grain were transported,
saving three hundred thousand strings of coins in cart hire fees.
According to the Old Treatise,
the Hánjiā Granary in the Eastern Capital stored grain from Jiāng and Huái.
It was loaded onto large carts
and transported westward to Shǎn Prefecture, a distance of three hundred lǐ.
The rate was one thousand coins in labor cost per two hú.
This is the large amount saved by Yàogīng.
"Ten coins"
is an error.
It should be
"one thousand coins"
as correct.
First,
jiàn is pronounced xiàn.
Jiù,
is pronounced jí jiù.
Shǎn,
is pronounced shī rǎn.
Gèng,
is pronounced gōng héng.
Textual Analysis says: The Old Treatise states
"four hundred thousand strings."
Here, we follow Yàogīng's biography.
The Old Treatise also states:
"The following year,
Yàogīng was appointed Palace Attendant,
and Xiāo Jiǒng succeeded him."
According to this, Yàogīng proposed this plan in the twenty-first year.
This year, he became Palace Attendant,
and the Héyīn Granary was first established.
It was only after three years that the results became apparent;
therefore, he did not leave this post when he became Palace Attendant.
Yàogīng said:
"This is the profit or loss of the state treasury.
How can one use it to curry favor!"
He memorialized to use all of it as funds for purchasing grain.
11 Zhāng Guǒ firmly requested to return to Héng Mountain.
An edict appointed him as Grand Master of Silver and Blue Light,
with the title Master of Profound Mysteries,
bestowed rich gifts, and sent him off.
Later, he died.
Those fond of the unusual reported that he had achieved liberation from the corpse.
Because of this, the emperor began to believe somewhat in immortals.
Emperor Míng changed the name of the Hall of Gathered Immortals to the Hall of Gathered Worthies,
which shows that initially he did not believe in immortals.
By this time, he began to believe somewhat,
and by his later years, he believed deeply.
The historian remarks that maintaining a correct mind is difficult,
and one can gradually fall into error without realizing it.
12 In winter,
the twelfth month,
on the Wùzǐ day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
13 On the Yǐsì day,
the Yōuzhōu Military Governor Zhāng Shǒuguī beheaded the Qìdān King Qūliè and Kětūgàn,
and sent their heads to the capital.
Textual Analysis says: The Old Biography of Shǒuguī
writes "Qūliè"
as
"Qūlà."
The Qìdān biography states that the heads were sent the following year in the first month.
Here, we follow the Veritable Records.
At that time, Kě Tūgān repeatedly caused trouble along the border for years,
and neither Zhào Hánzhāng nor Xuē Chǔyù could subdue him.
After Zhāng Shǒuguī took up his post,
he repeatedly defeated him.
Kě Tūgān, hard-pressed,
sent an envoy to feign surrender.
Shǒuguī dispatched his secretary Wáng Huǐ to pacify him.
When Huǐ arrived at his headquarters,
he observed that the Khitan leadership had no intention of surrendering at all,
but had merely shifted their camp slightly closer to the northwest,
secretly sending people to contact the Turks,
plotting to kill Huǐ and rebel;
Huǐ learned of this.
The staff officer Lǐ Guòzhé
(Textual Analysis: The Old Book of Tang's "Biography of the Khitan" records
"Yùzhé."
We now follow the Veritable Records and the "Biography of Zhāng Shǒuguī.")
was at odds with them over power struggles.
Huǐ persuaded Guòzhé to plot against them.
Guòzhé led troops at night and killed Qūliè and Kě Tūgān,
exterminating all their followers,
and led the remaining multitude to surrender.
Shǒuguī led his troops out to Zǐméng Prefecture,
where he held a grand military review to pacify and stabilize them.
The heads of Qūliè and Kě Tūgān were displayed south of Tiānjīn.
14 The Turkic Bilgä Qaghan was poisoned by his minister Méilù Chuò,
but did not die.
He then executed Méilù Chuò and his clan and followers.
After his death,
his son Yīrán Qaghan succeeded him.
He soon died,
and his brother Dēnglì Qaghan succeeded him.
On the gēngxū day,
they came to announce the mourning.
15 Begging in the capital was prohibited,
and infirmaries were established to provide for them.
At that time, infirmaries were set up in various temples,
using fields of compassion to care for the sick,
a practice originating from Buddhism.
Begging,
pronounced gài in ancient times.
1 In spring,
the first month,

We now follow the Old Book of Tang's biography.)
On the yǐhài day,
the Emperor plowed the Jítián (sacrificial field),

Push,
pronounced tuī.

and the capital city held a three-day feast.
The capital city,

Feast,
pronounced pú.

Gāo Lìshì reported that the Assistant Magistrate of Hénán, Yán Ānzhī, was strict in governance,
(Assistant Magistrates of the capital counties in the Tang were of the seventh rank, lower grade.)
Governance,
means to rule;
the Tang avoided the taboo character
"zhì" (治),

He requested that he be sent to control the crowd;

to compete for superiority.
The Prefect of Huáizhōu transported several hundred musicians in carts,
all dressed in embroidered silk,
and the oxen pulling the carts were adorned to look like tigers, leopards, rhinoceroses, and elephants.
(The "Greater East" ode in the Book of Songs says: "Bright is that Draught Ox, but he does not serve to draw the carriage."

means the side-bar of a cart.
"Xiāng" (箱),
means the box of a large cart.
The subcommentary says: The space between the two side-rails is called "xiāng."

The commentary on the Book of Documents says: "Long enough to fill the carriage."
This refers to the space inside the cart for holding things.
Master Qiū said: "Fúxiāng"

Dressed,
pronounced yì.
They linked sleeves and sang the "Yú Wěi."
Lǔshān,
the ancient Lǔ County,
was the place where, during the time of Kǒng Jiǎ of the Xià dynasty,
the dragon-keeper Liú Lěi moved.
During the Hàn, it was Lǔyáng County,
belonging to Nányáng Commandery.
The Later Wèi established Lǔyáng Commandery,
and the Sui restored it as Lǔ County,
belonging to Rǔzhōu.
In the Táng, it was Lǔshān County,
named after
Mount Lǔ in the county.
The "Yú Wěi,"
was a song composed by Yuán Déxiù.
Wěi,
pronounced wěi.
(Textual Analysis: The Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Mínghuáng records
"Yú Wěi,"
while the New Book of Tang's biography records

The exact meaning is unclear.
We now follow the Miscellaneous Records.)
"The people of Huáizhōu,
are they in dire straits!"
The Emperor immediately demoted the prefect to a sinecure post.
(Sinecure posts
had no substantive duties.
Sinecure,
pronounced sǎn.)
The scholar-officials all admired his integrity.
2 The Emperor admired Zhāng Shǒuguī's achievements,
and wanted to make him chancellor.
Zhāng Jiǔlíng remonstrated, saying:
"The chancellor
acts on behalf of Heaven to govern all things,
and is not an office for rewarding merit."
The Emperor said:
"What if we give him the title but do not let him perform the duties?"
He replied:
"That would not be permissible.
Only names and instruments of authority should not be lightly given to others,
as they are what the ruler personally controls."
(This records the words of Confucius from the Zuǒzhuàn.)
"Your Majesty is about to make him chancellor;
what will you do if he completely annihilates the Xī and the Jué?"
(The Xī and Jué refer to the Xī and the Turks.
Jué,
pronounced jué.)
The Emperor then desisted.
In the second month,
Shǒuguī went to the Eastern Capital to present news of victory.
He was appointed as General of the Right Yǔlín Guards,
concurrently Censor-in-chief,
and his two sons were given official posts,
with very generous rewards.
3. Earlier,
Palace Censor Yáng Wāng had killed Zhāng Shěnsù.
(This matter is recorded in the nineteenth year of the previous scroll.)
Shěnsù's two sons, Zhāng Huáng and Zhāng Xiù, were both young at the time.
They were sentenced to exile to the Lingbiǎo region;
soon after, they escaped and returned,
planning to find an opportunity to avenge their father.
In the third month,
on Dīngmǎo day,
they personally killed Wànqǐng in the capital.
They attached a statement to an axe,
detailing the injustice done to their father.
They intended to go beyond the river to kill those who had conspired with Wànqǐng to frame their father.
When they reached Sìshuǐ,
they were captured by the authorities.
Many commentators argued that the two sons' father had died unjustly,
and that their youthful filial fervor in avenging their father
deserved compassion and pardon;
Zhāng Jiǔlíng also wished to spare them.
Péi Yàoqīng and Lǐ Línfǔ believed that doing so
would undermine state law.
The Emperor also agreed with this view.
He said to Jiǔlíng:
"The feelings of a filial son
are such that duty overrides concern for death;
however, to pardon someone for killing
is a precedent that cannot be set."
He then issued an edict stating:
"The state establishes laws
with the aim of stopping killing.
If each were to fulfill his ambition as a son,
who would not be one who dies for filial piety?
If revenge spirals endlessly,
where would it end?
When Gāoyáo served as Minister of Justice,
the law had to be enforced.
Even if Zēng Shēn killed someone,
he could not be pardoned.
They should be handed over to the Hénán Prefecture to be beaten to death."
Scholars and commoners all pitied them.
They composed elegies and dirges for them,
posting them on the main roads.
Market people collected money to bury them at Běimáng.
Fearing that Wànqǐng's family might exhume the bodies,
they also made several decoy graves.
(They made many graves to create confusion,
so that no one would know the exact burial place.)
4. In the early Táng,
princesses' actual fiefs were limited to three hundred households.
During the reign of Emperor Zhōngzōng,
Princess Tàipíng's fief reached five thousand households,
generally with a limit of seven adult males per household.
Since the Kāiyuán era,
the Emperor's sisters were limited to one thousand households,
and the Emperor's daughters to half that,
all with a limit of three adult males per household.
Imperial sons-in-law were all appointed as supernumerary officials of the third rank,
but were not assigned substantive duties.
The income from the princesses' estates was so meager
that they could not even afford proper carriages and attire.
Some attendants remarked that this was too stingy.
The Emperor said:
"The common people's land taxes and corvée,
are not mine to own.
Soldiers exert themselves to the point of death,
yet their rewards do not exceed bolts of silk.
What merit do women have,
that they should enjoy the revenue of many households?
Moreover, I wish to make them understand frugality and thrift."
In autumn,
the seventh month,
Princess Xiányí was about to be married off.
(Princess Xiányí was married to Yáng Húi.)
The princess
was the daughter of Wǔ Huìfēi.
Consequently, all princesses had their households increased to one thousand.
5. In winter,
the tenth month,
on Wùshēn day,
the Tūqíshī invaded Běitíng and the Ānxī outpost city of Bōhuàn.
6. In the intercalary month,
on Rénwǔ day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
Textual Analysis says: The Old Annals record
"the eleventh month,
on Rénshēn day, the first day of the month."
According to the perpetual calendar,
the first day of the eleventh month was Rénzǐ.
Here we follow the Veritable Records and the Táng Calendar.
7. In the twelfth month,
on Yǐhài day,
the daughter of the former Shǔzhōu Household Registrar Yáng Xuányǎn was enfeoffed as consort to the Prince of Shòu.
(This was the basis for the Emperor later taking her into the inner palace, leading to disorder in the state.)
Textual Analysis says: The Veritable Records record the enfeoffment document,
stating
"the eldest daughter of Xuánjiǎo."
According to Chén Hóng's "Song of Everlasting Sorrow" biography:

The Old Biography of Consort Yáng says:
"Xuányǎn's daughter was orphaned early,
