It also says:
"Someone memorialized that Xuányǎn's daughter's beauty was peerless in her generation,
and she should be summoned for an audience.
At the time, she wore Daoist robes,
and was called Tàizhēn."
The New Biography says:
"She was first the consort of the Prince of Shòu...
She was then summoned into the inner palace.
Acting on his own idea,
he had her registered as a female official,
with the title Tàizhēn.
He then arranged for the Prince of Shòu to marry the daughter of Wéi Zhāoxùn,
and Tàizhēn gained favor."
The Old History likely concealed this.
(He was the great-grandson of Wāng.
Yáng Wāng appears in the twelfth year of the Suí Yángdì's Dàyè era, scroll 183.)
8. This year,
the Qìdān king Guòzhé was killed by his minister Nièlǐ,
along with all his sons.
One son, Làgān, fled to Āndōng and escaped.
Nièlǐ reported to the court,
saying that Guòzhé's use of punishments was cruel and tyrannical,
causing widespread discontent,
hence he had killed him.
The Emperor pardoned his crime,
and accordingly appointed Nièlǐ as Governor of Sōngmò.
He also sent a letter reprimanding him, saying:
"According to your tribal customs, there is often little loyalty to rulers and superiors.
This has been the case since ancient times,
and We are aware of it.
However, Guòzhé was your king.
To kill him as soon as he does wrong
makes being such a king
rather difficult, does it not?
We fear only that when you become king,
later people will act the same way.
If one cannot even ensure one's own safety,
who would wish to be king?
You should also consider the consequences for the future.
How can you seek only immediate gratification!"
The Turks soon led troops east to invade the Xī and Qìdān.
Nièlǐ and the Xī king Lǐ Guīguó defeated them.

the first month,

the Vice Director of the Bureau of Evaluations was in charge of administering the examinations for the presented scholars.

Commentators argued that the Vice Director's position was too lowly

In the third month,
on Rénchén day,
an edict ordered that from now on, the Vice Minister of Rites would be entrusted with administering the examinations for the presented scholars.
6 Zhāng Shǒuguī sent Pínglú Pacification Commissioner and Left Flank Guard General Ān Lùshān to suppress the rebels among the Xī and Qìdān tribes.
Lùshān, relying on his bravery, advanced rashly,
and was defeated by the enemy.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Xīnhài day,
Shǒuguī submitted a request to have him executed.
Lùshān, facing execution, cried out:
"Does the Grand Master not wish to exterminate the Xī and Qìdān?
Why kill Lùshān!"
Shǒuguī also regretted losing his valor,
so instead he had him arrested and sent to the capital.
Zhāng Jiǔlíng wrote a comment:
"In the past, Rángjū executed Zhuāng Jiǎ.
Records of the Grand Historian: Duke Jǐng of Qí appointed Sīmǎ Rángjū as general.
Rángjū said:
'I wish to have Your Majesty's favored minister to supervise the army.'
Duke Jǐng sent Zhuāng Jiǎ to go.
Jiǎ was habitually arrogant and esteemed.
Rángjū made an agreement with him,
to meet at the army gate at noon;
he arrived only in the evening.
Rángjū, because Jiǎ was late,
executed him,
to command the three armies.
Comment,
pī, pīmī fān,
means to judge,
what people today call 'critique and judgment.'
Sūn Wǔ, using military strategy, met King Hélú of Wú.
The King of Wú said:
'Can you drill troops with a small test using women?'
He said:
'Yes.'
So he brought out 180 beautiful women from the palace,
divided them into two teams,
with the king's two favorite concubines each as team leaders,
all ordered to hold halberds.
After the rules were announced,
repeated orders were given,
then he beat the drum,
and the women on the right laughed loudly.
Master Sūn said:
'If the rules are not followed,
and the orders are not familiar,
it is the fault of the commander.'
He repeated the orders and beat the drum again,
and the women on the left laughed again.
Master Sūn executed the left and right team leaders as a warning,
used the next in line as team leaders and beat the drum again,
and the women's movements—left, right, forward, backward, kneeling, rising—all matched the rules and standards.
Then the King of Wú knew that Master Sūn could command troops,
and appointed him as general.
Lùshān should not be exempted from death."
The Emperor valued his talent,
and issued an edict to dismiss him from office,
allowing him to lead troops as a commoner.
Jiǔlíng firmly argued,
saying:
"Lùshān violated military discipline and lost the army,
by law he must be executed.
Moreover, I observe his appearance bears signs of rebellion,
if not killed, he will surely bring future calamity."
The Emperor said:
"Do not, like Wáng Yífǔ recognizing Shí Lè,
wrongly harm a loyal and good man."
In the Jìn dynasty, Shí Lè at age fourteen,
followed villagers trading in Luòyáng,
leaned against the Shàngdōng Gate and whistled.
Wáng Yǎn saw him and found him unusual,
turned to his attendants and said:
"That young barbarian just now,
I observed his voice and gaze have an extraordinary ambition,
I fear he will become a calamity for the world."
He quickly sent someone to arrest him,
but Lè had already left.
Examination of discrepancies: Xuánzōng Veritable Records:
"In the fourth month,
on the Xīnhài day,
Zhāng Shǒuguī reported that Lùshān, in commanding the army, violated discipline,
damaging the army's prestige,
requested to execute him according to military law;
it was approved.
Lùshān, facing execution, declared loudly: 'The two barbarian tribes are not yet pacified,
how can you bear to kill a strong man!
Is this for the Grand Master's plan!'
Shǒuguī, because Lùshān had previously been successful in capturing enemies alive,
hearing his words,
then spared him,
and reported it."
Sùzōng Veritable Records says:
"Lùshān was a market broker,
caught stealing sheep,
Shǒuguī was angry,
pursued and captured him,
wanted to beat him to death.
Lùshān cried out loudly: 'Does the Grand Master not wish to exterminate the Xī and Qìdān, the two barbarian tribes!
Yet you kill a strong man!'
Shǒuguī marveled at his appearance,
admired his words,
and then released him."
Yáo Rǔnéng, writing the Account of Ān Lùshān,
his account of the sheep theft is the same as the Sùzōng Veritable Records.
Also says:
"In the twenty-first year,
Shǒuguī ordered Lùshān to report on affairs.
Zhōngshū Lìng Zhāng Jiǔlíng saw him,
said to Shìzhōng Péi Guāngtíng: 'The one who will bring chaos to Yōuzhōu is this barbarian.'"
Also says:
"In the twenty-fourth year,
Lùshān was a Pínglú general,
campaigned against the Xī and Qìdān and was defeated,
Shǒuguī requested to have him executed,
Jiǔlíng commented: 'When Rángjū went to war,
he certainly executed Zhuāng Jiǎ;
when Sūn Wǔ enforced orders,
he also executed palace women.
If Shǒuguī's military orders are to be enforced,
Lùshān should not be exempted from death.'
Xuánzōng valued his bravery and sharpness,
only ordered his dismissal from office,
to serve as a commoner.
Jiǔlíng firmly petitioned for his execution,
Xuánzōng said: 'Do you, like Wáng Yífǔ recognizing Shí Lè,
arbitrarily conclude that Lùshān is hard to control!'
In the end, he was not executed."
Sūn Qiáo, writing the Western Studio Record,
its preface says:
"Why does it say Zhāng Shǒuguī with Ān Lùshān rebelled?
Because pardoning punishment violates teaching,
nurturing the steps to calamity.
Lùshān was originally Zhāng Shǒuguī's subordinate general,
once violated orders,
Zhāng Qǔjiāng ordered Shǒuguī to execute him,
he did not comply,
and indeed caused chaos in the world;
therefore the record says: 'Zhāng Shǒuguī with Ān Lùshān rebelled.'"
Old Book, Biography of Zhāng Jiǔlíng says:
"Zhāng Shǒuguī, with deputy general Ān Lùshān, campaigned against the Xī and Qìdān,
was defeated,
arrested and sent to the capital,
requested to apply court law.
Jiǔlíng submitted a memorial of impeachment: 'When Rángjū went to war,
he certainly executed Zhuāng Jiǎ;
when Sūn Wǔ drilled troops,
he also executed palace women.
If Shǒuguī's military orders are to be enforced,
Lùshān should not be exempted from death.'
The Emperor specially pardoned him.
Jiǔlíng memorialized: 'Lùshān has the heart of a wolf and wild ambitions,
his face bears signs of rebellion,
I request to execute him for his crime,
hoping to cut off future calamity.'
The Emperor said: 'Do not, like Wáng Yífǔ knowing the story of Shí Lè,
mistakenly harm a loyal and good man.'
Then released him to return to the barbarian lands."
New Book biography mentions Péi Guāngtíng's affair as in the Account,
the arrest and sending to the capital affair as in the Old Book biography,
Old Book biography of Lùshān, the sheep theft affair as in the Account,
but without the defeat and request for execution affair;
New Book biography is also the same.
Old Book biography also says:
"In the twentieth year,
Shǒuguī was Yōuzhōu Jiéduìshǐ,
Lùshān's sheep theft was discovered."
According to Péi Guāngtíng died in the twenty-first year,
that winter,
Jiǔlíng then became chancellor,
saying he spoke with Guāngtíng,
is mistaken.
Sūn Qiáo says
"Qǔjiāng ordered Shǒuguī to execute him",
is especially inaccurate.
Veritable Records,
twenty-first year,
Shǒuguī was still in Lǒngyòu erecting a boundary stele with Tǔbō,
had not reached Yōuzhōu.
Old Book biography says
"twentieth year as Jiéduìshǐ",
is also mistaken.
According to if Lùshān initially was a market broker,
how could Shǒuguī know he would eventually bring chaos to the world,
and release him without killing him!
How could Sūn Qiáo hastily charge him with the crime of rebellion!
If as in the Old Book biography of Jiǔlíng,
Shǒuguī arrested and sent him to the capital,
Xuánzōng personally pardoned him,
then what crime did Shǒuguī have that people of the time blamed him!
If saying stealing sheep and losing the army,
two offenses deserving death,
then how could Lùshān merely use words and be exempted from two deaths!
If as in the Xuánzōng Veritable Records,
Shǒuguī requested to apply the law,
received a reply granting permission,
moved by his one statement,
then spared him,
then Shǒuguī certainly would not dare to so easily reverse like this.
Moreover, how could Jiǔlíng have seen his face,
and say his face bears signs of rebellion!
If saying Shǒuguī never requested to apply the law,
In the collected works of Zhāng Jiǔlíng, there is an imperial edict granted to Shǒuguī, which states:
“Lùshān and others underestimated our military might,
without careful consideration,
leading to losses;
they should indeed be executed.
Since you have carried this out,
it accords with military law.”
There is also an edict granted to the officers and soldiers of Pínglú, which states:
“The execution of Ān Lùshān
was due to excessive underestimation of the enemy.
Do not become fearful or cowardly because of this,
lest you lose future plans.”
This shows that at the time, the execution was permitted.
If it is said that Shǒuguī spared him on his own,
contrary to Xuánzōng’s intention,
then there is another edict granted to Shǒuguī, which states:
“Lùshān was brave but lacked strategy,
leading to defeat.
His armor and supplies fell into enemy hands,
damaging our military prestige.
Considering his underestimation of the enemy,
he should be severely punished.
However, upon first hearing of his brave combat,
there were also executions;
moreover, the enemy has not yet been eliminated,
and military orders must adapt to circumstances.
Therefore, I do not abandon him for a single defeat,
but intend to observe his future performance.
If no light punishment is imposed,
there will be no deterrent.
It is appropriate to temporarily suspend his official position,
and have him lead as a commoner.
You should further consider the original circumstances,
and handle the matter accordingly.”
Now, referencing various texts,
it appears that Lùshān violated military discipline,
and Shǒuguī requested to enforce the law.
Thus, the earlier edict stated:
“Since you have carried this out,
it accords with military law.”
It also stated:
“The execution of Lùshān
was due to excessive underestimation of the enemy.”
This seems to imply that Shǒuguī had already executed him.
Afterward, Shǒuguī was moved by his words,
and admired his bravery.
He could not bear to kill him,
but sparing him would contradict his earlier report to the emperor.
Moreover, he feared he might not satisfy the hearts of the officers and soldiers.
Perhaps the report had not yet arrived,
so he sent him to the capital,
for the emperor to decide his fate,
hoping the emperor would see his talent and pardon him,
similar to how Chén Píng captured Fán Kuài,
or Wèi Qīng imprisoned Sū Jiàn.
The emperor thus intended to pardon him,
but Jiǔlíng firmly memorialized:
“If Shǒuguī’s military orders are to be enforced,
Lùshān should not escape death.”
This was also an impeachment of Shǒuguī for indecision outside the capital,
and further, a pretext to shift responsibility to the emperor.
Jiǔlíng saw him because of this,
and said
“he has the appearance of a rebel.”
The emperor still intended to pardon him,
so Jiǔlíng had no choice but to draft an edict stating:
“You should further consider the original circumstances,
and handle the matter accordingly.”
Upon receiving this edict, Shǒuguī
spared him,
and reported it.
This aligns with the Veritable Records of Xuánzōng,
and seems closer to human sentiment.
Ān Lùshān
was originally a mixed-barbarian from Yíngzhōu,
initially named Ā Luòshān.
His mother
was a shaman.
The New Book states: Lùshān’s original surname was Kāng.
His mother lived among the Turks,
and prayed at Mount Yàluò,
which the barbarians call the god of war.
She then gave birth to Lùshān,
hence he took it as his courtesy name;
he adopted the surname Ān from his stepfather.
Ā,
pronounced wū gé fān.
Luò,
pronounced lǚ jiǎo fān.
His mother remarried the Turk Ān Yányǎn.
When their tribe scattered,
he fled together with Yányǎn’s nephew, Sīshùn,
thus adopting the surname Ān,
and the name Lùshān.
There was also a man named Shǐ Sūgān,
who lived in the same neighborhood as Lùshān,
and was born one day apart.
Examination of Discrepancies states: The Old Biography says:
“Sīmíng was born on New Year’s Eve,
Lùshān on New Year’s Day.”
According to the Records of Lùshān’s Deeds:
“On the twentieth day of the first month of the tenth year of Tiānbǎo,
the emperor and nobles celebrated Lùshān’s birthday,”
so this is not adopted.
They were close friends,
both serving as market brokers,
and were known for their bravery.
Market brokers
are intermediaries;
prices for goods from north and south
are determined by their words,
before trade occurs.
Lùshān often went out with a few horsemen,
and captured dozens of Khitan people to return.
He was cunning,
skilled at gauging people’s feelings.
Shǒuguī favored him,
and adopted him as a son.
Sūgān once fled into Xī territory to escape official debts,
and was captured by Xī scouts,
who intended to kill him.
Sūgān deceived them, saying:
“I
am a marriage envoy of the Táng,
if you kill me,
disaster will befall your country.”
The scouts believed him,
and sent him to the chieftain’s tent.
Sūgān met the Xī king,
bowed with hands clasped but did not kneel.
Though the Xī king was angry,
he feared the Táng,
and dared not kill him.
Instead, he treated him as a guest,
and sent a hundred men to accompany Sūgān to the court.
Sūgān said to the Xī king:
“Though you send many people,
I see their talents are insufficient to meet the Son of Heaven.
I hear you have an excellent general named Suǒgāo—
why not send him to the court!”
Suǒgāo
is likely a title for Xī chieftains,
not a personal name.
There was already a Lǐ Shī Suǒgāo mentioned earlier.
General,
pronounced jí liàng fān.
Court,
pronounced zhí yáo fān.
As Sūgān approached Pínglú,
he first sent someone to tell Military Commissioner Péi Xiūzǐ:
“The Xī envoy Suǒgāo is coming with elite troops,
claiming to go to court,
but actually intending to attack the military city.
You should prepare carefully,
and preemptively deal with them.”
Xiūzǐ then arrayed his troops to welcome them,
and upon reaching the guesthouse,
buried all their accompanying soldiers alive,
and captured Suǒgāo, sending him to Yōuzhōu.
Zhāng Shǒuguī considered Sūgān meritorious,
and recommended him for the position of Guǒyì,
later promoting him to general.
When he later reported to the court,
the emperor spoke with him,
was pleased,
and granted him the name Sīmíng.
The affairs of Ān and Shǐ begin here.
7 Wǔ Yōuwàng’s son, Wēn Shèn, former Sima of Liánzhōu,
was implicated in associating with powerful nobles,
and was beaten to death.
After the emperor pacified the Wěi clan,
Wǔ Yōuwàng was demoted and died.
Shèn,
pronounced shí rèn fān.
On Yǐchǒu
Xìn’ān Prince Lǐ Wěi, Military Commissioner of Shuòfāng and Hédōng, was demoted to Prefect of Qúzhōu;
Guǎngwǔ Prince Lǐ Chénghóng was demoted to Biéjià of Fángzhōu;
Prefect of Jīngzhōu Xuē Zìquàn was demoted to Biéjià of Lǐzhōu;
all because they associated with Wēn Shèn.
Chénghóng
was the son of Shǒulǐ.
Prince Bīn, Lǐ Shǒulǐ,
was the son of Crown Prince Zhānghuái, Lǐ Xián.
On Xīnwèi
Prefect of Púzhōu Wáng Jǔ was demoted to Prefect of Tōngzhōu;
because he exchanged letters with Lǐ Wěi.
8 In the fifth month,
the sorcerer Liú Zhìchéng of Lǐquán rebelled,
driving and plundering passersby,
heading toward Xiányáng.
Villagers fled to inform the county officials,
who burned bridges and blocked roads to resist them.
The rebels then dispersed,
and within a few days,
all were captured and executed.
9 In the sixth month,
monthly salaries for officials began to be distributed.
10. Initially,
the Emperor, taking advantage of the plowing ceremony pardon,
ordered the officials to deliberate on increasing the offerings of biān and dǒu vessels for the ancestral temples and on matters of mourning regulations that had not yet been clarified.
The Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, Wéi Tāo, petitioned that each shrine in the ancestral temples should have twelve biān and dǒu vessels.
The Vice Minister of War, Zhāng Jūn, and the Director of the Bureau of Operations, Wéi Shù, argued:
"The sages understood that the feelings of filial sons are profound, yet the variety of objects is limitless,
therefore they established regulations for them.
Human preferences inherently lack a fixed standard;
the delicacies for private feasts change with the times,
so the sages uniformly returned everything to ancient practices.
Qū Dào was fond of water caltrops,
but Qū Jiàn did not offer them in sacrifice,
believing that personal desires should not interfere with the state's rituals.
The Guóyǔ states: The Chu official Qū Dào was fond of water caltrops.
When he fell ill,
he summoned his clan elder and instructed him, saying:
'When sacrificing to me, you must use water caltrops.'
When the sacrifice was to be performed,
the clan elder was about to offer the water caltrops,
but Qū Jiàn ordered them removed,
saying:
'The ruler of a state has oxen for offerings,
a high minister has sheep as tribute,
a scholar has pig and dog offerings,
and commoners have roasted fish as offerings.
As for biān and dǒu vessels with dried meat and pickles,
these are shared by all ranks.
One should not be ashamed of lacking rare delicacies,
nor display excessive extravagance,
nor use personal desires to interfere with the state's rituals.'
Thus, they were not used.
Jì (芰),
pronounced with the initials qí and jì.
Líng (蔆),
another name for jì.
The Shuōwén states: In Chu it is called jì,
in Qín it is called jiègòu,
but nowadays it is commonly called língjì.
The Wǔlíng Jì states: Those with four or three corners are called jì,
those with two corners are called líng.
Hào (好),
pronounced hū dào.
Qù (去),
pronounced qiāng lǚ.
If all are used for sacrifices,
and one exceeds the old regulations,
where would the limit be!
The Shū says:
'Millet and grain are not the fragrance;
only bright virtue is the fragrance.'
These are the words of King Chéng's command to Jūn Chén.
If we follow what one is accustomed to in life,
and seek spirits without fixed methods,
why must we rigidly adhere to antiquity? Then fǔ and guǐ vessels could be discarded, and plates, bowls, cups, and trays should be used instead;
the Sháo and Huò music could cease, and kōnghóu, zhēng, and flutes should be played instead.
Shùn's music was called Sháo,
Tāng's music was called Huò.
Kōnghóu,
was made by the musician Hóu Diào at the command of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn;
some say it was made by Hóu Huī.
Now, examining its shape, it resembles a smaller sè,
with seven strings,
played with a plectrum like a pipa.
The Old Tángshū states: Kōnghóu
is a Hu (foreign) instrument.
Emperor Líng of Hàn was fond of it.
Its body is curved and long,
with twenty-three strings,
held upright against the chest,
played with both hands simultaneously,
commonly called
'bò kōnghóu'.
The phoenix-head kōnghóu has a neck with seven strings and tuning pegs,
made by Zhèng Shànzǐ,
presented during the Kāiyuán era,
shaped like a ruǎnxián,
with a small, tapered lower part and a larger body,
with small hooks on the side,
for ease of handling.
Another account: Kōnghóu originated from the music of Zhèng and Wèi;
because it was the music of a perished state,
it was called 'the marquis of an empty state',
also known as kǎnhóu.
The Fēngsú Tōng states: During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Qiū Zhòng made the flute.
According to the Zhōulǐ,
the master of sheng is in charge of teaching chí and suì.
It is also said
to have originated among the Qiāng people.
The transverse flute described by Mǎ Róng of the Later Hàn,
was hollow and bottomless,
with two holes carved,
five holes on one side and one on the back,
exactly like the present chǐbā.
Lǐ Shàn annotated it,
saying it had seven holes and was one chǐ four cùn long,
which is the present transverse flute.
The transverse flute mentioned in the Tàicháng's drum and wind section
is not the one described by Mǎ Róng.
Mǎ Róng's description:
'Yì Jīng Jūnmíng understood music theory,
so originally with four holes, he added one;
the hole added by Jūnmíng was at the back,
this is called the shāng note, completing the five notes.'
Shěn Yuē's Sòngshū also states
that Jīng Fáng completed the five notes.
The Zhōulǐ commentary by the master of sheng: Dù Zǐchūn said: Suì is the present five-holed suì.
Considering the records of Mǎ Róng and Shěn Yuē,
then the ancient suì should not have five holes;
Zǐchūn's explanation
is also not necessarily correct.
Now, the Sānlǐ Tú depicts the suì as also transverse with five holes,
but it is unclear what classical basis this has.
Suì,
is the same as flute.
Fǔ (簠),
pronounced fǔ.
Guǐ (簋),
pronounced jū wěi.
What would later generations observe!
The spirits,
with their essence and intelligence, oversee humans;
they do not seek abundance and grandeur.
If one errs in ritual,
what use is abundance!
How can we abandon the ritual classics to follow contemporary customs!
Moreover, the noble person loves others through ritual,
not seeking improper compliance;
especially in the ancestral temples,
how dare we forget the old regulations!"
The Crown Prince's Guest, Cuī Miǎn, argued:
"The origin of sacrificial offerings
dates back to remote antiquity.
When people ate hair and drank blood,
there were offerings of hair and blood;
before the advent of fermented grains,
there were offerings of dark wine.
The Sīxuǎn clan used a mirror to collect bright water from the moon for dark wine.
Niè (糵),
pronounced yú liè.
Ritual objects gradually became complete;
yet, to show reverence through the spiritual way,
one dare not neglect them.
The contents of biān, dǒu, fǔ, guǐ, zūn, and léi vessels
were all delicacies of the Zhōu people's time,
also used for feasting guests,
and when the Duke of Zhōu established rituals,
he offered them to ghosts and spirits along with hair, blood, and dark wine.
Our state establishes teachings based on ritual,
creating models according to the times.
The seasonal sacrifices at the Qīngmiào temple
fully display ritual delicacies,
following the Zhōu system.
Such as fǔ, guǐ, biān, dǒu, xíng soup, and the like.
Zhuàn (饌),
pronounced chú liàn,
also chú huǎn.
Seasonal delicacies are fully set out,
following the Hàn method.
Such as Shūsūn Tōng's request to offer cherries and the like.
Shàng (上),
pronounced shí zhǎng.
To bring distant things.
When there is something new, it must be offered,
following the seasonal commands.
Within the imperial parks,
what is harvested by personal plowing,
during hunting seasons,
what is personally shot and hit,
all are offered before being eaten,
to express utmost sincerity and reverence.
If it is already like this,
what more can be added!
We should only instruct the officials,
not to be negligent or slack,
then fresh, delicious, rich, and strong flavors
will all be present,
and there is no need to increase the number of biān and dǒu vessels."
From this point upward,
the arguments of these individuals
all elaborated on the old rituals.
The Emperor insisted on moderately increasing the varieties and flavors.
Tāo again petitioned to add six biān and dǒu vessels to each shrine,
to be filled in each season with new fruits and rare delicacies;
this was approved.
Tāo further memorialized:
"In mourning garments, 'for maternal uncles,
wear coarse hemp for three months;
for maternal aunts and maternal grandparents, all wear finer hemp for five months.'
Maternal grandparents are of the highest honor,
yet their mourning is the same as that for maternal aunts;
aunts and uncles are of the same rank,
yet the mourning garments differ in weight.
Aunts,
that is, maternal aunts.
Cóng,
pronounced as cái yòng fān.
If affection is severed, one does not wear mourning for them;
aunts by marriage come from external clans,
and do not share the rites of living together.
I humbly believe that the ancient meaning is still not fully expressed,
so I request that mourning for maternal grandparents be increased to nine months of heavy mourning,
for aunts and uncles to five months of finer hemp,
and for paternal uncles, paternal aunts, and aunts by marriage to be increased to baring the shoulder and wearing a mourning band."
The five degrees of mourning end with coarse hemp,
beyond which there is the mourning of baring the shoulder and wearing a band.
Baring the shoulder means
partially removing clothing to expose the shoulder;
wearing a band means
using a cloth one inch wide,
passing from the back of the neck to the front, crossing over the forehead,
and then turning back to wrap around the hair knot.
Tǎn,
pronounced dàn.
Miǎn,
pronounced wèn.
Cuī Mǐn deliberated:
"The way to rectify the family
cannot be divided;
unifying a single principle,
the rationale returns to the main lineage.
Therefore, within the family, there are heavy and light mourning garments,
while outside, all wear coarse hemp.
The honorific titles added
do not exceed one degree,
this is the unchanging way of the former kings.
I wish to uphold the clear decree of the eighth year,
adhering entirely to ancient rites."
What Cuī Mǐn referred to as the imperial decree
is seen in the seventh year of volume two hundred twelve;
calling it the eighth year
includes the year of the emperor's accession to the throne, counting from the Xiāntiān era.
Wéi Shù deliberated:
"The commentary on mourning garments says: 'Animals know their mother but not their father.
Rustic people say,

and soon after, it was moved from Dūshàng to Suíyáng.
In the twelfth year of the Zhēnguān era,
Lǐ Hóngjié pacified the Yí and Liáo peoples,
establishing Gǔzhōu,
which was placed under the jurisdiction of the Róngzhōu Dūdūfǔ.
It was argued that
"replacing the death penalty with caning
is an act of great mercy,
but to be flogged and humiliated
is a rather disgraceful matter.
This should only be applied to slaves and convicts,
and not to gentlemen."
The Emperor followed this advice.
9 On the Guǐwèi day,
an edict was issued stating that as the frontiers were now pacified,
the Zhōngshū and Ménxià departments, along with the military governors of the various circuits, were to assess the urgency and importance of military garrisons,
carefully determine the quotas for troops and defenses,
recruit able-bodied men from among the conscripts and registered households,
to serve permanently as frontier troops,
increase the allocation of farmland and housing,
and ensure they were well provided for.
10 On the Xīnchǒu day,
the Emperor ordered the relevant officials to select capable members of the imperial clan,
appointing them to positions in the central departments, judicial offices, and capital county administrations.
The edict stated:
"Those who violate the Way and disregard the norms
shall receive no leniency under the royal law;
those who cultivate themselves and demonstrate loyalty,
shall they not receive greater favor than others?
It is hoped that they will lead by example,
and inspire our customs."
11 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Jǐmǎo day,
Dàlǐ Shǎoqīng Xú Qiáo
(Textual note: The Old Annals record
"Xú Hù."
Here, the Legal Records and Tōngdiǎn are followed.)
reported: "This year, only fifty-eight death sentences were carried out in the empire.
In the courtyard of the Dàlǐ prison,
it has long been said that the aura of killing was too strong,
and birds would not roost there.
Now, magpies have nested in its trees."
Thereupon, all officials, believing that punishments were nearly unnecessary,
submitted memorials of congratulations.
The Emperor attributed the credit to his chief ministers.
On the Gēngchén day,
he enfeoffed Lǐ Línfǔ as Duke of Jìnguó,
and Niú Xiānkè as Duke of Bīnguó.
(Textual note: The Veritable Records state:
"In the seventh month,
on the Wùyín day,
the relevant officials reported a decrease in prisoners.
The Emperor praised his chief ministers,
issuing an edict: 'Only fifty cases of punishment,
nearly reaching a state of no penalties.'
He then enfeoffed the two."
Also:
"On the Bǐngwǔ day of the tenth month,
while attending to government affairs,
the Emperor inquired about the prisoners in the capital.
The officials reported there were fifty;
he was pleased,
and issued an edict: 'Previously, in the place of thorns,
crows and magpies came to nest.
Now, the total number of punishments
barely exceeds fifty.
The Vice Minister of Justice Zhèng Shǎowēi and others shall each be granted a middle-to-high evaluation.'"
It is unclear whether these are one event or two.
Here, the Old Annals are followed.)
The Emperor ordered Lǐ Línfǔ, Niú Xiānkè, and judicial officials to revise and compile the laws, statutes, regulations, and precedents.
In the ninth month,
on the Rénshēn day,
they were promulgated and implemented.
12 Previously,
several dozen prefectures in the northwest frontier had long stationed heavy troops,
and neither land taxes nor military farming could sustain them,
so the policy of government grain purchase (hédí) was first implemented.
There was a man named Péng Guǒ,
who, through Niú Xiānkè, presented a proposal,
requesting the implementation of the grain purchase policy in Guānzhōng.
On the Wùzǐ day,
an edict was issued stating that the abundant harvest and low grain prices harmed the farmers,
ordering an increase of ten to twenty or thirty percent above the current market price,
to purchase several million hú of grain from the eastern and western capital regions.
The eastern capital region
refers to the Dūjī area.
The western capital region
refers to the Jīngjī area.
Dí (purchase)
is pronounced tā lì fān.
From then on, Guānzhōng's reserves became abundant,
and the imperial carriage no longer needed to travel to the eastern capital.
On the Guǐsì day,
an edict ordered that taxes from Hé'nán and Héběi destined for the Hánjiā and Tàiyuán granaries
(according to Lǐ Bì's biography,
the Tàiyuán granary was located west of Shǎnzhōu)
be handled accordingly. 13 Tàicháng Bóshì Wáng Yú
submitted a memorial requesting the establishment of an altar to the Green Emperor to welcome spring;
this was approved.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Xīnchǒu day,
an edict decreed that from then on, the Emperor would personally welcome spring at the eastern suburbs on Lìchūn.
At that time, the Emperor was quite fond of worshipping spirits and ghosts,
so Wáng Yú specialized in sacrificial rituals to curry favor with the times.
The Emperor was pleased with him,
appointing him as Shìyùshǐ,
and put him in charge of sacrificial affairs.
Wáng Yú sometimes burned paper money during prayers,
resembling a shaman.
Since the Hàn dynasty, burial customs included burying coins,
and later, common folk gradually used paper as a substitute for money in ghost-related matters.
Shǐ (envoy)
is pronounced shū lì fān.
Xí (male shaman)
is pronounced xíng dí fān.
14 On the Rénshēn day,
the Emperor visited the hot springs at Líshān.
On the Yǐyǒu day,
he returned to the palace.
15 On the Jǐchǒu day,
Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī Guǎngpíng Wénzhēn Gōng Sòng Jǐng passed away.
16 In the twelfth month,
on the Bǐngwǔ day,
Consort Wǔ passed away,
and was posthumously honored as Empress Zhēnshùn.
17 That year,
the Emperor ordered Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng Kāng Qiānsù
to go to the eastern capital to demolish the Míngtáng.
"Qiān"
is the same as
"qiān"
(fault),
in ancient script.
The New Book's Treatise on Rites and Music records
"Qiānsù."
"Demolishing it would be labor-intensive;
I request removing the upper level,
making it ninety-five feet lower than the original,
and restoring it as the Qiányuán Hall."
This was approved.
18 For the first time, it was ordered that land-tax, corvée, and household taxes, as well as tax payments in kind,
all be delivered to the capital in local products.
The land-tax, corvée, and household taxes of the western and eastern capitals
followed the laws of Gāozǔ and Tàizōng;
tax payments in kind likely followed laws established since the Kāiyuán era.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the Yǐhài day,
Niú Xiānkè was appointed as Shìzhōng.
2 On the Dīngchǒu day,
the Emperor welcomed the vital energy east of the Chǎnshuǐ River.
3 An edict stated that since the long-term garrison troops in the border regions
had been sufficiently recruited,
from then on, no more garrison troops were to be dispatched,
and those already there were allowed to return.
4 It was ordered that schools be established separately in all prefectures, counties, and villages of the empire.
5 On the Rénchén day,
Lǐ Línfǔ was appointed to oversee the Deputy Ambassador of the Lǒngyòu military command,
with Shànzhōu Dūdū Dù Xīwàng acting as Liúhòu.
In the second month,
on the Yǐmǎo day,
Niú Xiānkè was additionally appointed as Deputy Ambassador of the Hé'dōng military command.
Niú Xiānkè had previously been in charge of Shuòfāng,
and now also held Hé'dōng.
6 On the Jǐwèi day,
Empress Zhēnshùn was buried at Jìnglíng.
Wǔ Huì was posthumously honored as Empress Zhēnshùn.
Jìnglíng was located forty lǐ southeast of Wànnián County in Jīngzhào.
7 On the Rénxū day,
an edict ordered that the Hú people of the six prefectures in Héqū who had been scattered and assigned to various prefectures due to Kāng Dàibīn's rebellion,
be allowed to return to their homeland,
and that Yòuzhōu be established between Yánzhōu and Xiàzhōu
to settle them.
(The relocation of the six Hú prefectures is mentioned in scroll 212, year ten.)
Now, the territories of the six Hú prefectures were merged to form Yòuzhōu.
According to the old records: Yòuzhōu was 1,100 lǐ from the capital.
Xià (summer)
is pronounced hù yǎ fān.
Chǔ (to settle)
is pronounced chāng lǚ fān.
8 In the third month,
the Tǔbō invaded Héxī,
and the military governor Cuī Xīyì defeated them.
The governor of Shànzhōu and acting commander of Lǒngyòu, Dù Xīwàng, attacked the Tǔbō's new city,
captured it,
and established the Wēiróng Army there.
Three hundred and fifty lǐ northwest of Xīngxiùchuān in Shànzhōu was the Wēiróng Army.
Textual analysis notes: The Old Book biography says
"Wǔwǔ Army,"
but here we follow the Veritable Records.
9 In summer,
the fifth month,
on the yǐyǒu day,
Lǐ Línfǔ was appointed concurrent military governor of Héxī.
He already held Lǒngyòu,
and now also took on Héxī.
On the bǐngshēn day,
Cuī Xīyì was appointed governor of Hénán Prefecture.
Cuī Xīyì felt remorse for breaking faith with the Tǔbō,
having violated his alliance with Qǐlìxú.
He died not long after.
10 After Crown Prince Yīng's death,
Lǐ Línfǔ repeatedly urged the Emperor to appoint Shòuwáng Mào.
The Emperor considered that Zhōngwáng Yù was older,
and moreover benevolent, filial, respectful, and cautious,
and fond of learning,
and intended to appoint him,
but hesitated for over a year without deciding.
He reflected that his years were advancing,
three sons had been executed on the same day,
his heir was undetermined,
and he was often unhappy and distracted,
his sleep and appetite diminished because of it.
Gāo Lìshì seized an opportunity to ask the reason.
The Emperor said:
"You,
an old servant of my household,
surely can guess my thoughts!"
Gāo Lìshì said:
"Is it not because the young master is undetermined?"
The Emperor said:
"Yes."
He replied:
"Why must Your Majesty trouble your sacred mind so needlessly?
Simply appoint the eldest,
who would dare dispute it!"
The Emperor said:
"Your words are right!
Your words are right!"
Thus it was settled.
In the sixth month,
on the gēngzǐ day,
Yù was appointed Crown Prince.
11 On the xīnchǒu day,
Xiāo Jiǒng, governor of Qízhōu, was appointed military governor of Héxī and overall acting commander;
Dù Xīwàng, governor of Shànzhōu, was appointed military governor of Lǒngyòu;
Wáng Yù, Minister of the Imperial Stud, was appointed military governor of Jiànnán.
Textual analysis notes: The Old Book biography says
"Wáng Hào,"
but here we follow the Veritable Records and Táng Calendar.
They also destroyed the previously erected Chìlǐng stele.
The erection of the stele
is seen in the previous scroll, year 21.
12 The Qaghan of the Tūjuéshī, Sūlù,
was originally frugal and honest.
Whenever he gained spoils from campaigns,
he would share them with the various tribes,
keeping no private hoard,
and thus the masses gladly served him.
After he married a Táng princess,
he also secretly communicated with the Tūjué and Tǔbō,
and the Tūjué and Tǔbō each gave him a daughter in marriage.
Sūlù took the daughters of the three states as his qatuns,
and appointed several sons as yabghus,
so his expenses gradually increased,
and thus the spoils from campaigns
were no longer shared.
In his later years he suffered from a wind ailment,
one hand became contracted,
and the various tribes became disaffected.
The chieftains Mòhè Dágàn and Dūmódù had the two strongest tribes,
and their tribes were further divided into the Yellow Surname and Black Surname,
mutually at odds.
The Tūjuéshī people themselves called those descended from Suōgé the Yellow Surname,
and Sūlù's tribe the Black Surname.
They killed him.
Dūmódù initially conspired with Mòhè Dágàn,
but later turned against him,
and installed Sūlù's son Gǔchuò as the Tǔhuǒxiān Qaghan to gather the remaining people,
and fought with Mòhè Dágàn.
Mòhè Dágàn sent an envoy to inform Gài Jiāyùn, military governor of Qìxī.
Qì,
pronounced qī jì.
Tǔhuǒxiān and Dūmódù occupied Suìyè City,
and the Black Surname Qaghan Ěrwēi Tèlè occupied Dáluósī City.
The Suìyè River extends a thousand lǐ,
westward connecting to Dáluósī City.
The city originally belonged to the Shíguó,
and Shí often stationed troops to guard it.
Gài,
pronounced gǔ gé.
Qí,
pronounced qí jì.
Kě,
entering tone from kān.
Hán,
pronounced hán.
Dá,
pronounced dāng gē.
Luó,
pronounced láng zuǒ.
Textual analysis notes: The Táng Calendar says
"Héngluósī."
Here we follow the Veritable Records.
13 When the Crown Prince was about to receive the investiture,
the ceremonial protocol included "inner strictness," "outer readiness," and crimson gauze robes.
Under Táng regulations,
on the day the Emperor fasted for a grand sacrifice,
one kè after the water clock marks the day,
the Attendant Secretary presents a tablet and requests inner strictness.
The various guards enter and array in the palace courtyard,
civil and military officials of the fifth rank and above in trousers and jackets attend in position,
various attending officials wear their regalia and implements,
various fasting attendants tie on pendants,
and proceed to the gate to receive.
Two kè,
the Attendant Secretary presents a tablet and announces outer readiness,
and the imperial carriage then proceeds to court assembly.
The various guards stand in formation,
the hundred officials take their positions,
and the Attendant Secretary also announces outer readiness,
without requesting inner strictness.
When the Emperor is about to depart,
seven kè before the carriage departs, one drum is struck for the first strictness;
five kè before, two drums are struck for the second strictness.
The Attendant Secretary presents a tablet and requests inner strictness,
the officials display the imperial procession,
two kè before, three drums are struck for the third strictness.
The various guards enter in order and stand in the palace courtyard,
officials stand in the court hall,
the Attendant Secretary, Secretariat Director, and below receive at the western steps,
the Attendant Secretary holds the seal,
the Chénghuáng official presents the carriage at the southern side of the western steps of the Tàijí Hall,
the Qiānniú General stands before the carriage facing north holding a long sword,
the Yellow Gate Attendant stands before the attending ministers,
with two ushers.
Once outer readiness is announced,
the Minister of the Imperial Stud lifts his robe and ascends,
stands upright holding the reins,
and the imperial carriage departs and mounts the carriage.
The Empress Dowager and Empress also have inner strictness and outer readiness,
both announced by the Chief Director of Ceremonies with a tablet.
For the Crown Prince's inner strictness and outer readiness,
the Left Supervisor of the Household presents the tablet.
When the Emperor wears the "communicating with heaven" crown,
he then wears crimson gauze robes,
for receiving New Year's congratulations at the winter solstice, returning from sacrifices, feasting officials, and venerating the aged.
When the Crown Prince wears the "far-roaming" crown,
he also wears crimson gauze robes,
for attending court and returning to the palace, entering court on the first day of the year and the first of the month, and for the Shìdiàn ceremony.
A memorial requested to change this.
Left Chancellor Péi Yàoqīng memorialized to halt inner strictness,
change outer readiness to outer preparation,
and change crimson gauze robes to Zhūmíng robes.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the jǐsì day,
the Emperor ascended the Xuānzhèng Hall,
and invested the Crown Prince.
Textual analysis notes: Yuán Zǎi's Veritable Records of Sùzōng says:
"On the rénchén day of the seventh month of the twenty-seventh year,
the ceremony was performed."
Here we follow the Xuánzōng Veritable Records.
The Crown Prince rode a carriage to the hall gate.
At this time,
the Crown Prince did not use the carriage,
but walked from his palace.
On this day,
a general amnesty was declared.
On the jǐmǎo day,
the wife of Zhōngwáng, Wéi, was invested as Crown Princess.
14 Dù Xīwàng led the troops of Shànzhōu to seize the Tǔbō's Héqiáo,
and built Yánquán City on the left bank of the river.
The Tǔbō dispatched thirty thousand troops to meet them in battle.
Dù Xīwàng's forces were few and no match,
and the officers and soldiers were all afraid.
Left Guard Commandant Wáng Zhōngsì led his troops to first assault their formation,
wherever he went the enemy gave way,
killing several hundred men,
and the enemy formation fell into chaos.
Dù Xīwàng unleashed his troops to take advantage,
and the enemy was greatly defeated.
He established the Zhènxī Army at Yánquán.
The Zhènxī Army was one hundred and eighty lǐ west of Hézhōu.
15 In the eighth month,
on the xīnsì day,
the King of Bóhǎi, Wǔyì, died,
and his son Qīnmào succeeded him.
On the 16th day of the ninth month,
the first day of the month was Bǐngshēn,
and there was a solar eclipse.
Previously,
during the Yífèng era,
Tǔbō captured and occupied Ānróng Fort.
Initially,
to the west of Màozhōu in Jiànnán, Ānróng Fort was built and garrisoned,
in order to block Tǔbō's southern border.
The Shēng Qiāng guided Tǔbō to capture it,
and they then held it,
subsequently annexing the various tribes of the Xī'ěrhé region.
To the east, it bordered Sōng, Mào, and Xī.
Táng repeatedly attacked it,
but could not conquer it.
The Jiànnán military governor Wáng Yù built two forts beside it,
stationing troops at the foot of Púpó Ridge.
The New Book records it as
"Péngpó Ridge".
Its location was beyond the Snowy Mountains,
as mentioned in Dù Fǔ's poem:
"Next, they took Péngpó's city beyond the snow."
This refers to it.
Tǔbō dispatched a large army to relieve Ānróng Fort,
and Yù's forces suffered a major defeat,
with several thousand men killed.
Examination of discrepancies: The Old Biography states,
"Tens of thousands of officers and soldiers
were all lost to the enemy."
Here we follow the Veritable Records.
Provisions, weapons, and military supplies were all abandoned.
Yù was demoted to prefect of Kuòzhōu,
and further demoted to a minor official at Gāoyāo, where he died.
On the Wùwǔ day,
Méng Guīyì of Nánzhào was enfeoffed as Prince of Yúnnán.
Commentary on the Water Classic: The Yúnnán commandery was originally the territory of Yúnshān County,
established as a commandery in the second year of the Jiànxīng era of Shǔ Liú.
From Kāibiān County in Róngzhōu of Táng, seventy lǐ south to Qūzhōu,
and another two thousand five hundred lǐ to Yúnnán City.
Guīyì's ancestors were originally from the Āiláo Yi territory.
The Āiláo Yi
submitted to the court during the reign of Emperor Míng of Hàn.
To the southeast, it bordered Jiāozhǐ;
to the northwest, it bordered Tǔbō.
In the barbarian language, a king is called a zhào.
Initially, there were six zhào: Méngshè,
Méngyuè,
Yuèxī,
Làngqióng,
Yàngbèi,
and Yuèdàn.
Examination of discrepancies: The New Book states
"The six zhào are Méngxī, Yuèxī, Làngqióng, Téngshǎn, Shīlàng, and Méngshè."
Here we follow Dòu Pāng's Yúnnán Biélù.
None could unify the others;
successive dynasties used this to divide their power.
Méngshè was the southernmost,
hence it was called Nánzhào (Southern Zhào).
During Emperor Gāozōng's reign,
Méngshè's Xìnúluó first came to court.
Xìnúluó begot Luóshèng,
Luóshèng begot Shèngluópí,
Shèngluópí begot Píluógé.
Píluógé gradually grew powerful,
while the other five zhào weakened;
he happened to have achieved merit in defeating the Mǐhé barbarians.
Mǐhé is the Xī'ěrhé.
Mǐ
is pronounced nǎi lì fān.
He sought to unite the six zhào into one.
Yù submitted a memorial requesting this on his behalf,
and the court approved it,
additionally bestowing upon him the name Guīyì.
He then used military force to subdue the Qí barbarians,
destroying those who did not submit,
and subsequently defeated Tǔbō,
moving his residence to Dàhé City;
later, this eventually became a border trouble.
The affairs of Nánzhào begin here.
Their ancestors were a separate branch of the Wūmán.
In the barbarian language, a sloping mountain is called hé,
hence it was called Dàhé City.
Zú,
zǐ xù fān.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Wùyín day,
the Emperor went to the hot springs at Líshān;
on the Rénchén day,
the Emperor returned to the palace.
This year,
along the roads between the Western Capital and the Eastern Capital,
over a thousand traveling palaces were built.
The Left and Right Yǔlín armies were divided to establish the Lóngwǔ Army,
with the Wànqí camp placed under its command.
The prefect of Rùnzhōu, Qí Huàn, memorialized:
"Crossing the river from Guābù is a detour of sixty lǐ.
I request to cross directly from below the Jīngkǒu Dam,
digging the Yīlóu River for twenty-five lǐ to reach Yángzǐ County,
and establishing the Yīlóu Dam."
This was approved.
In spring,
the first month,
on the Rényín day,
the Prince of Róng, Wǎn, Military Commissioner of Lǒngyòu, was ordered to personally go to his circuit to inspect and manage the various armies,
selecting and recruiting thirty to fifty thousand strong men from Guānnèi and Hédōng,
to go to Lǒngyòu for defense.
If there were no enemy incursions by late autumn,
they were permitted to return.
The ministers requested to add the honorific title Shèngwén;
in the second month,
on the Jǐsì day,
this was granted,
and a general amnesty was declared,
exempting the common people from this year's land tax.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Guǐyǒu day,
an edict was issued:
"All yīn-yāng arts and divination techniques,
except for selecting dates for weddings and funerals,
are prohibited."
On the Jǐchǒu day,
Niú Xiānkè was appointed as Minister of War and concurrently Palace Attendant,
Lǐ Línfǔ as Minister of Personnel and concurrently Secretariat Director,
overseeing the selection of civil and military officials.
This meant Niú Xiānkè oversaw military selection,
and Lǐ Línfǔ oversaw civil selection.
Xuǎn,
xū juàn fān.
In the sixth month,
on the Guǐyǒu day,
Vice Censor-in-Chief Lǐ Shìzhī was concurrently appointed military governor of Yōuzhōu.
The Yōuzhōu generals Zhào Kān and Báizhēntuóluó forged an order from military governor Zhāng Shǒuguī,
ordering the Pínglú military commissioner Wū Zhīyì to attack the remnants of the rebellious Xī north of Héngshuǐ;
Héngshuǐ should be
"Huángshuǐ".
The New Book records it as
"Huángshuǐ",
while the Old Book's biography of Zhāng Shǒuguī records it as
"Huángshuǐ",
and we follow that here.
Huángshuǐ is in the Liáo region,
within the boundaries of present-day Línhuáng Prefecture.
The records state,
from Yíngzhōu, cross the Sōngxíng Ridge and travel north four hundred lǐ to reach Huángshuǐ.
Shǐ,
shū lì fān.
Jiàng,
jí liàng fān.
Báizhēntuóluó forged an imperial decree to pressure him.
Zhīyì had no choice but to send out troops,
encountered the enemy,
won initially but was later defeated;
Shǒuguī concealed the defeat,
reporting it as a victory with captures.
The matter was somewhat exposed,
and the Emperor ordered the Palace Receptionist Supervisor Niú Xiāntóng to go and investigate.
The Palace Receptionist Supervisor,
a rank of sixth grade, lower class, in Táng,
was responsible for internal announcements and managing the registers of imperial relatives and titled ladies attending court assemblies,
sending the lists to the Palace Domestic Service.
The blame was placed on Báizhēntuóluó,
who was forced to hang himself.
Xiāntóng was favored by the Emperor,
and the other eunuchs resented him,
jointly exposing his affairs.
The Emperor was angry,
and on the Jiǎxū day,
ordered Yáng Sīxù to beat him to death with a staff.
Sīxù bound and restrained him,
struck him several hundred times,
cut out his heart,
and sliced his flesh to eat.
Shǒuguī was demoted to prefect of Kuòzhōu.
The Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent, Xiāo Sōng, had once bribed Xiāntóng with several qǐng of good farmland south of the city,
Lǐ Línfǔ exposed this,
and Sōng was demoted to prefect of Qīngzhōu.
In autumn,
the eighth month,
on the Yǐhài day,
the Qìxī military governor Gài Jiāyùn captured the Tūjuéshī Qaghan Tǔhuǒxiān.
Qì,
qī jì fān.
Gài,
gǔ gé fān.
Tǔhuǒxiān came out to fight,
was defeated and fled,
and was captured at Hèluó Ridge.
Separate detachments were sent: the Shūlè garrison commander Fūméng Língchá and the Báhànnà king Āxīlàndágàn secretly led troops to suddenly enter Dáluósī City,
capturing the Black Surname Qaghan Ěrwēi,
then entered Yèjiàn City,
and took Jiāohé Princess.
The affair of Jiāohé Princess began in the 12th year, scroll 212.
His might shook the western frontier.
7 On the Rénwǔ day,
the Tǔbō invaded the Báicǎo and Ānrén armies.
The Báicǎo Army was located west of the Yùrú River.

14. The Military Governor of Jiànnán, Zhāng Yòu,

According to old records,

I have examined the Táng system:
wherever there were local militia troops,
a Militia Commissioner was established.
At this time, Shǔ had local militia troops for town defense in the five prefectures of Lí, Yǎ, Qióng, Yì, and Mào,
hence a Deputy Militia Commissioner was established;
after the rebellions of Ān Lùshān and Shǐ Sīmíng,

15. Previously,
after the mourning period for Emperor Ruìzōng had concluded,
a xiá sacrifice was held at the Imperial Ancestral Temple;
from then on, a xiá sacrifice was held every three years,
and a dì sacrifice every five years.
This year,
a dì sacrifice had already been held in summer,
and a xiá sacrifice was due again in winter.
The Court of Imperial Sacrifices deliberated and believed that excessive sacrifices would be disrespectful,
and requested to suspend this year's xiá sacrifice.
From then on, it was calculated that over five years, one xiá and one dì sacrifice would be held,
and this was approved.
The historical record states that this arrangement then conformed to the principle of holding two major sacrifices within five years.

Textual Analysis: The Old History biography states:
"Jiāyùn wished to establish Huáidào's son Xīn as Kaghan to pacify and govern them.
Mòhè Dágān refused,
saying: 'The campaign to subdue Sūlù
was originally my fundamental plan.
If Shǐ Xīn is established as ruler,
then how will the state reward me!'
Therefore, Shǐ Xīn was not established,
and Mòhè Dágān was instead ordered to command the multitude."
In the twenty-seventh year,
Jiāyùn went to the court to present captives,
and still had Tǔhuǒxiān presented at the Imperial Ancestral Temple."
The Institutional History states:
"In the twenty-ninth year,
Xīn, grandson of Xièsèluó and son of Huáidào, was made Kaghan,
and troops were sent to escort him.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo,
when Xīn reached Jùlán City southwest of Suìyè,
he was killed by Mòhèduō Dágān.
In the third year,
the Military Governor of Ānxī, Mǎ Língchá, beheaded him,
and instead established their chieftain as the Yídìmǐlǐ Gǔduōlù Píqié Kaghan."
According to the Veritable Records:
"In the twenty-eighth year of Kāiyuán,
in the third month,
on the Jiǎyín day,
Gài Jiāyùn captured and brought Tǔhuǒxiān to present him;
in the fourth month,
on the Xīnwèi day,
(the court) enfeoffed the wife of the Ten Tribes Kaghan Āshǐnà Xīn, Lady Lǐ, as the Princess of Jiāohé;
in the twelfth month, on the Yǐmǎo day,
the Tūjuéshī Kaghan Mòhè Dágān led his wives, children, and over a hundred banner officials and chieftains to submit to our authority.
Previously,
Mòhè Dágān and Wūsū Wànluò incited various tribes to rebel against us,
the Emperor ordered Gài Jiāyùn to proclaim grace and summon them,
and they all submitted in succession."
The New History biography states:
"Dágān refused to establish Xīn,
and immediately incited the tribes to rebel;
an edict ordered Jiāyùn to summon them,
and then (Dágān) led his wives, children, and others to surrender,
and was subsequently ordered to command his multitude.
Several years later,
Xīn was again made Kaghan,
and troops were dispatched to escort him.
When Xīn reached Jùlán City,
he was killed by Mòhèduō;
Mòhèduō made himself Kaghan,
and the Military Governor of Ānxī, Fūméng Língchá, executed him."
If it were as stated in the Old History biography,
that Jiāyùn immediately made Mòhè Dágān the Kaghan to command the multitude,
then Mòhè should not have rebelled again.
Moreover, establishing a Kaghan must involve court enfeoffment and appointment;
how could Jiāyùn presumptuously establish one beyond the frontier!
If he was not yet made Kaghan,
then the Veritable Records entry for the twelfth month should not refer to him as the Tūjuéshī Kaghan Mòhè Dágān.
If it were as stated in the Institutional History,
that Xīn was only established as Kaghan in the twenty-ninth year,
then the Veritable Records entry for the fourth month of the twenty-eighth year should not already refer to Xīn as the Ten Tribes Kaghan.
It is likely that after Gài Jiāyùn pacified Tūjuéshī,
he immediately memorialized to establish Xīn as the Ten Tribes Kaghan,
hence Mòhè Dágān, dissatisfied, rebelled.
Emperor Míng then made Mòhè Dágān a lesser Kaghan,
only commanding the Tūjuéshī multitude,
and had Jiāyùn summon and instruct him,
so he came to surrender;
however, Xīn was the Ten Tribes Kaghan,
concurrently commanding all tribes,
so Emperor Míng dispatched troops to escort him,
but he was killed by Mòhè Dágān.
Perhaps this is how it happened.
But the Veritable Records are incomplete and omit details,
making it doubtful and impossible to be certain;
therefore, I have roughly gathered what is seen in various texts,
preserving a general outline and recording it.
In the fourth month,

Gài Jiāyùn, relying on his border achievements to ingratiate himself with the sovereign,

In the capital, he amused himself with wine and women instead of immediately proceeding to his post,

The historian uses the phrase "lingered idly" to describe this,

It was remarked:

Dèng Màn said:

will he not neglect preparations!'
Mò Áo indeed neglected preparations.
When he reached Luó,
Luó and the Lú Róng jointly attacked him,
and inflicted a major defeat.
Complacent,
pronounced as nǚ jiǔ fān.
Lù Dé Míng said: Sāo,
pronounced as yīn xiāo,
also pronounced as yīn sān.
Ultimately,
pronounced as zǐ xù fān.
I privately worry about this.
Moreover, the autumn defense is not far off,
yet he has not mentioned a departure date.
If he only leaves when matters arise,
then the soldiers will not yet be acquainted with him,
how can he control the enemy!
Furthermore, when a general receives his command,
he exits through the ominous gate;
but now he indulges in drinking day and night,
which is hardly the heart of one who worries for the state and cares for the people.
If he cannot be changed,
he should be swiftly dispatched on his journey,
and I still beg Your Majesty's grace to sternly admonish and urge him."
The Emperor then urged Gài Jiāyùn to depart.
Later, Gài Jiāyùn ultimately achieved no merit.
Gài Jiāyùn, being of small capacity and easily satisfied,
his will and spirit had grown slack,
how could he possibly achieve merit!

A note on discrepancies: According to the Veritable Records,
in this year
“on the yǐwèi day of the eighth month,

The Old Annals state:

and deputy military commissioner of Pinglǔ.”
The Institutional History states:

and this became the established rule.”
According to the Old Biography,
Lùshān was promoted from Pinglǔ military commissioner to Pinglǔ military commissioner,
likely because the Pinglǔ military commissioner also held the title of deputy military commissioner of Yōuzhōu.
The Veritable Records erroneously includes
the character “dà”
(great).
In the first year of the Tiānbǎo era,

The fifth year
(Bǐngxū, 746)
1 Spring,
first month,
Yǐchǒu,
Huángfǔ Wéimíng, Military Commissioner of Lǒngyòu, was concurrently appointed Military Commissioner of Héxī.
Lǐ Shìzhī was by nature careless and impetuous.
Lǐ Línfǔ once said to Shìzhī:

Another day,

The Emperor asked Línfǔ about it,

the month mid-autumn,
I received the abundant virtue of Shǎohào,

Línfǔ knew this meaning,

Royal,
pronounced 'wàng', with the tone 'yù'.

and Jiān,

Temple,

Línfǔ had Shènjīn, along with the Imperial Censor Wáng Hóng and the Legal Officer of the Capital Prefecture Jí Wēn, jointly interrogate them.
Textual analysis notes: The Old Tángshu biography of Línfǔ states:

The biography of Shènjīn states:

The two biographies contradict each other.
Now following the Táng Calendar.

2. Appointed Wáng Zhōngsì as the Military Commissioner of Héxī and Lǒngyòu,
concurrently overseeing the affairs of the Shuòfāng and Hédōng military commands.
When Zhōngsì was initially in Shuòfāng and Hédōng,
each time trade was conducted,
he would deliberately overestimate the price of horses.
Upon hearing this,
the various non-Han peoples competed to sell their horses to the Táng,
and Zhōngsì bought them all.
Consequently, the number of horses among the non-Han peoples decreased,
while the Táng army grew stronger.
When he was transferred to Lǒngyòu and Héxī,
he further requested to allocate nine thousand horses from the Shuòfāng and Hédōng commands to bolster his forces,
making his army strong as well.
Zhōngsì wielded authority over four commands,
controlling a territory of ten thousand *lǐ*,
with the empire's elite troops and strategic strongholds
all under his control.
He fought the Tǔbō at Qīnghǎi and Jīshí,
achieving great victories in both battles.
He also campaigned against the Tǔyùhún at the Mòlí Army garrison,
capturing their entire population and returning.
Tǔ,
pronounced with the entering tone of tūn.
Yù,
pronounced yù.
3. In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Guǐwèi day,
appointed the Xī chieftain Suōgù as Prince Zhāoxìn,
and the Qìdān chieftain Kǎiluò as Prince Gōngrén.
4. On the Jǐhài day,
an edict was issued:
"Henceforth, in each of the four beginning months of the seasons,
an auspicious day shall be selected to sacrifice to Heaven, Earth, and the Nine Palaces."
5. After Wéi Jiān and others were demoted,
the Left Chancellor Lǐ Shìzhī grew fearful
and requested a less significant post for himself.
On the Gēngyín day,
Shìzhī was appointed as Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent,
and relieved of his governmental duties.
His son, Lǐ Zhá, the Junior Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, once prepared a lavish feast to invite guests,
but the guests, fearing Lǐ Línfǔ,
throughout the entire day, not a single one dared to attend.
6. Appointed Chén Xīliè, Vice Director of the Chancellery and Grand Academician of the Chóngxuán Institute, as Tongpingzhangshi (Participant in Determining Governmental Matters).
The Later Wèi established the Chóngxuán Office,
responsible for Buddhist monks and nuns, and Daoist priests and priestesses.
The Suí placed the Chóngxuán Office under the Court of Diplomatic Relations.
The Táng established Supervisors for various temples and monasteries,
subordinate to the Court of Diplomatic Relations,
with one Supervisor for each temple or monastery;
during the Zhēnguàn era,
the Supervisors for temples and monasteries were abolished.
In the second year of the Shàngyuán era,
the Lacquer Garden Supervisor was established,
but soon abolished;
in the twenty-fifth year of the Kāiyuán era,
the Chóngxuán School was established at the Temple of the Mysterious Origin Emperor;
in the first year of the Tiānbǎo era,
one Professor and one Assistant Professor each were established in the two capitals.
In the second year,
the Chóngxuán School was renamed the Chóngxuán Institute,
Professors were renamed Academicians,
and Assistant Professors were renamed Assistant Academicians;
a Grand Academician was established,
filled by the Chancellor,
overseeing the Mysterious Origin Temples and Daoist monasteries in the two capitals.
Xīliè was from Sòngzhōu,
and advanced through lecturing on Lǎozǐ and Zhuāngzǐ,
exclusively using tales of immortals and auspicious omens to flatter the Emperor.
Lǐ Línfǔ, because Xīliè was favored by the Emperor
and was moreover pliant and obsequious, easy to control,
thus recommended him to become Chancellor;
all governmental matters were decided by Línfǔ alone,
Xīliè merely assenting and agreeing.
According to precedent,
Chancellors would leave the office only after six *kè* past noon,
but Línfǔ petitioned that,
as the times were peaceful and without incident,
he could return to his residence by the sì hour (9-11 AM),
and military and state affairs were all decided at his private residence;
the Secretariat Clerk would merely bring the completed documents to Xīliè for him to sign his name.
7. In the fifth month,
on the Rénzǐ day, the first day of the month,

8. On the Yǐhài day,

the seventh month,

After this, most of those exiled or demoted did not survive the journey.
10. Yáng Guìfēi was then in favor,

There were seven hundred weavers and embroiderers dedicated to supplying the Guìfēi's residence.
Inside and outside the court, people vied to present her with utensils, garments, and rare curios.
The Military Commissioner of Lǐngnán, Zhāng Jiǔzhāng,
and the Senior Assistant of Guǎnglíng, Wáng Yì,
(Guǎnglíng Commandery
is Yángzhōu.
Senior Assistant,
pronounced zhǎng.)
Jiǔzhāng was promoted to the third rank,

the entire empire followed this trend and became subservient.
A folk song circulated:
"When a boy is born, don't be glad; when a girl is born, don't be sad.
Just look now at how a girl can become the lintel of the door."
Generally, when people build a house,
those coming from outside,
upon seeing its lintel grand and spacious,
consider it imposing.
This means the Yáng family, because they bore a daughter, saw their clan's gate become lofty and illustrious.
Another saying: The door is supported by the lintel,
meaning a daughter can support the family's门户.
Each year, orders were given to have lychees delivered from Lǐngnán by express relay.
From Sū Shì and others onward,
all say that at this time lychees were delivered from Fúzhōu,
not from Lǐngnán.
Their color and flavor remained unchanged.
Bái Jūyì said: Lychees grow in the Bā and Xiá regions.
The tree's shape is rounded like a curtained canopy,
leaves like those of the holly,
flowers like those of the orange,
blooming in spring,
fruit like cinnabar,
ripening in summer,
clusters like grapes,
pits like loquats,
shells like red silk,
membranes like purple gauze,
flesh pure white like ice and snow,
juice sweet and sour like sweet wine and cheese.
Generally as described,
but the reality surpasses it.
If separated from the branch,
in one day the color changes,
in two days the fragrance changes,
and beyond four or five days, color, fragrance, and flavor are completely gone.
At this point,

That day,
the Emperor was displeased,

His attendants' actions failed to meet his wishes,

Gāo Lìshì, wishing to test the Emperor's mood,

amounting to over a hundred carts in total;
the Emperor also personally divided his own imperial meals to bestow upon her.
When night fell,

and thus the palace gates were opened and she entered.
The *Tang Liudian* states: The Gate Captain is in charge of the schedule for opening and closing the various gates of the capital city, the Imperial City, and the palace.
At the Chéngtiān Gate, the dawn drum is beaten;
after hearing the bell strike and waiting one *ke*,
when the drumbeats cease,
the Imperial City gates open.
When the first series of *dongdong* drumbeats ceases,
the Palace City gates, along with the Zuǒ Yánmíng Gate, Yòu Yánmíng Gate, and Qiánhuà Gate, open.
When the second series of *dongdong* drumbeats ceases,
the palace gates open.
At night,
when the first series of *dongdong* drumbeats ceases,
the palace gates close.
When the second series of *dongdong* drumbeats ceases,
the Palace City gates close,
and the Zuǒ Yánmíng Gate, Yòu Yánmíng Gate, and Imperial City gates close.
The opening and closing of the capital city gates
occurs at the same time as the Imperial City gates.
The drum-beating at the Chéngtiān Gate
all follows the clepsydra and tallies;
the drum is struck only when the tally arrives;
when the clepsydra station's plaque arrives,
the drumbeats then cease.
For all keys to the closed gates of the Imperial City,
they are taken out first at *yǒu* (5-7 PM)
and brought back in after *xū* (7-9 PM);
keys to the open gates
are taken out after *chǒu* (1-3 AM)
and brought back in at the end of the night.
For keys to the closed gates of the capital city,
they are taken out after *shēn* (3-5 PM)
and brought back in before *zǐ* (11 PM-1 AM);
keys to the open gates
are taken out after *zǐ* (11 PM-1 AM)
and brought back in before *mǎo* (5-7 AM).
If it is not the scheduled time
but there is an order to open or close,
then one goes to the Secretariat to report and receive confirmation,
and upon receiving the decree and matching the tally, the gates are opened or closed.
For palace gates and city gates,
if there is an edict to open them at night,
the recipient of the edict must record in detail which gates need to be opened,
and announce it to the Secretariat-Chancellery.
Zhì,
is pronounced *zhǐlǐ fān*.
Thereafter, no other consorts could gain favor.

Xià,

Yuèzhōu was 2,237 *li*;
Xiázhōu was 1,888 *li*;
Ānzhōu,

Bīn,

Juàn,

Juàn,

13 The Advisor of the Crown Prince's Household, Dù Yǒulín,
(The Tang dynasty's Advisor of the Crown Prince's Household,
rank 5a upper grade,
was responsible for remonstrating and admonishing the Crown Prince.)
In the Tang Crown Prince's inner household,
the Senior Concubine (Liángdì),
rank 3a.
Dì,
is pronounced *tè jì fān*.
Jì was unrestrained and careless by nature,
fond of merit and fame,
and delighted in associating with heroes and outstanding figures.
The Prefect of Zīchuān, Péi Dūnfù, recommended him to the Prefect of Běihǎi, Lǐ Yōng.
Běihǎi Commandery
was in Qīngzhōu.
Jì went to the capital,
and became friends with the Editorial Director, Wáng Zeng, and others,
all of whom were famous scholars of the time.
Jì was at odds with his wife's family,
and wishing to entrap them,
he spread rumors,
accusing Yǒulín of falsely claiming prophetic texts,
colluding with the Eastern Palace (the Crown Prince's household),
and criticizing the imperial carriage (i.e., the Emperor).
Lǐ Línfǔ ordered the Capital Prefecture Judicial Officer, Jí Wēn, and the Censorate to investigate the matter.
(The Judicial Officer, the Administrator of Judicial Affairs,
was in charge of ferries, bridges, boats, carts, residences, and crafts.)
Wēn ordered Jì to implicate Zeng and others in the case.
In the twelfth month,
on Jiǎxū day,
Yǒulín, Jì, and Zeng were all beaten to death,
and their corpses piled up at the Dàlǐ Temple.
*Kǎoyì* says: The *Old Tang History* annals and the *Tánglì* both record
"Xīnwèi day."
Here we follow the *Veritable Records*.
The *Veritable Records* say
"Jì and his accomplices were all executed according to law,"
but the imperial edict states:
"Yet we still leniently commute the extreme penalty,
allowing them to be sentenced to caning.
As for Wáng Zeng and others,
each shall receive one hundred heavy strokes;
Dù Yǒulín and Liǔ Jì, considering their distant kinship [with the Crown Prince],
are specially spared from death,
to receive one beating,
and be demoted to the position of Assistant Magistrate of Xīnxīng in Lǐngnán."
The biography of Jí Wēn, however, states:
"Jì and others were beaten to death,
and their corpses piled up at the Dàlǐ Temple."
It seems that although the edict prescribed caning,
in reality they all died under the beating.
The court and the country were shocked and terrified.
The heir to the Prince of Guó, Jù, was demoted to Military Administrator of Yìyáng.
Yìyáng Commandery
was in Shēnzhōu.
According to the old records: Shēnzhōu was 1,796 *li* from the capital.
He was the son of Yōng.
(Gāozǔ's son
was the Prince of Guó, Fèng.
Fèng's legitimate grandson was the heir to the Prince of Guó, Yōng.)
The Crown Prince also expelled his Senior Concubine, reducing her to commoner status.
On the Yǐhài day,
Wáng Jū, the Grand Administrator of Yèjùn, was demoted to Sima of Jiānghuá for corruption.
Yèjùn,
originally the Wèijùn of Xiàngzhōu,
was renamed in the first year.
Jiānghuá Commandery,
in Dàozhōu.
Both he and Lǐ Yōng considered themselves senior officials,
having long been posted outside the capital,
and were discontented.
Lǐ Línfǔ disliked their reliance on talent and willfulness,
so he used this incident to remove them.
Wáng Jū had served the Emperor when he was Crown Prince,
and assisted in the decision to execute Princess Tàipíng.
"Dislike" is pronounced wù.
[Pronunciation note omitted.]
Sixth Year
(Dīnghài, 747)
1 Spring,
first month,
Xīnsì day.
Lǐ Yōng and Péi Dūnfù were both beaten to death.
Lǐ Yōng's talent and skill were outstanding.
Lú Cángyòng once said to him:
"You are like the swords Gānjiàng and Mòyé,
difficult to contend with,
but I fear you may eventually break."
Lǐ Yōng did not heed this.
Lǐ Línfǔ further petitioned to send censors to the places of exile to bestow death upon Huángfǔ Wéimíng, Wéi Jiān and his brothers, etc.
Luó Xīshì traveled from Qīngzhōu to Lǐngnán,
killing exiled officials along the way.
Luó Xīshì had already killed Lǐ Yōng in Qīngzhōu,
then proceeded to Lǐngnán.
The dispatch notice for post horses arrived at Yíchūn.
When censors traveled,
commanderies and counties along the route provided post horses,
so before arrival there was a dispatch notice for horses.
[Lǐ Yīzhī] took poison and killed himself.
Arriving at Jiānghuá,
Wáng Jū took poison but did not die.
Hearing that Luó Xīshì had arrived,
he hanged himself.
Luó Xīshì also took a detour through Ānlù,
intending to frighten Péi Kuān to death.
Péi Kuān kowtowed to Luó Xīshì, begging for his life.
Luó Xīshì did not stay overnight and passed through,
so [Péi Kuān] was spared.
Lǐ Shìzhī's son Lǐ Zhá escorted his father's coffin to Dōngjīng.
Lǐ Línfǔ had someone falsely accuse Lǐ Zhá,
and he was beaten to death at the Hé'nán Prefecture office.
The Imperial Advisor Fáng Guǎn, for being friendly with Lǐ Shìzhī,
was demoted to Grand Administrator of Yíchūn.
Fáng Guǎn
was the son of Fáng Róng.
Fáng Róng appears in scroll 207, fourth year of Cháng'ān under Empress Wǔ.
Lǐ Línfǔ's hatred for Wéi Jiān did not cease.
He sent envoys to prefectures and counties along the Huán River and the Jiāng-Huái region to seek evidence of Wéi Jiān's crimes,
arresting
and imprisoning transport supervisors and boatmen.
The prisons overflowed.
Ten boats constituted one transport unit.
An official served as supervisor.
The boatmen,
were those who towed and piloted the boats.
This extended to neighboring households,
who were stripped and died in government offices,
continuing until Lǐ Línfǔ's death.
2 On Dīnghài day,
the Emperor offered sacrifices at the Imperial Ancestral Temple;
on Wùzǐ day,
he performed the joint sacrifice to Heaven and Earth at the southern suburb,
and pardoned the empire.
An edict exempted the people from this year's land tax.
He also ordered the removal of statutes on strangulation and beheading.
The Emperor, admiring the reputation of sparing life,
thus ordered that those sentenced to strangulation or beheading instead be severely beaten and exiled to Lǐngnán.
In reality, officials generally beat them to death.
He also ordered the empire to observe three years of mourning for a remarried mother.
The Emperor wished to broadly seek talented men from the empire,
ordering those proficient in at least one art to come to the capital.
Lǐ Línfǔ feared that scholars from the countryside might criticize his treachery and evil in their examination responses,
so he proposed:
"Most examinees are lowly and foolish,
and I fear vulgar speech might pollute the imperial hearing."
He then ordered commandery and county officials to rigorously test and train them,
and those truly outstanding
were to have their names sent to the ministry,
entrusted to the Minister for re-examination,
supervised by the Censor-in-chief,
and those whose names matched their actual talent were reported.
When they arrived, they were tested on poetry, rhapsodies, and essays,
and as a result, not a single one passed.
Lǐ Línfǔ then presented a memorial congratulating that no worthy was left in the wilds.
3 On Wùyín day,
Ān Lùshān, Military Commissioner of Fànyáng and Pínglú, was concurrently appointed Censor-in-chief.
Ān Lùshān was corpulent,
his belly hanging past his knees.
He once claimed his belly
weighed three hundred catties.
Outwardly he seemed foolishly straightforward,
but inwardly he was cunning.
He often had his general Liú Luògǔ remain in the capital to spy on the court's intentions,
reporting all movements;
if memorials were needed,
Liú Luògǔ would draft and submit them for him.
Each year he presented captives, miscellaneous livestock, rare birds, exotic beasts, and precious curios,
the flow never ceasing on the roads,
exhausting commanderies and counties with the transport.
Before the Emperor,
Ān Lùshān responded quickly and fluently,
mixing in humor.
The Emperor once playfully pointed at his belly and said:
"What is inside this barbarian's belly?
It is so large!"
He replied:
"Nothing else,
only a red heart!"
The Emperor was pleased.
He also once ordered him to see the Crown Prince,
but Ān Lùshān did not bow.
Attendants urged him to bow,
but Ān Lùshān stood with hands clasped and said:
"Your subject is a barbarian,
unfamiliar with court etiquette,
and does not know what office the Crown Prince holds?"
The Emperor said:
"He is the heir,
who after my passing,
will rule over you in my place."
Ān Lùshān said:
"Your subject is ignorant.
Previously I only knew of Your Majesty alone,
and did not know there was also an heir."
Reluctantly,
he then bowed.
