He also seized Tāo and others,
intending to flog them,
but then released them all,
saying:
"What I have long resented about you,
I wished not to speak of,
fearing you would harbor worries.
Now that I have spoken of it,
then there is no issue."
Only then did the army become settled.
Initially,
when Gāo Xiānzhī was the Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ,
a man from Yīshì named Fēng Chángqīng,
orphaned and poor from a young age,
slender and thin with a squint in his eyes,
and one foot slightly shorter than the other,
sought to become Xiānzhī's attendant,
but was not accepted.
Chángqīng waited daily for Xiānzhī's comings and goings,
never leaving his gate,
for several tens of days,
until Xiānzhī had no choice but to keep him.
It happened that the Dáxī tribe rebelled,
and Fūméng Língchá ordered Xiānzhī to pursue them,
killing or capturing nearly all.
Chángqīng privately drafted a victory report to show Xiānzhī,
which contained everything Xiānzhī wished to say,
and from then on, the entire command regarded him as extraordinary.
When Xiānzhī became a Jiédùshǐ,
he immediately appointed Chángqīng as Pànguān;
when Xiānzhī went on campaign,
Chángqīng often served as Liúhòu.
Among the various commissioners of the Táng,
the Pànguān ranked below the Deputy Commissioner,
but had overall charge of the command's affairs.
Furthermore, when a Jiédùshǐ was either on campaign,
or attending court,
or had died without a replacement,
there was always someone appointed to know the affairs of the Liúhòu;
later, this position came to be called Jiédù Liúhòu;
by our dynasty, the Liúhòu was made Chéngxuānshǐ,
filled by those whose seniority did not yet warrant the establishment of a command.
Xiānzhī treated him like a brother,
entrusting him with household affairs,
and his authority extended throughout the army.
Once, when Chángqīng was going out,
Liú Déquán galloped up from behind and rushed past him.
Chángqīng went to the Shǐyuàn,
the Shǐyuàn,
being the office where the Liúhòu conducted affairs;
the Jiédùshǐ, when conveniently seated to conduct affairs,
might also go to the Shǐyuàn.
Shǐ,
read as in the official transcription.
Passing through each gate,
he closed them one by one,
and upon arrival,
Chángqīng rose from his seat and said to him:
"Chángqīng originally came from humble and lowly origins,
as the Lángjiàng knows.
Today, the Zhōngchéng has ordered me to be Liúhòu;
how can the Lángjiàng publicly humiliate and rush past me among the crowd!"
Then he rebuked him, saying:
"The Lángjiàng must be temporarily executed to enforce military discipline."
Zàn,
same as zàn (temporary).
He had him face down on the ground,
and dragged him out.
Xiānzhī's wife and wet nurse wept and wailed outside the gate to save him,
but it was too late.
They then reported the matter to Xiānzhī,
who, upon reading it,
exclaimed in shock:
"Is he already dead?"
When he saw Chángqīng,
he said nothing further,
and Chángqīng did not apologize to him either.
The army feared him and held their breath in awe.
History records that Fēng Chángqīng was capable of governing military affairs,
also because Gāo Xiānzhī did not allow personal relationships to interfere with the law.
Tì,
read as tā lì fān.
Since the rise of the Táng,
frontier commanders were all loyal and honest famous ministers,
not holding long tenures,
not holding remote commands,
not concurrently commanding multiple areas,
and those with notable achievements often entered the court as chancellors.
Such as Lǐ Jìng, Lǐ Jì, Liú Rénguǐ, Lóu Shīdé, and the like.
Since the Kāiyuán era,
Xuē Nè, Guō Yuánzhèn, Zhāng Jiāzhēn, Wáng Jùn, Zhāng Yuè, Dù Xiǎn, Xiāo Sōng, Lǐ Shìzhī, and others,
also all entered the chancellorship from frontier commands.
Shuài,
read as suǒ lèi fān.
Even those with talent and strategy like Āshǐnà Shè'ěr and Qìbì Hélì were not given sole command of major generals,
but were always overseen by high officials serving as commissioners.
When Shè'ěr campaigned against Gāochāng,
Hóu Jūnjí was the Yuánshuài;
when Hélì campaigned against Gāolì,
Lǐ Jì was the Yuánshuài.
Jiàng,
read as jí liàng fān.
Qì,
read as qī qì fān.
Bì,
read as pí bì fān.
Shǐ,
read as in the official transcription.
The Son of Heaven harbored ambitions to swallow the Four Barbarians,
and frontier generals remained unchanged for over a decade,
beginning the practice of long tenures;
such as Wáng Jùn, Guō Zhīyùn, Zhāng Shǒuguī, and the like.
Among chancellors, Xiāo Sōng and Niú Xiānkè
began the practice of holding remote commands;
matters concerning the various princes are seen in the 213th scroll, the 15th year of Kāiyuán.
Xiāo Sōng's matter is seen in the 17th year,
Niú Xiānkè's matter is seen in the 214th scroll, the 24th year.
They began concurrently commanding multiple areas.
Gài Jiāyùn's matter is seen in the 214th scroll, the 28th year of Kāiyuán.
Wáng Zhōngsì's matter is seen in the previous scroll, the 5th year.
Gài,
read as gǔ hé fān.
Because the Hú people were illiterate,
he memorialized, saying:
"Civil officials as generals,
are timid in facing arrows and stones;
it is better to use low-born Hú people;
hán,
meaning lowly and humble.
Jùn,
those who have engaged in farming.
Jùn is pronounced jùn.
Those from humble clans are isolated and without factions;
if Your Majesty truly treats them with kindness and wins their hearts,
they will certainly be able to exhaust themselves in death for the court."
The Emperor was pleased with his words,
and began employing Ān Lùshān.
By this time,
the Jiédùshǐ of the various circuits were all Hú people,
Ān Lùshān, Ān Sīshùn, Gēshū Hàn, Gāo Xiānzhī,
all being Hú people.
The balance of power in the realm became skewed,
eventually causing Lùshān to overthrow the realm,
all stemming from Línfǔ's schemes to monopolize favor and secure his position.
Seventh Year
(Wùzǐ, 748)
1 Summer,
April,
Xīnchǒu,
Left Jiānmén Dàjiāngjūn, Zhī Nèishìshěng Shì Gāo Lìshì was promoted to Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn.
The position of Zhī Nèishìshěng Shì began from this.
The Táng system: there were twenty-nine ranks of merit,
with Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn at the head,
corresponding to the first rank.
Jiān,
read as gǔ xián fān.
Piào,
read as pǐ miào fān.
Jì,
read as qí jì fān.
Both inside and outside the court feared him,
the Crown Prince also called him elder brother,
the various princes and dukes called him elder,
and the sons-in-law directly called him grandfather.
From Lǐ Línfǔ, Ān Lùshān, and others, all used him to attain positions as generals and chancellors.
His family was wealthy beyond measure.
In the Western Capital, he built the Bǎoshòu Temple;
when the temple bell was completed,
Lìshì held a vegetarian feast to celebrate it,
and the entire court gathered.
If Sòng Jǐng were present,
he certainly would not have attended this gathering.
Cháo,
read as zhí yáo fān.
He donated one hundred strings of cash,
and those seeking to curry favor gave as much as twenty blows,
with the least not less than ten blows.
However, his nature was harmonious, cautious, and rarely at fault;
adept at observing the times and adapting,
he did not dare to be arrogant or overbearing,
therefore the Son of Heaven always trusted and employed him closely,
and scholar-officials also did not hate or despise him.
2 In the fifth month, on the Rénwǔ day,

the ministers presented the emperor with the honorific title "Kāiyuán Tiānbǎo Shèngwén Shénwǔ Yìngdào Huángdì" (Emperor of Opening the Prime Era, Heavenly Treasure, Sagely Literary, Divine Martial, and Responsive to the Way).
A general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
The land tax and corvée service for the coming year were exempted for the common people.
A descendant of the Later Wèi dynasty was selected to be one of the Sān Kè (Three Honored Ones).
Regarding the Sān Kè and the descendants of the Two Dynasties,
the annotation has been seen previously.
Dù Yòu said: When the Zhōu dynasty gained the empire,
it enfeoffed the descendants of the Xià and Yīn (Shāng) dynasties,
and also enfeoffed a descendant of Shùn,
calling them Kè.
Kè means "to respect";
the meaning derives from those whom the king respects,
hence they are called the Sān Kè.
In the thirteenth year of the Tiānbǎo era,
the dukes and ministers deliberated, saying: "Regarding the theory of the Sān Kè and the Two Kings,
there are three interpretations.
The first says that before the Two Kings,
the descendants of the Three Dynasties were further established as the Sān Kè.
This is based on the statement in the Yuèjì:
'King Wǔ conquered Shāng,
and before he had even dismounted from his chariot, he enfeoffed the descendants of Huángdì, Yáo, and Shùn;
after dismounting, he enfeoffed the descendants of the Xià and Yīn.'
The second says that before the Two Kings,
only one generation was preserved,
making the Two Kings together the Sān Kè.
This is based on the Zuǒzhuàn:
'He only enfeoffed Hú Gōng to complete the Sān Kè,'
clarifying that the former kings whom the king respects are two,
so he further enfeoffed one generation to complete the Sān Kè.
The third says that the descendants of the Two Kings constitute one Kè,
the parents of one's wife constitute the second Kè,
and the rulers of the barbarian tribes constitute the third Kè.
This is based on the statement
'The king has three whom he does not treat as subjects'
and is derived from that.
Cuī Líng'ēn of the Liáng dynasty said: Among the three theories, the first is the most valid.
However, regarding the Two Kings and the Sān Kè,
the classics lack explicit text.
Líng'ēn, based on the Lǐjì,
then considered it as preserving five generations together,
but I privately fear this is not appropriate.
The record states: 'In honoring the worthy, one does not go beyond two generations.'
As for the third generation,
although distant and difficult to emulate,
how can one fail to record their descendants?
Therefore, they are also preserved,
merely to show respect for their Way,
and thus they are called the Sān Kè.
Therefore, the Zuǒzhuàn states:
'He enfeoffed Hú Gōng to complete the Sān Kè.'
This is sufficient to know that there were not five generations.
Moreover, from past dynasties to the present,
all have taken the Three Dynasties as the Sān Kè.
Based on this examination,
it seems that a descendant of the Later Wèi, along with descendants of the Zhōu and Suí dynasties, were made the Sān Kè.
The following year,
the Wèi descendant was soon abolished;
the annotation is also seen later.
3 In the sixth month, on the Gēngzǐ day,
Ān Lùshān was granted an iron pledge.
4 The Vice Director of the Bureau of Revenue and Concurrent Censor Yáng Zhāo was adept at discerning the emperor's likes and dislikes and catering to them.
Through aggressive taxation and rapid promotion,
within a year he held over fifteen concurrent commissions.
On the Jiǎchén day,
he was promoted to Supervising Secretary and
concurrently Vice Censor-in-Chief,
solely in charge of revenue matters,
and his favor and influence grew daily.
Sū Miǎn commented: "The establishment of offices and division of duties
means each has its own jurisdiction.
Governance becomes constant and easy to maintain,
affairs return to their roots and are hard to lose—
the principle for long-term planning,
apart from this, what else is there to rely on?
But when treacherous ministers extensively speak of profit to seek favor,
establish many commissions to show宠爱,
oppress the lower people with heavy exactions,
inflate false numbers to present achievements;
the ruler's heart becomes unsettled and increasingly extravagant,
the people's resentment accumulates and turns to disaster;
causing the Son of Heaven's officials to hold their positions without performing their duties,
receiving generous salaries while their functions remain empty.
Yǔwén Róng first initiated this trend,
Yáng Shènjīn and Wáng Hóng followed in his footsteps,
and Yáng Guózhōng ultimately completed the chaos.
Confucius said: 'Better to have ministers who steal than ministers who exact heavy taxes.'
The Dàxué records: 'A family with a hundred chariots does not keep ministers who exact heavy taxes;
rather than have ministers who exact heavy taxes,
better to have ministers who steal.'
The front carriage has already overturned,
yet the following tracks remain unchanged—
to seek the fundamental transformation,
is it not difficult indeed!"
5 In winter, the tenth month, on the Gēngxū day,
the emperor went to Huáqīng Palace.
6 In the eleventh month, on the Guǐwèi day,
the emperor's elder sister who had married into the Cuī family was made Lady of Hánguó,
the one who had married into the Péi family was made Lady of Guóguó,
and the one who had married into the Liǔ family was made Lady of Qínguó.
All three were talented and beautiful.
The emperor called them his aunts.
They entered and left the palace precincts,
all receiving imperial favor,
and their influence overshadowed the empire.
Whenever ladies with titles entered for an audience,
even Princess Yùzhēn and others yielded and did not dare take their seats.
Princess Yùzhēn was the daughter of Emperor Ruìzōng.
Whenever they made requests or entrusted matters,
the prefectures and counties complied and welcomed them,
more urgently than with imperial decrees.
Gifts from all directions
converged at their gates like spokes to a hub,
each fearing to be late,
bustling like a market from morning till night.
For the marriages of the various princes of the Ten Residences and the Hundred Grandsons Court,
(the Ten Princes' Residences and the Hundred Grandsons Court
are mentioned in the 213th scroll, the fifteenth year of the Kāiyuán era.)
none failed to achieve their wishes.
What the emperor bestowed and what was presented from all directions
was divided equally among the five households.
They vied in building mansions and houses,
making them extremely magnificent.
The cost for a single hall
often exceeded ten million cash.
Once completed,
if they saw others had something superior to their own,
they would immediately demolish and rebuild it.
Lady Guóguó was especially extravagant and unrestrained.
One day,
she led workers and artisans to suddenly enter Wéi Sìlì's residence,
immediately tore down the old buildings,
and built a new mansion for herself,
merely giving the Wéi family a vacant plot of ten mǔ of land.
When the central hall was completed,
she summoned plasterers to apply the finish,
agreeing on a price of two million cash.
The craftsmen further requested a reward for their skill.
Lady Guóguó rewarded them with five hundred bolts of crimson silk,
but they scoffed and ignored it,
saying:
"Please bring some ants and lizards,
count them and place them in the hall.
If even one is missing,
we will not dare accept payment."
7 In the twelfth month, on the Wùxū day,
someone reported that Xuányuán Huángdì (the deified Lǎozi) had descended at the Cháoyuán Pavilion.
The emperor had built a Lǎojūn Hall within the Huáqīng Palace complex;
north of the hall was the Cháoyuán Pavilion.
Because someone said Lǎojūn had descended there,
it was renamed the Jiàngshèng Pavilion (Pavilion of the Descended Sage).
Xīnfēng County was abolished and merged into Zhāoyìng County.
On the Xīnyǒu day,
the emperor returned to the palace.
(From the Wēnquán Palace.
The character '还' is read as 'xuán' here,
but it can also be read with its usual pronunciation.)
8 Gēshū Hàn built the Shénwēi Army fortress on the shore of Qīnghǎi Lake.
When the Tibetans arrived,
Hàn attacked and defeated them.
He also built a city on Lóngjū Island in the middle of Qīnghǎi Lake.
(The character '吐' is pronounced 'tǔ', entering tone.)
Qīnghǎi Lake is eight or nine hundred lǐ in circumference.
There is a mountain in the middle.
When the ice freezes, mares are released to roam on it.
The next year, they give birth to foals,
which are called 'dragon seed,'
hence the name Lóngjū Island.
The Tibetans hid their traces and did not dare approach Qīnghǎi.
9 This year, the King of Yúnnán, Guīyì, died.
His son Géluófèng succeeded him,
and appointed his own son Fèng Jiāyì as Governor of Yángguā Prefecture.
Eighth Year
(Jǐchǒu, 749)
1. In spring,
in the second month,
on the Wùshēn day,
the Emperor led the officials to view the Left Treasury.
The Tang Liù Diǎn says: The Rites of Zhou had the position of Outer Storehouse Middle Officer.
He was in charge of the coin treasury located outside,
overseeing the income and expenditure of the state's currency,
to supply various goods and meet state expenses.
There were also the positions of Currency Officer Senior Officer and Middle Officer,
in charge of the income of coins and goods.
These are equivalent to the duties of the Left Treasury today.
By the Qin and Han dynasties,
the duties were divided between the Minister of Agriculture and the Privy Treasurer.
In the Later Han,
the Privy Treasurer's subordinate officials included the Director and Assistant of the Inner Storehouse Office,
in charge of the inner storehouse's silks, gold, silver, and goods;
the Wei dynasty followed this.
The Jin dynasty's Privy Treasurer had Directors of the Left and Right Treasuries.
In the Eastern Jin, there were nine censors,
each in charge of one bureau;
there was a Storehouse Bureau Censor.
Later, the Storehouse Bureau was further divided,
establishing the Outer Left Storehouse and Inner Left Storehouse.
Emperor Wén of the Song dynasty abolished the Outer Left Storehouse,
and the Inner Left Storehouse was simply called the Left Storehouse.
The Qi, Liang, and Chen dynasties had a Right Treasury Storehouse but no Left Treasury.
The Northern Qi's Court of the Imperial Treasury oversaw the Directors and Assistants of the Left and Right Treasuries.
The Northern Zhou had Senior and Middle Officers of the Outer Storehouse.
The Sui dynasty had Directors and Assistants of the Left and Right Treasury Offices.
The Tang Left Treasury had the Eastern Storehouse, Western Storehouse, and Court Hall Storehouse,
and also the Eastern Capital Storehouse.
I note according to the Yōng Lù: In the Tàijí Palace, there were the Eastern Left Treasury Storehouse
and Western Left Treasury Storehouse;
the Eastern Storehouse was east of the Gōnglǐ Gate,
the Western Storehouse was west of the Ānrén Gate.
In the Dàmíng Palace, there was a Left Treasury Storehouse,
located to the left of the Líndé Hall.
There was also a Director of the Right Treasury Office,
in charge of the state's precious goods and miscellaneous items;
while the regular tax revenue in money and goods from across the empire,
all went to the Left Treasury.
Treasury (藏)
is pronounced zàng;
the same applies to treasury (帑藏) below.
At this time, the prefectures and counties were prosperous,
with granaries and storehouses accumulating grain and silk,
often amounting to tens of thousands.
Yáng Zhāo petitioned to have the grain stored locally sold and converted into light goods,
and to have the poll tax and land tax all converted into cloth and silk for delivery to the capital;
he repeatedly reported that the treasuries were full to overflowing,
rarely matched in ancient or modern times.
Therefore, the Emperor led his ministers to view it,
and bestowed upon Zhāo a purple robe and a golden fish pouch as a reward.
The Emperor, because state funds were abundant,
thus regarded gold and silk as dirt,
bestowing rewards upon the families of the noble and favored,
without any limit.
2. In the third month,
the Military Commissioner of Shuòfāng and other duties, Zhāng Qíqiū, built the Héngsài Army at Mùlà Mountain, over five hundred li northwest of the Central Shòuxiáng Fortress,
appointing the Commander of the Zhènyuǎn Army, Guō Zǐyí of Zhèng, as the Commander of the Héngsài Army.
The Héngsài Army was originally named Kědūn Fortress.
According to Sòng Bái's Xù Tōngdiǎn: The Héngsài Army
was initially established at Fēihú,
later moved to Yùzhōu,
and in the sixth year of the Kāiyuán era, Zhāng Jiāzhēn moved it south of the ancient Dà'ān City of Dàijùn,
to serve as support for the Nine Surnames tribes.
In the twelfth year of the Tiānbǎo era, it was renamed the Tiāndé Army.
Consulting various texts,
the Héngsài Army is the Héngyě Army.
The first year of Tiānbǎo records
"the Héběi Military Command oversees the Héngyě Army,"
which is the one moved in the sixth year of Kāiyuán.
This construction of the Héngsài Army was at Kědūn Fortress.
The Zhènyuǎn Army was within the boundaries of the Shànyú Protectorate.
Zhèng County,
belonged to Jīngzhào in the Han dynasty,
the Later Wei established the Eastern Yōng Province there,
merging with Huàshān County.
The Western Wei changed it to Huà Province.
In the Sui dynasty, early in the Kāihuáng era, the commandery was abolished,
early in the Dàyè era, the province was abolished,
and Zhèng County was re-established,
belonging to Jīngzhào.
In the Tang, it belonged to Huà Province.
Commander (使)
is pronounced shǐ.
Shòu (降)
is pronounced xiáng.
Là (剌)
is pronounced là.
3. In summer,
in the fourth month,
the Grand Administrator of Qiánníng, Zhào Fèngzhāng,
(Qiánníng Commandery was originally Dānzhōu Dānyáng Commandery,
the commandery name was changed in the first year.)
Grand Administrator (守)
is pronounced shǒu.
before his memorial could reach the court,
Lǐ Línfǔ learned of it,
hinted to the censors to arrest him,
accusing him of spreading evil rumors,
and had him beaten to death.
4 Previously,
the military prefectures (zhéchōng fǔ) all had wooden tallies and bronze fish tallies.
When the imperial court issued a mobilization order,
it would send down an imperial edict, a tally, and a fish tally.
According to the Táng system: bronze fish tallies were used to raise armies.
Within the royal domain,
there were three on the left and one on the right.
Outside the royal domain,
there were five on the left and one on the right.
Those on the left were used for external operations.
Starting from the first one as the head,
subsequent matters required using the second one to issue them,
cycling back to the beginning.
Regarding the wooden tally system,
if the crown prince was overseeing state affairs,
then within the royal domain,
there were three each on the left and right;
outside the royal domain,
there were five each on the left and right;
for common officials guarding fortifications,
there were ten each on the left and right.
The Táng Liù Diǎn states: The Fúbǎo Láng was in charge of tallies and seals.
The wooden tallies
were used to emphasize the importance of guarding fortifications
and to carefully manage disbursements and receipts.
When the imperial carriage went on an inspection tour,
and the crown prince oversaw state affairs,
those who had troops and horses under their command
were given wooden tallies.
Also, for military campaigns involving leading five hundred soldiers or more and five hundred horses or more,
wooden tallies were issued.
For officials below the rank of the Three Dukes,
the commanders of the two capitals and the various prefectures who had troops and horses under their command,
wooden tallies were also issued.
The bronze fish tallies
were used to raise armies
and to change garrison commanders.
The commanders of the two capitals, the various prefectures, various armies, military prefectures (zhéchōng fǔ), places where troops were stationed for defense, and the palace directorates
were all issued fish tallies.
Chéng Dàchāng's Yǎnfánlù states:
In the Táng era,
besides the left fish tally, there was also an imperial edict accompanying it,
hence the combined name "fish document."
Xiān,
read as xī jiàn fān.
Xià,
read as xiá jià fān.
Only then were they dispatched.
Since the recruitment and establishment of the Guōqí cavalry,
(see Guōqí in the 212th year of the Kāiyuán era, year 13).
Guō,
pronounced Guō,
also pronounced Huò.
Those who died or deserted
were no longer replaced by the authorities;
their six pack-horses or oxen, equipment, and dry rations
were almost completely depleted.
The militia soldiers who entered the capital for guard duty,
were called "attendant officials" (shìguān),
meaning they were the emperor's personal guards.
Later, the original guards often lent them out to others,
using them like slaves;
the people of Cháng'ān were ashamed of this,
to the point of using it as an insult.
The Lǐjì·Rú Xíng says: Nowadays, people use "Confucian" as a term of mutual insult.
The commentary states: Using "Confucian" to mock each other,
hence joking with each other.
Gòubìng,
means shame and disgrace.
Dù Yù states: Joking to make someone feel ashamed is called jìn.
Gòu,
pronounced gòu,
also pronounced hū hòu fān.
Moreover, they were often harshly used by frontier generals,
who profited from their deaths and confiscated their property.
As a result, all those who were supposed to serve as militia soldiers fled and hid,
so that by now there were no soldiers to hand over.
In the fifth month,
on the Guǐyǒu day,
Lǐ Línfǔ memorialized to abolish the upper and lower fish documents of the military prefectures (zhéchōng fǔ);
thereafter, the militia system only had officials in name.
According to the Táng militia system,
ten men formed a "fire" (huǒ),
and the fire had a leader.
Each fire was equipped with six pack-horses.
All fire equipment, including black cloth, tent iron, horse troughs, cloth troughs, spades, hoes, chisels, mortars, baskets, axes, pliers, saws,
one each,
two armor stands,
two sickles.
Fifty men formed a "team" (duì).
Each team was equipped with one fire drill,
one chest horse rope,
three head halters and leg fetters each,
each man had one bow,
thirty arrows,
a quiver, horizontal knife, whetstone, large awl, felt hat, felt clothing, and leggings, one each,
nine pecks of wheat meal,
two pecks of rice,
all self-provided.
Their armor and military equipment were stored in the armory.
When there was a campaign,
they would be issued based on the individual;
those taking turns for guard duty in the capital
were only issued bows, arrows, and horizontal knives.
Now, all these were depleted and ruined,
no longer as they were before.
Moreover, there was no promotion for years,
and scholar-officials were also ashamed to serve in it.
As for the Guōqí cavalry system,
after the Tiānbǎo era,
it gradually changed and fell into disuse.
Those who responded to recruitment were all market peddlers and unruly youths.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: The Báihǔ Tōng states: Markets were set up around wells,
hence called "market wells" (shìjǐng).
Yìng Shào's Tōngsú Wén states: Market (shì),
means to rely on;
to support the old and young,
relying on it not to be lacking.
The common saying about market wells,
is that those going to the market wash their goods at the well to make them fragrant and clean,
and also dress themselves properly,
before going to the market.
Carefully note: In ancient times, twenty mǔ formed one well,
and because markets for trade were set up there,
it was called market wells.
Thus, originally, because trade markets were set up within the well-field system,
the markets in the capital were also called market wells.
According to the ritual system, nine men formed a well.
Yìng Shào's "twenty mǔ as a well"
is based on the Hànshū·Shíhuòzhì: one well for eight families,
each family having one hundred mǔ of private land,
ten mǔ of public land,
and the remaining twenty mǔ used for wells, stoves, huts, and houses,
hence saying twenty mǔ.
Setting up markets around wells,
might be as Yìng Shào said.
At that time, peace had lasted long,
and many discussants believed that military forces in the central plains could be disbanded.
Consequently, civilians were prohibited from possessing weapons;
if a son or younger brother became a military officer,
his father and elder brothers would shun him as unworthy.
Fierce generals and elite troops
were all concentrated in the northwest,
leaving the central plains without military preparedness.
5 The Tàibái Mountain man Lǐ Hún and others submitted a memorial
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: Wǔgōng County has the Tàiyī Mountain,
in ancient texts considered the Zhōngnán Mountain,
also called Zhōngnán,
also called Tàibái Mountain.
It is south of Wǔgōng County,
two hundred lǐ from Cháng'ān,
its height unknown.
A common saying goes:
"Wǔgōng, Tàibái,
three hundred [lǐ] from heaven."
Dù Yànyuǎn said: Tàibái Mountain connects to Wǔgōng Mountain in the south,
the most outstanding and magnificent among the mountains.
Snow accumulates winter and summer,
appearing brilliantly white from afar.
The Suíshuì states: Tàiyī Mountain is within the boundaries of Zhōuzhì County.
The Xīn Tángshū states: Tàibái Mountain is in Méi County.
They said that in the Jīnxīng Cave there was a jade tablet stone inscription recording auspicious signs of the sage ruler's fortune and longevity.
The emperor ordered the Censor-in-Chief Wáng Hóng to enter the Xiānyóu Valley to search for it, and he obtained it.
The emperor, considering that auspicious signs followed one after another,
all due to the glorious achievements of his ancestors,
in the sixth month,
on the Wùshēn day,
honored the Sage Ancestor with the title "Great Dào Mysterious Origin Emperor" (Dàdào Xuányuán Huángdì).
He posthumously honored Emperor Gāozǔ as "Divine Yáo Great Sage Emperor" (Shényáo Dàshèng Huángdì),
Emperor Tàizōng as "Civil and Military Great Sage Emperor" (Wénwǔ Dàshèng Huángdì),
Emperor Gāozōng as "Heavenly August Great Sage Emperor" (Tiānhuáng Dàshèng Huángdì),
Emperor Zhōngzōng as "Filial and Harmonious Great Sage Emperor" (Xiàohé Dàshèng Huángdì),
Emperor Ruìzōng as "Mysterious Perfection Great Sage Emperor" (Xuánzhēn Dàshèng Huángdì).
Empress Dowager Dòu and below were all given the additional posthumous title "Obedient Sage Empress" (Shùnshèng Huánghòu).
6 On the Xīnhài day,
the Minister of Justice and Capital District Governor Xiāo Jiǒng was demoted to Tàishǒu of Rǔyīn for accepting bribes.
Rǔyīn Commandery,
is Yǐng Prefecture.
7 The Emperor ordered the Longyou Military Commissioner Gēshū Hàn to lead troops from Longyou, Hexi, and the Turkic Abusi tribe,
supplemented by soldiers from Shuofang and Hedong,
totaling sixty-three thousand men,
to attack the Tibetan Stone Fortress City.
The city was precipitous and inaccessible on three sides,
with only a single path leading upward.
The Tibetans defended it with merely a few hundred men,
storing abundant provisions,
and stockpiling wooden beams and stones.
Tang troops had repeatedly attacked it before and after,
but were unable to capture it.
Hàn attacked for several days without success,
then summoned his subordinate generals Gāo Xiùyán and Zhāng Shǒuyú,
intending to execute them.
Gāo Xiùyán later defended Dàtóng for Ān Lùshān,
as both were generals from Shuofang and Hedong.
They captured it as scheduled,
capturing four hundred Tibetans including Tiěrèn Xīnuòluó.
Tens of thousands of Tang soldiers perished,
exactly as Wáng Zhōngsì had predicted.
Wáng Zhōngsì's words
are recorded in the sixth year of the previous volume.
Hàn also dispatched troops to open up military farms west of Chìlǐng,
stationing two thousand exiled soldiers to garrison Lóngjū Island.
When the ice froze solid in winter,
the Tibetans massed in great numbers,
and the entire garrison perished.
Advancing deep into enemy territory,
with no reinforcements available,
it is what military strategy calls "abandoning men to be captured."
8 In the intercalary month,
on Yǐchǒu,
Stone Fortress City was designated as the Shénwǔ Army,
and the Bǎoníng Protectorate was established at Suǒmò Chuān in the western mountains of Jiànnán.
The Bǎoníng Protectorate was established
to administer Zāngkē and Tibet.
9 On Bǐngyín,
the Emperor paid homage at the Tàiqīng Palace.
In the first month of the first year of Tiānbǎo,
a spiritual talisman was obtained,
and a temple for the Mysterious Origin Emperor was built at Dàníng Lane in the Western Capital.
In the Eastern Capital, it was established at the former residence of Línzī in Jīshàn Lane of the Eastern Palace.
Every commandery throughout the empire set up an image of the Mysterious Origin in their Kāiyuán Temples.
By the twelfth day of the third month of the second year,
the Mysterious Origin Palace in the capital was renamed Tàiqīng Palace,
in the Eastern Capital it became Tàijí Palace,
and in commanderies throughout the empire they became Zǐjí Palaces.
On Dīngmǎo,
the assembled ministers presented the Emperor with the honorific title "Kāiyuán Tiāndì Dàbǎo Shèngwén Shénwǔ Yìngdào Huángdì,"
and a general amnesty was declared.
From now on, the Dì and Xiá sacrifices would have positions arranged in proper order before the Sacred Ancestor at the Tàiqīng Palace.
10 In autumn,
the seventh month,
Yíbō of the Tūqíshī was enfeoffed as the Ten Tribes Khagan.
11 In the eighth month,
on Yǐhài,
King Luózhēntán of Hùmì came to court,
requesting to remain as an imperial guard;
this was granted,
and he was appointed General of the Left Martial Guard.
12 In winter,
the tenth month,
on Yǐchǒu,
the Emperor visited Huáqīng Palace.
13 In the eleventh month,
on Yǐwèi,
Shīlǐ Dágāluó, the Yèhù of Tǔhuǒluó, sent an envoy with a memorial stating:
"The king of Qièshī has allied with Tibet,
causing hardship to the garrison troops of Xiǎo Bólǜ,
blocking their supply routes.
I intend to defeat these vicious rebels,
and hope to dispatch Ānxī troops,
to reach Xiǎo Bólǜ by the first month of next year,
and Dà Bólǜ by the sixth month."
Qièshī,
also called Jiéshī,
is of Hu ethnicity;
it borders Tǔhuǒluó.
Dà Bólǜ,
also called Bùlù,
lies directly west of Tibet,
with Xiǎo Bólǜ to its north.
Ninth Year
(Gēngyín, 750)
1 In spring,
the first month,
on Jǐhài,
the Emperor returned to the palace.
2 The assembled ministers repeatedly petitioned for the fēng sacrifice at the Western Peak,
which was approved.
3 In the second month,
Consort Yáng again offended the Emperor's will,
and was sent back to her private residence.
Consort Yáng's initial offense
is recorded in the fifth year of the previous volume.
Fù,
read as fú yòu.
Wǔ,
read as wǔ gù.
"Women have short-sighted judgment,
and have offended Your Majesty's will.
Why does Your Majesty begrudge a mere space within the palace,
not letting her go to her death?
How can you bear to disgrace her by sending her to an outer residence?"
Jí Wēn's words
were intended to ingratiate himself with the Yáng family.
Yé,
read as yē.
A palace envoy was sent to bestow imperial meals upon her.
Weeping to the envoy, she said:
"My crime deserves death,
yet Your Majesty mercifully did not kill me but sent me home.
Now I shall be forever separated from the palace chambers.
The gold, jade, and precious curios
were all bestowed by His Majesty,
and are not worthy as offerings.
Only my hair was given by my parents,
and I dare to offer it as a token of sincerity."
She then cut off a lock of her hair and presented it.
The Emperor immediately sent Gāo Lìshì to summon her back,
and his favor and treatment of her grew even deeper.
At that time, the noble relatives competed in presenting food to the Emperor.
The Emperor appointed the eunuch Yáo Sīyì as the Inspector of Food Presentations.
Thousands of platters of land and sea delicacies
cost the wealth of ten middle-class families for a single platter.
Once, the Secretariat Drafter Dòu Huá was returning from court
when a princess was presenting food.
The procession lined the central avenue;
he had to announce his passage and rein in his horse to get through.
Several hundred palace garden attendants brandished clubs in front,
(Palace garden attendants
were under the command of the Palace Garden Commissioner.)
Tǐng,
read as dài dǐng.
4 Ānxī Military Commissioner Gāo Xiānzhī defeated Qièshī,
capturing its king Bótè Mò.
In the third month,
on Gēngzǐ,
Bótè Mò's elder brother Sùjiā was installed as king of Qièshī.
5 The Emperor ordered Censor-in-Chief Wáng Hóng to construct a road on Huà Mountain,
and to set up an altar platform atop it.
That spring,
Guānzhōng suffered drought;
on Xīnhài,
the temple at the peak was struck by disaster;
an edict was issued to cancel the fēng sacrifice at the Western Peak.
6 In summer,
the fourth month,
on Jǐsì,
Censor-in-Chief Sòng Hún was found guilty of embezzling an enormous sum,
and was exiled to Cháoyáng.
Cháoyáng Commandery was originally Cháozhou's Yì'ān Commandery,
renamed in the first year.
Jí Wēn advanced through Lǐ Línfǔ's patronage;
in the fourth year of Tiānbǎo,
Jí Wēn investigated the case of the Ministry of War,
and from then on gained advancement.
Wēn then abandoned Línfǔ and attached himself to Yáng,
devising for Yáng a strategy to replace Línfǔ in power.
Xiāo Jiǒng and Hún
were both favored by Línfǔ.
Wēn sought out their crimes,
had Yáng memorialize to have them expelled,
to cut off Línfǔ's trusted aides,
and Línfǔ was unable to save them.
7 In the fifth month,
on Yǐmǎo,
Ān Lùshān was enfeoffed with the title Prince of Dōngpíng Commandery.
This was the beginning of Tang generals and commanders being enfeoffed as princes.
8 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on Yǐhài,
the Guǎngwén Institute was established at the Directorate of Education,
to teach students preparing for the jìnshì examination.
At that time, the Guǎngwén Institute had two Erudites,
and one Assistant Instructor.
9 In the eighth month,
on Dīngsì,
Ān Lùshān was appointed concurrent Investigation and Disposal Commissioner of Héběi Circuit.
10 Shuofang Military Commissioner Zhāng Qíqiū mismanaged grain distribution,
angering the troops,
who assaulted his administrative assistant.
The Army Commander Guō Zǐyí shielded Qíqiū with his own body,
enabling him to escape harm.
The world only knows that Guō Zǐyí won the support of the masses,
and thus was able to shield and save Zhāng Qíqiū,
but does not realize that at this time,
what indeed was the state of military administration in the Tang!
On Guǐhài,
Qíqiū was demoted to Prefect of Jìyīn,
(Jìyīn Commandery
was Cáozhōu.)
Jì,
read as zǐ lǐ.
On the 11th day, Xīnmǎo,
the retired scholar Cuī Chāng submitted a memorial stating:
"Our state should inherit the line of the Zhōu and Hàn dynasties,
using Earth to replace Fire.
The Suí and Northern Zhōu were both illegitimate intercalary positions,
and it is not appropriate to have their descendants serve as the Two Dynasties' Heirs."
The matter was referred to the high ministers for collective deliberation.
Wèi Bāo, an Academician of the Jíxián Hall, submitted a memorial stating:
"On the night of the collective deliberation,
four stars gathered at the Tail constellation,
the will of Heaven is clear."
The Emperor then ordered to seek descendants of the Yīn, Zhōu, and Hàn dynasties to serve as the Three Honored Families,
abolishing the Dukes of Hán, Jiè, and Xī;
Hán was
the descendant of the Northern Wèi.
Jiè was
the descendant of the Northern Zhōu.
Xī was
the descendant of the Suí.
Xī,
pronunciation: hù guī.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: According to the ancient Zuǒzhuàn commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals: The Zhōu house enfeoffed the descendants of the Xià and Yīn (Shāng) kings as High Dukes,
and enfeoffed the descendants of the Yellow Emperor, Yáo, and Shùn,
calling them the Three Honored Families.
Master Zhèng said: The reason for preserving the descendants of the Two Kings
is to command them to perform the suburban sacrifice to Heaven with the rites of the Son of Heaven,
to sacrifice to the founding king who received the Mandate from their own lineage,
and to use their own calendar and ceremonial colors.
'Kè' means
'to respect'.
Respecting their former sages and enfeoffing their descendants,
they are not different from other feudal lords,
and cannot be compared to the descendants of the Xià and Yīn.
Bāo was appointed Vice Director of the Bureau of Forestry and Crafts.
On the 12th day, winter,
tenth month,
Gēngshēn,
the Emperor went to the Huáqīng Palace.
On the 13th day, Wáng Xuányì, a hermit from Tàibái Mountain, reported seeing the Mysterious Prime Emperor,
who said there was a marvelous treasure and a true talisman in the Bǎoxiān Cave.
Textual analysis note: The Old History states,
"Wáng Hóng memorialized that Xuányì saw the Mysterious Prime in the Bǎoxiān Cave,

and sent Hóng with Zhāng Jūn, Wáng Chuí, Wáng Jì, Wáng Yì, and Wáng Yuèlíng to the cave, where they obtained a jade casket, the Shàngqīng Hùguó Scripture, treasure tallies, records and registers, etc., and presented them."
Now we follow the Veritable Records.
They obtained them.
At that time, the Emperor revered Daoism,
longed for immortality,
so everywhere people vied to report auspicious signs and portents,
and sycophantic ministers submitted congratulatory memorials every month without fail.
Lǐ Línfǔ and others all requested to donate their residences to be converted into monasteries
to pray for the Emperor's longevity,
which pleased the Emperor.
On the 14th day, Ān Lùshān repeatedly enticed the Xī and Qìdān,
holding feasts for them,
and making them drink wine infused with làngdàng seeds.
The Běncǎo says: Làngdàng seeds grow in coastal valleys,
and are now found everywhere.
The plant stem is about two to three chǐ tall,
its leaves resemble those of dìhuáng and hónglán,
but are three fingers wide;
it flowers in the fourth month,
purple in color;
the stem has white hairs between the leaves;
it bears fruit in the fifth month,
with a shell shaped like an opium poppy pod,
like a small pomegranate;
the seeds inside are extremely fine,
greenish-white like grains of rice,
and very poisonous;
after boiling for one or two days, sprouts appear,
and if used to brew wine,
its toxicity is even greater.
Wéi,
pronunciation: yú wèi;
same for the following 'wéi'.
Yǐn,
pronunciation: yú zhèn.
Làng,
pronunciation: làng.
Dàng,
pronunciation: dàng.
He would then massacre several thousand people,
presenting the heads of their chieftains in boxes as tribute,
doing so four times in total.
At this time, he requested to come to court,
and the Emperor ordered the relevant officials to first build a mansion for him at Zhāoyìng.
At that time, princes and dukes all privately built mansions at Zhāoyìng,
but only Lùshān, due to imperial favor,
had a mansion built for him by official order.
Qiú,
pronunciation: cí yóu.
Zhǎng,
pronunciation: zhī liǎng.
Cháo,
pronunciation: zhí yáo.
Yáng Zhāo and his brothers and sisters all went to welcome him,
their carriages and canopies covering the fields;
the Emperor personally went to the Wàngchūn Palace to await him.
On Xīnwèi,
Lùshān presented eight thousand Xī captives,
and the Emperor ordered that on the day of performance evaluation, he be recorded with the highest grade.
Previously, Lùshān had been permitted to mint coins at five furnaces in Shànggǔ,
and Lùshān then presented a sample of one thousand strings of coins.
On the 15th day, Yáng Zhāo,
who was the nephew of Zhāng Yìzhī,
petitioned to clear the names of Yìzhī and his brothers.
The execution of Yìzhī and his brothers is recorded in the 207th scroll, in the first year of Shénlóng of Emperor Zhōngzōng.
On Gēngchén,
an edict cited the merit of Yìzhī and his brothers in welcoming Emperor Zhōngzōng back from Fánglíng,
(Welcoming Emperor Zhōngzōng
was not a proposal initiated solely by the two Zhāngs;
the event is recorded in the 206th scroll, first year of Shènglì of Empress Wǔ.)
Textual analysis note: The Táng Calendar places this on the 25th day of the seventh month.
Now we follow the Veritable Records.
Zhāo, because the prognosticatory texts contained
"golden knife" (which forms the character 'Zhāo'),
requested to change his name;
the Emperor bestowed upon him the name Guózhōng.
On the 16th day, twelfth month,
Yǐhài,
the Emperor returned to the palace.
On the 17th day, Wáng Nándé, the Guānxī Patrol Commissioner, attacked Tǔbō,
capturing Wǔqiáo,
and taking the Shùdūn city;
Nándé was appointed as Commander of the Báishuǐ Army.
On the 18th day, Gāo Xiānzhī, Military Governor of the Four Garrisons of Ānxī, pretended to make peace with the Shíguó,
then led troops to launch a surprise attack,
capturing their king and his people and returning with them,
slaughtering all the old and weak.
Xiānzhī was by nature greedy,
plundering over ten hú of green gems,
five or six camel-loads of gold,
and other goods, horses, and miscellaneous items of comparable value,
all of which went into his own household.
(This sets the stage for the prince of Shíguó to incite various states to destroy Xiānzhī's army.)
Chēng,
pronunciation: chǐ zhèng.
On the 19th day, Yáng Guózhōng felt indebted to Xiānyú Zhòngtōng,
(Xiānyú Zhòngtōng had provided financial support to Guózhōng,
and also recommended him,
events recorded in the fourth year of the previous scroll.)
Zhòngtōng was narrow-minded and impatient by nature,
losing the hearts of the barbarian tribes.
According to precedent,
the Nánzhào king would often visit the military governor together with his wife and children,
passing through Yúnnán,
where the Yúnnán prefect Zhāng Qiántuó would all have illicit relations with them.
He also made excessive demands,
and when the Nánzhào king Géluófèng did not comply,
Qiántuó sent people to insult and humiliate him,
and secretly memorialized his crimes.
Géluófèng, filled with resentment,
in this year,
raised troops in rebellion,
attacked and captured Yúnnán,
killed Qiántuó,
and took thirty-two barbarian prefectures.
Barbarian prefectures
refer to the loosely administered prefectures established for the southwestern barbarians who submitted and were assimilated.
Tenth year
(Xīnmǎo, 751)
1. Spring,
first month,
Rénchén,
the Emperor performed the court sacrifice at the Tàiqīng Palace;
on Guǐsì,
performed the court offering at the Imperial Ancestral Temple;
on Jiǎzǐ,
held the joint sacrifice to Heaven and Earth at the southern suburb,
pardoned the empire,
and exempted the empire from land tax for this year.
(The text above records Rénchén and Guǐsì,
and below records Dīngyǒu,
therefore
"Jiǎzǐ"
should be
"Jiǎwǔ".)
2. On Dīngyǒu,
appointed Lǐ Línfǔ to concurrently hold the post of Military Governor of Shuòfāng from a distance,
with the Vice Minister of Revenue Lǐ Wěi acting as the administrator of留守 affairs.
3. On Gēngzǐ,
the five Yang households went on a night excursion,
(Yáng Xiān, Yáng Qí, and the Ladies of Hán, Guó, and Qín constituted the five households.)
and with the Princess of Guǎngpíng,
(the New History records
"Guǎngníng";)
the princess
was the Emperor's daughter.
Cóng,
pronunciation: cái yòng.
The princess fell from her horse,
and her consort Chéng Chāngyì dismounted to help her up,
for which he also received several lashes.
The princess tearfully complained to the Emperor,
and the Emperor had the Yang family slave beaten to death for this.
The next day,
Chāngyì was dismissed from his post,
and forbidden to attend court audiences.
4 The emperor ordered the relevant officials to build a residence for Ān Lùshān in the Qīnrén Ward,
decreeing that it should be made as magnificent as possible,
with no limit on the expenditure.
When it was completed,
it was furnished with tents, canopies, and utensils,
filling the place to the brim.
There were two beds of white sandalwood,
each ten feet long
and six feet wide.
The Běncǎo Tújīng states: Sandalwood resembles the tan tree,
grows in the southern seas,
and comes in varieties of yellow, white, and purple.
Canopy,
pronounced yì.
Length,
pronounced zhí liàng fān.
The tent measured ten by six feet.
All items in the kitchen and storage rooms were decorated with gold and silver,
including two gold rice jars,
two silver rice-washing basins,
rice-washing basins,
used for rinsing rice.
There was one woven silver-wire basket and one strainer each;
other items were of comparable quality.
Even items used in the imperial palace
were hardly a match for these.
The emperor often ordered eunuchs to oversee the construction for Lùshān,
oversee,
meaning to supervise.
Eunuch,
pronounced shū lì fān;
same below.
He often warned them:
"The Hu man has big eyes,
do not let him laugh at me."
When Lùshān entered his new residence,
he held a banquet,
requesting an imperial edict to invite the chancellors to his home.
That day,
the emperor had intended to play polo downstairs,
but he abruptly halted the game
and ordered the chancellors to attend.
He daily sent members of the Yáng family to accompany Lùshān on scenic tours and banquets,
accompanied by music from the Líyuán and Jiàofǎng troupes.
Líyuán,
refers to the emperor's Líyuán disciples.
Jiàofǎng,
refers to the inner Jiàofǎng.
Whenever fresh game was caught during hunts in the rear gardens,
the emperor would immediately send eunuchs on horseback to deliver it to Lùshān,
with messengers shuttling back and forth on the road.
On the jiǎchén day,
Lùshān's birthday,
the emperor and Guìfēi bestowed generous gifts of clothing, precious vessels, wine, and delicacies.
Three days later,
Lùshān was summoned into the palace,
where Guìfēi had a large swaddling cloth made of brocade,
wrapped Lùshān in it,
and had palace maids carry him in a colorful sedan chair.
Hearing laughter from the rear palace,
the emperor asked the reason,
and his attendants replied that Guìfēi was bathing the three-day-old Lùshān.
The emperor went to see for himself,
was delighted,
rewarded Guìfēi with gold and silver coins for bathing the child,
and also bestowed generous gifts on Lùshān,
ending the event in great joy.
From then on, Lùshān was allowed to come and go freely in the palace,
sometimes dining with Guìfēi,
sometimes staying overnight without leaving,
leading to unsavory rumors spreading outside,
but the emperor remained unsuspicious.
5 Ānxī Jiedùshǐ Gāo Xiānzhī came to court,
presenting the captured Tūqíshī Kèhán, a Tibetan chieftain, the King of Shíguó, and the King of Qièshī.
Xiānzhī was granted the title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Soon after, Xiānzhī was appointed Héxī Jiedùshǐ,
replacing Ān Sīshùn;
Sīshùn incited the Hu people to cut their ears and slash their faces to plead for his retention,
and an edict was issued to keep Sīshùn in Héxī.
6 Ān Lùshān requested to concurrently serve as Hédōng Jiedùshǐ.
In the second month,
on the bǐngchén day,
Hédōng Jiedùshǐ Hán Xiūmín was appointed Zuǒ Yǔlín Jiāngjūn,
and Lùshān replaced him.
Hùbù Lángzhōng Jí Wēn, seeing Lùshān's favor,
attached himself to him,
and they pledged to become brothers.
Wēn advised Lùshān:
"Although Right Chancellor Lǐ has been treating you as a close elder brother due to current circumstances,
in the first year of Tiānbǎo,
Shìzhōng was changed to Zuǒxiàng,
and Zhōngshū Lìng to Yòuxiàng.
Lǐ Línfǔ was then Yòuxiàng,
the position of Zhōngshū Lìng,
the character 'chéng'
is redundant.
Ān Lùshān,
ranked third.
Advise,
pronounced shì ruì fān.
Although I have been employed by him,
I have never been promoted.
If you, elder brother, recommend me to the emperor,
I will then memorialize that you are fit for great responsibilities,
and together we can oust Línfǔ,
and you will surely become chancellor."
Lùshān was pleased with his words,
and repeatedly praised Wēn's talents to the emperor,
who also forgot his earlier words.
When Lùshān took charge of Hédōng,
he memorialized to appoint Wēn as Deputy Jiedùshǐ and Acting Liúhòu,

3 In the early Táng dynasty,

often waiting at the North Gate for instructions,
and people at the time called them
"North Gate Academicians."
During the reign of Emperor Zhōngzōng,
Shàngguān Zhāoróng was solely in charge of such matters.
When the current Emperor ascended the throne,
he established the Hànlín Academy,
located close to the forbidden palace grounds,

and even including monks, Daoists,
and masters of calligraphy, painting, qín, chess, and numerology, all housed there,

"Attendant Officials."
Minister of Justice Zhāng Jūn and his brother, Minister of Sacrifices Zhāng Jì, were both attendants at the Hànlín Academy.
In the Táng dynasty,
when the Son of Heaven was in Dàmíng Palace,
the Hànlín Academy was inside the Right Silver Platform Gate;
when in Xīngqìng Palace,
the academy was inside the Jīnmíng Gate;
if in the Western Palace,
the academy was inside the Xiǎnfú Gate;
if in the Eastern Capital or Huáqīng Palace,
there were also places for Attendant Officials.
Those who were Attendant Officials

Ān Lùshān sent his deputy general Hé Qiānnián to present a memorial,
requesting to replace thirty-two Han generals with foreign generals.
The Emperor ordered that the document be immediately submitted for imperial approval.
"Submitted for imperial approval" means
ordering the Secretariat to draft a "dispatch edict,"
which is then presented to the Emperor for his signature before implementation.
The Tang Liudian states: The Secretariat is in charge of the Emperor's decrees,
and there are seven types of edicts.
The fourth type is the "dispatch edict,"
which specifically refers to the dispatch edict signed by the Emperor;

it is used for increasing or decreasing officials, establishing or abolishing prefectures and counties, dismissing or stripping officials of their titles, and appointing officials of the sixth rank and below.
The character "将" (jiàng) is pronounced with the falling tone (jiàng).
Wéi Jiànsù said to Yáng Guózhōng:
"Lùshān has long harbored treacherous intentions,
and now he makes this request—
his rebellion is clear.
Tomorrow, I will speak out strongly;
if the Emperor does not consent,
you must follow up."
Guózhōng agreed.
On the Rénzǐ day,
Guózhōng and Jiànsù went to see the Emperor.
The Emperor greeted them and said:
"Do you gentlemen suspect Lùshān's intentions?"
Jiànsù then spoke at length about how Lùshān's rebellion was already evident,
and that his request should not be granted.
The Emperor was displeased;
Guózhōng hesitated and did not dare to speak.
In the end, the Emperor approved Lùshān's request.
Another day,
Guózhōng and Jiànsù said to the Emperor:
"We have a plan that can quietly thwart Lùshān's scheme.
If we now appoint Lùshān as a Grand Councilor,
summon him to the court,
and appoint Jiǎ Xún as the military governor of Fànyáng,
Lǚ Zhīhuì as the military governor of Pínglú,
and Yáng Guānghuì as the military governor of Hédōng,
then his power will be divided."
The Emperor agreed.
The edict was drafted,
but the Emperor kept it and did not issue it.
Instead, he sent the eunuch Fǔ Qiúlíng to present precious fruits to Lùshān,
secretly observing his movements.
Fǔ is a surname.
The Zuǒzhuàn records that
in the state of Jìn, there was a senior official named Fǔ Lì.
Also, Zhì Guǒ's branch adopted the surname Fǔ.
This refers to the incident mentioned earlier in the Kǎoyì where sweet oranges were given to Lùshān.
The character "璆" (qiú) is pronounced qiú.
Upon his return,
he spoke glowingly of how Lùshān was utterly loyal and devoted to the state,

The Emperor said to Guózhōng and others:
"I have placed my trust in Lùshān,

Jiànsù said: 'If you hold this view, the state is in danger.'

When Fǔ Qiúlíng delivered the sweet oranges,

If I were to offer admonishing words or bitter medicine, in my heart...'

Lùshān presented gifts to Qiú Lín.

The Commentary on the Poem of the Jīnyáng Gate says: Within the palace, besides the two main imperial baths,

further west the Yíchūn Bath,

The Veritable Records of Sùzōng state:

with ambitions to seize the throne.

recruit righteous volunteers,
hold Tǔmén in the west,
connect with Héshuò in the north,
and await reinforcements from across the empire.

and on the other, it will preserve our integrity as ministers.

ordered Lǚqiān to lead troops to guard Tǔmén,
ordered Jiǎ Shēn to defend the eastern route,

Lǚqiān brought Qīn còu's head to Gǎoqīng.
Gǎoqīng and Lǚqiān were pleased with the success of the operation,

what use is life?

how can we seek temporary safety under the Hú and Jié rebels?

what regrets can we have?'
Shortly after,
the magistrate of Gǎochéng, Cuī Ānshí, reported that Gāo Miǎo was coming from Lùshān's camp,

Miǎo fell,

the southern border reported that Hé Qiānnián was coming from the Eastern Capital and had spent the night in Zhàojùn Commandery.

The Old Biography states:

That same day, they bound the two rebel generals and brought them back to the commandery."
Consider that when Lùshān first led hundreds of thousands of troops south from Fànyáng,
Chángshān lay directly on his route.
If Gǎoqīng had not complied with his orders,
but had immediately resisted with just over a thousand men,
he would have been crushed instantly.
How could he have continued to hold his commandery?
Moreover, at that time, Lùshān was still using the pretext of eliminating Yáng Guózhōng,
and had not yet usurped the throne.
Gǎoqīng welcomed him at Gǎochéng,
accepted his gold and purple robes,
and could hardly have avoided doing so.
What is recorded in the Veritable Records of Sùzōng
was likely intended to preserve the integrity of loyal ministers.
However, Gǎoqīng was loyal, upright, and resolute,
sacrificing his body for the state,
choosing righteousness over life,
a rarity since ancient times.
How could he have written a letter flattering Lùshān,
comparing him to Hàn Gāozǔ and Wèi Wǔdì,
and advising him on strategies of seizing territory and annexation?
Even a person of modest intelligence would know this could not be true.
It is likely that Bāo Xū was the son of Chù Suì,
and wanted to claim that Gǎoqīng initially had no intention of opposing the rebels and upholding integrity,
but was persuaded to do so by his father's letter,
in order to exaggerate his father's merit.
Looking at the recorded letter from Gǎoqīng to Lùshān,
The memorials submitted by Chǔ Suì and others to Yán Gǎoqīng,
and the memorial submitted by Tián Chéngsì to Shǐ Cháoyì,
are identical in literary style,
which is sufficient to know that they were all composed by Bāo Xǔ.
Furthermore, Zhāng Tōngyōu's elder brother was a member of the rebel faction,
and he also instigated Wáng Chéngyè to seize Yán Gǎoqīng's achievements,
ultimately being executed for his duplicity;
his conduct was such;
yet Bāo Xǔ claims that he initially joined Chǔ Suì in submitting a memorial urging Yán Gǎoqīng to be loyal and righteous,
which is particularly difficult to believe.
The Old Biography states:
"Qīn Còu and Gāo Miǎo jointly defended Tǔmén,
and Qīn Còu dispatched Miǎo to Yōuzhōu."
Since the two generals both held troops and jointly garrisoned Tǔmén,
how could Qīn Còu arbitrarily dispatch Miǎo to Yōuzhōu!
Now following Yīn Liàng's Biography of Yán Gǎoqīng,
it was Ān Lùshān himself who dispatched Miǎo to conscript troops, which is correct.
The Héluò Chūnqiū states:
"He left behind a hundred men from the Tóngluó and Yèluòhé tribes,"
but they were garrisoning Jǐngxíng,
blocking the armies from Shānxī,
a heavy responsibility;
how could it be defended by merely a hundred men!
Yīn's biography states
"seven thousand men defended Tǔmén,"
yet these seven thousand men could not have been bound by Lǚ Qiān in a single night either.
It is likely that Ān Lùshān left a hundred elite troops to serve as Qīn Còu's trusted confidants and claws,
while the rest were all militia conscripts coerced into following,
thus Lǚ Qiān was able to get them drunk with wine,
executed Qīn Còu and the hundred men, and dispersed the rest.
The Héluò Chūnqiū states
"poison was placed in the wine,"
but consider that at the time Lǚ Qiān and others were drinking together with Qīn Còu,
how could poison have been placed only in the guests' wine!
This is not adopted now.
Both the Old Biography and Yīn's biography state that Qīn Còu's surname was Jiǎng,
but now following the Veritable Records of Xuánzōng and Sùzōng, and the Tánglì, his surname was Lǐ.

yáng to recruit Jiǎ Xún.

Jiá,
pronounced jiá.

"Ān Lùshān, bearing ingratitude and acting rebelliously,
though he has taken Luòyáng,
will ultimately be destroyed.
