The Emperor then appointed Zhōu Bì, the Héxī Military Commander, as the Military Commissioner of Héxī,
and Péng Yuányào, the Lǒngyòu Military Commander, as the Military Commissioner of Lǒngyòu,
sending them together with the Protector-General Sījié Jìnmíng and others to their posts.
The Eastern Turkic Gāolánzhōu and Xīngxīfǔ,
and the Sījié Diànlínzhōu, Jīnshuǐzhōu, Hèlánzhōu, and Lúshānfǔ,
were all loosely attached to Héxī.
Additionally, the Lǒngyòu Circuit had three Eastern Turkic prefectures,
and twenty-seven commanderies.
Sīlǐ was appointed as the Acting Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ at the imperial temporary residence.
10 On the Wùshēn day,
the commoners of Fúfēng, Kāng Jǐnglóng and others, led each other in attacking the rebel-appointed Xuānwèishǐ Xuē Zǒng,
and beheaded over two hundred people.
On the Gēngxū day,
the Magistrate of Chéncāng, Xuē Jǐngxiān, killed the rebel garrison commander,
captured Fúfēng, and held it.
11. Ān Lùshān did not expect the Emperor to suddenly head west to safety.
He sent envoys to halt Cuī Qiányòu’s troops and keep them stationed at Tóngguān.
For a full ten days
he then sent Sūn Xiàozhé to lead troops into Cháng’ān.
Textual analysis: The *Sùzōng Shílù* and *Ān Lùshān Shìjì* only record that on the *dīngmǎo* and *jǐsì* days of the seventh month,
Lùshān killed the various princes and princesses.
None of the other texts record the day the rebels entered Cháng’ān.
Only the *Luànlí Jì* states:
“On the twenty-third day of the sixth month,
Sūn Xiàozhé and others attacked and captured Cháng’ān,
killing the various princes, princesses, and imperial grandsons.
On the first day of the seventh month,
Lùshān sent Palace Censor Zhāng Tōngrú to serve as the military governor of the Western Capital.”
This book contains many contradictions,
and is not reliable as evidence.
However, calculating by the dates,
the rebels broke through Tóngguān on the eighth day of the sixth month,
so their entry into Cháng’ān must have been within that month.
The *New History* biography states:
“The rebels did not think the Son of Heaven could leave so suddenly;
they stationed troops at Tóngguān for ten days,
then marched west.
By then, the Emperor had already reached Fúfēng.”
According to this, Emperor Xuánzōng reached Fúfēng County on the sixteenth,
and Fúfēng Commandery on the seventeenth.
If the rebels were stationed at Tóngguān for ten days,
then at that time they could not yet have reached Cháng’ān.
It also states:
“Lùshān appointed Zhāng Tōngrú to guard the Eastern Capital,
and Tián Qiánzhēn as the Governor of the Capital District.”
It further states:
“Before Lùshān reached Cháng’ān,
the gentry had all fled into the mountains and valleys,
and the unruly plundered the Left Treasury and the Dàyíng Storehouse.
The treasuries of the various offices were exhausted,
and they set fire to what remained.
When Lùshān arrived,
he was enraged,
and ordered a massive search for three days.”
According to the *Old History* biography,
Tōngrú was the military governor of the Western Capital.
Examining all the texts thoroughly,
Lùshān never went to Cháng’ān after his rebellion,
so the *New History* biography is mistaken.
Cuī Guāngyuǎn served as the Governor of the Capital District;
he sent Ān Zhōngshùn
to lead troops and camp in the imperial gardens,
in order to secure Guānzhōng.
These were the imperial gardens of the Western Capital.
Xiàozhé was especially influential,
often contending for power with Yán Zhuāng.
Lùshān put him in charge of supervising the various generals in Guānzhōng,
and Tōngrú and others were all subject to Xiàozhé’s control.
Xiàozhé was extravagant and arrogant,
decisive in killing,
and the rebel faction feared him.
Lùshān ordered the search and arrest of all officials, eunuchs, palace women, and others.
Whenever several hundred were captured,
they were escorted under armed guard to Luòyáng.
Princes, marquises, generals, and ministers who had accompanied the imperial carriage but whose families remained in Cháng’ān
were executed, including their infants.
Chén Xīliè, having lost favor in his later years,
resented the Emperor,
and together with Zhāng Jūn and Zhāng Jì, surrendered to the rebels.
Chén Xīliè had been dismissed as chancellor and lost his position;
Zhāng Jūn and Zhāng Jì resented not being greatly employed,
so they all surrendered to the rebels.
The remaining court officials were all given official posts.
Thus, the rebel power grew greatly,
threatening Lǒng and Lǒng to the west,
invading Jiāng and Hàn to the south,
and seizing half of Hédōng to the north.
Capturing Fúfēng allowed them to threaten Lǒng and Lǒng to the west;
besieging Nányáng allowed them to invade Jiāng and Hàn to the south.
Cuī Qiányòu, capitalizing on the victory at Tóngguān,
captured Hédōng to the north.
(Pronunciation note: 隴, lǒng.)
After capturing Cháng’ān,
believing they had achieved their ambition,
they indulged in drinking day and night,
devoted entirely to music, women, and treasures,
with no further intention of marching west.
Thus, the Emperor was able to travel safely into Shǔ,
and the Crown Prince’s journey north also faced no pursuit or pressure.
12. Lǐ Guāngbì had besieged Bólíng but not yet captured it.
Hearing that Tóngguān was lost,
he lifted the siege and headed south.
Shǐ Sīmíng followed closely behind him,
but Guāngbì repelled him,
and together with Guō Zǐyí, led their troops into Jǐngxíng.
They left the Tàishǒu of Chángshān, Wáng Fǔ, to command the militia troops of Jǐngchéng and Héjiān in defending Chángshān.
The Pénglú Jīédùshǐ Liú Zhèngchén was about to attack Fànyáng,
but before he arrived,
Shǐ Sīmíng led troops to meet and attack him.
Zhèngchén was badly defeated,
abandoned his wife and children and fled,
with over seven thousand of his soldiers dead.
Earlier,
Yán Zhēnqīng, hearing that the Héběi Jīédùshǐ Lǐ Guāngbì had marched out of Jǐngxíng,
immediately gathered his troops and returned to Píngyuán,
to await Guāngbì’s orders.
Hearing that Guō and Lǐ had entered Jǐngxíng to the west,
Zhēnqīng began again to manage military affairs in Héběi.
13. After the Crown Prince had been at Píngliàng for several days,
the Liúhòu of Shuòfāng, Dù Hóngjiàn, the Six Cities Water and Land Transport Commissioner Wèi Shǎoyóu,
(The Shuòfāng command administered three Shòuxiáng Cities,
as well as the three cities of Fēng’ān, Dìngyuǎn, and Zhènwǔ,
all located beyond the Yellow River.
Both Líng and Yán prefectures had salt ponds,
hence the appointment of a Pànguān.)
said, “Píngliàng is an open area,
not a place to station troops.
Língwǔ has ample troops and provisions,
(Língwǔ Commandery,
Líng Prefecture,
was the seat of the Shuòfāng Jīédùshǐ.)
Gather troops from the northern cities,
mobilize crack cavalry from Hé and Lǒng to the west,
and march south to pacify the Central Plains.
This is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity.”
They then sent Hán to present a memorial to the Crown Prince,
and also listed the numbers of Shuòfāng soldiers, horses, armor, weapons, grain, cloth, and military supplies to offer him.
When Hán reached Píngliàng,
the Crown Prince was greatly pleased.
Meanwhile, the Héxī Sīmǎ Péi Miǎn had entered the capital to serve as Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
He reached Píngliàng to see the Crown Prince,
and also urged the Crown Prince to go to Shuòfāng.
The Crown Prince agreed.
Hóngjiàn
was a clansman of Xiān;
(Dù Xiān
served as chancellor during the Kāiyuán era.)
Miǎn was the great-grandson of Dào.
(Dào
was the son of the elder brother of Prince Xiàoji of Yǒng’ān,
and succeeded Xiàoji.)
They repaired lodgings,
prepared supplies and stores,
and went to meet the Crown Prince north of Píngliàng.
They advised the Crown Prince, saying:
“Shuòfāng
is the place of the empire’s strongest troops.
Now the Tǔbō have requested peace,
the Huíhé have submitted internally,
and the various commanderies and counties are largely holding firm against the rebels, awaiting restoration.
If Your Highness now marshals troops at Língwǔ,
drives forward with reins held high,
issues proclamations to all regions,
and gathers the loyal and righteous,
then the rebellious traitors will be easily crushed.”
Shǎoyóu lavishly constructed palaces and halls,
with curtains and canopies all imitating those of the imperial palace,
and feasts prepared with delicacies from land and sea.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the *xīnyǒu* day,
the Crown Prince reached Língwǔ
and ordered all these to be removed.
(The historian notes that Sùzōng thereby achieved the merit of restoration.)
14. On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
the Emperor reached Pǔ’ān.
(Pǔ’ān Commandery,
Jiàn Prefecture.)
When the Emperor departed from Cháng’ān,
many of his ministers did not know.
Upon reaching Xiányáng,
he said to Gāo Lìshì:
“Among the court ministers, who will come,
and who will not?”
Lìshì replied:
“Zhāng Jūn and his son Zhāng Jì have received the deepest favor from Your Majesty,
and are moreover connected to the imperial in-laws,
(meaning Jì had married a princess.)
(Jì,
pronunciation note: jì, tone 4.)
Contemporary opinion held that Fáng Guǎn should be made chancellor,
but Your Majesty did not employ him.
Moreover, Lùshān had once recommended him,
so I fear he may not come.”
The Emperor said:
“The matter is not yet certain.”
When Guǎn arrived,
the Emperor asked about the Zhāng brothers.
Guǎn replied:
“I urged them to come together,
but they lingered and did not advance.
Judging their intentions,
it seemed they had something on their minds but could not speak it.”
The Emperor looked at Lìshì and said:
“I already knew it.”
That same day,
he appointed Guǎn as Vice Minister of the Civil Ministry and Tóngpíngzhāngshì.
(In the eleventh year of the Tiānbǎo era,
the Ministry of Justice was renamed the Ministry of Statutes,
and the Ministry of Personnel was renamed the Civil Ministry.)
Initially,
Zhāng Jì married Princess Níngqīn,
who had been transferred from the Xìngxìn fiefdom,
and was the emperor's daughter.
She received unparalleled favor and affection.
Chén Xīliè requested to be relieved of his administrative duties,
an event recorded in the previous volume under the thirteenth year of the Tiānbǎo era.
The emperor asked who could serve as chancellor.
Jì did not respond.
The emperor said:
"None is better than my beloved son-in-law."
Jì descended the steps and performed a ceremonial dance of gratitude.
However, he was not appointed,
so Jì harbored resentment,
which the emperor also perceived.

At that time, the brothers Jūn and Jì, along with Yáo Chóng's son, the Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs Yì, Xiāo Sōng's son, the Vice Minister of War Huá, Wéi Ānshí's son, the Vice Minister of Rites Zhì, and the Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices Bīn,
all held high offices due to their talent and reputation.
The emperor once said:
"When I appoint a chancellor,
I should select from among the sons of former chancellors."
Yet, none were ultimately appointed.
From the initial mention of Zhāng Jì onward,
the history records these past events retrospectively.
Bīn
is pronounced bīn.
15 Péi Miǎn, Dù Hóngjiàn, and others submitted a memorial to the Crown Prince,
urging him to comply with the decision made at Mǎwéi
and ascend the throne as emperor.
The Crown Prince refused.
Miǎn and the others argued:
"The officers and soldiers are all from Guānzhōng,
longing day and night to return home.
The reason they have followed Your Highness through arduous journeys into distant desert frontiers
is their hope for even the slightest merit.
If they were to disperse one day,
they could never be reassembled.
We implore Your Highness to strive to comply with the will of the masses,
for the sake of the state!"
After five memorials were submitted,
the Crown Prince finally consented.
On that day,
Emperor Sùzōng ascended the throne at the south tower of Língwǔ city.
The assembled officials performed the ceremonial dance,
and the emperor wept with emotion.
From this point onward,
whenever 'the emperor' is mentioned in the text,
it refers to Emperor Sùzōng.
Xū
is pronounced xū.
Xī
is pronounced xì according to the Fǎnqiè method (xǔ jì fān),
and also pronounced xī.
A general amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed.
It was at this time that the fourteenth year of Tiānbǎo was changed to the first year of Zhìdé.
Péi Miǎn was appointed Vice Director of the Secretariat and given the additional title of Tóng Píngzhāng Shì (Participant in Determining Governmental Matters).
The Guānnèi Surveillance Commissioner was changed to Military Commissioner,
with the seat of government moved to Ānhuà,
and the former Púguān Defense Commissioner Lǚ Chóngbēn was appointed to the post.
The Guānnèi Surveillance Commissioner was held by a capital official concurrently,
without a fixed seat of government;
now changed to a military governorship,
governing from Ānhuà,
overseeing the five prefectures of Jīngzhào, Tóng, Qí, Jīn, and Shāng.
Ānhuà County was originally the Suí dynasty's Hónghuà County,
renamed in the first year of Tiānbǎo,
and concurrently, Qìng Prefecture's Hónghuà Commandery was renamed Ānhuà Commandery.
Púguān
is Pújīn Pass.
Shǐ (Commissioner)
is pronounced according to the Fǎnqiè shū lì fān.
He concurrently held the title of Defense Commissioner;
the Lǒngyòu Military Commissioner Guō Yīngyì was appointed Grand Administrator of Tiānshuǐ,
concurrently holding the title of Defense Commissioner.
Shǒu (Grand Administrator)
is pronounced according to the Fǎnqiè shì yòu fān.
Tiānshuǐ Commandery
is Qín Prefecture.
Only the old and weak remained to guard the borders,
civil and military officials numbered fewer than thirty,
they cleared the wilderness,
established a court,
institutions were rudimentary,
and military men were arrogant and disrespectful.
The senior general Guǎn Chóngsì, in the court hall,
sat with his back to the palace steps,
talking and laughing as usual.
The Investigating Censor Lǐ Miǎn submitted an impeachment memorial against him,
and he was imprisoned by the relevant authorities.
The emperor specially pardoned him,
sighing:
"With Lǐ Miǎn,
the court begins to command respect!"
Miǎn
was the great-grandson of Yuányì.
Prince Zhèng Yuányì
was a son of Emperor Gāozǔ.
Those who submitted and joined gradually increased in number.
Consort Zhāng Liángdì was clever and perceptive,
able to understand the emperor's intentions.
She followed the emperor to Shuòfāng.
At that time, the accompanying troops were few,
and whenever Liángdì slept,
she often positioned herself in front of the emperor.
The emperor said:
"Resisting bandits is not something a woman can do."
Liángdì replied:
"In a sudden crisis,
I can use my body to shield you,
allowing Your Highness to escape from behind."
Upon reaching Língwǔ,
she gave birth to a child;
three days later, she got up
to sew clothes for the soldiers.
The emperor tried to stop her,
but she replied:
"This is not the time for me to focus on recuperating."
The emperor therefore cherished her even more.
This sets the background for Liángdì later using her favor to seize power and bring about disaster.
Liángdì
held a rank of the third degree.
16 On the day Dīngmǎo,
the Retired Emperor issued an edict:
"Appoint the Crown Prince Hēng as Grand Marshal of All Armies Under Heaven,
overseeing the Military Commissioners of Shuòfāng, Hédōng, Héběi, and Pínglú,
to march south and capture Cháng'ān and Luòyáng.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
the Crown Prince ascended the throne at Língwǔ.
On Dīngmǎo,
the Retired Emperor issued this edict.
Presumably, because the distance between them was vast,
those in Shǔ had not yet learned of it.
Shuài (Marshal)
is pronounced according to the Fǎnqiè suǒ lèi fān.
Shǐ (Commissioner)
is pronounced according to the Fǎnqiè shū lì fān.
The Sīmǎ of Lǒngxī Commandery, Liú Zhì, was provisionally appointed Vice Director of the Right of the Household of the Crown Prince;
Lǒngxī Commandery
is Wèi Prefecture.
Liú Zhì must have been recommended by Fáng Guǎn.
Appoint the Director of the Palace Administration, Dòu Shào, as his Tutor,
and the Grand Administrator of Chángshā, Lǐ Xiàn, as Vice Grand Commissioner;
this refers to the Vice Grand Commissioner of the Military Commissions.
He oversaw the Military Commissions of the Jiāngnán East Circuit, Huáinán, Hénán, and other circuits.
Appoint the former Chief Clerk of the Jiānglíng Metropolitan Governor's Office, Liú Huì, as his Tutor,
and the Chief Clerk of Guǎnglíng Commandery, Lǐ Chéngshì, as Vice Grand Commissioner;
Guǎnglíng Commandery
is Yáng Prefecture.
He also oversaw the Military Commissions of the Héxī, Lǒngyòu, Ānxī, Běitíng, and other circuits.
Appoint the Grand Administrator of Lǒngxī, Jìyīn's Dèng Jǐngshān, as his Tutor,
and concurrently serve as Vice Grand Commissioner.
Each circuit had its own Military Commissioner;
appointing various princes as Grand Commissioners to oversee them;
for those who did not proceed to their posts,
the Vice Grand Commissioner acted in their stead.
Jì
is pronounced according to the Fǎnqiè zǐ lǐ fān.
And they were to supply themselves from their respective routes.
The original Military Commissioners of these various routes, such as Prince Guó Jù, etc., all continued in their posts as before.
Meaning they remained as Military Commissioners as before.
And they were permitted to make their own selections,
reporting after appointments were made."
At that time, Qí and Gǒng did not leave the palace,
only Lín proceeded to his post.
This sets the background for Lín later raising troops and causing rebellion.
He oversaw nine commanderies including Xiāngyáng.

Overseeing Xiāng Prefecture's Xiāngyáng Commandery, Dèng Prefecture's Nányáng Commandery, Suí Prefecture's Hàndōng Commandery, Táng Prefecture's Huái'ān Commandery, Jūn Prefecture's Wǔdāng Commandery, Fáng Prefecture's Fánglíng Commandery, (Ān Prefecture's Ānlù Commandery,) Jīn Prefecture's Ānkāng Commandery, Shāng Prefecture's Shàngluò Commandery.
He oversaw twenty-two commanderies including Nánhǎi.
The Wǔxī Frontier Command was elevated to the Qiánzhōng Military Commission,
overseeing various commanderies including Qiánzhōng.
Commentary is found in the previous year's records.
Qián
is pronounced qín.
The East Circuit oversaw Yúháng,
the West Circuit oversaw various commanderies including Yùzhāng.
Yúháng Commandery
is Háng Prefecture.
Yùzhāng Commandery
is Hóng Prefecture.
No one knew where the emperor had gone,
and when this edict was issued,
they finally learned the location of the imperial carriage.
Huì
was Zhì's younger brother.
17 Ān Lùshān sent Sūn Xiàozhé to kill the Elder Princess of Huò
The Elder Princess of Huò
was a daughter of Emperor Ruìzōng,
who married Péi Xūjǐ.
Zhǎng (Elder)
is pronounced according to the Fǎnqiè zhī liǎng fān.
He cut out her heart,
to sacrifice to Ān Qìngzōng.
The execution of Ān Qìngzōng is recorded in the previous volume under last year.
A total of eighty-three people,
some had their skulls smashed with iron clubs,
blood flowing in the streets.
On the day Jǐsì,
he also killed over twenty imperial grandsons and commandery and county princesses.
On the 18th day, Gēngwǔ,
the Retired Emperor arrived at Bāxī.
The Grand Administrator, Cuī Huàn, went out to welcome and pay his respects.
Lóng Prefecture's Bāxī Commandery,
in the second year of the Xiāntiān era, to avoid the Retired Emperor's personal name taboo,
was renamed Làng Prefecture.
In the first year of the Tiānbǎo era, it was renamed Làngzhōng Commandery.
Mián Prefecture's Jīnshān Commandery was renamed Bāxī Commandery.
Textual analysis notes: The Veritable Records of Sùzōng records this as
"Xīnwèi (the 19th day)."
I now follow the Veritable Records of Xuánzōng.
The Old Accounts of the Liǔ Family states:
"When the Emperor first entered the Xiégǔ valley,
it was still early in the day,
and the mist and fog were very thick.
The Provisioning Commissioner and Supervising Secretary Wéi Tì obtained a pot of newly brewed wine from a country estate,
and kneeling before the Emperor's horse, he offered it up four times.
The Emperor did not lift it to drink.
Tì became afraid,
so he poured it into another vessel,
filled a cup for himself, and drank it in front of the Emperor.
The Emperor said: 'You suspect me [of doubting the wine].
When I first ascended the throne and ruled the realm,
I once got heavily drunk,
which resulted in the death of a man.
I grieved for him,
and because of this, I took it as a warning.
For forty years now,
I have not tasted the pleasant flavor of wine.'
Pointing to Gāo Lìshì and his close attendants, he said,
'They all know this,
I am not deceiving you.'
Those who heard this among his followers
were all moved and pleased."
The Record of the Journey to Shǔ states:
"When the Retired Emperor was in Bāxī Commandery,
the chief ministers requested that Gāo Lìshì memorialize that the climate in Shǔ was warm and miasmic,
and that he should drink wine frequently.
The Retired Emperor ordered Gāo Lìshì to announce his decree: 'I was originally fond of wine,
but I gave it up long ago.
I will ultimately not drink again,
and I deeply regret disappointing your intentions.'
Lìshì then explained: 'In the fourth year of the Kāiyuán era, the Retired Emperor,
drunk and angry, killed a man.
The next day, he did not remember it at all,
and still summoned him.
His attendants fully reported what had happened.
The Emperor was sorrowful and silent,
then bestowed five hundred bolts of silk from the imperial treasury to cover the funeral expenses,
and further ordered me to go to the residence to announce a decree and conduct a sacrifice.
From then on, he abstained from wine.
Even when taking medicine,
he would not casually drink [wine with it].'"
Note: Xuánzōng was excessive in his indulgence in music and women,
nearly losing the empire.
The minor virtue of abstaining from wine—
what is there worth mentioning!
I do not adopt [these accounts].
[The Emperor] was pleased with him [Cuī Huàn],
and Fáng Guǎn again recommended him.
That very day,
he was appointed Vice Director of the Chancellery and Joint Manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery,
and Wéi Jiànsù was made Left Chancellor.
Huàn
was the grandson of Cuī Xuánwěi.
When Zhōngzōng was restored to the throne,
Cuī Xuánwěi's merit was ranked among the Five Princes.
19. Earlier,
Lǐ Mì of Jīngzhào,
from a young age was renowned for his talent and quick-wittedness.
Xuánzōng had him associate with the Prince of Zhōng.
When the Prince of Zhōng became Crown Prince,
Mì was already grown.
He submitted a memorial discussing affairs.
Xuánzōng wanted to give him an official post,
but he refused.
[Xuánzōng] had him form a friendship with the Crown Prince as a commoner,
and the Crown Prince often called him "Teacher."
Yáng Guózhōng disliked him,
and memorialized to have him transferred to Qíchūn.
Qíchūn Commandery
was Qí Prefecture.
Dislike: wù, pronunciation wūlù fān.
He resided in Yǐngyáng.
In the first year of the Zǎichū era of Empress Wǔ,
Wǔlín County was established by dividing off Yīquē and Sōngyáng from Hénán.
In the fifteenth year of the Kāiyuán era,
it was renamed Yǐngyáng,
belonging to Hénán Prefecture.
[The Emperor] sent an envoy to summon him,
and he had an audience at Língwǔ.
Textual analysis notes: The Old Biography states
"had an audience at Péngyuán."
I now follow the Family Biography of the Marquis of Yè compiled by his son Lǐ Fán,
which says
"it had been eight or nine days since the accession."
Audience: jiàn, pronunciation xián biàn fān.
When they went out, they rode side by side;
when they slept, their couches faced each other.
It was just like when he was Crown Prince.
Matters great and small were all consulted with him,
and his advice was never disregarded,
even to the point of discussing the advancement or dismissal of generals and ministers with him.
The Emperor wanted to make Mì Right Chancellor,
but Mì firmly declined,
saying:
"If Your Majesty treats me as a guest and friend,
that is nobler than being Chancellor.
Why must you bend my will!"
The Emperor then desisted.
Textual analysis notes: The Old Biography states:
"Mì called himself a mountain recluse,
firmly declined official rank,
so he was honored with a sinecure post.
(得 dé should be 特 tè.)
He first entered official service
and was appointed Silver青光祿大夫,
entrusted with managing pivotal affairs."
The Family Biography of the Marquis of Yè says:
"Initially, he wished to appoint him as Right Chancellor.
[Mì], fearing military affairs,
firmly declined the noble rank,
wishing to follow as a guest,
saying: 'If Your Majesty treats me as a guest and friend,
that is nobler than being Chancellor.
Why must you bend my will!'
The Emperor had no way to press him."
I now follow this.
20. The Tóngluó and Tūjué tribes who had followed Ān Lùshān in rebellion were encamped in the parks of Cháng'ān.
On the Jiǎxū day,
their chieftain Āshǐnà Cónglǐ led five thousand cavalry,
secretly taking two thousand government horses, and fled back to Shuòfāng,
planning to gather the various Hú tribes,
and seize the border regions by force.
The Emperor sent an envoy to pacify and reassure them,
and many surrendered.
Textual analysis notes: The Veritable Records of Sùzōng states:
"Suddenly it was heard that the Tóngluó and Tūjué had turned their backs on Lùshān and fled to Shuòfāng,
planning with the Six Prefecture Zhì Hú to seize Héběi,
and all the generals were afraid.
The Emperor said: 'If we take advantage of this to summon and instruct them,
it should increase our army's prestige.'
The Emperor sent someone to pacify and reassure them,
and indeed, more than half surrendered."
The Old Biography of Cuī Guāngyuǎn states:
"The Tóngluó turned against Lùshān,
and taking two thousand government horses, they went out to the Chǎn River.
Sūn Xiàozhé and Ān Shénwēi followed and summoned them,
but could not get them back;
Shénwēi died of worry."
Chén Hóng's Family Biography of the Prince of Fényáng states:
"Lùshān was full of deceit and cunning.
He further plotted to use the acculturated Fān of Héqū as his own followers.
He had the Fān general Āshǐnà Cónglǐ lead five thousand Tóngluó and Tūjué cavalry, falsely claiming to rebel,
then go over to Shuòfāng.
Going out beyond the frontier passes,
he persuaded the Nine Surname Prefectures and the Six Hú Prefectures,
and they all came over.
There were fifty thousand armored troops,
and five hundred thousand tribespeople,
swarming like ants north of the Jīnglüè Army."
Note: If the Tóngluó rebelled against the bandits,
they should have gone west,
how could they have reached the Chǎn River again!
This is an error in the Old Biography.
If Lùshān had Cónglǐ falsely rebel,
then why would Xiàozhé summon him?
Why would Shénwēi die of terror?
Moreover, they must have first sent a surrender message to Sùzōng.
If that were the case,
then the various generals should have been pleased, not afraid.
The bandits' secret plan—
was it merely to obtain the acculturated Fān of Héqū!
Probably the Tóngluó and others, having been long away from home, longed to return.
Therefore, they rebelled against Lùshān,
wishing to take advantage of the world's chaos,
gather the various Hú tribes,
and seize the border regions.
What the Veritable Records of Sùzōng calls
"planning together to seize Héběi"
refers to
wishing to seize the two circuits west of Héběi,
just like saying
"Hé and Lǒng."
Sùzōng followed up by recruiting them,
there certainly were those who surrendered;
but if it says the greater part,
that seems too many.
I now select and preserve the credible parts from these various texts.

they arrived at Língwǔ.

Cháo's soldiers competed to shoot them,
and only after a long time did they realize they were straw men.

Later, they again lowered men at night,

Cháo's army was thrown into chaos,
burned their fortifications, and fled,
pursued for over ten miles.

Rebel crossbowmen shot at him,

and sent a spy to inquire.
He was greatly astonished,
and from afar said to Xún:

but what can you do against the will of Heaven!"
Xún replied:

how can you know the will of Heaven!"
This means that by betraying the sovereign and joining the rebels,
he did not understand the ethics between ruler and subject.

Jiǔyù Zhì: In Zhōngmóu County of Kāifēng, there was Báishā Town.

Examination of discrepancies: In the Biography of Vice-Director Zhāng:
"From the second day of the third month,
Cháo arrived at the walls of Yōngqiū,
attacking and defending for over sixty days,
Cháo was greatly defeated and fled,"
thus it was already early May at that time.
It also states:
"Not long after,
Cháo again led troops to attack,
saying to Xún: 'Our court is in peril,
troops have not exited the passes,'"
meaning Tóng Pass had not yet fallen.
Also, Xún’s reply to Cháo’s letter:
"Our sovereign, due to Gēshū’s defeat,
has taken refuge in Western Shǔ;
the Filial and Righteous Emperor has gathered horses from Hé and Lǒng,
taken armor from Tàiyuán,
Fán and Hàn troops assembling like clouds,
no less than four hundred thousand strong,
arrived at Tǔmén on the twenty-seventh of last month.
Troops from Shǔ and Hàn,
and the brave warriors of Wú and Chǔ,
are descending along the river.
Yǒngwáng and Shēnwáng’s forces have already reached the southern gates of Shēn and Xī.
I reckon the roaming spirits of the Hú barbarians
will not last beyond the year’s end."
This would be after the fifteenth day of the seventh month, Dīngmǎo.
The statement
"on the twenty-seventh of last month,
troops arrived at Tǔmén,"
is likely an error in rumors within the besieged city.
It also states:
"Holding out for over forty days,
Cháo withdrew his troops into Chénliú,
not daring to come out,"
and then says:
"In May,
Lǔ Jiǒng was defeated at Yè.
In June,
Gēshū Hàn was defeated at Tóng Pass,
the Retired Emperor took refuge in Shǔ,
the Emperor traveled north to Língwǔ.
On the ninth day of June,
rebel general Qú Bóyù occupied Yǔchéng.
On the twelfth,
rebels stationed at Báishā Wō.
On the night of the fourteenth,
Xún attacked and defeated them.
On the twelfth day of July,
Cháo and Bóyù reached Yōngqiū,
and were again defeated,"
the dates and months are inconsistent,
making verification impossible.
Likely Lǐ Hàn also obtained this from hearsay,
and could not verify it precisely.
Now, we simply place events before the fall of the pass in May,
and events after the fall of the pass in July.
Over ten thousand households of people left the rebels and returned.

with the strategic Jǐngxíng Pass,
it can choke their throat.

Great General, your troops are elite and disciplined,

residing in a four-way thoroughfare and seeking peace,

Chéng'ēn,

Wū Chéngcǐ appears in the thirteenth year of the second hundred scrolls of Kāiyuán.
Cǐ,
pronounced as cǐ,

Textual Analysis: The *Veritable Records of Sùzōng* states:
"In the eighth month,
on Rénwǔ,
Guō Zǐyí and Lǐ Guāngbì both achieved a great victory over the rebels at Jiāshān in Chángshān Commandery.
Guō Zǐyí and others all received the imperial edict
and led fifty thousand troops from Héběi.
Guō Zǐyí was appointed to a certain office,
and Lǐ Guāngbì was appointed to a certain office."
The *Family Biography of Fényáng* states:
"On the eighth day of the sixth month,
they defeated Shǐ Sīmíng at the foot of Jiāshān.
Guō Zǐyí said to Lǐ Guāngbì: 'The rebels are scattered.
How many remain?
We can drive southward
to pacify the realm.'
That month,
they set out from Héngyáng
and reached Chángshān.
The eunuch envoy Xíng Yán'ēn arrived,
bearing an edict to take the Héběi route
and sweep southward.
At that time, Gēshū Hàn was defeated,
Xuánzōng fled to Shǔ,
and Sùzōng went to Shuòfāng.
Upon hearing this,
Guō Zǐyí alone led fifty thousand elite troops to rush to Sùzōng's temporary headquarters.
Xuánzōng issued a decree
appointing Sùzōng as successor to the imperial throne.
Sùzōng received the decree with sobs,
overcome with grief.
Guō Zǐyí remonstrated, etc.,
knelt and presented the imperial seal,
and on the thirteenth day of the seventh month, Sùzōng ascended the throne.
On the twenty-seventh day,
an imperial order: He was appointed Minister of War and Grand Councilor."
The *Record of the Flight to Shǔ* states:
"On the eleventh day of the sixth month,
Xuánzōng summoned Guō Zǐyí to the capital,
while Lǐ Guāngbì defended Tàiyuán."
The *Annals of Héluò* states:
"On the twenty-fifth day of the sixth month,
they achieved a great victory over the rebels at Jiāshān.
On the twenty-sixth day,
they redeployed their formations.
On the twenty-seventh day,
an edict reached Héngyáng,
stating: Tóngguān had fallen,
the emperor had fled to Jiànnán,
and the heir apparent had gone to Língwǔ.
Therefore, they withdrew their army and entered the Jǐngxíng Pass."
The *Records of Bīn* states:
"On the eighth day of the sixth month,
they defeated Shǐ Sīmíng at Jiāshān.
At that time, Tóngguān had fallen,
so the two commanders withdrew their troops."
The *Táng Calendar* states:
"On the twenty-eighth day of the seventh month,
Guō Zǐyí and Lǐ Guāngbì were both appointed Grand Councilors.
Another edict ordered Guō Zǐyí to withdraw his troops and proceed to Shuòfāng,
while Lǐ Guāngbì was to go to Tàiyuán."
The *Annals of Héluò* also states:
"Lǐ Guāngbì reached Tàiyuán,
executed Wáng Chéng'ēn,
and firmly defended Jìnyáng."
The Old Annals agree with the Veritable Records.
The Biography of Guō Zǐyí states:
"In the seventh month,
Sùzōng ascended the throne.
As the rebels occupied both capitals,
plans were being made for recovery.
An edict ordered Guō Zǐyí to withdraw his troops.
In the eighth month,
Guō Zǐyí and Lǐ Guāngbì led fifty thousand infantry and cavalry from Héběi."
The Biography of Lǐ Guāngbì states:
"Sùzōng was organizing troops at Língwǔ
and sent the eunuch envoy Liú Zhìdá to summon Lǐ Guāngbì and Guō Zǐyí to his temporary headquarters."
It also states:
"He led five thousand troops from Jǐngchéng and Héjiān to Tàiyuán."
The *Veritable Records of Xuánzōng* states:
"In the sixth month,
on Rénwǔ,
Lǐ Guāngbì and Guō Zǐyí defeated Shǐ Sīmíng at Jiāshān."
The Old Annals state:
"In the sixth month,
Guǐwèi was the first day.
On Gēngyín,
Gēshū Hàn was defeated at Língbǎo.
On that same day,
Lǐ Guāngbì defeated Shǐ Sīmíng at Jiāshān."
The biographies of Guō Zǐyí and Lǐ Guāngbì both state
"in the sixth month,"
without specifying a day.
The various texts record the events concerning Lǐ and Guō so differently.
According to the calendar for that year,
the sixth month began on Guǐwèi,
which matches the Old Annals.
The *Veritable Records of Xuánzōng* states Rénwǔ,
which is an error.
The *Veritable Records of Sùzōng*
states "the eighth month, Rénwǔ,"
which is the first day of the month.
It records that Guō Zǐyí and Lǐ Guāngbì both achieved a great victory over the rebels at Jiāshān,
and led troops from Héběi,
being appointed to certain offices.
It seems Rénwǔ was the day they were appointed to office,
and the text mentions previous events in connection with this.
Both the *Family Biography of Fényáng* and the *Records of Bīn* state they defeated Shǐ Sīmíng on the eighth day of the sixth month,
which matches the Old Annals.
The *Family Biography* states that Guō Zǐyí urged Sùzōng to ascend the throne
and presented the seal,
but this is likely incorrect.
Gēshū Hàn was defeated on the eighth day of the sixth month,
and it would have taken about ten days for the news to reach Héběi.
Sùzōng ascended the throne on the thirteenth day of the seventh month.
If they withdrew their troops on the twenty-seventh day of the sixth month,
how could they possibly have reached Língwǔ by the thirteenth day of the seventh month?
The *Annals of Héluò*
states the victory was on the twenty-fifth day,
which does not match any of the other texts,
and is likely too late.
Now, based on the Old Annals of Xuánzōng, the *Family Biography of Fényáng*, the *Records of Bīn*, and the *Táng Calendar*,
which all state that Shǐ Sīmíng was defeated on the eighth day of the sixth month,
this should be followed.
The *Record of the Flight to Shǔ*
states that on the eleventh day,
Xuánzōng summoned Guō Zǐyí and Lǐ Guāngbì.
This may be accurate.
However, both biographies state that Sùzōng summoned them.
It is likely that while the two were in Héběi,
they heard that Tóngguān had fallen,
and had already begun withdrawing their troops to aid the crisis, en route,
when they encountered Sùzōng's eunuch envoy,
and thus proceeded to Língwǔ.
We now follow the Old Biographies.
The *Táng Calendar* records their appointment as councilors on the twenty-eighth day of the seventh month,
the *Family Biography of Fényáng* on the twenty-seventh day,
and the *Veritable Records of Sùzōng* on the first day of the eighth month.
These three texts are not far apart.
The Biography of Guō Zǐyí states the eighth month,
though without a specific day,
which roughly corresponds with the Veritable Records.
We now follow the Veritable Records.
According to the Old Biographies,
Lǐ Guāngbì also went to Língwǔ.
It is suspected that the Shuòfāng troops all followed Sùzōng,
so Lǐ Guāngbì only led the Héběi troops to Tàiyuán.
The *Annals of Héluò* is particularly inaccurate regarding months and days.
Its statement about executing Wáng Chéng'ēn
and firmly defending Jìnyáng
is certainly erroneous.
30. The Uighur Qaghan and the Tibetan Tsanpo successively sent envoys requesting to assist the state in suppressing the rebels.
They were feasted, given gifts, and sent off.
31. On Guǐwèi,
the Retired Emperor issued an edict,
granting a general amnesty.
Textual Analysis: The *Veritable Records of Xuánzōng* and the Old Annals both state
"the eighth month, Guǐwèi is the first day."
The *Veritable Records of Sùzōng*, the *Táng Calendar*, the Old Annals, and the Long Calendar all state
"Rénwǔ is the first day."
We now follow this.
At this time, the Retired Emperor did not yet know that the Crown Prince had ascended the throne at Língwǔ.
Hèlán Jìnmíng, the Grand Administrator of Běihǎi, sent his Registrar and Army Consultant Dìwǔ Qí to Shǔ to report on affairs.
Dìwǔ Qí addressed the Retired Emperor,
stating:
"Now that we are engaged in military operations,
financial resources are of utmost urgency.
The regions producing the most wealth and taxes
are primarily Jiāngnán and Huáinán.
I beg to be entrusted with an office,
so that I can ensure the army does not lack supplies."
The Retired Emperor was pleased,
and immediately appointed Dìwǔ Qí as Investigating Censor and Commissioner of Taxes and Transport for Jiāngnán and Huáinán.
In the eleventh year of the Kāiyuán era,
Yǔwén Róng was appointed as Commissioner for Managing Taxes and Land Taxes.
This was the beginning of the office of Commissioner of Taxes and Transport.
Subsequently, Wéi Jiān and Yáng Guózhōng successively held the position.
32. Shǐ Sīmíng attacked Jiǔmén again.
On Xīnmǎo,
he captured it,
killing several thousand people.
He then led his troops east to besiege Gǎochéng.
33. Lǐ Tíngwàng led over twenty thousand troops of various ethnic groups to launch a surprise attack eastward on Nínglíng and Xiāngyì.
At night,
he set up camp thirty li away from the city of Yōngqiū.
Zhāng Xún led three thousand short-weapon troops in a surprise attack,
inflicting a major defeat,
killing and capturing more than half of them.
Tíngwàng gathered his remaining troops and fled under cover of night.
34. On Guǐsì,
an envoy from Língwǔ arrived in Shǔ.
(The Crown Prince) had ascended the throne on the Jiǎzǐ day of the seventh month,
and it had been thirty days by now,
before the envoy finally reached Shǔ.
"My son responds to Heaven and accords with the people,
what more have I to worry about!"
On Dīngyǒu,
an edict was issued:
"From now on, imperial decrees and commands shall be called 'proclamations' (gào),
and memorials and petitions shall address me as 'Grand Emperor'.
All military and state affairs throughout the land
shall first be decided by the Emperor,
and then reported to me for my knowledge;
once the capital is recovered,
I will no longer participate in governance."
On Jǐhài,
the Grand Emperor held court in the audience hall,
and ordered Wéi Jiànsù, Fáng Guǎn, and Cuī Huàn to take the imperial seal and jade tablets to Língwǔ to formally transfer the throne.
*Textual Analysis says: The Veritable Records of Sùzōng state:*
"On Guǐwèi,
the Emperor's memorial reached Shǔ."
*The Veritable Records of Xuánzōng state:*
"On the first day of the eighth month, Guǐwèi,
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
At that time, the Crown Prince had already reached Língwǔ,
having ascended the throne on the Jiǎzǐ day of the seventh month.
The roads were dangerous and difficult,
and memorials had not yet arrived.
After this edict was issued,
several days later,
an envoy from the north finally arrived,
fully explaining the ministers' earnest requests and the Crown Prince's initial refusal and deference.
On Xīnmǎo,
an edict was issued,
adopting the title 'Grand Emperor'.
On Gēngzǐ,
Wéi Jiànsù and others were dispatched to present the tablets."
*Now we follow the Old Annals and the Táng Calendar.*
35. On Xīnchǒu,
Shǐ Sīmíng captured Gǎochéng.
36. In the past,
whenever the Grand Emperor held grand banquets,
he would first have the Tàicháng Court's elegant music performed by the seated and standing sections,
followed by martial music, foreign music, Jiàofǎng music, and the variety shows and miscellaneous performances of the prefectures and counties;
the Tàicháng elegant music
was the music established in the early Táng by Zǔ Xiàosūn and Zhāng Wénshōu.
Emperor Xuánzōng divided the music into two sections: those performing standing in the courtyard below the hall,
were called the 'standing section performers';
those performing seated in the hall above,
were called the 'seated section performers'.
The standing section had eight pieces: first, the Ān Dance;
second, the Tàipíng Music;
third, the Pòzhèn Music;
fourth, the Qìngshàn Music;
fifth, the Dàdìng Music;
sixth, the Shàngyuán Music;
seventh, the Shèngshòu Music;
eighth, the Guāngshèng Music.
The seated section had six pieces: first, the Yàn Music;
second, the Chángshòu Music;
third, the Tiānshòu Music;
fourth, the Niǎogē Wànsuì Music;
fifth, the Lóngchí Music;
sixth, the Xiǎo Pòzhèn Music.
Martial music
refers to the náo songs and martial music tunes managed by the Director of the Martial Music Office.
Foreign music
refers to the music of the various states such as Qiūcí, Shūlè, Gāochāng, and Tiānzhú.
Jiàofǎng music
refers to the music of the Inner Training Bureau and the Líyuán Academy's Fǎqǔ.
Prefectural and county [music]
refers to that of Jīngzhào Prefecture and the two capital counties, Cháng'ān and Wànnián.
Variety shows,
are miscellaneous performances.
Pú (banquet),
is pronounced 'pú'.
Mountain carts
were carts with pavilions erected on them,
decorated with colorful silks,
to resemble mountains and forests.
Land boats
were made by binding bamboo and wood into the shape of a boat,
decorated with silks,
with people arranged inside,
carried along as they walked.
During Emperor Xuánzōng's time,
the Héxī military governor Yáng Jìngshù presented the 'Rainbow and Feather Garments Dance' music in twelve sections.
Usually, all pieces end abruptly,
but only the 'Rainbow and Feather Garments Dance' ends with a drawn-out, increasingly slow melody.
Popular legend had it
that the Emperor visited the Moon Palace,
saw several hundred white-robed maidens,
dancing in a vast courtyard,
the Emperor memorized the tune,
and upon returning composed the 'Rainbow and Feather Garments Dance' —
this is not true.
(At banquets) they would raise cups to offer longevity toasts;
the Emperor would have a hundred horses,
richly adorned,
divided into left and right groups,
with three-tiered platforms placed (on them),
and they would dance to the 'Tilted Cup' tune dozens of times;
strong men would lift the platforms,
and the horses would not move.
Liú Xù said: The Emperor, from within the palace,
would lead out thirty prancing horses,
to perform the 'Tilted Cup' music,
raising their heads and beating their tails,
moving horizontally and vertically in time with the rhythm.
He also placed three-tiered wooden beds,
mounted the horses onto them,
and they would turn and dance.
Some would bow,
some would dance.
Ān Lùshān saw this and was delighted by it.
After capturing Cháng'ān,
he ordered the search and capture of musicians,
the transport of musical instruments and dance costumes,
and drove the dancing horses, rhinoceroses, and elephants all to Luòyáng.
Your subject Guāng remarks: The sage considers virtue and morality as beauty,
benevolence and righteousness as joy;
therefore, even with thatched roofs and earthen steps,
coarse clothes and simple food,
he is not ashamed of their simplicity,
but only fears that excessive provisions might burden the people and waste resources.
Emperor Mínghuáng, relying on the peace of his reign,
gave no thought to future troubles,
exhausted himself with sensual pleasures,
pursued the ultimate in musical and artistic skills,
believing himself to surpass all emperors and kings in wealth and honor,
wanting to make it so that none before could match him,
and none after could surpass him,
not merely to amuse himself,
but also to boast to others.
How could he know that a great bandit was at his side,
already harboring covetous designs,
ultimately leading to the emperor's flight and exile,
and the people suffering extreme misery.
From this we know that when a ruler displays extravagant splendor to others,
it merely serves to attract great bandits.
37. Lùshān held a banquet for his ministers at the Níngbì Pond.
*The Six Codes of the Táng* states: Within the forbidden park of Luòyáng were the Fāngshù and Jīngǔ Pavilions,
and the Níngbì Pond.
The Líyuán disciples often sighed and wept,
(the Líyuán disciples are mentioned in scroll 211, the second year of the Kāiyuán era).
The musician Léi Hǎiqīng, unable to bear his grief and indignation,
threw his musical instrument to the ground,
and wailed facing west.
Lùshān was enraged,
had him bound in front of the Shìmǎ Hall,
and dismembered.
Lùshān heard that previously, many commoners had taken advantage of the chaos to loot the treasury.
After capturing Cháng'ān,
he ordered a massive three-day search,
and along with their private property, everything was plundered.
He also ordered the prefectures and counties to investigate and prosecute,
leaving no item, however small, unscrutinized,
involving and searching for people in connection,
the ramifications endless,
causing unrest among the people,
who increasingly longed for the Táng court.
After the emperor departed from Mǎwéi and headed north,
among the common people it was rumored that the Crown Prince had gone north to gather troops and would come to capture Cháng'ān.
The people of Cháng'ān looked forward to this day and night.
Sometimes they would startle each other, saying:
"The Crown Prince's great army has arrived!"
Then they would all flee,
leaving the markets and neighborhoods empty.
When the rebels saw dust rising in the north,
they would panic and want to flee.
Throughout the capital region, local heroes often killed rebel officials and officers,
responding from afar to the imperial army;
even when executed, they would rise again,
one after another without end,
and the rebels could not control them.
At first, from the capital region, Fū, Fāng, all the way to Qí and Lǒng, they all submitted to him.
By this time, outside the western gate, enemy fortifications were everywhere.
The western gate,
refers to the western gate of Cháng'ān city.
To the south, they did not venture beyond Wǔguān,
and to the north, not beyond Yúnyáng.
Yúnyáng County,
in the Han dynasty belonged to Féngyì,
in the Later Wei dynasty belonged to Běidì Commandery,
and from the Sui dynasty onward belonged to Jīngzhào.
Wǔgōng County,
in the Han and Jin dynasties belonged to Fúfēng,
in the Sui and Táng dynasties belonged to Jīngzhào.
Zhī,
means to go.
Shàngjīn,
in the Han dynasty was the territory of Chánglì County in Hànzhōng,
the Liáng dynasty established Nánluò Prefecture there,
the Later Wei dynasty changed it to Shàng Prefecture;
the Sui dynasty abolished the prefecture and made it Shàngjīn County,
in the Táng dynasty it belonged to Shāng Prefecture.
All this was due to the achievements of Xuē Jǐngxiān.
38 In the ninth month,
on the Rénzǐ day,
Shǐ Sīmíng besieged Zhào Commandery,
on the Bǐngchén day,
he captured it;
then besieged Chángshān,
after ten days,
the city fell,
and several thousand people were killed.
39 Prince Jiànníng, Lǐ Tán,
was by nature heroic and resolute,
and had talent and strategy.
Accompanying the emperor north from Mǎwéi,
their troops were few and weak,
and they frequently encountered bandits and rebels;
Tán personally selected the brave and valiant,
positioning them in front and behind the emperor,
fighting bloody battles to protect him.
If the emperor sometimes went past mealtime without eating,
Tán would weep bitterly, unable to control himself,
and all in the army would turn their eyes toward him.
The emperor wished to appoint Tán as the Grand Marshal of the Empire's Armed Forces,
to command the various generals on the eastern campaign.
Lǐ Bì said:
"Jiànníng is indeed a talent for the role of marshal;
however, Guǎngpíng,
is his elder brother.
If Jiànníng achieves success,
how could we make Guǎngpíng become like Wú Tàibó!"
The emperor said:
"Guǎngpíng,
is the primary heir.
Why must the position of marshal be considered so important!"
Bì said:
"Guǎngpíng has not yet been formally installed as Crown Prince.
Now, with the empire in difficulty,
what the hearts of the multitude turn to,
lies with the marshal.
If Jiànníng achieves great success,
even if Your Majesty wishes not to make him the heir apparent,
would those who shared in his achievements be willing to stop!
Tàizōng and the previous emperor,
are examples of this situation."
Meaning they both succeeded to the great succession due to their achievements in pacifying the empire.
The various generals all submitted to him.
Textual Analysis says: The Family Biography of the Marquis of Yè states:
"Appointed Lǐ Guāngbì as Left Wing Military Commander of the Marshal,
to march out Jǐngxíng,
to attack Chángshān,
and plan against Fànyáng.
Guō Zǐyí was appointed Right Wing Military Commander,
to lead the troops south to capture Féngyì and Hédōng."
According to the Family Biography of Fényáng,
at that time Guō Zǐyí was campaigning north against the Tóngluó,
and had not yet headed toward Hédōng.
The Family Biography of the Marquis of Yè also states:
"The emperor summoned Guāngbì and Zǐyí to discuss plans for the campaign,
the two men made delaying remarks.
The emperor was greatly angered,
his countenance changed as he rebuked them,
and both men fell to the ground,
unable to finish their words before being dismissed.
The emperor told the Duke: 'These two generals rose from junior officers,
within a year,
encountering the nation's crisis,
and I also ascended the throne here,
they thus reached the ranks of the Three Dukes, generals and ministers;
I see they already have an arrogant demeanor.
When discussing the campaign,
they wished to delay;
just now I rebuked them,
and they both fell down.
Just as we plan to recover the realm, the generals are already arrogant,
I am deeply worried about this.
I now entrust military affairs to you, sir.
When discussing matters in your headquarters,
you should demonstrate stern authority,
to make them know fear.'
He replied: 'If Your Majesty truly wishes to make them fear me,
the two have not yet seen Guǎngpíng.
I humbly hope you will order the Prince to also come temporarily to the headquarters.
When the two arrive,
as the weather is cold,
I will drink with them.
The two will certainly request an audience with the Prince,
I will then institute a drinking rule,
stipulating that they not rise.
When the Prince arrives,
we will merely talk and laugh,
and together with me put them at ease.
After the drinking ends,
then instruct them to pay their respects to the Marshal.
Thus, the two will see the Marshal, with the dignity of the emperor's son, humbly following my drinking rule,
and will understand that Your Majesty currently favors and trusts me,
that orders in the army must be obeyed,
and that if in the future they violate discipline,
I will have power over their life and death.'
The emperor praised this.
He further memorialized: 'I humbly hope you will speak to Guǎngpíng,
letting him know this is the imperial intention,
that we wish Lǐ and Guō to fear me,
not that I dare presume on favor to act thus.'
The emperor said: 'Between Guǎngpíng and you,
how could there be any formality!'
He replied: 'The imperial son, the heir to the state,
because of Your Majesty is close to me;
what kind of person am I,
how dare I not be apprehensive!'
The next day,
just before dawn,
the Prince also arrived.
When Lǐ and Guō arrived,
in full military attire,
paying their respects,
they then sat down to drink.
The two men mentioned they had not yet seen the Marshal,
so he sent word to the Prince.
As the Prince was about to arrive,
he held up a cup and set the rule,
that no one was permitted to rise.
When the Prince arrived,
the Duke (Lǐ Bì) said: 'We have just set a rule,
allowing the two ministers not to rise.'
The Prince said: 'This humble one dare not.'
He hastily took his seat to drink.
Lǐ and Guō changed color.
Talk and laughter were all joyful.
The Duke said: 'The two rose to give thanks.'
Guǎngpíng said: 'If you, sir, can treat the two ministers like this,
what more is there to worry about,
this humble one will also exert his full strength.
Now let us unite our hearts to accomplish the great plan for the ancestral temple and state,
to fulfill the imperial will.'
After they left,
Lǐ said to Guō: 'The drinking rule just now,
was not about military operations,
the intention was all from the emperor,
wishing to make us receive orders.'"
Analysis: Emperor Sùzōng was gentle and benevolent,
and the two dukes were steady and courageous.
There certainly was no incident of them being rebuked to their faces and falling to the ground.
This is not adopted here.
Thanking Bì, he said:
"This was indeed Tán's own wish!"
The Emperor and Lǐ Mì went out to inspect the army.
The soldiers pointed at them
and whispered among themselves:
"The one in yellow
is the Sage.
The one in white
is the Mountain Recluse."
The Emperor heard this
and told Lǐ Mì,
saying:
"In these difficult times,
I dare not force an official post upon you,
but you should at least wear a purple robe to dispel their doubts."
Lǐ Mì had no choice
but to accept it.
He put it on
and went in to thank the Emperor.
The Emperor laughed and said:
"Now that you are wearing this,
how can you be without a title!"
He took out an edict from his bosom,
appointing Lǐ Mì as Imperial Counselor for Military and State Affairs and Chief of Staff of the Marshal's Headquarters.
The position of Imperial Counselor was created specifically for Lǐ Mì.
The Emperor said:
"I do not presume to make you my minister,
but only to help us through these difficulties.
Once the rebels are pacified,
you may follow your lofty aspirations as you wish."
Lǐ Mì then accepted the appointment.
The Marshal's Headquarters was established within the palace precincts.
When Lǐ Chù entered, Lǐ Mì would be at the headquarters,
and when Lǐ Mì entered, Lǐ Chù would do likewise.
Lǐ Mì also said to the Emperor:
"The generals are in awe of Your Majesty's authority.
When they present military matters before Your Majesty,
they may not be able to fully express their thoughts.
If there is the slightest error,
the harm would be great.
I beg that you first order them to discuss matters thoroughly with me and Guǎngpíng,
and then I and Guǎngpíng will calmly report to you.
What is feasible can be implemented,
and what is not can be set aside."
The Emperor agreed.
At that time, military affairs were extremely busy,
with reports coming in from all directions.
From dusk till dawn, there was not a moment's respite.
The Emperor had them all sent to the headquarters.
Lǐ Mì would open and examine them first.
If there were urgent matters or beacon fire alerts,
he would reseal them
and have them passed through the gate for immediate submission,
while the rest would wait until morning.
The keys and tallies for the palace gates
were all entrusted to Lǐ Chù and Lǐ Mì to manage.
This sets the stage for Lǐ Mì's later request to return the keys and tallies.
40 Āshǐnà Cónglǐ persuaded and incited tens of thousands of Hu people from the Nine Surnames Prefecture and the Six Hu Prefectures,
gathering them north of the Jīnglüè Army.
At that time, the Hu people of the Nine Surnames all lived in the Héqū region,
and each still retained the names of their old prefectures.
According to the Old Book biography of Lǐ Jífǔ,
the Jīnglüè Army
was the Yòu Prefecture of the late Táng.
During the Tiānbǎo era, the Jīnglüè Army was moved inside the walls of Líng Prefecture,
and Yòu Prefecture was temporarily administered from the Jīnglüè Army.
In the ninth year of the Yuánhé era,
Yòu Prefecture was established at the old site of the Jīnglüè Army, comprising the Six Hu Prefectures,
and Yán'ēn County was established under its jurisdiction.
Sòng Bái said: The Jīnglüè Army
was located three hundred lǐ northwest of Xià Prefecture.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
Wáng Zhōngsì petitioned to establish an army at Yúduōlè City.
It now belongs to Língwǔ,
over six hundred lǐ from Língwǔ.
Shuì,
read as shuì.
The Emperor ordered Guō Zǐyí to go to the Tiāndé Army to mobilize troops to suppress them.
The Tiāndé Army was located at Dàtóng River.
In the twelfth year of Tiānbǎo, Ān Sīshùn petitioned to abolish the Héngsāi Army
and requested to build a city west of Dàtóng City to establish an army.
Emperor Xuánzong bestowed the name Tiān'ān Army;
after the Qiányuán era,
it was renamed Tiāndé Army.
It was two hundred lǐ southeast to the Middle Shòuxiáng Fortress,
crossing the river to the west,
one hundred and sixty lǐ to Fēng Prefecture,
one hundred and eighty lǐ west to the Western Shòuxiáng Fortress,
three hundred lǐ north to the desert pass,
and two hundred lǐ northwest to the Héngsāi Army.
Examination of discrepancies: The Family Biography of Fényáng states:
"Fifty thousand armored soldiers,
and five hundred thousand tribesmen."
We now follow the Old Book biography of Zǐyí.
The Family Biography of Fényáng also states:
"On the nineteenth day of the ninth month,
the imperial carriage was about to proceed to Péngyuán,
and the Duke was ordered to go to the Tiāndé Army
to attack the rebellious barbarians."
According to the Veritable Records,
"On Wùchén,
the imperial procession proceeded to Péngyuán."
Wùchén
was the seventeenth day.
The Fényáng biography is mistaken.
The army was defeated,
and they surrendered;
but later they fled back,
and Púgù Huái'ēn shouted at them and beheaded them.
The officers and soldiers trembled with fear,
and each fought like a hundred men,
thus defeating the Tóngluó.
Although the Emperor used the troops from Shuòfāng,
he wanted to borrow soldiers from foreign tribes to bolster his military strength.
He appointed Chéngcǎi, son of Bīn Prince Shǒulǐ, as the Prince of Dūnhuáng,
and sent him with Púgù Huái'ēn as envoys to the Huíhé to request troops.
He also mobilized troops from Báhánnà,
and had them relay messages to the various walled-city states,
as the northern barbarians were nomadic, following water and grass.
The various states of the Western Regions all had walled cities,
hence they were called the walled-city states.
They were to have the Ānxī troops come to aid.
Lǐ Mì advised the Emperor:
"For now, proceed to Péngyuán.
Wait until the northwestern troops are about to arrive,
then advance to Fúfēng to meet them.
By that time, the regular taxes and levies will also have been collected,
which can be used to supply the army."
The Emperor followed this advice.
On Wùchén,
they departed from Língwǔ.
41 The eunuch Biān Lìngchéng again escaped from the rebels and returned.
The Emperor had him executed.
42 On Bǐngzǐ,
the Emperor arrived at Shùnhuà.
The Emperor changed Ānhuà Commandery of Qìng Prefecture to Shùnhuà Commandery.
They presented the imperial seal and register,
but the Emperor refused to accept them,
saying:
"Recently, because the Central Plains were not yet pacified,
I temporarily took charge of all officials.
How dare I, in this perilous situation,
hastily proceed with the succession!"
The ministers insisted,
but the Emperor would not allow it.
He placed the seal and register in a separate hall,
attending to them morning and evening,
as if performing the rituals of evening reassurance and morning greeting.
The Book of Rites states: For all who are sons,
they provide reassurance in the evening and greet in the morning.
Fèngshàng,
read as fèngshàng.
Bǐ,
read as bǐ.
Shěng,
read as xǐng.
This matter is recorded in the thirteenth and fourteenth years of the Tiānbǎo era in the previous scroll.
He had long heard of Fáng Guǎn's reputation,
and treated him with an open mind.
When Fáng Guǎn met the Emperor and discussed current affairs,
his words were passionate and his sentiments fervent.
The Emperor's expression changed because of this,
and from then on, he often consulted Guǎn on military and state matters.
Guǎn also took the affairs of the world as his own responsibility,
doing everything he knew should be done;
the other chancellors merely stood by deferentially, avoiding him.
43 The Retired Emperor bestowed upon Consort Zhāng a saddle adorned with seven treasures.
Lǐ Mì said to the Emperor:
"Now that the empire is torn apart,
we should set an example of frugality for the people.
It is not fitting for the Consort to use this.
I request that the pearls and jade be removed and given to the treasury officials,
to be kept for rewarding those who achieve military merit."
The Consort spoke from within the chamber:
"We are old acquaintances from the same hometown,
how can you go this far!"
The Consort's maternal family was from Xīnfēng,
and Lǐ Mì resided in Jīngzhào,
hence she said this.
"The gentleman is acting for the sake of the state."
She immediately ordered it removed.
Prince Jiànníng, Lǐ Tán, wept in the corridor,
and his voice reached the Emperor.
The Emperor was startled,
summoned him, and asked him.
He replied:
"I have been constantly worried that the calamities and chaos would not cease.
Now that Your Majesty follows remonstrance as flowing water,
I will soon see Your Majesty welcome the Retired Emperor back to Cháng'ān.
That is why I am so overjoyed that I weep."
From then on, the Consort hated Lǐ Mì and Lǐ Tán.
This sets the stage for the Consort slandering Lǐ Tán to death
and Lǐ Mì feeling uneasy.
Wù,
read as wù;
the following wù is the same.
The Emperor once casually spoke with Lǐ Bì about Lǐ Línfǔ,
intending to issue an edict ordering the generals, after capturing Cháng'ān,
to open his tomb,
burn his bones, and scatter the ashes.
Lǐ Bì said:
"Your Majesty has just stabilized the empire;
why harbor enmity against the dead?
What does that dry bone know?
This would only show that Your Majesty's virtue is not magnanimous.
(Regarding Lǐ Línfǔ shaking the Crown Prince's position, see Volume 215, the fifth and sixth years of the Tiānbǎo era.)
Cóng,
read as qiān róng.
If they hear of this action,
I fear it will hinder their intention to reform themselves."
The Emperor was displeased and said:
"That traitor in the past used every means to endanger me.
At that time,
I could not guarantee my safety from morning to night.
That I survived
was solely due to heaven's favor!
Lǐ Línfǔ also hated you,
but he died before he could harm you.
Why show him pity!"
Lǐ Bì replied:
"How could I not know this!
The Supreme Emperor (Táng Xuánzōng) ruled the empire for nearly fifty years.
He enjoyed peace and pleasure.
Once he suffered disappointment,
he was sent far away to Bā-Shǔ.
The southern region is harsh.
The Supreme Emperor is advanced in years.
If he hears of Your Majesty's edict,
he will certainly think it is because of Wéi's affair.
(The deposition of the Wéi clan is also recorded in Volume 215, the fifth year of the Tiānbǎo era.)
If, by any chance, grief and indignation cause him to fall ill,
then Your Majesty, with the vastness of the empire, would be unable to bring peace to your father."
Before he finished speaking,
the Emperor, with tears streaming down his face,
descended the steps,
looked up to heaven, bowed, and said:
"I had not considered this.
It is heaven that made you, sir, speak of it!"
He then embraced Lǐ Bì's neck and wept incessantly.
On another evening,
the Emperor again said to Lǐ Bì:
"Liangdì's grandmother
was the younger sister of Empress Zhāochéng.
The Supreme Emperor cherished her.
When Xuánzōng was young, he lost Empress Zhāochéng.
He regarded Liangdì's grandmother as a mother,
and she nurtured him with deep affection and thorough care.
