and do not make it a priority."
Tán did not listen.
17. On the day Jiǎchén,
Prince Yǒng Lǐ Lín led his troops
on an eastern tour,
proceeding down the river,
with a very impressive military display,
yet still not revealing any plan to carve out a separate domain.
Lǐ Xīyán, Grand Administrator of Wú Commandery and concurrently Investigating Commissioner of the Jiāngnán Dōnglù circuit, sent an official dispatch to Lín,
questioning his intention in leading troops eastward.
Lín was angered,
and divided his forces, sending his general Hún Wéimíng to attack Xīyán in Wú Commandery,
and Jì Guǎngchēn to attack Lǐ Chéngshì, Chief Clerk of Guǎnglíng and Investigating Commissioner of Huáinán, in Guǎnglíng.
Lín advanced to Dāngtú.
Xīyán sent his general Yuán Jǐngyào and Grand Administrator of Dāntú Yán Jìngzhī to lead troops to resist him.
Present-day Dāngtú
was originally the territory of the Hàn dynasty's Dānyáng County.
The Jìn dynasty partitioned Dānyáng to establish Yúhú County.
Emperor Chéng, because refugees from the Dāngtú County north of the river were residing in Yúhú,
changed it to Dāngtú County,
and temporarily established the Huáinán Commandery there.
The Suí dynasty abolished Huáinán Commandery,
making the county belong to Dānyáng Commandery.
The Táng dynasty placed it under Xuānchéng Commandery.
Dāntú County was attached to Rùn Prefecture's Dānyáng Commandery.
The Táng dynasty never used Dāntú as a commandery name.
"Tú"
should be
"yáng".
Shǒu,
read as shì.
Lín attacked and beheaded Jìngzhī to warn others,
Jǐngyào and Chéngqìng both surrendered to Lín,
and the Jiāng and Huái regions were greatly shaken.
Gāo Shì met with Lái Tián and Wéi Zhì in Ānlù,
forming an alliance and swearing an oath with the masses to campaign against him.
Wéi Zhì was likely on his way to his post,
heard of the rebellion en route,
and thus met in Ānlù.
Xiáng,
read as xiáng.
Tián,
read as tiàn.
18. Shèng, King of Yútián, hearing that Ān Lùshān had rebelled,
ordered his younger brother Yào to administer state affairs,
and personally led five thousand troops to come to the aid.
The Emperor praised him,
appointed him Special Advance,
concurrently Palace Steward.
19. Líng Hú Cháo and Lǐ Tíngwàng attacked Yōngqiū,
but after several months could not take it.
They then established a prefecture
and built a city north of Yōngqiū
to cut off its grain supplies and reinforcements.
The rebels often numbered tens of thousands,
while Zhāng Xún's forces barely exceeded a thousand.
Yet in every battle, he was victorious.
The military governor of Hénán, Prince Guó Jù, was stationed at Péngchéng
and appointed Zhāng Xún as Vanguard Commander.
That month,
the commanderies of Lǔ, Dōngpíng, and Jìyīn fell to the rebels.
Péngchéng Commandery
was Xúzhōu.
Lǔ Commandery
was Yǎnzhōu.
Dōngpíng Commandery
was Yùnzhōu.
Jì
is pronounced zǐlǐ.
(Líng Hú Cháo and Lǐ Tíngwàng) planned to attack Nínglíng
to sever Zhāng Xún's rear.
Zhāng Xún therefore evacuated Yōngqiū
and moved east to defend Nínglíng to await them,
where he first met Xǔ Yuǎn, the Grand Administrator of Suīyáng.
That day,
Yáng Cháozōng arrived northwest of Nínglíng city.
Zhāng Xún and Xǔ Yuǎn engaged him in battle,
fighting several dozen engagements day and night.
They routed him utterly,
beheading over ten thousand,
with corpses floating down the Biàn River, blocking its flow.
The rebels gathered their troops and fled under cover of night.
An imperial edict appointed Zhāng Xún as Deputy Military Governor of Hénán.
As his officers and men had performed meritorious service,
Zhāng Xún sent an envoy to Prince Guó Jù to request blank commissions and rewards.
Jù only gave him thirty blank commissions for Zhéchōng and Guǒyì officers,
and did not give any rewards.
Zhāng Xún sent a letter reproaching Jù,
but Jù ultimately did not respond.
20. That year,
the Běihǎi Military Governorship was established,
overseeing four commanderies including Běihǎi;
it oversaw Běihǎi Commandery of Qīngzhōu,
Gāomì Commandery of Mìzhōu,
Dōngmóu Commandery of Dēngzhōu,
and Dōnglái Commandery of Láizhōu.
It oversaw three commanderies including Shàngdǎng;
it oversaw Shàngdǎng Commandery of Lùzhōu,
Chángpíng Commandery of Zézhōu,
and Yángchéng Commandery of Qìnzhōu.
It oversaw four commanderies including Shàngluò.
It oversaw Shàngluò Commandery of Shāngzhōu,
Ānkāng Commandery of Jīnzhōu,
and Fèngxiáng Commandery of Qízhōu.
The *Fāngzhèn Biǎo* only lists three commanderies;
the remaining one should be investigated.
In Méi County of Fèngxiáng Commandery, east of Yuán, there was originally an Xìngpíng Army,
which was then used to establish the military governorship.
21. Tibet captured the armies of Wēiróng, Shénwēi, Dìngróng, Xuānwēi, Zhìshèng, Jīntiān, Tiānchéng, and the cities of Shíbǎo, Bǎigǔ, and Diāokē.
The Dìngróng Army was north of Shíbǎo City,
separated by a ravine seven *li* away.
140 *li* southwest of Kuòzhōu were the Hóngjì Bridge and the Jīntiān Army;
80 *li* southeast of it was Bǎigǔ City.
80 *li* west of Hézhōu in Suǒgōngchuān was the Tiānchéng Army;
over a hundred *li* west was Diāokē City.
All were established in the 13th year of the Tiānbǎo era.
22. Earlier,
Fàn Zhēnlóng, the king of Línyì, was killed by his minister Móhē Mànduōjiā Dú,
who exterminated the entire Fàn clan.
According to the *New Book*,
this event occurred in the 19th year of the Zhēnguàn era.
It is recorded here to show the beginning of events.
Since the Jin dynasty,
the Fàn clan had held Línyì for generations,
and by this time, they were extinguished.
The people of the state established the daughter of their former king Tóulí as queen.
The woman could not govern the state,
so they instead established Zhūgě Dì, the son of Tóulí's paternal aunt,
calling him Huánwáng,
and married him to the queen.
Second Year
(Dīngyǒu, 757)
1. Spring,
first month,
the Retired Emperor issued an edict,
appointing Lǐ Lín, the Minister of Justice, as *Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì*,
to oversee all government offices.
He ordered Cuī Yuán to take the edict to Péngyuán.
Lǐ Lín
was a descendant of the Revered Ancestor.
The Revered Ancestor, Emperor Guāng,
personal name Tiānxī,
was the father of Tàizǔ.
Lǐ Lín
was a descendant of Qǐdòu, the second son of the Revered Ancestor.
2. Since starting his rebellion,
Ān Lùshān's eyesight had gradually deteriorated,
and by this time he could no longer see.
He also suffered from ulcers,
and his temper grew increasingly violent and irritable.
Those serving him
would, for the slightest dissatisfaction,
often be caned or whipped,
and sometimes killed.
After proclaiming himself emperor,
he remained secluded deep within the palace,
and his generals rarely saw his face,
all matters being reported through Yán Zhuāng.
Although Zhuāng was noble and wielded power,
he too could not avoid beatings.
The eunuch Lǐ Zhū'ér was beaten especially often.
The *Old Book* says: Lǐ Zhū'ér
came from a Qìdān tribe.
He served Lùshān from the age of ten or so,
and was very cunning and clever.
Lùshān personally took a blade and completely removed his genitals.
Blood spurted several *sheng*,
and he was near death.
Lùshān applied ash and fire to the wound,
and after a full day, he revived.
Thus becoming a eunuch,
he was subsequently trusted and employed.
Lùshān's favored concubine Duàn shì
bore a son, Qìng'ēn,
and (Lùshān) wished to replace Ān Qìngxù with him as heir.
Qìngxù constantly feared death,
not knowing what to do.
Zhuāng said to Qìngxù:
"There are matters that are unavoidable;
the opportunity must not be lost."
Qìngxù said:
"If elder brother has a plan,
I dare not respectfully comply?"
(Zhuāng) also said to Zhū'ér:
"The beatings you have received, front and back,
are they even countable?
If we do not undertake the great affair,
death is not far off!"
Zhū'ér also agreed.
Zhuāng and Qìngxù stood armed outside the tent at night,
while Zhū'ér took a knife and went straight into the tent,
slashing Lùshān's belly.
Those nearby were terrified,
and did not dare move.
Lùshān groped for the knife beside his pillow,
but could not find it.
The *Old Book* says: Lùshān could see nothing.
There was always a knife by his bedside.
He said:
"It must be a traitor from within the household."
His intestines had already spilled out several *dou*,
and he then died.
They dug several feet deep beneath the bed,
wrapped his corpse in felt, and buried it there,
warning those in the palace not to leak the news.
At dawn on the *yǐmǎo* day,
Zhuāng announced to the outside,
saying that Lùshān was critically ill.
They established Prince of Jin, Qìngxù, as Crown Prince,
and soon after he ascended the throne,
honoring Lùshān as Retired Emperor,
and only then issued the funeral announcement.
Qìngxù was dim-witted and cowardly,
and his speech was incoherent.
Zhuāng, fearing the multitude would not submit,
did not let him meet people.
Qìngxù daily indulged in wine and pleasure,
treating Zhuāng as an elder brother,
appointing him as Censor-in-Chief and Prince of Féngyì.
Matters great and small
were all decided by him;
he generously increased the official ranks and titles of the various generals to please their hearts.
3 The Emperor casually said to Lǐ Mì,
"Guǎngpíng has been the Commander-in-Chief for over a year.
Now I intend to appoint Jiànníng to lead the campaign exclusively,
but I fear it will divide the authority.
What if we establish Guǎngpíng as the Crown Prince?"
Lǐ Mì replied,
"I have already spoken of this before.
Military affairs are urgent and must be dealt with promptly;
but regarding family matters,
we should await the return of the Retired Emperor.
Otherwise,
how will future generations understand the intention behind Your Majesty's ascension to the throne at Língwǔ?
This must be someone trying to create a rift between me and Guǎngpíng.
I request to speak with Guǎngpíng about this;
I am sure he would not dare accept it."
Lǐ Mì went out
and told Guǎngpíng Prince Lǐ Chù.
Lǐ Chù said,
"This shows the gentleman truly understands my heart and wishes to subtly achieve what is best."
He then went in
and firmly declined,
saying,
"Your Majesty has not yet been able to serve the Retired Emperor morning and evening;
how could I dare accept the position of Crown Prince?
I wish to wait until the Retired Emperor returns to the palace;
that would be my good fortune."
The Emperor praised and comforted him.
Lǐ Fǔguó was originally a minor attendant in the Flying Dragon Stables.
All those serving in the stables, pastures, Five Offices, and imperial parks were called "minor attendants."
Lǐ Fǔguó, a eunuch slave, served as a minor attendant in the idle stables.
He served in the Crown Prince's palace,
and the Emperor trusted and relied on him.
Lǐ Fǔguó appeared outwardly respectful, cautious, and reticent but was inwardly cunning and treacherous.
Seeing that Zhāng Liángdì was favored,
he secretly attached himself to her,
and they collaborated closely.
Jiànníng Prince Lǐ Tán repeatedly denounced the misdeeds of these two before the Emperor.
The two slandered him to the Emperor, saying,
"Lǐ Tán resents not being made Commander-in-Chief."
(The Emperor did not appoint Lǐ Tán as Commander-in-Chief; see the previous volume, last year, ninth month.)
The Emperor was angered
and ordered Lǐ Tán to commit suicide.
The Textual Analysis states: The Family Biography of the Marquis of Yè says:
"After Emperor Sùzōng departed from Mǎwéi heading north,
he reached Tóngguān County
and ate at the home of the local magnate Lǐ Qiān.
Zhāng Liángdì claimed abdominal pain and could not ride a horse,
so she and her young daughter were left at Lǐ Qiān's home before they departed.
After the Emperor ascended the throne,
he sent someone to fetch them.
The messenger perhaps said something else,
and Jiànníng, hearing of it, repeatedly spoke out about it."
The Old Biography says:
"Lǐ Tán repeatedly said that Liángdì was quite domineering and willful,
and that she colluded with Hùguó (Fǔguó) internally and externally,
seeking to undermine the Crown Prince."
It is unclear which account is accurate.
The Veritable Records and the Old and New Tang Histories' Basic Annals do not record the year or month of Lǐ Tán's death.
The Biographies state:
"After Lǐ Tán died,
the following winter,
Guǎngpíng Prince recovered the two capitals."
Thus, Lǐ Tán died in the first year of Zhìdé.
According to the Family Biography of the Marquis of Yè:
"The Emperor casually said, 'Guǎngpíng has been Commander-in-Chief for a year;
now I intend to appoint Jiànníng as Commander-in-Chief.'"
This indicates Lǐ Tán was still alive in the second year of Zhìdé.
It also states:
"Emperor Dàizōng sent someone from Péngyuán to retrieve Lǐ Tán's remains."
Therefore, it is placed here.
"Hùguó"
should be
"Fǔguó."
Lǐ Chù plotted to remove Lǐ Fǔguó and Liángdì.
Lǐ Mì said,
"That cannot be done.
Has the Prince not seen the disaster that befell Jiànníng?"
Lǐ Chù said,
"I am secretly worried for you, sir."
Lǐ Mì said,
"I have an agreement with the Sovereign.
(The Emperor promised Lǐ Mì that after the rebels were pacified, he would be free to pursue his lofty aspirations. See the previous volume, last year, ninth month.)
Once I leave and return to the mountains,
I will likely avoid such troubles."
Lǐ Chù said,
"If you leave, sir, then I will be in even greater danger."
Lǐ Mì said,
"The Prince should simply fulfill his filial duties as a son.
Liángdì is a woman;
if the Prince handles her with tact and deference,
what can she really do?"
In my view, the reason Emperor Dàizōng ultimately avoided disaster from Empress Zhāng was because he followed Lǐ Mì's advice.
4 The Emperor said to Lǐ Mì,
"Now Guō Zǐyí and Lǐ Guāngbì are already Chancellors.
If they recapture the two capitals and pacify the realm,
there will be no official positions left to reward them with.
What should be done?"
Lǐ Mì replied,
"In ancient times, official positions were for appointing the capable,
and noble ranks were for rewarding merit.
Since the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
although commanderies and counties were used to govern the people,
those with merit were still enfeoffed with land,
to be passed on to their descendants.
This continued through the Zhōu and Suí dynasties.
In the early Táng,
as they had not yet gained control east of the passes,
noble titles were merely nominal,
and those receiving actual fiefs were given only silk and cloth.
(Táng system: For those receiving actual fiefs, each household provided the annual tax of one adult male.)
Emperor Tàizōng wished to restore the ancient system,
but discussions among the high ministers differed, and it was not done. (See scroll 195, the thirteenth year of Zhēnguān.)
Using official positions to reward merit has two harms:
if the recipient lacks talent, affairs are neglected;
if their power is great, they become difficult to control.
Therefore, meritorious officials who hold high positions
do not make long-term plans for their descendants,
but instead seize the momentary power to seek profit,
stopping at nothing.
If Ān Lùshān had possessed a domain of a hundred *lǐ*,
he would have cherished it to pass on to his descendants
and would not have rebelled.
For the present strategy,
once the realm is pacified,
nothing would be better than to grant noble titles and land to reward meritorious officials.
Even the largest fief would be no more than two or three hundred *lǐ*,
comparable to a small commandery today—how difficult would that be to control?
For the subjects, it would be a benefit for ten thousand generations."
The Emperor said,
"Excellent!"
5 The Emperor heard that troops from Ānxī, Běitíng, Báhánnà, Dàshí, and other states had reached Liángzhōu and Shànzhōu.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
he went to Bǎodìng. (Bǎodìng Commandery was originally Āndìng Commandery of Jīngzhōu; the commandery name was changed last year. Shàn is pronounced shàn, also pronounced shízhàn.)
6 On the day Bǐngyín,
Jiǎ Xiù and five thousand soldiers from Jiànnán plotted rebellion.
General Xí Yuánqìng and Línqióng Prefect Liǔ Yì attacked and executed them. (Línqióng Commandery was Qiōngzhōu. Qiōng is pronounced qúróng. Prefect is pronounced shìyòu.)
7 Héxī Army Commander Gài Tínglún
and Wǔwēi merchant Hú Ānménwù of the Nine Surnames killed Military Governor Zhōu Mì,

gathering a crowd of sixty thousand. (Within the great city of Wǔwēi, there were seven smaller cities. Wǔwēi Commandery was Liángzhōu, governing Gūzāng. The old city was built by the Xiōngnú, seven *lǐ* north-south and three *lǐ* east-west. When the Zhāng family held Héxī, they added four more cities, each enclosure a thousand paces, making five together with the old city. It is unknown who built the remaining two cities.)
They held two cities firmly.
Fiscal Manager Cuī Chēng and Palace Eunuch Liú Rìxīn used troops from the two cities to attack them,
and after seventeen days,
pacified them.
8. Shǐ Sīmíng from Bólíng,
Cài Xīdé from Tàiháng,
Gāo Xiùyán from Dàtóng,
and Niú Tíngjiè from Fànyáng,
led a combined force of one hundred thousand troops
to invade Tàiyuán.
Lǐ Guāngbì’s elite soldiers had all been sent to Shuòfāng,
leaving only hastily assembled, untrained troops numbering less than ten thousand.
Sīmíng believed Tàiyuán could be taken as easily as pointing at his palm,
and that once captured,
he would then drive straight on to seize Shuòfāng, Hézhōng, and Lǒngyòu.
The various generals in Tàiyuán were all afraid,
and proposed repairing the city walls to await the enemy.
Guāngbì said:
“The perimeter of Tàiyuán city is forty lǐ.
Tàiyuán’s capital city,
with the Fén River on the left and Jìn on the right,
and Qiánqiū Hill in the center,
measures four thousand three hundred twenty-one bù in length,
two thousand one hundred twenty-two bù in width,
with a perimeter of fifteen thousand one hundred fifty-three bù.
The palace city is northwest of the capital city,
with a perimeter of two thousand five hundred twenty bù.
East of the Fén River is called the Eastern City,
built in the eleventh year of the Zhēnguàn era by Chief Secretary Lǐ Jì.
Between the two cities is called the Central City,
built by Empress Wǔ.
The statement that combining with the Eastern City makes a perimeter of forty lǐ
refers only to the capital city.
This would be exhausting ourselves before even seeing the enemy.”
He then led soldiers and civilians to dig moats outside the city to fortify themselves.
They made several hundred thousand adobe bricks,
and no one knew what they were for;
when the bandits attacked the city from outside,
Guāngbì used them to reinforce the inner walls,
repairing any damage immediately.
Sīmíng sent men to fetch siege equipment from Shāndōng,
guarded by three thousand Hu soldiers for escort.
When they reached Guǎngyáng,
Guǎngyáng,
was Shàng’ài County in the Hàn dynasty,
renamed Shí’ài County in the Later Hàn,
and given its current name in the first year of the Tiānbǎo era,
belonging to Tàiyuán Prefecture.
Jǐngxíng Pass lies to its east,
and Wěizé Pass to its northeast,
both being routes to Shāndōng.
[Guāngbì’s men] killed them all.
Sīmíng besieged Tàiyuán
for over a month without capturing it,
so he selected swift and fierce troops as mobile units,
instructing them:
“When I attack the north, you secretly rush to the south;
attack east, then rush west;
exploit any gap you find.”
But Guāngbì’s army was strictly disciplined,
and even where the enemy did not reach,
sentry patrols never slackened,
so the bandits could not enter.
Guāngbì recruited within the army,
and anyone with even a minor skill
was selected,
assigned according to ability,
so everyone was put to use.
He obtained three mint workers from Ānbiān Army,
skilled at digging tunnels.
Ānbiān Army was in Xìngtáng County of Yùzhōu.
Yùzhōu had copper smelters,
and mint officials,
hence there were mint workers,
and at that time he obtained three of them.
Guāngbì sent men through tunnels to grab the enemy by their feet and pull them in,
then beheaded them at the city wall.
From then on, the bandits watched the ground as they walked.
The bandits used scaling ladders, rams, and earthen mounds to attack the city,
and Guāngbì dug tunnels to meet them,
causing them to collapse near the walls.
Initially, when the bandits pressed the city urgently,
Guāngbì built large catapults,
hurling huge stones,
each shot killing over twenty men.
With two or three out of ten bandits dead,
they withdrew and camped several dozen paces away,
beyond the range of the catapults.
Catapult,
pronounced pǐ mào fān.
Guāngbì sent men to feign an agreement with the bandits,
setting a date to surrender,
making the bandits happy
and unprepared.
Guāngbì had tunnels dug all around the bandit camp,
propped up with wood.
When the time came,
Guāngbì arrayed troops on the city walls,
and sent a deputy general leading several thousand men out,
as if surrendering,
drawing the bandits’ full attention.
Suddenly the ground in the camp collapsed,
killing over a thousand men.
The bandits panicked and fell into chaos,
and the government troops raised a clamor and attacked,
capturing and killing tens of thousands.
Meanwhile, Ān Lùshān died,
and Qìngxù ordered Sīmíng to return and guard Fànyáng,
leaving Cài Xīdé and others to besiege Tàiyuán.
9. Qìngxù appointed Yǐn Zǐqí as Prefect of Biànzhōu and Military Governor of Hénán.
On Jiǎxū,
Zǐqí led Guī, Tán, Tóngluó, and Xī troops totaling one hundred thirty thousand toward Suīyáng.
Guī,
should be Guī,
meaning Guīzhōu.
Various unofficial histories of the Táng often write Guī and Tán,
which is an error.
Toward,
pronounced qī yù fān.
Suī,
pronounced suī.
Xún led troops from Nínglíng into Suīyáng.
From Nínglíng east to Suīyáng is forty-five lǐ.
Combined with Yuǎn’s troops, they totaled six thousand eight hundred men.
The bandits pressed the city with their full force,
and Xún urged and encouraged the officers and soldiers,
fighting bitterly day and night,
sometimes up to twenty engagements in a single day.
Over sixteen days,
they captured over sixty enemy generals,
killed over twenty thousand soldiers,
and the troops’ morale doubled.
Yuǎn said to Xún:
“I, Yuǎn, am timid
and unskilled in warfare,
while you, sir, possess both wisdom and courage.
I ask to handle defense for you, sir,
and you, sir, please do the fighting for me.”
From then on,
Yuǎn only managed military provisions,
repaired weapons,
and handled internal coordination,
while all battle planning came from Xún.
The bandits then fled by night.
10. Guō Zǐyí considered Hédōng as lying between the two capitals,
and that capturing Hédōng would allow planning against both capitals.
Hédōng Commandery,
is Púzhōu.
Advancing from Hédōng to attack and capture Tóngguān
would cut the route between the two capitals,
after which they could be taken.
On Dīngchǒu,
Zǐyí secretly sent men into Hédōng
to conspire with Táng officials who had surrendered to the bandits,
waiting for the government army to arrive
to act as an internal response.
11. Earlier,
Liú Zhèngchén, Military Governor of Pínglú, was defeated and returned from Fànyáng,
as seen in the previous volume last year.
Lùshān appointed his follower Xú Guīdào as Military Governor of Pínglú,
and Xuánzhì again joined with Pínglú general Hóu Xīyì to attack and kill him;
he also sent military commander Dǒng Qín to lead troops crossing the sea on reed rafts,
joining with senior general Tián Shéngōng to attack Píngyuán and Lè’ān,
capturing them.
Lǐ Xiǎn, the Anti-Riverbandit Recruitment Commissioner, acting under imperial authority, appointed Qín as Grand Administrator of Píngyuán.
12. In the second month,
on Wùzǐ,
the Emperor arrived at Fèngxiáng.
13. Guō Zǐyí led troops from Luòjiāo towards Hédōng.
Sòng Bái said: Luòjiāo Commandery of Fūzhōu,
was the territory of Diāoyīn in the Upper Commandery of the Hàn dynasty.
In the Later Wèi, it was Dōng Qínzhōu,
later changed to Běi Huázhōu.
Emperor Fèi changed it to Fūzhōu,
taking the name from Fūzhì.
In the Suí dynasty, the seat was moved from Xìngchéng to Wǔjiāochéng.
In the Tiānbǎo era, it was changed to Luòjiāo Commandery,
governing Luòjiāo County,
named after the confluence of the Luò River.
Qù,
qī yù fān.
Féngyì Commandery,
Tóngzhōu.
By taking both Pú and Tóng,
one could straddle Hédōng and Héxī,
to plan for Guān and Shǎn,
and thus control the rebels.
Jǐchǒu,
Hán Mín, the Registrar of Hédōng, and others turned the city of Hédōng to welcome the imperial army.
New Records: The Registrar of the Household Section,

32 General Wáng Qùróng, due to a personal grudge, killed the magistrate of his own county.
He deserved death.
Wáng Qùróng
was a man of Fùpíng.
On the Rénchén day,
an imperial decree pardoned him from death,
ordering him to serve as a commoner in Shǎn Commandery.
At that time, Shǎn Commandery had just been recovered,
situated between the two capitals,
a place the rebels were certain to attack.
The Emperor wished to spare Qùróng's life and utilize his strength,
without considering that this would undermine the laws of the state.
Textual analysis notes: The Veritable Records says:
"To serve in the Chéngtiān Army in Hédōng."
According to the collected works of Jiǎ Zhì,
it was Shǎn Commandery.
We follow this now.
A memorial was submitted,
arguing:
"Qùróng acted without propriety,
killing the ruler of his own county.
The Yì Jīng says: 'When a minister kills his ruler,
or a son kills his father,
it is not due to causes of a single morning or evening;
that by which it comes about is gradual.'
This is the text of the Wén Yán commentary on the Kūn hexagram of the Yì Jīng.
One can say his nature developed gradually.
Those who discuss this say that Shǎn Commandery has just been recovered,
and without such a man it cannot be held.
But if that is so, how is it that other places without a Qùróng
were also able to hold firm?
If Your Majesty, for the single skill of operating catapults, immediately exempts someone from capital punishment,
then among the various armies today, those whose skills are peerless
are truly numerous.
They will surely rely on their abilities
to commit offenses against their superiors wherever they are;
how then can this be stopped!
If you only spare Qùróng and execute the others,
then the laws and commands are not uniform, and you entice people to commit crimes.
Now, if you cherish the talent of one Qùróng and do not kill him,
you will surely have to kill ten others with talent like Qùróng's.
Would not the harm then be even greater!
This Qùróng
is a man of rebellion and disorder.
How can one be rebellious here and compliant there,
disorderly in Fùpíng yet orderly in Shǎn Commandery,
treacherous towards a county magistrate yet not treacherous towards the great sovereign!
I humbly beg the enlightened ruler to consider the far-reaching and major principles in their entirety;
then calamity and disorder will be settled before many days pass."
The Emperor sent the matter down,
ordering all officials to deliberate on it.
The Grand Preceptor of the Heir Apparent, Wéi Jiànsù, and others deliberated,
believing:
"The law is the great code of heaven and earth,
and even the emperor dares not act arbitrarily in killing.
This is
a case where the power of a subject surpasses that of the sovereign.
If Qù Róng, having killed a person, does not face death,
then all those in the army with skills
will also consider themselves without worry,
and violence and tyranny will occur everywhere.
For those governing commanderies and counties,
would it not be difficult indeed!
Your Majesty is the ruler of the realm,
and your love should be without partiality between close and distant.
To gain one Qù Róng but lose the myriad people—
what benefit is there in that!
According to the statutes,
killing the magistrate of one's own county
is listed among the Ten Abominations.
In the early Táng,
Fáng Xuánlíng, following the Suì-established laws,
had the articles of the Ten Abominations: first, plotting rebellion;
second, plotting great sedition;
third, plotting treason;
fourth, plotting wicked sedition;
fifth, inhumanity;
sixth, great irreverence;
seventh, unfiliality;
eighth, discord;
ninth, unrighteousness;
tenth, internal disorder.
Those who commit the Ten Abominations
cannot rely on the precedents for deliberation and petition.
The article on unrighteousness
notes: it refers to killing one's own prefect, regional inspector, or county magistrate;
killing one's current teacher;
officials or soldiers killing a superior official of the fifth rank or above within their own department;
and upon hearing of a husband's death concealing it and not observing mourning,
or making music, removing mourning garments for auspicious occasions, or remarrying.
If the king's law is not implemented,
the principles of human relations will be compromised.
We, your subjects, having received the edict,
do not know what to follow.
The state is governed by law,
the army triumphs by law;
having kindness without authority,
even a loving mother cannot control her son.
Your Majesty richly supports the warriors, yet in every battle there is little advantage—
is it not because there is no law!
Now, although Shǎn Commandery is crucial,
it is not more urgent than the law.
With law, there is no worry within the seas that cannot be overcome,
let alone Shǎn Commandery!
Without law, even Shǎn Commandery cannot be held,
what benefit is there in gaining it!
Moreover, Qù Róng's minor skill
does not determine the survival or fall of Shǎn Commandery;
the presence or absence of the king's law
is what makes the state light or heavy.
This is why we, your subjects, earnestly wish Your Majesty to uphold the laws of the Zhēnguàn era."
The emperor ultimately spared him.
Zhì
was the son of Jiǎ Zēng.
Jiǎ Zēng appears in the two hundred and tenth scroll, first year of the Xiāntiān era.

the seventh month,

36 On Rénzǐ,
Yǐn Zǐqí again levied tens of thousands of troops,
attacking Suīyáng.
Previously,
Xǔ Yuǎn had stored up to sixty thousand dàn of grain in the city,
but the Prince of Guó, Jù, gave half of it to the two commanderies of Púyáng and Jìyīn.
Yuǎn firmly contested this,
but could not prevent it;
afterward, Jìyīn obtained the grain,
and then rebelled with the city,
so that by this time Suīyáng's food was exhausted.
The officers and men received a daily ration of one ge of rice per person,
mixed with tea leaves, paper, and tree bark for food,
while the rebel grain transport was unobstructed,
and troops were levied again after defeats.
The Suīyáng officers and men who died were not replaced,
and supplies and reinforcements from other armies did not arrive,
until the soldiers were reduced to sixteen hundred men,
all starving and sick, unable to fight,
and thus were besieged by the rebels.
Zhāng Xún then repaired the defensive equipment to resist them.
The rebels made cloud ladders,
shaped like half a rainbow.
Dù Yòu said: using large timber as a base,
with six wheels placed underneath,
and two upright posts on top,
the posts having rung ladders,
each section twelve feet long,
with four crosspieces,
the crosspieces spaced four feet apart,
slightly angled to interlock with each other,
flying among the clouds to spy into the city.
There were ladders for ascending the city wall,
the top crowned with double pulleys,
leaning against the wall to ascend,
called flying cloud ladders.
Pushed against the city wall,
they were intended to enable a leap inside.
Xún prepared by boring three holes in the wall,
and when the ladder was about to arrive,
from one hole he extended a large timber,
with an iron hook at the end,
hooking it to prevent retreat;
from one hole he extended a timber,
propping it to prevent advance;
from one hole he extended a timber,
with an iron cage at the end,
filled with fire to burn it,
so the ladder broke in the middle,
and the soldiers on the ladder were all burned to death.
The rebels also used hook carts to hook the wall sheds and pavilions,
the wall sheds being
wooden frames erected on the wall,
projecting four or five feet outside the wall,
with roofed structures on top,
to shelter from wind and rain,
where soldiers resided,
to face and resist external enemies,
what people today call enemy towers.
None did not collapse.
Xún used large timbers,
with chains attached at the end,
and large rings at the end of the chains,
to cover the hook heads,
and with leather-covered carts pulled them into the city,
cut off the hook heads, and released the carts to depart.
The rebels also made wooden donkeys to attack the city,
Xún melted metal and poured it on them,
and they melted upon impact.
The rebels also piled earth bags and firewood at the northwest corner of the city to make a stepped path,
intending to ascend the wall.
Xún did not contend with them for advantage,
but each night,
secretly threw pine torches and dry straw among them.
Pine torches are
pine that has dried but retains resin,
which can be burned to provide light.
Dry,
pronounced gān.
The rebels did not notice,
and then he sent troops out for a major battle,
having men hold fire and burn it with the wind,
so the rebels could not save it,
and after over twenty days,
the fire finally extinguished.
What Xún did
was all responded to with immediate solutions,
and the rebels admired his wisdom,
not daring to attack again.
They then dug three layers of moats outside the city,
erected wooden palisades to guard against Xún,
and Xún also made moats inside to resist them.
37 On Dīngsì,
the rebel general Ān Wǔchén attacked Shǎn Commandery,
Yáng Wùqīn died in battle,

With a solitary city situated between powerful bandits,

38 Cuī Huàn, in selecting and appointing officials south of the Yangtze,

Háng Prefecture,

The Suí established Háng Prefecture at Yúháng County,

40. The Prefect of Língchāng, Xǔ Shūjì, was besieged by the rebels,

he led his troops and fled to Péngchéng.
Examination of Discrepancies states: The Veritable Records say:
"He led his troops south to join the Suīyáng Commandery."
According to the Biography of Vice-Director Zhāng:

It seems Shūjì intended to join Suīyáng,

41. The remaining soldiers in Suīyáng, after casualties,
numbered only six hundred men.
Zhāng Xún and Xǔ Yuǎn divided the city to defend it,
with Xún guarding the northeast
and Yuǎn the southwest.
They ate the same tea and paper as the soldiers,
and never left the city walls.
When rebel soldiers attacked the city,
Xún would persuade them with arguments of loyalty and rebellion,
and they often abandoned the rebels to surrender,
fighting to the death for Xún,
totaling over two hundred men before and after.
At this time,
Xǔ Shūjì was in the Qiáo Commandery,
Shàng Héng was in Péngchéng,
and Hèlán Jìnmíng was in Línhuái.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn established Línhuái Commandery,
Emperor Míng of Later Hàn renamed it Xiàpī,
its territory was vast.
Liáng established Gāopíng Commandery on the land of the Hàn Xú County,
in the 18th year of the Suí Kāihuáng era,
the commandery was abolished and became Xúchéng County,
belonging to the Sìzhōu Xiàpī Commandery,
at that time Sìzhōu was administered from Sùyù.
In the 4th year of Empress Wǔ's Cháng'ān era,
the two southern districts of Xúchéng County were carved out,
and Línhuái County was established at Sháshú and Huáikǒu.
In the 23rd year of the Kāiyuán era,
Sìzhōu's administration was moved to Línhuái;
in the 1st year of the Tiānbǎo era,
it was renamed Línhuái Commandery.
As the city's situation grew more desperate by the day,
Xún then ordered Nán Jìyún to lead thirty cavalry to break through the siege and go out,
to urgently seek help from Línhuái.
Jìyún left the city,
and tens of thousands of rebels blocked him,
but Jìyún charged straight through their ranks,
shooting left and right as he galloped,
the rebel ranks scattered,
and he lost only two cavalrymen.
Upon reaching Línhuái,
he met Jìnmíng.
Jìnmíng said:
"Today, whether Suīyáng survives or falls is unknown,
what good would sending troops do!"
Jìyún said:
"If Suīyáng falls,
Jìyún begs to atone with his death before you, Grand Master.
Moreover, if Suīyáng is taken,
Línhuái will be next,
like fur depending on skin,
how can you not rescue it!"
Jìnmíng admired Jìyún's bravery and strength,
but did not heed his words,
instead forcefully detaining him,
prepared food and music,
and invited Jìyún to sit.
Jìyún, impassioned,
wept and said:
"When Jìyún came,
the people of Suīyáng had not eaten for over a month!
Even if Jìyún wished to eat alone,
he could not swallow it.
You, Grand Master, sit here with strong troops,
watching Suīyáng fall,
without the slightest intention to share its calamity and rescue it from disaster,
is this the behavior of a loyal minister and righteous man!"
Thereupon he bit off one of his fingers to show Jìnmíng,
Examination of Discrepancies states: Hán Yù's Postscript to the Biography of Vice-Director Zhāng says:

Those present often wept.
Jìyún observed that Jìnmíng ultimately had no intention to send troops,

Reaching Nínglíng,
he joined the City Commandant Lián Tǎn, and together they led three thousand infantry and cavalry.
Zhāng Xún had entered Suīyáng from Nínglíng,
likely having appointed Lián Tǎn to guard Nínglíng city.
City Commandant,
appointed by Xún.
To lead,
pronounced liàng.
Commandant,
pronounced shǐ.
On the night of Wùshēn,
they braved the encirclement,
fighting and advancing,
until they reached the city walls,

The officers and officials in the city, knowing there was no rescue,

The rebels, knowing aid was cut off,
besieged them even more fiercely.
Initially,
when Fáng Guǎn was chancellor,
he disliked Hèlán Jìnmíng,
the matter is seen in the tenth month of last year.
To dislike,
pronounced wù.
He appointed Xǔ Shūjì as Jìnmíng's Chief Commander of Troops and Horses,
both concurrently holding the title of Censor-in-chief.
Shūjì, relying on the elite troops under his command,
and his rank being equal to Jìnmíng's,
did not accept his command.
Therefore, Jìnmíng did not dare to divide his troops,

The history states that Fáng Guǎn, due to personal grievance against Jìnmíng,

1 In the ninth month, on
Dīngchǒu,
Cài Xīdé arrived at the city walls with light cavalry to issue a challenge.
Chéng Qiānlǐ led a hundred horsemen, opened the gates, and charged out,
intending to capture him.
However, enemy reinforcements arrived,
and he gathered his cavalry and retreated.
The bridge broke,
and he fell into the moat,
instead being captured by Xīdé.
A commander
must not rely on courage and act rashly.
Chéng Qiānlǐ wanted to capture Cài Xīdé
but was instead captured by Xīdé—
this is the disaster of relying on courage and acting rashly.
Cavalry (qí)
is pronounced like "qí jì".
To challenge (tiǎo)
is pronounced "tú liǎo".
To lead (shuài)
is read as "shuài".
"My misfortune in coming to this point
is Heaven's will!
Go back and tell the generals:
defend well,
it is better to lose the commander
than to lose the city."
Xīdé attacked the city
but ultimately could not take it.

where Ān Qìngxù appointed him as Tèjìn
and imprisoned him in the guest quarters.
2 Guō Zǐyí, considering the Huíhé troops elite,
advised the Emperor to further summon their soldiers to attack the rebels.
Huáirén Kèhán sent his son Yèhù and General Dìdé and others, leading over four thousand elite troops, to Fèngxiáng.
The Emperor received Yèhù in audience,
feasted, rewarded, and bestowed gifts upon him,
granting whatever he desired.
On Dīnghài,
Marshal Guǎngpíng Prince Lǐ Chù led the Shuòfāng army and others, along with Huíhé and Western Regions troops, totaling one hundred fifty thousand men,
claiming two hundred thousand,
and set out from Fèngxiáng.
Chù met Yèhù,
and they swore to be brothers.
Yèhù was greatly pleased
and addressed Chù as elder brother.
When the Huíhé reached Fúfēng,
Guō Zǐyí hosted a feast for three days.
Yèhù said:
"The state is in crisis,
we have come from afar to assist.
What need is there for feasting!"
After the feast concluded,
they immediately departed.
Each day, their army was supplied with two hundred sheep,
twenty oxen,
and forty hú of rice.
On Gēngzǐ,
all armies set out together.
On Rényín,
they reached the west of Cháng'ān
and deployed east of the Fēng River, north of Xiāngjī Temple.
This was all land of the Hàn dynasty's Shànglín Park.
The Geographical Treatise states: The Fēng River
originates from Fēng Valley south of Hù,
flows north past the southeast of Hàn Lóngtái Observatory,
and meets the Wèi River at Duǎnyīn Mountain.
Chéng Dàchāng said: Xiāngjī Temple,
according to Lǚ's map, is directly north and slightly west of Zǐwǔ Valley.
When Guō Zǐyí recovered Cháng'ān,
he deployed north of the temple,
near the Fēng River,
facing the great river.
The great river refers to
Shěn River and Jiāo River,
which is the Táng dynasty's Yǒng'ān Canal.
Thus, the temple is east of the Fēng River
and west of the Jiāo River.
Lǚ's map states it is north of the source of the Hào River,
then it is near Kūnmíng Pond.
Zǐyí had previously been defeated at Qīngqú.
Arriving here, he followed the southern mountains to emerge behind the capital,
seizing the terrain to await the enemy.
Deploy (chén)
is read as "zhèn";
the same applies below for "deployed at", "their deployment", "at the deployment", "the deployment then", and "rebel deployment".
Guō Zǐyí commanded the central army,
Wáng Sīlǐ commanded the rear army.
The rebel forces, one hundred thousand strong, deployed to their north.
Lǐ Guīrén came out to challenge,
the government troops pursued him,
pressing close to their deployment.
The rebel army advanced together,
the government troops retreated,
were exploited by the rebels,
and panic and disorder spread in the army.
The rebels rushed to seize the baggage train.
Lǐ Sìyè said:
"If we do not use ourselves as bait for the enemy today,
not a single man in the army will survive."
He then bared his torso, grasped a long sword,
and stood before the deployment,
shouting loudly and fighting fiercely.
Those struck by his blade
—men and horses alike—were shattered,
and he killed several dozen men.
The deployment then gradually stabilized.
Thereupon, Sìyè led the forward army, each man grasping a long sword,
advancing like a wall,
leading the charge personally,
crushing all in their path.
The Army Commander-in-Chief Wáng Nándé went to rescue his subordinate officer.
Wáng Nándé was the Fèngxiáng Army Commander-in-Chief;
at that time, the Emperor was in Fèngxiáng,
so he was likely a senior general of the imperial guard.
An arrow pierced his eyelid.
Nándé pulled out the arrow himself,
tearing away the skin,
blood streaming down his face,
yet he fought on without cease.
The rebels had hidden elite cavalry east of their deployment,
intending to attack the government troops from behind.
Scouts learned of this,
and Shuòfāng Left Wing Army Commander Púgù Huái'ēn led the Huíhé to attack them,
cutting them down almost entirely.
The rebels' morale plummeted as a result.
Lǐ Sìyè again led the Huíhé around behind the rebel deployment,
attacking together with the main army in a pincer movement.
From noon until dusk,
sixty thousand heads were taken,
and many more died filling the ditches and moats.
The rebels then suffered a great rout.
The remaining forces fled into the city.
As night fell,
the clamor did not cease.
Púgù Huái'ēn said to Guǎngpíng Prince Lǐ Chù:
"The rebels have abandoned the city and fled.
I request to pursue them with two hundred cavalry
and capture Ān Shǒuzhōng and Lǐ Guīrén."
Chù said:
"General, you must be weary from battle.
Rest for now,
and we will plan for tomorrow morning."
Huái'ēn said:
"Guīrén and Shǒuzhōng
are the rebels' fiercest generals.
Victorious one moment, defeated the next—
this is Heaven's gift to us.
How can we let them go!
If they regain their followers,
they will return to trouble us.
Regret will be too late then!
In war, speed is divine.
Why wait for tomorrow morning!"
Meaning, what use is waiting for tomorrow morning.
He was sent back to camp.
Huái'ēn insisted on his request,
going and returning,
four or five times in one night.
At dawn,
scouts arrived,
reporting that Shǒuzhōng, Guīrén, along with Zhāng Tōngrú and Tián Qiánzhēn, had all fled.
Had Guǎngpíng Prince heeded Púgù Huái'ēn's advice,
he certainly would not have needed the battle at Xīndiàn,
and could have directly taken the Eastern Capital.
On Guǐmǎo,
the great army entered the Western Capital.
初，

跪捧王足，

營於滻水之東。
過京城南，
歷安化門、明德門、啟夏門外，
遶京城東南角，
轉北，
歷延興、春明、通化三門之外，
至滻水。
滻水，
出藍田縣境之西，

音產。
皆泣曰：
「廣平王真華、夷之主！ 」
上聞之喜曰：
「朕不及也！ 」
俶整衆入城，
百姓老幼夾道歡呼悲泣。
俶留長安，
鎮撫三日，
引大軍東出。
東出京城門，
取洛陽。
俶，
昌六翻。
甲辰 ，
捷書至鳳翔，
百寮入賀。
上涕泗交頤，
即日，
遣中使啖庭瑤入蜀奏上皇；
命左僕射裴冕入京師，
告郊廟及宣慰百姓。
上以駿馬召李泌於長安。
既至，
上曰：
「朕已表請上皇東歸，
朕當還東宮復脩臣子之職。 」
泌曰：
「表可追乎？ 」
上曰：
「已遠矣。 」
泌曰：
「上皇不來矣。 」
上驚，
問故。
泌曰：
「理勢自然。 」
上曰：
「為之柰何？ 」
泌曰：
「今請更為㣥臣賀表，
言自馬嵬請留，
靈武勸進，
及今成功，
聖上思戀晨昏，
請速還京以就孝養之意，
則可矣。 」
上即使泌草表。
上讀之，
泣曰：
「朕始以至誠願歸萬機。
今聞先生之言，
乃寤其失。 」
立命中使奉表入蜀，
因就泌飲酒，
同榻而寢。
而李輔國請取契鑰付泌，
泌請使輔國掌之；
上許之。
泌掌契鑰，
見二百十八卷上年九月。
今付輔國，
宮禁之權盡歸之矣。
為輔國專⿰⺘亶張本。
泌曰：
「臣今報德足矣，
復為閒人，
何樂如之！ 」
上曰：
「朕與先生累年同憂患，
今方相同娛樂，
柰何遽欲去乎！ 」
泌曰：
「臣有五不可留，
願陛下聽臣去，
免臣於死。 」
上曰：
「何謂也？ 」
對曰：
「臣遇陛下太早，
陛下任臣太重，
寵臣太深，
臣功太高，
迹太奇，
此其所以不可留也。 」
上曰：
「且眠矣，
異日議之。 」
對曰：
「陛下今就臣榻臥，
猶不得請，
況異日香案之前乎！
唐制：凡朝日，
殿上設黼扆、躡席、熏爐、香案，
皇帝升御座，
宰執當香案前奏事。
是殺臣也。 」
上曰：
「不意卿疑朕如此，
豈有如朕而辦殺卿邪！
是直以朕為句踐也！ 」
對曰：
「陛下不辦殺臣，
故臣求歸；
若其既辦，
臣安敢復言！
且殺臣者，
非陛下也，
乃『五不可』
也。
陛下曏日待臣如此，
臣於事猶有不敢言者，
況天下既安，
臣敢言乎！ 」
上良久曰：
「卿以朕不從卿北伐之謀乎！ 」
謂不從使建寧王自媯、檀取范陽之策也。
肅宗以意言之。
「非也，
所不敢言者，
乃建寧耳。 」
上曰：
「建寧，
朕之愛子，
性英果，
艱難時有功，
謂馬嵬勸留，
及北赴靈武，
血戰以衞上也。
事見二百十八卷元載六月。
但因此為小人所教，
欲害其兄，
圖繼嗣，
朕以社稷大計，
不得已而除之，
事見上卷本年正月。
嗣，
祥吏翻。
對曰：
「若有此心，
廣平當怨之。
廣平每與臣言其冤，
輒流涕嗚咽。
臣今必辭陛下去，
始敢言之耳。 」
上曰：
「渠嘗夜捫廣平，
意欲加害。 」
對曰：
「此皆出讒人之口，
豈有建寧之孝友聰明，
肯為此乎！
且陛下昔欲用建寧為元帥，
臣請用廣平。
事見二百十八卷元載九月。
帥，
所類翻。
當深憾於臣；
而以臣為忠，
益相親善，
陛下以此可察其心矣。 」
上乃泣下曰：
「先生言是也。
既往不咎，
引論語孔子之言。
Bì said:

Zú,

'The melons are ripe, the seeds abundant: / Plucking one makes the melons thrive,

Hearing of Your Majesty's rise to power,
all wish to cleanse their hearts and submit to the sagely transformation.
If we now execute them all,
it will drive them to follow the rebels."
The Emperor immediately ordered their pardon.

Examination of discrepancies: People of the Táng all credit the preservation of the Jiāng and Huái entirely to the merit of Xún and Yuǎn.
However, although Suīyáng lies on the route to the Jiāng and Huái,
once the city was besieged,

How could Suīyáng have blocked them!
It is likely that Xún was skilled in using troops,

Unless they eliminated Xún, they dared not advance past him to the south.
If we flee, we certainly will not escape.
In ancient times, the feudal lords of the Warring States

The various commanders,

Shuài,

On the day Guǐchǒu,

Ghosts with no place to return become fierce.

When Zhāng Xún first defended Suīyáng,
his troops numbered only about ten thousand,
and the city's residents were also several tens of thousands.
Upon meeting them once and asking their names,
thereafter there was none he did not recognize.
In total, he fought over four hundred battles, large and small,
killing one hundred and twenty thousand enemy soldiers.
Zhāng Xún did not follow ancient methods in deploying troops;
when instructing in battle formations,
he ordered each commanding officer to teach his own men according to his own ideas.
"Běn jiàng"
refers to the commanding officer of one's own unit.
"Chén"
is read as "zhèn" (formation).
Zhāng Xún said:
"Now when fighting against the Hú barbarians,
they gather like clouds and scatter like birds,
their changes are not constant.
Within a few steps,
the situation can differ.
Responding to sudden changes on the spot,
happens in the space of a breath.
If one must consult the senior general for every move,
matters will not be timely,
and that is not understanding the changes of warfare.
Therefore, I make the soldiers understand their commander's intent,
and the commanders understand their soldiers' circumstances.
Deploy them, and they go,
like a hand moving its fingers.
Soldiers and commanders being accustomed to each other,
each man fighting for himself,
is that not acceptable!"
From the start of the campaign,
weapons, armor, and equipment were all taken from the enemy,
and he never had them made himself.
In every battle,
if officers and soldiers retreated or scattered,
Zhāng Xún would stand at the battle site
and say to the officers and soldiers:
"I will not leave this spot.
You go back for me and decide it."
The officers and soldiers dared not not return,
fought desperately,
and ultimately defeated the enemy.
Furthermore, he treated others with sincerity and trust,
without suspicion or concealment;
facing the enemy and adapting to changes,
his unexpected strategies were endless;
his orders were clear,
rewards and punishments trustworthy,
and he shared hardships, heat, and cold with the masses.
Therefore, his subordinates vied to exert their utmost strength unto death.
When Zhāng Hào heard that Suīyáng was urgently besieged,

Your subject Guāng remarks: As subjects of a ruler,
once they have recorded their names and pledged their service,
they should face death without disloyalty.
Xīliè and others were either honored as high ministers and chancellors,

yet in times of peace,

this is something even butchers and wine-sellers would be ashamed of,

If each of them were to keep their heads,
