Why should those who do good be unfortunate and those who do evil be fortunate,
why should the court treat loyalty and righteousness so meagerly and protect treachery and evil so generously!
As for lowly and insignificant subjects,
patrol officers of humble status,
who did not participate in planning and discussion,
and were not reached by orders,
who heard the decree of the imperial expedition in the morning,
and by evening had lost the place where the imperial guard was stationed—
the event is recorded in the 218th scroll, under the first year of Zhìdé.
Was it not also difficult for them!
To deliberate punishment in six grades,
this was also appropriate,
so why regret it!
29 Therefore, after Wéi shì was deposed and became a nun,
she resided within the palace,
and died this year.
The deposition of Wéi is recorded in the 215th scroll, under the sixth year of Tiānbǎo.
30 Established the Left and Right Shénwǔ Armies,
filling them with the sons and younger brothers of the original followers.
The sons and younger brothers of the original followers
refers to those who followed the Emperor north from Mǎwéi and returned to the capital from Língwǔ.
Follow,
pronounced as cái yòng fān.
Collectively called the Six Armies of the Northern Guard.
Left and Right Yǔlín,
Left and Right Lóngwǔ,
Left and Right Shénwǔ,
are called the Six Armies of the Northern Guard.
Divided into Left and Right Wings,
named the Yīngwǔ Army.
31 Promoted the Hézhōng Defense Commissioner to Jiedushi,
overseeing seven prefectures including Pú and Jiàng;
in the first year of Zhìdé,
established the Hézhōng Defense Commissioner and Pú Pass Garrison Commander,
now promoted to Jiedushi,
overseeing the seven prefectures of Pú, Jiàng, Xí, Cí, Jìn, Guó, and Tóng,
with headquarters in Pú Prefecture.
Examination of Discrepancies says: Various geographical records all mention a certain commandery,
and in the first year of Qiányuán, they were restored to a certain prefecture,
but it is not seen on which month and day.
In the twelfth month of this year, on the Wùwǔ day, an amnesty stated:
"The recently changed official titles, commandery names, and official names,
shall all revert to the old system."
This is likely the text regarding the restoration of commanderies to prefectures.
By the time it was promulgated throughout the land,
it was already into the next year.
Therefore, all record it as the first year of Qiányuán.
Dōngchuān oversaw twelve prefectures including Zǐ and Suì;
Dōngchuān oversaw the twelve prefectures of Zǐ, Suì, Mián, Jiàn, Lóng, Làng, Pǔ, Líng, Lú, Róng, Zī, and Jiǎn,
with headquarters in Zǐ Prefecture.
Oversaw five prefectures including Jīng and Lǐ;
Kuíxiá Jiedushi,
oversaw five prefectures including Kuí and Xiá;
Jīngnán Jiedushi originally oversaw ten prefectures,
now divided into two commands.
Jīnglǐ additionally oversaw Lǎng, Yǐng, and Fù,
totaling five prefectures.
Kuíxiá additionally oversaw Fú, Zhōng, and Wàn,
totaling five prefectures.
First year of Qiányuán
(Wùxū, 758)
The era name was changed in the second month of this year.
1 Spring,
first month,
Wùyín day,
the Retired Emperor held court at Xuānzhèng Hall,
conferred the imperial seal,
and added the honorific title.
Examination of Discrepancies says: The Veritable Records state:
"On the Wùyín day,
Xuánzōng held court at Xuānzhèng Hall,
and conferred upon the Emperor the imperial seal.
After the ceremony,
the Emperor was honored with an additional title.
The Emperor humbly declined, saying: 'I have received the sacred decree,
bestowing upon me the honorific title of Guāngtiān Wénwǔ Dàshèng Xiàogǎn Huángdì,
and conferring the imperial seal and the mandate seal, one each.'"
According to this, on the Guǐhài day of the twelfth month of last year,
the Emperor had already received the imperial seal,
and reported to the Tàiqīng Palace.
On the Jiǎzǐ day,
Xuánzōng held court at Xuānzhèng Hall,
conferred the imperial seal upon the Emperor,
and the Emperor wept and bowed to receive it below the hall.
Now it is again said that the seal was conferred,
the event seems repetitive.
Táng Lì, Tǒng Jì, Niándài Jì, and the Old Annals all state that the imperial seal was conferred in the twelfth month of last year,
and on the Wùyín day of the first month of this year, the honorific title was conferred.
Here, this version is followed.
The title of
"Dàshèng"
was not accepted by the Retired Emperor.
The Emperor honored the Retired Emperor as Tàishàng Zhìdào Shènghuáng Tiāndì.
While the rebel bandits had not yet been pacified,
and the imperial ancestral temples had not yet been restored,
yet between father and son, honorific titles were repeatedly added—
what was the purpose of this!
Previously,
after the imperial army had recaptured the capital,
many ritual vessels from the ancestral temples and resources from the treasury had been scattered among the people.
Envoys were dispatched to investigate and recover them,
causing considerable disturbance.
On the Yǐyǒu day,
an edict was issued to halt all such actions,
and Jīngzhào Yǐn Lǐ Xiàn was ordered to pacify the wards and markets.
2 In the second month,
on the first day, Guǐmǎo,
Diànzhōng Jiān Lǐ Fǔguó was additionally appointed as Tàipú Qīng.
Fǔguó attached himself to Zhāng Shū,
serving as Pàn Yuánshuài Fǔ Xíngjūn Sīmǎ,
and his influence overwhelmed both court and populace.
This laid the groundwork for Fǔguó gaining power and later falling out with Shū.
Cháo,
read as Yáo.
3 Néng Yuánhào, the Běihǎi Jiédù Shǐ appointed by Ān Qìngxù, led his forces to surrender.
He was appointed as Hónglú Qīng
and concurrently served as Héběi Zhāotǎo Shǐ.
4 On the Dīngwèi day,
the Emperor ascended the Míngfèng Gate.
The Táng Huìyào states: In the third year of Zhìdé,
Dānfèng Gate was renamed Míngfèng Gate,
Tōnghuà Gate was renamed Dálǐ Gate,
and Ānshàng Gate was renamed Xiāntiān Gate.
All ward names containing
"Ān"
were changed,
but soon reverted to their original names.
The era name was changed.
The era name was changed to Qiányuán.
The term "zǎi" was restored to "nián."
Changing "nián" to "zǎi"
began from the third year of Tiānbǎo during the reign of the Retired Emperor.
Fù,
read as Fúyòu.
5 On the Gēngwǔ day,
Wáng Xuánzhì, Deputy Dà Dūhù of Āndōng, was appointed as Yíngzhōu Cìshǐ,
concurrently serving as Pínglú Jiédù Shǐ.
6 In the third month,
on the Jiǎxū day,
Chǔ Wáng Chù was transferred and made Chéng Wáng.
7 On the Wùyín day,
Zhāng Shū was established as Empress.
8 Zhènxī, Běitíng Xíngyíng Jiédù Shǐ Lǐ Sìyè was stationed at Hénèi.
The Xíngyíng Jiédù Shǐ began from this.
On the Guǐsì day,
Běitíng Bīngmǎ Shǐ Wáng Wéiliáng plotted a rebellion.
Sìyè, together with Deputy General Lìfēi Yuánlǐ, attacked and executed him.
Lìfēi,
is a non-Hán compound surname.
The Xìng Pǔ states: Lìfēi,
is of the Western Qiāng ethnicity.
In the Suí dynasty, there was Lìfēi Xióng,
a native of Jīngzhōu.
9 When Ān Qìngxù fled north,
his Píngyuán Tàishǒu Wáng Jiǎn
and Qīnghé Tàishǒu Yǔwén Kuān both killed his envoys and surrendered.
Qìngxù sent his generals Cài Xīdé and Ān Tàiqīng to attack and capture them,
taking them alive and bringing them back.
They were executed in the market of Yè.
Anyone who plotted to surrender,
was executed along with their kindred and clan.
For non-Hán people, their kindred were executed;
for Huá people, their clans were executed.
Zhǒng,
read as Zhāngyǒng.
Many were implicated and put to death.
He also swore a blood oath with his close ministers south of Yè,
but people's hearts grew even more alienated.
Qìngxù heard that Lǐ Sìyè was at Hénèi.
In summer,
the fourth month,
together with Cài Xīdé and Cuī Qiányòu, he led twenty thousand infantry and cavalry,
crossed the Qìn River to attack him.
The Qìn River originates southeast of Qìnyuán County, Qìnzhōu,
flows eastward out of the mountains,
and passes north of Hénèi County.
Qìngxù attacked Hénèi from Yè,
needing to cross the Qìn River.
Qìn,
read as Qīyùn.
10 On the Guǐmǎo day,
Guó Wáng Jù, Tàizǐ Shǎoshī, was appointed as Hénán Yǐn,
concurrently serving as Dōngjīng Liúshǒu.
11 On the Xīnmǎo day,
"Xīnmǎo"
should be
"Xīnhài,"
an error in transcription.
The Xīn Tángshū Sùzōng Jì records
"the fourth month, Xīnhài,"
here also missing
"the fourth month"
two characters.
The ancestral tablet was respectfully brought from the Chánglè Hall into the Grand Ancestral Temple.
On the Jiǎyín day,
the Emperor offered sacrifices at the Grand Ancestral Temple,
then sacrificed to the Supreme God of Heaven;
on the Yǐmǎo day,
he ascended the Míngfèng Gate,
and pardoned the empire.
12 In the fifth month,
on the Rénwǔ day,
an order was issued to abolish the Cǎifǎng Shǐ,
and the Chùzhì Shǐ was renamed Guānchá Shǐ.
The Guānchá Shǐ began from this.
In the early Zhēnguàn period,
ten grand envoys were dispatched to inspect the provinces for floods and droughts,
thus there were the titles of Xúnchá, Ānfǔ, and Cúnfǔ.
In the second year of Shénlóng,
twenty officials of the fifth rank and above were appointed as Shí Dào Xúnchá Shǐ,
to investigate and report on prefectures and counties,
serving for two years before being replaced.
In the second year of Jǐngyún,
twenty-four Dūdū were established,
to oversee the conduct of Cìshǐ and below.
At the time, it was considered that their authority was too great and difficult to control,
so they were abolished,
and Shí Dào Ànchá Shǐ were established.
In the second year of Kāiyuán, they were called Shí Dào Ànchá Cǎifǎng Chǔzhì Shǐ.
In the fourth year, they were abolished.
In the eighth year, the Ànchá Shǐ were reestablished,
making inspections of prefectures and counties in autumn and winter.
In the twentieth year, they were called Cǎifǎng Chǔzhì Shǐ,
divided into fifteen circuits.
At the end of Tiānbǎo,
they also concurrently served as Chùzhì Shǐ.
This year, they were renamed Guānchá Chǔzhì Shǐ.
13 Zhāng Hào was by nature simple and unassuming,
and did not serve powerful eunuchs.
Zhōngyào,
refers to eunuchs holding powerful positions,
such as Lǐ Fǔguó and the like.
He memorialized:
"Sīmíng is vicious and treacherous,
having seized power amidst chaos.
When his strength is great, the masses attach to him;
when his power is stripped away, people desert him.
Though he has a human face,
his heart is that of a wild beast,
difficult to win over with virtue.
I hope you do not grant him authority and power."
He also said:
"Huázhōu Fángyù Shǐ Xǔ Shūjì,
is cunning and deceitful,
and will certainly change sides in times of crisis.
I request that he be summoned to serve in the palace guard."
Later, both Sīmíng and Shūjì acted exactly as Hào had predicted.
Huázhōu,
Língchāng Commandery.
Shǐ,
read as Shūlì.
Nàn,
read as Nǎidàn.
The Emperor favored and accepted Sīmíng,
"yǐ"
should be
"yǐ,"
people of the Táng often used yǐ and yǐ interchangeably.
But here, using
"yǐ"
makes the text unintelligible.
All said that Sīmíng and Shūjì were loyal and sincere, and could be trusted.
Sīmíng was in Fànyáng.
Huázhōu administered Báimǎ County,
an ancient county from the Hàn dynasty,
where Xǔ Shūjì was stationed.
On the Wùzǐ day,
Hào was dismissed and made Jīngzhōu Fángyù Shǐ;
Lǐbù Shàngshū Cuī Guāngyuǎn was appointed as Hénán Jiédù Shǐ.
14 Empress Zhāng gave birth to Xīng Wáng Shào,
who was only a few years old.
She wished to make him heir,
but the Emperor was hesitant and undecided.
Casually, he said to Kǎogōng Lángzhōng, Zhī Zhìgào Lǐ Kuí:
"Chéng Wáng is older,
and moreover has rendered service.
I wish to establish him as Crown Prince.
What is your opinion?"
Kuí bowed twice in congratulations and said:
"This is a blessing for the state,
I cannot contain my great joy."
The Emperor, pleased, said:
"My mind is made up."
On the Gēngyín day,
Chéng Wáng Chù was established as Crown Prince.
Kuí
was the great-great-grandson of Xuándào.
On the 15th day, Yǐwèi,
Cui Yuán was appointed as Junior Tutor of the Heir Apparent,
and Lǐ Lín as Junior Guardian,
both being relieved of their administrative duties.
The Emperor was quite fond of ghosts and spirits,
and the Junior Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, Wáng Yù,
exclusively relied on ghosts and spirits to curry favor.
Whenever discussing rituals and ceremonies,
he often mixed in elements of shamanistic prayers and vulgar customs.
The Emperor was pleased with him,
and appointed Yù as Vice Director of the Secretariat and Joint Manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery.
On the 16th day, the late Prefect of Chángshān, Yán Gǎoqīng, was posthumously awarded the title of Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
with the posthumous name "Loyal and Steadfast."
His son, Yán Wēimíng, was appointed as a Secretary of the Court of the Imperial Stud.
When Gǎoqīng died,
(Yán Gǎoqīng's death is recorded in the 217th scroll, in the first year of the Zhìdé era.)
(Shǒu,
read as shì.)
there was ultimately no commendation or posthumous award.
While the Emperor was in Fèngxiáng,
Yán Zhēnqīng served as the Censor-in-Chief.
He tearfully appealed to the Emperor,
who then demoted Lǐ Tōngyōu to Prefect of Pǔ'ān,
(Jiànzhōu Pǔ'ān Commandery.)
The Retired Emperor had Tōngyōu beaten to death with a staff.
Gǎoqīng's son, Yán Quánmíng, was detained by Wáng Chéngyè,
and consequently took up residence in Shòuyáng.
(Shòuyáng County was established during the Jin dynasty,
belonging to Lèpíng Commandery.
The Later Wei abolished Lèpíng Commandery,
placing Shòuyáng County under Tàiyuán Commandery.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is located 180 lǐ east of Tàiyuán Prefecture.
However, in our dynasty, the seat of Tàiyuán Prefecture has already been moved to Yángqū.
Sòng Bái said: Shòuyáng County was originally part of the territory of Yúcì County during the Han dynasty.
The Hòuwèi Fēngtǔ Jì records: At the end of the Jin dynasty,
the Shānróng invaded inland,
and the people of Tàiyuán fled east of the mountains.
The Rong then occupied the area.
In the 10th year of the Zhēnjūn era,
the households of Shòuyáng were moved out and resettled south of Dàlíng City,
establishing Shòuyáng County.
During the Sui dynasty's Kāihuáng era, Shòuyáng was renamed Wénshuǐ County,
and Shòuyáng County was re-established at the old Shòuyáng city site,
which is the present-day county.)
Last year, when Shǐ Sīmíng attacked Tàiyuán,
he captured Quánmíng.
He was sent to Fànyáng,
and it happened that Ān Qìngxù had just ascended to power,
issuing an amnesty,
so he was spared.
When Sīmíng surrendered,
he was able to return.
He searched for his father's body in the Eastern Capital,
found it,
and then together with Yuán Lǚqiān's body, placed them in coffins and brought them back.
Gǎoqīng's sisters, younger sisters, daughters, and Quánmíng's own sons were all scattered in Héběi.
Zhēnqīng was then the Prefect of Púzhōu.
He sent Quánmíng to search for them.
Quánmíng wept and wailed as he sought them out,
moving passersby to pity,
and after a long time, he found them.
Quánmíng begged relatives and old acquaintances for contributions,
and with whatever he obtained, he ransomed them,
prioritizing his aunts, sisters, and younger sisters before his own son.
His aunt's daughter had been seized by bandits.
Quánmíng had two hundred strings of cash,
and intended to ransom his own daughter,
but pitying his aunt's distress and憔悴,
he first ransomed his aunt's daughter.
By the time he obtained more money,
and went to search for his own daughter,
she was already missing.
He encountered his paternal cousins and younger sisters,
as well as the wives and children of his father's former officers and officials like Yuán Lǚqiān who were scattered and displaced,
and brought them all back with him,
totaling over fifty households,
more than three hundred people.
He shared his resources and provisions equally among them,
(meaning he divided the resources and provisions equally.
If there was any insufficiency,
he reduced the usual amount and distributed it equally.)
When they reached Púzhōu,
Zhēnqīng provided for them all.
After some time,
he assisted them according to where they chose to go.
Yuán Lǚqiān's wife suspected that Lǚqiān's burial clothes and coverings were too frugal and thin,
opened the coffin to look,
and found it no different from Gǎoqīng's,
only then feeling ashamed and convinced.
Yán Gǎoqīng's loyalty and steadfastness certainly shine through the ages,
and his son's filial piety and righteousness are also beyond what ordinary people can achieve.
On the 17th day of the sixth month,
Jǐyǒu,
a Tàiyī altar was erected east of the southern suburb.
(Emperor Wǔ of the Han first sacrificed to Tàiyī.
By the Táng dynasty,
sacrifices to him were resumed,
likely incorporating the theory of the Nine Palaces Noble Spirits.
Xiàng Ānshì said: The central palace has the celestial pole star,
its spirit is Tàiyī,
the most revered among the constellations.
The direction it presides over receives repeated auspicious responses.
Emperor Wǔ of the Han first sacrificed to it.)
The Emperor had previously been unwell,
and divination indicated mountains and rivers were causing the affliction.
Yù requested sending palace eunuchs and female shamans by post to pray separately at famous mountains and great rivers throughout the land.
The shamans, relying on their influence,
caused trouble and harassment in the prefectures and counties they passed through,
demanding and accepting bribes.
In Huángzhōu, there was a shaman,
in her prime and beautiful,
accompanied by dozens of unruly youths,
who caused particularly severe harm.
Upon reaching Huángzhōu,
they lodged at a post station.
The Prefect, Zuǒ Zhèn, arrived at the station in the morning.
The gate was locked,
and could not be opened.
Zhèn was furious,
broke the lock and entered,
dragged the shaman down the steps and beheaded her,
and killed all the youths accompanying her.
He confiscated their bribes,
amounting to several hundred thousand,
and reported the matter in detail,
requesting to use the confiscated bribes to substitute for the poor people's taxes.
He sent the palace eunuch back to the capital,
and the Emperor had no grounds to punish him.
On the 18th day, Lǐ Sìyè, who held the title of Kaifu Yitong Sansi, was appointed Prefect of Huáizhōu,
and concurrently served as Military Commissioner of the Zhènxī and Běitíng Campaign Headquarters.
(Lǐ Sìyè stationed Zhènxī and Běitíng troops in Huáizhōu,
and was thus appointed as its prefect,
to levy supplies for the army.
Sì,
read as sì.)
On the 19th day, the recluse Hán Yǐng revised the new calendar.
On Dīngsì,
the Yǐng calendar was first implemented.
(At that time, Hán Yǐng memorialized that the Dàyǎn calendar might have errors.
The Emperor was suspicious,
appointed Yǐng directly to the Directorate of Astronomy,
had him adjust the method,
adding two days to each solar term,
and renamed it the Zhìdé calendar.)
On the 20th day, Wùwǔ,
an edict was issued that officials in the two capitals who had surrendered to the rebels,
and whose cases were still under investigation by the Three Judicial Offices, were all to be released;
those to be demoted or degraded would be dealt with subsequently.
(Last year in the twelfth month, the Three Judicial Offices were first ordered to investigate officials who had surrendered to the rebels.
Chǔ,
read as chǔ.
Fēn,
read as fèn.)
On the 21st day, the Junior Tutor of the Heir Apparent, Fáng Guǎn, having lost his position,
(meaning he was dismissed from the chancellorship.)
often claimed illness and did not attend court,
yet guests filled his gate morning and evening.
His partisans spread rumors in the court, saying:
"Guǎn possesses both civil and military talents,
and should be greatly employed."
The Emperor heard this and disliked it,
issued an edict enumerating Guǎn's crimes,
and demoted him to Prefect of Bīnzhōu.
The former Director of the Imperial Academy, Liú Zhì, was demoted to Prefect of Làngzhōu,
and the Governor of the Capital, Yán Wǔ, was demoted to Prefect of Bāzhōu,
all being partisans of Guǎn.
(Làngzhōu is Làngzhōng Commandery.
Bāzhōu is Qīnghuà Commandery,
originally the territory of Dàngqú County in the Bā Commandery of the Han dynasty.
Làng,
pronounced làng.)
On the 22nd day, initially,
Shǐ Sīmíng served as a subordinate general under the Pinglú Army Commissioner Wū Zhīyì.
(Kǎo yì says: The Old History biography states,
"Zhīyì was the Military Commissioner."
According to this, Ān Lùshān first became the Pinglú Military Commissioner.
The Old History biography is mistaken.)
Zhīyì's son, Wū Chéng'ēn, was the Prefect of Xìndū,
and surrendered the commandery to Sīmíng.
(This event is recorded in the previous scroll, first year of Zhìdé.)
When Ān Qìngxù was defeated,
Chéng'ēn persuaded Sīmíng to surrender to the Táng.
(Event from last December.)
Chéng'ēn was trusted by Sīmíng,
but secretly plotted against him.
He also advised the Emperor to appoint Chéng'ēn as Deputy Military Commissioner of Fànyáng,
bestow an iron pledge to Āshǐnà Chéngqìng,
and order them to jointly plot against Sīmíng.
The Emperor followed this advice.
Chéng'ēn often used his personal wealth to recruit troops,
and repeatedly dressed in women's clothing to visit the camps of various generals to persuade and entice them.
The generals reported this to Siming,
but Siming was suspicious and did not investigate.
When Chéng'ēn went to the capital,
the emperor sent the eunuch Lǐ Sījìng to accompany him to Fànyáng to convey imperial condolences.
After Chéng'ēn had delivered the imperial decree,
Siming detained Chéng'ēn in a guesthouse within his residence,
screened his bed,
and hid two men beneath it.
Chéng'ēn's youngest son was in Fànyáng,
and Siming allowed him to visit his father.
During the night,
Chéng'ēn secretly said to his son:
"I have received orders to eliminate this rebellious barbarian,
and I will be appointed as military governor."
The two men under the bed shouted loudly and emerged.
Siming then arrested Chéng'ēn,
searched his baggage,
which consisted of all the traveler's belongings,
packed in bags and sacks,
hence called "zhuāng náng."
Those with a bottom are called "náng,"
those without a bottom are called "tuó."
"Suǒ,"
Shānkè fān.
A document stated:
"If Chéngqìng's mission succeeds, then grant him the iron tally;
otherwise,
it must not be granted."
They also found several hundred pages of registers,
listing the names of soldiers and officers who had previously rebelled with Siming.
Wū Chéng'ēn carried the iron tally into the unpredictable territory of the barbarians;
had Āshǐnà Chéngqìng's mission failed,
could Chéng'ēn have returned the iron tally to the emperor?
If Siming had indeed been executed,
then his accomplices should have been pardoned,
yet their names were recorded beforehand;
could they all have been executed?
I believe that Lǐ Guāngbì, with his wisdom, would certainly not have done this.
Rather, Siming, based on Chéng'ēn's words,
forged this document,
and submitted a memorial to accuse Guāngbì of crimes;
he also forged the registers,
recording the names of soldiers and officers to incite their anger,
ensuring they would rebel with him and have no other intentions.
"How have I wronged you that you would do this!"
Chéng'ēn apologized, saying:
"I deserve death,
this was all Lǐ Guāngbì's plan."
Siming then gathered his officers, officials, and civilians,
faced west, and wept loudly, saying:
"I surrendered to the court with 130,000 troops,
how have I wronged Your Majesty,
that you would seek to kill me!"
He then had Chéng'ēn and his son beaten to death,
and over two hundred others were implicated and executed.
Chéng'ēn's younger brother, Chéngcǐ, escaped and survived.
Siming imprisoned Sījìng,
and submitted a memorial detailing the situation.
The emperor sent a palace envoy to console Siming, saying:
"This was not the intention of the court or Guāngbì,
it was all Chéng'ēn's doing,
and it was good that you killed him."
When the deliberations of the Three Judicial Offices regarding the crimes of officials who had surrendered to the rebels reached Fànyáng,
Siming said to his generals:
"Chén Xīliè and others were all high-ranking court ministers,
yet the retired emperor abandoned them and fled to Shǔ,
and now they still cannot escape death;
how much more so for us, who originally followed Ān Lùshān in rebellion!"
Siming used this to further incite his soldiers and officers.
Siming followed this,
ordering his administrative officer Gěng Rénzhì and his colleague Zhāng Bùjīn to draft a memorial, stating:
"If Your Majesty does not execute Guāngbì for me,
I will lead my troops to Tàiyuán and kill him myself."
Bùjīn drafted the memorial and showed it to Siming,
and when it was about to be sealed in a case,
all memorials were sealed in cases.
The scribe who wrote the memorial reported this to Siming,
and Siming ordered the arrest and execution of the two men.
Rénzhì had served Siming for a long time,
and Siming pitied him,
wanting to spare his life.
He summoned him again,
and said:
"I have employed you for nearly thirty years,
today it is not I who have wronged you."
Rénzhì shouted loudly:
"Every person must die once,
to die for loyalty and righteousness,
is a good death.
Now, following you in rebellion,
I would merely prolong my life for a short while;
how could that compare to a swift death!"
Siming was enraged,
beat him indiscriminately,
until his brains spilled on the ground.
History records that Gěng Rénzhì turned from rebellion to loyalty,
preserving his integrity through death.
"Hū,"
huǒ gù fān.
Wū Chéngcǐ fled to Tàiyuán,
and Lǐ Guāngbì recommended him to be appointed Prince of Chānghuà Commandery,
and appointed as commander of the Shílǐng Army.
The Shílǐng Army was located in Xiùróng County of Xīn Prefecture.
23 Autumn,
seventh month,
on Bǐngxū,
the first casting of large coins worth ten,
inscribed with
"Qiányuán Heavy Treasure,"
the Qiányuán coin had a diameter of one cun,
each string weighed ten jin,
and circulated alongside the Kāiyuán Tōngbǎo coins.
24 On Dīnghài,
the Uighur Khagan was enfeoffed as the "Heroic, Martial, and Far-Reaching Píqiāquē Khagan,"
and the emperor's youngest daughter, Princess Níngguó, was given to him as a wife.
The Prince of Hànzhōng, Yǔ, the Director of the Palace Administration, was appointed as the Enfeoffment Ceremony Envoy,
with Vice Director of the Right Bureau of the Department of State Affairs Lǐ Xùn as his deputy;
Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs Péi Miǎn was ordered to escort the princess to the border.
On Wùzǐ,
Xiānyú Shūmíng, Vice Director of the Bureau of Honors, was also appointed as Yǔ's deputy.
Shūmíng
was the younger brother of Zhòngtōng.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
Xiānyú Zhòngtōng allied with Yáng Guózhōng,
and attained high rank and prominence.
On Jiǎzǐ,
the emperor escorted Princess Níngguó to Xiányáng,
and the princess bid farewell, saying:
"The affairs of the state are of great importance,
even if I die, I will have no regrets."
The emperor wept and returned.
When Yǔ and others arrived at the Uighur royal tent,
the Khagan wore a reddish-brown robe and a barbarian hat,
sitting on a couch inside the tent,
with very strict ceremonial guards,
and had Yǔ and others stand outside the tent.
Yǔ stood without bowing,
and the Khagan said:
"I and the Heavenly Khagan are rulers of two states,
there are rituals between ruler and subject,
how can you not bow?"
Yǔ and Shūmíng replied:
"In the past, when Táng married with various states,
all used daughters of the imperial clan as princesses.
Now the Son of Heaven, because the Khagan has rendered meritorious service,
has given his own daughter to the Khagan as wife.
The grace and courtesy are extremely great;
how can the Khagan, as a son-in-law, be arrogant toward his father-in-law,
sitting on a couch to receive the enfeoffment decree!"
The Khagan changed his expression,
stood up, and received the enfeoffment decree.
The next day,
he installed the princess as Khatun.
Since the founding of the Türk state,
the Khagan has called his principal wife "Khatun."
25 On Yǐwèi,
Guō Zǐyí entered the court.
Examination of discrepancies: The Veritable Records state:
"Guō Zǐyí captured the rebel general Ān Tàiqīng and sent him to the capital."
According to the first year of the Shàngyuán era,
Lǐ Guāngbì captured Huái Prefecture,
and only then captured Tàiqīng.
The Veritable Records are mistaken.
The Táng Calendar, Basic Annals, and others do not mention this.
The Old Biography of Zǐyí states:
"In the seventh month,
he defeated the rebels on the river,
captured Ān Shǒuzhōng,
and presented him."
Other books also do not mention this,
and it is not adopted here.
On the 26th day of the eighth month,
Rényín,
Xǔ Shūjì, the military commissioner of five prefectures including Qīng and Dēng, was appointed as the military commissioner of six prefectures including Huá and Pú.
Textual analysis: The Veritable Records states:
“Jì Guǎngchēn, the military commissioner of five prefectures including Qīng and Xú;
Xǔ Shūjì, the military commissioner of five prefectures including Qīng and Dēng.”
How could Qīng Prefecture belong to two military commissioners simultaneously?
Moreover, Guǎngchēn was previously the senior administrator of Jīng Prefecture,
and in the fifth month of this year, he was appointed as the Right Regular Attendant.
In the ninth month, during the campaign against Ān Qìngxù,
the Veritable Records refers to him as the military commissioner of Zhèng and Cài.
The Family Biography of Fényáng refers to Huáixī, Jīng, and Lǐ,
the Old Annals refer to Jīng Prefecture,
but he never governed Qīng or Xú.
The Veritable Records here refers to Qīng and Xú,
which is likely an error.
I note that according to the New Book’s Table of Regional Commands,
in the first year of Zhìdé, the Qīng-Mì military commissioner was established,
overseeing the four commanderies of Běihǎi, Gāomì, Dōngmóu, and Dōnglái.
In the first year of Qiányuán,
the Qīng-Mì military commissioner was additionally given jurisdiction over Huá and Pú prefectures.
The Qīng-Mì military commissioner,
which is the same as the previously mentioned Běihǎi military commissioner,
oversaw the four prefectures of Qīng, Mì, Dēng, and Lái.
With the addition of Huá and Pú,
this made him the military commissioner of six prefectures.
If the five prefectures of Qīng and Dēng were to have Huá and Pú added,
that would make seven prefectures,
which does not match the number.
On the 27th day, Gēngxū,
Lǐ Guāngbì entered the court.
On Bǐngchén,
Guō Zǐyí was appointed as the Secretariat Director,
and Guāngbì as the Palace Attendant.
On Dīngsì,
Zǐyí proceeded to the military camp.
On the 28th day, the Uighurs sent their minister Gǔchuò Tèlè and Dìdé, leading three thousand elite cavalry to assist in the campaign against Ān Qìngxù.
The Emperor ordered Púgù Huái’ēn, the Left Military Vanguard Commander of Shuòfāng, to lead them.
In the ninth month,
on Gēngwǔ, the first day,
Zhào Cǐ, the Grand General of the Right Yǔlín Guard, was appointed as the military commissioner of the three prefectures of Pú, Tóng, and Guó.
Last year, the Hézhōng military commissioner was established,
overseeing seven prefectures including Pú and Jiàng.
Now, Zhào Cǐ was only the military commissioner of the three prefectures of Pú, Tóng, and Guó.
This was because during the turmoil of war,
military commissioners were appointed separately to secure strategic points,
and the changes in their jurisdictions, whether expanded, reduced, divided, or merged,
were adapted according to the needs of the time.
On the 30th day, Bǐngzǐ,
Wáng Zhòngshēng, the Pacification Commissioner for the Dǎngxiàng, beheaded the Dǎngxiàng chieftain Tuòbá Róngdé
and sent his head to the capital.
After the Zhēnguàn era,
the Tǔbō grew increasingly powerful,
and the Dǎngxiàng and Tuòbá tribes, fearing their pressure,
requested to move inward.
An edict established the Jìngbiān Army Prefecture in Qìng Prefecture to settle them.
Additionally, the Fāngchí Chief Command was established within the boundaries of Huái’ān County in Qìng Prefecture,
administering ten minor prefectures,
to settle the Yělì clan of the Dǎngxiàng.
Since the Zhìdé era,
with the turmoil in the Central Plains,
the Dǎngxiàng took the opportunity to raid Bīn and Níng prefectures.
When Ān Qìngxù first arrived in Yè,
although his followers were scattered and divided,
he still controlled over sixty cities across seven commanderies:
Jí, Yè, Zhào, Wèi, Píngyuán, Qīnghé, and Bópíng,
totaling seven commanderies.
Qìngxù did not attend to governance personally,
but devoted himself entirely to constructing terraces, ponds, and towers, and indulging in heavy drinking.
His senior ministers, Gāo Shàng and Zhāng Tōngrú, among others, fought for power and were at odds,
leading to a complete breakdown of order.
Cài Xīdé was talented and strategic,
and his troops were elite and well-trained,
but he was stubborn by nature,
fond of speaking bluntly.
Tōngrú slandered him, leading to his execution;
several thousand of his subordinates fled and scattered,
and the various generals resented this and refused to serve effectively.
Cuī Gānyòu was appointed as the Commander of All Military Forces,
in charge of both internal and external troops.
Gānyòu was obstinate, cruel, and fond of killing,
and the soldiers did not support him.
On Gēngyín,

orders were given for the seven military commissioners—Guō Zǐyí of Shuòfāng, Lǔ Jiǒng of Huáixī, Lǐ Huàn of Xīngpíng, Xǔ Shūjì of Huá-Pú, Lǐ Sìyè of Zhènxī and Běitíng, Jì Guǎngchēn of Zhèng-Cài, and Cuī Guāngyuǎn of Hénán—along with Dǒng Qín, the military commander of Pínglú, to lead two hundred thousand infantry and cavalry to campaign against Qìngxù.
Additionally, orders were given for Lǐ Guāngbì of Hédōng and Wáng Sīlǐ of Guānnèi and Zélù
(Wáng Sīlǐ was previously the military commissioner of Guānnèi;
at this time, he concurrently held the position of military commissioner of Zélù,
stationed in Lù Prefecture). Textual analysis: The Veritable Records includes Lǐ Huàn
but omits Cuī Guāngyuǎn,
and states there were nine military commissioners in total.
The Family Biography of Fényáng includes Guāngyuǎn
but omits Huàn,
and also includes Xuē Jiānxùn, the military commander of Hédōng.
It is likely that the Veritable Records omitted Guāngyuǎn,
while the Fényáng Biography omitted Huàn’s name.
Jiānxùn was likely a subordinate general under Guāngbì;
before Guāngbì arrived,
he was first sent to Yè City.
The Fényáng Biography also refers to Jiǒng as being from Xiāng-Dèng,
and Guǎngchēn as being from Huáixī and Jīng-Lǐ.
The Old Basic Annals
state, “Guǎngchēn was from Jīng Prefecture.”
I now follow the Veritable Records.
The Fényáng Biography also states,
“The Duke left Luò on the twelfth day of the ninth month,
and the army crossed the river and marched east.”
I now follow the Veritable Records,
which states “shè gēng,”
meaning the twenty-first day.
I note that
“shè gēng”
should be
“Gēngyín.”
Since it was difficult to unify command,
no supreme commander was appointed.
The various armies advanced together,
with hundreds of thousands of infantry and cavalry,
yet no supreme commander was appointed.
Orders were not unified,
which led to the defeat at Ānyáng.
The title of “Army Supervisor” originated from this.
On the 32nd day, Guǐsì,
Guǎngzhōu reported: The Arabs and Persians besieged the prefectural city.
(Guǎngzhōu administered Nánhǎi County,
originally the Hànyuán Pānyú County of the Hàn dynasty.)
The armies of these two countries plundered the warehouses,
burned houses,
and then departed by sea.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on Jiǎchén,
the Crown Prince was formally installed.
Textual analysis: The Veritable Records states:
“A general amnesty may be proclaimed throughout the land.
Recently, grand ceremonies have been frequently held,
and special grace has been repeatedly bestowed.
Throughout the realm,
cleansing has been carried out multiple times.
Yet it is still feared that some may remain imprisoned nearby,
so all prisoners currently held for crimes below penal servitude
shall be released without exception.”
If it is said to be a general amnesty,
then even capital crimes should be pardoned.
How could only crimes below penal servitude be pardoned?
I suspect that
“A general amnesty may be proclaimed throughout the land”
is a redundant phrase.
Therefore, I do not record the amnesty here.
Initially,
in the year the Crown Prince was born,
Yùzhōu presented auspicious grain,
which was taken as an auspicious sign.
Consequently, his name was changed to Yù.
(Gēng,
pronounced gōng héng fān.)
There were no further gifts bestowed below,
but by this time,
newly minted large coins had begun to appear—
the Qiányuán Heavy Treasure coins.
34. Guō Zǐyí led his troops across the river from Xìngyuán,
advancing east to Huòjiā.
(The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Jí County in Wèi Prefecture has a Xìngyuán Town.)
Huòjiā County,
originally the Xīnzhōng Township of Jí County,
was where Emperor Wǔ of Hàn traveled to.
Upon hearing of the capture of Lǚ Jiā,
he established Huòjiā County;
during the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Huái Prefecture.
(The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Huòjiā County
is located ninety lǐ west of Wèi Prefecture.)
They beheaded four thousand enemies,
and captured five hundred prisoners.
Ān Tàiqīng fled to defend Wèi Prefecture,
and Guō Zǐyí advanced to besiege it;
on Bǐngwǔ,
he sent an envoy to report the victory.
Lǔ Jiǒng crossed from Yángwǔ,
and Jì Guǎngchēn and Cuī Guāngyuǎn crossed from Suānzǎo.
(Yángwǔ County
was established in the fourth year of Wǔdé at the site of the old Yuánwǔ City,
and belonged to Zhèng Prefecture.)
Ān Qìngxù mobilized all seventy thousand troops from Yèzhōng to rescue Wèi Prefecture,
dividing them into three armies:
with Cuī Gànyòu commanding the upper army,
Tián Chéngsì commanding the lower army,
and Ān Qìngxù personally commanding the central army.
Guō Zǐyí stationed three thousand skilled archers in ambush behind the ramparts,
ordering them:
"When we retreat,
the rebels will certainly pursue us.
You shall then ascend the ramparts,
beat drums and shout while shooting at them."
Soon after, they engaged Ān Qìngxù in battle,
feigned retreat,
and the rebels pursued them.
When the rebels reached the foot of the ramparts,
the ambushing troops rose and shot at them,
with arrows falling like rain.
The rebels turned and fled,
and Guō Zǐyí led his troops in pursuit.
Ān Qìngxù suffered a major defeat.
They captured his younger brother Ān Qìnghé
and executed him.
Subsequently, they captured Wèi Prefecture.
Ān Qìngxù fled,
and Guō Zǐyí and others pursued him to Yè.
Xǔ Shūjì, Dǒng Qín, Wáng Sīlǐ, and the Hedong military commander Xuē Jiānxùn all led their troops to join them.
Ān Qìngxù gathered his remaining troops to resist at Chóusī Gǎng.
(Chóusī Gǎng
is located west of Yè City.
According to the Oǔ Shǐ,
it is in Tāngyīn County of Xiàng Prefecture.
Xuē Jūzhèng said: Within the boundaries of Tāngyīn County, there is a ridge
that locals call Chóusǐ Gǎng.)
(The Kǎoyì states: The Fényáng Family Chronicle records:
"On the fifth day of the tenth month,
they fought at Chóu Gǎng."
According to the Shílù,
"On Guǐchǒu,
Guō Zǐyí defeated the rebels
and captured Ān Qìnghé."
Guǐchǒu
was the fourteenth day,
likely when the victory report first arrived.)
In total, they beheaded thirty thousand enemies
and captured a thousand prisoners.
Ān Qìngxù then entered the city to hold firm,
and Guō Zǐyí and others besieged him.
Ān Qìngxù, in dire straits,
sent Xuē Sōng to seek help from Shǐ Sīmíng,
even offering to yield his position to him.
Shǐ Sīmíng mobilized one hundred thirty thousand troops from Fànyáng to rescue Yè,
but hesitated and did not dare advance,
first sending Lǐ Guīrén to station ten thousand infantry and cavalry at Fǔyáng.
(Cí Prefecture governs Fǔyáng,
which is sixty lǐ south of Yè City.)
35. On Jiǎyín,
the Retired Emperor visited Huáqīng Palace;
in the eleventh month,
on Dīngchǒu,
he returned to the capital.
36. Cuī Guāngyuǎn captured Wèi Prefecture;
(Wèi Prefecture
governed from the city walls of Hàn Yuánchéng County.
Guìxiāng County was also established,
making two counties with Yuánchéng.)
On Bǐngxū,
the former Vice Minister of War, Xiāo Huá, was appointed as the defense commissioner of Wèi Prefecture.
At that time, Shǐ Sīmíng divided his army into three forces:
one advancing from Xíng and Míng,
one from Jì and Bèi,
and one from Huánshuǐ heading toward Wèi Prefecture.
(Huánshuǐ County
was originally the territory of Hàn Chánglè County.
The Wèi Jùn Guó Zhì states: In the sixth year of Jiàndé of the Zhōu dynasty,
Huánshuǐ County was established from the northeast of Línzhāng County,
located west of Wèi Prefecture.
Qù
is pronounced qī yù fān.)
In the twelfth month,
on Guǐmǎo,
an edict appointed Cuī Guāngyuǎn as the prefect of Wèi Prefecture.
37. On Jiǎchén,
the Zhèjiāng Xīdào military commissioner was established,
overseeing ten prefectures including Sū and Rùn,
with Shēng Prefecture prefect Wéi Huángcháng appointed to the position.
(The Zhèxīdào military commissioner concurrently served as the Jiāngníng military commissioner,
overseeing ten prefectures: Shēng, Rùn, Xuān, Shè, Ráo, Jiāng, Sū, Cháng, Háng, and Hú,
with headquarters in Shēng Prefecture.)
On Gēngxū,
the Zhèjiāng Dōngdào military commissioner was established,
overseeing eight prefectures including Yuè and Mù,
with the Minister of Revenue Lǐ Huán appointed to the position.
(The Zhèdōngdào military commissioner oversaw eight prefectures: Yuè, Mù, Qú, Wù, Tāi, Míng, Chù, and Wēn,
with headquarters in Yuè Prefecture.)
(This should be cross-referenced with the note on Commander-in-Chief Lǐ Huán in the first year of Shàngyuán in the following volume.)
38. On Jǐwèi,
the ministers requested that the Emperor be honored with the title "Qiángān Dàshèng Guāngtiān Wénwǔ Xiàogǎn Huángdì,"
which was granted.
39. Shǐ Sīmíng took advantage of Cuī Guāngyuǎn's recent arrival
to lead a large force down,
and Cuī Guāngyuǎn sent General Lǐ Chǔyín to resist him.
The rebel forces were strong,
and Lǐ Chǔyín suffered consecutive defeats,
retreating toward the city.
The rebels pursued him to the city walls,
shouting:
"Lǐ Chǔyín summoned us here,
why does he not come out!"
Cuī Guāngyuǎn believed this,
and had Lǐ Chǔyín executed by waist-cutting.
Lǐ Chǔyín
was a valiant general
on whom the troops relied.
After his death,
the troops lost their will to fight.
(If Yáo Sǒngfū had been alive,
he might not have been able to defend Hénán for the Sòng,
yet his death
was mourned by the Sòng people.
If Lǐ Chǔyín had been alive,
he might not have been able to defend Wèi Prefecture for the Táng,
yet his death
was mourned by the Táng people.
To execute one's own fighting general while facing the enemy
is to cut off one's own hands and feet.)
On Dīngmǎo,
Shǐ Sīmíng captured Wèi Prefecture,
killing thirty thousand people.
40. The Pínglú military commissioner Wáng Xuánzhì passed away.
The Emperor sent a palace envoy to console the officers and soldiers,
and to observe whom the army wished to appoint,
granting them the command insignia.
The Gāolì man Lǐ Huáiyù, a deputy general,
killed Wáng Xuánzhì's son
and supported Hóu Xīyì as the Pínglú military commissioner.
Hóu Xīyì's mother
was Lǐ Huáiyù's aunt,
which is why Lǐ Huáiyù supported him.
(It was Lǐ Huáiyù who installed Hóu Xīyì,
and it was also Lǐ Huáiyù who later expelled Hóu Xīyì.
Lǐ Huáiyù was later granted the name Zhèngjǐ.)
The practice of military commissioners being deposed and installed by soldiers began from this.
Your servant Guāng remarks: The people in their lives have desires;
without a ruler, there will be chaos.
These are the words from the "Announcement of Zhòng Huī" in the *Shū*.
From the Son of Heaven, the feudal lords, down to the high ministers, grandees, officers, and common people,
there is a distinction between noble and base,
and an order between great and small,
like the meshes and cords of a net supporting each other.
The *Shū*, in the "Charge to Yuè," says:
"It is like a net having its guiding cord;
there are cords in order and not confusion."
Jiǎ Yì said:
"Like the body employing the arms,
the arms employing the fingers,
there is none that is not controlled and obedient."
Thus, those below have no presumptuous ambitions.
In the *Zhōu Yì*,
"Above, heaven; below, the marsh:
Lǚ (Treading)."
The Xiàng commentary says:
"The noble man uses this to distinguish above and below,
and to settle the people's will."
This is what it means.
The reason why a ruler of men is able to possess his ministers and people
is because the eight handles reside with himself.
The *Zhōu Lǐ* states:
"The king uses eight handles to govern his various ministers: the first is rank,
to govern their nobility;
the second is emolument,
to govern their wealth;
the third is bestowal,
to govern their favor;
the fourth is appointment,
to govern their conduct;
the fifth is granting life,
to govern their fortune;
the sixth is deprivation,
to govern their poverty;
the seventh is dismissal,
to govern their offense;
the eighth is execution,
to govern their transgression."
If the power between them is equal,
how can he make those below obey!
Emperor Sùzōng encountered the mid-Táng decline,
and fortunately restored the state.
He should have rectified the rites between superior and inferior to order the four quarters;
yet he stole a moment's peace,
not considering the lasting troubles.
Appointing commanders and generals,
to govern the frontier regions,
is a great affair of the state.
Yet he entrusted it to a single envoy,
who followed the sentiments of the troops,
not inquiring whether they were worthy or unworthy,
but granting it to whomever they wished to have.
From this time onward,
the accumulated practice became the norm,
and ruler and ministers followed and upheld it,
considering it a successful strategy,
calling it "gūxī" (temporary appeasement).
"Gū"
means "for the moment";
"xī"
means "peace";
seeking peace for the present moment.
When they killed or expelled their commanding general,
he also did not punish their crime,
but consequently bestowed the position upon them.
If so, then rank and emolument, dismissal and appointment, execution and granting life, bestowal and deprivation—
these are precisely what the *Zhōu Lǐ* calls the eight handles.
"Zhì" (to govern)
is pronounced "zhí."
"Yǔ" (to bestow)
is read as "yǔ" (to give).
When chaos arises,
how can there be an end!
Moreover, those who possess a state
reward the good and punish the wicked,
so that those who do good are encouraged,
and those who do evil are deterred.
For those who are subordinates to kill or expel their superiors—
what wickedness is greater than this!
Yet to let them hold the command banner and grasp the battle-axe,
to lead and govern a region,
is to reward them.
Rewarding to encourage wickedness—
to what extremes will their wickedness not reach!
The *Shū* says:
"Make your plans far-reaching."
Words from the "Announcement to Kāng" in the *Shū*.
"Yóu"
means "plan."
"Because your plans are not far-reaching,
therefore I greatly admonish you."
Words from the poem "Bǎn" in the *Dàyǎ* section of the *Shī*.
"If a man takes no thought about what is distant,
he will find sorrow near at hand."
Seen in the *Lúnyǔ*.
How can one fully reckon such troubles and perils!
Consequently, those below often gaze sidelong, watching their superiors,
and if they find an opportunity, they attack and exterminate their clans;
those above often tremble with fear, apprehensive of those below,
and if they find an opportunity, they surprise and slaughter them;
these two phrases perfectly capture the situation of the late Táng provincial governors, generals, and soldiers.
"Jiàn" (opportunity)
is pronounced "jiàn."
"Zhuì" (to tremble)
is pronounced "zhuì,"
meaning an appearance of worry and fear.
There was no mutual nurturing for the sake of shared benefit and long-term survival.
To seek the peace of the world under such circumstances,
how could it be possible!
Tracing the origin of this calamity,
it began here.
This means the disaster began with appointing Hóu Xīyì as military commissioner of Pínglú.
Máo Cháng said: "Lì"
means "evil."
Master Zhèng said: Violating governance and creating evil is called "lì."
In ancient times, governing the army was always based on ritual,
so when Duke Wén of Jìn fought at Chéngpú,
seeing that his army, young and old, had ritual propriety,
he knew it could be used.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn*: Jìn and Chǔ fought at Chéngpú.
The Marquis of Jìn ascended the ruins of Yǒushēn to observe his army,
and said:
"Young and old have ritual propriety;
it can be used."
Then they fought,
and the Chǔ army was utterly defeated.
"Zhì" (to govern)
is pronounced "zhí";
the same below.
"Shào" (young)
is pronounced "shào."
"Zhǎng" (old)
is pronounced "zhǎng."
If soldiers are allowed to encroach upon their lieutenants,
and lieutenants to encroach upon their generals,
then for generals to encroach upon the Son of Heaven
is a natural tendency.
Jiǎ Yì's discussion of the steps of hierarchy
expresses precisely this idea.
Consequently, disasters and rebellions arose in succession,
warfare did not cease,
the people fell into utter misery,
with nowhere to appeal,
for over two hundred years,

The emperor was moved and awakened to the truth,
and praised his integrity;
many of Lǐ Fǔguó's actions

and his investigative activities were abolished.
Because of this, Lǐ Fǔguó yielded his position as Military Secretary,
requesting to return to his original office.
His original office

An edict was issued:
"Recently, due to the pressing nature of military and state affairs,
oral edicts were sometimes issued for handling matters.
All kinds of requisitions and the sentencing and exile of prisoners,
from now on, are all to cease.
Unless it is a properly proclaimed edict,
none shall be implemented.
Affairs, both internal and external,
shall each revert to their respective responsible offices.
The Yīngwǔ Army patrol officers, the various commissioners of the Six Armies, and the various internal offices,
who recently sometimes, due to disputes,
arbitrarily pursued and arrested people on their own authority,
(The Yīngwǔ Army
consisted of the palace archers,

The Six Armies
were the Six Armies of the Northern Gate.
The various commissioners

The various offices

Shǐ,
read as shū lì fān.
Lùn,
read as lú pí fān.
Tái,
refers to the Censorate.
Fǔ,
refers to the Capital Prefecture.
shall be allowed to submit memorials detailing the circumstances for the emperor's information.
Regarding the various laws and statutes, except for the Ten Abominations, murder, adultery, theft, and forgery,
all other cumbersome and trivial provisions shall be deleted,
and this task is still entrusted to the Secretariat, the Chancellery, and the judicial officials to deliberate, finalize, and memorialize for the emperor's approval."
Lǐ Fǔguó consequently bore a grudge against Lǐ Xiàn.
Examination of Discrepancies says: The Shílù biography of Lǐ Xiàn states:

12. On the jiǎchén day,
the military commissioner of Chén, Zhèng, and Bó was established,
with Lǔ Jiǒng, the prefect of Dèng Prefecture, appointed to the post;
Shàng Héng, the prefect of Xú Prefecture, was appointed military commissioner of Qīng and Mì and seven other prefectures;
(The seven prefectures
were Qīng, Mì, Dēng, Lái, Zī, Yí, and Hǎi.)
Jiǒng,
read as gǔ jiǒng fān.
They were each to maintain defense and guard posts within their respective borders.
Chén, Zhèng, and Bó had not previously established a military commissioner district;
Lǔ Jiǒng was appointed from Nányáng.
For the seven prefectures including Qīng and Mì,
Shàng Héng was promoted from Péngchéng to command them.
The Xīngpíng Army was originally established in Shǐpíng County of Yōng Prefecture,
and while Lǐ Huàn was in the field camp,
he was made to command the three prefectures of Yù, Xǔ, and Rǔ.
These were all temporary, regional military appointments,
not part of any fixed, established system.
When the nine military commissioners were defeated at Xiàngzhōu,
the troops under Lǔ Jiǒng's command plundered and looted particularly severely.
Hearing that Guō Zǐyí had retreated and stationed his troops at Héshàng,
and Lǐ Guāngbì had returned to Tàiyuán,
Lǔ Jiǒng felt ashamed and fearful,

13. Shǐ Sīmíng proclaimed himself Emperor of the Great Yān,
changed the era name to Shùntiān,
established his wife, Lady Xīn, as empress,
his son Cháoyì as Prince of Huái,
appointed Zhōu Zhì as chancellor,
Lǐ Guīrén as general,
changed Fànyáng to Yānjīng,
and changed all the prefectures to commanderies.
14. On the wùshēn day,
Lǐ Bàoyù, the Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, was appointed military commissioner of Zhèng, Chén, Yǐng, and Bó.
Lǐ Bàoyù
was a descendant of Ān Xìngguì.
(Ān Xìngguì
appears in the second year of the Wǔdé era of Emperor Gāozǔ, in the 187th scroll.)
He had repeatedly achieved military merits,
and personally expressed shame at sharing the surname Ān with Ān Lùshān,
so he was granted the imperial surname Lǐ.
15. The Píjiā Què Kèhán of the Huíhé died.
His eldest son, the Yèhù, had been killed earlier,
and the people established his youngest son,
who became the Dēnglǐ Kèhán.
The Huíhé wanted to have Princess Níngguó buried alive with the deceased.
The princess said:
"The Huíhé admired the customs of the Central Kingdom,
therefore they married a woman of the Central Kingdom as a wife.
If you wish to follow your own native customs,
why did you need to marry from ten thousand lǐ away!"
Nevertheless, she also cut her face and wept for him.
According to the customs north of the desert,
when someone died, the corpse was placed in a tent.
The sons, grandsons, and male and female relatives each killed oxen and horses,
displayed them before the tent as offerings,
then rode horses around the tent seven times,
approached the tent entrance,
used knives to cut their faces,
and wept,
with blood and tears flowing together.
After doing this seven times,
they stopped.
Wéi,
read as yú wèi fān.
Lí,
read as lǐ zhī fān.
16. The supervisor of the Mǎfāng in Fèngxiáng committed robbery.
The supervisor
was the official in charge of the Mǎfāng.
Tiānxīng County,
originally the ancient Yōng County,
in the second year of the Zhìdé era,
was renamed Fèngxiáng,
and Tiānxīng County was separately established,
attached to Fèngxiáng Prefecture.
Lǐ Fǔguó had originally come from the Flying Dragon Stables.
Lǐ Fǔguó was originally a minor attendant in the Flying Dragon Stables.
There was no injustice.
He also ordered the Censor-in-Chief Cuī Bóyáng, the Vice Minister of Justice Lǐ Yè, and the Chief Minister of the Court of Judicial Review Quán Xiàn to interrogate him.
This was what the Táng system called the "Minor Three Judicial Offices."
He still
did not submit.
He then ordered the Attendant Censor Máo Ruòxū of Tàipíng to interrogate him.
Tàipíng County,
belonged to Jiàng Prefecture.
Emperor Tàiwǔ of the Wèi established Tàipíng County.
The Zhōu changed it to Tàipíng,
named after the Tàipíng Pass city.
Seeking to comply with Fǔguó's wishes,
he attributed the guilt to Yífǔ.
Bóyáng was angered,
summoned Ruòxū to question and reprimand him,

Ruòxū first went to the Emperor on his own,
and the Emperor hid Ruòxū behind a curtain.
Bóyáng soon arrived,
stating that Ruòxū had colluded with the eunuchs,
and that his interrogation of the case was unjust.
The Emperor was angered,
shouted at him to leave.
Bóyáng was demoted to a captain in Gāoyào,
Xiàn was demoted to a captain in Guìyáng.
Guìyáng,
a Hàn county,
during the Suí and Táng, was attached to Lián Prefecture.
South of the mountains,
refers to the counties south of the mountains.
The history lost the names of the counties to which Yè and Xiàng were demoted,
hence it says they were all demoted to captaincies south of the mountains.
They were exiled to Bō Prefecture.
The Minister of Personnel and concurrent Tóngpíngzhāngshì Lǐ Xiàn memorialized that Bóyáng was not guilty,
and that the punishment was too severe.
The Emperor considered this factionalism.
In the fifth month,
on Xīnsì,
Xiàn was demoted to Prefect of Shǔ Prefecture.
The Right Sanqíchángshì Hán Zémù entered for an audience.
Sàn,
read as sǎndǎn.
Qí,
read as qíjì.
"Lǐ Xiàn sought to monopolize power.
Now demoted to Shǔ Prefecture,
I myself feel the application of the law was too lenient."
He replied:
"Lǐ Xiàn spoke straightforwardly,
it was not monopolizing power.
Your Majesty being lenient with him,
only enhances the sage virtue."
Ruòxū was soon appointed Censor-in-Chief,
his authority shook the court.
17. On Rénwǔ,
Xǔ Shūjì, the military governor of Huá and Pú, was appointed Prefect of Biàn Prefecture,
and concurrently military governor of the seven prefectures of Huá, Biàn, etc.;

The Table of Regional Commands: In the ninth year of the Kāiyuán era, the Shòufāng military governor was established,
overseeing the Protectorate of the Single Chief,

Bīn Prefecture was originally Bīn Prefecture.
In the thirteenth year of the Kāiyuán era, because
the character "Bīn"
resembled
the character "Yōu",

the seventh month,

His replacement of Zǐyí in commanding Shòufāng,

This likely only refers to this time.
Guāngbì, with five hundred cavalry from Hédōng, hurried to the Eastern Capital,
at night,
entered his army.
Guāngbì governed the army with strict discipline.
As soon as he arrived,
once the orders were issued,
the soldiers, fortifications, banners, and overall spirit all changed.
The history states that when Guāngbì entered the Shòufāng army,
the deployments all followed Zǐyí's original arrangements,
but the orders were issued with added strictness and discipline.
Govern,
read as zhízhī.
They feared Guāngbì's strictness.

Yòngjì said:

The Capital Military Commissioner Púgù Huái'ēn said:

Huái'ēn's words here,

Had the generals followed Zhāng Yòngjì in this evil deed,

Textual Analysis says: The Old Biography states:
"Yòngjì, accustomed to Zǐyí's leniency,
feared Guāngbì's strictness.
He and the other generals held considerable differing opinions,
and wanted to delay his troops.
Guāngbì led several thousand cavalry out and encamped at Sìshuǐ County.
Yòngjì came alone on horseback to meet him,
and was immediately beheaded at the camp gate.
The other generals were awed into submission,
and Xīn Jīnggǎo replaced him.
He also summoned the Capital Military Commissioner Púgù Huái'ēn.
Huái'ēn, fearful,
arrived ahead of schedule."
The Bīnzhì states:
"On the 23rd day of the fifth month,
an edict appointed the Hé dōng Jiedushi Lord Lǐ to replace Zǐyí and concurrently command the various armies.
After Lord Lǐ received the command,
he led five hundred cavalry from Hé dōng to the Eastern Capital,
and at night,
entered their camp.
Zhāng Yòngjì was at Héyáng.
Hearing of this, he said: 'The Shuòfāng army,
is not a rebel force.
Why is he so suspicious!'
He wanted to lead elite cavalry in a sudden assault into the Eastern Capital,
to expel Lord Lǐ,
and request Lord Guō [to return].
Lord Lǐ learned of this,
and thus remained in the Eastern Capital,
submitting a memorial requesting reinforcements at Héyáng.
In the winter tenth month,
Sīmíng led his troops across the river.
Lord Lǐ said: 'If Sīmíng crosses the river,
he will certainly plan to take Luòchéng.
I should guard the Wǔlǎo Pass,
and display troops on the Guǎngwǔ Plain to await him.'
He then led the army east and stationed at Sìshuǐ County.
He sent a dispatch summoning the generals from Héyáng.
Yòngjì arrived late.
Lord Lǐ enumerated his crimes and executed him,
appointing Xīn Jīnggǎo to replace him in his duties.
The next day,
he led the army into Héyáng."
According to the Veritable Records,
this month Guāngbì was appointed Deputy Commander-in-Chief,
and only in the ninth month did he move the army to Héyáng.

The history states that Huái'ēn made preparations before meeting Guāngbì.
Guāngbì, though aware of the situation, tolerated it and did not expose it.
Fù,
pronunciation fú yòu fān.
21 He appointed
the Lù-Qìn Jiedushi Wáng Sīlǐ
(Wáng Sīlǐ was Jiedushi of Zé, Lù, and Qìn prefectures.

sometimes as Lù-Qìn.)
Qìn,
pronunciation qī zhèn fān.
to concurrently serve as Běijīng Liúshǒu and Hé dōng Jiedushi.
He replaced Lǐ Guāngbì.
Earlier,
during the defeat at Tóngguān,
(events seen in scroll 118, first year of Zhìdé.)
a cavalry soldier from Zhōuzhì named Zhāng Guāngshèng dismounted and gave him [Sīlǐ] his horse,
[Sīlǐ] asked his name,
but he left without telling him.
Sīlǐ secretly remembered his appearance,
but searched for him without success.
When he arrived at Hé dōng,
someone slandered the Dàizhōu Cishi, Xīnyúnjīng from Héxī.
Yúnjīng
was from Jīnchéng, Lánzhōu,
which belonged to the Héxī circuit.
Yúnjīng was afraid,
and did not know what to do.
Guāngshèng was then under Yúnjīng's command.
He said:
"I, Guāngshèng, once did a favor for Lord Wáng.
I have never dared mention it,
ashamed to seek reward for it.
Now that you, Prefect, are in dire straits,
I, Guāngshèng, request to go see Lord Wáng.
I will certainly resolve this for you, Prefect."
Yúnjīng, pleased, sent him.
Guāngshèng paid a visit to Sīlǐ.
Before he could speak,
Sīlǐ recognized him and said:
"Ah!
Are you not my old acquaintance?
Why have we met so late!"
Guāngshèng told him the truth.
Sīlǐ was overjoyed.
He grasped his hand,
and said with tears:
"That I am alive today,
is entirely due to your efforts."
(Sīlǐ meant that Guāngshèng gave him his horse,
saving him from the soldiers,
allowing him to have this day.)
He led him to sit on the same couch,
and swore brotherhood with him.
Guāngshèng then calmly spoke of Yúnjīng's injustice.
Sīlǐ said:
"Yúnjīng's fault is also not minor,

That same day, he promoted Guāngshèng to Military Commissioner,
and bestowed upon him generous gifts of gold, silk, fields, and residences.
Zhāng Guāngshèng's conduct towards Wáng Sīlǐ
could be called that of a gentleman.
Later, when he served Dézōng,
due to losing his post and harboring resentment,
he threw in his lot with Zhū Cǐ.
How contradictory his actions were before and after!

the Emperor sent General Cáo Rìshēng to Xiāngzhōu to appease and instruct Kāng Chǔyuán.

27 In the ninth month,
on Jiǎwǔ,
Zhāng Jiāyán attacked and captured Jīngzhōu.
The Jīngnán Jiedushi Dù Hóngjiàn abandoned the city and fled.
Upon hearing this, officials of Lǐ, Lǎng, Yǐng, Xiá, Guī and other prefectures
vied to flee secretly into the mountains and valleys.
(At that time, the Jīngnán Jiedushi administered ten prefectures: Jīng, Lǐ, Lǎng, Yǐng, Fù, Kuí, Xiá, Zhōng, Wàn, and Guī.)
On the 28th day (Wùchén),
an order was issued to have Jiàngzhōu cast large coins of the "Qiányuán Zhòngbǎo" type.
During the Táng dynasty, coin casting
generally involved ninety-nine furnaces across the empire,
with thirty of them located in Jiàngzhōu.
The other furnaces
were either separated by rivers and mountains,
or had fallen into enemy hands,
so at that time, coin casting largely relied on Jiàngzhōu.
(The new coin) was valued at fifty times (the standard coin);
the large coin had a diameter of one inch and two fen,
and its inscription also read
"Qiányuán Zhòngbǎo".
The outer rim on the reverse side was a double ring.
Each string (of a thousand coins) weighed twelve catties,
and it was called the "heavy-ridged coin".
(The character) "heavy"
is pronounced with the rising tone.
Previously, because the armies had no salaries,
it was appropriate to use the new coins to provide their winter allowances.
Winter allowances
refer to the salary and allowance money that each official was entitled to receive in winter.
On the 29th day (Dīnghài),
Cuī Guāngyuǎn, the Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent, was appointed as the Pacification Commissioner of Jīngzhōu and Xiāngzhōu,
and concurrently as the Military Commissioner of the Shānnán Dōngdào region;
Wáng Zhòngshēng, the Military Commissioner of Chénzhōu, Yǐngzhōu, Bózhōu, and Shēnzhōu, was appointed as the Military Commissioner of the five prefectures including Shēnzhōu and Miǎnzhōu,
and put in charge of the military operations of the Huáinán Xīdào region.
At that time, the Huáixī Military Commissioner governed the five prefectures of Shēnzhōu, Guāngzhōu, Shòuzhōu, Ānzhōu, and Miǎnzhōu.

and ordered the prefects of various commanderies each to lead three thousand troops to follow him south towards Hénán,
dividing into four routes.

Shǐ Cháoyì from Báigāo,
and Zhōu Zhì from Húliáng to cross the river.
Báigāo and Húliáng were both key crossing points on the Yellow River,
located on the northwest bank of Huázhōu.
The character "liáng"
is sometimes written as
"liáng".
(The character) "pú"
is pronounced "bǔ".
Lǐ Guāngbì was just then inspecting the camps along the river.
Upon hearing the news,
he returned and entered Biànzhōu,
and said to Xǔ Shūjì, the Military Commissioner of Biànzhōu and Huázhōu:

The *Táng Lì* states:
"On the day Jiǎchén of the first month,
Lǐ Huáixiān captured Shǐ Cháoyì,
displayed his head,
presented it at the palace,
and surrendered all the territory under his control."
The *Niándài Jì* states:
"On the day Jǐhài of the twelfth month of the first year of the Bǎoyìng era,
Púgù Huáixiān reported: 'Shǐ Cháoyì was killed by mutinous soldiers,
and his head was sent to the capital.'
On the day Jiǎshēn of the first month of the second year,
Cháoyì's head was displayed at the palace."
The new annals state:
"On the day Jiǎshēn of the first month of the first year of the Guǎngdé era,
Cháoyì committed suicide,
and his general Lǐ Huáixiān surrendered with Yōuzhōu."
Considering that the various armies besieged Cháoyì at Mòzhōu
already at the end of the eleventh month of the previous year,
and the *Héluò Chūnqiū* says the city was besieged for forty days,
and the old biography of Huáixiān also says the attack and defense lasted over a month,
then Cháoyì's death
must clearly have been in the first month of this year.
Various texts all say Cháoyì was killed in the first month of this year,
but the *Shílù* places it in the eleventh month of the first year,
and the old annals follow this,
also omitting the characters for "eleventh month."
The biography of Huáixiān mistakenly gives the first month as the third month.
Jiǎshēn
is the tenth day of the first month;
Jiǎchén
is the thirtieth day.
The new basic annals probably rely on the *Niándài Jì*,
but the *Niándài Jì* says Cháoyì died on the day Jǐhài in the eleventh month of the first year,
which is the same as the *Shílù*.
If he was killed in the first month,
his head should not have reached Cháng'ān by the tenth day.
It is suspected that he committed suicide on Jiǎshēn,
and his head was sent to the palace on Jiǎchén.
The new annals only use the *Niándài Jì*'s Jiǎshēn arrival at the palace as the day of suicide,
it is unknown what this is based on.
Now following the *Táng Lì*,
taking Jiǎchén as the day his head was sent to the capital.

He ordered them executed.
Then he reported the defeat of the enemy and the recovery of the city."
The Old Biography of Zǐyí states:
"Quán Xù sent the former imperial guard general Wáng Fǔ into Cháng'ān,
secretly forming connections with local strongmen as an internal response.
One day,
they simultaneously beat drums at Zhūquè Street,
and the Tibetan army fled in panic."
It also says:
"The archery officer Wáng Fǔ appointed himself Governor of the Capital District,
gathered two thousand troops,
and caused disturbances in the capital city.
Zǐyí summoned Fǔ
and killed him.
An edict appointed Zǐyí as acting capital city garrison commander."
The Biography of the Tǔbō states:
"Remnants of the Tǔbō were still in the city.
The military officer Wáng Fǔ and Censor-in-chief Wáng Zhòngshēng led troops entering from the imperial park,
beat drums and shouted loudly.
Zhòngshēng's troops also entered the city,
and the Tǔbō all fled."
If it were as stated in the Records of Bīn,
then Zǐyí killed Fǔ and usurped his merit.
I reckon Zǐyí certainly would not do such a thing.
Zǐyí's achievements and deeds
are praised as supreme in both ancient and modern times.
Líng Zhǔn, in writing his book,
often attacked his shortcomings,
which suggests there was old enmity,
and [his account] cannot be fully believed.
Now I follow the Family Biography of the Duke of Fényáng and the Old Biography of Zǐyí.)
Bái Xiàodé and the Bīn-Níng Military Commissioner Zhāng Yùnqí led troops to station in the capital district counties.
(The Capital District Prefecture administered twenty counties.
Wànnián and Cháng'ān were the imperial counties,
and the remaining counties were all capital district counties.)
The capital region was thus pacified.
9. The eunuch and Guangzhou Maritime Trade Commissioner Lǚ Tàiyī raised troops and started a rebellion.
(The Táng established Maritime Trade Commissioners in Guǎngzhōu to collect profits from merchant ships,
and at that time eunuchs were appointed to the post.
舶,
pronunciation bó.)
(Old Records: From Guǎngzhōu west to Duān Prefecture is two hundred forty lǐ.)
Government troops attacked and pacified it.
10. The Tibetans retreated to Fèngxiáng.
The military governor Sūn Zhìzhí closed the city gates and held fast,
and the Tibetans besieged it for several days.
The military governor of Zhènxī, Mǎ Lín, heard that the imperial carriage had gone to Shǎnzhōu,
and led over a thousand elite cavalry from Héxī to come to the rescue.
Fighting his way through, he reached Fèngxiáng,
where he encountered the Tibetans besieging the city.
Mǎ Lín led his troops, bows drawn and facing outward,
and charged into the city.
Without removing his armor,
he went out from the city to fight,
riding alone ahead of his soldiers and fighting fiercely,
capturing and beheading a thousand or so before returning.
The next day,
the enemy again approached the city and requested battle.
Mǎ Lín opened the suspended gate to await them.
Dù Yù said: The suspended gate
is installed on the inner city gate.
According to this, the gates of border cities today
have doors that can be opened and closed.
As for the suspended gate,
it is installed outside the gate threshold,
normally suspended and not lowered.
When enemies arrive, it is lowered to block the gate,
serving as a strong double closure.
They said:
"This general does not fear death;
we should avoid him."
They then left
and settled in the regions of Yuán, Huì, Chéng, and Wèi.
Yuánzhōu
is Gāopíng Commandery;
Huìzhōu
is Huìníng Commandery;
Chéngzhōu
is Tónggǔ Commandery;
all occupied strategic positions along the Hé and Lǒng regions, overlooking Táng territory.
11. In the twelfth month,
on Dīnghài,
the imperial carriage departed from Shǎnzhōu.
The Left Assistant Director Yán Zhēnqīng requested that the Emperor first pay homage at the imperial tombs and temples,
and then return to the palace.
Yuán Zǎi did not agree.
Yán Zhēnqīng angrily said:
"How can the court withstand Your Excellency ruining it again!"
From then on, Yuán Zǎi bore a grudge against him.
On Jiǎwǔ,
the Emperor reached Cháng'ān.
Guō Zǐyí led the officials of the city and the various armies to welcome him east of the Chǎnshuǐ,
prostrating themselves to await punishment.
The Emperor consoled them, saying:
"I did not employ you earlier,
and so things came to this."
12. Yú Cháo'ēn was appointed as the Military Surveillance, Pacification, and Disposition Commissioner of the Empire,
commanding the imperial guard troops.
His power and favor were unmatched.
Yú Cháo'ēn, due to his service in welcoming and escorting the Emperor in Shǎnzhōu,
received excessive delegation of authority and favor.
Getting rid of a snake and gaining a tiger—
this is what is called getting rid of a snake and gaining a tiger.
Chù,
read as chāng lǚ fān.
Shǐ,
read as shū lì fān.
Cháo,
read as zhí yáo fān.
He stationed troops to guard against the Tibetans.
Luò Fèngxiān was appointed as the Hùxiàn City Construction Commissioner,
and subsequently commanded those troops.
13. On Yǐwèi,
Miáo Jìnqīng was appointed as Grand Guardian,
Péi Zūnqìng was appointed as Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent,
and both were relieved of their administrative duties.
The Director of the Imperial Clan, Lǐ Xiàn, was appointed as Vice Director of the Chancellery and Participating in Determining Governmental Matters.
After Péi Zūnqìng left,
Yuán Zǎi's power grew even greater.
He used bribes to befriend the palace attendant Dǒng Xiù,
and had the Chief Clerk Zhuó Yīngqiàn secretly communicate with him.
Whatever the Emperor's intentions were focused on,
the Chief Clerk
is a provincial clerk.
Xiàn,
read as hù diǎn fān.
Shǔ,
read as zhī yù fān.
they would discern the subtleties and comply with his wishes,
so their words never failed to match.
Because of this, the Emperor grew even fonder of him.
Yīngqiàn
was from Jīnzhōu.
Jīnzhōu
is Ānkāng Commandery.
14. After the Tibetans had left,
the Prince of Guǎngwǔ, Lǐ Chénghóng, fled and hid in the wilderness.
The Emperor pardoned him and did not execute him.
On Bǐngshēn,
he was exiled to Huàzhōu.
Huàzhōu is Huàyīn Commandery,
180 lǐ from the capital.
15. Chéng Yuánzhèn, having been found guilty,
returned to Sānyuán.
Hearing that the Emperor had returned to the palace,
he dressed in women's clothing
and secretly entered Cháng'ān,
hoping to be employed again.
The Jīngzhào Prefecture arrested him and reported it.
16. The Tibetans captured the three prefectures of Sōng, Wéi, and Bǎo, as well as the two newly built cities of Yúnshān.
Sōngzhōu is Jiāochuān Commandery,
named after the Gānsōng Ridge within its borders.
In the 28th year of the Kāiyuán era,
Fèngzhōu Yúnshān Commandery was established from Dìnglián of Wéizhōu.
In the 8th year of the Tiānbǎo era,
its administrative seat was moved to Tiānbǎo Army,
and it was renamed Tiānbǎo Commandery.
In this year, it fell to the Tibetans.
By the first year of the Qiányuán era,
the succeeding Prince of Guīchéng, Dǒng Jiājùn, brought the commandery back to allegiance,
and it was then renamed Bǎozhōu.
Also, according to this, in the 8th year of Tiānbǎo, Yúnshān County was established from part of Dìnglián.
At that time, two new cities were probably built in the county.
Consequently, the various prefectures west of the mountains in Jiànnán also fell to the Tibetans.
1. In spring,
the first month,
on Rényín,
an edict stated that Chéng Yuánzhèn had changed his clothes and traveled in secret,
plotting treason.
He was exiled to Qínzhōu.
The Emperor remembered Yuánzhèn's achievements,
and also remembered his service in protection.
2. On Guǐmǎo,
Jiànnán East and West Circuits were merged into one,
with the Vice Director of the Chancellery, Yán Wǔ, appointed as military governor.
The division of Jiànnán into East and West Circuits
is recorded in the 220th scroll, first year of the Zhìdé era of Emperor Sùzōng.
Textual analysis says: The Old Biography states:
"Yán Wǔ was Junior Governor of Jīngzhào.
Due to Shǐ Simíng's obstructing troops,
he did not take up the post,
and was sent out as Prefect of Miánzhōu.
He was promoted to military governor of Dōngchuān.
The Retired Emperor decreed that the two Chuān be merged into one circuit,
and Yán Wǔ was appointed military governor of Jiànnán."
The New Biography states:
"Yán Wǔ was Junior Governor,
implicated with Fáng Guǎn,
demoted to Bāzhōu.
After a long time,
he was transferred to Dōngchuān."
The rest is the same as the Old Biography.
According to this, Shǐ Simíng obstructed troops in Hé and Luò;
how could the Junior Governor of Jīngzhào not take up his post!
It was this year that East and West Chuān were first merged into one circuit;
how could it have been decreed by the Retired Emperor!
Both the New and Old Biographies are mistaken.
3. On Bǐngwǔ,
the Acting Minister of Justice, Yán Zhēnqīng, was sent to pacify the Shòufāng army camp.
When the Emperor was in Shǎnzhōu,

but the Emperor did not permit it.
By now,
the Emperor ordered Zhēnqīng to persuade Huái'ēn to come to court.
He replied:
"When Your Majesty was in Shǎnzhōu,
if I had gone
and admonished him with loyalty and righteousness,
urging him to come to the rescue,
there might still have been reason for him to come.
Now that Your Majesty has returned to the palace,
he cannot advance to serve the sovereign,
nor can he retreat and disband his troops.
To summon him now—
how would he be willing to come!
Moreover, those who say Huái'ēn is rebelling
are only Xīn Yúnjīng, Luò Fèngxiān, Lǐ Bàoyù, and Yú Cháo'ēn—four people.
All the other ministers say he is wronged.
Your Majesty would do better to replace Huái'ēn with Guō Zǐyí;

At that time, the Assistant Prefect of Fénzhōu, Lǐ Bàozhēn,
a paternal cousin of Bàoyù,
knew that Huái'ēn had treacherous intentions,

The Emperor was worried about Huái'ēn,

He replied:
"This is not worth worrying about.
The officers and soldiers of Shòufāng miss Guō Zǐyí
like children and younger brothers miss their fathers and elder brothers.
Huái'ēn deceived his troops, saying
that Guō Zǐyí had already been killed by Yú Cháo'ēn.
The troops believed it,
and so they serve him.
If Your Majesty truly appoints Zǐyí to lead Shòufāng,

The Emperor agreed.

the Ritual Commissioner Dù Hóngjiàn
(The Táng Huìyào states: At the time of Emperor Gāozǔ’s abdication and succession,

Shǐ,
read as shū lì fān.
“From now on, for sacrifices at the Circular Mound and Square Mound, we request that Tàizǔ be the accompanying deity;

According to the Táng system: the winter solstice sacrifice was held at the Circular Mound,
the summer solstice sacrifice at the Square Mound,

5 On the day Yǐmǎo,

“Huái’ēn and his son have deeply betrayed Us.

Xiàn,

Sàn,

Cháo,
read as zhí yáo fān.

12 Púgù Yáng besieged Yúcì,

Lǐ Guāngyì was garrisoned at Qíxiàn,

The troops could not advance,

Those lagging behind
were soldiers who could not keep up with the main force.
Shè,
read as ér yì fān;
the same applies to nǎi shè and shè zhī below.
“General, why are you shooting at people?”
Yù said:

so what harm is there in shooting them!”
Bái Yù and Jiāo Huī wanted to kill Yáng,

Yáng reprimanded them for being slow,
and a Hu soldier said:
“We are riding horses,
it is the Hàn soldiers who are not moving.”
Yáng beat the Hàn soldiers,
and the soldiers all became resentful and angry,

That evening,

When Púgù Huái’ēn heard of this,

what shall we do now!”
Huái’ēn did not reply,
but bowed twice and went out.
His mother picked up a knife and chased after him, saying:
“I will kill this traitor for the state,
and take his heart to apologize to the three armies.”
Huái’ēn fled quickly,
and escaped,
then crossed the river north with three hundred of his followers.
They crossed the river west from Fénzhōu,
heading north,
toward Língzhōu.
At that time, the general of Shuòfāng, Hún Shìzhī, was guarding Língzhōu.
When Huáién’s dispatch arrived,
stating that the entire army was returning to the garrison,
Shìzhī said:
“That is not so.
This must be a case of the troops collapsing.”

How can we not admit them!”
Shìzhī hesitated and could not decide.
Huáién moved swiftly,
arriving before the advance scouts,
and Shìzhī had no choice but to admit him.
Zhāng Sháo informed Huáién of Shìzhī’s plan,
and Huáién, taking Sháo as a spy,
killed Shìzhī and took command of his army.
The historian remarks that Hún Shìzhī brought disaster upon himself by failing to make a decisive judgment in the face of events.
The character 間 (jiàn)
is pronounced as in ancient times, like 莧 (xiàn).
Later, Huáién said:
“Shìzhī
was my uncle,
and yet he betrayed him.
How could he be loyal to me!”
Another day,
on some pretext, he had him beaten with a staff,
breaking his shinbone,
and left him in Mí’é City, where he died.
Zhāng Sháo’s death was well-deserved.
The character 折 (zhé)
is pronounced as 而設翻 (ér shè fān).
The character 脛 (jìng)

脛 (jìng)
means the stem of the leg.
The capital military inspector Zhāng Wéiyuè was in Qìnzhōu.

Zǐyí sent his staff officer Lú Liàng to Fénzhōu.
Military governors, prefectures, and government offices all had staff officers and traveling officers.
Staff officers served as attendants in the yamen,
while traveling officers were sent on missions throughout the land.
After the Five Dynasties period,
military officials were commonly reviled as “staff officers.”
Zǐyí ordered him to verify the report.
Zǐyí memorialized that Wéiyuè had killed Yáng.
The Examination of Discrepancies says: The Family Biography of Fényáng states:
“The official Lú Mǎng
was first sent by the Duke to Fénzhōu to console and instruct.

he slandered those who did not align with him
and favored those who bribed him.
