Guō Gōng reported that Rúyuè had killed Yáng,
and an imperial edict rewarded him.
The generals said this and that,
and Guō Gōng then investigated Liàng’s crime
and had him beaten to death.”
Now, taking both books into account,
Mǎng’s official title follows the Bīnzhì.
The ministers entered to offer congratulations,
but the Emperor looked sorrowful and displeased,
saying:
“I failed to trust others,
causing a meritorious minister to fall into ruin.
I am deeply ashamed of this.
What is there to congratulate?”
He ordered Huáién’s mother to be brought to Cháng’ān by carriage,
where she was treated with great generosity.
After more than a month,
she passed away from old age.
The historian says she died of old age
to clarify that she was not killed.
The meritorious officials were all moved and sighed.
On the day Wùyín,
Guō Zǐyí went to Fénzhōu.
The Examination of Discrepancies says: The Veritable Records state:
“On Dīngyǒu in the twelfth month of the first year of Guǎngdé,
Púgù Yáng was killed by his subordinate Zhāng Wéiyuè,
who led his troops to join Guō Zǐyí.
When Huáién heard of this,
he abandoned his camp and fled alone to the northern tribes.”
However, the reason the Shuòfāng troops did not support the Púgù clan
was because Zǐyí was their commander.
Even if it did not occur after Zǐyí was appointed military governor of Shuòfāng,
it should have happened after he was appointed deputy marshal of Hédōng.

Emperor Dàizōng held a banquet in the three halls to send him off.
On the twenty-sixth day,
he departed from the upper capital.
In the second month,
he arrived in Hézhōng,
concurrently serving as grand commissioner of Shuòfāng.
On Wùyín,
he went to Fénzhōu.
On Jiǎshēn,
he returned to Hézhōng.”
The Bīnzhì states:

In the second month,
Púgù Yáng led his troops to attack Yúcì,
but after more than ten days, he failed to capture it,”
and so on.
Thus, Yáng’s death certainly did not occur in the twelfth month of the previous year.
Now, in connection with Zǐyí’s going to Fénzhōu,
it is mentioned together.
All the troops returned to him,
and they were all moved to tears,

It ultimately turned out as Yán Zhēnqīng and Lǐ Bàozhēn had said.
He had him beaten to death.
The Emperor, seeing that Lǐ Bàozhēn’s words had proven true,
promoted him to deputy director of the Palace Administration.
13 When the Emperor fled to Shǎn,
Lǐ Guāngbì ultimately delayed and did not come.
The Emperor, fearing that this would create a rift,

repeatedly sent palace envoys to inquire after her.

The Emperor brought his mother to Cháng’ān,
provided for her generously,

14 On the day Wùzǐ,
a general amnesty was declared throughout the land.
15 Since the turmoil of the rebellion,
the Biàn River had silted up and fallen into disuse.
Those transporting grain by waterway had to go from the Jiāng and Hàn rivers to Liáng and Yáng,
a circuitous, perilous, and laborious route.
Ever since Ān Lùshān rebelled,
the roads through Guān and Luò were blocked,
and grain transport had to go upstream along the Jiāng River into the Hàn River,
reaching Liáng and Yáng.
Thus, the Biàn Canal silted up and was left unrepaired.
On the day Jǐyǒu,
the Crown Prince’s guest Liú Yàn was appointed transport commissioner for Hénán, Jiāng, and Huái regions,
and discussions were held to reopen the Biàn River.
On the day Gēngxū,
Yàn was also ordered to work with the military governors of the various circuits to equalize taxes and corvée duties,

spanning only seven days in total.
How could there be a situation where memorials and reports did not reach the court for over ten days!
Zǐyí was the commander-in-chief,
facing a strong enemy across the battlefield.
How could he abandon his army to enter the court!
The Fényáng family records also show no such event of entering the court at this time.
Therefore, it is not adopted here.
On the day Bǐngyín,
the Huíhé and Tǔbō forces joined together to besiege Jīngyáng.
Guō Zǐyí ordered his generals to strictly maintain defenses and not engage in battle.
By dusk,
the two enemy forces retreated and camped at Běiyuán,
which is north of Jīngyáng.
On the day Dīngmǎo,
they returned to the city walls.
At this time,
the Huíhé and Tǔbō, having heard of Púgù Huái'ēn's death,
were already contending for supremacy,
were not on good terms,
and camped separately.
Guō Zǐyí knew this.
The Huíhé were west of the city.
Guō Zǐyí sent his adjutant general Lǐ Guāngzàn and others to persuade them.
An adjutant general is
a commanding officer at the headquarters,
in charge of the commander's personal guards.
Persuade,
read as shuì;
the following instances of persuasion are the same.
The Huíhé did not believe it,
saying:
"Is Lord Guō really here?
You are deceiving me.
If he is truly here,
can we see him?"
Lǐ Guāngzàn returned to report.
Guō Zǐyí said:
"Now we are outnumbered and cannot match them,
making it difficult to overcome them by force.
In the past, we had a very strong covenant with the Huíhé.
It would be better for me to step forward and persuade them.
We might subdue them without fighting."
The generals requested to select five hundred armored cavalry as his escort.
Guō Zǐyí said:
"That would only cause harm."
Guō Xī grasped his horse's reins and remonstrated:
"They are
tigers and wolves;
you, sir,
are the nation's commander-in-chief.
How can you offer yourself as bait to the enemy!"
Guō Zǐyí said:
"If we fight now,
both father and son will die, and the state will be in danger.
If I go and speak to them with utmost sincerity,
perhaps they will fortunately listen,
and that would be a blessing for the entire realm!
Otherwise,
I alone will perish, but my family will be preserved."
This is how Guō Zǐyí carefully assessed the advantages and disadvantages and weighed the priorities.
"Go!"
He then rode out of the gate with a few horsemen,
sending someone to shout:
"Lord Lìng is coming!"
Guō Zǐyí was then the Zhōngshū Lìng,
hence he was called Lord Lìng.
Their great commander, Héhúlù Dūdū Yàogéluó,
who was the khan's brother,
stood before the battle line with his bow drawn and arrow nocked.
Guō Zǐyí removed his helmet, shed his armor, cast aside his spear, and advanced.
The Huíhé chieftains looked at each other and said:
"It is him!"
They all dismounted and bowed in a circle.
Guō Zǐyí also dismounted,
stepped forward, and took Yàogéluó's hand,
reproaching him:
"You, the Huíhé, have rendered great service to the Táng,
referring to raising troops to help the Táng pacify Ān and Shǐ.
Why did you break the covenant,
deeply enter our territory,
invade and press upon the capital's counties?
The counties subordinate to the Táng capital,
those attached to the city were called 'chì',
and 'cì chì'.
For example, Zhāoyìng, Fèngtiān, Lǐquán, and other counties were 'cì chì'.
The rest were capital counties.
You have created enmity,
turned your back on kindness and virtue, and aided a rebellious minister.
How foolish this is!
Moreover, Huái'ēn rebelled against his sovereign and abandoned his mother.
This refers to Huái'ēn amassing troops in Fén and Jiàng,
then later rebelling and returning to Língwǔ,
abandoning his mother in Fénzhōu.
Now I have come forward alone.
If you seize and kill me,
my officers and soldiers will certainly fight you to the death."
Yàogéluó said:
"Huái'ēn deceived me,
saying the Heavenly Khagan had passed away,
and Lord Lìng had also died,
that China had no ruler.
That is why I dared to come with him.
Now I know the Heavenly Khagan is in the Upper Capital.
Since the Zhēnguàn period, when the chieftains of the four barbarian tribes requested Tàizōng to be the Heavenly Khagan,
thereafter the barbarians generally referred to the Son of Heaven as the Heavenly Khagan.
The Upper Capital
is Cháng'ān.
Huái'ēn has also been killed by Heaven.
How could we be willing to fight Lord Lìng!"
Guō Zǐyí then persuaded him:
"The Tǔbō are unprincipled.
Taking advantage of the turmoil in our country,
they disregarded the kinship of uncle and nephew.
The Tǔbō married a Táng princess,
becoming a state with uncle-nephew relations.
Again,
read as fù.
Persuade,
read as shuì.
They burned and ravaged our capital region.
The wealth they plundered is immeasurable.
Horses, cattle, and various livestock,
stretching for hundreds of lǐ,
are scattered across the wilderness.
This is Heaven's gift to you.
Preserve your army and renew friendship,
defeat the enemy and seize riches.
Considering your interests,
what could be more advantageous than this!
Do not miss this opportunity."
Yàogéluó said:
"I was misled by Huái'ēn,
and have deeply wronged you, sir.
Now I ask to exert my full strength for you, sir,
to attack the Tǔbō and atone for my fault.
However, Huái'ēn's son
is the brother of the khatun.
I hope you will spare him and not kill him."
Guō Zǐyí agreed.
The Huíhé onlookers
formed two wings,
gradually advancing.
Guō Zǐyí's subordinates also advanced.
Guō Zǐyí waved his hand to make them retreat.
He then took wine and drank with the chieftains.
Yàogéluó asked Guō Zǐyí to first hold the wine and make a vow.
Guō Zǐyí poured wine on the ground and said:
"Long live the Great Táng Son of Heaven!
Long live the Huíhé Khagan as well!
Long live the generals and ministers of both states!
Whoever breaks this covenant,
may they fall in battle,
and their family perish."
When the cup reached Yàogéluó,
he also poured wine on the ground and said:
"As Lord Lìng has vowed!"
Then all the chieftains were greatly pleased and said:
"Previously, we had two shamans with the army.
The shamans said this campaign would be very safe,
that we would not fight the Táng,
but meet a great man and return.
Now it has indeed come true."
Guō Zǐyí gave them three thousand bolts of colored silk.
The chieftains divided it to reward the shamans.
Guō Zǐyí finally settled the covenant and returned.
When the Tǔbō heard of this,
that night,
they led their troops and fled.
The Huíhé sent their chieftain Shíyěnà and five others to see the Son of Heaven.
Yàogéluó led his troops in pursuit of the Tibetans,
and Guō Zǐyí sent Bái Yuánguāng to lead elite cavalry to join him;
on Guǐyǒu day,
they fought west of Língtái on the plains,
and inflicted a major defeat on them.
Língtái—
this was the location of Chúngū County in the Hàn dynasty.
In the first year of the Tiānbǎo era,
it was renamed Língtái.
According to the Jiǔyùzhì: Língtái County
is located ninety lǐ east of Jīngzhōu.
According to the Old History,
the place where the Tibetans were defeated
was fifty lǐ west of Língtái County,
at a place called Chìshān Ridge.
They recovered four thousand men and women who had been captured.
On Bǐngzǐ day,
they again defeated them east of Jīngzhōu.
Examination of discrepancies: The Veritable Records states:
"In the tenth month,
the Tibetans retreated to Bīnzhōu,
where they encountered the Uighurs,
and once again joined forces to raid.
On Xīnyǒu day,
they raided Fèngtiān.
On Yǐhài day,
the Uighurs, because Púgù Huái'ēn had died,
turned against the Tibetans.
On Dīngchǒu day,
Guō Zǐyí rode alone to the Uighur camp,
removed his helmet and spoke with the Uighur general,
reproaching him for breaking the agreement,
and then made a covenant with them.
On Jǐmǎo day,
the Uighur leaders Shíyěnà and five others came to court.
On Gēngchén day,
Zǐyí sent Bái Yuánguāng to lead elite troops and join with several thousand Uighur soldiers to inflict a major defeat on over a hundred thousand Tibetan troops west of Língtái County on the plains."
The Family Biography of Fényáng states:
"On the eighth day of the tenth month,
the Tibetans and Uighurs jointly besieged Jīngyáng,
encamping on the northern plains.
That night,
the Duke ordered each direction to clear two roads,
preparing for battle the next morning.
The next day,
the enemy arrived again,
with even greater numbers of troops and armor.
The Duke sent the commander Lǐ Guāngzàn and others to go out and admonish them,
but they would not accept it,
and requested a decisive battle.
The Duke, considering the enemy cavalry strong,
and also that he was outnumbered,
with a lone army and no reinforcements,
ordered the camp gates opened,
and rode out on a single horse.
The Vice Director of the Ministry of War Mǎ Xí and the Vice Director of the Bureau of Receptions Chén Hóng at the time followed on a single horse.
The Uighurs, together with the Dudu Yàogéluó and the chancellor, stood before the battle array,
with bows drawn and facing him,
the Duke went forward and rebuked them, etc.
Yàogéluó and the others were bewildered and ashamed,
prostrated themselves and asked for punishment,
and then made a covenant with them.
When the Tibetans heard of this,
at midnight,
they withdrew their troops and fled.
The Uighur Yàogéluó and others immediately pursued them,
and the Duke sent Bái Yuánguāng and others to follow,
on the fifteenth day,
they reached Língtái,
and defeated Shàngjiéxī's hundred thousand troops.
On the eighteenth day,
east of Jīngzhōu they again defeated them."
The Old Biography of Zǐyí states:
"Zǐyí arrived from Hézhōng,
and encamped at Jīngyáng,
but the enemy cavalry had already assembled.
Zǐyí's army numbered over ten thousand men,
and the various barbarians surrounded them in several layers.
Zǐyí sent Lǐ Guóchén and Gāo Shēng to hold the east,
Wèi Chǔyù to face the south,
Chén Huíguāng to face the west,
Zhū Yuáncóng to face the north,
and Zǐyí himself led two thousand armored cavalry to appear and disappear around the left, right, front, and rear.
The barbarians saw and asked:
'Who is that?'
They replied:
'It is Lord Guō.' The Uighurs said:
'Is Lord Guō still alive?
Púgù Huái'ēn said the Heavenly Khagan had abandoned the realm,
and Lord Guō had also passed away,
that China had no ruler,
and so we followed him here.
Now if Lord Guō is alive,
is the Heavenly Khagan alive?'
They replied:
'The Emperor lives ten thousand years without end.'
The Uighurs all said:
'Huái'ēn deceived us.'
Zǐyí again sent someone to admonish them, etc.
The Uighurs said:
'We were told Lord Guō had died,
otherwise,
why would he have come here!
If Lord Guō is truly alive,
how can we see him?'
Zǐyí was about to go out,
and the various generals advised against it.
Zǐyí said:
'Now our strength is certainly no match,
but utmost sincerity moves the spirits,
how much more so these barbarians!'"
The Biography of the Uighurs states:
"The Tibetan generals Mǎ Chóngyīng and others in the tenth month initially withdrew,
taking the old road back to Bīnzhōu.
The Uighur leaders Luódágān and others led over two thousand of their cavalry to Jīngyáng to request surrender,
Zǐyí agreed,
and led several thousand men in armor with bows drawn.
The Uighur interpreter said:
'We have come not with evil intent,
but to see Lord Guō.'
Zǐyí said:
'I am Lord Guō.'
The Uighurs said:
'Please remove your armor.'
Zǐyí then removed his helmet and spear armor,
spurred his horse forward and straightened his body.
The Uighur chieftains looked at each other and said:
'It is him!'
Then they dismounted and bowed in a circle.
Zǐyí also dismounted,
took the hands of the Uighur general Dudu Yàogéluó and others,
and reproached them, saying:
'The state knows the Uighurs have merit,
and has rewarded you greatly,
why did you break the agreement,
and invade the royal domain!
I must fight you,
why then do you surrender!
I have come alone into your camp,
you may capture me as you wish,
but my officers and soldiers below will certainly fight you.'
The Uighur interpreter again said:
'Huái'ēn was disloyal,
and came to report to the Khagan, saying,
"The Táng Son of Heaven has now gone to Jiāng and Huái,
and Lord Guō also does not command troops,"
and so we dared to come.
Now we know the Heavenly Khagan is at the upper capital,
and Lord Guō is the general,
and Heaven has also killed Huái'ēn,
we now request to pursue and kill the Tibetans,
take their sheep and horses,
to repay the state's kindness.'"
The Bīnzhì states:
"On the twenty-fourth day of the tenth month,
the Uighurs approached Jīngyáng,
arrayed west of the outer wall,
and one who spoke Chinese said:
'Who is the general in the city?'
The military officer replied:
'It is Lord Guō.'
The barbarians said:
'Lord Guō is dead,
you are deceiving us.'
Lord Guō heard this,
and alone with five or six household servants in ordinary clothes went to see them.
His son Guō Xī and others grabbed his horse's bridle to stop him,
the Duke struck their hands and said:
'Go away.'
He sent someone to inform the barbarians,
and reined in his horse and approached them.
The Uighurs looked closely and said:
'It is him!'
They dismounted and all bowed,
saying:
'At first we did not know Lord Guō was still alive,
today we surrender,
is that acceptable!'
Lord Guō entered their midst,
took wine and drank with them.
The barbarians again requested:
'We fear we are not trusted,
we wish to attack the Tibetans to prove ourselves.'
Lord Guō agreed.
The Uighurs attacked the Tibetans,
pursued them,
on the thirtieth day,
defeated the Tibetan troops at Língtái,
18. Initially,
Emperor Sùzōng appointed Guō Yīngyì, the military governor of Shǎnxī, to command the Divine Strategy Army,
with the eunuch Yú Cháo'ēn supervising the army.
When Yīngyì entered the capital to serve as Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
Cháo'ēn took sole command of the army.
When the emperor traveled to Shǎn,
Cháo'ēn led the troops stationed in Shǎn and the Divine Strategy Army to welcome and escort him,
all of which were then called the Divine Strategy Army,
and the emperor visited their camp.
After the capital was pacified,
Cháo'ēn brought the army back into the palace precincts,
personally commanding it,
but it still could not yet be ranked alongside the Northern Army.
The Northern Army refers to
the Six Armies of the Northern Gate.
Cháo'ēn stationed the Divine Strategy Army with the emperor in the imperial gardens,
and its power gradually grew,
being divided into left and right wings,
and it came to occupy a position superior to the Northern Army.
This records the origins of the Divine Strategy Army's rise to power.
19. Guō Zǐyí, fearing that Púgù Míngchén, Lǐ Jiànzhōng, and others—all fierce generals under Púgù Huái'ēn—might flee to foreign tribes,
requested to recruit them.
Míngchén was
Huái'ēn's nephew,
and at the time was in the Huíhé camp.
The emperor issued an edict pardoning the crimes of these and other former generals who had rendered meritorious service,
ordering the Huíhé to send them back.
On the rénwǔ day,
Míngchén surrendered with over a thousand cavalry.
Zǐyí sent Mùróng Xiūzhēn, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel, to deliver a letter persuading the Dǎngxiàng chieftains Zhèng Tíng and Hǎo Dé,
who all went to Fèngxiáng to surrender.
20. On the jiǎshēn day,
Zhōu Zhìguāng went to the court to present captives,
and after staying two nights, returned to his garrison.
Zhìguāng bore the unpunished crime of unauthorized killing—
referring to the crime of killing Zhāng Lín and the family members of Dù Miǎn.
Punish,
zhí zhī fān.
21. On the yǐyǒu day,
over two hundred Huíhé officials, including the Húlù Dudū, came for an audience,
and they were given a total of one hundred thousand bolts of silk as gifts;
the treasury was emptied,
and officials' salaries were taxed to provide for them.

Later
In the first year of Yǒngtài
(yǐsì, 765)
1. In the intercalary tenth month,
on the yǐsì day,
Guō Zǐyí came to court.
Zǐyí, citing that Língwǔ had only recently been recovered—
after Púgù Huái'ēn's death,
Língwǔ was recovered—
and the tribal settlements were not yet pacified,
requested that Lù Sìgōng, the military provisions commissioner of Sānyuán, be appointed to garrison it.
The military provisions commissioner
is the provisions commissioner.
The death of Yáng Zhìliè is recorded in the second year of Guǎngdé in the previous scroll.
The emperor agreed to all his requests.
2. On the dīngwèi day,
the officials requested to hand over their official fields to supply military provisions.
The Táng system: first-rank officials received twelve qǐng of official land,
second-rank ten qǐng,
third-rank nine qǐng,
fourth-rank seven qǐng,
fifth-rank six qǐng,
sixth-rank four qǐng,
seventh-rank three qǐng and fifty mǔ,
eighth-rank two qǐng and fifty mǔ,
ninth-rank two qǐng,
all located within a hundred lǐ.
For the governors, protectors, and officials of princely households in the various prefectures: second-rank twelve qǐng,
third-rank ten qǐng,
fourth-rank eight qǐng,
fifth-rank seven qǐng,
sixth-rank five qǐng,
seventh-rank four qǐng,
eighth-rank three qǐng,
ninth-rank two qǐng and fifty mǔ.
For officials of garrisons, forts, passes, ferries, mountains, and rivers: fifth-rank five qǐng,
sixth-rank three qǐng and fifty mǔ,
seventh-rank three qǐng,
eighth-rank two qǐng,
ninth-rank one qǐng and fifty mǔ.
For the Central Guard generals, superior prefecture commanders: six qǐng,
medium prefecture five qǐng and fifty mǔ,
inferior prefecture and generals five qǐng,
superior prefecture deputy commanders four qǐng,
medium prefecture three qǐng and fifty mǔ,
inferior prefecture three qǐng,
superior prefecture chief clerks and assistant commanders three qǐng,
medium and inferior prefectures two qǐng and fifty mǔ.
For princely household army commanders: five qǐng and fifty mǔ,
deputy army commanders four qǐng,
personal guards and imperial bodyguards three qǐng,
superior prefecture military officers two qǐng,
medium and inferior prefectures one qǐng and fifty mǔ,
colonels one qǐng and twenty mǔ,
majors one qǐng,
squad leaders and deputies eighty mǔ.
Below the rank of prince,
there were also permanent estates of one hundred qǐng.
For active-duty officials: first-rank sixty qǐng,
commandery prince, active-duty officials of sub-first-rank fifty qǐng,
duke of state, active-duty officials of sub-second-rank thirty-five qǐng,
commandery duke, active-duty officials of sub-third-rank twenty-five qǐng,
county duke, active-duty officials of sub-third-rank twenty qǐng,
marquis, active-duty officials of sub-fourth-rank twelve qǐng,
viscount, active-duty officials of sub-fifth-rank eight qǐng,
baron, active-duty officials of sub-fifth-rank five qǐng,
sixth and seventh ranks two qǐng and fifty-eight mǔ,
eighth and ninth ranks two qǐng.
Supreme Pillar of State thirty qǐng,
Pillar of State twenty-five qǐng,
Supreme Protector of the Army twenty qǐng,
Protector of the Army fifteen qǐng,
Supreme Commandant of Light Chariots ten qǐng,
Commandant of Light Chariots seven qǐng,
Supreme Commandant of Cavalry six qǐng,
Commandant of Cavalry four qǐng,
Valiant Cavalry and Flying Cavalry Commandant eighty mǔ,
Cloud Cavalry and Martial Cavalry Commandant sixty mǔ.
For titular officials of the fifth rank and above,
the allocation was the same as for active-duty officials.
3. On the wùshēn day,
the Vice Minister of Revenue, Lù Sìgōng, was appointed military governor of Shuòfāng.
Sìgōng cleared the thorns and brambles,
established the military headquarters,
and his authority and orders were greatly enforced.
4. On the jǐyǒu day,
Guō Zǐyí returned to Hézhōng.
Zǐyí returned to garrison Hézhōng after attending court in the capital.
Return,
cóng xuān fān,
also pronounced as the original character.
5. Initially,
the military governor of Jiànnán, Yán Wǔ, recommended General Cuī Gàn as prefect of Lìzhōu.
At that time, Jiànxīn was newly in turmoil,
with mountain bandits blocking the roads,
and Gàn suppressed them.
When Wǔ again became military governor of Jiànnán,
he bribed Zhāng Xiànchéng, the military governor of Shānnán Xīdào, to request Gàn.
Lìzhōu
was the ancient fief of the Marquis of Jū,
and in the Qín and Hàn dynasties, it was the territory of Jiāméng.
During Shǔ Hàn, it was Hànshòu County,
in Jìn it was Jìnshòu,
in Liáng it was Lízhōu,
and later changed to Lìzhōu;
in Tiānbǎo it was Yìchāng Commandery,
and in Qiányuán it was restored as Lìzhōu,
under the jurisdiction of Shānnán Xīdào.
Gàn,
gǔ dàn fān.
He went to Wǔ.
Wǔ appointed him prefect of Hànzhōu,
and had him lead troops to attack the Tǔbō in the Western Mountains,
capturing several of their cities in succession,
and expanding the territory by several hundred lǐ.
Hànzhōu
was the territory of Luò County, Shífāng, and Miánzhú in Hàn times,
established as Hànzhōu in Táng during Chuígōng,
in Tiānbǎo it was Déyáng Commandery,
and in Qiányuán it was restored as a prefecture.
When Wǔ died,
as recorded in the fourth month of the previous scroll,
the chief military commissioner Guō Yīnggàn,
Yīngyì's younger brother,
together with the chief inspector Guō Jiālín, requested Yīngyì as military governor.
Gàn, then the chief military commissioner of the Western Mountains,
together with his subordinates, requested the general Wáng Chóngjùn as military governor.
As the court had already appointed Yīngyì,
Yīngyì bore a grudge against him.
Upon arriving in Chéngdū a few days later,
he falsely accused Chóngjùn of a crime and executed him.
He summoned Gàn back to Chéngdū,
but Gàn declined, citing the need to guard against the Tǔbō,
and could not return.
Yīngyì grew even angrier,
cutting off his supplies to distress him.
Gàn moved deep into the mountains,
and Yīngyì personally led troops to attack him,
claiming to assist Gàn in defense.
A heavy snow fell,
with snow several feet deep in the valleys,
and many soldiers and horses froze to death.
Gàn led his troops out to attack,
and Yīngyì was badly defeated,
gathering his remaining troops,
barely a thousand men, and returned.
Yīngyì governed with
harshness, arrogance, and extravagance,
showing no concern for his soldiers,
causing widespread discontent and resentment.
When Emperor Xuánzōng left Shǔ,
he converted the traveling palace where he had stayed into a Taoist temple,
and even cast a golden statue of himself;
Yīngyì, admiring the lush beauty of its bamboo and trees,
petitioned to turn it into a military camp,
and thus moved the golden statue away,
taking up residence there himself.
Gàn declared that Yīngyì was rebelling,
for otherwise,
why would he move the golden statue and occupy the place himself!
Thereupon, he led over five thousand of his troops to attack Chéngdū.
On Xīnsì,
they fought west of the city,
and Yīngyì was utterly defeated.
Gàn then entered Chéngdū,
slaughtering Yīngyì’s family.
Yīngyì fled alone on horseback to Jiǎnzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Jiǎnzhōu
was the territory of the Hàn dynasty’s Niúbǐ County.
In the third year of the Rénshòu era of the Suí dynasty,
Yáng'ān and Píngquán from Yìzhōu,
and Zīyáng from Zīzhōu,
were separated to establish Jiǎnzhōu,
and the prefecture had a Làijiǎn Pond,
from which it derived its name.
(Yīngyì’s) head was sent to Gàn.
The adjutant of Qióngzhōu, Bǎi Màolín; the adjutant of Lúzhōu, Yáng Zǐlín; and the adjutant of Jiànzhōu, Lǐ Chāngnáo
Sòng Bái said: Qióngzhōu,
was the Hàn dynasty’s Línqióng County,
established as Qióngzhōu by Liáng’s Prince Wǔlíng Jì,
taking its name from the Qiónglái Mountain on its southern border.
Lúzhōu,
was the Hàn dynasty’s Jiāngyáng County,
established as Lúzhōu by Liáng,
taking its name from the Lú River.
Jiànzhōu,
was the Hàn dynasty’s Zǐtóng County of Guǎnghàn,
established as Ānzhōu by Liáng,
and renamed Shǐzhōu by Western Wèi;
in the second year of the Xiāntiān era of the Táng dynasty,
it was changed to Jiànzhōu,
taking its name from Jiàngé.

"The materials of the capital market"
refers to timber accumulated in the capital market.
South of the Lónghuá Nunnery in the Shēngdào Ward, on the third street east of the Imperial City and the fifth street east of the Zhūquè Street in Cháng'ān,
there was a winding stream,
called Qǔjiāng.
In the Qín dynasty, this place was the Yíchūn Garden and Gāizhōu;
in the Hàn dynasty, it was the Lèyóu Garden.
During the Kāiyuán era, it was dredged and excavated,
becoming a scenic spot.
To its south were the Zǐyún Tower and Fúróng Garden;
to its west were the Xìng Garden and Cí'ēn Temple.
Along the riverbanks, reeds and cattails grew lush and green,
willow shades gathered from all sides,
with clear waves and red lotus flowers,
reflecting each other in a delightful manner.
For Huáqīng Palace, see the sixth year of the Tiānbǎo era in scroll 215.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: The number "yì" (億) has two methods, large and small: the small method
takes ten as the base unit,
where one hundred thousand is one yì,
and ten yì is one zhào;
the large method
takes ten thousand as the base unit,
counting ten thousand to ten thousand,
so ten thousand ten-thousands is one yì,
and counting from yì to ten thousand again,
ten thousand yì is one zhào.
In summary, it was said:
"The late Empress's virtuous deeds
do not require a temple to enhance their glory;
the long-term plans of the state
should prioritize the people as the foundation.
Abandoning the people for the sake of a temple—
what kind of blessing is that!"
It was also said:
"It is better to have no temple than
to have no people!"
And further:
"Your Majesty should emulate the humble palaces of Xià Yǔ,
taking him as a model,
rather than following the fashion of Emperor Liáng Wǔ in erecting pagodas and temples!"
Another memorial stated,
summarizing:
"The wise kings of antiquity accumulated virtue to attain blessings,
not squandering wealth to seek blessings;
they cultivated virtue to avert disasters,
not exhausting the people to ward off calamities.
Now, construction is rushed,
with no rest day or night.
Those unable to meet the demands are flogged with rods and whips,
and cries of sorrow and pain fill the roads.
To expect blessings from this—
I fear it will not be so."
It also said:
"Your Majesty turns away from the right path within your heart,
seeking trivial aid from external things,
indulging in the misguided plans of those around you,
harming the grand strategies of imperial rule.
I privately grieve for Your Majesty!"
All these petitions were ignored without response.
Examination of discrepancies: In the collection of Yè's works,
the earlier memorial is dated the 25th day of the eighth month, and the later one the 12th day of the ninth month.
Here, it is mentioned in connection with the temple construction.
Initially,
the Emperor favored sacrificial rituals
but did not particularly esteem Buddhism.
When Yuán Zài, Wáng Jìn, and Dù Hóngjiàn served as chancellors,
all three were fond of Buddhism;
Jìn was especially devout,
abstaining from meat and blood.
"Hūn" (葷)
refers to pungent vegetables.
"Blood"
means taking it from slaughtered livestock.
"Hào" (好)
is pronounced with the fourth tone.
The Emperor once asked them,
"Buddhist teachings speak of retribution—
is it truly real or not?"
Zài and others replied:
"The enduring fortune of our state
must stem from accumulated merit in past lives.
How else could it be achieved!
Since this merit is already determined,
even if minor calamities occur occasionally,
they ultimately cannot cause harm.
Thus, when Ān Lùshān and Shǐ Sīmíng's rebellions were at their peak, both met with filial disasters—
meaning Ān Qìngxù killed Lùshān, and Shǐ Cháoyì killed Sīmíng.
They died of illness upon departure;
the Huíhé and Tǔbō launched large-scale invasions deep into our territory,
yet retreated without fighting—
events all recorded in the previous scroll of last year.
How can one say there is no retribution!"
The Emperor thus deeply believed in it,
often hosting over a hundred monks for meals in the palace.
When enemies approached, he would order monks to lecture on the Rénwáng Sūtra to ward them off—
the so-called "State-Protecting Rénwáng Sūtra."
The foreign monk Bùkōng
rose to the rank of a minister or supervisor,
was enfeoffed as a Duke of the State,
moved freely within the palace gates,
his influence swaying the powerful and noble.
The fertile fields and fine estates around the capital largely fell into the hands of Buddhist temples.
An edict forbade the whipping or dragging of monks and nuns.
The Jīngé Temple was built on Wǔtái Mountain—
in Wǔtái County of Xīnzhōu stood Wǔtái Mountain,
which Buddhist tradition holds as the bodhimaṇḍa of Mañjuśrī.
Detailed annotations are provided later.
The cost amounted to tens of billions;
"jù yì" (鉅億) means
billions upon billions.
This refers to the large-number method of counting yì.
Dozens of monks from Wǔtái were sent in all directions
to seek donations for its construction.
Whenever Zài and others attended the Emperor leisurely,
they often discussed Buddhist matters.
Consequently, officials and commoners, both inside and outside the court, followed this trend and transformed,
all neglecting human affairs to devote themselves to Buddhism,
leading to daily disorder in governance and punishments.
On the 7th day of the eighth month,
Gēngchén,
Lǐ Bàoyù, Military Commissioner of Fèngxiáng and other circuits, Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, and Participant in Determining Government Matters, came to court.
Lǐ Bàoyù served as Military Commissioner of Chénzhèng, Zélù, Fèngxiáng, and other circuits to guard against Tǔbō.
His words were earnest and sincere.
"Què" (確)
means firm
and steadfast.
On the Guǐchǒu day,
he again requested to relinquish the post of Fèngxiáng Military Commissioner,
but it was not permitted.
On the 8th day, Dīngyǒu,
Dù Hóngjiàn hosted a meal for a thousand monks,
to give thanks for his safe return from Shǔ.
In the ninth month,
tens of thousands of Tǔbō troops besieged Língzhōu,
with scouting cavalry reaching Pānyuán and Yílù.
Pānyuán
was originally the ancient Yīnpán County.
In the first year of the Tiānbǎo era,
it was renamed Pānyuán,
under Jīngzhōu.
The capital was placed under martial law.
On the Jiǎzǐ day,
Guō Zǐyí shifted his garrison to Fèngtiān.
Examination of discrepancies: According to the "Family Chronicle of Fényáng":
"On the 17th day of the eighth month,
Tǔbō reached west of Jīng.
On the 27th day,
an edict ordered him to lead ten thousand elite troops to join Mǎ Lín in attacking them."
Here, the Veritable Records are followed.
The Veritable Records state:
"On the Jiǎyín day,
they invaded Língzhōu.
On the Yǐmǎo day,
they invaded Yílù."
This likely records the dates the reports arrived.
Here, the Táng Calendar is followed.
On the 10th day, mountain Lǎo tribes captured Guìzhōu,
expelling Prefect Lǐ Liáng.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Wùyín day,
Lù Sìgōng, Military Commissioner of Shuòfāng, defeated Tǔbō forces under the walls of Língzhōu.
Examination of discrepancies: The Táng Calendar states:
"In the ninth month,
Tǔbō besieged Língwǔ.
On the Wùshēn day,
Sìgōng defeated Tǔbō."
According to the perpetual calendar,
Wùshēn
was the first day of the ninth month.
Here, the Veritable Records are followed.
Tǔbō forces withdrew.
On the twelfth month,
the Gēngchén day,
tomb robbers excavated the grave of Guō Zǐyí's father.
They were pursued,
but not captured.
People believed that Yú Cháo'ēn, who had long harbored animosity towards Zǐyí,
was suspected of having instigated it.
Zǐyí came to court from Fèngtiān.
The court was worried he might stage a rebellion.
When Zǐyí had an audience with the Emperor,
the Emperor mentioned the matter.
Zǐyí wept and said:
"Your subject has long commanded troops,
yet was unable to prevent violence.
Many soldiers in the army have excavated people's graves.
That it has reached this point today
is Heaven's punishment,
not a matter of human affairs."
The court then felt at ease.
In this year,
Zhènxī was again renamed Ānxī.
The change to Zhènxī is seen in scroll 220, the first year of the Zhìdé era of Emperor Sùzōng.
Fù,
read with the rising tone.
King Xiàn'ēng of Xīnluó died.
His son Qiányùn succeeded him.
In spring,
the first month,
on the Yǐchǒu day,
the Emperor visited Zhāngjìng Temple,
and ordained a thousand monks and nuns.
Jiànníng Prince Tán was posthumously honored as Prince of Qí.
Tán's death is seen in scroll 219, the second year of the Zhìdé era.
In the second month,
on the Guǐsì day,
Shāngzhōu military commander Liú Qià killed defense commissioner Yīn Zhòngqīng.
He was soon pacified by a punitive campaign.
On the Jiǎwǔ day,
Guō Zǐyí prohibited riding horses without reason in the army.
The son of the wet nurse of Lady Nányáng violated the prohibition.
Zǐyí's wife was enfeoffed as Lady Nányáng.
His sons tearfully complained to Zǐyí,
and spoke of the overbearing behavior of the capital patrol commander.
Yǔwén Tài served as Chancellor of Wèi,
and established the post of Patrol Commander-in-Chief.
Later generations followed this,
establishing the office of Patrol Commander.
Héng,
read with the departing tone.
The next day,
Zǐyí spoke of the matter to his aides and sighed,
saying:
"All my sons
are worthless slaves.
They do not commend their father's patrol commander, but pity their mother's wet nurse's son.
If they are not worthless slaves, then what are they!"
On the Gēngzǐ day,
the palace lady Dúgū was made a Guìfēi.
In the third month,
on the Yǐsì day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Wùyín day,
Shānnán Xīdào military governor Zhāng Xiànchéng,
due to illness, recommended his paternal cousin, Right Imperial Guard General Zhāng Xiàngōng, to succeed him.
The Emperor approved.
On the Rényín day,
Xīchuān military governor Cuī Gàn came to court.
Earlier,
the Emperor had sent a palace envoy to summon Lǐ Mì from Héngshān.
Mì's return to Héngshān is seen in scroll 220, the second year of the Zhìdé era.
He was again bestowed the golden seal and purple ribbon.
When Mì followed Emperor Sùzōng to Língwǔ,
he had already been granted the golden seal and purple ribbon.
After returning to Héngshān,
he resumed his original attire.
Now it was bestowed again.
Fù,
read with the rising tone.
Pénglái Hall is north of Zǐchén Hall.
North of Pénglái Hall is Tàiyè Pond,
within which is Pénglái Mountain.
Wéi,
read with the departing tone;
the following wéi for Mì is the same.
The sweat garment
was common attire for leisure at home.
Now, both noble and common wear it,
only the Emperor's is distinguished by being yellow.
The Zhìgǔzi says: At the Yān court,
with the formal headdress and robe, there was a white gauze inner garment,
and a bright garment,
both resembling the sweat garment,
used for performing sacrifices and receiving spirits.
When Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn fought with Xiàng Yǔ,
sweat soaked his inner garment,
so it was renamed the sweat garment,
worn by both noble and common.
Yī,
read with the entering tone.
Guò,
read with the level tone.
Jǐ and Shè refer to
the Jǐshìzhōng and Zhōngshū Shèrén,
both officials of the fifth rank in the Táng.
He discussed matters with them all.
He also had Yú Cháo'ēn build an outer residence for Mì at Báihuā Tún,
so he could meet with relatives and old friends.
The Emperor wished to make Mì a Vice Director of the Chancellery and Tóng Zhāngshì Shì,
but Mì firmly declined.
The Emperor said:
"The press of official duties is so heavy,
we cannot meet morning and evening.
It truly would be better for you to reside close by.
Why must you have your name on the edict to be considered Chancellor!"
Later, during the Duānwǔ Festival,
princes, dukes, and princesses each presented clothing and curios.
The Emperor said to Mì:
"Why have you alone presented nothing?"
He replied:
"Your subject resides within the palace.
From headband to shoes, all are bestowed by Your Majesty.
What remains is only this one body.
What is there to present!"
The Emperor said:
"What We seek is precisely this."
Mì said:
"Your subject's body does not belong to Your Majesty.
To whom then does it belong?"
The Emperor said:
"The late Emperor wished to humble you with the post of Chancellor but could not succeed.
See scroll 218, the seventh month of the first year of the Zhìdé era of Emperor Sùzōng.
Now it is only as We command.
It is not yours to have!"
Mì said:
"What does Your Majesty wish your subject to do?"
The Emperor said:
"We wish you to eat meat and drink wine,
to have a family,
to receive a salary and rank,
and to be a worldly man."
Mì wept and said:
"Your subject has abstained from grains for over twenty years.
Why must Your Majesty make me abandon my resolve!"
The Emperor said:
"What good is weeping!
You are within the ninefold palace gates.
Where do you wish to go?"
He then ordered a palace envoy to bury Mì's two parents,
and also had Mì marry a daughter of the Lú family as his wife.
The Kǎoyì says: The Family Biography of the Marquis of Yè states:
"On the Duānwǔ Festival of the first year of Yǒngtài,
the Emperor ordered Mì to eat meat and marry."
Below it states:
"Master Āzú stole felt shoes,
and placed them in Zǐchén Hall.
The Emperor wished to have palace women guard the lamps and candles.
Mì said: 'Your subject has been here six or seven years.'"
It also says:
"Moreover, newly bestowed with marriage."
From the Emperor's accession to Yǒngtài,
was only four years.
It also says,
"Because of this, he incurred slander,
and Yuán Zǎi then used the matter of Yú Cháo'ēn to expel him."
Thus, the marriage and Cháo'ēn's execution were not far apart.
Now it is all mentioned following the posthumous honors for Chéngtiān.
He bestowed a residence in Guāngfú Ward,
ordering Mì to stay at his residence for several days,
and at Pénglái Lodge for several days.
When the Emperor spoke with Mì about Prince Tán of Qí,
wishing to bestow generous posthumous honors,
Mì requested that he be posthumously honored as Crown Prince following the precedent for Princes Qí and Xuē.
The Emperor wept and said:
"My younger brother first proposed the plan at Língwǔ,
achieving the restoration of the dynasty.
The events are seen in scroll 219, the first year of the Zhìdé era of Emperor Sùzōng.
He exhausted his loyalty and filial piety,
yet was harmed by slanderers.
Had he still been alive,
We would certainly have made him Crown Prince.
Now We should honor him with an imperial title,
fulfilling Our long-held wish."
By the decree of the Yǐmǎo day,
Tán was posthumously given the title Emperor Chéngtiān.
On the Gēngshēn day,
he was buried at Shùnlíng.
When Cuī Gàn came to court,
he appointed his younger brother Kuān as Acting Military Governor.
In this year, on the Rényín day of the fourth month,
Cuī Gàn came to court.
Cháo,
read with the rising tone.
When the court heard of this,
they added to Gàn the honorary title of Acting Minister of Works,
bestowed upon him the name Níng,
and sent him back to his garrison.
On the 11th day of the sixth month,
Rénchén,
the Yōuzhōu military commissioner Zhū Xīcǎi, Deputy Military Commissioner Zhū Cǐ of Chāngpíng,
and Cǐ's younger brother Zhū Tāo together killed Military Commissioner Lǐ Huáixiān.
Xīcǎi proclaimed himself acting military commissioner.
In the intercalary month,
Chéngdé Army Military Commissioner Lǐ Bǎochén sent a general leading troops to attack Xīcǎi,
but was defeated by Xīcǎi.
The court had no choice but to pardon him.
Gēngshēn,
Wáng Jìn was appointed to concurrently hold the position of Lúlóng Military Commissioner.
Dīngmǎo,
Xīcǎi was appointed as
acting military commissioner of Yōuzhōu.
Cuī Kuān fought against Yáng Zǐlín,
suffering several defeats.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
Cuī Níng's concubine Rén shì contributed several hundred thousand strings of cash from her personal wealth,
recruited several thousand soldiers,
led them to attack Zǐlín,
and defeated him.
Zǐlín fled.
On the 13th day, Yǐhài,
Wáng Jìn went to Yōuzhōu.
Zhū Xīcǎi deployed strong troops and strict defenses to receive him.
Jìn proceeded calmly,
and Xīcǎi welcomed and paid his respects with great deference.
Jìn realized he ultimately could not control him,
so he inspected the troops,
and after over ten days, returned.
The 14th entry: The Kèhán's wife (Kèdūn) of the Huíhé died.
Gēngchén,
Right Sanqí Chángshì Xiāo Xīn was appointed as the envoy to offer condolences and sacrifices.
Sàn,
xī dǎn fān.
Qí,
qí jì fān.
Xīn,
xǔ jīn fān.
Shǐ,
shū lì fān.
"We have rendered great service to Táng.
How can Táng break faith,
purchase our horses,
and not return the payment on time?"
Xīn said:
"Táng has already repaid the Huíhé's service.
When Púgù Huái'ēn rebelled,
the Huíhé aided him,
allied with Tǔbō troops to invade,
and pressed close to our capital's outskirts.
After Huái'ēn died,
and Tǔbō fled,
then the Huíhé, in fear, requested peace.
Our Táng, not forgetting your former service,
showed kindness and let you go.
This matter is recorded in the first year of Yǒngtài in the previous scroll.
Not a single horse was returned.
It was the Huíhé who broke the agreement,
how can it be Táng breaking faith!"
The Huíhé were ashamed,
and sent him back with generous gifts.
The 15th entry: Bǐngxū,
a Yúlánpén was taken from the palace and bestowed upon Zhāngjìng Temple.
The Buddhist Yúlánpén Sūtra states: The monk Mùlián saw his deceased mother among the hungry ghosts.
Mùlián said to the Buddha: On the full moon of the seventh month,
for parents of seven generations suffering in hardship,
prepare a hundred delicacies and five fruits placed in a basin,
make offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions,
and then receive the food.
The Mèng Huá Lù says: On Zhōngyuán,
ghost utensils and colored clothes are sold.
A bamboo stand with three legs, shaped like a lamp niche,
is called a Yúlánpén.
Paper money and clothes are hung on it,
and burned.
The Shìshì Yàolǎn says: In Sanskrit, Yúlán,
here means 'saving those hanging upside down' basin.
Lù Yóu said: Customarily, on the full moon of the seventh month, vegetarian food is prepared to honor ancestors.
Bamboo is woven into basins and bowls,
paper money is stored inside,
placed on a bamboo and burned.
This is called a Yúlánpén.
Alas!
For Dàizōng to do this,
where did he think the spirits of the seven imperial temples were!
The imperial title was written on a banner,
and all officials welcomed and paid respects at the Guāngshùn Gate.
According to the palace version map of Dàmíng Palace: The Guāngshùn Gate is west of the Zǐchén Gate.
Inside the Guāngshùn Gate are the Míngyì Hall and Chénghuān Hall.
The 16th entry: In the eighth month,
Rénxū,
100,000 Tǔbō troops invaded Língwǔ.
Dīngmǎo,
Tǔbō's Shàng Zànmó with 20,000 troops invaded Bīnzhōu,
and the capital was placed under martial law.
Bīnníng Military Commissioner Mǎ Lín defeated them.
Tǔ,
cóng tūn rù shēng.
Bīn,
bēi mín fān.
Shǐ,
shū lì fān.
Lín,
lí zhēn fān.
The 17th entry: Gēngwǔ,
Hé dōng Military Commissioner and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì Xīn Yúnjīng died.
Wáng Jìn was appointed to concurrently hold the position of Hé dōng Military Commissioner,
his other titles remaining as before.
The 18th entry: In the ninth month,
Rénshēn,
Guō Zǐyí was ordered to lead 50,000 troops to station at Fèngtiān to guard against Tǔbō.
The 19th entry: Dīngchǒu,
Jì Prince Huán died.
Huán was Xuánzōng's son.
Jì,
zǐ lǐ fān.
The 20th entry: Rénwǔ,
Shuòfāng cavalry general Bái Yuánguāng attacked Tǔbō and defeated them.
Rénchén,
Yuánguāng again defeated 20,000 Tǔbō troops at Língwǔ.
Fèngxiáng Military Commissioner Lǐ Bàoyù sent his Right Army Commander Líntáo Lǐ Shèng to lead 5,000 troops to attack Tǔbō.
Shèng said:
"In terms of strength, 5,000 is insufficient;
in terms of strategy, it is too many."
So he led a thousand men
out of Dàzhèn Pass.
Reaching Líntáo,
he slaughtered the Tǔbō at Dìngqín Fortress.
Líntáo is Táozhōu.
Tǔbō aimed to swallow Qín territory,
hence built a fortress in Táozhōu,
naming it Dìngqín.
Táo,
tú dāo fān.
Shèng,
chéng zhèng fān.
He captured the fortress commander Mùróng Gǔzhǒng and returned.
When Tǔbō heard this,
they lifted the siege of Língzhōu and left.
Wùxū,
martial law in the capital was lifted.
The 21st entry: Yǐngzhōu Prefect Lǐ Hù offended Huáibó Military Commissioner Línghú Zhāng over some matter.
Zhāng sent his Military Judge Yáo Shì to inspect Yǐngzhōu,
intending to replace Hù in administering the prefecture,
and said:
"If Hù does not hand over authority,
kill him."
Hù learned of this,
incited his officers and soldiers to anger,
had them kill Shì,
over a hundred people dying along with Shì.
Hù fled to Biànzhōu to seek refuge with Hénán Military Commissioner Tián Shéngōng.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Yǐsì,
Zhāng submitted a memorial reporting the situation,
and Hù also submitted a memorial defending himself.
The Emperor ordered Jǐshìzhōng Hèruò Chá to go and investigate.
The 22nd entry: Dīngmǎo,
Guō Zǐyí came to court from Fèngtiān.
The 23rd entry: In the eleventh month,
Dīnghài,
Yōuzhōu Acting Military Commissioner Zhū Xīcǎi was appointed Military Commissioner.
The 24th entry: Guō Zǐyí returned to Hézhōng.
Having come to court from Fèngtiān,
he returned to Hézhōng.
Huán,
cóng xuān fān.
Also pronounced as the original character.
Mǎ Lín stationed the Four Garrisons' troops at Bīnníng,
his strength insufficient to resist,
while Guō Zǐyí with the heavy Shuòfāng troops garrisoned Hézhōng,
deeply situated in the secure interior region with no affairs.
So he discussed with Zǐyí and the various generals,
to transfer Lín to garrison Jīngzhōu,
and have Zǐyí use the Shuòfāng troops to garrison Bīnzhōu,
saying:
"If the border lands are desolate and ravaged,
and military funds are insufficient,
then use the tax revenues from the interior and transport gold and silk to assist."
The various generals all agreed.
In the twelfth month,
Jǐyǒu,
Mǎ Lín was transferred to be Jīngyuán Military Commissioner,
with Bīn, Níng, and Qìng prefectures placed under Shuòfāng.
Lín first went to fortify Jīngzhōu,
appointing Dū Yúhòu Duàn Xiùshí to act as Bīnzhōu Acting Military Commissioner.
初，
四鎮、北庭兵遠赴中原之難，
事見二百十九卷至德元載。
難，
乃旦翻。
數遷徙，
四鎮歷汴、虢、鳳翔，
北庭歷懷、絳、鄜然後至邠，
頗積勞弊。
及徙涇州，
衆皆怨誹。
刀斧兵馬使王童之謀作亂，
期以辛酉旦警嚴而發。
旦警嚴者，
將旦嚴鼓以警衆也。
周禮謂之發昫，
今人謂之攢點。
有告之者；
秀實陽召掌漏者，
怒之，
以其失節，
令每更來白，
掌漏者，
謂守漏之卒也。
令，
力丁翻。
更，
工衡翻。
遂四更而曙，
童之不果發。
秀實欲討之而亂迹未露，
恐軍中疑其冤。
告者又云，
「今夕欲焚馬坊草，
因救火謀作亂。 」
中夕，
火果起，
秀實命軍中行者皆止，
坐者勿起，
各整部伍，
嚴守要害。
童之白請救火，
不許。
及旦，
捕童之及其黨八人，
皆斬之。
下令曰：
「後徙者族，
流言者刑！ 」
遂徙于涇。
史言段秀實能弭亂。
令，
力丁翻。
25癸亥 ，
西川破吐蕃萬餘衆。
吐，
從暾入聲。
26平盧行軍司馬許杲
考異曰：舊傳作
「許果」 。
今從韓愈順宗實錄。
有窺淮南意，
淮南節度使崔圓令副使元城張萬福攝濠州刺史；
杲聞，
即提卒去，
止當塗。
此當塗縣，
宋屬太平州，
本漢丹陽縣地。
按漢書地理志，
當塗屬九江郡。
晉成帝時，
以江北之當塗縣流人過江者立當塗僑縣，
遂為實土。
上召萬福，
以為和州刺史、行營防禦使，
討杲。
萬福至州，
杲懼，
移軍上元，
按上元，
楚之金陵，
秦之秣陵，
吳之建業，
江左之建康。
晉分秣陵置臨江縣，
太康初，
又改為江寧，
至肅宗上元二年更今名，
屬昇州。
使，
疏吏翻。
許杲既去濠州，
南渡江而屯當塗。
及張萬福至歷陽逼之，
又移上元，
又自上元渡江而北，
掠楚州也。
未至淮陰，
杲為其將康自勸所逐。
自勸擁兵繼掠，
循淮而東，
萬福倍道追而殺之，
免者什二三。
元甫將厚賞將士，
萬福曰：
「官健常虛費衣糧，
無所事。
兵農既分，
縣官費衣糧以養軍，
謂之官健，
猶言官所養健兒也。
按唐六典：衞士之外，
天下諸軍有健兒。
舊健兒在軍皆有年限，
更來往，
頗為勞弊。
開元十五年，
敕以天下無虞，
宜與人休息，
自今已後，
諸軍鎮量閒劇、利害置兵防健兒，
於諸色征行人內及客戶中，
召募取丁壯情愿充健兒、長住邊軍者，
每年加常例給賜，
兼給永年優復，
其家口情願同者，
聽至軍州，
各給田地屋宅。
人賴其利，
中外獲安，
永無徵發之役。
此當時言兵農已分之利，
而養兵之害卒不可救，
以至于今。
不足過賞，
請用三分之一。 」
正月，
丙子 ，
郭子儀入朝，
魚朝恩邀之遊章敬寺。
元載恐其相結，
密使子儀軍吏告子儀曰：
「朝恩謀不利於公。 」
子儀不聽。
吏亦告諸將，
將士請衷甲以從者三百人。
杜預曰：衷甲，
謂在衣中。
從，
才用翻；
下同。
國之大臣，
彼無天子之命，
安敢害我！
若受命而來，
汝曹欲何為！ 」
乃從家僮數人而往。
朝恩迎之，
驚其從者之約。
子儀以所聞告，
且曰：
「恐煩公經營耳。 」
朝恩撫膺捧手流涕曰：
「非公長者，
能無疑乎！ 」
2 壬午 ，
流李岵於夷州。
3 乙酉 ，
郭子儀還河中。
朝而還也。
還，
從宣翻，
又如字。
4 辛卯 ，
賜李岵死。
5 二月，
壬寅 ，
以京兆之好畤、鳳翔之麟遊、普潤隸神策軍，
從魚朝恩之請也。
6 After Yáng Zǐlín was defeated and returned to Lúzhōu,
he recruited fugitives,
gathering several thousand men.
He then sailed eastward along the river,
claiming he was heading to the court.
Wáng Shǒuxiān, the garrison commander of Fúzhōu, laid an ambush at Huángcǎo Gorge,
but Yáng Zǐlín captured all of them.
He attacked Shǒuxiān at Zhōngzhōu,
and Shǒuxiān barely escaped with his life.
Yáng Zǐlín then killed Zhāng Zhōng, the deputy inspector of Kuízhōu,
and occupied the city.
Wèi Bóyù, the military governor of Jīngnán, sought to ally with him for support,
promising him Kuízhōu,
and petitioned the court on his behalf.
Liú Chāngyì of Yángqǔ
(old record: Yángqǔ County of the Former Hàn,
Dìngxiāng County of Táng’s Xīnzhōu was located there.
The Later Hàn moved Yángqǔ County to the Tàiyuán region,
and established Dìngxiāng County at the old Yángqǔ city site.
As for Tàiyuán’s Yángqǔ,
in the sixth year of the Suí dynasty’s Kāihuáng era,
it was renamed Yángzhí,
and in the sixteenth year,
it was renamed Fényáng,
due to aversion to the name Yángqǔ.
In the seventh year of the Wǔdé era,
it was restored as Yángqǔ County.)
Yáng Zǐlín followed his advice.
On the Yǐsì day,
Yáng Zǐlín was appointed as the militia commissioner of Xiázhōu.
Xiázhōu
was the Yílíng Commandery.
7 Earlier,
after Púgù Huái’ēn died,
(see the first year of Yǒngtài in the previous volume.)
his daughter was placed in the palace,
where she was raised as an imperial daughter.
The Huíhé requested her as their queen.
In summer,
the fifth month,
on the Xīnmǎo day,
she was enfeoffed as Princess Chónghuī
and married to the Huíhé khan.
On the Rénchén day,
Lǐ Hán, the vice minister of war, was sent to escort her.
Hán recommended Dǒng Jìn, the director of the bureau of sacrifices from Yúxiāng, as his deputy.
Yúxiāng
was the Xiè County of the Hàn dynasty.
The Later Wèi divided it to establish Yúxiāng County.
In the seventeenth year of the Zhēnguàn era,
Xiè County was abolished and merged into Yúxiāng.
In the twentieth year,
Xiè County was reestablished and Yúxiāng was abolished.
In the second year of the Tiānshòu era,
Xiè County was again divided to establish Yúxiāng County,
which belonged to Hézhōng Prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: In the ninth year of the Tàihé era of the Later Wèi,
Nánxiè County was established thirteen lǐ west of present-day Yúxiāng County.
Emperor Míng of the Zhōu dynasty abolished Nánxiè
and placed Yúxiāng County under Suíhuà Commandery,
which is the old Suíhuà city thirty-four lǐ west of the present county.
In the fourth year of the Bǎodìng era,
Suíhuà was renamed Yúxiāng County.
At the end of the Zhōu dynasty,
Xiè County was established east of present-day Yúxiāng city,
and another Yúxiāng County was established fifty lǐ west of Xiè County,
which is the present city.
On the Dīngyǒu day,
the princess bid farewell and departed,
arriving at the Huíhé headquarters.
The Huíhé came and said:
“The Táng agreed to trade horses with us,
but after the horses were delivered,
the payment returned to us was insufficient.
We shall take it from the envoy.”
Hán was frightened
and dared not reply.
He looked at Jìn,
who said:
“It is not that we lack horses and must trade with you;
have we not bestowed enough favors upon you?
Your horses arrive yearly,
and we count the hides and return payment,
meaning regardless of whether they are alive or dead,
we pay the full price for the horses.
The Son of Heaven, mindful of your service,
has thus issued an edict forbidding any encroachment upon you.
The various tribes, fearing that our great state supports you,
dare not contend with you.
That your fathers and sons live in peace and your horses multiply—
who but us has made it so?”
Thereupon, the crowd surrounded Jìn and bowed.
Then they lined up facing south and bowed in unison,
raising both hands and saying:
“We dare not harbor ill will toward the great state.”
This account of Jìn was written by the clerk Hán Yù,
and his words may be somewhat exaggerated.
Shuài
is read as shuài.
8 On the Wùshēn day,
Wáng Jìn submitted a memorial resigning as deputy commander-in-chief, overall commander, and campaign commissioner.
9 On the Xīnyǒu day,
Guō Zǐyí moved from Hézhōng to Bīnzhōu,
taking his elite troops with him.
The remaining troops were commanded by subordinate generals,
guarding Hézhōng and Língzhōu.
The soldiers had long been settled in Hézhōng,
and were quite unwilling to relocate.
Many fled back from Bīn;
the campaign secretary Yán Yǐng, in charge of the留守 office,
captured them all,
executed their leaders,
and only then did the troops settle down.
10 In autumn,
the ninth month,
the Tǔbō invaded Língzhōu.
On the Dīngchǒu day,
Cháng Qiānguāng, the acting military governor of Shuòfāng, repelled them.
11 The military commanders of Hédōng, Wáng Wúzòng and Zhāng Fèngzhāng, relying on their achievements, became arrogant and unruly.
Considering Wáng Jìn a mere scholar,
they looked down on him
and frequently violated orders.
Jìn received an edict to dispatch troops to Yánzhōu for autumn defense.
Yánzhōu
was the territory of the Hàn’s Wǔyuán Commandery.
The Suí established Yánzhōu,
governing Wǔyuán County.
The present prefecture extends south to the northern border of Mǎlǐng County in Qìngzhōu,
which was the territory of the Hàn’s Mǎlǐng County.
Fèngzhāng delayed and did not advance,
while Wúzòng used other pretexts to enter Tàiyuán city.
Jìn captured and executed them both,
along with seven of their accomplices.
Nearly all the fierce and rebellious generals were eliminated,
and the military administration finally stabilized.
12 In winter,
the tenth month,
Cháng Qiānguāng reported that the Tǔbō had invaded Wūshā,
stretching forty lǐ from front to rear.
Tǔ
is pronounced with the entering tone of tūn.
Wūshā County,
belonging to Língzhōu,
was originally the territory of the Hàn’s Fùpíng County.
Zǐyí personally led his troops to Qìngzhōu,
but upon hearing that the Tǔbō had retreated,
he returned.
13 Dù Hóngjiàn, the vice minister of the imperial secretariat and concurrent chief minister, resigned due to illness.
On the Rénshēn day,
it was approved.
On the Yǐhài day,
he passed away.
Hóngjiàn was gravely ill
and had a monk shave his head.
His will instructed that a pagoda be built for his burial.
14 On the Bǐngzǐ day,
Péi Miǎn, the left vice director of the imperial secretariat, was appointed chief minister.
Earlier,
when Yuán Zài was a county lieutenant of Xīnpíng,
Miǎn had recommended him.
Therefore, Zài recommended him as chief minister,
also finding it advantageous that his old age and illness made him easy to control.
At the moment of receiving the appointment,
Miǎn danced for joy and fell to the ground.
Zài hurried over to support him
and expressed gratitude on his behalf.
In the twelfth month,
on the Wùxū day,
Miǎn passed away.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the Jǐsì day,
the Qiāng chieftain Bái Duìpéng and others each led their tribes to submit.

2 Yú Cháo’ēn, the commissioner of army supervision, consolation, and administration, grand general of the left imperial gate guard, commissioner of the Shéncè Army, and director of the palace attendants,
exclusively commanded the imperial guards,
enjoying unparalleled favor and authority.
The emperor often discussed military and state affairs with him,
and his influence overwhelmed the court and the public.
Cháo’ēn enjoyed speaking freely about current politics in large gatherings,
insulting and belittling the chief ministers.
Although Yuán Zài was eloquent,
he could only remain silent and dared not respond.
The Divine Strategy Army's Dū Yúhòu Liú Xīxiān and
Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ Wáng Jiàhè
were both favored by Yú Cháo'ēn.
Xīxiān persuaded Cháo'ēn to establish a prison within the Northern Army.
The Left and Right Divine Strategy Armies,
the Left and Right Yǔlín Armies,
and the Left and Right Lóngwǔ Armies
were all referred to as the Northern Army.
(Persuade: shuì, pronounced shuō, read as shuì.)
(Xiāng: read as xiàng.)
(Xiāng: read as xiàng.)
(Xiāng: read as xiàng.)
(Xiān: read as xiān.)
(Xiān: read as xiān.)
They falsely accused people of crimes,
arrested and imprisoned them in underground dungeons,
interrogated and tortured them until they confessed,
confiscated their family assets for the army,
and distributed rewards to those who reported and captured them.
The location was within the forbidden and secretive area,
and no one dared to speak out.
Whenever Cháo'ēn reported matters,
he expected them to be approved without fail.
If there were court affairs he was not consulted about,
he would angrily say:
"Is there anything under heaven that does not go through me?"
The Emperor heard this,
and from then on, he was displeased.
Cháo'ēn's adopted son Lìnghuī was still young,
serving as an inner attendant.
He wore green robes.
According to the Táng system: inner attendants had no fixed number of positions,
and they belonged to the Palace Domestic Service.
Those without official rank
were called inner attendants,
responsible for managing the ledgers of items entering through various gates.
Sòng Bái said: They were in charge of the ledgers for items entering and exiting through various gates.
(Wear: yī, pronounced yì.)
(Yī: read as yì.)
He returned and told Cháo'ēn.
The next day, Cháo'ēn went to see the Emperor and said:
"My son's official rank is low,
and he is bullied by his peers.
I beg you to grant him purple robes."
Before the Emperor could respond,
the officials had already brought purple robes forward,
and Lìnghuī put them on,
bowing in gratitude.
The Emperor forced a smile and said:
"The child looks good in purple,
it must be very satisfying."
Yuán Zǎi discerned the Emperor's intention,
and took the opportunity to report that Cháo'ēn was acting arbitrarily and plotting treason.
(Opportunity: jiàn, read as jiàn.)
(Jiàn: read as jiàn.)
He requested to remove him.
The Emperor also knew that everyone in the empire resented and was angry with him,
so he ordered Yuán Zǎi to devise a strategy.
Whenever Cháo'ēn entered the palace,
he often had the archery general Zhōu Hào lead a hundred men to protect him,
and also had his ally, the Shǎnzhōu Jiedùshǐ Huángfǔ Wēn, hold troops outside as support.
Yuán Zǎi bribed them heavily to win them over,
so all of Cháo'ēn's secret plots and confidential conversations
were heard one by one by the Emperor,
but Cháo'ēn was unaware of this.
On Xīnmǎo,
Yuán Zǎi devised a plan for the Emperor:
transfer Lǐ Bàoyù to serve as the Shānnán Xīdào Jiedùshǐ,
and appoint Wēn as the Fèngxiáng Jiedùshǐ,
outwardly enhancing their authority,
but actually bringing Wēn closer to assist in the plan.
Yuán Zǎi also requested to assign Méi, Guó, Bǎojī, Hù, and Zhōuzhì to Bàoyù's jurisdiction,
and Xīngpíng, Wǔgōng, Tiānxīng, and Fúfēng to the Divine Strategy Army.
(Xīngpíng:
formerly called Shǐpíng,
in the first year of Jǐnglóng,
renamed Jīnchéng,
in the second year of Zhìdé,
renamed Xīngpíng,
belonging to Jīngzhào Prefecture.)
Cháo'ēn did not suspect Yuán Zǎi at all,
and remained as arrogant and domineering as before.
On the 3rd, Rénchén,
Zhāng Yánshǎng, the Governor of Hénán, was appointed as the Liúshǒu of Dōngjīng;
the deputy marshal of Hénán and other circuits was abolished,
and his troops were placed under the Liúshǒu.
(Yánshǎng:
the son of Zhāng Jiāzhēn.)
(Zhāng Jiāzhēn:
served as chancellor during the Kāiyuán era.)
On the 4th, in February,
on Wùxū,
Lǐ Bàoyù moved his garrison to Zhōuzhì,
relocating his troops to Zhōuzhì to concurrently govern Shānnán.
They plundered the wards and markets of Fèngxiáng,
and order was restored only after several days.
On the 5th, Liú Xīxiān began to sense a change in the Emperor's attitude,
and reported it to Yú Cháo'ēn.
Cháo'ēn started to feel suspicious and fearful.
However, whenever the Emperor saw him,
his favor and courtesy increased even more,
so Cháo'ēn also felt reassured by this.
When Huángfǔ Wēn arrived in the capital,
Yuán Zǎi detained him and did not let him leave,
and together with Wēn and Zhōu Hào, secretly plotted to kill Cháo'ēn.
(Examination of discrepancies: The Bīnzhì says:
"In the spring of the fifth year,
the Emperor summoned Lord Guō on the Cold Food Festival,
a festive season of abundant harvest,
wishing to enjoy himself with his ministers.
At that time, he intended to kill Cháo'ēn,
so he instructed Lord Guō,
'The Shuòfāng Army
has rendered meritorious service to the state,
so it is fitting for several thousand of its accomplished soldiers to come to the court.
I can then host a banquet and reward them,
and get to know them.'
In the first month,
Lord Guō led three thousand armored soldiers to the court.
Yú Cháo'ēn invited Lord Guō to visit the Zhāngjìng Temple,
and Lord Guō agreed.
Chancellor Yuán, thinking they were on good terms,
had someone hint to the Bīn officials to ask Lord Guō not to go.
The Bīn officials rushed from the Central Secretariat to inform Lord Guō:
'The Jūnróng intends to harm you,'
and also informed the generals.
Shortly after,
Cháo'ēn's envoy arrived,
and as Lord Guō was about to leave,
three hundred soldiers, wearing armor under their clothes, requested to accompany him,
wishing to guard against unexpected events.
Lord Guō angrily said:
'I am a high minister.
Unless he has a secret edict, how would he dare harm me?
If it is the Emperor's order,
what are you all doing?'
He went alone with only a dozen or so servants.
Cháo'ēn awaited him,
and exclaimed in surprise:
'How modest your entourage is!'
Lord Guō replied with what he had heard,
and added:
'I was afraid to trouble you with worry!'
The Jūnróng patted his chest and clasped his hands,
sobbing and wiping away tears, saying:
'If not for your magnanimity,
would there not be suspicion?'")
According to the Fényáng Family Chronicle,
Zǐyí entered the court in May,
and arrived in Bīnzhōu in July.
This might have been an event from the first month of the fourth year.
At that time, there was no plan to kill Cháo'ēn.
It is not adopted here.
The Family Chronicle also says:
"In March,
Lord Guō reported that Yú Cháo'ēn was secretly allying with Zhōu Zhìguāng as an external supporter,
and had long controlled the imperial guards.
If not dealt with early,
disaster would arise."
This is also not adopted.
In the third month,
on Guǐyǒu,
was the Cold Food Festival.
The Jīng Chǔ Suìshí Jì states: "One hundred and four, one hundred and five, and one hundred and six days after the winter solstice, fire is prohibited,
which is called the Cold Food Festival."
The Chūxué Jì says: The Qín Cāo records: Jìn Wéngōng and Jiè Zǐsuí fled together,
and when Wéngōng returned to the state,
Zǐsuí received nothing.
He composed the "Song of the Dragon and Snake" and went into seclusion.
Wéngōng sought him out,
but he refused to emerge,
so Wéngōng set fire to the trees around him.
Zǐsuí embraced a tree and died.
Wéngōng grieved for him,
and ordered that no fire be lit on the fifth day of the fifth month.
As for Zhōu Jǔ's letter, Wèi Wǔ's Míng Fá Lìng, and Lù Huì's Yèzhōng Jì,
they all state that the prohibition of fire during the Cold Food Festival originated with Zǐtuī.
The Zǐsuí mentioned in the Qín Cāo
is actually Tuī.
It also says the fifth day of the fifth month,
which differs from the present custom,
all due to popular transmission.
According to the Zuǒ Zhuàn and the Shǐ Jì, there is no record of Zǐtuī being burned to death.
However, the Zhōu Shū mentions the Sī Xuǎn shì,
who in mid-spring used wooden clappers to announce the fire prohibition throughout the state.
The commentary states: "This is because fire will be used in late spring."
Now, the Cold Food Festival,
according to the solar terms, falls at the end of mid-spring.
The Qingming Festival is at the beginning of the third month.
Thus, the fire prohibition is also a Zhōu dynasty institution.
Zǎi was in charge of the Zhōngshū Shěng.
After the banquet ended,
Cháo'ēn was about to return to camp,
but the Emperor detained him to discuss matters,
and then accused him of harboring rebellious intentions.
Cháo'ēn defended himself,
but his words were rather defiant and disrespectful.
Hào and the attendants seized and strangled him,
with no one outside knowing.
The Emperor issued an edict,
dismissing Cháo'ēn from his positions as Guān Jūnróng and other commissions,
while retaining his title as Nèishì Jiān.
It was falsely claimed
that "Cháo'ēn received an edict and then hanged himself."
His body was returned to his family,
and six million coins were bestowed for his burial.
On Dīngchǒu,
Liú Xīxiān and Wáng Jiàhè were promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
to reassure the hearts of the Northern Army.
On Bǐngxū,
prisoners in the capital region were pardoned,
and it was ordered that all of Cháo'ēn's associates be released,
with the Emperor stating:
"The generals and soldiers of the Northern Army,
are all my claws and teeth,
and should remain as before.
I am now personally commanding the imperial guards,
so do not worry or fear."
6 On Jǐchǒu,
the Dùzhī Shǐ and the Zhuǎnyùn, Chángpíng, and Yántiě Shǐ for Guānnèi and other circuits were abolished,
with the Dùzhī affairs entrusted to the Prime Minister.
7 Huángfǔ Wēn was ordered to return to his garrison in Shǎn.
After Yú Cháo'ēn was executed,
Wēn was no longer stationed in Fèngxiáng.
Shǎn,
is pronounced as Shī Rǎn fān.
8 After Yuán Zǎi executed Yú Cháo'ēn,
the Emperor favored and trusted him even more,
and Zǎi became increasingly arrogant and overbearing.
He often boasted in public,
claiming to possess both civil and military talents,
unmatched in ancient or modern times.
He manipulated power and played tricks,
allowing governance to be determined by bribery,
and lived extravagantly beyond all bounds.
The Lìbù Shìláng Yáng Wǎn,
who conducted official selections fairly,
was upright and principled by nature,
and did not attach himself to Zǎi.
The Lǐngnán Jiédùshǐ Xú Hào,
greedy and sycophantic,
used treasures from the south to bribe Zǎi.
Zǎi
appointed Wǎn as Guózǐ Jìjiǔ,
and promoted Hào to replace him.
Hào,
was from Yuèzhōu.
Zǎi had a father-in-law who came from Xuānzhōu,
seeking an official position from Zǎi.
Zǎi assessed that the man was not capable of handling affairs,
so he merely gave him a letter for Héběi and sent him away.
The father-in-law was displeased,
and upon reaching Yōuzhōu,
privately opened the letter to read it.
The letter contained not a single word,
only Zǎi's signature.
The father-in-law was furious,
but had no choice but to try visiting the local officials.
The officials,
who were subordinates of the military commissioner's office,
were greatly astonished.
The Pànguān,
the Jiédù Pànguān,
dispatched a senior officer to receive the letter in a box,
accommodated him in the finest guest quarters,
hosted him for several days of banquets,
and when he departed,
presented him with a thousand bolts of silk.
Such was the awe-inspiring power Zǎi commanded.
9 In summer,
the fourth month,
on Gēngzǐ,
the Húnán Bīngmǎ Shǐ Zāng Jiè killed the Guānchá Shǐ Cuī Guàn.
The Cízhōu Cìshǐ Yáng Zǐlín raised troops to suppress him,
but accepted a bribe and withdrew.
10 The Jīngyuán Jiédùshǐ Mǎ Lín repeatedly complained that his garrison was desolate and impoverished,
unable to support the army.
The Emperor hinted to Lǐ Bàoyù to cede Zhèng and Yǐng prefectures to him.
On Yǐsì,

11 On Gēngshēn,
