the Tibetans pressed upon Jīngzhōu.
To say they did not dare to violate the frontier for three or four years
is likely an exaggerated praise by the historians.
(Duàn Xiùshí) possessed authority and benevolence,
he maintained personal integrity and frugality,
had no concubines in his household,
and unless it was an official gathering,
he never drank wine or listened to music.
On the fifteenth day, an army of 80,000 Tibetans encamped at the Chángzéjian north of Yuánzhōu,
which is likely the Chángzé River.
The Tang dynasty had previously established a horse pasture here.
Tǔ,
follows the entering tone of tūn;
the same below.
On Jǐsì,
they captured Fāngqú.
Fāngqú
was a county in the Hàn dynasty,
belonging to the Běidì Commandery,
later abolished.
In the third year of Shénlóng of Emperor Zhōngzōng,
Fāngqú County was established by dividing from Mǎlǐng,
and belonged to Qìngzhōu.
Sòng Bái's Continuation of the Comprehensive Statutes: The Fāngqú Garrison of Língzhōu,
in the early Sòng dynasty, established the Tōngyuǎn Army.
The Qín Great Wall is one lǐ north of the city.
Guō Zǐyí sent his subordinate general Lǐ Huáiguāng to rescue them,
and the Tibetans retreated.
On Gēngwǔ,
the Tibetans invaded Fángzhōu.
In the winter,
tenth month,
on Yǐyǒu,
Cuī Nìng, the military commissioner of Xīchuān, reported a major defeat of the Tibetans at Wànghànchéng.
The Tibetans built a city on the Western Mountains to observe Shǔ,
hence it was named Wànghànchéng (City Observing Hàn).
Shǐ,
read as shū lì fān.
Previously,
due to autumn rains,
much of the pond salt in Hézhōng Prefecture was spoiled.
Under the jurisdiction of Hézhōng Prefecture were Ānyì and Xiè Counties,
both having salt ponds.
Xiān,
read as xī jiàn fān.
On Dīnghài,
a report stated that although the rain was heavy,
it did not harm the salt,
and auspicious salt was still produced.
The Emperor doubted this was true,
and sent the Remonstrance Official Jiǎng Zhèn of Yìxīng to go and inspect it.
Yìxīng,
was the location of Yángxiàn County in the Hàn dynasty,
the Jìn dynasty established Yìxīng Commandery and county,
the Suí dynasty abolished the commandery but kept the county,
placing it under Chángzhōu.
The Tibetans invaded Yánzhōu and Xiàzhōu,
and also invaded Chángwǔ;
Yílù County of Bīnzhōu had the Chángwǔ City.
At that time, Guō Zǐyí sent Lǐ Huáiguāng to build Chángwǔ City,
occupying the head of the plain,
overlooking the Jīng River,
commanding a view of the thoroughfare,
and from then on the Tibetans did not dare to lightly invade.
Sòng Bái said: Chángwǔ Garrison,
is within the boundaries of Línyóu County of Fèngxiáng Prefecture,
forty lǐ west to Jīngzhōu.
Xià,
read as hù yǎ fān.
Liú Qià, the Yāyá of the Yǒngpíng Army from Kuāngchéng, was appointed as Prefect of Sòngzhōu.
The Textual Analysis states: The Old Biography of Liú Xuánzuǒ says:
"When Lǐ Língyào occupied Biànzhōu,
Qià led troops and, taking advantage of his unpreparedness,
directly entered Sòngzhōu."
However, according to records, Liú Chāng, as a Yámén General of Sòngzhōu, persuaded Lǐ Sēnghuì to submit,
meaning Sēnghuì was already guarding Sòngzhōu for Língyào,
and the court accordingly appointed him Prefect of Sòngzhōu.
If Sēnghuì had not surrendered,
then Qià could not have taken Sòngzhōu;
if he had already surrendered,
then (Qià) would not dare to seize Sòngzhōu.
It is likely that after Sēnghuì was killed by Lǐ Zhōngchén,
Qià then led troops to occupy Sòngzhōu.
The Old Biography wished to attribute this as Qià's achievement,
hence it says so,
but in reality, it was not.
The Yǒngpíng Army was headquartered in Huázhōu.
The Capital Prefecture Governor Lí Gàn reported that autumn rains had damaged crops,
while Hán Huàng reported that Gàn's account was untrue;
the Emperor ordered a Censor to investigate.
On Dīngwèi,
he returned and reported,
"The total damage is over 30,000 qǐng."
The Magistrate of Wèinán, Liú Zǎo,
Wèinán County,
belonged to Huàzhōu in the early Táng,
at this time it belonged to Yōngzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Guō Yuánshēng's Account of Campaigns states: Wèinán County,
was established by the barbarians,
meaning the Fú and Yáo (states).
(Liú Zǎo) was said to have flattered and attached himself to Hán Huàng.
Dù,
read as tú luò fān.
Censor Zhào Jì's report was the same as Zǎo's.
The Emperor said:
"The heavy rain was widespread,
how could Wèinán alone have none!"
He then ordered Censor Zhū Áo to inspect it,
and the damage was over 3,000 qǐng.
The Emperor sighed for a long time,
and said:
"A county magistrate,
is an official who nurtures the people.
Even if there is no damage, he should still report damage,
how could he be so unkind!"
He demoted Zǎo to the position of Deputy of Nánpǔ.
The Northern Wèi divided Qú Rǔn County to establish Yúquán County,
the Northern Zhōu changed it to Wànchuān,
the Suí changed it to Nánpǔ,
and the Táng attached it to Wànzhōu.
But he did not question Huàng.
In the eleventh month,
on Rénzǐ,
Zhāng Xiàngōng, the military commissioner of Shānnán Xīdào, reported defeating over ten thousand Tibetan troops at Mínzhōu.
On Bǐngchén,
Jiǎng Zhèn returned,
and reported,
"The auspicious salt is indeed as Hán Huàng stated,"
and furthermore submitted a memorial of congratulations,
requesting it be announced to the Historiographers,
and bestowed with an auspicious name.
The Emperor complied,
bestowing the name Bǎoyìng Língyìng Pond.
The bestowed name
refers to the Ānyì Pond.
In the twelfth month,
on Bǐngxū,
Zhū Cǐ returned to the capital from Jīngzhōu.
Zhū Cǐ came to court from Yōuzhōu,
and then remained in the capital,
subsequently being sent for frontier defense and now returning.
Huán,
read as cóng xuān fān,
also pronounced as the usual reading.
On Dīnghài,
Cuī Nìng reported defeating over a hundred thousand Tibetan troops,
beheading over eight thousand.
Tǔ,
follows the entering tone of tūn.
On Gēngzǐ,
Zhū Cǐ was appointed concurrent military commissioner of Lǒngyòu,
and put in charge of the Héxī and Zélù field headquarters.
26. The Pinglú military governor Lǐ Zhèngjǐ originally held the territories of ten prefectures: Zī, Qīng, Qí, Hǎi, Dēng, Lái, Yí, Mì, Dé, and Dì.
During the rebellion of Lǐ Língyào,
various circuits combined their forces to attack him.
The lands they captured
were each taken for themselves.
Lǐ Zhèngjǐ further acquired the five prefectures of Cáo, Pú, Xú, Yǎn, and Yùn.
Consequently, he moved his administrative seat from Qīng Prefecture to Yùn Prefecture,
placing his son, the former prefect of Zī Prefecture, Lǐ Nà, to guard Qīng Prefecture.
Lǐ Zhèngjǐ employed severe punishments,
so that people everywhere dared not even speak in pairs;
however, his laws and decrees were uniform,
and the taxes were equitable and light.
He commanded a hundred thousand troops,
powerfully occupying the eastern region,
and neighboring military governors all feared him.
At this time, Tián Chéngsì held the seven prefectures of Wèi, Bó, Xiàng, Wèi, Míng, Bèi, and Chán.
Chán Prefecture
was located in the territory of Dùnqiū County, Hàndōng Commandery.
In the sixteenth year of the Suí dynasty's Kāihuáng era,
Dùnqiū was divided to establish Chányuān County.
The Táng changed its name to Chánshuǐ,
to avoid the personal name taboo of Emperor Gāozǔ.
In the fourth year of the Wǔdé era,
Chán Prefecture was established from Chánshuǐ of Lí Prefecture, Dùnqiū of Wèi Prefecture, and Guān Prefecture.
In the first year of the Zhēnguān era,
the prefecture was abolished.
In the seventh year of the Dàlì era,
Tián Chéngsì memorialized to re-establish Chán Prefecture
using Dùnqiū and Línhuáng from Wèi Prefecture.
Sì,
read as xiáng lì fān.
Xiàng,
read as xī liàng fān.
Míng,
pronounced as míng.
Chán,
read as shí lián fān.
Each commanded fifty thousand troops.
Liáng Chóngyì held the six prefectures of Xiāng, Dèng, Jūn, Fáng, Fù, and Yǐng,
with twenty thousand troops.
They mutually relied on each other, deeply entrenched and intertwined.
Although they nominally served the imperial court, they did not follow its laws and decrees.
Official titles, ranks, armor, weapons, taxes, levies, punishments, and executions were all decided by themselves.
The Emperor was lenient and benevolent,
allowing them to act as they pleased.
If the imperial court repaired a single city wall
or added a single soldier,
they would immediately voice complaints,
considering it suspicion and disloyalty,
often causing the projects to be halted.
Yet within their own territories, they ceaselessly built fortifications and trained troops.
Therefore, although nominally they were vassals within the Central Kingdom,
in reality, they were like foreign barbarian lands.
1. In spring,
the first month,
on Xīnyǒu,
an edict was issued to destroy the water-powered mills on the tributaries of the Bái Canal to irrigate the fields.
Princess Shēngpíng owned two mills.
She went to see the Emperor,
requesting to preserve them.
The Emperor said:
"I wish to benefit the common people.
If you understand my intent,
you should lead by example for the masses."
The princess destroyed them that very day.
2. On Wùchén,
the Huíhé invaded Tàiyuán.
Lǐ Zìliáng, the Yāyá of Hé dōng from Sìshuǐ, said:
"The Huíhé elite troops have come from afar seeking battle;
it is difficult to contend with them head-on.
It would be better to build two fortifications on their return route,
and garrison troops there.
When the enemy arrives,
fortify the walls and do not engage them in battle.
Once their army is worn out and returns,
then send out our troops to attack them.
With the two fortifications blocking them in front,
and our main army pressing them from behind,
we will be invincible."
The Liúhòu Bào Fáng did not listen.
He dispatched the senior general Jiāo Bóyú and others to meet them in battle.
On Guǐyǒu,
they encountered the enemy at Yángqū,
suffered a great defeat and retreated,
with over ten thousand dead.
The Huíhé troops rampaged and plundered extensively.
In the second month,
the Dàizhōu commander Zhāng Guāngshèng attacked and defeated them at Yángwǔ Valley,
and they then withdrew.
The Emperor also did not inquire into the reason for the Huíhé invasion,
and treated them as before.
3. On Jǐhài,
Tǔbō sent its general Mǎ Chóngyīng to lead forty thousand troops to invade Líng Prefecture.
Tǔ,
read as the entering tone of tūn.
Shuài,
read as shuài.
Shǐ Zhào said: The three canals refer to Zhènhàn Canal, Yùshǐ Canal, and Shàngshū Canal.
Zhèn,
read as zhèn.
4. In the third month,
on Jiǎxū,
a Huíhé envoy was returning,
passing through Hézhōng.
Shòufāng army soldiers plundered their baggage train.
These were Shòufāng army soldiers stationed in Hézhōng.
Shǐ,
read as shū lì fān.
Guò,
read as gǔ hé fān,
also read as gǔ wò fān.
Zī,
read as zhuāng chí fān.
Zhòng,

5. In summer,
the fourth month,
on Jiǎchén,
Tǔbō invaded Líng Prefecture.
The Shòufāng Liúhòu Cháng Qiānguāng attacked and defeated them.
6. In the sixth month,
on Wùxū,
the Lǒngyòu military governor Zhū Cǐ presented a cat and mice suckling together without harming each other, considering it an auspicious sign.
Cháng Gǔn led the officials in offering congratulations.
The Zhōngshū Shèrén Cuī Yòufǔ alone did not congratulate,
saying:
"When things go against their nature, it is an omen.
A cat catching mice
is its duty.
Now they suckle together;
this is an omen.
Why should we congratulate!
We should admonish judicial officials who fail to investigate crimes and border officials who fail to resist invaders,
to comply with Heaven's will."
The Emperor praised him.
Cuī Yòufǔ
was the son of Cuī Miǎn.
Cuī Miǎn was a famous minister of the Kāiyuán era.
Miǎn,
read as mí yǎn fān.
In the seventh month,
Cuī Yòufǔ was appointed to oversee the selection affairs of the Ministry of Personnel.
Yòufǔ frequently disputed official matters with Cháng Gǔn,
and because of this, Gǔn disliked him.
This laid the groundwork for Gǔn's memorial requesting Yòufǔ's demotion.
Xuǎn,
read as xū juàn fān.
Shù,
read as suǒ jiǎo fān.
Wù,
read as wū lù fān.
7. On Wùwǔ,
Guō Zǐyí memorialized that since the Huíhé were still north of the frontier,

This was approved.

8. On Xīnwèi,
the Tǔbō general Mǎ Chóngyīng with twenty thousand troops invaded Yán and Qìng Prefectures.

The bestowal of the surname Lǐ upon Bǎochén is recorded in the 222nd scroll, in the first year of the Bǎoyìng era.
Shǐ,
read as shū lì fān.
10. Twenty thousand Tǔbō troops invaded Yín and Lín Prefectures,

Tǔ,
read as the entering tone of tūn.
Yín Prefecture was located in the territory of Yínyín County, Hàn dynasty Xīhé Commandery.
Lín Prefecture was located in the territory of Xīnqínzhōng of the Hàn dynasty.
Dǎng,
read as dǐ lǎng fān.
Chù,
read as xǔ jiù fān.
11. The Emperor continuously mourned and missed Empress Zhēnyì.
Empress Zhēnyì was Dúgū,
who passed away in the tenth year.
For years he could not bear to bury her.
On Dīngyǒu,
she was finally buried at Zhuānglíng.
Zhuānglíng is located five lǐ northwest of Sānyuán County, Jīngzhào.
On the twelfth day of the ninth month,
Gēngwǔ,
ten thousand Tibetan cavalry descended from Qīngshí Lǐng
and pressed upon Jīngzhōu.
Qīngshí Lǐng is located west of Bǎodìng County in Jīngzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Línjìng City,
lies directly ninety *li* northwest of Jīngzhōu,
and within its boundaries is Qīngshí Lǐng.
Cavalry,
read as *qí jì*.
13 In winter,
the twelfth month,
Bǐngxū,
Lì Bù Shàngshū and Commissioner for Transport, Salt, and Iron, etc., Liú Yàn, was appointed Zuǒ Púyè,
while his duties overseeing the three selections and his commissioner posts remained as before.
14 Guō Zǐyí came to court,
and ordered his administrative assistant, Dù Huángcháng of Jīngzhào, to take charge of the留守 affairs.
Lǐ Huáiguāng secretly plotted to replace Zǐyí,
forged an imperial edict,
and intended to execute the senior general Wēn Rúyǎ and others.
Huángcháng detected the forgery,
and questioned Huáiguāng about it;
Huáiguāng broke into a sweat and confessed his crime.
Thereafter, regarding the generals who were difficult to control,
Huángcháng,假借 Zǐyí's orders,
sent them all out to external posts,
and only then did the military headquarters become peaceful.
15 Dù Yà, Jǐ Shì Zhōng, was appointed Jiāngxī Guānchá Shǐ.
16 The Emperor summoned Lǐ Bì, the判官 of Jiāngxī, for an audience,
and spoke to him about the matter of Yuán Zǎi,
saying:
"It has been eight years since parting with you,
and only now have I been able to punish this traitor.
I relied on the Crown Prince to uncover his阴谋,
so the credit belongs to the Crown Prince.
Spoke,
read as *yù*.
I almost did not see you again."
Bì replied:
"Your servant indeed spoke of this in the past.
If Your Majesty knew that a subject had evil intentions,
you should have removed him;
but your包容 was excessive,
hence it came to this."
The Emperor said:
"Matters should also be perfectly handled,
one cannot act lightly."
The Emperor then said:
"I personally entrusted you to Lù Sìgōng,
yet Sìgōng, following Zǎi's intention,
memorialized to appoint you as Biéjià of Qiánzhōu.
When Sìgōng first pacified Lǐngnán,
he presented a琉璃盘,
nine inches in diameter,
which I considered a supreme treasure.
But when Zǎi's household was raided,
we found a琉璃盘 given by Sìgōng to Zǎi,
one foot in diameter.
When he arrives,
I shall discuss this with you."
Bì said:
"Sìgōng's character is such that
he is cautious,
good at serving others,
fears authority and power,
diligent and meticulous in official duties but does not grasp the greater principles.
Formerly, as a county magistrate,
he had a reputation for capability;
Lù Sìgōng's original name was Jiànkè,
he served as magistrate of Xiāoguān,
was successively transferred to the two counties of Shénwū and Gūzāng,
and his performance evaluations were the best in the empire.
Emperor Xuánzōng considered him worthy to succeed Hàn's Lǔ Gōng,
hence bestowed this name upon him.
But as he was employed by Zǎi,
he therefore exerted his utmost for him.
If Your Majesty truly understands and employs him,
he will also exert his utmost for Your Majesty.
As for the Biéjià of Qiánzhōu,
your servant desired it himself,
it was not his fault.
Moreover, Sìgōng has newly achieved great merit,
referring to the merit of pacifying Lǐngnán.
The Emperor's mind was then appeased,
and he appointed Sìgōng as Bīng Bù Shàngshū.
17 Guō Zǐyí, because the Shuòfāng Jiédù Fùshǐ Zhāng Tán was by nature rigid and blunt,
believed that he, as a military man, looked down upon him,
and bore a grudge against him;
the孔目官 Wú Yào was trusted by Zǐyí,
each military prefecture had a孔目官,
to comprehensively manage all affairs,
an official position.
It means every single matter,
all are managed by him.
Zǐyí became angry,
falsely memorialized that Tán was煽动 the troops,
and had him executed.
The掌书记 Gāo Yǐng strenuously argued against it,

and memorialized to demote Yǐng to Assistant Magistrate of Yīshì.
Yīshì County,
belonged to Hézhōng Prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: Originally the territory of the state of Xún,
Yī Dùn started his wealth here,
hence called Yīshì.
Zǐyí regretted it,
and recommended them all to the court,
saying:
"Wú Yào misled me."
He then dismissed him.
History records that Guō Zǐyí could改正 his errors.
Court,
read as *cháo*.
18 Cháng Gǔn said to the Emperor:
"Your Majesty has long wished to employ Lǐ Bì.
In the past, when Hàn Emperor Xuāndì wished to employ someone among the公卿,
he would first test them in governing the people.
I request to temporarily appoint him as a刺史,
so that he may fully understand the benefits and ills among the people,
and after he reports on his administration, then employ him."
Tàigōng governed Qí,
and reported on his administration in five months.
Bóqín governed Lǔ,
and reported on his administration in three years.
Cháng Gǔn used this典故.
1 In spring,
the first month,
Rénxū,
Lǐ Bì was appointed Cìshǐ of Lǐzhōu.
2 In the second month,
Guǐwèi,
Tián Chéngsì, the Wèibó Jiédù Shǐ, passed away.
He had eleven sons,
but considered his nephew, the Zhōngjūn Bīngmǎ Shǐ Yuè, to be talented,
and had him take charge of military affairs,
with his sons assisting him.
Jiǎshēn,
Yuè was appointed Wèibó Liúhòu.
This sets the stage for Tián Xù killing Yuè.
3 Lǐ Zhōngchén, the Huáixī Jiédù Shǐ,
was greedy, cruel, and fond of women.
If the wives or daughters of his officers were beautiful,
he often forced himself upon them.
He entrusted all military and administrative affairs to his brother-in-law, the Jiédù Fùshǐ Zhāng Huìguāng.
Huìguāng, relying on his power, was暴虐 and overbearing,
causing suffering throughout the military prefecture.
Zhōngchén further appointed Huìguāng's son as a牙将,
who was even more暴虐 and overbearing than his father.
The Zuǒxiāng Dū Yúhòu Lǐ Xīliè,
a clansman of Zhōngchén,
was respected by the multitude.
Xīliè, taking advantage of the众心's resentment and anger,
in the third month,
Dīngwèi,
together with the senior general Dīng Gǎo and others,
killed Huìguāng and his son and drove out Zhōngchén.
Zhōngchén fled alone on horseback to the capital.
The Emperor, considering he had merit—
when the Tibetans invaded the capital,
Zhōngchén was the first among the various garrisons to come to the rescue,
and he also had merit in pacifying Lǐ Língyào—
appointed Xīliè as Cìshǐ of Càizhōu and Liúhòu of Huáixī.
This sets the stage for Lǐ Xīliè's rebellion with Huái and Cài.
He was additionally given jurisdiction over Biàn and Yǐngzhōu,
and his garrison was moved to Biànzhōu.
The Yǒngpíng Army was originally stationed at Huázhōu.
Biàn,
read as *biàn*.
4 Xīnyǒu,
Wáng Hóng, the Róngguǎn Jīnglüè Shǐ, was appointed Hézhōng Shǎoyǐn and Prefectural Administrator.
The deputy of the Hézhōng Deputy Yuánshuài Liúhòu, the部将 Líng Zhèng, was暴虐 and overbearing,
and Hóng restrained him.
Zhèng and his followers took advantage of the night to stage a rebellion.
Hóng learned of it,
so he deliberately shortened the water clock by several marks to错开 the timing.
The rebels were alarmed,
scattered and fled,
Zhèng was captured,
and executed,
and only then did the military prefecture become peaceful.
5 Zhāng Bǎochén, the Chéngdé Jiédù Shǐ, having already requested to resume his original surname,
last year Bǎochén requested to resume the surname Zhāng.
further requested to be bestowed a surname;
in summer,
the fourth month,
Guǐwèi,
he was again bestowed the surname Lǐ.
6 In the fifth month,
on the Guǐmǎo day,
the Emperor first fell ill.
On the Xīnyǒu day,
an edict was issued for the Crown Prince to oversee state affairs.
That evening,
the Emperor passed away in the inner hall of the Zǐchén Palace.
The Emperor was fifty-two years old.
The Zǐchén Hall is located north of the Xuānzhèng Hall and
south of the Pénglái Hall in the Eastern Palace.
On the Guǐhài day,
Emperor Dézōng ascended the throne.
While in mourning,
he strictly adhered to ritual laws.
Once, he summoned Prince Hán Jiǒng for a meal.
Jiǒng
was Dézōng’s younger brother.
No salt or dairy products were served.
Mǎchǐ
refers to purslane.
Lào,
pronounced luò,
means dairy products.
7 Cháng Gǔn had a stern and impatient temperament.
His governance was harsh and meticulous,
which did not align with public sentiment.
At the time, when court officials attended morning and evening mourning sessions,
Gǔn wept so intensely that he became exhausted,
and attendants sometimes had to support him.
The Secretariat Drafter Cuī Yòufǔ pointed this out to the crowd and said:
"When a minister weeps before his sovereign,
is there any ritual that permits being supported?"
When Gǔn heard this,
he resented him even more.
When the court officials discussed mourning attire,
Gǔn believed:
"According to ritual,
a minister wears the coarsest mourning for three years for his sovereign.
Emperor Wén of Hàn established a temporary regulation,
reducing it to thirty-six days.
This matter is recorded in the fifteenth volume of the Former Hàn Annals, in the seventh year of Emperor Wén’s later reign.
All followed the Hàn regulations.
During the mourning periods for Emperor Xuánzōng and Emperor Sùzōng,
it was first reduced to twenty-seven days.
Now, the testamentary edict states:
'All officials under heaven
shall remove their mourning attire after three days.'
In ancient times, high ministers and officials followed their sovereign in mourning.
Since the Emperor’s mourning period is twenty-seven days,
the court officials should also follow this."
Yòufǔ believed:
"The testamentary edict
makes no distinction between court officials and commoners.
Both inside and outside the court,
all are under heaven.
Every official in charge of affairs,

In the early Táng dynasty,

Those who had land paid the zū tax,

When the Ān Lùshān Rebellion broke out during the Zhìdé era,

The various tax-collecting agencies increased their demands without any unified oversight,

without any limits.
Wealthy households had many adult males,

Officials took advantage to nibble away at the people,
with taxes collected every ten days
and monthly deliveries,
making it unbearable and exhausting,
so many fled and became floating households,
with less than four or five out of a hundred remaining as registered residents.

and the Tibetans sent their minister Lùn Qīnmíngsī and others to present tribute.
30. In this year,
the Crown Prince's mother, Lady Wáng, was enfeoffed as Shūfēi.
31. The number of tax households in the empire was 3,085,076,
registered soldiers numbered over 768,000,
registered soldiers referring to
soldiers listed in the registers.
and grain stores amounted to over 2,157,000 hú.
1 Spring,
the first month,
on the Wùchén day,
the military governor of Chéngdé, Lǐ Bǎochén, passed away.
Héng and Jì
constituted the Chéngdé army.
The Textual Analysis states: The *Jiànzhōng Shílù* records:
"On the Dīngsì day of the second month,
Bǎochén died."
This is likely the date the report arrived.
Now we follow the *Dézōng Shílù*.
Gǔ Kuàng's *Yānnán Jì* states:
"In his final years, Zhōngzhì
only accepted deceitful individuals, along with those versed in yīn-yáng, divination, and flattering, opportunistic types.
They competed in presenting prognosticatory charts and texts,
claiming he possessed a noble position,
fraudulently creating vermilion grass and auspicious fungi,
and carving names on stones.
He also set up an altar in the rear courtyard,
observed a vegetarian fast,
and placed golden cups, jade goblets, and silver plates,
saying that sweet dew and divine wine would spontaneously appear within them.
He also claimed that celestial talismans descended.
Zhōngzhì believed his fate was aligned with Heaven,
and none of his officers dared to remonstrate.
He issued documents,
proclaiming to the prefectures and counties:
'Auspicious fungi and vermilion grass,
are auspicious signs for a true king.
They have spontaneously grown upon the altar,
their fragrance fills the courtyard.
Spiritual stones manifest good fortune,
celestial talismans fly in response.
Sweet dew is like honey,
divine wine fills the cups.
These were not sought by me,
yet they arrived unbidden.
Each document is sent to the commanderies and counties within the jurisdiction,
they should be made aware,
and join in the celebration.'
Subsequently, the deceitful men further deceived him, saying:
'Soon, a celestial deity will descend,
bearing a golden casket and jade seal.
Then you will ascend the great position,
bestowed by Heaven.
All regions will submit of their own accord,
no military campaigns will be needed,
and the realm will be peacefully settled.'
Zhōngzhì was greatly pleased.
He generously rewarded them with gold, silver, silks, brocades, and exotic goods.
The yīn-yáng practitioners and deceivers knew their claims were false
and feared exposure and execution.
They jointly said:
'Your Excellency should drink a decoction of sweet dew and auspicious fungus,
then the celestial deity will descend swiftly.'
Zhōngzhì, entirely trusting the deceivers,
thus had poison secretly added to the decoction.
After drinking it,
he immediately lost his voice
and died after three days."
The old biography also holds this view.
However, consider: the magicians and deceivers
were certainly disliked by the entire administration.
Their sole reliance was on Bǎochén alone.
If they poisoned Bǎochén,
being within the headquarters,
with nowhere to flee,
how could they escape death?
Even if the magicians were foolish,
they surely would not do this.
Probably contemporaries saw Bǎochén had drunk their decoction
and fell ill and died,
thus believed the magicians poisoned him,
and Gǔ Kuàng recorded it as such.
Because he was young and weak-minded,
he preemptively executed generals who were difficult to control,
such as Shēnzhōu Prefect Zhāng Xiànchéng and others,
resulting in over ten men dying on the same day.
Bǎochén summoned Yìzhōu Prefect Zhāng Xiàozhōng,
but Xiàozhōng did not go.
Bǎochén then sent Xiàozhōng's younger brother, Xiàojié, to summon him.
Xiàozhōng told Xiàojié to say to Bǎochén:
"What crime have the generals committed,
to be executed one after another?
Xiàozhōng fears death,
so he dares not come,
but he also dares not rebel.
His intention is just like yours in not attending court."
Xiàojié wept and said:
"If so,
Xiàojié will certainly die."
Xiàozhōng said:
"If you go, we both die.
While I am here,
he certainly will not dare to kill you."
Xiàojié then returned,
and Bǎochén did not punish him.
The military commissioner Wáng Wǔjùn,
though of low rank, was brave,
so Bǎochén particularly favored and loved him,
giving his daughter in marriage to Wǔjùn's son, Shìzhēn.
Shìzhēn, in turn, generously cultivated relationships with those around Bǎochén.
Therefore, Xiàozhōng and Wǔjùn alone were spared.
The historian remarks: one must not kill indiscriminately.
This also sets the stage for Xiàozhōng and Wǔjùn's later submission to the court.
Fù,
read as fú yòu fān.
When Bǎochén died,
the administrative officer Hú Zhèn
and the household servant Wáng Tānú advised Wéiyuè to conceal the death for over twenty days.
They forged a memorial from Bǎochén,
requesting that Wéiyuè be allowed to succeed him.
The Emperor did not permit it.
He dispatched the Supervising Secretary Bān Hóng, a man from Jí, to inquire about Bǎochén's illness
and convey instructions.
Wéiyuè tried to bribe Hóng heavily,
but Hóng did not accept,
and returned to report.
Wéiyuè then announced the death,
and assumed the position of acting military governor himself.
He had his officers jointly petition for the imperial insignia and commission,
but the Emperor again did not permit it.
Jí County
belonged to Wèi Prefecture.
Huán,
read as cóng xuān fān,
also pronounced as the character's usual sound.
Jiàng,
read as jí liàng fān.
Initially,
Bǎochén had allied with Lǐ Zhèngjǐ, Tián Chéngsì, and Liáng Chóngyì.
This matter is recorded in the previous volume, under the twelfth year of the Dàlì era of Emperor Dàizōng.
Sì,
read as xiáng lì fān.
Therefore, when Chéngsì died
(see the previous volume, fourteenth year of Dàlì),
he had the commission bestowed upon Tián Yuè.
Emperor Dàizōng complied.
When Yuè first succeeded,
he served the court with utmost respect.
The military governor of Hédōng, Mǎ Suì, memorialized that he would certainly rebel
and requested preparations be made in advance.
At this time, Yuè repeatedly petitioned for Wéiyuè's succession.
The Emperor wished to reform previous malpractices
and did not permit it.
Some advised:
"Wéiyuè already holds his father's domain.
If you do not顺势 appoint him,
he will certainly rebel."
The Emperor said:
"The root cause of bandits' ability to rebel
is that they all rely on our land
and borrow our titles and ranks
to gather their followers.
In the past, we often appointed them according to their desires,
yet rebellion increased daily.
This shows that bestowing titles and commissions cannot stop rebellion but rather fosters it."
Emperor Dézōng, determined to subdue the military governors, uttered these words.
They truly pinpointed the failings of the Sùzōng and Dàizōng eras.
Yet, in the end, he could not stop rebellion
and even provoked it,
because his actions did not match his words.
Zhǎng,
read as zhī zhàng fān.
"Appointing or not appointing amounts to the same thing."
He ultimately did not permit it.
Yuè then, together with Lǐ Zhèngjǐ, each sent envoys to Wéiyuè,
secretly plotting to mobilize troops and defy the imperial command.
The deputy military governor of Wèibó, Tián Tíngjiè, said to Yuè:
"You rely on your uncle's legacy.
Tián Chéngsì was Yuè's uncle.
To sit and enjoy wealth and honor—
is that not good enough?
Why, for no reason, join with Héng and Yùn to become a rebel?
The military governor of Chéngdé governed from Héng Prefecture,
the military governor of Zīqīng governed from Yùn Prefecture,
hence referring to them as Héng and Yùn.
Héng,
read as hù dēng fān.
Yùn,
pronounced yùn.
Who among those who commit treason and rebellion can protect their families?
If you are determined to pursue your ambition,
you should kill me first,
so that I do not witness the extermination of the Tián clan."
He then claimed illness and remained at home.
Yuè personally went to apologize,
Military Judge Shào Zhēn of Chéngdé, upon hearing of Lǐ Wéiyuè's plot,
tearfully admonished him, saying:
"The late Grand Councilor received great favor from the state.
While you, sir, are still in mourning attire,
to hastily betray the state
is absolutely unacceptable."
He urged Wéiyuè to seize the envoy of Lǐ Zhèngjǐ and send him to the capital,
and furthermore requested to campaign against him,
saying:
"If you do this,
the court will commend your loyalty, sir,
and then the command insignia might well be obtained."
Wéiyuè agreed with this,
and had Zhēn draft a memorial.
Senior Administrator Bì Huá said:
"Your late father maintained friendly relations with these two circuits for over twenty years.
How can we abandon them in a single day!
Moreover, even if we seize their envoy,
the court may not necessarily trust us.
If Zhèngjǐ suddenly attacks us,
with our isolated army having no reinforcements,
how will we withstand him!"
Wéiyuè then followed this advice instead.
Former Dìng Prefecture Governor Gǔ Cóngzhèng,
who was Wéiyuè's maternal uncle,
was courageous and resourceful,
and quite well-read.
Wáng Wǔjùn and others all respected and feared him.
He was resented by Lǐ Bǎochén,
so Cóngzhèng then claimed illness and shut his door to visitors.
Wéiyuè also resented him,
and did not consult him on planning matters,
instead day and night solely discussing plans with Hú Zhèn, Wáng Tānú, and others,
and distributing much gold and silk to please the officers and troops.
Cóngzhèng went to see Wéiyuè and said:
"Now, with peace throughout the land,
those who come from the Imperial Domain
— at this time, the military governors privately hold their territories,
comparing themselves to the feudal lords of antiquity,
they refer to the capital as the 'Imperial Domain'.
The Emperor's will is to achieve great peace,
and he deeply does not wish for the descendants of the military governors to monopolize territory.
You are now the first to disobey the imperial edict.
The Son of Heaven is certain to dispatch the various circuits to campaign against you.
The officers and troops have received rewards,
and all say they will exhaust themselves to the death for you, sir;
but if even one battle is not won,
each will cherish his own life,
and who will not become disloyal!
The senior generals who hold power,
taking advantage of the danger and watching for an opportunity,
will all think of capturing you to claim merit for themselves.
Furthermore, the senior generals of high rank killed by the late Grand Councilor
number nearly a hundred.
In times of defeat and chaos,
their sons and brothers who wish to seek revenge —
could they possibly be counted!
Also,
the Grand Councilor had a grievance with Yōu Prefecture,
referring to Lǐ Bǎochén's attack on Zhū Tāo.
This matter is seen in the previous volume, the tenth year of the Dàlì era of Emperor Dàizōng.
Now the Son of Heaven is certain to appoint him as general;
Tāo and we are within earshot of each other's watchmen's clappers,
The Zuǒzhuàn says: Lǔ's watchmen's clappers were heard in Zhū.
This means their borders are connected.
It would be like a tiger or wolf getting hold of prey —
how could we withstand it!
Later, the disasters and defeats of Lǐ Wéiyuè
all occurred as Gǔ Cóngzhèng had said.
Having personally experienced a hundred battles,
his ferocity was known throughout the land.
Defying the edict and raising troops,
he considered himself invincible;
but when Lú Zǐqī was captured,
and Wú Xīguāng returned to allegiance,
Chéngsì pointed to heaven and wept,
not knowing what to do with himself.
He relied on the late Grand Councilor halting the troops and not advancing,
and furthermore pleading for him,
and the late Emperor, being lenient and benevolent,
pardoned and did not execute him.
This matter is also seen in the previous volume, the tenth year of Dàlì.
Xiàng,
pronounced xiàng.
Wéi,
pronounced wèi.
Does the Tián family alone have a special seed!
Moreover, you grew up in wealth and honor,
your age and hair still young,
having not experienced hardship and danger,
yet you believe the words of your attendants,
and wish to imitate what Chéngsì did!
For your plan,
it would be better to decline before your officers,
have Wéichéng temporarily administer the military headquarters,
and personally go to court,
begging to remain for guard duty,
thereby stating that Wéichéng may temporarily stay to handle affairs.
The decree of grace rests with the imperial will;
the Emperor will certainly be pleased with your loyalty and righteousness.
Even if you do not obtain a high position,
you will not lose honor and emolument,
and be forever without worry.
If not,
great calamity will
befall you.
I also know you have always been distant and suspicious of me,
but considering our uncle-nephew bond,
with the situation critical,
I cannot but speak!"
Wéiyuè,
seeing his words were earnest,
disliked him even more.
Cóngzhèng then returned again,
shut his door and claimed illness.
Wéichéng was
Wéiyuè's elder half-brother,
modest, sincere, and fond of study,
and won the hearts of the multitude.
His maternal sister was the wife of Lǐ Zhèngjǐ's son.
'Maternal sister' means
Wéichéng's sister by the same mother.
Wéiyuè sent Wéichéng to Zhèngjǐ,
and Zhèngjǐ had him revert to the surname Zhāng,
whereupon he served in Zīqīng.
Wéiyuè dispatched Wáng Tānú to Cóngzhèng's home,
to observe his daily activities,
intending to kill him.
He made his intention known to him,
to have him take his own life.
As he was about to die,
he said:
"I do not fear death,
I grieve that the Zhāng clan will now be exterminated!"
Lǐ Bǎochén was originally Zhāng Zhōngzhì,
hence he spoke thus.
After Liú Wénxǐ's death,
Lǐ Zhèngjǐ, Tián Yuè, and others all felt uneasy;
after Liú Yàn's death,
Zhèngjǐ and others became even more fearful.
The deaths of Liú Wénxǐ and Liú Yàn are both seen in the previous year.
"Our crimes and evils,
how could they be compared with Liú Yàn's!"
Lǐ Zhèngjǐ and Tián Yuè did not say this to each other face to face,
but had people relay the message that these words were spoken.
Spreading it,
people in the east spread a rumor
that "the Emperor wishes to conduct the eastern fēng sacrifice,
therefore he is fortifying Biàn Prefecture."
Zhèngjǐ, fearful,
dispatched ten thousand troops to garrison Cáo Prefecture;
Cáo Prefecture,
under Lǐ Zhèngjǐ's jurisdiction,
bordered Biàn Prefecture.
Dù Yù said: 'Wán jù' means
to repair the city walls,
and gather the people.
The officials and people of Hénán were thrown into turmoil and alarm.
Yǒngpíng originally governed seven prefectures: Biàn, Sòng, Huá, Bó, Chén, Yǐng, and Sì.
This was after the pacification of Lǐ Língyào,
the territory under the jurisdiction of the Yǒngpíng Army.
According to this, in the seventh year of the Dàlì era of Emperor Dàizōng,
the Huá-Bó Army was granted the name Yǒngpíng;
in the eleventh year,
after pacifying Lǐ Língyào,
it was given additional jurisdiction over Sòng and Sì prefectures;
in the fourteenth year,
it was given additional jurisdiction over Biàn and Yǐng prefectures.
Before the Huá-Bó Army was granted its name,
it already governed Chén Prefecture,
making seven prefectures in total.
On the bǐngzǐ day,
Sòng, Bó, and Yǐng were separated to form a separate military governor,
with Sòng Prefecture Governor Liú Qià appointed to it;
Sì Prefecture was placed under Huáinán;
also, the Eastern Capital Retainer Lù Sìgōng was appointed military governor of four prefectures — Huái, Zhèng, Rǔ, and Shǎn — and the Sānchéng of Héyáng.
Within ten days,
Yǒngpíng Military Governor Lǐ Miǎn was further made commander-in-chief of the two circuits of Qià and Sìgōng,
and Zhèng Prefecture was also transferred to his jurisdiction.
Men who had formerly served as generals were selected as prefectural governors,
to guard against Zhèngjǐ and others.
2. Initially,
Gāo Lìshì had an adopted daughter who was widowed and living in the Eastern Capital,
and she was quite capable of speaking about matters within the palace.
The female official Lǐ Zhēnyī suspected that she was Empress Dowager Shěn,
and went to the envoy to describe her appearance in detail.
Last year, an envoy was dispatched to search for the Empress Dowager.
(The emperor) was pleasantly surprised.
At that time, the old acquaintances of the Shěn family had all passed away,
and there was no one who could recognize the Empress Dowager.
The emperor sent eunuchs and palace ladies to examine and observe her;
her age and appearance were quite similar.
The eunuchs and palace ladies did not carefully recognize the Empress Dowager,
and all said it was her.
The Gāo woman declined, claiming she was indeed not the Empress Dowager,
but those examining her grew even more suspicious,
and forcibly welcomed her into the Shàngyáng Palace.
The emperor dispatched over a hundred palace ladies,
bearing imperial carriages, garments, and utensils to serve at the Shàngyáng Palace.
Those around her coaxed and persuaded her in every possible way;
the Gāo woman’s heart wavered,
and she then claimed herself to be (the Empress Dowager).
The examiners galloped on horseback to report,
and the emperor was overjoyed.
In the second month,
on Xīnmǎo,
the emperor held court on an even-numbered day,
and all the ministers entered to offer congratulations.
According to Táng regulations: the Son of Heaven receives court congratulations on odd-numbered days.
Now, delighted at finding the Empress Dowager,
he therefore held court on an even-numbered day to receive congratulations.
The Gāo woman’s younger brother, Chéngyuè, was in Cháng’ān,
fearing that if he did not speak out,
he would eventually be punished,
and hastily recounted the whole story.
The emperor ordered Fán Jǐngchāo, the adopted grandson of Gāo Lìshì, to go and re-examine her.
Jǐngchāo saw the Gāo woman residing in the inner palace,
conducting herself as the Empress Dowager,
with guards and attendants around her in strict formation.
Jǐngchāo said to the Gāo woman:
“Aunt, why have you placed yourself on the chopping block!”
This means she would be punished for fraud and deception,
as if placing herself on a chopping block,
awaiting the knife.
Jǐngchāo raised his voice and declared:
“By imperial decree,
the Empress Dowager is fraudulent;
all attendants may step down.”
All attendants descended from the hall.
The Gāo woman then said:
“I was forced by others;
it was not of my own doing.”
She was taken back to her home in an ox cart.
The emperor feared that people would no longer dare to speak of the Empress Dowager,
so he did not punish any of them,
saying:
“I would rather be deceived a hundred times,
in hopes of finding her.”
From then on, from all directions, there were several reports of finding the Empress Dowager,
but none were true,
and the real Empress Dowager ultimately remained missing.
Zhī means
to go.
3. The Censor-in-Chief Lú Qǐ,
was the son of Lú Yì.
In the fourteenth year of the Tiānbǎo era,
Ān Lùshān captured Luòyáng,
and Lǐ Chéng and Lú Yì died there.
(Lú Qǐ’s) complexion was bluish,
and he was eloquent;
the emperor favored him.
On Dīngwèi,
he was promoted to Grand Master,
promoted to Censor-in-Chief.
Sentence.
His concubines never left his side.
(Lú Qǐ) once went to inquire about (Guō Zǐyí’s) illness,
and Zǐyí dismissed all his serving concubines,
waiting alone, leaning on a table.
Someone asked the reason,
and Zǐyí said:
“(Lú Qǐ) is ugly in appearance and treacherous at heart;
if the women see him, they will surely laugh.
If he achieves power in the future,
our clan will be wiped out!”
After Yáng Yán had Liú Yàn killed,
both court and commoners viewed him with suspicion and fear.
Lǐ Zhèngjǐ repeatedly submitted memorials requesting an investigation into Yàn’s crimes,
criticizing and condemning the court.
Yán grew fearful,
and sent trusted aides to various circuits,
under the pretext of conveying imperial consolation,
but actually to secretly instruct the military governors, saying:
“Yàn previously associated with treacherous villains,
and requested the establishment of Dúgū as Empress;
the emperor hated him for this and had him killed.”
The emperor heard of this and despised him,
and from then on harbored the intention to execute Yán,
but kept it hidden and did not act.
On Yǐsì,
Yán was transferred to be Vice Director of the Secretariat,
and Lú Qǐ was promoted to Vice Director of the Chancellery,
both serving as Tongpingzhangshi,
so Yán was no longer solely entrusted.
(Lú Qǐ) was short and ugly,
lacking literary talent;
Yán looked down on him,
often feigning illness and not joining the communal meals.
According to Táng regulations: all chancellors
dined together daily in the Administrative Hall.
(Lú Qǐ) was cunning and treacherous,
wanting to build his influence and establish authority;
anyone who showed even slight opposition, he sought to put to death.
He recommended Tàicháng Bóshì Péi Yánlíng to be a Zhíxuéshì of the Jíxián Hall,
and placed close trust in him.
This sets the stage for Lú Qǐ’s treachery leading to chaos.
However, as the catalyst for the Jiànzhōng calamities,
everyone knew it;
his recommendation of Péi Yánlíng to form a faction,
the disaster spread,
lasting until the final years of the Zhēnyuán era,
yet people did not realize his crime.
Therefore, the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn explicitly states it.
4. On Bǐngwǔ,
the Biànsòng Army was renamed Xuānwǔ.
According to this, at that time Lǐ Miǎn, as Military Governor of the Yǒngpíng Army, garrisoned Biànzhōu,
likely establishing Sòng, Bó, and Yǐng as the Xuānwǔ Army.
This should follow the New Book’s Regional Commands Table.
Gēng means
Gōng Héng’s annotation.
5. The Military Governor of Zhènwǔ, Péng Lìngfāng, was harsh and cruel,
and the Supervisor Liú Huìguāng was greedy and corrupt;
on Yǐmǎo,
the soldiers jointly killed them.
6. Dispatched twelve thousand troops from the Western Capital’s autumn defense to garrison Guāndōng.
At that time, the Tǔbō had made peace,
and the western border was without alarm,
but the various garrisons in Hénán and Hébèi joined forces in defying orders,
causing unrest in Guāndōng.
Therefore, troops from the Western Capital’s autumn defense were drawn to garrison Guāndōng.
The Wàngchūn Tower,
located west of the Bà River,
overlooked the Guǎngyùn Pond.
Only the Shéncè Army soldiers did not drink;
the emperor sent someone to question them,
and their general Yáng Huìyuán replied:
“When we departed from Fèngtiān,
Army Commander Zhāng Jùjì admonished us: ‘On this campaign, achieve great merit and fame;
on the day of triumphant return,
we shall celebrate together.’
Therefore, we dare not accept the order.”
According to the first year of Jiànzhōng,
Shéncè Army Commander Zhāng Jùjì was sent to lead imperial troops to assist Zhū Cǐ and others in suppressing Liú Wénxǐ.
Likely after Jīngzhōu was pacified,
Jùjì returned to garrison Fèngtiān.
Jié means
Qù Jí’s annotation.
Shuài means
Suǒ Lèi’s annotation.
Huán means
pronounced Xuán,
or also as the original character.
Officials set up wine and food along the route,
but only Huìyuán’s troops did not open their bottles and jars.
The emperor deeply admired and praised them,
bestowing a letter to commend them.
Huìyuán
was from Píngzhōu.
Píngzhōu,
Běipíng Commandery.
7. In the third month,
established Yīnzhōu at Yǎnchéng.
Wèi Shōu’s Treatise on Geography: Qūyáng County of Yǐngchuān Commandery had Yǎnchéng.
Later, the Northern Qí established the Línyǐng Commandery,
the Suí abolished the commandery,
making it Yǎnchéng County,
which belonged to Càizhōu in the Táng.
At that time, Yǎnchéng, Línyǐng, and the Yīn River of Chénzhōu were divided to establish Yīnzhōu.
Yīn,
pronounced Yújīn’s annotation.
Yǎn,
pronounced Yújiàn’s annotation.
8. On Xīnsì,
appointed Wáng Hóng, Governor of Fénzhōu, as Military Commissioner of Zhènwǔ and Deputy Commander of Zhènběi, Suí, Yín, and other prefectures.
9. Sent Diànzhōng Shǎojiān Cuī Hànhéng as envoy to the Tǔbō.
1 On the gēngyín day of the sixth month,
Hán Huàng, the Surveillance Commissioner of Eastern and Western Zhèjiāng and Prefect of Sūzhōu, was appointed as Prefect of Rùnzhōu and Military Commissioner of Eastern and Western Zhèjiāng.
Sūzhōu's
administrative seat was in Wú County.
Huàng,
is pronounced Huǎng.
Rùnzhōu's
administrative seat was in Jīngkǒu.
Commissioner (shǐ),
is pronounced shǐ.
2 Zhāng Zhù arrived in Xiāngyáng.
He had been dispatched in the fourth month of this year,
and now reached Xiāngyáng.
It seems Zhāng Zhù also suspected Liáng Chóngyì,
and thus delayed his advance.
(Liáng Chóngyì) arrayed his troops and received him.
Lìn Gǎo, upon receiving the imperial edict, did not dare to act,
(this refers to) the edict appointing him to Dèngzhōu.
He requested a pardon for his life.
In the end, he did not accept the edict.
Zhāng Zhù returned to report.
On the guǐsì day,
Lǐ Xīliè was promoted to the rank of Prince of Nánpíng Commandery.
(Nánpíng Commandery was in) Yúzhōu.
He was ordered to oversee the armies from various circuits to campaign against (Liáng Chóngyì).
Textual analysis note: The "Dé Zōng Shílù" records:
"On the jǐsì day of the fifth month,

Huáiníng Military Commissioner Lǐ Xīliè was granted the title Prince of Nánpíng Commandery and concurrently appointed as General-in-Chief and Pacification Commissioner of the armies south and north of the Hàn River."
The biography of Lǐ Xīliè states:

and together with Qià, Huán, and Chéng, rescue them.
At that time, the supplies and equipment for the Shuòfāng army had not arrived,
their banners and uniforms were worn and shabby,
the Xuānwǔ troops mocked them, saying:
"Can beggars defeat the rebels!"
Cháochén used these words to incite his soldiers,
and said:
"The Commander-in-Chief has ordered,
whoever first breaks the enemy camp,
everything in the camp will be given to him."
The soldiers were all enraged and fought with great fervor.
Chóngqìng and Wēn attacked Péngchéng,
but after twenty days they could not take it,
so they requested reinforcements from Nà;
Nà sent his general Shí Yǐnjīn with ten thousand men to assist them.
*Kǎoyì* says: The *Shílù* first writes
"Yǐnjīn,"
later it writes
"Yǐnquán."
We now follow the earlier version.
As dusk approached,
Qià led his troops to retreat slightly.
The Shuòfāng cavalry commander Yáng Cháochéng said to Táng Cháochén:
"You, sir, position your infantry with their backs to the mountain in formation,
to await the two armies.
I will hide the cavalry in the mountain's bend.
When the enemy sees your isolated force appears vulnerable,
they will certainly attack it.
I will then cut them off at the waist with the ambush,
and we are sure to defeat them."
Cháochén agreed.
Chóngqìng and others indeed led two thousand cavalry across the bridge to the west,
pursuing and attacking the government troops.
The ambush was sprung,
striking them from the side;
Chóngqìng's forces were cut in two,
and they retreated in disarray,
holding the bridge to resist the government troops.
Some of their soldiers, unable to seize the bridge,
crossed by wading through the water.
Cháochéng pointed at them and said:
"If they can wade across,
why can't we!"
So they waded through the water and attacked.
Those holding the bridge all fled,
and Chóngqìng's troops were utterly routed;
Qià and others pressed the advantage,
beheading eight thousand,
with over half drowning.
The Shuòfāng army captured all their baggage and supplies.
Their banners and uniforms were bright and splendid,
so they said to the Xuānwǔ men:
"How does the beggars' achievement
compare with Sòng's?"
Sòng
refers to the Xuānwǔ troops.
At that time, Sòng and Bó constituted the Xuānwǔ Army.
Liú Qià, from Prefect of Sòngzhōu, became Military Commissioner of Xuānwǔ,
hence the expression.
The government troops pursued the fleeing enemy in victory,
reaching the walls of Xúzhōu.
The Wèibó and Zīqīng armies lifted the siege and fled,
and the water transport from Jiāngnán and Huáidōng finally became passable.
On the 22nd, Jǐsì,
an edict was issued stripping Lǐ Wéiyuè of his offices and ranks;
it recruited those among his subordinates who would surrender,
pardoning and rewarding them.
On the 23rd, Jiǎshēn,
Chén Shàoyóu, Military Commissioner of Huáinán, sent troops to attack Hǎizhōu,
and its Prefect Wáng Shè surrendered the prefecture.
Hǎizhōu
was under Lǐ Nà's jurisdiction.
Shǐ,
read as *shū lì fān*.
Shǎo,
read as *shǐ zhào fān*.
Jiàng,
read as *hù jiāng fān*.
In the twelfth month,
Mǎ Wàntōng, Prefect of Mìzhōu under Lǐ Nà, requested to surrender;
on Dīngyǒu,
he was appointed Prefect of Mìzhōu.
Sòng Bái says: Mìzhōu borders the sea,
occupying the land of Yúyí mentioned in the *Tribute of Yu*.
During the Spring and Autumn period, it was the territory of Jǔ and Lǔ.
The prefectural seat,
is the Zhūchéng of Lǔ,
in Hàn times it was the Kingdom of Gāomì,
in Jìn times the Dōngguǎn Commandery was established,
in Later Wèi times Jiāozhōu was established;
Suí changed it to Mìzhōu,
taking the Mì River within its borders as the name.
Cuī Hànhéng reached Tibet,
Cuī Hànhéng's mission to Tibet,
see the third month of this year in the previous scroll.
Tǔ,
read as *cóng tūn rù shēng*.
He was received entirely according to the rituals for a subject;
furthermore,
west of Yúnzhōu,
the border should be at the Hèlán Mountains.
The *Wǔdài Zhì* states,
Língwǔ Hóngjìng County has the Hèlán Mountains.
Hóngjìng County
was renamed Bǎojìng in Táng.
Yúnzhōu
should be Língzhōu,
the text is mistaken.
On Dīngwèi,
Hànhéng sent his administrative assistant and a Tibetan envoy to report to the court.
The Emperor accordingly altered the imperial edict
and the territorial boundaries,
granting all their requests.
As military operations were underway in Guāndōng and Héběi,
there was no leisure to dispute with Tibet.
Mǎ Suì was additionally appointed Pacification Commissioner of Wèibó.
In spring,
the first month,
Lǐ Jiāo, Military Commissioner of Héyáng, led troops to press against Wèizhōu.
Tián Yuè's defending general Rèn Lǚxū feigned surrender,
but later rebelled again.
Wèizhōu,
administered from Jí.
Jiāo,
read as *jū bāo fān*.
Jiàng,
read as *jí liàng fān*.
Rèn,
read as *yīn rén*.
Jiàng,
read as *hù jiāng fān*.
Fù,
read as *fú yòu fān*,
also read as the usual pronunciation.
2 Mǎ Suì and other armies were stationed at the banks of the Zhāng River.
Tián Yuè sent his general Wáng Guāngjìn to build a crescent-shaped fortification to defend the Long Bridge.
The Long Bridge
was over the Zhāng River.
The crescent-shaped fortification,
with its two ends embracing the river,
was shaped like a half-moon.
Mǎ Suì linked several hundred carts with iron chains,
filled them with earth bags,
and blocked the river's lower flow.
The water became shallow,
allowing the various armies to wade across.
At that time, the army was short on provisions,
and Tián Yuè and others, behind deep fortifications, refused to engage in battle.
Mǎ Suì ordered the armies to carry ten days' worth of rations,
advanced, and stationed themselves at Cāngkǒu,
positioning his forces opposite Tián Yuè's across the Huán River.
Lǐ Bàozhēn and Lǐ Kuāng asked:
"With limited rations and advancing deep into enemy territory,
why?"
Mǎ Suì said:
"Limited rations favor swift battle.
Now the three military districts have joined forces but are not fighting.
The three districts
refer to Wèi-Bó, Zī-Qīng, and Chéng-Dé.
Kuāng,
pronounced with the initial 'j' and the rhyme 'bao', with the 'fān' tone.
Shǎo (few),
pronounced with the initial 'sh' and the rhyme 'shao', with the 'fān' tone.
If we divide our forces to attack his left and right,
Tián Yuè is sure to rescue them,
then we will be attacked from front and rear,
and the battle will certainly be unfavorable.
Therefore, advancing our army to press Tián Yuè
is what is called 'attacking what he is sure to rescue'.
Military strategy has this saying.
I will certainly defeat him for all of you."
He then built three bridges across the Huán River,
and daily went forth to challenge to battle,
but Tián Yuè did not come out.
Mǎ Suì ordered the armies to rise and eat at midnight,
and secretly led the troops along the Huán River straight towards Wèi Prefecture,
ordering:
"If the enemy arrives,
then halt and form battle arrays."
He left a hundred cavalrymen in the camp to beat drums and sound horns,
still holding firewood and torches.
Once the various armies had all departed,
they were to cease the drums and horns and hide nearby.
Once Tián Yuè's army had all crossed,
they were to burn the bridges.
The army had marched about ten lǐ,
when Tián Yuè heard of it.
He led forty thousand infantry and cavalry from Zī-Qīng and Chéng-Dé across the bridges to attack from the rear,
taking advantage of the wind to set fires,
and advancing with loud shouts.
Zào (clamor),
pronounced with the initial 'z' and the rhyme 'zao', with the 'fān' tone.
(Mǎ Suì's army) first cleared the grass and undergrowth for a hundred paces ahead to create a battlefield,
formed battle arrays, and waited.
They recruited over five thousand brave warriors to form the front ranks.
When Tián Yuè's army arrived,
the fires ceased,
and their momentum waned.
Mǎ Suì unleashed his troops to attack them,
and Tián Yuè's army was greatly defeated.
The Shéncè, Zhāoyì, and Héyáng armies retreated slightly.
Shéncè
refers to Lǐ Shèng's army.
Zhāoyì,
refers to Lǐ Bàozhēn's army.
Héyáng,
refers to Lǐ Kuāng's army.
They turned back to fight,
and again defeated (the enemy).
Pursuing the fleeing enemy to the river,
the three bridges were already burned.
The three bridges
were the ones over the Huán River.
Those who plunged into the water and drowned were too many to count,
over twenty thousand heads were cut off,
and more than three thousand were captured.
Corpses lay piled upon each other for over thirty lǐ.
Tián Yuè gathered his remaining troops, over a thousand men, and fled to Wèi Prefecture.
Mǎ Suì and Lǐ Bàozhēn were not in harmony,
and halted their troops at the Píngyì pagoda.
Tián Yuè arrived at the southern outer wall at night,
(this refers to) the southern outer wall of Wèi Prefecture.
He waited for the government troops.
After a long time,
as dawn was approaching,
Cháng Chūn then opened the gate and let him in.
Tián Yuè killed Cháng Chūn,
and prepared the city for defense.
The soldiers in the city numbered less than a few thousand.
The relatives of the dead
wailed and filled the streets.
Tián Yuè, worried and fearful,
then took his sword,
mounted his horse, and stood outside the gate of his headquarters.
He assembled all the soldiers and civilians,
and with tears said:
"I, Yuè, am unworthy.
I received the support and recommendation from the two elders of Zī-Qīng and Chéng-Dé,
and succeeded to my uncle's position.
(The elders were) Lǐ Zhèngjǐ of Zī-Qīng and Lǐ Bǎochén of Chéng-Dé.
Tián Yuè served them as elders.
The uncle
was Tián Chéngsì.
Zī,
pronounced with the initial 'zh' and the rhyme 'zhuang', with the 'chí' tone and the 'fān' tone.
Sì (to succeed),
pronounced with the initial 'x' and the rhyme 'xiang', with the 'lì' tone and the 'fān' tone.
Their sons could not inherit,
and I, Yuè, dared not forget the great kindness of the two elders.
Not measuring my own strength,
I rashly resisted the court's orders.
Having suffered defeat to this extent,
causing you gentlemen to have your livers and brains spilled on the ground,
it is all my crime.
I have an elderly mother,
so I cannot kill myself.
I wish you all to use this sword to cut off my head,
take it out of the city, and surrender to Vice Director Mǎ,
to seek your own wealth and honor.
Do not die together with me!"
Thereupon, he threw himself from his horse to the ground.
The officers and soldiers rushed forward to support and hold Tián Yuè, saying:
"Your Excellency raised troops for a righteous cause,
not for personal gain.
Victory and defeat,
are common occurrences for military men.
We have received your kindness for generations.
How can we bear to hear this!
We wish to follow Your Excellency into one more battle.
If we do not win, then we will follow with death."
Tián Yuè said:
"Since you all do not abandon me, Yuè, in my defeat,
even if I die,
how dare I forget your profound kindness in the underworld!"
Then he and the various generals each cut off a lock of hair,
swore to be brothers,
and pledged to live and die together.
He took out all that was in the government storehouses and collected wealth from the rich families,
obtaining over a million (units),
to reward the soldiers.
The hearts of the multitude began to settle.
Tián Yuè was adept at surviving defeat, not perishing.
This is the so-called 'even among robbers there is a code'.
He had them reorganize the troops,
repair the defenses,
and the army's momentum revived.
Tián Yuè did not employ Xíng Cáojùn.
See the previous year in the previous scroll.
Fù (again),
pronounced with the initial 'f' and the rhyme 'fu', with the 'yòu' tone and the 'fān' tone.
Also pronounced according to its usual reading.
Lǐ Nà stationed his army at Púyáng.
Pressed by the Hé'nán army,
he fled back to Pú Prefecture.
Textual analysis says: At that time, Pú Prefecture administered Juànchéng.
There was a separate Púyáng County.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì,
Púyáng County was ninety lǐ east of Pú Prefecture.
Pú,
pronounced with the initial 'b' and the rhyme 'bo', with the 'mù' tone and the 'fān' tone.
Tián Yuè sent the army envoy Fú Lín with three hundred cavalry to escort him.
Fú Lín's father, Lìngqí, said to Fú Lín:
"I am old.
Having observed all the rebels like Ān (Lùshān) and Shǐ (Sīmíng),
where are they now!
How long can the Tián family last!
You should take this opportunity to abandon rebellion and follow loyalty.
This will make your father's name praised by later generations."
He bit his arm in farewell.
Fú Lín then, with his deputy Lǐ Yáo, led his troops and surrendered to Mǎ Suì.
Tián Yuè arrested and executed his family.
Lìngqí cursed slowly and died.
Lǐ Yáo's father, Zàichūn, surrendered with Bó Prefecture.
Tián Yuè's cousin Áng surrendered with Míng Prefecture.
Wáng Guāngjìn surrendered with the Long Bridge.
Tián Yuè had entered the city for over ten days
when Mǎ Suì and the other armies finally arrived below the city walls.
They attacked,
but could not capture it.
3 On the bǐngyín day,
Lǐ Wéiyuè dispatched troops along with Mèng Yòu to defend Shùlù.
Shùlù,
was originally Lùchéng County.
When Ān Lùshān rebelled,
Emperor Xuánzōng changed the county's name to Shùlù to suppress him,
and it belonged to Shēn Prefecture.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: it was located 45 lǐ west of the prefectural seat.
Sòng Bái said: Shùlù County,
was originally the territory of Xīliáng County in the Hàn dynasty,
and the ruins of the old Xīliáng city still exist 60 lǐ south of the present county.
They advanced and besieged Shēn Prefecture.
Lǐ Wéiyuè was worried and fearful,
and his chief secretary, Shào Zhēn, again persuaded Wéiyuè,
to secretly prepare a memorial,
first sending his younger brother Wéijiǎn to the court;
then executing the generals who would not obey orders,
and personally going to the court,
having his father-in-law, Jì Prefecture Governor Zhèng Shēn, temporarily act as military commissioner,
to await the court's command.
After Wéijiǎn had departed,
Mèng Yòu learned of this plan,
and secretly sent word to Tián Yuè.
Tián Yuè was furious,
and sent his yá official Hù Jí to see Wéiyuè,
reproaching him, saying:
"The Minister raised troops,
precisely to seek the ceremonial banner and staff for you, Grand Master,
the matter began in the second year of the previous scroll.
Jí,
yú jí fān.
Shàng,
chén yáng fān.
Wèi,
yú wèi fān;
below, fēi wèi, xiāng wèi are the same.
Now you, Grand Master, actually believe Shào Zhēn's words,
send your brother to present a memorial,
placing all the crimes of rebellion on the Minister,
seeking to cleanse yourself,
how has the Minister wronged you, Grand Master, that it has come to this!
If you execute Shào Zhēn for me,
then I will treat you as before;
if not,
I will break with you, Grand Master."
Judge Bì Huá said to Wéiyuè:
"Minister Tián, for your sake, Grand Master, has plunged himself into a heavy siege,
if you, Grand Master, betray him one day,
it is most unrighteous.
Moreover, the troops of Wèibó and Zīqīng are strong and provisions are plentiful,
sufficient to resist the realm,
the outcome is still unknown,
how can you hastily adopt such an inconsistent plan!"
Wéiyuè was by nature timid,
and could not hold to his previous plan,
so he summoned Shào Zhēn,
and before Hù Jí, executed him;
he mobilized ten thousand troops from Chéngdé,
and together with Mèng Yòu, besieged Shùlù.
On the bǐngyín day,
Zhū Tāo and Zhāng Xiàozhōng fought them beneath the walls of Shùlù,
and Wéiyuè was badly defeated,
burning his camp and fleeing.
Examination of discrepancies: The Shílù and the old biography of Wéiyuè only mention one defeat for Wéiyuè.
According to Tāo's biography:
"Tāo and Xiàozhōng attacked him,
and heavily defeated Wéiyuè at Shùlù.
Tāo ordered a flank army to guard Shùlù,
and advanced to besiege Shēn Prefecture.
Wéiyuè then led over ten thousand troops and Tián Yuè's relief forces to besiege Shùlù.
Wéiyuè's general Wáng Wǔjùn led three thousand cavalry in a horizontal battle formation to advance.
Tāo had silk embroidered with images of suānní,
and had a hundred fierce warriors cover themselves with it,
beating drums and shouting as they charged fiercely,
the enemy horses were startled and thrown into chaos,
they followed with an attack,
heavily defeated them,
and Wéiyuè burned his camp and fled."
According to this,
then Wéiyuè was defeated twice.
The Yānnán Jì,
says Mèng Yòu was defeated first,
then Wéiyuè was defeated again.
This corresponds with Tāo's biography,
so we follow this now.
The military commissioner Wáng Wǔjùn was framed by those around him,
and Wéiyuè suspected him,
but valued his talent,
and could not bear to eliminate him.
During the battle at Shùlù,
he sent Wǔjùn as the vanguard,
who privately plotted, saying:
"If I defeat Zhū Tāo,
then Wéiyuè's military power will greatly increase,
and upon returning,
he will certainly kill me."
Therefore, he did not fight very hard and was defeated.
Zhū Tāo wanted to take advantage of the victory to attack Héng Prefecture,
but Zhāng Xiàozhōng led his army northwest,
and encamped at Yìfēng.
Yìfēng County,
belonged to Dìng Prefecture.
Xiàozhōng's officers all found this strange,
but Xiàozhōng said:
"Héng Prefecture still has many veteran generals,
they are not easy to underestimate.
If pressed, they will unite and fight to the death,
but if given respite, they will plot against each other.
You gentlemen just watch,
with our army at Yìfēng,
we can sit and wait for Wéiyuè's destruction.
Moreover, Minister Zhū talks big but has shallow insight,
one can start with him,
but it is difficult to finish with him!"
Zhū Tāo later indeed turned out as Zhāng Xiàozhōng had predicted.
He did not dare advance.
Wéiyuè's general Kāng Rìzhī surrendered Zhào Prefecture to the state,
making Wéiyuè even more suspicious of Wáng Wǔjùn,
and Wǔjùn was very afraid.
Someone said to Wéiyuè:
"The late Grand Councilor entrusted his trusted confidant to Wǔjùn,
the late Grand Councilor,
refers to Lǐ Bǎochén.
Xiàng,
xī liàng fān.
Moreover, there is a kinship bond.
This refers to Wǔjùn's son Shìzhēn being a son-in-law of the Lǐ family.
Now in this time of crisis,
you add suspicion and obstruction;
if not Wǔjùn,
whom do you want to use, Grand Master, to repel the enemy!"
Wéiyuè thought this reasonable,
so he sent the infantry commander Wèi Chángníng to attack Zhào Prefecture together with Wǔjùn,
and also sent Wáng Shìzhēn to lead troops and stay in the headquarters to protect himself.
4 On the guǐwèi day,
the Prince of Shǔ, Suì, changed his name to Sù.
5 The Huáinán military commissioner Chén Shǎoyóu captured Hǎi and Mì prefectures,
but Lǐ Nà attacked and recaptured them.
6. Wáng Wǔjùn, having already left Héngzhōu,
said to Wèi Chángníng:
"Wǔjùn is now fortunate to have escaped the tiger's mouth,
and will not return!
I should go north and submit to Minister Zhāng."
Chángníng said:
"The Grand Master is dim-witted and weak,
trusting his close attendants.
Judging by the situation, he will ultimately be destroyed by Zhū Tāo.
Now the Son of Heaven has issued an edict:
whoever obtains the head of the Grand Master
will be granted his official position and rank.
The Vice Censor-in-Chief has always been respected by the multitude.
Rather than fleeing into exile,
why not turn your weapons against him and seize the Grand Master,
transforming calamity into fortune?
It is as easy as turning over one's hand!
If the endeavor should fail,
then submit to Minister Zhāng—
it would not be too late."
Wǔjùn deeply considered this to be right.
It happened that Wéi Yuè sent the Yàojí official Xiè Zūn to the walls of Zhàozhōu.
The Yàojí official
was also a position in the military headquarters of the Tang dynasty's military governors.
In the second year of the Jǐngyún era of Emperor Zhōngzōng,
Xiè Wǎn served as the Grand Commander of Shuòfāng.

He dispatched the accompanying army Yàojí officials Héyáng Assistant Magistrate Zhāng Guànzōng, Féixiāng Magistrate Wéi Jǐngjùn, and Pǔ'ān Magistrate Yú Chùzhōng to inspect and manage the recruited soldiers of the three cities.
Thus, the Tang frontier garrisons had Yàojí officials for a long time.
Furthermore, according to the "Biographies of the Loyal and Righteous" in the New Book,
when Zhū Cǐ commanded the Yōuzhōu expeditionary camp
and served as the military governor of Jīngyuán and Fèngxiáng,
an edict appointed Cài Tíngyù, as the Junior Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, to be the Military Administrator,
and Zhū Tǐwēi to be the Yàojí.
Thus, the Yàojí
was indeed a trusted confidant of the military governor.
When Zhū Tāo and Wáng Wǔjùn became kings,
they changed the title of the Yàojí official to Chénglìng.
Zūn returned
and secretly informed Wáng Shìzhēn.
In the intercalary month,
on the jiǎchén day,
Wǔjùn and Chángníng led troops back from Zhàozhōu to launch a surprise attack on Wéi Yuè.
Zūn and Shìzhēn forged an order from Wéi Yuè
and opened the city gates to let them in.
At dawn,
Wǔjùn led several hundred cavalrymen to charge through the gates of the headquarters.
Shìzhēn responded from inside,
killing over ten people.
Wǔjùn issued an order:
"The Grand Master has rebelled.
Officers and soldiers who submit
—dare to disobey and resist will have their clans exterminated!"
None among the multitude dared to move.
They then captured Wéi Yuè,
arrested Zhèng Shēn, Bì Huá, Wáng Tānú, and others,
and executed them all.
Wǔjùn, because Wéi Yuè was the son of his former commander,
Lǐ Bǎochén had already died,
hence the term "former commander."
Shǐ (commander),
read as shū lì fān.
Chángníng said:
"If he sees the Son of Heaven,
he will again shift the crime of rebellion onto the Vice Censor-in-Chief."
They then strangled him to death
and sent his head to the capital.
This ultimately matched what Gǔ Cóngzhèng had said.
In the first year of the Guǎngdé era of Emperor Dàizōng,
Lǐ Bǎochén commanded Chéngdé.
It lasted for two generations, nineteen years, and then was destroyed.
Wéi Yuè's brother-in-law,
surrendered to Zhū Tāo.
Tāo had him reinstated to his position.
7. The state monopoly on wine was reinstated throughout the empire,
except in the Western Capital.
The abolition of the wine monopoly is recorded in the seventh month of the fourteenth year of the Dàlì era, in scroll 225.
Què (monopoly),
read as gǔ yuè fān.
8. In the second month,
on the wǔwǔ day,
Yáng Zhèngyì, the prefect of Dìngzhōu appointed by Lǐ Wéi Yuè, surrendered.
At that time, Héběi was largely pacified,
only Wèizhōu remained unconquered.
The various armies in Hénán attacked Lǐ Nà at Púzhōu,
and Nà's situation grew increasingly dire.
The court believed the empire could be pacified in no time.
On the jiǎzǐ day,
they appointed Zhāng Xiàozhōng as the military governor of Yì, Dìng, and Cāng prefectures,
Wáng Wǔjùn as the Military Commissioner and Surveillance Commissioner of Héngjì,
Kāng Rìzhī as the Military Commissioner and Surveillance Commissioner of Shēnzhào,
placed Dé and Dì prefectures under Zhū Tāo's jurisdiction,
and ordered him to return to his garrison.
Tāo firmly requested Shēnzhōu,
but it was not granted.
Consequently, he became resentful
and remained stationed in Shēnzhōu.
Zhū Tāo campaigned against Lǐ Wéi Yuè,
winning battle after battle.
Yet when the territories under Chéngdé's jurisdiction were divided to reward the surrendering generals,
not an inch of land
was allotted to Tāo.
Moreover, they wanted him to seize Dé and Dì prefectures.
This is why the Zuo Commentary knew King Huán would lose Zhèng!
Considering himself the one who personally executed Lǐ Wéi Yuè,
his merit was greater than Kāng Rìzhī's.
Yet Xiàozhōng was made military governor,
while he and Kāng Rìzhī were both made Military Commissioners,
and he also lost Zhào and Dìng prefectures.
He was also displeased.
Furthermore, an edict ordered three thousand shi of grain to be given to Zhū Tāo,
and five hundred horses to be given to Mǎ Suì.
Wǔjùn believed the court did not wish to make former subordinates military governors.
Wáng Wǔjùn
was an old general of Héngzhōu,
hence this statement.
They would certainly seize Héngjì,
so they divided the grain and horses to weaken him.
Suspicious,
he was unwilling to obey the edict.
Tián Yuè heard of this
and sent his administrative officers Wáng Yòu and Xǔ Shìzé by side roads to Shēnzhōu,
to persuade Zhū Tāo, saying:
"The Minister of Works, following the imperial edict, campaigned against Lǐ Wéi Yuè.
Within a short period,
you captured Shùlù,
took Shēnzhōu.
Wéi Yuè's situation became critical,

The Old Basic Annals, and the biographies of Zhū Tāo and Wáng Wǔjùn all state the eleventh month,
without specifying a day.
Only Tián Yuè's biography states,
"the first day of the eleventh month."

and converged at Chénzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: At the beginning of the Jiànzhōng era,
Dù Yòu changed the water transport route,
from ten *lǐ* west of Jùnyí,
its southern bank diverted water into Pípá Ditch,
passing through the Cài River,
to Chénzhōu converging with the Yǐng,
which was the old route of the Qín and Hàn dynasties.
Since the Suí opened the Biàn River,
benefiting travel to Yáng and Chǔ,
official transport no longer used this route,
but Yòu reopened it.
Up,
*shí zhǎng fān*.
37 In the twelfth month,
on Dīngchǒu,
Lǐ Xīliè proclaimed himself Grand Marshal of All Under Heaven, Grand Commandant, and King of Jiànxīng.
At that time, Zhū Tāo and others had been confronting the imperial army for months,
the imperial army had provisions supplied by the Ministry of Revenue,
and various circuits sent reinforcements,
while Tāo and Wáng Wǔjùn, with their isolated army deep in enemy territory,
relied entirely on Tián Yuè for supplies,
and both guest and host grew increasingly exhausted.
Guest,
refers to the armies of Tāo and Wǔjùn;
host,
refers to Tián Yuè.
They became quite resentful,
so together they planned to send an envoy to Xǔzhōu,
urging Xīliè to proclaim himself emperor,
and thus Xīliè proclaimed himself Grand Marshal of All Under Heaven.
38 The Deputy Director of the Astrological Service, Xú Chéngsì, requested to create a new Jiànzhōng Zhèngyuán calendar;
this was approved.
In the first year of Qiányuán,
the Bureau of the Grand Astrologer was renamed the Astrological Service,
with the Director as the Supervisor,
rank 3a,
Deputy Director,
rank 4a upper,
responsible for observing celestial phenomena and verifying calendars,
and for all anomalies of the sun, moon, stars, winds, clouds, and atmospheric colors,
leading his subordinates in divination.
During the reign of Emperor Sùzōng,
Hán Yǐng revised the Dàyǎn calendar to create the Zhìdé calendar.
In the first year of Bǎoyìng,
Emperor Dàizōng, because the Zhìdé calendar did not match celestial phenomena,
ordered the officials of the Astrological Service, Guō Xiànzhī and others, to reuse the Lìndé era's foundational principles,
reestablish the annual precession,
adjust the rates of lunar motion, eclipses, and planetary differences,
to transcribe the Dàyǎn method,
called the Wǔjì calendar.
By this time,
the Wǔjì calendar's seasonal markers and new moon times were slightly behind the heavens,
and its calculations of stellar positions differed considerably from the Dàyǎn's error rates,
so an edict ordered Chéngsì and others to combine the principles of the Lìndé and Dàyǎn calendars to create a new calendar,
named the Jiànzhōng Zhèngyuán calendar.
Deputy,
*shǐ zhào fān*.
Sì,
*xiáng lì fān*.
Create,
*gōng héng fān*.

Fourth Year of Jiànzhōng
(Guǐhài, 783)
1 Spring,
first month,
on Dīnghài,
the military governor of Lǒngyòu, Zhāng Yì, and the Tibetan Shang Jiezan swore an alliance at Qīngshuǐ.
On the Gēngyín day,
Lǐ Xīliè sent his general Lǐ Kèchéng to launch a surprise attack and capture Rǔzhōu,
seizing the Deputy Prefect Lǐ Yuánpíng.
Yuánpíng,
