but his nature was careless and arrogant,
daring to boast,
and fond of discussing military affairs;
Guān
Bò considered him extraordinary,
recommended him to the Emperor,
believing him to be a man of general and chancellor caliber.
As Rǔzhōu was closest to Xǔzhōu,
the Jiǔyù Zhì states: Rǔzhōu,
is two hundred and seventy lǐ southeast to Xǔzhōu.
The history remarks that Guān Bò employed men without talent.
Chancellor,
read xiàng.
He was appointed to administer the affairs of the prefecture.
When Yuánpíng arrived in Rǔzhōu,
he immediately recruited laborers to repair the city walls;
Xīliè secretly sent strong men to answer the recruitment and perform the labor,
several hundred entered,
and Yuánpíng did not notice it.
Xīliè sent Kèchéng with several hundred cavalry to suddenly arrive at the city walls,
general,
read jiàng,
also read as the usual pronunciation.
Cavalry,
read jì.
They bound Yuánpíng and galloped away with him.
Yuánpíng was a man of small stature,
beardless,
beard,
in ancient characters, the form was taken from the image,
using the category of hair on the face.
Later people followed and added
to form
the character "鬚"
this is a vulgar writing.
His urine and feces soiled the ground.
Xīliè scolded him, saying:
"A blind chancellor sent you to oppose me,
how they belittle me!"
He appointed Judicial Commissioner Zhōu Huǎng as Prefect of Rǔzhōu,
and also sent another general Dǒng Dàimíng and others to plunder in all directions,
capturing Wèishì,
Wèishì County,
belonged to Biànzhōu.
Jiǔyù Zhì: It is ninety lǐ south of the prefecture.
Plunder,
read chāo.
The government troops were repeatedly defeated by them.
Their patrol cavalry reached as far west as Péngpó,
causing the officials and people of the Eastern Capital to be shocked and terrified,
fleeing and hiding in the mountains and valleys;
the Defender-in-chief Zhèng Shūzé entered and secured the Western Park.
The Eastern Capital's Western Park,
was west of the Eastern Capital city.
Zhèng Shūzé likely prepared for an emergency to easily flee west.
Defender,
read shǒu.
The Emperor asked Lú for advice,
who replied:
"Xīliè is a young and valiant general,
relying on his achievements, arrogant and disrespectful,
his officers and aides dare not admonish or stop him;
if we could obtain a refined and dignified senior minister,
to convey and proclaim the imperial grace,
explaining to him the consequences of rebellion and loyalty, fortune and misfortune,
Xīliè is sure to reform his heart and repent of his errors,
and we could subdue him without the toil of armies.
Yán Zhēnqīng is a senior minister of three reigns,
Zhēnqīng served the Xuán, Sù, and Dài reigns.
Reign,
read cháo.
His reputation is great throughout the land,
trusted and respected by all,
he is truly the right man!"
The Emperor considered this correct.
On the Jiǎwǔ day,
he ordered Zhēnqīng to go to Xǔzhōu to convey imperial consolation to Xīliè.
When the edict was issued,
the entire court turned pale.
Zhēnqīng traveled by post to the Eastern Capital,
Zhèng Shūzé said:
"Going will certainly be unavoidable disaster,
it is better to stay a little,
and await a later command."
Zhēnqīng said:
"It is the sovereign's command,
how can one avoid it!"
And so he departed.
Lǐ Miǎn submitted a memorial stating:
"To lose a senior statesman,
is a disgrace to the state,
I beg to retain him."
He also sent someone to intercept Zhēnqīng,
but did not catch up.
Zhēnqīng wrote a letter to his son,
merely instructing him to
"serve the family temple, and care for the orphans."
That was all.
Upon reaching Xǔzhōu,
as he was about to proclaim the imperial decree,
Xīliè had over a thousand of his adopted sons surround him, cursing and reviling,
Lǐ Xīliè adopted strong men as sons,
called them adopted sons.
Surround,
read huán.
They made gestures as if to slice and eat him;
Zhēnqīng did not move his feet,
nor did his expression change.
Xīliè hastily shielded him with his own body,
motioned for the crowd to retreat,
and lodged Zhēnqīng, treating him with courtesy.
Xīliè intended to send Zhēnqīng back,
but it happened that Lǐ Yuánpíng was present,
Zhēnqīng reproached him,
Yuánpíng rose in shame,
and secretly reported to Xīliè;
Xīliè's mind then changed,
and he detained Zhēnqīng, not sending him back.
Zhū Tāo, Wáng Wǔjùn, Tián Yuè, and Lǐ Nà each sent envoys to Lǐ Xīliè,
presenting memorials declaring themselves his subjects,
urging him to ascend the throne.
The envoys performed the ceremonial bow and dance before Lǐ Xīliè,
and persuaded him, saying:
"The imperial court has been executing and exterminating meritorious ministers,
losing the trust of the realm.
Your Excellency, the Commander-in-Chief, possesses innate heroism and martial prowess,
with achievements that overshadow the age.
Yet you have already incurred the suspicion and jealousy of the court.
You are about to face the calamity that befell Hán Xìn and Bái Qǐ.
We urge you to swiftly assume the imperial title,
so that all subjects and people under heaven will know where to pledge their allegiance."
Lǐ Xīliè summoned Yán Zhēnqīng and showed him [the memorials], saying:
"Now, the Four Kings have sent envoys urging me [to take the throne],
acting in concert without prior consultation.
They call Zhū Tāo the Prince of Jì,
Wáng Wǔjùn the Prince of Zhào,
Tián Yuè the Prince of Wèi,
and Lǐ Nà the Prince of Qí.
Therefore, Lǐ Xīliè refers to them as the Four Kings.
Envoy,
(annotation: Shūlì fān).
Am I alone to be distrusted by the court, with no place to stand?"
Yán Zhēnqīng said:
"These are the Four Fiends,
what Four Kings!
Your Excellency does not strive to preserve your own achievements and legacy,
to be a loyal minister of the Táng,
but instead associates with rebellious ministers and traitorous villains,
seeking to share their utter destruction!"
Lǐ Xīliè was displeased,
and had Yán Zhēnqīng escorted out.
Another day,
he again feasted with the four envoys together.
The four envoys said:
"We have long heard of the Grand Preceptor's high prestige.
Now, just as the Commander-in-Chief is about to assume the great title, the Grand Preceptor has arrived.
This is Heaven bestowing a Chief Minister upon the Commander-in-Chief."
Yán Zhēnqīng held the title of Grand Preceptor of the Heir Apparent,
hence they all addressed him by this official title.
Chief Minister,
(annotation: Xì liàng fān).
"What Chief Minister!
Do you know of Yán Gǎoqīng, who cursed Ān Lùshān and died?
(The affair of Yán Gǎoqīng is recorded in the 217th scroll, the first year of the Zhìdé era of Emperor Sùzōng).
Curse,
(annotation: Chǐ lì fān).
I am eighty years old,
I only know to die preserving my integrity.
How could I submit to your lot's enticements and coercion!"
Shǐ Zhào said: Using profit to move someone is called enticement (yòu),
using force to pressure someone is called coercion (xié).
Entice,
(annotation: Yīn yǒu).
Lǐ Xīliè then ordered ten armored soldiers to guard Yán Zhēnqīng at the guesthouse,
dug a pit in the courtyard,
saying he intended to bury him alive.
Yán Zhēnqīng remained calm and composed.
He appeared before Lǐ Xīliè and said:
Calm and composed,
a demeanor of peace and harmony.
"Life and death are already determined,
why engage in so many schemes!
Quickly give me a sword,
would that not satisfy your heart's desire!"
Lǐ Xīliè then apologized to him.
Textual Analysis: The "Yán Family Conduct Record" states:
"When the Duke arrived in Xǔzhōu,
Lǐ Xīliè repeatedly forged memorials in the Duke's name,
dozens of times petitioning for Biànzhōu.
The Emperor knew of this and suppressed them."
The Old Biography of Yán Zhēnqīng states:
"Lǐ Xīliè forced him to draft a memorial,
ordering him to clear his own name,
and expressing willingness to disband his troops.
He repeatedly sent Yán Zhēnqīng's nephew Yán Xiàn and several accompanying officials successively to the capital.
The Emperor gave no response to any of them.
Lǐ Xīliè held a grand banquet for his rebellious faction,
where actors and performers disparaged the court's governance.
Yán Zhēnqīng flicked his sleeves and rose to leave.
Later, when Zhāng Bóyí suffered a defeat,
[Lǐ Xīliè] ordered the severed heads to be displayed boastfully.
Yán Zhēnqīng wailed in grief.
Zhōu Zēng plotted to support Yán Zhēnqīng,
and subsequently sent Yán Zhēnqīng to Lóngxīng Temple."
According to the analysis: Tāo and others urging Lǐ Xīliè to assume supremacy was last year.
Yán Zhēnqīng's mission to Xǔzhōu was in the first month of this year.
It seems Tāo and others initially urged Lǐ Xīliè to proclaim himself emperor,
but Lǐ Xīliè only styled himself Grand Marshal and Prince of Jiànxīng.
Therefore, this year Tāo and others again sent Fán Bō and others to urge him to assume the title of Commander-in-Chief.
Yán Zhēnqīng was resolute and unyielding,
maintaining his integrity unto death.
How could Lǐ Xīliè possibly force him to draft a memorial clearing his own name!
The Conduct Record states
"forged memorials and petitions,"
which is correct.
3 On Wùxū day,
[the Emperor] appointed Left Dragon Martial Grand General Gēshū Yào as Military Commissioner of Dōngdū and Rǔzhōu,
leading over ten thousand troops from the Fèngxiáng, Bīnníng, Jīngyuán, Fèngtiān, and Hǎozhì expeditionary camps to attack Lǐ Xīliè.
Fèngxiáng, Bīnníng, Jīngyuán,
troops from three military provinces.
Fèngtiān, Hǎozhì,
were Shence Army
garrison troops.
Gēshū Yào marched to Jiáchéng,
encountered Lǐ Xīliè's vanguard general Chén Lìzhēn,
defeated him;
Lǐ Xīliè's momentum was slightly checked.
Yào,
was the son of [Gēshū] Hàn.
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
when Ān Lùshān rebelled,
Gēshū Hàn was defeated and perished at Tóngguān.
Lǐ Xīliè sent his general Fēng Yǒulín to occupy Dèngzhōu,
thus cutting off the southern route's tribute deliveries,
and merchant travel was also blocked.
On Rényín day,
an edict was issued to repair the Shàngjīn mountain road,
establishing postal stations.
4 In the second month,
on Wùshēn, the first day of the month,
[the Emperor] ordered Court Minister for Dependencies Cuī Hànhéng to escort Ōu Jiá Zàn back to Tǔbō.
(The matter of Ōu Jiá Zàn's audience begins in the previous scroll, last year).
Court Minister for Dependencies,
(annotation: Líng rú fān).
5 On Bǐngyín day,
[the Emperor] established the Héyáng Army from the Héyáng Three Cities and Huái and Wèi Prefectures.
6 On Dīngmǎo day,
Gēshū Yào captured Rǔzhōu,
and captured Zhōu Huǎng.
7 In the third month,
on Wùyín day,
Military Commissioner of Jiāngxī, Prince Cáo Lǐ Gāo, defeated Lǐ Xīliè's general Hán Shuānglù at Huángméi,
and beheaded him;
on Xīnmǎo day,
he captured Huángzhōu.
At that time, Lǐ Xīliè's troops had fortified Càishān,
which was impregnable.
Lǐ Gāo announced he would march west to capture Qízhōu,
leading his naval forces upstream along the river.
Lǐ Xīliè's generals led their troops along the riverbank, following and engaging in battle.
After they had gone over three hundred lǐ from Càishān,
Lǐ Gāo then turned his boats around and sailed swiftly downstream,
launching a sudden attack on Càishān,
and captured it.
Lǐ Xīliè's troops turned back to rescue it,
but arrived too late and were defeated.
Lǐ Gāo then advanced and captured Qízhōu,
recommending Yī Shèn as Prefect of Qízhōu,
and Wáng È as Prefect of Jiāngzhōu.
8 The capital protector of Huáiníng, Zhōu Zēng, the commander of the garrison troops, Wáng Fēn, and the deputy commanders Yáo Dàn and Wéi Qīng secretly pledged allegiance to Lǐ Miǎn.
Lǐ Xīliè sent Zhōu Zēng and the deputy general Kāng Xiùlín to lead thirty thousand troops to attack Gēshū Yào.
They reached Xiāngchéng,
Xiāngchéng County,
which belonged to Yǐngchuān Commandery during the Hàn dynasty,
and to Xiāngchéng Commandery during the Jìn dynasty.
Later, during the Northern Zhōu dynasty, Rǔ Prefecture was established.
In the first year of the Zhēnguàn era of the Táng dynasty,
the prefecture was abolished,
and Xiāngchéng County was placed under Xǔ Prefecture.
In the eighth year of the Zhēnguàn era,
Yī Prefecture was renamed Rǔ Prefecture,
while Xiāngchéng remained under Xǔ Prefecture.
In the seventh year of the Tiānbǎo era,
it was again placed under Rǔ Prefecture.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: Xiāngchéng County
is located one hundred and fifty lǐ southeast of Rǔ Prefecture.
They intended to install Yán Zhēnqīng as the military governor,
with Wáng Fēn, Yáo Dàn, and Wéi Qīng acting as internal agents.
Lǐ Xīliè learned of this,
and sent the deputy general Lǐ Kèchéng to lead three thousand mule troops
(the Huáixī region had few horses,
so they fought on mules,
hence the name "Mule Army,"
which was exceptionally fierce and elite).
The character "將"
is pronounced jiàng (with the falling tone);
the "將" in Kèchéng's name is pronounced the same,
or it can also be pronounced according to its usual reading.
The character "騾"
is pronounced luó.
He killed them,
along with Wáng Fēn, Yáo Dàn, and their associates.
On the jiǎwǔ day,
an imperial edict was issued posthumously conferring official titles upon Zhōu Zēng and the others.
Initially,
Wéi Qīng had made an agreement with Zhōu Zēng and the others
that if the plot was exposed, they would not implicate each other,
which is why he alone escaped punishment.
Fearing that disaster would eventually befall him,
Wéi Qīng persuaded Lǐ Xīliè to send him to Zhū Tāo to request reinforcements.
Lǐ Xīliè dispatched him,
but when he reached Xiāngyì,
he fled to Liú Qià.
Xiāngyì County
belonged to Sòng Prefecture.
Liú Qià was then serving as the military governor of Xuānwǔ and stationed in Sòng Prefecture.
He shut the gates and remained inside for several days;
his partisans who were raiding Wèishì and Zhèng Prefecture heard of this
and also retreated.
Lǐ Xīliè then submitted a memorial to the throne, blaming Zhōu Zēng and the others,
and led his troops back to Cài Prefecture,
outwardly showing repentance and submission,
but in reality waiting for reinforcements from Zhū Tāo and others.
He placed Yán Zhēnqīng in Lóngxīng Temple.
The temple was likely located in Cài Prefecture.
On the dīngyǒu day,
the military governor of Jīngnán, Zhāng Bóyí, engaged the Huáiníng troops in battle at Ān Prefecture.
Ān Prefecture
was the location of the Hàn dynasty's Ānlù.
Zhāng Bóyí barely escaped with his life,
losing the ceremonial staff he held.
Lǐ Xīliè sent someone to show the staff and the captives and severed heads to Yán Zhēnqīng;
Yán Zhēnqīng wailed in grief and threw himself to the ground,
fainting and then reviving.
From then on, he no longer spoke with anyone.
9 In the summer,
during the fourth month,
the emperor appointed the commander of the Shéncè Army, Bái Zhìzhēn, as the capital recruitment commissioner,
to recruit imperial guards to suppress Lǐ Xīliè.
Bái Zhìzhēn requested that all those who had previously served as military governors, surveillance commissioners, or regional commanders,
regardless of whether they were alive or dead,
be compelled to have their sons, younger brothers, and servants provide their own horses and equipment to join the army,
and be granted the fifth-rank official title;
the poor suffered greatly from this,
and public sentiment began to waver.
The historian notes that Emperor Dézōng's relentless military campaigns
would soon lead to chaos.
10 The emperor ordered the chancellor and the minister of war to swear an oath with the Tibetan envoy Ōu Jiá Zàn at Fēngyìlǐ.
Ōu Jiá Zàn, citing that the borders had not been settled in the Qīngshuǐ alliance,
refused to finalize the oath.
In the spring of this year,
Zhāng Yì had sworn an oath with the Tibetans at Qīngshuǐ.
Sòng Bái said: The text of the oath between Zhāng Yì and the Tibetans stated:
"The current borders defended by the state
are: from Jīng Prefecture,
west to the western mouth of Tánzhēng Gorge;
from Lǒng Prefecture,
west to Qīngshuǐ County;
from Fèng Prefecture,
west to Tónggǔ County;
and east of the Dàdù River in the western mountains of Jiànnán,
which constitute the Hàn borders.
The Tibetan state
defends its territory in Lán, Wèi, Yuán, and Huì,
west to Líntáo,
and east to Chéng Prefecture,
reaching the western border of Jiànnán, the Móxiē tribes, and southwest of the Dàdù River,
which constitute the Tibetan borders."
The character "相"
is pronounced xiàng.
The character "尚"
is pronounced shàng.
The character "吐"
is pronounced tǔ.
The character "埸"
is pronounced yì.
On the jǐwèi day,
Cuī Hànhéng was sent into Tibet,
to seek a decision from the Tsanpo.
In the second month of this year,
Cuī Hànhéng was ordered to escort Ōu Jiá Zàn back,
likely intending to swear an oath with him before sending him off,
but the oath had not been settled for a long time.
Cuī Hànhéng was again sent into Tibet,
to seek a decision from the Tsanpo.
At this time, the Central Plains was exhausted by war,
and the Tibetans certainly had the opportunity to observe the Táng's weakness,
making the oath meaningless.
11 On the gēngshēn day,
Lǐ Miǎn, the overall commander of Yǒngpíng, Xuānwǔ, and Héyáng, was additionally appointed as the Huáixī pacification commissioner,
with the military governor of Dōngdū and Rǔ Prefecture, Gēshū Yào, as his deputy.
The military governor of Jīngnán, Zhāng Bóyí, was appointed as the Huáixī relief pacification commissioner,
with the military governor of Shānnán Dōngdào, Jiǎ Dān, and the military governor of Jiāngxī, Cáo Wáng Gāo, as his deputies.
The emperor urged Gēshū Yào to advance his troops.
Gēshū Yào reached Yǐngqiáo,
(according to the Jiǔyù Zhì: Xiāngchéng County had the Yǐngqiáo garrison),
but then retreated to defend Xiāngchéng.
Lǐ Xīliè sent his general Lǐ Guānghuī to attack Xiāngchéng;
Gēshū Yào repelled him.
12 In the fifth month,
on the yǐyǒu day,
Prince Yǐng, Jiǎo, passed away.
13 On the yǐwèi day,
the military governor of Xuānwǔ, Liú Qià, was additionally appointed as the Zīqīng pacification commissioner.
14 Li Shèng planned to seize the two prefectures of Zhuō and Mò,
in order to cut off the route of communication between Yōu and Wèi.
Together with Zhāng Xiàozhōng's son Shēngyún, he besieged Zhū Tāo's appointed Yì Prefecture governor Zhèng Jǐngjì at Qīngyuàn.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: The Xú River originates from Běipíng,
flows east past Qīngyuàn City,
then east to Gāoyáng,
and enters the river.
Liú Xù said: Qīngyuàn County,
was the Hàn dynasty's Lèxiāng County,
belonging to the Xìndū Kingdom.
In the Suí dynasty it became Qīngyuàn County,
belonging to Yíng Prefecture;
in the first year of the Táng dynasty's Jǐngyún era,
it belonged to Jì Prefecture;
by the Sòng dynasty,
Qīngyuàn County became the seat of Bǎo Prefecture's administration.
Sòng Bái said: Emperor Gāozōng of Hàn sought the descendants of Yuè Yì,
found Yuè Shū,
and enfeoffed him at Lèxiāng.
The Northern Qí abolished it,
and then moved Yǒngníng County from the boundaries of present-day Yì Prefecture's Mǎnchéng County,
to govern the northern city.
The Suí changed it to Qīngyuàn County,
named after the Qīngyuàn River in Mǎnchéng County's boundaries.
Tāo appointed his Minister of War Mǎ Shí as the garrison commander,
The Minister of War,
is equivalent to the imperial court's Minister of War.
and personally led fifteen thousand infantry and cavalry to rescue Qīngyuàn.
Li Shèng's army was greatly defeated,
and retreated to defend Yì Prefecture.
Tāo returned his army to Yíng Prefecture,
and Zhāng Shēngyún fled to Mǎnchéng.
Liú Xù said: Mǎnchéng County,
was the territory of the Hàn dynasty's Běipíng County,
the Later Wèi established Yǒnglè County there,
in the first year of the Tiānbǎo era,
it was changed to Mǎnchéng,
belonging to Yì Prefecture.
He led his army back to defend Dìng Prefecture.
The Examination of Discrepancies states: The Yānnán Jì says:
"Shèng, together with Zhāng Shēngyún and others, besieged Zhèng Jǐngjì at Qīngyuàn,
from the second month until the fourth month.
Tāo personally led fifteen thousand infantry and cavalry to rescue Qīngyuàn,
on the second day of the fourth month,
he set out from Guǎntáo Fort,
arriving within the fifth month.
Shèng went out to battle but was unsuccessful,
the defenders within the city also came out to attack Shèng,
and Shèng was defeated and withdrew.
Tāo, taking advantage of the victory, pursued Shèng and others,
and routed them completely.
Shèng fled to Yì Prefecture,
contracted an illness,
and did not venture out again."
The Veritable Records state:
"On the Gēngzǐ day,
Li Shèng retreated from Qīngyuàn to defend Yì Prefecture."
The Old Biography of Shèng states:
"From the first month until the fifth month,
Shèng happened to be severely ill,
and was unconscious on several occasions.
The military officers consulted together,
and then used a horse-drawn carriage to return him to Dìng Prefecture."

On that day,

Xiùshí suddenly rose in fury,
snatched Xiū's ivory tablet—
in the early years of the Wǔdé era,
following the old Suí system,
officials of the fifth rank and above held ivory tablets;
for those of the third rank and below, the front was tapered and the back straight,
while for those of the fifth rank and above, the back was curved.
From that time onward,
all uniformly had a round top and square bottom,
with no further distinction.
He then shouted loudly,
"Mad rebel!
I regret only that I cannot cut you into ten thousand pieces—
how could I ever follow you in rebellion!"
He then struck Cǐ with the tablet.
Cǐ raised his hand to block it,

Cǐ and Xiùshí grappled fiercely,
while those around them were caught off guard,

After Xiùshí's death,
Cǐ wept bitterly for him

According to this, if Lǐ Zhōngchén and others had already led five thousand troops to attack Fèngtiān,

Moreover, if Hǎibīn had been detected while drawing a dagger from his boot,

If he had been detected by the gatekeeper,

If the incident had been widely known,
and the rebels had taken precautions,

These several points
all seem difficult to believe.
Now, we only take the credible parts from *Duàn Gōng's Xíngzhuàng*, the *Xìng Fèngtiān Lù*, and the old biographies.

Ēnzhōu
was located within the territory of the Hàn dynasty's Hépǔ Commandery.
During the Southern Qí dynasty, it was the Qí'ān Commandery,
and in the Suí dynasty, the commandery was abolished and became Hǎi'ān County.
In the twenty-third year of the Táng dynasty's Zhēnguàn era,
Ēnzhōu was established from Xīpíng, Hǎi'ān, and Dùlíng of Gāozhōu,
with Hǎi'ān renamed as Ēnpíng;
during the Tiānbǎo era, it was called Ēnpíng Commandery,
and in the Qiányuán era, it was restored as Ēnzhōu.
After the Sòng dynasty pacified Wáng Zé,
Bèizhōu was renamed Ēnzhōu,
and this prefecture was subsequently referred to as Nán'ēnzhōu.
Sòng Bái stated that this Ēnzhōu bordered the sea,
and was extremely humid,
located along the maritime route to the five commanderies south of the sea.
This route involved sailing from Guǎngzhōu for several days before landing,
and people feared the sea waves,
so they did not take this route,
often traveling overland via Xīnzhōu instead.
Only couriers on urgent missions
and those delivering official documents
used this route.
Xīnzhōu,
administered from Xīnxīng County,
was established after the Qín dynasty captured the Lùliáng region and set up the Xiàng Commandery,
with the present prefecture located in that area.
During the Jìn dynasty's Yǒnghé era, it was separated from Cāngwú Commandery
to establish the Xīnníng Commandery,
and Emperor Wǔ of Liáng established Xīnzhōu.
The so-called Xīnxīng County
was Línyuán County of the Hàn dynasty's Hépǔ Commandery.
Furthermore, according to the Old Records: Ēnzhōu
was 6,600 lǐ southeast of the capital,
and bordered Guǎngzhōu sixty lǐ to the northwest.
Xīnzhōu was 5,052 lǐ from the capital.
Bōzhōu,
formerly Zāngkē County in the Suí dynasty,
was 4,450 lǐ south of the capital.
Zhào Guāngqí was trusted by the Emperor,

I hope Your Majesty will take the tracks of an overturned cart as a warning,
and truly bring boundless blessings to the ancestral temples."
25 On Dīngsì day,
the former Shānnán Dōngdào military governor Jiǎ Dān of Nánpí was appointed Minister of Works.
Previously,
Dān had sent his行军司马 Fán Zé to report matters at the imperial headquarters.
After Zé had completed his mission and returned,
just as a grand banquet was being held,
an urgent dispatch arrived,
appointing Zé to replace Dān as military governor.
The incident is recorded in the first year of the Xīngyuán era in the previous volume.
The banquet continued as before,
and his expression did not change;
after the banquet ended,
he summoned Zé and informed him,
and also ordered his officers and officials to pay their respects to Zé.
The牙将 Zhāng Xiànfǔ angrily said:
"The行军司马 went to inquire after the Son of Heaven's well-being on behalf of the Minister,
yet he dared to scheme for the commander's tally himself,
seizing the Minister's territory.
He serves his lord disloyally;
I request to kill him."
Dān said:
"What kind of talk is this!
It is the Son of Heaven's command,
so he is now the military governor!"
That very day he left his headquarters,
taking Xiànfǔ with him,
and the military administration was thus pacified.
Leaving his headquarters that very day
not only accorded with
"when summoned by the ruler's command,
one does not wait for the carriage"
principle,
but also served to curb the source of disorder.
Taking Zhāng Xiànfǔ with him
meant Fán Zé had no cause for suspicion or resentment,
and also served to protect Xiànfǔ.
Lí
is pronounced lì zhì fān.
26 Left Vice Director of the Secretariat Lǐ Kuí returned from Tǔbō,
on Jiǎzǐ day,
and died in Fèngzhōu.
Lǐ Kuí's mission to Tǔbō is recorded in the 228th volume, fourth year of the Jiànzhōng era.
Presumably, he was returning from Tǔbō to Xīngyuán,
and died upon reaching Fèngzhōu.
27 Hán Yóuguī led troops to join Hún Jiān at Fèngtiān.
28 On Bǐngyín day,
Pínglú military governor Lǐ Nà was given the additional title of Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
29 On Dīngmǎo day,
Prince Yì, Lǐ Cǐ, died.
Cǐ
was a son of Xuánzōng.
Cǐ
is pronounced cǐ,
also qiě lǐ fān.
30 Zhū Tāo attacked Bèizhōu for over a hundred days,
and Mǎ Shí attacked Wèizhōu for more than forty days as well,
but neither could capture it.
Jiǎ Lín again persuaded Wáng Wǔjùn on behalf of Lǐ Bàozhēn,
saying:
"Zhū Tāo's ambition is to swallow Bèi and Wèi.
Now, with Tián Yuè having been killed,
if we do not rescue them within ten days,
then Wèibó will all fall to Tāo.
Once Wèibó is taken,
then Zhāng Xiàozhōng will surely become his subject.
Zhāng Xiàozhōng was then stationed in Yì and Dìng.
The three circuits,
meaning Yōuzhōu, Yìdìng, and Wèibó.
At that time, the Huíhé sent troops to aid Tāo.
Héngzhōu Chángshān commandery,
where Wáng Wǔjùn resided.
How can this be allowed!
If Chángshān is not held,
then Zhāoyì will retreat to defend the western mountains.
From Chángshān south to Zhàozhōu,
all are under the jurisdiction of Héngjì.
Further southwest, reaching the boundary of Xíngzhōu,
that is under the jurisdiction of Zhāoyì,
relying on the mountains for defense.
It would be better to take advantage of Bèi and Wèi not yet having fallen,
and join forces with Zhāoyì to rescue them;
once Tāo is defeated and destroyed,
then Guānzhōng will lose morale,
and Zhū Cǐ will soon be destroyed.
Zhū Cǐ had usurped control of Guānzhōng;
if Tāo is defeated, then Cǐ will lose morale.
Sàng
is pronounced xī làng fān.
Among the various generals' merits,
who could rank above you, my lord!"
Wǔjùn was pleased
and followed his advice.
On the Wùchén day,
Wǔjùn encamped southeast of Nángōng.
Bàozhēn led troops from Línmíng to join him,
and their camps were ten lǐ apart.
The two armies still harbored mutual suspicion.
The next day,
Bàozhēn went with a few cavalrymen to Wǔjùn's camp.
His advisors all urged him not to go,
but Bàozhēn ordered his marching Sima Lú Xuánqīng to keep the troops ready and wait,
saying:
"My action this time
concerns the safety of the realm.
If I do not return,
leading the army to heed the court's commands will be up to you,
and inspiring the officers and men to avenge our shame will also be up to you."
Having spoken,
he departed.
Wǔjùn prepared strict defenses to await him.
Bàozhēn met Wǔjùn,
recounted the calamities that had befallen the state,
and the emperor's flight from the capital.
He held Wǔjùn and wept,
tears streaming down his face.
Wǔjùn was also overcome with grief,
and those around them could not look up.
Then he and Wǔjùn swore to become brothers,
vowing to destroy the rebels together.
Wǔjùn said:
"Your Excellency, Tenth Brother, your reputation is known throughout the land.
(Lǐ Bàozhēn was the tenth among his siblings, hence called Tenth Brother.)
I have been able to abandon rebellion and follow righteousness,
avoiding the crime of being minced into pickles,
and enjoying the glory of a prince or duke.
Now, without regard for my barbarian origins,
you humbly treat me as a brother.
How can I ever repay you!
What Tiāo relies on is the Huíhé,
but they are not fearsome.
On the day of battle,
I hope Tenth Brother will rein in his horse and observe.
I, Wǔjùn, vow to crush them for Tenth Brother."
Bàozhēn withdrew into Wǔjùn's tent
and slept soundly for a long time.
Wǔjùn was deeply moved,
and treated him with even greater respect.
Pointing to his heart and looking up to heaven, he said:
"I have already pledged this life to die for Tenth Brother!"
The historian says that Bàozhēn won Wǔjùn's loyalty with sincerity, thus achieving great success.
In Shānnán, the weather was warm.
As the troops had no spring clothing,
the emperor also wore lined garments himself.

Later
First Year of Xīngyuán
(Jiǎzǐ, 784)
1 In May,
the Salt and Iron Judge Wànnián Wáng Shào arrived with silks and fabrics from Jiāng and Huái.
Wànnián,
a capital county,
belonged to Jīngzhào.
Zēng,
pronounced cí líng.
Only then did the emperor wear a single-layer robe.
He changed from lined garments to a single-layer robe.
Shān,
a single-layer garment.
Jiàng,
pronounced jí liàng.
His staff officer Hé Shìgàn volunteered to go.
Huàng was pleased and said:
"If you can go on my behalf,
please cross the river today."
Shìgàn agreed,
returned home to bid farewell,
and found firewood and rice supplies already arranged at his doorstep.
When he boarded the boat,
supplies and equipment were already loaded on board.
Down to kitchen utensils,
kitchen utensils,

"toilet utensils."

Nothing was left unprepared.
For each porter,

Sōu,

the same below.
Shèng,

Textual analysis says: Liǔ Pín's narrative states:
"When the emperor first arrived in Liáng,
he was very pleased upon reading the memorial.
Knowing that Xīpíng must be short of grain supplies for gathering troops,

However, in early May, Liángzhōu still lacked spring clothing,
