Liáng and Rùn are several thousand lǐ apart.
How could an imperial order reach so quickly!
This is not adopted here.
Officers vied to lift it,
and it was completed in a short while.
Each boat was equipped with five crossbowmen for defense and support.
If bandits approached, they would beat the sides of the boat to alert others,
and five hundred crossbows would be ready.
By the time they reached the Wèi Bridge,
bandits did not dare approach.
At that time, Guānzhōng was plagued by war and famine,
and a dǒu of rice cost five hundred coins.
When Huàng's rice arrived,
the price dropped by four-fifths.
Huàng was a man of strong will, strict and resolute.
He lived frugally himself,
and his wife often wore a silk skirt
until it was worn out,
before changing it.
2 After the Tǔbō defeated Hán Mín and others,
Tǔ,
pronounced cóng tūn.
The defeat of Hán Mín is recorded in the fourth month of this year in the previous volume.
Zhū Cǐ sent Tián Xījiàn to bribe them heavily with gold and silk,
and the Tǔbō accepted it.
Hán Yóuhuái reported this.
Hún Jiān also memorialized:
"Shàngjiézàn repeatedly sent people to set a date for jointly capturing Cháng'ān,
but never showed up.
I heard that his troops suffered a great plague this spring,
and he has recently led his troops away."
The emperor, considering that Lǐ Shèng and Hún Jiān had few troops,
wanted to rely on the Tǔbō to recapture the capital.
Hearing that they had left,
he was very worried
and asked Lù Zhì about it.
Zhì believed that the Tǔbō were greedy and cunning,
harmful and unbeneficial,
and their departure
was truly something to celebrate.
He then submitted a memorial,
which roughly stated:
"The Tǔbō delayed and watched,
repeatedly changing their stance.
They penetrated deep into the capital's suburbs,
secretly accepting the rebels' bribes,
causing our commanders to worry about advancing or retreating.
If we abandon them and advance alone,
we fear they may harbor resentment and follow closely behind;
(taking advantage of our weakness and following closely behind).
Niè,
pronounced ní zhé.
If we wait for them, we suffer from their失信 and delays.
If the barbarians do not leave,
the rebels will never be eliminated."
He also said:
"The commanders suspect that Your Majesty does not trust them,
and fear that the barbarians will steal their achievements.
The soldiers fear that Your Majesty does not care for their past efforts,
and dread that the barbarians will monopolize the rewards.
The rebel faction fears the barbarians' victory,
knowing that if they do not die, they will all be captured.
The common people fear the barbarians' arrival,
knowing that their wealth will surely be plundered.
Thus, those who follow the royal transformation cannot help but slacken,
while those trapped in rebel territory cannot help but hold firm."
He also said:
"Now, Huáiguāng separately defends Pú and Jiàng,
and the Tǔbō have retreated far from our borders.
With the situation divided,
we have no worries about our front and rear.
Commanders like Jiān and Shèng
can fully exert their talents."
He also said:
"I only hope that Your Majesty will carefully manage relations
and diligently encourage your troops.
The great task of restoration
can be achieved in a matter of months.
You should not remain attached to these犬羊之㣥,
lest you lose the hearts of your officers and men."
The Emperor again sent word to Zhì, saying:
"Your discussion of the Tǔbō situation is excellent,
but regarding the armies of Jiān and Shèng, we should deliberate and plan,
ordering them to advance and attack.
I wish to send an envoy to proclaim my solace and concern,
you should carefully and thoroughly outline the arrangements
and report them to me."
Tiáo means
to divide.
Liú means
to branch.
"A wise ruler selects his generals,
entrusts them with responsibility and demands results,
thus he can achieve success.
Moreover, now between Qín and Liáng is a thousand lǐ,
Qín
refers to Xiányáng.
Cháng'ān
is the ancient land of Qínzhōng.
Liáng
refers to Liángzhōu.
To plan from afar,
may not be appropriate.
If they disobey orders, it diminishes the sovereign's authority;
if they follow orders, it harms military affairs.
Advancing or retreating, they are hindered and obstructed,
making success difficult;
Shǐ Zhào said: Jī,
is a horse's bridle.
Ài,
means what the bridle catches on and obstructs."
I believe what Zhì meant by jī'ài is,
that if they wish to advance, they are bridled and cannot advance;
if they wish to retreat, they are obstructed and cannot retreat.
If they are rewarded with extraordinary honors,
then the commanders will be moved and pleased,
and their wisdom and courage can be fully exerted."
He then submitted a memorial,
which in summary said:
"When blades and arrows clash on the plains yet decisions are made within the ninefold palace gates,
when opportunities change in an instant yet strategies are fixed from a thousand lǐ away,
employing and discarding hinder each other,
whether good or bad, both bring misfortune.
The Yì says: When an army sets out, it must have discipline;
without discipline, there is misfortune.
Wáng Bì's commentary says: To unite the multitude requires discipline;
losing discipline leads to dispersion.
Discipline must not be lost;
if discipline is lost yet the outcome is good,
how is that different from it being bad?
Disobeying orders yet achieving merit
is not pardoned by law.
Therefore, if an army sets out without discipline,
whether good or bad, both bring misfortune.
Lù Démíng's explanatory text says: Pǐ,
pronounced bǐ,
means bad.
Zāng,
pronounced zāng,
means good.
Mì Zǐjiàn became magistrate of Shànfǔ,
and requested officials from the Marquis of Lǔ.
The Marquis of Lǔ sent two officials to accompany him to Shànfǔ.
Zǐjiàn had the officials write while he pulled their elbows,
and if the writing was poor, he would then become angry with them.
The two officials returned
and reported this to the Marquis of Lǔ.
The Marquis of Lǔ said:
'This means I hampered his governance.'
The Art of War says: A general dies in retreat,
there is only advancing, no retreating.
'Hearsay differs from actual observation;
distant calculation differs from facing the situation.'"
He also said:
"Suppose among them there is one who indulges his feelings and violates orders;
can Your Majesty at that time execute him for disobeying the decree?
Thus, those who disobey orders are not actually punished,
and those who follow orders may not act appropriately.
It merely wastes empty words,
only troubles Your Majesty's wise consideration,
not only is it unbeneficial,
the harm is indeed great."
He also said:
"The sovereign's power
is uniquely different from that of his ministers.
Only by not acting on his own
can he employ others effectively."
3 On Guǐyǒu,
Prince Tǐng of Jīng passed away.
4 Gāo Chéngzōng, the observation commissioner of Xú, Hǎi, Yí, and Mì, died.
In the second year of Jiànzhōng,
Lǐ Wěi surrendered Xúzhōu to the state.
The following year,
he was made observation commissioner of Xú, Yí, and Mì.
After Wěi died,
Gāo Chéngzōng succeeded him.
On Jiǎxū
he had his son Míngyìng take charge of military affairs.
5 On Yǐhài,
Lǐ Bàozhēn and Wáng Wǔjùn encamped thirty lǐ from Bèizhōu.
Zhū Tāo heard the two armies were approaching,
urgently summoned Mǎ Shí,
and Shí traveled day and night to join him.
Someone advised Tāo:
"Wǔjùn excels at field battles;
we cannot withstand his vanguard.
We should move our camp slightly forward to press him,
and have the Huíhé cut off his supply routes.
We can sit and consume provisions from Dé and Dì,
arrayed by our camp.
If advantageous, we attack;
if not, we retreat to defend.
Wait until they are hungry and weary,
then we can control them."
Tāo hesitated, undecided.
Just then, Mǎ Shí's army arrived,
and Tāo ordered battle for the next day.
Shí said:
"The soldiers have endured the summer heat and are exhausted;
I request several days of rest before battle."
The Regular Attendant Yáng Bù
(Tāo imitated the imperial court by appointing Regular Attendants)
and the Dágān said:
"When the Huíhé in our homeland fought neighboring states,
we often used five hundred cavalry to defeat several thousand enemy cavalry,
like sweeping leaves.
Now we have received the Great King's gold, silk, oxen, and wine beyond count,
and wish to render service for the Great King.
This is the time.
Tomorrow,
may the Great King station his horse on a high hill,
and watch the Huíhé cut down Wǔjùn's cavalry for you,
leaving not a single horse to return."
Bù and Xióng said:
"Great King, your heroic strategy surpasses the age.
You raised the entire army of Yān and Jì,
intending to sweep south of the river,
and clear Guānzhōng.
Now, seeing a minor enemy, you hesitate and do not attack,
losing the hopes of those near and far.
How then will you achieve your hegemon's enterprise!
The Dágān's request for battle is correct."
Tāo was pleased,
and thus resolved to give battle.
At dawn on Bǐngzǐ,
Wǔjùn sent his military commander Zhào Lín with five hundred cavalry to ambush in the mulberry forest.
The location of the mulberry forest
is southwest of Jīngchéng.
Wǔjùn led his cavalry to the front,
personally facing the Huíhé.
The Huíhé unleashed their troops to charge them.
Wǔjùn had his cavalry control their horses and evade.
The Huíhé burst out behind them,
and as they were about to turn back,
Wǔjùn then unleashed his troops to attack them.
Zhào Lín emerged from the forest to strike them from the side.
The Huíhé were defeated and fled.
Wǔjùn pursued them urgently.
Tāo's cavalry also fled,
trampling their own infantry formations underfoot.
Infantry and cavalry all fled eastward.
Tāo could not control them,
and so fled towards his camp.
Bàozhēn and Wǔjùn combined forces and pursued them.
At that time, Tāo had led thirty thousand men to battle;
over ten thousand died,
and over ten thousand scattered in flight.
Tāo barely managed to enter his camp with several thousand men and defend it firmly.
As dusk fell,
a thick fog gathered,
and the two armies could not advance.
Bàozhēn stationed his army northwest of the camp,
and Wǔjùn stationed his northeast.
Tāo burned his camp at night,
led his troops out the south gate,
headed towards Dézhōu and escaped,
abandoning the plundered wealth piled mountain-high.
The two armies, because of the fog,
could not pursue.
Tāo killed Yáng Bù and Cài Xióng and returned to Yōuzhōu.
His heart was inwardly ashamed,
and he also feared that Liú Pēng, the留守 of Fànyáng, might take advantage of the defeat to plot against him.
Pēng deployed all the留守 troops lining the road for twenty lǐ,
prepared ceremonial guards,
and welcomed him into the headquarters.
Facing each other, they felt both grief and joy.
Many people at the time praised him for this.
6. Initially,
Zhāng Xiàozhōng surrendered Yìzhōu to the state.
An edict appointed Xiàozhōng as Military Commissioner of Yìwǔ,
placing the three prefectures of Yì, Dìng, and Cāng under his jurisdiction.
(This matter is recorded in the 227th scroll, in the third year of the Jiànzhōng era.)
(He was) the brother-in-law of Lǐ Wéiyuè.
(Lǐ Wéiyuè)
originally had the surname Zhāng,
but married a woman from the Lǐ family.
Xiàozhōng dispatched his garrison commander, Chéng Huá from Ānxǐ, to hand over the affairs of the prefecture.
(Ānxǐ County,
was Lúnú County in the Hàn dynasty,
belonging to the Zhōngshān Kingdom.
Mùróng Chuí, the ruler of Yān, renamed it Bùlián.
The Northern Qí changed it to Ānxǐ.
The Suí changed it to Xiānyú.
In the fourth year of the Wǔdé era of the Táng, it was restored to Ānxǐ,
attached to Dìng Prefecture.)
As (Lǐ Gùliè, the Cāng Prefect) was about to depart,
the soldiers clamored loudly, saying:
"The Prefect has swept clean the treasury's wealth to take with him,
leaving the officers and soldiers behind to suffer hunger and cold.
What are we to do!"
They then killed Gùliè,
and slaughtered his family.
Chéng Huá heard of the disorder,
escaped through a hole in the wall,
but the mutinous soldiers found him,
and requested him to take charge of the prefectural affairs.
Huá had no choice
but to comply.
When Xiàozhōng heard of this,
he immediately appointed Huá as acting Prefect of Cāng.
(Textual analysis notes: The Old Book biography of Zhāng Xiàozhōng states:
"He sent Huá to Cāng to inspect and hand over the treasury stores."
The biography of Chéng Rìhuá states:
"Xiàozhōng ordered Huá to go to Gùliè to hand over the commandery.
After Gùliè's death,
Xiàozhōng appointed Huá to manage the affairs of Cāng Prefecture."
The Yānnán Jì states:
"Xiàozhōng dispatched his garrison officer Chéng Huá to take over from Gùliè.
After Gùliè's death,
Xiàozhōng, upon hearing the news,
that very day sent someone with an official document,
ordering him to act as Prefect."
Considering that once Gùliè had left,
Cāng Prefecture would be without a leader,
how could Xiàozhōng have merely ordered Huá to inspect the treasury stores?
We now follow Huá's biography and the Yānnán Jì.)
(Huá) treated the officers and soldiers with sincere trust,
and they felt at ease with him.
At that time, Zhū Tāo and Wáng Wǔjùn rebelled,
and repeatedly sent people to recruit Huá,
but Huá refused them all.
At the time, Xiàozhōng was in Dìng Prefecture.
To travel from Cāng to Dìng,
one necessarily passed through Yíng Prefecture,
which was under Zhū Tāo's control,
making the road obstructed and difficult.
The Registrar of Cāng Prefecture, Lǐ Yǔ, advised Huá,
suggesting he submit a memorial stating the advantages and disadvantages,
and request to form a separate army.
Huá followed this advice,
and sent Yǔ to present the memorial at the imperial headquarters.
The Emperor immediately appointed Huá as Prefect of Cāng, Deputy Commissioner of the Héng Hǎi Army, and Administrator of Military Commissioner Affairs,
bestowing upon him the name Rìhuá.
He ordered Rìhuá to supply Yìwǔ with 120,000 strings of cash annually in tax revenue.
Wáng Wǔjùn again sent someone to persuade and entice him.
At the time, the army was short of horses.
Rìhuá deceived the envoy, saying:
"If Commissioner Wáng insists on allying with me,
he should send two hundred cavalry to assist me."
Wǔjùn provided them.
Rìhuá kept all the horses,
and sent the soldiers back.
Wǔjùn was furious,
but as he was then confronting Mǎ Suì and others,
he was unable to attack and seize (Cāng).
Thus, Rìhuá managed to remain intact.
Later, when Wǔjùn returned his allegiance to the state,
Rìhuá sent someone to apologize for his fault,
repaid the value of the horses,
and also bribed him.
Wǔjùn was pleased,
and resumed friendly relations with him.
7. On Gēngyín,
Lǐ Shèng arrayed his troops in a grand formation,
announcing his intent to recapture the capital.
Previously,
Yáo Lìngyán and others had repeatedly sent spies to scout the timing of Shèng's advance,
but all were captured by the patrol cavalry.
Shèng showed them his deployed troops,
and said to them:
"Go back and tell those rebels:
Strive hard to defend firmly,
do not be disloyal to the rebels!"
He gave them all wine to drink,
provided them with money, and released them.
He then led his troops to outside the Tōnghuà Gate,
displayed his military might, and returned,
the rebels not daring to come out.
Shèng summoned his generals,
asking from where the army should enter.
All requested
"first take the outer city,
occupy the wards and markets,
then attack the palace from the north."
Shèng said:
"The wards and markets are narrow and confined.
If the rebels ambush troops and engage in close combat,
the residents will panic and cause chaos,
which would not be advantageous for the imperial army.
Now the enemy's main forces are all concentrated in the imperial parks.
It would be better to attack them from the north of the parks,
crushing their core,
and the rebels will certainly flee.
In this way,
the palace will not be damaged,
and the wards and markets will not be disturbed.
This is the best strategy!"
All the generals said:
"Excellent!"
He then sent dispatches to Hún Jiān, Military Commissioner of Zhènguó Luò Yuánguāng, and Military Commissioner of Shāng Prefecture Shàng Kěgū,
setting a date to assemble beneath the city walls.
(Beneath the capital's walls.)
On Rénchén,
Shàng Kěgū defeated the rebel general Qiú Jìngzhōng west of Lántián,
and beheaded him.
On Yǐwèi,
Lǐ Shèng moved his army to Mǐcāng Village outside the Guāngtài Gate.
(The Guāngtài Gate
is the northeastern gate of the park walls.)
(Chéng Dàchāng said: The Guāngtài Gate is north of the Tōnghuà Gate,
the eastern gate of the small walled city.
Seven lǐ east of the gate is Chánglè Slope.
Lǚ Dàfáng's Map of Cháng'ān states: The Guāngtài Gate
is an eastern gate of the capital city,
east of the eastern park of the Dàmíng Palace.)
On Bǐngshēn,
as Shèng was personally supervising the construction of fortifications,
the rebel elite generals Zhāng Tíngzhī and Lǐ Xīqiàn led a large force arriving.
Shèng said to his generals:
"Initially, I worried the rebels would hide and not come out.
Now they come to deliver themselves to death.
This is Heaven aiding us.
We must not miss this opportunity!"
He ordered Deputy Commander-in-Chief's Army Commander Wú Shēn and others to unleash their troops and attack them.
At the time, the Huàzhōu camp was in the north,
with few troops.
(The Huàzhōu troops
were Luò Yuánguāng's soldiers.
Huà
is pronounced with the entering tone.
Shǎo
is pronounced with the rising tone.)
Shèng ordered the vanguard general Lǐ Yǎn and others to lead elite troops to rescue them.
Yǎn and others fought fiercely,
and the rebels were defeated and fled.
Yǎn and others pursued them,
and following up on the victory, entered the Guāngtài Gate.
They fought again,
and again defeated them.
As night fell,
Shèng gathered his troops and returned.
The remaining rebel forces fled into the Báihuá Gate.
(The gate of the Báihuá Hall.)
Sounds of wailing and crying were heard.
(Xīqiàn
was the younger brother of Xīliè.)
On the dīngyǒu day,
Lǐ Shèng once again dispatched troops.
His generals requested to wait for the western army to arrive and attack together.
The western army
refers to Hún Jiān's forces.
"The rebels have been defeated several times,
their courage is already broken.
If we do not seize the victory and take them,
allowing them to prepare their defenses,
it is not a good plan."
The rebels came out to fight again,
and the government forces achieved repeated victories;
Luò Yuánguāng defeated Zhū Cǐ's forces west of Chǎn River.
On the wùxū day,
Lǐ Shèng arrayed his troops outside the Guāngtài Gate.
He ordered Lǐ Yǎn and the commander of the forward cavalry, Wáng Bì, to lead the cavalry,
and the forward general Shǐ Wànqǐng to lead the infantry,
advancing directly to the Shénjiā Village by the garden wall.
According to the New Book biography of Lǐ Shèng,
Shénjiā Village was north of the imperial garden.
Jiā
is pronounced gǔ yá in ancient times.
By the time Lǐ Yǎn and others arrived,
the rebels had already erected a palisade blocking it,
and from within the palisade they stabbed and shot at the government troops,
preventing them from advancing.
Lǐ Shèng was furious,
and rebuked his generals, saying:
"If you let the rebels act like this,
I will first behead you all!"
Shǐ Wànqǐng was afraid,
and led his troops to advance first,
pulling up the palisade and entering.
Wáng Bì and Lǐ Yǎn led the cavalry to follow,
and the rebel forces were utterly routed.
The various armies entered from different routes simultaneously.
Yáo Lìngyán and others still fought fiercely,
but Lǐ Shèng ordered the commander of the decisive army, Táng Liángchén, and others to press them with infantry and cavalry,
fighting and advancing,
for over ten engagements in total,
until the rebels could no longer hold out.
Upon reaching the Báihuá Gate,
several thousand rebel cavalry appeared behind the government army.
Lǐ Shèng led over a hundred cavalry to turn back and defend against them.
His attendants shouted:
"The Grand Councillor is coming!"
The rebels were all startled and scattered.
The officers and soldiers of Jīngyuán had long feared and respected Lǐ Shèng,
hence upon hearing of his arrival they were startled and scattered.
Previously,
Zhū Cǐ had sent Zhāng Guāngshèng to station five thousand troops at Jiǔqū,
over ten lǐ from the Eastern Wèi Bridge.
Zhāng Guāngshèng secretly pledged allegiance to Lǐ Shèng.
When Zhū Cǐ was defeated,
Zhāng Guāngshèng urged Zhū Cǐ to flee.
Zhū Cǐ then fled west with Yáo Lìngyán and the remaining troops,
still numbering nearly ten thousand.
Zhāng Guāngshèng escorted Zhū Cǐ out of the city,
then returned,
and surrendered to Lǐ Shèng.
Lǐ Shèng sent the cavalry commander Tián Zǐqí to pursue Zhū Cǐ with cavalry.
Lǐ Shèng stationed himself in front of the Hányuán Hall,
lodging at the Right Jīnyǔ Guard post.
The Hányuán Hall
was the front hall of the Eastern Palace of the Táng.
The Left Jīnyǔ Guard post
was east of the hall;
the Right Jīnyǔ Guard post
was west of the hall.
"I, Shèng, rely on the strength of the officers and soldiers
to have cleared the palace grounds.
The gentry and commoners of Cháng'ān
have long been trapped under rebel rule.
If there is the slightest disturbance,
it would not align with the intent of comforting the people and punishing the guilty.
It will not be long before I, Shèng, and you all can reunite with your families.
For five days, no one is to send messages home."
He ordered the Capital Governor Lǐ Qíyùn and others to comfort the residents.
Lǐ Shèng's senior general Gāo Míngyào took a rebel courtesan,
and a soldier under Shàng Kěgū's command took a rebel horse.
Lǐ Shèng executed them both,
causing the army to tremble with fear.
Public and private affairs were undisturbed,
and not the slightest violation occurred.
In distant wards, some only learned the government troops had entered the city after a night had passed.
History records that Lǐ Shèng governed his army with strict discipline.
On that day,
Hún Jiān, Dài Xiūyán, and Hán Yóuguī also captured Xiányáng,
defeating over three thousand rebel troops.
Hearing that Zhū Cǐ was fleeing west,
they divided their forces to intercept him.
On the jǐhài day,
Lǐ Shèng ordered the Capital Western Cavalry Commander Mèng Shè to station troops at the Báihuá Gate,
and Shàng Kěgū to station troops at the Wàngxiān Gate.
The southern side of the Táng Dàmíng Palace had five gates.
The central one was called the Dānfèng Gate.
East of Dānfèng was the Wàngxiān Gate,
and further east was the Yánzhèng Gate.
West of Dānfèng was the Jiànfú Gate,
and further west was the Xīng'ān Gate.
Lǐ Shèng stationed three thousand of his forward troops at the Ānguó Temple.
Chéng Dàchāng said: The Zhāngjìng Temple
was outside the eastern city wall.
The Ānguó Temple
was southeast of the Dàmíng Palace.
He executed eight of Zhū Cǐ's partisans, Lǐ Xīqiàn, Jìng Hóng, Péng Yǎn, and others, in the marketplace.
8. After Wáng Wùjùn defeated Zhū Tāo,
he returned to Héngzhōu
and submitted a memorial declining the post of Military Governor of Yōuzhōu and Lúlóng.
The Emperor approved.
Wáng Wùjùn concurrently held the posts of Military Governor of Yōuzhōu and Lúlóng;
see the second month of this year in the previous scroll.
Héng
is pronounced hù dēng.
9. In the sixth month,
on the guǐmǎo day,
Lǐ Shèng sent his administrative secretary, Yú Gōngyì, a man from Wú, to draft a victory proclamation to be sent to the Emperor's temporary residence,
which said:
"Your servant has already purified the palace grounds,
and reverently paid respects at the imperial tombs.
The bells and stands remain unmoved,
and the ancestral temples appear as before."
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: Miào (temple) means mào (appearance).
The spirit of the deceased cannot be seen,
so we use the palace chambers and likeness from their lifetime to represent them.
The commentary to the Classic of Filial Piety states: Zōng
means to honor.
Miào
means mào (likeness).
"Heaven gave birth to Lǐ Shèng
for the sake of the state,
not for my sake alone."
When Lǐ Shèng was at the Wèi Bridge,
Mars was stationary near Jupiter.
Where Jupiter is located,
that state has fortune.
If Mars stations there,
it is a punitive star.
His aides and assistants all congratulated him,
saying:
"Mars has retreated from its station,
it is a blessing for the imperial house!
We should quickly advance the troops."
Lǐ Shèng said:
"The Son of Heaven is residing in the wilds,
his subjects only know to fight the enemy to the death.
The celestial phenomena are lofty and distant,
who can know them!"
After capturing Cháng'ān,
he then said to them:
"It was not that I disagreed with you earlier.
I have heard that the five planets advance and retreat irregularly.
The Treatise on Astronomy in the Book of Hàn states: If any of the five planets appears early, it is an advance;
advance signifies the guest.
If it appears late, it is a retreat;
retreat signifies the host.
The Treatise on Astronomy in the Book of Jìn states: Losing its sequence and moving upward is an advance;
losing its sequence and moving downward is a retreat.
If we had advanced at that time, our army would have collapsed without even fighting!"
They all apologized, saying:
"We could not have foreseen that!"
10. Zhū Cǐ intended to flee to Tǔbō.
His followers scattered and deserted along the way.
By the time he reached Jīngzhōu,
he had only over a hundred cavalry left.
Tián Xījiàn closed the city gates and refused him entry.
Zhū Cǐ said to him:
"Your command tally
was bestowed by me."
Zhū Cǐ had appointed Tián Xījiàn as Military Governor of Jīngyuán;
see the fourth month of this year in the previous scroll.
He ordered him to burn the city gate;
Tián Xījiàn took the command tally and threw it into the fire, saying:
"Return your tally to you!"
Zhū Cǐ's followers all wept.
The Jīngzhōu soldiers then killed Yáo Lìngyán,
and went to Tián Xījiàn to surrender.
Zhū Cǐ alone, with his Fànyáng personal guards and his clan members and guests, headed north towards the Yìmǎ Pass.
The Prefect of Níngzhōu, Xiàhóu Yīng, resisted him.
Upon reaching the western city garrison of Péngyuán,
Péngyuán
was originally Péngyáng County.
In the 18th year of the Suí dynasty's Kāihuáng era, its name was changed.
During the Táng, it belonged to Níngzhōu.
Hán Mín and others beheaded him,
and went to Jīngzhōu to surrender.
Yuán Xiū and Lǐ Zǐpíng fled to Fèngxiáng.
Lǐ Chǔlín executed them,
and all sent their heads to the Emperor's temporary residence.
The Emperor ordered Lù Zhì to draft an edict to be bestowed upon Hún Jiān,
instructing him to search for and retrieve the "wrapped-head palace women" who had been lost during the flight to Fèngtiān.
The "wrapped-head palace women"
were those who performed duties and errands within the palace.
Palace women who performed duties all wore headscarves,
hence they were called "wrapped-head palace women."
Lù Zhì believed:
"The great bandits have only just been pacified,
the exhausted and ailing populace,
the wounded and battered soldiers,
have not yet been comforted and tended to,
yet the first thing sought are women.
This is not the way to meet the expectations for a renewed era.
If a plan's beginning is perfectly sound,
it is rare that it can be carried through to the end;
if one does not plan at the beginning,
what will there be at the end!
Regarding the edict to be bestowed upon Jiān,
I dare not accept the imperial command."
The Emperor consequently did not issue the edict,
but in the end dispatched a palace envoy to search for them.
On the yǐsì day,
an edict appointed the Vice-Minister of Personnel Bān Hóng to serve as Commissioner of Pacification and Consolation,
to reward and inquire after the generals and soldiers,
and to comfort and soothe the multitudes of the people.
According to the annotations of the Shījīng commentaries: Zhēng
means multitude;
lí,
also means multitude.
Láo,
is pronounced with the tone 'lì dào fān'.
On the bǐngwǔ day,
Lǐ Shèng executed over ten civil and military officials who had enjoyed Zhū Cǐ's favor and appointments, including Cuī Xuān, Hóng Jīnglún, and others.
The Textual Analysis states: Yuán Hào's Xīngyuán Shènggōng Lù records Lǐ Shèng's memorial pleading for leniency for Guō Xī, which said:
"Xī, due to the recent movement of the imperial carriage,
hid in the mountains and valleys.
Known to the rebel bandits,
he was carried to the city;
coerced and forced into accepting an appointment,
there were many such instances before and after.
In the midst of haste and confusion,
the false orders still reached him;
if he firmly refused and maintained his integrity,
he would immediately fear severe punishment;
if he followed custom and accepted office,
it would damage his lifelong principles.
However, Xī, though already tainted by corrupt customs,
can still be shown to be clear.
Zǐyí's meritorious service,
is recorded in the princely archives.
The father being a pillar of the restoration,
the son bearing a name of suspicion and slander—
this does not only concern him alone,
but truly risks sullying the achievements of his illustrious ancestors.
Moreover, I command the troops and horses,
standing alone at the Wèi Bridge,
frequently received silk letters,
repeatedly expressing sincere loyalty."
According to Xī's old biography,
"Cǐ wanted to put him in charge of troops,
Xī feigned muteness.
Cǐ threatened him with soldiers,
but he ultimately did not speak.
The bandits knew he could not be used,
and so stopped.
Xī secretly fled to Fèngtiān,
and followed the imperial carriage back to the capital."
It does not say he ultimately served Cǐ;
yet Hào records Shèng's memorial,
fearing it is not factual.
It is not adopted here.
Liú Nǎi,
his affair is seen in the second month of this year in the previous scroll.
Jiǎng Yǎn,
his affair is seen in scroll 228, the fourth year of the Jiànzhōng era.
On the jǐyǒu day,
Lǐ Shèng was appointed Minister over the Masses and Secretariat Director,
Luò Yuánguāng and Shàng Kěgū were each promoted in office to varying degrees.
This was to reward their merit in recapturing the capital.
12 An edict changed the name of Liáng Prefecture to Xīngyuán Prefecture.
Using the reign era name as a prefecture name began here.
13 On the jiǎyín day,
Hún Jiān was appointed Palace Attendant,
Hán Yóuguī and Dài Xiūyán were each promoted in office to varying degrees.
This was to reward their merit in escorting and guarding.
14 When Zhū Cǐ was defeated,
Lǐ Zhōngchén fled to Fánchuān.
Lì Dàoyuán's Commentary on the Water Classic says: Fánchuān,
was Fán Township of Dù County.
When Hàn Gāozǔ returned to pacify the Three Qín,
because Fán Kuài's flooding of Fèiqiū was the greatest achievement,
he was granted an estate in this township.
According to this, the place was south of Cháng'ān in the Táng.
Chéng Dàchāng said: Fánchuān,
is thirty-five lǐ south of Wànnián County.
On the bǐngchén day,
he was executed.
15 The Emperor asked Lù Zhì:
"Now, upon reaching Fèngxiáng, there are armies welcoming the imperial carriage,
the situation is very imposing.
I wish to take this opportunity to send someone to replace Lǐ Chǔlín.
What do you think?"
Zhì submitted a memorial,
believing:
"Doing so would make the affair akin to coercion and seizure.
Speaking of eliminating disorder, it is not martial;
speaking of attending to governance, it is not sincere.
Using this as a time for inspection tours,
where will one enter afterwards!
The Shū·Zhōuguān says,
in the sixth year,
the king then made a seasonal inspection tour,
examining the institutions at the Four Peaks,
where the feudal lords each paid court at their respective directional peak.
Kǒng Ānguó said: East in spring, south in summer, west in autumn, north in winter,
hence it is called a seasonal inspection tour.
I privately do not understand the reasoning.
The meaning of 'expediency' (quán)
is analogous to a steelyard balance.
Héng,
is to weigh things evenly.
Quán,
then weighs the lightness and heaviness of things,
measuring them with the balance's level.
To first act with coercion and seizure,
exchanging one commander but damaging the righteousness of the Son of Heaven,
gaining one region but sowing suspicion throughout the land,
this is to make heavy what is light and make light what is heavy.
To call this 'expediency',
is it not contrary!
To take contrary ways as expediency,
to consider employing schemes as wisdom—
if the ruler above practices this, he will surely lose the multitude;
if ministers below use this, they will surely bring ruin upon themselves.
The reason why successive generations have had much chaos and disorder and prolonged treachery and evil
is due to this error.
Lù Zhì's discussion here
is to correct the Hàn Confucians' error of 'acting contrary to the constant norm to accord with the Way' as expediency.
Master Chéng said: The Hàn Confucians considered 'acting contrary to the constant norm to accord with the Way' as expediency,
hence there were theories of expedient change and expedient schemes,
all of which are incorrect.
Expediency is simply the character for 'constant norm'.
Since the Hàn dynasty onward, no one has understood the character for 'expediency'.
Sàng,
is pronounced 'xī làng fān'.
Zhǎng,
is pronounced 'zhī liǎng fān'.
To settle and rest peacefully in the capital,
Shǐ Zhào said: Diànzhěn,
means to rest peacefully.
Yángzǐ said: Settle and rest peacefully in the capital.
They, pleased by the grace and pardon,
will be rushing about without respite,
how would they dare to rashly offer collective resistance?
Shǐ Zhào said: Lǚ,
means multitude.
Jù,
means to resist.
It means leading the multitude to resist each other.
On the wùwǔ day,
the imperial carriage departed from Hànzhōng.
16 Lǐ Shèng comprehensively managed Cháng'ān to prepare for the various offices,
Shǐ Zhào said: Zōng,
is the heddle of a loom.
Lǐ,
means to govern.
It means to put affairs in order,
making everything have proper arrangement,
like the heddle organizing the threads on a loom.
The Emperor did not permit it.
The Palace Attendant-in-ordinary Yǐn Yuánzhēn, on a mission to Tóng and Huà,
went on his own to Hézhōng to summon and instruct Lǐ Huáiguāng.
This was the usual behavior of eunuchs in the mid-Táng period.
Huà,
is pronounced 'hù huà fān'.
"Yuánzhēn forged an imperial decree to pardon the arch-villain,
I request his crime be dealt with!"
Lǐ,
means to govern.
Avoiding Gāozōng's personal name taboo,
using
"lǐ"
for
"zhì".
17 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the bǐngzǐ day,
the imperial carriage reached Fèngxiáng,
and executed Qiáo Lín, Jiǎng Zhèn, Zhāng Guāngshèng, and others.
Lǐ Shèng believed that although Guāngshèng had served the bandits,
he had also contributed considerably to their destruction,
and wished to spare him;
the Emperor did not permit it.
18. Deputy Marshal's Judge Gāo Yǐng repeatedly urged Lǐ Huáiguāng to submit to the court.
Huáiguāng sent his son Lǐ Cuǐ to the imperial headquarters to apologize for his crimes,
requesting to surrender himself and return to the court.
On the Gēngchén day,
an edict was issued sending the Supervising Secretary Kǒng Cháofù to deliver the previous decree appointing Huáiguāng as Grand Preceptor of the Heir Apparent.
(The appointment of Huáiguāng is recorded in the previous volume, in the third month of this year.)
The officers and soldiers of the Shuòfāng Army all had their official titles and ranks restored as before.
(The Shuòfāng officers and soldiers were those under Huáiguāng's command.)
(Huáiguāng's forces.)
(Examination of discrepancies: The "Shènggōng Lù" of the Xīngyuán period contains Lǐ Shèng's memorial reporting Yǐng's urging of Huáiguāng to submit, stating:
"Now Huáiguāng wishes to surrender himself."
This likely stemmed from Yǐng's persuasion.
I adopt this account.)
19. On the Rénwǔ day,
the imperial carriage arrived at Cháng'ān.
Hún Jiān, Hán Yóuguī, and Dài Xiūyán led their troops as the imperial escort.
Lǐ Shèng, Luò Yuánguāng, and Shàng Kěgū led their troops to welcome the emperor.
There were over a hundred thousand infantry and cavalry,
with banners and flags stretching for dozens of miles.
Shèng paid his respects to the emperor at Sānqiáo.
(Sānqiáo
is east of the Wàngxián Palace
and west of the capital city.)
(See,
pronounced xiàn, with the meaning "to appear.")
Afterwards, he apologized for the delay in recovering the capital,
kneeling by the roadside to ask for punishment.
The emperor halted his horse to comfort and console him,
wiping away tears for him,
and ordered attendants to help him mount his horse.
Upon reaching the palace,
on every leisure day,
the emperor would feast the meritorious officials,
bestowing generous rewards.
Lǐ Shèng was foremost among them,
Hún Jiān next,
and the other generals and ministers after them.
20. Cáo Wáng Lǐ Gāo sent his generals Yǐ Shèn and Wáng È to besiege Ānzhōu.
Lǐ Xīliè sent his nephew Liú Jièxū with eight thousand infantry and cavalry to relieve it.
Gāo sent his deputy general Lǐ Bóqián to intercept
them at Yìngshān.
(Liú Xù said: Yìngshān
originally belonged to the Suí County territory of the Hàn Dynasty's Nányáng Commandery.
The Liáng Dynasty partitioned Suí County to establish Yǒngyáng County.
The Suí Dynasty changed it to Yìngshān,
named after the mountain north of the county.
In the Táng Dynasty, it belonged to Suízhōu.
The "Jiǔyù Zhì" states: Yìngshān County
is 108 lǐ north of Suízhōu.)
They captured Jièxū alive,
paraded him beneath the city walls,
and Ānzhōu subsequently surrendered.
Yǐ Shèn was appointed as the Prefect of Ānzhōu.
They also attacked Lǐ Xīliè's general Kāng Shūyè at Lìxiāng,
driving him away.
(The "Jì Fǎ" records: When the Lìshān clan possessed the empire,
their descendant, the Farmer,
was able to cultivate all the grains.
The commentary states: The Lìshān clan
was Emperor Yán,
who arose from Lìshān.
The commentary to the "Geography Treatise" of the "History of the Western Hàn" states: Suí
was the ancient state of Lì.
Huángfǔ Mì said: It is the present-day Lìxiāng in Suí.
The "Jiǔyù Zhì" states: Lìxiāng Village in Suízhōu has Lìshān.
Now, from Zǎoyáng to Lìxiāng,
the roads intersect,
and it is called the Ninety-Nine Ridges.)
21. On the Dīnghài day,
Kǒng Cháofù arrived at Hézhōng.
Lǐ Huáiguāng, dressed in plain clothes, awaited punishment,
but Cháofù did not stop him.
Many of Huáiguāng's attendants were non-Han people.
They all sighed, saying:
"The Grand Commandant has lost his office!"
(The non-Han people were unfamiliar with court protocol.
Seeing Huáiguāng in plain clothes awaiting punishment,
they therefore thought he had lost his office.)
"Who in the army can replace the Grand Commandant and lead the troops?"
Thereupon, Huáiguāng's attendants became angry and raised a clamor.
Before the proclamation of the edict was finished,
the crowd killed Cháofù and the palace envoy Dàn Shǒuyíng.
Huáiguāng also did not stop them.
(Examination of discrepancies: The "Bīnzhì" states:
"On the twelfth day of the seventh month,
the imperial carriage returned to Cháng'ān.
The emperor sent the Remonstrance Official Kǒng Cháofù and the palace official Tán Huáixiān with an edict pardoning Huáiguāng, saying: 'At the time of Fèngtiān,
without you, no one could have saved Us;
in today's matter,
without Us, no one can tolerate you.
You should entrust the army and come to the court,
to preserve your office and rank.'
As the envoys were about to arrive,
Huáiguāng secretly incited his soldiers to keep him.
The non-Han and Hún soldiers, following Huáiguāng's intention,
killed the two envoys,
wishing to eat their flesh.
Huáiguāng shielded and covered them,
reporting their intact bodies to the court."
I now follow the "Veritable Records.")
22. On the Xīnmǎo day,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
23. Earlier,
when Emperor Sùzōng was at Língwǔ,
(see volume 219, the first year of Zhìdé),
he studied literature under Lǐ Bì.
During the reign of Emperor Dàizōng,
Bì resided at the Pénglái Academy,
(see volume 224, the first year of Yǒngtài).
(Shǐ Zhào said: Bì,
pronounced bì, with the meaning "to seep.")
and the emperor also associated with him.
When the emperor was at Xīngyuán,
Bì was the Prefect of Hángzhōu.
The emperor urgently summoned him by edict,
and he went to the imperial headquarters together with the Prefect of Mùzhōu, Dù Yà.
On the Yǐwèi day,
Bì was appointed as Left Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
and Yà as Vice-Minister of Justice.
Bì was ordered to serve daily in the Western Secretariat to await audience.
(The Táng Dynasty's Chancellery is called the Eastern Secretariat,
and the Secretariat is called the Western Secretariat.)
The emperor asked Bì:
"Hézhōng is close to the capital.
The Shuòfāng troops have always been renowned for their elite prowess.
Men like Dáxī Xiǎojùn
are each a match for ten thousand.
We worry about them day and night.
What is to be done?"
He replied:
"There are indeed many things in the empire worthy of worry.
If it is only Hézhōng,
it is not worth worrying about.
In assessing an enemy,
one assesses the general, not the soldiers.
Now, Huáiguāng
is the general;
men like Xiǎojùn are merely soldiers.
Why should they be of concern!
After Huáiguāng lifted the siege of Fèngtiān,
seeing that Zhū Cǐ was a nearly defeated foe yet unable to capture him,
he instead allied with him,
allowing Lǐ Shèng to seize the achievement.
Now Your Majesty has already returned to the palace,
yet Huáiguāng does not surrender himself to accept punishment.
Instead, he brutally killed the envoys,
(referring to the killing of Kǒng Cháofù and Dàn Shǒuyíng).
(Shǐ,
pronounced shǐ, with the meaning "envoy.")
He is like a person in a nightmare!
I only fear that before long he will be beheaded by his own subordinates,
leaving the various generals with no means to accomplish anything."
Earlier,
the emperor had mobilized the Tǔbō to attack Zhū Cǐ,
(see volume 229, the first month of this year).
After Cǐ was executed,
the Tǔbō came to demand territory.
The emperor wished to summon the two garrison military commissioners Guō Xīn and Lǐ Yuánzhōng back to court.
(Xīn and Yuánzhōng are mentioned in volume 227, the second year of Jiànzhōng.)
Lǐ Bì said:
"Ānxī and Běitíng
have populations of fierce and hardy nature.
They control fifty-seven states of the Western Regions.
(The Western Regions
had thirty-six states during the Hàn Dynasty.
Later they gradually divided,
so that by the Táng Dynasty there were fifty-seven states.
The Western Turkic Khaganate had the Five Nǔshībì and the Five Duōlù,
totaling ten tribes.)
They prevent them from combining forces to invade eastward.
(Meaning invading eastward into Jīng, Bīn, Qí, Lǒng, and other prefectures.)
Moreover, the people of the two garrisons,
isolated and in a distant land,
have been utterly loyal and exerted all their strength,
firmly defending for the state for nearly twenty years.
(Early in Dàizōng's reign,
the Tǔbō captured Hé and Lǒng,
yet only Ānxī and Běitíng held firm for the Táng.)
(Wèi,
pronounced wèi, meaning "for.")
(Jìn,
pronounced jìn, meaning "near.")
If we suddenly abandon them and give them to the barbarians,
their hearts will certainly deeply resent the Central Kingdom.
In the future, when they follow the Tǔbō in invasion,
it will be like avenging a private grudge.
Furthermore, previously the Tǔbō watched and hesitated, not advancing,
secretly playing both sides,
plundering Wǔgōng extensively,
and accepting bribes before departing.
(See the previous volume, the fourth month of this year.)
The general opinion also considered this reasonable.
The emperor therefore did not cede the territory.
24. When Lǐ Xīliè heard that Lǐ Xīqiàn had been executed,
he was furious.
In the eighth month,
on the rén-yín day,
he sent a palace envoy to Càizhōu to kill Yán Zhēnqīng.
(Textual analysis note: According to the "Yán Family Chronicle":
"On the twenty-fourth day of the eighth month of that year,
Xīn Jǐngzhēn and others were again sent to harm the Duke at Lóngxīng Temple.")
It also states:
"After the initial calamity,
Sì Cáo Wáng Gāo submitted a memorial saying: 'I saw the messengers Zhāng Xīcàn and Wáng Shìkē, who had returned from Càizhōu, report that
on the twenty-fourth day of the eighth month last year,
they witnessed a sealed document in Càizhōu city.
There was a neighbor's child whose name is unknown,
who said that Lǐ Xīliè ordered the false imperial city commissioner Xīn Jǐngzhēn and Right Army commander Ān Huá to kill Yán Zhēnqīng at Lóngxīng Temple.'")
The Veritable Records and the Old Biography state
"on the third day."
We now follow this.
"There is an imperial decree."
Yán Zhēnqīng bowed twice.
The palace envoy said:
"Now you are granted death."
Yán Zhēnqīng said:
"This old minister has been remiss,
and my crime deserves death.
May I ask, how many days ago did the envoy depart from Cháng'ān?"
The envoy said:
"I came from Dàliáng,
not from Cháng'ān."
Yán Zhēnqīng said:
"Then you are a rebel,
how can you speak of an imperial decree!"
He was then strangled to death.
25. Lǐ Shèng considered that Jīngzhōu, being a border region,
had repeatedly harmed military commanders,
and was often a source of rebellion.
When the Emperor first ascended the throne,
there was the rebellion of Liú Wénxǐ in Jīngzhōu,
followed by the rebellion of Yáo Lìngyán,
and then Tián Xījiàn also killed Féng Héqīng.
(Commander,
pronounced as suǒ lèi fān;
the same below.
Govern,
means to administer.)
On the guǐ-mǎo day,
Lǐ Shèng was appointed concurrently as Military Commissioner of Fèngxiáng and Lǒngyòu, and Deputy Commander-in-Chief of the Four Garrisons, Beiting, Jīngyuán, and other expeditionary camps.
He was also advanced to the rank of Xīpíng Prince.
At that time, Lǐ Chǔlín came to court.
Lǐ Shèng requested to take him along to Fèngxiáng and execute him there,
to punish rebellion and disorder.
The Emperor, because the capital had just been recovered,
was focused on pacifying those with rebellious intentions,
and did not grant permission.
26. Previously,
the Emperor had ordered Hún Jiān and Luò Yuánguāng to attack Lǐ Huáiguāng's army in Tóngzhōu.
(The "Jiǔyù Zhì" states: Tóngzhōu is seventy-five lǐ from Hézhōng.)
(Previously,
pronounced as xī jiàn fān.)
Hún Jiān and others were repeatedly defeated by them,
and could not advance.
At that time, the Ministry of Revenue's funds were insufficient,
and many advisors requested to pardon Lǐ Huáiguāng,
but the Emperor refused.
Lǐ Huáiguāng sent his brother-in-law Yào Tíngzhēn to guard Jìnzhōu,
his officer Máo Cháoyáng to guard Xízhōu,
and Zhèng Kàng to guard Cízhōu.
Mǎ Suì sent people to persuade them to surrender.
(The three prefectures of Jìn, Xí, and Cí
all bordered the area under Mǎ Suì's jurisdiction,
hence he was able to persuade them to surrender.
Sòng Bái said: Cízhōu, Wénchéng Commandery,
was the state of the Chìdí Qiánggāorú.
Southwest of the commandery is Cǎisāng Ford,
where Lǐ Kè of Jìn defeated the Chìdí.
In the Hàn dynasty, it was Běiqū County.
In the Suí dynasty, it was Fēnzhōu.
In the Dàyè period, it was Wénchéng Commandery.
In the Táng dynasty, during the Zhēnguàn period, it became Cízhōu.
Because there was an old Cíwū garrison within the prefectural city,
it was named accordingly.
It administered Jíxiāng County,
which was Běiqū County in the Hàn dynasty.)
(Persuade,
pronounced as shì ruì fān.)
He was appointed Deputy Commander-in-Chief of the Hézhōng, Tónghuà, Shǎnguó expeditionary camps.
Mǎ Suì was additionally appointed Military Commissioner of Fèngchéng Army and Jìn-Cí-Xí,
and Deputy Commander-in-Chief of the various armies within his jurisdiction.
Together with Zhènguó Military Commissioner Luò Yuánguāng—
(In the second year of the Shàngyuán era of Sùzōng,
the Zhènguó Military Commission was established in Huàzhōu.
It was abolished in the first year of the Guǎngdé era,
and now it was re-established.)
Initially,
Wáng Wǔjùn urgently attacked Kāng Rìzhī in Zhàozhōu.
Mǎ Suì memorialized requesting an edict ordering Wáng Wǔjùn and Lǐ Bàozhēn to jointly attack Zhū Tāo,
assigning Shēnzhōu and Zhàozhōu to Wáng Wǔjùn,
and changing Kāng Rìzhī to Military Commissioner of Jìn, Cí, and Xí.
The Emperor agreed.
Before Kāng Rìzhī arrived, the three prefectures surrendered to Mǎ Suì,
so the Emperor had Mǎ Suì concurrently administer them.
Mǎ Suì memorialized to yield the three prefectures to Kāng Rìzhī,
and stated that granting them because of surrender
might cause future meritorious individuals
to follow this as a precedent,
and the Emperor praised and approved.
Mǎ Suì sent an envoy to welcome Kāng Rìzhī.
When he arrived,
Mǎ Suì registered the government storehouses and returned them to him.
27. On the jiǎ-chén day,
Fèngxiáng Military Commissioner Lǐ Chǔlín was appointed Left Imperial Guard General.
28. On the bǐng-wǔ day,
Hún Jiān was additionally appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Shuòfāng expeditionary camp.
29. Lǐ Shèng arrived at Fèngxiáng
to investigate the crime of killing Zhāng Yì.
(The killing of Zhāng Yì is recorded in the 228th volume, fourth year of the Jiànzhōng era.)
(Investigate,
pronounced as zhí zhī fān.
Yì,
pronounced as yì zhì fān.)
30. Zhū Tāo, attacked by Wáng Wǔjùn,
was almost unable to maintain his army,
and submitted a memorial awaiting punishment.
31. On the guǐ-wèi day,
Mǎ Suì led thirty thousand infantry and cavalry to attack Jiàngzhōu.
(Jiàngzhōu was then under Lǐ Huáiguāng.)
(Led,
pronounced as jí liàng fān,
also pronounced as usual.
Cavalry,
pronounced as qí jì fān.)
32. The Ministry of Revenue, because the tens of thousands of officers and soldiers under Lǐ Huáiguāng's command had rebelled along with him,
did not issue winter clothing.
The Emperor said:
"The Shuòfāng Army has been loyal and righteous for generations.
Now they are only controlled by Lǐ Huáiguāng.
What crime have the officers and soldiers committed!"
In winter,
the tenth month,
an edict was issued:
"For the Shuòfāng Army and the various armies under Lǐ Huáiguāng,
winter clothing and reward money should all be separately stored.
Once the roads are somewhat passable,
they shall be issued immediately."
33. Lǐ Miǎn repeatedly submitted memorials requesting self-demotion,
because he had lost his army and failed to defend against Lǐ Xīliè.
On the xīn-chǒu day,
Lǐ Miǎn was dismissed from the posts of Commander-in-Chief and Military Commissioner.
(During the Jiànzhōng era,
Lǐ Miǎn, as Yǒngpíng Military Commissioner, was Commander-in-Chief of the forces attacking Lǐ Xīliè.)
34. On the bǐng-chén day,
Lǐ Huáiguāng's officer Yán Yàn invaded Tóngzhōu.
The government forces were defeated at Shāyuàn.
An edict was issued to summon the army from Bīnzhōu,
and Hán Yóuguī led six thousand armored soldiers to join them.
35. On the yǐ-chǒu day,
Mǎ Suì captured Jiàngzhōu,
and divided his forces to take Wénxǐ, Wànquán, Yúxiāng, Yǒnglè, and Yīshì.
(In the first year of the Wǔdé era,
Yǒnglè County was established from part of Ruì County,
belonging to Ruìzhōu.
When the prefecture was abolished,
it belonged to Dǐngzhōu.
When Dǐngzhōu was also abolished,
the county was assigned to Hézhōng Prefecture.)
After Mǎ Suì took Yǒnglè,
his troops pressed close to Hézhōng.
(Lè,
pronounced as luò.)
36. Initially, after Yú Cháo'ēn was executed,
Emperor Dàizōng no longer allowed eunuchs to command troops.
(For the event, see scroll 224, the fifth year of the Dàlì era.)
Fù,
pronounced fú yòu fān;
the same below.
He entrusted all the imperial guard troops to Bái Zhìzhēn.
(Bái Zhìzhēn's given name was Bái Xiùguī. His command of the imperial guard troops first appears in scroll 225, the fourteenth year of the Dàlì era.)
(See scroll 229, the fourth year of the Jiànzhōng era.)
He accompanied the emperor to Shānnán,
and the two armies gradually assembled.
(The two armies refer to the Left and Right Shéncè Armies.)
He was quite wary of veteran generals who held large numbers of troops,
and gradually dismissed them.
On the Wùchén day,
he appointed Wén Chǎng as Supervisor of the Left Wing Cavalry and Infantry Commander of the Shéncè Army,
and Wáng Xīqiān as Supervisor of the Right Wing Cavalry and Infantry Commander,
thus beginning the practice of having eunuchs separately command the imperial guard.
From this point on, the eunuchs' grip on military power could no longer be wrested away.
Jiàng,
pronounced jí liàng fān.
Jiān,
pronounced gǔ xián fān.
Textual analysis: The Old Book biography of Dòu Wénchǎng states:
"Wénchǎng and Huò Xiānmíng separately commanded the imperial guard."
It seems Xīqiān was soon dismissed and Xiānmíng replaced him.
Now follow the Veritable Records.
37. In the intercalary month, on the Bǐngzǐ day,
Tián Xījiàn, the military governor of Jīngyuán, was appointed as Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
When Lǐ Shèng first arrived at Fèngxiáng,
Xījiàn sent an envoy to pay his respects.
Shèng said to the envoy:
"Jīng Prefecture is close to Tǔbō.
If they invade,
can the prefectural troops alone defend against them?
I wish to send troops for defense and support,
but I do not know Minister Tián's intentions."
The envoy returned
and reported this to Xījiàn.
Xījiàn indeed requested reinforcements,
and Shèng sent his trusted general Péng Lìngyīng and others to garrison Jīng Prefecture.
Shèng soon used the pretext of inspecting the border to go to Jīng Prefecture.
Xījiàn came out to welcome him,
and Shèng rode side by side with him into the city,
reminiscing about old times and fostering goodwill.
Xījiàn's wife, née Lǐ,
treated Shèng as an uncle,
and Shèng called him "Tián Láng."
Shèng ordered provisions for three days,
saying:
"After the inspection tour is completed,
I will return to Fèngxiáng."
Xījiàn no longer suspected anything.
Shèng held a banquet,
and Xījiàn and his officers all came to Shèng's camp.
Shèng had hidden armed men in the outer corridors.
After eating and drinking,
Péng Lìngyīng led the Jīng Prefecture generals down from the hall.
Shèng said:
"I have been separated from you all for a long time;
each of you should state your name."
Thus, he identified more than thirty people, including Shí Qí, who had participated in the rebellion.
He rebuked them, saying:
"You have repeatedly engaged in rebellion and treachery,
harming loyal and good officials.
This is certainly intolerable to heaven and earth!"
He had them all taken out
and executed.
Xījiàn was still seated.
Shèng looked at him and said:
"Tián Láng, you are not without fault either.
Because of our close relationship,
I will allow you to keep your body intact."
Xījiàn said:
"Yes."
He was then taken out
and strangled to death,
along with his son, Tián È.
Textual analysis: The Old Book biography of Shèng states:
"Shèng arrived at Jīng Prefecture;
Xījiàn came to pay his respects at the seat,
and Shèng captured and executed him.
Returning to his headquarters,
he recommended Lǐ Guān as military governor of Jīngyuán."
The Record of the Emperor's Sojourn in Fèngtiān states:
"On the tenth month, Dīngchǒu day,
Lǐ Shèng executed Tián Xījiàn at Jīng Prefecture."
The Veritable Records state:
"On the intercalary month, Guǐyǒu day,
Lǐ Guān was appointed military governor of Jīngyuán.
On the Bǐngzǐ day,
Xījiàn was appointed Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
On the Dīngchǒu day,
Shèng executed Xījiàn."
Now follow this.
He explained the reason for executing Xījiàn,
and the crowd trembled with fear,
not daring to move.
38. Lǐ Xīliè sent his general Zhái Chónghuī to besiege Chén Prefecture with all his troops.
After a long time,
he still could not capture it.
Lǐ Chéng, knowing that the troops in Dàliáng were few and unable to control Huá Prefecture,
burned the banners and insignia granted by Xīliè
and pledged to his troops to return to the allegiance of the state.
(Lǐ Chéng's request to surrender began in the previous scroll, last year.)
On the Jiǎwǔ day,
Chéng was appointed military governor of Biàn-Huá.
Textual analysis: In the second month, it was already stated that the emperor appointed Chéng as military governor of Huá Prefecture.
It seems that at that time, it was only promised.

39. Liú Qià, military governor of Sòng-Bó, sent his cavalry and infantry commander Liú Chāng and Qū Huán, military governor of the Lǒngyòu and Yōuzhōu expeditionary camps, among others, to lead thirty thousand troops to rescue Chén Prefecture.
In the eleventh month, on the Guǐmǎo day,
they defeated Zhái Chónghuī west of the prefecture,
beheading thirty-five thousand,
and captured Chónghuī to present as a trophy.
Taking advantage of the victory, they advanced to attack Biàn Prefecture.
Lǐ Xīliè, fearing for his safety,
fled back to Cài Prefecture.
Lǐ Chéng led his troops toward Biàn Prefecture,
but upon reaching north of the city,
he was timid and did not dare to advance.
Liú Qià's troops arrived east of the city.
On the Wùwǔ day,
Tián Huáizhēn, the defending general under Lǐ Xīliè, opened the gates and let them in.
The next day,
Chéng entered
and stayed at Jùnyí.
(Jùnyí was attached to Biàn Prefecture.
Lǐ Chéng likely stayed at the county seat.
The Geographical Records: Below Yímén,
east of Xīnlǐ,
north of Jùnshuǐ,
modeled and measured,
it was named as a city.
In the first year of Hànwǔ,
Xīnlǐ was abolished and Jùnyí County was established.)
Daily disputes arose.
Meanwhile, Sūn Yè, the defending general of Zhèng Prefecture under Lǐ Xīliè, surrendered to Chéng,
and Chéng led his troops to station at Zhèng Prefecture.
An edict appointed Bǎodǐng Xuē Yuè, the Chief Clerk of the Commander-in-Chief's Office, as Prefect of Biàn Prefecture.
(The Chief Clerk of the Commander-in-Chief's Office refers to the Chief Clerk of the Sòng, Huá, and Héyáng Commander-in-Chief's Office.
Bǎodǐng County belonged to Hézhōng Prefecture.
Originally Fényīn County,
in the tenth year of the Kāiyuán era, a precious tripod was discovered,
and the name was changed.
Yuè,
pronounced gǔ yuè fān.)
Li Miǎn arrived in Cháng'ān,
wearing plain clothes to await punishment;
many critics argued that
"Li Miǎn lost the defense of Dàliáng,
(the matter of Li Miǎn losing the defense is recorded in volume 229, fourth year of the Jiànzhōng era).
Lǐ Bì spoke to the emperor, saying:
"Li Miǎn is fair, loyal, and upright,
but military command is not his strength.
When Dàliáng fell,
nearly twenty thousand soldiers abandoned their wives and children to follow him,
which is enough to show that he has won the hearts of the masses.
Moreover, Liú Qià was once under Li Miǎn's command;
when Li Miǎn arrived in Suīyáng,
(Suīyáng,
Sòng Prefecture).
he ultimately pacified Dàliáng,
which is also Li Miǎn's achievement."
The emperor then ordered Li Miǎn to be restored to his position.
Critics also said:
"Hán Huàng, hearing that the imperial carriage was outside the capital,
gathered troops and fortified Shítóu City,
(the matter is recorded in volume 229, fourth year of the Jiànzhōng era).
The emperor was suspicious of this,
and asked Lǐ Bì about it,
who replied:
"Huàng is fair, loyal, and frugal,
ever since the imperial carriage left the capital,
Huàng has continuously presented tribute.
(The matter is recorded in the previous volume).
No bandits have arisen,
all due to Huàng's efforts.
(During the Táng dynasty, the territories under the Zhèjiāng East and West Circuits
consisted of only fourteen prefectures: Rùn, Shēng, Cháng, Hú, Sū, Háng, Mù, Yuè, Míng, Tái, Wēn, Qú, Chù, and Wù).
Previously, Huàng dispatched crossbowmen from Xuān and Rùn to aid Nínglíng,
(this indicates he also governed Xuān Prefecture,
making it fifteen prefectures in total).
Huàng, seeing the turmoil in the Central Plains,
believed Your Majesty might undertake a journey like the Yǒngjiā era,
(referring to the Yǒngjiā disorder during the Jìn dynasty when Emperor Yuán crossed south).
This is the loyal and sincere concern of a subject;
how can it be considered a crime!
Huàng's nature is stern and strict,
and he does not flatter the powerful,
so he faces much slander and defamation.
I hope Your Majesty will investigate this;
I dare guarantee he has no other intentions."
The emperor said:
"Outside criticism is rampant,
memorials are as numerous as hemp,
(as numerous as hemp,
meaning they are as plentiful as hemp that can be bundled).
Lǐ Bì replied:
"I have indeed heard of this.
His son, Hán Gāo, is an Assistant Director of the Bureau of Evaluations,
and now dares not return to visit his parents,
precisely because the slander is so intense."
The emperor said:
"Even his son fears like this;
how can you, Minister, guarantee him?"
Lǐ Bì replied:
"I know Huàng's intentions
very well.
I wish to submit a memorial clarifying that he has no other intentions,
and request it be announced in the Secretariat,
so that all court officials may know."
(Court officials,
refers to the multitude of officials at court).
(Court,
pronounced zhāo;
same below).
The emperor said:
"I am about to employ you, Minister;
how can one easily guarantee another!
Be careful not to go against the crowd,
lest it implicate you as well."
Lǐ Bì withdrew,
and then submitted a memorial,
pledging with his entire clan to guarantee Huàng.
Another day,
the emperor said to Lǐ Bì:
"You actually submitted the memorial;
I have kept it for you.
Although I know you and Huàng are close old friends,
how can you not cherish yourself!"
Lǐ Bì replied:
"How could I favor old friends to the detriment of Your Majesty!
It is simply that Huàng truly has no disloyal intentions;
my submitting the memorial
is for the court,
not for myself."
The emperor said:
"How is it for the court?"
Lǐ Bì replied:
"Now the empire suffers from drought and locusts,
in Guānzhōng, a peck of rice costs a thousand coins,
granaries are depleted,
yet Jiāngdōng has a bountiful harvest.
I hope Your Majesty will soon issue my memorial
to dispel the doubts of the court officials,
and personally instruct Hán Gāo to return for a visit,
(return for a visit,
means returning to visit his parents).
and quickly transport grain supplies;
is this not for the court!"
The emperor said:
"Good!
I understand deeply."
He immediately issued Lǐ Bì's memorial,
ordered Hán Gāo to request leave to return for a visit,
personally bestowed upon him crimson official robes,
and instructed him, saying:
"There have been slanders against your father recently,
but I now know the truth,
and am relieved, no longer believing them."
He further said:
"Guānzhōng lacks grain;
go back and tell your father,
(tell, pronounced yù).
Gāo arrived in Rùn Prefecture,
Huàng was moved and overjoyed, shedding tears,
and that very day,
personally supervised the shipment of a million hu of rice from the waterfront,
allowing Gāo to stay only five days before returning to court.
Gāo bid farewell to his mother,
his weeping could be heard outside;
Huàng was angry,
summoned him out,
beat him,
personally escorted him to the riverbank,
and sent him off braving wind and waves.
Soon after, Chén Shǎoyóu heard that Huàng had presented rice,
and also presented two hundred thousand hu.
(Chén Shǎoyóu was then stationed in Huáinán).
The emperor said:
"Hán Huàng can even influence Chén Shǎoyóu to present rice!"
Lǐ Bì replied:
"Not only Shǎoyóu,
the various circuits will compete to present tribute!"
The Minister of Personnel and concurrent Chief Minister, Xiāo Fù, returned from his mission in Jiāng-Huái,
(Xiāo Fù's mission is recorded in volume 229, first year of the Xīngyuán era, fourth month).
(returned,
pronounced huán,
or as the character reads).
After Li Miǎn and others withdrew,
Xiāo Fù alone remained,
and said to the emperor:
"Chén Shǎoyóu, holding both military and civil offices,
was the first to betray his duty as a subject,
while Wéi Gāo, a low-ranking staff officer,
alone upheld loyalty and righteousness,
(Wéi Gāo's matter is recorded in volume 228, fourth year of the Jiànzhōng era).
The emperor agreed.
Soon, he sent the palace envoy Mǎ Qīnxù to greet Liú Cóngyī,
whispered in his ear, and left.
The various ministers returned to their offices.
(The various ministers sat in the Hall of Government Affairs within the Department of State Affairs;
after withdrawing,
each resided in their respective offices).
Liú Cóngyī said to Xiāo Fù:
"Qīnxù conveyed the imperial decree,
ordering me to discuss with you, Minister, the matter mentioned this morning,
and then memorialize for implementation;
(morning,
pronounced zhāo;
same below for 'this morning').
May I ask what matter this is?"
Xiāo Fù said:
"In the times of Táng and Yú, promotions and demotions
were agreed upon by all regional chiefs.
(The matter is recorded in the Canon of Yáo and Canon of Shùn).
They were shared with the officials.
(Quoting the words of the Royal Regulations).
If not, then they were dismissed.
Since we hold the position of Chief Minister,
how can we not discuss court government affairs together, yet alone conceal this matter!
This is the greatest flaw of the present time.
This morning, the sovereign already mentioned this,
and I have already personally stated it is unacceptable;
I did not expect the imperial intention remains thus.
I do not mind memorializing with you, Minister, to implement it,
but I fear it may gradually become customary,
so I dared not inform you."
In the end, he did not tell Liú Cóngyī.
Liú Cóngyī memorialized this,
and the emperor became even more displeased.
Xiāo Fù then submitted a memorial resigning his position.
On the yǐchǒu day,
he was demoted to Left Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent.
Liú Qià captured Biàn Prefecture,
and obtained Lǐ Xīliè's court diary,
which stated:
"On such-and-such month and day,
Chén Shǎoyóu submitted a memorial pledging allegiance."
(The history thoroughly recounts the matter of Chén Shǎoyóu betraying his duty as a subject).
Chén Shǎoyóu fell ill,
and in the twelfth month,
on the yǐhài day,
he died.
He was posthumously awarded Grand Commandant,
and funeral and sacrificial rites were conducted according to regular protocol.
The general of Huáinán, Wáng Sháo, wanted to make himself the military governor,
ordering the officers and soldiers to recommend him to take charge of military affairs,
and moreover intended to carry out large-scale plundering.
Hán Huàng sent an envoy to tell him:
"If you dare to cause rebellion,
I will immediately lead the entire army across the river to execute you!"
Sháo and the others, in fear, stopped.
The emperor, hearing of this, was pleased,
and said to Lǐ Mì:
"Huàng not only pacified Jiāngdōng,
but also pacified Huáinán.
Truly, he is a man of great ministerial caliber.
You, sir, can indeed be said to know men!"
On the Gēngchén day,
Huàng was additionally appointed as Píngzhāngshì and Jiānghuái Zhuǎnyùnshǐ.
Huàng transported grain and silk from Jiāng and Huái into the tribute storehouses,
referring to the court's storehouses for receiving tribute and storing wealth.
The court relied on this,
and envoys with rewards and inquiries followed one after another;
the favor and treatment he received began to deepen.
In this year, locusts spread far and wide,
leaving no grass or trees untouched,
only not eating rice.
There was a great famine,
and corpses on the roads could be seen one after another.
The Odes say: "When walking, there are dead men;
still, perhaps bury them."
Jìn,
pronounced qú lìn fān,
means to bury a corpse;
also, those who starve to death are called jìn.
"Corpses on the roads could be seen one after another"
originally comes from a saying in the Zuǒzhuàn.
The first year of Zhēnyuán
(yǐchǒu, 785)
1 In spring,
the first month,

19. When Lǐ Mì first assumed office,
(this refers to his entry into the Administrative Affairs Hall to assume his duties).
On the Rényín day,
he, along with Lǐ Shèng, Mǎ Suì, and Liǔ Hún, entered for an audience.
The Emperor said to Lǐ Mì:
"You, in the past at Língwǔ,
should already have been appointed to this official position,
but you yourself declined and yielded.
(For details, see Volume 219, the first year of the Zhìdé era of Emperor Sùzōng).
I wish to make an agreement with you.
(This is also one instance revealing the Emperor's suspicion and jealousy).
For those who have shown you kindness, I shall repay them on your behalf."
Lǐ Mì replied:
"Your subject has always followed the Daoist teachings,
and does not bear grudges against others.
Lǐ Fǔguó and Yuán Zài were both those who harmed me,
but now they have perished by themselves.
As for those I have long been on good terms with and those who have shown me kindness,
most have already achieved prominence and success,
or many have passed away or declined,
so there is no one for your subject to repay."
The Emperor said:
"Even so,
for those who have shown even small kindnesses,
you should still repay them."
Lǐ Mì replied:
"Today, your subject also wishes to make an agreement with Your Majesty,
may I?"
The Emperor said:
"Why not!"
Lǐ Mì said:
"I wish that Your Majesty would not harm meritorious officials.
Your subject has received great kindness from Your Majesty,
and thus has no personal concerns.
Lǐ Shèng and Mǎ Suì have rendered great service to the state.
I have heard there are those who slander them.
Although Your Majesty certainly will not listen,
yet today, in the presence of these two men, I speak of this,
wishing that they would not harbor doubts themselves.
If by any chance Your Majesty were to harm them,
then the soldiers of the imperial guards,
and the ministers of the regional commands,
would all be filled with indignation and resentment, becoming restless and disloyal,
and I fear that turmoil within and without the court would arise again before long!
If a subject is fortunate enough to receive the ruler's affection and trust, that is already happiness;
what does an official position matter!
In the days when I was at Língwǔ,
I did not hold any official position,
yet generals and ministers all accepted my guidance and plans;
Your Majesty appointed Lǐ Huáiguāng as Grand Commandant, yet Huáiguāng became even more fearful,
and consequently rebelled.
These are all things Your Majesty has personally witnessed.
Now, Shèng and Suì already have ample wealth and honor.
If Your Majesty treats them with openness and sincerity,
allowing them to secure themselves without worries,
when the state has matters, they go forth to join campaigns;
when there are no matters, they attend court audiences,
what joy could compare to this!
Therefore, I wish that Your Majesty would not, because of these two ministers' great achievements, become suspicious of them,
and that these two ministers would not, because of their high positions, doubt themselves.
Then the world will forever be without troubles."
The Emperor said:
"When I first heard your words,
I was startled and did not understand what you meant.
But after listening to your analysis,
I realize this is the paramount strategy for the state!
I shall carefully inscribe it on my sash,
and these two great ministers should also jointly uphold it."
Lǐ Shèng and Mǎ Suì both stood up,
weeping and expressing gratitude.
The Emperor then said to Lǐ Mì:
"From now on, all matters concerning military affairs and grain reserves,
you shall be in charge;
civil appointments and rites shall be entrusted to Zhāng Yánshǎng;
criminal law shall be entrusted to Liǔ Hún."
Lǐ Mì said:
"That will not do.
Your Majesty, not considering me incompetent,
has made me serve as Chancellor, bearing the responsibility.
The duties of the Chancellor
cannot be divided.
It is not like the case of the Supervising Secretaries, who review civil and military appointments.
(The Ministry of Personnel and the Ministry of War are in charge of civil and military selections.
All memorials and proposals are reviewed by the Chancellery.
When various offices submit memorials and documents,
after the Palace Attendant-in-Chief has examined them,
the Supervising Secretaries read them aloud,
and if there are violations or errors, they correct and reject them.
Under the Táng system: there are six Secretariat Drafters,
who assist the Chancellor in reviewing cases,
and jointly sign before submission.
According to the Six Codes: six Secretariat Drafters,
each oversees one of the six bureaus.
All matters under heaven are jointly deliberated and managed.
If each has their own separate charge,
then they become mere departmental officials,
not Chancellors.)"
The Emperor laughed and said:
"I misspoke just now,
what you say is correct."
Lǐ Mì requested the reinstatement of the reduced prefectural and county officials.
In this year, during the intercalary month,
following Zhāng Yánshǎng's advice,
there was a major reduction of prefectural and county officials.
("Officials are appointed for the people.
Now the population has decreased by two-thirds compared to peaceful times,
yet the number of officials has increased instead.
Can this be right?")
Lǐ Mì replied:
"Although the population has decreased,
the affairs of government are more than ten times those of peaceful times.
How can the number of officials not increase!
Moreover, those reduced all had substantive duties, while the redundant officials without duties were not reduced.
This is why it was inappropriate.
Since the Zhìdé era, extra officials have been appointed,
amounting to one-third of the regular officials.
If they are allowed to calculate their tenure to receive seniority benefits before being dismissed,
and are additionally granted two selections to be appointed as regular officials of the same category.
(The character '停' [dismiss]
should be read as a separate phrase.
It means calculating their seniority based on their days in office,
and then dismissing them according to the reduced positions.
Furthermore, by adding two selections, civil and military,
appointing them as regular officials,
of the same category as their original positions.
Then not only will they not resent it,
but they will even be pleased.")
He also requested that princes who have not yet left the palace not be assigned staff officials for their princely establishments.
(These are the redundant officials without duties that Lǐ Mì mentioned were not reduced,
so he requested they be reduced and not appointed.)
On the Yǐmǎo day,
an edict was issued that all previously reduced officials
be restored to their former positions.

Shūmíng's son, Lǐ Shēng,

Establish reward regulations,
informants receive rewards according to the regulations, and punish those who conceal or embezzle.
“Your strategy is very far-sighted,

He replied:

The Emperor said:
“Excellent!”
He appointed the Vice Director of the Bureau of Revenue Yuán Yǒuzhí as the Commissioner for Investigating the Two-Tax Copper Cash and Silk in Hénán, Jiāng, and Huáinán.
Initially,
after Hé and Lǒng were lost to Tǔbō,
in the early years of Emperor Dàizōng,
Hé and Lǒng fell and were lost.
Tǔ,
follows the entering tone of tūn.
Those from Ānxī and Běitíng presenting affairs, as well as envoys from the Western Regions in Cháng’ān,
their return routes were cut off,
and their people and horses all relied on the Court of State Ceremonial for provisions.
The Court of State Ceremonial entrusted the prefectures and counties to supply them,
receiving payment from the Bureau of Revenue.
The Bureau of Revenue did not make payments on time,
and the markets of Cháng’ān could not bear the hardship.
Lǐ Mì learned that among the Hú guests who had stayed in Cháng’ān for a long time,
some for over forty years,
all had wives and children,
purchased fields and homes,
engaged in lending to obtain profits,
jǔ means
lending to obtain double or more interest.
zhì means
using goods as collateral for money,
calculating monthly interest.
He ordered an investigation to identify Hú guests who owned fields and homes and stop their provisions.
In total, four thousand people were found,
and he was about to stop their provisions.
The Hú guests all went to the government office to complain,
government office,
meaning the office of the chief minister.
“This has always been the fault of the chief ministers.

be granted official positions,
