Thereupon, not a single Hú guest was willing to return.
Mì assigned them all to the two Shéncè armies.
Princes and envoys became scattered cavalry officers or yāyá,
scattered,
read as sǎndǎn.
The imperial guards grew stronger.
The Court of State Ceremonial now provided for only a little over ten Hú guests,
saving five hundred thousand strings of cash annually from the Bureau of Revenue;
the market people were all pleased.
They were relieved from supplying provisions,
hence pleased.
The Emperor again asked Mì about the strategy to restore the fǔbīng system.
He replied:
“This year, one hundred seventy thousand troops were levied from Guāndōng to garrison Jīngxī.
Calculating their annual grain consumption amounts to two million four hundred thousand hú.
Currently, one dǒu of grain costs one hundred fifty cash,
amounting to three million six hundred thousand strings of cash.
The state has recently suffered famine and turmoil,
and financial resources are insufficient.
Even if we had the money,
there is no grain to purchase,
so there is no leisure to discuss restoring the fǔbīng system.”
The Emperor said:
“Then what should we do?
Quickly reduce the garrison troops and send them back,
how about that?”
He replied:
“If Your Majesty
adopts my words,
you can avoid reducing garrison troops,
avoid disturbing the common people,
have sufficient food supplies,
see grain and wheat prices drop daily,
and also accomplish the fǔbīng system.”
The Emperor said:
“If it can be like this,
why not adopt it!”
He replied:
“This must be done urgently.
After ten days, it will be too late.
Now Tǔbō has long resided between Yuán and Huì,
using oxen to transport grain.
Once the grain is exhausted,
the oxen will be of no use.
I request that inferior silk from the Left Treasury be dyed into colored patterned silk,
and through Dǎngxiàng, trade for them,
no more than two or three bolts per ox.
Calculating one hundred eighty thousand bolts,
we can obtain over sixty thousand oxen.
Also order the various smelters to cast farming tools,
purchase wheat seeds,
distribute them to the frontier military garrisons,
recruit garrison soldiers,
to cultivate wasteland and plant them,
agreeing to repay double the seeds next year after the wheat ripens,
and for the remainder, increase the price by one-fifth based on the market price,
with the government purchasing it.
Next spring, planting millet will follow the same method.
Guānzhōng soil is fertile and has long been fallow,
so the harvest will surely be abundant.
The garrison soldiers will gain profits,
and cultivators will gradually increase.
The resident population in the border areas is very small.
Soldiers monthly eat government grain,
and if grain and wheat have no outlet for sale,
their price will surely drop.
Though called increasing the price,
it will actually be much lower than this year’s prices.”
The Emperor said:
“Excellent!”
He immediately ordered it implemented.
Li Mì further stated:
"There are many vacancies among officials in the border regions.
I propose recruiting people who contribute grain to fill these positions,
which could suffice for this year's grain supply."
The Emperor also agreed to this.
He then asked:
"You mentioned that the militia system could also be restored,
how would that work?"
Li Mì replied:
"If garrison soldiers become wealthy through military farming,
they will settle on that land,
no longer thinking of returning home.
According to the old system,
garrison soldiers were replaced every three years.
When their term was nearing completion,
an order would be issued: those willing to stay
would be granted the land they had opened up as their permanent property.
If family members wished to join them,
their native prefecture would issue a long-term pass and provide provisions along the journey to send them.
For the families of garrison soldiers
being sent to the border fortresses,
their native prefecture would issue a long-term pass,
and the commanderies and counties they passed through would provide provisions,
until they reached the garrison post.
A report would be transferred to their home circuit.
Even the commanders of Héshuò would be spared the trouble of replacements,
and would be pleased to hear of this.
After no more than a few rotations,
the garrison soldiers
would become local inhabitants,
and then they could all be managed according to the militia system laws.
'Lǐ' here means
'to govern'.
The Emperor was pleased and said:
"If this is done,
there will be no more troubles in the empire."
The strategy for restoring the militia system proposed by Li Mì
should have been achieved gradually over time.
For the Emperor to hastily claim there would be no more troubles in the empire
shows he was merely pleased that the words sounded good, without realizing the matter could not be accomplished overnight.
"Not yet.
I can cause Tǔbō to become exhausted without using the central empire's troops."
The Emperor said:
"What is the plan?"
He replied:
"I dare not speak of it yet.
Wait until the wheat and grain harvest shows results,
then it can be discussed."
The Emperor pressed him further,
but he did not answer.
Li Mì's intention was to ally with Huíhé, Dàshí, and Yúnnán to jointly scheme against Tǔbō,
forcing Tǔbō to prepare on many fronts;
knowing the Emperor had long harbored hatred for Huíhé,
he feared the Emperor would be displeased upon hearing it,
and that even the military farming proposal would not be implemented,
hence he refused to speak.
Soon after, garrison soldiers responded to the recruitment,
with five or six out of ten willing to farm the military fields.
Since Li Mì became chancellor,
observing how he handled the empire's affairs,
there had been none like him since Yáo Chóng.
The historian-official stated that he moved in and out of the imperial palace,
served four sovereigns,
was often resented by powerful and favored officials,
yet always escaped by his wits.
He was fond of grand纵横家-style rhetoric,
yet often offered forthright remonstrance,
able to awaken and shift the ruler's mind.
However, he often upheld Huáng-Lǎo and鬼神 doctrines,
hence he was ridiculed by others.
I say that Li Mì escaping by his wits
is indeed as the historian-official said.
Yet his grand纵横家-style rhetoric,
upholding Huáng-Lǎo and鬼神 doctrines,
was also wisdom.
Li Mì navigated between Emperor Sùzōng and Emperor Dàizōng, father and son;
his discussions on the形势 of restoration,
there was no word that did not prove effective.
And between Zhāng and Lǐ,
the means by which he protected and assisted Emperor Dàizōng,
there was no word that was not acted upon.
As for Yuán Zǎi's slander and resentment,
he ultimately managed to save himself,
which can be called wisdom.
When it came to his discussions with Emperor Dézōng on the empire's affairs,
it was as clear as pointing at his palm.
That with Emperor Sùzōng and Emperor Dàizōng trusting him yet he refused to become chancellor,
and with Emperor Dézōng's suspicious and jealous nature yet he calmly accepted the position,
this too was wisdom.
Alas!
To serve and gain the ruler's favor,
with remonstrance implemented and words heeded,
then attaining the position of chief minister is fitting.
Having served three reigns,
keeping himself pure and avoiding harm,
as his physical strength began to decline,
only then did he enter the administration hall to join ranks with the newly honored.
The so-called strategies for statecraft,
which he had been unable to express fully for Emperor Sùzōng and Emperor Dàizōng,
he now fully expressed for Emperor Dézōng.
Could it be that Emperor Dézōng's magnanimity surpassed that of his grandfather and father?
Li Mì likely measured the situation before entering.
That Emperor Dézōng, suspicious, jealous, harsh, and mean,
even towards Xiāo and Jiāng,
accused them of belittling him and flaunting their integrity;
towards those with merit like Lǐ and Mǎ,
was jealous and placed them in idle positions;
yet Li Mì spoke freely and without fear.
In his heart, he regarded Li Mì as an old minister from his grandfather's time,
of unfathomable wisdom and strategy,
who greatly aided the mid-dynasty restoration,
and his respect and trust in him had been long-standing.
The reason Li Mì dared to assume the chancellorship
was that his self-assessment was also careful.
Was this not wisdom!
His upholding of Huáng-Lǎo and鬼神 doctrines
was the same old stratagem of Zhāng Liáng wishing to follow Chìsōngzǐ.
Only Zhāng Liáng did so after achieving merit,
while Li Mì was sincerely devoted to it from beginning to end.

3 Initially,
the Vice Minister of War and Tongpingzhangshi Liǔ Hún and Zhāng Yánshǎng both served as chancellors.
Liǔ Hún often disagreed in discussions,
so Zhāng Yánshǎng sent a close associate to tell him:

then your high position can be long-lasting."
Liǔ Hún said:

Liǔ Hún's head can be cut off,

From then on, they became enemies.
The Emperor appreciated refined elegance and含蓄,
but Liǔ Hún was blunt, straightforward, and frivolously informal,
lacking dignified bearing,
and often used vulgar language in the Emperor's presence.
The Emperor was displeased
and wanted to demote him to Chief Administrator of a princely establishment.
Li Mì said:
"Liǔ Hún is narrow-minded and straightforward, but has no other faults.

a dismissed chancellor does not become a Chief Administrator."

Jiǔyù Zhì: Liángyuán
is sixty lǐ southwest of Jīngzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Suí divided Āndìng and Chúngū to establish Liángyuán county,
thirty lǐ southwest there is a Liángyuán plain,
hence the name.
11. Yúnnán King Yì Móuxún wished to submit to the imperial court,
but did not dare to send an envoy himself.
First, he dispatched the Eastern Mán ghost-lords Piào Páng, Jū Mèngchōng, and Jū Wūxīng to have an audience.
In the fifth month,
on the yǐmǎo day,
they were feasted at the Líndé Hall,
bestowed with generous gifts,
enfeoffed as kings, given seals, and sent back.
Piào Páng was enfeoffed as the King of Héyì,
Jū Mèngchōng as the King of Huáihuà,
and Jū Wūxīng as the King of Shùnzhèng.
12. On the xīnwèi day,
Tàizǐ Bīnkè Wú Còu was appointed as the Fújiàn Observant Commissioner,
and Wú Shēn was demoted to Prefect of Fúzhōu.
13. More than thirty thousand Tibetan cavalry invaded the prefectures of Jīng, Bīn, Níng, Qìng, Fū, and others.
Previously,
the Tibetans often invaded in autumn and winter,
and retreated in spring due to widespread illness and epidemics.
By this time,
having captured Tang people,
they held their wives and children as hostages,
sent their generals to lead them,
and invaded in the height of summer;
the various prefectures all defended their walled cities,
none daring to engage in battle.
The Tibetans captured and plundered tens of thousands of people and livestock before leaving.
14. Yáng Chéng of Xiàxiàn County was renowned for his learning and conduct,
living in seclusion north of Liǔgǔ.
Lǐ Mì recommended him;
in the sixth month,
he was summoned and appointed as Remonstrance Advisor.
15. Hán Yóuhuái, because the Tibetans had breached the frontier,
had personally garrisoned Níngzhōu;
falling ill,
he requested a replacement to return.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the gēngxū day,
Hún Jiān was additionally appointed Deputy Commander-in-Chief of Bīnníng,
with Zuǒ Jīnyú General Zhāng Xiànfǔ appointed as Military Commissioner of Bīnníng,
and Chénxǔ Army Commander Hán Quányì appointed as Campaign Commissioner of Chángwǔ Fortress.
Before Xiànfǔ arrived,
on the rénzǐ night,
Yóuhuái, without informing the troops,
lightly rode back to court.
Garrison soldier Péi Mǎn and others, fearing Xiànfǔ's strictness,
taking advantage of the absence of a commander,
on the guǐchǒu day,
led their followers in rebellion,
saying:
"If Lord Zhāng does not come from our own army,
we will certainly resist him."
This meant that Zhāng Xiànfǔ was originally not from the Shuòfāng Army.
They surrounded the residence of the Army Supervisor Yáng Míngyì,
and had him petition to appoint Fàn Xīcháo as Military Commissioner.
The Capital Military Inspector Yáng Cháoshèng, having fled the turmoil and left the city,
upon hearing this,
re-entered,
saying:
"The request greatly accords with my own heart,
I have come to congratulate you!"
The rebellious soldiers gradually calmed.
Cháoshèng secretly plotted with the various generals,
at dawn marshaled troops,
summoned the rebellious soldiers and said:
"The request cannot be granted,
Lord Zhāng has already arrived at Bīnzhōu.
You who rebelled deserve death,
but not all can be killed.
You should yourselves identify those who led and instigated."
Thereupon, over two hundred were beheaded,
and the multitude welcomed Xiànfǔ.
The Emperor, hearing that the army wished to have Fàn Xīcháo,
intended to appoint him.
Xīcháo declined, saying:
"I came fearing the disaster of Yóuhuái.
Now to go and replace him [Xiànfǔ]
is not the way to guard against covetous designs
and pacify unrest."
The Emperor praised him,
promoted him to Prefect of Níngzhōu,
to serve as deputy to Xiànfǔ.
Yóuhuái arrived at the capital,
and was appointed Commander of the Right Lóngwǔ Guard.
16. Zhènwǔ Military Commissioner Táng Cháochén did not maintain strict patrols and sentries.
On the jǐwèi day,
the Xī and Shìwéi tribes invaded Zhènwǔ.
Lǐ Yánshòu said: The Shìwéi,
it seems those of the Qìdān in the south are the Qìdān,
those in the north are the Shìwéi.
Sòng Qí said: The Shìwéi,
are a separate branch of the Qìdān,
on the northern frontier of the Dōnghú,
likely descendants of the Dīnglíng.
Their land occupies the area north of Huánglóng,
bordering the Náoyuè River,
directly seven thousand lǐ northeast of Cháng'ān.
To the east are the Hēishuǐ and Mòhé,
to the west the Tūjué,
to the south the Qìdān,
to the north bordering the sea.
They plundered a great number of people and livestock and left.
At that time, the Uighur multitude escorting the princess was at Zhènwǔ.
Cháochén dispatched seven hundred cavalry along with several hundred Uighur cavalry to pursue them,
and the Uighur envoy was killed by the Xī and Shìwéi.
17. In the ninth month,
on the gēngshēn day,
the Tibetan Shàngzhì
Dǒng Xīng invaded Níngzhōu.
Zhāng Xiànfǔ repelled him;
the Tibetans turned to plunder Fū and Fāng before leaving.
18. Yuán Yǒuzhí audited the various circuits' extra-regular tax goods,
the matter first appearing in the previous year's scroll.
Jù,
pronounced gōu in ancient reading.
It then became a fixed regulation,
annually delivering over a million strings of cash and hu measures beyond the regular taxes,
which the people could not bear.
Many circuits personally appealed to the Emperor.
The Emperor realized the situation,
and issued an edict:
"What has already been collected this year and is in official hands shall be delivered to the capital;
what has not yet been collected shall all be given to the people.
From next year onward,
it is all exempted."
Thereupon, the people of the southeast returned to their peaceful occupations.
19. The Uighur Hé Gǔduōlù Kèhán, having obtained the Tang's consent to the marriage,
was greatly pleased.
He dispatched his younger sister, Princess Gǔduōlù Píjiā, along with the wives of ministers, the State Minister, the Dié Dudū,
and over a thousand others below them to welcome the Kèdūn.
Their words and courtesies were very respectful,
saying:
"Formerly we were brothers,
now I am your son-in-law,
a half-son.
If the Tibetans cause trouble,
the son shall eliminate it for the father!"
Thereupon, they reviled and insulted the Tibetan envoy to sever relations.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the wùzǐ day,
the Uighurs arrived at Cháng'ān.
The Kèhán further submitted a memorial requesting to change the name from Huíhé to Huíhú;
it was granted.
Textual analysis notes:
"The Old History Uighur Biography states:
'In the fourth year of Yuánhé,
Kèhán Lǐjiā sent an envoy requesting to change to Huíhú,
taking the meaning of wheeling and turning as swift and nimble as a falcon (hú).'"
Cuī Xuàn's Supplementary Essential Regulations states:
"In the seventh month of the fifth year of Zhēnyuán,
when the princess reached the headquarters tent,
the Uighur envoy Lǐ Yìjìn requested to change the character 'hé'
to 'hú.'"
This agrees with the Comprehensive Annals.
The Family Biography of the Marquis of Yè states:
"In the seventh month of the fourth year,
the Kèhán submitted a memorial requesting to change the character 'hé'
to 'hú,'"
agreeing with Lǐ Fán's Records of the Northern Wilderness Chieftains and the New History Uighur Biography.
Considering that Lǐ Mì died in the spring of the following year,
if the change occurred in the seventh month of the following year,
the Family Biography should not mention it.
Now we follow the Family Biography, the Records of the Chieftains, and the New History.
The Tǔbō (Tibetans) dispatched an army of one hundred thousand intending to invade Xīchuān (Western Sichuan),
and also called for troops from Yúnnán (Nanzhao).
Although Yúnnán had internally submitted to the Táng,
externally it did not dare to rebel against Tǔbō.
It also dispatched tens of thousands of troops to station north of the Lú River.
North of Lú,
means north of the Lú River.
The Lú River,
is the one that Zhūgě Liàng crossed in the fifth month.
(Wéi Gāo) then wrote a letter to the King of Yúnnán,
recounting the sincerity of his rebellion against Tǔbō and submission to (Táng) civilization,
stored it in a silver case,
and had the Dōngmán (Eastern Barbarians) forward it to Tǔbō.
Tǔbō then began to suspect Yúnnán,
and dispatched twenty thousand troops to station at Huìchuān.
Huìchuān,
was originally Qiōngdū County.
In the second year of the Shàngyuán era of Emperor Gāozōng, the county seat was moved to Huìchuān,
and consequently the name was changed.
New Annals: Huìchuān County belonged to Xīzhōu.
There was the Lújīn Pass,
located thirty *lǐ* southeast of Huìchuān.
Yúnnán was angered,
and led its troops back to its own country.
From then on, Yúnnán and Tǔbō greatly suspected and obstructed each other,
and Yúnnán's resolve to submit to the Táng grew firmer.
Tǔbō, having lost Yúnnán's assistance,
saw its military strength begin to weaken.
However, Tǔbō had already launched the invasion,
so it divided its forces: forty thousand attacked Liǎnglín and Piàopáng,
thirty thousand attacked the Dōngmán,
and seven thousand raided the Qīngxī Pass.
The Qīngxī Pass,
was within the boundaries of Xīzhōu.
From the pass southward, it was seven hundred and twenty *lǐ* to Xīzhōu.
Hóngyuán Annals: The Qīngxī Pass,
was on the southwestern border of Lízhōu.
New Annals: Lízhōu had eleven strategic cities including Tóngshān.
(Táng forces) defeated Tǔbō outside the Qīngxī Pass.
21 On the Gēngzǐ day,
(the emperor) issued the edict appointing Princess Xián'ān,
and added to the title of the Huíhé (Uyghur) Khagan
"Longevity and Celestial Kinship Khagan".
In the eleventh month,
Guān Bō, the Minister of Justice, was appointed as the envoy to escort Princess Xián'ān and confer the edict upon the Huíhé Khagan.
From this point onward,
the *Comprehensive Mirror* consistently follows the previous histories in writing
"Huíhé".
22 Tǔbō, ashamed of the previous defeat,
(referring to the defeat outside the Qīngxī Pass mentioned above),
attacked the Dōngmán with ten thousand troops;
Wéi Gāo ordered Wéi Jìn to defend the strategic city of Yàochōng,
and oversee the various armies to resist them.
Liú Cháocǎi, the Military Commissioner of Xīzhōu, went out from the pass and fought consecutive battles,
from the Yǐmǎo day to the Guǐhài day,
and inflicted a major defeat on them.
23 Lǐ Mì spoke to the Emperor, saying:
"The water transport from Jiāngnán and Huáidōng
takes Yǒngqiáo as its throat,
which lies within Xúzhōu,
bordering Lǐ Nà's territory.
Xúzhōu and the area under Lǐ Nà's patrol are neighboring territories.
Gāo Míngyìng succeeded in controlling Xúzhōu,
beginning in the first year of the Xīngyuán era, in the 231st scroll.
He is young,
(the character) 'shào' is pronounced as 'zhào'.
If he secretly seizes Xúzhōu,
then we will lose Jiāngnán and Huáidōng,
from where will the state's resources then come!
I request to transfer Zhāng Jiànfēng, the Regional Commander of Shòu, Lú, and Háo, to garrison Xúzhōu,
and carve out Háo and Sì to place under his command;
then return Lú and Shòu to Huáinán,
thus Zīqīng (i.e., Lǐ Nà) will be fearful and the transport route will remain constantly open,
and Jiāngnán and Huáidōng will be secure.
Now, while Míngyìng is young and foolish and can be replaced,
it is appropriate to summon him to be a General of the Imperial Guards.
If by chance someone else obtains it,
then it cannot be controlled again."
The Emperor followed this advice.
He appointed Jiànfēng as Military Governor of Xú, Sì, and Háo.
Jiànfēng governed with leniency and generosity, yet maintained discipline,
he did not pardon people based on the law.
For those who broke the law,
there was punishment without pardon.
24 Chéng Rìhuá, the Military Governor of Hénghǎi, died.
His son, Chéng Huáizhí, assumed the position of Acting Military Governor on his own authority.
25 Tǔbō repeatedly sent people to entice and coerce Yúnnán.
1 In spring,
the second month,
on the Dīnghài day,
Wéi Gāo sent a letter to Yì Móuxún,
stating:
"The Huíhé have repeatedly requested to assist the Son of Heaven in jointly destroying Tǔbō.
If Your Majesty does not settle on a plan early,
and one day the Huíhé take the initiative,
then Your Majesty's accumulated merits and reputation over generations will be vainly discarded.
Moreover, Yúnnán has long been humiliated and oppressed by Tǔbō.
If you do not take this opportunity now to rely on the power of the great state to repay grievances and wipe out shame,
you will regret it too late."
2 On the Wùxū day,
Chéng Huáizhí, the Acting Military Governor of Hénghǎi, was appointed as the Surveillance Commissioner of Cāngzhōu.
Huáizhí requested to separate Gāogāo and Jǐngchéng to form Jǐngzhōu.
Jǐngchéng County,
originally belonged to Cāngzhōu.
In the fourth year of the Wǔdé era, it belonged to Yíngzhōu.
In the first year of the Zhēnguān era, it belonged to Cāngzhōu.
In the seventh year of the Dàlì era, it belonged to Yíngzhōu.
Hénghǎi probably, following Zhū Tāo's defeat,
regained possession of it,
but it later soon belonged to Yíngzhōu again.
Gāogāo,
was an ancient Hàn county.
It was abolished during the Wèi and Jìn dynasties.
The Suí established Gāogāo County on the territory of the Hàn Gé County.
During the Táng, it belonged to Cāngzhōu.
The Emperor was pleased and said:
"There has been no such thing for thirty years!"
He then appointed the Vice Director Xuán Shēn as the Prefect of Jǐngzhōu.
3 Lǐ Mì, Vice Director of the Secretariat and Joint Manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery, repeatedly begged to have another chief minister appointed.
The Emperor wished to use Bān Hóng, the Vice Minister of Revenue.
Lǐ Mì said that although Hóng was upright and capable, his nature was often rigid and inflexible.
He then recommended Dòu Shēn as intelligent and capable,
who could concurrently handle the Finance Commission and Salt and Iron Monopoly;
and Dǒng Jìn as upright and principled,
who could serve in the Chancellery.
The Emperor considered them both unsuitable.
Shēn,
was the great-great-grandson of Dòu Dàn.
Dòu Dàn,
was the one who during the Wǔdé era advised Prince Qí, Yuánjí, to abandon Bìngzhōu.
Jìn was the Minister of Ceremonies.
At this time, Lǐ Mì's illness became severe,
and he again recommended these two men.
On the Gēngzǐ day,
Dǒng Jìn was appointed Vice Director of the Chancellery,
and Dòu Shēn was appointed Vice Director of the Secretariat concurrently as Commissioner of Finance and Transport,
both as Joint Managers of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery.
Bān Hóng was appointed as a Department Head,
remaining as before the Vice Commissioner of Finance and Transport.
Shēn was a person of resolute determination, harsh and severe,
lacking scholarly learning,
and full of cunning schemes.
Every time matters were reported to the throne,
after the other chief ministers left,
Shēn alone remained behind,
using the pretext of reporting on finance commission affairs,
but in reality monopolizing major governance,
extensively placing relatives and partisans in key positions,
using them as his eyes and ears;
Dǒng Jìn merely filled the post.
However, Jìn was a person of great caution,
what he said before the Emperor was never leaked to others.
His sons or younger brothers sometimes asked him,
Jìn said:
"If you wish to know whether a chief minister is capable or not,
look at the safety or danger of the realm.
As for the plans and discussions made before the Emperor,
they are not worth speaking of."
*Examination of Discrepancies* says: Hán Yù, in writing Jìn's biography, said:
"During the entire five years he held the chief minister's position,
what he reported before the Emperor
were all the ways of the Two Emperors and Three Kings;
from the Qín and Hàn dynasties onward, he never spoke of them.
Upon returning,
he never spoke to others about what he had said before the Emperor.
When sons or younger brothers privately inquired,
he said: 'The duty of a chief minister
is tied to the safety and danger of the realm.
The ability or inability of a chief minister can be seen.
If you wish to know whether a chief minister is capable or not,
looking at it this way is permissible.
As for all the plans and discussions made before the Emperor,
they are not worth speaking of.'
Therefore, the details of these matters ultimately were not heard."
Hán Yù, in writing the biography,
must extol the good and conceal the bad.
The account of his time as chief minister ends here,
from which his passive silence and merely filling the post can be known.
However, his great caution is also worthy of praise.
Now, the biography is briefly excerpted.
In the third month,
on the Jiǎchén day,
Lǐ Mì passed away.
Lǐ Mì had strategic acumen but was fond of discussing the mystical and supernatural,
and thus was looked down upon by his contemporaries.
Examination of Discrepancies states: Guó Shǐ Bǔ says:
"When Lǐ Mì served as chancellor,
he took it upon himself to engage in empty and fantastical talk.
He once told his guests to instruct his family to quickly sweep and clean,
saying that Hóngyá Xiānshēng would come to stay that night.
Someone sent him a jar of fine wine,
and when a guest arrived,
he said:
'Mágū has sent wine,
let us drink together.'
Before they finished drinking,
the gatekeeper said:
'A certain vice minister has come to retrieve the jar.'
Lǐ Mì ordered it to be returned,
showing no sign of shame."
The Old Biography of Lǐ Mì says:
"When Emperor Dézōng first ascended the throne,
he particularly despised shamans and those who spoke of strange tales.
By the end of the Jiànzhōng era,
with internal rebellions and foreign invasions,
Sāng Dàomào had proposed moving the capital to Fèngtiān.
The emperor began to pay attention to auspicious and inauspicious days,
and having heard that Lǐ Mì was skilled in mystical arts,
he recalled him from exile,
eventually appointing him to a high position.
Public opinion at the time was not favorable.
While serving as chancellor,
he adapted to circumstances without firm principles,
and there was little to commend.
He also associated with frivolous individuals like Gù Kuàng,
often becoming the subject of ridicule and mockery by court officials,
which brought much criticism.
Lǐ Mì was unrestrained, quick-witted, and eloquent,
fond of making grandiose statements.
Since entering the imperial court,
he was repeatedly envied and resented by powerful figures,
but he always managed to avoid harm through his wisdom.
In the end, through his persuasive speech,
he enlightened the sagely emperor,
and thus rose to the position of chancellor.
Earlier,
when Lǐ Mì was exiled to Jiāngnán,
he formed friendships with Liǔ Hún and Gù Kuàng,
enjoying poetry and a carefree life.
Liǔ Hún achieved success first,
so Lǐ Mì was able to return to court service.
Gù Kuàng was from Sūzhōu."
However, although Lǐ Mì was fond of discussing the mystical and supernatural,
his wisdom and strategies were truly exceptional.
As for assisting Emperors Sùzōng and Dàizōng in recapturing the two capitals,
declining the chancellorship and leaving,
and ensuring the safety of Emperors Dàizōng and Shùnzōng while they were crown princes,
all relied on Lǐ Mì.
These are the major virtues for which he should be respected.
The Old Biography criticizes him too harshly.
The family biography comes from his son,
and although it cannot be fully trusted,
how can it be entirely dismissed?
Now, I will select the credible parts and preserve them.
Earlier,
the emperor, recalling Lǐ Huáiguāng's contributions,
wished to pardon one of his sons.
The matter is recorded in the 232nd volume, under the first year of the Zhēnyuán era.
On the Wùchén day,
an edict was issued appointing Lǐ Huáiguāng's grandson, Yān Bābā, as his heir,
bestowing upon him the name Lǐ Chéngxù,
appointing him as Left Guard Commander and Armory Officer,
granting him a thousand strings of cash,
and ordering him to support Lǐ Huáiguāng's wife, Wáng Shì,
and guard his tomb and sacrifices.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Wéi Gāo sent his general Cáo Yǒudào to lead troops and fight against the Eastern Barbarians, the Two Forests Barbarians, and the Tǔbō's Qīnghǎi and Làchéng commanders at Táidēng Valley in Xīzhōu.
Táidēng was a Hàn dynasty county,
belonging to Xīzhōu in the Táng dynasty.
They beheaded two thousand enemies,
and those who fell off cliffs or drowned were countless.
They killed the enemy's Grand Military Commander, Qǐzàng Zhēzhē.
Qǐzàng Zhēzhē was a valiant general of the enemy.
After his death,
every fortress and stockade attacked by Wéi Gāo fell.
Within a few years,
the entire territory of Xīzhōu was recovered.
The Yìdìng military governor, Zhāng Xiàozhōng, raised troops and attacked Yùzhōu,
plundering people and livestock.
An imperial edict reprimanded him,
and after more than ten days, he returned to his garrison.
Since the Qiánfēng era, Qióngzhōu had been occupied by mountain bandits.
Qióngzhōu is located on a large island in the sea,
with Límǔ Mountain in the middle,
inhabited by the Lí people,
who did not pay taxes to the court.
The so-called mountain bandits were likely the Lí people.
Sòng Bái said: Fifteen lǐ north of Qióngzhōu,
one reaches the vast sea.
Sailing a large ship with a southwest wind,
it takes three days and three nights to reach a place called Yáshānmén.
Entering the river,
it takes one day to reach Xīnhuì County.
With favorable winds,
it takes ten days to reach Guǎngzhōu.
The Lǐngnán military governor, Lǐ Fù, sent his assistant, Jiāng Mèngjīng, and the Yázhōu prefect, Zhāng Shǎoqiān, to attack and capture it.
In the twelfth month,
on the Gēngwǔ day,
news arrived that the Tiānqīn Khagan of the Huíhé had passed away.
On the Wùyín day,
the Court of State Ceremonial Minister, Guō Fēng, was sent to confer the title of Dēnglǐluóméimìshījùlùzhōngzhēnpíjiā Khagan upon his son.
Previously, Ānxī and Běitíng had to pass through Huíhé territory to report to the court,
but this route was blocked by the Tǔbō,
making the Hé-Lǒng road impassable.
Thus, they had to go through Huíhé territory to submit reports.
Běitíng was especially close to Huíhé territory,
and the demands were endless.
Additionally, more than six thousand tents of the Shātuó people relied on Běitíng.
The Shātuó were a branch of the Western Turkic Chùyuè tribe,
living south of Jīnsuō Mountain,
east of Púlèi Sea.
There was a large desert called Shātuó,
hence they called themselves Shātuó.
The Three Gélù were the three tribes of Géluólù:
the first called Móulà,
the second called Póbó,
and the third called Tàshílì.
They were northwest of Běitíng,
west of Jīnshān.
The "White-Clothed Turks,"
recorded in the New Táng History as
"White-Eyed Turks."
The Tǔbō used the forces of the Gélù and White-Clothed Turks to attack Běitíng,
and the Huíhé Grand Chancellor, Jiégàn Jiāsī, led troops to rescue them.
Although Yúnnán had turned against the Tǔbō,
it did not dare to openly break with them.
On the Rénchén day,
Wéi Gāo again sent a letter to persuade them.
In spring,
an edict was issued to bring the Buddha's finger bone from the Wúyōuwáng Temple in Qíshān to the palace,
and then to various temples to show the people.
The entire capital came to pay homage,
donating vast sums of money.
In the second month,
on the Yǐhài day,
a palace envoy was sent to return it to its original resting place.
Earlier,
after Zhū Tāo was defeated at Bèizhōu,
as recorded in the 231st volume under the first year of the Xīngyuán era,
he offended Wǔ Jùn,
who summoned him but he did not come.
Tián Xù was cruel and ruthless.
His elder brother, Tián Cháo,
served Lǐ Nà as the prefect of Qízhōu.
Someone said that Lǐ Nà intended to install Tián Cháo in Wèi,
which frightened Tián Xù.
His assistant, Sūn Guāngzuǒ, and others devised a plan for Tián Xù:
bribe Lǐ Nà heavily,
and persuade him to recruit Zhào Gǎo to capture Dìzhōu to please him,
while requesting to send Tián Cháo to the capital.
Lǐ Nà agreed.
On the Dīngyǒu day,
Zhào Gǎo surrendered Dìzhōu to Lǐ Nà.
In the third month,
Wǔ Jùn sent his son, Wǔ Shìzhēn, to attack him,
but he was unsuccessful.
The younger brother of the Huíhé Zhōngzhēn Khagan assassinated Zhōngzhēn and declared himself khagan.
Examination of Discrepancies states: The New History says:
"The khagan was poisoned by the young Khatun, Princess Yè,
and the khagan's younger brother then declared himself khagan."
Now, I follow the Veritable Records.
In summer,
the fourth month,
the deputy chancellor led the people to kill the usurper and installed Zhōngzhēn's son, Ā Chuò, as khagan,
who was fifteen years old.
In the fifth month,
Wáng Wǔjùn stationed troops in Jìzhōu,
intending to attack Zhào Gǎo.
Zhào Gǎo led his followers and fled to Yùnzhōu;
Lǐ Nà sent troops to occupy it.
Tián Xù sent Sūn Guāngzuǒ to Yùnzhōu,
forging an imperial edict to place Dìzhōu under Lǐ Nà's jurisdiction.
Wǔ Jùn was enraged

When Dòu Cān's family was ruined,
I fortunately was able to fill a place in the palace.
Now that I serve before the Dragon Countenance,
it is as if I am in heaven.'
Emperor Dézōng said: 'Dòu Cān's crimes were not limited to harboring knights-errant and assassins;
he was also deeply corrupt.
Previously, he turned over an extremely large amount of silver vessels to the government.'
Shàngqīng said tearfully: 'Dòu Cān served successively as Vice Censor-in-chief, Commissioner of Finance, Minister of Revenue, and Commissioner of Salt and Iron,
rising to chancellor.
From beginning to end over six years,
his monthly income amounted to several hundred thousand strings of cash.
The untimely rewards and gifts he received before and after are also beyond count.
As for the silver objects turned over to the government from Chēnzhōu,
they were all bestowed by imperial favor.
On the day they were inventoried and recorded,
I was in Chēnzhōu.
I personally saw the prefectural and county officials, following Lù Zhì's intent,
scrape off the inscriptions of the military governors' official titles and names that were engraved on the silver vessels presented,
and falsely claim them as corrupt goods.
I beg Your Majesty to investigate this.'
Thereupon, the silver vessels of Dòu Cān that had been confiscated by the government were summoned for inspection.
Upon re-examining the places where the characters had been scraped off,
it was all as Shàngqīng had said.
This was in the twelfth year of the Zhēnyuán era.
Emperor Dézōng also asked about the matter of harboring knights-errant and assassins.
Shàngqīng said: 'There originally was none.
It was entirely Lù Zhì's陷害,
who had someone do it.'
Emperor Dézōng angrily said of Lù Zhì: 'This獠奴!
I took off his green robe and gave him a purple one to wear.
I also often called him Lù the Ninth.
Just when I had appointed Dòu Cān and he was beginning to perform satisfactorily,
I was made to wrongly kill him.
And when power fell into his hands,
he was weaker than a lump of clay.'
He then issued an edict rehabilitating Dòu Cān.
At that time, Péi Yánlíng, sensing that Lù Zhì's favor was waning,
was able to freely engage in slander and incitement.
Lù Zhì ultimately suffered condemnation and did not return to favor.
Later, Shàngqīng was specially granted an imperial decree written in cinnabar, allowing her to become a Daoist nun.
She eventually married Jīn Zhōngyì.
The world, because many of Lù Zhì's disciples held prominent and high positions,
did not dare to spread the story.
Therefore, this matter was completely unknown to anyone."
If this account is to be believed,
then Dòu Cān was being blackmailed by someone.
How could Emperor Dézōng instead say
"harboring knights-errant and assassins"!
Moreover, Lù Zhì was a worthy chancellor.
How could he be willing to do such a thing!
Even if he wanted to陷害 Dòu Cān,
his methods were certainly numerous.
How could he be willing to engage in such childish play!
It is completely contrary to human nature.
Therefore, it is not adopted here.

Zhào Jǐng, the Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, and Lù Zhì, the Vice Minister of War, were both appointed Vice Directors of the Secretariat and Co-managers of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery.
Jǐng
was the great-grandson of Rénběn.
8 Zhāng Pāng requested the old salt and iron administration registers from Bān Hóng,
but Hóng would not give them.
Pāng and Hóng together selected officials for the inspection offices,
but none were suitable.
Many positions remained vacant.
Pāng said to the Emperor:
"If this continues,
official duties will certainly be neglected,
and I will have no way to escape blame."
On the Bǐngwǔ day,
the Emperor ordered Hóng and Pāng to separately administer the empire's financial resources,
following the precedent of the Dàlì era.
In the first year of Dàlì,
Dìwǔ Qí and Liú Yàn were ordered to separately manage the empire's financial resources.
This matter is recorded in scroll 224.
9 On the Rénzǐ day,
Tibet invaded Língzhōu,
capturing the branch canals of the Shuǐkǒu,
and destroying the military agricultural colonies.
An edict ordered Hé dōng and Zhènwǔ to provide relief,
and dispatched two thousand troops from the six armies of the Divine Strategy to garrison Dìngyuǎn and Huáiyuǎn cities.
Huáiyuǎn County belonged to Língzhōu.
It was established during the Later Zhōu,
and the Sui dynasty's Wǔyuán Commandery was located within its boundaries.
Sòng Bái said: Dìngyuǎn County is 200 lǐ northeast of Língzhōu.
10 Lù Zhì requested that the chief officials of the various departments and bureaus each recommend their own subordinates,
recording their names in the imperial edict,
so that in the future, when assessing their performance as best or worst,
the recommenders would also be promoted or demoted accordingly.
In the fifth month,
on the Wùchén day,
an edict was issued implementing Lù Zhì's proposal.
Not long after,
someone said to the Emperor:
"All the recommendations made by the various departments involve personal connections or old friendships,
and some even involve accepting bribes;
thus, truly capable individuals are not being selected."
The Emperor secretly instructed Lù Zhì:
"From now on, regarding appointments and changes,
you should personally select them,
and not rely on the various departments."
The various departments,
refer to the chief officials of the Táishěng.
The gist of it was:
"In our dynasty, officials of the fifth rank and above
are appointed by imperial decree,
which is decided after deliberation and approval by the chancellor.
Officials of the sixth rank and below are appointed by imperial order,
meaning the Ministry of Personnel evaluates their qualifications and assigns positions,
and the imperial decree merely acknowledges the report without approval or disapproval.
For the appointment certificates of sixth-rank officials and below,
the character
'acknowledged'
is written.
Officials such as the Qǐjū, Yí, Bǔ, and Yùshǐ
are still listed together in the selection department.
This refers to the Qǐjū Láng, Shèrén, Shíyí, Bǔquē, and Yùshǐ,
all of whom are proposed by the Ministry of Personnel.
Selection,
must be carefully considered.
To discard collective deliberation and emphasize one's own authority,
to abolish public recommendations and practice private favoritism,
is to ensure that among the multitude of officials,
unless they align with the chancellor's intentions,
they cannot attain positions."
He also said:
"Since the implementation of this system,
only a dozen or so individuals have been recommended.
Evaluating their qualifications and reputation,
they are not inferior to their peers;
examining their conduct and abilities,
no failures have been heard of.
Yet critics hastily spread rumors,
troubling the Emperor's wise judgment.
The difficulty of implementing proper governance
can thus be understood!
I request that those who made the accusations specify the details:
who accepted bribes,
which recommendation involved personal connections,
and hand the matter over to the relevant authorities
to verify the truth;
those who made erroneous recommendations must be punished,
and those who falsely accused good people must also be held accountable for their crimes.
This means to impose reciprocal punishment for the crime.
Without cross-examination,
public discussion becomes biased,
and the names of the accusers are not disclosed.
The names of the accusers,
refer to the names of those who filed the accusations.
If the guilty are allowed to escape,
and the wrong and the right are treated alike,
what can the people rely on!
Moreover,
there are only a few chancellors,
how can they be familiar with all the talented individuals!
If they are to appoint all officials themselves,
they would inevitably have to inquire indirectly;
this would turn public recommendations into private referrals,
replacing open promotion with covert appointments.
The contrast between public and private, open and covert,
naturally reveals the logic.
This is the method of writing.
However,
the term 'open promotion'
originates from the Yúshū,
and the term 'covert appointments'
originates from the Hànshū.
In writing, one cannot lack sources.
In recent times, those who teach writing often follow this approach,
but writing is not limited to this alone.
The resulting弊端 becomes even more severe.
Therefore, in previous appointments of officials,
few escaped criticism.
Although the wielders of authority were not uniform,
some acted out of personal feelings,
but it was also due to privately consulting their close associates,
who then betrayed them.
The弊端 is not far off,
and the Emperor's wise discernment is clear."
He also said:
"Today's chancellors were formerly the chief officials of the Táishěng,
and today's chief officials of the Táishěng will be future chancellors.
It is merely a temporary difference in titles,
not a sudden change in conduct or recommendations.
Conduct and recommendations,
are made by the chief officials of the Táishěng,
and implemented by the chancellors.
When occupying the position of chancellor, one can select hundreds of subordinates;
public opinion is vast and varied,
and confusion is profound.
The higher-ups oversee the essentials,
while the lower ranks handle the details.
Thus, the sovereign selects his ministers,
and the ministers select the heads of various departments.
The heads of various departments,
refer to the leaders of the multitude of officials.
To ensure the right people are chosen,
there is no better method than this.
Seeking talent requires breadth,
while evaluating performance requires precision.
In the past, Zétiān, to win over the people's hearts,
promoted officials without regard to rank.
Zétiān,
refers to Empress Wǔ.
She also allowed officials to recommend their own talents.
However, as assessments were strict,
promotions and demotions were swift.
Thus, her era was praised for its discernment of people,
and successive dynasties relied on the talents she cultivated."
He also said:
"Zétiān's method of selection was overly simplistic but yielded capable people,
while Your Majesty's cautious selection rule
is stated in the Shū: 'Carefully select your officials.'
The Emperor ultimately rescinded the previous decree and did not implement it.
On the 11th day of the month, Guǐyǒu,
the military governor of Pínglú, Lǐ Nà, passed away.
The army supported his son, Lǐ Shīgǔ, to act as interim commander.
In the sixth month,
over a thousand Tibetan cavalry raided Jīngzhōu,
capturing more than a thousand soldiers from the agricultural garrison and leaving.
Agricultural garrison soldiers,
refer to troops engaged in land reclamation.
The military governor of Lǐngnán reported:
"Recently, foreign ships carrying rare treasures
have mostly conducted trade in Ānnán.
I wish to send an assistant magistrate to Ānnán to oversee trade,
and request that a palace eunuch accompany him."
The Emperor intended to agree.
Lù Zhì submitted a memorial,
arguing:
"Merchants from distant lands
seek only profit.
If treated leniently, they will come;
if harassed, they will leave.
Guǎngzhōu has long been a hub for foreign ships.
Now, they have suddenly shifted to Ānnán.
If this is not due to excessive exploitation,
then it must be because of improper handling of foreign relations.
Handling foreign relations,
means managing separation,
referring to losing the proper way to attract and manage foreign relations.
In the Zuǒzhuàn,
Guǎn Zhòng said: 'Attract foreigners with courtesy.'
In the Lúnyǔ,
Confucius said:
'I have never seen anyone who, upon seeing his own faults, inwardly accuses himself.'
The commentary states: Accuse,
means to blame,
meaning people who have faults are unable to blame themselves.
The Yuèlìng records: 'Do not create extravagant crafts to sway the ruler's heart.'
The commentary states: Sway,
means to动摇 it.
All land belongs to the king,
whether palace eunuchs or external officials,
all are the king's servants.
Why must we trust Lǐngnán and neglect Ānnán,
or prioritize palace eunuchs over external officials?
I hope the reported request will not be approved."
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the first day, Jiǎyín,
the Minister of Revenue and head of the Dùzhī, Bān Hóng, passed away.
Lù Zhì recommended appointing the former Húnán observation commissioner, Lǐ Xùn, as acting head of the Dùzhī,
and the Emperor agreed.
However, the Emperor later wanted to appoint the Vice Minister of the Court of the Imperial Granaries, Péi Yánlíng.
Lù Zhì submitted a memorial,
arguing:
"The current Dùzhī
oversees the balancing of all goods.
Excessive strictness breeds trouble,
while excessive leniency harbors corruption.
Péi Yánlíng is a deceitful and frivolous petty man;
appointing him would shock public opinion.
The responsibility for holding a sinecure
should rightly fall upon humble officials like me;
but the discernment of people,
I fear, would also harm the Emperor's wise judgment."
The Emperor did not listen.
On the sixth day, Jǐwèi,
Péi Yánlíng was appointed head of the Dùzhī.
This sets the stage for Péi Yánlíng's slander of Lù Zhì.
More than forty provinces including Hé'nán, Hé'běi, Jiāng, Huái, Jīng, Xiāng, Chén, and Xǔ suffered major floods,
with over twenty thousand people drowning,
and Lù Zhì requested to send envoys for relief and consolation.
The Emperor said:
"I hear the damage is quite minor;
if we immediately discuss generous relief,
I fear it may breed deceit and fraud."
Lù Zhì submitted a memorial,
which roughly stated:
"The flaw of common practice
is often to follow flattery and sycophancy,
exaggerating words to please those they wish to delight,
and downplaying matters they anticipate will be unwelcome to hear,
leading to improper preparations and provisions,
a constant ailment in this regard."
"Preparations and provisions"
means establishing measures according to circumstances and preparing in advance.
"Constant,"
pronounced with the hù-dēng tone.
"What is spent is material resources,
what is gained is the hearts of the people.
If we do not lose the people,
why worry about lacking resources!"
The Emperor agreed to send envoys,
but said:
"Since Huáixī has already suspended its tribute and taxes,
there is no need to send envoys there."
Lù Zhì submitted another memorial,
arguing:
"Your Majesty has ceased military action and endured humiliation,
pardoning their chief leaders.
'Chief'
means great.
'Leaders'
means commanders.
They should be shown compassion and relief.
In the past, even though Qín and Jìn were enemies,
Duke Mù of Qín still relieved their famine.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn records: When Jìn suffered famine,
Qín supplied them with grain.
When Qín suffered famine,
Jìn closed its grain markets;
Duke Mù attacked Jìn,
capturing Duke Huì.
When Jìn suffered famine again,
Duke Mù again supplied them with grain,
saying:
'I resent their ruler but pity their people.'
Only with virtue and righteousness
would one rather let others wrong me
than have me wrong others."
This reverses Cáo Cāo's saying,
and thus carries the bearing of an emperor.
He dispatched the Zhōngshū Shèrén Jīngzhào Xī Zhì and others to proclaim relief for the flood disasters in various circuits.
15. Appointed the former Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ Lǐ Shīgǔ as the Pínglú Jiédùshǐ.
16. Wéi Gāo attacked
Wéizhōu.
In the first year of the Guǎngdé era of Emperor Dàizōng,
Wéizhōu fell to Tǔbō.
17. Lù Zhì submitted a statement,
arguing that the inadequacy of border provisions
was due to improper arrangements
and misguided methods of accumulation and collection.
It roughly stated:
"The so-called improper arrangements refer to
garrison soldiers not being subordinate to the local commanders,
and local commanders not being under the overall command of the marshal.
This leads to a situation where
the general of a single city,
the troops of a single brigade,
each have a palace envoy overseeing them,
all appointed by separate imperial decrees.
They are stationed across a thousand lǐ of territory,
with no one to lead and follow;
along the border, an army of a hundred thousand is arrayed,
yet no chief strategist is appointed.
Whenever bandits arrive,
they must await instructions from the central government;
by the time they receive orders to mobilize and provide aid,
the bandits have already achieved victory and withdrawn.
Compared to China,
Tǔbō is outnumbered and unmatched,
and their skills are inferior,
yet they have surplus strength for attack,
while we lack sufficient strength for defense.
This is because their commands come from their generals,
while our control lies with the court,
and because their troops are united while ours are fragmented and divided.
The so-called misguided methods of accumulation and collection refer to
Your Majesty recently establishing the methods of 'army procurement' and 'harmonious grain purchase' to reduce transport,
and setting doubled prices to encourage agriculture.
When these orders were first implemented,
everyone was pleased and admired them.
These were the methods implemented by Lǐ Mì,
as recorded in
[two hundred thirty-two]
[Zhēnyuán].
However, the officials competed in being perfunctory,
focusing solely on petty frugality.
In years of good harvest, they did not collect and store in a timely manner;
in times of food scarcity, they forced purchases.
This allowed powerful families and greedy officials
to instead seize control of profitable authority,
buying cheaply from people in anticipation of shortages for both public and private needs.
Furthermore, influential figures, close relatives, and itinerant scholars
entrusted cheap grain purchases to the military garrisons,
while obtaining high prices in the capital,
and also receiving excessive amounts of coarse silk and linen as payment.
In the remote, cold border regions, these could not be worn,
and when sold, there was no market.
Since the superiors showed no trust toward the subordinates,
the subordinates also responded with deceit.
The price estimates from the Dùzhī became increasingly higher,
and grain prices in the military garrisons became increasingly expensive.
The Dùzhī considered selling stagnant goods at any price as achievement and profit,
while the military garrisons
regarded the added value from their obtained goods as surplus revenue.
Although inspection bureaus were established,
they instead became pockets for embezzlement.
On the twelfth day of the twelfth month in the fourth year of the Yuánhé era,
an edict stated:
'Distant provincial envoys
often act arbitrarily and violate laws,
and the central ministries have no way to fully know.
The Transport Commissioner and Dùzhī all have inspection bureaus;
they are entrusted to investigate and report to the central ministries on matters within their jurisdictions and prefectures,
including additional levies beyond the two-tax system and violations of regulations, decrees, and laws.'
It was Liú Yàn who first established inspection bureaus,
from the Jiāng and Huái regions reaching to the Hé and Wèi rivers,
and later they were also set up in the border circuits.
Falsely pointing to granaries,
the counted numbers exceed hundreds of millions,
It was also said:
"Under the old system, due to the high expenses in Guānzhōng,
grain taxes from the east were transported annually,
to the extent that there was a saying: 'A coin to transport a peck of rice.'
Those accustomed to old practices and unaware of current exigencies
would say: 'For major state affairs,
cost and loss should not be counted;
even if we know it is laborious and troublesome,
it cannot be abolished.'
Those accustomed to immediate gains and heedless of long-term troubles
would say: 'Every year at the autumn harvest,
simply order grain purchases within the capital region;
this is easy to accomplish,
and also sufficient to encourage agriculture.'
I believe both arguments
have their respective strengths and weaknesses.
To manage state expenditures,
one must weigh the relative importance.
If food is insufficient but wealth is abundant,
then relax accumulating wealth and focus on filling granaries;
if food is abundant but wealth is insufficient,
then slow down accumulating food and economize on currency.
In recent years, Guānfǔ has repeatedly had bountiful harvests;
public reserves are piled up,
sufficient to supply for several years.
This summer, the Jiāng and Huái rivers flooded,
rice prices doubled,
and many people became displaced laborers.
'Displaced'
means fleeing and migrating.
'Laborer'
means hired labor.
We should increase prices to purchase rice but have no money;
in Jiāng and Huái, due to expensive grain, people are distressed;
we should reduce prices to sell rice but have no rice.
Yet we transport what they lack
to add to what we have in surplus here—
this is precisely what is called being accustomed to old practices and unaware of current exigencies.
Now, a peck of rice in Jiāng and Huái costs one hundred and fifty coins;
transported to Dōng Wèiqiáo,
the freight cost is approximately another two hundred,
the rice is coarse and stale,
and especially cheap in the capital.
According to the market office's monthly estimates,
(the present Market Order Office
also monthly reports the figures of price fluctuations to the emperor).
Losing nine-tenths and keeping only one-tenth—
with Jiāng and Huái rice
combined with the freight cost of water transport,
roughly one peck amounts to three hundred and fifty coins,
while the capital's rice price is only thirty-seven coins per peck.
This is losing nine-tenths and keeping only one-tenth.
Managing affairs like this
can truly be called a grave error!
Recently, every year, 1.1 million hú of rice were transported from Jiāng, Hú, Huái, and Zhè
to Héyīn, where 400,000 hú were retained
and stored in the Héyīn granary.
To Shǎnzhōu, another 300,000 hú were retained
and stored in the Tàiyuán granary.
The remaining 400,000 hú were delivered to Dōng Wèiqiáo.
Now, the Héyīn and Tàiyuán granaries still have over 3.2 million hú of rice in stock.
In Jīngzhào counties, a peck of rice costs no more than seventy coins.
I request that next year, Jiāng and Huái transport only 300,000 hú to Héyīn;
from Héyīn and Shǎnzhōu, transport in sequence to Dōng Wèiqiáo.
As for the 800,000 hú of rice shipment suspended from Jiāng and Huái,
entrust the transport commissioner to sell it at eighty coins per peck in flood-stricken prefectures and counties,
to relieve the poor and needy.
This would yield 640,000 strings of coins,
and reduce freight costs by 690,000 strings.
I request that the Ministry of Revenue first allocate 200,000 strings to Jīngzhào,
ordering the purchase of rice to make up for the shortfall in the Wèiqiáo granary.
(The Wèiqiáo granary
is the Dōng Wèiqiáo granary.)
Increasing prices to purchase benefits agriculture.
Have them purchase a year's grain for 100,000 people;
the remaining 104,000 strings can be used for next year's grain purchase price.
The money from Jiāng and Huái rice and the freight costs should all be entrusted to the transport commissioner to exchange for líng, juàn, shī, and mián silk to deliver to the capital,
repaying the money previously borrowed from the Ministry of Revenue."
In the ninth month,
an edict ordered the northwestern frontier to purchase grain at high prices to fill granary reserves.
(Commentary: The Veritable Records states:
"A total of 330,000 hú of rice was stored."
According to Lù Zhì's memorial on defense preparations:
"Sitting and obtaining frontier reserves,
the number exceeds one million.
The various garrisons' grain purchases
are now nearing completion."
It also says:
"After another year,
we can accumulate three years' grain for 100,000 people."
Probably the Veritable Records refers
to this year's number,
while Zhì's memorial includes calculations for next spring.)
18 Winter,
eleventh month,
on the first day, rénzǐ,
there was a solar eclipse.
19 Tibet and Yúnnán grew increasingly suspicious of each other.
Whenever Yúnnán troops reached the border,
Tibet would also dispatch troops,
claiming to respond in coordination,
but actually preparing against them.
On xīnyǒu,
Wéi Gāo again sent a letter to the King of Yúnnán,
wishing to jointly attack Tibet,
and drive them beyond the Yúnlǐng mountains.
(The land of Yúnnán
originally was the Hàn dynasty's Yúnnán County.
In Hàn, it belonged to Yìzhōu Commandery;
in Later Hàn, it was divided under Yǒngchāng Commandery.
The Records of the Southern Regions says: West of Yúnnán County, high mountains are connected;
among the many mountains,
there is one particularly tall and large,
shaped like Fúfēng's Tàiyī Mountain,
lush and towering,
connected with clouds and mist.
Looking at it, one cannot see the mountain;
it is perpetually shaded and bitterly cold.
Even in the fifth month, at the height of summer, it is not hot.
This is the so-called Yúnlǐng.)
Solely with Yúnnán, build a large fortress on the border,
establish garrisons to protect each other,
forever united as one family.
The Left Aide to the Heir Apparent, Jiāng Gōngfǔ, had not been promoted for a long time.
He went to Lù Zhì to request a promotion.
Lù Zhì secretly told him:
"I have heard that Minister Dòu has repeatedly submitted proposals for your promotion,
but His Majesty has not approved them.
Nowadays, people say that when the imperial decree does not grant a request, it is called 'not approving,'
a phrase commonly heard in the words of the Tang people."
Gōngfǔ became fearful
and requested to become a Daoist priest.
The Emperor asked him the reason,
but Gōngfǔ did not dare to reveal Lù Zhì's words,
so he answered by citing what he had heard from Dòu Cān.
The Emperor was angry that Cān was shifting blame onto the sovereign.
On the day Yǐsì,
he demoted Gōngfǔ to the position of Assistant Prefect of Jízhōu.
He also sent a palace envoy to reprimand Cān.
Jiāng Gōngfǔ, living in an era of suspicion and jealousy, could not remain content with his fate and duty,
and by this, he aggravated Dòu Cān's offense.
This was also due to a single remark from Lù Zhì.
Textual Analysis states: According to the Veritable Records:
"Initially,
when Gōngfǔ was dismissed from his post as chancellor and made Left Aide to the Heir Apparent,
he was excused due to mourning,
and later reappointed as Right Aide to the Heir Apparent.
He repeatedly visited Dòu Cān privately,
and Cān several times proposed appointing Gōngfǔ to another official post;
the Emperor did not consent,
and spoke words of anger against Gōngfǔ.
Gōngfǔ became afraid
and requested to be relieved of his official post to become a Daoist priest.
After a long time,
there was no response.
He then brought it up during an audience at the Yányīng Hall,
and the Emperor asked him the reason.
Gōngfǔ answered by citing Cān's words.
The Emperor made it clear to him,
but he persisted stubbornly.
The Emperor became greatly enraged,
demoted him,
and issued an edict reprimanding Cān for shifting blame onto the sovereign."
The Biography of Gōngfǔ states:
"When Lù Zhì was in charge of government affairs,
due to their old association in the Hànlín Academy,
Gōngfǔ repeatedly approached Zhì seeking an official post.
Zhì secretly said to Gōngfǔ:
'I have often seen Minister Dòu from Chēnzhōu,
and he said he has proposed your appointment several times,
but the Emperor's will did not consent, and there were angry words about you.'
Gōngfǔ became fearful,
and submitted a memorial begging to resign his post and become a Daoist priest.
After a long time,
there was no response.
Later, he again brought it up in court,
and Emperor Dézōng asked him the reason.
Gōngfǔ did not dare to reveal Zhì's words,
so he answered by citing Cān's words.
The Emperor was angry,
demoted Gōngfǔ to Assistant Prefect of Quánzhōu,
and also sent a palace envoy bearing an edict to reprimand Cān."
The Biography of Zhì states:
"Jiāng Gōngfǔ memorialized:
'Dòu Cān often told me that Your Majesty is still angry with me.'
Emperor Dézōng was angry,
demoted Cān again,
and eventually had him killed.
Contemporary opinion held that Gōngfǔ obtained the words about Dòu Cān from Zhì,
and that Cān's death
was partly due to Zhì's influence."
According to Zhì's memorial requesting that senior officials recommend subordinate officials, it states:
"It is also because of privately consulting those close to one,
who then betray one,
the harm of which is not far off,
as Your Majesty's wise discernment clearly knows."
These were words to exonerate Cān.
And when Cān was about to be executed,
Zhì pleaded for his exoneration most earnestly.
From this perspective,
how could Zhì have had any intention to kill Cān!
Moreover, when Zhì spoke to Gōngfǔ,
how could he have known that Gōngfǔ would request to become a Daoist priest,
and then before the Emperor shift the crime of leaking words onto Cān!
This was Gōngfǔ's own intention,
not Zhì's intention.
People at the time,
seeing that there was discord between Cān and Zhì,
speculated according to their own views.
The historians who disliked Zhì
thus blamed Zhì for it.
This is not adopted here.
On the day Gēngwǔ,
Yán Zhèn, Military Governor of Shānnán Xīdào, reported defeating the Tibetans at Fāngzhōu and Hēishuǐ Fort.
Initially,
Lǐ Nà, because the salt profits from Géduī in Dìzhōu were lucrative,
fortified and occupied it;
he also garrisoned Sānchà Fort south of Dézhōu,
to maintain communication with Tián Xù.
When Lǐ Shīgǔ succeeded to his position,
Wáng Wǔjùn, considering him young,
looked down on him.
In this month,
he led troops to station at Dé and Dì,
intending to seize Géduī and Sānchà Fort;
Shīgǔ sent Zhào Hào to lead troops to resist him.
The Emperor sent a palace envoy to order them to stop,
and Wǔjùn then withdrew.
Initially,
when Liú Pēng died,
see the 232nd scroll, first year of the Zhēnyuán era.
Pēng,
pronounced Pǔ Méng.
Died,
pronounced Hū Gōng.
His younger brother by the same mother, Yōng, was at their father's side,
and by their father's order summoned Jì and handed over the military governorship to him.
Mòzhōu administered Mò County,
located 280 li south of Yōuzhōu.
Yōng,
pronounced Yú Yòng.
Yíngzhōu,
Héjiān Commandery,
was a major prefecture under the jurisdiction of Yōuzhōu,
its territory lying south of Yōuzhōu.
Later, Jì appointed his own son as Deputy Grand Marshal.
The three military governors of Héběi and Zīqīng all appointed their sons as Deputy Grand Marshals,
as reserve commanders.
Yōng reported to the court,
and sent a thousand soldiers for autumn defense.
Jì was angry,
dispatched troops to attack Yōng,
and defeated him.
The Grand General of the Left Shéncè Army, Bǎi Liángqì,
the Grand Generals of the Left and Right Shéncè Armies of the Tang,
were of the second rank.
Shǐ Zhào said: The Bóhuáng clan,
an ancient imperial title,
later became a surname.
Zhuānxù's teacher Bó Liàngfù,
was a descendant of Dì Kù's teacher Bó Chāozhī.
The Army Supervisor Dòu Wénchǎng disliked him.
It happened that a relative of Liángqì's wife got drunk,
and lodged overnight in the palace quarters.
Palace quarters,
were lodgings for those on duty in the palace.
The history states that the eunuchs disliked Bǎi Liángqì for performing his duties well,
and used his wife's relative's violation of palace guard prohibitions to fabricate a crime against him.
On the day Bǐngxū,
Liángqì was demoted to Right Commander of the Guards.
From then on, eunuchs began to monopolize military administration.
This laid the groundwork for eunuchs holding military power to coerce the Son of Heaven.
Right Commander of the Guards,
was one of the Sixteen Guards.
At that time, the various guards of the Southern Administration
were merely nominal positions.
The Northern Army controlled the imperial guards,
wielding great power,
hence Liángqì's demotion was considered a leftward move.
1. In spring,
on the first month,
on the Guǐmǎo day,
tea was taxed for the first time.
The Erya, in explaining trees, says: Jiǎ,
is bitter tea.
Guō Pú's commentary states: The tree is about the size of a gardenia,
its leaves grow in winter and can be boiled to make a soup for drinking.
Nowadays, those picked early are called chá,
those picked late are called míng,
also known as chuǎn.
What people in Shǔ call bitter tea refers to this.
Nowadays, it is generally called chá.
Chá and tú are similar in sound,
hence it is called so.
In mid-spring, tender leaves begin to grow;
they are steamed and roasted to remove the bitter water,
then ground into powder,
and only then can they be consumed.
This is quite different from how it was consumed in ancient times.
The Běncǎo Yǎnyì states: Wēn Qiáo of the Jìn dynasty submitted a memorial,
offering a tribute of one thousand jīn of chá,
and three hundred jīn of míng.
Guō Pú said: Early-picked leaves are called chá,
late-picked leaves are called míng.
Míng is also called chuǎn,
which refers to old tea leaves.
In ancient times, the buds were called "sparrow tongues" or "wheat grains,"
indicating their extreme tenderness.
There are also new buds,
which grow over an inch as soon as they sprout,
slightly thick like needles.
Only those with long buds are considered top quality,
as their roots and stems are nourished by abundant soil nutrients.
As for "sparrow tongues" and "wheat grains,"
they are of lower quality,
something earlier generations did not fully understand.
Historical records state that the taxation of tea began here,
thus opening a source of profit.
All were assessed for their value,
with a tax of one-tenth,
following the request of the Salt and Iron Commissioner Zhāng Pāng.
Zhāng Pāng memorialized:
"Last year, due to floods, taxes were reduced,
and state expenditures are insufficient.
I request the taxation of tea to make up for it.
From next year onward,
the revenue from tea taxes
shall be stored separately by the respective localities,
to be used in times of flood or drought,
in place of the people's land taxes."
From then on, an annual revenue of four hundred thousand strings of cash was collected from tea taxes,
though it was never actually used to relieve flood or drought.
The proposal for a tea monopoly
originated with Zhào Zàn,
and it was Zhāng Pāng who first implemented it.
Zhāng Pāng further memorialized:
"Cunning individuals melt down coins to make copper utensils for profit.
I request a complete ban on copper utensils.
Copper mines may be opened for mining by the people,
but private sales are prohibited."
2. In the second month,
on the Jiǎyín day,
Yìwǔ Army Acting Military Commissioner Zhāng Shēngyún was appointed as Military Commissioner.
3. Earlier,
after Yánzhōu had fallen,
(the fall of Yánzhōu is recorded in the 232nd scroll, second year),
the Tǔbō often blocked the route to Língwǔ,
and invaded and harassed Fūfāng.
They not only cut off the route to and from Língwǔ,
but also harassed the people of Fūfāng.
On the Xīnyǒu day,
an edict was issued to dispatch 35,000 troops to fortify Yánzhōu.
Examination of discrepancies: The Bīnzhì states:
"In the eighth year,
an edict summoned Lord Zhāng to discuss fortifying Yán and Xià.
Lord Zhāng memorialized: 'For the army's advance and capture,
skilled generals are urgently needed.
Among the Shence Army's irregular generals, there is Wèi Guāng,
a son of Shuòfāng,
whose martial skills are unparalleled.
With Guāng,
we can accomplish the task.'
The Emperor sent him.
Lord Zhāng appointed Guāng as the Bīnníng Army's cavalry commander.
In the third month,
the army and other forces arrived at Wǔyuán,
camping a hundred lǐ from the city.
Guāng alone led his cavalry straight to the city walls,
breached and entered the city,
drove out the Tǔbō,
and summoned the other forces to fortify it.
He then led his troops westward to raid the border areas,
moving back and forth on reconnaissance,
serving as the army's eyes and ears.
The Tǔbō masses dared not cross the border,
and the government forces fortified the two prefectures and returned."
In the notes to Bái Jūyì's ballad "Yánzhōu,"
it is also stated
"in the Rénshēn year of Zhēnyuán,
a special edict ordered its fortification."
However, the Veritable Records place it in the ninth year, second month.
It seems the edict to fortify it was issued the previous year,
and this year, Dù Yànguāng and others were ordered to carry it out.
The fortification was completed in twenty days.
Yánzhōu Military Commissioner Dù Yànguāng was ordered to garrison it,
and Shuòfāng Army Deputy Commander Yáng Cháochéng was ordered to garrison Mùbō Fort.
Mùbō Fort
is within the boundaries of Fāngqú County, Qìngzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Fāngqú,
renamed Tōngyuǎn County in the Sòng dynasty,
where Huánzhōu was established,
has Mùbō Town.
Xiàzhōu and Héxī thus gained peace.
4 The emperor sent someone to instruct Lù Zhì,
saying,
"Regarding important matters,
do not discuss them with Zhào Jǐng;
instead, seal them in a handwritten memorial and report them to me."
Also,
"Miáo Càn, because his father Miáo Jìnqīng previously acted as regent—
during the Bǎoyìng era,
there were successive national mourning periods,
and Jìnqīng acted as the chief minister.
His sons all share names with ancient emperors and kings.
Jìnqīng had ten sons: Fā, Pī, Jiān, Chuí,
which are the same as the names of emperors and kings.
His brothers have also been appointed to posts outside the capital;
do not let them be stationed near areas with garrisoned troops."
Also,
"You are excessively pure and cautious;
when various circuits send gifts,
you refuse them all.
I fear this may hinder the smooth handling of affairs.
As for things like whips and boots,
accepting them would do no harm."
Zhì submitted a memorial in response,
which roughly stated:
"Yesterday, what I reported
was heard only by Zhào Jǐng.
Your Majesty has already gone to great lengths,
taking elaborate precautions.
This means that even among those closest to you,
there are still constraints of formality.
When actions are the same but circumstances differ,
it is rarely effective.
I fear this may undermine the virtue of impartiality.
'Shuǎng' means 'to err.'
The *Book of Documents* says: 'Do not hesitate to correct your faults.'
'When enfeoffing someone, it must be done at court;
when punishing someone, it must be done in the marketplace,'
for fear that the multitude may not see it,
and the matter may not be made clear.
The *Records* say: 'Enfeoffing someone at court
is to share it with the multitude;
punishing someone in the marketplace
is to have the multitude reject them.'
'Cháo' is pronounced 'zhí yáo fān.'
The common people hear it without doubt or dispute;
those receiving rewards accept them without shame;
those facing punishment bear it without resentment.
This is how the sage kings proclaimed and clarified the statutes and regulations,
sharing them publicly with all under heaven.
Generally, slanderous accusations
are mostly not truthful words.
They benefit from causing harm
and fear public debate.
Some say that too much time has passed,
making it impossible to investigate thoroughly;
some say that the matter is sensitive,
requiring concealment and tolerance;
some say that the evil deeds are not yet exposed,
and another pretext should be used;
some say that simply removing the person is enough,
why must they be explicitly reprimanded and shamed?
The words all seem reasonable,
but the intent is truly wrapped in deception and falsehood.
Harming the good and promoting the wicked—
nothing is worse than this!
If Miáo Jìnqīng and his sons truly committed grave crimes,
then they should be judged publicly according to the law.
If they have been wrongfully accused,
how can they be secretly subjected to exile?
In hearing cases and discerning slander,
one must seek the truth and examine the evidence.
When the truth is revealed and the evidence is clear,
and the accused confesses and the reasoning is exhausted,
then punishment may be applied.
This way, there are no wronged people below,
and no erroneous judgments above."
He also said:
"Supervising officials accepting bribes
is punishable even for a foot's worth.
According to the law,
any supervising official
who accepts goods from those under their supervision
is to be caned forty strokes for one foot.
Any supervising official in charge who accepts bribes and perverts the law
is to be beaten one hundred strokes for one foot.
'Jiān' is pronounced 'gǔ xián fān.'
This should be strictly prohibited;
how much more so for those at the forefront of moral influence,
who should instead allow it to pass?
The forefront of moral influence
refers to the prime minister, from whom moral influence emanates.
If it spreads and grows worse,
starting with whips and boots,
it will inevitably extend to gold and jade.
'Xuē' is the same as 'boot.'
How can one restrain one's own heart?
An ancient saying goes:
'If one does not see what is desirable,
this heart will not be disturbed.'
How can one cut off such intentions in the middle?
This means that once one accepts private gifts,
it becomes difficult to refuse private requests.
The ravines and valleys will become disastrous."
He also said:
"If one accepts some things
and refuses others,
then those whose gifts are refused will suspect they are being rejected and that communication is blocked.
If one refuses all gifts,
then everyone will know that refusal is the norm,
and what suspicion or obstruction could there be?"
5 Earlier,
Dòu Cān disliked the Left Department Director Lǐ Xùn
and had him appointed as Prefect of Chángzhōu.
When Cān was demoted to Chēnzhōu,
Xùn became the Military Commissioner of Húnán.
Biànzhōu Military Commissioner Liú Shìníng sent Cān fifty bolts of silk,
and Xùn reported that Cān was colluding with a military governor.
The emperor was furious
and wanted to execute Cān.
Lù Zhì believed Cān's crime did not warrant death,
so the emperor refrained.
Later, he again sent a eunuch envoy to tell Zhì:
"Cān colluded both inside and outside the court;
his intentions are unfathomable.
Matters of the state are grave;
quickly submit a document for handling."
Zhì submitted a statement:
"Cān is a high-ranking court minister;
executing him cannot be without justification.
In the past, when Liú Yàn died,
his crime was not clear,
and to this day, public opinion remains indignant about it,
giving rebellious ministers a pretext.
See scrolls 226, years Jiànzhōng 1 and 2.
This is known throughout the land.
As for secretly harboring treacherous plans,
the evidence is ambiguous.
If no investigation is conducted
and severe punishment is hastily imposed,
the shock and unrest will not be minor.
Dòu Cān and I have no personal connection;
there is no bond of friendship in our words.
'Fèn' is pronounced 'fú wèn fān.'
It is not that I wish to rescue him,
but rather that I cherish the principle of not滥用 the legal punishments."
In March,
Cān was further demoted to Military Advisor of Huānzhōu,
and his sons and daughters were all exiled.
The emperor also ordered an investigation of his close associates.
'Lǐ' means 'to govern.'
"Crimes have principals and accomplices;
the law has severity and leniency.
'Shǒu' refers to the ringleader.
'Cóng' refers to the followers.
The ringleader is treated severely,
the followers leniently.
Close associates should also receive reduced punishment;
moreover, when Cān was first convicted,
his private associates were already implicated.
Public sentiment has long been settled;
I request that no further inquiries be made."
This was approved.
The emperor also wanted to confiscate his family's assets.
Zhì said:
"According to the law,
rebels have all their property confiscated,
while those guilty of corruption only have the proceeds of their crimes seized.
All must be convicted and sentenced
before confiscation takes place.
Now, the crime and punishment are not yet detailed,
and Your Majesty has already shown leniency.
If we inventory his family's property now,
I fear it may harm righteousness for the sake of wealth."
At the time, the eunuchs and attendants hated Cān deeply
and continued to slander and vilify him.
Before Cān reached Huānzhōu,
he was ultimately ordered to commit suicide on the road.
Dòu Shēn was beaten to death,
and his goods, wealth, and slaves were all sent to the capital.
'Zhuàn' is pronounced 'zhī liàn fān.'
6. The Coastal Prefecture Militia Commissioner, Zhāng Shēnglín,
was the younger brother of Shēngyún,
and the son-in-law of Lǐ Nà.
Because of his father's Great Auspicious Rite, he returned to Dìngzhōu.
Coastal Prefecture,
Dōnghǎi Commandery,
was under the jurisdiction of Zīqīng Circuit.
Lín,
read as lí zhēn.
Son-in-law,
read as xī jì.
Dìngzhōu,
was the seat of the Yìwǔ Military Governor.
A son in mourning for his father,
after two full years performs the Great Auspicious Rite.
Wǔjùn reported this.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Dīngchǒu day,
an edict was issued stripping him of his office,
and a palace envoy was dispatched to cane and imprison him.
Dìngzhōu was wealthy and populous,
Wǔjùn had long coveted it,
and taking this opportunity, he dispatched troops to raid and capture Yìfēng,
plundered Ānxǐ and Wújí, taking over ten thousand people captive,
and relocated them to Dézhōu and Dìzhōu.
Yìfēng,
belonged to Dìngzhōu.
Ānxǐ County,
was originally the seat of Dìngzhōu's administration,
it seems the prefectural seat had been moved.
Wújí,
an ancient county from the Hàn,
named after Mount Wújí,
belonged to Dìngzhōu in the Táng.
According to the Mount Wújí stele inscription:
"Mount Wújí came into being together with Heaven and Earth,
from its summit to its base,
it is about three lǐ,
with a stone forming its body,
about two zhàng and five chǐ.
The stone is blue-green on top,
yellow-white below,
the front is level and even,
enough to spread two large mats."
It is located thirty lǐ southwest of Wújí.
In the second year of the Jǐngfú era,
Wújí County was made Qízhōu.
Dì,
read as dà jì.
He repeatedly sent envoys to apologize,
and then stopped.
The Emperor ordered Lǐ Shīgǔ to dismantle the Sānchà Fortress.
Lǐ Nà had built the Sānchà Fortress,
see the previous year.
Chà,
read as chǔ jià.
However, he often recruited and gathered fugitives,
those who had offended the court,
he would all comfort and employ them.
7. In the fifth month,
on the Jiǎchén day,
