Zhōngshū Shìláng Zhào Jǐng was appointed Ménxià Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì;
Yìchéng Jíédùshǐ Jiǎ Dān was appointed Right Deputy Director;
Right Assistant Lú Mài retained his original office,
and both were appointed Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
Mài,
was a clansman of Hàn.
Jǐng suspected that Lù Zhì, relying on imperial favor,
wanted to monopolize major government affairs,
and had him sidelined to the Ménxià Bureau.
The Hall of Government Affairs was in the Zhōngshū Bureau,
now Jǐng was transferred to the Eastern Bureau,
hence he suspected Zhì was sidelining him.
The Right Deputy Director belonged to the Ménxià Bureau.
From this, a rift developed between him and Zhì.
This sets the stage for Zhào Jǐng's later attachment to Péi Yánlíng.
Examination of Discrepancies says: The Old Biography of Jǐng states:
"Jǐng and Lù Zhì jointly administered government affairs.
Zhì, relying on his long tenure in the palace precincts,
and being specially favored,
took state affairs as his own responsibility.
After barely a year,
he had Jǐng transferred to be Ménxià Shìláng.
Jǐng deeply resented this because of it,
repeatedly requested leave citing eye ailments,
and did not actively participate in government affairs,
leading to discord between them."
However, Jǐng's transfer to Ménxià still made him a chancellor,
and furthermore, Jiǎ Dān and Lú Mài were added,
how could Zhì monopolize government?
It seems Jǐng harbored this suspicion in his heart.
8. Lù Zhì submitted a memorial discussing the six failures in border defense,
believing:
"Deployment is misguided,
accountability and demands are deficient,
wealth is exhausted by excessive troops,
strength is divided among too many generals,
resentment arises from inequality,
and opportunities are lost due to remote control.
From 'deployment is misguided' onward,
these are the so-called six failures.
Submitted,
read as shí zhǎng.
General,
read as jí liàng;
same below.
The garrison troops from east of the passes,
unaccustomed to the local climate,
suffer physically in the desolate borderlands,
and fear the barbarian tribes in their hearts.
The state supports them like spoiled children,
and indulges them like hired men.
They count on their fingers the days until their return,
open their mouths waiting to be fed;
some hope for the imperial army's defeat,
taking advantage of the turmoil to flee eastward;
others abandon towns and forts,
shaking the resolve of people near and far.
Not only is this of no benefit,
it is actually harmful.
Furthermore, there are those exiled for committing crimes,
who are already of a bad sort,
and moreover, their longing for home is intensified,
hoping for chaos and calamity,
even more than the garrison troops.
This can be called misguided deployment.
This is the first failure.
Recently, authority has shifted to subordinates,
and control has been lost by the court.
The generals' orders are rarely carried out by the army,
and the state's laws and regulations cannot be applied to the generals.
They strive to accommodate and nurture each other.
Accommodate,
means to follow,
meaning they follow each other in nurturing wrongdoing.
If they wish to reward one who has merit,
they then worry that those without merit will become restless;
if they wish to punish one who is guilty,
they again worry that his accomplices will be anxious.
Crimes are concealed and tolerated, not exposed;
merits are viewed with suspicion and not rewarded.
The path of indulgence
has reached this point.
Therefore, those who forget themselves and exert loyalty are ridiculed by their peers,
those who lead the charge and scale walls first incur the resentment of the soldiers,
those who cause army defeat and state distress feel no shame or fear,
and those who delay rescue and miss deadlines consider themselves clever and capable.
This is why righteous men are pained at heart,
and brave men become disheartened.
This can be called deficient accountability and demands.
This is the second failure.
Whenever the barbarians invade,
the generals and commanders pass responsibility to each other,
with none daring to take charge.
They exaggerate the enemy's strength in reports to the court,
then claim their troops are too few to resist.
The court does not investigate this,
but only strives to levy and dispatch more troops.
This does not aid the work of defense,
but greatly increases the burden of supply.
Greatly,
read as zhí yòng.
Demands grow daily more numerous,
using the resources of registered households who are ruined and bankrupted,
combined with the profits from the officials' salt monopoly and liquor taxes,
all the income combined,
is spent annually on border affairs.
This can be called wealth exhausted by excessive troops.
This is the third failure.
The entire military force of Tibet,
is only comparable to that of a dozen or so large commanderies in China.
Yet when they move, China fears their numbers and dares not resist;
when they are still, China dreads their strength and dares not invade.
What is the reason for this?
It is truly because China's command is divided among many authorities,
while the barbarian foe's leadership is unified.
When leadership is unified,
the people's minds are not divided,
orders are not contradictory,
advances and retreats can be coordinated,
speed and slowness are as desired,
opportunities are not missed.
(Note: "Missed" means violated.)
This is how the few become many,
and the weak become strong.
During the Kāiyuán and Tiānbǎo eras,
controlling the two barbarian tribes in the northwest
relied solely on the three military governors of Shuòfāng, Héxī, and Lǒngyòu.
Since the restoration of the dynasty,
there has been no time for external campaigns,
and those resisting the two barbarian tribes are only the four military governors of Shuòfāng, Jīngyuán, Lǒngyòu, and Hédōng.
(Note: The term "two barbarian tribes in the northwest" is used to distinguish them from the two tribes of Xī and Qìdān.
Since the Kāiyuán and Tiānbǎo eras,
to the west was Tibet,
to the north was the Turks.
Since the restoration,
the so-called two barbarian tribes
are Tibet to the west
and the Uyghurs to the north.)
Those who established headquarters and held authority numbered three envoys.
(See Volume 225, the fourteenth year of the Dàlì era.)
(Note: "Envoy" is pronounced as shǐ, with the meaning of an official.)
The number now reaches forty,
all appointed by special imperial decree,
each with a eunuch supervisor assigned,
allowing them to rival each other,
with no one subordinate to another.
Only when border reports arrive urgently
are they ordered to coordinate military actions.
Since there is no military law imposed from above,
they are merely treated as guests.
Now, the use of military force
relies on momentum and morale;
when morale is concentrated, it is strong;
when dispersed, it dissipates;
when forces are united, they are powerful;
when divided, they become weak.
The current border defenses
are weak in force and low in morale,
which can be said to result from dividing strength among too many generals.
The key to managing the military
lies in examining and distinguishing between the excellent and the inferior,
establishing a system of clothing and food grades accordingly,
so that the capable strive to reach higher levels,
while the incapable resign themselves to their lot.
Although there are differences in treatment, there will be no grievances arising from envy.
Now, in the remote border regions,
the soldiers stationed there long-term
are all veterans of countless battles, scarred and wounded,
enduring extreme hardship and toil year-round.
Yet the clothing and rations provided to them
are only sufficient for themselves,
and are typically shared with their wives and children,
so they often appear cold and hungry.
Meanwhile, the garrison soldiers from Guāndōng
are timid in facing the enemy,
slack in performing duties,
yet the clothing and rations issued to them
exceed those of the border soldiers by several grades.
Moreover, there are those who were originally not imperial guards
but border troops,
whose officers craftily used flattering words
to request nominal affiliation with the Shéncè Army,
without leaving their original posts,
merely changing their
names.
As for the abundant provisions and rewards,
they thus gained threefold benefits.
When the duties are no different but the provisions vary greatly,
unless one has forgotten all sense of fairness,
who can avoid resentment?
This can be said to breed resentment from inequality.
In general, when selecting and appointing generals,
one must first examine their conduct and abilities.
Those suitable are sent;
those unsuitable are dismissed;
those doubtful are not employed;
those employed are not doubted.
Thus, when a general is in the army,
even the sovereign's commands may not always be followed.
(These are words from Sun Tzu's *The Art of War*.)
Now, decisions often come from the imperial heart;
when selecting and appointing military officials,
the priority is to find those easily controlled.
Their forces are divided by increasing their units,
their authority is weakened by lightening their responsibilities,
thus causing them to obey orders even when contrary to military circumstances,
and to obey orders even when contrary to practical needs.
The barbarian enemies charge and attack
as swiftly as wind and storm.
By the time urgent reports reach the court,
a month or more has passed.
Those defending the territory dare not resist the enemy due to insufficient troops,
while those in separate garrisons refuse to send troops without an imperial edict.
After the enemy has plundered and retreated,
they then report achievements and claim victory.
Their defeats and losses are reduced from a hundred to one,
while their captures are inflated from a hundred to a thousand.
The generals, fortunate to have overall control residing at court,
do not worry about being held accountable for offenses.
Your Majesty, in turn, believes that great authority lies in your own hands,
without investigating the actual situation.
This can be said to lose opportunities due to remote control.
This is the sixth failing.
I, in my foolishness, suggest that the system of sending troops from various circuits for autumn defense should be abolished.
Let each circuit provide only clothing and rations,
recruiting garrison soldiers willing to stay, along with barbarian and Han youths, to supply them.
Moreover, open more military farms,
with the government purchasing the harvest.
When the enemy arrives, each person fights for themselves;
when the season comes, each family farms with their own strength.
How can this be compared with those who come and go abruptly?
Also, select civil and military officials of ability to serve as the three commanders of Lǒngyòu, Shuòfāng, and Hédōng,
each overseeing the various military governors along the border.
Those that are not essential
should be merged according to convenience and proximity.
Then reduce wasteful and inflated expenses to enrich resources,
establish a system of clothing and ration grades to harmonize the masses,
broaden the way of delegation to expand their utility,
and uphold the laws of rewards and punishments to examine their achievements.
If this is done,
then the barbarian tribes will be awed and submit,
and the borders will be peaceful and tranquil!"
Although the Emperor could not fully adopt these suggestions,
he held them in high regard.
9 Wéi Gāo sent his general Dǒng Miǎn and others to lead troops out of the Western Mountains,
defeating the Tibetan forces
and capturing over fifty forts and stockades.
10 On Bǐngwǔ,
the Vice Director of the Chancellery and Tongpingzhangshì Dǒng Jìn was dismissed and made Minister of Rites.
11 The King of Yúnnán, Yì Móu Xún, sent three groups of envoys,

one through Róngzhōu (Sòng Bái said: Róngzhōu is located in the area of the Hàn dynasty's Bódào Nán'ān County. Liáng established Róngzhōu, meaning to pacify the barbarians. From the southwest, take the Qū and Xiézhōu route along with Nánníngzhōu, Ānníng, and Yánjǐng Road to reach the Yángjūmiē City where Nánzhào resides, a distance of 2,300 lǐ. According to old records: Róngzhōu is 3,104 lǐ southwest of the capital.),
one through Ānnán,

each carrying raw gold and cinnabar to Wéi Gāo (raw gold refers to unrefined gold ore; cinnabar is extracted from rocks by quarrying. Qián is pronounced qín. Cinnabar is used to show sincerity of heart),
dividing the letters given by Wéi Gāo into three parts as tokens,
all reaching Chéngdū.
Yì Móu Xún submitted a memorial requesting to abandon Tibet and return to the Táng,
and also sent a silk letter to Wéi Gāo,
calling himself the Táng

grandson of the King of Yúnnán, sworn brother of the Tibetan Tsanpo, and King of Rìdōng. (Tibet regarded the King of Yúnnán as a brother; see Volume 216, the tenth year of Tiānbǎo. Enfeoffed as King of Rìdōng; see Volume 226, the fourteenth year of Dàizōng's Dàlì era.)
He also submitted a memorial of congratulations.
The Emperor bestowed an edict upon Yì Móu Xún,
ordering Wéi Gāo to send an envoy to comfort and pacify him.
12 Jiǎ Dān, Lù Zhì, Zhào Jǐng, and Lú Mài served as chancellors.
When officials reported matters,
they yielded to each other and did not speak.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
they memorialized requesting to follow the precedent of the Zhìdé era,
with chancellors taking turns wielding the brush to handle administrative affairs (see Volume 219, the first year of Sùzōng's Zhìdé era, tenth month. Handle, pronounced chǔlǚ; similarly below).
An edict approved this.
Thereafter, they rotated daily.
13. In Jiànnán and the Western Mountains, the various Qiāng tribes had a queen named Tāng Lìzhì.
The queen
was also a different branch of the Qiāng.
To the east, her territory bordered Tǔbō, Dǎngxiàng, and Màozhōu.
To the west, it was adjacent to Sānbōhē.
To the north, it reached Yútián.
It was under the jurisdiction of Yǎzhōu.
The Luónǚ Mán and Báiláng Yí tribes
had a woman as their ruler.
She resided in Kāngyán Chuān,
an area surrounded by steep and perilous terrain on all sides,
with the Ruòshuǐ River flowing southward.
"Tāng Lìzhì"
is written as
"Tāng Lìxī" in the New Book.
According to the Dùyáng Biān: The people of the Nǚmán state
wore high topknots and golden crowns,
with strings of jewels adorning their bodies,
hence they were called Púsà Mán.
At that time, entertainers and musicians thus composed the Púsà Mán tune.
From the Gēlín tribe downward, all the various tribes
were scattered and lived in the Western Mountains.
The Western Mountains are the Snowy Mountains.
Today, in Bǎoníng County of Wēizhōu, there are Snowy Mountains,
connected to Rǔchuān and Báigǒu Lǐng.
They have nine peaks,
with accumulated snow that does not melt even in spring and summer.
Báigǒu Lǐng is connected to the Snowy Mountains.
Wēizhōu
was Wéizhōu in the Táng dynasty.
At this time, each tribe led their followers to submit to the interior.
Wéi Gāo settled them in Wéi, Bǎo, and Bàzhōu.
In the first year of the Tiānbǎo era,
the raw Qiāng tribes were recruited and attached,
and Bàzhōu was established.
Lìzhì, Tuóhū, and Pìhé came to court,
and all were appointed to official positions,
generously rewarded, and then sent back.
14. On Guǐmǎo,
the Vice Minister of Revenue, Péi Yánlíng, memorialized:
"Since I took charge of the Dùzhī,
I have examined and demanded over eight million strings of cash in arrears from the various prefectures,
collected three million strings of cash from the various prefectures' extraction fees,
and received over three hundred thousand strings worth of sample goods.
I request to establish a separate Arrears, Deficits, and Surpluses Quarterly Treasury to manage them."
"Hào"
means deficit or reduction.
"Shèng"
means surplus or profit.
"Shèng"
is pronounced with the yǐ zhèng fān,
and also with the shí zhèng fān.
Three months constitute one quarter.
At the end of every three months,
goods are deposited into the treasury,
hence it is called the Quarterly Treasury.
When goods are deposited monthly,
it is called the Monthly Treasury.
The arrears are all owed by poor people who have no means to repay,
merely leaving the numbers on record.
The extraction fee cash is used up as soon as it is allocated.
The sample goods and dyeing and refining materials are all proper goods of the Left Treasury.
Yánlíng merely placed them in a separate treasury,
inflating the numbers with empty names to confuse the Emperor.
The Emperor believed him,
thinking him capable of enriching the state and favored him,
but in reality, there was no increase.
"Yú shí zhě"
means regarding the actual situation.
In the marshy land west of the capital, several acres of reeds grew.
Yánlíng memorialized, claiming there were several hundred qǐng of marshlands in Cháng'ān and Xiányáng,
suitable for pasturing horses.
The Emperor ordered the relevant officials to inspect,
but there were none,
yet he was not punished.
The Left Supplements Officer Quán Déyú submitted a memorial,
(Quán originally descended from Zhuānxū,
was destroyed by King Wǔ of Chǔ,
and his descendants took the state name as their surname.)
"Shàng"
is pronounced shí zhǎng fān.
"Yánlíng takes the unused portions of regular tax expenditures to fill the 'surplus' and claims it as his own achievement.
For goods previously purchased by the officials,
he pays for them again,
using this to fill separate storage.
Since this spring, the border armies have not been supplied with rations.
If Your Majesty believes Yánlíng is uniquely loyal and independent,
and that people of the time malign the upright with slanderous rumors,
why not send trusted officials to re-inspect,
investigate the whole matter from beginning to end,
and clearly implement rewards and punishments?
Now, public sentiment and numerous voices are clamoring in the court and marketplaces;
could it be that all the scholars and commoners of the capital are forming factions?
Your Majesty should also slightly shift your sagely consideration and examine this."
The Emperor did not comply.
15. In the eighth month,
on Gēngxū,
the Grand Commandant, Secretariat Director, and Xīpíng Loyal and Martial Prince Lǐ Shèng passed away.
16. In winter,
the tenth month,
on Jiǎzǐ,
Wéi Gāo sent his Military Governor's Inspector Cuī Zuǒshí to carry an imperial edict to Yúnnán,
and also personally wrote a letter in reply on silk.
The Military Governor's Inspector
ranks below the Administrative Assistant and Judge,
and above the Yá Tuī.
17. In the eleventh month,
on Yǐyǒu,
the Emperor sacrificed at the Circular Mound,
and pardoned the empire.
18. Liú Shìníng had already become the Military Governor of Xuānwǔ.
(In the third month of the eighth year,
Liú Shìníng was appointed Military Governor of Xuānwǔ.)
Shìníng was licentious, chaotic, and cruel.
When he went hunting, he would often not return for several days,
causing suffering in the army.
The Capital Commander of Troops Lǐ Wànróng had won the hearts of the masses.
Shìníng suspected him,
stripped him of his military authority,
and ordered him to administer affairs in Biànzhōu.
In the twelfth month,
on Yǐmǎo,
Shìníng led twenty thousand troops to hunt in the outer wilderness.
Wànróng entered the headquarters early in the morning,
summoned the over one thousand personal troops left behind,
and deceived them, saying:
"An imperial decree summons the Grand Master to court,
and I am put in charge of the留守 affairs.
Each of you will be rewarded with thirty strings of cash."
The troops all bowed.
He also informed the outer camp troops,
who all obeyed his orders.
He then divided troops to close the city gates,
and sent someone galloping to inform Shìníng, saying:
"An imperial decree summons the Grand Master.
You should quickly take to the road.
'Jí'
means to proceed.
We will send your head as tribute."
Shìníng knew the troops would not serve him,
and fled back to the capital with five hundred cavalry.
By the time he reached the Eastern Capital,
all he had left were his servants and concubines.
Upon reaching the capital,
he was ordered to return to his residence to observe mourning,
and was forbidden to go out.
The Military Governor of Huáixī, Wú Shǎochéng, heard of the mutiny,
and dispatched troops to station at Yǎnchéng.
Yǎnchéng
was the Yǎn County of the Hàn and Jìn dynasties.
In the Later Wèi, it was abolished and merged into Qūyáng County.
In the early Suí Kāihuáng era, Yǎnchéng County was established,
belonging to Biànzhōu.
At that time, it belonged to Càizhōu,
the northern border of Cài.
To the east was the old city of the Hàn Zhàolíng County,
and to the southeast was the old city of the Later Hàn Zhēngqiāng County.
"Yǎn"
is pronounced yī zhàn fān.
He inquired about the reason for expelling Shìníng.
Wànróng replied with mocking words,
mocking him
to show he had no fear.
Previously,
the Tǔbō (Tibetans) and Huíhú (Uyghurs) contended for Běitíng,
engaging in a great battle,
with heavy casualties on both sides.
(The contention over Běitíng is recorded in the fifth and sixth years of the previous scroll.)
Xiān,
read as xī jiàn fān.
Yìmóuxún (Nanzhao king) declined on the grounds that his state was small,
requesting to send only three thousand men.
The Tǔbō considered this too few;
meaning they thought it insufficient.
Shǎo,
read as shī shào fān.
They then agreed.
Yìmóuxún dispatched five thousand men to advance first,
personally leading tens of thousands of troops to follow closely behind,
marching day and night,
and launched a surprise attack on the Tǔbō.
They fought at Shénchuān,
inflicting a major defeat,
capturing sixteen cities including Tiěqiáo.
Tiěqiáo,
is located southeast of Shīmán.
According to the New Book: In this battle,
Yìmóuxún defeated the Shī and Shùn barbarians,
captured their kings,
and established Báiyá Chéng.
Also according to the New Gazetteer: Traveling south from Kāibiān County, Róng Prefecture,
to Báiyá Chéng,
is nearly three thousand lǐ.
The Biography of Nánzhào states: Nánzhào resided between Yǒngchāng and Yáozhōu,
south of Tiěqiáo.
Jiàng,
read as jí liàng fān;
same below.
They forced the surrender of over a hundred thousand of the enemy's troops.
On Wùxū,
they sent an envoy to present the victory report.
3 The Governor of Yíng Prefecture, Liú Hòng, was pressured by his elder brother Liú Jì,
(The discord between Jì and Hòng began in the eighth year of the previous scroll.)
and thus led his troops of fifteen hundred men and over ten thousand men and women to the capital,
maintaining strict discipline,
with not a single person daring to take even a chicken or dog from others along the way.
The Emperor praised him,
and in the second month,
on Bǐngwǔ,
appointed him as Governor of Qín Prefecture and Military Commissioner of Lǒngyòu,
administering from Pǔrùn.
Lǐ,
means to govern.
Using Pǔrùn as the administrative seat.
He did not set up music or entertainment.
When soldiers fell ill,
Hòng personally attended to them,
and when they died, he mourned them.
4 On Yǐchǒu,
the Military Governor of Yìchéng, Lǐ Róng, passed away.
On Dīngmǎo,
Lǐ Fù, Governor of Huá Prefecture, was appointed as Military Governor of Yìchéng.
Fù,
was the son of Lǐ Qíwù.
Lǐ Qíwù,
was the grandson of Prince Huái'ān, Lǐ Shéntōng.
The Army Supervisor, Xuē Yíngzhēn, frequently interfered in military affairs,
but Tǎn (Lú Tǎn) always resisted him based on principle.
Yíngzhēn often said:
"What Attendant Censor Lú says is fair,
I certainly will not oppose."
Tǎn was later able to escape Yíngzhēn's slander.
Shìyù,
was Tǎn's nominal court rank,
the so-called Xiànxián (Censorate title).
5 The Military Governor of Hénghǎi, Chéng Huáizhí, came to court,
was richly rewarded, and sent back.
6 In summer,
the fourth month,
on Gēngwǔ,
the Xuānwǔ Army mutinied,
but the Acting Military Governor, Lǐ Wànróng, suppressed it.
Previously,
three hundred personal soldiers of Xuānwǔ had long been arrogant and unruly,
and Wànróng disliked them,
sending them to the western capital for autumn defense;
the personal soldiers resented this.
The generals Hán Wéiqīng and Zhāng Yànlín incited the personal soldiers to rebel,
attacking Wànróng;
Wànróng defeated them.
The personal soldiers looted and then dispersed,
many fleeing to Sòng Prefecture,
where the Governor of Sòng Prefecture, Liú Yìzhǔn, treated them generously.
(This shows that Lǐ Wànróng could not control Liú Yìzhǔn.)
Yànlín fled to the Eastern Capital.
Wànróng executed the wives and children of the rebels, numbering several thousand.
Several soldiers shouted in the market:
"Tonight a large army will arrive,
and the city will be breached."
Wànróng arrested and executed them,
reporting that it was the doing of Liú Shìníng.
In the fifth month,
on Gēngzǐ,
Shìníng was transferred to Chēn Prefecture.
7 The chieftain of the Qīnzhōu barbarians, Huáng Shǎoqīng, rebelled,
besieging the prefectural city.
Shǎoqīng,
was a chieftain of the Xīyuán Huángdòng barbarians.
Qiú,
read as cí yóu fān.
After the Shàngyuán period, the Yǒngguǎn Military Commissioner was established,
overseeing Yǒng, Guì, Dǎng, Héng, and other prefectures.
The Emperor sent a eunuch envoy to persuade him to desist.
8 Lù Zhì submitted a memorial stating:
"Nearly half a year has passed since the amnesty following the suburban sacrifices,
yet those who were exiled have still not received the imperial grace."
He then drafted three proposals to submit.
The Emperor sent someone to tell him:
"According to precedent,
demoted officials are to be transferred closer according to the amnesty,
Shǐ Zhào said: Yí,
means to move,
referring to those exiled for offenses who, upon amnesty, are moved to a nearer location.
The current proposals seem somewhat excessive,
and many are near military forces or prefectures and counties along the main routes,
(Dānglù prefectures and counties,
refers to those located along the route to the capital.)
Jìn,
read as qí jìn fān.
Zhì again submitted a memorial,
arguing:
"A ruler treats others with sincerity,
with reproach and anger but no suspicion or resentment,
with punishment and restraint but no hatred or jealousy.
Exiling them serves as a warning against disrespect,
while pardoning them encourages self-renewal;
without warning, authority and punishment gradually encroach,
without encouragement, further dismissals and demotions follow.
Although repeatedly promoted or demoted,
it is not due to favor or dislike.
Enforcing the law temporarily leads to demotion,
but considering talent gradually leads to promotion and reinstatement.
Knowing they may be reused,
who would not strive to improve!
What worry is there about disrupting norms,
what fear is there about harboring resentment!
If, because they were demoted,
they are immediately deemed treacherous and evil,
constantly kept under guard and surveillance,
forever subjected to exclusion and abandonment,
then those who repent have no way to make amends,
and those with talent never see it realized.
It is human nature,
when in dire straits, to think of change;
harboring grief and coveting disorder
may arise from this.
Qī,
means sorrow,
pain.
There are also cases where the territory does not leave the original circuit,
but the local conditions are worse than the old prefecture,
resulting in the hardship of moving households in vain,
actually increasing the disturbance of relocation.
Furthermore,
in the current prefectures and commanderies,
many have military troops,
and in the various territories,
few lack post stations,
causing people suspicion and worry,
which is also not magnanimous.
I humbly request further deliberation and judgment."
The emperor was by nature suspicious and jealous,
not entrusting authority to his ministers.
Regardless of an official's rank,
he would personally select and appoint them.
When the chief ministers submitted recommendations,
he rarely approved them.
And if a minister was once reprimanded or punished,
he was often never employed again for the rest of his life.
He favored appointing people based on their eloquence and quick wit,
failing to obtain sincere and substantial talents.
Advancement and appointment were difficult,
causing talented individuals to be obstructed and stranded.
Lù Zhì submitted a memorial to admonish him,
the gist of which said:
"Promotion is to encourage meritorious service,
'encourage'
means to urge.
'Meritorious service'
means achievement.
These two are used alternately,
the principle operates like a cycle.
If one commits an error after promotion, it serves as a warning for punishment;
after being punished and reforming, one is promoted again.
In this way, the law is not abandoned,
nor are people discarded.
Even minor faults must be punished, yet talents are not exhausted;
therefore, it can make those who are demoted strive diligently to seek reinstatement,
and those who are promoted remain vigilant and diligent in their posts.
'Diligent in their posts'
means to be reverently diligent in their official duties.
Thus, there will be no accumulated resentment below. "
He also said:
"An enlightened ruler does not judge people solely by their words,
nor select officials based on personal impressions.
If one likes goodness but does not choose whom to employ accordingly,
delights in words without verifying the corresponding actions,
promotions and demotions follow personal likes and dislikes,
closeness and distance depend on whether views align or differ,
this is like discarding the marking line and arbitrarily judging straightness and crookedness,
abandoning the scale and weighing lightness and heaviness by hand.
No matter how meticulous,
it cannot be free from error. "
'Yóu'
is the same as 'yóu' (like).
'Chuǎi',
initial reading 'chū wěi fān'.
"For people of average ability and above,
each has their own strengths in turn.
If distinctions are made appropriately,
appointments match their capabilities,
each suited to their nature,
each utilizing their abilities,
and when combined to achieve success,
it is no different from having complete talents.
It only requires clear discernment and magnanimity,
and governing them with proper methods. "
He also said:
"To consider someone capable based on a single pleasing remark
'qiè',
reading 'kǔ yè fān'.
and to hold someone at fault for a single act of opposition without examining their loyalty or treachery,
then if they are pleasing, they are entrusted with responsibilities beyond their limits,
without considering what they cannot achieve;
if they oppose, they are punished excessively,
without forgiving what they are incapable of.
Thus, within their official duties, there is no success,
and between ruler and minister, there is no fixed relationship. "
The emperor did not listen.
Lù Zhì also requested the equitable regulation of finances and taxes,
in six points altogether:
The first,
discussing the flaws of the Two-Tax System,
the gist of which said:
"The old system of taxation and corvée,
was called the Zu, Diào, and Yōng.
Each adult male received one hundred mǔ of land,
and annually submitted two dàn of grain,
called the Zu.
Each household, according to local conditions, submitted a total of two zhàng of silk, either juàn, líng, or shī,
and three liǎng of silk floss,
or in non-silk-producing regions, two zhàng five chǐ of cloth,
and three jīn of hemp,
called the Diào.
For each adult male's annual corvée service,
commutation was collected instead,
calculated at three chǐ of silk per day,
called the Yōng.
The empire was treated as one household,
laws and regulations were uniform,
even if people wanted to move around,
it prevented deceitful practices,
so people had no restless hearts and affairs had fixed regulations.
When the Jié and Hú barbarians threw Huá into chaos,
referring to Ān Lùshān and Shǐ Sīmíng.
population registers were lost due to people fleeing,
and the tax system was ruined by military demands.
At the beginning of the Jiànzhōng era,
all regulations were re-established,
those in charge knew the flaws needed reform but their actions also lost the original intent,
they knew simplification was desirable but their implementation missed the key points.
Generally, to remedy a flaw,
one must thoroughly trace its origin.
If it is a flaw of the times, then only address the times;
if it is a flaw of the law, then completely reform the law.
If the actions are appropriate,
regret will vanish.
The Yìjīng says: If reform is appropriate,
regret will vanish.
'Appropriate',
reading 'dīng làng fān'.
Unlimited demands for supplies,
this was a flaw of the times,
not a flaw of the law.
Yet they hastily changed the Zu, Diào, and Yōng system,
dispatched envoys separately,
to search and scrutinize the commanderies and counties,
checking account books,
taking the year with the highest levy during the Dàlì era in each prefecture as the fixed quota for the Two-Tax System.
The matter is recorded in the 226th scroll, first year of Jiànzhōng.
It must be based on human labor,
therefore, in the former kings' system of taxation,
they necessarily took adult males as the foundation.
Not increasing taxes because of diligent farming,
not reducing the Zu because of abandoning cultivation,
thus sowing and planting increased;
not increasing levies because of productive assets,
not exempting the Diào because of being itinerant,
thus attachment to the land was solidified;
not increasing corvée burdens because of diligence,
not exempting the Yōng because of laziness and neglect,
thus labor efforts were diligent.
In this way,
people were content in their dwellings,
and exerted their full strength.
The establishment of the Two-Tax System,
solely took assets as the criterion,
not taking the person as the foundation.
They never realized that among assets,
some are hidden in bosoms, bags, and boxes,
the items may be valuable but others cannot see them;
referring to merchants hoarding precious goods,
waiting for the right time to profit.
Their value may be low but the masses consider them wealthy.
Referring to those who farm diligently and store grain.
The quantity may be small but daily profits are calculated;
there are assets like houses and tools,
their price may be high but they yield no profit throughout the year.
Referring to those with beautiful residences, extravagant clothing and utensils, boasting for a time.
The categories are truly numerous,
yet uniformly calculating and estimating by strings of cash,
inevitably leads to unfairness and encourages falseness.
Consequently, those engaged in light, mobile assets and fond of moving around,
often escape corvée and taxes;
those devoted to fundamental occupations and establishing settled property,
are often burdened by exactions and demands.
This induces people towards deceit,
drives them to evade service,
labor efforts inevitably slacken,
and tax revenues inevitably fall short.
Furthermore, at the beginning of the system's creation,
'the beginning of the system's creation',
means at the start of legislation.
'Fù',
reading 'fú yòu fān'.
there were differences in the complexity of supplies,
local governors varied in ability,
the corvée and taxes in each locality,
differed greatly in weight,
the dispatched envoys,
held different opinions,
once the reported calculations were fixed,
there were additions but no deductions.
Moreover, items like military supplies and tribute offerings during the Dàlì era,
were already incorporated into the Two-Tax System,
yet now, outside the Two-Tax System,
they still exist concurrently.
I hope for a gradual implementation of equalization and reduction,
to save the devastated people. "
Second,
it is requested that the two taxes be set in terms of cloth and silk,
not calculated in monetary amounts.
The summary states:
"All state taxes
must be measured according to the people's capacity,
and levied according to the suitability of the land.
Therefore, what is collected consists only of cloth, hemp, silk fabrics, silk floss,
and various grains.
The former kings feared that the value of goods might become imbalanced,
and that transactions among people would be difficult to standardize.
Thus, they established the coinage system to regulate the appropriate weight and value.
Bān Gù said: Tàigōng established the Nine Treasuries Circular System for the Zhōu,
where treasure was in gold,
profit in knives,
circulation like springs,
distribution like cloth,
and binding in silk.
Additionally, Zhèng's commentary on the Zhōu Lǐ states: What is stored is called 'spring,'
what circulates is called 'cloth.'
It takes its name from water springs,
as its flow reaches everywhere.
It must pass through this system.
This is the great handle for managing wealth,
the state's authority over profit.
It is held by the officials,
not entrusted to the people.
Thus, grains and silk
are produced by the people;
coins and currency
are created by the state.
Therefore, the laws of our dynasty stipulate:
land tax is paid in grain,
corvée exemption in silk,
household tax in silk fabrics, silk floss, and cloth.
When has there ever been a prohibition on private coinage while using coins for taxation?
The current two-tax system
uniquely diverges from the old regulations.
It merely assesses assets to determine the levy,
then sets taxes in terms of coins and grain,
temporarily converting them into various goods for collection.
This means converting the value of coins and grain to levy other miscellaneous goods.
Convert,
zhī shé fān.
It only considers the convenience of obtaining profits,
without regard for the difficulty of provision.
What is levied is not what is produced,
what is produced is not what is levied.
Consequently, some must raise prices to buy what they lack,
or lower prices to sell what they have.
With one increase and one decrease,
much is already lost.
It is hoped that an investigation will be conducted into the silk and cloth collected in the initial year of the two-tax system in each prefecture,
to assess and compare it with current market prices,
adding where prices are low and reducing where they are high,
taking a moderate average,
and totaling the tax amount in coins,
converting it into a quantity of cloth and silk."
It further states:
"The productive capacity of the land has its limits.
If taken in moderation
and used with restraint,
it will always be sufficient.
If taken without moderation
and used without restraint,
it will always be insufficient.
The abundance or failure of produce depends on Heaven;
the amount of goods used depends on humans.
Therefore, the sage kings established standards,
measuring income to determine expenditure.
Even when encountering disasters,
the people were not impoverished.
When governance declines,
the opposite occurs.
Governance,
meaning the rule and transformation.
There is no consideration for what is lacking.
Jié used the resources of the entire realm and still had insufficiency;
Tāng used only seventy lǐ and had surplus.
This shows that sufficiency or insufficiency depends on whether there is restraint or not."
Third,
discussing how local officials are evaluated based on increasing households, raising taxes, and expanding farmland.
The summary states:
"Those governing the people rarely consider the principle of empathy by putting themselves in others' place,
nor do they embody the utmost impartiality and dedication to the state.
Instead, they repeatedly offer minor favors,
competing to lure cunning migrants,
considering it wisdom and ability to encroach upon neighboring regions,
and viewing the gathering of fugitives as good governance.
Those who leave one place for another are treated as newly registered households and granted exemptions,
gather,
meaning to assemble.
Exemption,
fāng mù fān.
Exemption,
meaning remission.
Only those who remain settled in their homeland,
never moving from beginning to end,
are burdened with increasingly heavy taxes,
and levies are added daily.
This forces the settled population to constantly bear the tax burdens for the idle and wandering,
no different from driving them to migrate
and teaching them deceit and cunning.
This results from local officials' lack of broad understanding,
each selfishly concerned only with their own jurisdiction."
It further states:
"Laws to regulate people
inevitably become flawed over time.
If those administering them do not know how to adjust, modify, and adapt appropriately,
then cunning and falseness will arise,
often fueled by obstruction and encouragement.
It is requested that the relevant authorities be instructed
to carefully establish evaluation criteria.
If within a jurisdiction,
the people become more prosperous,
and the set tax quota yields a surplus,
allow a reduction based on the number of households,
with the amount of reduction determining the grade in performance evaluation.
Comparing the overall tax goods within the jurisdiction,
a reduction of three-tenths per household is considered superior performance,
a reduction of two-tenths is next,
and a reduction of one-tenth is further down.
This does not take increasing households as the highest achievement,
but rather the ability to reduce the tax burden on settled households as the highest achievement.
For officials who increase taxes on existing households,
the comparison and penalties should be similarly applied."
Fourth,
discussing the urgency of tax deadlines.
The summary states:
"Establishing officials and building the state
is to nurture the people;
collecting taxes and acquiring wealth
is to support the state.
An enlightened ruler does not prioritize what supports the state at the expense of what nurtures the people.
Therefore, he must first consider the people's affairs and borrow their spare capacity,
first ensure household sufficiency before collecting surplus wealth."
It further states:
"When sericulture is just beginning,
silk taxes are already demanded;
when farming is not yet finished,
grain rents are hastily collected.
As superiors impose strict demands,
subordinate officials intensify their coercive pressure.
Those who have goods are forced to sell urgently at half their value,
while those without must borrow at double the cost.
It is hoped that tax collection deadlines will be reconsidered and set in detail."
Fifth,
proposing to use tea tax revenue to establish charitable granaries for flood and drought preparedness.
Tea tax,
see above, ninth year.
"Ancient texts speak of reserves for nine years or six years.
The Record of the King's System states: Three years of farming must yield one year's food reserve,
nine years of farming must yield three years' food reserve.
Using a thirty-year cycle to plan state expenditure,
measure income to determine outlay.
A state without nine years' reserves is called insufficient;
without six years' reserves is called precarious;
without three years' reserves is called not a state at all.
This certainly does not mean only enriching state granaries
while neglecting the common people.
Recently, officials proposed levying a tea tax,
estimated to yield about five hundred thousand guàn annually.
The original decree ordered it stored in the Ministry of Revenue,
to aid the people in times of famine.
Now using it to store grain
precisely fulfills the previous intent."
The sixth point,
discussing the powerful families who monopolize land,
whose private levies are heavier than the official taxes,
the summary states:
"Now within the capital region,
for each mu of land,
the official tax is five sheng,
yet private households collect rents that can reach up to one dan per mu,
which is twenty times the official tax.
Even for medium-grade land,
the rent is still half of that.
The land belongs to the sovereign,
and farming is the work of the peasants,
yet the monopolizing factions
unjustly reap the profits."
It further states:
"It is hoped that for all occupied land,
regulations should be established according to the outlined limits,
reducing rents,
and ensuring benefits for the poor.
The law should be valued for its enforcement,
caution should be exercised against severity,
its provisions should be generous to accommodate customs,
its decrees should be strict to punish violations,
slightly reducing the surplus of the wealthy,
and moderately favoring the insufficient.
This does not harm the wealthy,
yet the favor can relieve the poor.
This is the excellent principle of
pacifying the wealthy and comforting the poor,
and should not be abandoned."
The Rites of Zhōu, Office of Earth, states: "To nurture the myriad people with six forms of protection and sustenance: first, caring for the young;
second, supporting the elderly;
third, relieving the destitute;
fourth, comforting the poor;
fifth, being lenient toward the disabled;
sixth, pacifying the wealthy."
