Later Student Tiāntāi
In the tenth year of Zhēnyuán
(Jiǎxū, 794)
1 In the sixth month,
on the first day, Rényín,
Zhāoyì Military Governor Lǐ Bàozhēn passed away.
His son, Palace Censor Jiān, conspired with Bàozhēn's maternal nephew Yuán Zhòngjīng,
secretly concealing the death,
forging a memorial from Bàozhēn,
requesting that official duties be granted to Jiān;
they also forged a letter from his father,
sending Deputy General Chén Rǒng to Wáng Wǔjùn to borrow money and goods.
Wǔjùn angrily said:
"I was close friends with your father,
wishing to jointly support the royal house,
how could I join you in such evil deeds!
I have heard that your father has already died,
nǎi,
means 'you.'
gōng,
means 'elder.'
Yet you dare to inform me,
and even make requests!"
He sent Rǒng back,
conveying a message to reprimand Jiān.
zhì,
means 'to rectify.'
To reprimand with righteous principles.
Zhāoyì Infantry Commander Wáng Yánguì,
a native of Liáng in Rǔzhōu,
Liáng County,
belonged to Hénán Commandery during the Hàn and Jìn dynasties,
later, the Northern Wèi established Rǔběi Commandery,
Suí divided it to establish Chéngxiū County,
while Liáng County remained as before.
Táng placed Chéngxiū County under Rǔzhōu,
so Liáng County was located forty-five lǐ to its southwest.
The Emperor, knowing that Bàozhēn had died,
sent Palace Envoy Dìwǔ Shǒujìn to observe the situation,
and entrusted military affairs to Wáng Yánguì.
Shǒujìn arrived at Shàngdǎng,
the Zhāoyì Army
was headquartered at Shàngdǎng.
After three days,
Jiān led troops to meet Shǒujìn,
Shǒujìn said to him:
"The court already knows that the Grand Councilor has passed away,
juān,
means 'to abandon.'
It means the deceased has abandoned his residence and departed.
The Censor should announce the death and observe mourning."
Jiān was startled,
went out,
and said to the generals:
"The court does not permit Jiān to manage affairs,
what are your opinions?"
No one responded.
Jiān, fearful,
then returned to announce the death,
handing over the official seal and keys to the Military Supervisor.
The official seal,
is the seal of the Military Governor.
jiān,
pronounced as 'xián' in ancient times.
An oral decree was issued ordering him to assume duties,
orally conveying the received imperial decree,
hence called an oral decree.
He was urged to proceed to the Eastern Capital,
and return to his private residence.
qù,
read as 'cù.'
Yánguì attributed all blame to Zhòngjīng,
capturing and executing him.
An edict appointed Yánguì to temporarily manage Zhāoyì military affairs.
2 Yúnnán King Yì Móuxún sent his younger brother Còuluó Liàng
to present maps, local tribute, and the golden seal given by Tǔbō,
requesting to restore the title Nánzhào.
In the barbarian language, 'king' is called 'zhào.'
Their earlier chieftains numbered six,
calling themselves the Six Zhào,
namely Méngxī Zhào,
Yuèxī Zhào,
Làngqióng Zhào,
Téngshǎn Zhào,
Shīlàng Zhào,
Méngshè Zhào.
Méngshè Zhào was located south of the other tribes,
hence called Nánzhào.
Up to Méng Guīyì,
Xuánzōng enfeoffed him as King of Yúnnán,
hence the name Yúnnán.
On Guǐchǒu,
the Court of Sacrifices Vice-Director Yuán Zī was appointed as Envoy to Enfeoff Nánzhào,
Textual Analysis states: The Old Táng History, Nánzhào Biography:
"In the tenth year, eighth month,
Còuluó Liàng was sent to present the Tǔbō seal."
The New Táng History states:
"Yì Móuxún made a covenant with Cuī Zuǒshí at Diǎncāng Mountain,
and defeated the Turks at Shénchuān.
In the sixth month of the following year,
Yì Móuxún was enfeoffed as King of Nánzhào."
According to the Veritable Records,
it was in the sixth month of this year,
both the New and Old Histories are mistaken.
Wéi Gāo's memorials all refer to
"King of Yúnnán,"
while Dòu Pāng's Yúnnán Bié Lù states:
"Yuán Zī was ordered to enfeoff Yì Móuxún as Nánzhào."
This was in accordance with his request,
the name Nánzhào began from this.
In the barbarian language,
'zhào' means 'king.'
The New Táng History states
"King of Nánzhào,"
which is also mistaken.
I note that Yì Móuxún defeated Tǔbō at Shénchuān,
the Textual Analysis mistakenly writes
"Turks."
The inscription reads
"Zhēnyuán Enfeoffment Seal of Nánzhào."
When Zī arrived in their country,
Yì Móuxún knelt facing north to receive the enfeoffment seal,
kowtowing twice,
then feasted with the envoy,
bringing out two silver flat-engraved horse-head trays bestowed by Xuánzōng to show Zī.
He also pointed to an old flutist and a singing girl, saying:
"These are the Kuīcí music bestowed by the Emperor,
Táng's Ten Types of Music includes Kuīcí music,
with instruments: zither, vertical konghou, pipa, five-string, transverse flute, sheng, xiao, bìlì, dálà drum, máoyuán drum, dūtán drum, hóutí drum, jīlóu drum, waist drum, dān drum, qí drum,
each one set,
two bronze cymbals,
four dancers.
They set up five directional lions,
over ten feet tall,
decorated in directional colors,
each lion has twelve people,
in painted clothing,
holding red whisks,
with red stockings on their heads,
called lion attendants.
Kuīcí,
pronounced Qiūcí.
Zī said:
"Nánzhào should deeply remember its ancestors,
and for generations to come, remain loyal to Táng."
Yì Móuxún bowed and said:
"How dare I not respectfully follow the envoy's command!"
3 Yìwǔ Military Governor Zhāng Shēngyún was granted the name Màozhāo.
Textual Analysis states: The Old Táng History, in the account of his father Xiàozhōng's death, mentions the name change.
The Chronological Record places it in the ninth month of this year.
Now following the Veritable Records.
4. The Vice Censor-in-Chief Mù Zàn investigated a treasury official for corruption.
Péi Yánlíng wanted to exonerate him,
shielding the official,
and sought to clear him of the crime.
Péi Yánlíng slandered Mù Zàn,
who was demoted to Assistant Prefect of Ráozhōu.
Court officials feared Péi Yánlíng and averted their eyes.
They were afraid of him and dared not look directly.
(Mù Zàn was the son of Mù Níng.)
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
when Ān Lùshān rebelled,
Mù Níng raised troops in Héběi to suppress him.
5. Wéi Gāo reported defeating Tibet at Éhé Chéng.
In the first year of the Wǔdé era,
Yìzhōu was established on the territory of the former Hàn Cánlíng County,
and within its jurisdiction was Éhé Chéng.
6. In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the first day, Rénshēn,
Wáng Yánguì was appointed as Acting Military Governor of Zhāoyì,
and granted the name Qiánxiū.
Upon hearing that Qiánxiū had been made Acting Military Governor,
Yuán Yì, the Zhāoyì Campaign Commander and Acting Prefect of Míngzhōu,
felt discontent.
He submitted a request to separate Cí, Xíng, and Míng into a separate military district.
(The elite troops of Zhāoyì were mostly in Shāndōng.
The Zhāoyì army was stationed in Lùzhōu,
and referred to Cí, Xíng, and Míng as Shāndōng.)
The Emperor repeatedly sent eunuch envoys to instruct him,
but he did not comply.
The defending general of Línmíng, Xiàhóu Zhòngxuān, surrendered the city to Qiánxiū.
Qiánxiū sent the Prefect of Cízhōu, Mǎ Zhèngqīng, to supervise the deputy general Shí Dìngfān and others, leading five thousand troops to attack Míngzhōu.
Shí Dìngfān led his two thousand troops to defect and join Yuán Yì,
and Mǎ Zhèngqīng withdrew.
An edict appointed Yuán Yì as Prefect of Ráozhōu,
but Yuán Yì did not go.
Qiánxiū personally led troops to attack him,
diverting the Míng River to flood the city.
7. Huáng Shǎoqīng captured Qīn, Héng, Xún, Guì, and other prefectures,
and attacked Sūn Gōngqì in Yǒngzhōu.
8. In the ninth month,
Wáng Qiánxiū defeated Yuán Yì’s troops
and advanced to capture Jīzé.
(Jīzé was originally the territory of Guǎngpíng County in the Hàn dynasty.
In the fourth year of the Wǔdé era, Jīzé County was established,
belonging to Míngzhōu.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì, it is sixty lǐ northeast of the prefecture.)
9. Péi Yánlíng reported that there were too many officials,
and requested that from then on, vacant positions should not be filled,
and their salaries should be collected to enrich the treasury.
The Emperor wanted to repair Shénlóng Temple,
requiring pine trees fifty chǐ tall,
but none could be found.
Péi Yánlíng said:
"I recently saw a valley in Tóngzhōu
with several thousand trees,
all about eighty chǐ tall."
The Emperor said:
"During the Kāiyuán and Tiānbǎo eras, even searching for fine timber near the capital was impossible.
How could there be such trees now?"
Péi Yánlíng replied:
"Heaven produces precious timber
precisely to await a sage ruler to appear.
How could such timber have been found during the Kāiyuán and Tiānbǎo eras!"
Péi Yánlíng reported:
"The Left Treasury has many missing items.
Recently, while inspecting and establishing ledgers,
we found one hundred thirty thousand taels of silver in the dirt,
along with over a million bolts of silk and miscellaneous goods.
(If silk and miscellaneous goods
were left in the dirt,
they should have rotted and become unusable.
Even the most foolish person would know this claim is absurd.
Dézōng did not punish him for this.
What did Péi Yánlíng have to fear then?)
These are surplus items,
and should all be transferred to the miscellaneous treasury to fund special imperial expenditures."
The Vice Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury, Wéi Shàohuá, refused to comply,
and submitted a memorial stating:
"These are all items reported monthly as currently in stock.
I request a thorough investigation."
The chief ministers requested that the Three Judicial Offices conduct a detailed review.
The Emperor did not permit it,
nor did he punish Wéi Shàohuá.
Whenever Péi Yánlíng reported to the Emperor,
he indulged in deceitful and bizarre claims,
saying things others dared not mention and had never heard of,
yet Péi Yánlíng spoke without hesitation.
The Emperor was also quite aware of his absurdity,
but because he enjoyed slandering others,
the Emperor hoped to hear about external affairs through him,
and thus treated him with favor.
(Dézōng favored Péi Yánlíng
not only to hear about external affairs,
but also because his tribute offerings satisfied the Emperor’s desires.)
The court officials feared Yán Líng's favor with the emperor,
and none dared speak out.
Only the Salt and Iron Transport Commissioner Zhāng Pāng, the Governor of Jīngzhào Lǐ Chōng, and the Minister of Agriculture Lǐ Xiān,
whose official duties were related,
occasionally exposed his falsehoods.
Only Lù Zhì alone stood against him personally,
daily stating that he was unfit for use.
In the eleventh month,
on the day Rénshēn,
Zhì submitted a memorial exhaustively detailing Yán Líng's deceit and cunning,
enumerating his crimes and evils.
The summary stated:
"Yán Líng regards extortionate taxation as a superior strategy,
considers deceit and falsehood as excellent plans,
views oppressive exploitation that accumulates resentment as loyal service,
and sees quiet slander and embracing calumny as fulfilling one's duty.
(Zuo Zhuan: Shǎohào had an unworthy son,
who destroyed trust and abandoned loyalty,
glorified and adorned evil words,
embraced slander and harbored wickedness,
to defame great virtue.
The people of the world called him Qióngqí.)
He dares to take what the sages warned against as his conduct and ability.
He can be called the Gònggōng of the Yáo era.
(Shū, Yáo Diǎn: The Emperor said:
'Who can succeed me in my tasks?'
Huāndōu said:
'Gònggōng is widely gathering and displaying merit.'
The Emperor said:
'Alas!
His words are fair, but his actions are contrary;
he appears respectful, but is insolent to Heaven.')
(Gòng,
pronounced gōng.)
(Family Sayings of Confucius: When Confucius was Minister of Justice of Lǔ,
acting as prime minister,
after seven days he executed Shàozhèng Mǎo,
killing him beneath the two observation towers.
Zǐgòng came forward and said:
'This Shàozhèng Mǎo
was a well-known man in Lǔ.
You, Master, upon taking office, began by executing him.
Might this be a mistake?'
Confucius said:
'In the world there are five great evils,
and theft is not among them.
The first is a mind perverse and dangerous,
the second is conduct hypocritical and obstinate,
the third is speech false and sophistical,
the fourth is memory of the ugly and extensive,
the fifth is compliance with wrong and glossing it over.
These five,
if a person possesses even one,
he cannot avoid execution by the gentleman.
And Shàozhèng Mǎo possessed them all.
His dwelling was sufficient to gather followers and form factions,
his discourse was sufficient to adorn and glorify himself to the multitude,
his forceful resistance was sufficient to overturn what is right and stand alone.
This is a villainous hero among men,
who cannot be left unremoved.')
Day by day, month by month, he grows and multiplies.
His hidden secrets certainly have not all been revealed,
and his exposed transgressions are especially difficult to fully enumerate."
He also said:
"If Your Majesty suspects he is bearing slander,
then it is truly appropriate to urgently clarify it for him.
If Your Majesty knows he is without goodness,
how can you then wrongly tolerate and cover for him!"
He also said:
"Your Majesty, merely wishing to preserve and uphold him,
has never once interrogated him.
Yán Líng believes he can deceive and delude,
and no longer fears reflection;
shifting from east to west,
he makes it out as administrative achievement;
taking from here to supply there,
he calls it surplus revenue;
fooling the court,
as if playing children's games."
He also said:
"His capacity for crafty deception,
his words of false accusation,
whenever an affair arises, he immediately acts;
responding to speech, he instantly gives voice;
there is not a day without it,
not a time when he is not doing it.
It is also difficult to fully describe."
He also said:
"In the past, Zhào Gāo called a deer a horse.
(See scroll eight, the third year of Qín Èrshì.)
The principle of things was still the same;
how can it compare to Yán Líng covering up what exists as non-existent,
pointing to what is non-existent as existent?"
He also said:
"Yán Líng's vicious falsehoods
spread throughout the realm.
From high-ranking dukes, ministers, and close courtiers above,
down to the lowly servants and base ranks below—
(Zuo Zhuan: Qiǎn Yǐn Wúyǔ said: The king has the dukes as ministers,
the dukes have the senior officials as ministers,
the senior officials have the gentlemen as ministers,
the gentlemen have the zào as ministers,
the zào have the yú as ministers,
the yú have the lì as ministers,
the lì have the liáo as ministers,
the liáo have the pú as ministers,
the pú have the tái as ministers.)
counted by the tens of thousands in groups—
those able to speak to the emperor about him,
how many are there!
I, your servant, though lowly and mean,
hold the office of chief minister.
My feelings are stirred within my heart;
though I wish to desist, I cannot remain silent."
The memorial was submitted,
but the emperor was displeased,
and treated Yán Líng with even greater favor.
10 In the twelfth month,
Wáng Qiánxiū took advantage of the frozen moat to cross over
and urgently attacked Míngzhōu.
Yuán Yì sent troops to attack him,
and Qiánxiū, failing to win, returned;
at dusk the ice melted,
and more than half of his soldiers died.
11 The Vice Director of the Secretariat and Tongpingzhangshi Lù Zhì, because the emperor treated him with great favor and trust,
whenever affairs were not right,
often strenuously contested them.
Some of his close associates admonished him for being too sharp,
but Zhì said:
"Above, I do not betray the Son of Heaven;
below, I do not betray what I have learned.
I have no other concerns."
Péi Yánlíng daily disparaged Zhì before the emperor.
When Zhào Jǐng entered the ministry,
Zhì had actually recommended him.
Later, Jǐng bore a grudge against Zhì.
(The affair is seen in the previous scroll, years eight and nine.)
Therefore, Yánlíng was even more able to carry out his schemes,
and the emperor, because of this, believed Yánlíng and did not side with Zhì.
Zhì made an agreement with Jǐng to exhaustively discuss Yánlíng's villainy and deceit before the emperor,
but the emperor's anger showed on his face,
and Jǐng remained silent and said nothing.
On the day Rénxū,
Zhì was dismissed and made a Tutor of the Heir Apparent.
(Textual Analysis: Hán Yù's Veritable Records of Shùnzōng states:
"Dézōng had been on the throne for some time,
and increasingly took the reins of power into his own hands,
personally managing minor affairs,
losing the greater substance of a ruler's role.
The chief ministers increasingly could not perform their duties,
and yet commentators said this was because of Zhì."
In general, all who serve as chief minister wish to monopolize power;
how would they willingly seek to lose their posts?
Not employing the chief ministers
was Dézōng's error,
yet blaming it on Zhì—
is this human nature!
Also, Zhì's memorial on the vacancies among court officials states:
"Recently, the assisting ministers have rarely been competent,
yet they have been excessively tolerated and maintained,
merely filling the official posts,
causing Your Sagacious Thoughts to labor,
managing both great and small matters."
This was precisely admonishing Dézōng for not employing his chief ministers and personally managing minor affairs.)
12 Initially,
the King Wén of Bóhǎi, Qīn Mào, died.
His son Hóng Lín died early,
and his clansman Yuán Yì was established.
Yuán Yì was suspicious and cruel,
and the people of the state killed him,
establishing Hóng Lín's son Huá Yǔ,
who became King Chéng,
changing the era name to Zhōngxīng.
Huá Yǔ died,
and they again established Qīn Mào's youngest son Sōng Lín,
who became King Kāng,
changing the era name to Zhènglì.
Bóhǎi, since Dà Zuòróng established the state during the Kāiyuán period,
and his son Wǔ Yì succeeded him,
increasingly grew strong and prosperous.
The various eastern barbarians all feared and submitted to it.
(He changed the era name to Rén'ān.)
Through the Five Dynasties and until the Sòng,
though the Yēlǜ repeatedly sent armies against it,
they could not subdue it.
Therefore, the Comprehensive Mirror narrates its successive reigns in detail.
1 Spring,
second month,
on the day Yǐsì,
Sōng Lín was appointed by imperial edict as Governor of Hūhàn Prefecture and King of Bóhǎi.
(Textual Analysis: The Veritable Records states:
"On Yǐsì,
Dà Lǐng Sōng Lín was appointed King of Bóhǎi Commandery."
Now we follow the New History biography.)
2 After Lù Zhì was dismissed from the post of chancellor,
Péi Yánlíng slandered the Capital Governor Lǐ Chōng, the Commandant of the Guards Zhāng Pāng, and the former Minister of Agriculture Lǐ Xiān, accusing them of being part of Lù Zhì's faction.
At that time, there was a drought.
Péi Yánlíng submitted a memorial stating:
"Lù Zhì and others, having lost power, harbor resentment.
They have been saying among the people:
'There is a drought across the land,
the common people are about to become refugees,
the Ministry of Revenue owes large amounts of fodder and provisions to the various armies,
the soldiers and horses in the army have nothing to eat,
what is to be done about this matter!'
They are saying that the situation is such that nothing can be done about it.
Their intention is not merely to slander me."
A few days later,
the Emperor was hunting in the imperial park,
when it happened that a soldier of the Divine Strategy Army complained:
"The Ministry of Revenue is not providing horse fodder."
The Emperor believed Péi Yánlíng's words to be true,
and hurriedly returned to the palace.
In the summer,
the fourth month,
on the Rénxū day,
Lù Zhì was demoted to Vice Prefect of Zhōngzhōu,
Lǐ Chōng was demoted to Chief Clerk of Fúzhōu,
and Zhāng Pāng was demoted to Chief Clerk of Tīngzhōu.
In the 24th year of the Kāiyuán era,
the mountain caves in the regions of Fǔzhōu and Fúzhōu were opened up,
and Tīngzhōu was established.
According to old records: Zhōngzhōu
is 2,122 lǐ south of the capital.
Tīngzhōu
is 6,173 lǐ southeast of the capital.
Qiáo Zhōu's Bā Jì states: In the 6th year of the Chūpíng era of the Later Hàn,
Línjiāng County was established,
belonging to Yǒngníng Commandery.
This is the old Línjiāng city east of present-day Zhōngzhōu.
In the 2nd year of the reign of the deposed Emperor of the Later Wèi,
it was changed to Línzhōu,
named after Línjiāng County.
The Suí dynasty abolished the prefecture,
merging its territory into Bādōng Commandery.
In the 4th year of the Zhēnguàn era,
Zhōngzhōu was established,
named for its location bordering the Bā frontier,
signifying loyalty and trustworthiness.
Fúzhōu,
originally the territory of Fúlíng County in the Hàn dynasty,
was established as Fúzhōu in the Suí dynasty,
2,350 lǐ south of the capital.
Shàozhōu,
3,400 lǐ southeast of the capital.
Sòng Bái said: Shàozhōu,
was Zhāolíng County in the Hàn dynasty,
renamed Shàolíng by Wú,
and the northern part of Línglíng was separated to form Shàolíng Commandery.
The Suí dynasty established Jiànzhōu,
but soon abolished it,
placing Shàolíng County under Tánzhōu.
The Táng dynasty established Shàozhōu in the 11th year of the Zhēnguàn era.
Initially,
Yáng Chéng was summoned from being a recluse to serve as Remonstrance Advisor,
see the 232nd scroll, year 2.
Chǔ,
Chānglǚ fān.
Before he arrived at the capital,
people all looked forward to his demeanor,
saying:
"Yáng Chéng will certainly remonstrate and argue,
and die at his post."
When he arrived,
the various remonstrance officials were constantly speaking about trivial matters,
and the Son of Heaven became increasingly annoyed and weary of them.
Meanwhile, Yáng Chéng was day and night drinking heavily with his two younger brothers and guests,
and no one could discern his true intentions,
so they all thought he had gained his reputation falsely.
The former Jìnshì Hán Yù from Hénán wrote "Discourse on the Contentious Official" to satirize him,
but Yáng Chéng did not take it to heart.
If someone wanted to visit Yáng Chéng to ask questions,
xiè,
means clean,
or to care about.
Zào,
Qīdào fān.
he would forcibly give them wine.
Sometimes the guest would be the first to get drunk and fall on the mat,
sometimes Yáng Chéng would be the first to get drunk and lie in the guest's lap,
unable to listen to what the guest said.
When Lù Zhì and others were demoted,
the Emperor's anger had not subsided,
and everyone inside and outside the court was fearful,
thinking that the punishment might be severe,
and no one dared to rescue them.
Yáng Chéng heard about it and rose, saying:
"We cannot let the Son of Heaven trust treacherous ministers
and kill innocent people."
He immediately led the Remonstrators Wáng Zhòngshū, Guī Dēng, the Right Rectifiers Xióng Zhíyì, Cuī Bīn, and others to guard the Yányīng Gate.
Yányīng Gate,
is the gate of the Yányīng Hall.
Chéng Dàchāng said: According to the Six Codes,
west of the Xīshànggé Gate of the Xuānzhèng Hall Gate,
is the Yányīng Gate,
and to the left of the gate is the Yányīng Hall.
Therefore, when Yáng Chéng wanted to rescue Lù Zhì,
he arranged with Wáng Zhòngshū and others to guard the Yányīng Hall Pavilion and submit a memorial,
prostrating themselves at the pavilion and refusing to leave.
Shuài,
read as shuài.
Lù Zhì and others were innocent.
The Emperor was greatly angered
and wanted to punish Yáng Chéng and the others.
The Crown Prince interceded on their behalf,
and the Emperor's anger then subsided,
ordering the chancellor to instruct them to leave.
At that time, General of the Imperial Guards Zhāng Wànfú heard that the remonstrance officials were prostrating themselves at the pavilion to remonstrate,
hurried to the Yányīng Gate,
and loudly congratulated them:
"With upright officials in the court,
the world will surely be at peace!"
He then bowed to Yáng Chéng and Zhòngshū and the others one by one,
and then repeatedly shouted
"Long live peace!
Long live peace!"
Wànfú,
a military man,
over eighty years old,
from then on became famous throughout the land.
Dēng,
was the son of Chóngjìng.
Chóngjìng,
was well-versed in the study of rites,
and served four generations: Xuánzōng, Sùzōng, Dàizōng, and the current Emperor.
Yáng Chéng said:
"If Péi Yánlíng is appointed chancellor,
I, Yáng Chéng, will take the white hemp edict and tear it up."
According to Táng precedent,
the Secretariat used yellow and white hemp paper to distinguish the importance of imperial decrees.
Later, the Hanlin Academicians exclusively handled internal decrees,
the Secretariat used yellow hemp,
and all white hemp was kept in the Hanlin Academy,
used for appointing generals and chancellors, and for edicts of amnesty.
Sòng Bái said: According to Táng precedent,
white hemp edicts were all drafted within the inner court,
used for appointing chief ministers, appointing military governors, relieving disasters, and denouncing rebels;
the chancellor received them in the main court.
For edicts appointing chancellors,
the Receptionist received the imperial order,
and after it was proclaimed and praised,
it was then issued to the relevant office.

According to the Hanlin Records: For all amnesty edicts, imperial pronouncements, establishing empresses, appointing crown princes, carrying out major punitive campaigns, appointing or dismissing the Three Dukes and chancellors, and appointing generals,
white hemp paper was used,
without a seal.
Drafting was done on even-numbered days,
waiting until the pavilion gate was locked before being presented.
On odd-numbered days,
all officials assembled at the Xuānzhèng Hall,
the Privy Councilor brought the case,
and exited from the Dōngshànggé Gate.
If appointing or dismissing a chancellor,
it was immediately given to the Receptionist,
others were given to the Secretariat and the Chancellery,
and all were proclaimed by the Receptionist.
If urgent matters of state were involved,
it could also be done on even-numbered days.
For extremely urgent matters,
even on holidays,
officials were summoned to assemble for proclamation.
Àn,
refers to the decree case.
Cè,
refers to the investiture case.
The investiture of a princess also involved the case exiting from the pavilion gate.
Huài,
yīn guài.
There was a man named Lǐ Fán,
the son of Lì Bì.
Yáng Chéng listed all of Péi Yánlíng's faults and evil deeds,
intending to submit a secret memorial about them.
Because Fán was the son of an old friend,
Yáng Chéng's appointment as Remonstrance Advisor
was recommended by Lì Bì.
Fán directly reported this to Péi Yánlíng.
Péi Yánlíng went to see the Emperor first,
and explained everything himself.
When the memorial was submitted,
the Emperor considered it false,
and did not review it.
3 On the Bǐngyín day,
Yōuzhōu reported defeating the Xī king Chuòlì and over 60,000 of his troops.
4 The Uighur Fengchéng Khagan died.
He had no sons,
so the people of the state established his chancellor Gǔduōlù as khagan.
Gǔduōlù’s original surname was Diē.
He was eloquent, intelligent, brave, and strategic.
Since the time of Tiānqīn
(the Uighur Tiānqīn Khagan
was Hégǔduōlù),
the great ministers and various chieftains all feared and submitted to him.
After becoming khagan,
he adopted the surname Yàogěluó.
(The Uighur khagans used the surname Yàogěluó.
Gǔduōlù abandoned his original surname
and adopted this surname to succeed to the state.)
(Chieftain:
pronounced cí yóu.)
(Chief:
pronounced zhī liǎng.)
All the young and immature descendants from Tiānqīn Khagan and above
were brought into the imperial court.
(The imperial court of the Tang.)
5 In the fifth month,
on Dīngchǒu,
Lǐ Wànróng, the acting military governor of Xuānwǔ, and Wáng Qiánxiū, the left army supervisor and acting military governor of Zhāoyì, were both appointed as military governors.
6 On Jiǎshēn,
Lǐ Zìliáng, the military governor of Hédōng, passed away.
On Wùzǐ,
the army supervisor Wáng Dìngyuǎn memorialized requesting that the army commander Lǐ Yuè be appointed as acting military governor.
(Yuè
was a fifth-generation descendant of Shéntōng.
Huái’ān Prince Shéntōng
was a cousin of Emperor Gāozǔ,
who raised troops in Guānxī
and was the first to respond to the righteous banner.
Yuè
is pronounced as yuè;
the same below.)
7 On Gēngyín,
the Secretariat Director Zhāng Jiàn was sent to confer the title of Ténglǐluóyǔlùmòmìshīhéhúlùpíjiā Huáixìn Khagan upon the Uighur Khagan Gǔduōlù.
8 On Guǐsì,
Lǐ Yuè was appointed as the acting military governor of Hédōng
and put in charge of the prefectural affairs.
Yuè deeply felt indebted to Wáng Dìngyuǎn
and requested that an official seal be cast for the army supervisor.
The army supervisor having an official seal began with Dìngyuǎn.
9 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on Bǐngyín, the first day,
Yáng Chéng was demoted to the position of Director of the National University,
due to his remarks regarding Péi Yánlíng.
10 Wáng Dìngyuǎn, relying on his merit toward Lǐ Yuè,
monopolized the military and administrative affairs of Hédōng,
arbitrarily replacing various generals;
Yuè could not fully comply,
and thus a rift developed between them.
Dìngyuǎn, in a fit of personal anger, struck and killed the senior general Péng Lìngyīn,
burying him in horse dung.
The officers and soldiers were all enraged.
Yuè reported the situation,
and when Dìngyuǎn heard of it,
he went directly to Yuè,
drew a knife, and stabbed him;
Yuè fled and escaped.
Dìngyuǎn summoned the generals,
and with a box containing over twenty imperial edicts and letters of appointment,
(box:
a bamboo chest.
Contain:
pronounced dīng lǚ.)
said, “There is an imperial edict
ordering Yuè to go to the capital,
and appointing the army commander Lǐ Jǐnglüè as acting military governor.
(Lǐ Jǐnglüè was resented by Lǐ Yuè,
which likely originated from this.)”
Everyone bowed.
The senior general Mǎ Liángfǔ secretly looked into the box
and saw that all were Dìngyuǎn’s own letters of appointment and the edicts he had received.
He then signaled to the crowd, saying:
“The edicts and appointments are all fake,
and cannot be accepted.”
Dìngyuǎn fled and climbed the Qiányáng Tower.
(The Qiányáng Tower
was likely the south gate tower of the Jìnyáng Palace.)
No one responded,
and he jumped over the wall and fell,
injured by a dead tree stump and dying.
11 In the eighth month,
on Xīnhài,
the Minister of Education and Palace Attendant, Běipíng Zhuāngwǔ Prince Mǎ Suì, passed away.
12 In the intercalary month,
on Wùchén,
Yuán Yì pretended to surrender with Míng Prefecture;
Wáng Qiánxiū sent a deputy general with two thousand men into the city,
and Yì killed them all.
13 In the ninth month,
on Dīngsì,
Wéi Gāo was additionally appointed as the Pacification Commissioner of Yúnnán.
(Using the title of Pacification Commissioner to pacify Nánzhào.)
14 The military governor of Hénghǎi, Chéng Huáizhí,
showed no concern for his soldiers,
hunting in the wilds
for several days without returning.
Huáizhí’s cousin Huáixìn, who was the cavalry commander,
taking advantage of the soldiers’ resentment,
closed the gates and barred him;
Huáizhí fled back to the capital.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on Dīngchǒu,
Huáixìn was appointed as the acting military governor of Hénghǎi.
15 Nánzhào attacked the Tǔbō’s Kūnmíng City
and captured it.
(Kūnmíng City
was northwest of the Western Cuàn,
benefiting from salt ponds.
The Shī and Shùn barbarians
were both of the Wūmán tribe.
The Shī barbarians were northwest of Tiěqiáo,
residing in Dàshīshǎn and Liǎnxúnshǎn.
The Shùn barbarians were four hundred lǐ northwest of Jiànshǎn.
Shǎn:
pronounced shī rǎn.)
1 In spring,
the first month,
on Gēngzǐ,
Yuán Yì, Shí Dìngfān, and others led five thousand soldiers from Míng Prefecture and over ten thousand of their family members to flee to Wèi Prefecture;
the emperor pardoned them and did not inquire further,
ordering Tián Xù to pacify them.
2 On Yǐchǒu,
Hún Jiān and Wáng Wǔjùn were both concurrently appointed as Zhongshu Ling.
On Jǐsì,
Yán Zhèn, Tián Xù, Liú Jì, and Wéi Gāo were additionally appointed as Tongpingzhangshi;
all military governors and surveillance commissioners of the realm
were given additional honorary titles to please them.
3 In the third month,
on Jiǎwǔ,
Wéi Gāo reported the surrender of over twenty thousand southwestern barbarians, including Gāo Wàntáng.
4 On Yǐsì,
the Palace and Park Commissioner Lǐ Qíyùn was appointed as Minister of Rites,
(the Palace and Park Commissioner positions
were likely concurrently held by Lǐ Qíyùn),
while his commissioner duties remained unchanged.
Qíyùn had no talent, ability, or learning,
but solely relied on flattery to gain the emperor’s favor.
Whenever the chief ministers finished their audience,
Qíyùn would be the next to enter and decide on matters;
if he was ill and resting at home,
and the emperor wished to make appointments,
he would often send a palace eunuch to inquire of him.
5 On Bǐngzǐ,
Prince Xiān of Sháo passed away.
(Xiān
was the emperor’s younger brother.)
6 The military governor of Wèibó, Tián Xù, married Princess Jiāchéng;
he had three sons by concubines,
of whom Jì’ān was the youngest.
The princess treated him as her own son
and appointed him as deputy commander.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on Gēngwǔ,
Xù suddenly died;
his attendants concealed his death,
having Jì’ān take charge of military affairs.
(He was fifteen years old.)
On Yǐhài,
the funeral was held,
and Jì’ān was recommended as acting military governor.
7 On Gēngchén,
the emperor’s birthday,
according to precedent,
Buddhist monks and Daoist priests were ordered to debate at the Líndé Hall.
At this time,
Confucian scholars were first ordered to participate.
The Sìmén academician Wéi Qúmóu was witty and eloquent in debate.
(Later, Liú Fāng of the Northern Wèi memorialized: In the twentieth year of Tàihé,
Sìmén academicians were established, and schools were set up at the four gates.
According to the Book of Rites: The Son of Heaven established four schools.
Zhèng’s commentary states: These were the Yúxiáng schools in the four suburbs of Zhōu.
As they were considered too distant,
they were placed at the four gates.
He requested they be moved to the same location as the Imperial Academy,
and this was approved.
The Tang official records: Sìmén academicians
were of the seventh rank, upper grade,
responsible for teaching sons of marquises, earls, viscounts, and barons of the seventh rank and above, as well as commoners’ sons who were outstanding scholars.)
Within a month,
he was promoted to right supplementer,
and began to gain favor.
8 In the fifth month,
on Bǐngshēn,
the military governor of Bīnníng, Zhāng Xiànfǔ, suddenly died.
The army supervisor Yáng Míngyì requested that the capital patrol commander Yáng Cháoshèng temporarily act as military governor.
On Bǐngchén,
Cháoshèng was appointed as military governor of Bīnníng.
9 In the sixth month, on the yǐchǒu day,
the Director of the Left Shence Army, Dòu Wénchǎng, and the Director of the Right Shence Army, Huò Xiānmíng, were both appointed as Protectorate Army Central Commanders.
The Supervisor of the Left Shenwei Army, Zhāng Shàngjìn, and the Supervisor of the Right Shenwei Army, Jiāo Xīwàng, were both appointed as Central Protectorate Commanders.
Initially,
the Emperor established six unified armies,
equivalent to the six ministries,
to accommodate military governors who had been removed from their commands.
The six unified armies were established in the first year of the Xingyuán era;
the matter is recorded in scroll 229.
At this time,
Wénchǎng hinted to the chief ministers that the unified army commanders should be appointed by imperial edict.
The Hanlin Academician Zhèng Yīn
memorialized:
"According to precedent, only the enfeoffment of princes and the appointment of chief ministers use white paper edicts.
Now, if they are used to appoint central commanders,
I do not know whether Your Majesty is specially favoring Wénchǎng,
or if this will become an established regulation?"
"During the Wǔdé and Zhēnguàn eras,
eunuchs were at most supplementary generals with the same status as regular ones,
and very few wore crimson robes.
Since Lǐ Fǔguó,
the regulations have been corrupted.
I am now employing you,
not because there is no partiality.
If edicts are again used to proclaim this to the world,
people will surely say that you forced me to do it."
Wénchǎng kowtowed and apologized.
The edict was then burned,
and it was ordered that from now on, appointments of unified army commanders would be issued by the Secretariat through imperial decrees.
The next day,
the Emperor said to Yīn:
"The chief ministers could not refuse the eunuchs;
it was only upon hearing your words that I realized this."
At this time, Dòu and Huò held power that overshadowed both the court and the provinces.
Many military governors and generals came from the Shence Army,
and even important positions in the central government were filled by their protégés.
10 The Xuānwǔ military governor Lǐ Wànróng fell ill with a wind disorder,
becoming confused and unaware of affairs.
Huò Xiānmíng recommended that the Xuānwǔ deputy officer Liú Mù could be entrusted with military administration.
On the xīnsì day,
Mù was appointed as acting military commander.
11 The Xuānshè observation commissioner Liú Zàn died.
Initially,
because the Emperor had faced hardship and scarcity in Fèngtiān,
after returning to the palace,
he became especially focused on amassing wealth.
Many military governors used tributes to curry favor,
all claiming
"additional revenue beyond taxes" —
turning square into round,
meaning that beyond regular taxes,
they manipulated funds
to generate wealth.
"Surplus from expenditures" —
in reality, they either withheld regular taxes,
or increased levies on the people,
or reduced salaries and benefits,
or engaged in selling vegetables and fruits,
often keeping the proceeds privately,
with only one or two-tenths of the revenue being presented.
Lǐ Jiān in Jiāngxī had monthly tributes,
and Wéi Gāo in Xīchuān had daily tributes.
Later, the prefect of Chángzhōu, Péi Sù from Jìyuán, was promoted to observation commissioner of Zhèdōng due to his tributes;
prefects presenting tributes began with Sù.
When Liú Zàn died,
his administrative officer Yán Shòu took charge of the留守 affairs,
exhausting the government treasury to present tributes,
and was summoned to serve as a vice director in the Ministry of Justice.
Staff members presenting tributes began with Shòu.
Shòu was from Shǔ.
The historians could not ascertain his commandery or county,
so they simply said he was from Shǔ.
12 Lǐ Wànróng's illness worsened.
His son, Lǐ Nǎi, was the military commissioner.
On the jiǎshēn day,
Nǎi assembled the generals and reprimanded Lǐ Zhàn, Yīlóu Shuō, and Zhāng Pī for neglecting military affairs,
banishing them to outer counties.
The Emperor sent the eunuch envoy Dìwǔ Shǒujìn to Biànzhōu.
As soon as the proclamation of安抚 was completed,
over ten soldiers shouted:
"The military commissioner has worked hard without reward;
who is Liú Mù to become acting military commander!"
Mù, afraid,
feigned a stroke
and was carried out.
The soldiers also shouted:
"The granary official Liú Shūhé engages in fraud in disbursements."
They killed and ate him.
They also wanted to cut down Shǒujìn,
but Nǎi stopped them.
Nǎi also killed Yīlóu Shuō and Zhāng Pī.
The capital patrol commissioner, Dèng Wéigōng from Kuāngchéng, had been on good terms with Wànróng from the same hometown;
Wànróng often entrusted him with confidential matters,
and Nǎi also relied on him.
At this point,
Wéigōng conspired with the army supervisor Jù Wénzhēn,
captured Nǎi,
and sent him to the capital.
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the yǐwèi day,
the东都留守 Dǒng Jìn was appointed as同平章事,
concurrently serving as Xuānwǔ military governor,
while Wànróng was made junior guardian of the heir apparent,
and Nǎi was demoted to military advisor of Qiánzhōu.
On the bǐngshēn day,
Wànróng died.
After Dèng Wéigōng captured Lǐ Nǎi,
he took temporary charge of military affairs,
believing he would succeed Wànróng,
and did not send anyone to welcome Dǒng Jìn.
After Jìn received the imperial order,
he immediately set out for his command with only a dozen or so attendants,
without military escort.
When he reached Zhèngzhōu,
no one came to welcome him.
The "Jiǔyù Zhì" states: Zhèngzhōu is 150 lǐ east of Biànzhōu.
Some advised Jìn to stay and observe the situation.
Someone coming from Biànzhōu
said to Jìn:
"Do not enter."
Jìn did not reply
and proceeded.
Wéigōng, surprised by Jìn's swift arrival,
had no time to plan.
When Jìn was over ten lǐ from the city,
Wéigōng led the generals out to welcome him.
Jìn ordered Wéigōng not to dismount,
his demeanor very calm,
and Wéigōng felt somewhat reassured.
After entering,
Jìn still entrusted military administration to Wéigōng.
Initially,
Liú Xuánzuǒ increased the troops in Biànzhōu to 100,000,
treating them generously,
and Lǐ Wànróng and Dèng Wéigōng further increased the generosity.
The soldiers became arrogant
and uncontrollable.
To guard against them,
they camped under the eaves of the government hall,
armed with bows and swords,
and were frequently rewarded with wine and meat.
The day after Jìn arrived,
he abolished all of this.
Dǒng Jìn's reasoning was that these soldiers were the trusted men of the previous commander;
as the new commander, if he also relied on them as confidants,
they would not only fail to protect him but could even cause trouble.
By abolishing the special treatment, he treated all armies equally
and showed he harbored no suspicions.
13 On the wùxū day,
Prince Hán, Lǐ Jiǒng, died.
Jiǒng was the Emperor's younger brother.
14 On the rénzǐ day,
an edict was issued stating that because the Xuānwǔ generals and soldiers, including Dèng Wéigōng, had merit in capturing and sending Lǐ Nǎi,
each was promoted in rank and granted money.
Those who were coerced by Nǎi
to pressure the imperial envoys
were all not questioned.
Coercion refers to being forced to comply.
It means Lǐ Nǎi used his power to coerce his subordinates to pressure the eunuch envoys.
During the Táng dynasty, eunuch envoys were called敕使,
also known as制使.
15 In the eighth month,
on the bǐngwèi day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
16 On the jǐsì day,
Tián Jì'ān was appointed as military governor of Wèibó.
17 On the bǐngzǐ day,
the prefect of Rǔzhōu, Lù Chángyuán, was appointed as acting military commander of Xuānwǔ.
The court discussion held that Dǒng Jìn was gentle and accommodating,
fearing he might not be able to accomplish tasks.
Court discussion refers to deliberations within the court.
"Accommodating" means he complied with all requests,
unable to enforce rules and laws.
Chángyuán was rigid and harsh,
often changing old practices.
Jìn initially approved everything,
but when the plans were completed, he ordered them to be suspended,
thereby bringing stability to the army.
This sets the stage for Chángyuán's misfortune due to his rigidity and harshness.
On the 18th day, bingxu,
Zhào Jǐng, the Vice Director of the Chancellery and Concurrently Vice Director of the Secretariat, passed away.
Earlier,
the Emperor did not wish to have military governors replaced while they were still alive,
and often personally selected a marching commissioner to serve as the reserve commander.
The marching commissioner
was responsible for assisting in military administration,
training in hunting during peacetime,
and enforcing the laws of warfare and defense during campaigns.
He also had exclusive authority over weapons, provisions, military registers, and rewards.
The term "commander"
is pronounced similarly to "suì."
Lǐ Yuè was jealous of him.
When the Uighur envoy Méilù came to offer tribute,
he passed through Tàiyuán.
Lǐ Yuè hosted a banquet for him,
but Méilù argued over seating arrangements,
and Lǐ Yuè was unable to stop him.
Lǐ Jǐnglüè rebuked him,
and Méilù recognized his voice.
He hurried forward and bowed, saying:
"Is this not Lord Lǐ of Fēngzhōu?"
Lǐ Jǐnglüè's confrontation with Méilù
is recorded in the 233rd scroll, third year.
People of the Táng dynasty referred to imperial attendants as "Lord."
Lǐ Zhào's "Supplement to the National History" states:
Chancellors referred to each other as "Hall Elders,"
officials of the two departments as "Chamber Elders,"
Ministers of the Department of State Affairs as "Court Chiefs,"
and censors as "Lord."
Méilù then took a lower seat.
Everyone at the banquet fixed their gaze on Lǐ Jǐnglüè.
Lǐ Yuè grew even more resentful,
so he heavily bribed the Palace Army Commander Dòu Wénchǎng
to have Lǐ Jǐnglüè removed.
At that time, rumors spread that the Uighurs were about to invade,
and the Emperor was worried.
Since Fēngzhōu was in the path of the enemy,
he sought someone capable of defending it.
Dòu Wénchǎng recommended Lǐ Jǐnglüè.
In the ninth month,
on the jiǎwǔ day,
Lǐ Jǐnglüè was appointed as the Regional Defense Commissioner of Fēngzhōu.
The remote border was cold,
with poor soil and impoverished people.
Lǐ Jǐnglüè led the people with diligence and frugality,
and within two years,
supplies were ample and secure,
making the northern border strong.
Lú Mài suffered from a wind ailment,
and on the gēngzǐ day,
Jiǎ Dān observed a private mourning day.
The death anniversaries of parents, grandparents, and great-grandparents were considered private mourning days.
It was said that not a single chancellor was present in the court.
According to Táng regulations:
The chief clerk of the Department of State Affairs

hence he declined on the grounds that troops and provisions were not yet assembled.
This can be discussed with the wise.
11 The Chief Military Inspector of Shānnán West Circuit, Yán Lì, flattered and served Yán Zhèn.
When Zhèn fell ill,
he had Lì act as interim governor,
and in his posthumous memorial recommended him.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the yǐsì day,
Lì was appointed Military Governor of Shānnán West Circuit.
On the 12th day of the eighth month,
Qū Huán, the military governor of Chénzhōu and Xǔzhōu, passed away.
On the yǐwèi day,
Wú Shǎochéng sent troops to raid Línyǐng.
Línyǐng
was an ancient county from the Hàn dynasty,
and during the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Xǔzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is located sixty lǐ southeast of Xǔzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: In the fourth year of the Suí dynasty's Dàyè era,
the county seat was moved from the old city to Línyǐnggāo,
which is actually a hilly area.
(The court) sent the senior general Wáng Lìngzhōng with three thousand troops to rescue it,
but they were all captured by Shǎochéng.
On the bǐngwǔ day,
Shàngguān Sù was appointed as the military governor of Chénzhōu and Xǔzhōu.
Shǎochéng then besieged Xǔzhōu.
Sù wanted to abandon the city and flee,
but the deputy commissioner for army-agriculture colonies, Liú Chāngyì, stopped him, saying:
"The troops in the city are sufficient to deal with the enemy.
Just close the gates and do not engage them in battle.
In a few days,
the enemy's morale will naturally decline.
We, at full strength, can exploit their exhaustion,
and there is nothing we cannot overcome."
Miè
means "nothing" or "none."
Chāngyì recruited a thousand brave soldiers, had them tunnel out from the city wall, and launched a surprise attack on Shǎochéng,
inflicting a major defeat on him.
The city was thus preserved.
Chāngyì
was a man from Yǎnzhōu.
Shǎochéng also attacked Xīhuá.
Xīhuá
was a Hàn dynasty county,
and during the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Chénzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is located eighty lǐ west of the prefecture.
Ān Guóníng, the commander-in-chief of the Chénzhōu and Xǔzhōu armies, was at odds with Shàngguān Sù
and plotted to turn the city over to Shǎochéng.
Liú Chāngyì had him executed through a stratagem.
He summoned Guóníng's subordinates,
giving each two bolts of silk.
He then set ambushes in the alleys,
and anyone seen carrying silk was beheaded,
with none escaping.
On the 13th day, gēngchén,
Liú Quánliàng, the military governor of Xuānwǔ, passed away.
The army, remembering the kindness of Liú Xuánzuǒ,
supported his nephew, the commander-in-chief Hán Hóng of Kuāngchéng, as acting military governor.
When Hóng led troops,
he could discern their character, bravery, and cowardice,
and his commands always ensured they were up to the task.
On the 14th day, bǐngchén,
an edict was issued stripping Wú Shǎochéng of his official titles and ranks,
ordering the various circuits to advance troops to attack him.
On the 15th day, xīnyǒu,
Hán Hóng was appointed as the military governor of Xuānwǔ.
Previously,
Shǎochéng
had made an agreement with Liú Quánliàng to jointly attack Chénzhōu and Xǔzhōu,
with Chénzhōu to be given to Xuānwǔ.
Several of his envoys were still at the guesthouse.
Hóng drove them all out and beheaded them.
He selected three thousand soldiers
to join the other armies in attacking Shǎochéng near Xǔzhōu.
Shǎochéng thus lost his advantage.
(He lost his advantage) because he no longer had accomplices to aid him.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the yǐchǒu day,
Prince Yōng, Yuán, passed away.
He was the son of the Crown Prince,
and the Emperor loved him as his own son.
Upon his death,
he was posthumously honored as Crown Prince Wénjìng.

Yú Dì, military governor of Shānnán Dōngdào; Yí Shèn, military governor of Ānzhōu and Huángzhōu; Wáng Zōng, administrator of Shòuzhōu; along with Shàngguān Sù and Hán Hóng, advanced to attack Wú Shǎochéng,
repeatedly defeating him.
In the eleventh month,
on the rénzǐ day,
Yú Dì reported the capture of Wúfáng and Lǎngshān.
The Later Wèi established the Xiāngchéng Commandery in the area of the Hàn dynasty's Rǔnán and Xīpíng,
and also established the Suìníng County.
In the early Dàyè era of the Suí dynasty, it was renamed Wúfáng.
Wúfáng
was originally a county name from the Hàn dynasty.
Yīng Shào said: Originally the state of Fángzǐ,
the Chǔ state enfeoffed it to King Wú Fūgài,
hence the name Wúfáng.
Lǎngshān
was the location of the Hàn dynasty's Ānchāng County.
The Later Wèi established the Chū'ān Commandery there.
In the 18th year of the Suí dynasty's Kāihuáng era, Ānchāng was renamed Lǎngshān.
During the Táng dynasty, both belonged to Càizhōu.
In the Sòng dynasty, to avoid the taboo name of the Sacred Ancestor,
Lǎngshān was changed to Quèshān.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Wúfáng
is located seventy lǐ northwest of Càizhōu.
Lǎngshān
is located seventy-five lǐ southwest of Càizhōu.
In the twelfth month,
on the xīnwèi day,
the Secretariat Director and Prince of Xiánníng, Hún Jiān, passed away in Hézhōng.
Hún Jiān was enfeoffed as the Prince of Xiánníng Commandery.
Although he reached the highest ranks of general and minister,
he never showed an air of arrogance or self-importance.
Whenever presenting tribute, he always personally inspected it,
and when receiving imperial gifts, he behaved as if he were in the Emperor's presence.
Because of this, he was beloved by the Emperor.
After the Emperor returned from Xīngyuán,
even towards a single prefecture or garrison that had troops,
he always practiced appeasement.
Whenever Jiān submitted a memorial,
if it was not approved,
(according to Táng regulations: When a memorial is approved,
it passes through the Chancellery and the Secretariat;
if not approved,
the memorial is shelved and not forwarded),
he would say, "The Emperor does not doubt me."
Thus, he was able to maintain his reputation and achievements until the end.
The six prefectures of Dǎngxiàng had lived in Shízhōu since the Yǒngtài era.
After Emperor Dàizōng's Yǒngtài era,
the era name was changed to Dàlì.
The six prefectures of Dǎngxiàng tribes
were called Yělì Yuèshī,
Yělì Lóng'ér,
Yělì Juélǜ,
Ér Huáng,
Yě Hǎi,
Yě Sū, etc.
Those living in Qìngzhōu were called the Dōngshān tribe,
and those in Xiàzhōu were called the Píngxià tribe.
After the Yǒngtài era,
they gradually moved to Shízhōu.
The Táng dynasty established the Yǒng'ān garrison commander in Shízhōu
to pacify and control the Dǎngxiàng.
Jiǎn,
ancient pronunciation "gǔ xiàn fān."
The various armies attacking Wú Shǎochéng lacked a supreme commander.
Every time they sent out troops,
each man sought his own profit.
Guī
means to scheme for.
On the yǐwèi day,
the various armies collapsed on their own at Xiǎo Yǐnshuǐ.
Yǐn
is the same as Yǐn,
pronounced yīn,
also pronounced yǐn.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: The Yǐng River flows southeast past Línyǐng County,
where the Xiǎo Yǐn River flows into it.
It then flows east past the north of Xīhuá County,
then south past the north of Rǔyáng County,
then southeast past the north of Nándùn County,
where the Dà Yǐn River flows into it from the west.
Sòng Bái said: Rǔyáng County in Càizhōu
was renamed Yǐnshuǐ in the 17th year of the Suí dynasty's Kāihuáng era.
Nowadays, within its boundaries, there are rivers named Dà Yǐn and Xiǎo Yǐn.
That same year, another Rǔyáng County was established northeast of Shàngcài County.
(The areas) all came under Shǎochéng's control.
At this point, they began discussing the appointment of a commander-in-chief for the campaign.
Fifty thousand Tǔbō troops split up to attack Nánzhào and Xīzhōu.
Yì Móuxún and Wéi Gāo each dispatched troops to defend against them.
The Tǔbō returned without achieving anything.
In spring,
the first month,
the four armies of Héngjì, Yìdìng, Chénxǔ, and Héyáng engaged Wú Shǎochéng in battle,
but all were unsuccessful and retreated.
Hán Quányì, the military governor of Xiàsuí, originally came from the Shéncè Army.
The Palace Army Commander Dòu Wénchǎng favored and esteemed him,
recommending him to the Emperor,
to have him command the various armies against Wú Shǎochéng.
In the second month,
on the yǐyǒu day,
Quányì was appointed as the commander-in-chief of the campaign against Càizhōu from all sides,
with troops from seventeen circuits all under Quányì's command.
(This sets the stage for Hán Quányì's later military defeat.)
8. The military governor of Xú, Sì, and Háo, Zhāng Jiànfēng, had garrisoned Péngchéng for over ten years.
In the fourth year of the Zhēnyuán era,
Zhāng Jiànfēng was garrisoning Péngchéng.
He fell gravely ill,
and requested the appointment of a replacement.
On the Xīnhài day,
Wéi Xiàqīng, the prefect of Sūzhōu, was appointed as the marching commander of Xú, Sì, and Háo.
Before the imperial edict arrived,
Jiànfēng had already passed away.
Xiàqīng was
a cousin of Wéi Zhíyí.
The administrative assistant of Xúzhōu, Zhèng Tōngchéng, assumed the duties of acting governor.
Fearing a mutiny by the troops,
and as troops from Zhèxī were passing through Péngchéng,
Tōngchéng wanted to bring them into the city as reinforcements.
The soldiers were enraged.
On the Rénzǐ day,
several thousand men broke open the armory gates with axes,
took out armor and weapons and donned them,
surrounded the headquarters compound,
forced Zhāng Jiànfēng's son, the former military advisor of Guózhōu, Zhāng Yīn, to take charge of the military government affairs,
killed Tōngchéng and several senior officers including Duàn Bóxióng,
and imprisoned the army supervisor.
When the Emperor learned of this,
he appointed the Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel, Lǐ Hōng, as the imperial commissioner to Xúzhōu.
Hōng went directly to the army camp,
summoned the officers and soldiers to announce the imperial decree,
explained the consequences of good and bad actions to them,
removed the shackles from the army supervisor,
and reinstated him to his position.
The rebellious faction did not dare to oppose.
Yīn submitted a memorial requesting to be appointed as acting military governor.
Hōng, considering it not an imperial appointment,
did not accept it,
and had him remove the title,
only then accepting the memorial and returning.
9. Língzhōu forces defeated the Tǔbō at Wūlán Bridge.
The *Tángshū* Treatise on Geography states: Wūlán County in Huìzhōu had Wūlán Pass;
the bridge was likely outside the pass on the Huáng Hé.
10. On the Bǐngyín day,
Wéi Shìzōng re-entered Qiánzhōng.
Earlier this year in the fourth month,
Wéi Shìzōng had been driven out by his subordinate officer Fù Jìn.
Qián,
is pronounced qín,
also pronounced qílián.
11. The observation commissioner of Húnán, Lǚ Wèi of Hézhōng, reported that he had discovered Yáng Lǚ, the prefect of Yǒngzhōu, had taken bribes and embezzled;
Lǚ submitted a memorial claiming that all the collected goods were intended for tribute to the Emperor.
The Emperor summoned him to Cháng'ān.
On the Dīngchǒu day,
he ordered the three judicial commissioners to interrogate him.
When questioned about the whereabouts of the goods and their use,
Lǚ said:
"I have already purchased horses and presented them."
He was further questioned,
"Who was the horse owner?
How old were the horses?"
He replied:
"The horse owner
was a man from all directions,
and I do not know where he is now.
According to ritual,
inquiring about the age of the Emperor's horses is punishable,"
a saying from the *Qūlǐ*.
His replies were generally like this.
The Emperor was pleased with his mention of presenting tribute,
released him,
and only dismissed him from office.
Dézōng's suspicious nature was such that,
even though officials like Yáng Yán and Dòu Cān held the position of chief minister,
they all shifted blame onto the sovereign,
not placing it on the ground.
Yáng Lǚ, caught for corruption, claimed in his memorial it was for tribute,
can it be said this was not shifting blame onto the sovereign!
Dézōng was pleased with his mention of presenting tribute and pardoned his crime.
Now, a fondness for goods
is not a good reputation.
Even if someone is fond of goods,
if labeled with the name 'fond of goods,'
they would certainly be displeased and not accept it.
Why then did Dézōng accept this name so calmly!
I suspect that after Yáng Lǚ's corruption was exposed,
he must have presented something to avoid punishment,
and Dézōng was not merely pleased with his words.
12. On the Bǐngxū day,
Lǐ Shīgǔ, the military governor of Zīqīng, was given the additional title of Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
13. The mutinous soldiers in Xúzhōu submitted a memorial on behalf of Zhāng Yīn requesting the commander's insignia,
but the court did not grant it.
Instead, Dù Yòu, the military governor of Huáinán, was given the additional title of Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì,
and concurrently appointed military governor of Xú, Háo, and Sì,
and ordered to suppress the rebellion.
Yòu prepared a large fleet of boats and ships,
and sent his subordinate officer Mèng Zhǔn as the vanguard.
They crossed the Huái River but were defeated,
and Yòu did not dare advance.
Zhāng Pī, the prefect of Sìzhōu, led troops to attack Yǒng Bridge,
but was badly defeated and returned.
The court had no choice but to appoint Yīn as the Xúzhōu regimental training commissioner,
appoint Pī as acting governor of Sìzhōu,
and Dù Jiān, the prefect of Háozhōu, as acting governor of Háozhōu.
Yòu was additionally appointed concurrent observation commissioner of Háo and Sì.
Háo and Sì were placed under the jurisdiction of Huáinán,
to weaken the authority of Xúzhōu.
*Textual Analysis* states: According to the *Veritable Records*:
"On the Guǐmǎo day of the twelfth month,
Sìzhōu and Háozhōu
were ordered to be placed under the administration of the Huáinán observation commissioner."
This is now mentioned here to conclude the matter.
Jiān
was a fifth-generation descendant of Dù Zhènglún,
who served as chief minister under Tàizōng and Gāozōng.
When Jiànfēng's illness became critical,
Jiān secretly plotted to replace him,
and hurried from Háozhōu to the headquarters.
The staff officer Lǐ Fān and his colleagues
went in to inquire about Jiànfēng's illness.
Upon coming out and seeing Jiān,
Fān said tearfully:
"The Vice Director's illness is so critical,"
(Zhāng Jiànfēng held the title of Vice Director,
hence the address.)
"Now you abandon your prefecture and come here,
what is your intention!
You should leave quickly.
Otherwise,
I will report you."
Jiān, taken by surprise and caught off guard,
immediately returned.
After Jiànfēng's death,
Fān returned to Yángzhōu.
Jiān falsely accused Fān of stirring up unrest in the army following Jiànfēng's death.
The Emperor was furious,
and secretly ordered Dù Yòu to have him killed.
Yòu had always held Fān in high regard,
and kept the edict for ten days, unable to bring himself to carry it out.
He then engaged Fān in a discussion on Buddhist scriptures, saying,
"Buddhism speaks of karmic retribution,
does such a thing exist?"
Fān replied:
"It does."
Buddhist scriptures say,
the good and evil deeds a person commits are the cause,
and the fortune or misfortune that follows in response to those deeds is the effect.
"If this is truly so,
you should face events without fear."
He then showed Fān the edict.
Fān's expression did not change,
and he said:
"This is truly retribution."
Yòu said:
"Be careful not to speak of this.
I have already secretly petitioned,
and guaranteed you with the lives of my hundred relatives."
(It was common to refer to one's extended family as 'a hundred mouths.')
He summoned Fān to Cháng'ān.
Upon seeing Fān's dignified and composed demeanor,
the Emperor said,
"How could this man be an evildoer!"
He immediately appointed him as a secretary in the Imperial Library.
14. The king of Xīnluó, Jùnyōng, died,
and the people of the state installed his son, Chóngxī, as king.
15. In autumn,
the seventh month,
Wú Shǎochéng attacked Hán Quányì at Wǔlóu,
and the various armies were again badly defeated.
Quányì fled at night,
and took refuge in Yīnshuǐ County town.
Yīnshuǐ County
was located in the area of the Hàn dynasty's Rǔyáng County.
It was established as Yīnshuǐ County in the Suí dynasty,
and Rǔyáng was merged into it.
In the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Chénzhōu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: It was eighty *lǐ* southwest of the prefecture.
16. Liú Jì, the military governor of Lúlóng, had a younger brother named Yuán who was the prefect of Zhuōzhōu.
Yuán did not obey Jì's orders.
Jì led troops, attacked, and captured him.
17. In the ninth month,
on the Guǐmǎo day,
the military governor of Yìchéng, Lú Cóng, died.
On the Jiǎxū day,
Lǐ Yuánsù, the Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed to replace him.
Jiǎ Dān said:
"Whenever a military governor is appointed from within the army,
there are inevitably preferences and aversions, support and opposition,
with joy and fear being equally divided among the troops,
so the minds of the many are often unsettled.
From now on, I hope Your Majesty will only appoint people from the court,
so as to avoid other changes."
The Emperor agreed.

18. Zhèng Yúqìng, the Vice Director of the Secretariat and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì, was on good terms with Yú Pī, the Vice Director of the Ministry of Revenue and concurrently the Commissioner of Finance.
Regarding matters Pī memorialized about,
Yúqìng often urged the Emperor to approve them.
The Emperor believed they were forming a faction.
On the Gēngxū day,
Yúqìng was demoted to Military Advisor of Chēnzhōu,
and Pī to Registrar of Quánzhōu.
Pī
was the elder brother of Yú Dí.
On the 19th day (Guichou),
Wú Shǎochéng advanced to within several li of the Yīnshuǐ River and set up camp.
Hán Quányì once again led the various armies in retreating to defend Chénzhōu.
The Xuānwǔ and Héyáng troops privately returned to their own circuits.
Only the Chén-Xǔ general Mèng Yuányáng and the Shéncè general Sū Guāngróng led their troops to remain stationed at the Yīnshuǐ River.
Quányì used deception to lure the Zhāoyì general Xiàhóu Zhòngxuān, the Yìchéng general Shí Áng, the Héyáng general Quán Wénbiàn,
and the Hézhōng general Guō Xiāng,
and had them executed,
intending to intimidate the masses.
When Quányì reached Chénzhōu,
the prefect Liú Chāngyì ascended the city wall and said to him:
"The Son of Heaven commanded you, Duke, to attack Càizhōu.
Now you have come here instead.
Chāngyì dares not admit you.
I request that you lodge outside the city."
Afterwards, Chāngyì brought cattle and wine into Quányì's camp to reward the troops.
Quányì was pleasantly surprised,
and inwardly admired him.
On the Jǐwèi day,
Mèng Yuányáng and others engaged Wú Shǎochéng in battle,
killing over two thousand men.
On the 20th day (Gēngshēn),
Tài Cháng Qīng Qí Kàng was appointed as Zhōngshū Shèrén and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
(New Book, Table of Chancellors: Qí Kàng was Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.)
On the 21st day (Guǐhài),
Zhāng Yīn was appointed as Liúhòu of Xúzhōu.
22. In winter,
the tenth month,
Wú Shǎochéng led his troops back to Càizhōu.
Mèng Yuányáng had blunted his advance,
hence he retreated.
Wéi Gāo, hearing that the various armies' campaign against Shǎochéng had achieved nothing,
submitted a memorial stating:
"I request that Hún Jiān and Jiǎ Dān be appointed as Marshals,
to command the various armies. (Hún Jiān died in the twelfth month of last year. Wéi Gāo likely submitted this memorial before Jiān's death.)
(Chóng, meaning difficult.)
(To march out from Jīngchǔ to exterminate the wicked rebels.)
(Wéi Gāo wished to be Marshal,
but this was also grand talk to impress the court.
Would he ever be willing to leave Xīchuān?!)
If, taking advantage of his plea for pardon, he is pardoned,
and the armies of the two Hé regions are disbanded to allow both state and people to rest,
this would also be a secondary strategy.
If one day Shǎochéng's crimes become full and his wickedness ripe,
and he is killed by his subordinates,
then his title and position would again have to be conferred upon another.
This would be eliminating one Shǎochéng
only to create another Shǎochéng,
leading to endless trouble."
Jiǎ Dān said to the Emperor:
"The bandits' intention is likely also to hope for imperial grace and leniency.
I fear we must leave them a way out."
The Emperor agreed.
It happened that Shǎochéng sent a letter and gifts to the supervising army officials seeking vindication.
The supervising army officials reported this.
On the Wùzǐ day,
an edict was issued pardoning Shǎochéng and the officers and men of Zhāngyì,
and restoring their offices and ranks.
(Textual Analysis says: The Veritable Records state:
"On the ninth month, Rényín day,
the Chancellors had an audience in the Yányīng Hall.
Jiǎ Dān memorialized: 'Recently, when Hán Quányì retreated from Wǔlóu,
the bandits did not dare to pursue.
This likely indicates they hope for the state's grace and leniency.
I fear we must leave them a way out.'
The Emperor approved of this."
According to this, Quányì retreated from Wǔlóu to defend the Yīnshuǐ River.
Shǎochéng advanced to camp near the Yīnshuǐ River.
Quányì again retreated to defend Chénzhōu.
This was not a case of them not daring to pursue!
It also says:
"The various armies attacked Càizhōu,
never once forming proper battle arrays to engage the enemy,
yet the imperial armies repeatedly suffered setbacks and routs.
Wú Shǎochéng, knowing the imperial armies were incapable,
sent a letter and gifts to inform the supervising army officials,
wishing to seek vindication.
The Emperor, having accepted Jiǎ Dān's proposal,
and further receiving favorable reports from the supervising army officials,
then restored his offices and ranks."
According to this, if Shǎochéng knew the imperial armies were incapable,
he should have encroached even more.
How would he be willing to seek vindication through the supervising army officials?
It is likely that since Shǎochéng raised troops,
he could not avoid exhaustion,
and therefore sought rest.
This version is not adopted here.)
On the 23rd day (Jǐchǒu),
the Hé dōng Jié dù shǐ Lǐ Yuè died.
On the Jiǎwǔ day,
his Xíngjūn Sīmǎ Zhèng Dān was appointed as Jié dù shǐ.
The Emperor selected someone who could replace Dān,

and because the Xíngbù Yuánwàiláng Yán Shòu had previously presented tribute as a staff officer (Yán Shòu presenting tribute is recorded in the twelfth year of the Emperor's reign. The historian notes that Dézōng was fond of goods, and would firmly remember the names of those who presented tribute),
he was appointed as Xíngjūn Sīmǎ.
24. The Tǔbō were repeatedly defeated by Wéi Gāo.
This year,
their Nǎnggòng, Làchéng, and other nine Jiédùshǐ Yīng, Lóngguān Mǎ Dìngdé led their tribes to surrender.
Dìngdé was intelligent and resourceful.
When the various Tǔbō generals conducted military operations,
they all received his plans and strategies.
He often traveled by post relay to discuss matters.
At this time, because the military situation was repeatedly unfavorable,
he feared punishment,
and thus came to surrender.

(According to the Old Book, it says: The Tǔbō tribal chieftain and concurrently supervising commander of Nǎnggòng, Làchéng and other nine Jiédùshǐ Yǔnǚ Yǔnǚ, and Lóngguān Mǎ Dìngdé, along with eighty-seven of their great generals, led their tribes to surrender.
Dìngdé had plans and schemes.
Yǔnǚ Yǔnǚ understood military strategy and the topography of mountains and rivers.
At this time, because they had achieved no success on the frontier,
they feared punishment and came.
If so, then Yǔnǚ Yǔnǚ is one person,
and Lóngguān Mǎ Dìngdé is another.
Checking the dictionaries,
there is also no character
"Yǔnǚ".
However, the text recorded in the Comprehensive Mirror follows entirely the text from the biography of Wéi Gāo in the Old Book.
It seems the biography of Wéi Gāo and the biography of the Tǔbō in the Old Book contradict each other.
Shuài is read as lǜ.)
