Tiāntāi
The 17th Year of Zhēnyuán (Xīnsì, 801)
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the Jiǎyín day,
Hán Quányì arrived in Cháng'ān.
Dòu Wénchǎng covered up the traces of his defeat.
The Emperor treated him with great courtesy and honor.
Quányì claimed to have a foot ailment,
and was unable to attend court audiences.
He sent his Sīmǎ Cuī Fàng to respond on his behalf.
Fàng took the blame on Quányì's behalf,
apologizing for achieving no merit.
The Emperor said:
"Quányì, as the Zhāotǎo shǐ,
was able to induce Shǎochéng to come.
This is great merit.
Why must one kill people to be considered meritorious?" (Dézōng's perception was deafened and blinded by eunuchs, often like this.)
On the Jiǎxū day,
he returned to Xiàzhōu.
2. Wéi Shìzōng, having entered Qiánzhōu (Shìzōng re-entered Qiánzhōu last year; the event is recorded in the previous scroll. Qián, pronounced qújīn fān, also qílián fān.),
caused great disturbance among the people.
Shìzōng became fearful.
In the third month,
he fled alone to save his life.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Xīnhài day,
the Yòu Jiànyì Dàfū Péi Jí was appointed as Qiánzhōu Guānchá shǐ.
3. In the fifth month,
on the first day, Rénxū,
there was a solar eclipse.

4. The Shuòfāng Bīn, Níng, Qìng Jié dù shǐ Yáng Cháochéng (The Shuòfāng troops were stationed in Bīn, hence the Shuòfāng army title was still prefixed. In reality, he only commanded the three prefectures of Bīn, Níng, and Qìng.)
died on the Yǐyǒu day.
Previously,

Hún Jiān had sent the Bīngmǎ shǐ Lǐ Cháocǎi to lead troops to garrison Dìngpíng. (In the second year of Wǔdé, Dìngpíng County was established from part of Dìng'ān County of Níngzhōu, and still belonged to Níngzhōu. The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is sixty li south of the prefecture. Cháo, pronounced zhíyáo fān. Cǎi, pronounced cāngzǎi fān. Jiàng, pronounced jíliàng fān.)
Cháocǎi requested that his troops be attached to the Shéncè Army.
An edict granted permission.
When Yáng Cháoshèng was critically ill,
he summoned his staff and said:
"I, Cháoshèng, will certainly not recover.
Appointments for the commander of Shuòfāng have often come from within the army itself.
Although this accords with the sentiments of the troops,
it is entirely contrary to the dignity of the state.
Níngzhōu Prefect Liú Nánjīn
is well-versed in military affairs.
He should be made acting commander of the army,
and put in charge of military matters.
By the time the court selects a commander,
there will surely be no cause for concern."
He also handed a handwritten letter to the supervising eunuch Liú Yīngqiàn,
and Yīngqiàn reported it to the court.
The soldiers privately discussed:
"If the court appoints a commander,
we will accept him.
If they appoint Liú,
we will serve him.
But if they appoint a commander from another army,
he will certainly bring his own subordinates with him,
and we will be cast aside.
We must resist that."
On the day Jǐchǒu,
the Emperor sent a palace envoy to observe the mood of the army,
and most in the army favored Nánjīn.
On the day Xīnmǎo,
the Emperor again sent the high-ranking eunuch Xuē Yíngzhēn to carry an edict to Níngzhōu.
The Palace Domestic Service of the Táng had 1,966 high-ranking eunuchs.
Fù,
means again.
On the day Jiǎwǔ,
Yíngzhēn arrived at the army
and proclaimed the edict:
"The troops that Lǐ Cháocǎi commands were originally from the Shuòfāng Army.
Now we intend to merge them
to strengthen the army's power
and intimidate the Róng and Dí tribes.
We appoint Lǐ Cháocǎi as commander,
with Nánjīn as his deputy.
What does the army think of this?"
All the generals accepted the edict.
On the day Bǐngshēn,
the Chief Inspector of Discipline Shǐ Jīng said to the crowd:
"Commander Lǐ has ordered the collection of bows and swords, and is sending two thousand sets of armor."
The soldiers all said:
"Commander Lǐ wants to bring in two thousand of his own men as his trusted aides.
How can our wives and children be safe then!"
That night,
they went to Liú Nánjīn,
wanting to install him as commander.
Nánjīn said:
"To be a military governor is certainly what I desire,
but it cannot be done without the Emperor's command.
Are there no other generals in the army?"
The crowd said:
"Our bows and swords have all been collected by the authorities.
Only the Military Affairs Office still has armor and weapons."
The Military Affairs Office
is where the officer in charge of military matters resides.
Nánjīn said:
"If you gentlemen do not want Cháocǎi as commander,
you should report the situation to the imperial envoy.
To take up arms
is to defy an imperial edict."
He ordered the gates closed and did not let them in.
The soldiers left
and went to the Cavalry Commander Gāo Gù.
Gù fled and hid;
they searched and found him.
Gù said:
"If you gentlemen will follow my words, then it can be done."
The crowd said:
"We will obey your command."
Gù said:
"Do not kill anyone,
and do not plunder gold or silk."
The crowd said:
"Agreed."
Then they went together to the supervising eunuch
and requested that he memorialize the court.
The crowd said:
"Since Liú has already received the court's decree as deputy commander,
he will certainly obstruct our affairs."
They falsely claimed an order from the supervising eunuch,
summoning him to discuss matters,
and killed him when he arrived.
On the day Wùxū,
an imperial decree appointed Lǐ Cháocǎi as military governor of Bīnníng.
That same day,
a messenger reporting the mutiny in Níngzhōu arrived,
and the Emperor recalled the decree,
again sending Xuē Yíngzhēn to investigate the situation in the army.
On the day Rényín,
he arrived at the army.
The army requested that Gāo Gù be appointed,
and Yíngzhēn immediately issued an imperial order appointing Gù to take charge of military matters.
When the decree of Wùxū was reportedly delivered to Bīnzhōu,
the troops in Bīnzhōu were confused,
not knowing whom to follow.
Xuē Yíngzhēn had already ordered Gāo Gù to take charge of military affairs in Níngzhōu,
but then there was also a report that the decree appointing Lǐ Cháocǎi had arrived in Bīn.
Therefore, the troops stationed in Bīn were confused and did not know which order to follow.
And they were on the verge of mutiny.
The acting governor Mèng Zǐzhōu gathered all the elite armored troops inside the government compound,
feasted the soldiers daily,
inwardly to please the hearts of the multitude,
outwardly to intimidate the treacherous faction.
The troops in Bīn did not mutiny,
thanks to Zǐzhōu's strategy.
5. Since Lǐ Qí had gained control of the empire's financial power,
(In the fifteenth year, Lǐ Qí was appointed Commissioner for Salt and Iron Transport for all circuits;
see the previous volume.)
he used bribes to win over powerful nobles,
relying on this to act arrogantly and wantonly,
without any fear or restraint,
embezzling state property,
and officials under his jurisdiction were successively executed without crime.
A commoner from Zhèxī, Cuī Shànzhēn, went to the capital to submit a sealed memorial,
speaking of the evils of the Palace Market, tribute offerings, and the salt and iron monopoly,
and also spoke of Qí's unlawful actions.
The Emperor read it
and was displeased.
He ordered Shànzhēn shackled and sent to Qí.
Qí, hearing of his impending arrival,
first had a pit dug by the roadside.
On the day Jǐhài,
when Shànzhēn arrived,
he was thrown into the pit along with his shackles,
and buried alive.
Those who heard of it far and wide
trembled with fear.
Qí, furthermore, wanting to make plans for his own security,
increased and expanded his troops,
selecting strong and skilled archers, calling them "Wǎnqiáng" (Strong Pullers),
meaning their strength could pull a strong bow.
Dù Fǔ's poem says:
"When pulling a bow, pull a strong one."
Captured Hú and Xī tribesmen assigned to Jiāngnán,
Qí took in and supported.
The Transport Deputy Lú Tǎn repeatedly remonstrated without success,
and he, along with staff officer Lǐ Yuē and others, all left.
Yuē
was the son of Lǐ Miǎn.
Lǐ Miǎn served under Emperors Sùzōng, Dàizōng, and Dézōng,
and during the Zhēnyuán era became chancellor.
6. On the day Jǐyǒu,
Gāo Gù was appointed military governor of Bīnníng.
Gù
was a veteran general,
who won the hearts of the multitude through his generosity and kindness.
The military governor was jealous of him,
placing him in an idle post,
and his colleagues often slighted and insulted him.
But when he was raised to commander,
he took no revenge whatsoever,
and thus the army was pacified.
7. On the day Dīngsì,
the military governor of Chéngdé, Wáng Wǔjùn, passed away.
8. In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the day Wùyín,
the Tǔbō invaded Yánzhōu.
9. On the day Xīnsì,
the Vice Military Governor of Chéngdé, Wáng Shìzhēn, was appointed military governor.
10. On the day Jǐchǒu,
the Tǔbō captured Línzhōu,
killed Prefect Guō Fēng,
razed its walls,
and plundered the inhabitants and Dǎngxiàng tribes before leaving.
Fēng
was the son of Guō Yào.
Yào
was the son of Guō Zǐyí.
The monk Yánsù was captured by the enemy.
Among the enemy generals was one named Xú Shèrén,
who said to Yánsù:
"I am the fifth-generation descendant of Duke Yīng.
(Lǐ Jì
was enfeoffed as Duke of Yīngguó.)
My great-grandfather raised a righteous army but did not succeed,
(referring to Lǐ Jìngyè.
See the events in the second year of Empress Wǔ's Guāngzhái era, volume 202.)
Although for generations we have held official posts and commanded troops,
the thought of our origins has never been forgotten.
But considering the size of the clan,
there was no way to extricate ourselves.
Now I let you return."
And so he released him.
The emperor dispatched an envoy with an edict ordering Wéi Gāo to send troops deep into Tǔbō to divide their forces,
alleviating the threat on the northern frontier.
Alleviate,
means to ease.
They attacked the Wéi, Bǎo, and Sōng prefectures of Tǔbō, as well as the cities of Qījī and Lǎowēng.
Sòng Bái said: Bǎo Prefecture was originally Dìnglián County of Wéi Prefecture,
bordering Tǔbō to the south,
and was the farthest frontier outpost among the barbarian settlements.
In the 28th year of the Kāiyuán era,
the Qiāng barbarians submitted to the interior,
and Fèng Prefecture was established.
During the Tiānbǎo era, it was renamed Yúnshān Commandery,
and in the 8th year,
the administrative seat was moved to Tiānbǎo Army,
and it was renamed Tiānbǎo Commandery.
Soon after, it was lost,
but in the 1st year of the Qiányuán era, it returned and submitted again,
and was then renamed Bǎo Prefecture.
According to the biography of Wáng Yá: The western border of Wéizhōu's Wēifān Stockade reached Qījī City.
It was likely within the boundaries of Mào Prefecture.
11. The Hé dōng military governor Zhèng Dān died suddenly,
without having time to appoint a successor.
The army became clamorous,
and there was about to be a mutiny.
In the middle of the night,
over ten cavalrymen armed with weapons summoned the administrative secretary Lìnghú Chǔ to the army gate,
where the generals surrounded him,
ordering him to draft a final memorial.
Lìnghú Chǔ, amidst the gleaming blades,
took up the brush and completed it immediately.
Chǔ
was a clansman of Défēn.
Lìnghú Défēn served Tàizōng,
suspecting
that after the character "clan"
there should be
"grandson"
and
"great-grandson, great-great-grandson"
and other characters.
Fēn,
is pronounced fǔwén.
On the Wùwǔ day,
Yán Shòu, the marching commander of Hé dōng, was appointed military governor.
12. In the ninth month,
Wéi Gāo reported a great defeat of Tǔbō at Yǎ Prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: Yǎ Prefecture
was originally the territory of Yándào County of Qín,
and the Later Wèi established Méngshān Commandery,
while the Táng established Yǎ Prefecture.
According to the Records of Commanderies and States,
Hànyuán County had Lí Mountain,
which was excavated by the Shǔ governor Lǐ Bīng.
Lí,
is the ancient character for Yǎ,
and the prefecture was named after it.
Old records: Yǎ Prefecture
is 2,723 lǐ southwest of the capital.
13. The Left Shence Army commander Dòu Wénchǎng retired,
and his deputy Yáng Zhìlián replaced him.
14. Wéi Gāo repeatedly defeated Tǔbō,
fighting across a thousand lǐ,
capturing seven cities in total,
five military garrisons,
burning 150 forts,
beheading over ten thousand,
capturing six thousand prisoners,
and receiving the surrender of three thousand households,
and then besieged Wéi Prefecture and Kūnmíng City.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Gēngzǐ day,
Gāo was additionally appointed Acting Minister of Education and concurrently Secretariat Director,
and granted the title Prince of Nánkāng Commandery.
The Nánzhào king Yìmóuxún captured especially many,
and the emperor dispatched a palace envoy to console and reward him.
15. On the Wùwǔ day,
Yán Prefecture governor Dù Yànxiān abandoned the city and fled to Qìng Prefecture.
This was due to pressure from Tǔbō.
The construction of Yán Prefecture was only eight years before this year.
1. In spring,
the first month,
the king of Piào, Móluósīnuó, sent his son Xīlìyí to present tribute.
The state of Piào was 6,800 lǐ southwest of Nánzhào,
and the New Book states: Piào
was ancient Zhūbō,
located 2,000 lǐ south of Yǒngchāng,
and 14,000 lǐ from the capital.
Piào,
is pronounced pízhào.
Through Nánzhào, they had an audience,
and also presented their music.
2. Tǔbō dispatched its chief minister and concurrently military governor of the five eastern frontier circuits, Lùn Mǎngrè, leading 100,000 troops to relieve the siege of Wéi Prefecture.
The Xīchuān troops occupied strategic positions and set an ambush to await them.
When the Tǔbō forces arrived,
a thousand men were sent out to provoke battle,
and the barbarians pursued them with their entire force.
The ambush was sprung,
and the barbarian forces were greatly defeated,
with Lùn Mǎngrè captured,
and more than half of the soldiers killed.
Wéi Prefecture and Kūnmíng ultimately were not taken,
and the troops withdrew.
On the Yǐhài day,
Gāo sent an envoy to present Lùn Mǎngrè.
Examination of discrepancies: The Old Book biography of Wéi Gāo states:
"In the tenth month, an envoy was sent to present Lùn Mǎngrè,"
but now we follow the Veritable Records.
3. The Zhèdōng observation commissioner Péi Sù, having already advanced through presenting tribute,
Péi Sù obtained a carriage through presenting tribute,
as seen in the twelfth year of the previous scroll.
The official Qí Zǒng took over the subsequent duties,
according to the New Táng Book: Sù died in office,
and Qí Zǒng took over the subsequent duties.
In the third month,
on the Guǐyǒu day,
an edict promoted Zǒng to be governor of Qú Prefecture.
The supervising secretary of Cháng'ān, Xǔ Mèngróng, returned the edict sealed,
saying:
"Qú Prefecture has no other concerns,
and Qí Zǒng has no exceptional achievements.
Suddenly granting such an extraordinary reward
deeply shocks public sentiment.
If Zǒng indeed has something worthy of record,
I hope his merits and service will be clearly stated,
and then he may be promoted beyond his rank and transferred to office,
to resolve public doubts."
The edict was then kept within the palace.
On the Jǐhài day,
the emperor summoned Mèngróng,
and consoled and rewarded him.
4. In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Xīnwèi day,
the advisory officer of the Jiā royal household, Gāo Hóngběn, presented matters at the main court.
Prince Yùn of Jiā
was a son of Dàizōng.
Advisory officer,
rank 5a upper,
in charge of planning and discussing matters.
In the Táng Eastern Palace, Hányuán Hall was the main court,
and in the Western Palace, Tàijí Hall was the main court.
The Táng system: When the Son of Heaven resides, it is called yá;
when traveling, it is called jià.
Yá
is the same as yá.
Bū,
means to owe.
On the Yǐhài day,
an edict
stated: "From now on, dukes, ministers, and various officials should not present matters at the main court.
If there is something to present,
they should request an audience at the Yányīng Gate."
Commentators believed:
"Presenting matters at the main court
has not been changed since the Wǔdé era,
serving to communicate public sentiment
and discuss government affairs.
Hóngběn was ignorant,
and it would be acceptable to dismiss him,
but matters should not be abolished because of a person."
5. The Huáinán military governor Dù Yòu repeatedly submitted memorials requesting a replacement.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Dīnghài day,
the Minister of Justice Wáng È was appointed deputy military governor of Huáinán and concurrently marching commander.
6. On the Jǐyǒu day,
the Fūfāng military governor Wáng Qīyào died.
The central army general Hé Cháozōng plotted to start a rebellion,
and at night,
set fires.
The capital defense commander Péi Bīn secretly hid and did not fight the fires,
but at dawn,
captured Cháozōng,
and beheaded him.
Liú Gōngjì, governor of Tóng Prefecture, was appointed Fūfāng military governor,
and Bīn was appointed marching commander.
1. In spring,
the second month,
on the Dīnghài day,
the Ānhuáng Army was renamed Fèngyì.
This was to honor Yǐ Shèn.
2. On the Jǐhài day,
the Ānnán deputy general Wáng Jìyuán expelled its observation commissioner Péi Tài,
and Tài fled to Zhūyuān.
Liú Xù said: Zhūyuān
was a Hàn county name,
and its present location is the territory of Wújūn Píng County.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn renamed it Hǎipíng,
and the Eastern Jìn established Wǔpíng Commandery;
the Sui abolished the commandery and made it Zhūyuān County,
which belonged to Jiāo Prefecture in the Táng.
The Left Infantry and Cavalry Commander Zhào Yún beheaded Jìyuán and his accomplices,
and welcomed Tài back to restore him.
3. On the Jiǎchén day,
Dù Yòu entered the court.
He entered the court from Huáinán.
On the Rénzǐ day, the first day of the month,
Yòu was appointed Acting Minister of Works and concurrently participating in determining government matters;
and Wáng È was appointed Huáinán military governor.
4 The Minister of Ceremonies Wáng Quán requested to relocate the two ancestors, Xiànzǔ and Yìzǔ, to the temples of Démíng and Xīngshèng.
In the second year of the Tiānbǎo era of Emperor Xuánzōng,
Gāo Yáo was honored as Emperor Démíng,
and Liáng Wǔzhāo Wáng was honored as Emperor Xīngshèng,
with temples established in the capital.
Lú,
pronounced like "línrú."
To rectify the position of Tàizǔ facing east;
this was approved.
In the second year of the Jiànzhōng era,
Xiànzǔ was placed in the proper east-facing position,
as recorded in Volume 227.
5 On Yǐhài,
Lǐ Shí, the Minister of Agriculture, was appointed concurrently as the Governor of Jīngzhào.
Lǐ Shí governed with cruelty and tyranny,
yet the emperor favored and trusted him.
Relying on imperial favor, Lǐ Shí became arrogant and proud,
promising recommendations and promotions,
appointing officials out of order,
and falsely accusing and expelling others,
all of which were carried out as scheduled,
causing officials and scholars to fear him and avoid his gaze.
6 In summer,
during the fourth month,
Liú Chāng, the Military Commissioner of Jīngyuán, petitioned to move the seat of Yuán Prefecture to Píngliàng;
this was approved.
In the seventh year, Liú Chāng built Píngliàng,
as recorded in Volume 233.
Yuán Prefecture was originally administered from Gāopíng,
which was called Pínggāo County during the Táng dynasty,
but was captured by the Tǔbō.
7 On Yǐhài,
the Tǔbō sent their minister Lùn Jiárè to present tribute.
8 In the sixth month,
on Xīnmǎo,
Sūn Róngyì, the Deputy Commander of the Right Divine Strategy Army, was appointed as Commander,
and together with Yáng Zhìlián, they became arrogant, indulgent, and sought power.
Yáng Zhìlián was then the Commander of the Left Army.
The Examination of Discrepancies states: According to the Veritable Records:
"In the seventeenth year, sixth month,
the eunuch Yáng Zhìlián was appointed as the Commander of the Left Divine Strategy Army."
"On Bǐngxū in the seventh month,
the palace attendants Yáng Zhìlián and Sūn Róngyì were appointed as Deputy Commanders of the Left and Right Divine Strategy Armies."
"On Wùyín in the ninth month,
Zhìlián was appointed as Commander of the Left Divine Strategy Army."
"On Xīnmǎo in the sixth month of the nineteenth year,
Róngyì was appointed as Commander of the Right Divine Strategy Army."
"On Wùshēn in the tenth month of the twentieth year,
Zhìlián was appointed as Special Adviser, Right Supervisor General, and Commander of the Left Army."
The records are repetitive and contradictory in this manner.
It is likely that in the seventeenth year, sixth month, he was only acting commander,
and in the seventh month, he became deputy commander,
while in the ninth month and the nineteenth year, sixth month, he was formally appointed as commander.
In the twentieth year, tenth month, he was only promoted in rank and given additional titles.
The Old Biography also states:
"Previously, Dòu Wénchǎng retired,
and after the fifteenth year,
Zhìlián and Róngyì became commanders of the Left and Right Armies,
following Dòu's precedent."
This is likely a general account,
and it is not certain that they were appointed as commanders precisely in the fifteenth year.
I note
that "Right Supervisor General"
should be
"Right Gate Supervisor General."
The power of the eunuchs grew even stronger.
9 On Rénchén,
Xuē Pī, the Great General of the Right Dragon Martial Army, was sent as an envoy to the Tǔbō.
10 The Military Commissioner of Chén-Xǔ, Shàngguān Suì, passed away,
and his son-in-law Tián Chěng attempted to coerce his son into succeeding to military authority;
the officer Wáng Pèi,
also a son-in-law of Suì,
learned of the plot,
reported it to the Supervisor Fàn Rìyòng,
and they captured him.
On Yǐwèi,
Liú Chāngyì, the Military Secretary of Chén-Xǔ, was appointed as Military Commissioner.
Wáng Pèi
was from Xǔ Prefecture.
11 From the first month until the seventh month of autumn, there was no rain.
12 On Jǐwèi,
Qí Kàng, the Vice Director of the Secretariat and concurrent Chief Minister, was dismissed due to illness and appointed as a Guest of the Crown Prince.
13 Initially,
the Hanlin Attendant Wáng Pī was skilled in calligraphy,
and Shānyīn's Wáng Shūwén was skilled in chess.
Shānyīn,
an ancient county from the Hàn dynasty,
was abolished during the Suí dynasty and merged into Kuàijī County,
but during the early Táng dynasty, it was re-established as Shānyīn County from Kuàijī.
Both counties were located within the walls of Yuè Prefecture.
They entertained and served the Crown Prince.
Wáng Pī
was from Háng Prefecture.
Wáng Shūwén was cunning and full of schemes,
claiming to have studied and understood governance,
and often took opportunities to speak to the Crown Prince about the hardships of the common people.
Once, the Crown Prince discussed the palace market with his tutors and Wáng Shūwén,
and the Crown Prince said:
"I intend to speak out strongly about this."
Everyone praised him,
but only Wáng Shūwén remained silent.
After they withdrew,
the Crown Prince asked Wáng Shūwén to stay,
and said to him:
"Earlier, you alone remained silent.
Was there a reason?"
Wáng Shūwén replied:
"I am fortunate to serve Your Highness,
and if I have any insights,
I dare not keep them from you.
The duty of the Crown Prince is to attend to meals and inquire about well-being.
According to the records of the heir: morning and evening, he goes outside the main chamber's door,
and asks the attendants:
'How is His Majesty's health today?'
The attendants reply
'Well,'
and the heir shows a pleased expression.
If there is any discomfort,
the attendants inform the heir.
The heir's face shows worry and concern.
When the attendants report recovery,
the heir's expression returns to normal.
When meals are served morning and evening,
the heir must be present,
checking the temperature.
After the meal is finished,
he inquires about the dishes served,
ensuring he knows what was presented,
and instructs the kitchen steward,
before withdrawing.
If the attendants report illness,
the heir personally observes fasting and tends to the patient.
He must respectfully inspect
the food prepared by the kitchen steward.
For medicine during illness,
he must taste it himself.
If the food tastes good,
the heir can also eat;
if the food is bland,
the heir cannot eat his fill either.
Until recovery,
he maintains this practice.
His Majesty has been on the throne for a long time,
and if he suspects the Crown Prince of winning over people's hearts,
how will you defend yourself?"
The Crown Prince was greatly alarmed,
and tearfully said:
"Without you, sir,
I would never have realized this."
From then on, he greatly favored and trusted him,
and he and Wáng Pī became closely associated.
Wáng Shūwén then said to the Crown Prince:
"So-and-so could be appointed as minister,
so-and-so could be appointed as general,
and I hope you will employ them in the future."

He secretly formed alliances with Hanlin Academician Wéi Zhíyí and other prominent officials seeking rapid advancement, such as Lù Chún, Lǚ Wēn, Lǐ Jǐngjiǎn, Hán Yè, Hán Tài, Chén Jiàn, Liǔ Zōngyuán, and Liú Yǔxī,
establishing them as sworn friends.
Others like Líng Zhǔn and Chéng Yì further advanced through their faction,
associating with them daily,
their movements secretive,
with no one knowing their true intentions.
Some military governors secretly sent money and gifts,
forming connections with them.
Lù Chún,
from Wú,
once served as Vice Director of the Left Bureau;

Shīgǔ said to his administrative assistants Gāo Mù and Lǐ Gōngdù:
"Before I become confused,
before,
meaning while.
Illness leads to confusion.
After I die,
whom do you intend to support as commander?"
The two looked at each other and did not answer.
Shīgǔ said:
"Is it not Shīdào?
Human nature dictates that no one would treat their own flesh and blood poorly while treating others well.
However, if an unsuitable commander is installed,
it will not only ruin military administration
but also destroy our clan.
Shīdào is the descendant of a noble family,
yet he does not devote himself to training troops and governing people.
Instead, he specializes in the petty skills of lowly people, considering them his abilities.
Is he truly fit to be commander?
I hope you gentlemen will carefully consider this!"
In the intercalary month,
on Rénxū, the first day,
Shīgǔ passed away.
Mù and Gōngdù kept the death secret and did not announce the mourning,
secretly welcoming Shīdào from Mì Prefecture,
and installing him as deputy military governor.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on Guǐchǒu,
Gāo Chóngwén defeated ten thousand of Liú Pì's troops at Xuánwǔ.
Liú Xù said: Xuánwǔ
was the territory of the Dī people during the Hàn,
renamed Xuánwǔ in the Jìn.
Wǔdài Shǐ Zhì: Xuánwǔ,
formerly called Wǔchéng,
later, the Northern Zhōu established Xuánwǔ Commandery;
in the early Suí Kāihuáng era,
the commandery was abolished and the county renamed,
called Xuánwǔ,
belonging to Zǐ Prefecture in the Táng.
Jiǔyù Zhì: It is located ninety lǐ west of the prefecture.
On Jiǎwǔ,
an edict stated:
"All subsequent reinforcement troops for Xīchuān
shall be entirely placed under Chóngwén's command."
On Rényín,
the Emperor Zhìdé Dàshèng Dà'ān Xiào was buried at Fēnglíng,
Fēnglíng,
located thirty lǐ east of Fùpíng County in Jīngzhào, at Wèngjīn Mountain.
In the eighth month,
on Rénxū,
Lady Guō was made a Noble Consort.
On Dīngmǎo,
the Emperor's son Níng was established as Prince of Dèng,
Kuān as Prince of Lǐ,
Yòu as Prince of Suì,
Chá as Prince of Shēn,
Huán as Prince of Yáng,
Liáo as Prince of Jiàng,
Shěn as Prince of Jiàn.
These all used contemporary prefecture names as the names of their principalities.
Lǐ Shīdào took charge of military affairs,
but after a long time,
the court's appointment had still not arrived.
Shīdào consulted with his officers,
some suggested sending troops to raid the surrounding regions;
Gāo Mù firmly stopped this,
proposing instead to pay the two taxes,
report officials,
implement the salt monopoly,
to demonstrate careful service to the court,
and not to follow the court's actions.
Dù Huángshang requested to take advantage of the unsettled situation to divide the territory;
but as Liú Pì had not yet been pacified,
on Jǐsì,
Shīdào was appointed acting military governor of Pínglú and administrator of Yùn Prefecture affairs.
The Chief Clerk in the Secretariat, Huá Huàn, had long served in the Secretariat,
Chief Clerk in the Secretariat,
equivalent to today's Secretariat officials.
Huá,
pronounced 'hù',
is a surname.
When chancellors discussed matters and disagreed with Guāng Qí,
they would have Huàn convey their intentions,
often achieving what they desired.
Dù Yòu, Zhèng Yīn, and others all lowered their intentions and treated him well.
When Zhèng Yúqìng was discussing matters with the other chancellors,
Huàn pointed out right and wrong from the side,
Yúqìng angrily rebuked him;
not long after,
he was dismissed from his post as chancellor.
Bribes and gifts came to him from all directions without a day's break,
the Secretariat Drafter Lǐ Jífǔ spoke of his arbitrary and unrestrained behavior,
and requested his removal.
The Emperor ordered the chancellors to close the four gates of the Secretariat and conduct a search,
fully uncovering his treacherous activities.
In the ninth month,
on Xīnchǒu,
Huàn was demoted to Registrar of Léi Prefecture,
Sòng Bái said: Léi Prefecture,
was the territory of Xúwén County in the Hàn's Hépǔ Commandery,
Liáng established Hé Prefecture from it,
at the end of Dàtóng, because Héféi was made Hé Prefecture,
this was made Nánhé Prefecture,
renamed Léi Prefecture in the Táng.
His property was confiscated,
amounting to several tens of millions in total.
In this year,
the Uighurs came to offer tribute,
and for the first time brought Manichaeans with them.
Temples were established in China to accommodate them.
The Manichaeans of the Uighurs
were like the Buddhist monks of China;
their religion was also different from that of India.
According to the 19th volume of the Tángshū Huìyào: The Uighur khagan ordered Manichaean monks to advance their teachings into Tang.
On the 29th day of the sixth month of the third year of the Dàlì era,
an imperial edict granted the Uighur Manichaeans
the establishment of temples,
bestowing the name "Dàyún Guāngmíng" (Great Cloud Brightness).
In the first month of the sixth year,
an edict ordered the establishment of one Dàyún Guāngmíng temple each in Jīng, Hóng, Yuè, and other prefectures.
The Tángshǐ Bǔ volume states: The barbarians often discussed government affairs with Manichaean monks,
and temples were established for them in the capital.
Their practice was
to eat only in the evening,
drinking water and consuming vegetables but not dairy products.
The senior Manichaeans
traveled to and from their home country once every few years,
while the junior ones did so annually.
The Tángshǐ Huíhú Lièzhuàn states: In the early years of the Yuánhé era,
they came again to offer tribute,
and for the first time brought Manichaeans with them,
eating only in the evening.
The khagan often governed the state together with them.
Chǔ,
read as Chānglǚ.
They consumed vegetables but not dairy products.
The Uighurs believed in them,
and the khagan sometimes discussed state affairs with them.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the Xīnmǎo day,
the emperor performed sacrifices at the Yuánqiū altar;
he pardoned the empire.
2 The emperor, considering Dù Yòu advanced in years and of great virtue,
treated him with respect and ceremony,
often addressing him as Sītú (Minister Over the Masses) without using his personal name.
Dù Yòu, due to old age and illness,
requested to retire;
an imperial decree ordered that Dù Yòu need not attend court more than two or three times a month,

on other days, he was permitted to return to Fánchuān.
Dù Yòu had built pavilions and viewing towers at Fánchuān,

3 Ménxià Shìláng (Vice Director of the Chancellery) and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì (Participant in Determining Government Matters) Dù Huángcháng
possessed great talent for statecraft but paid little attention to minor matters of conduct,
and therefore could not remain long in the position of chancellor.
On the Yǐsì day,
Dù Huángcháng was appointed Tóng Píngzhāng Shì,

Upon hearing this, Lǐ Jífǔ was moved to tears,

"I, Jífǔ, wandered in Jiāng and Huái for

In the seventh year of the Zhēnyuán era of Emperor Dézōng,

Now that I have become chancellor,
it has been a total of sixteen years.
Jì,
read as Qíjì.
I think of how to repay this virtue,
and it lies solely in recommending the worthy.
However, among the junior officials at court,
I have had little contact or acquaintance,

Péi Jì took up a brush and listed over thirty people;
within a few months,

At the time, it was unanimously praised that Lǐ Jífǔ had obtained the right people.

The Huáng bandits

Chieftain,

Leader,

the fourth month,

Pǔrùn Garrison, Chóngxìn Fortress, Dìngpíng Garrison, □□□, Guīhuà Fortress, Dìngyuǎn Fortress, Yǒng'ān Fortress, and Héyáng County.

Now it says Yòu Shéncè;

This was to appoint border generals.

the eighth month,

Xià

Shǔ

This means to be cautious and fearful,

The Zhènhǎi military commissioner Lǐ Qí also felt uneasy,

The emperor considered this correct,

Lǐ Qí, his deception exhausted,
then plotted rebellion.
Once Wáng Dàn took charge of the acting affairs,

It happened that winter clothing was being distributed.
The Tang system for maintaining troops
included spring clothing and winter clothing.

They dragged him down,

they placed a blade against the imperial envoy's neck,

Before reaching Jīngkǒu,

Lǐ Qí
was a member of the imperial clan,

Troops from Xuānwǔ, Yìníng, and Wǔchāng were summoned

the New Book records it as
"Wǔníng,"

pronounced wǔ gè fān.)

At that time,

"I, Chóngwén,

wanted to seize it first.

The three men knew Lǐ Qí was bound to fail,

Péi Xínglì

(Xuānzhōu was Xuānchéng Commandery.)

The troops were pleased,

That very night,

wrapped him in a curtain,

The strong crossbowmen and foreign auxiliaries fought to kill themselves,
their corpses piled upon each other.
(The matter of Lǐ Qí maintaining strong crossbowmen and foreign auxiliaries is seen in the previous volume, the seventeenth year of the Zhēnyuán era of Emperor Dézōng.)
(Zhěn,
pronounced zhí rèn fān.
Jiè,
pronounced cí yè fān.)
On the Guǐyǒu day,
the army reported the matter.
(The army referred to is the Zhèxī Army.)

the assembled ministers offered congratulations in the Zǐchén Hall.
(The Zǐchén Hall
is located north of the Xuānzhèng Hall.)
The Emperor said:

there have repeatedly been those within the realm who violate the law.
I am ashamed,
what is there to congratulate!"
The chancellors deliberated on executing Lǐ Qí's relatives within the degree of mourning for "great service" and closer.
("Great service" refers to paternal uncles' sons and daughters, i.e., first cousins;
"and closer" refers to the degree of mourning for one year, i.e., uncles, aunts, siblings, etc.)
The Minister of Justice, Lǐ Yì, said:

are all descendants of the Prince of Huái'ān, Jìng.
(The Prince of Huái'ān, Lǐ Shéntōng, was posthumously titled Jìng.)
They are entitled to burial near the imperial tombs and to share in sacrifices at the ancestral temple.
(Lǐ Shéntōng raised troops in response to the righteous army,
and for his merit was buried near the Xiànlíng tomb,
and given a place in the sacrifices at Emperor Gāozǔ's temple.)
If you also wish to execute his brothers,
Yì said:
"Lǐ Qí's brothers
are the sons of the former Commander-in-chief Lǐ Guózhēn.
Guózhēn died in service to the throne,
(The event is recorded in the 222nd volume, the first year of the Bǎoyìng era of Emperor Sùzōng.)
The chancellors considered this reasonable.
On the Xīnsì day,
Lǐ Qí's paternal cousins, such as the Prefect of Sòngzhōu, Lǐ Xiān, and others, were all demoted and exiled.
On another day,
the Emperor summoned Lǐ Jiàng to an audience at the Yùtáng Hall.
In the Tang imperial palace, there was a Yùtáng Hall.
Since Emperor Dézōng, it had often been used as a residence.
Shěn Kuò said: The Yùtáng Hall was located north of the Hànlín Academy.
The Hànlín Academy had a separate northern gate,
to facilitate responding to summonses.
According to the Old Book's biography of Péi Yánlíng: Emperor Dézōng said to Yánlíng:
"One of the beams in the Yùtáng Hall where I reside,
due to its age,
appears to be damaged and worm-eaten,
but I have been unable to replace it."
From this, we know that Emperor Dézōng often resided in the Yùtáng Hall.
Chéng Dàchāng said: Shěn's claim that the northern gate of the Academicians' Institute
was south of the Yùtáng Hall,
to facilitate responding to summonses,
is mistaken.
The Academicians' Institute was west of the Zǐchén and Pénglái Halls.
The Yùtáng Hall itself was east of the Zǐchén Hall,
not south of the Academicians' Institute.
Many Tang academicians had audiences at the Yùtáng Hall.
Lǐ Jiàng's vehement criticism of the palace eunuchs,
and Liǔ Gōngquán's writing by dipping paper and continuing by candlelight,
all took place there.
However, neither the Six Codes nor Lǚ's maps mention this hall.
Yè Shìlín said: The claim that the northern gate of the Academicians' Institute
was south of the Yùtáng Hall,
to facilitate responding to summonses,
is likely inaccurate.
North of the Academicians' Institute was the Hànlín Academy,
and north of the Hànlín Academy was the Shàoyáng Institute.
Even if the Yùtáng Hall were here,
it would be separated by the sleeping halls and the three main halls,
making it impossible for a northern gate to connect directly.
The palace edition of the Tang map does show the Yùtáng Hall,
and its location is south of the Língqǐ Hall.
As for the Língqǐ Hall,
the Cháng'ān Zhì says,
it was east of the Pénglái Hall.
And the Academicians' Institute
was directly west of the Pénglái Hall.
Being separated east and west,
with many other halls in between,
there is no reason for a gate to connect them north-south.
The Cháng'ān Zhì records the Yùtáng Gate, Yùtáng Hall, and Yùtáng Courtyard,
and says Emperor Wénzōng once summoned Zhèng Zhù for an audience in this hall,
and also held audiences with academicians in the Yùtáng Hall.
There was also a separate Yùtáng Courtyard,
in the same location,
indicating it must have been within the Dàmíng Palace,
but its exact location is not specified.
Therefore, I believe the palace map's placement south of the Língqǐ Hall
is correct.
Yuán Zhěn's "Record of the Chief Councillor's Hall" provides further evidence:
It says: When the imperial carriage proceeds to the suburban altars or ancestral temple,
the Chief Councillor may ride a special horse,
following from the Yùtáng Hall through the inner court.
If foreign guests are received at the Lìndé Hall,
he remains on duty within the palace to await.
The inner court
refers to the Zǐchén Hall.
The Tang suburban altars and ancestral temple were south of the capital.
When the emperor performed ceremonies there,
if he did not exit through the Dānfèng Gate,
he would exit through the Chéngtiān Gate,
certainly not detour westward through the Xī Yíntái Gate.
Therefore, the Yùtáng Hall must have provided access to the inner court,
and the inner court must have led to the Dānfèng Gate.
This logic is certain;
and since it is said the hall was east of the Pénglái Hall,
it would be adjacent to the Zǐchén Hall,
which is also certain.
Thus, the palace map's placement
aligns with and elaborates on Yuán Zhěn's record,
and is highly credible.
As for foreign guests being received at the Lìndé Hall,
the Lìndé Hall was east of the Academicians' Institute,
so one could wait at the institute without joining the formal procession.
Considering both statements together,
the Yùtáng Hall must have been east of the Zǐchén Hall,
not west of it.
"There is an extremely strange matter,
which I have been reluctant to mention.
I discussed with Zhèng Yīn about ordering Cóng Shǐ to return to Shàngdǎng,
and later summoning him to court.
Yīn then leaked this to Cóng Shǐ,
who claimed Shàngdǎng lacked provisions,
and requested to obtain food in Shāndōng.
For a minister to betray me like this,
how should he be dealt with?"
Lǐ Jiàng replied:
"If this is true,
exterminating his clan would not be excessive!
However, Yīn and Cóng Shǐ would certainly not admit this themselves.
From whom did Your Majesty learn of it?"
The Emperor said:
"Jí Fǔ secretly memorialized."
Lǐ Jiàng said:
"I have privately heard discussions among officials,
praising Yīn as an excellent scholar.
I fear this may not be true.
Perhaps a colleague wishes to monopolize court affairs,
envying favor and resenting precedence.
I hope Your Majesty will investigate more thoroughly,
and not let people say the Emperor believes slander!"
After a long pause, the Emperor said:
"Indeed,
Yīn would certainly not go this far.
Were it not for your words,
I would have nearly made a mistaken decision."
The Emperor once also casually asked Lǐ Jiàng:
"Remonstrance officials often slander and ridicule court policies,
mostly without factual basis.
I wish to demote one or two of the worst offenders to warn the others.
What do you think?"
He replied:
"This is likely not Your Majesty's own intention,
but surely some treacherous minister is clouding Your Majesty's judgment.
A minister's life or death
depends on the sovereign's favor or displeasure.
How many dare to speak out with remonstrance!
Even those who do remonstrate
ponder day and night,
editing and reducing their words morning and evening,
until by the time it reaches the top,
not even two or three out of ten points remain.
Thus, even when a sovereign diligently seeks remonstrance,
he still fears it may not come,
how much more if he punishes it!
Acting thus
would seal the mouths of all under heaven,
which is no blessing for the state."
The Emperor approved his words and desisted.
On the 12th day, officials requested the Emperor accept the honorific title "The Sagely Civil and Martial Emperor of Profound Wisdom";
on the Bǐngshēn day,
he consented.
Bái Jūyì, the Wèi of Zhōuzhì and proofreader at the Jíxián Institute, composed over a hundred yuefu poems and other verses,

Pínglú Jiédùshǐ Lǐ Shīdào requested to redeem it with his private wealth.
The Emperor ordered Bái Jūyì to draft an edict.
Jūyì memorialized, saying:
"This matter concerns encouragement and moral suasion,
it should come from the court.
What kind of man is Shīdào,
that he dares to seize this virtuous act for himself!
I hope you will command the relevant office to use government funds to redeem it and return it to the descendant."
The Emperor followed this,
taking two thousand strings of cash from the inner treasury to redeem and bestow it upon Wèi Chóu,
and further prohibited mortgaging or selling it.
Chéng Dàchāng says: Wèi Zhēng's residence was in Dànfèng Ward,
directly facing south into Yǒngxīng Ward.
*Huìyào* says: In the fourth year of Yuánhé,
the Emperor, praising Wèi Zhēng's remonstrance,
issued an edict to seek out his former residence.
It had already been mortgaged and sold through several families,
and divided into nine households.
The Emperor took two million cash from the inner treasury to redeem it,
returning it to his family,
and prohibited its mortgage or sale.
10. Wáng Chéngzōng's paternal uncle, Shìzé, because Chéngzōng had presumptuously established himself,
feared disaster would reach the clan,
and along with his advisor Liú Qīchǔ, voluntarily returned to the capital.
*Kǎoyì* says: The Old Biography states:
"Qīchǔ served as an official in Zhènzhōu,
and Wáng Chéngzōng thought very highly of him."
We now follow the *Shílù*.
11. Hànlín Xuéshì Lǐ Jiàng and others memorialized, saying:
"Your Majesty has succeeded to the great treasure,
for four years now,
yet the heir apparent has not been established,
and the ceremonial investiture has not been carried out.
This opens the door for covetous designs,
and violates the principle of grave caution,
which is not the way to uphold the ancestral temple and weightily guard the altars of state.
We humbly hope you will restrain the minor virtue of excessive modesty,
and implement the great ceremony of utmost impartiality."
On the Dīngmǎo day,
an edict was issued establishing the eldest son, Dèng Wáng Lǐ Níng, as Crown Prince.
Níng
was the son of Consort Jì Měirén.
12. On the Xīnwèi day,
Língyán Jiédùshǐ Fàn Xīcháo memorialized requesting to supply the Shātuó
with clothing and provisions for six hundred Tàiyuán soldiers;
this was approved.
The Left Army Imperial Guard Commander Tǔtū Chéngcuǐ concurrently held the position of Commissioner of Meritorious Works.
In the early Tang dynasty,
the Office of Temple and Monastery Supervision was established,
and all Buddhist monks, nuns, Daoist priests, and female Daoist officials in the empire were under the jurisdiction of the Court of State Ceremonial.
Empress Wǔ placed monks and nuns under the Ministry of Sacrifices.
In the fourteenth year of the Kāiyuán era,
Daoist priests and female Daoist officials were placed under the Court of Imperial Clan Affairs.
In the second year of the Tiānbǎo era,
Daoist priests were placed under the Bureau of Titles,
and the Institute for the Veneration of the Mysterious established the position of Grand Academician,
which was held by the Chief Minister,
overseeing the Mysterious Origin Temples and Daoist monasteries in the two capitals.
In the fourth year of the Zhēnyuán era,
the Institute for the Veneration of the Mysterious abolished the Grand Academician position,
and established the Left and Right Street Commissioners of Great Meritorious Works and the Eastern Capital Commissioner of Meritorious Works,
to manage meritorious works,
with the commissioners overseeing the registers of monks and nuns as well as labor services.
In the second year of the Yuánhé era,
Daoist priests and female Daoist officials were placed under the Left and Right Street Commissioners of Meritorious Works.
The *Táng Huìyào* records: Ānguó Temple is located in Chánglè Ward.
In the first year of the Jǐngyún era, an imperial edict designated the former residence of the emperor before his accession as a temple,
and it was named Ānguó based on the original title.
Chéng Dàchāng said: Chánglè Ward
is on the fourth street east of the Vermilion Bird Street.
Its height was exactly modeled on the Huàyuè Stele.
Emperor Xuánzōng erected the Huàyuè Stele in front of the Huàyuè Shrine,
which was over fifty feet tall.
Huà,
pronounced as *huà* with a falling tone.
He requested an imperial order for an academician to compose an inscription,
and said,
"I have already prepared ten thousand strings of cash,
intending to pay for it."
The emperor ordered Lǐ Jiàng to compose it,
and Jiàng submitted a memorial stating:
"Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, and Tāng
never erected steles to proclaim their own sage virtues.
Only Qín Shǐhuáng, during his inspection tours,
carved stones to highly praise himself.
I am uncertain what Your Majesty wishes to emulate!
Moreover, describing the beauty of constructing a temple
merely emphasizes its grandeur and appeal for sightseeing—
how could that glorify and enhance Your Majesty's sage virtue!"
The emperor read the memorial,
and Chéngcuǐ happened to be at his side.
The emperor ordered the stele tower to be pulled down.
Chéngcuǐ said:
"The stele tower is very large,
and cannot be pulled down.
I request that it be dismantled gradually."
He hoped to delay
and find an opportunity to argue again.
The emperor said sternly:
"Use many oxen to pull it down!"
Chéngcuǐ then dared not speak further.
A total of one hundred oxen were used to pull it,
and it finally fell.

Fourth year of the Yuánhé era
(Jǐchǒu, 809)
1 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on Rénxū,
the Censor-in-Chief Lǐ Yíjiǎn impeached the Capital Governor Yáng Píng,
for being corrupt and extravagantly exceeding his authority when he previously served as Military Commissioner of Jiāngxī.
On Dīngmǎo,
Píng was demoted to Assistant Magistrate of Línhè.
Línhè
was a Hàn dynasty county,
belonging to Cāngwú Commandery,
named for being near the Línhè River.
Hence the name.
In the Táng dynasty, it was attached to Hè Prefecture.
He was a descendant of Yuányì in the fifth generation.
Prince Zhèng Yuányì
was a son of Emperor Gāozǔ.
Property, land, and gardens,
which people rely on for livelihood,
are called assets.
"According to old regulations,
unless for rebellion, one's household should not be confiscated."
The emperor then stopped.
None of Píng's relatives or friends dared to see him off,
except for Lìyáng Assistant Magistrate Xú Huì, who alone went to Lántián to bid him farewell.
The Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices Quán Déyù, who had long been on good terms with Huì,
said to him:
"Your sending off Yáng Línhè
is indeed generous,
but might it not bring you trouble?"
Huì replied:
"Since my humble days as a commoner, I received recognition and encouragement from Lord Yáng.
Now that he is being exiled far away,
how could I not bid him farewell?
If someday you, esteemed sir, were to be expelled by slanderers,
would I dare treat you as a mere stranger?"
Déyù sighed in admiration
and praised him at court.
A few days later,
Lǐ Yíjiǎn recommended him for the position of Investigating Censor.
Huì expressed his gratitude, saying:
"In my entire life, I have never had the honor of meeting you, sir.
How did you come to select me?"
Yíjiǎn replied:
"You did not fail Yáng Línhè;
would you be willing to fail the state?"

request officials,

The matter of Lǐ Shīdào
is recorded in the first year of this volume.
"Dé and Dì prefectures have belonged to Chéngdé

each worries about being divided in the future,

Lǚ
means multitude.
Lǚjù
means relying on the multitude to resist the emperor's command.
Chǔ,
pronounced as *chǔ* with a rising tone.
Sān,
pronounced as *sān* with a departing tone,
or as usual.

The Emperor further inquired:

If they were to pass away,
(Note on 'pass away' already seen in the Hàn Annals.)
Shǐ Zhào said: Yán Shīgǔ said: 'Pass away'
means death.
It says they become the same as ghosts and thus are 'past'.
Another explanation:
not wishing to speak bluntly,
one simply says all the things they used are now 'past'.

Shǔ

Therefore, those fawning, flattering, impetuous, and competitive men

frivolous.

contentious.)

The situation in Héběi is different from those two regions.
Why is that?
Xīchuān and Zhèxī were not places of rebellion and disloyalty.

(Arms and fingers:
using the sense of Jiǎ Yì's words,

Therefore, we subjects at the time also urged Your Majesty to execute them,

Chéngdé, however, is not like that.
Internally, they have been firmly entrenched for many years.
Externally, they are extensively connected and widespread in influence.
(Firmly entrenched:
like glue adhering solidly.)
(Extensively connected:
like creeping weeds spreading and linking together.)

refers to Tǔbō;
Northern Dí:
refers to Huíhé.)
(Opportunity:
pronounced like the ancient character for 'amaranth';

At that time, Wú Shǎochéng was gravely ill.

(Jiàng and others's words

and we are sure to gain the advantage regarding Shēncài."

was ancient Zhēndìng.)

called the Ten Princes' Mansions.
The Ten Princes were Qìng, Zhōng, Dì, È, Yí, Yǐng, Yǒng, Róng, Yán, and Jì.
[Correction: The numbers in the source text seem misaligned here. The translation follows the content.] Later, Shèng, Yí, Shòu, Fēng,
Héng, and Liáng, six more princes, upon receiving their fiefs, also moved into the inner mansions.
This was the beginning of the name Sixteen Mansions.
Those selected to marry imperial princesses were all chosen by the eunuchs,
generally achieving it through substantial bribes.
Lǐ Jífǔ submitted a memorial stating:
"Since ancient times, those marrying princesses were always chosen for their qualities,
only in recent times has this not been the case."
In the twelfth month,

17. On the Jǐchǒu day,
the Vice Minister of Revenue Lǐ Jiàng was appointed as Vice Director of the Secretariat and Participator in Determining Governmental Matters (Tóng Píngzhāng Shì).
Textual Analysis: The Old Biography says:
"Tǔtū Chéngcuǐ enjoyed favor and trust like no other.
That year, when the Emperor was about to appoint Jiàng as Chancellor,
the day before, he sent Cuǐ out as Army Supervisor of Huáinán;
the next day, the edict was issued
appointing Jiàng as Tóng Píngzhāng Shì."
The New Biography says:
"There was nothing Jiàng said that the Emperor did not heed. The Emperor wished to make him Chancellor.
But Chéngcuǐ's favor was at its peak,
and he was jealous of Jiàng's advancement,
secretly slandering and disparaging him.
The Emperor then sent Chéngcuǐ out as Army Supervisor of Huáinán;
the next day,
he appointed Jiàng as Tóng Píngzhāng Shì."
Now, according to the Veritable Records,
there were fifty-four days between sending Chéngcuǐ out and Jiàng becoming Chancellor.
The Old Biography saying
"the next day"
is mistaken.
[Lǐ Jífǔ] often nursed old grudges.
The Emperor was quite aware of this,
therefore he promoted Jiàng to be Chancellor.
Jífǔ was skilled at catering to the Emperor's wishes,
while Jiàng was outspoken and upright,
and they often argued before the Emperor.
The Emperor often sided with Jiàng and followed his advice,
because of this, the two men were at odds.
18. In the intercalary month,
on the Xīnmǎo day, the first day of the month,
Qiánzhōu reported: The rebel leader Zhāng Bójìng of Chén and Xù prefectures raided Bōzhōu and Fèizhōu.
19. The Probationary Crown Prince Messengers' Attendant Lǐ Shè
In the Tang, the Crown Prince Messengers' Attendant belonged to the Right Spring Quarters,
with a staff of eight,
rank 7b lower,
in charge of guiding palace officials in taking leave, receiving audiences, and conveying orders and greetings.
This was an administrative post.
As for Lǐ Shè, he held a probationary appointment.
then submitted a memorial via the petition box,
stating that
"Chéngcuǐ has merit,
Xīguāng was not guilty.
Chéngcuǐ has long been entrusted as a confidant,
he should not be abruptly discarded."
The Petition Box Commissioner and Remonstrance Official Kǒng Kuí saw the duplicate copy of his memorial,
questioned and reprimanded him, and did not accept it.
Shè then resorted to bribery,
going to the Guāngshùn Gate to submit it.
When Kuí heard of this,
he submitted a memorial strongly stating
"Shè is treacherous, dangerous, and deceives Heaven.
I request that he be publicly executed."
On the Wùshēn day,
Shè was demoted to Granary Officer of Xiázhōu.
Xiázhōu
was the ancient territory of Yílíng.
The Shu state established the Yídū Commandery.
The Liang established Yízhōu.
The Later Wei changed it to Tuòzhōu,
taking the meaning of 'opening up new territory'.
Emperor Wu of the Zhōu, because the prefecture controlled the mouth of the Three Gorges,
changed it to Xiázhōu.
Old Gazetteer: Xiázhōu
was 1,888 lǐ southeast of the capital.
He was the elder brother of Lǐ Bó;
Lǐ Bó was at that time living in seclusion on Shàoshì Mountain.
He was the son of Kǒng Cháofù.
Kǒng Cháofù died in the rebellion of Lǐ Huáiguāng.
20. On the Xīnhài day,
Crown Prince Huìzhāo, Lǐ Níng, passed away.
Níng was established as Crown Prince;
see the fourth year, third month, in the previous scroll.
21. This year,
the empire had a great harvest.
A peck of rice could cost as little as two coins.
1. In spring,
in the first month,
on the Xīnwèi day,
Yuán Yìfāng, the Governor of the Capital District, was appointed as Surveillance Commissioner of Fūfāng.
Earlier,
Yìfāng had curried favor with Tǔtū Chéngcuǐ.
Lǐ Jífǔ, wishing to ingratiate himself with Chéngcuǐ,
promoted Yìfāng to be Governor of the Capital District.
Lǐ Jiàng detested Yìfāng's character,
therefore he had him sent out.
Yìfāng went to thank the Emperor,
and took the opportunity to say
"Lǐ Jiàng shows favoritism towards his fellow graduate Xǔ Jìtóng,
appointing him as Junior Governor of the Capital District,
while sending me out to Fūfāng.
He arbitrarily wields power and influence,
deceiving Your Sagaciousness."
The Emperor said:
"I know Lǐ Jiàng is not like that.
Tomorrow,
I will question him."
Yìfāng left in fear and shame.
The next day,
the Emperor questioned Jiàng, saying:
"Do people necessarily have feelings towards their fellow graduates?"
He replied:
"Fellow graduates are people from all over the realm who happen to pass the examinations in the same year.
Some only become acquainted after passing the examinations.
What feelings could there be?
People of the Tang called those who passed the jìnshì examination in the same year 'tóngnián',
and it is still so today.
Holding the post of Chancellor,
the duty of a Chancellor lies in assessing talent and assigning posts.
If a person truly has talent,
even if he were among one's own brothers, sons, or nephews, one should still employ him,
let alone a fellow graduate!
To avoid suspicion and discard talent
is to benefit oneself,
not to serve the public."
The Emperor said:
"Well said.
I knew you would certainly not do such a thing."
He then urged Yìfāng to proceed to his post.
2. The Zhenwǔ River overflowed,
destroying the Eastern Shòuxiáng Fortress.
The Eastern Shòuxiáng Fortress bordered the river;
the river overflowed,
thus destroying the fortress.
3. In the third month,
on the bǐngxū day,
the Emperor held court at the Yányīng Hall.
Lǐ Jífǔ said:
"The realm is already at peace;
Your Majesty should indulge in pleasures."
Lǐ Jiàng said:
"During the reign of Emperor Wén of Hàn, when weapons were made of wood and had no blades,
and every household had ample supplies and people were well-fed,
Jiǎ Yì still likened the situation to placing firewood under a pile of kindling,
and said it could not be considered safe.
See the sixth year of Emperor Wén of Hàn in the fourteenth volume.
In Héběi and Hénán, there are over fifty prefectures;
the Quǎnróng barbarians, reeking of mutton,
are close to Jīng and Lǒng,
and beacon fires have repeatedly raised alarms;
The Táng Liù Diǎn states: The placement of beacon towers
generally follows a distance of thirty lǐ.
If there are mountains or ridges obstructing the view,
they must be placed as appropriate,
so that they can see each other,
and are not strictly limited to thirty lǐ.
Those near the border
are built as fortresses and manned,
with each beacon tower having one commander and one deputy.
The number of torches lit at the beacons varies from one, two, three, to four,
depending on the number of enemy troops.
Granaries are empty,
and this is precisely the time for Your Majesty to rise early and retire late,
how can it be called peace,
and how can you hastily indulge in pleasures!"
The Emperor said happily:
"Your words are exactly in line with my thoughts."
After retiring,
he said to his attendants:
"Jífǔ only seeks to flatter and please;
as for Lǐ Jiàng,
he is a true chancellor!"
The Emperor once asked his chancellors:
"During the Zhēnyuán era, governance was neglected;
how did it come to this?"
Lǐ Jífǔ replied:
"Emperor Dézōng relied on his own wisdom,
trusting others instead of his chancellors,
which allowed treacherous ministers to seize the opportunity to wield power and influence.
The neglect of governance
was due to this reason."
The Emperor said:
"However, this may not entirely be Emperor Dézōng's fault.
When I was young and by Emperor Dézōng's side,
I observed that when affairs had merits or faults,
the chancellors of that time did not repeatedly remonstrate or report,
but instead clung to their positions and sought comfort,
so how can we solely blame Emperor Dézōng today!
You should take this as a warning;
when affairs are improper,
you must forcefully and persistently state your views,
and not fear my reproach or anger and hastily stop."
Lǐ Jífǔ once said:
"A minister should not remonstrate too forcefully.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states: Gōng Zhīqí's character
was timid and unable to remonstrate forcefully.
Lù Déming's phonetic annotation says: qiáng,
pronounced as qí liáng fān,
also as qí liǎng fān.
Is this not admirable!"
Lǐ Jiàng said:
"A minister should risk offending the ruler and speak earnestly,
pointing out merits and faults.
If he leads the ruler into wrongdoing,
how can he be considered loyal!"
The Emperor said:
"Jiàng is right."
Jífǔ returned to the Zhōngshū Department,
lay down and neglected his duties,
only sighing deeply.
If Lǐ Jiàng went a long time without remonstrating,
the Emperor would question him, saying:
"Is it that I cannot tolerate criticism,
or that there is nothing to remonstrate about?"
Lǐ Jífǔ once again said to the Emperor:
"Rewards and punishments
are the two handles of a ruler,
and neither can be neglected.
Since Your Majesty ascended the throne,
your benevolence has been profound;
but威严 and punishments have not been strengthened,
and both inside and outside the court, there is slackness and laziness.
I hope you will impose stricter measures to rectify this."
The Emperor turned to Lǐ Jiàng and said:
"What do you think?"
He replied:
"The governance of a true king
emphasizes virtue over punishment.
How can we abandon the ways of Chéng, Kāng, Wén, and Jǐng and instead emulate Qín Shǐhuáng and his son!"
The Emperor said:
"Indeed."
Over ten days later,
Yú Dí had an audience with the Emperor
and also urged the Emperor to impose harsher punishments.
A few days later,
the Emperor said to his chancellors:
"Yú Dí is a great treacherous minister;
he urged me to impose harsher punishments.
Do you know his intention?"
They all replied:
"We do not know."
The Emperor said:
"He wants to make me lose the people's support."
Jífǔ turned pale,
and after retiring, he lowered his head and did not speak or smile all day.
The Emperor considered Yú Dí's advice on harsh punishments as treacherous,
so Jífǔ was ashamed of his earlier improper words.
4. In summer,
the fourth month,
on the bǐngchén day,
the Emperor appointed the Kùbù Langzhōng and Hànlín Academician Cuī Qí as Zhōngshū Shèrén,
while retaining his position as academician.
The Kùbù Lang
was in charge of weapons, ceremonial guards, and insignia,
and belonged to the Ministry of War.
The Emperor ordered the academicians:
"From now on, when submitting memorials,
you must obtain Cuī Qí's joint signature,

Cuī Qí said:
"All actions of the Hànlín Academy become precedents.
If this is done,
in the future, if there is a flattering and obsequious person serving as its head,
then subordinates with straightforward advice will have no way to present it."
He firmly refused to obey the order.
After submitting three memorials,
the Emperor relented.
5. In the fifth month,
on the gēngshēn day,
the Emperor said to his chancellors:
"You have repeatedly reported floods and droughts in Huái and Zhè last year,
but recently a censor returned from there
and said there was no disaster.
What is the actual situation?"
Lǐ Jiàng replied:
"According to the memorials from Huáinán, Zhèxī, and Zhèdōng,
they all reported floods and droughts,
with many people displaced,
and requested measures to recruit and安抚 them,
establishing laws and systems to recruit and安抚 the displaced people.
How could they falsely claim a disaster if there was none!
This must be the censor attempting to deceive and flatter to please Your Majesty.
I hope to learn his name
and hold him accountable according to the law."
The Emperor said:
"You are right.
The state relies on the people as its foundation.
Upon hearing of a disaster, we must urgently provide relief;
how can we still doubt it!
I was thoughtless earlier
and spoke improperly."
He ordered the immediate减免 of taxes and levies.
The Emperor once discussed governance with his chancellors in the Yányīng Hall.
As the day grew late,
the heat was intense,
and sweat soaked the Emperor's robes.
The chancellors feared the Emperor was tired
and requested to retire.
The Emperor stopped them, saying:
"When I return to the palace,
the only people I interact with are palace women and eunuchs.
So I enjoy discussing the essentials of governance with all of you,
and I am truly not tired."
"Wéi lǐ"
means the same as "wéi zhì" (to govern).
The Táng dynasty避讳 the name of Emperor Gāozōng,
so "zhì" was changed to "lǐ."
"Chǔ"
is pronounced as chāng lǚ fān.
"Lè"
is pronounced as luò.
6. In the sixth month,
on the guǐsì day,
the Minister over the Masses and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì Dù Yòu retired as Grand Guardian.
Soon, Tián Huái'àn being young and weak,
military and administrative affairs were all decided by the household servant Jiǎng Shìzé.
He repeatedly transferred and replaced various generals based on his personal likes and dislikes,
causing widespread anger among the troops.
The imperial court's orders had not arrived for a long time,
and the army was unsettled.
Tián Xīng entered the headquarters in the morning,
and several thousand soldiers clamored loudly,
surrounding Tián Xīng and bowing to him,
requesting that he become the acting military governor.
Tián Xīng, startled, fell to the ground,
but the crowd did not disperse.
After a long time,
Tián Xīng realized he could not avoid it,
and so said to the crowd:
"Are you willing to listen to my words?"
They all said:
"We will obey your command."
Tián Xīng said:
"Do not offend the Deputy Commissioner,
uphold the laws and decrees of the court,
submit the population registers,
and request the appointment of officials;
only then can it be done."
They all said:
"Yes."
Tián Xīng then killed Jiǎng Shìzé and more than ten others,
and moved Tián Huái'àn outside.
In the first year of the Guǎngdé era of Emperor Dàizōng,
Tián Chéngsì commanded Wèi-Bó,
for four generations,
lasting forty-nine years before its demise.

and only then grant it to them,
this would be repeating the faults of the Dàlì and Zhēnyuán eras.
For,

the following 'for', 'right for', 'estimate for', 'should for' are the same.
It would not originate from the sovereign,

Meaning, fearing they might not understand the Emperor's intention.

Shǎn,

"Wèi-Bó has not received the imperial transformation for over fifty years,

Its six prefectures,
Wèi, Bó, Bèi, Wèi, Chán, Xiàng.
were the nest of rebellion.

otherwise,
what is the point of merely storing them in the treasury!"
In the eleventh month,

their cheers like thunder.

Yǎnyùn,

Yùn,

"Our generations have had a covenant with the Tián clan to protect and aid each other.

5 The Emperor once said to the chief ministers at Yányīng Hall:
"You all should be sparing in granting official posts for my sake,
and not use them for personal relatives or old acquaintances."
Lǐ Jífǔ and Quán Déyù both apologized, saying they dared not.
Lǐ Jiàng said:
"Cuī Yòufǔ once said,

"It is indeed as you say."

Chǔ,

Fēn,

5 The Minister of Works and Chief Minister Yú Dí had long stayed in Cháng'ān,

Dí entered the court in the second year;
see scroll 232.
He claimed to be of the same clan as the Privy Councilor Liáng Shǒuqiān,
and could make requests on behalf of others.
Dí had his son, the Court Minister of Sacrifices Mǐn, heavily bribe Zhèngyán,
seeking an appointment as a military governor.
After a long time,
Zhèngyán's deceit gradually came to light.
Mǐn demanded the bribe back but could not get it,
so he lured Zhèngyán's servant,
dismembered him,
and threw him into a latrine.
When the matter was discovered,
Dí led his son, the Assistant Director of the Palace Administration Jìyǒu, and others in plain clothes to the Jiànfú Gate to plead guilty.
The gatekeepers would not let them in;
they retreated,
stood with their backs against the south wall,
and sent someone to submit a memorial.
The gate officials would not accept it because there was no official seal or introduction;
Táng regulations: all memorials from the four directions
were received by the gate officials and presented.
Dí was pleading guilty,
having neither an official seal
nor an internal introduction,
so it was not accepted.
The next day,
they came again.
On Dīngyǒu day,
Dí was demoted to Tutor of the Prince of Ēn,
and still barred from court audiences;
Mǐn was exiled to Léizhōu.
Old records: Léizhōu
is 6,512 lǐ from the capital.
Several of his servants and slaves were executed;
Mǐn died upon reaching Qínlǐng.
Going south from Lántián Pass, one crosses Qínlǐng.
The matter implicated the monk Jiànxū.
Since the Zhēnyuán era,
Jiànxū had used wealth to befriend powerful and favored officials,
accepted bribes from regional military governors,
lived in great luxury himself,
and officials dared not investigate him.
By this time,
the powerful and favored officials competed to speak on his behalf.
The Emperor intended to release him,
but the Censor-in-Chief Xuē Cúnchéng would not allow it.
The Emperor sent a palace envoy to the Censorate to proclaim his decree:
"I wish to interrogate this monk in person,
it is not to release him."
Cúnchéng replied:
"If Your Majesty insists on personally releasing this monk,
I beg you to first kill your servant,
and then take him.
Otherwise,
your servant will certainly not obey the decree."
The Emperor praised him and complied.
In the third month,
on the day Bǐngchén,
Jiànxū was caned to death,
and all his property was confiscated.
Textual analysis states: The Veritable Records places this in the second month.
According to the perpetual calendar,
the second month began on Yǐyǒu,
the third month began on Jiǎyín.
Bǐngchén
is the third day of the third month.
Jiǎzǐ
is when Wǔ Yuánhéng entered to take charge of government affairs,
which is the eleventh day.
The Veritable Records accidentally omitted writing the month.

the former Xīchuān military governor and concurrent Tóngpíngzhāngshì Wǔ Yuánhéng was summoned to enter and take charge of government affairs.

Wǔ Yuánhéng was sent out to govern Xīchuān,

the sixth month,

8 In autumn,
the seventh month,
the Zhènwǔ military governor Lǐ Guāngjìn requested to repair the Shòuxiáng City,

"Lǐ"
means to manage.
The river destroying Shòuxiáng City is mentioned in the seventh year of the previous scroll.
The old Tiāndé city
was located two hundred lǐ west of the Eastern Shòuxiáng City, at Dàtóngchuān.
After the Qiányuán era,
the Tiāndé Army was relocated to Yǒngjì Zhà.
Sòng Bái's Xù Tōngdiǎn records it as
"Yǒngqīng Zhà".
That city
was the old site of the Suí dynasty's Dàtóng city.
"Shòuxiáng City,
built by Zhāng Rényuàn,
the event is recorded in the 209th scroll, in the first year of Jǐnglóng under Emperor Zhōngzōng.
It occupied a strategic position against the barbarians,
had good water and grass,
a beneficial location for guarding the frontier.
Now, to avoid the river's danger,
retreating two or three lǐ would suffice.
How can we abandon a strategy for ten thousand generations of eternal peace,
and follow the convenience of temporary frugality!
Moreover, the old Tiāndé city is located in a remote and barren place,
extremely far from the river.
Beacon signals for urgent alerts cannot connect,
if the barbarians suddenly attack,
there would be no way to know the situation,
this is to shrink the state's territory by two hundred lǐ for no reason."
When the city commissioner Zhōu Huáiyì memorialized on the advantages and disadvantages,
his opinion was the same as Jiàng's and Tǎn's.
The Emperor ultimately adopted Jífǔ's strategy,
placing the Shòuxiáng City cavalry under the Tiāndé Army.
Lǐ Jiàng said to the Emperor:
"The frontier armies only have numbers on paper, not reality.
They waste clothing and grain,
and the generals only use them for private service.
'For private service' means
using the name of public service to employ them privately.
They have never been trained to prepare for unexpected events.
This is something that cannot be overlooked by Your Sage Attention in times of peace."
At that time, the Shòuxiáng City military register originally had four hundred men.
When handed over to the Tiāndé Army,
there were only fifty men.
Textual analysis states: The Veritable Records says:
"Lǐ Guāngjìn requested to repair the Eastern Shòuxiáng City and also manage the river defenses."
It also says:
"Place the Central Shòuxiáng City and the one thousand one hundred and forty cavalrymen under its jurisdiction under the Tiāndé Army."
The Old Biography says:
"Lú Tǎn and Lǐ Jiàng jointly proposed,
believing the Western City built by Zhāng Rényuàn
should not be abandoned."
These three accounts differ,
it is unclear which is correct.
Now we only say Shòuxiáng City,
leaving the doubt unresolved.
Also, Lǐ Sīkōng Lùn Shì says:
"The Central City originally belonged to Zhènwǔ,
with a garrison of four hundred men.
At that time, it was transferred to Tiāndé,
and only fifty men were handed over."
The numbers differ so much,
perhaps the one thousand one hundred and forty is the total number for the three cities.
The rest were similar.
Therefore, Jiàng mentioned it.
The Emperor was shocked and said:
"The frontier troops are actually this deficient!
You gentlemen should conduct inspections."
But then Jiàng was dismissed from the chancellorship and it stopped.

the Tiānwēi Army was abolished.

the Left and Right Shénwēi were combined into one army,

The Shénwēi Army

"Wěi"
means to assign,

11 Initially,
the Tibetans wanted to build the Wūlán Bridge.
The New Treatise: Huìzhōu Wūlán County had Wūlán Pass,
located southwest of the county.
The Tibetans built a bridge over the river.
Shuòfāng often secretly sent people to throw things into the river,

The barbarians knew that the Shuòfāng and Língyán military governor Wáng Bì was greedy,
so first bribed him heavily,
then concentrated their efforts to complete the bridge,

From then on, Shuòfāng had no respite from defending against invaders.
12 In winter,
the tenth month,
the Uighurs dispatched troops south across the desert,
and attacked the Tibetans west from Liǔgǔ.
The New Treatise: Two hundred and ten lǐ north of Xīzhōu Jiāohé County,
one passes through Liǔgǔ Crossing.
On the day Rényín,
Zhènwǔ and Tiāndé Army reported that several thousand Uighur cavalry had reached Pìtí Quán.
Pìtí Quán
is three hundred lǐ north of the Western Shòuxiáng City.
Pì,
pronunciation fú lì fān.
Tí,
pronunciation tú xī fān.
13 The Zhènwǔ military governor Lǐ Jìnxián
did not care for his soldiers.
His administrative assistant Yán Chè,
was the son of Yán Shòu,
at that time Yán Shòu was still alive.
Shòu,
pronunciation shòu.
Jìnxián sent the officer Yáng Zūnxiàn to lead five hundred cavalry to the Eastern Shòuxiáng City to guard against the Uighurs.
The supplies provided were mostly overvalued;
supplies were not given in kind,
their value was inflated,
and other goods were given instead.
Qù,
pronunciation qī yù fān.
Zūnxiàn stayed in a house
while the soldiers were exposed to the elements.
The crowd became angry.
At night,
they gathered firewood around his house and burned it,
rolled up their armor, and returned.
On the night of Gēngyín,
they burned the gate,
attacked Jìnxián.
Jìnxián climbed over the city wall and fled.
The soldiers slaughtered his family,
and also killed Yán Chè.
Jìnxián fled to the Jìngbiān Army.
The Jìngbiān Army was one hundred and eighty lǐ west of Yúnzhōu.
14 Court ministers repeatedly petitioned to establish Virtuous Consort Guō as Empress.
The Emperor, because her clan was powerful and prosperous,

The Emperor sighed at Yù's talent and excellence, saying:
"Déyú obtained Yù as a son-in-law,
but I, on the contrary, am not as fortunate!"
Previously, those who married imperial princesses were all chosen from families of noble relatives and meritorious ministers.

The Emperor now began to order the chief ministers to select sons and younger brothers of dukes, ministers, and high officials who were refined and elegant and could hold pure and prestigious positions.
Shǐ Zhào said: Guàn means affairs.
Qīngguàn is like saying a pure and prestigious post.

the seventh month,

on Guǐsì,

Zhìzhǐ means those who can be controlled, governed, and directed.

on Bǐngchén,
the Zhāngyì Military Governor Wú Shàoyáng died.
Examination of discrepancies: The Veritable Records place Shàoyáng's death under the entry for the intercalary month Jǐchǒu and above Rénchén,
and combine it with the mention of Yuánjì burning Wǔyáng.

Now we follow the New Annals.
He secretly gathered desperadoes,
raised horses and mules,
and from time to time raided the tea mountains of Shòuzhōu to supply his army.
Shòuzhōu had tea mountains.
Chāo, pronounced as in Chǔjiāo fān.

reported illness,

Since the Emperor pacified Shǔ,

the Huáinán Military Governor Lǐ Jífǔ submitted a memorial stating:

This matter is seen in the fourth and fifth years of the previous scroll.

Wú Shàoyáng's administrative assistants Sū Zhào, Yáng Yuánqīng, and senior general Hóu Wéiqīng all urged Shàoyáng to go to court.

Yuánjì killed Yuánqīng's wife and four sons and used their blood and flesh to plaster the archery target wall.

slaughtered Wǔyáng,

plundered Lǔshān and Xiāngchéng,

on Wùchén,

1. In spring,
the first month,

This refers to the region of the Eastern Capital.

"Cíqiū"
should be
"Cíqiū."

He fled into Táng Prefecture and defended it.

selected 6,000 soldiers to be placed under Tīng's command,

The one who commands all the armies of the various units

It was as if they were under his direct command.
Gōngchuò's orders were strict and orderly,
and his handling of military affairs

For soldiers in the campaign camp,
if their families fell ill or died,
he provided generous support.
If a wife committed adultery,
she was drowned in the river.
The soldiers all rejoiced, saying:
"The Vice Censor-in-Chief manages our households for us,
how can we not advance and die in battle!"
Thus, they achieved victory in every battle.
The horse Gōngchuò rode
kicked and killed a stableman.
Gōngchuò ordered the horse killed as a sacrifice.
Someone said:
"The stableman himself was not careful.
This is a fine horse—
what a pity!"

3. Liú Fǔ, a general of Hédōng, killed Yān Chónggàn, the prefect of Fēng Prefecture.
Wáng È executed him
along with his accomplices.
There is also the "Biography of Guo Tuótuó the Tree Planter" which says:
"The trees planted by Tuótuó
all grow and flourish.
Someone asked him about it,
and he replied: 'It is not that Tuótuó can make trees live long and multiply.
Generally, the nature of trees is such that
their roots desire to spread out,
and the soil should be the original soil.
Once they are planted,
do not disturb them or worry about them;
leave and do not look back.
When planting them, treat them as your own children;
when leaving them, treat them as if abandoned.
Then their natural state will be preserved and their nature fulfilled.
Other planters are not like this.
They curl the roots and change the soil;
they love them too dearly,
worry about them too diligently,
inspect them in the morning and pat them in the evening,
leave and then look back again.
Some even scratch the bark to test whether they are alive or dead,
or shake the trunk to observe how dense or sparse they are.
Thus, the nature of the trees is increasingly lost.
Though they say they love them,
in reality, they harm them;
though they say they worry about them,
in reality, they treat them as enemies.
That is why they are not as good as I am!
Governing is the same way.
I have seen officials in the countryside
who enjoy issuing numerous orders,
as if they deeply care for the people, but in the end, they bring disaster upon them.
Officials come morning and evening,
gather the people and order them about,
hurry them to plow and harvest,
supervise their sericulture and weaving.
We commoners have to interrupt our meals to serve the officials without respite—
how can we then multiply our livelihoods and settle our natures?
All sickness and weariness
are due to this.'"
Dù Yù said: "Zhí"
means "to be in charge of."
The "Biography of the Carpenter" is used to advise ministers,
and the "Biography of the Tree Planter" is used to advise local officials.
Therefore, Lord Wēn selected them,
as they are beneficial to governance.

raid the markets,
