and will surely achieve merit."
The Emperor was pleased.
(He was pleased because Dù said there was a certain prospect of victory.)
(Thus, he was pleased.)
The Examination Officer and Drafter Hán Yù submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Huáixī consists of three small prefectures—
three small prefectures,
namely Shēn, Guāng, and Cài.
Yet it withstands the full force of the empire;
its defeat can be expected at any moment.
(This is said in terms of the disparity in size and strength.)
It depends on whether Your Majesty is decisive or not."
He then detailed the advantages and disadvantages of the military campaign,
stating:
"Now, the various circuits each dispatch only two to three thousand soldiers.
Their strength is weak and isolated;
they are strangers in a foreign land,
unfamiliar with the enemy,
and cower at the mere sight of them.
The commanders treat them as auxiliary troops,
treating them poorly
and employing them harshly.
Sometimes their units are divided,
separating soldiers from their officers.
Their morale is low and their will timid,
making it difficult to achieve success.
Moreover, their original armies must provide supplies,
but the roads are long and distant,
doubling the labor and expense.
I have heard that in the prefectures of Chén, Xǔ, Ān, Táng, Rǔ, and Shòu, which border the rebel area,
the villagers all possess weapons,
are accustomed to fighting,
and understand the enemy's situation deeply.
So far, no arrangements have been made for them,
yet they are willing to provide their own clothing and food
to protect their hometowns.
If they are recruited,
an army can be formed immediately.
After the rebels are pacified,
they can easily be sent back to farming.
I request to disband all the troops from other circuits
and recruit local people to replace them."
He also said:
"The soldiers in Cài Prefecture are all subjects of the state.
If they are so desperate that they cannot cause harm,
there is no need for excessive slaughter."
10 On the Bǐngshēn day,
Lǐ Guāngyán reported defeating Huáixī troops at Shíqū.
Shíqū
is located southwest of Yīnshuǐ County in Chén Prefecture.
Defeated,
Bǔ Mài fān.
Guāngyán could not break out,
so he destroyed the left and right sides of his own stockade
and sent out cavalry to attack.
Guāngyán personally led several cavalrymen to charge the enemy formation,
going back and forth several times.
The rebels all recognized him,
and arrows struck his body like porcupine quills.
His son grabbed his reins to stop him,
(grabbed—
to seize with the hand).
At this, the soldiers fought desperately,
and the Huáixī troops were utterly defeated,
with several thousand killed.
The Emperor considered Péi Dù a good judge of character.
11 Since the death of Lǐ Jífǔ,
the Emperor had entrusted all military affairs to Wǔ Yuánhéng.
A retainer kept by Lǐ Shīdào advised him:
"The reason the Son of Heaven is determined to destroy Cài
is because Yuánhéng supports it.
I request to secretly go and assassinate him.
If Yuánhéng dies,
then other ministers will not dare to advocate the plan,
and they will urge the Son of Heaven to halt the campaign."
Shīdào agreed
and immediately provided resources and sent him off.
Wáng Chéngzōng sent his officer Yǐn Shǎoqīng to handle affairs,
lobbying on behalf of Wú Yuánjì.
Shǎoqīng arrived at the Central Secretariat,
and his words were disrespectful.
Yuánhéng shouted and expelled him;
Chéngzōng also submitted a memorial slandering Yuánhéng.
In the ninth month, on
Guǐyǒu,
Hán Hóng was appointed as the overall commander of the various armies in Huáixī.
Hóng enjoyed being self-reliant and
wished to rely on the rebels to enhance his own importance,
so he did not want Huáixī to be pacified quickly.
An examination of discrepancies states: The old biography says:
"Hóng defended Biànzhōu,
which was at the strategic point between the two rivers where rebel forces were active.
The court feared he had disloyal intentions,
so they wished to entrust him with military authority,
but had Lǐ Guāngyán and Wū Chóngyìn actually lead the troops.
Thus, Hóng was appointed as the overall commander of the various armies in the Huáixī campaign.
Although Hóng held the position of commander,
he often did not want the various armies to achieve merit,
secretly employing delaying tactics.
Whenever he heard of victories being reported,
he would be unhappy for several days.
Such was his way of endangering the state while seeking personal gain."
However, considering that Hóng took over after the accumulated chaos in Xuānwǔ,
he stabilized the region,
situated among powerful rebels,
and his prestige was considerable.
If he had disloyal intentions,
he could have allied with the various military governors and acted arrogantly,
as easily as turning over his hand.
Yet, observing his actions from beginning to end,
he never failed in his duties as a subject.
If the court suspected him of disloyalty and still appointed him as overall commander,
then Guāngyán and Chóngyìn would be under his command,
which would not be a way to guard against him.
Moreover, being unhappy for several days—
what evidence is there for this?
I fear this criticism may have exaggerated the facts.
Now, I follow what is credible.
Hóng wished to win his favor,
so he searched throughout Dàliáng city and found a beautiful woman.
The Xuānwǔ military governor's seat was at Dàliáng.
Search,
Shānkè fān.
He adorned her with pearls, jade, gold, and emeralds,
worth several million coins,
and sent an envoy to present her to him.
The envoy first delivered a letter to Guāngyán,
and a grand
feast was held for the officers and soldiers.
The envoy presented the courtesan,
whose beauty was unparalleled,
astonishing everyone present.
Guāngyán said to the envoy:
"The Prime Minister pities Guāngyán for being away from home,
and bestows upon me a beautiful courtesan.
I am deeply grateful for his kindness.
However, there are tens of thousands of soldiers
who have all left their homes and come from afar,
braving the edge of swords.
How could Guāngyán bear to enjoy music and beauty alone for his own pleasure?"
Then he shed tears,
and all those seated wept;
"Seated,"
I fear it should be
"sitting"
for the text to be coherent.
He returned the courtesan along with
the message:
"Please convey Guāngyán's deep gratitude to the Prime Minister.
Guāngyán has dedicated his life to the state,
and vows not to share the same sky with the rebellious traitors.
He will remain loyal unto death!"
18 In winter,
the tenth month, on
Gēngzǐ,
Shānnán Dōngdào was first divided into two military commands.
The Vice Minister of Revenue Lǐ Xùn was appointed as the military governor of Xiāng, Fù, Yǐng, Jūn, and Fáng;
and the Right Yǔlín Grand General Gāo Xiáyù was appointed as the military governor of Táng, Suí, and Dèng.
The court deliberated that since Táng bordered Cài,
Xiáyù was to focus solely on attack and combat,
while Xùn was to allocate the taxes from the five prefectures to supply him.
19 On Xīnchǒu,
the Vice Minister of Justice Quán Déyú memorialized:
"Since the 25th year of the Kāiyuán era when the statutes, regulations, laws, and ordinances were compiled and categorized,
the Táng Liùdiǎn records the names of legal texts:
24 chapters of regulations,
33 chapters of ordinances,
12 chapters of laws,
and 27 chapters of statutes.
The Huìyào states: In the 25th year of Kāiyuán, the laws were edited into 12 chapters,
the legal commentaries into 30 chapters,
the ordinances into 20 chapters,
and the new Kāiyuán regulations into 10 chapters.
Also, the statutes, regulations, laws, and ordinances were compiled into 40 chapters,
categorized for
ease of reference.
Recently, they have been edited into 30 chapters,
and I request their implementation."
This was approved.
The Huìyào: In the 19th year of Kāiyuán,
Péi Guāngtíng and others memorialized to have the relevant officials compile six chapters of long-standing edicts following the regulations.
Now, the long-standing edicts after the 25th year have been edited into 30 chapters.
20 Although the Emperor had severed Wáng Chéngzōng's tribute and diplomatic relations,
he had not issued an edict to attack him.
The military governor of Wèibó, Tián Hóngzhèng, stationed troops at the border,
and Chéngzōng repeatedly defeated him.
Hóngzhèng was angered,
and petitioned to attack him,
but the Emperor did not permit it.
After ten petitions,
he was allowed to advance to Bèizhōu.
On Bǐngwǔ,
Hóngzhèng's army was at Bèizhōu.
21 On Gēngxū,
the Eastern Capital reported that thieves had burned the Bóyá granary.
Sòng Bái said: Héqīng County has the Bóyá fortress.
Dù Yòu said: The Bóyá fortress,
built by Hóu Jǐng,
is west of Héqīng County.
22 In the eleventh month,
the prefect of Shòuzhōu, Lǐ Wéntōng, reported defeating Huáixī troops.
On Rénshēn,
Hán Hóng requested that all armies jointly attack Huáixī;
this was approved.
Lǐ Guāngyán and Wū Chóngyìn defeated Huáixī troops at Xiǎo Yīnshuǐ,
and captured their city.
On Yǐhài,
Yán Shòu was appointed as Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
This was because he had achieved no merit in the campaign against Huáixī.
Thieves burned the military supplies stored in a Buddhist temple in Xiāngzhōu.
All the stored hay in the capital city was moved to the four suburbs to guard against fire.
On Dīngchǒu,
Lǐ Wéntōng defeated Huáixī troops at Gùshǐ.
Gùshǐ,
was the Jìn County of Rǔnán Commandery in the Former Hàn,
the Jìnqiū of the Spring and Autumn period,
renamed Gùshǐ in the Later Hàn,
and belonged to Guāngzhōu in the Táng.
The Jiǔyùzhì: It is 145 lǐ northeast of the prefecture.
On Wùyín,
thieves burned the resting palace and the eternal lane of the Xiànlíng tomb.
23 An edict was issued to dispatch 2,000 troops from Zhènwǔ
to join the Yìwǔ army in attacking Wáng Chéngzōng.
24 On Jǐchǒu,
the Tǔbō requested trade at the Lǒngzhōu frontier,
asking to establish mutual markets,
and this was permitted.
25 Earlier,
Wú Shàoyáng heard of the reputation of Wú Wǔlíng from Xìnzhōu,
and invited him to be a guest and friend,
but Wǔlíng did not respond.
When Yuánjì rebelled,
Wǔlíng wrote to admonish him, saying:
"Do not think, sir, that your subordinates will not deceive you.
Human nature is the same for you as for others.
If you rebel against the Son of Heaven,
others will also wish to rebel against you.
Consider this from another perspective,
and the situation will be clear."
26 On Dīngyǒu,
the military governor of Wǔníng, Lǐ Yuàn, reported defeating the forces of Lǐ Shīdào.
At that time, Shīdào repeatedly sent troops to attack Xúzhōu,
devastating several counties such as Xiāo and Pèi.
Yuàn entrusted all infantry and cavalry to the capital officer Wēn Rén Wáng Zhìxīng,
who defeated them.
In the twelfth month, on
Jiǎchén,
Zhìxīng again defeated Shīdào's forces,
beheading over 2,000,
and pursuing the fleeing enemy as far as Píngyīn before returning.
Píngyīn,
was the ancient state of Féizi,
the territory of Féichéng County in the Hàn.
In the 14th year of the Suí's Kāihuáng era, Yúshān County was established.
In the early Dàyè era, it was renamed Píngyīn,
taking its name from the ancient Píngyīn city within its borders.
At that time, it belonged to Yùnzhōu.
The Jiǔyùzhì: It is 120 lǐ northeast of the prefecture.
Return,
Cóng Xuān fān,
or also read as the original character.
He was the son of Shèng.
27 The Eastern Capital defense commissioner Lǚ Yuányīng requested recruiting mountain dwellers to guard the palace city,
and this was approved.
28 On Yǐchǒu,
the military governor of Hédōng, Wáng È, passed away.
29 Wáng Chéngzōng allowed his troops to plunder in all directions,
causing suffering to the three military districts of Yōu, Cāng, and Dìng.
They vied to submit memorials requesting permission to attack Chéngzōng.
The Emperor wished to grant this,
but the Vice Director of the Secretariat and Tongpingzhangshi Zhāng Hóngjìng believed
"two campaigns launched simultaneously,
two campaigns,
meaning attacking Huáixī
and also attacking Héngjì.
I request that we concentrate our efforts on pacifying Huáixī first,
and then campaign against Héngjì."
The Emperor did not stop because of this,
so Hóngjìng requested to be relieved of his duties.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the day Jǐsì,
Zhāng Hóngjìng was appointed as Tóng Píngzhāng Shì [Joint Manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery]
and concurrently served as the military governor of Hédōng.
2 Liú Zǒng, the military governor of Yōuzhōu, reported defeating the troops of Chéngdé,
capturing Wǔqiáng,
and beheading over a thousand men.
3 On the day Gēngchén,
Qián Huī, a Hanlin Academician and Zhōngshū Shèrén [Secretariat Drafter],
and Xiāo Fǔ, a Director of the Bureau of Carriages and Coachmen and Zhī Zhìgào [Draftsman],
were each relieved of their duties
and retained only their substantive offices.
At that time, many court ministers requested to halt the military campaigns,
which troubled the Emperor,
so he demoted Huī and Fǔ to warn the others.
Huī
was from Wú.
4 On the day Guǐwèi,
an edict was issued stripping Wáng Chéngzōng of his official titles and noble rank,
and ordering the six circuits of Hédōng, Yōuzhōu, Yìwǔ, Hénghǎi, Wèibó, and Zhāoyì to advance and attack.
Wéi Guànzhī repeatedly requested to first capture Wú Yuánjì and then campaign against Chéngzōng,
saying:
"Has Your Majesty not seen what happened during the Jiànzhōng era?
It began with campaigns against Wèi and Qí,
and then Cài, Yān, and Zhào all responded,
ultimately leading to the rebellion of Zhū Cǐ.
The events are recorded in scrolls 226
It ended,
with Zǐ Xù turning the pages.
This was because they desired the achievement of peace to be swift."
The Emperor did not listen.
Those who delight in arms are instruments of ill omen.
The words of Zhāng Hóngjìng and Wéi Guànzhī should not be overly criticized.
5 On the day Jiǎshēn,
thieves broke forty-seven halberds at the gate of the Jiànlíng mausoleum.
6 In the second month,
Xīchuān reported that the Tibetan Tsanpo had died,
and the new Tsanpo, Kělíkězú, had ascended.
7 On the day Yǐsì,
Lǐ Féngjí, a Zhōngshū Shèrén, was appointed as Ménxià Shìláng [Vice Director of the Chancellery] and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
Féngjí
was the great-grandson of Lǐ Xuándào.
Lǐ Xuándào served under Emperor Tàizōng,
as a scholar of the Literary Institute.
8 On the day Yǐmǎo,
Xī Shìměi, the military governor of Zhāoyì, reported defeating the troops of Chéngdé,
beheading over a thousand men.
9 Quàn Lóngshèng of Nánzhào was licentious, cruel, and unprincipled,
causing resentment and hatred among both high and low,
so Wáng Cuōdiān, the military commissioner of Nòngdòng, assassinated him
and established his younger brother, Quàn Lì, [in his place].
Quàn Lì was grateful to Cuōdiān,
bestowing upon him the surname Méng,
and called him
"Dàróng."
Róng
means "elder brother" in the Mán language.
Nánzhào established the Nòngdòng military commissioner in the territory of the Táng's Yáozhōu.
Chéng Dàchāng said: Nánzhào had six military commissioners,
named Nòngdòng, Yǒngchāng, Yínshēng, Jiànchuān, Tuòdōng, and Lìshuǐ.
The kings of Nánzhào bore the surname Méng.
Cuō,
is pronounced zuó hé.
Diān,
is pronounced diān.
10 On the day Jǐwèi,
Liú Zǒng defeated the troops of Chéngdé,
beheading over a thousand men.
11 The ancestral tombs of Yuán Zī, the military governor of Jīngnán, were in Lǎngshān.
Yuán Zī
was a descendant of Yuán Xiàn of Chén.
After the fall of Chén,
Xiàn entered the Central Plains,
and later resided in Lǎngshān County, Càizhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Lǎngshān
was the Hàn's Ānchāng County,
renamed Lǎngshān at the end of the Hàn,
named after the Lǎng Mountain within its borders.
Liú Xù said: Lǎngshān
was the Hàn's Ānchāng County,
renamed Lǎngshān in the Suí.
Dù Yòu said: Lǎngshān
was the Hàn's Lǎnglíng County,
and the Sòng, to avoid the taboo of the Sacred Ancestor,
changed Lǎngshān to Quèshān.
[Yuán Zī] wished to persuade the Emperor to halt the military campaigns.
When he reached Dèngzhōu,
he heard that Xiāo Fǔ and Qián Huī had been demoted;
upon meeting the Emperor,
he instead urged that victory was certain,
and barely managed to return to his garrison.
12 On the day Xīnyǒu,
Wèibó reported defeating the troops of Chéngdé,
capturing its Gùchéng;
on the day Yǐchǒu,
they further reported capturing its Yāchéng.
Gùchéng and Yāchéng
were likely within the boundaries of Nángōng County, Jìzhōu.
13 In the third month,
on the day Gēngwǔ,
the Empress Dowager passed away.
The Empress Dowager, née Wáng,
was the Emperor's mother.
On the day Xīnwèi,
an edict was issued that due to national mourning,
all official matters of the various departments were to be temporarily handled by the Secretariat-Chancellery,
with only the chief ministers participating in the decision-making for the affairs of the hundred departments.
Chǔ,
is pronounced chǎng lǚ.
Fēn,
is pronounced fú wèn.
Since the mid-Táng period,
upon the death of the Son of Heaven,
a Regent Grand Steward was appointed,
imitating the ancient system where all officials reported to the Grand Steward,
but they were unable to fully implement the ancient ways.
14 Lǐ Wéntōng, the Tuanlian Commissioner of Shòuzhōu, reported defeating Huáixī troops at Gùshǐ,
capturing a mountain.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
Gāo Xiáyù, the military governor of Tángdèng, reported defeating Huáixī troops at Lǎngshān,
beheading over a thousand men,
and burning two stockades.
15 Liú Zǒng, the military governor of Yōuzhōu, besieged Lèshòu.
16 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day Gēngzǐ,
Lǐ Guāngyán and Wū Chóngyìn reported defeating Huáixī troops at the Língyún stockade.
The Língyún stockade
was southwest of Yīnshuǐ
and northeast of Yǎnchéng.
The men of Cài established a stockade here,
naming it Língyún.
17 On the day Xīnhài,
Huángfǔ Bó, the Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury, was appointed concurrently as Vice Censor-in-Chief and acting Commissioner of Public Revenue.
Bó began to gain favor through his methods of amassing wealth.
18 On the day Yǐmǎo,
Liú Zǒng reported defeating Chéngdé troops at Shēnzhōu,
beheading 2,500 men.
On the day Yǐchǒu,
Hún Hào, the military governor of Yìwǔ, reported defeating Chéngdé troops at Jiǔmén,
killing over a thousand men.
Hào
was the son of Hún Jiān.
Hún Jiān served with great merit under Emperors Sùzōng, Dàizōng, and Dézōng.
19 The army at Yòuzhōu mutinied,
expelling the prefect Luò Yí;
Tián Jìn, the military governor of Xiàzhōu, quelled it.
20 In the fifth month,
on the day Rénshēn,
Lǐ Guāngyán and Wū Chóngyìn reported defeating Huáixī troops at the Língyún stockade,
beheading over two thousand men.
21 In the sixth month,
on the day Jiǎchén,
Gāo Xiáyù suffered a major defeat at Tiěchéng,
barely escaping with his life.
According to the Old Book: Xiáyù advanced from Xiāobēi to Wénchéng stockade,
where he encountered an ambush and was defeated.
It is likely that Tiěchéng was Wénchéng stockade,
and because it was so坚固不可破,
it was called Tiěchéng [Iron City].
Sòng Bái said: Tiěchéng
was northeast of the Xīnxīng stockade.
The Xīnxīng stockade
was southwest of Wúfáng County,
northeast of Wénchéng.
In victory, they exaggerated their kills and captures;
in defeat, they concealed it;
this time,
the defeat was so great it could not be hidden,
and only then was it reported to the Emperor,
causing shock and alarm both inside and outside the court.
The chief ministers entered for an audience,
intending to advise the Emperor to halt the military campaigns,
but the Emperor said:
"Victory and defeat are common in warfare.
Now we should only discuss military strategy,
identify and replace generals and commanders who are incompetent,
and assist where troops and provisions are insufficient.
How can we discuss halting the campaigns just because one general has suffered a defeat!"
Thus, he solely adopted the advice of Péi Dù,
and others who spoke of halting the campaigns gradually fell silent.
On the day Jǐyǒu,
Xiáyù retreated to defend Tángzhōu.
The Emperor reprimanded Gāo Xiáyù for his defeat,
and Xiáyù claimed that Lǐ Xùn had failed to provide support.
Lǐ Xùn was in charge of provisions,
so Xiáyù’s army was able to shift the blame onto him.
In the seventh month,
Xiáyù was demoted to Prefect of Guīzhōu.
Guīzhōu
was ancient Zǐguī.
The state of Wú established Jiànpíng Commandery there,
and the Táng set up Guīzhōu,
located 2,268 lǐ south of the capital.
Ēnwáng Lián,
son of Emperor Dàizōng.
Yuán Zī, Military Governor of Jīngnán, was appointed Military Governor of Zhāngyì and Surveillance Commissioner of Shēn, Guāng, Cài, Táng, Suí, and Dèng,
with Tángzhōu as his administrative seat.
On the rénwǔ day,
the Xuānwǔ Army reported defeating 20,000 troops at Yǎnchéng,
killing over 2,000,
and capturing over 1,000.
Tián Hóngzhèng reported defeating Chéngdé troops at Nángōng,
killing over 2,000.
Wéi Guànzhī, Vice Director of the Secretariat and Co-Director of the Chancellery,
was aloof and reserved by nature,
fond of distinguishing social ranks,
and repeatedly requested halting military campaigns.
Left Rectifier of Omissions Zhāng Sù slandered him before the Emperor,
accusing him of forming factions.
In the eighth month,
on the rényín day,
Guànzhī was dismissed and made Vice Minister of Personnel.
The various armies campaigning against Wáng Chéngzōng watched each other without advancing,
but only Xī Shìměi, Military Governor of Zhāoyì, led elite troops to press on his border.
On the jǐwèi day,
Shìměi reported a major victory over Chéngzōng’s forces at Bǎixiāng,
killing over 1,000,
with a similar number surrendering,
and built three fortifications encircling Bǎixiāng.
Bǎixiāng
was a Hàn-dynasty county,
belonging to Jùlù Commandery.
Its old city was located 17 lǐ southwest of the present county seat,
which now lies north of the Péngshuǐ River,
established in the Suí dynasty,
under Zhàozhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Bǎixiāng County in Zhàozhōu
was the territory of the Jìn-era Hào settlement in the Spring and Autumn period.
The Hàn established Hào County,
which Emperor Guāngwǔ renamed Gāoyì.
In the sixth year of the Tiānbǎo era of Northern Qí, Gāoyì County was moved to the eastern border of the Hàn-era Fángzǐ County,
which is present-day Gāoyì County.
In the sixteenth year of the Kāihuáng era of Suí,
Bǎixiāng County was established 18 lǐ south of the old Hàn county seat,
adopting the distant name of the Hàn-era Bǎixiāng.
In the Sòng dynasty, Bǎixiāng was abolished as a town,
placed under Gāoyì.
Huán
is pronounced huàn.
On the gēngshēn day,
Empress Zhuāngxiàn was buried at Fēnglíng.
She accompanied Emperor Shùnzōng.
In the ninth month,
on the yǐhài day,
Right Omissions Corrector Dúgū Lǎng was implicated for requesting an end to military campaigns
and demoted to Granary Officer of Xīngyuán Prefecture.
Lǎng
was the son of Dúgū Jí.
Dúgū Jí served under Emperor Dàizōng,
skilled in argumentative writing.
Ráozhōu suffered a great flood,
sweeping away 4,700 households.
On the bǐngzǐ day,
Wéi Guànzhī was appointed Surveillance Commissioner of Húnán,
still implicated for his previous actions.
Previous actions
refer to his request to halt military campaigns.
On the xīnsì day,
Vice Minister of Personnel Wéi Yǐ, Examination Officer Wéi Chǔhòu, and others were all appointed as prefects of distant prefectures,
slandered by Zhāng Sù,
who claimed they were Guànzhī’s faction.
Yǐ
was the grandson of Wéi Jiànsù;
Wéi Jiànsù
served as chancellor at the end of the Tiānbǎo era.
He was the ninth-generation descendant of Wéi Xiòng.
Wéi Xiòng
was the elder brother of Wéi Xiàokuān of Later Zhōu.
Xiòng
is pronounced xuānzhèng fān.
On the yǐyǒu day,
Lǐ Guāngyán and Wū Chóngyìn reported capturing Wú Yuánjì’s Língyún Stockade.
On the dīnghài day,
Guāngyán also reported capturing the Shí and Yuè stockades;
Shòuzhōu reported defeating forces at Yīnchéng,
capturing six stockades.
Yīnchéng
was the Hàn-era Qīsī County,
belonging to Rǔnán Commandery.
The Sòng established Bāoxìn County,
renamed Yīnchéng in the Suí,

Twelfth year of the Yuánhé era

1. In spring,
the first month,
on Jiǎshēn,
Yuán Zī was demoted to Fǔzhōu Prefectural Governor.
Lǐ Sù arrived at Tángzhōu.
The army, having suffered defeats and losses,
had soldiers who all feared battle.
Sù understood this.
When some came out to greet him,
Sù said to them:
"The Son of Heaven knows that I, Sù, am gentle and timid,
capable of enduring humiliation,
and therefore sent me here to comfort you all.
As for launching attacks and advancing to seize territory,
that is not my business."
The multitude believed him and felt at ease.
Sù personally went to inspect the soldiers,
caring for the wounded and sick,
and did not act with stern authority.
Some criticized him for lax military discipline,
but Sù said:
"It is not that I am unaware.
Minister Yuán exclusively used kindness and favor to win over the rebels,
so the rebels underestimated him.
Upon hearing of my arrival,
they are bound to increase their preparations.
I therefore deliberately show them laxness.
They will certainly think I am timid and negligent,
and then we can devise a plan."
The people of Huáixī, having previously defeated the two commanders Gāo and Yuán,
looked down on Sù due to his lowly reputation and position,
and consequently made no preparations.
This set the stage for Sù to take advantage of their weakness and capture Cài.
Examination of discrepancies: The Old Biography states:
"Sù was deep, brave, and far-sighted,
treating his men with sincerity,
thus he could utilize his seemingly weak position
to strike the rebels unexpectedly.
After half a year,
knowing his men were usable,
he then planned the surprise attack on Cài,
submitting a memorial requesting reinforcements;
an edict added two thousand cavalry from Hézhōng and Fūfāng to his forces."
Zhèng Xiè's Píng Cài Lù states:
"On the 24th day of the first month, Jiǎshēn,
the Duke arrived at his command.
Previously,
the soldiers, having experienced defeats at Wànshèng, Xiāobēi, Tiěchéng, and Xīnxīng,
were all fearful in heart,
not daring to speak of battle.
The Duke pretended, saying,
'Warfare is not something I am capable of.'
Afterwards, he secretly summoned his senior generals to plan the matter.
At that time,
the Duke submitted a memorial requesting to directly attack Wú Yuánjì,
and everyone laughed at his proposal.
He then sent his observation judge, Wáng Nǐ, to request troops at the court.
An edict summoned a total of two thousand infantry and cavalry from Yìchéng, Hézhōng, and Fūfāng to fill his shortage."
According to this,
then he requested additional troops immediately upon arrival.
Also, in the second month,
he captured Díng Shìliáng,
and induced Wú Xiùlín to surrender.
This shows he did not wait half a year before knowing his men were usable.
The Old Biography is probably mistaken.
However, Sù's secret plan to surprise Cài—
how could he have revealed it beforehand?
And saying
"he submitted a memorial requesting to attack Yuánjì,
and everyone laughed at his proposal,"
would mean everyone knew about it.
This is probably not true!
It is not adopted here.

1 In the second month,
Lǐ Tīng attacked Hǎizhōu,
capturing the counties of Dōnghǎi, Qúshān, and Huáirén, among others.
Hǎizhōu,
with its administrative seat at Qúshān,
was originally the Qú County of the Hàn dynasty,
to which later people added
the character
"shān" (mountain).
Dōnghǎi,
was the territory of Gànyú County in the Hàn dynasty.
The Later Qí established Dōnghǎi County,
which belonged to Dōnghǎi Commandery.
The Suí dynasty abolished the commandery and the county,
incorporating it into Guǎngráo County.
In the first year of the Rénshòu era of the Suí dynasty, Guǎngráo was renamed Dōnghǎi,
to avoid the taboo of the crown prince's name.
In the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Hǎizhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is located ten lǐ east of the prefecture.
Huáirén County,
was established during the Liáng dynasty as the two Qīngzhōu, northern and southern.
The Eastern Wèi abolished the prefecture,
establishing Yìtáng Commandery and Huáirén County.
The Suí dynasty abolished the commandery,
and the county was placed under Hǎizhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is located eighty lǐ north of the prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: Huáirén County of Hǎizhōu,
was originally the territory of Gànyú County in the Hàn dynasty.
According to this, Hàn Gànyú,
is the old Gànyú city located thirty lǐ northeast of the present county.
The Liáng dynasty established the Huángguō garrison here,
and the Later Wèi established Yìtáng Commandery,
administering Huángguō City,
and governing the three counties of Yìtáng, Guīyì, and Huáirén.
The Northern Qí moved Yìtáng Commandery and Huáirén County to the area of present-day Jǔ County in Mìzhōu.
The Suí dynasty abolished the commandery during the Kāihuáng era,
and moved Huáirén County to administer here,
which is the present county seat.
They captured Chéng County.
Chéng,
was a Hàn dynasty county.
The Later Wèi established Lánlíng Commandery,
and the Suí dynasty abolished the commandery, making it Lánlíng County.
In the fourth year of the Wǔdé era, it was renamed Chéng County,
and later belonged to Yízhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is located one hundred and eighty lǐ southwest of the prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: Chéng,
is an old Hàn county,
and was the state of Céng during the Spring and Autumn period.
The Jìn dynasty established Lánlíng Commandery,
administering Chéng City.
According to this, the previous seat of Chéng County was located one lǐ west of the present county,
which is the old city of Hàn Chéng County.
In the sixteenth year of the Suí Kāihuáng era, Céngzhōu and Chéng County were established,
but soon the prefecture and county were abolished,
and Lánlíng County was moved to the old city of the abolished Céngzhōu.
In the mid-Táng period, Lánlíng was again renamed Chéng County.
Northwest of the county is the Chéng River.
Defeated,
pronunciation: bǔ mài fān.
Chéng,
pronunciation: shí zhèng fān.
Lǐ Shīdào heard that the imperial army was encroaching and pressing close,
so he conscripted civilians to repair the walls and moats of Yùnzhōu City,
and to prepare defenses,
even involving women in the labor,
causing the people to become increasingly fearful and resentful.
The Chief Military Commissioner Liú Wù,
was the grandson of Liú Zhèngchén.
Liú Zhèngchén appears in scroll 217, first year of the Zhìdé era of Emperor Sùzōng.
Wù was dedicated to being lenient and benevolent,
allowing the soldiers to act as they pleased,
and was nicknamed "Father Liú" in the army.
When Tián Hóngzhèng crossed the river,
Wù's army was unprepared,
and they suffered several defeats in battle.
Someone said to Shīdào:
"Liú Wù does not enforce military discipline,
but instead focuses on winning the hearts of the masses.
I fear he has other intentions,
and you should deal with him early."
Shīdào summoned Wù to discuss matters,
intending to kill him.
Someone advised against it, saying:
"Now the imperial armies are closing in from all sides,
and Wù has shown no signs of rebellion.
If you kill him based on one person's words,
which generals will be willing to serve you?
This would be like removing your own claws and teeth."
Shīdào kept Wù for ten days,
then sent him back,
giving him generous gifts of gold and silk to appease him.
Wù knew of this,
and upon returning to camp,
secretly made preparations.
Shīdào, because Wù was leading troops outside,
appointed Wù's son, Cóngjiàn, as a ménxià biézòu.
A ménxià biézòu is
someone placed among the staff at the yámén,
waiting to be appointed to an official position.
The Táng Liù Diǎn states: For all military garrison commanders-in-chief,
of the third rank or above,
there are twenty-five attendants,
and ten biézòu;
for deputy commanders,
there are twenty attendants,
and eight biézòu.
For commanders,
of the third rank or above,
there are eighteen attendants,
and six biézòu;
for deputy commanders,
of the fourth rank or above,
there are eleven attendants,
and three biézòu.
For expeditionary, defensive, and patrol deputy commanders,
the number of attendants is reduced by three according to rank,
and biézòu are reduced by two.
For commanders and deputy commanders,
the number of attendants is reduced by two according to rank,
and biézòu are reduced by one.
If there is no deputy commander for garrison commanders or those subordinate to large military garrisons,
the attendants and biézòu for the commander and below are reduced by one-fourth,
and the attendants and biézòu to be filled are to be recruited by themselves.
Cóngjiàn learned of the secret plot,
and secretly wrote to inform his father.
Another person said to Shīdào:
"Liú Wù will ultimately be a problem,
it would be better to eliminate him early."
On the bǐngchén day,
Shīdào secretly sent two messengers with a warrant to the deputy commander of the field army, Zhāng Xiān,
ordering him to behead Wù and present his head,
and commanding Xiān to temporarily take command of the field army.
At that time, Wù was on a high hill, with a tent set up and wine laid out,
two or three lǐ away from the camp.
The two messengers arrived at the camp,
and secretly gave the warrant to Xiān.
Xiān had always been on good terms with Wù,
so he pretended to discuss with the messengers, saying:
"Since Wù returned from the commander's headquarters,

We cannot act hastily.
I request to go first and inform him,

and also has gifts to bestow.
Please, Commander, return quickly.'
In the army, the commander is called the dūtóu.
Pass on the message,
meaning the words conveyed by the messengers sent by Shīdào.
Then he will not suspect anything,
and we can proceed with the plan."
The messengers agreed.
Xiān took the warrant and hurried to Wù,
dismissing others to show it to him.
Wù secretly sent people to first seize the two messengers,
and killed them.
By then, it was nearly dusk.
Wù reined in his horse and rode slowly back to camp,
sat in his tent,
and stationed troops to protect himself.
He summoned the generals,
and sternly said to them:
"Wù and all of you have fought against the imperial army without regard for death,
truly without betraying the Sikōng.
Now the Sikōng believes slanderous words,

If Wù dies,
you will be next.
Moreover, what the Son of Heaven wishes to punish is only the Sikōng alone.
Now the military situation is worsening daily,
why should we follow him to the destruction of our clans?
I wish to join all of you in rolling up the banners and bundling the armor,
roll,
same as juǎn.
to carry out the Son of Heaven's command,
meaning to carry out the imperial decree,
to punish Lǐ Shīdào.
Wealth and honor can be attained.
What do all of you think?"
The military commissioner Zháo Chuíjí stood at the front of the crowd,

"Will this matter

Wù immediately cursed him in response:
"Are you conspiring with the Sikōng?"
And immediately beheaded him.
He asked each of the others in turn,

The rest all trembled with fear,

Then he ordered the soldiers, saying:
"Upon entering Yùnzhōu,

As for the property of the official residence and the homes of the rebel faction,
you may freely plunder them;
the official residence,

Have all the soldiers eat their fill and take up arms,
at midnight,
listen for the drum,

detain them,

Several li from the city,

at daybreak,

He declared
"Commander Liú is entering the city under orders."
Official documents from the commander-in-chief issued to the various generals are called orders.

Report to the commissioner,

Commissioner,
Shūlì fān.
All fled and hid;

By the time they arrived,
the inner city gates were already wide open,

Wù led troops up to the audience hall,

Shīdào and his two sons hid under a toilet bed,

Shīdào still harbored hopes of surviving,

Soon all were beheaded.
In the first year of the Yǒngtài era of Emperor Dàizōng,
Lǐ Zhèngjǐ obtained Zīqīng,
for four generations,
fifty-four years, then it was destroyed.
Wù then ordered the two capital patrol commanders to inspect the wards and markets,
prohibiting plundering,
and order was immediately restored.
He gathered a large assembly of soldiers and civilians at the polo ground,

Wù saw Lǐ Gōngdù,

When Wù turned his troops from Yánggǔ towards Yùnzhōu,

rú zì,

thought he would obtain all twelve prefectures,

At this time, the emperor was deeply immersed in feasting,
paying no attention to the affairs of the realm.
Cuí Zhí and Dù Yuányǐng lacked long-term vision,
unaware of the major principles of security and peril.
They merely wished to honor and elevate Lǐ Hóngjìng,
so they only carved out the two provinces of Yíng and Mò,
placing Zhāng Shìméi in charge of them,
while all the rest were placed under Hóngjìng's command.
Zhū Kèróng and others had long been stranded in the capital,
even to the point of begging for clothing and food.
They went daily to the Secretariat seeking official posts,
but Zhí and Yuányǐng paid them no heed.
When Hóngjìng was appointed to Yōuzhōu,
they ordered Kèróng and his ilk to return to their original armies for assignment,
which filled Kèróng and the others with resentment and anger.
Previously,
the military governors of Héběi had personally endured cold and heat,
sharing toil and leisure with their soldiers.
But when Hóngjìng arrived,
he was dignified, proud, and noble,
riding in a sedan chair amid the multitude,
astonishing the people of Yān.
"Astonishing" means
seeing it and being shocked and suspicious.
Yān
is pronounced Yúxián;
the same below.
Only once every ten days would he emerge to sit and decide matters.
Guests, generals, and officials rarely heard him speak;
he did not connect with their sentiments,
and mostly delegated governmental affairs to his staff officers.
Moreover, the assistant officials he appointed, such as Wéi Yōng, were mostly young and frivolous men,
fond of drink and unrestrained in their arrogance.
When they went out or returned, their retinue made a great clamor;
sometimes they returned at night with torches lighting up the streets,
all things the people of Yān were unaccustomed to.
An edict granted a million strings of cash to reward the officers and soldiers,
but Hóngjìng kept two hundred thousand strings for miscellaneous expenses of the military headquarters.
Yōng and his ilk further reduced the soldiers' grain allowances,
restraining them by law,
and repeatedly insulted and scolded the officers and soldiers as rebel captives.
They said to the soldiers:
"Now the realm is at peace;
you lot may be able to draw a two-dàn bow,
but that's not as good as recognizing a single character!"
From this, everyone in the army harbored resentment and anger.
To pacify the wild and fierce,
spreading virtue and transformation,
one must adapt to their customs and govern appropriately to achieve success easily.
To startle them with what they have never seen,
to frighten them with what they have never heard,
rarely fails to hasten disaster.

Shǐ Xiànchéng secretly harbored treacherous intentions,
and taking advantage of the troops’ discontent,
he sowed discord and incited them.
Using the troops’ sentiments as a metaphor for fire,
fire inherently has a fierce nature,
and if bellows are used to blow on it,
and fans are used to fan it,
it becomes even fiercer.
Jiàn,
pronounced as in ancient times, like xiàn.
He was ordered to rescue Shēnzhōu,
on the gēngzǐ day,
Tián Bù’s army was utterly defeated,

meaning to follow the example of Tián Chéngsì and Lǐ Bǎochén.

Tián Bù had no way to deal with them,

“The task will not be accomplished!”
That same day,
he wrote a final memorial detailing the situation,
roughly stating:
“I observe the troops’ intentions,

since I have achieved no merit,
I dare not forget to die immediately.
Jí,
means to approach.
If not,
loyal officials and righteous men will all be slaughtered by Héshuò!”
He presented the memorial weeping loudly,

as a filial son mourning his parent,
he set up a table and mat,
morning and evening prepared water for washing,
offered food and drink,
serving him as if he were alive,
commonly called the spirit table.
“Above, to apologize to the sovereign and father,
below, to show the three armies.”
Then he stabbed his heart and died.
When Shǐ Xiànchéng heard that Tián Bù had died,
he informed his troops,
to follow the old ways of Héběi.
The troops were pleased,
and supporting Shǐ Xiànchéng, they returned to Wèi,
and installed him as acting military governor.
On the wùshēn day,
Wèizhōu reported Tián Bù’s suicide.
On the jǐyǒu day,
Shǐ Xiànchéng was appointed as the military governor of Wèibó.
Although Shǐ Xiànchéng was pleased to obtain the symbols of command,
outwardly he served the court,
but inwardly he actually colluded with Yōu and Zhèn.
2 On the gēngxū day,
Dézhōu prefect Wáng Rìjiǎn was appointed as the military governor of Hénghǎi.
Wáng Rìjiǎn,
was originally an officer of Chéngdé.

Even Lǐ Guāngyán merely closed his fortifications and defended himself.
The soldiers gathered their own firewood and fodder,

Chén,
means old.
Rice that has been stored for a year is called old rice.
Sháo,
pronounced as zhí lüè fān,
also pronounced as shí zhuó fān.
According to the Rites of Zhōu: the carpenter makes drinking vessels,
one sháo equals one shēng.
However, a sháo of one shēng
is a drinking vessel,
not for measuring rice.
In general measurement,
ten sháo make one gě,
ten gě make one shēng,
ten shēng make one dǒu.
In terms of measurement,
if each person is given a daily ration of one sháo of old rice,
they would only starve to death.
The historian is likely exaggerating the extreme scarcity,
similar to the phrase in Wǔ Chéng “blood flowed enough to float pestles.”
The court had no alternative,
in the second month,

When the emperor first ascended the throne,

that in military garrisons where there were troops,

Some by desertion,
some by death,
removing them from the registers.
Miǎn,
pronounced as miǎn.

An edict was issued to summon troops from various circuits to suppress them,

a motley crowd;
moreover,
since the various military governors had supervising eunuchs,
those leading separate armies also had palace eunuchs supervising the formations,
the commanding generals could not fully control orders,
if they achieved a minor victory, swift couriers would report the victory,
claiming credit for themselves,
if they were defeated, they would pressure the commanding generals,
and blame them for the defeat;
they selected all the bravest soldiers in the army for their own protection,

Also, in all military operations,
every move was directed by strategies issued from the palace,

so they did not know what to follow;
without considering feasibility,
they only urged them to fight quickly.
Palace eunuchs filled the roads like weaving,

They took side roads to travel,

Péi Dù was a senior minister of great reputation,

Cui Zhi and Du Yuányǐng served as
chancellors,

The historical record strongly states the reasons for the Táng's second loss of Héběi and Shuòfāng.

Fù,
pronounced fú yòu fān.

Lè,
pronounced luò.

Textual analysis says: According to the Veritable Records:

and that month,

However, Déyù held prestigious and important positions throughout the Yuánhé era,
so he was not unpromoted.
At this time, Yuán Zhěn became chancellor,
while Féngjí was in Huáinán,

This likely stems from the words of Déyù's partisans.
Thus, it is not adopted here.

The New Book biography later states
"Minister of Education,"

"As military operations had not yet ceased,

"If the government sells salt itself,

The term "suǒyóu"

"Order the chief ministers to oversee the Salt and Iron Commission."

"Those who jointly signed the petition"
refers to those who signed their names together on the complaint.
Hán Yù, Vice Minister of War, submitted a memorial,

"Outside the city walls,
there is little cash
to buy salt,
which should belong to the previous sentence.
Salt merchants, however, accept all kinds of goods,

'Dài'
means to borrow.
Both parties benefit and find it convenient.
Now, if clerks are ordered to sit in shops and sell salt themselves,
displaying goods for sale is called a 'shop.'
'Pù,'
pronounced pǔ gù fān.
They will certainly not dare to accept goods.
In this way,
the poor will have no means to obtain salt,
naturally leading to a loss of regular revenue.
How can there be doubled profits?

Furthermore,
the duties of prefects and county magistrates lie in sharing the emperor's concerns.
The ruler worries about the people,
and when some cannot make a living,

They should not be assessed solely on their administrative performance!

poor households consume very little salt,

If salt is distributed according to household,

officials, fearing punishment,
will certainly use threats and penalties.
I fear this will cause unrest everywhere,

Wéi Chùhòu, a Secretariat Drafter, argued,

Dòu Shēn's case is recorded in the annals of Dézōng.
Huángfǔ Bó's case is recorded in the annals of Xiànzōng.
'Zú,'
pronounced zǐ xù fān.
Refers to beating to death the ringleaders who lodge complaints,
and caning the back of those who jointly signed.
Such a policy will certainly not succeed;
prohibiting what people are bound to violate,

An examination of discrepancies: The Veritable Records, due to the event of Zhāng Píngshū's promotion to Vice Minister of Revenue on Rényín in the third month,

It is now appended at the end of the fourth month.

Now, observing Emperor Mùzōng's bestowals,

The two biographies contradict each other.
Féngjí's connection with Shǒuchéng

Lǐ Ràngyí was a partisan of Lǐ Déyù,

Furthermore, Zhāng Yòuxīn and Lǐ Xùzhī being Féngjí's subordinates during his governorship
occurred after Féngjí was reassigned to govern Xiāngyáng,
and was not the case at this time.
This account is not adopted here.

Chéng Dàchāng states: In the seventh year of the Zhēnyuán era of Emperor Dézōng
, an edict was issued that each time the Emperor held court in the Yányīng Hall,

to be consulted on governmental affairs.
This was called "xúnduì."
Thus, besides the "dàizhì" officials,
there was also a separate "xúnduì."
It seems that "dàizhì" properly referred to
the chief officials of the various departments.
Those called "xúnduì"
were not chief officials but were among the regular court audience officials,
and could also take turns being summoned for audience.
The term "cìduì guān"
refers to the "xúnduì" officials,
who were permitted to wait for audience after the "dàizhì" officials.
Therefore, "cìduì" cannot be precisely equated with "dàizhì."
When people nowadays write,
whenever they mention "dàizhì,"
they all refer to it as "cìduì."
This is likely not accurate.
However, since the term has become customary,
even people of the Táng dynasty themselves did not distinguish clearly.
During the Kāichéng era,
an imperial order stated that henceforth, on days when the Emperor held court in the inner hall,
the "cìduì" officials should not immediately leave with their regular groups.
Instead, they should stand together under the pine trees on the eastern steps,
and after the chief ministers finished reporting and withdrew,
they were to approach the incense table together and each report on their department's official business.
The Left and Right Historiographers waited until the "cìduì" officials finished reporting before leaving together.
This account refers to the chief officials of various departments who served as "dàizhì"
being called "cìduì guān."
If one examines the system closely,
it actually mistakenly treats "dàizhì" as "cìduì guān."
I have examined that after the mid-Táng period,
when the chief ministers faced the Emperor in the Yányīng Hall,
after they withdrew,
both the "dàizhì" officials and the "xúnduì" officials could be granted an audience.
Collectively, they could be called "cìduì guān."
The so-called "cìduì guān"
means those who obtained an audience after the chief ministers,
not those who entered for audience after the "dàizhì" officials.
The people of the Táng dynasty were not mistaken;
Chéng Tàizhī himself was mistaken.
According to Sòng Bái's record,
the edict of the eleventh month in the seventh year of Zhēnyuán
states that "cìduì guān" referred to regular court audience officials who took turns for audience.

This is because the compilers of the *Veritable Records of Emperor Mùzōng* detested Shēn,
