Ānnán reported that the Huángmán were invading.
The Huángmán,
are the Huángdòngmán.
24. The Governor of Lóngzhōu, Yùchí Ruì, submitted a memorial stating:
"Mount Niúxīn has long been renowned as a place of divine wonder.
There is a spot where it has been excavated and severed;
I request that it be repaired and filled."
This was approved.
Tens of thousands of laborers were conscripted for work in this extremely perilous location,
causing exhaustion and hardship in Dōngchuān.
(Wéi,
read as yúwèi.)
25. In the ninth month,
on the day Dīngwèi,
Lǐ Sūshā of Persia presented timber for a pavilion made of chénxiāng (aloeswood).
Left Reminder Lǐ Hàn submitted a memorial stating:
"How is this any different from the Jade Terrace or Jasper Chambers!"
Although the Emperor was angered,
he treated him with leniency.
Dù Yòu said: Chénxiāng comes from Línyì.
The local people cut the wood,
and after accumulating it over many years,
the rotten parts fall away, leaving only the heartwood and knots.
When placed in water, it sinks,
hence it is called chénxiāng (sinking fragrance).
According to the Zhū Fān Zhì: Chénxiāng comes from various places,
its forms are diverse and its names also vary:
Some resembling a rhinoceros horn are called xījiǎo chén;
some resembling a swallow's beak are called yànkǒu chén;
some resembling monkshood (fùzǐ) are called fùzǐ chén;
some shaped like a shuttle are called suō chén;
those with hard grain and fine texture are called héngyáng chén.
Now, timber that can be used to build a pavilion
indicates pieces far surpassing these other types of chén.
(Lǐ Hàn was the sixth-generation descendant of Lǐ Dàomíng.
Dàomíng
was the younger brother of Huáiyáng Prince Lǐ Dàoxuán.)
26. In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Wùxū,
Hanlin Academician Wéi Chǔhòu admonished the Emperor about his feasting and excursions, saying:
"The late Emperor brought illness upon himself and shortened his lifespan through wine and women.
The reason I did not remonstrate unto death at that time
was because Your Majesty was already fifteen years old.
Now the Crown Prince is barely one year old;
how dare I, fearing death, not remonstrate!"
The Emperor was moved by his words
and bestowed upon him a hundred bolts of brocade and four silver vessels.
27. In the eleventh month,
on the day Wùwǔ,
Ānnán reported: The Huángmán people, allied with Huánwáng, attacked and captured Lùzhōu,
killing Governor Gé Wéi.
28. On the day Gēngshēn,
the Ruìshèng Wénhuì Xiào Emperor was buried at the Guānglíng tomb;
(Guānglíng
is located fifteen li north of Yáoshān in Fèngxiān County, Tóngzhōu.)
29. Wáng Bò bribed Wáng Shǒuchéng with one hundred thousand strings of cash,
seeking to regain control over the salt and iron monopolies.
(In the fourth month of this year,
Wáng Bò had been dismissed from the post of Salt and Iron Transport Commissioner.)
On the day Guǐwèi,

Remonstrance Officials Dúgū Lǎng and Zhāng Zhòngfāng, Diarists Liǔ Gōngquán and Sòng Shēnxī, and Reminders Lǐ Jǐngràng and Xuē Tínglǎo requested an audience at the Yányīng Hall to discuss his treacherous nature.
The Emperor asked:
"Are those who previously argued at court not among them?"
That same day,
Liú Qīchǔ was appointed as a Remonstrance Official.
(Jǐngràng
was the great-grandson of Lǐ Chéng.
Lǐ Chéng
defended the Eastern Capital at the end of the Tiānbǎo era
and died during Ān Lùshān's rebellion.
Chéng,
read as zhílíng.)
(Liú Qīchǔ was a man of Hézhōng.)
30. In the twelfth month,
on the day Gēngyín,
Tiānpíng Military Governor Wū Zhòngyìn was given the additional title of Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
31. On the day Yǐwèi,
Xúsì Observation Commissioner Wáng Zhìxīng, on account of the Emperor's birthday,
(According to the Táng Huìyào: The Emperor was born on the ninth day of the sixth month in the fourth year of the Yuánhé era.)
now requested the establishment of an ordination platform in the twelfth month,
making the request in advance.)
ordained Buddhist monks and nuns to accumulate blessings;
(According to Buddhist law,
all newly ordained monks and nuns
must go to an ordination platform to receive the precepts.
Those who have not received the precepts are called śrāmaṇeras;
ignorant people and those seeking to avoid taxes and corvée labor flocked to it.)
(In Sìzhōu there was a great sacred pagoda,
which people revered and served,
hence Wáng Zhìxīng requested to establish the ordination platform there.)
Since the Yuánhé era,
imperial decrees had prohibited this abuse,
but Zhìxīng, wishing to amass wealth,
was the first to request its establishment.
Consequently, people converged from all directions,
especially from Jiāngnán and Huáinán.
Wáng Zhìxīng's family wealth thereby accumulated to tens of millions.
Zhèxī Observation Commissioner Lǐ Déyù submitted a memorial stating:
"If this is not checked,
and it only stops on the Emperor's birthday,
it is estimated that Liǎngzhè and Fújiàn will lose six hundred thousand adult males."
When the memorial arrived,
the practice was abolished that very day.
32. This year,
the Huíhé Chóngdé Kèhán died.
His younger brother, Hésà Tèlè, succeeded him.
First Year of the Bǎolì Era
(Yǐsì year, 825)
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the day Xīnhài,
the Emperor performed the suburban sacrifice at the southern altar;
upon returning,
he ascended the Dānfèng Tower,
proclaimed a general amnesty,
and changed the reign era.
Previously, the Magistrate of Hù County, Cuī Fā, heard a commotion outside,
inquired about it,
and was told:
"Men from the Five Stables are beating commoners."
Fā became angry,
ordered them seized and brought in,
and dragged them into the courtyard.
As it was already dark,
it was only after a long while,
upon interrogation,
that he realized they were palace eunuchs.
The Emperor was furious,
arrested Fā,
and imprisoned him in the Censorate.
On that day,
as Fā stood with other prisoners beneath the golden rooster,
(Under Táng regulations: Whenever a state pardon was to be granted,
the Ministry of Justice would first assemble the prisoners before the palace gate.
The Guard Command would erect a golden rooster
and place a drum to the right of the palace gate.
When the prisoners arrived, the drum would be beaten.
Only after the decree was proclaimed were the prisoners released.)
(In the thirteenth year of Xuánzōng's Tiānbǎo era,
the Palace Domestic Service established 1,696 high-ranking officials
and 2,932 low-ranking and unranked officials,
all being eunuchs.)
they beat him until his face was broken and teeth shattered;
he lost consciousness and they left.
After a few hours he revived,
but then others came seeking to beat him again.
The prison officials shielded him with mats,
and he barely escaped.
The Emperor ordered Fā imprisoned again in the Censorate prison.
(The Censorate prison
is the prison of the Censorate.)
14 The court received Liú Wù's posthumous memorial.
Many in the discussions argued that the Shangdang region was an internal military command,
different from Héshuò,
and should not be granted.
Left Vice Director Lǐ Jiàng submitted a memorial,
believing:
"Military strategy values speed,
authority and decisiveness prize firmness.
When people's sentiments are not unified,
then one can attack their plans.
Liú Wù has been dead for several months,
yet the court has still not made arrangements.
The minds of those inside and outside the court
all regret the missed opportunity.
Now, the troops of the Zhāoyì army
certainly will not all share Liú Cóngjiàn's plans.
Even if half agree with him,
there is still the other half who remain loyal.
Liú Cóngjiàn has not long commanded troops,
his authority and favor have not been extended to the people.
Furthermore, this region has always been poor;
speaking of the Zhāoyì circuit,
it has always been impoverished and weak,
not as wealthy as other circuits.
If the court now quickly appoints a general near Zé-Lù to serve as Military Governor of Zhāoyì,
ordering him to travel day and night to take up his post,
before Liú Cóngjiàn can make arrangements,
the new commissioner will have already arrived in Lùzhōu.
This is the so-called 'forestalling others to seize their hearts'.
Once the new commissioner arrives,
the army's morale will naturally have something to rely on;
Liú Cóngjiàn holds no official position,
what name does he have to take charge?
Even if he schemes to obstruct the court's orders,
his officers and soldiers will certainly not follow him.
Now, the court has long made no arrangements,
that army does not understand the court's intentions.
That army,
refers to the Zhāoyì army.
If they wish to join in evil, they fear another person might be appointed;
in their hesitation,
if there are treacherous men who scheme for them,
falsely promising large sums of reward money,
the soldiers, coveting these rewards,
will be especially difficult to command.
I humbly hope for a swift decision,
and first issue a clear decree,
a clear decree,
meaning a clear imperial edict.
Decide,
Dīng luàn fān.
Issue,
Xiá jià fān.
Commending their longstanding loyalty and integrity,
speaking of the Zé-Lù army,
since Lǐ Bàozhēn's time,
has been utterly loyal and devoted to the court.
Grant them rewards;
subsequently appoint Liú Cóngjiàn as a Prefect.
Since Liú Cóngjiàn would have gained something roughly,
he will certainly choose what is advantageous and act accordingly,
and will absolutely not dare to resist.
If he does not obey the command,
I also believe there is no need for attack and suppression.
Why?
I have heard that Liú Cóngjiàn has already forbidden the soldiers of the three prefectures east of the mountains from privately keeping weapons,
the Zhāoyì subordinate prefectures Xíng, Míng, Cí,
are all east of the mountains.
Matters within his own tent are also not beyond doubt.
Meaning within his tent there are certainly those who plot against Liú Cóngjiàn to gain merit.
There is absolutely no reason to immediately confer authority upon Liú Cóngjiàn."
At that time, Lǐ Féngjí and Wáng Shǒuchéng had already settled their plans,
and in the end did not adopt Lǐ Jiàng's strategy.
Examination of discrepancies says: The Veritable Records:
"Cóngjiàn bribed those in power with gold and silk."
The Old Biography of Cóngjiàn says:
"Lǐ Féngjí and Wáng Shǒuchéng accepted his bribes,
and wrongfully petitioned on his behalf."
Whether these events occurred is difficult to ascertain,
and are not adopted here.
On Xīnchǒu,
Cóngjiàn was appointed as Interim Military Governor of Zhāoyì.
Liú Wù had been oppressive and harsh,
Cóngjiàn alleviated this with leniency and generosity,
and the masses became quite attached to him.
15 Lǐ Jiàng was fond of speaking frankly,
and Lǐ Féngjí detested him.
According to precedent,
on the day the Vice Director assumed office,
the Chief Ministers would escort him,
all officials would stand in ranks,
the Vice Censor-in-Chief would take his position in the court,
and officials of the rank of Department Head and below would attend the monthly assembly.
Assembly,
means assembly attendance.
When Yí Shèn served as Vice Director,
the Erudite of the Grand Court of Imperial Sacrifices Wéi Qiān submitted that the old ceremonial was too heavy,
and it was abolished.
The Vice Censor-in-Chief Wáng Bó, relying on Féngjí's influence,
when encountering Jiàng on the road,
did not yield to him.
Jiàng cited precedent and submitted:
"The Vice Director,
at the founding of the state, served as the principal Chief Minister.
In the early Táng,
when Tàizōng served as Head of the Department of State Affairs,
his ministers did not dare occupy that position,
and from then on it was not appointed,
using the Left and Right Vice Directors as the heads of the Department of State Affairs,
their duty being that of principal Chief Minister.

Those called Participants in Deliberations of Court Governance, Participants in Knowledge of Important Matters, and Joint Managers of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery, although all are duties of the Chief Minister,
are not the principal Chief Minister.
If a person is unworthy of the position,
naturally another worthy should be appointed;
if the court orders one to maintain the office,
how can the laws and institutions be impaired?
I request that the matter be submitted to all officials for detailed deliberation."
Most in the discussion agreed with Jiàng's opinion.
The Emperor ordered the old ceremonial to be followed.
On Jiǎzǐ,
because Jiàng had a foot ailment,
he was appointed as Junior Mentor of the Heir Apparent, with duties in the Eastern Capital.
16 Many who spoke on affairs praised Péi Dù's worthiness,
and that he should not be relegated to a provincial command.
The Emperor repeatedly sent envoys to Xīngyuán to console and inquire after Dù,
secretly indicating the time for his return;
Dù therefore requested to enter the court,
and the faction of Féngjí was greatly afraid.
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the Rénchén day,
Péi Dù entered the court from Xìngyuán.
The faction of Lǐ Féngjí used every means to slander him.
Previously, there was a folk ballad that said:
"The child in crimson clothes bares his belly,
The mouth in the sky is driven away."
Crimson clothes,
refers to the character 'Péi'.
The mouth in the sky,
refers to the character 'Wú'.
It was said that Péi Dù could capture Wú Yuánjì,
and his talent could be employed.
Within Cháng'ān city, there were six ridges running across,
resembling the hexagram Qián.
Péi Dù's residence happened to be situated on the fifth ridge.
The six ridges running across,
resemble the six lines of the Qián hexagram.
Péi Dù's mansion in Pínglè Ward happened to be on the fifth ridge.
Chéng Dàchāng said: When Yǔwén Kǎi planned the Suí capital,
he said: The Zhūquè Street runs north-south to the outer walls,
with six high slopes,
symbolizing the six lines of the Qián hexagram.
Therefore, on the second line (jiǔ èr), palaces were placed to represent the dwelling of the emperor.
On the third line (jiǔ sān), various government offices were established to correspond to the number of gentlemen.
The fifth line (jiǔ wǔ) is a noble position,
not intended for ordinary people to reside,
so Xuándū Temple and Xìngshàn Temple were placed there to suppress the location.
Liú Yǔxī's poem "Viewing Flowers" refers to this.
Péi Dù's residence was east of Zhūquè Street,
from north to south, it was the fourth ward,
named Yǒnglè Ward,
roughly opposite Xuándū Temple from east to west.
However, his mansion, compared to the temple's foundation,
was set back two wards to the north,
not directly opposite.
The Táng Veritable Records state: Péi Dù was in Xìngyuán,
and requested to enter the court for an audience.
Among Lǐ Féngjí's faction was a man named Zhāng Quányú who opposed him,
believing that
"Péi Dù's name corresponds to prophecies,
his residence occupies the Qián ridge,
he comes without being summoned,
his intentions are evident."
What Quányú called "his residence occupies the Qián ridge"
refers to the remaining influence of the fifth slope of Lóngshǒu.
However, where Péi Dù resided,
Zhāng Yuè's mansion was to its west,
even closer to Xuándū Temple.
And Zhāng Jiāzhēn's mansion was precisely north of the ward,
why single out Péi Dù for occupying the Qián ridge!
Petty men using personal grudges to deceive the ruler are all like this.
"Péi Dù's name corresponds to prophecies,
his residence occupies the ridge plain,
he comes without being summoned,
his purpose is evident."
Textual analysis states: The old biography of Féngjí says:
"In the early Bǎolì era,
Péi Dù repeatedly submitted memorials requesting an audience,
Féngjí's faction felt uneasy,
as if arrows were piercing their bodies,
so they conspired together,
wanting to prevent his coming.
Zhāng Quányú composed the ballad 'Non-clothed Child'
[the ballad],
spreading it in the streets and alleys,
saying Péi Dù's appearance had a heavenly mandate,
his name corresponded to the ballad prophecy."
However, Wéi Chùhòu analyzed before the emperor the words composed by Quányú.
Consider: If Quányú composed the ballad,
he should have added more malicious words,
not merely saying
"The mouth in the sky is driven away"
and that's all.
Probably the folk had this ballad first,
Quányú then said Péi Dù's name corresponded to the ballad prophecy,
he did not compose it.
[The emperor] thoroughly investigated the false accusations and slander,
and treated Péi Dù even more generously.
When Péi Dù first arrived in the capital,
court officials filled his door,
Péi Dù kept guests for drinks.
The Capital Prefect Liú Qīchǔ leaned close to Péi Dù's ear to whisper,
the Attendant Censor Cuī Xián raised a cup to penalize Péi Dù, saying:
"The Chancellor should not allow subordinate officials to whisper in the ear."
The Capital Prefect manages numerous and complex affairs,
hence people in the Táng dynasty called prefectural and county officials 'subordinate officials'.
Xiàng Ānshì's Family Explanation says: Today, public servants in wards and markets are called 'subordinate officials'.
Whisper,
pronounced chì shè fān.
Murmur,
pronounced ér shè fān.
Whispering and murmuring,
means speaking softly,
the mouth moves but the sound is not heard far away.
Qīchǔ felt uneasy,
and hurried out.
In the second month,
on the Dīngwèi day,
Péi Dù was appointed as Minister of Works and Grand Councilor.
While Péi Dù was in the Secretariat,
his attendants suddenly reported the seal was lost,
those who heard turned pale.
Péi Dù continued drinking as usual;
after a while,
his attendants reported the seal was found again in its original place,
Péi Dù did not respond.
Someone asked him the reason,
Péi Dù said:
"This must be a clerk stealing it to stamp documents,
if pressed urgently, he would throw it into water or fire,
if dealt with leniently, it would return to its original place."
Someone asked:
"When the attendants reported finding the seal,
could he not have immediately questioned the person about where the seal was found?"
The answer was:
"Lord Jìn (Péi Dù) handling this must have his reasons,
please consider it carefully yourself."
2. Since ascending the throne,
the emperor wanted to visit the Eastern Capital,
many grand councilors and court officials admonished against it,
the emperor did not listen to any,
determined to go,
and had already ordered the Vice Minister of Revenue Lú Zhēn to inspect
and repair the Eastern Capital palaces and waystations along the route.
From Cháng'ān through Huà, Shǎn to Luò,
along the route there were waystations,
such as the Qióngyuè Palace and Jīnchéng Palace in Huàyīn,
the Shéntái Palace in Zhèng County,
the Xiùlǐng Palace in Shǎn County,
the Fāngguì Palace in Miǎnchí,
the Fúchāng Palace in Fúchāng,
the Qíxiù Palace and Lánfēng Palace in Yǒngníng,
and the Liánchāng Palace and Xìngtài Palace in Shòu'ān.
"The state originally established two capitals to prepare for imperial tours,
since the many troubles arose,
this matter was abandoned.
Now the palaces, barracks, and various office buildings are mostly dilapidated,
if Your Majesty wishes to travel,
you should order the relevant officials to gradually complete repairs over time,
then you may go."
The emperor said:
"Those who have spoken on this matter all said I should not go,
but as you said,
not going is also acceptable."
It happened that Zhū Kèróng and Wáng Tíngcòu both offered to send soldiers and craftsmen to assist in repairing the Eastern Capital.
In the third month, on the Dīnghài day,
an edict was issued stating that repairing the Eastern Capital was troublesome,
and it was cancelled.
The historian states that the Eastern Capital repair project,
was not cancelled due to the admonitions of loyal ministers,
but specifically because of fear of Yōu and Zhèn raising troops.
At that time, the incident arose suddenly.
Wáng Shǒuchéng, considering that the Hanlin Academician Wéi Chǔhòu was broadly learned in ancient and modern affairs,
discussed all arrangements for that night
together with him.
Shǒuchéng and others wanted to issue orders to the court and the regions,
but were uncertain about the wording to use.
Chǔhòu said:
"To rectify the name and punish the crime,
what objection can there be in terms of righteousness?
How can one be indecisive
and avoid something out of taboo!"
They also asked:
"How should Prince Jiāng ascend the throne?"
Chǔhòu said:
"Tomorrow morning,
we should announce to the court and the regions by the Prince's instruction that the internal crisis has been pacified.
Then, the assembled ministers should present three memorials urging his accession,
and he should be enthroned as emperor by the decree of the Grand Empress Dowager."
At that time, everyone followed his words.
There was no time to consult the relevant offices again,
so all ceremonial regulations
came from Chǔhòu,
and none were inappropriate.
On the Guǐmǎo day,
Péi Dù was appointed Acting Grand Steward.
All officials paid their respects to Prince Jiāng at the outer corridor of the Zǐchén Hall,
where the Prince, in plain clothes, wept.
On the Jiǎchén day,
he received the various military commissioners at the Shàoyáng Court.
The Shàoyáng Court,
judging by its location and status,
should be in the northeast corner of the palace city,
where the Crown Prince resides,
also called the Eastern Palace.
Now, according to the palace map of the Dàmíng Palace: the Shàoyáng Court is east of the Yùtáng Hall,
with the Wēnshì, Xuānhuī, Qīngsī, Tàihé, and Zhūjìng Halls further north.
It is not exactly in the northeast corner of the palace city.
Examination of discrepancies: Wèi Mó's Veritable Records of Emperor Wénzōng
places the reception of the military commissioners after the reception of all officials,
not specifying a separate day.
Now, we follow the Veritable Records of Emperor Jìngzōng.
All were exiled to Lǐngnán or border regions.
On the Yǐsì day,
Emperor Wénzōng ascended the throne,
and changed his name to Áng.
On the Wùshēn day,
he honored his mother, Lady Xiāo, as Empress Dowager,
and Empress Dowager Wáng as the Bǎolì Empress Dowager.
At that time,
Empress Dowager Guō resided in the Xīngqìng Palace,
Empress Dowager Wáng in the Yì'ān Hall,
and Empress Dowager Xiāo within the main palace.
The Emperor was filial and respectful by nature,
serving the three palaces equally.
From this point onward,
whenever "the Emperor" is mentioned,
it refers to Emperor Wénzōng.
He first offered sacrifices at the suburban altars and ancestral temple,
then served the three palaces,
and only afterward attended to his own affairs.
Empress Dowager Xiāo
was from Mǐn.
On the Gēngxū day,
Hanlin Academician Wéi Chǔhòu was appointed Vice Director of the Secretariat and Joint Manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery.
Since his time as a prince,
the Emperor had deeply understood the failings of the two previous reigns,
referring to the reigns of Emperors Mùzōng and Jìngzōng.
Reign,
pronounced zhāo;
same below.
He exerted himself to seek good governance,
eliminating extravagance and embracing frugality.
He issued an edict that all palace women without official duties be sent out,
resulting in over three thousand leaving.
The falcons and hounds of the Five Offices,
following the precedent of the Yuánhé era,
were kept only in limited numbers for hunting,
and the rest were released.
The annual supplies for the palace provided by the relevant offices
all followed the precedent of the Zhēnyuán era.
He reduced over twelve hundred positions in the Music Academy, Hanlin Academy, and various directorates,
the directorates
referring to the Park Directorates.
The various offices,
meaning the various internal offices.
Their clothing and grain allowances,
which were excessive grants from Emperor Jìngzōng's reign,
were all returned to the relevant offices.
The previous practice of demanding embroidered, carved, and engraved items
was entirely abolished.
During Emperor Jìngzōng's reign,
court audiences were held no more than once or twice a month.
The Emperor now restored the old system,
holding court audiences on every odd-numbered day without fail,
consulting with the chief ministers and assembled officials on government affairs,
often for a long time before concluding.
Officials on standby duty, though previously established,
had never been summoned for audience;
now they were frequently invited for consultation.
Court suspensions or cancellations were all on even-numbered days.
Both court and regions rejoiced together,
believing that peace and prosperity could be hoped for.
Rulers who truly desire good governance do not appear in every generation.
When a ruler first administers,
if there are one or two actions sufficient to renew the people's perspective,
the hopes of the world are greatly placed upon him.
Yet, in the end, he fails to meet the world's expectations—
such were Cáo Máo (Duke of Gāoguìxiāng) of Wèi, Emperor Huái of Jìn, Emperor Dézōng of Táng, and Emperor Wénzōng.
First year of Tàihé
(Dīngwèi, 827)
1. Spring,
second month,
on the Yǐsì day,
a general amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed.
2. Lǐ Tóngjié (dǎn) occupied Cāngjǐng,
and the court did not address it for a year.
Last year in the third month,
Lǐ Tóngjié (dǎn) assumed the post of Acting Military Governor of Hénghǎi.
In the third month,
on the first day, Rénxū,
he sent his administrative secretary Cuí Cóngcháng to present a memorial and, together with his brothers Tóngzhì and Tóngxùn, come to court,
requesting to obey the court's orders.
3. Although the Emperor humbly listened and accepted advice, he could not be resolute.
After deciding matters with the chief ministers,
he would soon change his mind.
Summer,
fourth month,
on the Bǐngchén day,
Wéi Chǔhòu strongly argued this point at the Yányīng Hall,
and requested to resign;
the Emperor repeatedly consoled and encouraged him.
4. The military governor of Zhōngwǔ, Wáng Pèi, passed away.
On the Gēngshēn day,
the Minister of the Imperial Stud, Gāo Yǔ, was appointed military governor of Zhōngwǔ.
Since the Dàlì era,
military governors had mostly come from the imperial guards.
Senior generals of the imperial guards
all borrowed money from wealthy families at double interest,
"double" meaning
the interest equaled the principal.
"Equal" meaning
the interest matched the principal.
Equal,
pronounced chēng.
Often exceeding hundreds of millions,
they then obtained their posts,
never through the administration;
upon arriving at their commands,
they heavily taxed to repay their debts.
When Pèi died,
Péi Dù and Wéi Chǔhòu finally recommended Yǔ as his replacement.
Court and regions congratulated each other, saying:
"From now on, there will be few debt-commanders!"
5. Fifth month,
on the Bǐngzǐ day,
Wū Zhòngyìn, military governor of Tiānpíng, was appointed military governor of Hénghǎi,
and the former deputy military governor of Hénghǎi, Lǐ Tóngjié, was appointed military governor of Yǎnhǎi.
The court still worried that military governors north and south of the Yellow River might incite Tóngjié to defy orders,
so they additionally granted Shǐ Xiànchéng of Wèibó the title Joint Manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery.
On the Dīngchǒu day,
Lǐ Zàiyì of Lúlóng, Kāng Zhìmù of Pínglǔ, and Wáng Tíngcòu of Chéngdé were granted honorary titles.
6. The Salt and Iron Commissioner, Wáng Bō, came to court from Huáinán,
striving for high office.
He presented silverware numbering in the thousands,
and silks and gauzes numbering in the hundred thousands.
Sixth month,
on the Guǐsì day,
Bō was appointed Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs and Joint Manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery.
7. Autumn,
seventh month,
on the Guǐyǒu day,
Emperor Ruìwǔ Zhāomǐn Xiào was buried at Zhuānglíng;
Zhuānglíng
is located five lǐ northwest of Sānyuán County in Jīngzhào.
8. Lǐ Tóngjié pretended to be detained by his officers and troops,
and did not accept the edict.
On the Yǐyǒu day,
the military governor of Wǔníng, Wáng Zhìxīng, memorialized requesting to lead his own army of thirty thousand men,
self-supplied with five months' provisions, to attack Tóngjié.
This was approved.
Eighth month,
on the Gēngzǐ day,
Tóngjié was stripped of his offices and ranks.

Wū Zhòngyìn, Wáng Zhìxīng, Kāng Zhìmù, Shǐ Xiànchéng, Lǐ Zàiyì, along with the military governor of Yìchéng, Lǐ Tīng, and the military governor of Yìwǔ, Zhāng Fán, were ordered to each lead their own armies to attack him.
Tóngjié sent his sons and nephews with treasures, antiques, and female entertainers to bribe the various military governors of Héběi.
On the Wùwǔ day,
Lǐ Zàiyì captured his nephew
and presented him along with the bribes.
Shǐ Xiànchéng was related by marriage to Lǐ Quánlüè.
When Lǐ Tóngjié rebelled,
Xiànchéng secretly supplied him with provisions.
Péi Dù was unaware of his actions,
and believed Xiànchéng harbored no disloyalty.
Xiànchéng sent a trusted subordinate to the Secretariat to request instructions.
Wéi Chǔhòu said to him:
"Duke Jìn guaranteed your master's loyalty with the lives of his entire clan before the Emperor;
Péi Dù was enfeoffed as Duke of Jìn.
A military governor is the master of a circuit,
hence his subordinate officials refer to him as 'master'.
Shǐ,
read as shū lì fān.
We merely await his actions,
for the court's laws will naturally be applied!"
Xiànchéng became fearful,
and dared not communicate further with Tóngjié.
Wáng Tíngcòu, having failed to obtain the symbols of authority for Tóngjié,
then assisted him in his rebellion,
deploying troops on the border to harass the Wèi army;
he also sent envoys with lavish bribes to the Shatuo chieftain Zhūyé Zhíyí,
wishing to join forces with him.
Zhíyí refused and did not accept.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Tiānpíng and Hénghǎi Military Governor Wū Chóngyìn attacked Tóngjié,
repeatedly defeating him.
In the eleventh month,
on the bǐngyín day,
Chóngyìn died.
On the gēngchén day,
Bǎoyì Military Governor Lǐ Huán was appointed as Hénghǎi Military Governor.
In the third year of the Chángqìng era of Emperor Mùzōng,
the two prefectures of Jìn and Cí were made the Bǎoyì Army.
In the twelfth month,
on the gēngxū day,
Wáng Zhìxīng was additionally appointed as Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
In spring,
the third month,
on the jǐmǎo day,
Wáng Zhìxīng attacked Dì Prefecture,
burning its three gates.
Since the end of the Yuánhé era,
the eunuchs had become increasingly overbearing,
establishing and deposing emperors at their whim.
Both Emperor Mùzōng and the current Emperor were installed by eunuchs.
No one dared speak of it.
The Emperor
personally presided over the special imperial examination.
The Virtuous and Upright candidate Liú Fén from Chāngpíng
submitted his policy response,
vehemently denouncing this calamity.
The gist of it said:
"What Your Majesty should first worry about is
upheaval in the palace, danger to the altars of state, the empire's collapse, and turmoil throughout the land."
It also said:
"If Your Majesty wishes to prevent the seeds of usurpation and regicide,
then occupy the rightful position and draw near to upright men.
Keep at a distance those base men of the blade and saw,
and be close to those of straightforward and upright character.
Let the chief ministers fully exercise their responsibilities,
and let the various officials properly perform their duties.
How can you allow five or six intimate attendants to control the empire's great governance!
Disaster ripens within the palace walls,
and treachery is born behind the curtains.
I fear that Cáo Jié and Hóu Lǎn are reborn today."
Cáo Jié and Hóu Lǎn are mentioned in the annals of Emperor Huán of Hàn.
Fù,
read as fú yòu fān.
"Loyal and worthy men are not entrusted with your confidence,
while the palace gatekeepers hold the power to depose and install.
They caused your late father not to meet a proper end,
and led to Your Majesty not having a proper beginning."
This refers to the eunuchs assassinating Emperor Jìngzōng and installing the current Emperor.
The Gǔliáng Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals says: In the first year of Duke Dìng,
spring, the king is not mentioned in the first month,
because Dìng had no proper beginning.
Why did Dìng have no proper beginning?
The end of Duke Zhāo
was not a proper end;
the beginning of Duke Dìng
was not a proper beginning.
Since Zhāo had no proper end,
therefore Dìng had no proper beginning.
"Imperial authority declines,
and regional commanders act arrogantly.
Some, ignorant of the proper conduct of a minister,
initiate rebellion under the pretext of pacifying the sovereign;
others, failing to grasp the subtle principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
take up arms claiming to expel evil.
Wēi,
refers to the subtle intent of the Spring and Autumn Annals.
These two phrases,
Fén likely feared that powerful regional commanders would initiate rebellion and raise troops,
using the name of expelling wicked ministers close to the sovereign.
Military campaigns will inevitably originate from the feudal lords."
In the reign of Emperor Zhāozōng,
Qí and Biàn engaged in warfare,
using the pretext of punishing eunuchs,
ultimately fulfilling Liú Fén's prediction.
"Why does Your Majesty not block the paths of covert evil,
dismiss those familiar and frivolous ministers,
curb their encroaching, oppressive, and coercive hearts,
restore the duties of sweeping and cleaning to the gatekeepers,
beware what should be bewared,
and worry about what should be worried!
If you could not govern properly before,
you should govern properly hereafter;
if you could not rectify the beginning,
you should rectify the end.
Then you can reverently uphold the statutes and codes,
and be able to inherit the great legacy.
In the past, Qín perished due to its excessive violence,
while Hàn perished due to its excessive weakness.
Excessive violence causes treacherous ministers, fearing death, to harm their sovereign."
This refers to Zhào Gāo.
Gāo was also a eunuch.
This refers to maternal relatives and eunuchs.
Fén's meaning specifically points to eunuchs.
"Do not nip it in the bud.
I humbly hope Your Majesty deeply grieves over the worries of Hàn's demise,
to prevent its gradual occurrence."
Fén likely meant that Emperor Jìngzōng lost his life due to recklessness and violence,
and also feared that the current Emperor, being benevolent and weak, would be unable to control the eunuchs.
"Then the distant tracks of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors can be followed."
Sān, wǔ,
refers to the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors.
"I have heard that when Emperor Yuán of Hàn first ascended the throne,
he changed over seventy regulations,
the gist of which can be seen in the 28th scroll, first and second years of the Chūyuán era of Emperor Yuán of Hàn.
His reputation was most excellent,
yet afterwards, laws and discipline daily fell into disorder,
the state's fortune daily declined,
traitors and villains daily grew stronger,
and the common people daily suffered hardship.
This was because he could not select the worthy and enlightened and employ them,
losing his grip on the reins of power."
Citing Emperor Yuán as a warning,
likely because the Emperor's rejection of extravagance and embrace of frugality resembled Emperor Yuán,
and his indecisiveness and procrastination also resembled Emperor Yuán.
"If Your Majesty can truly lift up the state's power and return it to the chief ministers,
and grasp the military authority and return it to the generals,
then your intentions will be fully communicated,
and your actions will be entirely trustworthy."
It also said:
"Laws should be uniform,
and offices should have proper names.
Now the establishment of separate officials for the outer court and the inner court,
and the setting up of separate bureaus for the Southern Administration and the Northern Administration—
the hundred officials who go to the Southern Yá for court audiences,
are called outer officials,
also called the Southern Administration.
The eunuchs have their bureaus arrayed inside the Xuánwǔ Gate.
The two Army Supervisors command the various camps within the imperial gardens.
They are called inner officials,
also called the Northern Administration.
Sometimes, when proper punishment is applied in the outer court, the law is broken in the inner court.
Laws issue from many sources,
leaving the people with nowhere to turn.
This truly stems from the differing circumstances of soldiers and farmers, and the different laws applied inside and outside the palace."
It also said:
"Now the Ministry of War does not know the military registers,
limiting itself to ceremonial court attendance;
the Six Armies do not manage military affairs,
limiting themselves to nurturing ranks of merit.
The Ministry of War,
holds the ancient office of the Minister of Summer.
The Six Armies—
the Senior Generals, Great Generals, Generals, and Commanders all use them to nurture ranks of merit.
Military regulations are attached to the duties of the inner court officials."
This refers to the Army Surveillance Commissioners and the various Army Supervisors.
"They hate civil officials like enemies;
as soon as one sets foot in an army camp,
they regard farmers as worthless as weeds.
Their schemes are insufficient to eradicate vicious rebels, yet their deceit is ample to manipulate authority and fortune.
Their courage is insufficient to protect the altars of state, yet their violence is ample to invade and harass villages and neighborhoods.
They restrain the regional commanders,
offend and encroach upon the chief ministers,
destroy and rend the royal standards,
and confuse and disorder court regulations.
Flaunting the might of military men,
they use it above to control the sovereign and his father;
borrowing the emperor's command,
they use it below to command the heroes and elite.
They harbor hearts that conceal treachery and watch for opportunities,
but lack the duty to maintain integrity and die for a just cause.
How can this be the intent of the former kings' weaving civil and military principles!"
It also said:
"I am not unaware that speaking out will bring calamity upon me,
and that my plans being carried out will lead to my execution.
But I grieve over the peril of the altars of state,
and lament the suffering of the living people.
How could I bear to indulge the taboos of the time,
and secretly enjoy the favor of a single appointment from Your Majesty!"
The Rites of Zhōu states: One appointment receives an office.
Later generations considered conferring an initial official rank as one appointment.
3 In the intercalary month,
on the first day, the bingxū day,
Shǐ Xiànchéng reported that he had dispatched his son, Vice Commissioner Táng, and Chief Military Commander Qí Zhìshào, leading 25,000 troops to head for Dézhōu to campaign against Lǐ Tóngjié.
At that time, Xiànchéng intended to assist Tóngjié,
but Táng tearfully remonstrated,
and requested to dispatch troops to campaign against him;
Xiànchéng could not oppose this.
4 On the jiǎwǔ day,
the virtuous and upright candidates Péi Xiū, Lǐ Hé, Lǐ Gān, Dù Mù, Mǎ Zhí, Cuī Xū, Wáng Shì, Cuī Shènyóu, and others,
twenty-two in total, passed the imperial examination,
and all were appointed to official positions.
The examiners, Left Adviser Féng Sù and others, upon seeing Liú Fén’s policy essay,
all sighed in admiration,
but fearing the eunuchs,
did not dare to select him.
When the edict was issued,
public opinion clamored in protest, calling it unjust.
Remonstrance officials and censors wished to submit memorials discussing this,
but the chief ministers suppressed them.
Lǐ Hé said:
“Liú Fén failed the examination,
while we, his peers, passed.
How can we not feel deeply ashamed!”
He then submitted a memorial,
stating:
“The policy essay Fén submitted
has no equal since the Hàn and Wèi dynasties.
Now the responsible officials, because Fén’s essay directly criticized those in power,
did not dare to report it,
fearing that the path for loyal and good men would be blocked,
and law and order would thereby be severed.
Moreover, the essay I submitted is far inferior to Fén’s.
I beg that the appointment granted to me be rescinded to honor Fén’s integrity.”
There was no response.
Consequently, Fén was unable to serve in the imperial court,
and ended his career as a Censor in a military commissioner’s headquarters.
The commissioner’s headquarters
refers to the military commissioner’s administrative office.
The title Censor
was a nominal salary-grade official position held by staff members,
also called a surveillance official.
(Péi Xiū was) Péi Yòu’s grandson;
(Mǎ) Zhí
was Mǎ Xūn’s son;
Dù Yòu served through the reigns of Dézōng, Shùnzōng, and Xiànzōng,
reaching the position of a high minister.
For Mǎ Xūn, see Volume 230, Dézōng Zhēnyuán 1st Year.
Textual analysis notes: The Old History biography
writes “Xūn”
as
“Xūn”,
which is an error.
Xūn’s affairs are recorded in the Dézōng Veritable Records.
(Wáng Shì was) Wáng Qǐ’s grandson;
(Cuī) Shènyóu
was Cuī Róng’s great-great-grandson.
For Wáng Qǐ, see Volume 241, Mùzōng Chángqìng 1st Year.
Cuī Róng was renowned for his literary compositions during Empress Wǔ’s reign.
5 In summer,
the sixth month,
Jìn Prince Pǔ passed away;
on the xīnyǒu day,
he was posthumously honored
as Crown Prince Dàohuái.
6 Earlier,
Empress Dowager Xiāo left her hometown when young,
and had one younger brother;
after the Emperor ascended the throne,
he ordered the Fújiàn Observation Commissioner to search for him,
but his whereabouts were unknown.
There was a tea transport laborer named Xiāo Hóng.
Generally, tea merchants transporting tea
would organize their goods into groups of a certain size called “gāng” to pay taxes to the authorities.
A merchant named Zhào Zhěn brought him to meet Lǚ Zhāng’s wife, a close relative of the Empress Dowager,
but she also could not verify his identity,
and went with him to see the Empress Dowager.
The Emperor, believing he had found his true maternal uncle,
on the jiǎzǐ day,
appointed him as a Crown Prince’s Assistant.
This sets the stage for Xiāo Hóng’s fraud being discovered, leading to his exile and death.
Xiān,
is pronounced xī.
7 Fēngzhōu Prefect Wáng Shēngcháo rebelled;
on the gēngchén day,
Ānnán Protector-General Hán Yuē of Wǔlíng campaigned against and executed him.
Old Records: Fēngzhōu is 11,500 lǐ from the capital.
Sòng Bái said: Fēngzhōu
administered Jiāníng County,
the area of the Hàn dynasty’s Mílěng County.
Wǔlíng,
was the area of the Hàn dynasty’s Línyuán County,
the Suí dynasty established Wǔlíng County,
and the Táng dynasty attached it to Lǎngzhōu.
Shēng,
is pronounced zhí yáo.
8 Wáng Tíngcòu secretly provided troops, salt, and grain to assist Lǐ Tóngjié,
and the Emperor wished to campaign against him;
in autumn,
the seventh month,
on the jiǎchén day,
an edict ordered the Secretariat to assemble all officials to deliberate on the matter.
From the Chief Ministers down, none dared to oppose,
but Guard Commandant Yīn Yòu alone believed:
“Although Tíngcòu has attached himself to the villains,
his actions are not yet fully exposed.
It is appropriate to tolerate him for now,
and focus the campaign solely against Tóngjié.”
On the jǐsì day,
an edict was issued listing Tíngcòu’s crimes,
ordering neighboring circuits each to strictly garrison their defenses,
and to allow him to reform himself.
9 In the ninth month,
on the dīnghài day,
Wáng Zhìxīng reported capturing Dìzhōu.
10 Lǐ Huán led troops from Jìnzhōu to his garrison,
but did not restrain his soldiers,
who committed atrocities along the way.
Upon arrival, he massed his troops and did not advance,
merely sitting and demanding provisions.
On the gēngyín day,
Huán was appointed as Xiàsuí Military Commissioner.
11 On the jiǎwǔ day,
an edict stripped Wáng Tíngcòu of his offices and titles,
and ordered the various armies to advance and attack from all sides.
12 Wáng Zhìxīng was additionally appointed as Acting Minister of Education,
and former Xiàsuí Military Commissioner Fù Liángbì was made Héng Hǎi Military Commissioner.
13 Yuè Prince Gǔn passed away.
14 On the gēngxū day,
the Róngguǎn administration reported a military mutiny in Ānnán,
which expelled Protector-General Hán Yuē.
15 In winter,
the tenth month,
Yáng Prince Xīn passed away.
Xīn
was Xiànzōng’s son.
16 Wèibó forces defeated Héng Hǎi troops at Píngyuán,
and subsequently captured it.
17 In the eleventh month,
on the first day, the guǐwèi day,
Yìdìng Military Commissioner Liǔ Gōngjì reported attacking Lǐ Tóngjié’s Jiāngù Stronghold,
and capturing it;
Tóngjié had built the stronghold west of Cāngzhōu,
to resist the imperial army,
and named it “Jiāngù” (Firm and Solid).
At that time, the various armies north and south of the Huáng Hé campaigning against Tóngjié had long been unsuccessful.
Whenever they achieved a minor victory,
they would exaggerate the number of enemy heads taken to seek substantial rewards.
The court exhausted its resources to supply them,
causing depletion and hardship in Jiāngnán and Huáinán.
18 Fù Liángbì reached Shǎnzhōu and passed away.
On the yǐyǒu day,
Left Imperial Guard General-in-Chief Lǐ Yòu was appointed as Héng Hǎi Military Commissioner.
19 On the jiǎchén day,
a fire broke out at the Zhāodé Temple within the palace grounds.
A fire caused by heaven is called a “zāi” (calamity),
a fire caused by humans is called a “huǒ” (fire).
Several hundred people died in the blaze.
20 In the twelfth month,
on the dīngsì day,
Wáng Zhìxīng reported that Military Commander Lǐ Jūnmóu led troops across the river,
and captured Wúdì.
Wúdì
was the northern border of the ancient Qí state,
the extent of the territory granted to Tàigōng by the Zhōu king;
during the Hàn dynasty it was Yángxìn County;
within its boundaries was the Wúdì Channel,
connecting to the sea;
during the Táng dynasty it was Wúdì County,
belonging to Cāngzhōu.
The Nine Regions Gazetteer states: It is 107 lǐ southeast of the prefecture.
21 On the rénshēn day,
Secretariat Vice Director and Chief Minister Wéi Chǔhòu passed away.
22 Lǐ Tóngjié’s military situation grew increasingly dire daily,
and Wáng Tíngcòu was unable to rescue him.
He then sent someone to persuade Wèibó General Qí Zhìshào
to kill Shǐ Xiànchéng and his son and seize Wèibó;
Zhìshào consequently rebelled,
leading his 20,000 troops back to press upon Wèizhōu.
On the dīngchǒu day,
Remonstrance Official Bǎi Qí was ordered to pacify and reassure Wèibó,
and also to dispatch Yìchéng and Héyáng troops to campaign against Zhìshào.
23 On the wùyín day,
Hanlin Academician Lù Suí was appointed as Secretariat Vice Director and Chief Minister.
24 On the xīnsì day,
Shǐ Xiànchéng reported that Qí Zhìshào’s troops were stationed at Yǒngjì.
During Dàizōng’s Dàlì 7th Year,
Tián Chéngsì partitioned Línqīng from Wèizhōu to establish Yǒngjì County,
attaching it to Bèizhōu.
An edict ordered Yìchéng Military Commissioner Lǐ Tīng to lead the various armies of the Cāngzhōu campaign headquarters to campaign against Zhìshào.
Punctuated by Róng Zhàozǔ, proofread by Niè Chóngqí
Compiled by Imperial Order
by Sīmǎ Guāng
Later Student from Tiāntāi
Third Year of Tàihé
(Jǐyǒu, 829)
1. Spring,
the first month,
Qí Zhìshào joined forces with Chéngdé to raid Bèi Prefecture.
Bèi Prefecture
is located 210 li north of Wèi Prefecture.
2. Three thousand soldiers from the Yìchéng campaign army were originally stationed in Qí Prefecture.
They were sent to Yǔchéng.
"Zhī"
means "to go to."
One version
writes "stationed."
Yǔchéng
was the territory of Zhù'ā County in the Hàn dynasty.
In the first year of the Tiānbǎo era, it was renamed Yǔchéng,
because west of the county there was the ancient city of Yǔxī.
It belonged to Qí Prefecture.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is 130 li northwest of the prefectural seat.
Héng Hǎi military governor Lǐ Yòu attacked and executed them.
3. Lǐ Tīng and Shǐ Táng combined forces to attack Qí Zhìshào,
and defeated him.
Zhìshào led his 5,000 troops and fled to Zhèn Prefecture.
4. Lǐ Zàiyì reported attacking Chānglú in Cāng Prefecture,
and captured it.
Cāng Prefecture
administered Qīngchí County.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Chānglú town belonged to Qīngchí.
5. On the jiǎchén day,
Zhāoyì reported that 15,000 remaining troops of Qí Zhìshào surrendered to their original command,
and they were settled in Luò
Prefecture.
6. In the second month,
Héng Hǎi military governor Lǐ Yòu led the campaign armies of various circuits to attack Lǐ Tóngjié,
defeated him,
and advanced to attack Dé Prefecture.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Dé Prefecture
is 230 li northeast to Cāng Prefecture.
7. Wǔníng's "capture alive" military commander Shí Xióng
was brave and fierce,
and cared for his soldiers.
Wáng Zhìxīng was cruel and oppressive,
and the army wanted to expel Zhìxīng and establish Xióng.
Zhìxīng knew this,
and because Xióng had achieved merit,
he petitioned to have him appointed as a prefect.
On the bǐngchén day,
Xióng was appointed as prefect of Bì Prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: Bì Prefecture was originally the territory of Dàngqú County in the Hàn dynasty.
During the Dàtǒng era of the Later Wèi, the Nuòshuǐ County was established at the current prefectural seat.
In the eighth year of the Wǔdé era of the Táng, Bì Prefecture was established,
named after the Bì Mountain one li west of the county.
It is 1,822 li southwest of the capital.
8. Shǐ Xiànchéng heard that Cāngjǐng was about to be pacified and became fearful.
His son, Táng, urged him to go to court.
On the bǐngyín day,
Xiànchéng sent Táng to present a memorial requesting to come to court,
and also requested that his administered territory obey commands.
9. After Shí Xióng had left,
Wǔníng's Wáng Zhìxīng killed over a hundred people in the army who were on good terms with Xióng.
Summer,
the fourth month,
on the wùwǔ day,
Zhìxīng reported that Xióng was unsettling military morale,
and requested his execution.
The Emperor knew Xióng was not guilty,
spared him from death,
and exiled him to Bái Prefecture.
This sets the stage for Emperor Wǔzōng's later reuse of Shí Xióng.
In the third year of Wǔdé,
Bóbái County was established from land partitioned from Hépǔ County.
In the fourth year, Nán Prefecture was established.
In the sixth year, it was renamed Bái Prefecture.
It is 6,715 li from the capital.
The prefecture and county were both named after the Bóbái River.
10. On the wùchén day,
Lǐ Zàiyì reported attacking Cāng Prefecture,
and breached its outer wall.
The outer wall
is the outer city wall.
Over 3,000 officers and soldiers from the city fled to Zhèn Prefecture.
Lǐ Tóngjié sent a letter to Yòu requesting to surrender.
Yòu forwarded his letter in a memorial.
Remonstrance official Bǎi Qí received an edict to proclaim imperial grace and offer reassurance.
Qí liked to exaggerate his authority and power to intimidate and control the various generals in the campaign army,
and the generals already disliked him.
When Lǐ Tóngjié requested to surrender to Yòu,
Yòu sent his senior general Wàn Hóng to guard Cāng Prefecture in his stead.
Qí suspected Tóngjié's surrender was a ruse,
and personally led several hundred cavalry to gallop into Cāng Prefecture.
Using an incident as pretext, he executed Hóng,
and took Tóngjié and his family members to the capital.
On the yǐhài day,
they reached Jiānglíng.
Jiānglíng
was the territory of Āndé County in the Hàn dynasty.
The Suí partitioned Āndé,
and established a county at the old city of Jiānglíng.
In the Táng, it belonged to Dé Prefecture.
There, he beheaded Tóngjié,
and sent his head
for display. Cāngjǐng was completely pacified.
In the fifth month,
on the gēngyín day,
Lǐ Zàiyì was given the additional title of Tóngpíngzhāngshì.
Textual analysis notes: The Veritable Records writes
"gēngyín,"
which is an error.
For three years,
they had barely managed to subdue it.
The Emperor, in the first year of his reign, began the campaign against Tóngjié,
and by now it was three years.
Qí took credit for himself,
and the various generals resented him,
competing to submit memorials criticizing him.
On the xīnmǎo day,
Qí was demoted to Registrar of Xún Prefecture.
Xún Prefecture
was the ancient territory of Lóngchuān.
The Suí established Xún Prefecture.
Textual analysis notes: The Veritable Records states:
"In the fourth month,
Lǐ Yòu captured Dé Prefecture,
and Tóngjié requested to surrender to Yòu.

it was as if he had personally traveled through all of it.
The emperor ordered Déyù to repair and block the Qīngxī Pass to cut off the route of invasion by Nánzhào.
In places where there was no soil,
they used stones to build fortifications.
Déyù submitted a memorial stating:
"There are numerous small paths leading to the barbarian regions,
making it impossible to block them all.
Only by stationing heavy troops for defense
can we ensure safety.
However, from Lízhōu and Yǎzhōu onward, we need ten thousand men,
and Chéngdū requires twenty thousand men.
If these troops are rigorously trained,
the barbarians will not dare to act.
Moreover, the border troops should not be too numerous;
they must be strong enough to enforce control.
Cuī Gàn's killing of Guō Yīngyì
is recorded in the 224th scroll, in the first year of the Dàizōng era's Yǒngtài reign.
It is also recorded in the 229th scroll, in the fourth year of the Dézōng era's Jiànzhōng reign.
At that time, the northern troops had all returned to their own provinces,
leaving only three thousand men from Hézhōng and Chénxǔ in Chéngdū.
An edict ordered them to return in March of the following year,
causing panic among the people of Shǔ.
Déyù petitioned to request five hundred men from Zhènghuá and a thousand from Chénxǔ to garrison Shǔ.
He further stated:
"The troops of Shǔ are weak and fragile,
having recently been harassed by barbarian invaders.
They are all terrified,
and are unfit for military service or garrison duty.
The morale of victorious troops
is boosted a hundredfold,
while defeated soldiers
never recover their spirit—
this is precisely the case here.
'Fragile'
is pronounced as 'cuì' here.
If we do not take action, the situation will be no different from when Dù Yuányǐng was in charge,
and Shǔ will be impossible to defend.
I fear that some officials may argue that since the barbarian invasion, Shǔ has already increased its troops.
However, when the barbarian invaders were approaching,
Yuányǐng hastily recruited civilians as soldiers,
obtaining over three thousand men.
They were merely a number on paper,
and were practically useless.
Guō Zhāo recruited northern troops but managed to gather only a little over a hundred men.
I myself recruited another two hundred or so,
but aside from these, the rest are all old troops from Yuányǐng's time.
I also fear that some officials may cite the saying, 'One man can hold the pass,'
meaning that one man guarding the pass
can stop ten thousand from advancing.
This is how people in the past described the strategic importance of Shǔ.
However, after consulting veteran generals in Shǔ,
I learned that beside the Qīngxī Pass,
there are three main roads
and countless small paths.
All of these were temporarily opened by the Eastern Barbarians.
Wùdēng, Fēngpá, and Liǎnglín
are all Eastern Barbarian tribes.
'Wéi'
is pronounced as 'wèi' here.
To claim otherwise would be deceiving the court.
What is needed is to build another city north of the Dàdù River,
extending it to connect with Lízhōu.
The 'Jiǔyù Zhì' states: Lízhōu is one hundred lǐ south of the Dàdù River.
Sòng Bái said: Lízhōu
is the ancient land of Chénlí.
'Yǐ'
is pronounced as 'yǐ' here.
'Lǐ'
is pronounced as 'lǐ' here.
Moreover, I have heard that Nánzhào bribed Tǔbō with two thousand captured Shǔ people and gold and silk.
If these two enemies learn of Shǔ's vulnerabilities,
they may join forces to invade,
which is a cause for serious concern.
As for the court officials who offer suggestions,
since the disaster does not affect them personally,
I request that each of them submit a written statement
to be kept in the official records.
The 'táng'
refers to the Council of State.
'Àn'
refers to official documents.
I should not be the only one held accountable for the laws of the state."
'Xiàn'
means law.
'Bài'
is pronounced as 'bài' here.
Déyù then trained the soldiers,
repaired fortifications and barriers,
and stockpiled grain and supplies to prepare for border defense,
bringing a measure of stability to the people of Shǔ.
12 In this year,
Bóhǎi's King Xuānwáng Rénxiù passed away.
His son Xīndé had died early,
so his grandson Yízhèn succeeded him,
changing the era name to Xiánhé.
1 Spring,
first month,
on the day Dīngsì,
the emperor bestowed the name Yìchāng Army upon the Cāng, Qí, and Dé military commands.
Zhāng Xiàozhōng appointed Chéng Rìhuá as the governor of Cāngzhōu.
During the rebellion of Zhū Tāo,
Cāngzhōu and Dìngzhōu were cut off from each other,
but Rìhuá managed to maintain communication between Cāngzhōu and the imperial court.
In the third year of the Zhēnyuán era,
Rìhuá was appointed as the military governor of the Héng Hǎi Army,
overseeing Cāngzhōu and Jǐngzhōu.
In the thirteenth year of the Yuánhé era,
Wáng Chéngzōng offered Dézhōu and Dìzhōu,
and the Héng Hǎi Army came to oversee Cāng, Jǐng, Dé, and Dìzhōu.
In the first year of the Chángqìng era,
Jǐngzhōu was abolished.
The following year,
Jǐngzhōu was reinstated under its jurisdiction.
In the first year of the Tàihé era,
Qízhōu was added to its jurisdiction.
The following year,
Dìzhōu was transferred to the Zīqīng and Pínglú military commands.
The year after that,
the Héng Hǎi military command was abolished,
and the Qí Dé military command was established instead.
Shortly after, Lǐ Tóngjié was pacified,
and Cāngzhōu was regained,
leading to the renaming as the Cāng, Qí, Dé military command.
In this year,
it was bestowed the name Yìchāng Army.
2 On the day Gēngshēn,
the Lúlóng military supervisor reported that Lǐ Zàiyì was feasting with an imperial envoy in the backyard of the polo field when
deputy military commander Yáng Zhìchéng and his followers raised a clamor and started a rebellion.
Zàiyì and his son Zhèngyuán fled to Yìzhōu.
Zhìchéng also killed the governor of Mòzhōu, Zhāng Qìngchū.
Sòng Bái said: Yōuzhōu
is two hundred and eighty lǐ south of Mòzhōu.
Niú Sēngrú said:
"Since the time of Ān Lùshān and Shǐ Sīmíng,
Fànyáng has not truly belonged to the state.
Liú Zǒng temporarily offered the land,
as recorded in the 241st scroll, in the first year of the Mùzōng era's Chángqìng reign.
Today, Zhìchéng has taken it,
just as Zàiyì took it before.
In the second year of the Jìngzōng era's Bǎolì reign,
Lǐ Zàiyì gained control of Fànyáng,
as recorded in the previous scroll.
As long as he defends against the northern barbarians,
there is no need to consider his loyalty or rebellion."
The emperor followed this advice.
Zàiyì traveled from Yìzhōu to the capital.
The emperor, recognizing Zàiyì's achievements in pacifying Cāngzhōu and Jǐngzhōu,
as recorded in the third year of the previous reign,
in the second month,
on the day Rénchén,
appointed Zàiyì as Grand Guardian,
while retaining his position as co-chief of the Council of State.
Yáng Zhìchéng was appointed as the acting military governor of Lúlóng.
Commentary by Minister Guāng: In ancient times, the sages followed the principles of heaven and understood human nature.
Knowing that the common people could not govern themselves,
they appointed leaders to guide them.
Knowing that officials could not command one another,
they established feudal lords to control them.
Knowing that the various states could not submit to one another,
they established the Son of Heaven to unify them.
From the leaders up to the Son of Heaven,
the so-called leaders
are the officials closest to the people.
'Zhǎng'
is pronounced as 'zhǎng' here.
They must praise the good and punish the evil,
suppress the strong and support the weak,
pacify the obedient and punish the rebellious,
prohibit violence and eliminate chaos.
Only then can they issue commands that are followed throughout the land.
'Shuài'
means to follow.
'Cóng'
means to obey.
Another interpretation: to follow the commands of the superior together.
"Diligently, our king
governs the four directions."
These are words from the 'Dàyǎ · Yùpǔ' poem in the Book of Songs.
Zàiyì had contributed to the state,
yet he was driven out without any crime by Zhìchéng.
This is a matter the Son of Heaven should address.
If no action is taken,
and instead the land and titles are bestowed upon the rebel,
then the appointment, dismissal, life, and death of generals would all be determined by the soldiers.
Even if the Son of Heaven is above,
what purpose does he serve?
The establishment of military commands in the state
is not merely for the benefit of collecting taxes!
Sēngrú's words
are nothing but a policy of appeasement and temporary peace.
How can this be the way for a prime minister to assist the Son of Heaven in ruling the world?
3 The king of Xīnluó, Yànshēng, passed away,
and his son Jǐnghuī succeeded him.
4 The emperor conspired with Sòng Shēnxī to eliminate the eunuchs.
Shēnxī recommended the Vice Minister of Personnel, Wáng Fán, to serve as the governor of the capital region,
and secretly informed him of the emperor's intentions.
However, Fán leaked the plot,
and Zhèng Zhù and Wáng Shǒuchéng learned of it,
secretly preparing themselves.
The emperor's younger brother, Prince Li Còu of Zhāng, was virtuous
and enjoyed popular support.
Zhèng Zhù ordered the commander of the Shence Army's capital patrol, Dòulú Zhù, to falsely accuse Sòng Shēnxī of plotting to enthrone Prince Li Còu of Zhāng.
On the Wùxū day,
Wáng Shǒuchéng reported this.
The emperor believed it to be true
and was extremely angry.
Prince Li Còu of Zhāng was someone the emperor had long been wary of.
To slander and create discord by exploiting the emperor's wariness—
this was why Sòng Shēnxī could not avoid punishment.
The Feilong Commissioner Mǎ Cúnliàng firmly argued:
"If we do this,
the capital itself will fall into chaos!
We should summon other ministers to discuss the matter."
Judging from Mǎ Cúnliàng's role in quelling Zhāng Sháo's rebellion and his argument in the Sòng Shēnxī affair,
Sīmǎ Guāng's selection of Cúnliàng
was certainly not based on just one incident.
The Feilong Commissioner
was in charge of the Feilong stables.
On that day,
it was the Xúnxiū holiday.
A month is divided into three xún.
At the end of each xún, officials would leave their posts to rest and bathe.
This was called Xúnxiū,
which is what we now call the xún holiday.
A palace eunuch said:
"The name of Lord Sòng is not among those summoned."
Shēnxī knew he had incurred guilt.
He looked toward the Yányīng Hall,
touched his forehead to his hu tablet, and withdrew.
According to the Dàmíng Palace map from the Gé edition: Between the Zhōngshū Secretariat and the Yányīng Hall,
there were only the Outer and Inner Courts of the Diànzhōng Bureau in between.
The emperor showed them the memorial submitted by Shǒuchéng.
The ministers looked at each other in stunned disbelief.
The emperor ordered Shǒuchéng to arrest the palace market official Yàn Jìngzé from the Sixteen Estates and Shēnxī's personal attendant Wáng Shīwén, among others, as accused by Dòulú Zhù,
and interrogate them within the palace.
Personal attendants
were those who constantly remained by one's side.
Even today, chief ministers, executives, and attendants
still have personal attendant officials.
In the third month,
on the Gēngzǐ day,
Shēnxī was dismissed and made a Right Aide of the Heir Apparent.
None of the chief ministers or high officials dared to openly speak of his innocence.

Only the Capital Prefect Cuī Guǎn and the Chief Minister of the Court of Judicial Review Wáng Zhèngyǎ successively submitted memorials requesting that the internal prison case be handed over to the outer court for verification.
The interrogation was conducted within the palace,
hence it was called the internal prison.
Zhèngyǎ
was the son of Wáng Hóng.
Wáng Hóng
appears in the Annals of Emperor Dézōng.
It was claimed that Shēnxī sent Wáng Shīwén to convey his intentions to the prince,
to establish a connection for future recognition.
Once the case was concluded,
on the Rényín day,
the emperor summoned all officials from the Tutors of the Heir Apparent down, as well as ministers from the various departments, bureaus, and courts, to question them in person.
At the wǔ hour,
the wǔ hour
refers to the beginning of the wǔ watch,
not precisely noon.
They begged that the prison case be handed over to the outer court for reinvestigation.
The emperor said:
"I have already discussed this with the ministers."
He repeatedly ordered them to leave,
but they did not withdraw.
Dòu Xuánliàng kowtowed, weeping, and said:
"Even when executing a commoner, one cannot but exercise the utmost caution,
let alone a chief minister!"
The emperor's resolve softened slightly.
He said:
"I will discuss it again with the chief ministers."
He then summoned the chief ministers back in.
Niú Sēngrú said:
"For a subject, there is no position higher than chief minister.
Now Shēnxī is already a chief minister.
Even if he had plotted as alleged,
what more could he
seek?
Shēnxī would hardly have gone to such lengths!"
Fearing that a reinvestigation would expose the fraud, Zhèng Zhù
then advised Shǒuchéng to request that only demotion and dismissal be carried out.
On the Guǐmǎo day,
Prince Li Còu of Zhāng was demoted to Duke of Cháoxiàn,
and Sòng Shēnxī was demoted to Military Advisor of Kāizhōu.
Cúnliàng requested retirement that very day.
Above "Cúnliàng"
there should be another
character "Mǎ"
to
make the name clearer.
It is noted that Mǎ Cúnliàng, knowing Sòng Shēnxī was innocent yet unable to save him,
and detesting Wáng Shǒuchéng's tyranny yet unable to remove him,
requested retirement that very day.
Though a eunuch, he possessed the demeanor of the ancients.
He was from Cízhōu.
Wáng Zhì
was the fifth-generation descendant of Wáng Tōng.
Wáng Tōng appears in the 179th year of Emperor Wén of Suí's Rénshòu era;
he was known as Master Wénzhōng.
Wáng Yì was the son
of Jiǎng Yì. Jiǎng Yì appears in the 235th year of Emperor Dézōng's Zhēnyuán era.
He was from Jiāngzhōu.
Yàn Jìngzé and others were sentenced to death or exile, numbering in the dozens to a hundred.
Shēnxī ultimately died at his place of exile.
5 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Jǐchǒu day,
Lǐ Zàiyì was appointed Military Commissioner of Shǎnnánxīdào,
and Yáng Zhìchéng was appointed Military Commissioner of Yōuzhōu.
6 In the fifth month,
on the Xīnchǒu day,
the emperor, because two chambers of the Imperial Ancestral Temple had been leaking for over a year without repair,
penalized the Directors of the Palace Buildings, the Revenue Commissioners, and the Chief Minister of the Imperial Clan by withholding their salaries.
The Director of the Palace Buildings
was in charge of construction and craftsmen.
The Revenue Commissioner
was in charge of disbursements and allocations.
The Chief Minister of the Imperial Clan
was in charge of the fasting officials of the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
The Imperial Temple was not maintained,
hence all were penalized by salary withholding.
Salary
is pronounced fú yòng fān.
He halted construction projects within the palace and used the materials to repair the temple.
Left Reminder Wéi Wēn remonstrated,
believing that:
"The state establishes various offices,
each with its own responsibilities.
If officials neglect their duties,
they should be dismissed,
and replaced with capable individuals.
Now, those who neglect their duties are merely penalized by salary withholding,
while matters of urgent concern are entrusted to palace eunuchs.
This treats the Imperial Temple as Your Majesty's private concern and renders all officials mere figureheads."
The emperor approved his words,
immediately recalled the palace eunuchs,
and ordered the relevant officials to carry out the repairs.
7 On the Bǐngchén day,
the Xīchuān Military Commissioner Lǐ Déyù memorialized that he had sent an envoy to Nánzhào to demand the return of captured people,
and retrieved four thousand individuals.
Textual analysis notes: Lǐ Déyù's *Southwestern Border Defense Record* states:
"Nánzhào returned 5,364 captured men and women to us."
The *Old History* biography states:
"He also sent people into Nánzhào to seek captured artisans,
retrieving over four thousand monks, Daoists, and skilled craftsmen,
who returned to Chéngdū."
According to the *Veritable Records*,
it says "approximately four thousand people."
We follow this.
8 In autumn,
the eighth month,
on the Wùyín day,
Cuī Yān, the Surveillance Commissioner of Shǎnguó, was appointed Surveillance Commissioner of Èyuè.
The land of Èyuè is surrounded by mountains and girded by rivers,
situated at the confluence of Bǎiyuè, Bā, Shǔ, Jīng, and Hàn.
The region had many gangs of bandits,
who plundered passing boats,
killing everyone aboard, old and young, without exception.
When Yān arrived,
he trained troops and prepared the army,
constructing méngchōng ships to pursue and attack them.
Méngchōng
were warships.
To govern
is pronounced zhí zhī fān.
He executed them all.
While in Shǎn,
Yān governed with leniency and benevolence,
sometimes going a full month without caning a single person.
But upon arriving in È,
he enforced strict punishments.
When asked the reason,
Yān said:
"Shǎn's land is barren and its people poor.
I have no time but to comfort them,
still fearing they might be alarmed.
È's terrain is perilous and its population mixed.
The barbarian customs are fierce and cunning, given to villainy.
Without employing威严 and punishment,
good governance cannot be achieved.
Governance values knowing when to adapt—
this is what it means."
9 The Military Commissioner of Xīchuān, Lǐ Déyù, submitted a memorial:
"Among the Shǔ troops, the weak, sick, old, and feeble
have never been screened out for their entire lives.
I ordered the establishment of a standard of five chi and five cun,
and screened out over 4,400 men.
(Screen means to select.)
(Out means to remove.)
(Qiè, read with the Lǚ tone.)
The northern soldiers recruited have already reached 1,500 men.
They live intermixed with the local soldiers,
training and learning from each other,
becoming increasingly proficient and well-drilled day by day.
Furthermore,
the weapons made by Shǔ craftsmen
merely pursue ornate decoration and are unusable;
I now employ craftsmen from other circuits to manufacture them,
and they are all sturdy and sharp."
In the ninth month,
the Deputy Commissioner of Wéizhōu of Tǔbō, Xīdámóu, requested to surrender,
leading all his followers to flee to Chéngdū.
Déyù dispatched the Acting Prefect of Wéizhōu, Yú Cángjiǎn, to lead troops and occupy the city.
On Gēngshēn,
he submitted a detailed report of the situation,
and stated:
"I wish to send 3,000 Qīngqiāng tribesmen
to burn the Thirteen Bridges,
striking at the very heart of the Western Rong,
which could wash away a long-standing disgrace—
this is what Wéi Gāo, to his dying day, regretted being unable to achieve!"
(During the reign of Dézōng,
Wéi Gāo repeatedly sent troops to attack Wéizhōu
but could not capture it.)
The Emperor assembled all officials for deliberation,
and they all requested to follow Déyù's strategy.
Niú Sēngrú said:
"The territory of Tǔbō
extends ten thousand li in all four directions.
Losing one Wéizhōu
cannot damage its power.
Recently, we have been cultivating friendly relations,
agreeing to withdraw garrison troops.
For the Central Plains to defend against the Rong,
keeping trust is paramount.
If they come to reproach us, saying,
'Why have you broken faith?'
and then pasture their horses at Yùrú Chuān—
(Yuánzhōu's Xiāoguān County has the Yùrú River.
West of the river is the Báicǎo Army.
Yù,
read as Yūwù.)
—deploying ten thousand cavalry to link up with Huízhōng,
with furious words and direct accusations,
they could reach the Xiányáng Bridge in less than three days.
At that time, what use would gaining a hundred Wéizhōus,
thousands of li away in the southwest, be to us!
We would merely abandon good faith,
with harm and no benefit.
This is something even a common man would not do,
let alone the Son of Heaven!"
The Emperor considered this correct.
He issued an edict ordering Déyù to return the city to Tǔbō,
and to seize Xīdámóu and all those who came with him and hand them over entirely.
Tǔbō executed them all at the border,
with extreme cruelty.
Déyù's resentment towards Sēngrú deepened from this.
(This serves as the basis for Lǐ Déyù's later re-examination of the Wéizhōu affair during the reign of Wǔzōng.)
10 In winter,
the tenth month,
on Wùyín,
Lǐ Déyù reported that Nánzhào had invaded Xīzhōu,
capturing three counties.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on Rénzǐ,
an edict was issued to reduce sentences for prisoners due to floods and droughts.
The ministers offered the Emperor the honorific title 'Grand Harmony Civil and Martial Utmost Virtue Emperor.'
Right Rectifier of Omissions Wéi Wēn submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Now that floods and droughts are causing disasters,
I fear this is not the time to glorify and adorn with fine titles."
The Emperor approved of this,
and declined to accept the title.
2 In the third month,
on Xīnchǒu,
Wǔníng Military Commissioner Wáng Zhìxīng was concurrently appointed as Shìzhōng,
and assigned as Zhōngwǔ Military Commissioner;
Bīnníng Military Commissioner Lǐ Tīng was appointed as Wǔníng Military Commissioner.
3 The Huíhé Zhāolǐ Kèhán was killed by his subordinates,
and his nephew Hútèlè succeeded him.
4 Before Lǐ Tīng's previous appointment to govern Wǔníng,
he had a servant who served as a Yájiàng.
(Examining the New and Old Histories,
Lǐ Tīng had not previously governed Wǔníng.
I suspect this servant likely followed Tīng's elder brother Yuàn, who had long governed Wǔníng,
and thus became a Yájiàng.)
Tīng first sent a close official to Xúzhōu to console the officers and soldiers.
The servant did not want Tīng to come again,
and incited the soldiers
to kill his close official,
cutting him into pieces and eating him.
Tīng, fearful,
firmly declined on grounds of illness.
On Xīnyǒu,
the former Zhōngwǔ Military Commissioner Gāo Yǔ was appointed as Wǔníng Military Commissioner.
5 In summer,
the fifth month,
on Jiǎchén,
Lǐ Déyù memorialized about repairing the Qiónglái Pass and moving the administrative seat of Xīzhōu to Táidēng City.
(The Qiónglái Pass,
sometimes written as Qióngxiá Pass,
is an error.
The Qiónglái Pass is in Róngjīng County of Yǎzhōu,
the so-called Qiónglái Nine-Bend Slope,
where Wáng Zūn shouted to his carriage driver.
Zhù Mù said: The Qiónglái Pass is ninety li north of Xīzhōu.
Xīzhōu was originally administered from Yuèxī County.
Sòng Bái said: Yuèxī
is the area of the Hàn dynasty's Qióngdū.
Táidēng
is the area of the Hàn dynasty's Máoniú.
Lǐ Xīnchuán said: The Qiónglái Pass
is near Róngjīng,
sixty li from Lízhōu.)
6 In autumn,
the seventh month,
Prince Yuán Kuí passed away.
(Kuí
was a son of Dàizōng.)
7 In winter,
the tenth month,
on Jiǎzǐ,
Lǔ Prince Yǒng was established as Crown Prince.
Initially,
the Emperor, considering Jìn Prince Pǔ
(the eldest son of Jìngzōng),
to be prudent and sincere,
wished to make him heir;
but he happened to pass away.
(Jìn Prince Pǔ
passed away in the second year of Tàihé,
see the previous volume.)
Therefore, the establishment of an heir was long not discussed,
and it was only now carried out.
8 In the eleventh month,
on Yǐmǎo,
Jīngnán Military Commissioner Duàn Wénchāng was appointed as Xīchuān Military Commissioner.
The Xīchuān Army Supervisor Wáng Jiànyán entered to take charge of the Privy Council.
He repeatedly said to the Emperor:
"Binding and sending Xīdámóu to please the enemy's heart,
cutting off future surrenders,
is not a good plan."
The Emperor also regretted it,
and particularly blamed Secretariat Vice-Director and Tongpingzhangshi Niú Sēngrú for his misstep.
Those attached to Lǐ Déyù therefore said
"Sēngrú had a grudge against Déyù,
and harmed his achievement."
The Emperor grew more distant from him.
(To blame means to consider it a fault.)
(To be distant means feelings are not close.)
It happened that the Emperor was holding court at Yányīng Hall,
and said to the chief ministers:
"When will the world ever be at peace?
Do you, gentlemen, also have any intention towards this?"
(Reproaching them for holding office idly and eating for free,
lacking the heart to assist in governance and promote transformation.)
"There is no fixed sign of great peace.
Now, the four barbarians are not invading each other,
the common people are not scattered and displaced;
although this is not the ultimate governance,
(ultimate governance means the highest order.)
it is peaceful.
(Peaceful means tranquil.)
it is not something we ministers can achieve."
After withdrawing,
he said to his colleagues:
"The Sovereign's expectations and reproaches are like this;
how can we remain long in these positions?"
Consequently, he repeatedly submitted memorials requesting to be relieved.
In the twelfth month,
on Yǐchǒu,
Sēngrú was appointed as Tongpingzhangshi,
and assigned as Huáinán Military Commissioner.
Your servant Guāng remarks: When the ruler is enlightened and the ministers are loyal,
when superiors issue commands and subordinates obey,
when the worthy and capable are in office,
when the flattering and wicked are dismissed and kept at a distance,
when rites are cultivated and music is performed,
when punishments are clear and governance is equitable,
when treachery and villainy are eliminated and subdued,
when weapons of war are laid aside and stored,
when the feudal lords submit and adhere,
when the barbarians of the four quarters cherish and submit,
when households are provided for and people have enough—
this is the image of great peace.
Yet at this time,
eunuchs monopolized power,
coercing the ruler within the palace,
and he was unable to keep them at a distance;
the military governors held armed forces,
acting arrogantly and disrespectfully beyond the capital,
and he was unable to control them;
soldiers killed or expelled their commanding generals,
defied orders and established themselves independently,
and he was unable to interrogate them;
military campaigns were launched year after year,
taxes and levies grew more urgent by the day,
