Your subject Guāng says: The incompatibility of gentlemen and petty men
is like ice and charcoal, which cannot coexist in the same vessel.
Thus, when gentlemen gain positions, they expel petty men;
when petty men gain power, they exclude gentlemen.
This is the natural order.
However, gentlemen promote the worthy and dismiss the unworthy.
Their intentions are public-minded,
and their actions are based on facts.
Petty men praise those they favor,
and slander those they despise.
Their intentions are selfish,
and their actions are deceitful.
Those who are public-minded and factual are called upright,
while those who are selfish and deceitful are called factions.
It is up to the ruler to distinguish between them.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler on the throne: assesses virtue to assign positions,
and measures ability to confer offices.
These are the words of Xún Qīngzǐ.
"Assess"
is pronounced tuó luò fān.
"Measure"
is pronounced yīn liáng.
The guilty are punished;
deception cannot confuse him,
and flattery cannot sway him.
If this is the case,
how could factions arise!
But the foolish ruler is not like this.
His clarity cannot illuminate,
his strength cannot decide;
the wicked and the upright are promoted together,
slander and praise come in waves;
choices are not in his own hands,
and authority and favor secretly shift to others.
Thus, slanderers achieve their ambitions, and the discourse of factions arises.
When wood rots, worms are born;
when vinegar turns sour, flies gather.
Therefore, if there are factions in the court,
the ruler should blame himself and not blame his ministers.
If Emperor Wénzōng was troubled by the factions among his ministers,
why did he not examine whether their slander and praise were factual
or deceitful,
whether those promoted were worthy
or unworthy,
whether their intentions were public-minded
or selfish,
and whether they were gentlemen
or petty men!
If they were factual,
worthy,
public-minded,
and gentlemen,
not only should their words be heeded,
but they should also be promoted.
If they were deceitful,
unworthy,
selfish,
and petty men,
not only should their words be discarded,
but they should also be punished.
If this were done,
even if they were driven to form factions,
who would dare!
Instead of doing this,
he complained about the difficulty of managing his ministers,

If the factions in the court cannot be eliminated,
how much less the rebels in Héběi!

and by the Hàn dynasty, it became the Lèyóu Garden.
Its foundation was the highest,
offering a broad and open view in all directions.
When the Suí dynasty built the capital city,

deliberately left this area undeveloped for residential neighborhoods,
and instead excavated it into a pond to suppress unfavorable influences.
Additionally, the Huángqú River water came from the south outside the city,

During Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's reign,

Its location was south of the Lónghuá Temple in Shēngdào Ward in the southeast of the city.
Kūnmíng Pond,
excavated by Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,

with a circumference of forty lǐ.
Sānfǔ Old Tales states: The pond covered three hundred and twenty qǐng.
Cháng'ān Records states: It is now farmland.
Since it could be made into farmland,
it was no longer a water-filled area.
So where did the Hàn dynasty get the water from?
Cháng'ān Records quotes the Classic of Waterways: The Jiāo River flows west to the Shí'è Dam,
which was built when Emperor Wǔ excavated Kūnmíng Pond.
There was a stone sluice gate,
located thirty-two lǐ southwest of the county seat.
Thus, the Kūnmíng Pond covering over three hundred qǐng
used water from this dam.
The foundation of Kūnmíng Pond was high,
so its downstream flow could still be dammed and channeled for use by the capital city.
Thus, three branches were separately dredged alongside the city,
benefiting both inside and outside the city.
This pond still existed.
Kuòdìzhì states: The Fēng and Hào rivers were both dammed into Kūnmíng Pond,
and no longer had separate courses.
Kuòdìzhì was compiled during Tàizōng's reign,
indicating that the damming was still maintained and not abandoned in the early Táng,
and by Emperor Wénzōng's time, it was still dredged.
However, the compilation of local records likely occurred after Emperor Wénzōng,
hence it dried up and became farmland.
4. In the third month,
Prince Jì Qiú passed away.
Qiú,
was a son of Emperor Shùnzōng.

It happened that Déyù had already left Zhèxī.
Governess,

Provide,

Leave,

Déyù was summoned from Zhèxī; see the third year of the previous volume,
governed Shǔ; see the fourth year,
the Sòng Shēnxī affair; see the fifth year.
The chronology is inconsistent,
and should be examined.
Vice Director of the Left Wáng Fán and Vice Minister of Revenue Lǐ Hàn memorialized that Déyù had bribed Zhòngyáng heavily,

Kuǎn's memorial against Zhù; see the previous year in the previous volume.
Textual analysis: The Sweet Dew Record states:
"Some contemporary opinions said Kuǎn outwardly sought a reputation for integrity while secretly serving Zhù."
However, Kuǎn's impeachment of Zhù exposed his hidden evils,
how could someone who treated another like this secretly collude with him!
This was all because mediocre people at the time saw Zhù recommending Kuǎn as his replacement,
and thus had such suspicions.
This is not adopted here.
Laughing without breaking into a smile is called shěn.

the Capital Prefect, Jiǎ Sù from Hénán,

On the Shangsi Festival,

In ancient times, the Shangsi Festival
was precisely held on the first sì day of the third month;
from the Wèi dynasty onward, it was simply held on the third day of the third month,
no longer using the sì day.
During the Táng Zhēnyuán period, three seasonal festivals were established,
allowing officials to choose scenic spots for enjoyment,
the third day of the third month being one of them.
The Prefect dismounted outside the gate,
and bowed to the censors.
Sù, relying on his noble status and power,
rode his horse straight in.
Palace Censors Yáng Jiǎn and Sū Tè argued with him,

Sù felt ashamed,

when Sòng Shēnxī was found guilty,

Although the Emperor outwardly appeared tolerant,

Lǐ Xùn and Zhèng Zhù then took it upon themselves to eliminate the eunuchs.

According to the Supplement to the National History:
"Xǔ Kāngzuǒ presented the newly annotated sixty-chapter Spring and Autumn Annals of the States.

The Veritable Records state:

on the first day, yǐsì,

Thus, the Emperor's plot with Lǐ Xùn to eliminate the eunuchs must have occurred around this time.

They deliberated day and night,

Zhèng Zhù was often in the palace,

Outsiders only knew that Lǐ Xùn and Zhèng Zhù relied on eunuch power to act arrogantly,

When the Emperor ascended the throne,

People were all pleased that Shòuchéng, who had accepted flattery, met his end, and they detested the cunning and deceit of Xùn and Zhù.

Those promoted and supported by Lǐ Xùn

However, he also occasionally selected men of great reputation in the empire to appease public sentiment.
For instance, Péi Dù, Líng Hú Chǔ, and Zhèng Tán were all esteemed veterans of successive reigns
who had long been suppressed by those in power
and relegated to insignificant posts.
Xùn promoted them all to high positions.
Consequently, some scholar-officials also hoped that he could truly bring about peace and prosperity,
and not only was the Emperor deluded by him.
However, those with discernment saw his excessive arrogance

on the day Bǐngwǔ,
Guō Xíngyú, the Chief Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, was appointed as the military governor of Bīnníng.
On the day Guǐchǒu,

On the day Dīngsì,

Shí was
the fifth-generation descendant of Shén Fú.

was the younger brother of Shéntōng, Prince of Huái'ān.

Initially,
Zhèng Zhù and Lǐ Xùn plotted that
upon reaching his garrison,
Zhù would select several hundred strong men,
all armed with white clubs,
concealing axes,
to serve as his personal guards.
In this month,
on the day Wùchén,
Wáng Shòuchéng was buried by the Chǎnshuǐ River.
According to the Yōnglù: The source of the Chǎnshuǐ is in the western region of Lántián County.
It flows slightly northward to the west of Báilùyuán,
then heads towards the capital city.
Wáng Shòuchéng was likely buried southwest of Báilùyuán.
Zhù planned to bring his personal guards with him.
He would then request that all palace eunuchs, from the commanders of the Shence Army down, gather at the Chǎnshuǐ River to attend the funeral.
Zhù would then close the gates,
order his personal guards to axe them,
leaving none alive.
Once this plan was settled,
Xùn plotted with his associates:
"If this succeeds,
then Zhù will claim all the credit.
It would be better to have Xíngyú and Fán, under the pretext of departing for their garrisons,
recruit many strong men as their private troops,
and also utilize the officers and soldiers of the Imperial Guard and the Censorate.
They would first eliminate the eunuchs ahead of schedule,
and afterward, remove Zhù as well."
Xíngyú, Fán, Lìyán, Yuē, and the Vice Censor-in-Chief Lǐ Xiàoběn
were all men Xùn had long favored,
so he placed them in key positions.
He only plotted with these few men and Shū Yuányú,
and no one else knew about it.
On the day Rénxū,
the Emperor held court at the Zǐchén Hall.
After the officials had taken their positions in order,
Hán Yuē did not report "all is peaceful."
According to Táng regulations: At court,
after the Emperor ascends the throne,
the General of the Imperial Guard reports:
"Peace reigns within and without the left and right wings."
"Last night, sweet dew appeared on the pomegranate tree behind the office of the Left Imperial Guard.
I submitted a report through the gate."
This means that during the night, upon hearing the report,
the palace gates were already locked,
so the report was passed through the closed gate for submission.
The chief ministers also led the officials in offering congratulations.
Xùn and Yuányú urged the Emperor to go personally to observe it,
to receive Heaven's blessing,
and the Emperor agreed.
The officials withdrew
and formed ranks at the Hányuán Hall.
Zǐchén
is the inner hall;
Hányuán
is the front hall.
The Emperor intended to go observe the sweet dew,
so the officials withdrew from Zǐchén and came out,
forming ranks at the Hányuán Hall,
because the guards of the Left and Right Imperial Guard were stationed to the left and right in front of the Hányuán Hall.
The Emperor rode in a soft carriage out of the Zǐchén Gate.
A soft carriage
is made by piling cushions and mattresses,
with a wooden frame underneath,
carried by men.
He first ordered the chief ministers and officials from the two departments to go to the left guard post to inspect it,
and they returned after a long while.
Xùn reported:
"I and the others have examined it,
and it seems it is not genuine sweet dew.
It should not be hastily announced."
The Textual Analysis states: Considering that Xùn and Hán Yuē conspired together,
fabricating the sweet dew,
yet Xùn himself said he feared it might not be a true auspicious sign,
likely intending to make all the eunuchs go to the Imperial Guard to re-examine it,
so that soldiers lying in ambush could kill them.
Therefore, the decree drafted by Líng Hú Chǔ on the 22nd also states
"the chief culprit still requested a re-examination."
Now, we follow the Veritable Records.
The Emperor said:
"How could this be!"
He turned and ordered the Left and Right Shence Army commanders Qiú Shìliáng and Yú Zhìhóng to lead the eunuchs to go inspect it.
After the eunuchs had left,
Xùn hastily summoned Guō Xíngyú and Wáng Fán, saying:
"Come and receive the imperial decree!"
Fán's legs trembled, and he dared not advance,
only Xíngyú bowed below the hall.
At that time, the private troops of these two men, numbering several hundred,
were all holding weapons and standing outside the Dānfèng Gate.
Xùn had already sent someone to summon them earlier,
ordering them to enter and receive the decree.
Only the eastern troops entered—
these were the troops from Hédōng.
The character "east"
above is missing
the character "river."
[Chapter note: The Kǒng edition correctly has
the character "river."
Qiú Shìliáng and others arrived at the Left Arsenal to inspect the Sweet Dew,
Hán Yuē's complexion changed and he was sweating profusely.
Shìliáng, finding this strange, said:
"General, why are you like this?"
Suddenly, a gust of wind blew the curtains open,
revealing many armed men,
and the clanging of weapons was heard.
Shìliáng and the others, startled and terrified, fled.
The gatekeepers tried to close the gates,
but Shìliáng shouted at them,
and the crossbar could not be put in place.
The crossbar,
is the bolt of the gate.
"Put in place,"
is pronounced as "shàng" at that time;
the following "shàng" is the same.
Lǐ Xùn saw this,
and urgently called to the Imperial Guards:
"Those who come up to the hall to protect the imperial carriage,
will be rewarded with a hundred strings of cash each!"
The eunuchs said:
"The situation is critical,
we request Your Majesty to return to the palace!"
They immediately lifted the soft carriage,
welcomed the Emperor, helped him ascend the carriage,
broke through the fúsī screen at the back of the hall,
and hurried northward.
The fúsī in the Táng palace halls
were made of silk,
shaped like a net,
to block swallows and sparrows,
unlike the fúsī of the Hàn palace towers.
Now that the eunuchs could break through it and escape,
this can be understood.
Chéng Dàchāng said: Fúsī
are carved from wood,
with open spaces inside,
allowing light to pass through.
Some are square openings,
some are interlocking patterns,
their appearance is sparse and branching,
hence called fúsī,
pronounced like "fúsī,"
akin to saying "bushy and not bushy."
By imagining its original form based on its shape,
it becomes clear.
Once the name fúsī was established,
it was then applied according to its use and location to give it a name.
When in palace towers, it is called tower fúsī;
when ministers come to see the sovereign,
upon reaching the tower, they again think of what to report, hence the name.
When on tomb walls, it is called tomb fúsī;
Wáng Mǎng chopped away the tomb fúsī,
saying it was to make people no longer think of Hàn, hence the name.
Looking back to ancient times,
the "shū píng" in the Book of Rites is also this object.
"Shū" means
carved with cloud patterns and hollowed out intricately.
There is also "wǎng hù,"
carved with continuous patterns,
linked together,
shaped like a net.
Sòng Yù said,
"Net doors with red trimmings, carved in square links,"
refers to this.
Since it is said to be carved,
then it is carved from wood,
shaped like a net.
Later generations thus directly wove silk nets and hung them under eaves and windows to protect against birds.
During the Sweet Dew Incident of Emperor Wénzōng,
they exited through the northern gate of the hall,
tore through the fúsī and left,
which was a real net.
This is also following the Chǔcí tradition and applying nets.
Yuán Zhěn, when serving as Academician, wrote a poem:
"Few know the depths of Ruǐzhū,

I have privately heard that over the past few months,
the Music Bureau has selected and tested hundreds of women,
and the Estate Bureau continues to purchase them without cease.
(The various offices within the Tang court included the Music Bureau Commissioner and Estate Bureau Commissioner,
both positions held by eunuchs.)
Without regard for imperial relatives,
this has stirred widespread public criticism.
I privately regret this.
In the past, when Emperor Guangwu of Han once glanced at a screen painted with virtuous women,
Sòng Hóng sternly admonished him,
and Guangwu immediately had it removed.
(During Emperor Guangwu's reign,
Sòng Hóng served as Grand Minister of Works.
Once, during a banquet audience,
the imperial seat had a new screen painted with images of virtuous women.
The emperor repeatedly glanced at it.
Sòng Hóng solemnly said:
'I have never seen one who loves virtue as much as he loves beauty!'
The emperor immediately had it removed.
Smiling, he said to Sòng Hóng:
'Upon hearing righteousness, I submit—is this acceptable?'
Sòng Hóng replied:
'Your Majesty advances in virtue;
I could not be more delighted!')
How could Your Majesty wish to be inferior to Emperor Guangwu?"
The emperor then released Lǐ Xiàoběn’s daughters.
(Textual analysis states: The Veritable Records first says
'took two daughters of Xiàoběn into the palace,'
but later, in Wèi Mó's memorial, it says
'took one younger daughter of Xiàoběn into the palace.'
The reason for this discrepancy is likely that both of Xiàoběn’s daughters were conscripted into the Right Army.
The elder daughter was first taken into the palace,
which Wèi Mó did not know about.
When the younger daughter was also taken,
Wèi Mó learned of it and submitted his memorial.
The emperor said:
'I selected and purchased women to bestow upon the princes.
I pitied Xiàoběn’s daughters,
orphaned and helpless in their youth,
so I took them into the palace to care for them.
Wèi Mó was able to speak forthrightly even in matters of suspicion;
he can be said to love me and does not disgrace his ancestors!')
He ordered the Secretariat to draft a generous edict to reward him.
Wèi Mó was the fifth-generation descendant of Wèi Zhēng.
(Wèi Zhēng served Tàizōng with integrity.)
17. Xiāo Hóng, Military Commissioner of Fūfāng, falsely claimed to be the younger brother of the Empress Dowager.
(This matter began in the 243rd scroll, in the second year of the Tàihé era.)
In the eighth month, on the day Jiǎchén,
he was exiled to Huānzhōu and
died en route by imperial decree.
Zhào Zhěn, Lǚ Zhāng, and others were all exiled to Lingnán.
Initially, Lǐ Xùn knew of Xiāo Hóng’s deception.
Xiāo Hóng, fearing exposure,
appointed Lǐ Xùn’s elder brother, Zhòngjīng, to his staff.
Previously, when someone from the Divine Strategy Army was appointed as a military commissioner,
the army would provide him with travel funds.
Upon reaching his post,
he would repay threefold.
Someone from the Left Army (the Left Divine Strategy Army) was appointed to Fūfāng.
The army demanded repayment from Xiāo Hóng,
but Xiāo Hóng, relying on Lǐ Xùn’s influence, refused.
When the army demanded repayment from the deceased’s son,
Xiāo Hóng instructed the son to appeal to the chancellor himself.
Lǐ Xùn ruled to reject the claim.
Qiú Shìliáng thus harbored resentment toward Xiāo Hóng.
The Empress Dowager had a half-brother in Mǐnzhōng,
who was weak and unable to make himself known.
A man from Mǐn named Xiāo Běn learned from him the names of his inner and outer clans
and, through Qiú Shìliáng, presented himself to the emperor,
exposing Xiāo Hóng’s fraud.
Xiāo Hóng was thus punished.
The emperor, believing Xiāo Běn to be the true younger brother of the Empress Dowager,
on the day Wùshēn, promoted him to Right Advisor of the Heir Apparent.
18. In the ninth month, on the day Dīngchǒu,
Lǐ Shí spoke to the emperor about Sòng Shēnxī’s loyalty and integrity,
how he was slandered by malicious individuals,
exiled to distant lands, and died without being exonerated.
The emperor bowed his head for a long time, then shed tears and said with emotion:
"I have long known this matter was wrong.
Treacherous men pressured me, citing the great matter of the state.
I almost could not protect my own brother" (referring to Prince Zhāng, Còu).
(Jī, pronounced jūyī.)
"I barely managed to preserve my life.
It was not only the inner officials;
outer court officials also aided them.
All this was due to my lack of clarity.
Had I encountered an emperor like Hàn Zhāodì,
such injustice would certainly not have occurred!" (Referring to Hàn Zhāodì’s awareness of the deceit of Yān, Gài, and Shàngguān.)
The emperor felt deep regret and showed a ashamed expression.
On the day Gēngchén, an edict was issued to fully restore Shēnxī’s official titles and ranks,
and his son, Shènwēi, was appointed as Chénggù County Lieutenant. (Chénggù County belonged to Xīngyuán Prefecture.)
19. Lǐ Shí appointed Hán Yì, Vice Director of the Bureau of Treasury, to handle the Ministry of Revenue’s cases. (Àn, same as "case," referring to documents. This is a sentence break.)
Hán Yì was imprisoned.
Lǐ Shí said: "I initially used Yì because he was quite knowledgeable about finances, but I did not know he was so corrupt!"

The emperor said: "A chancellor should employ people based on their abilities and punish them for their faults. This way, capable people can be easily found. Your willingness to expose the faults of those you employ can be called utmost impartiality. Previous chancellors preferred to conceal the faults of those they employed and did not want others to impeach them—this is a grave flaw!"
In winter, the eleventh month, on the day Dīngsì, Hán Yì was demoted to Registrar of Wúzhōu. (Wúzhōu was named after Cāngwú Commandery, located 5,500 lǐ from the capital.)
(Hǎo, pronounced hūdào. Hé, pronounced hùgài, also hùdé.)

20. Since the Sweet Dew Incident, the emperor had been dispirited and unhappy. Gatherings for polo and kickball in the two armies decreased by sixty to seventy percent. Even during banquets with music and performers filling the hall, he never smiled. In his leisure time, he would sometimes pace and gaze into the distance or sigh and speak to himself.
On the day Rénwǔ, the emperor said to the chancellors at the Yányīng Hall: "Whenever I discuss matters of the realm with you, I cannot help but feel sorrow."
They replied: "Governance cannot be achieved hastily." (Wéilǐ means the same as wéizhì, "to govern.")
The emperor said: "Whenever I read books, I feel ashamed of being an ordinary ruler."

Lǐ Shí said: "Among the officials both inside and outside the court, there are still many petty men who harbor doubts and create obstacles. I hope Your Majesty will govern them with even greater leniency. For those who are as impartial, upright, and law-abiding as Liú Hóngyì and Xuē Jìléng, Your Majesty should also reward them to encourage good conduct."

On the day Jiǎshēn, the emperor again said to the chancellors: "When I discuss matters of the realm with you, there are situations where action cannot be taken. Afterward, I can only drink strong wine to seek drunkenness!"
They replied: "This is all our fault."
21. The officials reported that the Left Treasury had long been plagued by malpractices,
and requested an inspection and audit.
They also stated that for officials and clerks whose crimes occurred before the amnesty,
they requested leniency.
The Emperor approved.
Subsequently, they indeed found silk fabrics falsely claimed to be stained and soiled.
An imperial decree was issued to pardon them.
The Supervising Secretary Dí Jiānmó returned the sealed decree, saying:
"Officials and clerks guilty of corruption,
in principle, should not be pardoned!"
The Emperor instructed him:
"When the officials initially requested the inspection,
I already approved it.
Rather than break my word,
I would rather let the guilty go unpunished.
You are capable of fulfilling your duties,
I greatly commend you!"
22. In the twelfth month,
on the Gēngxū day,
Lú Jūn, the Governor of Huá Prefecture, was appointed Military Governor of Lǐngnán.
Lǐ Shí said to the Emperor:
"Regarding Lú Jūn's appointment to Lǐngnán,
all court officials congratulated each other.
They consider Lǐngnán a rich and prosperous region,
and in recent years, appointments there were obtained through heavy bribes to the Northern Bureau;
now that the Northern Bureau does not interfere with court authority,
Your Majesty should also have a way to commend them.
This would encourage both internal and external officials to uphold the law,
which is the foundation for achieving good governance."
The Emperor followed this advice.
When Lú Jūn arrived at his post,
he became renowned for his integrity and benevolence.
23. On the Jǐwèi day,
Prince Shū, Zòng, passed away.
Zòng,
was a son of Emperor Shùnzōng.
1. In spring,
the second month,
on the Jǐwèi day,
the Emperor said to the chief ministers:
"When recommending people, do not ask whether they are close or distant.
I heard that when Dòu Yìzhí was chief minister,
Dòu Yìzhí served as chief minister during the Chángqìng and Bǎolì reigns.
If relatives or old acquaintances are truly talented,
to avoid suspicion and discard them,
that is also not the utmost fairness."
2. Prince Jūn, Wěi, passed away.
Wěi,
was a son of Emperor Shùnzōng.
3. In the third month,
a comet appeared in the constellation Zhāng,
over eighty zhàng in length.
On the Rénshēn day,
an edict was issued to suspend music and reduce the imperial meals,
using one day's provisions to cover ten days.
4. In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Jiǎchén day,
the Emperor received the Secretariat Drafter, Hanlin Academician, and Concurrent Attendant-Calligrapher Liǔ Gōngquán in the informal hall.
Liǔ Gōngquán was previously appointed Hanlin Attendant-Calligrapher Academician,
now he serves as Hanlin Academician concurrently as Attendant-Calligrapher.
"This garment has already been washed three times!"
Everyone praised the Emperor's frugal virtue;
only Liǔ Gōngquán remained silent.
The Emperor asked him the reason,
he replied:
"Your Majesty is honored as the Son of Heaven,
possessing the wealth of the four seas.
You should promote the worthy and dismiss the unworthy,
accept remonstrance and criticism,
clarify rewards and punishments,
then you can achieve harmony and prosperity.
Wearing washed clothes
is merely a minor detail."
The Emperor said:
"I know that a Secretariat Drafter should not concurrently serve as Remonstrance Official,
Dù Yǒu's Tōngdiǎn states: The Secretariat Drafter
is the ultimate post for literary scholars,
a prestigious selection of the court,
no other official position compares.
I must trouble you to take this post."
On the Yǐsì day,
Liǔ Gōngquán was appointed Remonstrance Official,
retaining his other positions.
5. On the Wùxū day,
the Hanlin Academician and Vice Minister of Works Chén Yíxíng was appointed Tongpingzhangshi (chief minister).
6. In the sixth month,
the Héyáng army mutinied.
The Military Governor Lǐ Yǒng fled to Huái Prefecture;
the soldiers burned the government offices,
killed Lǐ Yǒng's two sons,
and plundered extensively for several days before stopping.
Lǐ Yǒng,
was a man from the Cháng'ān market,
who registered in the Imperial Guard,
obtained a military governorship through bribery,
wherever he went, he relied on his connections,
was greedy, cruel, and unlawful,
his subordinates could not endure his commands,
hence they rebelled.
On the Dīngwèi day,
Lǐ Yǒng was demoted to Assistant Prefect of Lǐ Prefecture.
Lǐ Prefecture,
is 1,893 lǐ southeast of the capital.
Lǐ,
pronounced lǐ.
On the Wùshēn day,
Left Jinwu General Lǐ Zhífāng was appointed Military Governor of Héyáng.
7. In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Guǐhài day,
Zhènwǔ reported that over three hundred tents of Dǎngxiàng tribes had plundered and fled.
8. Supervising Secretary Wéi Wēn served as Tutor to the Crown Prince.
He went to the Eastern Palace in the morning,
but only managed to see the Crown Prince at noon.
Wéi Wēn remonstrated:
"The Crown Prince should rise at cockcrow,
inquire after [his parents'] well-being and oversee the meals.
The Record states: When King Wén was Heir Apparent,
at first cockcrow he dressed,
went to the door of the bedchamber,
and asked the attending inner attendant:
'How is [the ruler's] health today?'
The inner attendant said:
'Well.'
King Wén was then pleased.
If there was any discomfort,
then the inner attendant would inform King Wén,
King Wén would look worried,
and walk unable to step properly.
Until recovery,
then he also returned to normal.
When food was presented, he would certainly observe whether it was warm or cool."
Shǐ Zhào said: Cooked food is called yōng,
prepared food is called shàn.
Shàn means good.
The Crown Prince did not follow his advice,
setting the stage for the Crown Prince's unfortunate end.
On the Xīnwèi day,
[Wéi Wēn] was relieved of this duty and returned to his original post.
9. One hundred and fifty tents of Turks in Zhènwǔ rebelled,
plundering the military farms;
on the Wùyín day,
Military Governor Liú Miǎn defeated them.
10. In the eighth month,
on the Gēngxū day,
Lady Wáng, the Zhaoyi, was made Dé,
and Lady Yáng, the Zhaorong, was made Xián.
The Táng followed the Sui system,
having one each of Guì, Shū, Dé, and Xián,
as Ladies,
rank Zheng Yīpǐn.
Zhízhōng was made Prince of Xiāng,
Yán Yáng was made Prince,
Chéngměi was made Prince of Chén.
On the Guǐchǒu day,
the Emperor's son Zōngjiǎn was established as Prince of Jiǎng.
Jiǎng,
is the name of an ancient state.
Zuǒzhuàn: Fán, Jiǎng, Xíng, Máo, Zuò, Zhài.
11. After the Héyáng soldiers had expelled Lǐ Yǒng,
they daily incited each other,
wanting to rebel.
In the ninth month,
Lǐ Zhífāng apprehended over seventy of the chief instigators,
and executed them all.
The remaining accomplices were distributed to other garrisons,
and only then was order restored.
12. In winter,
the tenth month,
the stone classics at the Directorate of Education were completed.
Liú Xù said: At that time, the Emperor was fond of literature,
Zhèng Tán, as chief minister overseeing the Directorate of Education,
following the Later Hàn's Cài Yōng who had inscriptions carved and erected at the Imperial Academy,
initiated the carving of the Nine Classics on stone tablets,
with various scholars correcting errors.
The Emperor also ordered the Hanlin engraving officials to check the calligraphic style,
but it further deviated from the master's method.
Therefore, several decades after the stone classics were erected,
renowned scholars did not even look at them,
considering them crude and burdensome.
13. Fújiàn reported that a commoner from Jìnjiāng, Xiāo Hóng, claimed to be a relative of the Empress Dowager.
Jìnjiāng,
originally the territory of Jìn'ān County, Jìn'ān Commandery.
The Wú established Dōng'ān County,
the Jìn changed it to Jìn'ān,
the Sui changed it to Nán'ān,
in the eighth year of the Kāiyuán era, Jìnjiāng County was established from part of Nán'ān,
attached to Quán Prefecture.
14. On the Wùshēn day,
the Vice Director of the Chancellery and Tongpingzhangshi Lǐ Gùyán was appointed Tongpingzhangshi,
and sent as Military Governor of Xīchuān.
15. On the Jiǎyín day,
the Censorate reported that Xiāo Hóng's claim was fraudulent;
an edict ordered him escorted back to his hometown,
instructing that he be provided food along the way while being escorted back.
Hoping to find the true one.
Punctuated by Zhōu Yīliáng, proofread by Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí.
9. Earlier, at the end of the Taihe era,
Dù Cóng served as the military governor of Fèngxiáng.
An edict was issued to reduce the number of monks and nuns.
This matter is recorded in the previous volume under the eighth year of Taihe.
Near Fǎmén Temple,
rumors spread among the people that the Buddha’s bone had manifested an auspicious sign.
The Buddha’s bone was housed at Fǎmén Temple,
hence the saying.
The supervising eunuch wanted to report this to the throne,
but Dù Cóng said:
“Changes in clouds and atmospheric phenomena—what constancy do they have?
If the Buddha truly cared for the monks and nuns,
it would manifest in the capital.”
Not long after,
a white rabbit was captured.
The supervising eunuch again wanted to report it,
saying:
“This is an auspicious sign from the west.”
Dù Cóng said:
“The wild beast is not yet tamed;
it should be kept for now.”
After ten days, it died.
The supervising eunuch was displeased,
believing that Dù Cóng was concealing the emperor’s virtuous influence.
He alone drew a picture of it and presented it to the throne.
When Zhèng Zhù replaced Dù Cóng as military governor of Fèngxiáng,
according to the previous volume of the Comprehensive Mirror,
in the eighth year of Taihe,
in the ninth month,
on the Gēngshēn day,
Lǐ Tīng, the military governor of Fèngxiáng, was appointed military governor of Zhōngwǔ,
replacing Dù Cóng.
On the Dīngmǎo day,
Zhèng Zhù was appointed military governor of Fèngxiáng.
Zhèng Zhù falsely accused Lǐ Tīng of corruption and cruelty while in Fèngxiáng.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the Yǐhài day,
Lǐ Tīng was appointed Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent with a sinecure in the eastern capital,
and Dù Cóng was again made military governor of Zhōngwǔ.
If it is as recorded in the previous volume,
then Dù Cóng was governing Zhōngwǔ,
not in Fèngxiáng.
Zhèng Zhù also presented a white pheasant.
That year,
in the eighth month,
sweet dew fell on the cherry trees in front of the Zǐchén Hall.
The emperor personally picked and tasted it,
and all officials offered congratulations.
In the eleventh month of that year,
the Sweet Dew Incident involving the Imperial Guards occurred.
When Dù Cóng later served as Minister of Works and concurrently oversaw state finances,
Hézhōng reported the appearance of a zōuyú.
Commentary on the Classic of Poetry: The zōuyú is a righteous beast,
a white tiger with black markings.
It does not eat living creatures
and appears in response to the utmost virtue of sincerity.
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú’s “Fēngshàn Memorial” says: “The splendid beast delights in our sovereign’s park; white in substance and black in pattern, its appearance is pleasing.”
Yán Shǐgǔ’s commentary states: This refers to the zōuyú.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas says: The zōuyú resembles a tiger,
is five-colored,
and has a tail longer than its body.
The emperor said to Dù Cóng:
“Lǐ Xùn and Zhèng Zhù both used auspicious signs to advance their rebellions.
Now I know that auspicious objects are not necessarily blessings for the state.
You, earlier in Fèngxiáng, did not report the white rabbit—truly a prescient judgment.”
Dù Cóng replied:
“In ancient times, the River produced the Chart, and Fúxī used it to draw the Eight Trigrams;
the Luo produced the Writing, and the Great Yǔ used it to order the Nine Categories.
Both were beneficial to humanity, hence they are worthy of esteem.
As for auspicious signs involving birds, beasts, plants, or trees—when have they ever been absent?
Liú Cōng was tyrannical and rebellious, yet yellow dragons appeared three times.
Shǐ Jìlóng was cruel and oppressive, yet obtained sixteen gray qílín and seven white deer to pull his carriage canopy.
Shí Hǔ, courtesy name Jìlóng; the Táng avoided the temple name taboo, hence his courtesy name is used.
Do auspicious signs truly depend on virtue?
Emperor Xuánzōng once served as Assistant Prefect of Lùzhōu.
During Emperor Zhōngzōng’s reign,
Emperor Xuánzōng was Assistant Prefect of Lùzhōu.
Lùzhōu reported nineteen auspicious signs.
Emperor Xuánzōng said: ‘When I was in Lùzhōu, I only knew to diligently attend to my duties. I was unaware of such auspicious objects.’
I hope Your Majesty will focus solely on the prosperity and peace of the common people as the true blessing of the state.
All else is not worth pursuing.”
The emperor approved of this.
Another day,
he said to the chief ministers:
“Seasonal harmony and abundant harvests—these are the supreme auspicious signs.
Fine grain and numinous fungi—what benefit do they truly bring to affairs?”
The chief ministers accordingly said:
“The Spring and Autumn Annals records disasters and anomalies to warn rulers,
but does not record auspicious signs—precisely for this reason!”
This was likely Zhèng Tán’s words.
In summer,
in the fifth month,
on the Yǐhài day,
an edict was issued:
“If any circuit has auspicious signs, none may report them,
nor submit documents to the relevant offices.
The year-end sacrifices at the Imperial Ancestral Temple
(Táng system: sacrifices at the Imperial Ancestral Temple were held at the beginning of each season and at year-end.
The Táng used the Yín day for the year-end sacrifice.)
and at the Tàiqīng Palace
(In the second year of Tiānbǎo, Emperor Xuánzōng designated the Xuányuán Emperor Temple in the western capital as the Tàiqīng Palace.)
are all suspended.”
The Six Codes: All major auspicious signs were to be reported by memorial immediately,
and civil and military officials would proceed to the palace to offer congratulations.
Others were to be reported collectively at year-end by memorial;
the relevant office would announce them at the temple,
and officials would proceed to the palace to offer congratulations.
Also, the Regulations on Ceremonies stated: Major auspicious signs were to be reported by memorial immediately;
medium and minor auspicious signs were to be reported to the relevant offices,
and announced on New Year’s Day.
Now all these are suspended.
Examination of discrepancies: The Veritable Records state:
“Earlier, the emperor said to the chief ministers: ‘Abundant harvests and peaceful people—are these not the supreme auspicious signs?’
The chief ministers accordingly mentioned that the Spring and Autumn Annals does not record auspicious signs.
The emperor deeply agreed, and hence issued this edict.”
The Supplement to the National History attributes it to Dù Cóng’s advice.
Here both accounts are combined.
10. Earlier,
Wáng Yànpíng, military governor of Língwǔ, embezzled over seven thousand strings of cash.
The emperor, considering that his father Wáng Zhìxīng had rendered meritorious service
(Wáng Zhìxīng had merit in suppressing Héng Hǎi),
sentenced him to perpetual exile to Kāngzhōu.
Wáng Yànpíng secretly petitioned the three military governors of Wèi, Zhèn, and Yōu
(the Wèi commander was Hé Jìntāo;
the Zhèn commander was Wáng Yuándá;
the Yōu commander was Shǐ Yuánzhōng).
The emperor had no choice.
In the sixth month,
on the Rényín day,
he changed the sentence to Registrar of Yǒngzhōu.
11. In the eighth month,
on the Jǐhài day,
Prince Jiā, Yùn, passed away.
Yùn was a son of Emperor Dàizōng.
The mother of Crown Prince Yǒng, Wáng Dé, was not favored and
died after being slandered by Yáng Xián.
The Táng dynasty followed the Suí system,
with one each of Guì, Shū, Dé, and Xián,
as consorts,
of the first rank.
During the Kāiyuán era,
Emperor Xuánzōng considered the four stars of the empress,
one being the empress herself;
having an empress and then establishing four more
was not according to the statutes.
So he established Huì, Lì, and Huá
to replace the three consorts.
Later, the Guì consort was reinstated,
thus restoring the early Táng system of four.
Being close to petty men,
Xián slandered him day and night.
In the ninth month,
on the Rénxū day,
the Emperor opened the Yányīng Hall,
summoned the chief ministers, officials from the two departments, the Censorate, and court officials,
listed the crown prince's faults and misdeeds,
and discussed deposing him,
saying:
"Is this one fit to be the Son of Heaven?"
All the ministers said:
"The crown prince is young,
and may yet reform his faults.
The foundation of the state is of utmost importance,
how can it be lightly shaken!"
The Vice Censor-in-Chief Dí Jiānmó argued most earnestly,
even to the point of weeping.
The Supervising Secretary Wéi Wēn said:
"Your Majesty has only one son,
and failing to instruct him,
you have led him to this state—
is it solely the crown prince's fault!"
On the Guǐhài day,
six Hanlin Academicians and sixteen commanders of the six armies of the Shéncè Army again submitted memorials discussing the matter,
and the Emperor's resolve softened somewhat.
That evening,
the crown prince was finally able to return to the Shàoyáng Hall;
the Rújīng Commissioner Wáng Shàohuá and others
(the Táng established the Rújīng Commissioner,
appointing military officers to the post,
an inner court position,
but it is unknown what duties it entailed.)
13 The Yìwǔ military governor Zhāng Pán had been in his post for fifteen years;
in the third year of Emperor Mùzōng's Chángqìng era,
Pán replaced Chén Chǔ as governor of Yìwǔ.
When he fell ill,
he requested to come to court.
Before the court could make arrangements,
his illness worsened,
and he instructed his son Yuányì to lead the entire family back to the court,
and not to follow the precedent of Héběi.
After his death,
the army wished to install Yuányì,
but the acting military governor Lǐ Shìjì refused,
and the multitude killed him,
also killing more than ten senior officers.
On the Rénshēn day,
Lǐ Zhòngqiān, the prefect of Yìzhōu, was appointed military governor of Yìwǔ.
The Yìwǔ cavalry commander Hé Qīngcháo broke away and returned to court,
and on the Guǐyǒu day,
he was appointed prefect of Yízhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Liáozhōu, the Lèpíng commandery,
was established as Liáozhōu in the third year of the Wǔdé era of the Táng,
renamed Jīzhōu in the eighth year,
and in the second year of the Xiāntiān era,
due to Emperor Xuánzōng's name taboo,
was renamed Yízhōu.
14 The court considered that the Yìchāng military governor Lǐ Yànzuǒ had been in his post for a long time;
in the sixth year of the Tàihé era,
Lǐ Yànzuǒ replaced Yīn Yòu as governor of Yìchāng.
On the Jiǎxū day,
Liú Yuē, the prefect of Dézhōu, was appointed deputy military governor,
intending to have him replace Yànzuǒ.
15 Since the Kāichéng era began,
promotions of Shéncè Army officers and officials
were often not reported,
but directly sent to the Secretariat for review and implementation,
with promotions and changes occurring almost daily.
After the Gānlù incident,
the eunuchs' arbitrary conduct had reached this point.
On the Guǐwèi day,
an edict was finally issued that all promotions of Shéncè Army officers and officials must first be reported,
with the documents sent to the Secretariat,
and only then reviewed and implemented.
First reported to the Emperor,
the palace would send the documents to the Secretariat,
which would then review the records and implement them.

the tenth month,

Wūjiè at that time moved his tent to protect Cuòzǐ Shān.
They were sent by the khan.
It is appropriate to point out that these troops claim not to accept the khan’s command,
and they plunder the border regions.
Secretly order Liú Miǎn and Zhòngwǔ
(Zhòngwǔ,
that is Zhāng Zhòngwǔ)
if they can attack and drive them away,
there will also be justification for the action.
Destroying this one branch,
the khan will certainly become fearful on his own.”
Summer,
fourth month,
Gēngchén,
Tiāndé Regional Defense Commissioner Tián Móu reported:
“The Uighurs have been invading and harassing without cease.
Without waiting for court orders,
I have already dispatched three thousand troops to resist them.”
Rénwǔ,
Lǐ Déyù reported:
“Tián Móu knows nothing about military affairs.
The Róngdí are skilled in field battles
but weak in siege warfare.
Móu should only defend firmly and wait for the troops from various circuits to assemble.
Now, the entire army has gone out to fight.
If by any chance they are defeated,
the city will be empty,
and how will they defend themselves?
I hope an imperial envoy is urgently sent to stop him.
If they have already engaged in battle,
then order the Qiāng and Hún from Yún, Shuò, Tiāndé, and beyond to each send troops to vigorously attack the Uighurs.
All captured goods
should be allowed to be taken by themselves.
The Uighurs have been wandering for two years,
their food supplies are exhausted,
and their morale is easily shaken.
It is appropriate to order Tián Móu to recruit and lure those who surrender,
provide them with food, and transfer them to Tàiyuán.
They must not be kept at Tiāndé.
Although the sincerity of Wòmòsī is still unknown,
it is nevertheless important to grant him an official position and reward early.
Examination of Discrepancies says: The Collected Works of the First Rank, Preface to the Biography of Loyalty from Foreign Lands, states:
“In the second year,
fourth month,
Jiǎshēn,
the Uighur Great Tèlè Wòmòsī led his country’s Tèlè, ministers, and others to submit internally.”
However, this memorial on the eighteenth day of the fourth month already mentions Wòmòsī sending a message of surrender.
Probably Wòmòsī had already sent a message of surrender to Tián Móu when he intended to kill Chìxīn,
and on the twentieth day, he led his followers to Tiāndé.
Therefore, the edict appointing him as Left Imperial Guard General states:
“He repeatedly offered sincerity,
communicating with the border generals;
soon captured the rebel barbarians,
not abandoning his ruler and kin.
He gathered his starving followers,
without the slightest violation.
Observing his actions,
his great integrity is very clear.”
Probably when the Uighurs were in chaos and collapse,
Wòmòsī originally came to submit to the Táng along with Chìxīn and others,
but the border officials were suspicious and obstructive,
so Chìxīn and others became angry and intended to invade the border.
And Wòmòsī first informed the border officials,
lured Chìxīn’s followers to flee eastward,
and Wòmòsī led his followers to surrender to the Táng.
This is also sufficient to serve as counterintelligence.
Moreover, to reward his loyalty and righteousness,
and to create a justification for punitive campaigns,
so that the various distant and nearby barbarians know that we only blame the khan for his rebellion,
and do not intend to completely exterminate the Uighurs.
Shí Xióng is skilled in battle and unmatched,
I request that he be appointed as Tiāndé Regional Training Vice Commissioner,
to assist Tián Móu in military affairs.”
The Emperor followed all of his suggestions.
Initially,
during the Tàihé period,
the Dǎngxiàng in Héxī harassed the border.
Emperor Wénzōng summoned Shí Xióng from Báizhōu.
(Shí Xióng was exiled to Báizhōu; see the 244th volume, third year of Tàihé.)
He repeatedly achieved military merits,
but because of Wáng Zhìxīng’s influence,
he was not greatly promoted.
At this time,
Déyù recommended and employed him.
Jiǎshēn,
Wòmòsī led his country’s Tèlè, ministers, and others, more than two thousand two hundred people, to surrender.
Examination of Discrepancies says: The Collected Works of the First Rank,
the memorial of Wòmòsī Tèlè and others was submitted on the fourth day of the fifth month.
The Veritable Records places it on Bǐngshēn of the fifth month,
probably based on the date the report arrived.
Now, follow the Preface to the Biography of Loyalty.
8 The Emperor trusted Lǐ Déyù,
and the Army Surveillance Commissioner Qiú Shìliáng disliked him.
It happened that the Emperor was about to receive an honorific title,
and would proclaim an amnesty from the Dānfèng Tower.
Someone informed Shìliáng,
saying that the宰相 and the Ministry of Revenue were discussing drafting an edict to reduce the clothing and food rations for the Imperial Guard and the fodder for their horses.
Shìliáng publicly declared to the crowd:
“If this is the case,
on that day,
the soldiers will certainly clamor in front of the tower!”
Déyù heard of this.
Yǐyǒu,
he requested to open the Yányīng Hall to personally explain.
The Emperor was angry,
and immediately sent an imperial envoy to proclaim to the two armies:
“The amnesty edict originally had no such matter.
Moreover, the amnesty edict is entirely my own intention,
not from the宰相.
How can you say such things!”
Shìliáng then became fearful and ashamed, offering apologies.
Dīnghài,
the ministers presented the honorific title of “Benevolent, Holy, Civil, Martial, Supreme, Divine, and Greatly Filial Emperor” to the Emperor;
an amnesty was proclaimed throughout the land.
9 In the fifth month, on the Wùshēn day,
the Court sent the Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Zhāng Jiǎ, to pacify Wàméisī and others.
Wàméisī was appointed as General of the Left Imperial Guard and Prince of Huáihuà Commandery.
The other chieftains were also rewarded with various official positions.
Their tribe was granted 5,000 hu of rice
and 3,000 bolts of silk.
Nàxiéchuò led his forces from Zhènwǔ and Dàtóng,
eastward through the Shìwéi and Hēishā regions,
and then southward toward the Xióngwǔ Army,
with the intention of spying on Yōuzhōu.
The Military Governor of Lúlóng, Zhāng Zhòngwǔ, sent his younger brother Zhòng Zhì with 30,000 troops to intercept them.
He inflicted a major defeat on them,
with countless beheadings and captives taken.
He completely subdued their 7,000 tents,
and distributed them among various circuits.
Nàxiéchuò fled,
but was captured and killed by the Uyghur Khagan, Wūjiè.
Commentary: The *Record of Suppressing Rebellions* states:
"Zhòngwǔ successively recruited over 30,000 deserters from Chìxīn's defeated troops and tribes under the Khagan,
distributing them among various circuits,
causing the Uyghur tribe to become greatly weakened."
Both the new and old annals lack records of Zhòngwǔ defeating the Uyghurs.
The old *History of the Uyghurs* states:
"Zhòngwǔ inflicted a major defeat on Nàxié's forces,
completely subduing 7,000 tents,
and killing or capturing a total of 90,000 people, young and old.
Nàxié was struck by an arrow,
but secretly escaped by hiding among camels.
Wūjiè captured and killed him."
The *Stele of Meritorious Deeds in Yōuzhōu* from the *Collected Works of the First Rank* states:
"The Duke successively accepted the surrender of 30,000 people, two Tèlè, one elder sister of the Khagan, and four Grand Commanders and external chancellors,
with other subordinate kings and cavalry generals too numerous to fully record."
None of the texts mention the specific month and day of Zhòngwǔ's defeat of Nàxiéchuò,
so it is appended here.
At that time, although Wūjiè's forces had diminished,
they still claimed to number 100,000,
and were encamped north of the Lǘmén Mountain in the Dàtóng Army region.
Yáng Guān returned from the Uyghurs,
and the Khagan submitted a memorial requesting grain, cattle, and sheep,
which was sent along with Yáng Guān's return.
An imperial edict replied:
"Regarding grain, you are permitted to purchase 3,000 shi from Zhènwǔ using the price of horses.
Since the Sùzōng and Dàizōng eras, the Uyghurs have traded horses with China,
with payment made according to their value.
As for farming resources,
China prohibits the slaughter of cattle.
Sheep are scarce in China,
and come from the northern border tribes.
The state has never levied them as taxes.
Since the initial defeat of his own state, Wàméisī
first sought refuge at the border,
and has not followed the Khagan for nearly two years,
fearing suspicion and resentment.
The previous Khagan was precisely overthrown due to suspicion and cruelty, lacking close allies,
leading to internal division and external rebellion.
Now that the Khagan has lost his territory and is a distant guest,
he should especially deeply correct his previous faults.
If he again engages in fratricide,
then which of the Khagan's trusted ministers would dare to consider themselves safe!
We strive to show equal care,
and have already accepted his surrender.
This refers to accepting Wàméisī's surrender.
For the court, this avoids compromising trust and righteousness.
Would this not achieve a mutually beneficial outcome,
deeply aligning with a wise plan!"
10 Wàméisī came to the court.
In the sixth month, on the Jiǎshēn day,
the forces under Wàméisī were organized into the Guīyì Army,
with Wàméisī appointed as General of the Left Imperial Guard
and made Army Commissioner.
11 The Vice Director of the Chancellery and Concurrent Chief Minister, Chén Yíxíng, was dismissed and made Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
the Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs, Lǐ Ràngyí, was appointed as Vice Director of the Secretariat and Concurrent Chief Minister.
12 Tián Mǎnchuān of Lánzhōu occupied the prefectural city and rebelled,
but Liú Miǎn suppressed and executed him.
13 Wàméisī requested to establish his household in Tàiyuán,
pledging to join his brothers in defending the border with all their strength.
An edict ordered Liú Miǎn to provide care for his family.
The Uyghur Khagan Wūjiè again sent his chancellor to submit a memorial,
requesting troops to assist in restoring his state,
and also requesting the Tiāndé Fortress.
An edict refused these requests.
Initially,
the Khagan traveled between Tiāndé and Zhènwǔ,
plundering the Qiāng and Hún tribes,
and also stationed north of Pátóu Fēng.
Sòng Bái said: Pátóu Fēng is in Shuòchuān.
An order was issued for him to return south of the desert,
but the Khagan did not comply with the decree.
Lǐ Déyù believed that
"Nàxiéchuò is stationed north of the mountains,
and Wūjiè fears that he might conspire with the Xī and Qìdān to intercept him,
so he dares not venture far from the frontier.
It is hoped that Zhāng Zhòngwǔ will be ordered to instruct the Xī and Qìdān to join forces with the Huíhú to eliminate Nàxiéchuò,
so that he can return north."
After Nàxiéchuò died,
the Khagan still did not leave.
Some officials believed that the Huíhú were waiting for payment for their horses;
an edict was issued to fully compensate them for the horses,
yet they still did not leave.
In August,
the Khagan led his troops south of Pátóu Fēng,
suddenly entered Dàtóng Chuān,
drove away tens of thousands of cattle and horses from the various tribes in Hédōng,
and fought their way to the gates of Yúnzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Yúnzhōu,
the ancient territory of Píngchéng,
is three hundred li north of the Great Wall, which marks the border with the foreign tribes.
Today, Dàtóng Fǔ of the Great Yuán administers Dàtóng County,
overseeing the two counties of Yúnzhōng and Báidēng;
there is also Yúnnèi Zhōu,
overseeing the two counties of Róufú and Mánchuān.
The Tǔyùhún and Dǎngxiàng tribes all fled into the mountains with their families to avoid them.
On Gēngwǔ,
an edict was issued to dispatch troops from Chén, Xǔ, Xú, Rǔ, Xiāngyáng, and other regions to station in Tàiyuán, Zhènwǔ, and Tiāndé,
waiting until the following spring to drive out the Huíhú.
Examination of discrepancies: The Veritable Records state:
"In June,
the Huíhú invaded Yúnzhōu,
and Liú Miǎn led troops from Tàiyuán to defend against them."
It also states:
"Liú Miǎn went to rescue Yúnzhōu,
but was defeated by the Huíhú."
In July, it further states:
"Wūjiè passed through Tiāndé,
reached Pátóu Fēng,
suddenly entered Dàtóng Chuān,
drove away tens of thousands of cattle and horses from the Tàiyuán tribes,
and fought their way to Yúnzhōu."
The New Annals state:
"In January,
the Huíhú invaded Héngshuǐ Zhà,
plundered Tiāndé and Zhènwǔ Jūn.
In March,
the Huíhú invaded Yún and Shuò.
In June,
Liú Miǎn fought the Huíhú at Yúnzhōu,
and was defeated."
According to the "Memorial on Huíhú Affairs" from the Yīpǐn Collection:
"We have heard from Yáng Guān that
because many of the Huíhú Chìxīn's troops are scattered north of the mountains,
the Khagan fears they might join forces with the Xī, Qìdān, and Shìwéi to intercept him,
so he dares not venture far away.
Now, by issuing an edict to Zhòngwǔ,
he is instructed to convey the court's intentions.
Since the Huíhú have previously shown loyalty and service,
and are now in a state of ruin,
having submitted to the state,
the court must show compassion and care.
Now, if the Xī and Qìdān join forces with them,
to eliminate the scattered troops of Chìxīn,
the Khagan can gradually move out of the Hàn border,
avoiding further delays."
Although this memorial lacks a date,
it likely occurred after Yáng Guān returned from the Huíhú, after Chìxīn's death, and before Nàxiéchuò's defeat.
Another letter to the Khagan states:
"Recently, several envoys returned,
all saying that the Khagan was only waiting for payment for the horses.
But when arrangements were made for the payment,
it was heard that his location had changed repeatedly."
This indicates that the Khagan was demanding payment for the horses,
and the court had fully compensated him.
Another memorial dated July 19 states:
"We hope to send a letter to the Khagan: 'We have received Wòméisī's memorial,
stating that while in his own country, each had their allotted horses,
and the silk payment for the horses should be deducted,
to be used as tribute.
Since the Khagan's country is in ruins,
and he has long been on the frontier,
we have already generously compensated Wòméisī,
and the silk payment for the horses allotted to Wòméisī and below,
will be given to the Khagan.'"
Thus, the payment for the horses must have been made before July 19.
At that time,
the Huíhú had certainly not invaded Yúnzhōu,
defeated Liú Miǎn,
suddenly entered Dàtóu Chuān,
or plundered Tàiyuán's cattle and horses.
Therefore, the court reluctantly complied with his demands,
hoping he would leave the frontier early and return north,
and had not yet considered launching an attack.
The Veritable Records also state:
"In August,
on the first day, Rénxū,
Lǐ Déyù memorialized requesting to send Shí Xióng to raid the camp and capture the princess,
and seize the Khagan.
On Wùchén,
he again memorialized to halt the raid for the time being.
On Xīnwèi,
an edict was issued to dispatch troops from Chén, Xǔ, Xú, Rǔ, Xiāngyáng, and other regions to station in Tàiyuán, Zhènwǔ, and Tiāndé for reinforcement."
According to the Yīpǐn Collection,
Lǐ Déyù's memorial on attacking the Huíhú states:
"I have repeatedly received imperial decrees,
as the Huíhú are gradually approaching Pátóu Fēng,
an early attack is necessary.
I have heard that the barbarians do not understand siege warfare,
and only know how to charge on horseback.
I estimate they have no scouts or ambushes,
nor do they know how to raid camps.
If Shí Xióng leads the Yìwǔ cavalry along with the Tuìhún cavalry,
selects elite infantry as support,
and launches a surprise night attack with gagged soldiers,
success will surely be easy."
This memorial lacks a date.
The Veritable Records, based on the memorial of the 7th, state,
"Regarding the plan for Shí Xióng to raid the camp discussed on the 1st of this month,
we hope to halt it for now,"
so it was recorded on the first day.
At that time, it was still said that they were gradually approaching Pátóu Fēng,
meaning it was not yet known that they had crossed south of Pátóu Fēng.
Another memorial on Huíhú affairs dated August 7 states:
"Since the Huíhú arrived north of Pátóu Fēng,
several weeks have passed,
with no reports,
and no further invasions.
Observing their situation,
it is no different from when they were at the borders of Tiāndé and Zhènwǔ.
Regarding the plan for Shí Xióng to raid the camp discussed on the 1st of this month,
we hope to halt it for now,
and further assess the situation."
Based on the intent of this memorial,
it is clear that they were unaware the Khagan had deeply invaded and attacked Yúnzhōu.
Another memorial dated August 10 requesting the dispatch of troops from Chén, Xǔ, and other regions states:
"We have already reported to the emperor in the Yányīng Hall yesterday,
requesting to reinforce the defenses of Tàiyuán, Zhènwǔ, and Tiāndé,
and to further mobilize troops from Chén, Xǔ, Xú, Rǔ, Xiāngyáng, and other regions.
By the time the river freezes,
we deeply fear the Khagan might suddenly cross the river,
and even ally with the Tǔbō,
which would cause no small trouble,
and requires careful preparation.
The mobilization of troops from various regions must not be halted,
and they must arrive at their destinations
before the river freezes."
Thus, the Huíhú's sudden entry into Dàtóng Chuān and attack on Yúnzhōu must have occurred at the beginning of August.
On the 1st and 7th, it was still unknown,
and the report only arrived on the 9th,
hence the decision to dispatch troops for defense and expulsion.
The Veritable Records and the New Annals are both incorrect.
Now, we follow the Old Annals.
On Dīngchǒu,
Wòméisī and his brothers Ālìzhī, Xíwùchuò, and Wūluósī were all granted the surname Lǐ,
with the given names Sīzhōng, Sīzhēn, Sīyì, and Sīlǐ.
Wòméisī was named Sīzhōng,
Ālìzhī was named Sīzhēn,
Xíwùchuò was named Sīyì,
and Wūluósī was named Sīlǐ.
Examination of discrepancies: The Old Annals state:
"In June,
Wòméisī and others arrived in the capital,
and an edict was issued appointing Wòméisī as commander of the Guīyì Jūn,
granting him the surname Lǐ and the given name Sīzhōng.
The Huíhú chancellor Shòuxiéwù was appointed deputy commander of the Guīyì Jūn,
and granted the surname Lǐ and the given name Hóngshùn."
The Old Huíhú Biography states:
"In the winter of the second year,
and the spring of the third year,
seven Huíhú tribes totaling thirty thousand people surrendered to Yōuzhōu one after another,
and were assigned to various regions.
Wòméisī, Shòuxiéwù, and other tribes surrendered to Zhènwǔ,
and were all granted the surname Lǐ,
with the given names Sīzhōng, Sīzhēn, and Sīyì."
Now, we follow the Veritable Records.
The given name is Hóngshùn;
and Hóngshùn was still appointed deputy commander of the Guīyì Jūn.
The emperor dispatched the Uighur Shí Jièzhí to return to his country,
bestowing a letter upon the khan,
*Kǎoyì* states: The old annals place this edict under the entry for Liú Miǎn and Zhāng Zhòngwǔ being appointed as campaign commanders.
According to the *Yīpǐn Jí* memorial of the 18th day of the eighth month:
"In the past two days, we have privately heard external discussions saying that
Shí Jièzhí has long been in the capital city,
and no matter how great or small the affairs,
there is nothing he is not thoroughly familiar with.
Recently, because he was taken into the Court of State Ceremonial,
fearing the court's handling,
he thus sought a diplomatic mission,
his intention being to escape."
It also says:
"Shí Jièzhí previously had two sons who fled,
they must have already entered Uighur territory,
we estimate that on this journey, how could he be willing to exert his utmost effort!
We humbly hope for a swift edict to Liú Miǎn,
to intercept and turn him back wherever he is."
However, dispatching Shí Jièzhí to bestow the letter upon the khan must have been before this memorial,
it is unknown whether he was indeed intercepted and turned back later.
"Since your country was defeated by the Qìgēsī,
and you came to rely on our border regions,
our reception and acceptance of you has been all-encompassing.
Now the khan still remains near these frontier passes,
with no discussion of returning to your homeland,
sometimes invading and plundering Yún, Shuò, and other prefectures,
sometimes raiding and attacking the Qiāng, Hún, and various tribes.
From afar we surmise your deep intention,
it seems you rely on the feelings of marital alliance;
believing that by holding the Grand Princess Tàihé hostage, you can coerce the Central Kingdom.
Surmise,
*chū wěi fān*.
Alliance,
*hū dào fān*.
In truth, you harbor plans for swift raids.
The generals and ministers, both within and without, all request your extermination,
but Our feelings are deeply inclined to humble Ourself,
and We cannot bear to take advantage of your calamity.
The khan should swiftly choose a proper course,
lest you incur later regret!"
The emperor also ordered Lǐ Déyù to draft a reply on behalf of Liú Miǎn to the Uighur minister Jiégàn Jiāsī,
stating:
"The Uighurs have come from afar to rely on and submit,
they should emulate Hūhányé by sending a son to serve as attendant,
and personally come to court themselves.
The affair of Hūhányé is seen in the annals of Emperor Xuān of Hàn.
Pleading pitifully and begging for mercy,
then Our relief and compassion,
would leave nothing to be ashamed of in Our heart.
This means there would be nothing to be ashamed of in the heart.
Acting arrogantly and willfully as before,
making excessive demands beyond expectation,
as if still in your own homeland,
and moreover deeply penetrating the border regions,
incessantly invading and ravaging,
seeking aid and continuing friendly relations—
how could it be appropriate to act like this!
Your letter also says the Hu people are easily agitated and difficult to pacify,
if they are caused to become angry,
they cannot be controlled again.
The Uighurs were defeated by the Qìgēsī,
the bones of your entire country's generals and ministers were abandoned in the wilderness,
the tombs of successive generations of khans,
lie separated at the ends of the earth,
the Uighurs' angry hearts,
do not vent upon them,
Them,
meaning the Qìgēsī.
Yet you give free rein to your ambitions against the Central Kingdom,
how could Heaven, Earth, and the deities tolerate this!
In the past, Zhìzhī did not serve the Great Hàn,
and ultimately brought about his own destruction,
the affair is seen in the annals of Emperor Xuān and Emperor Yuán of Hàn.
Can you not bear this in mind!"
On the *wùzǐ* day,
Lǐ Déyù and others submitted a memorial stating,
"If according to the previous edict,
the three circuits of Hédōng and others strictly garrison and prepare defenses,
The three circuits are Hédōng, Lúlóng, and Zhènwǔ.
Taking advantage of the time when the Uighur people are exhausted and horses emaciated,
and also the government troops avoid the hardship of severe cold,
then the Yōuzhōu troops should be ordered to halt and garrison within their own circuit to await the imperial command.
If concerned that once the river ice solidifies,
the Uighurs will again have the means for swift raids,
and they must be driven out early,
then we should take advantage while the weather is not yet cold,
and decide on a strategy within a few
months.
Using Hébīng troops to reinforce the Hédōng troops,
we can certainly ensure success is achieved within two months.
Now we hear external discussions are numerous and confused,
with differing opinions among them,
if we do not uniformly inquire about the actual situation,
we will ultimately be misled by empty words.
We hope to order the dukes and ministers to assemble for deliberation!"
An edict followed this.
At the time, most deliberators believed it appropriate to wait until the coming spring.
In the ninth month,
Liú Miǎn was appointed concurrent Commissioner for Pacifying the Uighurs,
if it became necessary to drive them out,
the various expeditionary armies' troops were to be placed under his command;
Zhāng Zhòngwǔ was appointed Eastern Commissioner for Pacifying the Uighurs,
the expeditionary troops of his own circuit and the Xī, Qìdān, Shìwéi, etc., were all to be under his own command.
Lǐ Sīzhōng was appointed Dūjiàng of the Héxī Dǎngxiàng and Southwest Commissioner for Campaigning Against the Uighurs;
This Héxī,
refers to west of the Northern River.
Liú Miǎn was ordered to garrison Yànmén Pass.
Yànmén Pass is in Yànmén County of Dàizhōu,
which is Xínglíng Pass.
Earlier,
the Xī and Qìdān were loosely attached to the Uighurs,
each had supervising envoys,
who annually oversaw their tribute and taxes,
and also spied on Táng affairs.
Zhāng Zhòngwǔ dispatched his staff officer Shí Gōngxù to control the two tribes,
and they killed over 800 people including the Uighur supervising envoys.
Zhāng Zhòngwǔ defeated Nàjiéchuò,
and captured the wives and children of the Shìwéi chieftain.
The Shìwéi offered gold, silk, sheep, and horses to ransom them,
but Zhāng Zhòngwǔ did not accept,
saying:
"Only if you kill
the supervising envoys will I return them!"
On the *guǐmǎo* day,
Lǐ Déyù and others memorialized:
"The Hédōng reporting official Sūn Chóu has just arrived,
saying the Uighurs have moved their camp forty *lǐ* closer south.
Liú Miǎn believes this must be because the Qìdān are not acting in concert with them,
and they fear being attacked by surprise.
Based on this situation,
it is precisely the time to drive them out.
We asked Sūn Chóu,
if joining forces with Yōuzhōu,
to press and drive out the Uighurs,
how many more troops would be needed.
Chóu said not many more troops are needed,
only the Dàtóng troops are few,
getting a thousand men from Yìdìng to assist would suffice."
The emperor followed all of this.
An edict ordered Hédōng, Yōuzhōu, Zhènwǔ, and Tiāndé each to dispatch large armies,
move their camps slightly forward,
to press the Uighurs.
14 The emperor, hearing of the reputation of the Crown Prince's Junior Tutor Bái Jūyì,
wished to make him chancellor,
and asked Lǐ Déyù about it.
Lǐ Déyù had always disliked Bái Jūyì,
so he said Bái Jūyì was frail and ill,
and unable to endure court audiences.
His paternal cousin, Left Department Vice Director Bái Mǐnzhōng,
his literary talent is not inferior to Bái Jūyì's,
and moreover he has capacity and discernment.
On the *jiǎchén* day,
Bái Mǐnzhōng was appointed Hanlin Academician.
This sets the stage for Mǐnzhōng later opposing Déyù.
15 Lǐ Sīzhōng requested to join forces with six thousand cavalry of the Qìbì, Shātuó, and Tǔyùhún to attack the Uighurs.
On the *yǐsì* day,
Yínzhōu Prefect Hé Qīngcháo and Yùzhōu Prefect Qìbì Tōng were ordered to separately lead the Hédōng tribal troops to Zhènwǔ,
to receive command under Lǐ Sīzhōng.
Tōng,
is the fifth-generation descendant of Hé Lì.
The Qìbì tribal tents,
during the Tàihé period attached themselves to Zhènwǔ;
Qìbì Hé Lì,
came to court during Tàizōng's time,
and subsequently remained in the imperial guard.
Yù,
*yū wù fān*.
Qì,
*qī qì fān*.
16 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the *dīngmǎo* day,
the emperor's son Xiàn was established as Prince of Yì,
and Qí as Prince of Yǎn.
Upon reaching Wèizhōu,
he encountered the State Minister Shàng Sīluó, who was stationed at Bóhán Mountain.
Kǒngrè attacked him,
and Sīluó abandoned his baggage and fled westward to Sōngzhōu.
Wáng Yá said: From Lóngzhōu Qīngchuān Town, entering the Tǔbō border, one goes straight to the old city of Sōngzhōu,
which was where Tǔbō had previously established a military governorship.
Sīluó mobilized troops from Sūpí, Tǔyùhún, Yángtóng, and others,
totaling eighty thousand,
to defend the Táo River,
burning the bridges to block the enemy.
When Kǒngrè arrived,
he spoke across the water to the Sūpí and others, saying:
"Traitorous ministers have thrown the state into chaos,
and Heaven has sent me to punish them.
Why are you aiding the rebels?
I am now the Prime Minister,
and I command all the troops in the country.
If you do not submit,
I will annihilate your tribes!"
The Sūpí and others hesitated and did not fight.
Kǒngrè then led his elite cavalry across the river,
and the Sūpí and others all surrendered.
Sīluó fled westward,
was pursued and captured,
and killed.
Kǒngrè absorbed all his troops,
totaling over one hundred thousand.
From Wèichuān
to Sōngzhōu,
wherever he passed, he wrought devastation,
with corpses piled upon one another.

Compiled by Sīmǎ Guāng
