Later Scholar from Tiāntāi
The third year of Huìchāng
(Guǐhài, 843)
1 Spring,
First Month,
the Uyghur Khagan Wūjiè led his forces to invade and press upon Zhènwǔ.

Liú Miǎn dispatched Shí Xióng, the Prefect of Línzhōu, and Wáng Féng, the Commander-in-Chief of the Army, leading the three tribes of the Shatuo Zhūyé Chìxīn, as well as three thousand cavalry from Qìbì and Tuòbá, to attack his headquarters.
Tuòbá
refers to the Dǎngxiàng tribes.
Shuài,
pronounced as shuài.
Qì,
pronounced as qī.
Textual analysis notes: The Old History of the Uyghurs says Shí Xióng was the Prefect of Fēngzhōu.
The Annals of the Later Táng Xiànzǔ says Shí Xióng was the Prefect of Shízhōu.
At that time, Tián Móu was the Prefect of Fēngzhōu.
Here, the Veritable Records are followed.
Shí Xióng arrived at Zhènwǔ,
climbed the city wall to observe the size of the Uyghur forces,
and saw several dozen felt-covered carts,
felt-covered carts,
meaning carts covered with felt as a canopy.
Shèng,
pronounced as shèng.
resembling those of the Chinese;
he sent spies to inquire,
and they said:
"That is the Princess's tent."
Shí Xióng sent spies to inform her:
"Princess, you have come here,
this is your home,
you should seek a way to return!
We are about to send troops to attack the Khagan.
Please stay hidden with your attendants,
and keep your cart still!"
Shí Xióng then dug more than ten tunnels through the city wall,
led his troops out at night,
and directly attacked the Khagan's headquarters.
When they reached his tent,
the enemy finally noticed them.
The Khagan was greatly alarmed,
not knowing what to do,
abandoned his baggage and fled,
and Shí Xióng pursued him.
On Gēngzǐ,
he heavily defeated the Uyghurs at Shāhú Mountain,
Shāhú Mountain is also known as Hēi Mountain.
The Khagan fled with several hundred cavalry,
and Shí Xióng welcomed Princess Tàihé back.
Textual analysis notes: The Old Biography of Shí Xióng says:
"In the third year,
the Uyghurs extensively raided Yún and Shuò.
Liú Miǎn stationed the Tàiyuán troops at Yúnzhōu.
Miǎn said to Xióng: 'The state, because of the Princess, does not wish to attack hastily.
We are defending the border,
and as long as we can eliminate the threat,
we may act on our own authority.'
Xióng accepted the instruction,
personally selected elite cavalry,
gathered the Shatuo tribes,
along with Qìbì, Tuòbá, and other mixed tribes,
set out from Mǎyì at night,
and headed straight for Wūjiè's headquarters.
At that time, the enemy tents were close to Zhènwǔ.
After Xióng entered the city,
he climbed the battlements to observe the enemy's numbers,
saw several dozen felt-covered carts, etc.
Then he welcomed the Princess back to Tàiyuán."
The Biography of the Uyghurs:
"Wūjiè set up camp eighty li from Yōuzhōu.
That night,
Liú Miǎn of Hédōng suddenly arrived with troops.
Wūjiè fled in panic,
heading northeast to camp near Héjiě Shìwéi,
and did not have time to take Princess Tàihé with him.
Shí Xióng's troops encountered the Princess's tent,
and thus welcomed her back to the state."
The Annals of the Later Táng Xiànzǔ says:
"Miǎn recommended the Emperor as the vanguard.
The Uyghur Khagan set up his headquarters at Shāhú Mountain.
The Emperor and Shí Xióng advanced silently at night,
surrounded his headquarters,
and Khagan Wūjiè fled lightly equipped on horseback.
The Emperor paid his respects to Princess Tàihé at the headquarters,
and escorted her back to the state."
According to the Yīpǐn Collection,
in a memorial dated the seventeenth day of the tenth month of the second year of Huìchāng:
"It is heard that Liú Miǎn is quite experienced in border affairs,
but when it comes to making decisions on the spot,
he tends to hesitate.
I fear that excessive caution
may gradually cause him to miss opportunities.
I hope to issue an edict to Liú Miǎn: 'Previously, because the Uyghurs had not yet invaded or harassed,
we focused on pacification and appeasement.
Now that they have killed our border people,
driven off our cattle and horses,
repeated edicts have been issued to quickly expel them.
You should assess the situation yourself,
respond flexibly to circumstances,
and not be overly hesitant,
always waiting for instructions from the court.
Since you have been given the authority,
and appointed to command the various armies,
border affairs are all entrusted to you.
Henceforth, if you need to move camps or advance troops,
you may act entirely at your own discretion,
and need not always await orders!'"
The Veritable Records: On Wùyín,
an edict was issued to Liú Miǎn as mentioned above.
Based on Déyù's memorial,
how could Miǎn dare not await the imperial edict
and hastily send Shí Xióng to attack the Khagan's headquarters,
especially since there was already an edict not requiring prior reporting?
The Old Biography of Déyù:
"Déyù said: 'North of Bàtóu Beacon is the desert.
Fighting in the open there requires cavalry.
If we use infantry against them,
it is logically difficult to ensure victory.
Now, what Wūjiè relies on is the Princess.
If we send brave generals with cavalry
to seize the Princess,
the enemy will collapse on their own.'
The Emperor agreed,
and immediately ordered Déyù to draft an edict for action."
The Record of Suppressing Rebels says:
"The Emperor asked about plans for a surprise attack.
Déyù memorialized: 'If we use infantry to engage the Uyghurs in open battle,
there is certainly no chance of victory.
The Uyghurs often keep the Princess with them as a hostage.
I have thought of a plan.
I reckon the Uyghurs are unaware of a night raid.
Shí Xióng is brave and unmatched.
If he is ordered to select elite troops from the Fān, Hún, and Hàn,
advance silently at night,
he will surely capture the Princess,
and the Khagan can also be captured.'
The Emperor agreed.
Then he ordered Shí Xióng to lead Fān, Hún, and Hàn troops to advance at night.
The Uyghurs indeed had no patrols or ambushes,
and only realized when the troops reached their tents.
Thus, the Princess was captured,
and only the Khagan fled lightly equipped on horseback."
However, Déyù later requested to take charge of the night raid himself,
but Shí Xióng saw the Princess's tent from the city wall and welcomed her back,
not because of Déyù's strategy.
This is not adopted here.
More than twenty thousand of their tribesmen surrendered.
On Bǐngwǔ,
Liú Miǎn's victory report arrived.
Lǐ Sīzhōng came to court.
Being a surrendered Uyghur general himself,
he feared suspicion from border generals,
and requested that he, his younger brother Sīzhēn, and others, as well as Ài Hóngshùn, all return to the capital.
On Gēngxū,
Shí Xióng was appointed as the Regional Defense Commissioner of Fēngzhōu.
This was a reward for his victory over the Uyghurs.
The Khagan Wūjiè fled and took refuge among the Hēichēzi tribe.
Hú Qiáo said: North of Xiájiá are the Shànyú Tūjué,
and further north are the Hēichēzi.
They are skilled at making carts and tents.
Their people understand filial piety and righteousness.
Their land is poor and produces nothing.
Upon detailed examination of the Old and New Histories,
the Hēichēzi are one type of Shìwéi.
According to the edict conferring titles upon Xiájiásī at that time,
the Hēichēzi were over a thousand *li* from the Han border.
*Kǎoyì* states: The Old History's *Huíhé Biography* says:
"Wūjiè fled in alarm to the northeast, about four hundred *li* away,
and camped under the protection of Héjiě Shìwéi.
He married his younger sister to the Shìwéi,
and attached himself to them."
Now we follow the *Fápàn Jì*, the *Shílù*, and the New History's biography.
The Old History's *Zhāng Zhòngwǔ Biography* also says:
"After Wūjiè was defeated,
he then relied on Kāngjū to seek survival,
moving all his remaining people to entrust themselves to the Hēichēzi."
This is probably based on Lǐ Déyù's *Jìshènggōng Bēi*, which says:
"Wūjiè, together with Dīnglíng, sought peace,
relied on Kāngjū to seek survival,
moved all his remaining people,
and submitted his will to the Hēichēzi."
The term "Kāngjū" used there
is an allusion to the story of Zhìzhī;
this led to the error.
2 In the second month,
on the first day, Gēngshēn,
there was a solar eclipse.
3 An edict was issued to disband the Guīyì Army,
(the establishment of the Guīyì Army is mentioned in the previous year's section of the previous volume).
Generous provisions of grain and rewards were given.
4 On Xīnwèi,
Xiájiásī sent the envoy Zhùwú Hé Suǒ to present two famous horses.
The New History says: Zhùwú
is a barbarian surname.
Hé means fierce,
Suǒ means left,
referring to a warrior fierce and skilled at shooting with the left hand.
"Suǒ"
is written
as "Suǒ".
Sòng Bái said: Suǒ
is pronounced with a rising tone.
On Jiǎxū,
the Emperor summoned him for an audience,
placing his rank above that of the envoy from Bóhǎi.
The Emperor wanted to order Zhào Fān to go to Xiájiásī to request Ānxī and Běitíng.
Lǐ Déyù and others submitted a memorial saying:
"Ānxī is over seven thousand *li* from the capital,
Běitíng over five thousand *li*.
Even if we obtained them,
we would have to re-establish a Protectorate,
and garrison them with ten thousand Táng troops.
It is unclear from where these troops could be recruited and dispatched,
or through which route supplies could be transported.
This would be using real expenses to exchange for an empty name,
and is not a good plan."
*Kǎoyì* states: The biography of Déyù says:
"In the second month of the third year,
Zhào Fān reported that Xiájiásī was attacking the Ānxī and Běitíng Protectorates,
and we should send troops to provide support."
Déyù's memorial's wording is the same as this.
The *Xiàntì Jì* says:
"In the third year,
on the eleventh day of the second month,
at the Yányīng Hall,
Déyù memorialized: 'On the ninth day, we received the imperial command,
ordering us to instruct Zhào Fān
to demand Ānxī and Běitíng from Xiájiásī.
We deeply fear this cannot be done,'"
and the following wording is also the same as this.
According to the *Shílù*:
"On Xīnwèi,
Zhùwú Hé Suǒ first arrived,
and Zhào Fān was ordered to host and reward him.
On Bǐngzǐ,
the Secretariat-Chancellery memorialized that on the ninth day they had received the imperial command,"
and the wording is also the same as in the *Xiàntì Jì*.
It is unknown from which book Sòng obtained these dates Xīnwèi and Bǐngzǐ.
For now, we omit the specific day,
and place it after Zhùwú Hé Suǒ's audience to convey the uncertainty.
5 The Vice Director of the Secretariat and Tongpingzhangshi Cuī Gǒng was dismissed and made Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs.
6 Xiájiásī requested investiture.
Lǐ Déyù memorialized,
saying it was appropriate to establish friendly relations with them,
and order them to lead troops themselves to seek out and punish the criminals who killed the envoy.
(Xiájiásī had sent an envoy to escort the Princess Tàihé,
who was killed by the Huíhé;
the event is recorded in the previous year's section of the previous volume.)
The Emperor feared that if he granted them the title of Khagan, they would not observe the rituals of a subject,
and would follow the precedent of the Huíhé in requesting annual gifts and horse trading,
and so he hesitated and could not decide.
Déyù memorialized:
"Xiájiásī has already proclaimed itself Khagan.
Now, if we wish to make use of their strength,
I fear we cannot begrudge them this title.
The Huíhé had merit in pacifying Ān and Shǐ,
so they were annually granted twenty thousand bolts of silk,
and also allowed to trade.
Xiájiásī has not yet rendered any service to China,
how would they dare to suddenly seek bribes and gifts!
If we are concerned about their not being submissive,
we should make an agreement with them,
stipulating that they must, like the Huíhé, declare themselves subjects,
before we perform the investiture;
we should also mention the shared surname to draw them closer,
making them observe the rituals of descendants."
The Emperor followed this advice.
7 On Gēngyín,
the Princess Tàihé arrived at the capital,
and was redesignated as the Princess Āndìng Dàzhǎng.
(The Princess Tàihé was married to the Huíhé in the first year of Chángqìng,
and only now returned.)
"Āndìng"
is written in the New History as
"Dìng'ān".
Zhǎng
is pronounced zhī zhàng fān.
The princess went to the Guāngshùn Gate,
removed her ceremonial attire,
took off her hairpins and earrings,
and apologized for the Huíhé's ingratitude and for her failure in the peace marriage.
Táng princesses who married into foreign tribes were called
"peace marriage princesses".
Now the Princess Tàihé, because the Huíhé had invaded the border,
thus apologized for her failure in the peace marriage.
Qù
is pronounced qiǎng lǚ fān.
Afterwards, she entered the palace.
The six
princesses, including Yáng'ān, did not come to console the Princess Āndìng,
and each was fined a portion of their stipend goods and silk from their estates.
(The Princess Yáng'ān
was a daughter of Emperor Shùnzōng.)
Sòng Bái said: Those who did not come were the six [seven] princesses: Yáng'ān, Xuānchéng, Zhēnníng, Yìníng, Línzhēn, Zhēnyuán, and Yìchāng.
8 The Military Commissioner of Wèibó, Hé Chóngshùn, was granted the name Hóngjìng.
9 In the third month,
the Grand Coachman Zhao Fan was appointed as the Pacification Commissioner to the Qìjiásī.
The Emperor ordered Lǐ Déyù to draft a letter to be bestowed upon the Qìjiásī Khagan,
instructing him that
"In the twenty-first year of the Zhēnguàn era, the former lord of the Qìjiásī personally came to court.
'Twenty-first year'
should be
'twenty-second year'.
Up until the Tiānbǎo era,
tribute was continuously offered.
Recently, they were cut off by the Huíhú,
who oppressed and mistreated the various tribes.
The Khagan was able to avenge grievances and wipe away resentments,
his magnificent achievements and heroic integrity
are unmatched in recent times.
Now, the remaining Huíhú soldiers number less than a thousand,
scattered and hiding in the mountains and valleys.
Since the Khagan has already become their enemy,
he must completely annihilate them;
if any remnants are left,
they will surely cause future troubles.
It is also heard that the origin of the Khagan's clan name
is the same as ours.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: The Son of Heaven bestows surnames and clan names;
feudal lords may only be bestowed clan names,
not surnames,
as they are inferior to the Son of Heaven.
Therefore, in the eighth year of Duke Yǐn in the Zuǒ Zhuàn, it is said: When Wúhài died,
the Duke asked Zhòng Zhòng about the clan.
Zhòng Zhòng replied:
'The Son of Heaven establishes virtue,
and based on birth bestows a surname,
grants land and assigns a clan name.
Feudal lords use their posthumous names as clan names,
and thus form clans.
If an office has hereditary merit,
then there is an official clan;
the same applies to fiefs.'
From this, it can be said
that the Son of Heaven bestows a surname based on the ancestry of the feudal lords.
Dù Yù's annotation states: For example, Shùn was born in Guīruì,
and was bestowed the surname Guī;
Shùn's descendants were enfeoffed in Chén,
and the land of their enfeoffment was used to assign their clan name.
Thus, Shùn's descendants had the surname Guī and the clan name Chén.
Therefore, Zhèng Xuán refuted the different interpretations, saying: Emperor Yán's surname was Jiāng,
bestowed by Tàihào.
Emperor Huáng's surname was Jī,
bestowed by Emperor Yán.
Thus, Yáo bestowed Bóyí with the surname Jiāng,
bestowed Yǔ with the surname Sì,
bestowed Qì with the surname Zǐ,
bestowed Jì with the surname Jī,
as recorded in the classics and commentaries.
According to Zhèng's words,
this is the Son of Heaven bestowing surnames.
Feudal lords bestow clan names upon their ministers and officials.
If they are of the same surname,
the son of a duke is called Gōngzǐ,
the son of a Gōngzǐ is called Gōngsūn,
and the descendants of Gōngsūn are already distant in kinship,
unable to directly connect to the duke,
so they use their grandfather's courtesy name as their clan name.
If they are sons of the principal wife,
then they use the courtesy names of the fifty characters Bó, Zhòng as clan names,
such as Zhòngsūn and Jìsūn of Lǔ.
If they are sons of concubines or secondary wives,
then they use the twenty characters as clan names,
such as Zāngshì and Zhǎnshì.
If they are of a different surname,
then they use their father's or grandfather's official title or the fief they received as their clan name: those using official titles as clan names,
are like Sīmǎ, Sīchéng;
those using fiefs as clan names,
are like Hán, Zhào, Wèi.
In general, bestowing clan names
is done when one becomes a minister,
and those with great merit are bestowed a clan during their lifetime,
such as Shūsūn Décén.
Even if they are Gōngzǐ themselves,
if they have great merit and virtue,
then their courtesy name as Gōngzǐ is bestowed as their clan name,
such as Xiāng Zhòng Suì.
If they have no merit or virtue,
their clan name is bestowed after death,
such as Wúhài.
If descendants become ministers,
and their ruler does not bestow a clan name,
they use their grandfather's courtesy name as their clan name.
Clan names and lineages,
when contrasted, are distinct,
but in general usage, they are interchangeable.
Therefore, in the Zuǒ Zhuàn, when asking Zhòng Zhòng about the clan, it is said below,
'The Duke ordered to use the courtesy name as the Zhǎn clan'
is an example.
Surnames and clan names are also interchangeable in general usage,
hence in the Spring and Autumn Annals, there are Jiāngshì, Zǐshì,
where Jiāng and Zǐ are surnames but referred to as clans.
The Khagan is a descendant of the Commandant.
The Grand Administrator of Běipíng,
refers to Lǐ Guǎng.
Commandant,
refers to Lǐ Líng.
Their status of high and low can be understood.
Now, we intend to confer a patent of appointment upon the Khagan,
specially adding an honorable title,
but as we do not yet know the Khagan's intentions,
we are first sending this to convey our regards.
Once Zhào Fān returns,
we will separately appoint an envoy to perform the ceremony."
From the time the Huíhú arrived at the frontier and the Qìjiásī offered tribute,
whenever there were imperial edicts,
the Emperor often ordered Lǐ Déyù to draft them.
Lǐ Déyù requested to delegate this to the Hanlin Academicians,
but the Emperor said:
"The Academicians cannot fully capture my intentions,
you must do it yourself."
10 Liú Miǎn reported:
"More than three thousand Huíhú soldiers of the Guīyì Army and forty-three chieftains, in accordance with the imperial decree, were to be assigned to various circuits.
They all shouted loudly,
camped together along the Hūtuó River,
and refused to comply with the orders.
They have all been executed.
The Huíhú who surrendered to Yōuzhōu totaled more than thirty thousand people,
and they have all been dispersed and assigned to various circuits."
11 Lǐ Déyù revisited the matter of Xīdámóu of Wéizhōu.
The event is recorded in the 244th volume, in the fifth year of the Tàihé era of Emperor Wénzōng.
"Wéizhōu is situated on a high mountain peak,
facing the river on three sides,
located at a strategic point on the plains of the barbarian tribes,
and is the route for Han troops to enter.
Initially,
when Hézhōu and Lǒngzhōu were both lost,
only this place remained.
The Tǔbō secretly married women to the gatekeepers of this prefecture,
and twenty years later,
when the two sons grew up,
they secretly opened the fortress gate,
leading troops in at night,
and thus it was captured,
and named Wúyōu City.
From then on, they were able to concentrate their forces on the western front,
with no further worries about the southern route.
Concentrating forces on the western front,
refers to the Tǔbō concentrating their forces to attack Qí, Lǒng, Bīn, Jīng, Líng, and Xià.
No worries about the southern route,
refers to Xīchuān being south of the Tǔbō.
From Cháng'ān's perspective,
Xīchuān is also south of Jiànguān.
If the Tǔbō invaded Shǔ,
the southern route would be through Wéi and Mào,
and the northern route through Xīzhōu.
This caused anxiety for several reigns.
During the Zhēnyuán era,
Wéi Gāo wanted to manage Hézhōu and Huángzhōu,
and needed this city as a starting point.
With tens of thousands of troops at full strength,
they attacked fiercely for several years.
Although they captured Lùn Mǎngrè and returned,
the city was strong and ultimately could not be taken.
See the 236th volume, the seventeenth and eighteenth years of the Zhēnyuán era of Emperor Dézōng.
Ultimately,
zú, read as xù.
When I first arrived in Western Shǔ,
I externally promoted the nation's prestige,
and internally secured the border defenses.
The people of Wéizhōu, familiar with my trustworthy commands,
abandoned their walls and came to submit.
I initially accepted their surrender.
The southern barbarians were awed and intimidated,
and the eight states west of the mountains
all wished to become internal dependencies.
The Tǔbō cities of Héshuǐ, Qījī, and others,
as well as the Héjiāng Shǒuzhuō fortress in Yìzhōu,
were originally all Táng territory,
lost to the Tǔbō.
Naturally, they should be reclaimed,
allowing the reduction of garrison troops at eight locations,
and effortlessly recovering over a thousand lǐ of former land.
Moreover, the year before Wéizhōu surrendered,
the Tǔbō were still besieging Lǔzhōu.
Lǔzhōu
was one of the six Hú states in Héqū,
located on the western border of Yòuzhōu.
When I accepted the surrender,
I swore by heaven,
personally promising to report it to the court,
and that each would receive rewards.
Those who at the time did not side with me,
hearing rumors, hastily accused me.
An edict ordered me to arrest and send Xìdámóu and others to be executed by them.
How could I bear to abandon trust and seek ease at the cost of over three hundred lives!
I repeatedly submitted memorials arguing my case,
begging for compassion and leniency.
The reply edict was stern and severe,
ultimately ordering me to send them back.
Their bodies were bound with three types of restraints,
carried on bamboo baskets.
As they were about to set off on the road,
their wrongful cries were mournful.
The officers and officials facing me
could not help but shed tears.
Those escorting them were further ridiculed and mocked by the Tǔbō commanders,
who said, "Since you have already surrendered to them,"
(this refers to the Tǔbō calling China 'them').
Shuaì,
pronounced suǒ lèi fān.
They then executed these surrendered men on the Hàn border,
wantonly committing cruelty,
using this to solidify the wavering;
meaning those barbarians with wavering hearts inclined towards us,
fearing the Tǔbō's brutal slaughter,
would not dare harbor thoughts of rebellion again,
thus using terror and cruelty to firmly control them.
They were impaled on spears and lances.
This severed the path of loyal sincerity,
gratified the feelings of the vicious and cruel,
and since ancient times,
there has never been such a thing.
Although more than a decade has passed,
and the fortune belongs to a thousand years,
(meaning a once-in-a-thousand-years opportunity).
Shǔ,
pronounced zhī yù fān.
They should each be posthumously honored and awarded! "
An edict posthumously awarded Xìdámóu the title of General of the Right Guard.
Your subject Sīmǎ Guāng remarks: Commentators often doubt the decision regarding Wéizhōu's capture or abandonment,
unable to determine the right and wrong between Niú and Lǐ.
I believe that in the past, when Xún Wú besieged Gǔ,

"If someone uses our city to betray,

what do I alone gain from it!

He made the people of Gǔ kill the traitors and repair their defenses.
See the Spring and Autumn Annals, Zuǒzhuàn.
Speaking in terms of benefit,
then Wéizhōu is small but trust is great;
speaking in terms of harm,
then Wéizhōu is a slow concern while Guānzhōng is urgent.
So then, for those planning for the Táng,
which should come first?
Xìdámóu, from the Táng perspective, was turning towards civilization,
but from the Tǔbō perspective, he could not avoid being a traitorous minister.
His execution—what is there to pity!
Moreover, what Lǐ Déyù spoke of was benefit,
while what Lǐ Shēngrú spoke of was righteousness.
Even a commoner who pursues profit and forgets righteousness is ashamed of it,

It is like a neighbor's ox
escaping and entering one's home.
Some advise the elder brother to return it,
others advise the younger brother to seize it.
Those advising return say:
"Seizing it is unrighteous,
and will lead to lawsuits."
Those advising seizure say:
"He once seized our sheep,
why be constrained by righteousness!
An ox is a large animal,
selling it can enrich the family."
From this perspective,
the right and wrong of Niú and Lǐ,
can clearly be seen.
At the beginning of the Yuányòu era,

the fourth month,

13. Earlier,
the Zhāoyì military governor Liú Cóngjiàn had repeatedly submitted memorials speaking of Qiú Shìliáng's crimes,

When the present Emperor ascended the throne,
Liú Cóngjiàn had a horse nine chǐ tall,

The Emperor did not accept it.
According to the Zhōulǐ: Horses over eight chǐ are called lóng (dragons),
over seven chǐ are called lái,
over six chǐ are called mǎ (horses).
A horse nine chǐ tall
was probably rare.
Gāo,
pronounced gǔ bào fān.

He then recruited fugitives,
repaired and completed weapons and armor,

Cóngjiàn monopolized horse pastures and merchant travel,
earning fifty thousand strings of cash annually.
He also sold iron and boiled salt, earning tens of thousands more.
Major merchants were all given nominal military titles,
yá zhí,
meaning positions as officers in the yá (headquarters) troops.
and thereby engaged in trade.
Merchants relied on Cóngjiàn's power,

So he plotted with his advisors Zhāng Gǔ and Chén Yángtíng to emulate the various Héběi military governors,
appointing his younger brother Right Flank Guard General Liú Cóngsù's son Liú Zhěn as the Yánèi Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ (Commander of the Internal Headquarters Troops),

Bīngmǎshǐ (Commander of the Personal Guard Troops),

Gǔ

Cóngjiàn soon died,

Wáng Xié advised Zhěn, saying:

He sent the Yāyá officer Jiāng Yín to petition for a court physician.

Gòngfèngguān
are also eunuchs.
The Emperor consulted with his ministers regarding the matter of Zélù.
Most of the ministers believed:
"The remnants of the Huíhú have not yet been extinguished,

Lǐ Déyù alone said:
"The situation in Zélù is different from that of the three Héshuò provinces.

(The capture of Lú Cóngshǐ is recorded in Volume 238, the third year of the Yuánhé era of Xiànzōng.)

Cóngjiàn was arrogant and difficult to control,

(Examination of discrepancies: According to the old annals, biographies, and the Veritable Records, the words of Déyù all come from the *Record of Campaigning Against Rebels*. The *Record of Campaigning Against Rebels* places this at the time of Liú Cóngjiàn's death in the fourth month. By this point, the intention of the sovereign and minister to suppress the rebellion was already decided. The assembly of officials for discussion and the ministers' further deliberations were merely formalities. Déyù's words should belong to the initial stage of the affair. The Veritable Records placing them here is an error.)

According to the Yīpǐn Jí,
a memorial submitted on the twenty-second day of the second month of the fourth year of Huìchāng stated:
"Because Lǐ Huí and others reported that the envoy of Xiájiásī said,
'This winter, we definitely intend to go to Hēichēzǐ to eliminate the remaining forces of the Uighur Khan,
and earnestly hope for the support of the state's troops.'
When the Xiájiásī envoy returns, an imperial edict has already been bestowed,
permitting Yōuzhōu, Tàiyuán, Zhènwǔ, and Tiāndé to each dispatch troops to strategic routes to intercept."
It also said:
"Also order the various armies of Dàiběi to prepare and arrange in order."
It also said: The troops of Yōuzhōu are extremely numerous,
there is no need to order them to prepare in advance,
wait until early winter, then further send a palace envoy to bestow an edict.
The Xiájiásī envoy came in the second month of the fourth year,
and the terms 'this winter,' 'autumn defense,' and 'early winter' mentioned in Déyù's memorial
all refer to events of the fourth year.
It is unlikely that it was not until the second month of the fifth year that Méng was appointed as the Border Inspection Commissioner.
Méng's mission should have been in the spring or summer of this year,
but the exact month and day are unknown,
so it is attached here.
Also ordered Tiāndé, Zhènwǔ, and Hédōng to train soldiers and sharpen weapons,
to await the attack of Xiájiásī on the Uighurs this autumn,
and to intercept the defeated crowds fleeing southward,
all entrusted to Méng to discuss in detail with the Military Governors and Túanliàn Commissioners and report.
Méng
was the grandson of Yàn.
Liú Yàn died due to slander at the beginning of the Jiànzhōng era.
11 The Taoist priest Zhào Guīzhēn was appointed as Yòujiē Dàomén Jiàoshòu Xiānshēng.
12 Lùn Kǒngrè's general, Jízàng Fēngzàn, disgusted by Kǒngrè's cruelty,
surrendered to Shàng Bìbì.
Kǒngrè dispatched troops to attack Bìbì at Shànzhōu,
and Bìbì divided his troops into five routes to resist him.
Kǒngrè retreated to defend Dōnggǔ,
Jiǔyù Zhì: Dōnggǔ Fort is fifteen lǐ southeast of Hézhōu,
established in the seventh year of Xīníng of the Sòng dynasty.
They cut off his water source.
Kǒngrè led over a hundred cavalry to break through the encirclement and fled to defend Bóhán Mountain,
and the remaining troops all surrendered to Bìbì.
13 In summer,
the fourth month,
Wáng Zǎi attacked Zézhōu.
14 The Emperor was fond of immortals,
and the Taoist priest Zhào Guīzhēn gained favor,
prompting repeated remonstrances from the advising officials.
On the Bǐngzǐ day,
Lǐ Déyù also remonstrated:
"Guīzhēn
was a criminal during the reign of Emperor Jìngzōng,
see the second year of Bǎolì in scroll two hundred and forty-three.
The Emperor said:
"When I have nothing to do in the palace, I talk about the Dao with him to cleanse my烦恼.
As for governmental affairs,
I always ask you all and the secondary audience officials,
even a hundred Guīzhēns could not迷惑 me."
Déyù said:
"Petty men, seeing where advantage lies,
rush toward it,
like moths flying into a flame at night.
I have heard that in the past ten days or so,
at Guīzhēn's door,
carriages and horses have gathered like spokes.
I hope Your Majesty deeply guards against this!"
15 On the Wùyín day,
Zuǒ Púshè Wáng Qǐ was appointed Tóng Píngzhāng Shì,
and assigned as the Military Governor of Shānnán Xīdào.
Qǐ, being a civil official who had never held administrative power,
was directly appointed as an Envoy with the title of Grand Councilor,
a precedent unmatched before,
so he firmly declined;
In the mid-Táng period and after,
a Military Governor with the title Tóng Píngzhāng Shì was called an Envoy with the title of Grand Councilor.
Bǐ,
pronounced pí zhì fān,
means precedent.
"There is no distinction between internal and external for Grand Councilors,
if I have any shortcomings,
you may send a flying memorial to inform me!"
16 Lǐ Déyù considered the number of assistant officials in prefectures and counties too large,
and submitted a memorial requesting the Secretary of the Ministry of Personnel, Liǔ Zhòngyìng, to reduce them.
In the sixth month,
Zhòngyìng reported a reduction of one thousand two hundred and fourteen positions.
Textual analysis note: According to the Xiàntì Jì:
"Reduced by two thousand and two positions."
The New History biography says:
"Abolished over two thousand positions."
The Old History biography of Liǔ Zhòngyìng says:
"Reduced by one thousand two hundred positions,"
now follow this.
He was the son of Gōngchuò.
Liǔ Gōngchuò served under Emperors Xiàn and Mù,
holding positions as Regional Military Governor and Capital Prefect,
with notable achievements and reputation.
17 A eunuch exposed Qiú Shìliáng's past evils,
and several thousand weapons were found in his home.
An edict was issued stripping him of his official titles and ranks,
and confiscating his family property.
In the autumn of the 18th year,
in the seventh month,
on the day Xīnmǎo,
the Emperor discussed with Lǐ Déyù about having Wáng Féng lead troops to station at Yìchéng.
The Emperor said:
"I have heard that Féng enforces military law too strictly.
Is this true?"
Déyù replied:
"I have also questioned him about this.
Féng said: 'When facing naked blades ahead,
if the law is not strict,
who would be willing to advance!'"
The Emperor said:
"His words also have reason.
You should summon him again and caution him!"
Déyù then stated that Liú Zhěn should not be pardoned.
The Emperor said:
"That is certainly so."
Déyù said:
"In the past, when Lǐ Huáiguāng had not yet been pacified,
the capital suffered from locusts and drought,
a peck of rice cost a thousand coins,
and the imperial granary's rice could not supply the Emperor and the six palaces for even a few tens of days.
Emperor Dézōng assembled all the officials
and sent the palace eunuch Mǎ Qīnxù to inquire.
Left Sanqí Chángshì Lǐ Mì took a paulownia leaf, tore it apart,
and handed it to Qīnxù to present.
Dézōng summoned him and asked the reason.
He replied: 'The relationship between Your Majesty and Huáiguāng,
like this leaf, cannot be rejoined!'
From this, Dézōng's resolve was fixed.
After Huáiguāng was defeated,
he was then appointed as chancellor,
and was solely entrusted for several years."
See the Annals of Dézōng.
"He was indeed a remarkable man!"
Lǐ Mì's achievements as chancellor
were outstanding and praiseworthy.
Observing this, it can be believed,
and those Táng people who slandered him were all wrong.
On the 19th, the Emperor heard that courtesans in Yángzhōu were skilled at drinking games,
and ordered the Huáinán military supervisor to select seventeen and present them.
The supervisor requested the military governor Dù Cóng to jointly select,
and moreover wanted to choose beautiful women from good families,
train them, and present them.
Cóng said:
"The supervisor received the order himself;
Cóng dares not participate or hear of it!"
The supervisor repeatedly requested him,
but he did not comply.
The supervisor was angry,
and submitted a memorial detailing the situation.
The Emperor read the memorial and remained silent.
Those around him requested that the military governor also be ordered to jointly select.
The Emperor said:
"Ordering a regional command to select courtesans to enter the palace—
how could this be done by a sage Son of Heaven!
Dù Cóng did not comply with the supervisor's wishes,
he upheld the dignity of a high minister.
He truly has the talent of a chancellor.
I am deeply ashamed!"
He immediately ordered the supervisor to cease the selection.
On the day Jiǎchén,
he appointed Cóng as Tóngpíngzhāngshì.
Textual analysis says: The New Tables
record Cóng's appointment as chancellor in the intercalary month on the day Rénxū.
Now we follow the Veritable Records.
When Cóng gave his formal thanks,
after receiving the appointment and entering to give thanks,
it was called "zhōngxiè."
"You did not follow the supervisor's words;
I know you have the heart to serve your sovereign.
Now I make you chancellor,
it is like obtaining a Wèi Zhēng!"
This was how Emperor Wǔzōng placed his hopes in Dù Cóng.
However, during Cóng's tenure as chancellor,
his remonstrances and advice
are not praised in the histories.

Fourth year of Huìchāng
(Jiǎzǐ, 844)
1 Intercalary month,
on the day Rénxū,
he appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng, Tóngpíngzhāngshì Lǐ Shēn as Tóngpíngzhāngshì,
and concurrently Military Governor of Huáinán.
2 Lǐ Déyù memorialized:
"The reporting official Gāo Dí from Zhènzhōu
(regional commands dispatched officers to report matters,
thus called 'reporting officials')
believes that 'the rebels are adept at the tactic of secretly moving troops,
stealthily drawing troops from various places and concentrating them in one location.
Government troops often pursue them closely,
leading to defeat;
after one or two months,
they secretly move the troops to another place.
Government troops must know this situation.
Unless they come to attack our fortifications,
we must be careful not to engage in battle.
Their stay will not exceed three days,
and they must disperse and return to their original stations.
If they return empty-handed several times like this,
their morale will naturally decline.
Government troops should secretly send spies to detect where they are drawing troops from,
and attack the vacated places.
There will be no victory not achieved.'
Secondly,
'Although the stationed troops of Zhèn and Wèi are numerous,
they ultimately cannot divide the rebel forces.
Why?
They encamp without leaving their original positions,
and every two or three months make a deep incursion,
burning and plundering before leaving.
The rebels merely firmly guard their city walls and fortifications;
as for the people outside the city,
the rebels do not cherish them either.
We should order our troops to advance and occupy strategic points,
gradually pressing them.
If we only act as we do today,
the rebels are certainly not afraid.'
I hope to issue an edict to inform all the generals!"
Liú Zhěn's trusted general Gāo Wénduān surrendered.
He said that within the rebel ranks food was scarce,
and they ordered women to rub grain and pound it to supply the army.
Déyù asked Wénduān for strategies to defeat the rebels.
Wénduān believed:
"If government troops now directly attack Zézhōu,
I fear many soldiers will be killed,
and the city will not be easily taken.
Zézhōu has about fifteen thousand troops.
The rebels often divide more than half their forces
to lie hidden in the mountains and valleys.
When they see the government troops exhausted from attacking the city,
they gather from all sides to rescue it,
and the government troops are sure to be defeated.
Now I request that the Chén-Xǔ army cross the Gānhé and establish a camp,
and from the camp city continuously construct a double-walled city,
encircling Zézhōu.
Each day, dispatch a large army to form battle arrays outside to block rescue troops.
When the rebels see the siege about to close,
they are sure to come out for a major battle.
Wait until they are defeated,
then take advantage of the momentum to capture the city."
Déyù memorialized requesting an edict to instruct Wáng Zǎi.
Wénduān also said:
"The Gùzhèn stronghold has cliffs on all four sides, extremely steep,
making it impossible to attack by force.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Wǔ'ān County of Cízhōu has the Gùzhèn town.
West of Wǔ'ān,
it is over three hundred lǐ north to Liáozhōu.
They all drink from stream water,
located about one lǐ east of the stronghold.
We should order Wáng Féng to advance his troops and press them,
cutting off their water supply.
In no more than three days,
the rebels are sure to abandon the stronghold and flee.
The government troops can then pursue closely.
Fifteen lǐ ahead is the Qīnglóng stronghold,
also with cliffs on all four sides, extremely steep.
Water is outside the stronghold,
so it can be taken by the previous method.
Fifteen lǐ east of that is Qìnzhōu city."
Qìnzhōu administered Qìnyuán County,
the location of the Hàn dynasty's Shàngdǎng commandery's Gǔyuǎn County.
Qìn
is pronounced qìnm.
Wénduān also said:
"Dūtóu Wáng Zhāo led ten thousand troops garrisoning Luòzhōu.
After Liú Zhěn exterminated Xuē Màogīng's clan,
he also executed the Xíng-Luò rescue forces commander Tán Cháoyì and his two brothers.
Zhāo from then on was suspicious and fearful.
Zhěn sent an envoy to summon him,
but Zhāo refused to enter.
The soldiers all made an uproar.
Zhāo certainly will not be used by Zhěn.
However, Zhāo and his soldiers' families are all in Lùzhōu,
and the soldiers fear that if they surrender, they will be killed by government troops.
If we summon them, they certainly will not come.
Only by conveying our intent to Zhāo,
having him lead troops into Lùzhōu to capture Zhěn,
and on the day the task is accomplished,
promising to appoint him as military governor of another circuit,
along with generous rewards,
might he be willing to comply."
Déyù memorialized requesting an edict for Hé Hóngjìng to secretly send someone to convey this intent to him.
Liú Zhěn was young and weak-willed.
Yāyá Wáng Xié and the commander of the household troops Lǐ Shìguì held power,
focusing solely on amassing wealth and goods.
The government storehouses were overflowing,
yet when soldiers and officers achieved merit, they received no rewards.
Consequently, people's hearts grew alienated and resentful.
Liú Cóngjiàn's wife, Péi shì,
was a descendant of Péi Miǎn's lineage.
Péi Miǎn served as chancellor during the reigns of Emperor Sùzōng and Emperor Dàizōng.
Her younger brother, Péi Wèn,
commanded troops east of the mountains.
She intended to summon him to take charge of military affairs.
Lǐ Shìguì feared that Péi Wèn's arrival would strip him of his own authority
and expose his treacherous conduct,
so he said:
"The affairs east of the mountains rely entirely on the Fifth Maternal Uncle.
If we summon him,
it would mean losing the three prefectures."
Thus, the plan was halted.
The three prefectures
were Xíng, Míng, and Cí.
Wáng Xié recommended Wáng Zhāo as the Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ of Míng Prefecture.
Wáng Zhāo had won the hearts of the masses,
but often did not comply with the commands of the military headquarters.
His colleagues Gāo Yuánwǔ and Ān Yù claimed he had disloyal intentions.
Liú Zhěn summoned him,
but Wáng Zhāo declined, saying:
"I have not yet achieved even a small merit since arriving in Míng Prefecture,
and I am truly ashamed and regretful.
I beg to remain for a few more months,
and then I will proceed to the headquarters."
This was permitted.
Wáng Xié proposed taxing merchants.
Each prefecture dispatched one military officer to oversee it.
It was called merchant taxation,
but in reality, it registered the assets of registered households.
Registered households
means the registered populace.
Jiàng,
read as liàng.
All assets were assessed in terms of bolts of silk,
with two-tenths taken as tax,
and the assessments were generally inflated.
The people exhausted their movable property and dry provisions to pay,
yet still could not meet the demands,
leaving everyone anxious and uneasy.
Movable property refers to wealth not tied to land,
which can be exchanged to generate profit.
Qiǔ,
read as qiǔ.
Xiōng,
read as xiōng.
The military officer Liú Xī was particularly greedy and cruel.
Liú Cóngjiàn had dismissed him and not employed him.
Liú Xī heavily bribed Wáng Xié.
Since Xíng Prefecture had the most wealthy merchants,
Wáng Xié put Liú Xī in charge there.
The troops commanded by Péi Wèn were called
"Night Flyers."
Many were sons of wealthy merchants.
When Liú Xī arrived,
he detained all their fathers and elder brothers.
The soldiers complained to Péi Wèn.
Péi Wèn made a request on their behalf,
but Liú Xī refused,
replying with disrespectful language.
Péi Wèn grew angry,
secretly conspiring with his subordinates to kill Liú Xī and defect to the imperial court.
He also informed Prefect Cuī Gǔ,
who agreed.
On Bǐngzǐ,
Cuī Gǔ and Péi Wèn closed the city gates,
executed four senior generals within the city,
and requested to surrender to Wáng Yuándí.
At that time, Gāo Yuánwǔ was at Dǎngshān.
Upon hearing this,
he also surrendered.
"Dǎngshān"
likely should be
"Yáoshān."
Previously, the military headquarters had granted cloth to the soldiers of Míng Prefecture,
one duàn per person.
Soon after, an order was issued to deduct it from the winter stipend.
Just as the military officer for merchant taxation was about to arrive in Míng Prefecture,
Wáng Zhāo, taking advantage of the people's unrest,
said to the soldiers:
"The Liúhòu is young,
and governance does not stem from himself.
Now the storehouses are full and ample,
sufficient to last ten years.
How can we not distribute a little
to comfort the hardworking troops!
That order should not be followed."
He then opened the storehouses,
granting each soldier one bolt of silk
and twelve dàn of grain.
The soldiers were greatly pleased.
Wáng Zhāo then closed the city gates and requested to surrender to Hé Hóngjìng.
Ān Yù was in Cí Prefecture.
Hearing that the two prefectures had surrendered,
he also surrendered to Hé Hóngjìng.
The Yáoshān Dūzhī Bīngmǎshǐ Wèi Yuántán and others surrendered to Wáng Yuándí.
Because they had long resisted surrender,
Wáng Yuándí executed them all.
In the eighth month,
on Xīnmǎo,
Zhèn and Wèi reported the surrender of Xíng, Míng, and Cí prefectures.
The chancellors entered to offer congratulations.
Lǐ Déyù said:
"The foundation of Zhāoyì lies entirely east of the mountains.
With the three prefectures surrendered,
changes in Shàngdǎng will occur within days."
The Emperor said:
"Guō Yì will surely behead Liú Zhěn to redeem himself."
Lǐ Déyù said:
"It truly is as Your Majesty predicts."
The Emperor said:
"What matter should be prioritized now?"
Lǐ Déyù requested that
Lú Hóngzhǐ be appointed as Liúhòu of the three prefectures.
Textual analysis note: The Old History's Annals and Biographies both write
"Hóngzhèng."
The Veritable Records and the New History's Annals and Biographies all write
"Hóngzhǐ."
We follow the latter here.
"If by chance Zhèn and Wèi request control of the three prefectures,
the court will find it difficult to decide."
The Emperor agreed.
An edict ordered Lú Jūn, the Jiédùshǐ of Shānnán Dōngdào concurrently overseeing Zhāoyì, to proceed by post-horse to his headquarters.
The people of Lù, hearing of the surrender of the three prefectures,
were greatly frightened.
Guō Yì and Wáng Xié plotted to kill Liú Zhěn to redeem themselves.
Liú Zhěn's second cousin, the Zhōngjūnshǐ Liú Kuāngzhōu, also served as Yāyá.
Second cousin
means sharing the same great-grandfather.
Cóng,
read as cóng.
He said to Liú Zhěn:
"The Thirteenth Young Master is in the Yáyuàn.
Liú Kuāngzhōu
was the thirteenth.
Yáyuàn
is the office where the Yāyá conducts affairs.
The generals fear being suspected by the Thirteenth Young Master and incurring punishment,
which is why we lost the region east of the mountains.
If we can truly ensure the Thirteenth Young Master does not enter,
then the various generals will dare to speak fully,
and by gathering opinions from the multitude,
we are sure to obtain a sound strategy."
Liú Zhěn summoned Liú Kuāngzhōu and instructed him,
ordering him to claim illness and not enter.
Liú Kuāngzhōu angrily said:
"While I am in the office,
the various generals dare not harbor treacherous designs.
If I leave the office,
our family will surely be destroyed!"
Liú Zhěn insisted on his request.
Liú Kuāngzhōu had no choice
and left with a snap of his fingers.
Guō Yì ordered Liǔ Zhěn's confidant Dǒng Kěwǔ to persuade Liǔ Zhěn, saying:
"The rebellion east of the mountains
was caused by your fifth uncle.
Who among the people in the city dares to guarantee each other's safety now!
What does the Acting Military Governor intend to do?"
Fifth uncle
refers to Péi Wèn.
Liǔ Zhěn had appointed himself Acting Military Governor,
hence he was addressed as such.
"There are still fifty thousand men in the city now,
we should just close the gates and hold firm."
Kěwǔ said:
"That is not a good plan.
It would be better for the Acting Military Governor to surrender himself and submit to the court,
like Zhāng Yuányì did.
The matter of Yuányì is recorded in the 246th volume, in the third year of the Kāichéng era of Emperor Wénzōng.
And let Guō Yì serve as Acting Military Governor.
Once he obtains the command,
he can gradually escort the Grand Lady and your family, along with gold and silk, back to the Eastern Capital.
Would that not be good?"
Grand Lady
refers to Liǔ Cóngjiàn's wife, Lady Péi.
"Would Yì really agree to such a thing?"
Kěwǔ said:
"Kěwǔ has already made a solemn oath with him,
he will certainly not betray it."
He then brought Yì in.
After Zhěn and Yì had secretly agreed on the plan,
Zhěn informed his mother.
His mother said:
"Submitting to the court is indeed a good thing,
but I regret it is already too late.
I could not even protect my own brother—
referring to Péi Wèn surrendering Xíngzhōu.
You must plan for yourself!"
Zhěn then put on plain clothes and went out the gate,
and on his mother's order, appointed Yì as the Chief Military Commissioner.
Wáng Xié had already ordered the generals to line up in the outer hall.
After Yì bowed and thanked Zhěn,
after,
meaning finished.
Zhěn packed his belongings in the inner hall.
Lǐ Shìguì heard of this,
and led several thousand troops from the rear courtyard to attack Yì.
Yì rebuked them, saying:
"Why not take the rewards for yourselves,
instead of wanting to die with Lǐ Shìguì!"
The soldiers then retreated,
and together killed Shìguì.
Yì replaced the generals and officials,
deployed the troops,
and everything was settled in a single night.
The next day,
he sent Dǒng Kěwǔ to visit Zhěn, saying:
"Please discuss official matters."
Zhěn said:
"Why not speak of it!"
Kěwǔ said:
"I fear alarming the Grand Lady."
He then led Zhěn on foot out of the yámén,
to the northern residence.
Northern residence,
refers to the separate residence of the Zhāoyì Military Governor,
located north of the governor's residence,
hence called the northern residence.
When they were deep in drink,
he then said:
"Today's affair is to preserve the entire family of the Grand Commandant—
Liǔ Wù was posthumously granted the title of Grand Commandant.
Then the court will surely show compassion."
Zhěn said:
"If it is as you say,
it is also Zhěn's wish."
Kěwǔ then stepped forward and seized his hand,
while Cuī Xuándù beheaded him from behind.
They then rounded up Zhěn's clan,
from Kuāngzhōu down to infants in swaddling clothes, and killed them all.
Swaddling,
pronounced with two rising tones.
Clothes,
pronounced bǎo.
In the first year of the Chángqìng era of Emperor Mùzōng,
Liǔ Wù first commanded Zhāoyì.
For three generations,
twenty-six years, until they were destroyed.
They also killed twelve families closely associated with Liǔ Cóngjiàn and his son, including Zhāng Gǔ, Chén Yángtíng, Lǐ Zhòngjīng, Guō Tái, Wáng Yǔ, Hán Màozhāng, Màoshí, Wáng Wò, and Jiǎ Xiáng,
along with their sons, nephews, sons-in-law, and brothers-in-law, leaving none.
Zhòngjīng
was the elder brother of Xùn;
Tái
was the son of Xíngyú;
Yǔ
was the grandnephew of Yá;
Màozhāng and Màoshí
were the sons of Yuē;
Wò
was the son of Fán;
Xiáng
was the son of Sù.
During the Gānlù Disturbance,
Zhòngjīng and others fled to join Cóngjiàn,
who took them in and cared for them.
Lǐ Zhòngjīng and others barely escaped the disaster of Gānlù,
only to end up slaughtered along with the clan of Liǔ Cóngjiàn.
It seems Heaven gathered them to be annihilated.
Yì executed people daily,
and the blood flowed like mud.
He then placed Zhěn's head in a box,
and sent an envoy to present a memorial and letter,
surrendering to Wáng Zǎi.
When the head passed through Zézhōu,
Liǔ Gōngzhí led the entire camp in wailing,
and also surrendered to Zǎi.
On the yǐwèi day,
Zǎi reported the situation.
On the bǐngshēn day,
the chief ministers entered to offer congratulations.
Lǐ Déyù memorialized:
"Now there is no need to appoint Acting Military Governors for Xíng, Míng, and Cí again.
Just send Lú Hóngzhǐ to pacify and inspect the three prefectures, as well as the two circuits of Chéngdé and Wèibó."
The Emperor said:
"How should Guō Yì be dealt with?"
Déyù said:
"Liǔ Zhěn was nothing but a foolish youth.
The armed resistance and defiance of orders
were all masterminded by Yì.
When he became isolated and powerless,
he then sold out Zhěn to seek reward.
If such a person is not executed,
how can evil be punished!
We should take advantage of the armies being in the region
to execute Yì and the others together!"
The Emperor said:
"My thoughts are also thus."
An edict was then issued ordering Shí Xióng to lead seven thousand men into Lùzhōu,
to fulfill the prophecy.
The prophecy is recorded in the third year of the previous volume.
It was said that Yì and others could be pardoned,
but the Emperor stared intently and did not respond.
Déyù said:
"Earlier this year, when Zé-Lù was not yet pacified,
and Tàiyuán was again in turmoil,
if not for Your Majesty's firm resolution,
how could the two rebels have been pacified!
Outside opinions suggest that if this were in the previous reign,
they would have been pardoned long ago."
The Emperor said:
"You do not know that Emperor Wénzōng's disposition did not align with yours,
how could he have deliberated on this!"
Lú Jūn was relieved of his post in Shānnán Dōngdào,
and appointed solely as the Military Governor of Zhāoyì.
On the wùxū day,
Liǔ Zhěn's head was delivered to the capital.

the first month,

a different path.

(A note on discrepancies: The Old History biography states
"the twelfth year,"

(He was the son of Liu Zhongying.

The Emperor wished to visit the Huaqing Palace.

The court entertainer Zhu Hanzhen
was witty and quick-tongued.
(The Suoyin commentary on the Records of the Grand Historian states: "Hua" means chaotic;
"ji" means same.
It refers to eloquent and quick people whose words turn "is" into "is not" and "is not" into "is," able to confuse similarity and difference.
Cui Hao said: "Hua" is pronounced "gu."
"Ji" is a wine vessel.
Pouring and spitting wine,
ceaseless all day.
It means words flow like a finished composition,
with inexhaustible rhetoric,
like the "guji" wine vessel spilling wine.
Therefore, Yang Xiong's "Rhapsody on Wine" says:
"The leather wine bag 'guji,'
its belly large like a pot,

That is it.
Also, Yao Cha said: "Guji" means comic banter.
"Hua" is read as the common character.
"Ji" is pronounced "ji."
It means words are smooth and witty,
his clever schemes emerge swiftly,

His improvisations seemed precomposed,

One day,

"In the eleventh year of the Dazhong era,
seventh month,
Hanwang Qianyu was demoted to Lingwai.

I now follow the "Remaining Affairs of Zhenling.")
The musician Luo Cheng
excelled at the pipa

The Emperor was well-versed in music theory,
and Luo Cheng was especially favored.
Relying on this favor, Luo Cheng acted violently and tyrannically,
killing someone over a minor grievance.
He was imprisoned in the capital jail.
The other musicians wished to plead for him.
When the Emperor visited the rear garden for music,
they set up an empty seat,
placed a pipa on it,
and bowed in a circle in the courtyard,

The Emperor asked the reason.
They replied:

deserving ten thousand deaths.

The Emperor said:

the tenth month,
on the Jǐsì day,
Lǐ Chéngxūn, the defense commissioner of Qínchéng, was appointed as the military governor of Jīngyuán.
Chéngxūn
was the grandson of Lǐ Guāngbì.
The character "xūn"
is the same as "xūn" (勳).
The Tibetan chieftain Shàng Yánxīn surrendered with the tribes of Hé and Wèi prefectures,

Chéngxūn coveted the wealth of his sheep and horses,
lured him into Fènglín Pass,
north of Fènglín County in Hé Prefecture, there is Fènglín Pass.
Fènglín
was the territory of Báishí County in the Hàn dynasty,

The character "yòu" (誘)
is pronounced as "yǒu."
Chéngxūn conspired with his generals to capture Yánxīn,

Yánxīn learned of this,
and during a military banquet hosted by Chéngxūn,
he said to Chéngxūn in the midst of the gathering:
A banquet held in the army is called a military banquet.
The character "zuò" (坐)
is pronounced as "cuò."
"Hé and Wèi prefectures
have vast lands and sparse populations,
leading to famine and epidemics.
Many Táng people have moved inland to the three river valleys,
the three river valleys
refer to Píngliàng Chuān, Wèirú Chuān, and Luòmén Chuān.

there is not a trace of human habitation.
I, Yánxīn, wish to enter the court to see the Son of Heaven,

Zhāng Yìcháo surrendered Shā, Guā, and other prefectures to the Táng.
Chéngxūn hesitated and did not agree,

"Once Yánxīn enters the court,
and the tribes relocate inland,
it is only regrettable that Qín Prefecture will no longer have anything to rely on."
Chéngxūn and his generals looked at each other in silence.
The next day,
the generals said to Chéngxūn:
"Your Excellency was the first to establish military farms,
set up the commissioner's office,
command ten thousand troops,
and rely on the Ministry of Revenue for supplies.
The commissioner's office
refers to the defense commissioner's office of Qín and Chéng.
The character "yǎng" (仰)
is pronounced as "niú xiàng fān."
There are benefits from farming and trade.
Farming
refers to the profits from military farms.
Trade

Chéngxūn agreed,
and immediately memorialized to appoint Yánxīn as the commander of the patrol forces of Hé and Wèi,
allowing him to govern his people there.
The history records that the Táng frontier garrisons,
from the commanders down to the junior officers,
were meticulous in their personal schemes,
but neglectful of state affairs.
Thus, the barbarians could see through their intentions,
and also carry out their own plans for self-preservation.
An examination of discrepancies: This event comes from the Supplementary National History.
According to it, Zhāng Yìcháo surrendered with eleven prefectures,
and Hé and Wèi were among them.
Now Yánxīn surrendering Hé and Wèi again
is because Yìcháo led Hàn people,
while Yánxīn led Tibetan tribes.
Moreover, the Supplementary National History does not specify the year or month of Yánxīn's surrender.
The New History biography only mentions Zhāng Yìcháo's surrender,
and later, the Tibetan general Shàng Yánxīn of Hé and Wèi prefectures, due to the collapse of his state,

Gāo Pián, the prefect of Qín Prefecture, lured Yánxīn and ten thousand tents of the Húnmò tribe to surrender,

Pián recovered Fènglín Pass,

According to the Old History biography,
Gāo Pián did not become the prefect of Qín Prefecture until the reign of Emperor Yìzōng.
The New History biography is mistaken.
Now, we follow the Supplementary National History.
Because Chéngxūn was transferred to Jīngyuán,
the matter of Yánxīn is placed here.

1 In spring,
the first month,

An examination of discrepancies: The Old History Annals record Wáng Shì's appointment to Ānnán in the second month.

Upon arriving in Jiāozhǐ,

and planted bamboo outside the trenches,

Fàn Chéngdà's Guìhǎi Yúhéng Zhì records: Lè bamboo

densely covered with sharp thorns.

Lambs and piglets could not pass through,

It is said that the outer walls of Jiāozhǐ were also made of this bamboo,

The character "lè" (竻)
is pronounced as "lú dé fān."
Shortly after,
a large force of southern barbarians arrived,

according to Táng regulations: For land travel,
a horse covers seventy lǐ per day,
walking or by donkey covers fifty lǐ per day,
and by cart covers thirty lǐ per day.
For water travel,
heavily loaded boats going upstream on rivers cover thirty lǐ per day,
on the Yangtze River forty lǐ per day,
and on other waters forty-five lǐ per day.
Empty boats going upstream on rivers cover forty lǐ per day,
on the Yangtze River fifty lǐ per day,
and on other waters sixty lǐ per day.
Boats going downstream,
regardless of load, follow the same rule:
on rivers, one hundred fifty lǐ per day,
on the Yangtze River one hundred lǐ per day,
and on other waters seventy lǐ per day.
He sent an interpreter to persuade them,

They sent someone to apologize, saying:

not to raid."
Luó Xínggōng, the senior officer of Ānnán,

The term "senior officer"
is equivalent to "commander."
The character "lǎo" (獠)
is pronounced as "lǔ hào fān."
The character "xiào" (校)
is pronounced as "hù jiào fān."
The central army of the protector-general had only a few hundred weak soldiers;

the Vice Minister of Revenue and Commissioner of Finance, Liú Zhuàn,

At the time, he was serving as the Military Governor of Hédōng,

On the Wǔwǔ day,

Textual Analysis states: The Dōngguān Zòujì says:

the Emperor personally issued an edict recalling him.
Upon his arrival,
he was appointed Vice Minister of Revenue and Commissioner of Finance.
On the seventeenth day of the twelfth month,
during his audience,
the Emperor handed Zhuàn the imperial calendar from the imperial desk,
instructing him to select an auspicious day from the latter part of the month.
Zhuàn did not understand the Emperor's intention.
The Emperor said:
'Simply choose a day suitable for appointing an official.'
Zhuàn knelt and replied:
The Emperor smiled and said:
'The twenty-fifth day is very auspicious.'
'On that day, I shall appoint you as Chancellor.'
This was kept secret,
and no one in the world knew of it.
Gāo Shí was an assistant in Fèngxiáng,
and Shí was an old colleague of Zhuàn's.
On the twenty-fourth day,
he took his leave of Zhuàn at Zhuàn's private residence in Xuānpíng Ward.
Shí said:

The next morning,

The Shílù and
Zhuàn's biography state:
"On the seventeenth day of the first month of the following year,
during his audience,
the Emperor handed Zhuàn the calendar,
instructing him to select an auspicious day.
Zhuàn knelt and replied: 'The twenty-fifth day.'"
We follow this account.
He was a fifth-generation descendant of Liú Rénguǐ.

holding both military and ministerial positions.
Zhuàn and Cuī Shènyóu were discussing governance before the Emperor.
Shènyóu said:
"We should only distinguish and classify the ranks and statuses,

Zhuàn said:
"In the past, Wáng Yífǔ revered and promoted superficial elegance,
Wáng Yǎn, styled Yífǔ of the Jìn dynasty.
leading to the desolation of the Central Plains.
Now, in this prosperous and enlightened court,
we should demand reality in accordance with names,
ensuring that all officials fulfill their duties appropriately.
To hastily prioritize the classification of ranks and statuses—

Shènyóu had no reply.
3. Xuānyuán Jí arrived at Cháng'ān.
The Emperor summoned him into the palace
and asked:
"Can longevity be learned?"
He replied:
"If a ruler suppresses desires and honors virtue,
then he will naturally receive great
and far-reaching blessings.
Why seek longevity elsewhere!"
He stayed for several months
and firmly requested to return to the mountains.
The Emperor then sent him off.
Xuānyuán Jí's request to return
was due to the lessons from the events at the end of the Huìcháng era.
4. In the second month,
on the Jiǎzǐ day, the first day of the month,
the practice of high officials paying morning respects at the Guānglíng tomb and offering incense on death anniversaries was abolished,
and all palace women were relocated to the various imperial tombs.
This was to attribute the crime of regicide to Emperor Mùzōng.
In the early Táng dynasty,
the emperor had the ritual of visiting the imperial tombs.
If the Son of Heaven did not personally visit,
then the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices would perform the tomb visit.
In the fifth year of the Xiǎnqìng era of Emperor Gāozōng,
an edict was issued for inspections in the spring and autumn seasons each year,
to be conducted by the Three Dukes for tomb visits,
with the Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices assisting.
The Court of Imperial Sacrifices provided the ceremonial guard,
and this was recorded in the statutes.
Initially,
according to the Zhēnguàn ritual code, tomb inspections were conducted in the middle months of spring and autumn each year.
By the time of Empress Wǔ,
envoys were dispatched to the tombs in the four seasonal months, on birthdays, and death anniversaries to pay respects.
In the fourth year of the Zhēnyuán era,
the Director of the Imperial Academy, Bāo Jí, stated:
"In the second and eighth months each year,
high officials pay morning respects at the various imperial tombs.
The tomb officials
guide them to the foot of the tombs.
The ritual is brief,
and there is no way to fully express reverence."
Thereupon, the Court of Imperial Sacrifices drafted a ceremony based on the old rituals,
and the high officials and various officers performed it in order,
paying morning respects before returning.
Offering incense on death anniversaries
was the ritual of visiting the tombs to pay respects.
There was also the ritual of offering incense at Buddhist temples on death anniversaries.
Sòng Bái said: According to Táng regulations:
For national mourning incense offerings,
initially, they were only conducted at temples and monasteries in the capital.
In the fifth year of the Zhēnyuán era,
in the eighth month,
an imperial decree ordered that all superior prefectures in the empire should follow the regulations for national mourning incense offerings.
Whenever an emperor passed away,
palace women without children were all sent to the mountain tombs to serve morning and evening,
preparing washing and combing utensils,
arranging quilts and pillows,
serving the dead as they would the living.
Cháo,
read as zhí yáo fān.
5. On the Wùchén day,
Cuī Shènyóu, the Vice Minister of the Secretariat and Tongpíngzhāngshì, was appointed Military Governor of Dōngchuān.
Textual Analysis states: The Táng Quēshǐ says:
"Chancellor and Grand Guardian Cuī once attended an audience in the informal hall.
The Emperor intended to ascend the tower to proclaim a general pardon.
The Grand Guardian submitted a memorial, etc.
Ten days later,
he was dismissed from his ministerial duties."
The Old Biography states:
"Initially,
Shènyóu and Xiāo Yè were both in the Hànlín Academy,
and their relationship was not harmonious.
When Shènyóu became chancellor,
he dismissed Yè from the Academy.
Soon after, Yè rose from Commissioner of Finance
to become Tongpíngzhāngshì,
and the Emperor's favor towards him grew increasingly profound.
Yè recommended Zhuàn to jointly handle governmental affairs,
and as a result, Shènyóu was sent out to Dōngchuān."
The Dōngguān Zòujì states:
"After Liú Zhuàn entered the chancellorship,
he and Shènyóu discussed governance before the Emperor.
Shènyóu said:
'We should only distinguish and classify the ranks and statuses.'
Zhuàn said, etc.
Shènyóu could not reply.
Because of this, the Emperor's favor gradually declined,
and soon he was dismissed as chancellor and appointed Military Governor of Dōngchuān,
with the Tongpíngzhāngshì title removed."
We now follow the Táng Quēshǐ.
The Emperor intended to ascend the tower to proclaim a general pardon.
In the early Táng dynasty,
the Son of Heaven resided in the Western Palace,
and general pardons were usually proclaimed from the Chéngtiānmén tower.
After Emperor Gāozōng,
the Son of Heaven resided in the Eastern Palace,
and general pardons were usually proclaimed from the Dānfèngmén tower.
"Ascending the tower to proclaim a pardon involves extensive expenses;
such an act requires justification.
Moreover, pardons should not be frequent."
According to Táng regulations: Whenever a general pardon is proclaimed from the tower,
the Six Armies and Twelve Guards all receive generous rewards,
hence the statement about extensive expenses.
Liú Wēnsǒu said: According to precedent,
unless a major amnesty is proclaimed, the tower is not ascended,
and the military and common people all receive grants.
Shù,
read as suǒ jiǎo fān.
The Emperor said:
"From what can I derive justification!"
Shènyóu said:
"Your Majesty has not yet established an heir apparent,
and all within the Four Seas look to you with hope.
If you were to perform this ritual,
even suburban sacrifices would be permissible,
let alone ascending the tower!"
At the time, the Emperor was taking medicines from alchemists
and had already begun to feel restless and thirsty,
though outsiders did not yet know.
Suspicion and jealousy ran deep.
Upon hearing this,
he lowered his head and spoke no more.
The historian states that Emperor Xuānzōng did not early establish the foundation of the state,
allowing Wáng Zōngshí to establish the elder [as heir] and secretly claim the merit of deciding the succession.
Fù,
read as fú yòu fān.
Shènyóu was dismissed from the chancellorship.

On the Guǐwèi day,
On the Gēngzǐ day,
the military commander of Lǐngnán, Wáng Lìnghuán, rebelled,

was from Sūzhōu.
