Cease the lecture sessions,
and personally devote yourself diligently to government affairs."
Although the emperor praised and rewarded him,
in the end he could not follow his advice.
11 The military governor of Lingnán Xīdào, Cài Jīng, governed with harsh cruelty,
employing the punishment of roasting on a hot pillar,
causing resentment throughout the entire region.
Consequently, he was driven out by the soldiers of Yǒngzhōu.
Lingnán was divided into two military commands,
with the Western Circuit governing from Yǒngzhōu.
Téngzhōu,
originally the territory of the Hàn dynasty's Měnglíng County,
was established as Téngzhōu in the Táng dynasty,
located five thousand six hundred lǐ from the capital.
Cài Jīng recruited local militiamen and neighboring native troops to attack Yǒngzhōu.
His forces were a motley assembly,
prone to collapse at the slightest movement,
so he went to seek refuge in Guìzhōu.
The people of Guìzhōu resented him for causing the division,
and refused to accept him.
This was because he had separated the patrol jurisdictions of Guìguǎn and placed them under the Western Circuit military governor.
An imperial decree demoted him to Registrar of Yázhōu,
but he refused to take up the post;
on his way back,
upon reaching Línglíng,
an imperial decree ordered him to commit suicide.
Zhèng Yú, the Surveillance Commissioner of Guìguǎn, was appointed as the military governor of Lingnán Xīdào.
12 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the first day, Bǐngshēn,
the emperor's son Yì was enfeoffed as Prince of Wèi,
Tǐng as Prince of Liáng,
and Jí as Prince of Shǔ.
13 In the eleventh month,
Shùnzōng's son Jī was enfeoffed as Prince of Qí,
and Xiànzōng's son Fèn as Prince of Róng.
14 Nánzhào led fifty thousand Mán tribesmen to invade Ānnán.
The Protector-General, Cài Xí, urgently reported the situation,
and an imperial decree dispatched two thousand troops from the Jīngnán and Húnán circuits,
along with three thousand volunteer soldiers from Guìguǎn,
to Yǒngzhōu.
The term "volunteer soldiers"
referred to those who responded to the recruitment call to join the army.
15 Wéi Zhòu, the military governor of Lingnán Dōngdào, memorialized:
"The Mán invaders will surely head toward Yǒngzhōu.
If we do not protect it first
but hastily embark on a distant campaign,
I fear the Mán may later take advantage of the emptiness to cut off our supply routes."
An imperial decree then ordered Cài Xí to station his troops at Hǎimén.
A note on discrepancies: According to the Veritable Records:
"The edict ordered Xí to temporarily stay at Hǎimén."
This meant abandoning Jiāozhǐ
and retreating to station at Hǎimén.
However, when Xí died, he was still in Jiāozhǐ.
It is likely that by the time the edict arrived,
Xí was already besieged,
and communication was impossible.
In the twelfth month,
Xí again requested reinforcements,
and an imperial decree ordered Shānnán Dōngdào to send a thousand crossbowmen to assist him.
By then, Nánzhào had already besieged Jiāozhǐ,
and Xí defended the city firmly,
but relief troops could not reach him.
16 Prince Yì, Chǎn, passed away.
17 That year,
the Wàmò began to offer tribute.
The Wàmò
were slaves of the Tǔbō.
Whenever the Tǔbō mobilized troops,
wealthy households often sent slaves to accompany them,
sometimes with over ten slaves from a single family,
which contributed to the large numbers of Tǔbō forces.
After Lùn Kǒngrè rebelled,
many slaves were left without masters,
so they banded together to form tribes,
scattered across Gān, Sù, Guā, Shā, Hé, Wèi, Mín, Kuò, Dié, and Dàng,
and even weaker Tǔbō people came to rely on them.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day Gēngwǔ,
the emperor performed sacrifices at the Circular Mound;
a general amnesty was declared.
2 On that day,
Nánzhào captured Jiāozhǐ.
All of Cài Xí's attendants perished,
and he fought on foot with great effort,
his body pierced by ten arrows.
He tried to reach the eunuch supervisor's boat,
but the boat had already left the shore,
so he drowned in the sea and died.
His staff member, Fán Chuò, carried his official seal and swam across the river.
From Bóbái County in Báizhōu, one hundred lǐ southwest to Běishù Tān,
exiting at Mǎmén River,
crossing the sea,
one reaches the border of Ānnán.
The river where Fán Chuò crossed with the seal
was this very river.
They fled to the waters east of the city,
where Yuán Wéidé, a military officer from Jīngnán, said to the troops:
"We have no boats;
entering the water means death.
It would be better to turn back toward the city and fight the Mán.
If each of us trades one life for two Mán,
it would still be advantageous."
So they turned back toward the city
and entered the Eastern Luó Gate.
The Eastern Luó Gate
was the east gate of Ānnán's outer wall.
Wéidé and others led their troops in killing over two thousand Mán.
A note on discrepancies: According to the Veritable Records:
"In the second month,
Ānnán's Military Commissioner Cài Xí reported: 'The Mán rebels Yáng Sījiàn and Má Guānggāo, the magistrate of Fúyé County in Luófúzhōu, led five to six thousand of their troops
to camp at the western corner of the city.'
The military governor of Lingnán Dōngdào, Wéi Zhòu, reported: 'On the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month,
the Mán rebels approached the city of Ānnán.
The Military Commissioner and Acting Minister of Works, Cài Xí, led troops to engage in battle,
resulting in equal casualties on both sides.
On the third day of the first month,
the rebel forces besieged the city,
attacking fiercely.
Xí used mounted crossbows on the city walls to shoot at them.
By the seventh day,
the city fell.
Xí was struck by a crossbow arrow in his right arm and died.
His family and over seventy followers all perished at the hands of the rebels.
His staff member, Fán Chuò, carried the seal and crossed the river.
The troops from Jīngnán, Jiāngxī, Èyuè, and Xiāngzhōu rushed to the waters east of the city,
but having no boats, they turned back
and together entered the Eastern Luó Gate,
killing only one to two thousand Mán.
By night,
rebel reinforcements arrived,
and they slaughtered the city.'"
These two reports seem to have been compiled later from Mán records,
and they contain many discrepancies.
For example, Yáng Sījiàn
appears twice in the Mán records,
both times written as
"Yáng Sījìn,"
likely a clerical error from cursive script turning it into
"jiàn"
Even though they are barbarians,
why would they name someone
"Sījiàn"
The "Old Accounts of Zhāng Jǐnlǐ" records a letter from Gāo Pián to Yúnnán,
also mentioning Yáng Sījìn,
the military governor of Shànlán.
The New Book also mistakenly follows this as
"jiàn."
Moreover, what the Mán records refer to as Sījìn and Guānggāo leading
were five to six thousand Táohuā Mán,
not the entire force of Mán tribesmen.
The Supplementary National History states that fifty thousand Mán troops attacked Ānnán,
not merely five to six thousand.
Also, on the twenty-first day of the twelfth month,
the Luǒxíng Mán, Máng Mán, and Táohuā people were already at the city walls,
so how could they only approach Ānnán on the twenty-seventh!
The Mán records mentioning the twenty-seventh as the day they approached the city
only record the day they saw the Hé Mán and Xúnchuán Mán;
and mentioning the second and third days of the first month
only records the day they used mounted crossbows to shoot the Jǔzǐ,
not the day the siege began.
Moreover, during the chaos of the city's fall and the rush to escape,
unless Fán Chuò was personally present,
how could he know the details!
The number of enemies killed by the four-circuit troops entering the city
was only known because of the monk Wú Hàn's account.
Wéi Zhòu was in Guǎngzhōu;
how could his report be exactly like Fán Chuò's records?
Its falseness is evident.
The New Biography states:
"That night,
the Mán slaughtered the city,"
also mistakenly following the Veritable Records.
The Mán general Yáng Sījìn then emerged from the inner city to rescue them.
The inner city
refers to the small city within the main walls.
Nánzhào captured Jiāozhǐ twice,
killing or capturing nearly one hundred and fifty thousand people.
They left twenty thousand troops behind,
placing Sījìn in charge of Jiāozhǐ City,
and the various mountain tribes, both near and far, all surrendered to him.
An imperial decree recalled all troops from various circuits that had been sent to Ānnán,
and they were reassigned to defend Lingnán
Western Circuit.
3 The emperor indulged in excessive feasting and entertainment.
Left Reminder Liú Tuì submitted a memorial stating:
"Currently, the construction of fortifications in Xīliáng is underway,
and decisions regarding support or abandonment have not yet been settled.
Xīliáng,
refers to Liángzhōu,
likely because at this time, plans were being made to advance and construct fortifications there.
Weapons and armor are all scattered along the roads.
Over the past month or so,
there has been no lack of significant events.
If Your Majesty does not outwardly show concern and compassion to demonstrate it to both near and far,
how can you demand that they exert their utmost effort unto death!
I hope you will moderate your entertainment and excursions,
and wait until the distant people are pacified and secure;
it will not be too late then."
This means that after the distant people are pacified and secure,
then engaging in entertainment and excursions
would still not be too late.
4 In the second month,
on the first day, Jiǎwǔ,
the emperor paid respects to the sixteen imperial mausoleums.
The sixteen mausoleums
refer to the Xiàn, Zhāo, Qián, Dìng, Qiáo, Tài, Jiàn, Yuán, Chóng, Fēng, Jǐng, Guāng, Zhuāng, Zhāng, Duān, and Zhēn mausoleums.
An examination of discrepancies notes: Paying respects to the sixteen mausoleums
could not be completed in a single day,
yet the old histories do not record the date of return to the palace.
The Táng Nián Bǔ Lù states: In the second month,
on Gēngzǐ.
Paying respects to sixteen mausoleums in one day
is particularly difficult to believe.
5 The Tiānxióng Army was established in Qínzhōu.
Emperor Dàizōng indulged Tián Chéngsì,
bestowing the title of Tiānxióng Army to honor Wèi-Bó,
but soon, due to his arrogance and defiance,
it was revoked.
Now, the Tiānxióng Army was reestablished in Qínzhōu.
By the end of the Táng dynasty,
Wèi-Bó regained the title of Tiānxióng Army,
while Qínzhōu no longer held the title Tiānxióng.
Former Left Jinwu General Wáng Yànshí was appointed as the Tiānxióng Military Observer.
Yànshí
was the son of Zǎi.
Zǎi’s father, Zhìxīng, adopted him as a son,
as seen in the 247th volume, fourth year of the Huìchāng era.
6 In the third month,
Guīyì Military Commissioner Zhāng Yìcháo reported that he personally led seven thousand Tǔbō and Hàn troops to recapture Liángzhōu.
7 The Nánmán invaded the Left and Right Rivers,
gradually approaching Yōngzhōu.
Zhèng Yú was frightened
and stated that as a civil official, he lacked military strategy,
requesting that a military official be appointed instead.
The court summoned Yìwǔ Military Commissioner Kāng Chéngxùn to the capital,
intending to have him replace Yú.
An edict was also issued for him to select several military officers and several hundred soldiers to accompany him.
This selection was to be made from within the Yìwǔ Army.
The character for officer (校)
is pronounced xiào.
8 Secretariat Vice Director and Tongpingzhangshi Bì Xián, due to his colleagues frequently acting selfishly and unlawfully,
pleaded illness and resigned from his post.
In the summer,
fourth month,
he was removed and appointed as Minister of War.
9 On Gēngxū,
bandits entered Xúzhōu,
killing officials;
Prefect Cáo Qìng suppressed them.
10 Kāng Chéngxùn arrived at the capital
and was appointed as Military Commissioner of Lǐngnán Xīdào.
Ten thousand troops from the Jīng, Xiāng, Hóng, and È circuits were mobilized to accompany him.
11 In the fifth month,
on Wùchén,
Hanlin Academician Recipient of Edicts and Vice Minister of War Yáng Shōu was appointed Tongpingzhangshi.
Shōu
was the younger brother of Fā.
Emperor Xuānzōng, due to the opening of Hé and Huáng,
posthumously added honorific titles to Emperors Shùn and Xiàn.
The relevant officials discussed remaking the ancestral temple tablets,
inscribing the new posthumous titles.
Fā believed that creating new tablets
had no precedent in ancient texts,
and firmly opposed it.
Those knowledgeable in rites considered him correct,
and he became well-known because of this.
Hence, he was able to become chancellor.
12 On Yǐhài,
the Róngguǎn was abolished,
and placed under Lǐngnán Xīdào.
Additionally, Gōng and Xiàng prefectures were reassigned to Guìguǎn.
The previous year, Gōng and Xiàng had been placed under Lǐngnán Xīdào.
13 On Wùzǐ,
Menxia Vice Director and Tongpingzhangshi Dù Shěnquán was appointed Tongpingzhangshi,
and concurrently appointed as Military Commissioner of Zhènhǎi.
14 In the sixth month,
the Ānnán Protectorate was abolished,
and a provisional Jiāozhōu was established at Hǎimén Garrison.
Right Gate Guard General Sòng Róng was appointed as Provisional Prefect of Jiāozhōu,
and Kāng Chéngxùn was put in charge of Ānnán and various military camps.
15 In the intercalary month,
Menxia Vice Director and Tongpingzhangshi Dù Cóng was appointed Tongpingzhangshi,
and concurrently appointed as Military Commissioner of Fèngxiáng.
Vice Minister of War and Commissioner of Finance Hénán Cáo Què was appointed Tongpingzhangshi.
16 In autumn,
seventh month,
on the first day, Xīnmǎo,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the 24th day of the twelfth month,
Nánzhào invaded Xīchuān.
On the 25th, Shěn Xún, the military governor of Zhāoyì, had a slave named Guī Qín
who had an affair with one of Xún's maids.
Xún intended to kill him,
but did not succeed.
On the yǐyǒu day,
Guī Qín conspired with some junior officers to rebel,
attacked the official residence,
and killed Shěn Xún.
1 In spring,
the first month,
Lǐ Pín, the governor of Jīngzhào, was appointed as the military governor of Zhāoyì.
He took Guī Qín's heart and liver to sacrifice to Shěn Xún.
2 Lìnghú Táo, the military governor of Huáinán, appealed for redress of grievances on behalf of his son Lìnghú Hào.
Zhāng Yún was demoted to deputy governor of Xìngyuán,
and Liú Tuì to magistrate of Huàyīn.
An imperial edict stated:
"Although we commend their loyal and outspoken advice,
they cannot escape the blame for their negligence and carelessness."
3 On the bǐngwǔ day,
Xīchuān reported
that Nánzhào had invaded Xīzhōu,
but the prefect Yù Shìzhēn defeated them,
capturing over a thousand men.
Considering that Yù Shìzhēn lost the defense the following year due to greed and cunning,
this victory was likely an exaggerated report of achievements.
Yán Qìngfù, a senior general of Zhōngwǔ, requested the construction of two cities, Xīn'ān and Èróng,
which was approved.
These two cities
were built within the boundaries of Xīzhōu.
4 Zhāng Yīn, the military commissioner of Róngguǎn, was additionally put in charge of Jiāozhōu affairs;
the garrison at Hǎimén was increased to 25,000 men,
and Zhāng Yīn was ordered to advance and capture Ānnán.
5 In the second month,
on the jǐsì day,
Lǐ Fú, the Minister of Justice and commissioner for salt and iron transport, was appointed as a chief minister and concurrently military governor of Xīchuān.
6 On the jiǎshēn day,
the former military governor of Xīchuān, Xiāo Yè, was demoted to surveillance commissioner of Shānnánxīdào.
7 In the third month,
on the dīngyǒu day,
a comet appeared in the constellation Lóu,
three chi in length.
On the jǐhài day,
the director of the Bureau of Astronomy memorialized:
"According to the classic of stars,
this is called the 'Hányù' star,
an auspicious star."
The emperor was greatly pleased.
The director of the Bureau of Astronomy in the Táng,
of the third rank,
was responsible for observing astronomical phenomena and verifying calendars.
The history states that by the end of the Táng, the astronomical officials were confused about celestial signs,
treating ominous phenomena as auspicious.
"We request that this be announced throughout the court and the country,
and recorded in the historical annals."
This was approved.
8 Kāng Chéngxùn arrived at Yōngzhōu,
where the barbarian incursions were intensifying.
An edict ordered troops from eight circuits—Xǔ, Huá, Qīng, Biàn, Yǎn, Yùn, Xuān, and Rùn—to be placed under his command.
Chéngxùn did not set up scouts;
Nánzhào, leading nearly 60,000 Mán troops, invaded Yōngzhōu.
As they were about to enter the territory,
Chéngxùn then dispatched about 10,000 troops from six circuits to resist them,
using Liáo tribesmen as guides,
who deceived them.
When the enemy arrived,
no defenses were prepared.
Eight thousand troops from five circuits were annihilated,
only the Tiānpíng army, which arrived a day later,
escaped.
The Tiānpíng army
consisted of troops from Yùn.
Chéngxùn was terrified and did not know what to do.
The deputy military governor Lǐ Xíngsù led the troops in repairing the moats and palisades,
which were just completed
when the Mán army surrounded them.
After four days,
as the Mán were preparing siege equipment,
some generals requested to launch a night raid on the Mán camp in separate columns,
but Chéngxùn refused.
A junior officer from the Tiānpíng army strenuously argued for it repeatedly,
and only then did he consent.
The junior officer led 300 brave warriors,
who at night
were lowered by ropes from the walls,
scattered to set fire to the Mán camps,
and beheaded over 500 men.
The Mán were greatly alarmed,
and after a day,
they lifted the siege and withdrew.
Chéngxùn then sent several thousand troops in pursuit,
killing or capturing fewer than 300 men,
all of whom were coerced followers from the溪獠 tribes.
Chéngxùn sent a swift memorial reporting victory,
claiming a great defeat of the barbarian bandits,
and congratulations came from both the court and the country.
9 In summer,
the fourth month,
Xiāo Zhì, the Vice Minister of War and concurrently in charge of the Ministry of Revenue, was appointed as a chief minister.
Zhì
was the grandson of Xiāo Fù.
Xiāo Fù served as chief minister under Emperor Dézōng.
10 Kāng Chéngxùn was awarded the additional title of Acting Vice Director of the Right,
as a reward for defeating the barbarians.
Among those who received rewards for reported achievements,
all were Chéngxùn's relatives or close associates;
the officers who led the fire attack on the camp were not promoted a single rank.
Consequently, there was resentment and anger in the army,
and rumors spread along the roads.
11 In the fifth month,
an edict stated:
"The local customs of Xúzhōu are vigorous and strong,
and its armored soldiers are elite and powerful.
Recently, due to the abolition of the military governorship,
many have gone into hiding.
It is appropriate to order the Xú-Sì training commissioner to select and recruit 3,000 soldiers to go to Yōngzhōu for garrison duty.
Once matters beyond the mountains are pacified,
they shall be replaced and return home."
12 In autumn,
the seventh month,
Xīchuān reported that the ghost chieftain of the Liǎnglín tribe intercepted the Nánzhào Mán,
and defeated them.
Shǐ Zhào said: The Liǎnglín tribe
was part of the Dōngmán state,
located seventy lǐ from the Wùdèng state.
Although their territory was small, they were acknowledged as leaders by various tribes,
and were called the great ghost chieftain.
'Defeated'
is annotated as bǔ mài fān.
Dù Shǒulián, the commander of Bǎosāichéng, did not submit to Nánzhào,
and led his troops to surrender at Lízhōu.
13 Wéi Zhòu, the military governor of Lǐngnándōngdào, was fully aware of Kāng Chéngxùn's actions,
and wrote to inform the chief ministers.
Chéngxùn also became suspicious and fearful himself,
and repeatedly submitted memorials pleading illness to resign.
Consequently, Chéngxùn was appointed as General of the Right Guard of the Militant Guards and assigned to a sinecure post in the eastern capital.
Examination of discrepancies: According to the Supplementary National History,
"Wéi Zhòu, the military governor of Lǐngnándōngdào, concurrently oversaw military supply.
He secretly ordered officials and officers stationed in Yōngzhōu
to report to him,
so no matter how great or small the affairs,
he knew everything.
Furthermore, upon investigation, he found that most of the reports of victories were false,
and he informed the chief ministers of all he had heard.
Chéngxùn had already become suspicious and fearful,
and pleaded illness to avoid blame,
and was appointed General of the Right Guard of the Militant Guards and assigned to a sinecure post in the eastern capital."
The biography of Kāng Chéngxùn in the Veritable Records of Emperor Xīzōng states:
"When the southern barbarians captured Jiāozhǐ,
Chéngxùn was appointed military governor of Lǐngnánxīdào.
After over a year,
he pacified the region,
and was awarded the additional title of Acting Vice Director of the Right.
He was at odds with the neighboring military governor,
and was dismissed and returned as General of the Right Guard of the Militant Guards."
This likely came from his family's biographical account.
We now follow the Supplementary National History, the Veritable Records of Emperor Yìzōng, and the New History biography.
The four prefectures of the Róngguǎn region were again made a separate military commission.
According to the New History's Table of Military Governors,
in the first year of the Xiántōng era,
the Róngguǎn commission was abolished,
and its subordinate prefectures were placed under the jurisdiction of Yōngguǎn.
13. Gāo Pián besieged Jiaozhǐ for over ten days.
The Man people were in extreme distress,
and the city was about to fall.
However, he received a dispatch from Wáng Yànquán,
stating that he and Lǐ Wéizhōu had already led a large army from Hǎimén.
Pián then handed over military affairs to Wéi Zhòngzǎi
and returned north with over a hundred of his subordinates.
Earlier,
Zhòngzǎi had sent the minor envoy Wáng Huìzàn,
and Pián had sent the minor officer Zēng Gǔn to report the victory at Jiaozhǐ.
While at sea,
they saw banners and flags approaching from the east.
They asked a patrol boat,
a patrol boat,
a scouting vessel.
The two men plotted:
"Wéizhōu will surely seize our report and detain us."
So they hid on an island.
After Wéizhōu passed,
they hurried to the capital.
The emperor received their memorial,
was greatly pleased,
and immediately appointed Pián as Acting Minister of Works,
reinstating him to pacify Ānnán.
Pián reached Hǎimén and then turned back.
Wáng Yànquán was dim-witted and cowardly,
acting only on Lǐ Wéizhōu's orders.
Wéizhōu was cruel and greedy,
and the generals refused to serve under him.
Consequently, the heavy siege was lifted,
and the majority of the Man forces escaped.
When Pián arrived,
he again urged and encouraged the officers and soldiers to attack the city,
and eventually captured it.
He killed Duàn Qiúqiān and the local Man leader Zhū Dàogǔ, who had guided Nánzhào,
beheading over thirty thousand.
Textual analysis: The Old Annals state: In the tenth month,
Pián reported that the Man rebels were completely pacified.
The Veritable Records:
"In the ninth month,
Pián reported killing the Man chieftains Duàn Qiúqiān, Zhū Dàogǔ, and beheading over three thousand."
Under the entry for the bǐngshēn day of the tenth month,
it also says
"Pián reported the recovery of Ānnán,
and the Man rebels fled and scattered."
It also says
"defeated Yáng Jīsī, Duàn Qiúqiān, Zhū Dàogǔ,
killing over thirty thousand."
The New Annals:
"In the tenth month,
Gāo Pián captured Ānnán."
Note: 'Guīshǒuqiān'
is an error for Duàn Qiúqiān.
The Supplementary National History's account of capturing the city and defeating Jīsī and others are the same event.
The Veritable Records splits them across two months,
and it is unclear what source this is based on.
The New Book of Nánzhào states:
"In the seventh year,
sixth month,
Pián reached Jiaozhōu.
After several victorious battles,
the soldiers fought fiercely,
beheading their general Zhāng Quán.
Lǐ Zhǎolóng surrendered with ten thousand troops.
They captured the three fortifications of Bōfēng.
Jīsī came out to fight but was defeated,
and fled back to the city.
The soldiers pursued him,
scaled the battlements and entered,
beheaded Qiúqiān, Nìxiē, Nuòméi,
presenting thirty thousand heads.
Ānnán was pacified."
This is likely because Pián reached Ānnán in the sixth month,
and the account concludes there,
but Ānnán was not actually pacified in the sixth month.
Now follow the New and Old Annals.
Pián also defeated two caves of local Man people allied with Nánzhào,
executed their chieftains,
and seventeen thousand local Man leaders and their followers surrendered.
14. In the eleventh month,
on the rénzǐ day,
a general amnesty was declared throughout the land.
An edict ordered the armies of Ānnán, Yǒngzhōu, and Xīchuān to each defend their own territories,
and not to attack Nánzhào further.
Liú Tóng was entrusted to explain this clearly.
If they could restore the old friendly relations,
all past matters would be overlooked.
15. The Jìnghǎi Army was established in Ānnán,
with Gāo Pián as its military governor.
From then until the Sòng dynasty,
Ānnán remained the Jìnghǎi Army military district.
The troubles in Ānnán had lasted nearly ten years,
and were only now pacified.
Pián built the city of Ānnán,
with a circumference of three thousand paces,
and constructed over four hundred thousand buildings.
16. In the twelfth month,
Xiájiásī sent General Yǐzhī Liánjǐ to present tribute,
requesting the dispatch of horses and saddles to welcome the envoy for conferring titles and asking for the calendar for the hài year.
This year was bǐngxū;
hài
refers to the next year.

Some urged Yǎn Céng to flee to Yǎnzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: From Xúzhōu north to Yǎnzhōu is 360 lǐ.
"I am the commander-in-chief,"
he said, "if the city falls, I die—
that is my duty!"
He immediately beheaded the speaker.
On the Dīngchǒu day,
the rebels reached the city walls.
Their forces numbered six or seven thousand men,
and their drumming and shouting shook the earth.
As for the common people living outside the city walls,
the rebels all comforted and pacified them,
committing no acts of plunder or harassment.
Consequently, people vied with each other to submit to them.
Before long,
they captured the outer city.
Yǎnzēng retreated to defend the inner city.
The outer city
refers to the large outer wall.
The inner city
refers to the small inner wall.
They pushed carts of straw to block the gates and set them on fire,
and the city fell.
An examination of discrepancies states: According to the Old Annals:
"In the ninth month,
on the Yǐwèi day,
Páng Xūn captured Xúzhōu,
killing the military governor Cuī Yǎnzēng, administrative assistant Jiāo Lù, and others.
The rebels ordered the deputy commander Liáng Pī to guard Sùzhōu,
and also dispatched Liú Xíngjí, Dīng Jǐngcóng, and Wú Jiǒng to attack and besiege Sìzhōu."
The present account follows the *Record of the Turmoil at Péngmén* and the New Annals.
The biography of Yǎnzēng in the Old History states:
"On the fourteenth day of the ninth month of the ninth year,
the rebels pressed upon Xúzhōu.
After the fifteenth day,
heavy fog occurred every morning.
On the sixteenth day,
Yǎnzēng executed the families of the rebellious soldiers.
On the seventeenth day,
the fog was especially thick at dusk,
and the rebels broke through the gates from all sides and entered."
The *Veritable Records*
places all events from after Xūn learned of the Xúzhōu troops' retreat to Fúlǐ
in the eleventh month.
The present account follows the *Record of the Turmoil at Péngmén*.
They captured Yǐn Kān, Dù Zhāng, and Xú Xíngjiǎn,
disemboweled and chopped them into pieces,
cutting open their bellies and chopping them into inch-long segments.
Xūn sat in the audience hall,
which was the official hall of the Xúzhōu observation commissioner.
The character "tīng"
is pronounced as "tīng" (hall).
Civil and military officials and officers prostrated themselves in audience,
none daring to look up.
That very day,
over ten thousand people in the city expressed their willingness to join and follow him.
On the Wùyín day,
Xūn summoned Wēn Tínghào,
ordering him to draft a memorial requesting the imperial insignia of authority.
Tínghào said:
"This matter is of great importance;
it cannot be accomplished in a moment.
I request to return home and draft it at leisure."
Xūn granted his request.
The next morning,
Xūn sent someone to urge him,
and Tínghào came to see Xūn, saying:
"The reason I did not refuse immediately yesterday
was because I wished to see my wife and children one last time.
Now that I have parted from my wife and children,
I have come respectfully to meet my death."
Xūn stared at him intently,
then laughed and said:
"A scholar dares to act like this—
are you not afraid of death?
Páng Xūn was able to capture Xúzhōu;
why worry about finding no one to draft a memorial!"
He then released him.
There was a man named Zhōu Zhòng,
who always prided himself on his talent and strategy.
Xūn welcomed him as a distinguished guest.
Zhòng drafted a memorial for Xūn,
which stated:
"My army
is located in the land where the Hàn dynasty's rise to kingship began.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn rose from Pèi.
In the Táng dynasty, Pèi County was part of Xúzhōu,
hence he referred to it to boast and exaggerate.
Punishments and rewards were improperly administered,
leading to the forced expulsion.
This means that the reason the soldiers expelled their commander
was entirely due to his own actions.
The extermination of an entire army
is recorded in the third year of the previous volume.
Innocent lives were unjustly taken beyond count.
Now, hearing that the local authorities intend to execute and exterminate us again,
the officers and soldiers are overwhelmed with grief and indignation.
They have provisionally appointed me as the military governor-in-waiting,
to control an army of a hundred thousand,
and pacify the lands of four prefectures.
I have heard that recognizing advantage and seizing opportunity
are the foundations of imperial rule.
I do not fail to recognize advantage,
nor do I hesitate when opportunity arises.
I humbly beg Your Majesty's graciousness
to bestow upon me once more the imperial insignia of authority.
Otherwise,
wielding spears and dragging halberds,
I shall march to the capital gates without delay!"
On the Gēngchén day,
he dispatched the officer Zhāng Guǎn to present the memorial at the capital.
Xūn appointed Xǔ Jí as the chief inspector,
Zhào Kělì as the chief patrol commissioner,
and assigned his followers to various military posts,
dividing command of the armies among them.
He also dispatched the former general Liú Xíngjí with fifteen hundred men to garrison Háozhōu,
Lǐ Yuán with two thousand men to garrison Sìzhōu,
and Liáng Pī with a thousand men to garrison Sùzhōu.
As for other crucial counties and towns,
he fully repaired and garrisoned their defenses.
The people of Xúzhōu believed that the imperial insignia of authority would arrive within a month or so,
and those willing to offer their services and strategies converged from near and far.
Even bandits from Guāng, Cài, Huái, Zhè, Yǎn, Yùn, Yí, and Mì
all rushed to join him by forced marches,
filling the outer city to overflowing.
Within ten days,
the price of a peck of rice reached two hundred cash.
Many people came to join the rebellion,
hence the price of rice soared.
The memorial roughly stated:
"The violent soldiers of one army
can all be exterminated;
the ignorant people of five counties
should each be assigned as bondsmen."
The five counties
refer to Péngchéng, Xiāo, Fēng, Pèi, and Téng.
In accordance with their request,
it was disseminated throughout the region.
The people of Xúzhōu believed it,
and all directed their resentment toward the imperial court,
saying:
"If not for the Guìzhōu officers and soldiers turning their weapons around,
we would all have been slaughtered like fish and meat!"
Liú Xíngjí led his troops to Wōkǒu.
From Wōkǒu to Háozhōu,
only the Huái River lay between.
The character "wō"
is pronounced "gē."
The troops in Háozhōu numbered only a few hundred,
and the prefect Lú Wànghuí had never made any preparations,
not knowing what to do.
So he opened the gates and prepared oxen and wine to welcome them.
Xíngjí entered the city,
imprisoned Wànghuí,
and assumed the duties of prefect himself.
An examination of discrepancies states: According to the Old Annals, the *Veritable Records*, and the New Annals,
the fall of Háozhōu occurred in the eleventh month.
However, Háozhōu was originally a subordinate prefecture of Xúzhōu.
As soon as Xūn captured Xúzhōu,
he dispatched Xíngjí to seize it.
Wànghuí had not yet had time to prepare,
so how could it have been as late as the eleventh month?
The present account follows the *Record of the Turmoil at Péngmén*.
They completed defensive preparations to await them
and also sought aid from Jiāngnán and Huáinán.
Lǐ Yuán dispatched a hundred elite soldiers to enter Sìzhōu first,
to seal the government storehouses.
Tāo sent people to welcome and console them,
lured them into the city,
and had them all executed.
The next day,
Yuán arrived,
immediately leading his troops to besiege the city.
Arrows and stones rained down from the city walls,
and several hundred rebels were killed.
They then gathered their troops and encamped west of the city.
Since Xūn considered Sìzhōu a crucial point between Jiāngnán and Huáinán,
he dispatched more troops to assist Yuán in attacking it.
Their numbers reached over ten thousand,
but they ultimately could not capture it.
The history here briefly mentions the final outcome;
the details of the events are elaborated below.
Earlier,
when the imperial court heard that Páng Xūn had turned back from Rènshān toward Sùzhōu,
they dispatched the high-ranking eunuch Kāng Dàowěi to deliver an imperial edict to pacify and console him.
In the eleventh month,
Dàowěi arrived at Péngchéng.
Xūn went out to the suburbs to welcome him.
From Rènshān to the inner city, a distance of thirty *li*,
he arrayed a grand display of armored troops.
The sounds of orders, gongs, and drums reverberated through the mountains and valleys.
All able-bodied men in the city
were driven to man the walls.
He feasted Dàowěi at the polo ground,
having several thousand people pretend to be bandits surrendering,
and dozens of messengers from various camps reporting victories.
He also composed another memorial requesting the imperial insignia of authority,
which he entrusted to Dàowěi to present to the court.
初，
辛雲京之孫讜，
辛雲京見二百二十二卷肅宗寶應二年。
讜，
多曩翻。
喜任俠，
年五十不仕；
與杜慆有舊，
聞龐勛作亂，
詣泗州，
勸慆挈家避之，
慆曰：
「安平享其祿位，
危難棄其城池，
吾不為也！
且人各有家，
誰不愛之？
我獨求生，
何以安衆！
誓與將士共死此城耳！ 」
讜曰：
「公能如是，
僕與公同死！ 」
乃還廣陵，
與其家訣，
壬辰 ，
復如泗州。
時民避亂，
扶老攜幼，
塞塗而來，
見讜，
皆止之曰：
「人皆南走，
子獨北行，
取死何為！ 」
讜不應。
至泗州，
賊已至城下，
讜急棹小舟得入，
慆即署團練判官。
城中危懼，
都押牙李雅有勇略，
為慆設守備，
帥衆鼓譟，
四出擊賊，
賊退屯徐城，
衆心稍安。
龐勛募人為兵，
人利於剽掠，
爭赴之，
至父遣其子，
妻勉其夫，
皆斷鉏首而銳之，
執以應募。
鄰道聞勛據徐州，
各遣兵據要害，
而官軍尚少，
賊衆日滋，
官軍數不利。
賊遂破魚臺近十縣。
宋州東有磨山，
民逃匿其上，
勛遣其將張玄稔圍之。
會旱，
山泉竭，
數萬口皆渴死。
或說勛曰：
「留後止欲求節鉞，
當恭順盡禮以事天子，
外戢士卒，
內撫百姓，
庶幾可得。 」
勛雖不能用，
然國忌猶行香，
唐自中世以後，
每國忌日，
令天下州府悉於寺觀設齋焚香。
開成初，
禮部侍郎崔蠡以其事無經，
據奏罷之，
尋而復舊。
畢仲荀幕府燕閒錄曰：國忌行香，
起於後魏。
唐會要曰：天寶七年，
敕華、同等州僧、尼、道士，
國忌日各就龍興寺行道散齋。
至貞元五年，
處州奏，
「當州不在行香之數，
乞同衢、婺等州行香。 」
有旨
註又見前。
凡方鎮大饗將士，
必朝服，
帥將佐西向望闕謝恩，
言皆出於君賜也。
癸卯
勛聞敕使入境，
以為必賜旌節，
衆皆賀。
明日，
敕使至，
但責崔彥曾及監軍張道謹，
貶其官。
勛大失望，
遂囚敕使，
不聽歸。
詔以右金吾大將軍康承訓為義成節度使、徐州行營都招討使，
神武大將軍王晏權為徐州北面行營招討使，
羽林將軍戴可師為徐州南面行營招討使，
考異曰：舊紀：
「十年正月，
以神武大將軍王晏權為武寧節度使。
晏權，
智興之從子也。
以右神策大將軍康承訓充徐泗行營都招討使，
凡十八將，
分董諸道之兵七萬三千一十五人。
正月一日，
進軍攻徐州。 」
又曰：
「承訓大軍攻宿州，
賊將梁伾出戰，
屢敗，
乃授承訓義成節度使。 」
實錄：
「九年十二月，
以右金吾大將軍康承訓為義成軍節度使、充徐泗行營兵馬都招討使。
承訓不赴鎮，
以節度副使陳魴句當留後，
以王晏權為徐、泗、濠、宿等州觀察使、充徐州北面行營招討等使，
羽林將軍戴可師為徐州南面行營招討等使。 」
彭門紀亂、新紀，
承訓等除招討使皆在十一月。
唐年補錄：
「十一月庚申 ，
以太原節度使康承訓為都統，
討徐州。 」
按庚申乃十二月一日，
承訓舊官亦非太原節度使。
補錄誤也。
今從彭門紀亂、新紀。
承訓奏乞沙陀三部落使朱邪赤心
沙陀、薩葛、安慶分為三部。
詔許之。
Páng Xūn, because Lǐ Yuán had long failed to capture Sìzhōu,
sent his general Wú Jiǒng to replace him.
On the bǐngwǔ day,
they again attacked Sìzhōu,
ceaselessly day and night.
At that time, the imperial envoy Guō Hòuběn
(Textual Analysis: The Old Annals and Veritable Records say
"Xī Hòuběn,"
but here we follow the Pénɡmén Jìluàn and the Old Biography.)
reached Hóngzé,
(Jiǔyù Zhì: Huáiyīn County of Chǔzhōu had a Hóngzé town.)
but dared not advance.
Xīn Dǎng requested to go and seek aid,
and Dù Tāo agreed.
On the dīngwèi night,
he took a small boat and secretly crossed the Huái River,
reaching Hóngzé,
where he tried to persuade Hòuběn,
but Hòuběn would not listen.
By dawn,
he returned again.
On the jǐyǒu day,
the rebels attacked the city even more fiercely,
intending to burn the water gate.
The city was almost unable to defend itself;
Dǎng requested to go again to seek aid.
Tāo said:
"You went before and returned in vain;
what good will it do to go now?"
Dǎng said:
"If I obtain troops on this trip, I will return alive;
if not, I will die there."
Tāo parted from him in tears.
Dǎng again took a small boat, carrying a door shield, and broke through the siege,
meeting Hòuběn,
and explaining the advantages and disadvantages to him.
Hòuběn was about to agree,
when the Huáinán capital commander Yuán Gōngbiàn said:
"The rebels' momentum is like this;
we fear we cannot even protect ourselves—
how can we spare the effort to save others!"
Dǎng drew his sword, glared at Gōngbiàn, and said:
"The rebels attack the city from a hundred directions;
it will fall any moment.
You have received an imperial edict to provide relief, yet you delay and do not advance—
is this not only betraying the state's grace above!
If Sìzhōu is not held,
then Huáinán will become a bandit's territory.
How could you survive alone then!
I should kill you first and then stop!"
He rose,
intending to strike him.
Hòuběn stood up,
embraced and stopped him,
and Gōngbiàn barely escaped.
Dǎng then turned to look toward Sìzhōu,
wailing bitterly all day long.
The soldiers all wept for him.
Hòuběn then agreed to give him five hundred men,
and asked the officers and soldiers,
who were all willing to go.
Dǎng prostrated himself,
kowtowing to thank the officers and soldiers,
then led them to the southern bank of the Huái River.
Seeing the rebels attacking the city,
a military officer said:
"The rebels' momentum seems to have already entered the city;
it would be better to turn back."
Fearing the rebels, he dared not advance the troops,
saying that returning the army would be more convenient for the matter.
Dǎng grabbed him by the topknot,
(Grab means to seize and hold.)
and the soldiers together tried to rescue him,
saying:
"He is a judge of fifteen hundred men;
you cannot kill him."
Dǎng said:
"Speaking recklessly before battle to confuse the masses—
he must not be spared!"
The crowd pleaded but could not persuade him,
so they tried to seize him together.
Dǎng was naturally very strong,
and the crowd could not take him from him.
Dǎng said:
"If the officers and soldiers just board the boats,
I will release this man."
The crowd rushed to board the boats,
and he then released him.
Any soldier who looked back
was beheaded.
He drove them to the north of the Huái River,
deployed the troops, and attacked the rebels.
Tāo deployed troops on the city walls to coordinate with them,
and the rebels were then defeated and fled.
They beat drums and shouted as they pursued them,
returning only at dusk.
Páng Xūn dispatched his general Liú
Jí to lead several thousand elite troops to assist Wú Jiǒng in attacking Sìzhōu.
Liú Xíngjí, from Háozhōu, sent his general Wáng Hónglì to lead troops to join them.
On the day Wùwǔ,
Dù Shěnquán, the Jìedùshǐ of Zhènhǎi,
(the Zhènhǎi army headquarters was in Rùnzhōu).
On the day Jǐwèi,
Xíngyuē led his troops to Sìzhōu.
The rebels intercepted and attacked them south of the Huái River,
surrounding them.
The troops in the city were few,
and could not rescue them.
Xíngyuē and his soldiers all perished.
Previously,
Línghú Táo had sent Lǐ Xiāng with several thousand troops to rescue Sìzhōu.
He joined forces with Guō Hòuběn and Yuán Gōngbiàn and encamped at Dūliáng Chéng.
Dūliáng Chéng
was located on Dūliáng Shān, north of Xūyí County in Sìzhōu.
Xiàng Ānshì said: Dūliáng County had a small hill,
where the water on the hill was extremely clear and shallow.
The entire hill produced láncǎo (orchid grass),
with green leaves and purple stems.
It was commonly called "dūliáng" for orchid,
hence the county was named after it.
After the rebels defeated Zhái Xíngyuē,
they took advantage of the victory to surround them.
In the twelfth month,
on the day Jiǎzǐ,
Lǐ Xiāng and others led their troops out to battle,
suffering a great defeat.
The rebels then captured Dūliáng Chéng,
seizing Lǐ Xiāng and Guō Hòuběn and sending them to Xúzhōu.
Textual analysis notes: The Old Annals state:
"In the tenth month,
as the rebel attack on Sìzhōu intensified,
Línghú Táo, fearing the loss of Sìkǒu,
ordered the senior general Lǐ Xiāng to go to its aid,
and the entire army was lost.
Lǐ Xiāng and the military supervisor Guō Hòuběn were both captured by the rebels,
and sent to Xúzhōu."
The Biography of Línghú Táo states:
"When the rebels heard Lǐ Xiāng was coming to aid,
they sent someone with a letter to Táo,
the wording of which was humble and submissive,
saying, 'The court has repeatedly issued edicts of pardon and amnesty,
it is only two or three individuals who are resisting,
we plan to remove them soon,
and then will submit ourselves and beg for our lives,
we hope the Grand Councilor will guarantee us.'
Táo immediately reported this to the court,
requesting that Páng Xūn be granted the symbols of authority (jiéyuè),
and instructed Lǐ Xiāng merely to garrison Huáikǒu,
as the rebels had already offered to surrender,
he must not act differently.
Consequently, Lǐ Xiāng's army removed their armor and rested peacefully,
abandoning alerts and defenses,
daily facing the rebel army,
laughing and conversing with them.
One day,
the rebel army seized an opportunity and their infantry and cavalry directly entered Lǐ Xiāng's camp.
Five thousand soldiers from Huái were all captured alive,
and sent to Xúzhōu,
where they were steamed and eaten by the rebels.
Lǐ Xiāng and the supervising army officer Guō Hòuběn had their hands and feet cut off by Páng Xūn,
and were displayed to Kāng Chéngxùn's army.
At that time, Dù Shěnquán of Zhèxī dispatched a thousand troops,
who had arranged to join forces with Lǐ Xiāng.
The senior general Zhái Xíngyuē was renowned for his bravery.
Before the Zhèxī army arrived, Lǐ Xiāng's army was defeated.
The rebels then divided their forces,
raised Huáinán banners,
creating the appearance of a battle,
Xíngyuē's army saw this,
hurried towards them,
and the thousand men were all captured by the rebels,
and sent to Xúzhōu.
After Táo lost his army,
the court appointed Mǎ Jǔ to replace Táo as the Huáinán Jìedùshǐ."
The Biography of Xīn Dǎng states:
"Lǐ Xiāng led five thousand men to come to the rescue,
the rebels feigned surrender,
(Lǐ Xiāng) was defeated at Huáikǒu,
Lǐ Xiāng and Guō Hòuběn were both captured by the rebels."
The Péngmén Jìluàn states:
"Because Sìzhōu held firm,
Páng Xūn sent Liú Jí to jointly plan an attack to capture it.
At that time, the three circuits of Huáinán, Xuān, and Rùn had dispatched troops to garrison the old city of Dūliáng Shān,
which was separated from Sìzhōu only by the Huái River.
The rebel forces then secretly crossed the Huái River by night,
and by dawn were pressing close to the city.
The rebel commander Liú Xíngjí from Háozhōu also sent Wáng Hónglì to raid Huáinán.
They then combined their forces for a fierce attack,
and the government troops abandoned the city to come out and fight.
On the thirtieth day of the eleventh month,
the rebels heavily defeated the government army,
killing two thousand men,
capturing alive seven or eight hundred,
and also seizing their general Lǐ Xiāng and others,
all of whom were sent to Xúzhōu.
The rebels then occupied Huáikǒu,
cutting off the courier route."
It also says:
"After the rebels defeated Dài Kěshī,
Línghú Táo became fearful,
and sent an envoy to entice and persuade them,
promising to memorialize the court requesting the symbols of authority for them."
The Xù Huángwáng Bǎoyùn Lù states:
"On the twenty-ninth day of the eleventh month,
Dù Shěnquán, Jìedùshǐ of Zhèxī, sent the Dūtóu Zhái Xíngyuē with two thousand troops to rescue them.
On the thirtieth,
as Xíngyuē was leading his troops intending to enter Sìzhōu,
he was again rushed upon by the rebels.
Xíngyuē occupied a hill,
but was soon completely surrounded.
The soldiers in the city could not come out to rescue him.
The rebels then opened the encirclement,
Xíngyuē, not realizing it was a trick,
tried to flee and leave,
but ran into the ambush troops at the foot of the hill.
In a short time he was killed,
not a single horse remained.
The rebels then surrounded the Huáikǒu garrison.
The Huáinán Dūyāyá Lǐ Xiāng and garrison commander Yuán Gōngbiàn, leading three thousand infantry and cavalry, were surrounded.
From the thirtieth day of the eleventh month to the fifth day of the twelfth month,
Lǐ Xiāng donned his armor and led the army out,
but they were ambushed and all killed.
Those who retreated back into the garrison
were made to raise a surrender flag.
Over ten thousand soldiers, elderly, and children within the garrison
were seized and driven to Háozhōu.
Guō Hòuběn was killed at this time."
I now follow the Xù Bǎoyùn Lù.
(Huáikǒu is) the mouth where the Sìshuǐ enters the Huái.
This means the route for southeastern water transport and courier stations to the capital was cut off.
Kāng Chéngxùn stationed his army at Xīnxīng.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Xīnxīng Town was in Nínglíng County of Sòng Prefecture.

Fāngchéng,

He had no time to eat or drink,
and upon reaching Qí,
Qí,
an ancient county from the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
was established as Qiáo Commandery during the Sòng,
and became Běiqiáo Commandery during the Qí.
At that time, it was a county
under Sùzhōu.
Commentary: According to the "Jiǔyù Zhì," it is 36 lǐ south of the prefecture.
Lǐ Gǔn destroyed the bridge,
and deployed troops to resist them.
The rebels were bewildered and did not know where to go.
When they reached west of the county,
government troops gathered in large numbers,
launched an attack,
killing nearly ten thousand rebels,
while the rest drowned.
Only about a thousand surrendered.
Xūn also died, but no one recognized him.
Several days later,
his corpse was recovered.
Commentary: The "Péngmén Jì Luàn" states:
"Initially,
when Páng Xūn sought an official appointment,
he hoped to obtain it within the year.
Thus, children in the villages competed to sing: 'Whether he gets the appointment or not,
it will not go beyond the twelfth month.'
Páng Xūn rebelled on the seventeenth day of the tenth month of the ninth year,
and was executed on the nineteenth day of the ninth month of the tenth year.
Including the intercalary month,
it was exactly one year before his defeat."
Commentary: On the sixth day,
Chéng Xùn learned that Xūn was plundering Bózhōu and Sòngzhōu,
and immediately pursued him,
catching up with him at Qí County.
It is likely that this did not occur on the nineteenth day,
but rather on the ninth day.
The "New Annals" record
that on the Guǐyǒu day of the ninth month,
Páng Xūn was executed.
This follows the "Péngmén Jì Luàn."
Sùqiān
was originally Sùyù County during the Jìn dynasty.
To avoid the taboo of Emperor Dàizōng's name during the Táng,
it was renamed Sùqiān,
and placed under Xúzhōu,
located 180 lǐ southeast of Xiàpī.
Wú Jiǒng alone held Háozhōu and did not surrender.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Zhāng Xuánrěn was appointed Right Commander of the Rapid as Tigers Guard and Grand Master of Remonstrance.
Mǎ Jǔ attacked Háozhōu,
but from summer to winter, he could not capture it.
The city ran out of food,
and the defenders resorted to cannibalism.
The government troops dug deep trenches and surrounded the city tightly.
On the Xīnchǒu night,
Wú Jiǒng broke through the siege and fled.
Jǔ led his troops in pursuit,
killing or capturing nearly all of them.
Jiǒng died in Zhāoyì.
Kāng Chéngxùn was appointed Military Commissioner of Hédōng and Concurrently Manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery.
Dù Tāo was appointed Military Commissioner of Yìchéng.
The emperor praised Zhūyé Chìxīn for his achievements,
established the Dàtóng Army in Yúnzhōu,
and appointed Chìxīn as its Military Commissioner.
During the Huìchāng era,
a Dàtóng Army Training Commissioner had already been established in Yúnzhōu.
It was later made a defense command,
and now it was elevated to a military prefecture.
He was retained as Grand General of the Left Imperial Guard,
granted the surname Lǐ and the personal name Guóchāng.
Later, Lǐ Guóchāng and his son eventually raised troops in Yúnzhōu,
likely because they were soon sent back to govern the prefecture.
Commentary: The "Old History" states: Chìxīn was granted the surname and name,
and was registered under the lineage of the Prince of Zhèng.
See
Xián Biàn's annotation.
Xīn Dǎng was appointed Prefect of Bózhōu.
While in Sìzhōu,
Dǎng had broken through the siege to welcome troops and supplies,
making twelve round trips in total.
Upon his appointment to Bózhōu,
he submitted a memorial stating:
"My achievements
would not have been possible without Dù Tāo!"
Cuī Yōng, Prefect of Hézhōu, was ordered to commit suicide,
for opening the city gates to the rebels.
Commentary: The "Old Annals" record:
"In the eighth month,
Shí Móu and others, defense officials of Hézhōu, accused Yōng of crimes.
That month,
he was ordered to commit suicide."
The "Veritable Records" place the accusation in the eighth month,
and the order to commit suicide in the tenth month.
I follow this.
His five brothers were all exiled to distant places.
16 The emperor indulged in feasting and pleasure,
neglecting government affairs,
and entrusted power to Lù Yán.
Yán was extravagant and wasteful,
accepted many bribes,
and his associates wielded power.
Chén Pánsǒu, Magistrate of Zhìdé, submitted a memorial and was summoned for an audience.
Commentary: In the first year of the Zhìdé era of Emperor Sùzōng,
Zhìdé County was established from parts of Póyáng and Qiūpǔ,
and placed under Ráozhōu.
"If we confiscate the property of Biān Xián's family alone,
it could sustain the army for two years."
The emperor asked:
"Who is Xián?"
He replied:
"He is a close subordinate of Lù Yán."
The emperor was enraged,
and exiled Pánsǒu to Àizhōu.
From then on, no one dared to speak out.
17 Initially,
Nánzhào sent an envoy, Yáng Qiúqìng, to thank the court for releasing Dǒng Chéng from imprisonment.
Commentary: The release of Dǒng Chéng is recorded in the seventh year of the previous scroll.
However, they killed Qiúqìng.
The senior generals of Xīchuān resented Lǐ Shīwàng for dividing the administrative regions,
referring to the separation of Qiōng, Xī, and other prefectures from Xīchuān to establish the Dìngbiān Army,
as recorded in the sixth month of the ninth year of the previous scroll.
They incited the barbarians to invade.
Shīwàng was greedy and cruel,
amassing private wealth amounting to millions.
The garrison troops were resentful and angry,
wishing to eat him alive,
but Shīwàng managed to escape by stratagem.
The court recalled him,
and appointed Dòu Pāng, Junior Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury, to replace him.
Pāng was even more greedy and cruel than Shīwàng,
so even before the barbarian invasion arrived,
Dìngbiān was already in dire straits.
In this month,
the Nánzhào king Piàoxìn Qiúlóng launched a full-scale invasion,
leading tens of thousands of troops to attack the Dǒng Chūnwū tribe,
and defeated them.
The Dǒng Chūnwū tribe
were Mán people attached to the frontier of Xīchuān.
The Mán advanced and invaded Xīzhōu.
Ān Zàiróng, the Dìngbiān capital commander, defended Qīngxī Pass.
The Mán attacked him,
and Zàiróng retreated and stationed north of the Dàdù River,
where they faced each other across the water, shooting arrows
for nine days and eight nights.
The Mán secretly divided their army and opened
a path,
crossed Xuěpō,
and suddenly arrived at Mùyuán River.
Xuěpō
is the slope of Xuělǐng.
Mùyuán River lies within the boundaries of Luómù County in Jiāzhōu.
In the second year of the Líndé era,
they opened up the territory of the raw Lǎo people,
and established Luómù County and Mùzhōu.
Later, Mùzhōu was abolished,
and Luómù was placed under Jiāzhōu.
In the Sòng dynasty, Luómù was further abolished and made a town,
belonging to Éméi County.
Also, today in Qiánwéi County of Jiāzhōu, there is Mùchuān Town.
The entire army was annihilated.
In the twelfth month,
on Dīngyǒu,
the Mán dressed in the clothing of Yǎnhǎi,
pretending to be defeated soldiers,
reached the riverbank and called for boats.
Once they had crossed,
the crowd then realized it,
and they subsequently captured Qiánwéi,
unleashing their troops to burn and plunder the territories of Líng and Róng prefectures.
Qiánwéi,
a commandery name from the Hàn,
was established as Wǔyáng County in the Later Zhōu,
and in the early Kāihuáng era of the Suí,
was renamed Qiánwéi,
named after the mountain.
In the Táng, it belonged to Jiāzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is 120 lǐ southeast of the prefecture.
Qián
is pronounced as jiān.
The Mán army gathered in large numbers at Língyún Temple,
which faced Jiāzhōu across the river.
Jiāzhōu
was the territory of Nán'ān County in the Hàn's Qiánwéi Commandery.
Emperor Wǔ of the Liáng opened up the outer frontier,
established Qīngzhōu,
taking Qīngyī as its name.
The Western Wèi changed Qīngzhōu to Méizhōu,
taking Éméi Mountain as its name.
The Later Zhōu again called it Qīngzhōu,
and then changed it to Jiāzhōu,
taking the Hàn's Jiājiā Commandery as its name.
The Suí again changed it to Méizhōu,
and the Táng restored it as Jiāzhōu,
separately establishing Méizhōu in the territory of the Hàn's Wǔyáng County.
Língyún Temple is on the southern mountain of Jiāzhōu.
During the Kāiyuán era,
the monk Hǎitōng, at the confluence of the Dú River, Mòshuǐ, and Méngshuǐ—the three rivers,
beside the fierce currents and raging waves,
carved the mountain into a great statue of Maitreya,
over 360 chǐ tall,
and built a seven-story pavilion to cover it.
They joined with Zhāng Yǔnqióng, the Dìngbiān army supervisor, in leading troops to resist them.
The Mán secretly dispatched surprise troops to cross from Dōngjīn,
attacking the government forces from both sides,
killing Yán Qìngshī, the Zhōngwǔ capital general,
and the remaining troops all fled,
while Mǐn and Yǔnqióng escaped with their lives.
On Rénzǐ,
they captured Jiāzhōu.
Qìngshī
was the younger brother of Qìngfù.
Dòu Pāng personally led troops to resist the Mán at the Dàdù River.
The Piàoxìn deceitfully sent several Qīngpíngguān to Pāng to negotiate peace.
Before Pāng had finished speaking with them,
the Mán, using boats and rafts, vied to cross.
The Zhōngwǔ and Xúsù armies formed battle arrays to resist them.
Xúsù,
formerly the Wǔníng Army,
because its troops repeatedly rebelled,
had its military governorship abolished.
Chén
is read as zhèn.
He attempted to hang himself in his tent.
Miáo Quánxù, a general from Xúzhōu, released him,
saying:
"Commander, why go to this extent!"
Quánxù, together with Ān Zàiróng and the Zhōngwǔ general, led troops out to fight,
and Pāng then fled alone on horseback at night.
The three generals plotted, saying:
"Now we are outnumbered and cannot match the enemy.
If we fight again tomorrow morning,
we will all perish.
It would be better to attack them under cover of night,
causing them panic and chaos,
and then withdraw."
Thereupon, they entered the Mán camp at night,
firing bows and crossbows wildly.
The Mán were greatly alarmed,
and the three generals then led their entire army away.
The Mán advanced and captured Lí and Yǎ,
the people fleeing and hiding in the mountains and valleys,
while the defeated troops burned and plundered wherever they were.
Pāng fled to Dǎojiāng.
Dǎojiāng
was originally Dū'ān County established by Liú Shǔ,
later changed to Wènshān by the Later Zhōu,
and renamed Dǎojiāng in the Táng,
belonging to Péngzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is 90 lǐ west of the prefecture.
When the Mán arrived,
the city was already empty,
and they passed through without hindrance.
An examination of discrepancies: Zhāng Yún's Xián Tōng Jiě Wéi Lù states:
"In the tenth year,
tenth month,
the Nán Mán masses attacked the Dǒng Chūnwū tribe,
overturning their nest and den.
Chūnwū defended the northern stockade with his people.
Soon after, the Mán suddenly arrived at Mùyuán River,
then pressed on to Jiāzhōu,
and from the south, via Qīngxī Pass, invaded Lí and Yǎ."
Zhāng Jǐn's Lǐ Qí Jiù Chuán states:
"In the eleventh year,
on Gēngyín,
the military governor Lǔ Púshè Dān.
In winter,
tens of thousands of Yúnnán Mán invaded the border,
broke through Qīngxī Pass,
attacked the Dàdù River,
then advanced and captured Shěnlí,
burst into Qiónglái,
and went straight to Yǎ and Qióng."
According to the Jiě Wéi Lù, the new and old annals all place it in the tenth year winter,
when the Mán invaded;
but this alone places it in the eleventh year winter,
which is an error.
The new biography states:
"In the tenth year,
they then invaded,
using troops to pin down Qīngxī Pass,
secretly leading the masses to cut trees and open a path,
going directly via Xuěpō.
In midsummer,
2,000 soldiers died from the cold,
and they emerged at Mùyuán,
to spy on Jiāzhōu."
According to this, the Mán reached Mùyuán River in the eleventh month,
not midsummer,
so the new biography is in error.
The Shílù also states:
"The Piàoxìn left Shànchǎn on the third day of the tenth month,
each man only carrying one dǒu of fried rice with him.
An edict was then issued ordering Gāo Pián to take advantage of their country being without military preparations,
to attack Shànchǎn,
in order to relieve the conflict."
According to this, Pián was at that time the military governor of Yùnzhōu,
not in Ānnán,
so the Shílù is likely in error.
An edict ordered Yán Qìngfù, General of the Left Shénwǔ Army, to lead troops to assist.
