Sīmǎ Guāng
Compiled by Imperial Command
Later Student Tiān Tái
The eleventh year of the Xián Tōng era
(Gēngyín, 870)
1 Spring,
first month,
on Jiǎyín, the first day,
the assembled ministers presented the honorific title "Emperor of Profound Literature, Martial Prowess, Illustrious Virtue, Ultimate Benevolence, Great Sage, and Vast Filial Piety";
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
2 The people of Xīchuān, hearing that the Mán invaders were about to arrive,
rushed to enter Chéngdū.
At that time, Chéngdū only had the inner city,
and no moat either.
The space each person occupied
was no more than about a mat's worth.
When it rained, they wore bamboo hats and earthenware basins for shelter;
moreover, water was scarce,
so they took mud from the Móhē Pond,
let it settle, and drank it.
The Chéngdū Records state: Móhē Pond is located within the inner city built by Zhāng Yí.
Suí dynasty Prince of Shǔ, Xiù, took earth to expand the inner city,
and thus a pond was formed.
A foreign monk saw it and said:
"Móhē gōng pí luó."
It seems the foreign monk considered
"Móhē"
to mean great,
and "gōng pí luó"
to mean dragon,
meaning this pond was vast and had a dragon.
Hence it was named Móhē Pond.
Some say it was dug by Xiāo Móhē,
but that is incorrect.
The pond is now located twelve lǐ southeast of Chéngdū County.
The officers and soldiers were not accustomed to military preparations.
The military governor Lú Dān summoned Wú Xínglǔ, the prefect of Péngzhōu, to act as staff officer,
and together with the former prefect of Lúzhōu, Yáng Qìngfù
Textual Analysis says: The New History states
"Lúzhōu prefect Yáng Qìng".
The Old Tales of Jǐnlǐ states
"Jiāzhōu",
which is an error.
We now follow the Record of the Siege Lifted.
They selected officers,
assigned duties,
erected defensive sheds,
prepared catapults and rolling logs,
manufactured weapons and equipment,
and enforced strict patrols and alerts.
Previously,
many officers in Xīchuān held nominal titles,
and received no salaries either.
At this time,
notices were posted recruiting brave and valiant men,
filling positions with actual duties,
and providing generous rations and rewards.
Responders gathered like clouds.
Qìngfù then instructed them, saying:
"You are all sons of the army,
young, talented, and brave.
In ordinary times, you had no way to advance yourselves.
Now the Mán invaders are encroaching upon us,
this is your season to gain wealth and honor.
Can you not strive hard!"
All cheered and leapt with enthusiasm.
Then they arrayed weapons in the courtyard,
had each man demonstrate his abilities,
pitted them in pairs to compete for victory,
observed their bravery or timidity to promote or demote them,
and thus selected three thousand soldiers,
named them
"the Assault Corps".
Xínglǔ
was a man of Péngzhōu.
On the Wùwǔ day,
the Mán reached Méizhōu.
Dān sent Deputy Military Governor Wáng Yǎn and others bearing a letter to meet their minister in power, Dù Yuánzhōng,
to negotiate peace with him.
The Mán replied:
"Our movements
depend entirely on your noble sentiments."
3 Lù Yán and Wéi Bǎohéng memorialized:
"When Kāng Chéngxùn campaigned against Páng Xūn,
he delayed and did not advance,
nor did he completely eliminate the remaining rebels,
moreover, he was greedy for spoils,
and did not report achievements promptly."
On the Xīnyǒu day,
he was demoted to Tutor to the Prince of Shǔ, with an assignment to the Eastern Capital branch of the government;
the Prince of Shǔ, Jí,
was an imperial prince.
Textual Analysis says: The New History states:
"Chief Ministers Lù Yán and Wéi Bǎohéng impeached Chéngxùn for delaying during the campaign against the rebels,
being greedy for spoils,
and not reporting achievements promptly,
demoting him to Tutor to the Prince of Shǔ, assigned to the Eastern Capital branch."
However, at this time Bǎohéng was not yet Chief Minister.
Probably because he was married to a princess,
the Emperor heeded his words,
hence he was able to push Chéngxùn aside.
4 Nánzhào advanced its army to Xīnjīn.
Xīnjīn,
was Wǔyáng County in Hàn times,
later changed to Xīnjīn in the Later Zhōu,
and belonged to Shǔzhōu in Táng.
The Nine Regions Gazetteer: It is seventy lǐ southeast of the prefecture.
Lú Dān sent Deputy Military Governor Tán Fèngsì to deliver a letter to Dù Yuánzhōng,
inquiring about the reason for their coming;
the Mán detained him and did not let him return.
Dān sent a messenger to urgently report to the court,
and requested to send an envoy to make peace,
to alleviate the immediate crisis.
The court appointed Zhī Sìfāngguǎn Shì, Grand Minister of the Imperial Stud, Zhī Xiáng, as the Commissioner for Proclamation and Peace Negotiations.
Yàn Gōng's Categorized Essentials states: According to old protocol,
among the Tōngshì Shèrén,
the most senior one was appointed to oversee the affairs of the guesthouse,
called the Host of the Guesthouse.
All tributes and memorials from the four quarters were received and presented by him.
From the mid-Táng period onward,
officials from other posts began to be appointed to manage the affairs of the Sìfāngguǎn.
They also delayed for him,
and thus Chéngdū's defenses became roughly complete.
On the Jiǎzǐ day,
the Mán drove northward in full force,
capturing Shuāngliú.
Shuāngliú,
was the territory of Guǎngdū County in Hàn times,
established as Shuāngliú County in Suí,
and belonged to Chéngdū Prefecture in Táng.
The Nine Regions Gazetteer: It is forty lǐ south of the prefecture.
On the Gēngwǔ day,
Dān sent Deputy Military Governor Liǔ Pán to see them.
Dù Yuánzhōng handed Pán a document,
saying:
"This is the protocol for the meeting between the Piàoxìn and the military governor's headquarters after peace is established."
The protocol presumed the status of a king for themselves,
and the language was extremely arrogant.
They also sent men carrying colored curtains to the south of the city,
saying they intended to set them up in the Shǔ Prince's Hall to house the Piàoxìn.
When Suí dynasty Prince of Shǔ, Xiù, governed Shǔ,
he built an audience hall,
which was extremely magnificent.
Hall,
is pronounced tīng.
On the Guǐyǒu day,
the Dìngbiān Army was abolished,
and the seven prefectures were returned to Xīchuān.
The seven prefectures
are Qióng, Méi, Shǔ, Yǎ, Jiā, Lí, and Xī.
On that day,
the Mán army reached the walls of Chéngdū.
The day before,
Lú Dān had sent Vanguard Patrol Commander Wáng Zhòu to Hànzhōu to scout for the relief army,
and to urge them on.
At that time, six thousand men from Xīngyuán and four thousand from Fèngxiáng had already reached Hànzhōu.
Meanwhile, Dòu Pāng, with four thousand men from Zhōngwǔ, Yìchéng, and Xú-Sù, fled from Dǎojiāng to Hànzhōu,
joining the relief army for his own survival.
On the Dīngchǒu day,
Wáng Zhòu, with over three thousand troops from Xīngyuán, Zī, and Jiǎn, encamped at Píqiáo.
Píqiáo
is on the southern border of Hànzhōu.
Engaging in battle, they fared poorly,
and retreated to defend Hànzhōu.
At that time, Chéngdū daily hoped for the arrival of the relief army.
But Dòu Pāng, considering he had lost territory,
meaning he lost the Dìngbiān Army,
whenever a relief force arrived from the north,
would persuade them, saying:
"The Mán multitude outnumbers the imperial troops by several tens of times.
The imperial troops have come from afar, weary and exhausted,
and cannot easily advance hastily."
The various generals believed him,
and all hesitated and did not advance.
A minor officer of Chéngdū, Lǐ Zìxiào, secretly communicated with the Mán,
intending to burn the eastern granary as an inside response.
He was captured in the city and killed.
Several days later,
the Mán indeed attacked the city.
After a long while,
with no response from within the city,
they stopped.
In the second month,
on the first day, guǐwèi,
the Man tribes combined ladders and battering rams to attack Chéngdū from all sides.
On the city walls, they used hooks and loops to pull them close.
Tī refers to
scaling ladders;
chōng refers to
battering rams.
Huán,
pronounced yú shàn fān,
means bending the rope into a looped hook,
attached to its end.
All the attackers were killed.
Lú Dān ordered Yáng Qìngfù and acting Left Capital Commander Lǐ Xiāng to each lead assault troops out to fight,
killing or wounding over two thousand Man tribesmen.
As dusk fell,
they burned over three thousand of the enemy's siege equipment and returned.
The people of Shǔ were naturally timid,
but the assault troops had recently been encouraged and promoted by Qìngfù,
and were also motivated by generous rewards,
so their courage doubled.
Those who could not go out to fight
were all indignant and eager to exert themselves.
A few days later,
the enemy took bamboo fences from the people,
piled them up, soaked them, and bent them
to make shelters,
placing men underneath,
lifting them to the city walls to dig through.
Arrows and stones could not penetrate,
and fire could not burn them.
Rán
is the same as rán,
meaning to burn.
The attackers were again killed.
On the third day, yǐyǒu,
Zhī Xiáng sent an envoy to negotiate peace with the Man tribes.
On the fifth day, dīnghài,
the Man tribes gathered their troops and requested peace.
On the sixth day, wùzǐ,
they sent an envoy to welcome Zhī Xiáng.
At that time, Yán Qìngfù was about to arrive with reinforcements,
so Xiáng said to the Man envoy:
"I received an edict to go to Dìngbiān to negotiate peace,
but now Yúnnán is besieging Chéngdū,
which differs from the previous imperial decree.
Moreover, the reason the court seeks peace
is in the hope that they will not attack Chéngdū.
Now arrows and stones are exchanged day and night—
how can this be called peace!"
When the Man tribes saw that the peace envoy did not arrive,
on the eighth day, gēngyín,
they resumed their attack on the city.
On the ninth day, xīnmǎo,
troops from the city went out to attack them,
and they retreated.
Earlier,
Wéi Gāo recruited Nánzhào to defeat Tǔbō.
Later, the Man tribes complained about lacking armor and crossbows,
so Gāo sent craftsmen to teach them.
After a few years,
the armor and crossbows among the Man tribes became excellent.
Also,
the three eastern Man tribes—Jū Nàshí, Wù Dèng, and Mèng Chōng—assisted Gāo in defeating Tǔbō and made contributions.
This matter is recorded in the 233rd volume, in the fifth year of Emperor Dézōng's Xīngyuán reign.
The eastern Man tribes deeply resented the Táng,
so they attached themselves to Nánzhào,
often following Nánzhào on invasions,
exerting their utmost efforts,
and when they captured Táng people,
they all tortured and killed them.
The court demoted Dòu Pāng to Kāngzhōu Registrar,
appointed Yán Qìngfù as Military Governor of Dōngchuān,
and placed all troops sent to aid Shǔ
under Qìngfù's command.
On the eleventh day, guǐsì,
Qìngfù arrived at Xīndū.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: Xīndū County is located forty-five lǐ north of Chéngdū Prefecture.
On the twelfth day, jiǎwǔ,
he encountered the Man army,
and Qìngfù heavily defeated the Man troops,
killing over two thousand men.
Several thousand Shǔ civilians vied to wield sickles and wooden clubs to assist the government troops,
their shouts shaking the wilderness.
On the thirteenth day, yǐwèi,
tens of thousands of Man infantry and cavalry returned.
At that time, Right Guard General-in-Chief Sòng Wēi arrived with two thousand Zhōngwǔ troops,
and immediately joined the other armies in battle.
The Man army was heavily defeated,
with over five thousand dead,
and retreated to defend Xīngxiù Mountain.
Wēi advanced his troops to Tuójiāng Station.
Tuójiāng Station
is located in Xīnfán County, Chéngdū Prefecture.
According to the Yǔgòng,
the Jiāng originates from Mínshān,
and branches off to form the Tuó.
Tuó
is pronounced tú hé fān.
The Man tribes sent their minister Yáng Dìngbǎo to Zhī Xiáng to request peace.
Xiáng said:
"You should first lift the siege and withdraw your troops."
Dìngbǎo returned,
but the Man tribes continued the siege as before.
The people in the city did not know that reinforcements had arrived,
but seeing the enemy repeatedly request peace,
they realized the reinforcements must be winning.
On the sixteenth day, wùxū,
the Man tribes again requested peace,
with envoys going back and forth ten times.
The city also gave ambiguous replies.
The Man tribes, knowing reinforcements were nearby,
attacked the city even more urgently,
with the Piàoxìn and others personally standing amidst arrows and stones.
On the eighteenth day, gēngzǐ,
government troops arrived at the city and fought the Man tribes,
capturing their Shēngqiān Bridge.
Shēngqiān Bridge
is also known as Shēngxiān Bridge.
It was originally built by Lǐ Bīng during the Qín period,
and was formerly called Qīxīng Bridge.
The Man tribes burned their own siege equipment and fled.
By dawn,
the government troops realized it.
Earlier,
the court had sent Yán Qìngfù to rescue Chéngdū,
ordering Sòng Wēi to station at Mián and Hàn as backup.
Mián and Hàn
are the names of two prefectures.
Wēi contributed greatly to defeating the Man army,
which made Qìngfù jealous.
Wēi fed his troops and wanted to pursue the Man army,
and the soldiers in the city also wanted to join forces with the northern troops to advance together.
However, Qìngfù sent an order to Wēi,
taking away his command,
and forcing him to return to Hànzhōu.
When the Man tribes reached Shuāngliú,
they were blocked by the newly dug river.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: Xīnjīn County in Shǔ Prefecture has a Xīnchuān Town.
They were in disarray and lost their composure.
"Lost their composure" means
they lost their usual demeanor.
After a bridge was built,
they managed to cross,
then destroyed the bridge and left.
Weapons, armor, and supplies were abandoned along the road,
much to the regret of the Shǔ people.
Lízhōu Prefect Yán Shīběn gathered several thousand scattered troops to defend Qiōngzhōu.
The Man tribes besieged it,
but after two days,
failed to capture it,
and also abandoned the siege and left.
Yán Qìngfù then taught the people of Shǔ to build yōngmén walls.
Outside the city gates,
additional walls were built to shield the gates,
called yōngmén,
which people today call "eight trigrams walls."
They also planted deer antlers,
and divided into camps and posts.
They cut wood into deer antlers,
planted them outside the city,
to hinder assaults,
which people today call "pái chà."
They set up separate barracks,
called camps,
to house soldiers.
On the city walls, small huts were built,
where guards stayed to keep watch,
called posts.
Pù
is pronounced pǔ gù fān.
From then on, they no longer attacked Chéngdū.
Previously,
officers in the Western Chuān army had duties but no official titles.
After repelling Nánzhào,
four of them were awarded the title of Investigating Censor for their merits,
which is what is meant by "official titles."
Each person had to pay three hundred strings of cash as a hall fee;
the poor suffered greatly from this.
Being awarded an official title for merit but being forced to pay money—
the historian notes that Táng's discipline was severely corrupted.
5 In the third month,
Left Vice Director and Tongpingzhangshi Cáo Què was appointed Tongpingzhangshi
and Military Governor of Zhènhǎi.
6 In the summer,
fourth month,
on the twenty-fourth day, bǐngwǔ,
Hànlín Academician Recipient of Edicts and Vice Minister of War Wéi Bǎohéng was appointed Tongpingzhangshi.
7 Remnants of the Xú rebels still gathered in villages to commit banditry,
scattered across Yǎn, Yùn, Qīng, and Qí.
An edict ordered Xúzhōu Observer Xiàhóu Tóng to recruit and persuade them.
8 In the fifth month,
on the twenty-sixth day, dīngchǒu,
Qiōngzhōu Prefect Wú Xínglǔ was appointed Acting Military Governor of Western Chuān.
9 The people of Guāngzhōu expelled Governor Lǐ Ruòwēng,
and Ruòwēng fled to Xīnxì.
Xīnxì,
an ancient county from the Hàn dynasty,
was under Càizhōu in the Táng dynasty.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: It is located 155 lǐ southeast of the prefecture,
and 90 lǐ from Guāngzhōu.
"If a governor is unprincipled,
and the people suffer injustice,
they should appeal to the imperial court,
so that he may be dealt with according to the law.
How can they gather in factions,
take matters into their own hands and expel him,
disrupting the distinction between superior and subordinate!
This trend must not be allowed to grow;
severe punishment should be imposed to serve as a warning for the future."
10 The Emperor ordered all officials to discuss the appropriate arrangements for Xúzhōu.
In the sixth month,
on Bǐngwǔ,
Tàizǐ Shǎofù Lǐ Jiāo and others submitted a memorial stating:
"Although Xúzhōu has repeatedly been the source of turmoil and rebellion,
referring to the Silver Sabre and the Guìzhōu garrison soldiers.
This was due to improper leadership and control,
which allowed treacherous elements to seize the opportunity.
Now, although its official title has been downgraded,
referring to the downgrade from military governor to observation commissioner.
Shǐ,
Shūlì fān.
If it is made a subordinate prefecture, then military provisions will be insufficient;
if it is placed under another commandery, the people's hearts will not submit.
Perhaps old grievances will combine,
leading to even greater turmoil.
Only Sìzhōu, due to past attacks and defenses,
has formed deep enmity,
as seen in the ninth and tenth years of the previous volume.
This would likely be mutually beneficial."
An edict followed this recommendation.
Xúzhōu remained an observation commissioner,
governing Xú, Háo, and Sù prefectures.
Sìzhōu was made a defense commissioner,
and placed under Huáinán.
11 Yōuzhōu military governor Zhāng Yǔnshēn was additionally appointed Shìzhōng.
12 In autumn,
the eighth month,
on Yǐwèi,
Princess Tóngchāng passed away.
The Emperor was endlessly grief-stricken,
and had over twenty Hanlin medical officials, including Hán Zōngshào, executed.
He also arrested over three hundred of their relatives and imprisoned them in the Jīngzhào jail.
Zhōngshū Shìláng, Tóng Píngzhāng Shì Liú Zhān summoned the remonstrance officials and urged them to speak out,
but none dared.
So he submitted a memorial himself, stating:
"The length of one's life is predetermined by fate.
Previously, when the Princess was ill,
Your Majesty's compassion was deeply moved.
When Zōngshào and others were diagnosing and treating her,
they sought only her recovery,
employing all possible methods and techniques.
They were not lacking in diligence,
yet fortune and misfortune are difficult to alter,
and ultimately a misstep occurred.
Considering their circumstances,
they are also deserving of pity.
Yet over three hundred people, old and young, have been shackled and imprisoned.
Public opinion is seething,
and there is lamentation on the roads.
How can a ruler who understands principle and knows fate
incur the slander of being violent and unreasonable!
This is likely due to complacency without considering danger,
and anger without considering difficulty.
I humbly beg Your Majesty to reconsider slightly,
and leniently release those imprisoned."
The Emperor read the memorial
and was displeased.
Zhān, together with Jīngzhào Yǐn Wēn Zhāng, forcefully remonstrated before the Emperor;
the Emperor was greatly angered
and shouted at them to leave.
13 Wèibó military governor Hé Quánhào was young,
arrogant, violent, and fond of killing,
and also reduced the clothing and grain rations of the officers and soldiers.
The officers and soldiers mutinied,
Quánhào fled alone on horseback,
and they pursued and killed him.
Hé Jìntāo obtained Wèibó,
which was passed down for three generations,
lasting forty-two years before its demise.
Chéngdé military governor Wáng Jǐngchóng petitioned for an appointment;
in the ninth month,
on Gēngxū,
Jūnxióng was appointed Wèibó Liúhòu.
14 On Bǐngchén,
Liú Zhān was appointed Tóng Píngzhāng Shì
and concurrently appointed Jīngnán military governor.
Wēn Zhāng was demoted to Zhènzhōu Sīmǎ.
Zhāng sighed:
"I was born at the wrong time;
what is there to regret in death!"
That evening,
he took poison and died.
An imperial decree stated:
"If he had not been a harmful pest,
how could it have come to this!
His wickedness was indeed full,
and even in death his guilt remains.
He shall be temporarily buried outside the city within three days.
Only after an act of grace and pardon
will he be permitted to be returned for proper burial,
so that both inside and outside the court may be satisfied,
and treacherous villains may know fear."
On Jǐsì,
Yòu Jiànyì Dàfū Gāo Xiāng, Bǐbù Lángzhōng Zhī Zhìgào Yáng Zhīzhì, Lǐbù Lángzhōng Wèi Dàng, and others were demoted to Lǐngnán,
all because they were on good terms with Liú Zhān
and were expelled by Wéi Bǎohéng.
Zhīzhì
was the son of Rǔshì;
Rǔshì
was the elder cousin of Yúqīng,
see Volume 241, Mùzōng Chángqìng First Year.
Fú's son.
Wèi Fú see Volume 248, Xuānzōng Dàzhōng Third Year.
It was said they conspired with the medical officials,
mistakenly administering poison;
slanderous words claimed the mistaken administration of poison
led to Princess Tóngchāng's death.
However, since it was said to be a mistake,
how could it also be considered a conspiracy!
On Bǐngzǐ,
Zhān was demoted to Kāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Kāngzhōu is 5,750 lǐ from the capital.
"Secure a residence of a few acres,
yet it is still not one's own;
refuse bribes from all directions,
only fearing others might know."
Yán said to Tián:
"The Shìláng has recommended Minister Liú!"
He was demoted to Wúzhōu Cìshǐ.
Wúzhōu,
the location of Guǎngxìn County, the seat of Cāngwú Commandery in the Hàn dynasty,
was established as Wúzhōu in the Táng dynasty,
5,500 lǐ from the capital.
He was also demoted to Tīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Lù Yán had long held differing opinions with Liú Zhān in discussions.
After Zhān was demoted to Kāngzhōu,
Yán was still dissatisfied.
Consulting the Shídào Tú,
and seeing that Huānzhōu was ten thousand lǐ from Cháng'ān,
he further demoted Zhān to Huānzhōu Sīhù.
Huānzhōu,
by land route to Cháng'ān is 12,452 lǐ,
by water route 17,000 lǐ.
Examination of discrepancies: The Shílù and Xīn Zhuàn both state:
"Yán intended to kill him,
but relied on Yōuzhōu military governor Zhāng Gōngsù submitting a memorial arguing Zhān's innocence,
and thus stopped."
According to this, at that time Zhāng Yǔnshēn was stationed in Yōuzhōu.
Mentioning Gōngsù
is likely an error.
15 In winter,
the tenth month,
on Guǐmǎo,
Xīchuān Liúhòu Wú Xínglǔ was appointed military governor.
16 In the eleventh month,
on Xīnhài,
Bīngbù Shàngshū, Yántiě Zhuǎnyùn Shǐ Wáng Duó was appointed Lǐbù Shàngshū, Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
Duó
was the nephew of Qǐ.
Wáng Qǐ see Volume 241, Chángqìng First Year.
Duó,
was the son of Qǐ's elder brother Yán.
17 On Dīngmǎo,
Xúzhōu was again made the Gǎnhuà Army military governor.
Xúzhōu was originally the Wǔníng Army,
but experienced the Silver Sabre rebellion,
and the military governorship was abolished, making it an observation commission.
Now it was restored as the Gǎnhuà Army.
18 In the twelfth month,
Chéngdé military governor Wáng Jǐngchóng was additionally appointed Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
Zuǒ Jīnwú Shàng Jiāngjūn Lǐ Guóchāng was appointed Zhènwǔ military governor.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on Xīnyǒu,
Princess Wényì was buried.
Princess Tóngchāng was posthumously titled Wényì.
Her gold and silver were sifted.
An imperial edict ordered sacrifices to be held in the courtyard of the Wéi family,
hence it was called a courtyard sacrifice.
Tài (汰) means
to wash or sift.
Each type of item filled one hundred and twenty carriages,
with brocades, embroideries, pearls, and jade used as ceremonial guards and burial objects,
their brilliance stretching over thirty-some *lǐ*;
The *Record of the Rites: Tángōng* notes: Confucius said that those who make burial objects
understand the way of mourning,
preparing objects but making them unusable.
Calling them burial objects (明器)
is to treat them as for the spirits,
what need is there for brilliance and splendor!
Forty camel-loads of cakes and pastries,
were used to feed the laborers.
The Emperor and Consort Guō could not cease mourning the princess,
the court musician Lǐ Kějí composed the "Lament of a Hundred Years" tune,
its sound mournful and plaintive.
The "Lament of a Hundred Years" tune
narrates a person's life from youth,
to prime,
to old age;
the beauty of youth,
the pursuit of pleasure and utmost joy in prime,
and the state of decline in old age;
its sound is sorrowful,
moving people's hearts.
Wǎn (惋) is pronounced wǎn.
Treasures from the inner treasury were distributed for her head ornaments,
and eight hundred bolts of silk were used as a floor carpet.
When the dance ended,
pearls covered the ground.
2 Hán Jūnxióng, the acting military governor of Wèi-Bó, was appointed military governor.
3 The Vice Director of the Chancellery and Tongpingzhangshi Lù Yán and Wéi Bǎohéng had always supported each other,
their influence overwhelming the realm.
Later, they contended for power,
gradually developing a rift.
Bǎohéng then spoke ill of Yán before the Emperor.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on Guǐmǎo,
Yán was appointed Tongpingzhangshi
and assigned as military governor of Xīchuān.
As Yán left the city,
people on the road threw tiles and stones at him.
The acting Capital Prefect Xuē Néng
had been promoted by Yán.
Yán said to Néng:
"Upon my departure,
I am troubled by your sending me off with tiles and stones!"
Néng slowly raised his tablet and replied:
"In the past, when a chief minister departed,
the prefectural offices had no precedent of dispatching people for protection."
"Prefectural offices"
refers to the offices under the jurisdiction of the Capital Prefecture.
Néng
was from Fénzhōu.
4 In the fifth month,
the Emperor visited Ānguó Temple,
bestowing upon monks Chóngqiān and Chèché two lecture platforms of aloeswood and sandalwood,
each twenty feet high.
These were lecture platforms made of aloeswood and sandalwood.
Chén (沈) is pronounced chén.
Gāo (高) is pronounced gāo.
5 In autumn,
the seventh month,
Lú Dān, the Minister of War, was appointed Tongpingzhangshi
and assigned as military governor of Shānnán Dōngdào.
6 In winter,
the tenth month,
Liú Yè, the Vice Minister of War and Commissioner for Salt and Iron Transport, was appointed Minister of Rites and Tongpingzhangshi.
1 In spring,
the first month,
Zhāng Yǔnshēn, the military governor of Yōuzhōu, suffered a wind-induced illness,
and requested to entrust military affairs to seek medical treatment;
this was granted,
and his son Jiǎnhuì was made acting military governor.
As his illness worsened,
he sent an envoy to submit a memorial returning his insignia of command;
on Bǐngshēn,
he passed away.
Yǔnshēn governed Yōuzhōu for twenty-three years.
In the fourth year of Xuānzong's Dàzhōng era,
Zhāng Yǔnshēn succeeded Zhōu Chēn as military governor of Yōuzhōu.
The borders were without alarm,
and high and low were at peace.
2 In the second month,
on Dīngsì,
Yú Cóng, the Vice Minister of War and Tongpingzhangshi, was appointed military governor of Shānnán Dōngdào,
and Zhào Yǐn, the Vice Minister of Justice and concurrently Director of the Revenue Department from Fèngtiān, was appointed Vice Minister of Revenue and Tongpingzhangshi.
3 Zhāng Gōngsù, the prefect of Píngzhōu,
had long enjoyed prestige and reputation,
and was respected by the people of Yōuzhōu.
After Zhāng Yǔnshēn's death,
Gōngsù led his prefectural troops to attend the funeral.
Zhāng Jiǎnhuì, fearing him,
in the third month,
fled to the capital,
and was appointed as a general of the imperial guards.
Generally referred to as a general of the imperial guards,
without specifying which guard,
the history records it briefly.
4 In summer,
the fourth month,
the Emperor's son Bǎo was enfeoffed as Prince of Jí,
Jié as Prince of Shòu,
and Yǐ as Prince of Mù.
5 Zhāng Gōngsù was appointed acting military governor of Pínglú.
"Pínglú"
should be
"Lúlóng".
6 In the fifth month,
Wéi Yīnyù, the Director of the National University, went to the palace gate to report on the secret affairs of Guō Jìngshù, the younger brother of Consort Guō and Commissioner of the Inner Workshops;
the Commissioner of the Inner Workshops
was one of the commissioners of the inner departments,
in charge of manufacturing weapons for the inner treasury.
Yīnyù was beaten to death with a rod,
and his family property was confiscated.
*Kǎoyì* says: The *Continued Record of Precious Fortune* states:
"The Inner Workshop Commissioner Guō Jìngshù frequently drank with chief ministers Wéi Bǎohéng and Zhāng Néngshùn in the inner residence,
secretly communicating with Consort Guō,
their debauchery quite severe.
Each time they submitted documents in a golden box,
falsely claiming it contained fruit,
internally connecting with Consort Guō and Guō Jìngshù,
externally colluding with Zhāng Néngshùn and Wéi Yīnyù, Director of the National University,
plotting to overthrow the imperial throne,
and establish another crown prince.
When the affair was exposed,
they were hastily demoted.
On the fourteenth day of the fifth month,
an inner edict
demoted Yán Qí, the Minister of Works, to prefect of Chēnzhōu,
Lǐ Kuàng, the Supervising Secretary, to prefect of Qínzhōu,
Zhāng Duó, the Supervising Secretary, to prefect of Téngzhōu,
and Lǐ Jìngzhòng, the General of the Left Imperial Guard, to Registrar of Dānzhōu.
Wéi Yīnyù, Director of the National University,
was ordered by the Capital Prefecture to be given one severe beating with the heavy rod,
executed,
his family property, wife, and daughters confiscated by the government.
Also demoted were Wéi Jūnqīng, prefect of Xùzhōu, to County Defender of Chóngpíng County in Àizhōu,
and Zhāng Zhífāng, Vice Director of the Right and Commander of the Right Yǔlín Army, to Registrar of Kāngzhōu.
Subsequently, the Emperor's son-in-law Yú Cóng was also implicated in the conspiracy with Wéi Bǎohéng and others for treason.
On the seventeenth day of that month,
also demoted were Lǐ Dāng, Vice Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs, to prefect of Dàozhōu,
Wáng Fěng, Vice Minister of Personnel, to prefect of Jiànzhōu,
Lǐ Dū, the Left Regular Attendant, to prefect of Hèzhōu,
Zhāng Tí, the Hanlin Academician Receiver of Edicts, to Registrar of Fēngzhōu,
Fēng Yànqīng, a Secretariat Drafter, to Registrar of Cháozhōu,
and Yáng Shú, a Remonstrance Official, to Registrar of Xīnzhōu.
The Emperor's son-in-law Wéi Bǎohéng was demoted to prefect of Léizhōu,
then further to County Defender of Chéngmài County in Dānzhōu,
then further to a commoner exiled to Huānzhōu,
then ordered to commit suicide,
his family property confiscated by the government,
and his three clans forbidden from holding office in the court."
Its account is chaotic and unsubstantiated.
We now follow the *Veritable Records*.
On Yǐhài,
Tián Xiànxiān, the Commissioner of the Palace Gates, was stripped of his purple robe,
and reassigned as Commissioner of the Qiáolíng Mausoleum,
because he had accepted Yīnyù's petition.
Yīnyù's father-in-law, Vice Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury Cuī Yuányìng,
his wife's cousin, Secretariat Drafter Cuī Hàng,
and his younger uncle Jūnqīng were all demoted to posts in Lǐngnán;
Dù Yìxiū, the Supervising Secretary, was implicated for being friendly with Yīnyù,
and was also demoted to Registrar of Duānzhōu.
Hàng
was the son of Cuī Xuàn.
Cuī Xuàn appears in the 247th scroll, in the third year of Wǔzōng's Huìchāng era.
He was the son of Cóng.
5 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the Wǔyín day,
the Emperor’s illness took a critical turn. The Left Army Commander-in-Chief Liú Xíngshēn and the Right Army Commander-in-Chief Hán Wényuē established the youngest son, Prince Pǔ Lǐ Yǎn, as heir.
Commentary: Fàn Zhì’s Wǔdài Tōnglù records:
“Liáng’s Lǐ Zhèn said to Hán Yífàn, the Protector of Shǎnzhōu:
‘When Emperor Yì first passed away,
Commander-in-Chief Hán killed the elder and established the younger to benefit his own power,
thus throwing the empire into chaos.
Now, General, do you intend to do the same?’
Yífàn
was Wényuē’s grandson.”
Note: Emperor Yìzōng had eight sons;
Emperor Xīzōng was the fifth.
The other sons’ birth order is not recorded in the Old or New Histories,
nor is it stated what became of them,
so it is unclear which prince was actually killed.
On the Gēngchén day,
an edict was issued:
“Establish Yǎn as Crown Prince.”
Commentary: The Xù Bǎoyùn Lù states:
“That day,
the chief ministers, such as Xiāo Yè, went directly to the imperial bedchamber to inquire about the Emperor’s illness.
The Emperor faintly uttered the word ‘zhèn’
three times and then stopped.
The attending ministers could not help but weep aloud,
and all within and outside the palace shed tears.”
Note: At that time, the chancellor Wéi Bǎohéng held the highest position;
Xiāo Yè was not a chancellor.
This account is not adopted here.
On the Xīnsì day,
the Emperor passed away in the Xiánníng Hall.
He was forty-one years old.
Emperor Xīzōng ascended the throne.
In the eighth month,
on the Dīngwèi day,
his mother, Consort Wáng, was posthumously honored as Empress Dowager.
Liú Xíngshēn and Hán Wényuē were both enfeoffed as Dukes of the State.
6 Floods occurred in Guāndōng and Hénán.
7 In the ninth month,
the relevant officials presented the posthumous title of the late Empress Dowager as Huì’ān.
The late Empress Dowager
refers to the Emperor’s mother, Consort Wáng.
The Emperor
was then in charge of governance.
8 The Minister over the Masses, Vice Director of the Chancellery, and Tongpingzhangshi Wéi Bǎohéng
was accused of secret misconduct by his enemies,
and was demoted to Prefect of Hèzhōu.
The court musician Lǐ Kějí was exiled to Lǐngnán.
Kějí had been favored by Emperor Yìzōng.
Once, when he was marrying off his son,
Emperor Yìzōng bestowed upon him two silver wine pots.
When opened, they contained no wine but were solid inside.
The Right Army Commander-in-Chief Xīmén Jìxuán repeatedly remonstrated about this,
but Emperor Yìzōng would not listen.
Kějí once received a large quantity of gifts,
which were transported in official carriages.
Jìxuán said to him:
“On the day your family is ruined,
these items will have to be transported back in official carriages.
This is not receiving gifts,
but merely troubling the oxen’s feet!”
When Kějí was exiled to Lǐngnán,
his family property was confiscated,
exactly as Jìxuán had predicted.
The history records that when petty men receive excessive favor, disaster follows.
9 Lù Yán, Military Governor of Xīchuān, was concurrently appointed Shìzhōng;
Wáng Jǐngchóng, Military Governor of Chéngdé, was appointed Zhōngshūlìng;
Hán Jūnxióng, Military Governor of Wèibó; Zhāng Gōngsù, Military Governor of Lúlóng; and Gāo Pián, Military Governor of Tiānpíng, were all appointed Tongpingzhangshi.
Jūnxióng was additionally granted the name Yǔnzhōng.
Commentary: The Old History biography records
“Yǔnzhōng.”
The Veritable Records and the New History biography both record
“Yǔnzhōng.”
The latter is followed here.
10 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the Yǐwèi day,
Xiāo Fǎng, Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed Vice Director of the Chancellery and Tongpingzhangshi.
11 Wéi Bǎohéng was further demoted to Magistrate of Chéngmài in Yázhōu.
Chéngmài
was a county established in the Suí dynasty,
and belonged to Qióngzhōu in the Táng.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is located fifty-five lǐ west of the prefecture.
His younger brother, Wéi Bǎoyì, a Hanlin Academician and Vice Minister of War, was demoted to Registrar of Bīnzhōu.
His associate, Liú Chéngyōng, a Hanlin Academician and Vice Minister of Revenue, was demoted to Military Advisor of Fúzhōu.
Chéngyōng
was the son of Liǔ Yǔxī.
Liǔ Yǔxī appears in the 236th scroll, in the first year of the Yǒngzhēn era of Emperor Shùnzōng.
12 On the Guǐmǎo day,
a general amnesty was declared.
13 Lù Yán, Military Governor of Xīchuān,
was fond of music, women, and pleasure outings.
He entrusted the administration of the military government to his close subordinates Biān Xián and Guō Chóu,
who often acted first and reported afterward,
so that both superiors and subordinates feared them.
Once, during a grand military review,
the two men discussed matters,
writing silently on paper, showing it to each other, and then burning it.
The army suspected they had treacherous intentions,
and became alarmed and unsettled.
When the court heard of this,
in the eleventh month,
on the Wùchén day,
Yán was transferred to be Military Governor of Jīngnán.
Xián and Chóu secretly learned the reason,
and subsequently fled.
14 Xiāo Yè, Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed Tongpingzhangshi
and assigned as Military Governor of Hédōng.
15 In the twelfth month,
on the Jǐhài day,

"two."
He called him
"Father."
Lìngzī was fairly well-read,
and full of clever schemes.
He monopolized power and accepted bribes,
appointing officials and granting crimson and purple robes without reporting to the emperor.
Whenever he had an audience,
he often prepared two trays of fruits and food himself,
and ate and drank with the emperor facing each other,
taking his time before withdrawing.
The emperor was intimate with the young attendants of the inner gardens,
and rewarded musicians and entertainers,
the expenses often amounting to tens of thousands,
until the treasury was completely depleted.
Lìngzī persuaded the emperor to confiscate the precious goods of merchants from the two markets and deliver them all to the inner treasury.
Those who protested
were handed over to the Jīngzhào Prefecture to be beaten to death.
From the councilors down,
all were silenced and dared not speak.
5. Gāo Pián arrived at Chéngdū.
The next day,
he dispatched five thousand infantry and cavalry to pursue Nánzhào forces,
reaching the Dàdù River,
where they killed and captured many,
seizing several dozen of their chieftains.
They were brought to Chéngdū
and beheaded.
He repaired the fortifications at Qiōnglái Pass, the Dàdù River, and other towns and stockades.
He also built a city at Mǎhú Town in Róng Prefecture,
naming it the Píngyí Army.
Mǎhú Town
was strategically located along the Mǎhú River.
These were all key routes for the Man tribes entering Shǔ,
and each was garrisoned with several thousand troops.
From then on, the Man tribes did not invade again.
Gāo Pián summoned Huáng Jǐngfù
and reprimanded him for the loss of the Dàdù River defenses,
then had him executed by waist-cutting.
Textual Analysis states: The *Qíjiù Zhuàn* says:
"On the fifteenth day of the third month of the first year of Qiánfú,
the former Lí Prefecture Governor, concurrently Commander of the Dàdù River Garrison and Indigenous Forces, Huáng Jǐngfù, was dealt with."
The *Shílù* states:
"In the third month of the second year of Qiánfú,
Gāo Pián reported the execution of Jǐngfù."
Now, the event follows the *Qíjiù Zhuàn*,
while the year follows the *Shílù*.
"This command"
refers to the Xīchuān troops.
The imperial edict did not permit it.
Previously,
Nánzhào's Dūshuǎng had repeatedly sent dispatches to the Zhōngshū Secretariat.
Among Nánzhào's Qīngpíngguān,
below the Tǎnchuò, Bùxiè, and Jiǔzàn,
there was the Mùshuǎng,
in charge of military affairs;
the Cóngshuǎng,
in charge of household registration;
the Císhuǎng,
in charge of rites;
the Fáshuǎng,
in charge of punishments;
the Quànshuǎng,
in charge of officials;
the Juéshuǎng,
in charge of labor;
the Wànshuǎng,
in charge of finances;
the Yǐnshuǎng,
in charge of guests;
the Héshuǎng,
in charge of merchants: all were also Qīngpíngguān.
Shuǎng
is akin to saying "ministry."
Dūshuǎng
oversaw the three ministries.
"Xiān"
is pronounced "xī jiàn fān."
The Zhōngshū Secretariat did not reply.
Lú Xié memorialized, stating:
"If this continues,
the Man tribes will grow more arrogant,
thinking the Táng has no response.
We should enumerate the ten generations who received our grace and reprimand them.
The ancestor of Nánzhào was Xìnūluó.
During Gāozōng's reign,
he sent envoys to court.
He begot Luóshèngyán,
who begot Yángé.
When Yángé died,
his younger brother Shèngluópí succeeded him.
Shèngluópí begot Píluógé,
whom Xuánzōng bestowed the name Guīyì.
During the Kāiyuán period, he unified the six Zhào into one,
and the state began to grow strong.
Guīyì's son was Gélúofèng,
whose son was Fèngjiāyì,
whose son was Yìmóuxún,
whose son was Xúngéquàn,
whose son was Quànlóngshèng,
whose younger brother was Quànlì,
whose younger brother was Fēngyòu.
After Fēngyòu died, Qiúlóng succeeded him.
From Xìnūluó to Qiúlóng, there were thirteen generations.
Among them, Fèngjiāyì died before succeeding,
while Fēngyòu and Qiúlóng were enemies of the Táng.
Thus, ten generations received grace.
"Shǔ"
is pronounced "suǒ jù fān."
This would imply treating them as equals,
so I request that edicts be bestowed upon Gāo Pián and the Lǐngnán Military Commissioner Xīn Dǎng,
instructing them to copy the edict's text
and send it to them via dispatch."
"Copying the edict's text"
is what is now called
"lùbái"
6. In the third month,
Hán Jiǎn, the Acting Military Commissioner of Wèibó, was appointed Military Commissioner.
7. Last year,
the Gǎnhuà Army dispatched troops to Língwǔ for autumn defense.
When Nánzhào invaded Xīchuān,
an imperial order sent them to reinforce it.
After the Man tribes retreated,
they were ordered to return.
Upon reaching Fèngxiáng,
they refused to proceed to Língwǔ
and wanted to return directly to Xúzhōu.
The eunuch Wáng Yùběn and the general Liú Féng searched for and arrested the eight ringleaders, including Hú Xióng,
and beheaded them.
"Nèiyǎng"
also refers to eunuchs.
"Shuài"
is read as "lǜ";
the same applies below.
8. Initially,
when Nánzhào besieged Chéngdū,
Yáng Qìngfù recruited elite assault troops with high-ranking positions and generous provisions to defend against them,
as seen in the eleventh year of Xiánzōng's Xiántōng era above.
"Jiàng"
is pronounced "jí liàng fān";
the same applies below.
When Gāo Pián arrived,
he ordered them all to surrender their appointment documents.
"Dié"
refers to appointment documents.
Before people resumed their duties,
he suspended their provisions.
Having taken away their appointment documents
and stopped their generous provisions...
Gāo Pián was fond of sorcery.
Whenever he dispatched troops to pursue the Man tribes,
he would set up flags and formations at night,
burn paper cutouts of men and horses before the officers and soldiers,
and scatter small beans,
saying:
"The Shǔ troops are cowardly,
so I am sending the Mysterious Goddess's divine troops ahead."
The brave soldiers in the army were ashamed of this.
Gāo Pián's fondness for sorcery
ultimately led to his downfall because of this.
He suspended all of it.
He ordered the common people to use full strings of cash.
Those whose strings were short were arrested,
accused of bribery,
and both givers and receivers were executed.
His punishments were severe and cruel,
causing discontent among the people of Shǔ.
In summer,
the fourth month,
the assault troops mutinied,
noisily storming into the government offices.
Gāo Pián fled and hid in a latrine.
The assault troops searched for him
but could not find him.
The Tiānpíng Army general Zhāng Jié led several hundred of his armored troops into the offices to attack the assault troops.
Gāo Pián had moved from Tiānpíng to Xīchuān,
so Zhāng Jié was likely a former subordinate commander.
"Bèi"
is pronounced "pí yì fān."
In front of the Military Commissioner's headquarters,
weapons were displayed to enhance authority and appearance.
Fighting with furious strength,
the Tiānpíng Army could not withstand them
and retreated to their camp.
The assault troops pursued them,
but the camp gates were closed,
and they could not enter.
The army supervisor sent someone to persuade them,
promising to restore their ranks and provisions.
After a long time,
they agreed to return to camp.
The Tiānpíng Army then opened the gates and came out,
making as if to pursue them.
Reaching the northern part of the city,
where a polo field was under construction at the time,
with several hundred laborers,
the Tiānpíng Army beheaded them all,
returned,
and went to the government offices,
claiming
"the rebels have been executed."
Gāo Pián came out to see them
and richly rewarded them with gold and silk.
The next day,
he posted a notice apologizing to the assault troops,
fully restoring their ranks, clothing, and provisions.
From then on, he ordered the troops from various circuits who had come with him to take turns on duty in the offices daily,
strictly guarding for self-defense.
This was to prevent the assault troops from rebelling again.
"Gēng"
is pronounced "gōng héng fān."
9. Wáng Jǐngchóng, the Chéngdé Military Commissioner, was additionally appointed as a Zhōngshū Lìng.
10. Wang Ying, the garrison commander of Lángshān in Zhèxī, and sixty-eight others had performed meritorious service in battle.
(Today, Lángshān is south of Jìng Hǎi County in Tōngzhōu.
It consists of five connected mountains,
reaching up to the Great River [Yangtze] and
descending to the vast sea.
Crossing the river southward,
one reaches Fúshān Town in Chángshú County, Sūzhōu.
Following the river eastward leads to Chóngmíng Shoal.
Hoisting sails to catch favorable winds,
one can reach south to Dìnghǎi County in Míngzhōu.
This is what Táo Yǐnjū [Tao Hongjing] called
"the five Láng mountains facing the shore of Jùzhāng.")
Wang Ying and the others appealed for recognition but did not receive it,
so they plundered the armory and rebelled,
gathering followers until their numbers neared ten thousand.
They attacked and captured Sū[zhōu] and Cháng[zhōu].
(Sū[zhōu] and Cháng[zhōu] are the names of two prefectures,
located one hundred and eighty *li* apart.)
They sailed down the river into the sea,
then turned to plunder the two Zhè [circuits],
reaching as far south as Fújiàn,
becoming a great scourge to the people.
*Textual Analysis* says: The *New [Tang] History Basic Annals* records:
"Wang Ying, a vanguard commander of Zhèxī, rebelled.
In the fifth month,
the Right Longwu Grand General Sòng Hào was dispatched to suppress him."
According to [records for] the fourth month of the fourth year [of this reign],
after Wang Ying captured Lǔ Shí,
Hào was then ordered to attack him.
Placing it here [in the fifth month] is an error.
Chéng Kuāngróu's *Táng Bǔ Jì* says:
"In the sixth month,
Wang Ying, a vanguard commander of Zhèxī, rebelled,
amassing a following of ten thousand,
burning and plundering Sū[zhōu] and Cháng[zhōu].
In the third year,
first month,
Sūzhōu Prefect Lǐ Huì was demoted
because he had abandoned the city during Wang Ying's rebellion."
The *Old [Tang] History Basic Annals* records:
"In the second year,
fourth month,
the sea bandit Wang Ying attacked and plundered the commanderies and towns of Zhèxī."
The *Veritable Records* record:
"In the third year of Qiánfú,
second month,
Zhèxī reported that vanguard commander Wang Ying and sixty-eight others had plundered the armory and rebelled.
In the third month,
Zhèxī reported that Wang Ying had gathered a multitude of ten thousand,
attacking and capturing prefectures and counties."
The *Continued Bǎoyùn Record* says:
"In the first year,
Wang Ying rebelled in Liǎngzhè.
An imperial edict dispatched Shānběi troops to attack him.
Within a month, he was defeated,
and was then beheaded at the palace gates."
I now follow the *Old [Tang] History Basic Annals*.
11. In the fifth month,
Lìng Hú Táo, the Grand Tutor and Head of the Department of Ministries, was appointed Tongpingzhangshi [chief minister]
and concurrently Military Commissioner of Fèngxiáng.
12. Xiāo Fǎng, the Minister of Works and Tongpingzhangshi, died.
*Textual Analysis* says: The *Old [Tang] History Biography* states:
"Soon after, bandits arose in Hénán,
eunuchs held military power,
and the imperial court was in turmoil and disorder.
Fǎng was forthright and outspoken in his views,
which his colleagues resented.
He was removed from his administrative post
and sent out to serve as Prefect of Guǎngzhōu and Military Commissioner of Lǐngnán.
Encountering disturbances,
he died before reaching the capital."
The *Old [Tang] History Basic Annals* records:
"In the third year,
spring,
first month,
on the *jǐmǎo* day of the first month,
Fǎng was excused due to illness
and removed [from his post] to become Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent."
The *New [Tang] History Basic Annals* records his death this month.
The *New [Tang] History Biography* also says he died in office,
and that his service as Military Commissioner of Lǐngnán was earlier.
The *Old [Tang] History Basic Annals* and Biography are both mistaken.
I now follow the *Veritable Records*.
13. In the sixth month,
Censor-in-Chief Lǐ Wèi was appointed Vice Director of the Secretariat and Tongpingzhangshi.
14. On the *xīnwèi* day,
Gāo Pián secretly compiled a register of the names of the vanguard commanders [*tūjiàng*]
and had men raid and arrest them at night,
surrounding their homes,
breaking through walls and doors to enter.
The old, young, pregnant, and sick
were all driven out and killed.
Infants were either dashed against the steps
or smashed against pillars.
Blood flowed in streams,
and the sound of wailing shook the heavens.
Several thousand people died.
That night,
carts were used to carry the corpses and dump them into the river.
There was one woman who,
at the moment of execution,
pointed her finger like a halberd and loudly cursed:
"Gāo Pián!
You unjustly stripped meritorious officers and soldiers of their ranks, clothing, and rations,
inciting the anger of the multitude.
Fortunately, you escaped [their wrath],
yet you do not reflect on your own faults.
Instead, you further use deceit to slaughter nearly ten thousand innocent people!
How can Heaven, Earth, and the spirits
tolerate you acting like this!
I will surely accuse you before the Supreme Emperor [of Heaven],
so that one day your entire household will be slaughtered like mine is today,
suffer injustice and humiliation like I do today,
and live in terror and fear like I do today!"
After speaking,
she bowed to Heaven
and calmly submitted to execution.
Some time later,
there were vanguard commanders who returned from garrison duty.
Pián again wanted to exterminate their entire clans.
A long-serving personal aide named Wáng Yīn admonished him:
"Your Excellency follows the Dao,
you should cherish life and abhor killing.
(*Yuáncóng* means having served Gāo Pián for many years,
not being a recent subordinate.
*Cóng* is pronounced *cái yòng fān*.
*Hào* is pronounced *hū dào fān*.
*Wù* is pronounced *wū lù fān*.)
These men were not involved in the initial plot.
If you kill them again,
then those who feel endangered will be many!"
Pián then stopped.
15. Wáng Xiānzhī and his associate Shàng Jūncháng attacked and captured Púzhōu and Cáozhōu.
Their followers grew to several tens of thousands.
Xuē Chóng, the Military Commissioner of Tiānpíng, led troops to attack them
but was defeated by Xiānzhī.
Huáng Cháo from Yuānqú also gathered several thousand followers in response to Xiānzhī.
(Yuānqú was a Hàn dynasty county,
under Táng it belonged to Cáozhōu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: It is located forty-five *li* west of the prefecture.
Yán Shǐgǔ said: *Qú* is pronounced *qú*.
Huáng Cháo began here.)
Cháo was skilled in horsemanship and archery,
fond of championing justice,
and had a rough familiarity with books and histories.
He repeatedly sat for the *jìnshì* examinations but never passed,
and subsequently became a bandit.
Together with Xiānzhī, he attacked and plundered prefectures and counties,
rampaging through Shāndōng.
People suffering under heavy taxes and levies vied to join him.
Within a few months,
his followers grew to several tens of thousands.
16. Zhāng Gōngsù, the Military Commissioner of Lúlóng,
was by nature cruel and violent,
and was not supported by the troops.
The senior general Lǐ Màoxūn
was originally from the Ābùsī clan of the Uighurs.
After the Uighurs were defeated,
he surrendered to Zhāng Zhòngwǔ.
(Lǐ Màoxūn's surrender likely occurred during the Huìcháng period.)
He had repeatedly performed meritorious service
and was granted a [Chinese] surname and name.
There was a certain Chén Gòngyán, the Commissioner of the Army for Receiving Surrenders
(the Army for Receiving Surrenders was located at Dīnglíng River in Yōuzhōu),
a veteran general of Yōuzhōu,
who was trusted and respected by the troops.
[Màoxūn] spread word that Gòngyán
was leading troops toward Jì[zhōu].
Gōngsù went out to fight but was defeated,
and fled to the capital.
Màoxūn entered the city,
and the multitude then realized it was not Gòngyán.
Having no alternative,
they supported him and established him [in power].
The court accordingly appointed him
as Acting Military Commissioner.
In the autumn of the 17th year,
in the seventh month,
locusts came from the east and moved westward,
blotting out the sun.
Wherever they passed, the land was left barren.
This indicates the great number of locusts;
wherever they passed, they devoured the leaves of plants and trees, as well as the five grains, leaving nothing behind.
"The locusts entered the capital region,
but did not eat the crops;
instead, they all clung to thorns and brambles and died."
The chief ministers all offered congratulations.
Yáng Guózhōng had claimed that continuous rain did not harm the crops,
Hán Huàng had claimed that continuous rain did not ruin the salt,
and now Yáng Zhīzhì claimed that the locusts did not eat the crops but clung to thorns and brambles and died.
The ministers of the Táng dynasty had formed a habit of deceiving their ruler,
and this had been going on for a long time.
In the eighth month of the 18th year,
Lǐ Màoxūn was appointed as the military governor of Lúlóng.
Below "eighth month,"
there should be
the character
"yǐ"
In the ninth month,
the Right Supplementer Dǒng Yǔ admonished the emperor against excessive hunting and riding donkeys to play polo;
the emperor rewarded him with gold and silk to commend him.
The military governor of Bīnníng, Lǐ Kǎn, submitted a request for an official posthumous title for his adoptive father, the Huáqīng Palace Commissioner Dào Yǎ.
Lǐ Kǎn was the adoptive son of a eunuch.
"Wèi"
is pronounced "yú wèi fān."
His words somewhat offended the eunuchs.
The Privy Commissioners Yáng Fùgōng and others lined up to complain to the emperor.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Yǔ was demoted to the position of Military Administrator of Chēnzhōu.
Gǔ Yǒng exclusively attacked the emperor's person,
yet he did not lose his position as one of the Nine Ministers.
Wáng Zhāng denounced Wáng Fèng,
and died in prison.
Alas,
there is a reason for this!
He was the adopted grandson of Qīnyì.
Yáng Qīnyì appears in the 246th volume, in the fifth year of the Kāichéng era of Emperor Wénzōng.
The Zhāoyì army rebelled;
the general Liú Guǎng expelled the military governor Gāo Shí,
and made himself the acting military governor.
Cáo Xiáng, the Grand General of the Left Imperial Guard, was appointed as the military governor of Zhāoyì.
The Huíhé returned to Luóchuān.
Táng's Níngzhōu Zhēnníng County
was Suí's Luóchuān County,
and its location was the same as the Yángzhōu County of Shàngjùn in the Hàn dynasty.
In the second year of the Dàzhōng era of Emperor Xuānzōng,
the Huíhé fled westward,
and only now did they return.
They sent an envoy, Tóngluó Yúlù, to present tribute;
they were granted ten thousand bolts of silk for relief.
Bandits spread rampantly,
"qīn"
should be "jìn."
Reaching as far as Huáinán,
the larger groups numbered over a thousand,
the smaller ones several hundred;
an edict ordered the military governors and supervisors of the five armies—Huáinán, Zhōngwǔ, Xuānwǔ, Yìchéng, and Tiānpíng—to urgently suppress, capture, and pacify them.
In the twelfth month,
Wáng Xiānzhī invaded Yízhōu.
Sòng Wēi, the military governor of Pínglú, submitted a request to lead five thousand infantry and cavalry as a separate commander,
concurrently commanding the troops of his own circuit to suppress the bandits wherever they were.
Still,
Wēi was appointed as the Commissioner for Pacifying the Grass Bandits of the Various Circuits' Field Headquarters,
and was additionally given three thousand imperial guards and five hundred armored cavalry.
Consequently, an edict ordered that all commanders sent by the military governors of Hénán to suppress bandits were to be placed under Wēi's command.
In spring,
the first month,
the Tiānpíng army reported sending the officer Zhāng Yàn and others to rescue Yízhōu.
On their return,
when they reached Yìqiáo,
they heard that bandits had risen again in the northern region,
and they were ordered to stay and defend.
Yàn and others refused to comply,
and clamorously rushed toward Yùnzhōu.
The commanders Zhāng Sītài and Lǐ Chéngyòu rode out of the city,
tore their sleeves and made a pact with them,
using their salaries to prepare wine and food to appease and persuade them,
after which order was restored.
An edict ordered the army to pacify them in every way,
and not to pursue the matter further.
An order
was issued to the surveillance commissioners and prefects of Fújiàn, Jiāngxī, Húnán, and other circuits,
to train their soldiers;
it also commanded all villages in the empire to equip themselves with bows, knives, drums, and clappers to prepare against bandits.
The military governor of Yǎnhǎi was granted the title Tàiníng Army.
In the third month,
the military governor of Lúlóng, Lǐ Màoxūn, requested that his son, the Left Adjutant of Yōuzhōu, Lǐ Kějǔ, be made acting military governor,
while he himself sought retirement.
An edict granted Màoxūn retirement with the title Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs,
and appointed Kějǔ as acting military governor of Lúlóng.
The Vice Director of the Chancellery and Tongpingzhangshi Cuī Yànzhāo was dismissed and made Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent;
Wáng Duó, the Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, was concurrently appointed Vice Director of the Chancellery and Tongpingzhangshi.
Nánzhào sent an envoy to Gāo Pián to seek peace but continued to raid the borders;
Pián executed the envoy.
When the Mán captured Jiāozhǐ,
as recorded in the 250th volume, in the sixth year of the Xiántōng era of Emperor Yìzōng.
Yáo
was a distant relative of the imperial clan.
The Mán sent Yáo back,
delivering a wooden tablet to Pián,
"dì dié,"
meaning it was enclosed in wood,
hence called a wooden tablet.
Fàn Chéngdà's Guìhǎi Yúhéng Zhì states: In the first year of the Shàoxīng era,
when Ānnán communicated with the Guangxi military commissioner and Yǒng,
they used two lacquered boards to enclose documents,
with characters carved on them,
calling it a wooden tablet.
According to Sòng Bái's Xù Tōngdiǎn,
when the various circuits, prefectures, and surveillance offices transmitted imperial edicts,
they all used wooden tablets.
Thus, wooden tablets were also used in the Central Plains.
"Wèi"
is pronounced "wéi jì fān."
"The Dūshuǎng sent a dispatch to the military governor of Xīchuān,"
the wording was extremely arrogant.
Pián sent Yáo to the capital.
On the jiǎchén day,
he sent a reply to Nánzhào,
enumerating their crimes of betraying the accumulated grace and virtue of the sage emperors, violently invading the borders, and committing atrocities and deception,
as well as their defeats at Ānnán and Dàdù,
to humiliate them.
The prefect of Yuánzhōu, Shǐ Huáicāo, was greedy and cruel;
in summer,
the fourth month,
the army rebelled,
and drove him out.
A secret edict was issued to the military governors of Xuānwǔ and Gǎnhuà and the defense commissioner of Sìzhōu,
ordering them to select several hundred elite troops to patrol within their jurisdictions,
to guard the tribute transport ships,
and to report every five days on the safe transport of tribute money and grain.
The three garrisons of Biàn, Xú, and Sì,
through which the Biàn River flows,
were the route for all tribute transport from the southeast to the capital.
All followed this route.
Bandits were rampant,
and there was fear they would be plundered,
hence the secret edict to select troops for patrol and defense.
In the fifth month,
Prince Zhāo Ruì passed away.
Ruì
was a son of Emperor Xuānzōng.
The acting military governor of Lúlóng, Lǐ Kějǔ, was appointed as military governor.
In the sixth month,
Prince Fǔ Hóng passed away.
Hóng
was a son of Emperor Shùnzōng.
An earthquake split the earth in Xióngzhōu,
water gushed forth,
destroying the city walls and all public and private buildings completely.
Xióngzhōu
is located 180 lǐ southwest of Língzhōu.
"Huài"
is pronounced "guài."
In autumn,
the seventh month,
the former prefect of Yánzhōu, Gāo Jié, was appointed as General of the Left Rapid as Tigers Guard,
and concurrently Commander of the Coastal Naval Forces.
According to the New Annals: In the second year of the Tiàolù era,
Yánzhōu was established by dividing Héngzhōu and Guìzhōu,
setting up Yánzhōu,
named after the north of Yángāng.
Prince È Rùn passed away.
Rùn
was a son of Emperor Xuānzōng.
The military governor of Wèibó, Hán Jiǎn, was granted the additional title Tongpingzhangshi.
16. Sòng Wēi attacked Wáng Xiānzhī at the foot of Yízhōu's city walls,
and inflicted a major defeat on him.
A note of examination: According to the Veritable Records,
in the twelfth month of last year,
"Sòng Wēi advanced from Qīngzhōu with Deputy Commissioner Cáo Quánzhěng to attack Wáng Xiānzhī,
and Xiānzhī was defeated and fled."
However, if Xiānzhī had been defeated and fled in the twelfth month of last year,
how could he have remained inactive for half a year in between?
It is likely that the Veritable Records,
upon mentioning Sòng Wēi's appointment as Pacification Commissioner,
connected the events. In reality, Xiānzhī's defeat occurred this month,
not in the twelfth month.
Sòng Wēi reported that Wáng Xiānzhī was dead,
dismissed the troops from various circuits,
and returned to Qīngzhōu himself.
All officials entered the court to offer congratulations.
After three days,
prefectures and counties reported that Wáng Xiānzhī was still alive,
and continued his plundering raids as before.
At that time, the troops had just been disbanded,
and an edict was issued to mobilize them again,
causing the soldiers to become resentful and inclined toward rebellion.
In the eighth month,
Wáng Xiānzhī captured Yángzhái and Jiáchéng.
An edict ordered Cuī Ānqián, Military Commissioner of Zhōngwǔ, to dispatch troops to attack him.
Ānqián
was the younger brother of Shènyóu.
Cuī Shènyóu
served as Chancellor under Emperor Xuānzōng.
Military Commissioner of Yìchéng, Cáo Xiáng, led five thousand infantry and cavalry, along with Yìchéng troops, to guard the Eastern Capital's palace.
Zēng Yuányù, Left Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, was appointed Deputy Pacification Commissioner,
to defend the Eastern Capital.
Another edict ordered Lǐ Fú, Military Commissioner of Shānnán East Circuit, to select two thousand infantry and cavalry to guard the strategic routes of Rǔzhōu and Dèngzhōu.
Wáng Xiānzhī advanced and threatened Rǔzhōu.
An edict ordered Lǐ Kǎn, Military Commissioner of Bīnníng, and Línghú Táo, Military Commissioner of Fèngxiáng, to select one thousand infantry and five hundred cavalry to guard Shǎnzhōu and Tóngguān.
17. Wáng Jǐngchóng, Military Commissioner of Chéngdé, was additionally appointed Secretariat Director.
18. In the ninth month,
on the first day, yǐhài,
a solar eclipse occurred.
19. On the bǐngzǐ day,
Wáng Xiānzhī captured Rǔzhōu
and seized its Prefect, Wáng Liào.
Liào
was a paternal cousin of Duó.
The Eastern Capital was greatly shaken.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: Rǔzhōu is 160 lǐ north of the Eastern Capital.
On the yǐyǒu day,
an imperial decree pardoned Wáng Xiānzhī and Shàng Jūnzhǎng of their crimes,
and offered them official posts
to induce their surrender.
Wáng Xiānzhī captured Yángwǔ,
and attacked Zhèngzhōu.
Léi Yīnfú, Surveillance Commissioner's Judge of Zhāoyì, was stationed at Zhōngmóu.
Zhōngmóu
is an ancient county from the Hàn dynasty.
During the Suí dynasty, it was called Jiáchéng.
In the first year of the Dàyè era,
it was renamed Pǔtián.
In the third year of the Wǔdé era of the Táng dynasty,
it was renamed Zhōngmóu
and placed under Zhèngzhōu.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: It is 70 lǐ west of Biànzhōu.
Léi Yīnfú defeated and drove them away.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Wáng Xiānzhī attacked southward, targeting Tángzhōu and Dèngzhōu.
20. Gāo Pián, Military Commissioner of Xīchuān, constructed the outer wall of Chéngdū.
He had the monk Jǐngxiān oversee the planning and measurements.
The circumference was 25 lǐ.
All county magistrates were summoned to organize laborers and assign duties.
The Chéngdū Prefecture administered ten counties: Chéngdū, Huáyáng, Xīndū, Xīpǔ, Xīnfán, Shuāngliú, Guǎngdū, Pí, Wēnjiāng, and Língchí.
Pǐ
is pronounced pǐ bì fān,
meaning "to prepare."
Fù
means "to distribute";
it refers to distributing and assigning them to labor.
The soil in Shǔ is loose and poor,
so it was faced with bricks.
Soil was taken from within ten lǐ around the city,
and all mounds and hillocks were leveled flat.
No pits were allowed to be dug that would harm farming.
Laborers were replaced after no more than ten days of work.
The people were pleased with the fairness,
and the project was completed without the need for whipping or beating.
Construction began on the guǐchǒu day of the eighth month,
and was completed on the wùzǐ day of the eleventh month.
When the labor project first began,
Gāo Pián feared that Nánzhāo might spread rumors of an invasion.
Even if they did not actually come,
the laborers would surely be alarmed and disturbed.
So he petitioned to send Jǐngxiān, under the pretext of traveling, into Nánzhāo
to persuade the Pyu Shin to submit to China,
and even promised him marriage to a princess.
The New History says
"the Buddhist monk Jǐngxiān."
Written this way,
the meaning is clearer.
Shuō
is pronounced shuì ruì fān.
Qī
is pronounced qī xì fān.
The matter dragged on without resolution.
Gāo Pián also spread word that he intended to inspect the border,
with beacon fires lit day and night,
reaching the Dàdù River.
But in reality, he did not go,
causing anxiety and fear among the barbarians.
As a result, until the city wall was completed,
there were no alarms of border disturbances.
Previously,
when officials and generals from Xīchuān entered Nánzhāo,
the Pyu Shin would sit and receive their bows.
Gāo Pián, knowing their custom revered Buddhism,
sent Jǐngxiān instead.
The Pyu Shin indeed led his ministers to welcome and bow to him,
and trusted his words.
21. Wáng Xiānzhī attacked Yǐngzhōu and Fùzhōu,
and captured them.
22. Wáng Zhēng, through the intercession of Lǔ Shí, Prefect of Wēnzhōu, requested to surrender.
Shí repeatedly submitted memorials on his behalf,
and an imperial decree ordered Zhēng to come to the capital.
However, Zhēng delayed with his troops,
and did not arrive for half a year.
He firmly requested to be appointed Commissioner of Wànghǎi Garrison.
The court did not grant this,
but instead appointed him as Commander of the Right Guard Command.
The Táng had ten Guard Commands,
and the Commander of the Right Guard Command was one of them.
All the wealth he had previously plundered
was ordered to be returned to him.
23. In the twelfth month,
Wáng Xiānzhī attacked Shēnzhōu, Guāngzhōu, Lúzhōu, Shòuzhōu, Shūzhōu, Tōngzhōu, and other prefectures.
According to the Tángshū Geographical Records,
Tōngzhōu belonged to the Shānnán East Circuit,
which is Dázhōu in the Sòng dynasty.
Later, Emperor Shìzōng of the Later Zhōu established Tōngzhōu from the Southern Táng's Jìnghǎi Army,
which is the Tōngzhōu in Huáidōng today.
In the Táng dynasty, its territory was the eastern part of Hǎilíng County in Yángzhōu.
During the Táng, there was no Tōngzhōu in the Huáinán Circuit.
This must be an error.
Referring to the text below,
"Tōng"
should be
"Qí."
An imperial decree ordered Xuē Néng, Military Commissioner of Gǎnhuà, to select several thousand elite troops to assist.
Zhèng Tián, seeing that his advice was not followed,
pleaded illness and requested to retire.
This was not permitted.
He then submitted a memorial stating:
"Since the report of victory from Yízhōu,
referring to Sòng Wēi's report of defeating Wáng Xiānzhī at the foot of Yízhōu's city walls.
Shàng
is pronounced shí zhǎng fān.
they have slaughtered and captured five or six prefectures,
wreaking havoc across several thousand lǐ.
Sòng Wēi is old, frail, and often ill.
Since his false report,
he has been particularly resented by the various circuits,
referring to his false report
that Wáng Xiānzhī was dead.
and shows no intention of advancing to suppress the rebels.
Zēng Yuányù, with troops in Qízhōu and Huángzhōu,
only looks for opportunities to retreat and shrink back.
If the rebels capture Yángzhōu,
then the Jiāngnán region will also be lost to the state.
Cuī Ānqián's prestige surpasses others,
Zhāng Zìmiǎn is a brave and outstanding general,
and Palace Garden Commissioner Lǐ Zhuàn,
grandson of Xīpíng Prince Shèng,
is strict and courageous.
I request that Ānqián be appointed Field Commander,
Zhuàn be appointed Pacification Commissioner to replace Wēi,
and Zìmiǎn be appointed Deputy Commissioner to replace Yuányù."
A note of examination: Although the Veritable Records records Tián's submitted memorial this month,
it does not mention whether it was implemented or not.
The New History Annals then state here
"Ānqián was appointed Field Commander of the Various Circuits,
Lǐ Zhuàn was appointed Pacification Commissioner for the Grass Bandits,
and Zhāng Zìmiǎn was his deputy."
However, the following year,
Wēi and Yuányù remained as Commissioner and Deputy as before.
The New History Annals are mistaken.
24. Troops from Qīngzhōu and Cāngzhōu were garrisoning Ānnán.
Qīngzhōu
was the Pínglú Army;
Cāngzhōu
was the Yìchāng Army.
Upon reaching Guìzhōu,
they expelled Observation Commissioner Lǐ Zàn.
Zàn
was the son of Zōngmǐn.
Lǐ Zōngmǐn
served as Chancellor during the Dàhé era.
The military supervisor of Guìguǎn, Lǐ Wéizhōu, was arrogant and overbearing.
Zàn (likely referring to a local official) ingratiated himself with him,
gradually becoming unable to control him.
Guìguǎn had eight hundred soldiers,
of which the defense commissioner only commanded one hundred,
the rest all belonged to the military supervisor.
Furthermore, he participated in the plot to expel the commander,
forcibly seizing the two commissioner seals.
The two commissioner seals
refer to the seals of the observation commissioner and the defense commissioner.
Shuài (commander),
pronounced as suǒ lèi fān.
Shǐ (commissioner),
pronounced as shū lì fān;
same below.
[Unclear character/action]
He seized the "send-to-commissioner" funds of Zhāozhōu.
According to the Táng system,
the taxes of each prefecture were divided into three parts: one was "supply to the court,"
sent to the capital;
the second was "send to the commissioner,"
sent to the circuit;
the third was "retained by the prefecture,"
kept for the prefecture's expenses.
Yǔmó,
was the son of Chè.
Zhāng Chè appears in Volume 242, the first year of the Chángqìng era of Emperor Mùzōng.
25 The deputy commander and overall supervisor Yáng Fùguāng reported that Shàng Jūncháng's younger brother Ràng was occupying Cháyá Mountain,
and the government troops retreated to defend Dèngzhōu.
Fùguāng
was the adopted son of Xuánjià.
Yáng Xuánjià appears in Volume 250, the fourth year of the Xiántōng era of Emperor Yìzōng.
26 Wáng Xiānzhī attacked Qízhōu.
The prefect of Qízhōu, Péi Wò,
was a jìnshì promoted by Wáng Duó when he served as examination administrator.
Wáng Liào was among the rebels,
and wrote a letter to Wò on behalf of Xiānzhī to persuade him.
Wò made an agreement with Xiānzhī,
to gather troops and not fight,
promising to petition for an official position for him;
Liào also persuaded Xiānzhī to agree to the terms.
Wò then opened the city gates and invited Xiānzhī and Huáng Cháo, along with over thirty others, into the city,
held a banquet,
and presented them with a large display of goods and valuables as gifts,
submitting a memorial detailing the situation.
Many of the chief ministers said:
"The late emperor did not pardon Páng Xūn,
and within a year he was finally executed.
The event is recorded in the previous volume, the ninth and tenth years of Xiántōng.
Zú (finally),
pronounced as zǐ xù fān.
Xiānzhī is not comparable to Páng Xūn.
Pardoning his crimes and granting him an official post
would only encourage villainy and lawlessness."
Wáng Duó firmly requested it,
and it was approved;
Xiānzhī was thus appointed as Left Shence Army Officer in Charge of Security and concurrently Investigating Censor,
and a palace envoy was sent to bestow the certificate of appointment upon him in Qízhōu.
Xiānzhī was very pleased upon receiving it,
and Liào and Wò
both congratulated him.
Before they had even withdrawn,
Huáng Cháo, angered that he had not received an official position himself,
became furious and said:
"In the beginning we made a great oath together,
to rampage across the empire.
Now you alone take an official post and go to the Left Army,
what is to become of these more than five thousand followers!"
Examination of discrepancies: When Xiānzhī and Cháo first rose up,
it was said their followers reached tens of thousands within months.
Here there are only five thousand,
likely because they were a motley crew,
gathering and dispersing irregularly.
He injured Xiānzhī's head,
and the followers clamored incessantly.
Xiānzhī, fearing the anger of the masses,
thus did not accept the appointment,
plundered Qízhōu extensively,
half the people in the city
were driven out and half were killed,
and their houses were burned.
Wò fled to Èzhōu,
the imperial envoy fled to Xiāngzhōu.
The imperial envoy
refers to the palace envoy who bestowed the certificate of appointment.
The rebels then divided their army, with over three thousand following Xiānzhī and Shàng Jūncháng,
and over two thousand following Cháo,
each taking separate routes and departing.
Examination of discrepancies: Wáng Kūn's Jīng Tīng Lù says:
"In the fourth year of Qiánfú,
Dīngyǒu,
mid-summer,
heaven displayed a comet.
The bandits Huáng Cháo and Shàng Jūncháng rampaged,
which was the fifth year, Wùxū.
The violent bandit Wáng Xiānzhī arose from Yùn and Fēng,
and invaded Rǔ and Zhèng.
The great bandits Huáng Cháo and Shàng Jūncháng, along with the chieftains of the bandit leaders,
numbered only a little over a thousand men,
and captured Rǔzhōu"
and so on.
It also says:
"Huáng Cháo headed towards Mǐn and Guǎng,
Xiānzhī headed south towards Yùnzhōu,
and Shàng Jūncháng aimed for the area between Chén and Cài.
According to the wishes of these vicious men,
over three thousand bandits belonged to Xiānzhī and Jūncháng,
and over two thousand were under Huáng Cháo's command."
The following year,
in the second month,
Xiānzhī captured Èzhōu,
and Cháo captured Yùnzhōu,
so it was not Cháo heading for Mǐn and Guǎng,
nor Xiānzhī heading for Yùn.
Wáng Kūn's book
contains many errors in dates and events,
so we only select the credible parts to adopt.
