Compiled by Imperial Order by
Sīmǎ Guāng
Later Scholar from Tiāntái
Fourth Year of Qiánfú
(Dīngyǒu, 877)
1 Spring,
first month,
Wáng Yīng lured Lǔ Shí onto his boat,
and captured him. (Wáng Yīng had requested surrender through Lǔ Shí,
the event is recorded in the previous volume, last year.)
The court heard of this,
and appointed Right Longwu Grand General Sòng Hào as the various circuits south of the Yangtze recruiting commissioner.
In addition to the troops already levied from various circuits,
they further mobilized troops from the Zhōngwǔ, Xuānwǔ, and Gǎnhuà three circuits.
Chén-Xǔ
is the Zhōngwǔ Army;
Biàn-Sòng,
is the Xuānwǔ Army;
Xúzhōu,
is the Gǎnhuà Army.
The new and old troops totaled over fifteen thousand men,
all placed under Hào's command.
Second month,
Yīng captured Wànghǎi Garrison,
plundered Míngzhōu,
and also attacked Tāizhōu,
capturing it;
the prefect Wáng Bǎo retreated to defend Tángxīng.
Tángxīng
is present-day Tiāntái County,
located 110 lǐ west of Tāizhōu.
2 Wáng Xiānzhī captured Èzhōu.
3 Huáng Cháo captured Yùnzhōu,
killing the military governor Xuē Chóng.
4 Since Qiúlóng succeeded to the throne of Nánzhào,
he had been a border trouble for nearly twenty years. (Qiúlóng ascended in the thirteenth year of Dàzhōng of Emperor Xuānzōng.
Qiú,
pronounced cí yóu fān.)
But his own country was also exhausted.
Qiúlóng died,
posthumously titled Emperor Jǐngzhuāng;
his son Fǎ succeeded him,
changing the era name to Zhēnmíng, Chéngzhì, Dàtóng,
and the state name to Hètuò,
also called Dà Fēngrén.
Examination of discrepancies: Xú Yúnqián's Nánzhào Lù says:
"Nánzhào is also called Hètuò,
and later also called itself Dà Fēngrén,"
thus using Fēng as the state name.
Fǎ enjoyed hunting and heavy drinking,
entrusting state affairs to his ministers.
Intercalary month,
the military governor of Lǐngnán West Circuit Xīn Dǎng reported that Nánzhào had sent Tuóxī Duàn Cuōbǎo and others to request peace. (Tuóxī is a Nánzhào official title,
similar to a Chinese pànguān.)
Cuō,
pronounced qī hé fān,
also qī kě fān.
"The troops from various circuits have been garrisoning Yōngzhōu for years,
the cost of provisions,
exhausts the Central Kingdom.
I request that their peace offer be accepted,
to allow the weary and afflicted to rest."
An edict approved it.
Dǎng sent his general Dù Hóng and others bearing letters and gifts,
to escort Cuōbǎo back to Nánzhào,
only leaving the troops from Jīngnán and Xuān-Shè to garrison Yōngzhōu,
reducing the troops from the other circuits by seventy percent.
5 Wáng Yǐng rampaged through Zhèxī.
Péi Qú, the military governor of Zhènhǎi, strengthened his defenses with strict military preparations,
and did not engage him in battle.
Instead, he secretly recruited Wáng Yǐng's follower Zhū Shí to surrender,
dispersing six to seven thousand of his followers,
and seizing over two hundred thousand weapons and equipment,
with ships, grain, and silk cloth in similar quantities.
An imperial decree appointed Zhū Shí as General of the Imperial Guards.
Consequently, Wáng Yǐng's faction disintegrated.
Wáng Yǐng gathered his remaining forces
and fled east to Míngzhōu,
where Liú Jùróng, the garrison commander of Yǒngqiáo, shot and killed him with a tube arrow.
Liú Jùróng, as the garrison commander of Yǒngqiáo in Sùzhōu, led troops to suppress Wáng Yǐng.
The tube arrow
was just over a foot long.
It was placed inside a bamboo tube,
fitted onto the bowstring,
and the bamboo tube was tied to the wrist.
When the bow was drawn and released,
the tube would swing backward,
propelling the arrow to shoot the enemy,
piercing them through.
For details, see the section on corrections.
In the second year of Qiánfú,
Wáng Yǐng rebelled,
and by this time, he was pacified.
Shè,
pronounced similarly.
Qú,
was the great-grandson of Péi Xǔ.
Péi Xǔ appears in the fourteenth year of Dàlì, during the reign of Emperor Dàizōng, in the 206th volume.
Cóng,
pronounced as such.
6 In the third month,
Huáng Cháo captured Yízhōu.
7 In summer,
on the fourth month,
on the first day, Rénshēn,
there was a solar eclipse.
8 The rebel leader Liǔ Yànzhāng plundered Jiāngxī.
9 The army in Shǎnzhōu mutinied,
expelling the observation commissioner Cuī Jié.
Cuī Jié was demoted to the position of military advisor in Huáizhōu.
10 Huáng Cháo and Shàng Ràng joined forces and defended Cháyá Mountain.
An examination of discrepancies: The Old Annals state:
"In the third month of the fourth year,
Cháo captured Yùnzhōu.
In the seventh month,
he entered Cháyá Mountain
and joined Wáng Xiānzhī.
In the second month of the fifth year,
Shàng Jūncháng and Wáng Xiānzhī both died.
Shàng Ràng, because his elder brother was killed,
rampaged through Huáinán."
The Old Biography states:
"In the eighth month of the fifth year,
Wáng Duó executed Wáng Xiānzhī.
Prior to this,
Shàng Ràng, the younger brother of Shàng Jūncháng, because his brother was killed while on a mission,
led his troops into Cháyá Mountain.
Huáng Cháo, Huáng Kuí, and their six brothers led several thousand bandits to join Shàng Ràng."
According to the Veritable Records,
in the second year of Qiánfú,
when Wáng Xiānzhī captured Cáo and Pú,
Huáng Cháo had already risen in response.
In the twelfth month of the third year,
the deputy surveillance commissioner Yáng Fùguāng reported:
"The bandit Shàng Ràng occupies Cháyá Mountain,
and the government troops have retreated to defend Dèngzhōu."
In the fourth month of the fourth year,
Huáng Cháo led his forces to defend Cháyá Mountain.
That winter,
Shàng Jūncháng was killed.
The Jīngtīng Lù states:
"Cháo and Xiānzhī both entered Qízhōu.
Cháo became angry because Xiānzhī alone accepted an official position,
and he beat Xiānzhī, injuring his face.
From then on, they split into separate groups."
At that time, Shàng Jūncháng was also present,
so it was not after Xiānzhī's death
that Cháo joined Shàng Ràng.
Also, according to the Old Annals,
after Xiānzhī's death,
Wáng Duó was appointed commander-in-chief to suppress the bandits.
However, the Old Biography states
"Wáng Duó executed Xiānzhī,"
and earlier it says
"he killed Zhāng Lín,
then captured Guǎngzhōu,"
and earlier still
"he captured Huázhōu,
then attacked Tóngguān."
The narrative is disordered and inconsistent.
Now, we follow the Veritable Records.
11 In the fifth month,
on the day Jiǎzǐ,
Yáng Sǔn, the supervising secretary, was appointed observation commissioner of Shǎnguó.
Upon taking office,
Yáng Sǔn executed the ringleaders of the mutiny.
Sǔn
was the son of Yáng Sìfù.
Yáng Sìfù served under Emperor Wénzōng.
12 Earlier, Lǐ Zàn, the observation commissioner of Guìguǎn, misgoverned,
and his assistant Xuē Jiānshí repeatedly admonished him to correct his ways,
but Lǐ Zàn would not listen.
After Lǐ Zàn was expelled,
(Lǐ Zàn's expulsion is recorded in the previous volume, last year.)
Bèi,
pronounced as such.
Xuē Jiānshí sent documents to neighboring regions,
prohibiting the mutinous soldiers from causing trouble,
bringing peace to the area.
An imperial decree promoted Xuē Jiānshí to erudite of the National University.
13 In the sixth month,
Liǔ Yànzhāng attacked and captured Jiāngzhōu,
capturing the prefect Táo Xiáng.
He forced Táo Xiáng to submit a memorial,
and Liǔ Yànzhāng also attached his own petition for surrender.
An imperial decree appointed Liǔ Yànzhāng as General of the Right Gate Guard,
ordering him to disband his followers and proceed to the capital.
Liú Bìngrén, General of the Left Martial Guard, was appointed prefect of Jiāngzhōu.
Liǔ Yànzhāng did not comply.
Instead, he fortified Péngjiāng with over a hundred warships, establishing a water stronghold.
Péngjiāng is located outside Jiāngzhōu city,
connecting to the great river,
hence it is called Péngjiāng.
Péng,
pronounced as such.
14 The general Lǐ Kěfēng of the Zhōngwǔ Army returned from garrison duty at the border.
Upon reaching Bīnzhōu,
he coerced the commanding officer,
demanding payment of arrears in grain and salt,
and stayed for four days,
causing alarm throughout the region.
In autumn,
on the seventh month,
he returned to Xǔzhōu,
where the military governor Cuī Ānqián arrested and executed him.
15 On the day Gēngshēn,
Wáng Xiānzhī and Huáng Cháo attacked Sòngzhōu.
Three armies engaged them in battle
but were defeated.
(The three armies were from Pínglú, Xuānwǔ, and Zhōngwǔ.)
On the day Jiǎyín,
Zhāng Zìmiǎn, General of the Left Martial Guard, led seven thousand Zhōngwǔ troops to rescue Sòngzhōu,
killing over two thousand bandits.
The bandits lifted the siege and fled.
Wáng Duó and Lú Xié wanted Zhāng Zìmiǎn to place his troops under the command of Sòng Wēi.
However, Zhèng Tián believed that Sòng Wēi and Zhāng Zìmiǎn already harbored suspicion and resentment toward each other,
and if Zhāng Zìmiǎn were under Sòng Wēi's command,
he would certainly be killed.
Therefore, Zhèng Tián refused to endorse the memorial.
In the eighth month,
on the day Xīnwèi,
Wáng Duó and Lú Xié complained to the emperor,
requesting to be dismissed.
On the day Gēngchén,
Zhèng Tián requested to return to Chǎnchuān to recuperate from illness.
(Chǎnchuān is east of Cháng'ān.)
Chǎn,
pronounced as such.
The historian remarks that Emperor Xīzōng was unable to establish proper state policies.
16 Wáng Xiānzhī captured Ānzhōu.
17 The army in Yánzhōu mutinied,
expelling the prefect Wáng Chéngyán.
An imperial decree sent the high-ranking eunuch Niú Cóngguī to pacify and instruct them.
Wáng Chéngyán was demoted to the position of household registrar in Xiàngzhōu.
Wáng Chéngyán and Cuī Jié had always been known for their good governance,
but because they were strict, they were expelled by arrogant soldiers.
The court demoted them alongside those who caused chaos through greed and tyranny,
which was lamented by contemporaries.
The historian remarks that in the late Táng dynasty, rewards and punishments were inappropriate,
and due to the ruler's incompetence and political chaos,
capable officials not only could not fully utilize their talents
but also could not avoid punishment.
The army requested that the general Wáng Zōngchéng be appointed prefect.
An imperial decree summoned Wáng Zōngchéng to the capital,
pardoned the officers and soldiers,
and still granted them generous provisions.
18 On the day Yǐmǎo,
Wáng Xiānzhī captured Suízhōu,
capturing the prefect Cuī Xiūzhēng.
Lǐ Fú, the military governor of Shānnán Dōngdào, sent his son with troops to rescue Suízhōu,
but he died in battle.
Lǐ Fú requested reinforcements,
and the court sent Lǐ Chāngyán, General of the Left Martial Guard, with five hundred cavalry from Fèngxiáng to assist him.
Wáng Xiānzhī then plundered Fùzhōu and Yǐngzhōu.

The Textual Analysis states: According to the Old Annals:
"In the seventh month of the thirteenth year of the Xiántōng era,
Lú Jiǎnfāng, the former Military Governor of Yìchāng, was appointed as Minister of the Court of Imperial Stud.
In the twelfth month,
Lǐ Guóchāng, the Military Governor of Zhènwǔ, was appointed as Prefect of Yún Prefecture and Defense Commissioner of the Dàtóng Army.
Lǐ Guóchāng claimed illness
and declined the military duties.
Consequently, Lú Jiǎnfāng, the Minister of the Court of Imperial Stud, was appointed as Prefect of Yún Prefecture
and concurrently Defense Commissioner of the Dàtóng Army.
The Emperor summoned Lú Jiǎnfāng to the Sīzhèng Hall
and said to him:
'You, having served as Military Governor of Cāng Prefecture,
are now humbly stationed in Dàtóng.
However, I am troubled by the Shātuó and Tuìhún tribes disturbing the border regions.
Since you previously served in Yúnzhōng,
and your benevolence reached the tribes,
I ask you to endure this hardship and undertake this journey on my behalf.
Fully convey my intentions,
reassure Lǐ Guóchāng,
and prevent any suspicion or resentment.'
In the first month of the fourteenth year,
on the Xīnwèi day,
due to the turmoil in Yún and Shuò Prefectures
and the unrest in the Dàiběi region,
an edict was bestowed upon Lú Jiǎnfāng, stating:
'Recently, it has been learned that the Dàtóng Army is unstable,
and Duàn Wénchǔ has been killed.
Lǐ Guóchāng's youngest son, Lǐ Kèyòng, is now in command of the military authority.'
It further stated:
'If Lǐ Kèyòng temporarily refrains from leading the troops
and awaits the court's appointment of a replacement,
then this would be a matter of expediency
and not cause for suspicion.
However, if he seeks to seize military power
and intends to occupy Dàtóng,
then the trouble would be long-lasting,
and it would be difficult to comply.
I trust that Lǐ Guóchāng, loyal and devoted,
must have already issued instructions.'
Lú Jiǎnfāng conveyed the edict's message accordingly,
but Lǐ Guóchāng did not comply.
Consequently, an edict ordered Cuī Yànzhāo, the Military Governor of Tàiyuán, and Zhāng Gōngsù, the Military Governor of Yōuzhōu, to lead troops to attack him.
In the third month,
Lú Jiǎnfāng was appointed as Military Governor of Zhènwǔ.
He died upon reaching Lán Prefecture."
The Veritable Records states that Lú Jiǎnfāng was appointed to Dàtóng in the twelfth month of the first year of the Qiánfú era.
The edict was bestowed in the first month of the second year,
and it does not mention ordering Cuī Yànzhāo and Zhāng Gōngsù to attack him.
It seems that both the Old Annals and the Veritable Records, after recording the death of Duàn Wénchǔ,
included the appointment of Lú Jiǎnfāng and the edict
to maintain narrative continuity.
However, these accounts may not be reliable.
The Old Annals' mention of Tàiyuán and Yōuzhōu attacking him
likely refers to later events.
The reason the Veritable Records did not adopt this
is that the court was still attempting to appease him at the time,
and an attack was not necessarily imminent.
The Record of Things Seen and Heard from the Late Táng further states:
"In the fourth month of the fifth year,
an imperial decree appointed Lú Jiǎnfāng as Military Governor of Zhènwǔ.
In the fifth month,
he died."
The Veritable Records also places it in the fifth year,
but states he died in the sixth month.
This likely refers to the month the report arrived.
We now follow the Record of Things Seen and Heard from the Three Reigns.
5. Yáng Zhīwēn was demoted to the position of Military Advisor of Chēn Prefecture.
This was because Wáng Xiānzhī attacked Jiānglíng,
and the city nearly fell.
Many officials and civilians were killed or captured.
6. Zēng Yuányù reported a major victory over Wáng Xiānzhī at Huángméi.
Huángméi County
belonged to Qí Prefecture.
Sòng Bái stated: During the Sòng dynasty, the Nán Xīncài Commandery was established from part of the Jiāngxià Commandery.
In the eighteenth year of the Suí dynasty's Kāihuáng era,
it was renamed Huángméi County.
Within its borders lies Huángméi Mountain,
from which the name derives.
Huang Chao was attacking Bózhōu but had not yet captured it.
Shàng Ràng led the remaining forces of Wáng Xiānzhī and joined him.
They acclaimed Huáng Cháo as their leader,
bestowing upon him the title "Heaven-Storming General."
He changed the reign era to "Wángbà."
*Kǎoyì* states: The *Xù Bǎoyùn Lù* records:
"In the first year of Qiánfú,
Huáng Cháo gathered a multitude in Kuàijí and rebelled,
establishing the reign era as the first year of Wángbà."
The *Old Biography* states:
"Previously,
Shàng Jūncháng's younger brother Ràng, because his elder brother had been executed,
led his followers into Cháyá Mountain.
Huáng Cháo, Huáng Kuí, and their six brothers led several thousand bandits to join Ràng.
After more than a month,
their numbers reached tens of thousands.
They captured Rǔzhōu,
captured the prefect Wáng Liào,
and plundered extensively east of the Hángu Pass.
The government forces intensified their campaign against them,
but were repeatedly defeated by them.
Their followers numbered over one hundred thousand.
Shàng Ràng then, together with the various bandits, acclaimed Huáng Cháo as king,
calling him the Heaven-Storming General.
He then appointed officials and staff.
The provincial military governors were unable to control them."
The *New Biography* states:
"Shàng Jūncháng's younger brother Ràng led the scattered remnants of Wáng Xiānzhī's forces and joined Huáng Cháo.
They acclaimed Huáng Cháo as king,
bestowing upon him the title Heaven-Storming General.
He appointed and conferred offices upon his officials and staff.
He drove over one hundred thousand people from Hénán and Shānnán,
plundered Huáinán,
and established the reign era Wángbà."
We now follow this account.
Huáng Cháo attacked and captured Yízhōu and Púzhōu.
Subsequently, he was repeatedly defeated by government forces.
He then sent a letter to Tiānpíng military governor Zhāng Yáng,
requesting that he memorialize the court on his behalf.
An edict appointed Huáng Cháo as General of the Right Guard,
ordering him to disband his troops at Yùnzhōu.
Huáng Cháo ultimately did not go.
*Kǎoyì* states: The *Old Biography* records:
"After Wáng Xiānzhī was defeated,
Huáng Cháo attacked Bózhōu in the east but could not capture it.
He then attacked and captured Yízhōu and occupied it.
The remaining partisans of Wáng Xiānzhī all submitted to him."
The *Veritable Records* state:
"Huáng Cháo proclaimed himself King Huáng,
established the reign era Wángbà,
was successively defeated by the imperial army,
went to Tiānpíng to beg for surrender,
was appointed General of the Right Guard,
then rebelled and left again.
From then on, the army could not control him."
The *New Biography* states:
"Zēng Yuányù defeated the bandits at Shēnzhōu,
killing ten thousand men.
The Emperor considered Sòng Wēi's execution of Shàng Jūncháng to be unjust,
and moreover, his campaign against the bandits had achieved no merit.
An edict ordered him to return to Qīngzhōu,
appointing Yuányù as commander-in-chief,
and Zhāng Zìmiǎn as his deputy.
Huáng Cháo captured Kǎochéng,
took Púzhōu.
Yuányù's army was at Jīng and Xiāng,
and the relief forces were blocked.
Zìmiǎn was further appointed as commander-in-chief of the northeastern front army,
to supervise the various armies in urgently capturing Huáng Cháo.
Huáng Cháo was then plundering Xiāngyì and Yōngqiū.
An edict ordered Huázhōu military governor Lǐ Yì to fortify Yuánwǔ.
Huáng Cháo raided Yè and Yángdí,
intending to spy on the Eastern Capital.
At that time, Left Shenwu General-in-Chief Liú Jǐngrén led five thousand troops to reinforce the Eastern Capital,
and Héyáng military governor Zhèng Yánxiū stationed three thousand troops at Héyīn.
Huáng Cháo's forces in Jiāngxī were defeated by Zhènhǎi military governor Gāo Pián.
Those raiding Xīnzhèng, Jiá, Xiāngchéng, and Yángdí were driven away by Cuī Ānqián.
Those in Zhèxī had two of their leaders beheaded by military governor Péi Qú,
and many were killed.
Huáng Cháo was greatly discouraged and fearful.
He then went to the Tiānpíng Army to beg for surrender.
An edict appointed Huáng Cháo as General of the Right Guard.
Huáng Cháo reckoned that the provincial military governors were not united,
and could not sufficiently control him.
He immediately rebelled and left,
turning to raid Zhèdōng,
and captured observation commissioner Cuī Qiú."
This differs in sequence from the *Veritable Records*.
We now follow the *Veritable Records*.
7. Shānnándōngdào military governor Lǐ Fú was granted the title Tóng Píngzhāng Shì,
as a reward for his merit in rescuing Jīngnán.
8. In the third month,
various bandits captured Lǎngzhōu and Yuèzhōu.
Lǎng and Yuè are 550 *lǐ* apart.
Yuányù was stationed at Jīng and Xiāng.
Jīng and Xiāng are 340 *lǐ* apart.
The bandits raided Sòng and Biàn.
Huázhōu is 210 *lǐ* south to Biànzhōu.
Biànzhōu is 350 *lǐ* east to Sòngzhōu.
Huáng Cháo attacked Wèinán.
The Sui dynasty established Chǔqiū County at the site of the ancient Chǔqiū city.
Because Cáo had a Chǔqiū,
it was renamed Wèinán.
During the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Huázhōu.
An edict dispatched one thousand troops from Héyáng to the Eastern Capital,
to join two thousand troops from Xuānwǔ and Zhāoyì in guarding the palace gates;
this was to guard the palace gates of the Eastern Capital.
They were to command the troops of the three military commands.
The three commands were:
Héyáng, Xuānwǔ, and Zhāoyì.
Jǐngrén
was the grandson of Liú Chāng.
Liú Chāng appears in the *Annals of Dézōng*.
Three thousand troops from Yìchéng were dispatched to guard Huányuán, Yīquē, Héyīn, and Wǔláo.
In Gōushì County, Hénán,
to the north is the old Huányuán Pass.
North of Yīquē County is the old Yīquē Pass.
Sìshuǐ County in Mèngzhōu has the Hǔláo Pass.
The Táng dynasty avoided the taboo of an ancestor's name,
changing
"hǔ" (tiger)
to
"wǔ" (martial).
9. Wáng Xiānzhī's remaining partisan Wáng Chóngyǐn captured Hóngzhōu.
Jiāngxī observation commissioner Gāo Xiāng fled to Húkǒu.
Sixty *lǐ* northeast of Jiāngzhōu is Húkǒu Town,
situated at the mouth where Pénglí Lake enters the river.
The Sòng dynasty established Húkǒu County there.
Another commander, Cáo Shīxióng, plundered Xuān and Rùn.
An edict ordered Zēng Yuányù and Yáng Fùguāng to lead troops to rescue Xuān and Rùn.
10. There was a mutiny in the Húnán army.
The capital commander Gāo Jié expelled observation commissioner Cuī Jǐn.
Jǐn
was the son of Cuī Yǎn.
Cuī Yǎn appears in the 244th fascicle, under the fifth year of Wénzōng's Tàihé reign.
Yǎn,
pronounced yǎn.
11. Huáng Cháo led his troops across the river,
attacking and capturing prefectures such as Qián, Jí, Ráo, and Xìn.
12. The imperial court, considering that Lǐ Kèyòng occupied Yúnzhōng,
in the summer,
in the fourth month,
appointed the former Dàtóng Army defense commissioner Lú Jiǎnfāng as the Zhènwǔ military governor,
and appointed the Zhènwǔ military governor Lǐ Guóchāng as the Dàtóng military governor,
believing that Kèyòng would certainly have no means to resist.
At that time, court discussions held that by sending Lǐ Guóchāng to act as a father overseeing his son,
the son would certainly have no means to resist,
but who knew that Lǐ Guóchāng and his son wished to occupy both military commands simultaneously.
Examination of discrepancies says: The Tángmò Jiànwén Lù records:
"The Zhēlǔ Army and Dàizhōu reported emergencies,
Minister Dòu dispatched five hundred Uighur cavalry for border patrol,
and by the third day of the fourth month,
they advanced to the north of Wǔlǐ Hòu.
Deputy general Kāng Shūtán, relying on his drunkenness, rebelled,
shot and wounded commander Zhào Guīyì, cut and wounded staff officer Yán Jiànhóng, and captured and bound them to take into the prefectural headquarters.
The minister ordered their entire families executed at the southern gate of the yámen,
and the military commission dispatched deputy cavalry commander Zhào Yuánlüè to lead the cavalry in advancing,
while Yán Jiànhóng was escorted to Hǎixī.
Within that month, an imperial edict and ceremonial insignia arrived,
appointing the former Dàtóng Army defense commissioner Lú Jiǎnfāng to serve as the Zhènwǔ military governor,
and appointing the Zhènwǔ military governor Minister Lǐ to serve as the Dàtóng Army military governor."
The Veritable Records state:
"On the Wùchén day,
they appointed Jiǎnfāng to Zhènwǔ,
and Guóchāng to Dàtóng."
This probably mistakenly takes the day of Kāng Shūtán's rebellion as the day Jiǎnfāng and others received their ceremonial insignia.
The New Táng History's Shātuó Biography says:
"After Lǐ Kèyòng killed Duàn Wénchǔ,
the various officers together begged for Kèyòng to be made acting defense commissioner of Dàtóng,
but this was not granted,
and troops from various circuits were dispatched to advance and capture him.
The various circuits did not exert much effort,
and just then Huáng Cháo was leading troops across the river,
so the court reckoned it could not control him,
and thus pardoned him,
appointing Guóchāng as defense commissioner of the Dàtóng Army.
Guóchāng did not accept the appointment,
and an edict ordered the Hézhōng military governor Cuī Yànzhāo and the Yōuzhōu governor Zhāng Gōngsù to jointly attack him,
but they achieved no success."
According to this,
then he was defense commissioner of Dàtóng,
not military governor.
Xuē Jūzhèng's Historical Records of the Five Dynasties states:
"After the Martial Emperor killed Duàn Wénchǔ,
the various generals submitted a petition reporting the matter,
requesting to confer upon the Martial Emperor the ceremonial insignia of command,
but the court did not consent,
and summoned troops from various circuits to campaign against him.
In the fifth year of Qiánfú,
when Huáng Cháo crossed the river,
his momentum grew rampant,
and the Son of Heaven then realized the situation,
appointing the Martial Emperor as military governor of the Dàtóng Army and Junior Guardian of the Ministry of Works."
This means Kèyòng was military governor of the Dàtóng Army,
not Guóchāng.
The Veritable Records' biography of Guóchāng, the Niánlù of the Revered Ancestor, and the Old Táng History's Basic Annals all do not mention Guóchāng being military governor of Dàtóng;
only the Veritable Records mentions it here.
Below, in the fifth month, it also says
"Guóchāng killed the supervising eunuch,
and refused to be replaced."
This must have some basis.
Probably both Guóchāng and his son refused to accept replacement,
and the court thought that using Guóchāng to replace Kèyòng,
he would certainly not defy the order,
therefore transferred Guóchāng to be military governor of the Dàtóng Army,
and appointed Lú Jiǎnfāng to govern Zhènwǔ.
The two men ultimately did not accept their appointments,
so Jiǎnfāng could not proceed to his command and died in Lánzhōu,
and Guóchāng also never proceeded to Dàtóng.
13. An edict, because the military supplies in the Eastern Capital were insufficient,
ordered loans of money and grain from merchants, travelers, and wealthy people to cover expenses for several months,
and further bestowed five blank certificates of appointment for Palace Censors,
and ten blank certificates for Investigating Censors,
to be awarded to those who could contribute substantial private wealth to aid the state.
At that time, consecutive years of drought and locusts,
rampant banditry and rebellion,
half of farming and sericulture abandoned,
insufficient tax revenue,
the inner treasury empty and exhausted,
left nothing to rely on for assistance.
The Vice Minister of War and concurrent Director of Finance Yáng Yán submitted three memorials stating his own shortcomings in ability,
that he could not manage the affairs,
his language extremely sorrowful and earnest,
but an edict did not permit it.
When people see a desirable official post,
who does not want it?
Yet there were those who resigned but were not permitted,
from which one can observe the state of the world.
14. Cáo Shīxióng raided Húzhōu.
Cáo Shīxióng advanced from Xuānzhōu and Rùnzhōu to raid Húzhōu.
Wáng Chóngyǐn died,
and his general Xú Tángjǔ occupied Hóngzhōu.
Cáo Shīxióng and Wáng Chóngyǐn
were both partisans of Wáng Xiānzhī.
15. Ráozhōu general Péng Yòuzhāng combined with the Righteous Camp troops and recaptured Ráozhōu.
Ráozhōu had recently been captured by Huáng Cháo.
The Righteous Camp troops
were those from Ráozhōu who had risen in righteous uprising.
16. Nánzhào sent its chief minister Zhào Zōngzhèng to request a marriage alliance,
(Nánzhào officials included the position of chief minister,
below the senior generals,
above the jiǔzǎn,
also a high-ranking minister.)
(Chief,
pronunciation: cí yóu fān.)
but only had the Dūshuǎng office send a document to the Secretariat,
requesting to be considered a younger brother and not to be called a subject.
An edict ordered the hundred officials to discuss it.
The Vice Minister of Rites Cuī Dàn and others considered:
"Nánzhào is arrogant, presumptuous, and without propriety.
Gāo Pián does not understand the greater principles,
and instead, through a monk's whispering and humble words, enticed their envoy to come.
If we comply with their request,
I fear we will be laughed at by later generations."
Examination of discrepancies says: The Veritable Records places Dàn's discussion between the second and fourth months.
It also says,
"Nánzhào sent chief minister Zhào Zōngzhèng to court,
and also to discuss peace and friendly relations."
Now, because of the dispute between Lú and Zhèng over the barbarian affairs, this is placed here.
Gāo Pián submitted a memorial disputing with Cuī Dàn,
and an edict was issued to explain and resolve it.
Dàn
was the son of Cuī Yú.
Yú
was the younger brother of Cuī Gǒng.
Gǒng served as chancellor under Emperor Wǔzōng.
In the fifth month,
on the first day, bǐngshēn,
Zhèng Tián and Lú Xié discussed matters concerning the southern barbarians.
Xié wanted to arrange a marriage alliance to make peace with them,
but Tián firmly argued that this was unacceptable.
Xié became angry,
flung his sleeves and rose,
his sleeve catching on an inkstone and knocking it to the ground,
breaking it.
The Emperor heard of this
and said:
"When high ministers revile each other,
how can they serve as models for the empire!"
On the second day, dīngyǒu,
both Tián and Xié were dismissed from their posts and made Advisors to the Heir Apparent with separate offices.
Textual analysis: The Old Annals state:
"In the sixth year, fifth month,
the bandits besieged Guǎngzhōu.
They sent letters to Lǐ Tāo and Cuī Qiú,
requesting the authority of the Tiānpíng military commissioner.
Tián and Xié argued in the Secretariat,
their language disrespectful.
Both were dismissed
and given separate offices."
Tián's biography says:
"In the fifth year,
Huáng Cháo crossed east over the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
his followers numbering a million,
and repeatedly captured commanderies and cities along his route.
In the sixth year,
he captured the Ānnán Protectorate
and occupied it.
He sent a letter to Cuī Qiú, the Surveillance Commissioner of Zhèdōng, requesting the authority of the Yùnzhōu military commissioner.
Qiú said: 'The bandits' momentum is difficult to overcome;
it would be appropriate to grant it to them,
in order to end their ambition to look north.'
The Son of Heaven ordered the officials to deliberate.
Earlier,
when Huáng Cháo arose,
Chief Minister Lú Xié, because Gāo Pián, the Surveillance Commissioner of Zhèxī, had a history of military achievements,
recommended him as Military Commissioner of Huáinán,
ordering him to block the bandits' advance.
Soon after, Pián was made Commander-in-Chief of the various circuits' expeditionary camps.
When Cuī Qiú made his proposal,
the court officials deliberated on it,
and some requested to grant the authority to alleviate the crisis.
Tián, considering the various opinions,
wanted to use the authority of the Nánhǎi military commissioner to restrain them.
Xié, because he had initially employed Gāo Pián,
wanted him to achieve merit and plan for victory,
saying: 'Gāo Pián's military strategy is unmatched,
and the Huái region's troops are very sharp.
Now the armies of the various circuits are just assembling;
this petty, insignificant bandit
is not difficult to pacify and exterminate.
Why should we abandon this and show weakness,
causing the various armies to disintegrate!'
Tián said: 'The disorder caused by the bandit Cháo
originally arose from a year of famine;
people joined for profit,
and thus their numbers became truly large.
South of the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
they have gradually consumed nearly half the land.
The state has long not used military force,
and all have forgotten warfare.
The regional commanders everywhere shut their gates and defend themselves;
they cannot even hold out.
It would be better to release them from blame and be tolerant,
temporarily bestowing imperial favor.
They originally joined together in a year of famine for profit;
once they encounter a plentiful year,
who would not long for their homeland!
Once their followers disperse,
then the bandit Cháo is merely meat on a chopping block.
If at this time we do not use strategy to attack,
but rely entirely on military force,
I fear the empire's troubles will not cease!'
The assembly considered this reasonable.
But the Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, Yú Cóng, said: 'Nánhǎi has the profits from maritime trade,
and annually contributes pearls and jade.
If we allow the demon bandits to possess it,
the state treasury will gradually be exhausted.'
The Emperor also hoped for Gāo Pián's success,
so he followed Xié's proposal.
When the Secretariat discussed the drafting of the edict,
Tián said: 'The demon bandits, a million strong,
run rampant across the empire.
Lord Gāo delays and toys with the bandits,
having no intention to exterminate them.
If we further protect them like this,
they will have achieved their plan.
The safety of the state's destiny
rests on the planning of the three or four of us.
You rely on Huáinán to use troops;
I do not know where we will find rest!'
Xié became angry,
flung his sleeves and rose,
staining his sleeve on the inkstone,
and then threw it.
Emperor Xīzōng heard of this
and angrily said: 'When high ministers revile each other,
how can they serve as models for the empire!'
Both men were dismissed from administrative affairs."
Xié's biography says:
"In the fifth year,
Huáng Cháo captured the outer walls of Jīngnán and Jiāngxī, and the prefectures of Ráo, Jí, Qián, Xìn, etc.
From Zhèdōng he captured Fújiàn,
then reached Lǐngnán,
captured Guǎngzhōu,
killed the Military Commissioner Lǐ Tāo,
and then defiantly submitted a memorial requesting the authority of a military commissioner.
Earlier,
when Wáng Xiānzhī arose in Hénán,
Xié recommended Sòng Wēi, Qí Kèràng, and Zēng Gǔn, who had military strategy,
and they were appointed as Pacification Commissioners.
After Sòng Wēi killed Shàng Jūnzhǎng,
causing the bandits to become rampant,
the court then made the Chief Minister Wáng Duó the Commander-in-Chief,
which Xié deeply resented.
The Zhè commander Cuī Qiú and others submitted a memorial requesting that Huáng Cháo be granted the authority of the Guǎngzhōu military commissioner.
The Emperor ordered the chief ministers to deliberate.
Xié, because Wáng Duó was the commander-in-chief,
wanted to provoke Huáng Cháo's anger,
firmly stating that the bandits should not be granted the authority of a military commissioner,
and that they should only be granted the post of a Guard Commander;
he argued with his colleague Zhèng Tián,
threw an inkstone on the ground,
and because of this both were dismissed."
The Veritable Records state:
"Fifth year, fifth month,
first day, bǐngshēn.
On this day,
Chief Ministers Zhèng Tián and Lú Xié discussed matters concerning the southern barbarians.
Xié requested to send down a princess to establish peaceful relations.
Tián firmly argued that this was unacceptable,
vehemently debating right and wrong.
Xié became angry,
flung his sleeves and rose,
his sleeve staining the inkstone,
and then threw and smashed it.
On the second day, dīngyǒu,
Tián and Xié were both made Advisors to the Heir Apparent with separate offices."
The annotation states:
"The Old History and various accounts all say 'Tián and Xié deliberated on granting Huáng Cháo the authority of a military commissioner,
argued angrily, and were dismissed.'
But Zhèng Yánchāng, who composed Tián's conduct record, says 'they deliberated on barbarian matters,'
and there is nothing to verify this.
However, what was recorded at the time is probably not mistaken."
Also, Tián's biography says:
"At that time, Huáng Cháo attacked and captured the Jiāng and Zhè regions,
and submitted a memorial begging for the authority of a military commissioner.
Tián and his colleague Lú Xié planned strategies for attack and the promotion of generals and commanders,
but their opinions often differed.
Also, the Nánzhào barbarians requested a princess for peace and friendly relations.
Tián firmly argued that this was unacceptable,
and vehemently debated it.
Consequently, he and Xié were both dismissed from the chief ministership."
Also, Xié's biography says:
"Xié's appearance was very ugly,
and his speech was also not proper.
He and Zhèng Tián were both grandsons of Lǐ Áo,
and when they jointly assisted in governance,
their discussions did not harmonize.
Earlier,
when Wáng Xiānzhī arose in Hénán,
Xié recommended Sòng Wēi, Qí Kèràng, and Zēng Gǔn, who had military strategy,
and they were appointed as Pacification Commissioners.
They all failed to achieve merit in fighting the bandits,
causing the bandits to become rampant.
Also, he supported Gāo Pián's request
to use a princess to make peace with the Nánzhào barbarians.
Zhèng Tián opposed this,
considering it unacceptable.
They argued angrily before the Emperor,
and because of this both were dismissed."
The Old Annals state:
"Sixth year, fifth month,
the bandits besieged Guǎngzhōu.
They also sent letters to Lǐ Tāo, the Military Commissioner of Guǎngnán, and Cuī Qiú, the Surveillance Commissioner of Zhèdōng,
seeking their recommendation,
and begged for the authority of the Tiānpíng military commissioner.
Qiú and Tāo submitted memorials discussing this.
Chief Ministers Zhèng Tián and Lú Xié argued in the Secretariat,
their language disrespectful.
Both were dismissed and made Advisors to the Heir Apparent with separate offices in the Eastern Capital."
Note: According to the Old and New biographies and the Old Annals, the dismissal of Tián and Xié from the chief ministership occurred in the sixth year.
The Veritable Records, the New Annals, and the tables place it in the fifth year, fifth month.
The Veritable Records and the New Book are both self-contradictory.
However, the Sòng family has many books,
and knowing that the two men were dismissed in the fifth month,
they must have had some basis,
so I follow that here.
The Vice Minister of Personnel, Cuī Hàng, was made Vice Minister of Revenue,
and both were made Participating Chancellors with Separate Offices.
At that time, there was a chancellor who was fond of giving alms.
He often had people follow him with cloth bags filled with coins,
to distribute to beggars.
Every time he went out,
the road would be filled with ragged people.
A court official wrote a letter admonishing him, saying:
"Now the common people are exhausted and impoverished,
and bandits and robbers are rampant.
Your Excellency should promote the worthy and appoint the capable,
regulate all affairs,
eliminate unnecessary expenses,
block the door to private petitions,
so that all things may find their proper place.
Then every household will be well-supplied and every person satisfied,
and naturally there will be no poor people.
Why must you act in such a way, bestowing petty favors?"
The chancellor was greatly angered.
17. The Dàjiàng of Yōngzhōu, Dù Hóng, escorted Duàn Cuōbǎo to Nánzhào,
and returned after more than a year.
Dù Hóng escorted Duàn Cuōbǎo last year in the intercalary second month.
He returned,
following Xuān's interpretation.
On the jiǎchén day,
Xīn Dǎng again dispatched Acting Patrol Officer Jiǎ Hóng, Dàjiàng Zuǒ Yú, and Cáo Lǎng as envoys to Nánzhào.
18. Lǐ Guóchāng wanted father and son to jointly control two military commands.
Upon receiving the imperial edict for Dàtóng,
he destroyed it,
killed the supervising army eunuch,
and refused to be replaced.
He joined forces with Lǐ Kèyòng and captured the Zhēlǔ Army.
The Zhēlǔ Army was northeast of Hónggǔ,
also called Zhēlǔ Píng.
West of Huáiróng County in Guīzhōu was the Níngwǔ Army,
not this one;
this should have been south of Zhēlǔ Píng.
Lángǔ County in Lánzhōu had the Kělán Army.
According to Sòng Bái's Xù Tōngdiǎn,
from Yúnzhōu eastward, taking the Níngwǔ and Guīzhōu route,
it was seven hundred lǐ to Yōuzhōu.
From Shuòzhōu west to the Kělán Army was two hundred and twenty lǐ.
This Lǐ Guóchāng combined the troops of Yún and Shuò to attack east and west,
having already captured Zhēlǔ,
he attacked Níngwǔ to the east,
and Kělán to the west.
This was the Níngwǔ Army west of Guīzhōu.
The Kělán Army was one hundred lǐ northeast of Lánzhōu.
Kě,
is pronounced kū wǒ fān.
Lán,
is pronounced lú hán fān.
He reached Lánzhōu and died.
On the dīngsì day,
Hé dōng Jiédùshǐ Dòu Huàn conscripted civilians to dig a moat at Jìnyáng.
On the jǐwèi day,
he appointed Dū Yāyá Kāng Chuànguī as Prefect of Dàizhōu,
and also dispatched one thousand local militia troops to Dàizhōu.
The militia reached the north of the city,
halted their ranks and refused to advance,
demanding generous rewards.
At that time, the government treasury was empty and exhausted.
Huàn sent Mǎbù Dū Yúhòu Dèng Qián to go and appease them.
The militia troops [AS-FE47] Dèng Qián,
carried his corpse into the government office on a bed.
Huàn and the supervising army eunuch personally went out to appease them,
giving each person three hundred coins,
and one bolt of cloth.
The crowd then calmed down.
Yāyá Tián Gōng'è distributed the money and cloth to the mutinous troops.
The crowd then seized him and made him their Dūjiàng,
and proceeded to Dàizhōu.
Huàn borrowed fifty thousand strings of coins from merchants to aid the army.
Textual analysis: Tángmò Jiànwén Lù states:
"In the fifth month,
Zhènwǔ disregarded the separate imperial decree,
and did not accept the replacement.
Minister Lǐ recaptured the Zhēlǔ Army,
and advanced to attack Níngwǔ and the Kělán Army;
Dàizhōu reported an emergency.
On the twenty-second day,
orders were given within the three cities of the prefecture,
to conscript one laborer from each household to dig the moats on all four sides.
Minister Lú set out for Zhènwǔ,
reached Lánzhōu,
and died there.
On the twenty-fourth day,
Dū Yāyá Kāng Chuànguī was appointed Prefect of Dàizhōu.
Also, one thousand local militia youths conscripted from Tàiyuán and Jìnyáng counties were sent to be stationed in Dàizhōu.
When they reached north of the city,
they halted their ranks and refused to advance,
demanding generous rewards for the campaign.
Mǎbù Dū Yúhòu Dèng Qián was sent to appease them,
but was soon [AS-FE47] and killed,
his coffin carried into the government office on a bed.
The Minister and the supervising army eunuch personally went out to appease them,
deciding to give each person three hundred coins,
and one bolt of cloth.
Yāyá Tián Gōng'è was sent to distribute them,
but was not allowed to return.
He was then requested by the troops to serve as Dūjiàng,
and sent to the front lines.
The Commissioner's office posted a notice,
borrowing fifty thousand strings of coins from merchants to aid the army."
The Veritable Records state:
"In the fifth month,
Lǐ Guóchāng killed the supervising army eunuch,
refused to be replaced,
raised troops and advanced to attack Níngwǔ and the Kělán Army.
Dàizhōu dispatched troops to resist him.
Initially,
Guóchāng sent Kèyòng to lead troops in a surprise attack on Dàtóng.
The three armies petitioned for Kèyòng to be appointed Liúhòu.
The court did not approve,
and instead ordered Guóchāng to take command,
hoping his son would be unable to refuse.
At that time, Guóchāng coveted that territory,
wanting father and son to separately govern,
hence he defied the order."
The Veritable Records state:
"In the sixth month,
on the first day, yǐchǒu,
Lánzhōu reported that the newly appointed Zhènwǔ Jiédùshǐ Lú Jiǎnfāng had died.
Tàiyuán Prefecture Dū Yāyá Kāng Chuànguī was appointed Prefect of Dàizhōu.
One thousand local militia troops from Tàiyuán and Jìnyáng were dispatched to garrison Dàizhōu.
When they reached north of the city,
they halted their ranks and refused to advance,
demanding generous rewards.
Mǎbù Dū Yúhòu Dèng Qián went to appease them,
and was killed by the crowd.
Jiédùshǐ Dòu Huàn personally went out to pacify them,
and they were then calmed.
Initially,
the treasury of Tàiyuán Prefecture was empty and exhausted.
Whenever there were rewards to be given,
they necessarily had to be levied from the people's households.
By this time, it was especially straitened,
so a notice was posted to borrow fifty thousand strings of coins from merchants to aid the army."
All of this is based on a summary of Tángmò Jiànwén Lù,
but the dates are later, based on when the memorials arrived.
Tángmò Jiànwén Lù also states:
"On the eleventh day of the sixth month,
Zuǒ Sǎnqí Chángshì Zhī Mó received the imperial decree and arrived at the prefecture,
to serve as Dàtóng Army Zhìzhìshǐ,
concurrently acting as Hé dōng Jiédù Fùshǐ, and co-commander of military affairs at the front."
This refers to the day he arrived at the prefecture.
But the Veritable Records state:
"On the jiǎxū day,
Mó was appointed Zhìzhìshǐ."
Jiǎxū was the tenth day of the sixth month,
which is also an error.
In the sixth month,
former Zhāoyì Jiédùshǐ Cáo Xiáng was appointed Hé dōng Jiédùshǐ.
19. Remnants of Wáng Xiānzhī's band plundered Zhèxī.
The court, because Jīngnán Jiédùshǐ Gāo Pián had previously established a formidable reputation in Tiānpíng,
Gāo Pián's formidable reputation
came from defeating the Man barbarians at Jiāozhǐ and then being transferred to Tiānpíng,
and the people of Yùn consequently feared him.
So Pián was transferred to be Zhènhǎi Jiédùshǐ.
20. The Shātuó burned Tánglín and Guō County,
and entered the territory of Xīnzhōu.
In the first year of Zhèngshèng of Empress Wǔ,
Wǔtái and Guō were divided to establish Wǔyán County.
In the first year of Tánglóng,
it was renamed Tánglín.
Guō,
was an ancient county of the Hàn,
and at that time both belonged to Dàizhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Tánglín was originally the territory of Guǎngwǔ County of the Hàn.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Guō was fifty lǐ southwest of the prefecture.
Guō,
is pronounced guō.
21. In autumn,
the seventh month,
Cáo Xiáng arrived at Jìnyáng.
On the jǐhài day,
thirteen members of the militia who had killed Dèng Qián were arrested,
and executed.
The Yìwǔ troops arrived at Jìnyáng,
did not remove their armor,
and clamored noisily, demanding generous rewards.
Huān,
is the same as xuān.
They were then pacified.
Troops from Yìchéng, Zhōngwǔ, Zhāoyì, and Héyáng were assembled at Jìnyáng,
to defend against the Shātuó.
In the eighth month,
on the wùyín day,
Cáo Xiáng led troops to rescue Xīnzhōu.
The Shātuó attacked the Kělán Army,
captured its outer city,
and defeated the government troops at Hónggǔ.
Hónggǔ was south of the Kělán Army.
Defeated,
bǔ mài fān.
22. Huáng Cháo invaded Xuānzhōu.
Wáng Níng, the Xuānshè observation commissioner, resisted him,
but was defeated at Nánlíng.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: Nánlíng County is located 105 lǐ west of Xuānzhōu.
Huáng Cháo then led his troops to attack Eastern Zhèjiāng,
opening a mountain road for 700 lǐ,
and plundered the various prefectures of Fújiàn.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì,
from Wùzhōu to the border of Qúzhōu is 190 lǐ.
From the seat of Qúzhōu to Jiànzhōu is 705 lǐ.
Could this road have been first opened by Huáng Cháo?
Plunder,
pronounced piào.
23. In the ninth month,
the Pínglú Army reported that the military governor Sòng Wēi had died.
Dying of old age and illness
was certainly fitting for him.
The history records Sòng Wēi's death
as a warning against holding military power and toying with bandits, failing to serve the state.
24. On Xīnchǒu,
Zēng Yuányù, the overall campaign commander of the various circuits, was appointed to concurrently hold the position of Pínglú military governor.
25. On Rényín,
Cáo Xiáng died suddenly.
On Bǐngwǔ,
the Zhāoyì troops plundered Jìnyáng on a large scale.
The residents of the wards and markets joined forces to attack them,
killing over a thousand men,
and the troops then scattered.
26. Lǐ Wèi, Vice Director of the Secretariat and concurrently Grand Councilor, was dismissed to become the defender of the Eastern Capital.
Zhèng Cóngdǎng, the Minister of Personnel, was appointed Vice Director of the Secretariat and concurrently Grand Councilor.
Cóngdǎng
was the grandson of Zhèng Yúqìng.
Zhèng Yúqìng first appears in the fourteenth year of the Zhēnguán era of Emperor Dézōng, in scroll 235.
27. Lǐ Dū, the Minister of Revenue and concurrently in charge of the Ministry of Revenue, was appointed Grand Councilor and concurrently military governor of Hézhōng.
28. In winter,
the tenth month,

an edict ordered Lǐ Jūn, the military governor of Zhāoyì; Lǐ Kějǔ, the military governor of Yōuzhōu; the Tǔyùhún chieftains Hèlián Duó, Bái Yìchéng; the Shatuo chieftain Ān Qìng; and the Sàge chieftain Mǐ Hǎiwàn,
to combine their forces and attack Lǐ Guóchāng and his son at Yùzhōu.
Consulting the New and Old Histories,
Ān Qìng and Sàge
are both names of tribes.
This can be seen by comparing with the mention of Ān Qìng commander Shǐ Jìngcún in the first year of the Guǎngmíng era.
Chieftain,
pronounced cí yóu.
Leader,
pronounced zhī zhàng.
Sà,
pronounced sāng gě.
The Kělán Army turned the city over to the Shatuo.
On Dīngwèi,
Cuī Jìkāng, the Xuānwèi commissioner of Hézhōng, was appointed military governor of Hézhōng and overall campaign commander of the Dàiběi campaign.
The Shatuo attacked Shízhōu.
On Gēngxū,
Cuī Jìkāng went to its relief.
29. In the twelfth month,
on Jiǎxū,
Huáng Cháo captured Fúzhōu.
The observation commissioner Wéi Xiù abandoned the city and fled.
30. The Nánzhào envoy Zhào Zōngzhèng returned to his country.
In the fourth month of this year,
Zhào Zōngzhèng came to request peace.
Only the letter from Cuī Ānqián, the military governor of Western Chuān, was used,
instructing Ānqián to reply to him.
31. Cuī Jìkāng and Zhāoyì military governor Lǐ Jūn fought Lǐ Kèyòng at Hónggǔ.
The armies of the two garrisons were defeated,
and Lǐ Jūn died in battle.
The Zhāoyì troops retreated to Dàizhōu.
The soldiers plundered,
and the people of Dàizhōu killed almost all of them.
The remaining troops fled back to Shàngdǎng via the Yāmíng Valley.
Yāmíng Valley is located northeast of Xiùróng County in Xīnzhōu.
Examination of discrepancies: The Old Annals state:
"Hézhōng military governor Cuī Jìkāng and the northern campaign commander Lǐ Jūn fought the Shatuo Lǐ Kèyòng at Hónggǔ in the Kělán Army.
The imperial army was greatly defeated,
and Lǐ Jūn died from a stray arrow.
On Wùxū,
they reached Dàizhōu.
The Zhāoyì army mutinied,
and were almost completely killed by the people of Dàizhōu."
The Veritable Records for this year are roughly the same.
The Veritable Records for the eighth month of the first year of Guǎngmíng:
"Hézhōng reported that Zhāoyì military governor Lǐ Jūn was killed by the Měnghǔ Army."
It also says:
"An edict ordered him to lead his own circuit's troops out through Yànmén to attack Yúnzhōu.
He fought the bandits,
was defeated and returned,
and was killed by his subordinates."
The New Annals:
"On Gēngchén,
Cuī Jìkāng and Lǐ Jūn fought Lǐ Kèyòng at Hónggǔ,
and were defeated."
Xuē Jūzhèng's Historical Records of the Five Dynasties states:
"In the spring of the sixth year of Qiánfú,
the court appointed Zhāoyì military governor Lǐ Jūn as the northern campaign commander.
He led the troops of Shàngdǎng and Tàiyuán past the Shílǐng Pass,
and encamped at Dàizhōu,
joining with Yōuzhōu's Lǐ Kějǔ and Hèlián Duó to attack Yùzhōu.
The Revered Ancestor defended with one army,
and the Martial Emperor led one army south to Zhēlǔ Fortress to resist Lǐ Jūn.
That winter,
there was heavy snow.
Bows and crossbows snapped and broke.
The southern army suffered from the bitter cold,
and was greatly defeated in battle.
They fled back to Dàizhōu,
and Lǐ Jūn died from a stray arrow."
The Táng Mò Jiàn Wén Lù states:
"On the nineteenth,
Minister Cuī set out for the Kělán Army,
requesting that a separate edict appoint Acting Minister Jiǎ Jìngsì as acting military governor,
and observation judge Lǐ Shào as acting observation commissioner.
Zhāoyì military governor Lǐ Jūn led his circuit's troops to Dàizhōu.
The army mutinied,
and they were almost completely slaughtered by Dàizhōu.
Lǐ Jūn was captured.
The remaining army scattered,
and each returned to their own circuit via the Yāmíng Valley."
Regarding the Zhāoyì army mutiny,
it certainly was not something Lǐ Jūn did.
The people of Dàizhōu captured Lǐ Jūn,
but it is unknown how they dealt with him.
I now follow the Old Annals.
32. Regarding the rebellion of Wáng Yīng,
the events began in the second year of the previous scroll,
and ended in the fourth year of this scroll.
He was appointed to fill the position of Shíjìng Fort commander.
In the fourth year of Chuígōng,
the lands of Yúháng and Yúqián were divided,
and Lín'ān County was established at the old Línshuǐ city,
belonging to Hángzhōu.
There are Shíjìng Mountain and Shíjìng Fort.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: Lín'ān County is 120 lǐ west of the prefecture.
According to the Lín'ān Zhì: Shíjìng Mountain is 1 lǐ south of Lín'ān County.
Qián Liú later changed its name to Yìjǐn Mountain.
Cáo Shīxióng invaded the two Zhè regions.
Hángzhōu recruited a thousand militiamen from each county to attack him.
Dǒng Chāng, along with Qiántáng's Liú Mèng'ān, Ruǎn Jié; Fùyáng's Wénrén Yǔ; Yánguān's Xú Jí; Xīnchéng's Dù Léng; Yúháng's Líng Wénjǔ; and Línpíng's Cáo Xìn each became their respective commanders,
known as the Eight Battalions of Hángzhōu.
Qiántáng and Yúháng were both Hàn dynasty counties.
Fùyáng
was the Hàn dynasty Fùchūn County.
During the Jìn, to avoid a taboo,
it was changed to Fùyáng.
Xīnchéng
was a Wú dynasty county.
Yánguān
was on the site of the Hàn dynasty Hǎiyán County.
There was a salt official,
and the Wú dynasty thus named the county.
Línpíng Town
is north of Qiántáng.
The Suí dynasty's Yúháng County
established Hángzhōu.
Later, the prefectural seat was moved to Qiántáng,
and later again moved west of Liǔpǔ,
which is the present prefectural city.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: Fùyáng is 73 lǐ southwest of the prefecture.
Yánguān is 129 lǐ east of the prefecture.
Xīnchéng is 130 lǐ southwest of the prefecture.
Yúháng is 72 lǐ northwest of the prefecture.
Commander,
pronounced jí liàng.
The same below.
Later, Yǔ died,
and Qiántáng's Chéng Jí replaced him.
Lín'ān's Qián Liú served Dǒng Chāng with bravery.
For his achievements, he was made Shíjìng Battalion commander of the army.
The affairs of Qián Liú begin here.
Liú,
pronounced lì qiú.
1. In spring,
the first month,
the Prince of Wèi, Yì, died.
Yì
was a son of Emperor Yìzōng.
2. Gāo Pián, the military governor of Zhènhǎi, sent his generals Zhāng Lín and Liáng Zuǎn
Examination of discrepancies: The Old Annals
write "Zhāng Lín"
as
"Zhāng Lín".
The New Annals, biographies, and Veritable Records write it as
"Lín".
I now follow the Old History's biographies of Gāo Pián and Huáng Cháo, as well as the Táng Nián Bǔ Lù, Yāo Luàn Zhì, Táng Bǔ Jì, and Xù Bǎo Yùn Lù.
The Old Annals
write "Liáng Zuǎn"
as
"Liáng Jì".
I now follow the majority of texts.
They repeatedly defeated him,
and his generals Qín Yàn, Bì Shīduó, Lǐ Hǎnzhī, Xǔ Qíng, and several dozen others surrendered.
Huáng Cháo then headed for Guǎngnán.
Yàn
was from Xúzhōu.
Shīduó
was from Yuānqú.
Hǎnzhī
was from Xiàngchéng.
3. Jiǎ Hóng and others had not yet reached Nánzhào when
they died one after another on the journey.
Last year in May,
Xīn Dǎng had sent Jiǎ Hóng as an envoy to Nánzhào.
(He) died.
(Note on pronunciation for the character "卒": zú, with the tone falling and rising.)
At that time, Xīn Dǎng was already suffering from wind paralysis.
He summoned the acting patrol officer Xú Yúnqián,
grasped his hand, and said:
"I, Dǎng, have already petitioned the court to send an envoy to Nánzhào,
but the envoys have died one after another.
What is to be done?
Since you, sir, have entered official service, you should think of serving the state.
Can you undertake this journey?
I, Dǎng, regret that my wind paralysis prevents me from bowing to you."
Then, choking with sobs, he shed tears.
Yúnqián said:
"A scholar dies for one who understands him!
An ancient saying goes: 'A man of worth dies for one who appreciates him,
a woman makes herself beautiful for one who delights in her.'
(Note on pronunciation for the character "為" in this context: wèi, with the falling tone.)
(Tone falling.)
I regret having no means to repay your kindness.
How dare I not accept your command!"
Dǎng was pleased
and provided him with generous funds and equipment before sending him off.
The history records that Xīn Dǎng, even on his deathbed, did not forget the affairs of the state.
In the second month,
on the day Bǐngyín,
Yúnqián arrived at Shànchǎn City.
The Biāoxìn received the chief envoy with equal courtesy
but accepted bows from the deputy envoy and those below him.
On the day Jǐsì,
the Biāoxìn sent Cí Shuāngyǔ and Yáng Zōng to the guesthouse to say to Yúnqián:
"Your prefecture's dispatch wishes the Biāoxìn to declare himself a subject,
presenting memorials and offering local products as tribute.
The Biāoxìn has already sent people from Xīchuān into Táng,
to agree with Táng to be as brothers,
or else as uncle and nephew.
Between brothers or uncle and nephew,
it is only a matter of correspondence and gifts.
What need is there for memorials and tribute?"
Yúnqián said:
"Since the Biāoxìn wishes to be a younger brother or a nephew,
(note: The Biāoxìn is the son of Jǐngzhuāng.
Did Jǐngzhuāng not have brothers?
Qiúlóng was posthumously titled Emperor Jǐngzhuāng.)
When the Biāoxìn became ruler,
then all his uncles became his subjects.
How much more so for a younger brother or a nephew!
Moreover, the ancestors of the Biāoxìn
received the mandate of the Great Táng,
enabling them to unite the six Zhào into one.
(This event is recorded in scroll 214, the 26th year of the Xuánzong era's Kāiyuán period.)
The minor grievances in between
were the fault of the border officials.
(Referring to Nánzhào and Xīchuān contending over trivial matters,
leading to the outbreak of war.)
How can you go against the established practice of your ancestors!
Obeying one's ancestors is filial piety;
(this is) filial piety.
Serving a great state is righteousness;
(this is) righteousness.
Ceasing warfare is benevolence;
(this is) benevolence.
Clarifying names and statuses is propriety;
(this is) propriety.
These four
are all excellent virtues.
Should you not strive for them!"
The Biāoxìn treated Yúnqián with great courtesy.
Yúnqián stayed in Shànchǎn for seventeen days before returning.
The Biāoxìn gave Yúnqián two wooden tablets:
one addressed to the Secretariat-Chancellery,
and one a dispatch to the Lǐngnán West Circuit.
However, he still refused to present memorials and offer tribute.
4. On the day Xīnwèi,
the HéDōng army arrived at Jìnglè.
(Note: Jìnglè was the location of the Hàn dynasty's Fényáng County.
During the Qí and Zhōu periods, it was renamed Kělán.
In the 18th year of the Suí dynasty's Kāihuáng era, it was renamed Fényuán.
In the 4th year of the Dàyè era, it was renamed Jìnglè.
During the Táng, it belonged to Lán Prefecture.
The "Jiǔyù Zhì" states: It is fifty *li* northeast of the prefectural seat.)
They killed the record-keeping official Shí Yù and others.
On the day Rénshēn,
Cuī Jìkāng fled back to Jìnyáng.
On the day Jiǎxū,
the detachment commanders Zhāng Kǎi and Guō Pò led the camp troops to attack the Dōngyáng Gate,
entered the headquarters,
and killed Jìkāng.
On the day Xīnsì,
(the court) appointed the Shǎn-Guó observation commissioner Gāo Fén as military governor of Zhāoyì;
and appointed the Bīn-Níng military governor Lǐ Kǎn as military governor of HéDōng.
(Textual analysis note: The "Táng Mò Jiàn Wén Lù" records:
"On the 20th,
the pacification commissioner arrived at the headquarters.
Lǐ Kǎn was appointed military governor of HéDōng."
The "Shílù" therefore states
"on Gēngyín, Kǎn was appointed,"
which is an error.)
5. In the third month,
the military governor of Tiānpíng, Zhāng Tì, died.
The officer-in-charge Cuī Jūnyù took over the administration of the prefecture himself.
The prefect of Zī Prefecture, Cáo Quánzhěng, attacked and executed him.
6. In summer,
the fourth month,
on the first day, Gēngshēn,
there was a solar eclipse.
7. When the Xīchuān military governor Cuī Ānqián assumed his post, he did not investigate bandits,
which puzzled the people of Shǔ.
Ānqián said:
"If the officials in charge do not connive with them, bandits cannot operate.
(Note: 'Officials in charge' refers to the officers responsible for capturing bandits.)
Searches and arrests would only cause unnecessary disturbance."
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
he took 1,500 strings of cash from the treasury
and distributed them among the three markets.
(In the Chéngdū city, those selling flowers, fruits, and silkworm equipment gathered in one place, called the 'Silkworm Market';
those selling incense and medicine gathered in one place, called the 'Medicine Market';
those selling utensils were called the 'Seven Treasures Market'.)
He proclaimed: "Whoever can report and capture one bandit
will be rewarded five hundred strings of cash.
A bandit cannot act alone;
he must have accomplices.
If an accomplice reports and captures (the bandit),
he will be pardoned for his crime,
and rewarded the same as an ordinary person."
Not long after,
someone brought in a captured bandit.
The bandit protested, saying:
"You and I were bandits together for seventeen years.
The loot was always divided equally.
How can you capture me!
You and I will die together."
Ānqián said:
"Since you knew I had posted this proclamation,
why didn't you capture him first!
Then he would have been executed,
and you would have received the reward.
Since he got ahead of you,
what excuse do you have for not dying!"
He immediately ordered the reward money to be given to the captor,
made the bandit watch it,
and then had the bandit dismembered in the market,
also exterminating his family.
Thereupon, the various bandits and their accomplices became suspicious of each other.
Finding no place to set foot,
they did not wait for dawn
but scattered and fled beyond the borders.
Subsequently, there was not a single bandit within the territory.
Ānqián considered the Shǔ soldiers timid and weak.
He petitioned to send a general with documents to Chén and Xǔ to recruit strong men,
to mix them with the Shǔ people,
train and use them.
They obtained three thousand men,
divided into three armies.
They also wore yellow caps,
and were called the "Yellow Head Army."
(This imitated the name of the Zhōngwǔ Yellow Head Army.)
They taught the Shǔ people to use crossbows, shooting pellets while running.
A thousand men were selected,
called the "Divine Crossbow Battalion."
From then on, the Shǔ soldiers gradually grew stronger.
I have often said that the strength of an army lies with the general, not the soldiers.
With the soldiers of Qín being the strongest in the land,
yet Hàn Gāozǔ used Shǔ soldiers to pacify the Three Qín.
Since the Táng dynasty,
Shǔ soldiers have been known as cowardly and timid.
However, Wéi Gāo used them to subdue Tǔbō with ease,
never borrowing skilled men from other circuits.
It was with Lǐ Déyù that they began recruiting skilled men from other circuits to manufacture weapons.
Cuī Ānqián probably imitated Lǐ Déyù's old strategy.

"The Vice Director of the Astrological Service, Hóu Chāngyè, submitted a memorial,
which roughly stated:
'Your Majesty does not heed the advice of Lǐ Wèi and Dù Xī'áo;'
and also said:
'I openly pray to the Five Paths,
and secretly invoke the underworld officials,
trembling with fear among the ranks of officials,
wishing to soon pass from this world of Jambudvīpa;'
and also said:
'Receiving titles not from a virtuous ruler,
bearing halberds often in service to a lawless sovereign;'
and also said:
'I do not hope for the years of Yáo and Shùn,
but only to share the days of the late Emperor;'
and also said:
'Openly taking orders from Yǐn Xīfù,
secretly accepting petitions from Wáng Shìchéng,
forcibly seizing treasures from Persia,
extorting pearls from tea shops,
plundering warehouses wholesale,
and transporting entire cities;'
and also said:
'Is it that the Táng dynasty's allotted years are exhausted,
or that Your Majesty's lifespan has reached its limit?'
And also said:
'I humbly beg Your Majesty
to temporarily cease entertainments and rewards,
to rescue and aid the common people,
to establish a Vajradhātu altar within the palace,
and to use selfless wealth to make offerings to all Buddhas,
thereby aiding the world's fortune,
and jointly striving to ward off disasters.'
When the memorial was presented,
the Sacred Emperor's dragon-like wrath shook with rage,
and the attending ministers were terrified.
The Commissioner of the Palace Reception declared: 'Hóu Chāngyè is to be handed over to the Palace Domestic Service,
awaiting further instructions.'
At noon the next day,
the palace attendant Liú Jìyuǎn proclaimed an oral decree: 'Hóu Chāngyè, born of humble origins,
was elevated to a pure and close position.
Unable to cultivate caution,
he recklessly presented trivial words,
slandering the sovereign of ten thousand chariots,
and vilifying the hundred officials and ministers.
According to our constant laws,
this cannot be tolerated!
Hóu Chāngyè shall be ordered to take his own life.'"
The Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán states:
"After the Guāngmíng era of the Táng dynasty,
eunuchs monopolized power,
establishing Commissioners for Appointments and Dismissals in the north and south.
The Army Supervisor Tián Lìngzī possessed the power to reverse heaven's will,
and both inside and outside the court, people watched with sidelong glances.
Meanwhile, Wáng Xiānzhī and Huáng Cháo plundered Jiāng and Huái,
causing the court great concern.
The Left Reminder Hóu Chāngyè submitted a memorial vehemently criticizing the maladies of the time.
It was retained within the palace and not released,
and he was ordered to be executed within the palace guard.
Later, there were rumors that the wording of Hóu Chāngyè's memorial did not match the gravity of the matter,
and its conclusion stated:
'I request the opening of a Vajradhātu altar to dispel the calamities of war,'
resembling something fabricated by mediocre monks.
If Hóu Chāngyè indeed offended the sovereign with such shallow insight,
his death was fitting." The present account follows this.

Examination of discrepancies: The Xù Bǎoyùn Lù records Pián's memorial and the imperial reply, stating:
"Now We appoint you as Dūtǒng of the various circuits;
all generals, soldiers, and horses of the expeditionary camps
shall receive your command."
Before the imperial decree arrived,
the court grew suspicious and distrustful,
issuing a subsequent edict:
"However, you are not permitted to conduct military campaigns;
you are only to firmly guard your borders,
and must not rashly undertake punitive expeditions."
Thereupon, Gāo Pián diverted the Huái River to encircle Jiāngdū City with three layers of water,
sat armored and did not attack,
and Huáng Cháo's power grew increasingly strong from this point onward.
The Old Annals and Biographies state:
Wáng Duó was sent out to govern Jīngnán,
also serving as Dūtǒng of the various circuits' expeditionary camps.
However, the Veritable Records and the New Annals and Tables
all say
"served as Dūtǒng of the Southern Front expeditionary camps."
The Old Annals state:
"In the sixth month of the fourth year of Qiánfú,
Pián was appointed as Zhènhǎi Jiedùshǐ and Jiāngxī Zhāotǎoshǐ.

In the third month of the first year of Guǎngmíng,
because Wáng Duó had achieved no success in commanding the masses,
the court then conferred upon Pián the title of Dūtǒng of the various circuits' expeditionary camp troops and horses."
Pián's biography states:
"In the fourth year,
he served as Zhènhǎi Jiedùshǐ,
and soon was appointed Dūtǒng of the various circuits' troops and horses.

Lú Xié's biography says:

his Dūtǒng title was revoked,
and Gāo Pián replaced him."
The Veritable Records state:
"In the sixth month of the fifth year,
Pián was transferred to Zhènhǎi.
In the first month of the sixth year,
Pián was appointed Dūtǒng of the various circuits' expeditionary camp troops and horses,"
and the imperial edict bestowed was as recorded in the Bǎoyùn Lù.
In the eighth month, Pián's memorial also mentioned this.
In the tenth month, Pián was transferred to Huáinán,
continuing to serve as Dūtǒng as before.
According to Pián's memorial requesting to recall Láng Yòufù to defend Zhèxī,
this occurred while he was at Zhènhǎi.
The edict states
"having served in six garrisons,"
meaning after Pián had already been transferred to Huáinán.
The six garrisons
refer to Ānnán, Tiānpíng, Xīchuān, Jīngnán, Zhènhǎi, and Huáinán.
Furthermore, the edict states,
"Now We appoint you as Dūtǒng of the various circuits,"
which seems to indicate he became Dūtǒng only after being transferred to Huáinán.
It is suspected that while in Zhèxī, Pián was initially Zhāotǎoshǐ;
after repeatedly defeating Cháo's army,
he took the eradication of Cháo as his own responsibility,
submitting a memorial requesting the deployment of various armies,
intending to personally attack Cháo in Guǎngzhōu.
After Wáng Duó's defeat,
Lú Xié then replaced him with Pián.
Xié wanted to increase his authority,
hence making him Dūtǒng of the various circuits.
If Pián had already been Dūtǒng of the various circuits earlier,
and Duó was merely Dūtǒng of the Southern Front,
then Duó would have been under Pián's command,
and Pián could have directed him;
his memorial would not need to say
'I beg to issue an edict to command Duó'
Moreover, Duó, as a chancellor, commanded the various generals to suppress the bandits,
hence establishing the title of Dūtǒng;
there should not have been two Dūtǒng simultaneously.
The reason he held the title of Jiāngxī Zhāotǎoshǐ while in Zhèxī
was because Huáng Cháo was then plundering Qián, Jí, Ráo, and Xìn.
Now we follow the Old Annals and Lú Xié's biography.

Wéi Zhíyí’s *Hanlin Old Practices* states: According to old practices,
the Secretariat used yellow and white hemp paper,
to distinguish the importance of imperial decrees.
Recently, only yellow hemp paper was issued;
the white hemp paper was all kept in the Hanlin Academy.
Unless it was a matter of great national importance,
such as appointing generals or chancellors, or issuing imperial pardons,
white hemp paper was not used.
The historian notes that in the late Tang, eunuchs were unrestrained and arrogant,
and Army Supervisors and Commissioners of the Bureau of Military Affairs
received honors and treatment equal to those of generals and chancellors.
Chéng Dàchāng said: Whenever white hemp paper edicts were to be issued,
