Now follow the Yúnnán Affairs Account.
The Yúnnán Affairs Account also states:
"The Secretariat memorialized: 'Xuánzōng enfeoffed Méng Guīyì as King of Yúnnán,
his son Géluófèng surrendered to Tǔbō,
his grandson Yìmóuxún returned to the court,
personally requested to change his title to King of Yúnnán,
and was granted the title Nánzhào.
Dézong complied.
To his great-grandson Méng Fēngyòu,
Dù Cóng memorialized that because too many people were coming to court,
he reduced the number,
later demanded hostages,
gradually leading to contempt and disrespect.'"
At the end of the scroll, letters from Chén Jìngxuān to Yúnnán are recorded,
sometimes addressed to Hètuò,
sometimes to Dàfēngrén.
The Yúnnán Affairs Account does not record the compiler's name,
it seems to be a draft memorial by Lú Xié.
A letter was also sent to them,
and additional gold and silk were bestowed.
Sì Cáowáng Guīnián was appointed Vice Minister of the Court of the Imperial Clan to serve as envoy,
with Xú Yúnqián as deputy envoy,
separately sending a palace envoy,
together they carried the edict to Nánzhào.
Palace envoy,
means a eunuch envoy.
29 In autumn,
the seventh month,
Huáng Cháo crossed the river from Cǎishí,
and besieged Tiāncháng and Liùhé.
Cǎishí garrison,
is located northwest of Dāngtú County in Xuānzhōu,
crossing the river enters Hézhōu territory.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo,
land from Jiāngdū, Liùhé, and Gāoyóu counties was divided,
to establish Qiānqiū County,
in the seventh year of Tiānbǎo,
it was renamed Tiāncháng.
Liùhé,
originally land of the Hàn dynasty Tángyì County,
belonged to Qín Commandery in the Eastern Jìn,
the Northern Qí changed it to Qínzhōu,
the Later Zhōu changed it to Fāngzhōu,
the Sui made it Liùhé County,
the Táng placed it under Yángzhōu.
Sòng Bái states: Liùhé County,
was the Tángyi of Chǔ during the Spring and Autumn period,
Qín destroyed Chǔ,
and made Tángyi a county.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Tiāncháng is 110 li west of Yángzhōu.
Liùhé is 70 li northwest of Zhēnzhōu.
Huáinán general Bì Shīduó said to Gāo Pián:
"The court relies on you for security,
now the bandits, several hundred thousand strong, are advancing swiftly on the momentum of victory,
meaning they are riding the victorious momentum from killing Zhāng Lín.
If we do not occupy strategic terrain to attack them,
and allow them to cross the Huái River,
they will become uncontrollable,
and will certainly become a great calamity for the Central Plains."
Pián, because the armies of the various circuits had already dispersed,
and Zhāng Lín was also dead,
judged that his own strength was insufficient to control them,
and, fearful and timid, did not dare to send out troops.
He merely ordered his generals to prepare strict defenses,
to protect themselves,
and moreover submitted a memorial reporting the emergency,
stating:
"The bandits, over six hundred thousand strong, are encamped at Tiāncháng,
less than fifty li from my city."
Previously,
Lú Xié had said
"Pián has great civil and military talent,
if full military authority is entrusted to him,
Huáng Cháo can easily be pacified."
Although some at court and among the people believed Pián was not reliable,
they still placed some hope in him.
When Pián's memorial arrived,
high and low were disappointed,
and people were greatly alarmed.
An imperial edict reprimanded Pián for dispersing the armies of the various circuits,
allowing the bandits to cross the river unopposed.
Pián submitted a memorial stating:
"I memorialized requesting to send them back,
it was not done on my own authority.
Now I am exhausting my strength to protect this region,
and certainly can manage the situation;
but I fear the bandits may advance gradually across the Huái,
you should urgently order the generals and soldiers of the eastern circuits to prepare proper defenses."
Eastern circuits,
refers to the circuits east of the pass.
He did not go out to fight again.
30 An edict ordered the various circuits of Hénán to dispatch troops to garrison ⿰⺡Yīnshuǐ,
Tàiníng military governor Qí Kèràng garrisoned Rǔzhōu,
to prepare against Huáng Cháo.
31 On Xīnyǒu,
Cáo Quánzhěng, Prefect of Zīzhōu, was appointed Tiānpíng military governor and concurrently Deputy Commander of the Eastern Front.
32 Liú Hànhóng requested to surrender;
on the Wùchén day,
he was appointed as the prefect of Sùzhōu.
Examination of discrepancies: According to the Veritable Records:
"Hànhóng invaded and harassed Jīng and Xiāng;
Wáng Duó sent the former prefect of Háozhōu, Cuī Kè, to recruit him.
At this time,
he finally surrendered.
On the Xīnwèi day,
Hànhóng submitted a memorial requesting to surrender by turning his weapons in Háozhōu,
and an edict was issued praising him."
According to Duó's flight to Xiāngyáng,
Hànhóng began plundering Jiānglíng and rebelled.
Duó was soon assigned to a separate office;
it was likely before this assignment that he sent Kè to recruit him.
Also, on the Wùchén day, Hànhóng was appointed to Sùzhōu,
and it is said that he surrendered at this time,
meaning he had already surrendered.
On the Xīnwèi day, it is further stated that he requested to surrender in Háozhōu.
The court heard of his surrender,
and on the Wùchén day, he was already appointed to office.
However, Hànhóng's memorial only arrived on the Xīnwèi day.
33 Lǐ Kèyòng led his troops back from the Xióngwǔ Army to attack Gāo Wénjí in Shuòzhōu.
Lǐ Kějǔ sent the marching commander Hán Xuánshào to intercept him at Yào'ér Ridge.
Yào'ér Ridge
is located west of the Xióngwǔ Army.
They killed over seven thousand people,
and Lǐ Jìnzhōng and Chéng Huáixìn both died.
Jìnzhōng and Huáixìn
were those who had risen with Kèyòng in Yù and Shuò.
They killed ten thousand people.
Lǐ Zhuó and Hèlián Duó attacked Yùzhōu,
and Lǐ Guóchāng was defeated in battle.
His troops all scattered,
and he alone, along with Kèyòng and their clan, fled north into the Dáddá.
Sòng Bái said: The Dáddá
were originally a tribe from the northeast,
likely a branch of the Mòhé.
After the Zhēnyuán and Yuánhé eras,
as the Xī and Qìdān gradually grew stronger,
they frequently attacked and plundered,
causing the tribes to disperse.
Some submitted to the Qìdān,
some relied on Bóhǎi,
and some gradually migrated to Yīnshān.
Their language became corrupted,
and they were thus called Dáddá.
At the end of the Táng Xiántōng era,
there were chieftains such as Měi Xiāngwēn and Yúyuè Xiāngwēn,
who set up tents south of the desert,
following the grass for herding.
When Lǐ Kèyòng was besieged by the Tǔhún,
he once went to rely on them,
and the Dáddá treated him well.
When he was appointed as the military governor of Yànmén,
the two Xiāngwēn led their tribes to follow Kèyòng.
They helped recover Cháng'ān,
pursued Huáng Cháo in Hénán,
and all contributed to the battles with merit.
As a result, they were allowed to set up camp between Yún and Dài,
where they freely herded.
The Tǔyùhún Bái Yìchéng was appointed as the prefect of Yùzhōu;
"Bái Yìchéng"
is also written as
"Bái Yìchéng."
Lǐ Kějǔ was additionally appointed as a Zhōngshū Shìláng.
The Dáddá were originally a branch of the Mòhé,
residing in Yīnshān.
Ōuyáng Xiū said: The Mòhé were originally northeast of the Xī and Qìdān,
but were later attacked by the Qìdān,
causing the tribes to disperse.
Those who settled in Yīnshān called themselves Dáddá.
Hóng Jǐnglú said: When translating foreign languages into Chinese,
one can only approximate the sounds.
Tiānzhú
is phonetically transformed into Juāndǔ or Shēndú;
Tūfà
is transformed into Tǔbō;
Dáddá
is actually Mòhé.
Qìdān is pronounced like "chī,"
and only the New Book of Táng provides this pronunciation.
Mòdú is pronounced like "mòtū,"
and only the annotations of the Book of Jìn provide this.
Hèlián Duó secretly bribed the Dáddá,
urging them to capture Lǐ Guóchāng and his son.
Lǐ Kèyòng learned of this,
and while hunting with their chieftains,
he placed a horsewhip on a leaf,
or shot needles hanging from it,
never missing.
The chieftains were impressed.
He also drank with them,
and when they were drunk,
Kèyòng said:
"I have offended the Son of Heaven,
and though I wish to serve loyally, I cannot.
Now I hear that Huáng Cháo is coming north,
and he will surely bring disaster to the Central Plains.
If one day the Son of Heaven pardons my crime,
and I can join you in marching south to achieve great deeds,
would that not be joyous?
Life is short;
who would want to grow old and die in the desert?"
The Dáddá realized he had no intention of staying,
and so they stopped.
Hèlián Duó had likely persuaded the Dáddá chieftains
that Lǐ Kèyòng and his son were talented and brave,
and if they stayed long among the Dáddá,
they would inevitably take over their tribe.
Therefore, he urged them to kill him.
However, Kèyòng told the chieftains
that he wished to march south with them to serve the emperor.
The Dáddá chieftains realized his ambitions were great,
and he would certainly not stay long in Yīnshān
to plot taking over their tribe.
Since he had no intention of plotting against them,
why should they kill him?
Thus, they stopped.
34 In the eighth month,
on the Jiǎwǔ day,
the former military governor of Xīchuān, Cuī Ānqián, was appointed as a Tàizǐ Bīnkè and assigned to a separate office.
This was because Lú Xié disliked him.
35 In the ninth month,
the Eastern Capital reported:
"The five hundred soldiers recruited from Rǔzhōu, including Lǐ Guāngtíng, returned from Dàizhōu,
passed through the Eastern Capital,
burned the Ānxǐ Gate,
looted the markets,
and left through the Chángxià Gate."
They burned the northeastern gate of Luòchéng
and left through the southeastern gate.
36 Huáng Cháo's forces numbered around one hundred and fifty thousand.
Cáo Quánzhěng led his six thousand troops to fight them,
inflicting significant casualties;
but due to being outnumbered,
he retreated and stationed his troops at Sìshàng.
Sìshàng
refers to Sìzhōu.
He gathered his forces to attack;
however, Gāo Pián ultimately did not send aid,
and the rebels attacked Quánzhěng,
defeating him.
37 Xúzhōu sent three thousand troops to Yīnshuǐ,
passing through Xǔchāng.
The Xú troops were notoriously unruly and violent.
The military governor, Xuē Néng,
who had previously governed Péngchéng,
in the early Qiánfú era,
Néng governed Xúzhōu,
and now governed Xǔ.
He quartered them at the polo field.
By evening,
the Xú troops caused a great uproar.
Néng climbed the inner city tower to inquire,
and they replied that their provisions were inadequate.
He comforted them for a long time,
and they finally calmed down;
but the people of Xǔ were greatly frightened.
At the time, the Zhōngwǔ Army had also sent the general Zhōu Jí to Yīnshuǐ.
He had not gone far
when he heard of this.
At night,
he led his troops back,
and by dawn,
he entered the city,
attacked the Xú troops,
and killed them all.
Resenting Néng's favoritism toward the Xú troops,
they drove him out.
Néng attempted to flee to Xiāngyáng,
but the mutinous troops pursued and killed him,
along with his family.
Jí declared himself acting military governor.
The defense commissioner of Rǔ and Zhèng, Qí Kèràng, fearing an attack from Jí,
led his troops back to Yǎnzhōu.
Qí Kèràng was originally the military governor of Tàiníng,
and he led his troops back to his garrison.
The troops stationed along the way to Yīnshuǐ all dispersed.
Huáng Cháo then led all his forces across the Huái River.
As they passed, they did not plunder,
but only recruited able-bodied men to strengthen their army.
Their goal was to attack Cháng'ān.
38 Previously, the military governor of Zhènwǔ, Wú Shītài, was summoned to serve as the Left Imperial Guard General,
and Zhūgě Shuǎng replaced him.
Shītài, seeing the court was troubled,
had the soldiers and civilians submit a petition to keep him.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Shītài was reappointed as the military governor of Zhènwǔ,
and Shuǎng was appointed as the military governor of Xiàsuí.
39 Huáng Cháo captured Shēnzhōu,
then entered the territories of Yǐng, Sòng, Xú, and Yǎn.
Wherever they went, officials and civilians fled in panic.
Forty bandits captured Lǐzhōu,
killing Prefect Lǐ Xún and Administrative Assistant Huángfǔ Zhèn.
Huángfǔ Zhèn had taken the imperial examinations twenty-three times,
failing to pass.
He presented himself to the Ministry of Rites twenty-three times,
yet never succeeded.
Truly, he grew old in the examination halls.
Shàng,
read as shǎng.
Zhòng,
read as zhúzhòng.
When the bandits arrived,
the city fell,
and Zhèn fled.
He asked someone:
"Has the Governor escaped?"
The reply was:
"The bandits have captured him."
Zhèn said:
"Having received such recognition from him,
where else could I go?"
He then returned to the bandits,
and ultimately died alongside him.
A scholar dies for one who knows his worth;
Huángfǔ Zhèn exemplified this.
How could the imperial examination system possibly encompass all the talented scholars of the realm?
Punctuated by Róng Zhàozǔ, proofread by Niè Chóngqí
Compiled by Sīmǎ Guāng
by imperial decree
Postface by Zuò Tiāntái
First year of the Guǎngmíng era
(Gēngzǐ, 880)
1 In November,
Wáng Chóngróng, the Metropolitan Commandant of Hézhōng, rebelled,
plundering until both the wards and markets were emptied.
2 Liú Hànhóng, Prefect of Sùzhōu, resented the meager rewards from the court.
Hànhóng's surrender was recorded in the seventh month of the previous scroll.
Rewarding bandits, yet the bandits complain the rewards are too small—
they certainly had grounds to look down upon the court.
On Jiǎyín,
Hànhóng was appointed Military Governor of Zhèdōng.
This sets the stage for Hànhóng's later defeat by Qián Liú.
3 An edict ordered Zhèng Cóngdǎng, Military Governor of Hédōng, to assign troops from his circuit to Zhūgě Shuǎng and Zhū Méi, Prefect of Dàizhōu,
for a southern campaign against Huáng Cháo.
On Yǐmǎo,
Lǐ Zhuó, Commander-in-Chief of Dàiběi, was appointed Military Governor of Héyáng.
With Dàiběi pacified,
Lǐ Zhuó was transferred inward,
also to prepare against Huáng Cháo.
4 Earlier, when Huáng Cháo was about to cross the Huái River,
Dòulú Zhuàn requested that the Tiānpíng military authority be granted to Cháo.
Huáng Cháo had initially sought the Tiānpíng command;
Dòulú Zhuàn intended to satisfy his desire with this.
Lú Xié said:
"Bandits are insatiable.
Even if we grant him the command,
it will not stop his plundering.
It would be better to urgently dispatch troops from various circuits to hold Sìzhōu,
with the Biànzhōu Military Governor as Commander-in-Chief.
If the bandits cannot advance into the passes,
they will surely turn back to plunder Huái and Zhè,
eking out an existence on the coastal islands!"
This was adopted.
Subsequently, urgent reports came successively from north of the Huái.
Xié claimed illness and did not appear.
Examination of discrepancies: The Jīngtīng Lù states:
"Chief Minister Dòulú Zhuó memorialized: 'Since Huáinán is only nine postal stations from Sìzhōu,
I fear Gāo Pián will firmly defend his fortifications
and not intercept the major bandits.
If Huáng Cháo crosses the Huái,
it will be a missed opportunity to capture him.
Moreover, conscripting troops will be too late;
we must temporarily lure him.
I request to bestow the command,
appointing him Military Governor of Yùnzhōu.
Once he arrives,
suppressing him will not be difficult.'
Chief Minister Lú Xié argued this was unacceptable,
memorializing that 'Huáng Cháo has long been a scourge to the state.
Previously, when granted the Jiāngxī command,
he took the authority and marched,
attacking Jīngnán.
We then stripped him of the command,
merely conscripting brave warriors from various circuits
to guard Sìzhōu.'
Therefore, no imperial envoys were dispatched,
the establishment of dual banners was halted,
and envoys were sent to the various circuits instead.
Soon, urgent reports from Biànzhōu and Xúzhōu circuits reached the capital,
reporting Huáng Cháo had crossed the Huái.
Lú Xié feigned illness and did not appear."
Note: The court never granted Huáng Cháo the Jiāngxī command;
even if it had, how could it be taken back?
This Jīngtīng Lù is not credible.
On Gēngshēn,
the Eastern Capital reported Huáng Cháo had entered Rǔzhōu territory.
5 On Xīnyǒu,
Wáng Chóngróng was provisionally appointed Acting Military Governor of Hézhōng,
while Lǐ Dū, Military Governor of Hézhōng and concurrent Chief Minister, was made Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent.
Because Wáng Chóngróng rebelled and could not be controlled,
Lǐ Dū was recalled,
and Hézhōng was entrusted to him.
6 Qí Kèràng, Commander-in-Chief of the Rǔzhèng Defense, memorialized that Huáng Cháo had proclaimed himself General Who Supplements Heaven,
and circulated a dispatch to the various armies stating,
"Each should guard its fortifications,
and not oppose my vanguard!
I will enter the Eastern Capital,
then proceed to the capital region.
I wish to demand accountability myself;
it does not concern the multitude."
Meaning he wished to hold the court accountable,
and it did not concern the people.
Dòulú Zhuàn and Cuī Hàng requested deploying garrisons from within the passes and the two Divine Strategy Armies to guard Tóngguān.
On Rénxū,
the winter solstice.
The Emperor opened the Yányīng Hall,
facing his ministers in tears.
With great bandits approaching
and no means to resist them,
ruler and ministers facing each other shedding tears—what good did it ultimately do?
"I request to select crossbowmen from the Left and Right Divine Strategy Armies to guard Tóngguān,
and I myself will serve as Commander-in-Chief of Defense."
The Emperor said:
"The imperial guard officers and soldiers
are unaccustomed to campaign warfare;
I fear they may not be adequate."
Lìngzī said:
"In the past, when Ān Lùshān rebelled,
Emperor Xuánzōng went to Shǔ to avoid him."
Cuī Hàng said:
"Lùshān's forces numbered only fifty thousand;
compared to Huáng Cháo,
it is not worth mentioning."
Dòulú Zhuàn said:
"Gēshū Hàn with one hundred fifty thousand troops could not hold Tóngguān.
This matter is recorded in the annals of Emperors Xuánzōng and Sùzōng.
Moreover, Tóngguān now lacks even Gēshū's troops.
If Lìngzī considers the altars of state,
the military governors of the Three Rivers are all Lìngzī's confidants."
Referring to Chén Jìngxuān, Yáng Shīlì, and Niú Xù.
Shuài,
read as suǒlèi.
The Emperor was displeased.
Although Emperor Xīzōng was childish and ignorant,
at this moment, with this sentiment,
how could he not know the pleasure of resting easy in the capital,
and the worry of fleeing to the wilderness?
To worry only after disaster strikes—
then it is too late.
Ancient enlightened rulers dwelled in safety yet thought of danger,
thus they could long preserve their safety.
"You shall dispatch troops to guard Tóngguān for me."
That day,
the Emperor visited the Left Divine Strategy Army,
personally reviewing the officers and soldiers.
Lìngzī recommended Zhāng Chéngfàn, General of the Left Army Cavalry; Wáng Shīhuì, General of the Right Army Infantry; and Zhào Kē, Military Commissioner of the Left Army.
The Emperor summoned the three,
appointing Chéngfàn as Vanguard Commander and concurrent Commander of Tóngguān Defense,
Shīhuì as Commissioner of Pass Fortifications and Supplies,
Kē as Commissioner of Camp Palisades,
Lìngzī as Commander-in-Chief of the Left and Right Divine Strategy Armies' internal and external eight garrisons and all circuit troops, with authority over recruitment and campaigns,
and Yáng Fùgōng, Commissioner of the Flying Dragon Stables, as Deputy Commander.
On Guǐhài,
Qí Kèràng memorialized:
"Huáng Cháo has already entered the Eastern Capital's territory.
I have withdrawn my troops to defend Tóngguān,
establishing a camp outside the pass.
The officers and soldiers have repeatedly engaged in battle;
supplies have long been lacking.
The prefectures and counties are devastated,
human habitation nearly extinct.
East, west, north, and south—no imperial presence is seen.
Cold and hunger press together;
weapons are worn and damaged.
Each thinks of his hometown;
I fear they may suddenly disband and flee.
I beg for early dispatch of supplies and reinforcements."
The Emperor ordered the selection of two thousand eight hundred crossbowmen from the two Divine Strategy Armies,
commanding Zhāng Chéngfàn and others to lead them to the front.
On Dīngmǎo,
Huáng Cháo captured the Eastern Capital.
Liú Yǔnzhāng, the Imperial Representative, led the officials in welcoming him.
Cháo entered the city,
merely offering greetings and inquiries,
and the neighborhoods remained peaceful.
Yǔnzhāng
was the great-grandson of Liú Nǎi.
Liú Nǎi appears in Scroll 230, first year of Emperor Dézōng's Xīngyuán era.
Yǔnzhāng could be said to have disgraced his ancestor.
On the Xīnwèi day,
Shǎnzhōu reported that the Eastern Capital had fallen.
On the Rénshēn day,
Tián Lìngzí was appointed as the commander-in-chief of Rǔ, Luò, Jìn, Jiàng, Tóng, and Huà,
leading the Left and Right Armies to campaign eastward.
(These were the Left and Right Divine Strategy Armies.)
Shǎn,
(pronounced as shī rǎn).
Huà,
(pronounced as hù huà).
The rebels captured Guózhōu.
(According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: Guózhōu is 85 lǐ northeast to Shǎnzhōu.)
7. Luó Yuángǎo, a Divine Strategy general, was appointed as the military governor of Héyáng.
(Luó Yuángǎo was also a trusted confidant of Tián Lìngzí.)
8. Zhōu Jí was appointed as the military governor of Zhōngwǔ.
(After Zhōu Jí killed Xuē Néng,
the Zhōngwǔ military governorship was thus conferred upon him.)
Jí,
(pronounced as nì jí).
Xuē Néng had dispatched his officer Qín Zōngquán from Shàngcài to mobilize troops in Càizhōu.
Upon hearing of the chaos in Xǔzhōu,
Qín Zōngquán claimed he was responding to the emergency,
recruited soldiers in Càizhōu,
then expelled the prefect,
and seized the city.
When Zhōu Jí became military governor,
he appointed Qín Zōngquán as the prefect of Càizhōu.
(This laid the groundwork for Qín Zōngquán’s later military actions and self-proclamation of imperial title in Càizhōu.)
9. On the Yǐhài day,
Zhāng Chéngfàn and others led the Divine Strategy crossbowmen out of the capital.
The Divine Strategy soldiers were all sons of wealthy families in Cháng’ān,
who had bribed eunuchs to enroll in the army roster,
receiving generous provisions and rewards.
(Lǐn means to provide.)
(Lǐncì means provisions and rewards.)
(Nùmǎ refers to whipping a horse to make it angry and gallop fast.)
They had never experienced battle formations;
upon hearing they were to go on campaign,
fathers and sons gathered weeping,
and many used gold and silk to hire poor people from the infirmaries to go in their stead.
(The Táng established infirmaries in the capital to care for the sick.)
(According to the Huìyào: In the fifth year of Kāiyuán,
Sòng Jǐng and others memorialized:
"The Bēitián infirmaries,
since Cháng’ān, have had commissioners specifically in charge.
We request their abolition."
By the twenty-second year,
beggars in the capital who fell ill
were distributed among various temple infirmaries.
In the second year of Zhìdé,
both capitals established Pǔjiù infirmaries.
The establishment of infirmaries
had a long history.)
On that day,
the Emperor personally saw them off at the Zhāngxìn Gate tower.
(Commentary: The New History states:
"The Emperor feasted Lìngzí at the Zhāngxìn Gate,
bestowing lavish gifts."
However, although Lìngzí was appointed commander-in-chief,
and received gifts and emblems of authority,
he actually never left the palace precincts.
Those dispatched that day were Chéngfàn and others.
The New History’s statement about feasting Lìngzí is erroneous.)
"I hear Huáng Cháo commands hundreds of thousands of troops,
advancing westward with drums.
Qí Kèràng relies on ten thousand starving soldiers outside the pass,
and now you send me with just over two thousand men to station at the pass,
with no word on provisions.
To resist the rebels with this,
I am secretly chilled with fear.
I hope Your Majesty will urgently order elite troops from various circuits to provide reinforcements soon."
The Emperor said:
"You just proceed;
troops will arrive shortly!"
On the Dīngchǒu day,
Chéngfàn and others reached Huàzhōu.
The prefect, Péi Qiányú, had been transferred to become the observation commissioner of Xuānshè,
and the soldiers and civilians had all fled into Huàshān.
The city was desolate,
the prefectural treasury contained only dust and rat tracks,
but fortunately the granary still had over a thousand hú of rice.
The soldiers wrapped three days’ rations and marched on.
In the twelfth month,
on the first day, Gēngchén,
Chéngfàn and others reached Tóngguān.
They searched the thickets,
(thickets are places with dense grass),
(Shǐ Zhào said: forest thickets),
had people transport stones and draw water,
preparing defenses.
Both Chéngfàn’s and Qí Kèràng’s armies ran out of food,
and the soldiers lost all will to fight.
That day,
Huáng Cháo’s vanguard reached the pass,
white flags covering the fields,
endless to the sight.
Kèràng engaged them in battle,
and the rebels retreated slightly.
Soon Huáng Cháo arrived,
and the entire army gave a great shout,
its sound shaking the Hé and Huà rivers.
Kèràng fought fiercely,
from noon until dusk before the battle eased.
The soldiers were starving,
so they clamored,
set fire to the camp, and fled in disarray.
Kèràng fled into the pass.
To the left of the pass was a valley,
normally closed to traffic
to levy taxes,
called
the "Forbidden Pit."
The rebels arrived so suddenly
that the government troops forgot to guard it.
The fleeing soldiers entered through the valley.
The valley was densely woven with shrubs and ancient vines.
(Shrubs are clustered trees;
ancient vines are what we now call wànsuì vines.)
Chéngfàn distributed all his baggage and supplies to the soldiers.
(Zīnáng refers to baggage and personal belongings.
Baggage means military supplies;
personal belongings mean private luggage.)
He memorialized:
"I left the capital six days ago;
not a single soldier has been added to my ranks,
and there is no news of provisions.
On the day I reached the pass,
the great rebels had already arrived.
With just over two thousand men to resist six hundred thousand,
the outer army starved and collapsed,
trampling open the Forbidden Pit.
(Tà is the same as tread.)
I would willingly face the cauldron;
but the court’s planning ministers—
where will they hide their shameful faces?
I have heard that Your Majesty is already discussing a western tour
(meaning considering flight to Shǔ).
If so, the state will collapse from top to bottom.
I dare, with my still-living body, to risk uttering words of death:
I hope you will consult closely with your inner circle and chief ministers,
urgently summon troops to rescue the pass defenses.
Then the legacy of Gāozǔ and Tàizōng may still be upheld.
Should Huáng Cháo follow Ān Lùshān’s path to destruction,
may your humble servant surpass Gēshū Hán in death!"
On the Xīnsì day,
the rebels fiercely attacked Tóngguān.
Chéngfàn resisted with all his strength,
from dawn until late afternoon.
When arrows on the pass ran out,
they threw stones to strike the enemy.
Outside the pass was a deep moat.
The rebels drove over a thousand people into it
to dig earth and fill it.
In a short while,
it was leveled,
and they led troops across.
At night,
they set fires, completely burning the pass towers.
Chéngfàn dispatched eight hundred soldiers,
ordering Wáng Shīhuì to guard the Forbidden Pit.
By the time they arrived,
the rebels had already entered.
At dawn on the Rénwǔ day,
the rebels attacked Tóngguān from both sides.
The soldiers on the pass all fled in disarray.
Shīhuì committed suicide.
Chéngfàn changed clothes and led the remaining troops in escape.
At Yěhúquán,
they encountered two thousand reinforcement troops from Fèngtiān arriving belatedly.
Chéngfàn said:
"You have come too late!"
The Bóyě and Fèngxiáng armies, returning to Wèiqiáo,
(the Bóyě army was the one that Lǐ Huán led back to the capital in the second year of Mùzōng’s Chángqìng reign;
see scroll 242),
(shuài is pronounced as shuài),
and the new army (the men from the wards and markets that Tián Lìngzí recruited to supplement the two armies),
said: "What merit do these people have to receive such treatment,
while we suffer cold and hunger!"
So they plundered them,
and then acted as guides for the rebels
toward Cháng’ān.
When the rebels attacked Tóngguān,
the court appointed the former Jīngzhào Prefect Xiāo Lǐn as the Eastern Circuit Transport and Provisions Commissioner;
Lǐn pleaded illness,
requested to retire from office,
and was demoted to Registrar of Hè Prefecture.
Hè Prefecture,
was Línhè County of Cāngwú Commandery in the Hàn dynasty,
the Wú dynasty established Línhè Commandery,
the Táng dynasty established Hè Prefecture,
located 4,130 lǐ southeast of the capital.
Huáng Cháo entered Huá Prefecture,
leaving his general Qiáo Qián to guard it.
Wáng Chóngróng, the acting military governor of Hézhōng, requested to surrender to the rebels.
On Guǐwèi,
an imperial decree appointed Huáng Cháo as Military Commissioner of Tiānpíng.
On Jiǎshēn,
Wáng Huī, Academician of the Hànlín Academy and Vice Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed Vice Minister of Revenue,
and Péi Chè, Academician of the Hànlín Academy and Vice Minister of Revenue, was appointed Vice Minister of Works,
both were also given the additional title of Tongpingzhangshi (Participant in Determining Governmental Matters).
Lú Xié was appointed as a Tutor to the Heir Apparent and assigned to the Eastern Capital.
Tián Lìngzī, hearing that Huáng Cháo had already entered the pass,
feared the emperor would blame him,
so he shifted the blame onto Xié and had him demoted,
recommending Huī and Chè as chancellors.
That evening,
Xié drank poison and died.
Chè
was the nephew of Péi Xiū.
Péi Xiū appears in the 249th scroll, in the sixth year of the Dàzhōng era of Emperor Xuānzōng.
The officials had just retired from court,
when they heard that rebel soldiers had entered the city,
and they fled and hid along the roads.
"Bù lù" means
to take separate paths.
"Cháo"
is pronounced "zhí yáo fān".
Only the four princes—Fú, Mù, Zé, and Shòu—and a few imperial consorts followed the emperor,
and none of the other officials knew about it.
The emperor fled day and night without rest,
and many of the accompanying officials could not keep up.
After the imperial carriage departed,
soldiers and the people of the wards and markets rushed into the government storehouses to steal gold and silk.
In the late afternoon,
Huáng Cháo's vanguard general Chái Cún entered Cháng'ān,
and the General of the Imperial Guards Zhāng Zhífāng led several dozen civil and military officials to welcome Cháo at Bàshàng.
Cháo rode in a gold-decorated sedan chair,
his followers all wore their hair loose,
tied with red silk,
dressed in brocade and embroidery,
and followed with weapons in hand,
armored cavalry flowed like a river,
supply wagons clogged the roads,
stretching unbroken for a thousand lǐ.
The people gathered along the roads to watch,
and Shàng Ràng repeatedly admonished them, saying:
"King Huáng raised an army,
originally for the sake of the common people,
unlike the Lǐ family who did not love you all.
You all should just live in peace and have no fear."
Cháo took up residence at Tián Lìngzī's mansion,
his followers had been bandits for a long time,
and could not bear wealth,
so when they saw the poor,
they often gave them things.
After a few days,
they went out in groups to plunder on a large scale,
burning markets and shops,
killing people until the streets were filled with corpses,
and Cháo could not stop them;
they especially hated officials,
and killed all they captured.
The emperor hastened to Luò Valley,
and the Military Commissioner of Fèngxiáng, Zhèng Tián, paid his respects to the emperor along the way.
Examination of Discrepancies says: According to the Xù Bǎoyùn Lù:
"On Wùzǐ,
the emperor reached the Xuèshuǐ Station in Luò Valley,
and issued an edict to Niú Yǐng, Yáng Shīlì, and Chén Jìngxuān,
saying that on the seventh day of this month,
he had already reached Xuèshuǐ Station in Luò Valley."
According to this month, the first day was Gēngchén,
so Wùzǐ was the ninth day,
but the edict says the seventh day,
"nine"
was mistakenly written as
"seven"
The Veritable Records say:
"On Xīnmǎo,
the imperial carriage stopped at Fèngxiáng,
and Zhèng Tián waited to pay his respects on the road."
The Old Biography of Tián says he waited for the imperial carriage at Xié Valley.
The New Annals say:
"On Xīnmǎo,
he stopped at Fèngxiáng.
On Dīngyǒu,
he reached Xīngyuán."
According to this, on Jiǎshēn the emperor left Cháng'ān,
and on Xīnmǎo he first stopped at Fèngxiáng,
which is too slow,
and on Dīngyǒu he had already reached Xīngyuán,
which is too fast.
Also, if the route went through Luò Valley, then he would not pass through Fèngxiáng or Xié Valley.
It seems the imperial carriage passed through the territory of Fèngxiáng,
and Tián went to see him there,
not at Fèngxiáng or Xié Valley.
The Veritable Records say:
"The rebels pursued the imperial carriage westward with tens of thousands of troops."
But they do not say whether they caught up or not,
nor do they say who repelled them and caused them to turn back.
None of the other books mention this.
Therefore, it is not adopted here.
The emperor said:
"I do not wish to be close to the great bandits,
and will temporarily go to Xīngyuán,
to gather troops and plan the recovery.
You shall defend against the rebel vanguard in the east,
pacify the various tribes in the west,
unite with neighboring circuits,
and strive to achieve great merit."
Tián said:
"The roads are blocked,
and it is difficult to send memorials and reports,
I request to be allowed to act according to circumstances."
This was granted.
On Wùzǐ,
the emperor reached Xuèshuǐ.
The Jiǔyù Zhì says: Xīngdào County of Yáng Prefecture has a Xuèshuǐ Town,
it is said that the immortal Táng Gōngfǎng ascended to heaven with his entire family,
but his son-in-law could not ascend with them,
hence the water was named after him;
this is absurd.
He informed them that the capital could not be held,
and he would temporarily go to Xīngyuán,
if the rebel situation remained strong,
he would go to Chéngdū,
and they should prepare in advance.
On Gēngyín,
Huáng Cháo killed all members of the Táng imperial clan in Cháng'ān without exception.
On Xīnmǎo,
Cháo first entered the palace.
On Rénchén,
Cháo ascended the throne as emperor at the Hányuán Hall,
painting black silk to make imperial robes,
and beating several hundred war drums to replace the music of bells and chimes.
He ascended the Dānfèng Tower,
and issued a general amnesty;
the state was named Dà Qí,
and the era name was changed to Jīntǒng.
He said that the era name Guǎngmíng,
by removing the lower part of the character 'Táng' and adding the sun and moon of the Huáng family,
was an auspicious sign for himself.
Táng officials of the third rank and above were all dismissed from their posts,
while those of the fourth rank and below retained their positions.
He made his wife, Lady Cáo, empress.
Examination of Discrepancies says: The Veritable Records and the Biography of Cháo say he made his wife, Lady Qū, empress.
Now we follow the New Biography.
Zhào Zhāng was made Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant),
Cuī Qiú and Yáng Xīgǔ were both made Tongpingzhangshi,
Mèng Jiě and Gài Hóng were made Left and Right Vice Directors of the Department of State Affairs, in charge of left and right military affairs,
and Fèi Chuángǔ was made Privy Commissioner.
Tài Cháng Bóshì (Erudite of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices) Pí Rìxiū was made Academician of the Hànlín Academy.
Lù Yóu's Lǎoxué'ān Bǐjì says: The Gāiwén Lù says Pí Rìxiū was captured by Huáng Cháo and made an Academician of the Hànlín Academy,
and when Cháo was defeated,
he was executed;
now the Tángshū includes this account.
According to Yǐn Shīlǔ's epitaph for Pí Zǐliáng, the Dàlǐ Sìchéng (Assistant Minister of the Court of Judicial Review):
"His great-grandfather Rìxiū,
avoiding the disaster of the Guǎngmíng era,
moved his household registration to Kuàijī,
relied on the Qián family,
served as Tài Cháng Bóshì,
and was posthumously awarded the title of Minister of Rites.
His grandfather Guāngyè
was Chancellor of Wúyuè.
His father Càn
was a Judge in the Marshal's Office.
Three generations all excelled in literature in Jiāngdōng."
According to this,
Rìxiū was never captured by Huáng Cháo, made his Academician of the Hànlín Academy, and executed.
Fiction is full of absurdities,
there is nothing it does not include.
Shīlǔ's writings have been passed down through the ages,
and he was upright and principled,
not one to deceive later generations.
Cuī Qiú was the son of Cuī Bīn,
Cuī Bīn was the elder brother of Cuī Yǎn,
during the reign of Emperor Dézōng, he served as Yòu Bǔquē (Right Omissioner),
and once criticized Péi Yánlíng,
earning a reputation for integrity.
"Zǐ"
probably should be
"sūn".
In Cháng'ān,
Cháo captured him and made him chancellor.
When Qiú was in Zhèdōng,
he certainly had messengers coming and going with Cháo,
and also submitted memorials to the court on his behalf.
Zhūgě Shuǎng led the troops of the Dàiběi expeditionary camp to station at Yuèyáng.
Huáng Cháo's general, Zhū Wēn from Dàngshān, stationed at the Dōngwèi Bridge.
Dàngshān,
located within the boundaries of the Hàn dynasty's Dàng County,
was established as Ānyáng County during the Later Wèi,
with its seat at Máchéng.
In the 18th year of the Suí dynasty's Kāihuáng era, it was renamed Dàngshān.
During the Táng, it belonged to Sòng Prefecture.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is 90 lǐ southeast of Shàn Prefecture.
Dàng,
pronunciation: tú láng fān.
Zhū Wēn begins here.
Shuǎng then surrendered to Cháo.
Wēn was orphaned and poor in his youth.
He, along with his elder brothers Yù and Cún, followed their mother, née Wáng, and relied on the family of Liú Chóng in Xiāo County.
Chóng often whipped and humiliated him.
According to the History of the Five Dynasties,
Wēn was fierce, brutal, and untrustworthy.
Chóng was troubled because Tàizǔ (Zhū Wēn) was lazy and idle, not engaging in proper work,
and often whipped and reprimanded him.
Only Chóng's mother pitied him.
She often combed his hair and washed him herself,
and warned her family, saying:
"Zhū Sān is no ordinary man.
You should treat him well."
Shù,
pronunciation: suǒ jiǎo fān.
She warned her family, saying:
"Zhū Sān is no ordinary man.
You all must treat him well."
Zhū Wēn was the third son.
When Shuǎng proceeded to his garrison,
Luó Yuángǎo dispatched troops to resist him.
The soldiers all discarded their armor and welcomed Shuǎng.
Yuángǎo fled and ran to the imperial temporary headquarters.
11 Zhèng Tián returned to Fèngxiáng.
He summoned his officers to discuss resisting the rebels.
They all said:
"The rebels' momentum is currently fierce.
We should proceed calmly and wait for troops to assemble,
then plan the recovery."
Tián said:
"Are you gentlemen urging me, Tián, to submit to the rebels?!"
Thereupon, he fainted from distress and fell to the ground,
bruising his face on the brick paving.
Zhèng Tián, because his officers were negligent in their duty to aid the emperor,
his loyal indignation surged all at once,
to the point of fainting and collapsing to the ground,
thus bruising his face on the brick paving.
Zhòu,
pronunciation: zé jiù fān,
means brick.
He was still unable to speak.
It happened that Cháo's envoy arrived with a letter of pardon.
The supervising eunuch Yuán Jìngróu and the officers stood in order to proclaim and display it,
drafting a memorial on Tián's behalf, signing it to thank Cháo.
The supervising eunuch feasted with Cháo's envoy.
When music was played,
the officers and below all wept.
The envoy found this strange.
A staff advisor, Sūn Chǔ, said:
"It is because the Lord Minister is afflicted with wind paralysis and cannot come,
hence their sorrow."
Among the common people who heard this, none failed to weep.
Tián, hearing of it, said:
"I always knew the people's hearts had not yet grown weary of the Táng.
The day the rebel loses his head is not far off!"
He then pricked his finger and wrote a memorial in blood,
sending a trusted person by a secret route to the imperial temporary headquarters.
He summoned his officers and explained to them the difference between rebellion and loyalty.
They all obeyed his command.
Again he pricked his finger and swore a blood oath with them.
Then he repaired the city walls and moats,
prepared weapons and equipment,
trained the soldiers,
and secretly made pacts with neighboring circuits to combine forces and attack the rebels.
The neighboring circuits all promised to dispatch troops,
to rendezvous at Fèngxiáng.
At that time, several tens of thousands of imperial guards were still stationed separately throughout Guānzhōng.
The imperial guards stationed separately in Guānzhōng
were the troops of the eight Shéncè garrisons.
Having nowhere to return to,
Tián sent people to recruit them.
They all went to follow Tián.
Tián distributed wealth to win their hearts.
The army's momentum greatly revived.
12 On Dīngyǒu,
the imperial carriage reached Xīngyuán.
An edict was issued ordering each circuit to dispatch its entire army to recover the capital.
To have all the troops under one's command march out
is called the "entire army."
13 On Jǐhài,
Huáng Cháo issued an order:
Any officials who went to Zhào Zhāng's residence to submit their name and title
would have their offices restored.
Míngxián:
writing one's official position and name.
Those who hid among the common people,
when Cháo searched and captured them,
were all killed.
Princess Guǎngdé said:
"I am a daughter of the Táng imperial house.
I vow to die together with the Vice Director Yú!"
She grasped the rebel's blade and would not let go.
The rebels killed her as well.
They exhumed Lú Xié's corpse
and displayed it in the marketplace.
The Director of the Palace Buildings, Zhèng Qí, and the Vice Director of the Treasury Bureau, Zhèng Xì, in righteousness would not submit to the rebels.
Their entire households committed suicide.
The Táng had repeatedly undergone mourning and turmoil.
Reaching the Guāngmíng era,
there were still no lack of those whose entire households died for the state.
This was because kindness and righteousness had long bound them.
(Someone) harbored many fugitives,
hiding high officials and nobles in double walls.
Cháo killed him.
14 Earlier,
the Bureau of Military Affairs Commissioner Yáng Fùgōng recommended the retired scholar Zhāng Jùn from Héjiān.
He was appointed Erudite of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
and later promoted to Vice Director of the Bureau of Budgets.
When Huáng Cháo approached Tóng Pass,
Jùn took refuge from the turmoil at Shāng Mountain.
When the Emperor went to Xīngyuán,
there were no provisions along the way.
The Magistrate of Hànyīn, Lǐ Kāng, used mules to carry several hundred loads of dried provisions and presented them.
Hànyīn:
originally the territory of Ānyáng County in Hànzhōng.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn changed it to Ānkāng County.
In the 2nd year of the Táng's Zhìdé era, it was renamed Hànyīn County,
belonging to Jīn Prefecture.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is 165 lǐ northwest of the prefecture.
Tuó,
pronunciation: tú hé fān.
Using donkeys or horses to carry goods is called a tuó.
In Táng postal transport,
each tuó was 100 catties.
The Emperor asked Kāng:
"You are a county magistrate.
How were you able to do this?"
He replied:
"Your subject could not have managed this.
It was Vice Director Zhāng Jùn who instructed your subject."
The Emperor summoned Jùn to the imperial temporary headquarters
and appointed him Vice Director of the Ministry of War.
The vice directors of the various Táng ministries
were rank 5b.
Assistant directors
were rank 6b.
15 The Yìwǔ military governor Wáng Chùcún, hearing that Cháng'ān had been lost,
wailed for days on end.
Without waiting for an imperial command,
he raised his army and went to its aid,
dispatching 2,000 men by a secret route to Xīngyuán to guard the imperial carriage.
16. Huáng Cháo sent envoys to requisition supplies from Hézhōng,
totaling several hundred people over time,
causing unbearable hardship for officials and commoners alike.
Wáng Chóngróng addressed the crowd, saying:
“Initially, I humbled myself to alleviate the troubles of the military command.
Humbling myself
meant submitting to the rebels.
Alleviate,
pronounced as in Shāngjū,
means to ease.
Now they are about to conscript troops again;
our demise is imminent!
It would be better to raise troops and resist them.”
Everyone agreed,
so they drove out all of Huáng Cháo’s envoys and killed them.
Huáng Cháo dispatched his general Zhū Wēn from Tóngzhōu,
and his brother Huáng Yè from Huàzhōu,
to combine forces and attack Hézhōng.
Wáng Chóngróng engaged them in battle,
inflicting a major defeat,
capturing forty boats of grain and weapons.
He sent an envoy to form an alliance with Wáng Chùcún,
and led his troops to camp north of the Wèi River.
Examination of discrepancies: The Old Book biography of Wáng Chùcún states:
“At that time, Lǐ Dū was defending Hézhōng
and surrendered to the rebels.
When Wáng Chóngróng executed the false envoys,
he sent an envoy to Wáng Chùcún,
and they swore an alliance,
camping north of the Wèi River.
At that time, Huáng Cháo had usurped the title,
and many regional governors across the land accepted his false mandates.
Only Zhèng Tián held Fèngxiáng,
Zhèng Cóngdǎng held Tàiyuán,
and Wáng Chùcún and Wáng Chóngróng were the first to advocate righteous action.
Soon after, Zhèng Tián defeated the rebel vanguard,
and Wáng Duó arrived from the imperial camp,
so the various governors changed their plans,
sending out troops to rescue the emperor.”
According to this, Wáng Duó did not arrive until the second year of Zhōnghé,
so it was not yet time.
The biography of Wáng Chóngróng states:
“Initially,
Wáng Chóngróng was the commander of infantry and cavalry in Hézhōng.
When Huáng Cháo’s rebels occupied Cháng’ān,
the Pú commander Lǐ Dū could not resist,
so he submitted to the rebels.
The rebels falsely appointed Wáng Chóngróng as deputy military commissioner.
Wáng Chóngróng, because the rebels’ demands were endless,
wanted to resist them.
Lǐ Dū said: ‘Our troops are few and weak;
cutting them off will bring immediate disaster.
I wish to entrust the military authority to you.’
The next day,
Lǐ Dū returned to the imperial camp,
and Wáng Chóngróng took charge as acting governor.
He then executed the rebel envoys
and sought aid from neighboring governors.”
Běimèng Suǒyán states:
“Wáng Chóngróng initially served as a staff officer.
When Huáng Cháo invaded the capital,
the commander Lǐ Dū submitted to the false regime.
Fearing Wáng Chóngróng,
as many followed him,
he recommended him as deputy.
One day,
Wáng Chóngróng suddenly said to Lǐ Dū: ‘Your Excellency assists the rebels,
plunging the region into disloyalty,
and daily increases exactions.
With public discontent growing,
if a sudden change occurs,
how can it be stopped?’
He immediately ordered the execution of the false envoys.
Lǐ Dū had no reply,
so he handed over the military seal to Wáng Chóngróng and left.
When Lǐ Dū reached the imperial camp,
the court also sent the former Jīngzhào Yin Dòu Hù, who arrived via back roads to Hézhōng to replace Lǐ Dū.
Wáng Chóngróng welcomed him.
Dòu Hù had previously been Jīngzhào Yin,
known for his cruelty,
and was nicknamed ‘Duǒdié’ at the time.
Upon his arrival,
the next day,
he summoned the military officers to the hall,
saying: ‘The Son of Heaven has sent a high minister to command this garrison,
to block the rebels’ advance.
How can you lightly discuss expelling him and making him leave by the north gate!
Moreover, the troublemakers are only one or two individuals;
you may name them.’
Dòu Hù did not know that the military officers were all Wáng Chóngróng’s partisans.
No one responded.
Wáng Chóngróng then straightened his clothes, wore his sword, and ascended the steps,
saying to Dòu Hù: ‘If there is a troublemaker, who else but me!’
He then summoned Dòu Hù’s attendants to bring his horse to the steps,
requesting to follow the precedent set by Lǐ Dū,
and said, ‘Leave quickly!’
Dòu Hù did not dare to look up,
leaped onto his horse, and again left by the north gate.”
The New Book adopts this account.
According to records, on the first day of the eleventh month, Xīnhài,
Wáng Chóngróng had already rebelled,
plundering the markets.
On Xīnyǒu,
Wáng Chóngróng was appointed acting governor,
and Lǐ Dū was made Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent,
indicating that Lǐ Dū had already left Hézhōng.
As for Huáng Cháo’s invasion of the capital,
Lǐ Dū never submitted to the false regime,
nor was it heard that Dòu Hù replaced Lǐ Dū.
This account is not adopted here.
17. Chén Jìngxuān heard that the imperial carriage had fled,
and sent three thousand infantry and cavalry to welcome it,
submitting a memorial requesting the emperor to proceed to Chéngdū.
At that time, the accompanying troops were increasing,
and supplies in Xīngyuán were insufficient.
Tián Lìngzī also urged the emperor;
the emperor agreed.
First year of Zhōnghé
(Xīnchǒu, 881)
The era name was changed in the seventh month of this year.
1. Spring,
first month,
the imperial carriage departed from Xīngyuán.
Niú Xù was appointed Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
Chén Jìngxuān found the accompanying attendants arrogant and difficult to control.
A young attendant from the inner garden who had arrived earlier in Chéngdū,
In the Táng dynasty, those who served in the workshops and inner gardens
were all called ‘young attendants.’
laughed and said:
“People say Xīchuān is barbaric,
but looking at it today,
it’s not bad!”
Chén Jìngxuān seized him and had him beaten to death.
Examination of discrepancies: The New Book biography states:
“Chén Jìngxuān killed fifty people,
and displayed their corpses in the streets.”
Jǐnlǐ Qíjiù Zhuàn states:
“Three young attendants from the inner garden walked hand in hand,
circling the temporary palace several times.
One of them laughed and said such and such.
The patrolmen beat them indiscriminately
and seized them.
Chén Jìngxuān scolded them: ‘Today I intend to beat to death thirty or fifty of your kind,
and I will not let it go wrong.’”
The phrase ‘thirty or fifty of your kind’
was Chén Jìngxuān’s words,
not an actual killing of fifty people.
The New Book is mistaken.
Chén Jìngxuān went to greet the emperor at Lùtóu Pass.
On Xīnwèi,
the emperor reached Miánzhōu,
where the Dōngchuān military commissioner Yáng Shīlì paid his respects.
Dōngchuān’s seat was at Zǐzhōu,
168 lǐ north to Miánzhōu.
‘See’
is pronounced as in Xiánbiàn.
On Rénshēn,
the Vice Minister of Works and Commissioner of Finance Xiāo Gòu was appointed Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
2. Zhèng Tián arranged with the former Shuòfāng military commissioner Táng
Hóngfū and the Jīngyuán military commissioner Chéng Zōngchǔ to jointly attack Huáng Cháo.
Huáng Cháo sent his general Wáng Huī to deliver an edict summoning Zhèng Tián.
Zhèng Tián executed him,
and sent his son Zhèng Níngjì to the imperial camp.
Zhèng Níngjì caught up with the emperor at Hànzhōu.
From Miánzhōu southwest to Hànzhōu is 190 lǐ.
3. On Dīngchǒu,
the imperial carriage reached Chéngdū.
From Hànzhōu southwest to Chéngdū is 85 lǐ.
4. The emperor sent
envoys to urge Gāo Pián to attack Huáng Cháo.
Envoys were seen on the roads continuously,
but Gāo Pián never sent troops.
When the emperor reached Shǔ,
he still hoped Gāo Pián would achieve merit.
An edict authorized Gāo Pián to appoint, within his jurisdiction, prefects and generals who had merit,
from Investigating Censor to Regular Attendant,
using informal edicts, and report afterward.
5. Péi Chè fled from the rebels to the imperial camp.
At that time, officials had not yet gathered,
and there was a lack of people to draft edicts.
Right Omissioner Yuè Péngguī paid respects to Tián Lìngzī and bowed to him,
and was thus promoted to Academician of the Hànlín Academy.
Zhāng Jùn had earlier also bowed to Tián Lìngzī.
Tián Lìngzī once invited chief ministers and high officials to drink.
Zhāng Jùn felt ashamed to bow to Tián Lìngzī in front of the crowd,
so he first visited Tián Lìngzī to thank him for the wine.
When all the guests had gathered,
Tián Lìngzī said:
“Lìngzī and Gentleman Zhāng are of different streams, clear and turbid.
I have previously received his support inside and outside,
inside and outside
means working in concert with him.
Why fear to change?
Today, thanking for the wine in a hidden place is again unacceptable.”
Zhāng Jùn was ashamed and fearful, with nowhere to hide.
6. Second month,
on Yǐ
mǎo, the first day,
Heir Apparent’s Junior Tutor Wáng Duó was appointed Defender of the Minister over the Masses and concurrently Vice Director of the Chancellery and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
7 On the bǐngshēn day,
Zhèng Tián was appointed as tóng píngzhāngshì.
8 Huái’nán Jiedushi Gāo Pián was additionally appointed as Dōngmiàn Dūtǒng,
and Hé dōng Jiedushi Zhèng Cóngdǎng was additionally appointed as concurrent Shìzhōng,
continuing to serve as the Xíngyíng Zhāotǎoshǐ.
The Jiānjūn of Dàiběi, Chén Jǐngsī
(Textual Analysis states: The Veritable Records records
"Jǐng Sī,"
but here we follow Xuē Jūzhèng's History of the Five Dynasties.)
arrived at Jiàngzhōu,
intending to cross the river.
The Cìshǐ of Jiàngzhōu, Qú Zhěn,
was also a Shatuo,
and said to Jǐngsī:
"The bandits' momentum is currently strong,
we should not advance lightly.
It would be better to return to Dàiběi to recruit troops."
So he returned to Yànmén together with Jǐngsī.
9 The Shūmìshǐ Yáng Fùguāng was appointed as Jīngxī Nánmiàn Xíngyíng Dūjiān.
10 Huáng Cháo appointed Zhū Wēn as Dōngnánmiàn Xíngyíng Dūyúhòu,
leading troops to attack Dèngzhōu.
In the third month,
on the xīnhài day,
it was captured,
and Cìshǐ Zhào Jiè was seized.
They then garrisoned Dèngzhōu to control Jīng and Xiāng.
(Jiǔyùzhì: Dèngzhōu is 180 lǐ south to Xiāngzhōu,
and Xiāngzhōu is 457 lǐ south to Jīngzhōu.)
11 On the rénzǐ day,
Chén Jìngxuān was appointed as tóng píngzhāngshì.
On the jiǎyǐn day,
Jìngxuān memorialized that he had dispatched Zuǒ Huángtóu Jūnshǐ Lǐ Chán to lead troops to attack Huáng Cháo.
(The Xīchuān Huángtóu Army
was established by Cuī Ānqián,
the matter first appears in the sixth year of Qiánfú in the previous volume.)
(Chán
is pronounced as shí yán fān.)
12 On the xīnyǒu day,
Zhèng Tián was appointed as Jīngchéng Sìmiàn Zhūjūn Xíngyíng Dūtǒng.
An edict was bestowed upon Tián:
"All Fán and Hàn generals and soldiers who go to aid the crisis and achieve merit,
shall be appointed to office according to mòchì."
Tián memorialized to appoint Jīngyuán Jiedushi Chéng Zōngchǔ as Deputy Dūtǒng,
and former Shuòfāng Jiedushi Táng Hóngfū as Xíngjūn Sīmǎ.
Huáng Cháo sent his generals Shàng Ràng and Wáng Bō to lead a crowd of 50,000 to raid Fèngxiáng.
("Wáng Bō"
is recorded as
"Wáng Fán" in the New Book.)
Tián himself led several thousand soldiers,
displaying many banners and flags,
and spread out his formation on a high ridge.
The bandits, considering Tián a mere scholar,
looked down upon him.
They advanced beating drums,
with no proper formation.
An ambush was sprung,
and the bandits were greatly defeated at Lóngwěi Bēi.
(Both the New and Old Books record
"Lóngwěi Pō,"
only the Old Annals records
"Bēi.")
(Fèngxiáng Fǔ Qíshān Xiàn,
in the early Táng had its seat at Zhāngbǎo,
in the seventh year of Wǔdé it was moved to Lóngwěi Chéng,
which is northeast of the old Píngyáng city.)
Corpses lay strewn for tens of lǐ.
13 Someone wrote a poem on the gate of the Shàngshū Shěng to mock the bandits.
Shàng Ràng was enraged,
and had all the officials in the Shěng and the gate guards
have their eyes gouged out and hung upside down.
A great search was conducted in the city for those capable of writing poetry,
and they were all killed.
Those who were literate were given menial tasks.
In total, over 3,000 people were killed.
14 Qú Zhěn and Lǐ Yǒujīn arrived at Dàizhōu.
After recruiting troops for over ten days,
they gathered 30,000 men,
all being various northern Hú tribes.
They encamped west of Guō,
(that is, west of Guō Xiàn in Dàizhōu.)
(Guō,
pronounced guō.)
Zhěn and Yǒujīn could not control them.
Yǒujīn then persuaded Chén Jǐngsī, saying:
"Now although we have a multitude of tens of thousands,
if there is no general of prestige and authority to command them,
we will ultimately not succeed.
My elder brother, the Sītú, and his son,
surpass others in courage and strategy,
and are respected by the multitude.
If the Piàojì truly memorializes the Son of Heaven to pardon their crimes,
and summons them to be commanders,
(Lǐ Guóchāng was appointed Jiàoxiào Sītú for his merit in suppressing Páng Xūn.
Piàojì
is the highest rank in the Táng system of military honorary titles.
Since Gāo Lìshì in the Táng,
many eunuchs have held the office of Piàojì,
hence this is used to refer to Jǐngsī.)
then the mad bandits are not enough to be pacified!"
Jǐngsī considered this correct,
and sent an envoy to the imperial temporary residence to speak of it.
An edict was issued granting the request.
Yǒujīn took five hundred cavalry to carry the edict to the Dádá to welcome them.
(Lǐ Kèyòng entered the Dádá,
see the first year of Guǎngmíng in the previous volume.)
(Textual Analysis states: The Veritable Records:
"Chén Jǐngsī carried the edict into the Dádá to summon Lǐ Kèyòng,
and the army encamped at Yùzhōu.
Kèyòng then greatly plundered the military towns north of Yànmén."
Xuē Jūzhèng's History of the Five Dynasties:
"Previously,
Jǐngsī and Lǐ Yǒujīn dispatched five thousand cavalry from the Shatuo tribes to head south to the capital.
Yǒujīn
was a paternal uncle of Wǔhuáng.
In the second month of the first year of Zhōnghé,
Yǒujīn's army reached Jiàngzhōu.
As they were about to cross the river,
Cìshǐ Qú Zhěn said to Jǐngsī: 'The Cháo bandits are currently strong,
it would be better to return to Dàiběi for now,
and slowly plan advantages and disadvantages.'
In the fourth month,
Yǒujīn turned his army back to Yànmén.
Qú Zhěn reached Dàizhōu,
and within half a month,
recruited 30,000 troops,
encamping west of Guō Xiàn.
This army was all from the five northern tribes,
unfamiliar with military discipline,
and Qú Zhěn and Lǐ Yǒujīn could not control them.
Yǒujīn said to Jǐngsī such and such,
Jǐngsī agreed,
and urged a memorial to the imperial temporary residence.
The Son of Heaven then appointed Wǔhuáng as Yànmén Jiedushi,
and ordered him to use his own army to attack the bandits.
Lǐ Yǒujīn dispatched five hundred cavalry to carry the edict to summon Wǔhuáng from the Dádá,
and Wǔhuáng immediately led ten thousand men from the Dádá tribes towards Yànmén."
Note: Jǐngsī spoke of pardoning Guóchāng and his son,
but only Kèyòng came.
This is probably because Guóchāng was already old,
and only Kèyòng was sent.
This year,
Kèyòng only attacked and plundered Tàiyuán,
and also captured Xīn and Dài prefectures.
In the twelfth month of the following year,
he was appointed Yànmén Jiedushi from the position of Liúhòu of Xīn and Dài.
It seems that at this time only his crimes were pardoned,
and he was restored as Dàtóng Fángyùshǐ.
After he captured Xīn and Dài,
he proclaimed himself Liúhòu.
The court summoned him again,
and only then appointed him as Yànmén [Jiedushi].
Xuē's History is mistaken.
(The New Tables state,
"In the second year of Zhōnghé,
the two prefectures of Xīn and Dài in Hédōng were placed under Yànmén Jiedushi,
and Dàtóng Jiedushi was changed to Yànmén Jiedushi,
with its seat at Dàizhōu."
This is evidence.)
15 The officials who followed the imperial carriage gradually gathered in Chéngdū.
Nearly two hundred officials from the Nán and Běi Sī attended court.
Tribute from various circuits and the Four Barbarians continued without cease.
The treasuries in Shǔ were full,
no different from the capital.
Rewards and gifts were not lacking,
and the soldiers were pleased.
16 Huáng Cháo captured Wáng Huī,
and forced him to take office.
Huī feigned muteness,
and did not comply.
After over a month,
he escaped and fled to Hétóng.
He sent someone by a hidden path to present a silk memorial to the imperial temporary residence.
(Jiàn,
pronounced gǔ xiàn fān.)
17 The former Xiàsuí Jiedushi Zhūgě Shuǎng again submitted a memorial from Héyáng offering his allegiance.
(Last year when Huáng Cháo entered the pass,
Zhūgě Shuǎng surrendered to him.)
18. Tuòbá Sīgōng, Prefect of Yòuzhōu.
In the 16th year of the Kāiyuán era,
Yòuzhōu was established with the remnants of the Six Hú Prefectures.
In the 1st year of the Qiányuán era,
its administration was located at the Jīnglüè Army,
and later moved to govern Chángzé County.
Chángzé
was the territory of Sānfēng County in the Shuòfāng Commandery during the Hàn dynasty.
Textual criticism notes: Oūyáng Xiū's History of the Five Dynasties writes
"Tuòbá Sījìng,"
implying that the Old History of the Táng avoided the imperial taboo.
However, according to the Old Book of Táng and the Veritable Records, both write
"Sīgōng."
The Veritable Records state:
"In the 9th month of the 2nd year of the Tiānfù era,
Lǐ Sījìng, Military Commissioner of the Wǔdìng Army, surrendered the city to Wáng Jiàn.
Sījìng's original surname was Tuòbá,
and he was the younger brother of Sīgōng, Military Commissioner of Fūxià, and Sīxiào, Military Commissioner of Bǎodà.
Sīxiào retired from office,
and Sījìng was appointed as the Deputy Military Commissioner of Bǎodà,
later promoted to Military Commissioner,
and then transferred to the Wǔdìng Army."
The New Book of Táng's Account of the Dǎngxiàng states:
"Sīgōng served as Military Commissioner of Dìngnán,
and upon his death,
his younger brother Sījiàn succeeded him as Military Commissioner.
Sīxiào served as Military Commissioner of Bǎodà,
and due to old age,
recommended his younger brother Sījìng as Deputy Military Commissioner of Bǎodà,
who soon became Military Commissioner."
Thus, Sīgōng and Sījìng were two different persons.
Sījìng later attached himself to Lǐ Màozhēn,
and was possibly granted the imperial surname,
hence changing his surname to Lǐ.
Oūyáng Xiū combined them into one person,
which is an error.
The New Book states: The Dǎngxiàng were divided into tribes by surname,
and the Tuòbá clan was the strongest.
They formed an alliance to suppress the rebels.
Qí Kèjiǎn, Commissioner of Fèngtiān Garrison, sent an envoy to Zhèng Tián to offer his service.
On the jiǎzǐ day,
Tián issued a proclamation to all military governors across the land,
calling for a joint effort to suppress the rebels.
At that time, the Son of Heaven was in Shǔ,
and imperial decrees could not reach the regions,
so the people believed the court could no longer recover.
However, upon receiving Tián's proclamation,
they vied to send troops in response.
The rebels, fearing this,
dared not again look toward the western capital.
19. In summer,
the 4th month,
on the 1st day, wùyín,
Wáng Duó was additionally appointed as Shìzhōng.
20. Tuòbá Sīgōng was appointed as Acting Military Commissioner of Xiàsuí.
This laid the foundation for the Tuòbá clan's rise to power and eventual domination of Western Xià.
21. Huáng Cháo appointed his general Wáng Méi as Military Commissioner of Bīnníng.
Zhū Méi, General of the Tōngsāi Garrison in Bīnzhōu, raised troops and killed him,
yielding the position of Military Commissioner to another general, Lǐ Chónggǔ,
and personally led troops to attack Cháo.
At this time,
Táng Hóngfū was stationed north of the Wèi River,
Wáng Chóngróng at Shāyuàn,
Wáng Chùcún at the Wèi Bridge,
Tuòbá Sīgōng at Wǔgōng,
and Zhèng Tián at Zhōuzhì.
Hóngfū, taking advantage of the victory at Lóngwěi,
advanced and approached Cháng'ān.
On the rénwǔ day,
Huáng Cháo led his forces eastward in retreat.
Chéng Zōngchǔ first entered through the Yánqiū Gate,
as the imperial park of Cháng'ān had a gate
facing west called the Yánqiū Gate.
Chùcún led 5,000 elite troops and entered the city at night.
The residents of the wards and markets rejoiced,
rushing out cheering to welcome the imperial troops,
some throwing tiles and stones at the rebels,
others gathering arrows to supply the imperial army.
Zōngchǔ and others, fearing that other generals would share their merit,
did not report to Fèngxiáng and Fūxià.
Sentence break.
They plundered gold, silk, singing girls, and concubines.
Chùcún ordered his soldiers to tie white bands as identification,
but young men in the wards and markets stole these bands to plunder people.
The rebels camped in the open at Bàshàng.
Camping without shelter is called "camping in the open."
Moreover, the various armies failed to support each other,
so the rebels turned back and launched a surprise attack,
entering through various gates,
and a great battle ensued within Cháng'ān.
Zōngchǔ and Hóngfū died.
Textual criticism notes: The Old Annals and Biographies, as well as the New Biographies, all state that Hóngfū's defeat occurred in the 2nd month of the 2nd year.
However, the Jīngtīng Lù, Táng Nián Bǔlù, New Annals, and Veritable Records all place it in the 4th month of this year.
The New Annals provide particularly detailed dates,
so we follow that here.
Thus, the defeat was severe,
with eight or nine out of ten dead.
Chùcún gathered the remaining troops and returned to camp.
On the dīnghài day,
Cháo re-entered Cháng'ān.
Enraged by the people's support for the imperial army,
he unleashed his troops to slaughter them,
until blood flowed like rivers,
calling it "washing the city."
Thereupon, all imperial armies retreated,
and the rebels' power grew even stronger.
Wáng Pǔ, Prefect of Tóngzhōu appointed by the rebels, Qiáo Qiān, Prefect of Huázhōu, and Sòng Yán, Prefect of Shāngzhōu, hearing that Cháo had abandoned Cháng'ān,
all led their forces to flee to Dèngzhōu.
Zhū Wēn executed Pǔ and Qiān,
but released Yán,
sending him back to Shāngzhōu.
22. On the gēngyín day,
Tuòbá Sīgōng and Lǐ Xiàochāng engaged the rebels at the Tǔ
Bridge,
but were unsuccessful.
23. An edict appointed Wáng Chóngróng, Deputy Military Commissioner of Hézhōng, as Military Commissioner.
24. The rebel masses honored Huáng Cháo with the title "Emperor Who Responds to Heaven's Mandate, Initiates Sagely Rule, and Manifests Military Prowess."
25. A pair of pheasants gathered at the government offices of Guǎnglíng.
Diviners considered the arrival of wild birds
an omen that the city would be emptied.
Gāo Pián, disturbed by this,
issued a proclamation to all regions,
stating he would march to suppress Huáng Cháo.
He mobilized all 80,000 troops within his jurisdiction,
with 2,000 ships,
displaying grand banners and armor.
In the 5th month,
on the yǐ
wèi day,
he set out and stationed at Dōngtáng.
Dōngtáng
was located east of present-day Yángzhōu city,
namely the embankment area from Wāntóu to Yílíng.
Ship,
pronounced sōu.
Textual criticism notes: The Record of Strange Rebellions states:
"From the 12th day of the 5th month when he left for Dōngtáng,
until the 6th day of the 9th month when he returned to the prefectural seat,
over ninety days,
this was to avert the omen of the pheasants' gathering."
However, from the 12th day of the 5th month to the 6th day of the 9th month
is actually 163 days,
not over ninety days.
We now follow the Old Biography.
Pián used wind and waves as an excuse,
or claimed the timing was inauspicious,
and ultimately did not set out.
26. Lǐ Kèyòng sent a dispatch to Hédōng,
stating he had received an edict to lead 50,000 troops to suppress Huáng Cháo,
and ordered provisions to be prepared.
Setting up food and drink along the route for the army is called "dùn,"
and establishing postal stations is called "dì."
Kèyòng stationed east of Fén,
and Wáng Cóngdǎng provided rewards and provisions,
supplying funds and grain.
However, Kèyòng delayed his departure for days.
Kèyòng personally went to the city walls and shouted loudly,
demanding to meet with Cóngdǎng.
Cóngdǎng ascended the wall to apologize.
On the guǐhài day,
Kèyòng again demanded rewards for his army's departure,
and Cóngdǎng gave him a thousand strings of cash and a thousand hu of rice.
On the jiǎzǐ day,
Kèyòng allowed the Shātuó to plunder the residents,
causing great panic in the city.
Cóngdǎng sought help from Qìbì Zhāng, Military Commissioner of Zhènwǔ,
who led Turks and Tǔyùhún to rescue him,
destroying two Shātuó camps.
Kèyòng pursued and fought south of Jìnyáng city,
and Zhāng led his troops into the city.
The Shātuó plundered Yángqū and Yúcì before withdrawing.
When Huáng Cháo captured Cháng'ān,
Zhōu Jí, the military governor of Zhōngwǔ, surrendered to him.
In the eleventh month of last year, Zhōu Jí was appointed to the Zhōngwǔ command.
In the twelfth month, Huáng Cháo captured Cháng'ān.
Zhōu Jí urgently summoned the army supervisor Yáng Fùguāng.
Previously, Yáng Fùguāng had been appointed as the supervisor of the Zhōngwǔ Army,
stationed in Dèngzhōu,
to block the rebels' right flank.
After Huáng Cháo occupied Cháng'ān,
he sent Zhū Wēn to garrison Dèngzhōu.
Yáng Fùguāng then went to Xǔzhōu to join Zhōu Jí,
hence Zhōu Jí summoned him for a night banquet.
"Lord Zhōu has submitted to the rebels,
and may harm the Palace Attendant.
You must not go."
In the Táng dynasty, the Palace Attendants Directorate was headed by the Palace Attendant Supervisor,
with the Palace Attendant as the deputy,
hence his attendants referred to Fùguāng by this title.
"The situation is already like this,
for righteousness, I cannot seek personal safety."
He then went to see him.
When the wine was flowing freely,
Zhōu Jí spoke of the imperial court,
and Yáng Fùguāng shed tears.
After a long while,
he said:
"What moves a true man is gratitude and righteousness!
You rose from a commoner to become a duke and marquis.
How can you abandon the Son of Heaven of eighteen generations and serve a rebel?"
From Gāozǔ to Xīzōng, there were eighteen reigns.
"I alone could not resist the rebels,
so I outwardly submitted while secretly planning against them.
Today I summoned you
precisely for this purpose."
They then poured wine and swore an oath.
Shǐ Zhào said: This means to pour wine drop by drop.
Yáng Fùguāng sent his adopted son Shǒuliàng to kill the rebel envoy at the postal station.
At that time, Qín Zōngquán occupied Càizhōu
and did not obey Zhōu Jí's orders.
Yáng Fùguāng led three thousand Zhōngwǔ troops to Càizhōu,
to persuade Zōngquán to jointly raise an army against Huáng Cháo.
Zōngquán sent his general Wáng Shū with three thousand troops to follow Fùguāng in attacking Dèngzhōu.
Wáng Shū delayed and did not advance.
Fùguāng executed him,
merged his army,
and divided the eight thousand Zhōngwǔ troops into eight corps.
He sent the subordinate generals Lù Yànhóng, Jìn Huī, Wáng Jiàn, Hán Jiàn, Zhāng Zào, Lǐ Shītài, and Páng Cóng, eight men in total, to command them.
Textual analysis notes: Liú Shù's *Shíguó Jìnián* states: Regarding the eight corps,
only the names of seven men including Wáng Jiàn are recorded,
because the other texts cannot be verified.
Wáng Jiàn's story begins here.
He was from Wǔyáng;
Hán Jiàn,
from Chángshè;
Yànhóng, Huī, Zào, and Shītài
were all from Xǔzhōu.
Fùguāng led the eight corps to battle Zhū Wēn,
defeated him,
and thus captured Dèngzhōu.
They pursued the fleeing enemy north to Lánqiáo before returning.
Lánqiáo
is south of Lántián Pass.
Return,
read as cóng xuān fān,
or also as rú zì.
28 Gāo Yún, the military governor of Zhāoyì, joined forces with Wáng Chóngróng to attack Huàzhōu,
and captured it.
29 In the sixth month,
on the Wùxū day,
Zhèng Tián was appointed as Minister of Works, concurrently Vice Director of the Chancellery and Tongpingzhangshi,
retaining his position as overall commander.
30 Lǐ Kèyòng encountered heavy rain,
led his troops back north,
captured Xīnzhōu and Dàizhōu,
and then stayed in Dàizhōu.
Textual analysis notes: *Tángmò Jiànwén Lù* states:
"On the thirtieth day of the sixth month,
the Shatuo army turned back,
and recaptured Xīnzhōu and Dàizhōu."
*Tàizǔ Jìnián Lù* states:
"They encountered heavy rain,
and on the twenty-third day of the sixth month,
withdrew their army to Yànmén."
Xuē Jūzhèng's *Wǔdài Shǐ* agrees with *Jìnián Lù*.
Note: Xīnzhōu and Dàizhōu originally belonged to Hédōng,
and were transferred to Yànmén in the second year of Zhōnghé.
Here we follow *Jiànwén Lù* and the Veritable Records.
31 The deputy military governor of Bīnníng, Zhū Méi, stationed troops at Xīngpíng.
Xīngpíng County
is eighty-five lǐ west of Cháng'ān.
Yú Jìng said: Zhōu Zhàngqiū
is present-day Xīngpíng.
They besieged Xīngpíng,
and Zhū Méi retreated to station at Fèngtiān and Lóngwěi Bēi.
32 Lǐ Chán, commander of the Huángtóu Army in Xīchuān, led ten thousand men,
and Gǒng Xián led five thousand men.
Gǒng
is a surname.
Examples include Duke Jiǎn of Gǒng, a minister of the Zhōu court,
and Gǒng Shuò, a senior official of Jìn.
They established two camps,
fought against Huáng Cháo,
and repeatedly achieved victories.
Chén Jìngxuān sent the Divine Mechanism Camp commander Gāo Rénhòu with two thousand men to reinforce them.
The Divine Mechanism Camp

36. Initially,

The Shǔ army harbored considerable resentment.

Lìngzī held a banquet for the commanders of the local and guest armies.
The local army refers to the Shǔ army.
The guest army refers to the various armies accompanying the imperial carriage.
In the mid-Táng period,
the overall commander of the armies was called the commander.
Later on,
a single unit of the army was called a "dū,"

He then bestowed rewards upon them,

Only Guō Qí, the commander of the Huángtóu Army of Xīchuān, did not accept.
He stood up and said:
"The various generals receive monthly salaries and allowances,
which are ample and more than sufficient.
I often think of how difficult it is to repay such favor;
how dare I be insatiable!
However, the Shǔ army shares the same guard duties as the other armies,
yet the rewards are vastly unequal.
They feel deeply aggrieved,
and I fear this may lead to a mutiny.
I hope, Military Commissioner, that you will reduce the rewards for the generals and distribute them equally to the Shǔ army,
so that local and guest troops are treated as one.
This would be a great blessing for both superiors and subordinates!"
Lìngzī remained silent for a while,
then said:
"What merit have you ever achieved?"
He replied:
"I grew up in Shāndōng,
served in campaigns and garrisoned the border regions.
I fought the Dǎngxiàng seventeen times
and the Qìdān over ten times,
my body covered with wounds.
I also campaigned against the Tǔyùhún,
was wounded in the side, my intestines protruding,
yet I stitched them up with thread and returned to battle."
Lìngzī then personally poured wine from a separate vessel and offered it to Qí.
Qí knew it was poisoned,
but having no choice,
he bowed twice and drank it.
Upon returning,
he killed a maidservant,
sucked her blood to detoxify himself,
and vomited several shēng of black fluid.
He then led his troops in rebellion.
On the dīngmǎo day,

Lìngzī escorted the Son of Heaven to the east city for protection,

Qí led his troops back to camp.
Chén Jìngxuān ordered the chief adjutant Ān Jīnshān to lead troops to attack him.
Qí broke through the encirclement at night and fled to Guǎngdū.
The Suí dynasty changed Guǎngdū County to Shuāngliú County.
In the second year of the Lóngshuò era of the Táng dynasty, Guǎngdū County was re-established from Shuāngliú,
belonging to Chéngdū Prefecture.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is forty-five lǐ west of the prefectural seat.
Only one office clerk followed and rested with him on the riverbank.
Qí said to the clerk:
"Lord Chén knows I am innocent;
however, the military headquarters is in turmoil,
and it cannot be left unsettled.
You have served me faithfully from beginning to end,
and now I have a way to repay you.
Take my seal and sword to Lord Chén and say:
'Guō Qí fled across the river.
I struck him with the sword,
and he fell into the water.
His corpse drifted downstream with the current.
I obtained his seal and sword to present them.'
Lord Chén will surely act according to your words,
posting a notice and hanging the seal and sword in the market to reassure the public.
You will receive a generous reward,
and my family will also be kept safe.
I am now heading to Guǎnglíng
to return to Lord Gāo."
This means he intended to flee to Yángzhōu and submit to Gāo Pián.
"You can secretly inform my family of this."
He then removed his seal and sword, handed them over, and escaped.
The clerk presented them to Jìngxuān,

The Emperor spent day and night exclusively with eunuchs,

"In times of peace and order, those near and far should still be of one mind;

Last winter, the imperial carriage traveled west,

causing all from the Grand Councilors and Vice Directors down to be slaughtered by the rebels."
This refers to Dòu Lú Zhuàn, Cuī Hàng, and Yú Cóng, among others.
"Moreover, those court officials who have now arrived
have all braved death through perilous journeys
to serve their sovereign and parents from afar.
From now on, they should share both joy and hardship together.
I observe that the night before last, the Huángtóu Army rebelled.
Your Majesty alone, with Lìngzī, Jìngxuān, and the various inner court officials, closed the city gates and ascended the tower,
and did not summon Wáng Duó and those below him, nor admit the court officials into the city.
The next day,
you did not meet with the Grand Councilors,
nor did you console the court officials."
"The next day" means the following day.
"To this day, it is unknown whether Your Sacred Person is safe or not,
let alone those more distant!"
"If subjects do not care for their sovereign,
their crime certainly deserves execution;
but if Your Majesty does not show compassion for your subjects,
where then does righteousness lie!
The empire is the empire of Gāozǔ and Tàizōng,
not the empire of the Northern Administration.
The Son of Heaven is the Son of Heaven of all within the Four Seas and Nine Provinces,
not the Son of Heaven of the Northern Administration.
The Northern Administration is not necessarily entirely trustworthy;
the Southern Administration is not necessarily entirely useless.
How can the Son of Heaven and the Grand Councilors have no connection whatsoever,
and court officials be treated like strangers on the road!
If this continues,
I fear the time for recovery
will still trouble Your Sacred Thoughts,
while those holding sinecures
will be able to feast in peace.
I personally have received favor and honor,
and my duty lies in offering beneficial advice.
Although past events cannot be admonished,
future ones can still be pursued."
These two phrases are originally from the Analects.
Lìngzī withheld the memorial and did not present it.
On the xīnwèi day,
he forged an edict demoting Zhāotú to Registrar of Jiāzhōu
and had someone drown him at the Máyí Ford.
Máyí Mountain is seven lǐ east of Méishān in Méizhōu.
The mountain's shape resembles a toad's jaw, hence the name.
The mountain overlooks a river ford;
today there is a shrine to Reminder Mèng.
When a Son of Heaven kills a remonstrating minister,
his state is sure to perish.
For a eunuch to arrogate the authority to kill a remonstrating minister
is unprecedented since ancient times.
This not only harms your state,
but indeed also brings misfortune upon your own person.
Thus, before the Táng perished, Lìngzī himself perished first.
