Bówén Lù: There is etched gold foil, legal gold, and graded gold beaten into large thin sheets,
mixed with one liang of yellow alum, one liang of chicken-dropping alum, half a liang of blue vitriol, one fēn of borax, one liang of arsenic soil, and one liang of red soil, ground together,
then applied to the gold sheets with saltpeter water, dried over fire,
and reapplied and reheated;
after repeating this three times,
cover with a layer of cow dung ash,
place a layer of a separator underneath and heat over a strong fire for one day, then remove,
and wash with warm water.
What remains is gold,
and what is etched out is silver.
"This is due to the Grand Preceptor's benevolence and wisdom,
Chén Jìngxuān was Acting Grand Preceptor,
hence the address.
Are you trying to bring disaster upon me with this gift?"

were east of the mountains relative to Lùzhōu.
Estimate,
pronounced tuò.

This set the stage for Lùzhōu's rebellion against Mèng Fānglì.
An examination of discrepancies: The Veritable Records state:
"In the first month of the fourth year of Zhōnghé,
Yìchéng campaign army commander Zhèng Chāngtú was appointed as a secretary of the Central Secretariat.
In the third month,
a mutiny broke out in Xíngzhōu,
killing its commander Chéng Lín,
and secretary of the Central Secretariat Zhèng Chāngtú was temporarily appointed as the interim military governor of Zhāoyì."
However, Chéng Lín had already been killed by Mèng Fānglì earlier,
and he was not in Xíngzhōu,
as Xíngzhōu was under Fānglì's control.
Moreover, by that time, Lùzhōu was already occupied by Lǐ Kèxiū,
so how could Chāngtú go there to serve as interim military governor?
Also, in the fifth month of that year,
Right Vice Director Wáng Huī was appointed as a joint manager of affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery,
to serve as the military governor of Zhāoyì.
Huī submitted a memorial earnestly explaining the impracticality,
and he was reinstated to his original position as caretaker of the Dàmíng Palace.
The Old Book biography of Wáng Huī states:
"Initially,
a mutiny broke out in Lùzhōu,
killing Chéng Lín,
and Vice Minister of War Zhèng Chāngtú was temporarily appointed to administer the military affairs of Zhāoyì.
At that time, Mèng Fānglì had carved out the three eastern prefectures,
establishing a separate military command,
leaving only Zézhōu as a subordinate prefecture of Shàngdǎng,
and most of the military personnel sided with Fānglì,
so Chāngtú could not control them.
The chief ministers proposed appointing a senior minister to govern the region,
so Huī was appointed as acting Left Vice Director and joint manager of affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery,
to serve as the surveillance commissioner of Zé, Lù, Xíng, Míng, and Cí.
At that time, the imperial carriage had not yet returned,
bandits were gathering east of the passes,
and Lǐ Kèyòng of Hé dōng was contending with Mèng Fānglì over Zé and Lù,
so Huī believed that the court's military strength was insufficient to intervene.
He submitted a memorial stating: 'Zhèng Chāngtú has been in charge for several months,
and his roots have grown deep;
Mèng Fānglì exclusively controls the three prefectures,
leading to accumulated grievances.
Appeasing those outside would cause resentment among the people of Lù,
while placating those within would further arouse suspicion among the generals of Xíng.
The disaster is already ablaze,
and there is no way to remedy what has been lost.
We must observe the outcome of the conflict,
before deciding on stability.
I humbly request Your Majesty to broadly seek the opinions of the court,
choose someone suitable to entrust,
and handle the matter with a long-term perspective.'
The Son of Heaven then appointed Chāngtú to govern the region,
and Huī was appointed as the commissioner for taxes and military supplies for all circuits."
The New Book biography of Mèng Fānglì states:
"Fānglì attacked Chéng Lín,
beheaded him,
and carved out Xíng, Míng, and Cí as a separate command,
establishing Xíng as the headquarters,
and naming it the Zhāoyì army.
The people of Lù requested the supervising army officer Wú Quánxù to act as the interim military governor.
At that time, Wáng Duó was the overall commander of the campaign armies of all circuits,
and because Lù was unstable,
he issued an unauthorized imperial edict appointing Fānglì to administer affairs in Xíngzhōu.
Fānglì did not accept the appointment,
imprisoned Quánxù,
and sent a letter to Duó,
requesting that a Confucian scholar be appointed to govern Lù.
Duó sent his advisor, secretary of the Central Secretariat Zhèng Chāngtú, to administer the interim affairs of Zhāoyì,
intending for him to become the military governor.
Emperor Xīzōng personally appointed the former chief minister Wáng Huī to serve as the military governor.
At that time, the Son of Heaven was in Xīhé,
and Guānzhōng was in turmoil,
with Fānglì carving out territory while Lǐ Kèyòng eyed Lùzhōu.
Huī estimated that the court could not control the situation,
so he firmly declined in favor of Chāngtú.
Chāngtú governed for less than three months
and then left.
Fānglì then petitioned for Lǐ Yīnruì to be appointed as prefect,
and moved the headquarters to Lónggāng.
When Kèyòng became the military governor of Hé dōng,
the Zhāoyì army officer Qí Shěnhái requested troops,
seeking to restore the Zhāoyì army,
so Kèyòng killed Yīnruì,
annexed Lùzhōu,
and petitioned for Kèxiū to be appointed as interim military governor."
However, Wáng Duó was removed as overall commander in the first month of the third year,
so Chāngtú's appointment as interim military governor of Zhāoyì must have occurred in the second year.
Chāngtú left Lù within less than three months,
and since Huī declined the appointment in favor of Chāngtú,
Huī's appointment to Zhāoyì could not have been in the fifth month of the fourth year.
The dates in the Veritable Records are all incorrect.
If Fānglì had already declared himself the interim military governor of Zhāoyì,
and moved the army headquarters to Xíngzhōu,
then he was not merely carving out the three prefectures.
If he intended to establish a separate command,
he should have given it a different army name,
and certainly would not have shared the name Zhāoyì with Lùzhōu.
If he only regarded Lù as a subordinate prefecture,
he would have appointed his own prefect,
and would not have written to Wáng Duó requesting a Confucian scholar;
even if he had requested one,
Duó would have appointed Chāngtú as the prefect of Lùzhōu,
not as the administrator of Zhāoyì military affairs,
nor could he have treated Zézhōu as a subordinate prefecture.
It seems that after Fānglì killed Chéng Lín,
because Xíngzhōu was his hometown,
he wanted to move the headquarters there,
so he went to Xíngzhōu,
but the people of Lù did not comply,
so they requested Quánxù to serve as interim military governor.
Fānglì, seeing that public sentiment was not yet aligned,
did not dare to declare himself,
so he imprisoned Quánxù,
outwardly showing deference,
using the pretext that a eunuch could not serve as military governor to request from Wáng Duó
the appointment of a Confucian scholar;
his intention was that a Confucian scholar would be easier to control,
so he could outwardly respect him as military governor while monopolizing military and administrative power,
gradually planning to replace him.
After Chāngtú arrived in Lù,
he wanted to exercise the authority of military governor,
but the three eastern prefectures were already under Fānglì's control,
and they did not accept his command,
leaving only Zézhōu in the south,
where he could still issue orders.
Therefore, Wáng Huī's memorial stated:
"Chāngtú has been in charge for several months,
and his roots have grown deep."
This meant that Chāngtú had been in Zé and Lù for a long time,
and the people's hearts were gradually leaning toward him,
making him superior to Huī.
It also stated:
"Fānglì exclusively controls the three prefectures,
leading to accumulated grievances."
This meant that Chāngtú wanted to exercise the authority of military governor,
but Fānglì did not submit to his command,
leading to mutual suspicion and rivalry,
hence the accumulated grievances.
It further stated:
"Appeasing those outside would cause resentment among the people of Lù,
while placating those within would further arouse suspicion among the generals of Xíng."
This meant that by then, Xíng and Lù were already in conflict,
and if Huī went there and favored Xíng, the people of Lù would resent him for favoring the enemy,
while favoring Lù would make the generals of Xíng suspect he was plotting against them.
It also stated:
"We must observe the outcome of the conflict,
before deciding on stability."
This meant that only if Chāngtú could defeat Fānglì
would Zhāoyì become stable.
Chāngtú remained uneasy in Lù,
so he handed over the military command to Fānglì and left.
Only then did Fānglì declare himself interim military governor,
move the army headquarters to Xíngzhōu,
treat Lù as a subordinate prefecture,
and petition for Yīnruì to be appointed as prefect.
Therefore, the New Book biography places the move to Lónggāng after Yīnruì's appointment as prefect,
which serves as evidence.
This caused resentment among the people of Lù, who summoned the Shatuo,
and when Huī was appointed as military governor,
Kèyòng had not yet dared to contend for Zé and Lù.
Wú Quánxù
was likely the supervising army officer when Fānglì first entered Lù,
so Wáng Duó appointed him as interim military governor.
After Fānglì imprisoned him,
it is likely he was dismissed.
Qí Shěnhái was probably the supervising army officer during Zhèng Chāngtú's time.
The Chronological Record of the Founding Emperor states:
"Fānglì captured Shěnhái,
and declared himself interim military governor."
Xuē Jūzhèng's Old History of the Five Dynasties biography of Fānglì states:
"Mèng Fānglì established Xíngzhōu as his headquarters,
and appointed Shěn Huì to administer Lùzhōu."
Various accounts differ.
Moreover, having already captured Shěn Huì,
he certainly would not have appointed him to administer Lùzhōu.
Mèng Fānglì recommended Lǐ Yīnruì to be prefect,
while Shěn Huì remained in his old position,
so he must have been a later-appointed military supervisor.
Mèng Fānglì, because he had never opposed him,
therefore did not suspect him.
If he had once been imprisoned and captured,
he certainly would not have been kept.
The falseness of this
is clearly evident.
I suspect that in the late Táng, the Zhāoyì command repeatedly expelled its commanders;
Liú Guǎng and Chéng Lín rebelled and were killed,
which everyone knew.
Those recording events did not carefully investigate and correct,
sometimes taking the earlier for the later,
the later for the earlier,
resulting in discrepancies and inconsistencies,
hence many books contradict and do not agree.
Furthermore, the biography of Ān Chóngruǎn in the Old History of the Five Dynasties states:
"Ān Wényòu initially served as a Yámén general in Lùzhōu.

Moreover, during the Guāngqì era,

When Wényòu came,
he should have fought Kèxiū,

This matter is likely false,
