so as not to implicate each other.
Yòngzhī resented him for this.
Right Xiāoxióng Army Commander Yáo Guīlǐ
was straightforward and dared to speak out,
and particularly detested Yòngzhī's actions.
He often enumerated his crimes to his face,
and constantly wanted to kill him with his own hand.
On the night of Guǐwèi day,
Yòngzhī and his gang were meeting at a courtesan's house.
Guīlǐ secretly sent someone to set fire to the house,
killing several people who resembled him in appearance.
Yòngzhī changed clothes and escaped.
The next morning,
(Yòngzhī) thoroughly investigated the matter,
and caught the arsonists,
who were all soldiers from the Xiāoxióng Army.
Yòngzhī then day and night slandered the two generals to Pián.
Not long after,
Pián sent the two generals to lead three thousand Xiāoxióng soldiers to attack bandits in Shèn County.
(Shèn County
was the location of Jùnqiú County of Jiǔjiāng Commandery in the Hàn dynasty.
The old city was south of the present county.
The Suí dynasty established Shèn County.
In the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Lúzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is 60 lǐ northeast of the prefecture.
Jǐ,
read as jūqǐ.)
(Yòngzhī told Pián) "Gōngchǔ and Guīlǐ want to attack Lúzhōu."
Xíngmǐn dispatched troops to ambush them.
The two generals were unprepared,
and their entire army was annihilated.
(Xíngmǐn) reported to Pián that the two generals had plotted rebellion.
Pián did not know it was Yòngzhī's scheme,
and richly rewarded Xíngmǐn.
(This lays the foundation for Yáng Xíngmǐn's rise from Lúzhōu.)
13 On Jǐchǒu day,
Zhū Quánzhōng, Deputy Commander of the Hézhōng Campaign Pacification Army, was appointed Xuānwǔ Military Commissioner,
to await the recapture of Cháng'ān,
and then proceed to his post.
14 On Guǐsì day,
Lǐ Kèyòng and others captured Huàzhōu.
Huáng Kuí abandoned the city and fled.
15 Liú Hànhóng divided his troops to garrison the three towns of Huánglǐng, Yánxià, and Zhēnnǚ.
(These three towns
were all likely between Wù and Yuè.)
(Qián Liú) crossed the river from Fùchūn to attack the three towns.
(Fùchūn was Fùyáng County.)
He captured Yánxià Town Commander Shǐ Biàn and Zhēnnǚ Town Commander Yáng Yuánzōng.
Hànhóng stationed elite troops in Zhūjì.
Liú again attacked and defeated them,
and Hànhóng fled.
Zhuāng Mèngdié fought against Hán Xiùshēng and Qū Xíngcóng,
and was again defeated.
His defeated soldiers fled in disarray,
and though efforts were made to comfort and admonish them along the way,
they could not be stopped.
Encountering Gāo Rénhòu on the road,
he shouted at them,
and they immediately halted.
Gāo Rénhòu beheaded one commander,
and ordered the troops to reorganize their ranks.
He then summoned the village elders,
inquiring about the mountain paths and the locations of the rebel camps.
Delighted, he said:
"The enemy's elite troops are all on their boats,
leaving only the old and weak to guard the camps.
Their supplies and provisions are all stored in the camps.
This is what is called focusing on offense while neglecting defense—
their defeat is certain!"
He then displayed his troops along the river,
feigning an intention to cross.
The rebels prepared defenses day and night,
and sent troops to challenge them to battle.
Gāo Rénhòu did not engage them.
Instead, he secretly dispatched a thousand brave soldiers armed with weapons and carrying straw,
and at night,
they attacked the rebel camps via hidden paths,
setting them on fire.
When the rebels saw this,
they divided their forces to go and rescue the camps,
but it was too late.
Their supplies and provisions were completely destroyed,
and their morale was shaken.
Gāo Rénhòu further recruited skilled swimmers to bore holes in the enemy boats,
which then sank one after another.
The rebels were thrown into confusion,
unable to aid each other.
Gāo Rénhòu sent troops to ambush them at key points,
while also calling for their surrender.
The rebel forces all surrendered.
When Hán Xiùshēng and Qū Xíngcóng saw their troops disintegrating,
they swung their swords wildly,
trying to stop them,
but this only angered the troops further.
Together, they seized the two men and brought them before Gāo Rénhòu.
Gāo Rénhòu interrogated them, saying:
"Why did you rebel?"
Hán Xiùshēng replied:
"Since the Dàzhōng Emperor passed away,
(the Dàzhōng Emperor
refers to Emperor Xuānzōng.)
the bonds have loosened and the order has collapsed.
Today, those who rebel—
am I the only one?
Success is deemed right, failure is deemed wrong.
I am but meat on the chopping block,
to be cooked or minced as you please!"
Gāo Rénhòu looked solemn,
and ordered that they be well-fed before being shackled.
In the summer,
during the fourth month,
on the Gēngzǐ day,
they were presented at the imperial headquarters,
and executed.
Commentary on Discrepancies: The "Old Biography of Zhāng" states:
"In the fourth year of Zhōnghé,
Vice Director Gāo led a thousand infantry,
setting out on the fifth day of the third month.
Minister Zhuāng advanced together on the twentieth day of the third month.
On the fourteenth day of the fourth month,
reports from the Xiá region stated that on the first day of the fourth month,
the Xiá rebels were heavily defeated."
Jù Yánqìng's "Old Biography" states:
"In the third year,
on the Gēngwǔ day of the fourth month,
Hán Xiùshēng was captured,
and the victory report reached the headquarters."
According to the calendar, this month began on Dīngyǒu,
so there is no Gēngwǔ day.
The "Veritable Records" state:
"In the fourth month of the third year of Zhōnghé,
on the Gēngzǐ day,
Gāo Rénhòu captured Hán Xiùshēng,
and presented him at the imperial headquarters.
Initially,
when Gāo Rénhòu arrived in Xiá,
he engaged the rebels in battle,
and their forces were heavily defeated.
A junior officer among the rebels bound Hán Xiùshēng and surrendered him."
According to the collection of Zhèng Tián,
there is a memorial from Chén Shēn, the Surveillance Commissioner of Qiánnán, regarding Hán Xiùshēng of Fúzhōu plotting rebellion, stating:
"Hán Xiùshēng plundered and harmed the Qián region,
captured and looted officials,
occupied Fúlíng,
blocked the river routes,
harbored ambitions of usurpation,
and sought to be appointed as an inspector.
Chén Shēn then ordered Máo Píng to lead armored soldiers straight to their lair,
quickly breaching the city walls,
pursuing the ringleaders,
and exterminating the rebel faction."
However, various accounts all state that Gāo Rénhòu was the one who captured him.
The "New History" states:
"The troops, enraged,
seized Hán Xiùshēng and surrendered him.
Gāo Rénhòu sent him in a caged cart to the imperial headquarters,
where he was executed in the marketplace."
The "Old Biography of Zhāng" states:
"In the second year of Zhōnghé,
in the third month,
Qiān Néng rebelled.
In the eighth month,
Luó Húnqíng rebelled.
In the tenth month,
Jù Húsēng rebelled.
In the twelfth month,
Luó Fūzǐ rebelled.
In the third year,
reports from the northern route stated that Huáng Cháo was defeated and fled on the tenth day of the first month,
and Cháng'ān was recovered.
In the first month,
Qiān Néng sent Luó Húnqíng to set up twenty-seven camps at Xīnchuānbà,
cutting off the official land and water routes.
In the sixth month,
Hán Qiú rebelled,
and Qiān Néng, the rebel leader from Qióngzhōu, gradually encroached into the territory of Shǔzhōu.
In the ninth month,
Hán Xiùshēng of the Xiá region rebelled.
In the tenth month,
Qū Xíngcóng of the Xiá region rebelled.
The regional commander, Grand Mentor Chén, dispatched officer Zhuāng Èrmèng with two thousand troops,
who set out on the twentieth day of the tenth month to suppress Hán Xiùshēng, Qū Xíngcóng, and others in the Xiá region.
On the fifth day of the eleventh month,
Gāo Rénhòu set out to suppress Qiān Néng.
On the ninth day,
he captured the various camps within Qióngzhōu.
On the tenth day,
the prefectures and counties were pacified.
On the twenty-second day,
he returned to court for an audience.
On the third day,
a grand feast was held.
On the fifth day,
merits were discussed,
and he was appointed as the Prefect of Méizhōu.
In the third month of the fourth year,
Zhuāng Mèngdié retreated to Zhōngzhōu.
The regional commander dispatched Gāo Rénhòu with troops,
who set out on the fifth day of the third month.
Minister Zhuāng advanced together on the twentieth day of the third month.
On the fourteenth day of the fourth month, reports stated that on the first day of the fourth month, the Xiá rebels were heavily defeated,
and Hán Xiùshēng and others were captured.
On the fifteenth day,
Yáng Shīlì of Dōngchuān rebelled."
Jù Yánqìng's "Old Biography" is merely a copy and revision of Zhāng's biography,
with no additional information,
except that he moved Luó Húnqíng's rebellion to the fifth month of the second year of Zhōnghé,
Jù Húsēng and Luó Fūzǐ's rebellion to the sixth month,
Hán Qiú's rebellion to the seventh month of that year,
and Zhuāng Mèngdié's campaign against Hán Xiùshēng and Qū Xíngcóng to the Guǐchǒu day of the tenth month of that year.
Gāo Rénhòu's suppression of Qiān Néng and the other five rebels and his return to court for an audience
occurred on the Wùyín day of the twelfth month of that year.
In the second month of the third year,
Zhuāng Mèngdié was defeated by the rebels.
The regional commander dispatched Gāo Rénhòu with troops,
who set out on the Xīnchǒu day of the third month.
On the Gēngwǔ day of the fourth month, Hán Xiùshēng was captured,
and the victory report reached the headquarters.
In that month,
Yáng Shīlì rebelled.
In the fourth year,
reports from the northern route stated that Huáng Cháo was defeated and fled on the tenth day of the first month,
and Cháng'ān was recovered.
It is unclear whether Jù Yánqìng altered the dates based on other sources,
or simply did so arbitrarily.
As for Yáng Shīlì's rebellion in the third year
and the recovery of Cháng'ān in the fourth year,
these discrepancies are even more egregious.
The "Veritable Records"
regarding the affairs of Qiān Néng, Hán Xiùshēng, and others
largely follow Jù's biography,
but mistakenly place Hán Xiùshēng's rebellion in the seventh month,
and Gāo Rénhòu's campaign against Qiān Néng in the tenth month.
It omits the Wùyín and Xīnchǒu days,
and changes Gēngwǔ to Gēngzǐ.
These are the differences from Jù's biography.
The "New History Annals" state:
"On the Rénshēn day of the eleventh month of the third year,
Gāo Rénhòu, the Military Commander of Xīchuān, fought Qiān Néng at Qióngzhōu,
and defeated him."
The "Continued Record of Precious Fortunes" states:
"In the third year of Zhōnghé,
Hán Xiùshēng of Fúzhōu rebelled.
In the winter,
Qiān Néng rebelled,
and Gāo Rénhòu suppressed him."
According to Jiǎ Wěi's "Supplementary Records of the Táng Dynasty" and the iron amnesty certificate text recorded in the "Veritable Records," it states:
"In the third year of Zhōnghé, the cyclical year being Guǐmǎo,
the tenth month beginning on Jiǎwǔ,
on the sixteenth day, Jǐyǒu,
the Emperor bestowed an iron amnesty certificate upon the meritorious official Chén Jìngxuān."
The text contains
"Slaughtering Qián Néng was like cutting grass,
eliminating Hán Xiùshēng was like burning a nest."
Thus, the defeat of Xiùshēng
must have occurred before this date.
According to Zhāng's account, Xiùshéng was defeated in the fourth month of the fourth year.
On the tenth day of the tenth month of that same fourth year,
it also records the granting of an iron pledge to the Lord of Chuān, the Grand Preceptor,
which states:
"In the third year of Zhōnghé, the cyclical year being Guǐmǎo,
the tenth month, with the first day being Jiǎzǐ,
the fifth day being Wùchén."
The text matches the supplementary records and the Veritable Records,
showing such confusion and senility.
Jù's account takes Zhāng's events but changes the year,
while the Veritable Records uses Jù's year but changes the day.
The rise and fall of Qián Néng, Hán Xiùshēng, and others
cannot be precisely dated.
I now follow the Veritable Records.
17 Lǐ Kèyòng, along with the Zhōngwǔ general Páng Cóng, the Hézhōng general Bái Zhìqiān, and others, led their troops to advance first,
engaging Huáng Cháo's army at Wèinán,
fighting three battles in one day,
all victorious;
the Yìchéng, Yìwǔ, and other armies followed,
and the rebel forces fled in great disarray.
On Jiǎchén,
Kèyòng and others entered the capital through the Guāngtài Gate,
Huáng Cháo fought fiercely but could not prevail,
and he set fire to the palace buildings before fleeing.
Examination of Discrepancies: The Old Annals state:
"In the fourth month,
on Gēngzǐ,
the Shātuó and other armies advanced toward Cháng'ān,
the rebels resisted them at the Wèi Bridge,
were heavily defeated, and retreated.
Lǐ Kèyòng pursued them in victory.
On Jǐmǎo,
Huáng Cháo gathered his remaining forces,
and fled through the Lántián Pass.
On Gēngchén,
the capital was recaptured,
and Yáng Fùguāng reported the victory."
According to the calendar, the first day of that month was Dīngyǒu,
so there was no Jǐmǎo or Gēngchén.
Jìng Xiáng's Liáng Tàizǔ Biān Yílù states:
"On the fourth month, Yǐsì,
Cháo burned the palace halls, government offices, and residences almost entirely,
and fled over Lántián with his remaining followers.
The next day,
His Majesty and the various armies recaptured Cháng'ān."
The Veritable Records state:
"On Jiǎchén,
Lǐ Kèyòng, along with the loyal general Páng Cóng, the Hézhōng general Bái Zhìqiān, the Héngyě general Mǎn Cún, and the Cháoyì general Kāng Shīzhēn, defeated the rebels three times at the Wèi Bridge,
routing them completely.
The Yìchéng, Yìwǔ, and other armies advanced in succession.
On Yǐsì,
Cháo's rebels set fire to the Cháng'ān palace buildings,
gathered their remaining forces, and fled east through the Guāngtài Gate,
escaping via the Lántián Pass.
The various armies advanced and recaptured the capital."
The New Annals state:
"On the third month, Rénshēn,
Lǐ Kèyòng engaged Huáng Cháo in battle at Língkǒu,
defeating him.
On the fourth month, Jiǎchén,
he defeated him again at the Wèi Bridge.
On Bǐngwǔ,
the capital was recovered."
The Old Biography states:
"On the eighth day of the fourth month,
Kèyòng joined forces with the Zhōngwǔ cavalry general Páng Cóng and encountered the rebels at Wèinán,
fought three decisive battles,
and heavily defeated the rebel army.
On the night of the tenth,
Cháo's forces scattered and fled.
At dawn,
Kèyòng entered through the Guāngtài Gate,
recaptured the capital,
and Cháo's rebels fled east through Lántián and the Qīpán Road toward Guāndōng."
The New Biography states:
"Kèyòng sent his subordinate general Yáng Shǒuzōng to lead the Hézhōng general Bái Zhìqiān, the Zhōngwǔ general Páng Cóng, and others in the first attack on the rebels at the Wèi Bridge,
fighting three battles and routing them three times.
Thereupon, the troops of all the military governors were emboldened,
and none dared to lag behind.
They entered through the Guāngtài Gate,
the rebels collapsed,
they pursued the fleeing enemy to Wàngchūn,
and entered the gates of the Shēngyáng Hall.
Cháo fled by night,
his forces still numbering one hundred and fifty thousand,
claiming to head toward Xúzhōu,
exiting Lántián,
and entering Shāngshān."
Chéng Kuāngróu's Táng Bǔ Jì states:
"Yáng Fùguāng led over twenty thousand soldiers from the ten-circuit campaign, including military governors Wáng Chóngróng and Lǐ Kèyòng, to enter and attack through the Guāngtài Gate,
pursuing them to the Shēngyáng Hall,
killing over ten thousand rebels.
Huáng Cháo's army was defeated,
fled from the battlefield,
and escaped through the Lántián Pass."
The Later Táng Tàizǔ Jìnián Lù states:
"On Yǐsì,
Cháo was defeated,
burned the palace buildings, and fled east,
and Tàizǔ advanced to recapture the capital."
The Táng Nián Bǔ Lù states:
"On the eighth day,
Kèyòng and others fought at Wèinán,
defeating the rebel army three times.
On the ninth day,
Cháo fled."
According to Yáng Fùguāng's victory proclamation:
"On the eighth day of this month,
Yáng Shǒuzōng and others followed Kèyòng in entering the capital first through the Guāngtài Gate."
It also states:
"The rebels still formed a strong formation,
resisting the government troops.
From mǎo to shēn,
the fierce enemy was heavily routed,
immediately fled,
and entered Shāngshān to the south."
Thus, the government troops entered the city on the eighth day,
the rebels fought unsuccessfully and fled,
this is the most reliable account,
and I now follow it.
The battle at Wèinán
must have occurred before the eighth day,
and all other texts are mistaken.
The government troops plundered violently,
no different from the rebels,
leaving few houses and people remaining in Cháng'ān.
Cháo entered Shāngshān from Lántián,
having previously sent troops to block the Lántián road,
thus enabling his escape via this route.
The government troops scrambled to seize the spoils,
not pursuing urgently,
allowing the rebels to escape.
Yáng Fùguāng sent an envoy to report the victory,
Examination of Discrepancies: Zhāng's Old Biography states:
"In the third year of Zhōnghé,
the northern route reported that Huáng Cháo was defeated and fled on the tenth day of the first month,
and Cháng'ān was fully recaptured.
In the third month,
the northern route campaign recaptured the city,
and the officers and soldiers all turned back."
Jù Yánqìng's Old Biography states:
"In the fourth year,
the northern route reported that Huáng Cháo was defeated and fled on the tenth day of the first month,
and Cháng'ān was recaptured.
In the third month,
the northern route campaign defeated Huáng Cháo, and the officers and soldiers all returned."
Yánqìng shifted all events of the fourth year to the third year,
and events of the third year to the fourth year,
without changing the months and days,
making the errors even greater.
I now only mention the report of victory,
without specifying the month and day.
An edict ordered the retention of twenty thousand soldiers from the Zhōngwǔ and other armies,
entrusted to the Dàmíng Palace留守 Wáng Huī and the Jīngjí制置使 Tián Cóngyì for deployment,
to guard Cháng'ān.
In the fifth month,
Zhū Méi, Lǐ Kèyòng, and Dōngfāng Kuí were appointed as Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
Shǎnzhōu was elevated to a military governorship,
with Wáng Chóngyíng appointed as military governor.
Yánzhōu was also established as the Bǎosài Army,
with the Bǎodà campaign行军司马 and Yánzhōu刺史 Lǐ Xiàogōng appointed as military governor.
These were rewards for defeating Huáng Cháo and recapturing the capital.
Among all the generals, he was the youngest,
yet he defeated Huáng Cháo,
recaptured Cháng'ān,
his merit was foremost,
his military strength was the strongest,
and all the other generals feared him.
Kèyòng had one slightly impaired eye,
and people of the time called him
the "One-Eyed Dragon."
An edict ordered that Cuī Qiú, coming from a noble family and holding high status,
who served as Huáng Cháo's chancellor for three years,
neither fleeing nor hiding,
be executed wherever he was found.
18 Huáng Cháo sent his brave general Mèng Kǎi to lead ten thousand men as the vanguard,
to attack Càizhōu.
The military governor Qín Zōngquán engaged them in battle but was defeated;
the rebels advanced to attack his city,
and Zōngquán then declared his allegiance to Cháo,
joining forces with him.
Initially, when
Huáng Cháo was in Cháng'ān,
the Prefect of Chénzhōu, Wǎnqiū's Zhào Chōu, said to his generals and aides:
Wǎnqiū,
was the Xiàng County of the Later Wèi,
renamed Wǎnqiū in the Suí dynasty,
and belonged to Chénzhōu in the Táng;
under its jurisdiction was Xiàngchéng County,
which was the territory of Mòlíng County established by the Eastern Wèi as a relocated administrative seat,
renamed Xiàngchéng in the Suí dynasty.
Chōu,
pronounced Chāng Niú.
"If Huáng Cháo does not die in Cháng'ān,
he will certainly flee eastward,
and Chénzhōu lies in his path.
Moreover, Huáng Cháo has long been an enemy of the Zhōngwǔ Army,
since his initial uprising,
he has repeatedly battled Sòng Wēi, Zhāng Zìmiǎn, and others,
all of whom were Zhōngwǔ troops."
He thus fortified the city walls and moats,
repaired armor and weapons,
and stockpiled fodder and grain;
within a sixty-li radius,
any commoners who had provisions and grain
were all moved into the city.
He recruited many brave warriors,
placing them under the command of his younger brothers Zhào Chǎng and Zhào Xǔ, and his son Zhào Lín.
After Mèng Kǎi captured Càizhōu,
he shifted his troops to attack Chénzhōu,
encamping at Xiàngchéng;
Zhào Chōu first feigned weakness,
waited until they were unprepared,
launched a surprise attack,
killing or capturing nearly all of them,
captured Mèng Kǎi alive,
and executed him.
When Huáng Cháo learned of Mèng Kǎi's death,
he was alarmed and fearful,
and stationed all his troops at Yīnshuǐ,
In the sixth month,
he joined forces with Qín Zōngquán to besiege Chénzhōu,
digging five layers of trenches,
and attacking from a hundred directions.
The people of Chénzhōu were greatly terrified,
but Zhào Chōu exhorted them:
"The Zhōngwǔ Army has long been renowned for its righteousness and bravery,
and Chénzhōu is known for its strong soldiers.
Moreover, my family has long enjoyed the emoluments of Chénzhōu,
and I vow to live or die with this prefecture.
A true man should seek life amidst death;
and to die for one's country
is surely better than living as a subject of bandits!
Anyone who disagrees shall be executed!"
He repeatedly led elite troops to open the gates and attack the rebels,
defeating them.
Huáng Cháo grew even more furious,
encamping north of the prefecture,
and establishing palaces and various offices,
planning for a prolonged campaign.
At that time, the common people had no accumulated stores,
so the rebels seized people to use as food,
throwing them alive into mortars and mills,
consuming them along with their bones.
The place where provisions were supplied was called
"the Pounding and Grinding Camp."
The Pounding and Grinding Camp,
was where the mortars and mills were set up.
Mortars were used for pounding,
mills for grinding.
Grinding,
pronounced Mò Wò.
From the dozens of prefectures such as Hénán, Xǔ, Rǔ, Táng, Dèng, Mèng, Zhèng, Biàn, Cáo, Pú, Xú, Yǎn, and others,
all suffered from this atrocity.
This Hénán,
refers to Hénán Prefecture of Luòzhōu.
Suffered,
pronounced Pí Yì.
19 Initially,
Liú Qiān of Shàngcài served as a minor officer in Lǐngnán,
and the military governor Wéi Zhòu, impressed by his talent,
during the Xiāntōng era,
Wéi Zhòu governed Lǐngnán.
Liú Qiān attacked bandits,
repeatedly achieving merit.
On the Xīnchǒu day,
he was appointed Prefect of Fēngzhōu.
This marks the beginning of Liú Qiān's rise.
20 The military governor of Dōngchuān, Yáng Shīlì, was additionally appointed Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
21 The military governor of Xuānwǔ, Zhū Quánzhōng, led several hundred of his troops to his garrison,
in autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Dīngmǎo day,
he arrived at Biànzhōu.
At that time, Biànzhōu and Sòngzhōu were suffering from repeated famines,
both public and private resources were exhausted,
internally
the arrogant troops were difficult to control,
externally they were attacked by formidable enemies,
fighting occurred daily,
the hearts of the people were filled with fear and anxiety,
yet Zhū Quánzhōng's courage grew even more resolute.
An edict was issued stating that since Huáng Cháo had not yet been pacified,
Zhū Quánzhōng was additionally appointed as the Dōngběimiàn Dū Zhāotǎo Shǐ.
This set the stage for Zhū Quánzhōng using the Xuānwǔ troops to annex various garrisons and ultimately shift the Táng dynasty's mandate.
22 Nánzhào sent the official Yáng Qígōng to welcome the princess.
An edict ordered Chén Jìngxuān to write a letter,
declining on the grounds that
"the imperial carriage is on an inspection tour,
the ceremonial objects are not yet prepared,
wait until we return to the capital,
then she will be sent in marriage."
Yáng Qígōng did not comply,
proceeding directly to Chéngdū.
23. Lǐ Kèyòng led his troops from Cháng'ān back to Yànmén.
Soon an imperial edict arrived,
appointing Kèyòng as the military governor of Hédōng,
and summoning Zhèng Cóngdǎng to the emperor's temporary residence.
Kèyòng then traveled via the eastern route past Yúcì,
and went to Yànmén to visit his father.
Kèyòng soon issued a proclamation in Hédōng,
comforting the soldiers and civilians, saying:
"Do not dwell on past grievances,
each of you should settle down to your family occupations."
Because the people of Hédōng had fought against Kèyòng several times before,
he feared they would not feel secure,
hence he issued this proclamation to instruct them.
Textual Analysis: The Old Annals state:
"In the fifth month,
Lǐ Kèyòng was appointed military governor of Hédōng.
In the seventh month,
an edict ordered Zhèng Cóngdǎng to proceed to the emperor's temporary residence."
The New Annals state:
"In the fifth month,
Cóngdǎng was made Minister of Works and Grand Councillor."
Jiǎ Wěi's Táng Nián Bǔ Lù states:
"In the fifth month,
an edict: 'Lǐ (name omitted) may be appointed Grand Councillor,
and serve as military governor of Hédōng.'
(Note states:
"According to the Old History of the Five Dynasties,
in the sixth year of Tiānfú of the Jìn dynasty,
second month,
Jiǎ Wěi presented his Táng Nián Bǔ Lù to the throne."
It also says:
"Jiǎ Wěi,
a native of Huòlù, Zhēndìng,
because the Veritable Records of the Táng emperors
were incomplete and unrecorded from Emperor Wǔzōng onward,
gathered recent hearsay and stories from various unofficial histories, arranging them by year and month,
compiled them into the Táng Nián Bǔ Lù,
totaling sixty-five volumes.
He served under the Táng, Jìn, Hàn, and Zhōu dynasties,
therefore he dared not use Kèyòng's personal name."
) The Old Biography of Cóngdǎng states:
"In the third year,
Kèyòng was appointed military governor of Hédōng,
replacing Cóngdǎng.
On the fifteenth day of the fifth month,
Cóngdǎng left Tàiyuán.
The roads were full of bandits,
and when he reached Jiàngzhōu,
he stayed there for several months.
In winter,
an imperial envoy pursued him to the emperor's temporary residence,
and he resumed assisting in governance."
The Táng Mò Jiàn Wén Lù states:
"In the fifth month,
an imperial decree appointed Lǐ Shàngshū as military governor of Yànmén.
On the twenty-fifth day of the sixth month,
the military governor of Yànmén, Lǐ Púyè, passed by the eastern road of the prefectural capital.
Within the sixth month,
an appointment list arrived,
the Grand Councillor was replaced and summoned to the court,
and the military governor of Yànmén, Lǐ Xiànggōng, was appointed military governor of Hédōng.
On the fifteenth day,
the Grand Councillor departed via the Xīmíng Gate.
Within that month,
the new governor, Lǐ Xiànggōng, issued a proclamation,
pacifying the soldiers and commoners within the city,
saying: 'Do not harbor thoughts of the past,
let each of you settle your families.'"
It also says:
"The Prince of Jìn (personal name Kèyòng),
on the first day of the fifth month of the third year of Zhōnghé,
was appointed Grand Councillor from the position of military governor of Yànmén,
and served as military governor of Hédōng."
Regarding the appointment of Kèyòng to Hédōng and Cóngdǎng's resumption of assisting governance,
the various texts differ on the months and days.
The Old Annals record Kèyòng's appointment in the fifth month,
and Cóngdǎng proceeding to the emperor's residence in the seventh month,
but do not mention him becoming a councillor.
The New Annals record him already being a councillor in the fifth month,
which is especially erroneous.
The Old Biography of Cóngdǎng states
he left Tàiyuán on the fifteenth day of the fifth month,
which also contradicts the Annals.
The Táng Nián Bǔ Lù records an edict in the fifth month,
only praising and rewarding Kèyòng, Zhū Méi, and Dōngfāng Kuí,
the wording of the edict is vulgar,
casting doubt on its authenticity.
The Táng Mò Jiàn Wén Lù first says he was appointed to Hédōng in the sixth month,
but later says it was on the first day of the fifth month.
According to the Veritable Records, the Later Táng Tàizǔ Jì Nián Lù, and Xuē Jūzhèng's History of the Five Dynasties, all place it in the seventh month,
so we follow that here.
Cóngdǎng was appointed Defender of the Eastern Capital in the ninth month of this year,
and did not become a councillor again until the second month of the second year of Guāngqǐ.
24. The General of the Left Rapid as Tigers Guard, Yáng Fùguāng, died in Hézhōng.
Fùguāng was passionate and loyal to righteousness,
skilled at comforting his soldiers,
and the army mourned him for days.
The eight commanders, including Lù Yànhóng, each dispersed with their troops.
Tián Lìngzī had always feared and resented him,
and upon hearing of his death,
was greatly pleased.
He then dismissed Fùguāng's elder brother, the Bureau of Military Affairs Commissioner Yáng Fùgōng, to the position of Commissioner of the Flying Dragon Stables.
Lìngzī monopolized power,
and no one dared oppose him,
except Fùgōng who often disputed with him over gains and losses.
Therefore, Lìngzī hated him,
and Fùgōng consequently pleaded illness and retired to Lántián.

25. The acting military governor of Chéngdé, Wáng Róng; the acting military governor of Wèibó, Lè Xíngdá; and the acting military governor of Tiānpíng, Zhū Xuān, were appointed as the regular military governors of their respective circuits.
26. The Minister over the Masses, Vice Director of the Chancellery, and Grand Councillor, Zhèng Tián,
even during the emperor's flight,
still strictly adhered to regulations.
Tián Lìngzī requested a court official position for his administrative assistant, Wú Yuán.
(Wú Yuán
was a subordinate official of Tián Lìngzī.
For [the character] "wèi"
read "yú wèi".) Chén Jìngxuǎn wished to be ranked above the councillors.
Tián, citing precedent,
stated that although the rank and status of military governors holding councillor titles were high,
they all stood below the actual councillors,
and firmly argued against it.
(In the late Táng,
any military governor concurrently holding the title of Grand Councillor or serving as an honorary head of one of the Three Departments, one of the Three Dukes, or one of the Three Preceptors,
was called a "military governor-councillor.")
"The military situation is suspicious and jealous,
Tián should not be allowed to accompany the emperor past here."
In the first year,
they openly spoke of expelling Tián to seize Fèngxiáng,
so these two men incited others to submit memorials,
leading to Tián's dismissal from the councillorship.
From then on,
the court's appointment and dismissal of councillors
were largely controlled by the military governors.
(For the character "cóng"
read "cái yòng".)
He was then dismissed to become Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent.
Furthermore, his son, the Vice Minister of War, Zhèng Níngjì, was appointed Prefect of Péngzhōu,
so that Tián could go there to be cared for.
(Sòng Bái said: In the third year of Chuígōng of the Táng,
Péngzhōu was established from the Jiǔlǒng County of Yìzhōu,
named after the ancient Tiānpéng Pass.
For the character "yǎng"
read "yáng shàng".)
27. In the eighth month,
on the day Jiǎchén,
Lǐ Kèyòng arrived at Jìnyáng.
(From this point, Lǐ Kèyòng used Jìnyáng as the base for contending for the empire.)
He garrisoned Dàizhōu.
28. Húnán was elevated to the Qīnhuà Army,
and the Surveillance Commissioner, Mǐn Xù, was appointed its military governor.
29. In the ninth month,
Chén Jìngxuǎn was additionally appointed as President of the Chancellery,
and his noble rank was advanced to Prince of Yǐngchuān Commandery.
30. The military governor of Gǎnhuà, Shí Pǔ, encamped at Yīnshuǐ;
to block Huáng Cháo's troops,
and also to provide support for Chénzhōu.
31. The acting military governor of Jīngnán, Chén Rú, was appointed as the regular military governor.
32. The Zhaoyi military governor Mèng Fānglì,
considering Lù Prefecture's terrain perilous and its people fierce,
and that its commanders had repeatedly been usurped,
wished to gradually weaken it.
Therefore, he moved his administrative seat to Xíng Prefecture.
(For details, see the previous year.)
The term "commander" (帥)
is pronounced as "shuài" (所類翻).
The people of Lù were displeased.
The supervising eunuch Qí Shěnhài, taking advantage of the people's unrest,
secretly had Ān Jūshòu, the garrison commander of Wǔxiāng, send a message sealed in wax to Lǐ Kèyòng requesting troops,
asking to restore the military headquarters in Lù Prefecture.
Wǔxiāng bordered Liáozhōu, which was under the jurisdiction of Hédōng,
hence he had its garrison commander request troops.
Thereafter, military governors generally established garrison commanders in various counties,
and county magistrates could no longer perform their duties effectively.
Sòng Bái said: Wǔxiāng County was originally the territory of Niè County in the Han Dynasty.
The Jìn Dynasty first established Wǔxiāng Commandery,
and the county belonged to it.
In the tenth month,
Lǐ Kèyòng sent his general Hè Gōngyǎ and others to respond,
but they were defeated by Mèng Fānglì.
He then sent Lǐ Kèxiū to attack.
On the Xīnhài day,
they captured Lù Prefecture.
Textual analysis note: According to the Veritable Records:
"Lǐ Kèyòng petitioned to appoint Lǐ Kèxiū as military governor,
and thus divided the five prefectures of the Zhaoyi Army into two military commands."
Xuē Jūzhèng's Old History of the Five Dynasties, Biography of Mèng Fānglì, states:
"The people of Lù secretly requested troops from the Martial Emperor (Lǐ Kèyòng).
In the tenth month of the third year of Zhōnghé,
the Martial Emperor dispatched Lǐ Kèxiū with troops to aid them.
Mèng Fānglì resisted and fought,
but was greatly defeated.
Consequently, they successively captured the two commanderies of Zé and Lù,
and thus appointed Kèxiū as military governor."
According to Xuē Jūzhèng's Old History, Biography of Zhāng Quányì:
"Zhūgě Shuǎng recommended Zhāng Quányì as prefect of Zé Prefecture.
After Shuǎng's death,
Lǐ Hǎnzhī occupied Zé Prefecture."
It appears that Lǐ Kèxiū only obtained Lù Prefecture,
while Zé was taken by Héyáng.
Thereafter, Lǐ Kèyòng sent troops every year to contend for the area east of the mountains,
and half the population of the three prefectures were captured or killed,
leaving the fields without crops.
(The three Zhaoyi prefectures of Xíng, Míng, and Cí were located east of the mountains.)
33. A daughter of the imperial clan was made Princess Ānhuà.
(Ānhuà Commandery was in Qìng Prefecture.)
34. Liú Hànhóng led over a hundred thousand troops out of Xīlíng,
intending to attack Dǒng Chāng.
On the Wùwǔ day,
Qián Liú crossed the river to meet them in battle,
and inflicted a major defeat.
Liú Hànhóng changed his clothes, took a kitchen knife, and fled.
(This was so that if the enemy saw him, they would think he was a cook,
and not suspect he was Liú Hànhóng.)
On the Jǐwèi day,
Liú Hànhóng gathered his remaining forty thousand troops and fought again,
but Qián Liú again defeated him,
killing his brother Liú Hànróng and the general Xīn Yuē.
35. In the eleventh month,
on the Jiǎzǐ day, the first day of the month,
Qín Zōngquán besieged Xǔ Prefecture.
36. The Zhōngwǔ general Lù Yànhóng led his troops south from Hézhōng, plundering Xiāng, Dèng, Jīn, and Yáng,
slaughtering and destroying wherever they passed,
claiming they were heading west to join the imperial court.
Sòng Bái said: Jīn Prefecture
was Xīchéng County of the Hàn Dynasty's Hànzhōng Commandery.
Emperor Wén of Wèi established Xīchéng Commandery,
later renamed Wèixīng Commandery.
The Liáng Dynasty established Běiliáng Prefecture,
soon renamed Nánliáng Prefecture.
The Western Wèi established Dōngliáng Prefecture,
and because gold was produced there,
it was renamed Jīn Prefecture.
Yáng Prefecture
was the territory of Chénggù County in the Hàn Dynasty.
In the Later Hàn, Bān Chāo was enfeoffed here.
In the Jìn Dynasty, it was Nánxiāng County,
soon renamed Xīxiāng.
The Western Wèi established Yáng Prefecture.
The term "led" (帥)
is pronounced as "shuài" (率).
The character "洋" (Yáng)
is pronounced "xiáng" (祥).
Upon reaching Xīngyuán,
he expelled the military governor Niú Xù,
who fled to Lóngzhōu Xīshān.
(Lóngzhōu Xīshān was on the border of Sōng and Mào prefectures,
and was already occupied by barbarians at that time.)
Lù Yànhóng declared himself acting military governor.
37. The Wǔníng military governor Shí Pǔ
("Wǔníng"
should be
"Gǎnhuà".)
suspected his administrative assistant Lǐ Nínggǔ and killed him.
Lǐ Nínggǔ's father, Lǐ Sǔn,
was a Right Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
residing in Chéngdū.
Shí Pǔ memorialized that Lǐ Nínggǔ had conspired with his father.
Tián Lìngzī accepted bribes from Shí Pǔ,
and ordered the Censorate to investigate.
The Investigating Censor Wáng Huà argued for Lǐ Sǔn's innocence.
Tián Lìngzī forged an imperial edict to transfer Lǐ Sǔn to the Shéncè Army prison,
but Wáng Huà refused and would not send him.
Xiāo Gòu memorialized:
"The accusation that Lǐ Nínggǔ administered poison is
based on ambiguous circumstances.
He has already been killed by Shí Pǔ.
His father Lǐ Sǔn has been separated from him for several years,
with no communication between them.
How can he be falsely accused of conspiracy!
Shí Pǔ, relying on his merit, violates the law,
insults and despises the court,
and wishes to kill the Son of Heaven's attending officials.
If we yield to his desires,
it will extend to officials like us.
How can the court maintain its authority!"
Because of this, Lǐ Sǔn escaped death,
and returned to his hometown.
At that time, Tián Lìngzī monopolized power,
and officials dared not look at him directly in opposition,
only Xiāo Gòu repeatedly argued with him.
The court relied on him.
38. Zhèdōng was elevated to the Yìshèng Army,
with Liú Hànhóng appointed as its military governor.
39. Zhào Chōu secretly sent messengers by side roads to seek aid from neighboring commands.
Consequently, Zhōu Jí, Shí Pǔ, and Zhū Quánzhōng all led troops to rescue him.
Zhū Quánzhōng fought Huáng Cháo's forces at Lùyì,
defeated them,
beheading over two thousand,
and then led his troops into Bó Prefecture and occupied it.
(Lùyì was Wǔpíng County of Chénliú Commandery in the Later Wèi.
In the eighteenth year of the Suí Dynasty's Kāihuáng era,
it was renamed Lùyì,
and belonged to Bó Prefecture in the Táng.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is located 130 lǐ west of the prefectural seat.)
The term "defeated" (敗)
is pronounced "bài" (補邁翻).
1. In spring,
the first month,
Lù Yànhóng was appointed acting military governor of Xīngyuán.
2. The Wèibó military governor Lè Xíngdá was granted the name Yànzhēn.
3. The Dōngchuān military governor Yáng Shīlì, observing the great power and favor enjoyed by the brothers Chén Jìngxuān,
(Tián Lìngzī and Chén Jìngxuān were brothers.)
and that when Chén Jìngxuān dispatched Gāo Rénhòu to suppress Hán Xiùshēng (see the second month of this year),
he said, "Upon your successful return,
I will report to the Son of Heaven,
and request Dōngchuān as your reward."
When Yáng Shīlì heard this,
he angrily said:
"We are both equal regional commanders,
yet he rashly promises my territory to others.
This shows no regard for Heaven and Earth!"
Tián Lìngzī, fearing he would rebel,
used his failure to dispatch troops for defense as a pretext,
and summoned Yáng Shīlì to court as Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.
4. Huáng Cháo's forces were still strong,
and Zhōu Jí, Shí Pǔ, and Zhū Quánzhōng could not hold out.
They jointly sought aid from the Hédōng military governor Lǐ Kèyòng.
In the second month,
Lǐ Kèyòng led fifty thousand foreign and Han troops out of Tiānjǐng Pass.
The Héyáng military governor Zhūgě Shuǎng declined, citing the incomplete state of the river bridge,
(referring to the Héyáng Bridge).
Lǐ Kèyòng therefore turned back and led his troops east, crossing the river via Shǎn and Hézhōng.
Textual analysis note: The Tángmò Jiànwén Lù states:
"The Prince of Jìn dispatched a large army on the thirteenth day of the third month to attack Huáng Cháo."
The Tàizǔ Jìnián Lù states:
"In the first month,
Tàizǔ (Lǐ Kèyòng) led fifty thousand troops from Zélù, intending to descend through Tiānjǐng Pass.
Héyáng had troops stationed at Wànshàn,
so he changed route and crossed the river via Pú and Shǎn."
Xuē Jūzhèng's Old History of the Five Dynasties only states "spring of the fourth year."
Considering that they already fought Huáng Cháo in the fourth month,
dispatching from Jìnyáng on the thirteenth of the third month
seems too late.
Also, Lǐ Kèyòng's memorial states:
"In the second month last year,
I frequently received letters from Chén, Xǔ, Xú, and Biàn."
I follow the Old Annals here.
Also, Lǐ Kèyòng's memorial of self-defense states:
"I therefore proceeded via Shǎn territory,
and went directly to Xǔtián."
This indicates that troops crossed via both the Pú and Shǎn routes.
5 Yang Shili received the imperial edict,
became enraged,
and refused to be replaced.
He killed the official announcement envoy and the supervising army commissioner.
The official announcement envoy
was the one who had come bearing the appointment document for the Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs to summon Yang Shili.
The supervising army commissioner
was the supervisor of the Eastern Chuan region.
Using the pretext of attacking Chen Jingxuan,
he executed any senior officer who dared to advise against it,
and advanced to station his troops at Fúchéng.
Fúchéng
was located in the area of the former Hàn dynasty Fú County.
During the Eastern Jìn, the Shǐpíng Commandery was established there.
The Later Wèi changed it to Fúchéng and Tóng County.
The Suí changed Tóng to Fúchéng.
In the early Táng, it belonged to Mián Prefecture,
later it belonged to Zǐ Prefecture.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is located 55 lǐ northwest of the prefectural seat.
Fú
is pronounced "fú".
He was unsuccessful.
On the bǐngwǔ day,
Chen Jingxuan was appointed as Commander-in-Chief, Pacification Commissioner, and Disposal Commissioner for Western Chuan, Eastern Chuan, and Shǎnnán West Circuit.
In the third month,
on the jiǎzǐ day,
Yang Shili circulated a proclamation to the officials at the imperial court's temporary location and to the officers, officials, soldiers, and commoners of the various circuits,
enumerating Chen Jingxuan's ten crimes.
The Textual Analysis states: The Zhāng Qíjiù Zhuàn says:
"In the fourth year of Zhōnghé,
on the fifteenth day of the fourth month,
Yang Shili of Eastern Chuan rebelled."
Below, it records Yang Shili's proclamation,
which says
"on the third day of the third month,"
contradicting itself.
We now follow the Shílù.
Shǔ
means to enumerate.
According to the Xīn Táng Shū biography of Lù Yán,
when Yán commanded Western Chuan,
he established the Dìngbiān Army at Qióng Prefecture,
to control the Dàdù area,
and administered the old pass.
He recruited the sons and younger brothers of the Tán troops,
taught them combat skills,
and had them fill the military colony registers.
Thus, the Tán troops
were the local militia in the border commanderies of Shǔ.
Also, according to Lù Zhèn's Jiǔ Guó Zhì,
Shí Chùwēn served Mèng Zhīxiáng,
and was appointed as the Inspector and Commander of the various Tán troops within Wàn Prefecture's jurisdiction.
This shows that all the commanderies in Shǔ had Tán troops.
An edict was issued stripping Yang Shili of his offices and ranks.
Gāo Rénhòu, the Méi Prefecture defense commissioner, was appointed as the acting military governor of Eastern Chuan,
leading five thousand troops to attack him.
Yáng Màoyán, a Western Chuan officer, was appointed as the deputy commander of the expeditionary force.
6 Zhū Quánzhōng attacked Huáng Cháo's Wǎzǐ Stronghold,
and captured it.
Huáng Cháo had dismantled civilian houses to build the fort's structures,
hence it was called the Wǎzǐ (Tile) Stronghold.
7 Wù Prefecture resident Wáng Zhèn arrested the prefect Huáng Jié,
and surrendered to Qián Liú.
Liú Hànhóng sent his general Lóu Lài to kill Wáng Zhèn and replace him.
The Pǔyáng garrison commander Jiǎng Huái summoned Qián Liú's troops to jointly attack Wù Prefecture.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: The Pǔyáng River originates from Wūshāng County,
flows east past Zhūjì County,
and merges with the Xiè Creek.
Táng dynasty Wù Prefecture
was located in the area of the Hàn dynasty Wūshāng.
In the thirteenth year of the Tiānbǎo era,
Yìwū and Lánxī counties of Wù Prefecture and Fùyáng county of Háng Prefecture were separated
to establish Pǔyáng County.
Jié
was a man from Mǐn.
8 Gāo Pián's nephew, the Left Rapid as Tigers Guard General-in-Chief Yù,
wrote a memorial listing over twenty crimes of Lǚ Yòngzhī,
and secretly presented it to Pián.
He wept and said:
"Yòngzhī, internally, uses the pretext of immortality arts
to delude Your Excellency's judgment;
externally, he usurps the authority of military command,
and brutalizes the common people.
The officers and commanders fear for their lives,
and none dare to speak out.
As time passes,
his power is about to become entrenched.
If he is not eliminated,
I fear the accumulated merits of the Gāo family for generations
will be wiped out in a single day!"
He then choked with sobs, unable to control himself.
Pián said:
"Are you drunk?!"
He ordered him to be led out.
The next day,
Pián showed Yù's memorial to Yòngzhī.
Yòngzhī said:
"The Fortieth Gentleman once complained to me about being impoverished,"
Yù was the fortieth in his generation.
"Hence he bears this grudge."
He then produced several sheets of Yù's handwritten letters and presented them.
Pián was greatly ashamed,
and subsequently forbade Yù from leaving or entering.
Over a month later,
he appointed Yù to administer Shū Prefecture affairs.
The bandit Chén Rú attacked Shū Prefecture.
Yù sought help from Lú Prefecture.
Yáng Xíngmǐn lacked the strength to rescue him,
so he consulted his general Lǐ Shénfú.
Shénfú requested to drive them away without using a single blade.
He then took many banners and flags,
and entered Shū Prefecture via a side road.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Lú Prefecture is 420 lǐ south to Shū Prefecture.
Jiàn
is pronounced like the ancient character for "between."
He led Shū Prefecture troops out, displaying Lú Prefecture banners and flags,
pointed and sketched the terrain,
as if deploying a large battle formation.
The bandits became fearful
and fled overnight.
The bandits feared Lú Prefecture troops,
hence they fled overnight.
In warfare, there is the concept of first establishing a fearsome reputation and then applying real force;
this is close to that.
Chén
is read as "zhèn" (battle array).
He was a man of Míng Prefecture.
Lù Zhèn's Jiǔ Guó Zhì says: Lǐ Shénfú,
a man of Míng Prefecture,
was registered in the Shàngdǎng army.
When Gāo Pián was concurrently Commander-in-Chief of the various circuits' expeditionary camps,
Shénfú followed his prefectural commander to garrison the Huáihǎi region,
and subsequently joined Yáng Xíngmǐn.
After some time,
the bandits Wú Jiǒng and Lǐ Běn again attacked Shū Prefecture.
Yù could not hold it,
abandoned the city and fled.
Pián sent someone to kill him.
Yáng Xíngmǐn sent his generals Héféi's Táo Yǎ and Qīngliú's Zhāng Xùn, among others, to lead troops to attack Wú Jiǒng and Lǐ Běn.
They captured and executed them.
Héféi,
an ancient county from the Hàn,
was attached to Lú Prefecture in the Táng.
Qīngliú,
located in the area of the Hàn dynasty Quánjiāo County,
was established as Qīngliú County in the Suí,
and attached to Chú Prefecture in the Táng.
Qín Zōngquán sent his younger brother to lead troops to raid Lú Prefecture.
They occupied Shūchéng.
In the twenty-third year of the Kāiyuán era,
Héféi and Lújiāng were divided to establish Shūchéng County,
belonging to Lú Prefecture.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is 110 lǐ southwest of the prefectural seat.
9 The former Háng Prefecture prefect Lù Shěnzhōng was residing as a guest in Huáng Prefecture.
Lù Shěnzhōng had been rejected by Dǒng Chāng,
see the first year of the current scroll.
He recruited three thousand soldiers and entered to occupy it.
The Huáng Prefecture officer Dù Hóng also expelled the Yuè Prefecture prefect and replaced him.
10 Huáng Cháo besieged Chén Prefecture for nearly three hundred days.
Zhào Chōu and his brothers fought him in several hundred battles, large and small.
Although their troops and provisions were nearly exhausted,
the morale of the people grew even more steadfast.
Lǐ Kèyòng assembled the armies of Xǔ, Biàn, Xú, and Yǎn at Chén Prefecture.
At that time, Shàng Ràng was stationed at Tàikāng.
Tàikāng,
was the Hàn dynasty Yángxià County.
The Suí changed its name to Tàikāng,
because there was an ancient Tàikāng city east of the county.
It belonged to Chén Prefecture in the Táng.
In the fourth month,
on the guǐsì day,
the various armies advanced and captured Tàikāng.
Huáng Sīyè was stationed at Xīhuá.
Xīhuá,
a Hàn dynasty county,
belonged to Chén Prefecture in the Táng.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is 80 lǐ west of the prefectural seat.
Sīyè fled.
Huáng Cháo heard this and became fearful.
He withdrew his army to Gùyánglǐ.
Gùyánglǐ
was north of Chén Prefecture city.
Zhū Quánzhōng heard that Huáng Cháo was approaching,
so he led his army back to Dàliáng.
In the fifth month,
on the Guǐhài day,
heavy rain fell,
flooding the plains to a depth of three feet.
Huáng Cháo's camp was swept away by the water,
and upon hearing that Lǐ Kèyòng was about to arrive,
he led his troops northeast toward Biànzhōu,
slaughtering the people of Wèishì.
Shàng Ràng, with five thousand elite cavalry, advanced to threaten Dàliáng,
reaching as far as Fántái.
Fántái,
originally known as Master Kuàng's Chuītái,
was expanded by Prince Xiào of Liáng.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: Chuītái
is located to the right of the Mùzé marsh, south of Jùnyí city.
Mùzé,
now known as Púguānzé,
refers to this marsh.
Fēng,
a county established in the Hàn dynasty,
belonged to Xúzhōu during the Táng.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is located 140 lǐ northwest of Xúzhōu.
On the Bǐngyín day,
Kèyòng and Tián Cóngyì, the military supervisor of Zhōngwǔ, set out from Xǔzhōu.
On the Wùchén day,
they caught up with Huáng Cháo at Wángmǎndù, north of Zhōngmóu.
According to the Old Book's Imperial Annals,
Wángmǎndù was a ferry crossing along the Biàn River.
They launched a fierce attack,
inflicting a major defeat,
killing over ten thousand men,
and the rebels subsequently collapsed.
Shàng Ràng led his followers to surrender to Shí Pǔ,
while other commanders—Línjìn's Lǐ Dǎng, Qūzhōu's Huò Cún, Juànchéng's Gě Cóngzhōu, Yuānqú's Zhāng Guībà, and
his younger brother Guīhòu—led their troops to surrender to Zhū Quánzhōng.
Línjìn,
an ancient place name,
was separated from Yīshì during the Suí dynasty,
establishing Sāngquán County.
In the thirteenth year of the Tiānbǎo era,
it was renamed Línjìn,
belonging to Hézhōng Prefecture.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is located 65 lǐ north of the prefecture.
Qūzhōu,
an ancient county from the Hàn dynasty,
was abolished in the middle period,
reestablished by separating from Míngshuǐ during the Suí,
belonged to Míngzhōu during the Táng,
and was demoted to a town during the Sòng,
belonging to Jīzé County.
"Juànchéng"
should be written as
"Juànchéng",
also an ancient Hàn county,
attached to Púzhōu during the Táng.
History records that Zhū Quánzhōng later annexed various military governors,
often employing surrendered commanders from Huáng Cháo's forces.
Juàn,
pronounced as "juàn".
The Kǎoyì states: The Chóngwén Academy holds the Liáng Dynasty Meritorious Officials Biographies,
whose author is unknown,
stating:
"Zhāng Guīhòu,
grandfather Xīng,
father Chǔràng.
At the end of the Zhōnghé era, Guīhòu
came with his elder and younger brothers from Yuānqú to join."
Xuē Jūzhèng's History of the Five Dynasties states:
"Zhāng Guībà's grandfather Jìnyán,
father Shí."
Guīhòu's biography does not mention his father or grandfather,
only stating that he and his elder brother Guībà came to surrender.
According to the Liáng Dynasty Meritorious Officials Biographies,
their fathers and grandfathers differ from Guībà's,
so he was likely a younger cousin.
On the Jǐsì day,
Kèyòng pursued and attacked them at Fēngqiū,
again defeating them.
On the night of the Gēngwǔ day,
heavy rain fell once more,
and the rebels, alarmed, fled eastward.
Kèyòng pursued them,
passing through Zuòchéng and Kuāngchéng.
Zuòchéng,
originally Nányān County in the Hàn,
was renamed Zuòchéng during the Suí,
belonging to Huázhōu during the Táng.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is located 90 lǐ south of the prefecture.
Sòng Bái states: Zuòchéng County,
originally the ancient state of Zuò,
also the ancient state of Yān,
was Nányān County during the Hàn.
Emperor Wén of Suí, upon reviewing memorials,
saw the name Nányān County,
and remarked:
"Now the realm is unified under one rule,
how can there be a 'Southern Yān'!"
Thus, he changed it to Zuòchéng.
The rebels fled east toward Yǎnzhōu.
On the Xīnwèi day,
Kèyòng pursued them as far as Yuānqú.
Only a few hundred cavalrymen could keep up,
marching over 200 lǐ day and night.
Both men and horses were exhausted,
and provisions were depleted.
He thus returned to Biànzhōu,
intending to gather supplies and resume the pursuit.
He captured Huáng Cháo's young son, along with imperial carriages, utensils, garments, tallies, and seals,
and rescued about ten thousand men and women who had been plundered,
releasing them all.
11 On the Guǐyǒu day,
Gāo Rénhòu encamped at Déyáng.
Yáng Shīlì dispatched his commanders Zhèng Jūnxióng and Zhāng Shì'ān to hold Lùtóu Pass and resist him.
12 On the Jiǎxū day,
Lǐ Kèyòng arrived at Biànzhōu,
encamping outside the city.
Zhū Quánzhōng insisted on inviting him into the city,
lodging him at the Shàngyuán Post Station.
In the fifth year of the Jìn Tiānfú era,
the Shàngyuán Post Station in the Eastern Capital was renamed the Dūtíng Post Station.
Music, feasts, and utensils were all exquisite and abundant,
and the courtesy shown was extremely respectful.
However, Kèyòng, emboldened by drink, became arrogant,
and his words were rather offensive,
causing Quánzhōng displeasure.
As dusk fell,
the drinking ceased.
Kèyòng's attendants were all thoroughly drunk.
"Thoroughly drunk"
means heavily intoxicated,
with robes soaked,
unable to maintain composure.
Cóng,
pronounced as "cóng".
Carts were linked and barricades erected to block the roads,
and troops were sent to surround and attack the post station,
with battle cries shaking the earth.
Kèyòng, drunk,
heard nothing.
About ten of his personal guards, including Xuē Zhìqín and Shǐ Jìngsī, fought desperately.
An attendant, Guō Jǐngzhū, extinguished the candles,
helped Kèyòng hide under the bed,
splashed water on his face,
and gradually informed him of the danger.
Only then did Kèyòng open his eyes, grab his bow, and rise.
Zhìqín shot at the Biàn troops,
killing several dozen.
Soon,
smoke and fire closed in from all sides.
Fortunately, heavy rain and thunder struck,
darkening heaven and earth.
Zhìqín helped Kèyòng, leading a few men,
scale the wall and break through the encirclement.
They advanced by the light of lightning.
Biàn troops held the bridge,
but they fought their way across.
Shǐ Jìngsī covered the rear,
fighting to the death.
Kèyòng ascended the Wèishì Gate.
The Wèishì Gate,
the southern gate of Biàn city,
was renamed the Gāomíng Gate in the first year of the Liáng Kāipíng era,
and changed to the Xūnfēng Gate in the third year of the Jìn Tiānfú era.
The eunuch supervisor Chén Jǐngsī and over three hundred others
were all killed by the Biàn troops.
Yáng Yànhóng said to Quánzhōng:
"When barbarians are in a hurry, they ride horses.
Shoot anyone you see on horseback."
That evening,
Yànhóng happened to be on horseback in front of Quánzhōng.
Quánzhōng shot him,
killing him.
Li Keyong's wife, Lady Liú,
was highly intelligent and resourceful.
When those who had escaped earlier returned and reported that the Bianzhou troops had rebelled,
Lady Liú remained unperturbed,
immediately executed them,
secretly summoned the senior generals to issue orders,
and planned to safeguard the army for their return.
By dawn,
Li Keyong arrived,
intending to lead his troops to attack Zhū Quánzhōng.
Lady Liú said:
"You have been fighting for the state against the rebels,
rescuing the eastern lords in their hour of need.
Now the people of Bianzhou, acting without principle,
have plotted to harm you.
This should naturally be reported to the imperial court.
If you hastily raise troops to attack them,
then who in the empire will be able to determine right from wrong?
Moreover, it would give them a pretext."
Li Keyong heeded her advice,
led his troops away,
and merely sent a letter reprimanding Zhū Quánzhōng.
Zhū Quánzhōng replied in a letter:
"Regarding the incident the other night,
I was unaware of it.
The imperial court itself dispatched envoys to conspire with Yáng Yànhóng.
Since Yáng Yànhóng has already been punished for his crime,
I hope you will understand and investigate."
Li Keyong's adopted son, Lǐ Sìyuán,
was seventeen years old at the time.
He followed Li Keyong out from amidst the arrows and stones at Shàngyuán,
and was the only one completely unharmed.
Sìyuán was originally a Hu tribesman,
named Miǎojíliè,
with no surname.
This was the beginning of Lǐ Sìyuán.
Jí,
pronounced jí with the jí initial.
(Li Keyong) adopted many as sons.
He named the son of the Uighur Zhāng Zhèng as Lǐ Cúnxìn.
According to Xuē Jūzhèng's History of the Five Dynasties,
Cúnxìn's original name was Zhāng Wūluò.
He named Wáng Xián of Xǔzhōu as Lǐ Cúnxián,
and Ān Jìngsī as Lǐ Cúnxiào.
They all assumed the surname Lǐ.
These were the so-called "righteous sons."
Ōuyáng Xiū said: The Táng dynasty, starting with the Shatuo from north of Dàizhōu,
those who joined them were all heroic and fierce warriors of the time.
They often adopted them as sons,
calling them the "Righteous Sons Army."
On the day Bǐngzǐ,
Li Keyong reached the old camp at Xǔzhōu,
and requested provisions from Zhōu Jí.
Zhōu Jí declined, citing a lack of grain.
So (Li Keyong) crossed the river from Shǎnzhōu and returned to Jìnyáng.
13 Zhèng Jūnxióng and Zhāng Shì'ān held firm within their walls and did not come out.
Gāo Rénhòu said:
"To attack them would benefit them and injure us;
to besiege them would exhaust them while we rest."
He then set up twelve camps surrounding them.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
at the second watch of the night,
the second watch of the night,
is the second watch of the night.
Those keeping the watch sound the drum once for each watch,
so for the second watch they sound it twice.
Therefore, the second watch is called the second drum,
also known as the yǐ night.
Yáng Màoyán could not hold his position,
led his troops, abandoned the camp, and fled.
Several nearby camps, seeing the deputy commander flee,
also fled.
The Dōngchuān troops concentrated their forces and attacked southward against the central army.
Gāo Rénhòu, hearing of this,
threw open the gates of his camp,
set up torches to illuminate the area,
and personally led soldiers to lie in ambush on both sides of the road.
When the enemy arrived,
seeing the gates open,
they dared not enter,
and turned back.
Gāo Rénhòu then unleashed his ambush and attacked them.
The Dōngchuān troops fled in great disorder.
He pursued them to the city walls,
pressed them into the moat,
and inflicted heavy casualties before returning.
Gāo Rénhòu, considering that many of those who had abandoned their camps and fled would face execution the next morning,
the next morning, a great many would deserve execution,
secretly summoned the record-keeper Zhāng Sháo,
and instructed him:
"You must quickly dispatch several dozen foot scouts to pursue the deserters along different routes.
Foot scouts
are sent on foot to spy on the enemy,
hence the name.
Tàn,
pronounced tàn with the tàn initial.
(Tell them) all not to worry,
(and that) Gāo Rénhòu, for his merit in pacifying Qián Néng and others,
has been promoted to Acting Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
Come tomorrow morning for the muster at headquarters,
do not worry.'"
Generally, all generals in the field army
report to the commander's headquarters for muster each morning.
The troops believed this,
and by the fourth watch,
all had returned to camp;
only Yáng Màoyán had fled as far as Zhāngbǎ,
where he was finally caught up with.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Qīxiàn in Zǐzhōu has a Zhāngpá garrison.
"Bǎ"
should be
"pá".
(Gāo Rénhòu) said happily:
"They have all returned!"
The next morning,
when the generals gathered for muster,
they thought Gāo Rénhòu truly did not know.
After they had been seated for a long while,
Gāo Rénhòu said to Yáng Màoyán:
"Last night I heard that the deputy commander personally led the troops,
fleeing all the way to Zhāngpá.
Is this true?"
He replied:
"Last night, hearing that the enemy was attacking the central army,
my attendants said that you, the Vice Director, had already left,
so I mounted my horse and followed to join you.
Later, ascertaining the situation was false,
I returned to camp."
Gāo Rénhòu said:
"I and the deputy commander both received orders from the Son of Heaven
to lead troops against the rebels.
If I had fled first,
the deputy commander should have ordered me off my horse,
enforced military law,
taken command of the army in my place,
and then reported it to the court.
Now that the deputy commander fled first,
and furthermore attempted deception,
what, in principle, should be done?"
Yáng Màoyán bowed with clasped hands and said:
"I deserve death."
Gāo Rénhòu said:
"Indeed!"
He ordered his attendants to take him down,
and executed him.
The other generals trembled with fear.
Gāo Rénhòu then summoned several dozen of the prisoners captured the previous night,
untied them, and set them free to return.
Releasing the captives
to go back and tell of these events.
(The captives) said:
"Their military discipline is so strict and orderly,
from now on we must not send troops out again!"
The Zuǒzhuàn states: When the Jìn attacked Zhèng,
they held a military review and then returned,
following the plan of Zhōngháng Huánzǐ.
He said:
"Show them our orderliness,
and let them plan accordingly and come."
Zhèng then became fearful.
Later, they finally sought peace with Jìn.
Using troops with strict orderliness,
makes the enemy fear them.
This has been so since ancient times.
Fù,
pronounced fù with the fù initial.
14 On the day Gēngchén,
Shí Pǔ sent his general Lǐ Shīyuè to lead ten thousand troops in pursuit of Huáng Cháo.
15 On the day Guǐwèi,
Gāo Rénhòu deployed his troops beneath the walls of Lùtóu Pass.
Zhèng Jūnxióng and others led out all their forces to give battle.
Gāo Rénhòu set an ambush behind his battle lines,
feigned defeat and fled,
Zhèng Jūnxióng and others pursued him,
the ambush was sprung,
and Zhèng Jūnxióng and others were badly defeated.
That night,
they fled back to Zǐzhōu.
Chén Jìngxuān dispatched three thousand troops to reinforce Gāo Rénhòu's army,
which then advanced to besiege Zǐzhōu.
Punctuated by Róng Zhàozǔ, proofread by Niè Chóngqí
Compiled by
Sīmǎ Guāng
by Imperial Command
Later Student from Tiāntāi
Fourth year of the Zhōnghé era
(Jiǎchén, 884)
1 In the sixth month, on the Rénchén day,
Gāo Rénhòu, the acting military governor of Dōngchuān, reported that Zhèng Jūnxióng had beheaded Yáng Shīlì and surrendered.
Gāo Rénhòu had besieged Zǐzhōu for a long time without capturing it.
He then wrote a letter, shot it into the city,
and addressed the city's generals and officers, saying:
"I, Rénhòu, cannot bear to see the city's jade and stone destroyed together.
For your sakes, I will delay the attack for ten days,
allowing you to achieve the merit yourselves.
If within ten days you do not send Shīlì's head,
I will divide my troops into five shifts.
Each shift will attack day and night.
For us, this will be very easy;
for you, it will certainly be exhausting.
If after five days the city still does not fall,
we will advance from all four sides,
and capture it is assured.
Consider this carefully!"
A few days later,
Zhèng Jūnxióng shouted to the masses:
"The Son of Heaven only wishes to punish the chief culprit;
others are not involved."
The crowd shouted "Long live!"
made a great clamor,
rushed into the headquarters,
and Yáng Shīlì committed suicide.
Zhèng Jūnxióng took his head and went out to surrender.
Commentary on Discrepancies: The "Old Biography of Zhāng Qí" states:
"In the fourth year, on the first day of the seventh month,
Vice Director Gāo sent a military dispatch into the city, etc.,
and Shīlì committed suicide.
On the third day of the seventh month,
Generals Zhāng and Zhèng brought Shīlì's head out and surrendered.
On the seventh day of the seventh month,
Vice Director Gāo entered Dōngchuān."
The biography by Jù Yánqìng states: "In the third year, in the fifth month,
Lord Gāo advanced his army to the walls of Dōngchuān,
sent a swift dispatch into the city,
and Shīlì cut his own throat.
On the Xīnyǒu day of the seventh month,
Shīlì's head arrived in Chéngdū."
The Veritable Records state:
"On the Bǐngshēn day of the sixth month,
Gāo Rénhòu reported that Dōngchuān general Zhèng Jūnxióng had beheaded Yáng Shīlì
and sent the head to the imperial headquarters.
On that day,
an edict appointed Rénhòu as military governor of Dōngchuān."
The "Continued Record of Precious Destiny" states:
"In the second month,
Zǐzhōu observation commissioner Yáng Shīlì rebelled.
An imperial order dispatched Shǔ general Gāo Rénhòu and others to suppress it.
On the third day of the sixth month,
Zǐzhōu was captured and Yáng Shīlì's head was brought before the imperial carriage."
The New Annals state:
"On the Xīnyǒu day of the seventh month,
Yáng Shīlì was executed."
I now follow the "Continued Record of Precious Destiny" for the date,
and the Veritable Records for the event.
Chén Jìngxuān had Shīlì's son nailed to the city's north wall.
Jìngxuān's three sons went out to watch.
The nailing official shouted:
"This matter will soon reach you fellows;
you fellows later must strive to receive it!"
The three sons rode their horses back.
Gāo Rénhòu was appointed military governor of Dōngchuān.
2 On the Jiǎchén day,
Wǔníng general Lǐ Shīyuè and Shàng Ràng pursued Huáng Cháo to Xiáqiū
and defeated him.
Sòng Bái said: In the Spring and Autumn period, the Earl of Zhū, Yì, was brought here and imprisoned at Fùxiá.
Dù Yù's commentary states: It was a town of Lǔ.
In Gāopíng commandery, south of Nánpíngyáng County northwest, there was the Xiáqiū city.
In the Hàn, it was Xiáqiū County.
Defeated,
read as bǔ mài.
Huáng Cháo fled to Lánghǔ Valley.
Lánghǔ Valley
is located in the Láiwú region southeast of Mount Tài.
On the Bǐngwǔ day,
Huáng Cháo's nephew Lín Yán beheaded Huáng Cháo, his brothers, wife, and children,
and was about to take them to Shí Pǔ.
He encountered the Shātuó-Bóyě army,
which seized them,
and also beheaded Lín Yán, presenting the heads to Pǔ.
Huáng Cháo raised troops as a bandit in the third year of Qiánfú.
By now, it was ten years in total before his destruction.
Commentary on Discrepancies: The "Continued Record of Precious Destiny" states:
"Shàng Ràng surrendered to Xúzhōu. Huáng Cháo fled to Jiéshān.
Pressed hard by pursuing armies on the road,
he said to his nephew Zhū Yànzhī, etc.
The nephew repeatedly could not bear to do it.
Huáng Cháo then cut his own throat and passed it to his nephew.
As the nephew was about to arrive,
the Shātuó-Bóyě army seized it on the road,
and along with the nephew's head, sent them at once to the commander-in-chief's army."
The Old Annals state:
"In the seventh month, on the Guǐyǒu day,
the bandit general Lín Yán beheaded Huáng Cháo, Huáng Kuí, and Huáng Bǐng, three heads, and surrendered."
The Old Biography states:
"Huáng Cháo entered Mount Tài. Xú commander Shí Pǔ sent general Zhāng Yǒu with Shàng Ràng's troops to capture him.
At Lánghǔ Valley,
Huáng Cháo's general Lín Yán beheaded Huáng Cháo and his two younger brothers, Yè and Kuí, seven heads in total, along with his wife and children, placed them in a box, and sent them to Xúzhōu."
The New Annals state:
"On the Rénwǔ day of the seventh month,
Huáng Cháo was executed."
The New Biography states:
"Huáng Cháo, in desperate straits, said to Lín Yán: 'If you take my head and present it to the Son of Heaven, you can obtain wealth and honor. Do not let others benefit.'
Yán was Huáng Cháo's nephew and could not bear to do it.
Huáng Cháo then cut his own throat but did not die.
Yán therefore beheaded him,
placed the head in a box, and was about to take it to Shí Pǔ,
but the Tàiyuán-Bóyě army killed Yán and presented both his and Huáng Cháo's heads."
I now follow the New Biography.
3 Càizhōu military governor Qín Zōngquán unleashed his troops in all directions,
invading and devouring neighboring regions.
Tiānpíng military governor Zhū Xuān had thirty thousand troops.
His paternal cousin Zhū Jǐn was the bravest in the army.
Xuānwǔ military governor Zhū Quánzhōng was attacked by Zōngquán
and was in a very difficult situation.
He sought help from Xuān,
who sent Jǐn with troops to rescue him,
defeating Zōngquán at Héxiāng.
Quánzhōng was grateful to him
and swore brotherhood with Xuān.

Zhū Quánzhōng was a petty man of shifting allegiances. When his military strength was weak, he became sworn brothers with Zhū Xuān. Once his military strength became strong, he turned against him as an enemy, inevitably slaughtering him to satisfy his ambition. Can one share merit and fame with such a man?
4 In autumn, in the seventh month, on the Rénwǔ day,
Shí Pǔ sent an envoy to present the heads of Huáng Cháo, his family members, and his concubines.
The Emperor received them at the Dàxuán Tower.
The Dàxuán Tower was the main south gate tower of the outer wall of Chéngdū.
When Gāo Pián built the outer wall of Chéngdū,
after the work was completed, he divined using the "Book of Changes"
and obtained the hexagram Dàxù.
Pián said:
"'Xù' means to nurture.
Aided by strength, health, sincerity, and solidity,
brilliance and daily renewal—what greater auspiciousness!
The text should remove the lower and preserve the upper."
Therefore, he named it Dàxuán City.
The Emperor asked: "You are all daughters of meritorious and noble families,
generation after generation receiving the state's grace.
Why did you follow the bandit?"
The one at the forefront replied:
"The mad bandit was violent and rebellious.
The state, with a million troops,
lost the ancestral temples
and fled to Bā and Shǔ.
Now Your Majesty, unable to resist the bandit, blames a woman.
Where does that place the dukes, ministers, generals, and commanders?"
The Emperor asked no further
and had them all executed in the marketplace.
People vied to give them wine.
The others were all sorrowful, terrified, and stupefied by drink.
Only the one at the forefront neither drank nor wept.
When it came to the execution,
her expression was solemn.
Commentary on Discrepancies: The "Old Biography of Zhāng Qí" states:
"In the third year of Zhōnghé, on the twentieth day of the fifth month,
the northern route army advanced and presented Huáng Cháo's head, wife, and sons."
I do not adopt its date but adopt the event.
5 Zhū Quánzhōng attacked Qín Zōngquán
and defeated Zōngquán at Yīnshuǐ.
6 Lǐ Kèyòng arrived at Jìnyáng,
where he extensively prepared armor and weapons.
He dispatched Lǐ Chéngsì, the garrison commander of Yúcì from Yànmén, to present a memorial to the emperor at his temporary residence,
stating on his own behalf:
"I have rendered great service in defeating Huáng Cháo,
yet was plotted against by Zhū Quánzhōng.
I barely managed to escape with my life,
and over three hundred of my officers and subordinates who followed me,
along with the tally and seal, were all lost and have not returned.
In ancient times, when officials were appointed and granted seals with ribbons,
they would always wear them on their person,
and upon leaving office, they would return the seal and ribbons.
It was not until the Táng dynasty that official seals were established,
where those holding the office
would pass them on for use.
The seal was kept in a box,
and the officeholder would place it in his private quarters.
A separate tally was made,
entrusted to a clerk for safekeeping,
to strictly control access.
When the seal was taken out, the tally would be brought in;
when the tally was taken out, the seal would be brought in.
Hence, it was called the tally and seal.
It is said that I have died,
and the troops from the expeditionary camp have dispersed.
Orders were given to intercept and slaughter them wherever they were found,
to prevent any from escaping.
My officers and soldiers all wept and cried out in grievance,
pleading to avenge the wrongs.
I, believing in the utmost impartiality of the court,
awaited the imperial decree,
comforting and restraining them,
and have now returned to my own jurisdiction.
I beg you to send an envoy to investigate,
dispatch troops to punish and suppress,
and I have sent my younger brother, Kèqín, with ten thousand cavalry to await orders in Hézhōng."
At that time, the court, considering that the great rebellion had just been quelled,
was focused on appeasement.
Upon receiving Lǐ Kèyòng's memorial,
they were greatly alarmed,
