was an ancient county of the Hàn dynasty,
named after Wújí Mountain.
During the Táng, it belonged to Dìngzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is located 90 lǐ south of the prefecture.)
Kèyòng sent his general Kāng Jūnlì and others to lead troops to rescue them.
10. In the intercalary month,
Qín Zōngquán sent his brother Zōngyán to invade Jīngnán.
11. Earlier,
Tián Lìngzī, while in Shǔ, recruited a new army of 54 dū,
each dū consisting of 1,000 men,
divided and attached to the two Shéncè Armies,
forming ten armies to command them.
Furthermore, the officials of the Southern Administration and Northern Bureau totaled over ten thousand.
At that time, the military governors each monopolized the taxes,
and Hé’nán, Héběi, Jiāng, and Huái no longer submitted tribute.
The Three Departments responsible for transportation had nowhere to requisition supplies.
The Bureau of Revenue only collected taxes from the capital region and a few prefectures like Tóng, Huá, and Fèngxiáng,
which were insufficient to cover expenses.
Rewards and gifts were not distributed on time,
and the soldiers began to complain.
Lìngzī was troubled by this
and did not know what to do.
Previously,
the salt from the two ponds of Ānyì and Xièxiàn were both under the Salt and Iron Commission,
with officials appointed to monopolize them.
(Sòng Bái states: The salt administration of the two ponds
was originally under the Bureau of Revenue,
and its duties were handled by the various circuit inspection offices.
In the 16th year of Zhēnyuán [800 AD],
Shǐ Móu, as Director of the Bureau of Revenues, took charge of the pond administration
and subsequently petitioned to establish the Salt Monopoly Commissioner.
解,
pronounced hù mǎi fān.
榷,
pronounced qì yuè fān.)
Hézhōng military governor Wáng Chóngróng monopolized them.
When the Son of Heaven fled to Shǔ,
all the internal and external offices lost their administrative functions.
Wáng Chóngróng secretly occupied Hézhōng
and gained exclusive control over the profits from the salt ponds.
Lìngzī petitioned to restore the old system of placing them under the Salt and Iron Commission.
In summer,
the fourth month,
Lìngzī personally assumed the concurrent post of Salt Monopoly Commissioner for the two ponds.
(The Táng Huìyào states: In the 15th year of Yuánhé [820 AD],
the Héběi Tax Salt Commissioner was changed to Salt Monopoly Commissioner.
Later, after Héběi was lost again,
the Salt Monopoly Commissioner was established only for the two ponds of Ānyì and Xièxiàn.
) Chóngróng submitted memorials repeatedly arguing and protesting.
The emperor sent a palace envoy to instruct him,
but Chóngróng would not comply.
At that time, Lìngzī often sent his confidants to spy on the military governors.
If any did not submit to him,
he would plot against them.
Lìngzī's adopted son Kuāngyòu was sent to Hézhōng.
Chóngróng treated him with great courtesy,
but Kuāngyòu was extremely arrogant,
causing the entire army to become furious.
Chóngróng then enumerated Lìngzī's crimes and evils,
reprimanding him for his lack of propriety.
The army supervisor tried to mediate,
and Kuāngyòu barely managed to escape.
Upon returning,
Kuāngyòu reported this to Lìngzī
and urged him to plot against Chóngróng.
In the fifth month,
Lìngzī transferred Chóngróng to be Tàiníng military governor,
appointed Tàiníng military governor Qí Kèràng as Yìwǔ military governor,
and appointed Yìwǔ military governor Wáng Chùcún as Hézhōng military governor.
Furthermore, an edict was issued ordering Lǐ Kèyòng to use his Hé’dōng troops to assist Chùcún in taking up his post.
(This sets the stage for Lǐ Kèyòng and Wáng Chóngróng joining forces to attack the capital.)
12. The Lúlóng troops attacked Yìzhōu.
Deputy general Liú Réngōng tunneled into the city,
and thus captured it.
(Réngōng
was from Shēnzhōu.)
Lǐ Kèyòng personally led troops to rescue Wújí,
defeating the Chéngdé troops.
The Chéngdé troops retreated to defend Xīnchéng.
Kèyòng advanced to attack again,
routing them heavily,
capturing Xīnchéng.
The Chéngdé troops fled,
pursued to Jiǔmén,
where over ten thousand heads were taken.
After the Lúlóng troops captured Yìzhōu,
they became arrogant and lax.
Wáng Chùcún sent 3,000 soldiers at night, covered in sheepskins, to approach the city walls.
The Lúlóng troops thought they were sheep,
and rushed out to seize them.
Chùcún launched a fierce attack,
routing them heavily,
and recaptured Yìzhōu.
Lǐ Quánzhōng fled.
13. Shǎnguó military governor Wáng Chóngyíng was given the additional title of Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
14. After Lǐ Quánzhōng lost his army,
fearing punishment,
he gathered his remaining troops and returned to attack Yōuzhōu.
In the sixth month,
Lǐ Kějǔ, in dire straits,
led his entire family to climb a tower and burned themselves to death.
(In the second year of Qiánfú [875 AD],
Lǐ Màoxūn gained control of Yōuzhōu.
After two generations,
it was destroyed in eleven years.)
15. The Eastern Capital留守 Lǐ Hǎnzhī and Qín Zōngquán's general Sūn Rú confronted each other for several months.
Hǎnzhī had few troops and exhausted supplies,
so he abandoned the city,
retreating west to defend Miǎnchí.
Zōngquán captured the Eastern Capital.
(The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Miǎnchí County is located 156 lǐ west of the capital city.
澠,
pronounced mí yǎn fān.)
(Sūn Rú captured the Eastern Capital,
but it is attributed to Zōngquán
because Rú
was Zōngquán's general.)
16. In autumn,
the seventh month,
Lǐ Quánzhōng was appointed as Lúlóng acting military governor.
On the 17th day, Yǐsì,
Right Rectifier of Omissions Cháng Jùn submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Your Majesty has been excessively lenient towards the military governors.
Regarding right and wrong, merit and fault,
they stand shoulder to shoulder,
speaking of uniformity in right and wrong,
and equalizing merit and fault,
making no distinctions whatsoever.
If you still do not awaken to this,
how can you not recall the hardships and perils of Luògǔ,
and again entertain plans of looking westward?
You should slightly invigorate the statutes and penalties to awe the four quarters."
Tián Lìngzī's faction said to the Emperor:
"If this memorial circulates among the military governors,
will it not cause them suspicion and resentment!"
On the Gēngxū day,
Jùn was demoted to Registrar of Wànzhōu,
and soon after was ordered to commit suicide.
Sòng Bái said: Wànzhōu,
was the territory of the Kuí state during the Spring and Autumn period,
and during the Qin and Han dynasties, it was the territory of Qúrǔn County.
Later, the Northern Wei divided the land of Qúrǔn to establish Ānxiāng and Yúquán counties.
The Northern Zhou established Wànchuān Commandery and concurrently established Nánzhōu.
The Tang established Pǔzhōu.
In the early Zhēnguàn era,
it was changed to Wànzhōu,
taking the old name of Wànchuān Commandery as its designation.
Textual analysis notes: The Veritable Records do not say who Lìngzī's partisans were.
According to the memorial submitted by Xiāo Gòu and others requesting Lìngzī's execution, it states:
"Wéi Zhāodù lacks the heart to serve the sovereign and pledge loyalty to the state,
and has many traces of vilifying the upright and associating with the obstinate."
Lìngzī's partisans,
likely refer to Zhāodù.
The Continued Record of Precious Fortune states:
"On the third day of the seventh month,
the memorial was submitted.
The Emperor read it
and was displeased.
Turning to his attending officials, he said:
'If the military governors see this memorial,
they will be deeply resentful.
From this, suspicion and estrangement will arise; how can this be endured!'
On the 28th day,
an edict was issued demoting Jùn to Registrar of Wànzhōu."
It is suspected that 'third day' is an error,
and should be the 23rd day.
We now follow the Veritable Records.
18. A mutiny occurred in Cāngzhōu,
expelling Military Governor Yáng Quánméi,
and establishing Acting Commander Lú Yànwēi as Provisional Military Governor.
Quánméi fled to Yōuzhōu.
Cáo Chéng, Commander of the Bǎoluán Army, was appointed Military Governor of Yìchāng.
Bǎoluán,
was one of the fifty-four armies of the Divine Strategy Army.
19. Sūn Rú occupied the Eastern Capital for over a month,
burning palaces, government offices, and civilian residences,
plundering extensively and sweeping everything away before departing.
The city was left silent, without even chickens or dogs.
Lǐ Hǎnzhī again led his troops into the Eastern Capital,
building a fortified camp west of the market and residing there.
The city was large and difficult to defend,
and moreover, there were no inhabitants,
so he built a camp to protect and gather his forces.
20. Wáng Chóngróng, considering himself meritorious for recovering the capital,
see the third year of Zhōnghé in the previous scroll.
was unwilling to go to Yǎnzhōu.
He repeatedly submitted memorials arguing that Lìngzī was sowing discord between sovereign and ministers,
enumerating Lìngzī's ten crimes.
Lìngzī allied with Military Governor of Bīnníng, Zhū Méi, and Military Governor of Fèngxiáng, Lǐ Chāngfú, to oppose him.
Wáng Chùcún also submitted a statement:
"The troops of Yōu and Zhèn have only recently withdrawn,
and your subject dares not leave Yì and Dìng.
The troops of Yōu and Zhèn,
refer to the troops of Lǐ Kějǔ and Wáng Róng.
'Lí' [to leave],
is pronounced with the initial 'l' and the rhyme 'i'.
He has rendered great service to the state,
and should not be lightly transferred."
An edict urged him to take to the road.
In the eighth month,
Chùcún led his army to Jìnzhōu.
Governor Jì Jūnwǔ closed the city gates and did not admit him, so he returned.
The Military Governor of Hézhōng governed Jìn, Jiàng, Cí, Xí, and other prefectures.
Jūnwǔ was under Chóngróng's jurisdiction.
The surname Jì,
originated from Jì Ruì, a senior official of Jin,
who took his fief as his surname.
'Huán' [to return],
is pronounced according to the Xuān rhyme,
or also according to its usual pronunciation.
21. Governor of Míngzhōu, Mǎ Shuǎng,
was at odds with Xī Zhōngxìn, Army Supervisor of Zhāoyì.
He raised troops and stationed them south of Xíngzhōu,
pressuring Mèng Fānglì to request Zhōngxìn's execution.
Soon after, his forces disintegrated,
and Shuǎng fled to Wèizhōu.
Zhōngxìn sent someone to bribe Lè Yànzhēn, who had him killed.
22. Qín Zōngquán attacked over twenty neighboring prefectures,
capturing them.
Only Chénzhōu, about a hundred *li* from Cài,
with very weak military strength,
saw its Governor Zhào Chōu daily engaging Zōngquán in battle,
yet Zōngquán could not subdue him.
An edict appointed Chōu as Military Governor of Càizhōu.
Chōu was grateful for Zhū Quánzhōng's aid.
Since the third year of Zhōnghé,
when Huáng Cháo attacked Chénzhōu,
and later when he was attacked and pressured by Qín Zōngquán,
he relied solely on Zhū Quánzhōng for support.
Whatever Quánzhōng requisitioned or dispatched,
Chōu complied with immediately.
23. Wáng Xù arrived at Zhāngzhōu.
Due to the treacherous roads and scarcity of provisions,
he ordered the army
"not to bring along the old and weak.
Violators will be executed!"
Only Wáng Cháo and his brothers supported their mother, Dǒng shì, and followed the army through difficult terrain.
Xù summoned Cháo and others and reprimanded them:
"An army must have laws;
there has never been an army without laws.
If you violate my order and are not punished,
then there are no laws."
The three sons said:
Wáng Cháo and his two brothers followed Xù.
"All men have mothers;
there has never been a man without a mother.
How can the General make people abandon their mothers!"
Xù was enraged
and ordered their mother executed.
The three sons said:
"We, Cháo and others, serve our mother as we serve the General.
Since you have killed our mother,
what use are her sons?
We ask to die before our mother."
The officers and soldiers all pleaded for them,
and so he spared them.
There was an observer of auras who said to Xù:
"There is a royal aura in the army."
Thereupon, Xù, seeing officers and soldiers whose courage and strategy surpassed his own or who had imposing physiques, had them all killed.
Liú Xíngquán also died.
Everyone felt endangered,
saying:
"Xíngquán was a relative,
Xíngquán
was Xù's brother-in-law,
hence this statement.
and yet he was not spared,
how much more so us!"
When they reached Nán'ān,
Wáng Cháo persuaded the vanguard commander, saying:
"We have left behind our ancestral graves,
abandoned our wives and children,
and sojourned in foreign lands as bandits,
meaning they left Guāng and Shòu to enter Mǐn.
This was because we were coerced by Xù.
Now Xù is suspicious, harsh, and unkind,
arbitrarily killing the innocent.
Those in the army who stand out are being executed, nearly all of them.
'Jiéjié' [standing out],
describes a solitary, independent appearance.
Your horsemanship and archery are peerless,
and you are also the vanguard commander.
I privately fear for your safety!"
The vanguard commander grasped Cháo's hand and wept,
asking what plan he proposed.
Cháo devised a plan for him.
Dozens of strong men were hidden in a bamboo thicket.
When Xù arrived,
they drew their swords, shouted loudly, and leapt out.
'Tǐng jiàn' [drawing swords],
means to unsheathe swords.
'Hū' [to shout],
is pronounced with the initial 'h' and the rhyme 'u'.
They bound Xù and paraded him.
The army all shouted "Long live!"
In the first year of Zhōnghé,
Wáng Xù raised troops and became a bandit.
By now, he had been imprisoned by Wáng Cháo.
According to the New Book biography of Wáng Cháo,
the one who bound Wáng Xù was Liú Xíngquán,
which differs slightly from this account.
The Comprehensive Mirror's record
is based on Lù Zhèn's *History of the Nine States*.
The vanguard commander said:
"Today, we are not fish on the chopping block,
all due to Lord Wáng's efforts.
Heaven intends Lord Wáng to be our leader;
who would dare precede him!"
After several rounds of deferring to each other,
they finally offered the position of general to Cháo.
Xù sighed:
"This man was in my net, yet I could not kill him.
Is this not Heaven's will!"
Chao led his troops and was about to return to Guangzhou.
He made an agreement with his subordinates,
that along the way, not even the slightest harm would be done.
When they reached Shāxiàn,
in the sixth year of the Yǒnghuī era,
Shāxiàn was established from a division of Jiàn’ān,
belonging to Tīngzhōu.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: it is located 124 li west of Nánjiànzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Shāxiàn
is the ancient remnant of Nánpíng.
During the Jìn dynasty, it was Yánpíngxiàn.
In the fourth year of the Tàiyuán era,
it was changed to Shāshù;
at the beginning of the Wǔdé era of the Táng dynasty,
it was established as Shāxiàn.
The elders and leaders offered cattle and wine, blocking the road,
requesting Cháo to stay and serve as the regional general.
Cháo then led his troops to besiege Quánzhōu.
24 In the ninth month,
on Wùshēn,
Chén Jìngxuān was appointed as the overall commander and military commissioner of Sānchuān and the various prefectures within the Xiá region.
The Táng dynasty divided Sānchuān into separate military commands,
and the various prefectures within the Xiá region, Guī and Xiá,
belonged to the Jīngnán military command.
Now Chén Jìngxuān was given command and authority over all of them,
thanks to Tián Lìngzī’s support.
25 The Cài army besieged Jīngnán.
The Cài army
was the army sent by Qín Zōngquán, under Qín Zōngyán.
In the first month of this year,
Zhāng Huái imprisoned Chén Rú.
Huái
killed Kuāng and Rú.
26 In winter,
the tenth month,
on Guǐchǒu,
Qín Zōngquán defeated Zhū Quánzhōng at Bājiǎo.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: Biànzhōu’s Jùnyíxiàn had the town of Bājiǎo.
Defeated,
bǔ mài fān.
27 Wáng Chóngróng sought help from Lǐ Kèyòng.
Examination of discrepancies: The Tàizǔ Jìnián Lù states:
“Zhū Méi and Lǐ Chāngfú repeatedly allied to visit the Son of Heaven,
pointing out advantages and disadvantages,
planning strategies,
not supporting Tàizǔ,
but siding with the rebellious Wēn.
Tàizǔ’s anger grew increasingly intense.
At that time, Tián Lìngzī hated Tàizǔ’s close alliance with Hézhōng,
and memorialized: ‘Wáng Chóngróng has allied with Tàiyuán in the north,
his intentions are clear,
he should not be stationed near the capital.
Wáng Chùcún of Dìngzhōu is loyal and filial,
I request that he be appointed as the commander of Pú,
and Chóngróng be transferred to Dìngzhōu.’
The Son of Heaven agreed.
Chóngróng was furious and displeased,
and reported to Tàizǔ: ‘The sovereign has just returned to the throne,
and ministers are being cast aside.
At this time, I, innocent, am suddenly being exiled.
You, illustrious lord, should understand the deeper intentions.
Where can I go now!’
At that time, Tàizǔ was angry with Zhū Méi and his ilk,
and immediately replied: ‘I will join you, beating the drums out of Sìshuǐ Pass,
and after eliminating the rebellious bandits,
we will sweep away these rats,
like a strong wind blowing away a goose feather.’
Chóngróng said: ‘My territory is close to Bīn and Qí.
If you, lord, lead troops east of the pass,
the two villains will certainly press upon my city walls.
It would be better to first eliminate one villain,
removing him from the sovereign’s side.’”
Ōuyáng Xiū’s Wǔdài Shǐ states:
“Chóngróng sent someone to deceive Kèyòng, saying: ‘The Son of Heaven has ordered Chóngróng,
to wait until Kèyòng arrives,
and together with Chùcún, execute him.’
He then showed Kèyòng a forged edict, saying:
‘This is Zhū Quánzhōng’s plot.’
Kèyòng believed it.”
At that time, the court was suspicious and wary of Chóngróng,
and Kèyòng also knew this,
so it is unlikely such an event occurred.
Now, following the Jìnián Lù.
Zhū Quánzhōng attacked Kèyòng at Shàngyuán Station,
and the court was unable to punish him for his crime,
so Kèyòng held a grudge.
Gathering various Hu tribes,
he discussed attacking Biànzhōu,
and replied:
“Wait until I first eliminate Quánzhōng,
then I will sweep away these rats like autumn leaves!”
Chóngróng said:
“By the time you return from east of the pass,
I will have been captured.
It would be better to first remove the evil at the sovereign’s side,
and then capturing Quánzhōng will be easy.”
At that time, Zhū Méi and Lǐ Chāngfú also secretly allied with Zhū Quánzhōng.
Kèyòng then memorialized:
“Méi and Chāngfú collaborate with Quánzhōng,
intending to jointly destroy me.
I have no choice but to defend myself.
I have already gathered 150,000 barbarian and Han troops,
and have decided to cross the river next year,
marching from north of the Wei to attack the two commands.
I will not approach the capital,
ensuring no disturbance.
Once the two commands are eliminated,
I will turn my troops to destroy Quánzhōng and avenge this disgrace.”
The sovereign sent envoys to persuade and resolve the matter,
resolve, meaning to settle.
Xiāo Gòu, through the Bīnníng Circuit's memorial affairs judge Lǐ Sōngnián, arrived at Fèngxiáng.
In the late Táng, when a military governor sent a subordinate to report matters,
they were all called memorial affairs officials.
A judge,
was a high-ranking position in the military headquarters.
Zhū Méi sent him to report matters at the imperial court's temporary location,
hence he was called the memorial affairs judge,
to distinguish him from ordinary memorial affairs officials.
Xiāo Gòu was the chancellor,
yet when the Son of Heaven was fleeing and displaced, he did not escort him.
How could he be without fault!
Zhū Méi soon harbored treacherous intentions,
Xiāo Gòu could neither control him,
nor die for his principles.
He suffered punishment for his crimes,
which began from this.
On Guǐsì day
Méi led five thousand infantry and cavalry to Fèngxiáng.
Kǒng Wěi went to see the chancellors,
wishing to proclaim an edict summoning them;
Xiāo Gòu and Péi Chè, because Tián Lìngzí was by the emperor's side,
did not want to go,
and declined on grounds of illness, refusing to see him.
Wěi ordered officials from the Censorate to urge all officials to go to the imperial court's temporary location,
but they all declined, citing lack of court robes and tablets.
Wěi summoned the censors from the three bureaus.
Táng records: The Censor-in-chief had three bureaus under him: the first was the Terrace Bureau,
to which the Attendant Censors belonged;
the second was the Palace Bureau,
to which the Palace Censors belonged;
the third was the Investigation Bureau,
to which the Investigating Censors belonged.
"Even if commoners, relatives, or old friends are in urgent need,
one should still go to their aid.
How can it be that when the Son of Heaven is covered in dust,
as his ministers and subjects,
they are repeatedly summoned yet do not go!"
The censors requested a few days to prepare their baggage before departing.
Wěi flicked his sleeves and rose, saying:
"My wife is critically ill and near death, yet I do not attend to her.
You gentlemen plan well for yourselves,
I bid you farewell from here!"
He then went to Lǐ Chāngfú,
requesting cavalry escorts to send him to the imperial court's temporary location.
Chāngfú, considering this righteous,
gave him money for travel expenses,
and dispatched cavalry to escort him.
The troops of Bīnníng and Fèngxiáng pursued and pressed close to the imperial carriage,
defeating the Divine Strategy Commandant Yáng Shèng at Pānshì.
The sounds of gongs and drums were heard at the temporary palace.
Tián Lìngzí escorted the emperor in departing from Bǎojī,
leaving imperial guards to defend Shíbí as a rear guard.
Pānshì,
was northeast of Bǎojī.
Shíbí,
was southwest of Bǎojī,
also called Língbì.
Sū Shì said: Wǔchéng Town in Bǎojī County, Fèngxiáng Prefecture,
is what is commonly called Shíbí Stockade.
It was a city built by Marquis Wǔ Zhūgě Liàng,
thirty lǐ from Bǎojī.
Yáng Shèng was appointed military governor,
to defend Sànguān.
Xīngzhōu,
was the territory of Jǔ County in the Hàn dynasty's Wǔdū Commandery.
From Jìn through Sòng and Wèi, it was the state of the Wǔxīng Fan Prince of the Yáng clan.
Wèi destroyed the Yáng clan,
and established the Wǔxīng Garrison.
It was soon renamed Dōngyìzhōu.
In the Táng it was Xīngzhōu.
The present prefectural city is the ancient Wǔxīng City.
Fèngzhōu,
was the territory of the two counties Gùdào and Héchí in the Hàn dynasty's Wǔdū Commandery.
In the Later Wèi it was the Qiúchí Garrison.
During the Xiàochāng era, Nánqízhōu was established.
In the third year of the deposed emperor's reign,
it was renamed Fèngzhōu,
named after the Fènghuáng Mountain on its western border.
Arrows and blades crisscrossed.
Wáng Jiàn and Jìn Huī of the Divine Strategy Army were appointed as Road-Clearing and Chopping Envoys.
Jiàn, leading five hundred long swordsmen, charged ahead and fought fiercely,
allowing the imperial carriage to advance.
Examination of discrepancies: Máo Wénxí's "Record of Events of Wáng Jiàn" states:
"In the second year of Guāngqǐ,
on the first month, Xīnsì day,
the imperial carriage stopped at Chéncāng.
On the second month, Xīnhài day,
Zhū Méi sent troops to attack and press the imperial court's temporary location.
On Gēngshēn day,
they captured Guó County.
On the third month, Jiǎwǔ day,
as they were about to move the imperial presence to Liáng and Yáng,
the emperor appointed him as Road-Clearing and Chopping Envoy.
On Wùxū day,
the Bīn army reached Shíbí.
On Jǐhài day,
Shíbí was not held.
On Gēngzǐ day,
the enemy pressed Bǎojī.
On Xīnchǒu day,
the imperial carriage headed south."
Now we only take the events,
not the specific months and days.
They ascended Dàsàn Ridge.
Lǐ Chāngfú burned over a zhang of the plank road,
about to collapse it.
Wáng Jiàn supported and helped the emperor leap across through the smoke and flames.
At night,
they rested beneath planks.
The emperor rested his head on Jiàn's knee and slept.
After waking,
he then began to eat.
He took off his imperial robe and bestowed it upon Jiàn, saying:
"Because it has tear stains on it."
The imperial carriage had just entered Sànguān,
when Zhū Méi had already surrounded Bǎojī.
The Shíbí army collapsed.
Méi advanced swiftly and attacked Sànguān,
but did not capture it.
The Prince of Xiāng, Yūn,
was the great-great-grandson of Emperor Sùzōng.
Yūn,
was the great-grandson of Emperor Sùzōng's son, the Prince of Xiāng, Guàng.
Pronunciation: yún,
also yùn.
He could not keep up with the emperor,
and stayed at Zūntú Station.
According to Yūn's biography,
Zūntú Station was at Shíbí,
also called Shíbí Station.
He returned to Fèngxiáng with them.
On Gēngxū day,
Lǐ Kèyòng returned to Tàiyuán.
3 In the second month,
Wáng Chóngróng, Zhū Méi, and Lǐ Chāngfú again submitted a memorial requesting the execution of Tián Lìngzí.
4 The former Eastern Capital留守 Zhèng Cóngdǎng was appointed as Grand Mentor and concurrently Palace Attendant.
Examination of discrepancies: The "New Table of Chancellors" states
Cóngdǎng entered the Three Dukes' gate,

According to the "New Biography",
he was appointed Minister of Works,
again took charge of government,

The "New Table" is mistaken.
5 Zhū Méi and Lǐ Chāngfú ordered the Shānnán West Circuit military governor Shí Jūnshè to build stockades and block the strategic passes,
and burn the postal stations.
The emperor proceeded via other routes;
the mountain valleys were rugged.
The Bīn army pressed from behind,
the Bīn army,
was Zhū Méi's army.
They barely reached Shānnán.
In the third month,
on Rénwǔ day,
Shí Jūnshè abandoned his garrison and fled back to Zhū Méi.
Shí Jūnshè was allied with Bīn and Qí.
When the imperial carriage suddenly arrived,
he therefore abandoned his garrison and fled.
On Guǐwèi day,
the officials at Fèngxiáng, Xiāo Gòu and others, enumerated the crimes of Tián Lìngzí and his associate Wéi Zhāodù,
requesting their execution.
Earlier,
Zhāodù, through the court-supplied monk Chè, connected with the eunuchs,
and obtained the chancellorship.
Zhāodù becoming chancellor,
see the first year of Guāngmíng, scroll 254.
Whenever Zhāodù went with his colleagues to see Zhīxuán,
they all bowed to him.
Zhīxuán gestured for them to go to Chè to drink tea.
The Supervisor of the Army of Shǎnnán Xīdào, Yán Zūnměi of Féngyì, welcomed the Emperor at Xī County.
Since the Military Commissioner had already fled,
the Supervisor of the Army personally went to welcome the imperial carriage.
During the Later Wei, Bōzhǒng County was established by dividing Hànmiǎn County.
In the early years of the Sui dynasty's Dàyè era,
it was renamed Xī County,
and during the Táng, it belonged to Xīngyuán Prefecture.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: the county is located one hundred lǐ west of the prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: Xī County was originally called Báimǎ City,
also known as Jìnjiāng City.
During the Sòng, the Huáyáng Commandery was temporarily established here,
and during the Later Wei, Bōzhǒng County was established.
In the third year of the Sui dynasty's Dàyè era, it was renamed Xī County.
On Bǐngshēn,
the imperial carriage arrived at Xīngyuán.
Examination of discrepancies: According to Pí Guāngyè's Jiànwén Lù:
"On the first month, Yǐyǒu,
the imperial carriage stopped at Bǎojī."
According to Wáng Jiàn's Jìshì:
"On the first month, Xīnsì,
they stopped at Chéncāng.
On the second month, Xīnhài,
Zhū Méi's general [AS-FEBA] [AS-FBED] Jídiē Shīyǔ threatened the imperial presence,
defeating Yáng Shèng at Pānshì.
On Gēngshēn,
they captured Guó County.
On the third month, Jiǎwǔ,
Emperor Xīzōng was about to move to Liáng and Yáng,
on Wùxū,
the Bīn army reached Shíbí.
On Jǐhài,
Shíbí was lost.
On Gēngzǐ,
the enemy threatened Bǎojī.
On Xīnchǒu,
the imperial carriage moved south.
On the fourth month, Gēngshēn,
they reached Bāozhōng."
According to the Old Annals:
"On the first month, Wùzǐ,
Tián Lìngzī forced the imperial carriage to go to Xīngyuán.
On Gēngyín,
they stopped at Bǎojī.
On Guǐsì,
Zhū Méi reached Fèngxiáng.
When Lìngzī heard that the Bīn army had arrived,
he escorted the Emperor into Sǎnguān.
On the third month, Bǐngshēn,
the imperial carriage arrived at Xīngyuán."
According to the Táng Nián Bǔlù:
"On the seventeenth day of the third month,
the imperial carriage arrived at Xīngyuán,"
which is Bǐngshēn.
According to the Veritable Records:
"On the first month, Yǐyǒu,
the imperial carriage stopped at Bǎojī,"
Wùzǐ, Guǐsì, and the third month Bǐngshēn,
are the same as in the Old Annals.
According to the New Annals:
"On the first month, Wùzǐ,
they went to Xīngyuán.
On Guǐsì,
Zhū Méi rebelled,
and invaded Fèngxiáng.
On the third month, Bǐngshēn,
they stopped at Xīngyuán."
The various texts differ in their dates like this.
If we follow the New and Old Annals and the Veritable Records,
then it took sixty-four days from Bǎojī to reach Xīngyuán,
which seems too slow.
If we follow Jìshì,
then Bǎojī was a place of danger and threat,
and the imperial carriage stayed there for eighty days,
which seems too long.
In summary,
since the plank roads were burned and cut off,
Emperor Xīzōng had to travel through rugged paths to reach Shǎnnán,
it is possible that it took over sixty days;
as for staying at Bǎojī for eighty days,
that is certainly unreasonable.
Now we follow the New and Old Annals.
On Wùxū,

Kǒng Wěi, the Grand Master of Remonstrance, and Dù Ràngnéng, the Academician Recipient of Edicts and Minister of War, were both appointed as Vice Ministers of War and participated in determining governmental matters.
The commander of the Bǎoluán Army, Lǐ Chán, and others defeated the Bīn army at Fèng Prefecture.
An edict was issued adding Wáng Chóngróng as the Commissioner for Supplying Provisions,
and ordering him to transfer 150,000 hú of grain from his own circuit to aid the state's needs.
Chóngróng submitted a memorial stating that as long as Lìngzī was not executed,
he would not obey the edict.
Lú Wò, the Vice Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed as Minister of Revenue,
and served as the Interim Military Commissioner of Shǎnnán Xīdào.
Yán Zūnměi was appointed as the Commissioner of the Palace Command,
and Wáng Jiàn was sent to lead his troops to garrison Sānquán.
In the fourth year of the Wǔdé era,
Sānquán County was established by dividing Miángǔ County of Lì Prefecture,
and at that time, it belonged to Xīngyuán Prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: Sānquán County was originally part of the territory of Jiāmēng County during the Hàn,
during the Zhèngshǐ era of the Later Wei,
Sānquán County was established,
named after the Sānquán Mountain within its boundaries.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: it is located 210 lǐ southwest of the prefecture.
The character "shuài"
is read as "lǜ."
Of the five armies accompanying the Emperor,
Wáng Jiàn led one army to garrison Sānquán,
while Huī and Zào led the other four armies to station at Hēishuǐ.
Hēishuǐ
is located at Tàibái Mountain northwest of Chénggù County in Xīngyuán,
flowing south into the Hàn River.
It is the place mentioned in Zhūgě Liàng's letter:
"Depart from Nánzhèng in the morning,
and rest at Hēishuǐ in the evening."
Wáng Jiàn was appointed as the remote titular Prefect of Bì Prefecture.
The practice of generals and commanders holding remote titular appointments to prefectures and towns began from this.
6. Chén Jìngxuān suspected Gāo Rénhòu, the Military Commissioner of Dōngchuān,
and wanted to remove him.
The Prefect of Suí Prefecture, Zhèng Jūnlì,
raised an army and captured Hàn Prefecture,
advancing toward Chéngdū;
Jìngxuān sent his general Lǐ Shùnzhī to engage in battle,
and Jūnlì was defeated and died.
Jìngxuān also dispatched the Qiāng army from Wéi and Mào to attack Rénhòu,
and killed him.
Examination of discrepancies: According to Zhāng Qí's Jiù Zhuàn, it does not mention how Rénhòu died.
It only lists six mistakes of Jìngxuān:
"The Grand Tutor killed Gāo Rénhòu,
that is one mistake."
It also says:
"Minister Gāo was resourceful, wise, and brave,
and repeatedly rendered great service to the Grand Tutor,
and was extremely loyal and filial.
If he were alive,
Minister Wáng would not have passed beyond Zǐtóng."
According to the Veritable Records of Emperor Zhāozōng,
in the eighth month of the first year of the Wéndé era,
Rénhòu, Yáng Shīlì, Luó Yuángǎo, and Wáng Shīběn were all posthumously awarded official titles,
stating that they were all wrongly convicted on suspicion in the previous reign.
Now we follow the New Annals and the New Biography,
and refer to these two texts,
but there is no further information about Rénhòu's other affairs.
7. Zhū Méi believed that as long as Tián Lìngzī remained by the Emperor's side,
he could never be removed,
and said to Xiāo Gòu:
"The Sovereign has been wandering for six years,
while the generals and soldiers of the Central Plains have braved arrows and stones,
and the common people have supplied provisions,
with many dying in battle or from starvation,
reducing their numbers by seven or eight out of ten,
only to recover the capital.
Just as the world was rejoicing that the imperial carriage had returned to the palace,
the Sovereign instead bestowed the glory of the imperial commissioners with the merit of rescuing the throne.
As for the merit of rescuing the throne,
Yáng Fùguāng actually shared in it.
Tián Lìngzī, because he came from the Northern Bureau,
deluded the Sovereign into thinking it was his own glory.
This caused the collapse of laws and order,
disturbed the military commissioners,
and brought about chaos and disaster.
I, Méi, previously received your esteemed command to welcome the imperial carriage,
meaning Gòu summoned Méi to welcome the imperial carriage.
Instead, it seemed like coercing the Sovereign.
Our loyalty to the state is utmost,
and our strength in fighting the enemy is exhausted.
How can we bow our heads and submit,
to be controlled by the hands of eunuchs!
There are still many descendants of the Lǐ family,
why don't you, Minister, change your plans for the benefit of the state?"
Gòu said:
"The Sovereign has been on the throne for over ten years,
without any major faults;
it is precisely because Lìngzī monopolized power at his side,
causing him to sit uneasily on the throne.
Every time the Sovereign speaks of this,
he cannot stop weeping.
Recently, the Sovereign initially had no intention of leaving,
but Lìngzī deployed troops in front of his tent,
forcing and threatening him to leave,
not allowing him to wait until dawn.
The blame lies entirely with Lìngzī,
who doesn't know this!
You, sir, have devoted yourself to the royal house,
it would be proper to lead your troops back to your garrison,
and submit a memorial to welcome the imperial carriage.
Deposing and establishing a sovereign is a grave matter,
even Yī Yǐn and Huò Guāng found it difficult.
I, Gòu, dare not accept such a command!"
Méi left,
and declared:
"I will establish a prince of the Lǐ family,
anyone who dares to disagree will be executed!"
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Rénzǐ day,
Zhū Méi forced the officials at Fèngxiáng to support Prince Xiāng Lǐ Yùn in temporarily overseeing military and state affairs.
Acting under imperial authority, he appointed commanders and
also sent high officials into Shǔ to welcome the imperial carriage.
He swore an oath with the officials at Shíbí Station.
Zhū Méi had Xiāo Gòu draft the investiture document,
but Gòu declined, citing his literary skills as rusty;
so he had the Vice Minister of War and concurrent Director of the Revenue Ministry, Zhèng Chāngtú, compose it instead.
On the Yǐmǎo day,
Yùn received the investiture.
Zhū Méi personally assumed the concurrent posts of Commissioner of the Left and Right Shencè Ten Armies.
The Textual Analysis states: The Veritable Records say:
“Zhū Méi appointed himself Grand Chancellor.”
However, the Táng dynasty had no such office.
Furthermore, in the following fifth month,
Zhū Méi added for himself the title of Shìzhōng.
It is likely that writers of minor narratives in the late Táng period
sometimes referred to the Píngzhāngshì or Shìzhōng as Grand Chancellor,
and the Veritable Records mistakenly followed that wording.
Matters having reached this point,
Xiāo Gòu had no place to hide between heaven and earth.
The character 帥 [commander]
is read as 率 [to lead].
He appointed deputy commissioners for each,
and entrusted all affairs of the Three Departments to them.
The officials at Hézhōng, such as Cuī Ānqián and others, submitted a memorial to Prince Xiāng,
congratulating him on receiving the investiture.
When the Emperor left Cháng'ān,
the officials did not accompany him;
those who fled to Hézhōng
were called the Hézhōng officials.
8 Tián Lìngzī, knowing that he was not tolerated by the empire,
recommended the Bureau of Military Affairs Commissioner Yáng Fùgōng as Left Shencè Central Guard and Army Surveillance Commissioner,
while appointing himself as the Xīchuān Military Supervisor.
The Textual Analysis states: The Old Annals and the Veritable Records both say

Lìngzī was made Xīchuān Military Supervisor.”
The Old Biography says:

recommended Yáng Fùgōng to replace himself,

The New Biography says:

This likely follows Zhāng’s account.
According to the Records of Wáng Jiàn’s Affairs:

on the Gēngshēn day,
they reached Bāozhōng.
Lìngzī, his crimes and offenses overflowing,

thereupon appointed himself Xīchuān Military Supervisor,
to avoid being singled out for blame,
and again schemed to make a nest with Jìngxuān.”
We now follow this.
This sets the stage for the joint fate of Jìngxuān and Lìngzī.
He sent Wáng Jiàn out as Prefect of Lìzhōu,
Jìn Huī as Prefect of Jízhōu,
Zhāng Zào as Prefect of Wànzhōu,

Wáng Jiàn and others had submitted to Tián Lìngzī,

9 In the fifth month,
Zhū Méi made the Secretariat Vice Director and Tóng Píngzhāngshì Xiāo Gòu Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent,
while adding for himself the titles of Shìzhōng and Commissioner for Salt and Iron, Transport, etc.;
he added Péi Chè as concurrent Director of Finance,

acting as Commissioner for Jiāng-Huái Salt and Iron, Transport, etc., and Commander-in-Chief of the Various Circuits’ Campaign Armies;
he made the Huáinán Right Capital Guard Commander and Hézhōu Prefect Lǚ Yòngzhī Military Commissioner of Lǐngnán East Circuit;

About six or seven out of ten accepted his commands,
and Gāo Pián still submitted a memorial urging the Prince to ascend the throne.
The historian states: After Emperor Xīzōng’s second flight to Shānnán,
the empire had already lost hope;
his ability to return was a matter of fortune.
Lǚ Yòngzhī established his headquarters and opened his command tent,
exactly like Pián.
All of Pián’s trusted confidants and officers capable of handling affairs
he forced to follow him.
In all his actions,
he no longer consulted or reported.
Pián became quite suspicious of him
and secretly wished to strip him of his power,
but his roots were already deep and firm,
and there was nothing he could do.
Yòngzhī learned of this
and was greatly afraid.
He consulted his partisans, former Finance Inspector Zhèng and former Administrator of Lúzhōu Dǒng Jǐn,
who said:
“This is indeed too late.”
Meaning Pián had not realized it earlier.
They said:
“Cáo Mèngdé had a saying: ‘Rather I betray others,
than others betray me.’”
At the end of the Later Hàn,
Cáo Cāo, fleeing the troubles of Dǒng Zhuó,
traveled east by back roads to return home.
Passing by his old friend Lǚ Bóshē,
Bóshē sent out his five sons to prepare the host-guest rites.
Cáo heard the sounds of eating utensils
and thought they were plotting against him.
Drawing his sword, he killed eight people and left.
Afterwards, he said sorrowfully:
“Rather I betray others,
than others betray me.”
Mèngdé
was Cáo Cāo’s courtesy name.
Zhèng was likely urging Yòngzhī to plot against Pián.
He and Jǐn together wrote a sealed letter and gave it to Yòngzhī.
Its words were secret,
and no one knew them.
The plots of Zhèng and Jǐn are seen below in the third year of Guāngqǐ.
Xiāo Gòu, pleading illness, returned to Yǒnglè.
According to the New History,
Gòu’s younger brother Qú was Magistrate of Yǒnglè,
and Gòu went to join him.
Yǒnglè County
belonged to Hézhōng Prefecture,
established in the early Wǔdé period.
Sòng Bái says: Yǒnglè County was originally on the territory of Hàn’s Héběi County.
In the second year of Wǔchéng of Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu,
it was changed to Yǒnglè.
In the second year of Bǎodìng it was abolished,
and its territory was attached to Ruìchéng.
In the second year of Táng Wǔdé,
it was separated from Ruìchéng and re-established.
The pronunciation of 樂 [in Yǒnglè]
is luò.
Initially,
the Fèngxiáng Military Commissioner Lǐ Chāngfú conspired with Zhū Méi to enthrone Prince Xiāng.
Afterwards, Méi made himself chancellor and monopolized power;
Chāngfú became angry,
refused his appointment,
and instead communicated with Xīngyuán.
An edict added for Chāngfú the title of Acting Minister of Works.
Zhū Méi sent his general Wáng Xíngyú to lead fifty thousand troops from Bīnníng and Héxī in pursuit of the imperial carriage.
Since the time of Emperor Dàizōng,
Héxī had been lost to Tǔbō.
Emperor Xuānzong recovered Hé and Huáng,
Zhāng Yìcháo recaptured Liángzhōu,
and Héxī again became loosely attached to Táng.
They abandoned Sànguān Pass and fled.
Xíngyú advanced and stationed his troops at Fèngzhōu.
At this time,
the tribute and taxes from the various circuits mostly went to Cháng'ān,
not to Xīngyuán.
The character 之
means “to go to.”
The Emperor wept,
not knowing what plan to adopt.
Dù Ràngnéng said to the Emperor:
“Yáng Fùguāng and Wáng Chóngróng together defeated Huáng Cháo
and recaptured the capital;
they were close and friendly.”
This matter is seen above in the third year of Zhōnghé.
If we send an important minister to explain the great righteousness to him,
and also convey Fùgōng’s intentions,
he should reconsider and return to the state.”
The Emperor followed this.
He sent the Right Admonisher Liú Chóngwàng as envoy to Hézhōng,

Chóngróng immediately obeyed the command,
sent an envoy to present a memorial offering one hundred thousand bolts of silk,

On the Wùxū day,
Prince Xiāng Yùn sent an envoy to Jìnyáng to bestow an edict upon Lǐ Kèyòng,
saying
“The Emperor, having reached halfway on the road,

Kèyòng, hearing that the plot all came from Méi,

His senior general Gài Yù advised Kèyòng:

He burned the edict,
imprisoned the envoy,

Yù
was a man of Yùzhōu.
10. Qín Xián invaded Sòngzhōu's Biànzhōu,

the emperor appointed the Escort Guard capital commander Yáng Shǒuliàng as military commissioner of Jīnshāng and commissioner for establishment of the capital region,

was also one of the fifty-four capitals of the Divine Strategy Army.

the people in Shānnán all said that Kèyòng had allied with Zhū Méi,

The emperor sent Yáng Fùgōng to write a letter instructing him, saying:
"Wait until matters in the Three Adjuncts are pacified,
the Hàn dynasty considered Jīngzhào, Féngyì, and Fúfēng as the Three Adjuncts,

Huáixī general,

13. Zhènhǎi military commissioner Zhōu Bǎo sent his staff officer Dīng Cóngshí to launch a surprise attack on Chángzhōu.

Yù fled to Hǎilíng.

Zhāng Yù captured Chángzhōu.
Bà,
was a general under Gāo Pián,
garrisoned Hǎilíng,
with 50,000 households

14. In autumn,
the seventh month,
Qín Zōngquán captured Xǔzhōu,

Yànhóng occupied Xǔzhōu,

Màozhēn
was from Bóyě,

The promotion of the Húnán observation to the Qīnhuà Army is recorded in the previous scroll, the third year of Zhōnghé.
Gēng,
pronounced gōng héng fān.
17. In the eighth month,
Lúlóng military commissioner Lǐ Quánzhōng died,
and his son Kuāngwēi was appointed as acting military commissioner.
18. Wáng Cháo captured Quánzhōu,
killing Liào Yànruò.
Last year in the eighth month, Wáng Cháo besieged Quánzhōu,
and by this time he captured it.
Textual analysis states: The New Annals record:
"In the eighth month,
Wáng Cháo captured Quánzhōu,
and prefect Liú Yànruò died there."
According to various texts, it is all
"Liào Yànruò".
The New Annals record
"Liǔ",
which is probably an error.
Not daring to violate the territory of Fúzhōu,
he sent an envoy to surrender to them.
Yán recommended Cháo to be appointed as prefect of Quánzhōu.
Cháo was calm, brave, and resourceful.

he recruited and comforted the scattered people,

19. In the ninth month,
Zhū Méi's general Zhāng Xíngshí attacked Dàtáng Peak,

Jīnwǔ general Mǎn Cún fought with the Bīnzhōu army,
defeated them,
recaptured Xīngzhōu,

20. Lǐ Kèxiū attacked Mèng Fānglì.
On Jiǎwǔ,

was similar to the death of Zhāng Shénjiàn.
Several thousand people died.
On that day,
heavy snow fell,
and the ground outside the temple for several blocks turned red.
Gāo Wǎng fled,
but the next day,
he was captured and killed.
As for Lǚ Yòngzhī in Tiāncháng,
in the fifth month of this year,
Yòngzhī surrendered to Xíngmì at Tiāncháng.
"Yòngzhī had fifty thousand ingots of silver,
buried at his residence.
On the day the city is captured,
I hope to provide it for a feast for your troops."
On Gēngxū,
Xíngmì reviewed the soldiers,
looked at Yòngzhī, and said:
"The Vice Director promised these men silver,
why break your word!"
He then had him seized, shackled, and imprisoned,
ordering Tián Yūn to interrogate him.
Yòngzhī said:
"Together with Zhèng and Dǒng Jǐn, we plotted to invite Gāo Pián to his residence on the night of the Mid-Year Festival to hold a Huánglù Fast.
According to Daoist texts, the fifteenth day of the first month is the Upper Prime Festival,
the fifteenth day of the seventh month is the Mid-Year Festival,
and the fifteenth day of the tenth month is the Lower Prime Festival.
The Huánglù Grand Fast
summons all heavenly deities, earthly spirits, and human ghosts to set up a sacrificial altar,
to repent for the roots of sins,
hoping to ascend to the immortal realm,
believing that the merit is inconceivable,
but these are all absurd claims.
What Daoism calls 'entering stillness'
is similar to the Buddhist 'entering meditation,' with slight differences.
'Entering stillness' means
staying quietly in a room,
dismissing attendants,
clearing the mind and calming thoughts,
without thinking or scheming,
hoping to connect with heavenly deities.
Claiming to ascend to heaven.
Therefore, he ordered the commander of the Mòyé Army to lead the troops in supporting Yòngzhī as military commissioner."
On that day,
Yòngzhī was executed by waist-cutting,
and his enemies carved him up until nothing remained.
His clan and associates were also executed.
Soldiers searched his main hall
and found a wooden figure,
with Gāo Pián's name written on its chest,
shackled and nailed.
Yuán Xí said to Xíngmì:
"Guǎnglíng is already severely plagued by famine,
and if the Cài bandits come again,
the people will surely suffer even more.
The Cài bandits refer to Sūn Rú.
'Again' means once more.
'Suffer' means to endure hardship.
On Jiǎyín,
Xíngmì sent the Hézhōu general Yánlíng Zōng back to Hézhōu with his two thousand troops.
These were troops sent by Sūn Duān to assist Yáng Xíngmì,
and now they were sent back.
On Yǐmǎo,
he also ordered the commander Cài Chóu to lead a thousand soldiers
and several thousand carts of supplies
back to Lúzhōu.
This laid the groundwork for Cài Chóu's betrayal of Yáng Xíngmì.
42 Zhào Huī occupied Shàngyuán,
and after Zhōu Bǎo's defeat,
many defeated soldiers from Zhèxī joined him.
Zhōu Bǎo's defeat is recorded in the previous volume of this year.
Shàngyuán County is near Jīngkǒu,
so many defeated soldiers from Zhèxī joined him.
Huī then became arrogant and overbearing,
repairing the Southern Dynasties' palace city and residing there.
After Suí conquered Chén,
they completely destroyed the palace city of Jiànkāng,
leveling and plowing the land,
and instead established Jiǎngzhōu at Shítóu City.
The Táng abolished Jiǎngzhōu,
and placed the area under Rùnzhōu.
In the second year of Guāngqǐ,
Shēngzhōu was reestablished,
with its seat at Shàngyuán County.
It seems the palace city had long been abandoned.
'Repair' means to restore.
Zhāng Xióng was at Dōngtáng,
and Huī did not communicate with him;
when Xióng sailed up the river,
Huī blocked the middle of the river with troops.
Xióng was furious,
and on Wùwǔ,
attacked Shàngyuán,
capturing it.
Huī fled to Dāngtú,
but before arriving,
he was killed by his subordinates.
The remaining troops surrendered,
and Xióng buried them all alive.
In the summer of this year,
Zhāng Xióng sent Zhào Huī to occupy Shàngyuán,
and now, angered by his resistance, he buried the surrendering troops alive.
'Surrender' means to yield.
43 Zhū Quánzhōng sent the inner guest general Zhāng Tíngfàn to convey the court's orders to Yáng Xíngmì.
This refers to the court orders from the intercalary month.
He also appointed the Xuānwǔ marching secretary Lǐ Fán as the acting military commissioner of Huáinán,
and sent the officer Guō Yán with a thousand troops to escort him.
The military commissioner of Gǎnhuà, Shí Pǔ, considered himself senior to Quánzhōng,
holding the position of commander-in-chief,
yet he was unable to govern Huáinán,
while Quánzhōng obtained it,
which made him deeply resentful.
Quánzhōng sent a letter requesting passage through Pǔ's territory,
but Pǔ refused.
When Fán reached Sìzhōu,
Pǔ attacked him with troops.
Guō Yán fought fiercely and managed to escape and return.
Thus began the enmity between Xú and Biàn.
From this point on,
it was not only Xú and Biàn that became enemies.
Zhū Quánzhōng, having received the court's orders,
then contended with Yáng Xíngmì for Huáinán,
engaging in battles twice but failing to achieve his aims both times,
after which he gave up.
Fán is pronounced as Fú Yuān.
8 The military governor of Wèibó, Lè Yànzhēn,
was arrogant, extravagant, and lawless.
He conscripted the people of six prefectures
(the six prefectures:
Wèi, Bó, Bèi, Xiàng, Chán, and Wèi)
to build an outer wall
(the outer wall of Wèizhōu)
with a circumference of eighty *li*.
His son, Lè Cóngxùn,
was especially cruel and treacherous.
After he killed Wáng Duó
(the event is recorded in the fourth year of the Zhōnghé era, in the previous volume),
Cóngxùn gathered over five hundred fugitives to serve as his personal guard,
calling them the "Zǐjiàng."
The Yájūn (the professional army) grew suspicious of this,
and rumors and unrest spread.
(The Wèibó Yájūn originated with Tián Chéngsì,
and they were accustomed to deposing and appointing their commanders.
Now that Lè Cóngxùn had established a personal guard,
the Yájūn suspected he was plotting against them,
hence their unease.)
(Jiàng is pronounced with the falling tone, like *liàng*.)
Cóngxùn changed his clothes and fled,
stopping in a nearby county.
Yànzhēn therefore appointed him as the prefect of Xiàngzhōu.
Cóngxùn sent people to Wèizhōu to transport armor, weapons, gold, and silk,
creating a constant flow of traffic on the roads,
which further increased the Yájūn's suspicions.
Yànzhēn grew fearful
and requested to step down from his position.
He retired to Lóngxīng Temple to become a monk.
(Lè Yànzhēn gained control of Wèibó in the third year of Zhōnghé;
he met his downfall at this time.)
*Kǎoyì* (Textual Analysis) states: The Old Biography says:
"Yànzhēn died in fear and danger."
The *Shílù* (Veritable Records) states:
"Yànzhēn, fearing for his life,
sought to step down voluntarily
and retired to Lóngxīng Temple,
where the troops forced him to become a monk."
The Old Annals state:
"The Wèibó army mutinied
and expelled Yànzhēn."
If he had died,
it should not say "expelled."
I follow the *Shílù*.
Cóngxùn led thirty thousand troops to the city walls.
Zhào Wényǎn did not come out to fight,
and the troops killed him as well.
They promoted the junior officer Luó Hóngxìn of Guìxiāng to act as the interim military governor.
Previously,
there had been a rumor
that "a white-bearded old man appeared,
saying that Hóngxìn would become the local ruler."
After Wényǎn's death,
the troops gathered and shouted:
"Who wants to be the military governor?"
Hóngxìn stepped forward and responded:
"The white-bearded old man has already appointed me."
The crowd looked around and said:
"That will do."
They then established him.
Hóngxìn led his troops out
and fought against Cóngxùn,
defeating him.
(The Old Book's Imperial Annals record that in this year, the Wèibó army mutinied
and expelled their commander Lè Yànzhēn.
Yànzhēn's son, the prefect of Xiàngzhōu, Cóngxùn, led his troops to attack Wèizhōu.
The Yájūn established their junior officer Luó Zōngbiàn as the interim military governor
and sent troops to resist him.
This seems to combine the names Zhào Wényǎn and Luó Hóngxìn into one person.)
(Bài is pronounced with the falling tone, like *mài*.)
Nèihuáng
was a county established in the Hàn dynasty,
at that time belonging to Wèizhōu.
*Jiǔyùzhì*: The county is located 124 *li* southwest of the prefectural seat.
Sòng Bái said: Wèi considered the area north of the Yellow River as "inner" (nèi) and south of the river as "outer" (wài).
Since there was a Wàihuáng in Chénliú,
this was called Nèihuáng.
The old county town was located nineteen *li* northwest of the present county seat.
Previously,
when Zhū Quánzhōng was about to campaign against Càizhōu,
he sent his staff officer Léi Yè with ten thousand taels of silver to Wèi to purchase grain.
After the Yájūn expelled Yànzhēn,
they killed Yè at the guesthouse.
After Cóngxùn was defeated,
he sought aid from Quánzhōng.
9 Initially,
the military governor of Héyáng, Lǐ Hǎnzhī, and
Zhāng Quányì swore an oath by cutting their arms,
and they got along very well.
Hǎnzhī was brave but lacked strategy,
and his nature was greedy and violent.
He looked down upon Quányì,
and upon hearing of Quányì's diligence, frugality, and efforts in farming,
he laughed and said:
"This is just a country bumpkin!"
Quányì heard this
but did not take offense.
Hǎnzhī repeatedly demanded grain and silk from him,
and Quányì gave them all to him.
However, Hǎnzhī's demands were insatiable.
Hénán could not keep up,
and if his wishes were not fully met even slightly,
he would have the officials of Hénán shackled and brought to Héyáng to be caned.
(*Jiǔyùzhì*: Hénán is 85 *li* northeast of Héyáng.)
Quányì would say:
"If Grand Marshal Lǐ
asks for something,
how can we not give it!"
He served Hǎnzhī with all his might,
appearing as if he feared him,
which made Hǎnzhī even more arrogant.
Hǎnzhī's troops did not engage in farming
but relied solely on plunder for supplies,
even resorting to cannibalism for food.
At this time, he led all his troops to attack Jiàngzhōu.
The prefect of Jiàngzhōu, Wáng Yǒuyù, surrendered to him.
He then advanced to attack Jìnzhōu.
The military governor of Hùguó, Wáng Chóngyíng, secretly allied with Quányì to plot against him.
Quányì secretly mobilized his garrison troops
(Zhāng Quányì governed Hénán, establishing a garrison commander in each of the eighteen counties to lead the garrison troops. The garrison troops were the militia.)
and took advantage of the emptiness to attack Héyáng.
At dawn,
he entered the three cities
(Héyáng had the Southern City, Northern City, and Middle Sandbar City).
Quányì captured all of Hǎnzhī's family
and thus also took over the position of military governor of Héyáng.
Hǎnzhī fled to Zézhōu.
(*Jiǔyùzhì*: Héyáng is 90 *li* north of Zézhōu.)
10 In the third month,
on the first day, Wùxū,
there was a solar eclipse,
which was total.
*Kǎoyì* states: The Old Annals record:
"For Emperor Xīzōng, the hundred officials presented the honorary title 'Holy, Cultured, Wise, Virtuous, Martial, and Filial Emperor.'
In the third month,
on the first day, Wùxū,
he held court in the main hall to receive the ceremonial tablets."
The Annals of Emperor Zhāozōng record:
"In the first year of Dàshùn,
in the first month,
on the first day, Wùzǐ,
the hundred officials presented the honorary title 'Holy, Cultured, Wise, Virtuous, Martial, and Filial Emperor.'"
How could the honorary titles of two emperors be exactly the same?
I now follow the New Annals,
which state that this was only Emperor Zhāozōng's honorary title.
11 On Jǐhài,
the Emperor's illness recurred.
On Rényín,
his condition became critical.
The Emperor's younger brother, Prince Jí, Bǎo,
was the eldest and virtuous,
and the ministers placed their hopes on him.
The Army Supervisor of the Ten Armies, Yáng Fùgōng, requested that the Emperor's younger brother, Prince Shòu, Jié, be established.
On that day,
an edict was issued
establishing Jié as the Imperial Younger Brother (heir apparent)
to oversee military and state affairs.
*Kǎoyì* states: *Táng Nián Bǔlù* records:
"After Emperor Xīzōng held court,
his illness recurred,
and he died suddenly.
Yáng Fùgōng and others concealed the death and did not announce it.
At that time, the various princes from the Sixteen Estates were accompanying the Emperor,
so they promoted the Emperor (Zhāozōng) to be the Regent in the main estate.
Above the Emperor were Prince Shèng and Prince Yí,
both sons of Emperor Yìzōng,
and the Emperor was the third among those residing in the Six Estates."
The Old Annals record:
"The ministers considered Prince Jí the most virtuous
and also senior to Prince Shòu,
and intended to establish him.
Only Yáng Fùgōng requested that Prince Shòu be made Regent."
Note: Emperor Zhāozōng
was the seventh son of Emperor Yìzōng.
Prince Jí, Bǎo,
was the sixth.
The New and Old Biographies list eight sons for Emperor Yìzōng,
with no Prince Shèng or Prince Yí.
I follow the Old Annals.
The Emperor had eight brothers.
Tǐng died early.
There were six princes,
residing in the Six Princes' Estate.
The Grand Councilors and others went to see them.
On Guǐmǎo,
the Emperor passed away in the Língfú Hall.
He was twenty-seven years old.
The Imperial Younger Brother, Jié, changed his name to Mǐn,
and appointed Wéi Zhāodù to act as the Chief Minister.
When Emperor Zhāozōng ascended the throne,
his appearance was bright and pure,
possessing an air of heroism.
He was fond of literature and learning.
Seeing that Emperor Xīzōng's authority and commands were ineffective,
and the court's prestige was declining daily,
he harbored the ambition to restore the former glories.
He respected and treated ministers with courtesy,
dreaming of recruiting worthy and heroic talents.
At the beginning of his reign,
both the court and the populace were joyful.
People's hearts were weary of chaos and longed for order.
Following Emperor Xīzōng's reign,
witnessing the initial governance of Emperor Zhāozōng,
they believed he was capable of great achievements.
12. Zhū Quánzhōng gathered provisions in Sòngzhōu,
intending to attack Qín Zōngquán.
At that time, Yuè Cóngxùn came to report an urgent situation,
so he shifted his army to station at Huázhōu.
He dispatched Chief Yá Officer Lǐ Tángbīn and others to lead thirty thousand infantry and cavalry to attack Càizhōu,
and sent Chief Commander Zhū Zhēn and others to divide their forces to rescue Yuè Cóngxùn.
Textual analysis notes: Xuē Jūzhèng's "History of the Five Dynasties: Biography of Zhēn" states:
"Zhēn's army was at Nèihuáng,
defeating over ten thousand of Yuè Cóngxùn's troops."
According to this, Zhēn went to rescue Cóngxùn, yet it says he defeated Cóngxùn,
which is an error.
The biography of Gě Cóngzhōu states:
"He followed Tàizǔ across the river,
capturing towns such as Líyáng, Lǐgù, and Línhé,
reaching Nèihuáng,
where he defeated over ten thousand Wèi troops."
Based on the annals and biographies in Xuē's history,
it is said that Tàizǔ sent Zhū Zhēn and others to rescue Cóngxùn.
Only Cóngzhōu's biography states he followed Tàizǔ,
which is likely an error.
They captured the three towns of Líyáng, Línhé, and Lǐgù.
The "Yuánfēng Jiǔyù Zhì" records,
Chánzhōu had Línhé County,
located sixty *li* west of the prefecture.
Wèizhōu's Wèi County had the town of Lǐgù.
Xuē's history, Jìn annals: West of Yè there was a stockade called Lǐgù,
where the Qīng and Qí rivers converged nearby.
They defeated over ten thousand Wèi troops,
capturing their generals Zhōu Rú and nine others.
13. Lǐ Kèyòng appointed his general Kāng Jūnlì as the Southern Front Recruitment Commissioner,
overseeing five generals—Lǐ Cúnxiào, Xuē Ātán, Shǐ Yǎn, Ān Jīnjùn, and Ān Xiūxiū—with seven thousand cavalry,
to assist Lǐ Hǎnzhī in attacking Héyáng.
Zhāng Quányì defended the city,
and when food in the city ran out,
he sought help from Zhū Quánzhōng,
offering his wife and children as hostages.
14. Wáng Jiàn attacked Péngzhōu,
and Chén Jìngxuǎn came to its rescue,
so he withdrew.
Wáng Jiàn extensively plundered Xīchuān,
and all twelve prefectures suffered from his actions.
Xīchuān governed the twelve prefectures of Yì, Péng, Shǔ, Hàn, Jiā, Méi, Qióng, Jiǎn, Zī, Yǎ, Lí, and Mào.
Suffered,
pronunciation according to the *pí* tone.
15. In summer,
the fourth month,
on the *gēngwǔ* day,
the emperor's mother, Wáng shì, was posthumously honored as Empress Gōngxiàn.
16. On the *rénwǔ* day,
Sūn Rú attacked Yángzhōu,
capturing it.
Textual analysis notes: The Veritable Records place Rú's capture of Yángzhōu in the fifth month,
likely based on the date the report arrived.
Now, according to the Old Annals, it says the first day of the fourth month was *rénwǔ*,
the New Annals say *wùchén*,
and the "Records of Rebellions and Chaos" say the first day of the fourth month was *guǐwèi*,
and on *jiǎshēn*,
Rú captured Yángzhōu.
The "Wú Records" and "Ten Kingdoms Chronicle" do not specify a day,
only stating the fourth month.
Now, follow the Old Annals and the Chronicle.
Rú proclaimed himself Military Commissioner of Huáinán.
Yáng Xíngmì was about to flee to Hǎilíng,
but Yuán Xí advised him to return to Lúzhōu,
to plan for further advances,
and he followed this advice.
17. Zhū Quánzhōng sent his generals Dīng Huì, Gě Cóngzhōu, and Niú Cúnjié to lead tens of thousands of troops to rescue Héyáng.
Lǐ Cúnxiào ordered Lǐ Hǎnzhī to attack the city with infantry,
while he personally led cavalry to engage in battle at Wēn.
Wēn County,
belonged to Mèngzhōu.
Mèngzhōu administered Héyáng.
The "Jiǔyù Zhì" states: Wēn is seventy *li* east of Héyáng.
Led,
read as *shuài*.
Ān Xiūxiū, fearing punishment,
fled to Càizhōu.
The Biàn troops divided their forces intending to cut off the Tàiháng Road,
and Kāng Jūnlì and others, fearing this,
led their troops back.
Zhū Quánzhōng recommended Dīng Huì as the Interim Military Commissioner of Héyáng,
and reappointed Zhāng Quányì as Governor of Hénán.
Huì was from Shòuchūn;
Cúnjié was from Bóchāng.
Quányì was grateful to Quánzhōng for rescuing him,
and from then on, he wholeheartedly attached himself to him.
By this time, Zhū Quánzhōng had also annexed Luò and Mèng.
Quányì was responsible for supplying him with provisions and weapons without shortage.
Lǐ Hǎnzhī was appointed Prefect of Zézhōu,
concurrently holding the position of Military Commissioner of Héyáng.
Hǎnzhī left his son Qí to serve Kèyòng,
while he himself returned to Zézhōu,
focusing entirely on plundering and raiding.
For several hundred *li* between Huái, Mèng, Jìn, and Jiàng,
there were no prefects in the prefectures,
no magistrates in the counties,
no wheat or grain in the fields,
and no smoke from hearths in the settlements.
This lasted nearly ten years.
Between Hézhōng and Jiàngzhōu was Móyún Mountain,
extremely high,
where people gathered for protection.
Bandits and robbers could not approach,
but Hǎnzhī attacked and captured it.
People at the time called him
"Lǐ Móyún".
18. Yuè Cóngxùn moved his army to Huánshuǐ,
and Luó Hóngxìn sent his general Chéng Gōngxìn to attack Cóngxùn,
beheading him.
Both he and his father, Yuè Yànzhēn, had their heads displayed at the army gate.
On the *guǐsì* day,
he sent an envoy with generous gifts to reward Quánzhōng's army,
requesting to establish friendly relations.
Quánzhōng then recalled his army.
An edict appointed Luó Hóngxìn as Acting Interim Military Commissioner of Wèibó.
19. Guīzhōu Prefect Guō Yǔ attacked Jīngnán,
expelling Wáng Jiànzhào.
Wáng Jiànzhào had occupied Jīngnán the previous year.
An edict appointed Yǔ as the Interim Military Commissioner of Jīngnán.
After the turmoil of war in Jīngnán,
only seventeen households remained.
Yǔ diligently governed,
comforting and gathering the devastated people,
promoting commerce and encouraging agriculture.
By his later years, the population had nearly reached ten thousand households.
In the third year of the Tiānfù era of Emperor Zhāozōng,
Chéng Ruì was defeated and killed by Huáinán general Lǐ Shénfú.
The so-called later years
likely refer to this time.
Governed,
pronunciation according to the *zhí lì* tone.
He took nurturing the people as his primary task,
while only Huàzhōu Prefect Hán Jiàn recruited and settled the displaced,
encouraged agriculture and sericulture.
Within a few years,
the people were prosperous and the army well-supplied.
People at the time called them "Northern Hán, Southern Guō".
Qín Zōngquán's subordinate general Cháng Hòu occupied Kuízhōu,
and Yǔ, along with his general Xǔ Cún from Rǔyáng, attacked and seized it.
After some time,
the court appointed Yǔ as Military Commissioner of Jīngnán,
and Jiànzhào as Military Commissioner of Wǔtài.
Qiánzhōu was the Wǔtài Army.
Yǔ's memorial regarding his name is recorded in the first year of the Guāngqǐ era in the previous volume.
20. Lǐ Kèyòng was additionally appointed as *Shìzhōng*.
21. In the fifth month,
on the *jǐhài* day,
Zhū Quánzhōng was additionally appointed as *Shìzhōng*.
22. After Zhào Déyīn lost Jīngnán,
Jīngnán was then seized by Chéng Ruì.
On the *rényín* day,
he surrendered the Shānnán East Circuit.
In the fourth year of the Zhōnghé era,
Qín Zōngquán sent Zhào Déyīn to occupy Xiāngyáng,
and by now he surrendered.
Surrendered,
pronunciation according to the *hù jiāng* tone.
Quánzhōng submitted a memorial requesting Déyīn serve as his deputy.
An edict established the Shānnán East Circuit as the Zhōngyì Army,
appointing Déyīn as its Military Commissioner,
and concurrently Deputy Commander of the Càizhōu Four Fronts Campaign Headquarters.
23. After Zhū Quánzhōng gained Luò and Mèng,
he had no worries about the west,
so he launched a major attack on Qín Zōngquán,
heavily defeating Zōngquán south of Càizhōu.
The Old Book's Imperial Annals state: The Càizhōu campaign headquarters reported a major defeat of the bandits at Lóngbēi,
then advanced troops to press the bandit city.
Zōngquán garrisoned Zhōngzhōu,
Zhōngzhōu,
refers to the central city of Càizhōu.
24. Fèngxiáng Military Commissioner Lǐ Màozhēn was additionally appointed as Acting *Shìzhōng*.
At that time, Chén Jìngxuān was engaged in conflict with Wáng Jiàn,
causing the payment of tribute and taxes to be interrupted.
This indicates that Chén Jìngxuān had previously regularly submitted tribute and taxes,
but was now hindered by military affairs,
leading to their cessation.
Wáng Jiàn used this as a charge against Chén Jìngxuān and questioned him.
Having no territory to plunder upon retreat,
Wáng Jiàn considered withdrawing his troops.
However, Zhōu Xiáng and Qíwú Jiàn believed this was inadvisable.
Zhōu Xiáng said:
"The walls and moats of Qióngzhōu are solid and complete,
and its provisions can last for several years.
We can occupy it as a base."
Wáng Jiàn replied:
"Having long been in the military,
I have observed that those who wage war, if they do not rely on the authority of the Son of Heaven,
will find it easy for the hearts of the masses to drift away.
It would be better to detail Chén Jìngxuān's crimes in a memorial,
petitioning the imperial court,
to appoint a high minister as commander and assist him.
Then success might be achieved."
He then had Zhōu Xiáng draft the memorial,
requesting to campaign against Chén Jìngxuān to atone for his own crimes,
and also seeking control of Qióngzhōu.
Gù Yànlǎng also submitted a memorial requesting the pardon of Wáng Jiàn's crimes,
and the transfer of Chén Jìngxuān to another military command to pacify the two Chuān regions.
Wáng Jiàn raised troops within the jurisdiction of Dōngchuān to attack Xīchuān,
leading to a protracted war with no resolution,
causing unrest in both Chuān regions.
Earlier,
during the rebellion of Huáng Cháo,
the Emperor was then the Prince of Shòu,
accompanying Emperor Xīzōng in his flight to Shǔ.
For details, see the first year of the Guāngmíng era of Emperor Xīzōng in scroll 254.
Many of the imperial princes had to travel on foot through the mountain valleys.
The Prince of Shòu, exhausted,
could not proceed,
and lay down on a large rock.
Tián Lìngzī arrived from behind
and urged him to move.
The Prince said:
"My feet hurt.
I hope the Army Supervisor can provide a horse."
Tián Lìngzī said:
"This is a remote mountain area,
where can we find a horse!"
He then whipped the Prince to make him move forward.
The Prince looked back but said nothing,
harboring resentment in his heart.
After ascending the throne,
the Emperor sent someone to oversee the Xīchuān army,
but Tián Lìngzī did not obey the edict.
Tián Lìngzī relied on Chén Jìngxuān,
refusing to leave Xīchuān.
The Emperor intended to subdue him by force.
Coincidentally, he received the memorials from Gù Yànlǎng and Wáng Jiàn.
Realizing that what Tián Lìngzī relied on was Chén Jìngxuān,
in the sixth month,
he appointed Wéi Zhāodù concurrently as Zhōngshū Lìng,
and made him Military Governor of Xīchuān,
concurrently serving as Pacification Commissioner and other posts for the two Chuān regions.
He summoned Chén Jìngxuān to serve as Commander of the Lóngwǔ Army.
Wáng Jiàn's army was stationed at Xīndū.
At that time, local magnates from Miánzhú such as Hé Yìyáng and Fèi Shīqín from Ānrén
(In the third year of the Wǔdé era,
Ānrén County was established from parts of Línqióng and Yīzhèng,
belonging to Qióngzhōu.
According to the "Jiǔyù Zhì": It is located 38 li northeast of the prefecture.
Fèi,
pronounced as fèi.
Qín,
pronounced as qín.)
commanded followers, some numbering ten thousand,
others a thousand.
Wáng Jiàn sent Wáng Zōngyáo to persuade them,
and they all led their followers to join Wáng Jiàn,
providing him with supplies and provisions.
Wáng Jiàn's army thus regained strength.
26. The Yòuguó Army was established in Hénán Prefecture,
with Zhāng Quányì appointed as its Military Governor.
27. In autumn,
the seventh month,
Lǐ Hǎnzhī led Hé dōng troops to raid Héyáng,
but was repelled by Dīng Huì.
28. Fèngzhōu was elevated to a military governorship,
with Xīngzhōu and Lìzhōu placed under its jurisdiction.
Mǎn Cún, the Defensive Commissioner of Fèngzhōu, was appointed Military Governor and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
(In the second year of the Zhōnghé era of Emperor Xīzōng,
the Gǎnyì Army was established with Xīngzhōu and Fèngzhōu,
with Yáng Shèng as Military Governor,
tasked with defending Sǎnguān.
However, the military governorship was not formally established.
After Yáng Shèng was defeated and fled,
no new commander was appointed.
Now, the military governorship was formally established in Fèngzhōu,
and Mǎn Cún was appointed as Military Governor.)
29. Luó Hóngxìn, acting as Interim Military Governor of Wèibó, was appointed as Military Governor.
30. In the eighth month,
on the Wùchén day,
Zhū Quánzhōng captured the southern city of Càizhōu.
31. Yáng Xíngmì, fearing pressure from Sūn Rú,
considered leading a light force to raid Hóngzhōu.
Yuán Xí said:
"Zhōng Chuán has long secured Jiāngxī.
(In the second year of the Zhōnghé era,
Zhōng Chuán occupied Hóngzhōu.)
He is not easy to contend with.
Zhào Huò has newly obtained Xuānzhōu.
(Last year, Zhào Huò gained Xuānzhōu.
Huò,
pronounced as huò.)
The hearts of the people are not yet attached to him.
You should use humble words and generous gifts
to persuade Sūn Duān from Hézhōu and Zhāng Xióng from Shàngyuán
to cross the river from Cǎishí and invade his territory.
He will certainly come to engage them,
and you can cross the river from Tóngguān to join them."
(Now, Tónglíng County, 140 li northeast of Chízhōu, has Tóngguānzhǔ.)
Yáng Xíngmì followed this advice,
leaving Cài Cháo to defend Lúzhōu,
and leading his generals to cross the river from Sǎntán.
(According to the "Jiǔyù Zhì": Wúwéi County in the Wúwéi Army has the Sǎntán town.
Now, traveling by river from the Sǎntán estuary eastward, one passes the Níchà estuary,
and further east, the Zhàjiāng estuary.
Shuài,
pronounced as shuài;
similarly below.
Sǎn,
pronounced as sǎn.)
Sūn Duān and Zhāng Xióng were defeated by Zhào Huò.
Zhào Huò's generals Sū Táng and Qī Lǎng led 20,000 troops to station at Héshān.
(In Dāngtú County of Xuānzhōu, there is Héshān to the southwest,
with Dōngliángshān to its east.)
"You should lead troops swiftly towards Héshān,
fortify your position and defend it.
When they cannot engage in battle,
they will think we are timid.
Taking advantage of their laxness,
we can defeat them."
Yáng Xíngmì followed this advice.
Sū Táng and others were heavily defeated,
and Xuānzhōu was besieged.
Zhào Huò's elder brother, Zhào Gānzhī, led troops from Chízhōu to rescue Xuānzhōu.
(In the fourth year of the Wǔdé era,
Chízhōu was established from the Qiūpǔ and Nánlíng counties of Xuānzhōu.
In the first year of the Zhēnguān era,
the prefecture was abolished.
In the first year of the Yǒngtài era,
Chízhōu was re-established from Qiūpǔ and Qīngyáng of Xuānzhōu, and Zhìdé of Ráozhōu.
According to the "Jiǔyù Zhì": Chízhōu is 325 li east of Xuānzhōu.)
He was defeated.
Jiǔhuáshān
is located within the boundaries of Qīngyáng County, Chízhōu.
It was originally named Jiǔzǐshān.
Lǐ Bái, seeing that its peaks resembled lotus flowers,
renamed it Jiǔhuá.
Yáng Xíngmì appointed Zhāng Yǎ as the Military Commissioner of Chízhōu.
32. In the ninth month,
due to interrupted supply lines,
and considering that Qín Zōngquán's remaining forces were too devastated to pose a serious threat,
Zhū Quánzhōng led his troops back.
On the Bǐngshēn day,
he sent Zhū Zhēn with 5,000 troops to escort Liú Zàn, the newly appointed Prefect of Chǔzhōu, to his post.
(Zhū Quánzhōng, considering himself concurrently in charge of Huáinán,
regarded Chǔzhōu as within his jurisdiction,
hence he appointed the prefect himself.)
33. Qián Liú sent his cousin Qián Qiú to lead troops to attack Xú Yuē in Sūzhōu.
34. In winter,
the tenth month,
Xú troops intercepted Zhū Zhēn and Liú Zàn, preventing them from advancing.
(Xú troops refer to the forces of Shí Pǔ.)
They captured Pèi and Téng counties,
inflicting tens of thousands of casualties and captures.
35. Mèng Fānglì sent his general Xī Zhōngxìn with 30,000 troops to raid Liáozhōu.
(Liáozhōu originally comprised the territories of the Hàn dynasty's Shàng'ài and Zhān counties.
The Jìn dynasty established the Lèpíng Commandery.
In the third year of the Wǔdé era,
Liáozhōu was established.
In the eighth year,
it was renamed Jīzhōu.
In the first year of the Xiāntiān era,
to avoid the personal name of Emperor Xuánzōng,
it was renamed Yízhōu.
In the third year of the Zhōnghé era,
it was renamed Liáozhōu.)
He was heavily defeated,
and Xī Zhōngxìn was captured and sent to Jìnyáng.
36. On the Xīnmǎo day,
Emperor Huìshèng Gōngdìng Xiào was buried at the Jìnglíng tomb.
(Jìnglíng is located 10 li northeast of Fèngtiān County, Jīngzhào Prefecture.)
37. Upon hearing that Wéi Zhāodù was about to arrive,
Chén Jìngxuān and Tián Lìngzī trained troops and fortified the city to resist him.
In the eleventh month,
Shí Pǔ personally led 70,000 infantry and cavalry to camp at Wúkāngzhèn.
According to Xuē Jūzhèng's History of the Five Dynasties,
Zhū Zhēn attacked Fēng,
and captured it.
Shí Pǔ gathered his entire army to engage in battle south of Fēng at Wúkānglǐ.
He was utterly defeated.
Zhū Quánzhōng also sent a separate general to attack Sùzhōu,
and its prefect Zhāng Yǒu surrendered to him.
On the bǐngshēn day,
a separate general of Qín Zōngquán attacked and captured Xǔzhōu,
seizing the loyal military interim governor Wáng Yùn,
and retook Xǔzhōu.
Last year, Zōngquán was defeated by Quánzhōng,
and abandoned Xǔzhōu.
Wáng Yùn was likely appointed by Quánzhōng.
In the twelfth month,
the Cài general Shēn Cóng captured Zōngquán,
broke his legs and imprisoned him,
then surrendered to Quánzhōng.
Quánzhōng recommended Cóng as the interim governor of Càizhōu.
Earlier,
the Gǎnyì military commissioner Yáng Shèng, after losing Xīng and Fèng,
see the second year of the Guāngqǐ era in the previous scroll.
Wáng Jiàn attacked Xīchuān,
Tián Lìngzī, because Shèng was his former general,
appointed him acting military commissioner of Wēiróng,
and had him defend Péngzhōu.
Yáng Shèng
was formerly a Shéncè commandant.
Chén Jìngxuān's Méizhōu prefect Shān Xíngzhāng led 50,000 troops to fortify Xīnfán in order to rescue him.
Xīnfán
was the Fán county of the Hàn dynasty.
The Later Sovereign of Shǔ added
the character
"new"
to it,
and it belonged to Chéngdū prefecture in the Táng.
Sòng Bái said: Xīnfán was originally the Fán county of the Hàn.
In the tenth year of the Yánxī era of the Shǔ Later Sovereign,
a Hú chieftain from Liángzhōu led his followers to surrender to Shàn,
and settled in Fán county.
The population was moved here,
and it was commonly called Xīnfán.
The county name was changed according to custom.
On the dīnghài day,
Wéi Zhāodù was appointed as the campaign pacification commissioner,
with the Shānnán Xīdào military commissioner Yáng Shǒuliàng as his deputy,
and the Dōngchuān military commissioner Gù Yànlǎng as the campaign military administrator;
the prefectures of Qióng, Shǔ, Lí, and Yá were separated to establish the Yǒngpíng army,
with Wáng Jiàn appointed as its military commissioner,
governing from Qióngzhōu,
and serving as the commander of all campaign armies.
On the wùzǐ day,
Chén Jìngxuān was stripped of his official titles and ranks.
The Shānnán Xīdào military commissioner Yáng Shǒuhòu
captured Kuízhōu.
According to the New Book,
Yáng Shǒuliàng was then commanding Shānnán Xīdào,
and Shǒuhòu was the prefect of Miánzhōu.
Could it be that Yáng Shǒuliàng sent Shǒuhòu to capture Kuízhōu?
