Later Student of Tiāntāi
First year of Lóngjì
(Jǐyǒu, 889)
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the guǐsì day, the first day of the month,
a general amnesty was proclaimed,
and the era name was changed.
Textual analysis says: The Táng Nián Bǔlù states:
"In the first month,
on the guǐsì day,
the second year of Wéndé was changed to the first year of Lóngjì,
and all officials presented the imperial honorific title of Shèngwén Ruìdé Guāngwǔ Hóngxiào Huángdì."
The New and Old Annals and the Veritable Records
state that the honorific title was presented in the first month of the following year.
The Bǔlù is mistaken.
The Old Annals also states:
"The Jiànnán Xīchuān military commissioner and Liǎngchuān pacification and control commissioner Wéi Zhāodù was appointed as the guardian of the Eastern Capital."
According to this, Zhāodù became guardian in the second year of Dàshùn.
The Old Annals is mistaken.
Now all follow the Veritable Records.
2 Hànlín academician recipient of edicts and vice minister of war Liú Chóngwàng was appointed tóng píngzhāng shì.
3 The Biàn general Páng Shīgǔ captured Sùqiān,
and stationed his army at Lǚliáng.
Jiǔyùzhì: Péngchéng county of Xúzhōu has a Lǚliáng flood control town.
He was badly defeated,
and retreated to defend Péngchéng.
4 On the rénzǐ day,
the Cài general Guō Fán killed Shēn Cóng,
and sent Qín Zōngquán to Biàn,
reporting to Zhū Quánzhōng:
"Cóng plotted to re-establish Zōngquán."
Quánzhōng appointed Fán as the interim governor of Huáixī.
Zhū Quánzhōng thus annexed Huáixī to connect with Xiāng and Dèng,
and his power grew even stronger.
5 On the wùshēn day,
Wáng Jiàn heavily defeated Shān Xíngzhāng at Xīnfán,
killing and capturing nearly ten thousand men,
and Xíngzhāng barely escaped with his life.
Yáng Shèng, fearing,
moved his camp to Sānjiāo,
while Xíngzhāng camped at Méngyáng,
and they faced off against Jiàn.
In the second year of the Yífèng era,
Méngyáng county was established from parts of Jiǔlǒng, Luò, and Shífāng counties,
and belonged to Péngzhōu.
Jiǔyùzhì: It is located 31 lǐ east of the prefectural seat.
Sòng Bái said: The county is north of the Méng River,
hence the name Méngyáng.
6 In the second month,
Zhū Quánzhōng sent Qín Zōngquán to the capital,
and he was executed at Dúliǔ.
Textual analysis says: The Old Annals:
"On the jǐchǒu day of the second month,
Biànzhōu campaign military administrator Lǐ Fán supervised the delivery of Qín Zōngquán and his wife Lady Zhào for presentation,
and they were executed at Dúliǔ."
The Veritable Records:
"In the third month,
Quánzhōng presented Zōngquán,
who was executed at Dúliǔ."
The New Annals:
"On the wùchén day of the second month,
Zhū Quánzhōng captured Zōngquán and presented him.
On the jǐchǒu day,
Zōngquán was executed."
Considering that Zōngquán left Biàn in the first month,
he should not have reached Cháng'ān only in the third month;
if he was presented as a captive on wùchén,
he should not have been executed only on jǐchǒu.
Therefore, it is simply stated as the second month.
Zōngquán, from inside the cage cart, stretched out his head and said to Kuí:
"Your Excellency, consider whether Zōngquán is truly a rebel?
It is only that my loyalty was not effective."
The onlookers all laughed.
Kuí
was a clansman descendant of Sūn Tì.
Sūn Tì served up to vice minister of justice,
and Kuí was his fifth-generation descendant.
7 In the third month,
Zhū Quánzhōng was additionally appointed Zhōngshū Lìng,
and advanced in rank to Prince of Dōngpíng.
Textual analysis says: The Old Annals places this in the fourth month,
with the enfeoffment as Prince of Dōngpíng.
Xuē Jūzhèng's History of the Five Dynasties places it in the third month,
also stating he was enfeoffed as Prince of Dōngpíng.
Now following the Veritable Records,
he was only appointed Zhōngshū Lìng.
According to the textual analysis,
then
the six characters "advanced in rank to Prince of Dōngpíng"
should be omitted.
However, according to the Old Book's imperial annals,
in the first year of Guāngqǐ,
Quánzhōng was enfeoffed as Prince of Pèijùn.
At this time, although he had not been advanced to Prince of Dōngpíng,
he was certainly already a prince.
His military power grew even stronger.
Fèngguó military commissioner Zhào Déyīn was additionally appointed Zhōngshū Lìng.
In the second year of the Zhōnghé era of Emperor Xīzōng,
Càizhōu was made the Fèngguó army,
and Qín Zōngquán was appointed its military commissioner.
In the first year of Wéndé,
Xiāngzhōu was made the Zhōngyì army,
and Zhào Déyīn was appointed its military commissioner.
After Zōngquán perished,
the Fèngguó commission was never conferred on anyone else,
and Zhào Déyīn also never held the Fèngguó commission concurrently.
Therefore,
"Fèngguó"
should be changed to
"Zhōngyì."
He was appointed as the Zhōngwǔ military commissioner,
with Chénzhōu as the seat of his administration.
Zhōngwǔ was originally administered from Xǔzhōu;
Zhào Chōu,
a native of Chén,
and who had defended Chén with merit,
therefore moved the administrative seat to Chén.
Chōu,
pronunciation Chāng Niú.
He fully entrusted the military and prefectural affairs to his younger brother Chǎng,
and submitted a request to retire due to old age.
An edict appointed Chǎng to replace him as Zhōngwǔ military commissioner.
Not long after,
Chōu passed away.
8 On the Bǐngshēn day,
Qián Liú
captured Sūzhōu.
Last winter,
Qián Liú had attacked Sūzhōu;
the matter is recorded in the previous scroll.
In the third year of the Guāngqǐ era,
Xú Yuē had seized Sūzhōu,
and now he fled and died.
9 In summer,
the fourth month,
the Shǎn-Guó army was granted the honorary title "Bǎoyì".
10 In the fifth month,
on the Jiǎchén day,
Ruǎn Jié, the Military Commissioner of Rùnzhōu, died.
Qián Liú appointed Chéng Jí, the commander of the Jìngjiāng capital guards, to replace him.
11 Lǐ Kèyòng launched a major military campaign,
sending Lǐ Hǎnzhī and Lǐ Cúnxiào to attack Mèng Fānglì.
In the sixth month,
they captured the two prefectures of Cí and Míng.
Mèng Fānglì sent his generals Mǎ Gài and Yuán Fèngtāo with tens of thousands of troops to resist them.
They fought at Liúlíbēi,
and Mèng Fānglì's army was heavily defeated.
Both generals were captured,
and Lǐ Kèyòng took advantage of the victory to advance and attack Xíngzhōu.
Mèng Fānglì was suspicious and jealous by nature,
and many of his generals resented him.
By this time, none were willing to serve under Mèng Fānglì.
Mèng Fānglì felt ashamed and fearful,
and drank poison to die.
In the second year of the Zhōnghé era,
Mèng Fānglì had seized Xíngzhōu.
He had always won the hearts of the soldiers,
and the masses supported him as Acting Military Governor.
An examination of discrepancies: The Veritable Records state:
"Lǐ Kèyòng had his younger brother Lǐ Kèxiū guard Lùzhōu,
and sent Ān Jīnjùn, the prefect of Zézhōu, to attack Mèng Fānglì.
Mèng Fānglì then allied with various military governors to seek aid.
His general Xī Zhōngxìn attacked Liáozhōu.
Lǐ Kèyòng again sent Lǐ Hǎnzhī and others to launch a fierce attack.
Mèng Fānglì's general Mǎ Gài went out to fight
and was captured by Lǐ Hǎnzhī.
Mǎ Gài said to him: 'If you wish to seize Xíngzhōu,
you must first take Cízhōu.'
When the combined forces besieged Cízhōu,
Mèng Fānglì and Xī Zhōngxìn led their troops into a major battle.
The army was defeated,
and Cízhōu fell.
Mèng Fānglì returned alone on horseback to Xíngzhōu,
and Xī Zhōngxìn died there.
Mèng Fānglì felt ashamed about this,
and then plotted his own death.
The three armies established his younger brother Mèng Qiān,
and sought aid from Biànzhōu.
Zhū Quánzhōng sent Wáng Qiányù to assist them,
and Wáng Róng of Zhènzhōu sent a letter to Lǐ Kèyòng to mediate, after which he withdrew."
The Supplementary Records of the Tang Years states:
"Mèng Fānglì's strategist Shí Yuánzuǒ was captured by Ān Jīnjùn.
Ān Jīnjùn questioned him,
and Shí Yuánzuǒ suggested attacking Cízhōu,
to defeat Xī Zhōngxìn.
Ān Jīnjùn then killed him.
Mèng Fānglì indeed joined Xī Zhōngxìn in leading troops into Cízhōu.
Ān Jīnjùn fought them,
inflicting a major defeat.
Xī Zhōngxìn died,
and Mèng Fānglì entered Xíngzhōu alone on horseback.
Ashamed to face the elders,
he then took his own life."
Xuē Jūzhèng's Old History of the Five Dynasties, Biography of Mèng Fānglì, states:
"In the sixth month,
Lǐ Cúnxiào captured the two prefectures of Míng and Cí.
Mèng Fānglì sent Mǎ Gài and Yuán Fèngtāo with all their troops to engage in battle at Liúlíbēi.
Lǐ Cúnxiào attacked them,
annihilating them all,
and captured Mǎ Gài and Yuán Fèngtāo alive.
Initially,
Mèng Fānglì was harsh and impatient by nature,
and his kindness did not extend to his subordinates.
After the siege had lasted for several weeks,
he personally patrolled the city at night to comfort and exhort the troops,
but those guarding the battlements were all arrogant.
Mèng Fānglì knew the situation was hopeless,
so he drank poison and died.
His cousin Mèng Qiān, the prefect of Míngzhōu,
had always won the hearts of the soldiers,
and the masses thus recommended him as Acting Military Governor,
seeking aid from Biàn.
At that time, Liáng Zǔ was attacking Shí Pǔ,
and no relief troops were sent."
Note: Lǐ Hǎnzhī attacked and captured Cízhōu,
then advanced to attack Míngzhōu,
and only then captured Mǎ Gài.
The Veritable Records state
"Mǎ Gài advised Lǐ Hǎnzhī to seize Cízhōu,"
which seems to mistakenly identify Shí Yuánzuǒ as Mǎ Gài.
Also,
Xī Zhōngxìn had already been captured by Lǐ Kèxiū the previous year,
yet it says
"joined Mèng Fānglì in leading troops into a major battle,"
which is also an error.
The Old Annals state:
"In the sixth month,
Mèng Fānglì, the Military Governor of Xíng and Míng, died.
The three armies recommended his younger brother Mèng Qiān, the prefect of Míngzhōu, as Acting Military Governor,
and Lǐ Kèyòng sent troops to attack him."
The New Annals state:
"In the sixth month,
Lǐ Kèyòng invaded Xíngzhōu.
Mèng Fānglì, the Military Governor of the Zhāoyì Army, died.
His younger brother Mèng Qiān declared himself Acting Military Governor."
Note: The Supplementary Records of the Tang Years records a memorial from Wáng Róng reporting the statements of the major generals of Xíng and Míng,
stating that
"Mèng Fānglì suddenly passed away in this illustrious era,

and the three armies and common people together recommended his younger brother, the acting prefect of Míngzhōu, Mèng Qiān, to temporarily take charge of military affairs as Acting Military Governor."
Both the New and Old Annals, the Veritable Records, and Xuē Jūzhèng's History, Biography of Mèng Fānglì, all say that his younger brother Mèng Qiān was established.
Only the Chronological Records of Tàizǔ and Xuē Jūzhèng's History, Annals of Wǔhuáng, say that his nephew Mèng Qiān was established,
which is likely an error.
I now follow the various other texts.
Zhū Quánzhōng requested passage through Wèibó,
but Luó Hóngxìn refused.
Zhū Quánzhōng then sent his general Wáng Qiányù with several hundred elite armored troops,
to enter Xíngzhōu via a side road and jointly defend it.
12 Yáng Xíngmì besieged Xuānzhōu.
Food in the city was exhausted,
and people resorted to cannibalism.
The commander Zhōu Jìnsī seized the city and expelled Zhào Huáng.
Zhào Huáng intended to flee to Guǎnglíng,
but Tián Jūn pursued and captured him.
Not long after,
the people in the city seized Zhōu Jìnsī and surrendered.
Yáng Xíngmì entered Xuānzhōu.
The various generals competed to seize gold and silk,
but Xú Wēn alone occupied the granary,
making porridge to feed the starving.
Xú Wēn
was from Qúshān.
Zhào Huáng's general, Zhōu Běn of Sùsōng,
was the bravest in the army.
Yáng Xíngmì captured him but released him,
appointing him as a deputy general.
Sùsōng
was the territory of the Hàn dynasty's Wǎn County.
The Liáng dynasty established the Gāotáng Commandery there,
which the Suí dynasty abolished.
The Suí established Sùsōng County,
which belonged to Shūzhōu in the Táng dynasty.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is located 140 lǐ southwest of the prefecture.
Sòng Bái states: Sùsōng County
was called Sōngzī County during the Yuánshǐ era of the Hàn dynasty,
belonging to the Lújiāng Commandery.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn, because there was a Sōngzī County in Jīngzhōu,
changed it to Sùsōng.
Guàn
is pronounced gǔ wàn fān.
Zhào Huáng's attendants all scattered,
only Lǐ Déchéng followed Zhào Huáng and did not leave.
Yáng Xíngmì gave him a daughter of his clan as a wife.
Lǐ Déchéng
was from Xīhuá.
Yáng Xíngmì submitted a memorial to the court,
and an imperial edict appointed Yáng Xíngmì as the Surveillance Commissioner of Xuān and Shè.
Zhū Quánzhōng had an old relationship with Zhào Huáng,
and sent an envoy to request him.
Yáng Xíngmì consulted Yuán Xí,
and Yuán Xí said:
"It would be better to behead him and send his head."
Yáng Xíngmì followed this advice.
Not long after,
Yuán Xí died.
Yáng Xíngmì wept for him, saying:
"Does Heaven not wish me to achieve great deeds?
Why does it break my arms and legs!
I prefer leniency, yet Yuán Xí often urged me to kill—
is this why he did not live long!"
Sūn Rú sent troops to attack Lúzhōu,
and Cài Cháo surrendered the prefecture to him.
13 Zhū Zhēn captured Xiāo County,
occupied it,
and confronted Shí Pǔ.
Zhū Quánzhōng intended to go there personally to oversee the situation.
Zhū Zhēn ordered all armies to repair their horse stables;
only Yán Jiāo, a subordinate general under Lǐ Tángbīn, was lazy and negligent.
The military officer reprimanded him,
and Lǐ Tángbīn became angry.
He went to see Zhū Zhēn to complain about it;
Zhū Zhēn also became angry,
considering Lǐ Tángbīn disrespectful,
drew his sword and killed him.
Zhēn and Tángbīn had long been at odds;
seizing the moment of anger to kill him,
he acted without further consideration.
It was said that Tángbīn was plotting rebellion.
Jìng Xiáng, the Left Simǎ of Huáinán,
fearing that Quánzhōng might act rashly in anger,
and handle the matter inappropriately in haste,
therefore detained the messenger,
waited until nightfall,
and then calmly reported it.
Quánzhōng was indeed greatly shocked.
Xiáng then devised a strategy for him,
pretending to arrest Tángbīn's wife and children and imprison them,
and dispatched cavalry to console and pacify the troops.
Quánzhōng followed his advice,
and the army began to settle.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
Quánzhōng went to Xiāo County.
Before he arrived,
Zhēn came out to greet him,
but Quánzhōng ordered warriors to seize him,
accused him of unauthorized killing, and executed him.
Jìng Xiáng devised a plan for Quánzhōng to deal with Zhū Zhēn,
still using the previous strategy.
Quánzhōng became angry,
threw a bed at him,
and he withdrew.
Had Quánzhōng not killed Zhū Zhēn,
would Zhēn have been willing to serve under Quánzhōng?
Huò Cún and others pleaded for him,
but it was not considered.
Wéi,
pronounced as yú wèi fān.
On Dīngwèi day
he arrived at Xiāo County,
and appointed Páng Shīgǔ to replace Zhēn as the Chief Commanding Officer.
In the eighth month,
on Bǐngzǐ day,
Quánzhōng attacked Shí Pǔ's fortifications,
but encountered heavy rain,
and withdrew his troops.
14 In winter,
the tenth month,
Wáng Jìngwǔ, the Military Governor of Pínglú, passed away;
his son, Shīfàn,
aged sixteen,
was recommended by the army to act as Interim Governor,
but Zhāng Chán, the Prefect of Dì Prefecture, refused to comply.
An edict appointed Cuī Ānqián, concurrently the Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent, as Grand Councilor,
and appointed him as the Military Governor of Pínglú.
Chán welcomed Ānqián to the prefecture,
and together they planned to attack Shīfàn.
This laid the groundwork for Wáng Shīfàn to kill Zhāng Chán.
15 Dù Rúxiū, the Supervising Secretary, was appointed as Prefect of Sū Prefecture.
Qián Liú was displeased,
and appointed Shěn Càn, who was in charge of prefectural affairs, as the Military Commissioner and Commanding Officer.
Shěn Càn controlled the military authority,
while Dù Rúxiū was merely a nominal figure.
16 Yáng Xíngmì dispatched Tián Jūn, the Commander of Cavalry and Infantry, and others to attack Cháng Prefecture.
At that time, Dù Léng, a general under Qián Liú, was defending Cháng Prefecture.
17 In the eleventh month,
the Emperor changed his name to Yè.
18 The Emperor was about to perform sacrifices at the Circular Mound.
According to precedent,
the Palace Commanders and Privy Counsellors all wore informal robes when attending;
during Emperor Xīzōng's reign,
they already wore official robes and held tablets;
by this time,
the Emperor further ordered the relevant officials to prepare ceremonial robes for them,
ceremonial robes,
meaning court attire with swords and pendants.
The Emperor personally wrote a note instructing them:
"Your opinions are most appropriate.
Matters may require flexibility,
do not let minor flaws hinder the grand ceremony."
Thereafter, the eunuchs began to wear swords and pendants when attending sacrifices.
Examination of discrepancies: According to records, although Tián Lìngzī and Yáng Fùgōng held authority that overshadowed the sovereign,
their official ranks did not exceed General of the Imperial Guard,
so the other eunuchs must have been of lower rank.
However, various texts do not specify the rank of ceremonial robes the eunuchs desired at that time.
On Jǐyǒu day
sacrifices were performed at the Circular Mound,
and a general amnesty was declared.
While still a prince,
the Emperor had always detested eunuchs.
After ascending the throne,
Yáng Fùgōng relied on his merit in supporting the Emperor's accession,
(the support for accession is mentioned in the previous volume of the previous year).
The Emperor was displeased;
he often consulted with the chancellors on governmental affairs.
Kǒng Wěi and Zhāng Jùn advised the Emperor to follow the precedent of the Dàzhōng era to suppress the power of eunuchs.
Fùgōng often rode in a sedan chair to the Tàijí Hall.
The Tàijí Hall,
is the front hall of the Western Palace.
When the Emperor and his chancellors were discussing rebels from various regions,
Kǒng Wěi said:
"There are those around Your Majesty who are about to rebel,
let alone those in the regions!"
The Emperor, startled, asked him to explain,
and Wěi pointed at Fùgōng and said:
"Fùgōng is Your Majesty's family servant,
yet he rides a sedan chair to the front hall,
raises many strong men as adopted sons,
puts them in charge of the imperial guards,
or appoints them as regional governors—
if this is not rebellion, what is it!"
Yáng Fùgōng appointed his adopted son Shǒulì as Commander of the Tiānwēi Army,
Shǒuxìn as Commander of the Yùshān Army,
Shǒuzhēn as Military Governor of Lóngjiàn,
Shǒuzhōng as Military Governor of Wǔdìng,
Shǒuhòu as Prefect of Mián Prefecture,
and many other adopted sons served as prefects,
known as the "Outer Residence Gentlemen."
He also had six hundred adopted sons,
supervising armies in various circuits.
"I raise strong men as sons
to win the hearts of the warriors,
and to defend the state—
how could this be rebellion!"
The Emperor said:
"If you wish to defend the state,
why not have them take the surname Lǐ instead of Yáng?"
Fùgōng had no reply.
Yáng Fùgōng's adopted son, Yáng Shǒulì, Commander of the Tiānwēi Army,
originally surnamed Hú,
named Hónglì,
was the bravest in the Six Armies,
and everyone feared him.
The Emperor intended to move against Fùgōng,
but feared Shǒulì might cause trouble.
He said to Fùgōng:
"I wish to have your adopted son Hú by my side."
Fùgōng presented Shǒulì to the Emperor,
who bestowed upon him the name Lǐ Shùnjié,
and put him in charge of the keys to the Six Armies.
The Six Armies of the Northern Command
were all stationed in the palace gardens,
each camp had its own gate,
opened and closed morning and evening.
He was promoted to Chief of the Tiānwǔ Army,
concurrently serving as Military Governor of Zhènhǎi,
and soon was additionally appointed Tongpingzhangshi.
The Tiānwǔ Army was also one of the fifty-four units of the Shéncè Army.
Qī,
pronounced as jī.
The officials of the Censorate requested that he receive the assembled officials in order of rank,
but Kǒng Wěi ruled against gathering them;
he ruled on the Censorate's petition,
not allowing the assembly of all officials.
Shùnjié appeared displeased.
Another day,
he hinted at the matter,
and Wěi said:
"The chancellor is the leader of all officials,
hence there is an assembly in order of rank.
Your position is Chief of the Army,
yet you wish to receive all officials in the Hall of Government Affairs in order of rank—
do you find this appropriate?"
Shùnjié dared not mention it again.
Zhū Quánzhōng requested to oversee the salt and iron monopoly,
but Kǒng Wěi alone firmly opposed it,
saying to the reporting official:
"If Lord Zhū wants this position,
he will have to raise an army!"
Quánzhōng then desisted.
The history records that Kǒng Wěi, as chancellor of Táng,
sought to restore order and discipline,
but it is regrettable that constrained by the times,
he could not realize his aspirations.
19 Tián Jūn attacked Cháng Prefecture,
digging a tunnel into the city;
at midnight,
flags, armor, and weapons emerged from the bedroom of Dù Léng, the Military Commissioner,
and he was captured,
with thirty thousand troops garrisoning Cháng Prefecture.
20 Zhū Quánzhōng sent Páng Shīgǔ to lead troops from Yǐngshàng toward Huáinán,
to attack Sūn Rú.
During the Sòng dynasty, Lóufán County was established within the boundaries of Rǔyīn Commandery,
later the Northern Wèi used the county as the seat of Xiàcài Commandery,
the Northern Qí abolished the commandery,
the Suí dynasty changed it to Yǐngshàng County,
and the Táng dynasty placed it under Yǐng Prefecture.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: it is 117 lǐ east of the prefecture.
Qū,
pronounced as qī yù fān.
On the 21st day of the twelfth month,
the day Jiǎzǐ,
Wáng Jiàn defeated Shān Xíngzhāng and the Western Chuān cavalry general Sòng Xíngnéng at Guǎngdū;
Xíngnéng fled back to Chéngdū,
and Xíngzhāng retreated to defend Méi Prefecture.
On the day Rénshēn,
Xíngzhāng requested to surrender to Jiàn.
On the 22nd day, the day Wùyín,
Sūn Rú led troops from Guǎnglíng across the river,
and on the day Rénwǔ,
he drove Tián Yūn away,
captured Cháng Prefecture,
and appointed Liú Jiànfēng to guard it.
Rú then returned to Guǎnglíng,
and Jiànfēng further drove Chéng Jí away,
capturing Rùn Prefecture.
Chéng Jí had been guarding Rùn Prefecture for Qián Liú.
23. When the former Shānnán Dōngdào military governor Liú Jùróng was in Xiāngyáng,
a man named Shēntú Shēng taught him to refine medicine into gold.
When Tián Lìngzī's younger brother passed through Xiāngyáng,
Jùróng showed him the gold.
After Jùróng took up residence in Chéngdū,
in the fourth year of the Zhōnghé era,
Jùróng fled from Xiāngyáng to Chéngdū.
He did not give it to him,
and Lìngzī resented this.
That year,
Lìngzī killed Jùróng,
exterminating his clan.
The first year of the Dàshùn era
(Gēngxū, 890)
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the first day, Wùzǐ,
the officials presented the emperor with the honorific title "Holy, Cultured, Wise, Virtuous, Glorious, Martial, and Filial Emperor";
the era name was changed.
2. Lǐ Kèyòng urgently attacked Xíng Prefecture.
Mèng Qiān exhausted his food and strength,
captured Wáng Qiányù and the Biàn troops and surrendered.
In the second year of the Zhōnghé era of Emperor Xīzōng,
Mèng Fānglì occupied the three prefectures of Xíng, Cí, and Míng,
and by this time, they were lost.
Examination of discrepancies: The Táng Mò Jiàn Wén Lù states:
"In the first year of the Lóngjì era,
the main army defended and captured Xíng Prefecture city,
Mèng Qiān surrendered,
and Lǐ Cúnxiào was appointed as the prefect of Xíng Prefecture.
In the eleventh month,
on the fourth day,
Mèng Qiān was appointed as a supplementary training commissioner."
The Tàizǔ Jì Nián Lù and Xuē Jūzhèng's Wǔdài Shǐ Tàizǔ Jì both say:
"In the first year of the Dàshùn era,
Lǐ Cúnxiào urgently attacked Xíng Prefecture,
the Xíng commander Mèng Qiān surrendered the three prefectures of Xíng, Míng, and Cí to us,
capturing Zhū Wēn's general Wáng Qiányù and three hundred others to present,"
but without specifying the month.
The Tàizǔ Jì Nián Lù also says:
"Tàizǔ relocated Mèng Qiān to Tàiyuán,
appointing the general Ān Jīnjùn as the Xíng-Míng training commissioner."
Xuē Shǐ's Mèng Qiān biography says:
"In the first year of the Dàshùn era,
in the second month,
Qiān captured Wáng Qiányù and others and begged to surrender,
and Wǔhuáng ordered Ān Jīnjùn to replace him."
Now, we follow the Veritable Records.
Xuē Shǐ's Qiányù biography says:
"At that time, Tàizǔ's main army was campaigning against Yǎn and Yùn,
and before aid could arrive,
the people of Xíng were in distress and turned against him,
so Qiān bound Qiányù and sent him to Tàiyuán,
where he was soon killed."
According to this, at that time, Quánzhōng was attacking Shí Pǔ,
not campaigning against Yǎn and Yùn.
The Qiányù biography is mistaken.
3. On the day Rényín,
Wáng Jiàn attacked Qióng Prefecture.
Chén Jìngxuān sent his general Péngchéng Yáng Rú to lead three thousand troops to assist the prefect Máo Xiāng in defending it.
Xiāng went out to fight
but was repeatedly defeated.
Yáng Rú climbed the city wall,
saw the strength of Jiàn's troops,
and sighed:
"The Táng dynasty's mandate is exhausted.
Lord Wáng governs the masses
with strictness but not cruelty;
perhaps he can protect the people!"
He then led his troops out to surrender.
Jiàn adopted him as a son,
changing his name to Wáng Zōngrú.
On the day Yǐsì,
Jiàn left the Yǒngpíng military judge Zhāng Lín as the Qióngnán pacification commissioner,
and led his troops back to Chéngdū.
He again attacked Chén Jìngxuān.
He was from Xǔ Prefecture.
Chén Jìngxuān distributed troops and set up camps in Xīpú, Pí, Dǎojiāng, and other counties.
In the second year of the Chuígǒng era,
Xīpú County was established from part of Chéngdū County.
Pí
is an ancient Hàn dynasty county,
and in the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Chéngdū Prefecture.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Pí County is forty-five lǐ west of the prefectural seat.
Regardless of the number of able-bodied men in each household,
one man was conscripted from each household.
They gathered bamboo and wood,
transported bricks and stones,
and at night, they climbed the city walls,
striking clappers and patrolling,
without rest.
Wéi Zhāodù camped at Táng Bridge,
and Wáng Jiàn camped outside the eastern Chāng Gate;
Jiàn served Zhāodù with great respect.
On the day Xīnhài,
the Jiǎn Prefecture general Dù Yǒuqiān captured the prefect Yuán Qiánsōng and surrendered to Jiàn.
Jiàn appointed Yǒuqiān to administer the prefecture.
4. The Biàn general Páng Shīgǔ and others, with a force said to number one hundred thousand,
crossed the Huái River,
claiming to rescue Yáng Xíngmì,
and captured Tiāncháng.
On the day Rénzǐ,
they captured Gāoyóu.
"Captured" means
they surrendered and captured it.
5. In the second month,
on the day Jǐwèi,
the Zī Prefecture general Hóu Yuánchuò captured the prefect Yáng Kān and surrendered to Wáng Jiàn.
Jiàn appointed Yuánchuò to administer the prefecture.
6. On the day Yǐchǒu,
Zhū Quánzhōng was additionally appointed as the concurrent Zhōngshū Lìng.
7. Páng Shīgǔ led his troops deep into Huáinán.
On the day Jǐsì,
he fought Sūn Rú at Língtíng.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Tài Prefecture's Xīnghuà County has Língtíng Town.
8. Yáng Xíngmì sent his general Mǎ Jìngyán to lead five thousand troops,
taking advantage of the emptiness to attack and occupy Rùn Prefecture.
Lǐ Yǒu led twenty thousand troops to camp at Qīngchéng,
preparing to attack Cháng Prefecture.
Ān Rényì, Liú Wēi, and Tián Yūn defeated Liú Jiànfēng at Wǔjìn.
Last year,
Sūn Rú had sent Liú Jiànfēng to occupy Cháng and Rùn.
In the Jìn dynasty, Wǔjìn County was established from part of Qū'ē County.
In the Liáng dynasty, it was renamed Lánlíng.
In the Suí dynasty, it was abolished.
In the second year of the Táng dynasty's Chuígǒng era,
Wǔjìn County was again established from part of Jìnlíng,
belonging to Cháng Prefecture.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states
the county has Qīngchéng Town.
Yǒu
was from Héféi;
Wēi
was from Shèn County.
9. Lǐ Kèyòng led troops to attack the Yún Prefecture defense commissioner Hèlián Duó,
capturing its eastern city.
Duó sought help from the Lúlóng military governor Lǐ Kuāngwēi,
and Kuāngwēi led thirty thousand troops to aid him.
On the day Bǐngzǐ,
the Xíng-Míng training commissioner Ān Jīnjùn was hit by a stray arrow and died,
and the Hé dōng Wànshèng Army commissioner Shēn Xìn rebelled and surrendered to Duó.
When the Yōuzhōu army arrived,
Kèyòng withdrew and returned.
10. Shí Pǔ sought help from Hé dōng,
and Lǐ Kèyòng sent his general Shí Jūnhé with five hundred cavalry to aid him.
11. Lǐ Kèyòng inspected Lù Prefecture.
Because the provisions were not generous,
he became angry with the Zhāoyì military governor Lǐ Kèxiū,
scolding and caning him.
Kèxiū, ashamed and resentful, fell ill,
and in the third month,
he died.
Examination of discrepancies: The Tàizǔ Jì Nián Lù states:
"Tàizǔ sent Lǐ Hǎnzhī and Lǐ Cúnxiào to attack Xíng Prefecture.
In the tenth month,
he ordered the army to withdraw,
returning via Shàngdǎng.
Kèxiū was stingy by nature.
Tàizǔ's attendants demanded bribes from Kèxiū,
and within ten days,
tens of thousands were spent,
yet they still considered the provisions insufficient.
Seizing on this matter,
he caned Kèxiū and returned to Tàiyuán.
Soon after, Kèxiū, resentful and ashamed, fell ill."
Xuē Shǐ's Kèxiū biography says:
"In the first year of the Lóngjì era,
Wǔhuáng launched a major campaign against Xíng and Míng,
and upon withdrawing the army,
he pacified the territory of Shàngdǎng."
According to the Tàizǔ Jì, only Hǎnzhī and Cúnxiào were sent to attack Xíng Prefecture,
not that he personally went.
It seems that while Hǎnzhī and Cúnxiào besieged Xíng Prefecture,
Kèyòng only stationed the main army at the border to provide support,
and in the tenth month, he returned first.
Hǎnzhī and Cúnxiào were still besieging Xíng Prefecture,
so Mèng Qiān surrendered in the first month.
This sets the stage for Lù Prefecture's rebellion against Kèyòng.
12. The Xuānshè army was granted the name Níngguó,
and Yáng Xíngmì was appointed as its military governor.
In the summer of the 13th year,
in the fourth month,
Zhāng Jūn, a general of Sùzhōu, expelled the prefect Zhāng Shàoguāng
and attached himself to Shí Pǔ.
In the previous year, Zhū Quánzhōng had captured Sùzhōu.
Shí Pǔ sent troops to raid Dàngshān.
Zhū Quánzhōng dispatched his Yánèi Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ Zhū Yǒuyù to attack them,
killing over three thousand men
and capturing Shí Jūnhé.
The Examination of Discrepancies states: According to the *Veritable Records of Emperor Tàizǔ of the Later Liáng*,
it first says on the bǐngchén day of the fourth month,
and later says on the yǐmǎo day, Shí Pǔ sent out troops.
Checking the perpetual calendar,
the yǐmǎo day
is the last day of the fourth month.
The *Veritable Records* is mistaken.
(Zhū Yǒuyù was) the son of Zhū Quánzhōng.
On the yǐchǒu day of the 14th,
Chén Jìngxuān sent Rèn Cónghǎi, the prefect of Shǔzhōu, with twenty thousand troops to rescue Qióngzhōu.
They were defeated in battle,
and (Rèn Cónghǎi) intended to surrender Shǔzhōu to Wáng Jiàn.
Chén Jìngxuān had him killed
and appointed Xú Gōngshí to replace him as prefect of Shǔzhōu.
On the bǐngyín day,
Zhū Shí, the prefect of Jiāzhōu, surrendered his entire prefecture to Wáng Jiàn.
On the bǐngzǐ day,
Wénwǔ Jiān, a powerful local from Bódào, captured Xiè Chéng'ēn, the prefect of Róngzhōu, and surrendered him to Wáng Jiàn.
Bódào
was the former state of the Bó Marquis.
The Hàn established it as a county,
which became the seat of the Qiánwéi commandery.
The Liáng established Róngzhōu there.
Bó
is pronounced pú běi.
15. Hèlián Duó and Lǐ Kuāngwēi submitted a memorial requesting permission to campaign against Lǐ Kèyòng.
(They were) taking advantage of his misfortune.
"Kèyòng will ultimately be a calamity for the state.
Now, taking advantage of his defeat,
I request to lead the armies of Biàn, Huá, and Mèng."
(The three garrisons of) Biàn, Huá, and Mèng
were all under Zhū Quánzhōng's control at that time.
Shuài
is read as shuài.
The three garrisons of Héběi
refer to Lúlóng under Lǐ Kuāngwēi, Chéngdé under Wáng Róng, and Wèibó under Luó Hóngxìn.
Previously,
Zhāng Jùn had advanced through the influence of Yáng Fùgōng,
(an event) seen in the 254th scroll, the first year of the Guāngmíng era of Emperor Xīzōng.
Later, he attached himself to Tián Lìngzī and slighted Fùgōng.
When Fùgōng regained power,
he deeply resented him.
During the rebellion of Prince Xiāng, Yùn,
Tián Lìngzī went to rely on Chén Jìngxuān.
From then on,
Fùgōng regained power.
(The Emperor) particularly favored and relied on him.
The Examination of Discrepancies states: The Old Biography says:
"When (the Emperor) again took refuge in Shānnán,
Fùgōng replaced Lìngzī as Commander of the Shence Armies,
and dismissed Jùn from his administrative post.
When Emperor Zhāozōng was still a prince,
he deeply hated the eunuchs.
Fùgōng had the great merit of supporting his accession,
and, relying on this favor, managed affairs,
which displeased the Emperor.
At that time, many of those seeking advancement said that Jùn had strategies
and could plan great schemes.
He was reappointed as chancellor
and put in charge of finances."
According to the Old Annals, the Veritable Records, the New Annals, and the Tables,
Jùn was appointed Grand Councilor in the ninth month of the third year of the Guāngqǐ era,
and was demoted due to military defeat in the second year of the Dàshùn era.
In between, he was never dismissed.
The Old Biography is mistaken.
We now follow the New Biography.
(Zhāng Jùn) often compared himself to Xiè Ān and Péi Dù.
When Kèyòng was campaigning against Huáng Cháo and stationed in Hézhōng,
(an event) seen in the 255th scroll, the 23rd year of the Zhōnghé era of Emperor Xīzōng,
Wáng Duó was the commander-in-chief,
and Zhāng Jùn was his administrative assistant.
Hearing that Jùn had become chancellor,
(Kèyòng) privately said to an imperial envoy:
"Lord Zhāng is fond of empty talk and lacks practical ability;
he is a man who brings ruin.
The sovereign has selected him by reputation and employed him.
In the future, the one who will throw the world into chaos
is certainly this man."
Jùn heard of this and bore a grudge.
The Emperor leisurely discussed order and disorder throughout history with Jùn.
Jùn said:
"Your Majesty is so intelligent and wise,
yet both the court and the provinces are controlled by powerful ministers."
(Meaning) internally controlled by eunuchs,
externally controlled by regional commanders.
The Emperor asked him what was most urgent at present.
He replied:
"Nothing is more important than strengthening the military to subdue the realm."
The Emperor therefore extensively recruited soldiers in the capital,
reaching a total of one hundred thousand men.
When Quánzhōng and others requested permission to campaign against Kèyòng,
the Emperor ordered officials of the fourth rank and above in the Three Departments and the Censorate to deliberate on it.
The Three Departments are: the Department of State Affairs, the Chancellery, and the Secretariat.
Fourth rank and above:
the Left and Right Vice Directors of the Department of State Affairs and the Vice Ministers of the Six Ministries,
in the Chancellery and Secretariat, those from the Left and Right Remonstrance Counselors upward,
in the Censorate, those from the Vice Censor-in-Chief upward,
are all of the fourth rank.
Dù Ràngnéng and Liú Chóngwàng also considered it inadvisable.
Dù Ràngnéng and Liú Chóngwàng
were the two chancellors.
If the chancellor controls the military,
then the power of the outer court becomes weighty.
Jǐ
is pronounced zǐ xì,

Moreover, in the first year of Lóngjì, Sūn Rú was at the height of his power,

How could he have seized Yáng Prefecture and held it for over a year!
The recently compiled Tángshū biography of Yáng Xíngmì

They raised troops without the emperor's command,
hence it is called reckless.
They sent letters to Dù Ràngnéng and Xīmén Jūnsuì,
showing contempt for the court.
The emperor could not tolerate this,
and held court at Yányīng Hall,
summoning the chancellors and remonstrance officials to discuss the matter.
At the time, there were eunuchs secretly colluding with the two military governors,
so the chancellors looked at each other and dared not speak,
displeasing the emperor.
Jǐshìzhōng Niú Huī said:
"In the previous reign, during many difficulties,
Lǐ Màozhēn indeed had the merit of protecting and defending;
this refers to the time when Emperor Xīzōng fled to Shānnán twice.
Difficulty,
pronounced nàn.
He quickly launched attacks,
his intention also being to eradicate evil,
but it was inappropriate not to await an imperial edict.
Recently, it is heard that his troops have passed through Shānnán,
causing many casualties.
If Your Majesty does not appoint him as Zhāotǎoshǐ,
and use state laws to restrain him,
then the people of Shānnán will be completely wiped out!"
The emperor said:
"These words are correct."
He then appointed Lǐ Màozhēn as Shānnán Xīdào Zhāotǎoshǐ.
Niú Huī's words
served above to guide and support his sovereign,
and below to patch up relations with the fierce generals;
but if considered as a strategy for the state, they were not adequate.
8 On Jiǎshēn,
Zhū Quánzhōng arrived at Wèinán.
Zhū Xuān led ten thousand infantry and cavalry to raid Dǒumén,
and Zhū Yǒuyù abandoned his camp and fled.
Zhū Xuān occupied his camp.
Zhū Quánzhōng was unaware of this.
On Yǐyǒu,
he led troops toward Dǒumén,
and all who arrived were killed by the Yùnzhōu men.
Zhū Quánzhōng retreated his army to Hùhé.
Jiǔyùzhì: Léizé County in Púzhōu had a Hùhé Town.
On Dīnghài,
Zhū Xuān attacked Zhū Quánzhōng,
defeating him heavily,
and Zhū Quánzhōng fled.
Zhāng Guīhòu fought fiercely in the rear,
and Zhū Quánzhōng barely escaped.
Kǎoyì says: The biography of Guīhòu says it was in the eleventh month,
which is incorrect.
Now following the Liángjì.
9 Zhū Quánzhōng memorialized to demote Héyáng Jiedùshǐ Zhào Kèyù.
Kǎoyì says: The Shílù places this at the end of the first month,
saying
"Zhū Quánzhōng wanted Zhāng Quányì to obtain Héyáng,
so he memorialized that Zhào Kèyù had slanderous words and demoted him."
The Xīnjì says,
"On Jǐwèi,
Zhū Quánzhōng captured Mèngzhōu,
and expelled Héyáng Jiedùshǐ Zhào Kèyù."
Now following the Biānyílù.
Both military governors at the time were subordinate to Zhū Quánzhōng,
whether demoted or concurrently appointed,
it was solely according to his memorials.
10 Sūn Rú besieged Xuānzhōu.
Initially,
Liú Jiànfēng guarded Chángzhōu for Sūn Rú,
leading troops to follow Sūn Rú in attacking Yáng Xíngmì's Gānlù Fort.
He ordered Chén Kěyán to lead a thousand troops from his command to occupy Chángzhōu.
On the earthen hill at the eastern corner of Rùnzhōu's city wall was Gānlù Temple,
facing Běigù Mountain in front,
and backed by the great river behind.
During the Bǎolì era,
Lǐ Déyù built the temple,
and it happened that sweet dew fell,
hence it was named accordingly.
Sūn Rú likely established Gānlù Fort because of this temple.
Shuài,
read as shuài.
Chén Kěyán hastily went out to welcome them,
and Zhāng Xùn killed him with his own hand,
thus capturing Chángzhōu.
Kǎoyì says: The Xīnjì:
"In the second month of the second year of Jǐngfú,
Yáng Xíngmì captured Chángzhōu."
According to this, Yáng Xíngmì returned from Xuān to Yáng,
passed Chángzhōu,
and already praised Zhāng Xùn's achievement;
the Xīnjì is incorrect.
Now following the Shíguó Jìnián.
From then on, Yáng Xíngmì held Rùnzhōu,
and contended with the Qián clan for Chángzhōu.
11 Zhū Quánzhōng attacked Shí Pǔ for years in a row.
In the third year of Guāngqǐ,
the armies of Xú and Biàn first engaged in battle.
Troops from Yǎn, Yùn, and Hédōng came to his rescue,
but all were unsuccessful.
Moreover, floods occurred,
and six or seven out of ten people died.
Shí Pǔ was in dire straits,
and sought peace with Zhū Quánzhōng.
Zhū Quánzhōng said:
"You must transfer to another military governorship before it can be done."
Shí Pǔ agreed.
Zhū Quánzhōng then memorialized requesting to transfer Shí Pǔ to another military governorship,
and still ordered a high minister to guard Xúzhōu.
An edict appointed Ménxià Shìláng, Tóngpíngzhāngshì Liú Chóngwàng as Tóngpíngzhāngshì,
and concurrently Gǎnhuà Jiedùshǐ,
appointing Shí Pǔ as Tàizǐ Tàishī.
Shí Pǔ feared that Zhū Quánzhōng was deceiving him to kill him,
so he occupied the city and did not obey the edict.
Liú Chóngwàng reached Huáyīn and returned.
12 Zhōngyì Jiedùshǐ Zhào Déyīn died,
and his son Zhào Kuāngníng succeeded him.
Kǎoyì says: The Shílù,
before this month,
Zhōngyìjūn Jiedùshǐ Zhào Kuāngníng was restored from mourning to a certain office,
but does not state when Zhào Déyīn died.
The Xīnzhuàn and Xuēshǐ only say
"Zhào Kuāngníng was Tángzhōu Cìshǐ concurrently Qīzhōu Mǎbùjūn Dūxiào;
and when Zhào Déyīn died,
he made himself Liúhòu of Xiāngzhōu,
and the court then bestowed upon him the symbols of authority."
They also do not state the year and month.
Now appended here.
13 Fàn Huī was arrogant and extravagant, losing the hearts of the people.
Fàn Huī occupied Fúzhōu,
see the previous volume, last year.
His younger brother Wáng Shěnzhī was Dūjiān,
leading troops to attack Fúzhōu.
The people voluntarily requested to transport rice to supply the army,
and the Pínghú Cave and coastal barbarians all assisted with warships.
Pínghú Cave was outside the boundaries of Pútián County in Quánzhōu.
Jiǔyùzhì says: The present Dàfēi Mountain in Xīnghuàjūn,
the land was originally several qǐng of flat lake,
one night a storm suddenly arrived,
and in the morning this mountain was seen towering,
also called Dàfēi.
On the 14th day, Xīnchǒu,

Wáng Jiàn dispatched his clansman, Jiāzhōu Prefect Wáng Zōngyù, Yǎzhōu Prefect Wáng Zōngkǎn, Weìxìn Capital Commandant Huá Hóng, and Màozhōu Prefect Wáng Zōngyáo to lead an army of fifty thousand to attack Péngzhōu.
According to the Jiǔyùzhì, Péngzhōu is over ninety lǐ from Chéngdū.
This shows their territories were contiguous,
with the smoke of their cooking fires visible to each other.
This is the so-called
"how can one allow another to snore asleep
beside one's own bed?"
How could Wáng Jiàn not urgently attack it!
Zōngyù and others besieged it.
Yáng Shǒuliàng sent his general Fú Zhāo to rescue it,
who headed directly for Chéngdū,
and encamped at Sānxué Mountain.
Jiàn urgently summoned Huá Hóng back.
Hóng rushed swiftly and arrived.
Among Jiàn's generals at that time, only Huá Hóng possessed ample wisdom and strategy,
and was relied upon by Jiàn.
Therefore, he was urgently summoned to defend against Fú Zhāo.
Huá,
read with the hù and huà pronunciations.
With several hundred men, he went at night to a place several lǐ from Zhāo's camp,
and had many watch drums beaten;
Zhāo, thinking the Shǔ army had arrived in great force,
led his troops and fled under cover of night.
On the 15th day, in the third month,
Zhèng Yánchāng, the Minister of Revenue, was appointed as Zhongshu Shilang and Tong Zhongshu Menxia Pingzhangshi.
Yánchāng
was a paternal cousin of Zhèng Cóngdǎng.
During the Qiánfú era of Emperor Xīzōng,
Zhèng Cóngdǎng governed Hé dōng with a notable reputation and achievements.
Cóng,
read with the cái and yòng pronunciations.
The Left Shéncè Yǒngshèng Three Capital Commandants Yáng Zǐshí, Zǐqiān, and Zǐzhāo,
were all adopted sons of Shǒuliàng.
The Yǒngshèng Three Capitals
were also among the fifty-two Shéncè capitals.
Knowing Shǒuliàng would certainly be defeated,
on the Rénzǐ day,
they led their twenty thousand troops and surrendered to Wáng Jiàn.
Lǐ Kèyòng and Wáng Chùcún joined forces to attack Wáng Róng.
On the Guǐchǒu day,
they captured the Tiāncháng Garrison.
The Tiāncháng Garrison
was located northeast of the Hūtuó River.
On the Wùwǔ day,
Róng fought them at Xīnshì,
and inflicted a major defeat upon them,
killing and capturing over thirty thousand men;
Xīnshì
was an ancient Hàn county,
which the Táng merged into Jiǔmén County of Zhènzhōu.
On the Xīnyǒu day,
Kèyòng retreated and stationed his troops at Luánchéng.
An imperial edict mediated peace between the four military commands of Hédōng, Zhèn, Dìng, and Yōu.
Yáng Shèng sent letters to Yáng Shǒuzhēn, Yáng Shǒuzhōng, and Yáng Shǒuhòu,
urging them to attack Dōngchuān to relieve the siege of Péngzhōu.
Shǒuzhēn and the others complied.
The Shéncè Supervising General Dòu Xíngshí was garrisoning Zǐzhōu.
Shǒuhòu secretly induced him to act as an inside agent;
when Shǒuhòu reached Fúchéng,
Xíngshí's plot was exposed,
and Gù Yànhuī executed him.
The Kǎoyì states: According to the Shílù,
"In the first month of the following year,
Yáng Shǒuhòu attacked Dōngchuān,
using Dòu Xíngshí as an inside agent.
The affair was exposed,
Xíngshí died,
and Shǒuhòu fled."
This was because Lǐ Màozhēn and Wáng Jiàn were contending for Dōngchuān,
and they recounted the events of this year.
Now we follow the Shíguó Jìnián.
When Shǒuzhēn and Shǒuzhōng's armies arrived,
they had nowhere to return to,
and lingered between Mián and Jiàn.
Mián and Jiàn
are the names of two prefectures.
Sòng Bái said: Miánzhōu
was the territory of Fúchéng County in the Hàn,
the Western Wèi established Tóngzhōu there;
the Suí established Miánzhōu,
named after the Mián River.
The Jiǔyùzhì states: Miánzhōu is two hundred and ninety-four lǐ northeast to Jiànzhōu.
They defeated them.
On the Guǐhài day,
the Xīchuān general Lǐ Jiǎn intercepted and attacked Shǒuzhōng at Zhōngyáng.
The Jiǔyùzhì states: Bāxī County of Miánzhōu had the Zhōngyáng Garrison.
In summer,
the fourth month,
Jiǎn also defeated Shǒuhòu at Tóngmóu,
killing and capturing over three thousand men,
and forcing fifteen thousand to surrender;
Shǒuzhōng and Shǒuhòu both fled.
On the Yǐyǒu day,
the Wǔshèng Army was established in Hángzhōu,
with Qián Liú appointed as its Defense Commissioner.
The Tiānwēi Army Commander Jiǎ Déshèng,
because of Lǐ Shùnjié's death,
harbored considerable resentment and indignation.
(Lǐ Shùnjié's death is recorded in the previous scroll of the previous year.)
He was denounced and killed.
Over a thousand cavalry under Déshèng's command fled to Fèngxiáng,
and Lǐ Màozhēn thereby grew even stronger.
Lǐ Kuāngwēi sent troops to invade Yún and Dài.
On the Rényín day,
Lǐ Kèyòng finally led his troops back.
He led them back from Zhènzhōu.
Shí Pǔ sent troops to invade southward,
reaching Chǔzhōu.
Yáng Xíngmì's generals Zhāng Xùn and Lǐ Déchéng defeated them at Shòuhé,
and then captured Chǔzhōu,
seizing its Prefect Liú Zuàn.
(Zhū Quánzhōng appointed Liú Zuàn as Prefect of Chǔzhōu,
see scroll 257, the third year of the Guāngqǐ era of Emperor Xīzōng.)
After Zhāng Xùn and others defeated the Xú troops,
they took advantage of the victory to capture Biàn's Chǔzhōu.
The Kǎoyì states: According to the Xīn Jì,
"On the Yǐsì day of the third month,
Yáng Xíngmì captured Chǔzhōu,
and seized Prefect Liú Zuàn."
The Shíguó Jìnián states,
"In the third month,
Shí Pǔ dispatched thirty thousand troops to invade southward, reaching Chǔzhōu;
in the fourth month,
Yáng Xíngmì's generals Zhāng Xùn and Lǐ Déchéng defeated the Xú troops at Shòuhé,
capturing and beheading three thousand,
took Chǔzhōu,
and seized Zuàn."
Now we follow this.
The
Bīnníng Military Commissioner Wáng Xíngyú was additionally appointed as Zhongshu Ling.
Yáng Xíngmì repeatedly defeated Sūn Rú's troops,
overrunning his Guǎngdé camp.
(The Guǎngdé camp was Sūn Rú's military camp at Guǎngdé.)
Defeated,
read with the bǔ and mài pronunciations.
They severed his supply routes.
In the second year of the Yìníng era,
Shěn Fǎxīng partitioned Wúchéng to establish Ānjí County,
the Táng continued it,
and it belonged to Húzhōu.
The Jiǔyùzhì states: It is one hundred and seventy-one lǐ southwest of the prefecture.
Severed,
read with the duǎn sound.
A great epidemic broke out among the soldiers,
and he dispatched his generals Liú Jiànfēng and Mǎ Yīn to lead separate forces to plunder the various counties.
In the sixth month,
Xíngmì heard that Rú was ill with malaria.
On the Wùyín day,
he unleashed his troops to attack him.
It happened to be raining heavily and very dark,
Rú's army was badly defeated,
Ān Rényì overran more than fifty of Rú's stockades,
Tián Jūn captured Rú in battle,
beheaded him,
and sent his head to the capital.
Many of Rú's troops surrendered to Xíngmì.
In the third year of the Guāngqǐ era,
Sūn Rú began to engage in battle with Xíngmì,
and by now was defeated.
Sūn Rú attacked Xíngmì with forces ten times larger,
and his wisdom and courage were also not greatly inferior,
yet he ultimately perished at Xíngmì's hands because
Rú focused solely on killing and plundering,
failing to win the people's hearts,
and furthermore had no secure rear base.
Although Xíngmì was hard-pressed by Rú,
he separately dispatched Zhāng Xùn and Lǐ Déchéng to seize territory in Huái and Zhè to expand his own domain,
and also distributed surplus grain to feed the starving people.
Having thus won the people's hearts,
and possessing a secure base,
this is why he prevailed.
They fled south to Hóngzhōu,
and elected Jiànfēng as their commander,
with Yīn as Vanguard Commandant,
and Zhāng
Jí as chief strategist.
By the time they reached Jiāngxī,
their forces numbered over a hundred thousand.
On the Dīngyǒu day,
Yáng Xíngmì led his troops back to Yángzhōu.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Bǐngchén day,
he reached Guǎnglíng.
He memorialized to have Tián Jūn defend Xuānzhōu,
and Ān Rényì defend Rùnzhōu.
Previously,
Yángzhōu's wealth and prosperity were the greatest in the land,
and people of the time spoke of "Yáng One, Yì Two,"
meaning Yángzhōu ranked first,
and Yìzhōu was second.
(Qín Yàn, Bì Shīduó, Sūn Rú, and Yáng Xíngmì.)
For a thousand lǐ east and west, the land was utterly swept clean.
Wáng Jiàn besieged Péngzhōu,
but for a long time could not capture it.
The people all fled and hid in the mountains and valleys.
The various camps would go out daily to capture and plunder,
calling it
"sifting the captives."
The commanders would first choose the best among them,
and the rest would be divided among the soldiers.
This became the usual practice.
There was a soldier named Wáng Xiānchéng,
a man of Xīnjīn,
originally a scholar.
Due to the turmoil of the times,
he became a soldier.
Considering that among the generals, only Wáng Zōngkǎn of the northern camp was the most virtuous,
he went to persuade him, saying:
"Péngzhōu was originally a subordinate of Xīchuān.
Chén and Tián summoned Yáng Shèng,
ceding four prefectures to grant him,
as seen in the 257th scroll, the first year of Wéndé.
Chén and Tián
refer to Chén Jìngxuān and Tián Lìngzī.
They joined with him to resist the court's orders.
Now Chén and Tián have been pacified, but Shèng still holds it.
The people of the prefecture all know that Xīchuān is their superior command
—the subordinate prefectures
regard the military governor's office as the superior command,
also called the assembly command.
At that time, the court ordered Wáng Jiàn to be the acting minister,
hence he is referred to as such.
The people do not enter the city but hide in the mountains and valleys to avoid it,
awaiting amnesty.
Now the army has been here for many months,
yet no order of amnesty has been heard.
The soldiers, moreover, follow by plundering them,
no different from bandits.
They seize their property,
drive away their livestock,
and separate the old, weak, women, and children to make them slaves.
They cause fathers and sons, brothers to be scattered, filled with sorrow and resentment.
Those in the mountains are exposed to the summer rains,
injured by snakes and tigers,
isolated, endangered, hungry, and thirsty,
with nowhere to turn for redress.
At first, they did not follow Yáng Shèng because he was not their rightful lord.
Now, if the acting minister does not show care and compassion,
they will think back to the Yáng clan."
Zōngkǎn was moved with pity,
unconsciously moving his seat forward repeatedly.
He asked him,
and Xiānchéng said:
"There is something even worse than this: now the various camps send out six to seven hundred people each morning,
entering the mountains to sift captives,
and return only at dusk.
'Bó'
means pressing close.
They rely on the city being empty.
What if someone wise among them devises a strategy,
having them take advantage of the emptiness to charge forth,
first concealing a thousand elite soldiers inside the gate,
climbing the city wall to watch as those sifting captives go a bit farther,
then sending out a hundred archers and a hundred artillerymen each,
attacking one side of the camp,
followed by five hundred laborers,
carrying firewood and earth to fill the moat and make a path,
then sending out elite soldiers to attack fiercely,
and also burning their camp.
Moreover, on the other three sides of the city, they each send out troops to demonstrate,
the demonstrating troops
are to dazzle the enemy so they do not know where to prepare.
With no time to rescue each other,
the city can send out additional troops in succession.
If this happens,
can we avoid defeat?"
Zōngkǎn was startled and said:
"This indeed could happen.
What should we do about it?"
Xiānchéng requested to list the items in a memorial to report to Wáng Jiàn.
Zōngkǎn then ordered Xiānchéng to draft it.
The main points stated:
"Regarding the matters reported today,
they must be coordinated across all four sides.
At that time, the Xīchuān troops were besieging Péngzhōu,
with camps set up on all four sides.
Zōngyù, Zōngkǎn, Huá Hóng, and Zōngyáo each commanded one side.
If the reported matters are acceptable,
I beg that they be implemented through the yá-jǔ."
Yá-jǔ
refers to having the commander's office examine and implement them.
"First,
I beg to pacify and recruit the people in the mountains.
Second,
I beg to prohibit all soldiers and their dependents in the camps from going out to plunder.
Additionally, mark an area within seven lǐ around each camp where gathering firewood and grazing are permitted.
Anyone daring to cross the markers shall be executed.
Third,
I beg to establish a Pacification Camp,
capable of accommodating several thousand people,
to settle the recruited civilians.
Zōngkǎn requests to select prudent and capable officers from his own troops to serve as Pacification Officers,
leading thirty men each, armed and patrolling day and night for defense.
Fourth,
the pacification efforts must be entrusted to one person for overall leadership.
Now that notices have been issued,
each camp will inevitably send soldiers into the mountains to recruit civilians.
When the people see them, they will undoubtedly be frightened and suspicious,
like mice seeing a wildcat.
Who would be willing to come forward?
A wildcat
is a creature that catches mice.
When mice see a wildcat, they know they are certain to die.
They only regret that they cannot escape.
How could they willingly approach it?
Hence, this is used as a metaphor.
I hope to issue an order authorizing Zōngkǎn to take sole charge of this matter.
Fifth,
I beg to strictly order the four camp commanders
to gather all the men, women, old, and young from Péngzhōu previously captured and assemble them in the training grounds.
If there are fathers and sons, brothers, or husbands and wives who recognize each other, allow them to stay together immediately.
Record the numbers in a register,
and send them in groups to the Pacification Camp.
Anyone daring to secretly hide a single person shall be executed.
Additionally, I beg to order all battalions in the prefectural headquarters,
also to conduct strict searches.
Prefecture
refers to Chéngdū Prefecture.
Search,
Shānkè fān.
Provide them with provisions and supplies according to their needs,
and send them all in groups back to the Pacification Camp.
Sixth,
I beg to establish a Jiǔlǒng Branch County within the Pacification Camp.
Péngzhōu administers Jiǔlǒng County.
Since Péngzhōu has not yet been captured,
I beg to establish a branch county.
Jiǔlǒng was originally the location of Fán County in the Hàn dynasty.
Later, during the Wèi dynasty, it was renamed Jiǔlǒng,
named after the Jiǔlǒng Mountain to the west of the prefecture.
Jiǔlǒng
consists of: first, Fúlǒng;
second, Dòulǒng;
third, Qiūlǒng;
fourth, Lóngbēnlǒng;
fifth, Zǒumǎlǒng;
sixth, Luòtuólǒng;
seventh, Qiānqiūlǒng;
eighth, Jiàochēlǒng;
ninth, Héngdānlǒng.
Nánzhèng,
an ancient county from the Hàn dynasty,
was under the jurisdiction of Xīngyuán Prefecture in the Táng dynasty.
Pacify and comfort the people,
select the strong among their young men,
and give them notices to enter the mountains themselves to recruit their relatives: When they learn that the Minister strictly prohibits plundering,
and that those previously captured by soldiers
have all been settled safely,
they will surely cheer and leap for joy,
leading each other down the mountain,
like children returning to their mother.
In no time, they will all come out.
Seventh,
Péngzhōu's land is suitable for growing hemp.
According to the Yìzhōu Records: Péngzhōu is called 'Little Pí,'
meaning its land is fertile and excellent,
comparable to Pí County.
Order the county magistrate to instruct them
to each return to their fields and villages,
take out the retted hemp and sell it,
using the proceeds for provisions and supplies.
They will surely gradually resume their livelihoods."
When Jiàn received this, he was greatly pleased
and immediately implemented it,
exactly as proposed.
Examination of discrepancies: The Old Biography of Zhāng states:
"On the twentieth day of the fifth month,
the various army cavalry and infantry soldiers arrived at the walls of Péngzhōu.
By the beginning of the seventh month,
more than fifty days had already passed.
The soldiers of the various armies had just arrived
and were harvesting wheat for provisions.
By the beginning of the seventh month,
the wheat was exhausted,
with not a single grain left.
The soldiers merely used the pretext of seeking food
to go far into the mountains every day,
plundering the fleeing civilians.
There was one soldier
who was originally a Confucian scholar.
He went to the northern camp to persuade the commander"
and so on.
The Ten States Chronicle:
"Wáng Xiānchéng said to Wáng Zōngkǎn, etc.
Xiānchéng submitted seven matters for pacification and recruitment,
all of which Jiàn adopted.
Xiānchéng
was from Xīnjīn in Shǔ Prefecture."
According to the Ten States Chronicle,
Wáng Jiàn sent Wáng Zōngyù and others to attack Yáng Shèng from Xīnchǒu in the second month,
and they then besieged Péngzhōu.
Also, Shèng wrote in a letter to Yáng Shǒuzhōng:
"Although my humble city is small,
it has been besieged and defended for three years."
However, Zhāng states that they only besieged Péngzhōu on the twentieth day of the fifth month.
Could it be that they besieged it initially without success and then went again?
Zhāng only mentions 'one soldier,'
while the Ten States Chronicle gives the surname Wáng and the name Xiānchéng.
It is unknown which book this originally came from.
The next day,
when the notices arrived,
the authority of the orders was awe-inspiring,
and no one dared to violate them.
Within three days,
the people in the mountains competed to come out,
flocking to the Pacification Camp like going to the market.
The camp could not accommodate them all,
so it was expanded.
Gradually, a market district emerged,
and they also brought out hemp to sell.
When the people saw that the villages were free from the threat of plunder and violence,
they gradually bid farewell to the county magistrate
and resumed their former livelihoods.
After over a month,
the Pacification Camp was completely empty.

Examination of discrepancies: According to the Veritable Records:
"In the tenth month of the first year of the Dàshùn era,
Lǐ Cúnxiào, the general of Tàiyuán and prefect of Xíng Prefecture, led his troops from Jìn Prefecture to occupy Xíng Prefecture."

"In the eleventh month,
on the first day, Guǐchǒu,
Lǐ Cúnxiào, the general of Tàiyuán and prefect of Xíng Prefecture, relying on his merit of capturing Sūn Kuí,
thought he should be appointed as the military governor of Zhāoyì,
and resented Kèyòng for appointing Kāng Jūnlì instead.
Cúnxiào led his troops from Jìn Prefecture back to Xíng Prefecture,
occupied the city,
submitted a memorial to the court expressing his allegiance,
and sent letters to Zhāng Jùn and Wáng Róng seeking aid."
The Tángmò Jiànwén Lù records:
"On the twenty-fourth day of the tenth month,
Lǐ Cúnxiào led troops to attack Jìn Prefecture,
then fled back to Xíng Prefecture,
and rebelled.
He wrote to Chancellor Zhāng Jùn: 'I have governed the three prefectures
for nearly two years.'
He also said: 'I often think of Ān Zhījiàn's days here,
and the time he submitted to the court.
Without support from the neighboring regions,
my family would have suffered calamity.
Because of this hesitation,
I dared not declare my intentions,
and thus last year I abruptly severed friendly relations with my neighbors.
This was not my wish,
but was due to Lǐ Mǒu's orders.'
He also said: 'Since the battles this spring,
I have truly wished to cease hostilities.
From the fifteenth day of the ninth month onward,
Lǐ Mǒu's men
urged me to advance southward to Zhào Prefecture.
They coerced Lǐ Mǒu
to enter via the Tǔmén route,
directly reaching Zhèn Prefecture.
On the fourteenth day of this month,
the soldiers and people of the Zhāoyì army requested that I temporarily act as military governor,
and submit to the court.'
When the Prince heard of Cúnxiào's rebellion,
he was greatly enraged and displayed his might.
He issued orders,
first dispatching a general to advance his army,
quickly reaching Xíng Prefecture.
They were to await further orders,
and were not to engage in battle without authorization.
They were only to surround the small fortress,
and await the main army.'"
According to the Táng Tàizǔ Jìnián Lù, Xuē Jūzhèng's Wǔdài Shǐ Jì and biographies, the Veritable Records, and the New Annals,
all state that in the tenth month of the first year of the Jǐngfú era,
Cúnxiào rebelled against Tàiyuán
and submitted to the court.
However, the Old Annals and the Tángmò Jiànwén Lù place it in the tenth month of the first year of the Dàshùn era.
The Old Annals likely conflated events that occurred later.
According to the second year, in the third month,
Ān Zhījiàn had just rebelled against Tàiyuán,
yet this letter already mentions Zhījiàn.
It also says:
"I have governed the three prefectures
for nearly two years."
Cúnxiào became the military governor of Xíng, Míng, and Cí only in the second year of the Dàshùn era.
By the first year of the Jǐngfú era,
it would indeed be two years.
Thus, the Veritable Records stating that the prefect of Xíng Prefecture occupied Xíng Prefecture
is also due to the error in the Old Annals.
The letter from Cúnxiào recorded in the Jiànwén Lù
was likely addressed to Wáng Róng,
and mistakenly said to be to Zhāng Jùn.
An edict appointed Cúnxiào as the military governor of Xíng, Míng, and Cí,

37. The Xuānmíng calendar gradually became inaccurate.
When Emperor Mùzōng ascended the throne,
he believed that as successive generations inherited the throne,
the calendar must be revised.
He thus ordered the calendar officials to revise the calendar methods,
naming it Xuānmíng.
In the twelfth month,
it was presented.
It was named the Jǐngfú Chóngxuán calendar.
Biān Gāng, along with Hú Xiùlín, the Deputy Director of the Astrological Service, and Wáng Chí, the Sima of Jūn Prefecture, revised and created the new calendar,
but the methods were entirely devised by Gāng.
Gāng was skilled in calculations,
adept at maneuvering through multiplication and division,
leading to the rise of simplified, expedient, and shortcut methods,
while the grand and systematic methods of the past declined.
Although these methods were convenient for calculation,
they were all obscure regarding their fundamental principles.
