Kuāngwēi, drunk, violated her.
In the second month,
Kuāngwēi returned from Zhènzhōu,
and upon reaching Bóyě,
Kuāngchóu seized the military headquarters and declared himself military governor-in-waiting,
using tallies to recall the troops from the field camp.
Kuāngwēi's troops scattered and returned,
and he remained in Shēnzhōu only with his close associates.
Shēnzhōu is located 150 li southeast of Bóyě.
He sent his administrative assistant Lǐ Bàozhēn
to report to the court,
requesting to return to the capital.
The capital had repeatedly experienced great turmoil,
and upon hearing Kuāngwēi was coming,
the wards and markets were thrown into great panic,
saying:
"The golden-headed king is coming to seize the state."
Officials and commoners fled and hid in the mountains and valleys.
Wáng Róng was grateful to him for losing his territory because of him,
grateful that he had rescued him, resulting in the loss of Yōuzhōu.
He built a mansion for him,
and served him as a father.
On the 10th, Liǔ Pín, the Prefect of Yúzhōu, was appointed as the Prefect of Lúzhōu.
The "Jiǔ Yù Zhì" states: From Yúzhōu west to Lúzhōu is 760 li.
Pín,
(pronounced) bù tián fān.
Textual analysis notes: The New History biography states:
"Pín was demoted to Prefect of Lúzhōu due to an incident,
and died there."
The "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán" also says he was demoted and appointed to Lúzhōu.
Both the New and Old Histories
do not record the year and month of Pín's demotion.
Now, based on the Veritable Records,
this month Pín was transferred from Yúzhōu to be Prefect of Lúzhōu.
It must be that he was first demoted to Yúzhōu and later transferred to Lúzhōu;
the New History biography and "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán" are mistaken.
For generations, his family was esteemed by scholar-officials for their filial piety, fraternal duty, and adherence to ritual propriety.
It is said that since the Yuánhé era, they have been a renowned family.
The Emperor wanted to make him Chancellor,
but the eunuchs detested him,
so he was long exiled to provincial posts.
Pín once admonished his sons and nephews, saying:
"When one's family status is high,
it is something to be feared, not relied upon.
In establishing oneself and conducting one's affairs,
if one makes a single mistake,
the offense is heavier than for others.
Upon death, one would have no face to meet one's ancestors in the underworld.
This is why it is to be feared.
High status easily breeds arrogance;
a powerful clan invites jealousy from others.
Even with fine conduct and genuine talent,
people may not believe it.
With the slightest flaw or blemish,
everyone points at it:
This is why it cannot be relied upon.
Therefore, children of noble families
should study with even greater diligence,
and conduct themselves with even greater effort,
merely to match others!"
If the sons and nephews of the Liǔ family could always abide by Pín's admonition,
each striving to cultivate and rectify themselves,
they could remain a renowned family even to this day.
Wáng Jiàn repeatedly requested permission to kill Chén Jìngxuān and Tián Lìngzī,
but the court would not allow it.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the yǐhài day,
Wáng Jiàn had someone report that Chén Jìngxuān was plotting a rebellion,
and killed him at Xīnjīn.
(Chén Jìngxuān resided at Xīnjīn;
see the second year of Dàshùn in the previous scroll.)
He died in prison.
Wáng Jiàn had his Military Judge Féng Juān draft a memorial to report this, stating:
"'Opening the cage and letting the tiger out'—
Confucius did not blame others.
'Cutting the snake on the road'—
Sūn Shū'áo did so not for his own benefit.
The Analects records Confucius reproaching Rǎn Yǒu and Jì Lù, saying:
'When a tiger or rhinoceros escapes from its cage,
whose fault is it?'
When Sūn Shū'áo of Chǔ was a child,
he returned from an outing,
worried and unable to eat.
His mother asked the reason.
Weeping, he replied:
'Today I saw a two-headed snake.
I fear my death is imminent.'
His mother said:
'Where is the snake now?'
He said:
'I heard that whoever sees a two-headed snake dies.
I feared others might see it again,
so I have already buried it.'
His mother said:
'Do not worry,
you will not die.
I have heard that
Heaven repays hidden virtue with good fortune.'
When people heard of this,
they all understood his benevolence.
I acted preemptively, fearing to miss the opportunity while the arrow was in the bow."
Juān
was the grandson of Féng Sù.
(Féng Sù's affairs are recorded in scroll 245, the first year of Kāichéng.)
Juān,
(pronounced) guī yuān fān.
The Biàn army attacked Xúzhōu
for several months without capturing it.
(They had been attacking Xúzhōu since the eleventh month of last year,
and it was now the fifth month.)
"The timing for advancing the army was inauspicious,
hence there is no achievement."
Quánzhōng considered this reasonable.
Jìng Xiáng said:
"Now we have besieged the city for months,
expending vast resources.
The people of Xú are already exhausted,
and it will fall any day.
If the officers and soldiers hear these words,
they will slacken in their assault."
Quánzhōng then burned the letter.
On the guǐwèi day,
Quánzhōng personally led troops to Xúzhōu.
On the wùzǐ day,
Páng Shīgǔ captured Péngchéng.
Shí Pǔ led his entire family to ascend the Swallow Tower and burned themselves to death.
(In the first year of Emperor Xīzōng's Zhōnghé era,
Shí Pǔ seized control of Xúzhōu.
He perished at this time.)
When Zhāng Jiànfēng governed Xú,
he had a beloved courtesan named Pànpàn.
After Jiànfēng's death,
there was a small tower in the old Zhāng residence
named Swallow Tower.
Pànpàn, cherishing her old love, did not marry.
She lived in this tower for over ten years,
secluded and melancholy.
(From Bái Jūyì's collected works.)
Textual analysis notes: The Veritable Records state:
"In the fifth month,
Biànzhōu reported the capture of Xúzhōu."
The Old History Annals state:
"In the fourth month,
Biàn generals Wáng Chóngshī and Niú Cúnjié captured Xúzhōu."
The Old History biography states:
"Pǔ sought aid from Zhū Jǐn of Yǎnzhōu.
Jǐn dispatched troops to rescue him,
but encountered heavy snow.
With provisions exhausted, they returned.
Biàn generals Wáng Chóngshī and Niú Cúnjié scaled the walls by ladders at night and entered.
Pǔ, with his wife and children, ascended a tower and burned themselves to death.
This was in the second year of Jǐngfú."
The New History Annals state:
"In the fourth month,
on the wùzǐ day,
Zhū Quánzhōng captured Xúzhōu.
Shí Pǔ died there."
Xuē Jūzhèng's Old History of the Five Dynasties, Liang Annals states:
"On the dīnghài day,
Shīgǔ captured Péngmén
and presented Pǔ's severed head."
The "Táng Tàizǔ Jìnián Lù" states:
"In the fourth month,
Lǐ Hǎnzhī of Zézhōu reported: 'Surrendered men from Huáimèng reported that Biàn general Páng Shīgǔ captured Xúzhōu on the 8th of this month.
Xú commander Shí Pǔ and his entire family perished.'"
After Wēn captured Xú,
he falsely requested the court appoint a military governor.
Emperor Zhāozōng then appointed the Minister of War Sūn Chǔ as military governor of Xú.
Later, Wēn found another pretext to dismiss him
and installed his own general to govern it.
The 8th day of the fourth month
is likely an error in the HéDōng reports.
I now follow the "Biān Yí Lù" and the New History Annals.
On the jǐchǒu day,
Quánzhōng entered Péngchéng.
He appointed Sòngzhōu Prefect Zhāng Tíngfàn as acting Military Commissioner of Gǎnhuà,
13. Lǐ Kuāngwēi was in Zhènzhōu,
repairing the city walls and moats for Wáng Róng,
mending armor and weapons,
treating him like a son.
Kuāngwēi, considering Róng young,
and also enjoying the local customs of Zhēndìng,
secretly plotted to seize his position.
Lǐ Bàozhēn, returning from the capital,
devised a strategy for him,
secretly winning over the officers and soldiers with favors.
The Wáng family had been in Zhènzhōu for a long time,
and the people of Zhènzhōu loved them,
and did not follow Kuāngwēi.
On the anniversary of Kuāngwēi's parents' death,
Róng went to his residence to offer condolences.
The day one's parents pass away,
the son considers it the anniversary.
Residence refers to
the temporary residence of Lǐ Kuāngwēi.
Ambushers seized him,
and Róng rushed to embrace Kuāngwēi, saying:
"Róng was besieged by the Jìn people,
and nearly perished.
Jìn people
refers to the troops of Lǐ Kèyòng from Hédōng.
Nearly,
jū yī fān.
If you, sir, wish to obtain the four prefectures,
this is indeed Róng's wish as well.
The four prefectures of Zhèn, Jì, Shēn, and Zhào.
I will yield my position to you, sir,
then the officers and soldiers will have no one to resist."
Kuāngwēi thought this reasonable,
and rode side by side with Róng.
Riding side by side
means riding abreast.
Suddenly, there was a great storm with thunder and rain,
and the roof tiles all shook.
Kuāngwēi entered the eastern side gate,
this was the eastern side gate of the inner city of Zhènzhōu.
After entering the gate, he was shut in by the Zhènzhōu soldiers,
cutting off those who followed him.
They punched and beat Kuāngwēi's armored guards,
placed Róng on a horse,
and carried him up onto the roof.
After the people of Zhènzhōu secured Róng,
they attacked Kuāngwēi,
killed him,
along with his clan and followers.
Examination of discrepancies: According to the Veritable Records,
Kuāngwēi was killed in the fifth month,
likely based on reports received.
The Old Annals state:
"On the yǐmǎo day of the sixth month,
Lǐ Kuāngwēi of Yōuzhōu plotted to harm Wáng Róng,
and the three armies of Héngzhōu attacked Kuāngwēi,
killing him."
The Old Biography and the Tang Tàizǔ Jìnián Lù both say the fifth month.
The New Annals say
the dīnghài day of the fourth month.
According to Kuāngchóu's memorial, it was the nineteenth day of the fourth month.
That month began on the jǐsì day,
the nineteenth day
was dīnghài.
We now follow this.
Róng's body was thin and frail,
and as he was carried by Jūn Hé,
his neck hurt and his head was tilted for several days.
Lǐ Kuāngchóu memorialized that Róng had killed his elder brother,
and requested to raise troops to seek revenge;
the imperial edict did not permit it.
14. The Yōuzhōu general Liú Réngōng led troops to garrison Yùzhōu.
When their tour of duty expired and they were not relieved,
the soldiers longed to return home.
When Lǐ Kuāngchóu assumed power,
the garrison troops supported Réngōng as their commander,
and turned back to attack Yōuzhōu.
When they reached the Jūyōng Pass,
they were defeated by the prefectural troops.
Prefectural troops
refers to the troops of the Yōuzhōu military governor's headquarters.
Defeated,
bǔ mài fān.
Lǐ Kèyòng treated him generously.
This sets the stage for Lǐ Kèyòng's later capture of Yōuzhōu.
15. Lǐ Shénfú besieged Lúzhōu.
On the jiǎwǔ day,
Yáng Xíngmì personally led troops to Lúzhōu,
and Tián Jūn led troops from Xuānzhōu to join him.
Earlier,
the Càizhōu man Zhāng Hào, known for his bravery, served Qín Zōngquán.
Later he followed Sūn Rú.
After Rú's defeat,
he defected to Xíngmì.
Xíngmì treated him generously,
and sent him to lead troops garrisoning Lúzhōu.
When Cài Cháo rebelled,
Hào switched to serving him.
When the siege became critical,
Hào climbed over the wall to surrender.
Xíngmì placed him under the command of Yuán Zhěn, commander of the Silver Spear Corps.
Zhěn, considering Hào treacherous,
reported to Xíngmì,
requesting to kill him.
Xíngmì, fearing Zhěn could not tolerate him,
placed him in his personal guard.
This sets the stage for Zhāng Hào later killing Yáng Wò.
He was from Chénzhōu.
16. Wáng Yànfù and Wáng Shěnzhī attacked Fúzhōu,
but could not capture it for a long time.
Last year in the second month,
Wáng Cháo sent Yànfù and others to attack Fúzhōu.
In the third year of the Zhōnghé era of Emperor Xīzōng,
the Zhèdōng observation commissioner was promoted to Yìshèng military governor;
in the third year of the Guāngqǐ era,
it was changed to Wēishèng military governor.
He dispatched five thousand troops from Wēn, Tāi, and Wùzhōu to rescue it.
Yànfù and Shěnzhī, considering the city walls strong,
and relief troops about to arrive,
with many soldiers dead or wounded,
reported to Wáng Cháo,
wishing to withdraw troops and plan another attempt later.
Cháo did not permit it.
They requested Cháo to come personally to the camp.
Cháo replied:
"If troops are exhausted, add more troops;
if generals are exhausted, add more generals;
when both troops and generals are exhausted,
I will come myself."
Yànfù and Shěnzhī, afraid,
personally braved arrows and stones to attack urgently.
In the fifth month,
when food in the city ran out,
Huī knew he could not hold it.
At night,
he handed the seal to the army supervisor,
abandoned the city and fled.
The relief troops also withdrew.
On the gēngzǐ day,
Yànfù and others entered the city.
On the xīnchǒu day,
Huī fled to the Coastal Command,
and was killed by the officers and soldiers.
In the second year of the Wéndé era,
Fàn Huī seized Fúzhōu.
Cháo declared himself acting military governor,
buried Chén Yán in plain clothes,
married his daughter to Yán's son Yánhuī,
and generously provided for his family.
Tīng and Jiàn prefectures surrendered,
and over twenty bands of bandits between the mountains and the sea either surrendered or dispersed.
This means the bandits either surrendered or dispersed.
From then on, the Wáng family came to possess the Seven Mǐn.
Surrendered,
hù jiāng fān.
17. In the intercalary month,
Qián Liú, the Wǔshèng defense commissioner, was appointed as Sū-Háng observation commissioner.
Qián Liú had annexed Sūzhōu with Hángzhōu,
hence this appointment.
Lǐ Chán, commander of the Yàodé Corps, was appointed as Zhènhǎijūn military governor;
Sūn Wéishèng, commander of the Xuānwēi Corps, was appointed as Jīngnán military governor.
Yàodé and Xuānwēi
were also among the fifty-two corps of the Shéncè Army.
Qián,
qú jīn fān.
Chán,
yīn chán.
Chén Pèi, commander of the Pěngrì Corps, was appointed as Lǐngnán Dōngdào military governor,
all concurrently holding the title of tóng píngzhāngshì.
At that time, Lǐ Màozhēn was arrogant and domineering.
The Emperor, considering military men difficult to control,
wished to replace them with imperial princes.
Therefore, Chéng and the other three were all granted favors,
relieved of their military authority,
and ordered to proceed to their posts.
Later, it is not heard that these four men reached their posts,
likely because others had already seized control of those areas,
and the four could not proceed to take up their posts.
Examination of discrepancies: The Old Annals state:
"On the gēngzǐ day of the third month,
Chén Pèi was appointed Lǐngnán Dōngdào military governor,
Cáo Chéng was appointed Qiánzhōng military governor,
Lǐ Chán was appointed Zhènhǎi military governor,
Sūn Wéishèng was appointed Jīngnán military governor.
At that time, the court considered Màozhēn arrogant and disrespectful of the imperial command,
and military men difficult to control,
therefore they stripped these five generals of their authority."
Now following the Veritable Records,
it was only four generals.
18. Lǐ Kuāngchóu sent troops to attack Wáng Róng's Lèshòu and Wǔqiáng,
to avenge the shame of Kuāngwēi's killing.
On the 25th day of the month (Bǐngchén),
Yáng Xíngmì sent Tián Jūn to lead twenty thousand troops from Xuānzhōu to attack Shèzhōu.
Péi Shū, the prefect of Shèzhōu, defended the city,
and it could not be taken for a long time.
At that time, many of the generals serving as prefects were greedy and cruel,
but only Táo Yǎ, the Tuanlianshi of Chízhōu, was generous and kind, winning the people's hearts.
The people of Shèzhōu said:
"If Táo Yǎ were made our prefect,
we would submit."
Yáng Xíngmì then appointed Táo Yǎ as the prefect of Shèzhōu,
and the people of Shèzhōu accepted him.
Táo Yǎ treated Péi Shū with full courtesy,
and sent him back to the court.
Péi Shū
was the great-grandson of Péi Zūnqìng.
(Péi Zūnqìng appears in the 222nd volume, second year of the Shàngyuán era of Emperor Sùzōng.)
On the 26th day, Zhū Quánzhōng ordered Páng Shīgǔ to move his troops to attack Yǎnzhōu.
He fought with Zhǔ Jǐn,
and repeatedly defeated him.
In the ninth month,
on the Dīngmǎo day,
Qián Liú was appointed as the Jiedushi of Zhènhǎi.
The Wǔshèng defense commissioner of Hángzhōu was promoted to the Jiedushi of Zhènhǎi.
Originally, the Táng dynasty established the Zhènhǎi army in Rùnzhōu.
Now it was conferred upon Qián Liú in Hángzhōu.
By the first year of the Guānghuà era,
Qián Liú requested to move the army to Hángzhōu.
(Commentary: In the fifth month of this year,
Lǐ Tǐng was appointed as the Jiedushi of Zhènhǎi,
and ordered to proceed to his post.
Now Qián Liú is appointed again.
According to this, at that time Ān Rényì had already occupied Rùnzhōu,
and Sūn Wéichéng was appointed to Jīngnán,
while Chéng Ruì had already occupied Jīngnán.
How could these two men proceed to their posts?
It seems the intention was only to strip them of their military authority,
and in reality, they did not reach their posts but returned.
The Veritable Records state,
"The title of the Zhènhǎi army was also moved to Hángzhōu."
According to the Wúyuè Bèishǐ,
in this year, Qián Liú was first appointed as the Jiedushi of Zhènhǎi,
still concurrently holding the post of prefect of Rùnzhōu.
By the first year of the Guānghuà era,
the Zhènhǎi army was moved to Hángzhōu.
The Veritable Records are mistaken.)
On the 28th day, Lǐ Cúnxiào attacked Lǐ Cúnxìn's camp at night,
capturing Sūn Kǎolǎo, the commander of the Fèngchéng army.
Lǐ Kèyòng personally led troops to attack Xíngzhōu,
digging trenches and building fortifications to encircle it.
Lǐ Cúnxiào occasionally sent troops to assault the trenches and fortifications,
but they could not be completed.
Yuán Fèngtāo, a staff officer of Hédōng, secretly sent someone to tell Lǐ Cúnxiào:
"The Prince is only waiting for the trenches to be completed before returning to Jìnyáng.
What you, Minister, fear is only the Prince.
(Lǐ Kèyòng was at that time enfeoffed as the Prince of Lǒngxī Commandery.
Lǐ Cúnxiào also held the title of Minister.)
If the Prince returns,
how can these shallow trenches
hinder the sharpness of your, Minister's, advance?"
Lǐ Cúnxiào thought this reasonable,
and halted his troops, not launching attacks.
After ten days,
the trenches and fortifications were completed,
and not even birds could fly over them.
Lǐ Cúnxiào was thus trapped.
Dèng Jìyún, a general of Biàn, who had followed Lǐ Kèyòng in attacking Xíngzhōu,
escaped back on a light horse.
(Dèng Jìyún was captured;
see the first year of the Dàshùn era in the previous volume.)
He was made to command the personal guard.
On the Yǐhài day,
Prince Sìzhōu of Tán led thirty thousand imperial guards to escort Xú Yǎnruò, the Jiedushi of Fèngxiáng, to his post,
camping at Xīngpíng.
Lǐ Màozhēn and Wáng Xíngyú combined their forces, nearly sixty thousand men,
and camped at Zhōuzhì to resist them.
The imperial guards were all newly recruited young men from the markets and streets,
while the troops led by Lǐ Màozhēn and Wáng Xíngyú were seasoned border veterans.
On the Rénwǔ day,
Lǐ Màozhēn and others advanced to press on Xīngpíng.
The imperial guards all fled in panic at the mere sight of them.
Lǐ Màozhēn and others took advantage of the victory to attack Sānqiáo.
The capital was thrown into great alarm,
with officials and commoners fleeing in all directions.
The market people again gathered at the palace gate, demanding the execution of those who had first proposed the military campaign.
Cuī Zhāowěi, harboring ill will against Dù Ràngnéng, the Grand Preceptor, Menxia Shilang, and Tongpingzhangshi,
secretly sent a letter to Lǐ Màozhēn, saying:
"The military campaign was not the Emperor's intention;
it all came from Grand Preceptor Dù."
On the Jiǎshēn day,
Lǐ Màozhēn arrayed his troops at Língāo Station.
(Língāo Station
is west of Cháng'ān city.)
He demanded the execution of Dù Ràngnéng.
Dù Ràngnéng said to the Emperor:
"I had indeed spoken of this beforehand.
I beg that I be made the scapegoat."
(Meaning to place the blame on Ràngnéng to resolve the military conflict.)
The Emperor said:
"I bid you farewell!"
That day,
Dù Ràngnéng was demoted to prefect of Wúzhōu.
(Wúzhōu is 5,500 li from the capital.
Sòng Bái said: Emperor Wǔ of Hàn established Cāngwú Commandery,
with its seat at Guǎngxìn County;
the Suí dynasty established Cāngwú Commandery,
with its seat at Cāngwú County;
the Táng made it Wúzhōu.)
(The edict read:) "Abandoning the good counsel of the ministers,
creating deep conflicts with the regional commanders,
and during consultations,
obstinately persisting even more."
Furthermore, Xīmén Jūnsuì, the Army Surveillance Commissioner, was exiled to Dānzhōu;
Lǐ Zhōutóng, the Inner Privy Commissioner, to Yázhōu;
and Duàn Xǔ to Huānzhōu.
On the Yǐyǒu day,
the Emperor went to the Ānfú Gate,
and executed Xīmén Jūnsuì, Lǐ Zhōutóng, and Duàn Xǔ.
Dù Ràngnéng was further demoted to Registrar of Léizhōu.
An envoy was sent to tell Lǐ Màozhēn:
"Those who misled me into launching the military campaign
were these three men;
it was not Ràngnéng's fault."
The eunuchs Luò Quánguàn and Liú Jǐngxuān were appointed as Left and Right Army Commandants.
On the Rénchén day,
Wéi Zhāodù, the Liúshǒu of the Eastern Capital, was appointed as Minister over the Masses, Menxia Shilang, and Tongpingzhangshi.
Cuī Yǐn, the Vice Censor-in-Chief, was appointed as Vice Minister of Revenue and Tongpingzhangshi.
Cuī Yǐn
was the son of Cuī Shènyóu.
(Cuī Shènyóu served under Emperors Wén, Wǔ, and Xuān,
and became Chancellor during the Dàzhōng era.)
He formed a deep alliance with Cuī Zhāowěi,
and thus became Chancellor.
His uncle Cuī Ānqián said to those close to him:
"My father and elder brother worked hard to establish our family's standing,
but in the end, it will be ruined by Zīláng!"
(Zīláng
was Cuī Yǐn's childhood name.)
Li Maozhēn maintained his troops without dispersing them,
demanding the execution of Dù Ràngnéng before returning to his garrison.
Cuī Zhāowěi further pushed for this.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Ràngnéng and his younger brother, the Vice Minister of Revenue Hóng Huī, were ordered to commit suicide.
An examination of discrepancies states: The Continued Record of Bǎo Yùn says:
"In the second year of Dàshùn,
Chief Ministers Dù Ràngnéng and Kǒng Wěi, facing the frequent turmoil and disorder in the capital,
with court governance in disarray and decline,
at that time, complying with the wishes of the various circuits,
assembled an imperial escort of fifty-four military units,
filling every ward,
and together with the neighboring military governors,
intending to launch a punitive campaign,
personally led the armies.
As for Lǐ Màozhēn of Qíyáng,
he was enfeoffed as Crown Prince by the previous court,
his original surname was Sòng,
he was the Governor of Yángzhōu,
his ancestors had merit in quelling Liú Cóngjiàn of Zhāoyì,
and his descendants received continuous noble titles and rewards.
After Shòuwáng ascended the throne,
he dispatched Vice Minister of Rites Xuē Tíngguī bearing the imperial seal and documents with full ceremony,
to confer upon him the title of Prince of Qí.
Màozhēn, earlier during the Zhōnghé era,
submitted himself to the Army Surveillance Commissioner Tián Lìngzí to be adopted as a foster son,
taking the surname Tián and the name Yànbīn,
essentially currying favor with his power.
Zhū Wēn of Biànzhōu was enfeoffed as Prince of Dōngpíng by the previous court,
and up to the present emperor,
Xuē Tíngguī was again dispatched as the Ceremonial Commissioner,
with Prince Yán as the Enfeoffment Commissioner,
to enfeoff him as Prince of Liáng.
Moreover, the Prince of Qí and the Northern Bureau,
their relations were just harmonious,
but they were very discordant with the Chief Ministers,
repeatedly submitting memorials stating: 'Your subject now encamps his banners at Xiányáng,
not daring to enter the Secretariat to demand accountability,
[but] requests that Dù Ràngnéng and others be subjected to the severest punishment.'
When the memorial was presented,
the Emperor was displeased,
and thus issued an edict ordering Chief Ministers Kǒng and Dù to go to Xiányáng to apologize;
when the two chief ministers arrived at Xiányáng to see the Prince of Qí,
they trembled and could not speak.
The Prince of Qí was greatly angered,
and instead ordered them to return to the Secretariat to reflect on their faults.
Just upon returning to the Secretariat,
the Emperor again dispatched them,
ordering them to beg forgiveness from the Prince of Qí.
This back and forth happened three times.
The Prince of Qí again memorialized: 'The two chief ministers, upon seeing your subject,
did not utter a single word.
Such neglect of official duty,
brings disgrace to the sagely age,
I request the implementation of court discipline,
to select other worthy and talented individuals.'
The Emperor was unhappy,
but issued an edict relieving them of their administrative duties,
and reluctantly appointed Kǒng Wěi as Military Commissioner of Jīngnán,
and Dù Ràngnéng as Military Commissioner of Hézhōng;
three days later,
they were demoted to Lǐngbiǎo;
thirty li outside the capital gates,
both were ordered to commit suicide.
At that time, the Prince of Qí led five thousand elite troops stationed at Xiányáng,
and after the two chief ministers were demoted,
he withdrew."
These are all erroneous accounts.
Now we follow the Veritable Records.
It states
"Ràngnéng promoted the crooked and dismissed the upright,
using the words of Confucius from the Analects,
meaning he promoted the crooked,
and dismissed the upright, not employing them.
In a court of decline and disorder,
how could there be public right and wrong!
Cuò (dismiss),
is pronounced qiāngù.
He sold judgments and official posts,
amassing wealth exceeding tens of thousands."
From then on, every movement and rest of the court had to be reported to Bīn and Qí,
and officials of the Southern and Northern Bureaus often attached themselves to these two garrisons to seek favors.
There were Cuī Chán and Wáng Chāo,
who served as administrative assistants to the two garrisons.
Whenever the Son of Heaven had any approval or disapproval,
those who were discontented
would immediately appeal to Chán and Chāo.
The two would then instruct Màozhēn and Xíngyú to submit memorials arguing the matter.
If the court showed the slightest hesitation,
their language would already be disrespectful.
An edict reinstated Màozhēn as Military Commissioner of Fèngxiáng and concurrently Military Commissioner of Shānnán Xīdào, and Acting Secretariat Director,
whereupon Màozhēn possessed all fifteen prefectures including Fèngxiáng, Xīngyuán, Yáng, and Lǒng-Qín.
Fèngxiáng was originally one garrison,
Xīngyuán (Shānnán Xīdào) was another garrison,
Yángzhōu (Wǔdìng Army) was another garrison,
Qín-Lǒng (Tiānxióng Army) was another garrison;
the history states that Lǐ Màozhēn concurrently possessed the territories of four garrisons.
30. On Wùxū,
Wáng Cháo, the Prefect of Quánzhōu, was appointed as Surveillance Commissioner of Fújiàn.
31. Ní Zhāng, the Prefect of Shūzhōu, abandoned the city and fled.
Ní Zhāng had allied his troops with Cài Chóu.
Chóu had already been defeated,
therefore Zhāng fled.
32. Wáng Xíngyú, Military Commissioner of Bīnníng, Acting Palace Attendant, and concurrently Secretariat Director, requested to be appointed as President of the Department of State Affairs.
Wéi Zhāodù secretly memorialized:
"Emperor Tàizōng, having served as President of the Department of State Affairs,
subsequently ascended the great throne.
Since then, it has not been conferred upon subjects.
Only Guō Zǐyí, due to his great merit, was appointed President of the Department of State Affairs,
but he declined it for life.
How can Xíngyú lightly propose this!"
In the eleventh month,
Xíngyú was appointed Grand Preceptor,
granted the title Shàngfù,
and also bestowed an iron certificate.
33. In the twelfth month,
Zhū Quánzhōng requested to relocate the Salt and Iron Commission to Biànzhōu to facilitate military supply.
Cuī Zhāowěi believed that Quánzhōng had recently defeated Xú and Yùn,
doubling his military strength.
If he further controlled the Salt and Iron Commission,
he could no longer be restrained,
and thus an edict was issued to explain and persuade him.
34. Gé Cóngzhōu, a general under Biàn, attacked Zhū Wēi, the Prefect of Qízhōu.
Zhū Xuān and Zhū Jǐn,
led troops to rescue him.
According to the Table of Military Governors,
Qízhōu at that time belonged to the Pínglú military district.
Judging from the incident in the third year of Qiánníng when Zhū Qióng surrendered to Biàn,
Qízhōu had already been annexed by Yǎn and Yùn.
An examination of discrepancies states: The Compiled Supplementary Record says the tenth month, Yǐwèi.
Now we follow Xuē Jūzhèng's Old History of the Five Dynasties, Annals of Liáng.
35. Earlier,
Zhōu Yuè, Military Commissioner of Wǔ'ān, killed Mǐn Xù,
and occupied Tánzhōu.
See the second year of the Guāngqǐ era of Emperor Xīzōng, in scroll 256.
When the various generals entered to offer condolences,
Dèng Chùnè said:
"I and you gentlemen all received great kindness from the Vice Director.
Mǐn Xù was Acting Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs of the Right and Military Commissioner of Qīnhuà.
He appointed Chùnè as Prefect of Shàozhōu,
hence the statement of receiving kindness.
According to Lù Zhèn's History of the Nine States,
Dèng Chùnè, from the Qiánfú era of the Táng,
followed Mǐn Xù to campaign against the barbarians in Ānnán.
When Xù commanded Tán,
he appointed Chùnè as Military Commissioner-in-waiting of Shàozhōu.
Chù,
is pronounced chānglǚ.
I wish to join with you gentlemen to exhaust the strength of one prefecture,
to avenge the Vice Director.
Is this acceptable?"
They all said:
"Good!"
Thereupon, they trained soldiers and sharpened weapons.
After eight years,
they allied with Léi Mǎn, the Prefect of Lǎngzhōu.
Léi Mǎn had a grudge with Zhōu Yuè over a dispute about meat.
They defeated him,
beheaded Yuè,
and Chùnè proclaimed himself Commissioner-in-waiting.
Dèng Chùnè had just obtained Tánzhōu,
when Liú Jiànfēng and Mǎ Yīn were already eyeing his rear.
First year of Qiánníng
(Jiǎyín, 894)
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the first day of the month, Yǐchǒu,
a general amnesty was declared for the realm,
and the era name was changed.
2. Lǐ Màozhēn came to court,
arraying a large number of troops for self-protection,
and returned to his garrison after several days.
3. Lǐ Kuāngchóu was appointed Military Commissioner of Lúlóng.
4. In the second month,
Zhū Quánzhōng personally led troops to attack Zhū Xuān's army at Yúshān.
Yúshān
is located between Xūchāng and Dōng'ē counties of Yùnzhōu.
The armies of Yǎn and Yùn were heavily defeated,
with over ten thousand dead.
5. Zhèng Qǐ, the Right Sanqí Chángshì, was appointed as Lǐbù Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Qǐ enjoyed humor
and often wrote xiēhòu poems,
satirizing current affairs.
Xiēhòu means
stating the reason for the poem but omitting the concluding phrase.
The emperor personally annotated the court roster,
ordering him to be made chancellor.
The court roster
lists the names of those serving at court.
A clerk went to inform him,
and Qǐ laughed, saying:
"Gentlemen are greatly mistaken.
Even if there were no one else left in the world,
it would not come to Zhèng Qǐ!"
The clerk said:
"This specifically comes from the emperor's intention."
Qǐ said:
"If it is truly so,
what can be done about people laughing!"
Soon after, congratulatory guests arrived,
and Qǐ, scratching his head, said:
"Xiēhòu Zhèng the Fifth becomes chancellor—
Zhèng Qǐ was the fifth among his brothers,
and because he wrote xiēhòu poems,
he was called 'Xiēhòu Zhèng the Fifth style' at the time.
He repeatedly declined but could not avoid it,
so he took up his duties.
6. Dèng Chùnè, the Shàozhōu Cìshǐ, was appointed as Wǔ'ān Jiédùshǐ.
7. Zhāng Jūn, the Zhāngyì Jiédùshǐ, died,
and he recommended his elder brother Zhāng Fán to be Liúhòu.
At that time, Jīngzhōu was made the seat of the Zhāngyì Jiédù.
Fán,
pronunciation: fú yuán fān.
8. In March,
Wú Tǎo, the Huángzhōu Cìshǐ, surrendered the entire prefecture to Yáng Xíngmì.
Huángzhōu was then under Èyuè,
Èyuè,
which was the Wǔchāng Army.
According to the Xīn Tángshū biography of Dù Hóng,
Wú Tǎo
was a commoner from Yǒngxīng County in Èzhōu,
who rose as a leader of the local militia,
and seized Huángzhōu.
9. In Xíngzhōu city, food was exhausted.
On Jiǎshēn,
Lǐ Cúnxiào climbed the city wall and said to Lǐ Kèyòng:
"I, your son, received the king's grace to attain wealth and honor.
If not for being trapped by slander and wickedness,
how could I have abandoned father and son to follow enemies!
I wish to see the king once,
and I would die without regret!"
Kèyòng sent Lady Liú to see him.
The lady led Cúnxiào out to meet Kèyòng.
Cúnxiào kowtowed and apologized, saying:
"I, your son, had barely achieved some small merits,
but Cúnxìn pressured me,
leading to this misstep!"
Kèyòng rebuked him, saying:
"You sent letters to Zhū Quánzhōng and Wáng Róng,
slandering me in countless ways—
was that also taught by Cúnxìn!"
He imprisoned him,
sent him back to Jìnyáng,
and had him torn apart by chariots at the yámén.
Examination of discrepancies: The Tàizǔ Jìniánlù states:
"First capturing Biàn generals Dèng Jūn, Ān Kāngbā, army clerk Liú Ǒuzi, and the captured供奉官 Hán Guīfàn from Lùzhōu,
all were implicated with Cúnxiào,
and executed on the same day.
Cavalry general Xuē Ātán, fearing for himself,
committed suicide."
According to the Jiù Tángshū annals,
Kèyòng captured Guīfàn,
but soon sent him back,
and he submitted a memorial pleading his innocence;
it is not heard that he went to Jìnyáng again.
Xuē Jūzhèng's Wǔdài Shǐ biography of Dèng Jìjūn states
that he later escaped from Xíngzhōu back to Biàn.
The Jìniánlù is mistaken.
The biography of Cúnxiào says:
"Wǔhuáng marched out of Jǐngxíng,
approaching Zhēndìng.
Cúnxiào personally met Wáng Róng,
discussing military plans.
Wǔhuáng flew into a rage,
and executed the previously captured Biàn general Ān Kāngbā."
In Kèyòng's army, no one could match him;
he often led cavalry as the vanguard,
invincible wherever he went.
Clad in heavy armor,
with a bow at his waist and a lance at his side,
he alone would dance with an iron mace and break through formations,
causing ten thousand to retreat.
He always had two horses with him;
when a horse grew slightly tired,
meaning the horse was somewhat fatigued and lacking strength,
he would change mounts, moving like the wind.
Kèyòng regretted his talent.
He thought that at the execution, the generals would surely plead for him,
and he would then release him.
However, the generals were jealous of his ability,
and in the end, not one spoke up.
After he died,
Kèyòng did not attend to affairs for ten days,
privately resenting the generals,
yet he did not reprimand Lǐ Cúnxìn at all.
There was also Xuē Ātán,
whose bravery matched Cúnxiào's.
The generals were jealous of him,
so he was often discontented.
He secretly communicated with Cúnxiào;
after Cúnxiào was executed,
fearing the matter would be exposed,
he committed suicide.
From then on, Kèyòng's military power gradually weakened,
while Zhū Quánzhōng alone grew strong.
History says that Kèyòng cut off his own wings,
hence he could not compete with Biàn.
10. Zhū Quánzhōng sent army officer Zhāng Cónghuì to pacify Shòuzhōu.
Cónghuì insulted and bullied Cìshǐ Jiāng Yànwēn and drank at night with the generals;
Yànwēn suspected they were plotting against him.
The next day,
he killed all the generals at the banquet,
then wrote a letter to Quánzhōng apologizing and committed suicide.
The army recommended his son Jiāng Cóngxū to take charge of the military and prefectural affairs.
Quánzhōng had Cónghuì executed by waist-cutting for this.
11. In May,
Qián Liú, the Zhènhǎi Jiédùshǐ, was granted the additional title of Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
12. Liú Jiànfēng and Mǎ Yīn led troops to Lílíng.
"Lí"
should be
"Lǐ."
Lǐlíng
was within the boundaries of the Hàn dynasty's Línxiāng County.
Later, the Eastern Hàn dynasty established Lǐlíng County,
which was abolished during the Suí dynasty.
In the fourth year of Wǔdé,
Lǐlíng County was established from part of Chángshā,
belonging to Tánzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is 160 lǐ east of the prefecture.
Yīn arrived first at the pass,
and sent an envoy to Jiǎng Xūn.
Xūn and others provided oxen and wine to reward the army.
Yīn's envoy persuaded Xūn, saying:
"Liú Xuān is both wise and brave beyond others.
Later, Yáo Yànzhāng said to Mǎ Yīn:
'You and Liú Lóngxiāng are like one person,'
so here the character
'Lóng'
is likely missing.
Shuì,
pronunciation: shì ruì fān.
Yì and Zhěn
correspond to the Chǔ and Jīngzhōu divisions;
Chángshā enters the Zhěn constellation at 16 degrees.
His elite troops are invincible.
Yet you, with several thousand local militia, resist him—
it is difficult.
According to the Xīn Tángshū,
Jiǎng Xūn and Dèng Jìchóng were both local magnates of Shàozhōu,
and the troops they led were all locals,
hence they were called local militia.
To seek wealth and honor,
and return to your hometowns—
would that not be good!"
Xūn and others agreed.
He said to the troops:
"The eastern army allows us to return."
Liú Jiànfēng and others' troops came from the east,
so Jiǎng Xūn and others called them the eastern army.
They abandoned their banners, armor, and weapons and fled.
Jiànfēng ordered the vanguard to wear their armor,
display their banners,
and head toward Tánzhōu.
The people of Tán thought the Shàozhōu troops were returning,
and did not prepare.
Jiànfēng went straight into the prefectural headquarters.
Dèng Chùnè was feasting at the time,
and was captured and beheaded.
On Wùchén,
Jiànfēng entered Tánzhōu,
and declared himself Liúhòu.
The Zhaoyi military governor Kāng Jūnlì went to Jìnyáng to visit Lǐ Kèyòng.
On the Jǐwèi day,
Kèyòng gathered his generals for drinking and gambling.
When the wine was flowing freely,
Kèyòng spoke of Lǐ Cúnxiào,
and could not stop shedding tears.
Jūnlì had always been on good terms with Lǐ Cúnxìn,
and with one remark that went against Kèyòng's wishes,
Kèyòng drew his sword and struck him,
imprisoning him in the Cavalry and Infantry Bureau.
At the end of the Tang, all military governors established prisons in the Cavalry and Infantry Bureau,
which today is called the Military and Horse Bureau.
Wǔ,
pronounced as wǔ gù fān.
On the Gēngshēn day, the first day of the month,
he was released,
but Jūnlì was already dead.
Examination of discrepancies: Xuē Jūzhèng's Old History of the Five Dynasties states:
"After Lǐ Cúnxiào died,
Wǔhuáng deeply regretted it,
and was angry that none of the generals could relieve his sorrow;
Jūnlì, with one remark that went against his wishes,
was given poisoned wine by Wǔhuáng and died."
The Record of Seen and Heard at the End of the Tang says:
"On the thirtieth day of the eighth month,
the Grand Councillor was drinking at night in his residence on Left Street,
drew his sword and wounded the Zhaoyi military governor Kāng Jūnlì,
had him sent to the Cavalry and Infantry Bureau for imprisonment,
and by the first day of the ninth month,
when he was released,
he soon died."
Xuē's History mentioning poisoned wine
is likely embellishing the event.
26 In winter,
the tenth month,
the emperor enfeoffed his son Xǔ as the Prince of Dì,
Xì as the Prince of Qián,
Yīn as the Prince of Yí,
and Yī as the Prince of Suì.
27 Liú Réngōng repeatedly offered strategies to Lǐ Kèyòng through Gài Yù,
wishing to lead ten thousand troops to capture Yōuzhōu.
Kèyòng was then attacking Xíngzhōu,
so he divided off several thousand troops,
intending to install Réngōng in Yōuzhōu,
but did not succeed.
This refers to events before the eleventh month of this year.
He repeatedly invaded the territory of Hédōng.
Kèyòng was angered,
and in the eleventh month,
launched a large-scale attack against Kuāngchóu,
capturing Wǔzhōu,
and advancing to besiege Xīnzhōu.
Xīnzhōu
administered the four counties of Yǒngxīng, Fánshān, Huái'ān, and Lóngmén.
History has lost the record of when it was established,
but its location was northwest of Guīzhōu.
Examination of discrepancies: The Chronological Record of Táng Tàizǔ states:
"In the eleventh month,
on the Rénchén day,
the main army captured Jiékòu,
and advanced to take Yángmén and Jiǔzǐ;
on the Wùxū day,
they took Wǔzhōu.
On the Jiǎyín day,
they attacked Xīnzhōu,
encamping at its northwestern corner."
According to the calendar, the first day of the eleventh month was Jǐwèi,
so there were no Rénchén, Wùxū, or Jiǎyín days.
The Chronological Record is mistaken.
We now follow the Veritable Records.
28 Appointed Zhāng Xuān, the acting military governor of Jīngyuán, as the military governor of Zhāngyì.
29 Zhū Quánzhōng sent an envoy to Sìzhōu,
who insulted
and belittled the prefect Zhāng Liàn,
leading Liàn to surrender the entire prefecture to Yáng Xíngmì.
Sìzhōu
was originally under the jurisdiction of Xúzhōu,
but from this point on, it became part of Yáng Xíngmì's domain.
Quánzhōng detained the envoy Lìng Huí,
seizing all his tea.
This marked the beginning of discord between Yáng and Biàn.
This sets the stage for Quánzhōng's later attacks on Xíngmì.
30 In the twelfth month,
Lǐ Kuāngchóu sent a senior general leading tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry to relieve Xīnzhōu.
Lǐ Kèyòng selected elite troops to engage them at Duànzhuāng,
where he routed them decisively.
Duànzhuāng
was southeast of Xīnzhōu.
He captured three hundred officers alive,
bound them with ropes,
and paraded them beneath the city walls.
That evening,
Xīnzhōu surrendered.
On the Xīnhài day,
he advanced to attack Guīzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Guīzhōu is two hundred eighty lǐ southeast to Yōuzhōu,
and two hundred forty lǐ southwest to Yùzhōu.
Guī,
pronounced as jū wéi fān.
On the Rénzǐ day,
Kuāngchóu again dispatched troops through the Jūyōng Pass.
Kèyòng had elite cavalry engage them head-on to tire them out,
while sending infantry general Lǐ Cúnshěn to outflank them from the rear via another route for a pincer attack.
The Yōuzhōu troops were heavily defeated,
with tens of thousands killed or captured.
On the Jiǎyín day,
Lǐ Kuāngchóu fled with his family to Cāngzhōu.
The Yìchāng military governor Lú Yǎnwēi, coveting his baggage train, concubines, and singers,
sent troops to attack him at Jǐngchéng,
killing him,
and capturing all his followers.
Cúnshěn's original surname was Fú;
he was from Wǎnqiū,
and Kèyòng adopted him as a son.
According to Xuē's History,
Fú Cúnshěn initially followed Lǐ Hǎnzhī;
when Hǎnzhī was pressured by Zhūgě Shuǎng,
and withdrew to defend Huáizhōu,
his followers scattered,
and Cúnshěn then joined Lǐ Kèyòng.
On the Bǐngchén day,
Kèyòng advanced his army to Yōuzhōu,
and its senior generals requested to surrender.
Kuāngchóu had always been dim-witted and cowardly.
When he first seized control of the military headquarters,
his elder brother Kuāngwēi heard of it
and said to his generals:
"What the elder brother lost, the younger brother gained;
it has not left our family,
so what is there to regret!
I only regret that Kuāngchóu's talent is limited,
and he cannot hold on to it;
if he can last two years,
that would be fortunate."
In the second year of the Jǐngfù era,
Kuāngchóu gained control of Yōuzhōu,
and by now it had been barely two years.
31 Added the title of Acting Palace Attendant to the Kuāngguó military governor Wáng Xíngyuē.
32 Wú Tǎo feared pressure from Dù Hóng.
Dù Hóng's attack on Wú Tǎo was mentioned above in the fifth month.
Xíngmì appointed the vanguard commander Qú Zhāng as acting prefect of Huángzhōu.
This sets the stage for Qú Zhāng being attacked and captured by Biàn troops.
33 This year,
twenty thousand Huánglián Cave barbarians besieged Tīngzhōu.
Huánglián Cave
was south of Nínghuà County in Tīngzhōu,
which is the present-day Tánfēi Qì area.
The barbarians withdrew,
and Chéngxūn pursued and attacked them,
reaching Jiāngshuǐkǒu,
where he defeated them.
The Mǐn region was largely pacified.
Cháo sent his subordinates to tour the prefectures and counties,
encouraging agriculture and sericulture,
setting land taxes,
establishing friendly relations with neighboring regions,
defending the borders and giving the people rest,
and the people of Mǐn felt secure.
34 The prefect of Fēngzhōu, Liú Qiān, died.
His son Liú Yǐn observed mourning by the Hè River.
The Hè River's source is at Shílóng in Fùchuān County, Hèzhōu;
it flows
and
merges with the Guìlǐng River,
forming what is called the Hè River.
Over a hundred local people plotted a rebellion,
but Yǐn exterminated them all in a single night.
The Lingnán military governor Liú Chóngguī summoned and appointed him as Right Capital Guard Commander and concurrent commander of the Hèshuǐ Garrison;
not long after,
he recommended him as prefect of Fēngzhōu.
This marks the beginning of Liú Yǐn's rise.
In the second month, on the Xīnmǎo day,
Dǒng Chāng donned the imperial crown and robes and ascended the tower of the inner city gate,
where he proclaimed himself emperor.
He displayed all the auspicious objects in the courtyard to show the masses.
Previously, towards the end of the Xiántōng era,
rumors spread in the Wú and Yuè regions that a great bird had appeared in the mountains,
with four eyes and three feet,
whose cry sounded like
"Luópíng Tiāncè."
It was said that anyone who saw it would suffer misfortune,
so many among the common people painted its image and made offerings to it.
When Dǒng Chāng usurped the imperial title,
he declared:
"This is my yuèzhuó."
He then proclaimed himself ruler of the Great Yuè Luópíng State,
changing the reign era to Shùntiān.
[Textual note:] The Wú Yuè Bèishǐ states:
"On the Guǐmǎo day,
Dǒng Chāng usurped the title of emperor,
establishing the reign era Shùntiān,
and the state name Luópíng."
Some sources record the reign era as Tiāncè,
others as Dàshèng,
but both are incorrect.
Luó Yǐn, in his "Wú Yuè Campaign Proclamation," wrote:
"Luópíng is the name for founding the state;
Shùntiān is the beginning of the established reign era."
He further stated:
"The general's gate is called the Tiāncè Tower,
and the administrative headquarters serves as the Xuānshì Hall.
He clearly announced his self-proclamation,
stating, 'I temporarily assume the position of the Luópíng State.'
Dǒng Chāng's seal inscription read 'Seal for Governing the State in Accordance with Heaven.'"
The Shíguó Jìnián also records
"the reign era Shùntiān."
The Kuàijī Lù records Tiāncè,
which is likely an error.
I follow the Bèishǐ here.
He ordered his subordinates to refer to him as
"the Sage."

He appointed the former Hángzhōu Prefect Lǐ Miǎo, the former Wùzhōu Prefect Jiǎng Huái, the Deputy Commissioner of Salt and Iron for the Two Zhè Circuits Dù Yǐng, and the former Director of the Bureau of Imperial Farms Lǐ Yú as chancellors.
He also appointed Wú Yáo and others as Hanlin Academicians, and Lǐ Chàngzhī and others as Grand Generals.
Dǒng Chāng sent a letter to Qián Liú,
informing him that he had temporarily assumed the position of the Luópíng State,
and appointed Qián Liú as Military Commissioner of the Two Zhè Circuits.
Qián Liú sent a letter to Dǒng Chāng, stating:
"Rather than closing your gates and proclaiming yourself Son of Heaven,
bringing your nine clans and the common people into misery and ruin,
would it not be better to open your gates and serve as a military governor,
enjoying wealth and honor for life?
If you repent now,
it is still not too late!"
Dǒng Chāng did not listen.
Qián Liú then led thirty thousand troops to the walls of Yuèzhōu city,
arriving at the Yíng'ēn Gate
(the Yíng'ēn Gate was the west gate of Yuèzhōu city).
He bowed twice and said:
"Great King, you hold both military and ministerial positions;
why abandon safety for danger?
I have brought troops here
to await your correction of this error.
Even if you, Great King, do not value your own life,
what crime have the local gentry and common people committed
that they should be exterminated along with your clan?"
Dǒng Chāng grew fearful.
He sent two million cash to reward the army,
arrested the chief instigator Wú Yáo and several shamans, and handed them over to Qián Liú,
requesting to await punishment from the Son of Heaven.
Qián Liú led his troops back
and reported the situation to the court.
Wáng Chóngyíng's son, Bǎoyì Military Governor Wáng Gǒng,
(Wáng Chóngyíng had previously governed Shǎn-Guó;
after Wáng Chóngróng was killed by his subordinates,
Chóngyíng replaced him in governing Hézhōng,
and his son Gǒng succeeded him in governing Shǎn-Guó.
Shǎn-Guó was known as the Bǎoyì Army.
[Pronunciation note:] Gǒng is pronounced with the initial j and the final iong, with a rising tone.)
and Huázhōu Prefect Wáng Yáo raised troops to attack Wáng Kē,
submitting a memorial stating that Kē was not a son of the Wáng family.
In a letter to Zhū Quánzhōng,
he wrote:
"Kē was originally a servant of our household;
he should not be the heir."
Wáng Kē submitted a memorial presenting his own case
and sought aid from Lǐ Kèyòng.
The Emperor sent a palace envoy to mediate and resolve the dispute.
The Emperor valued Lǐ Xī's literary talent.
On the Yǐwèi day,
he reappointed Lǐ Xī as Vice Minister of Revenue and Grand Councilor.
(Last year, the Emperor had appointed Lǐ Xī as chancellor,
but Liú Chónglǔ obstructed it, causing it to stop.
This matter is recorded in the previous scroll.)
Zhū
Quánzhōng stationed his army at Shànfù.
(Shànfù County was attached to Shànzhōu at that time.
[Pronunciation note:] Shàn is pronounced shàn;
fù is pronounced fǔ.)
Zhū Yǒugōng was then besieging Zhǔ Jǐn in Yǎnzhōu.
Lǐ Kèyòng recommended Liú Rén'gōng as the Liúlóng Acting Military Governor,
leaving troops to garrison there.
On the Rénzǐ day,
he returned to Jìnyáng.
The Gūizhōu natives Gāo Sījì and his brothers
possessed military prowess
and were respected by the people of Yān.
Lǐ Kèyòng appointed them all as capital commanders,
dividing command of the Yōuzhōu troops among them.
The soldiers under their command
were all powerful figures from north of the mountains.
(Gūi, Tán, and other prefectures were all located north of the mountains of Yōuzhōu,
also called "beyond the mountains.")
After some time,
the Hézhōng troops garrisoning Yōuzhōu became violent and oppressive.
The Gāo brothers restrained them according to law,
executing a great many.
Lǐ Kèyòng grew angry
and reprimanded Liú Rén'gōng over this.
Liú Rén'gōng reported that it was the doing of the Gāo brothers,
so Lǐ Kèyòng had them all killed.
Liú Rén'gōng, wishing to win the hearts of the Yān people,
brought the Gāo brothers' sons back into his tent,
treating them generously and kindly.
(This sets the stage for Liú Rén'gōng's later rebellion against Lǐ Kèyòng.
[Pronunciation note:] Fù is pronounced fú, with a rising tone;
the same applies below.)
Cuī Zhāowěi formed deep connections with Lǐ Màozhēn and Wáng Xíngyú.
Whenever he learned of the Emperor's faults
or confidential matters of the court,
he would inform them of everything.
Bīnníng Deputy Military Governor Cuī Chán
was a clansman of Cuī Zhāowěi.
When Lǐ Xī was reappointed as chancellor,
Cuī Zhāowěi sent Cuī Chán to tell Wáng Xíngyú:
"Previously, the appointment as Minister of Works had already been issued,
but Wéi Zhāodù obstructed it.
(This matter is recorded in the second year of the Jǐngfù era in the previous scroll.)
Together they confused the Sage's hearing,
and I fear another incident like that of Grand Tutor Dù may occur."
(Regarding Dù Ràngnéng,
this matter is also recorded in the second year of the Jǐngfù era in the previous scroll.)
"Wéi Zhāodù lacks the qualifications to be chancellor;
he should be dismissed to a sinecure position."
([Pronunciation note:] Sǎn is pronounced sǎn.)
"As for military affairs,
I will consult with the military governors;
but the appointment of chancellors
should come from my own will."
Wáng Xíngyú and others continued to argue and criticize.
In the third month,
Lǐ Xī was again dismissed and made Junior Tutor of the Heir Apparent.
Wáng Gǒng and Wáng Yáo requested the court to appoint a military governor for Hézhōng.
An edict was issued appointing Vice Director of the Secretariat and Grand Councilor Cuī Yìn as Grand Councilor
and concurrent Military Governor of the Hùguó Army;
and appointing Vice Minister of Revenue and Manager of the Bureau of Revenue Wáng Tuán as Vice Director of the Secretariat and Grand Councilor.
Wáng Kē
was the son-in-law of Lǐ Kèyòng.
Lǐ Kèyòng submitted a memorial stating that Wáng Chóngróng had rendered meritorious service to the state
(referring to the defeat of Huáng Cháo and the removal of the Prince of Xiāng;
Wáng Chóngróng had contributed to both).
Wáng Gǒng cultivated close ties with the three military governors Wáng Xíngyú, Lǐ Màozhēn, and Hán Jiàn.
They repeatedly submitted memorials claiming that Wáng Kē was not a son of the Wáng family,
requesting that Kē be appointed to Shǎnzhōu and Gǒng to Hézhōng.
The Emperor informed them that he had already approved Lǐ Kèyòng's memorial,
and would not grant their request.
([Note:] Yǔn means to approve.)
(This sets the stage for the three military governors raising troops to enter the capital,
and for Lǐ Kèyòng's execution of Wáng Yáo and campaign against the three military governors.
[Pronunciation note:] Shǎn is pronounced shǎn.)
Wáng Róng was additionally appointed as Palace Attendant.
15. Yáng Xíngmì floated along the Huái River to Sìzhōu.
The defense commissioner Tái Méng prepared lavish furnishings and tents for him.
The surname compendium states: The surname Tái
derives from Tái Tái.
In the Later Hàn, there was the high-minded scholar Tái Tóng.
In the Jìn, there was the occultist Tái Yàn.
In the Former Zhào, there was the Special Counselor Tái Yángāo.
The term "furnishings"
is pronounced jū yòng fān.
After Yáng Xíngmì departed,
Tái Méng found a patched garment in the bedchamber
and sent a messenger galloping to return it.
The character "zhàn"
should be written as
"zhàn",
pronounced zhàng xiàn fān.
"Zhàn"
also means to mend.
The term "messenger"
is pronounced shū lì fān.
Yáng Xíngmì said, "I was poor and humble in my youth,
and I dare not forget my origins."
Tái Méng felt deeply ashamed.
Yáng Xíngmì attacked Háozhōu,
captured it,
and seized the prefect Zhāng Suì.
Zhāng Suì's allegiance to Zhū Quánzhōng is mentioned in the first year of Jǐngfú in the previous scroll.
Yáng Xíngmì's soldiers plundered and obtained the son of a man from Xúzhōu surnamed Lǐ,
who was eight years old.
Yáng Xíngmì adopted him as his son.
The Southern Táng historical account states: Lǐ Biàn
was from Xúzhōu,
the son of Lǐ Róng.
Lǐ Róng encountered turmoil and his whereabouts became unknown.
Lǐ Biàn was orphaned young
and drifted between Háo and Sì.
Yáng Xíngmì obtained him while attacking Háozhōu
and adopted him as his son.
Yáng Xíngmì said to his general Xú Wēn:
"This child's disposition and intelligence
are quite different from others.
I estimate that Wò will certainly not tolerate him.
I now bestow him upon you as your son."
Xú Wēn named him Zhīgào.
Zhīgào served Xú Wēn
with diligence and filial piety surpassing Xú Wēn's other sons.
Once he offended Xú Wēn,
and Xú Wēn caned him and drove him away.
When he returned,
Zhīgào greeted and bowed at the gate.
Xú Wēn asked,
"Why are you still here?"
Zhīgào tearfully replied,
"Where else would a son go after leaving his parents?
If a father is angry and returns to the mother,
it is a common human sentiment."
Xú Wēn thus loved him even more,
put him in charge of household affairs,
and no one in the family voiced dissent.
When he grew up,
he enjoyed books and was skilled in archery,
possessing outstanding insight and bearing.
Yáng Xíngmì often said to Xú Wēn:
"Zhīgào is outstanding;
none of the other generals' sons can compare to him."
The affairs of Xú Zhīgào begin here.
Later, he resumed his original surname Lǐ,
and was named Biàn.
On Dīnghài,
Yáng Xíngmì besieged Shòuzhōu.
16. The Emperor, because there were many bandits in the capital suburbs,
to the extent that some scaled walls to enter the palace or encroached upon the imperial tombs,
wished to order the imperial clan princes to lead troops in patrols and inspections,
and also wanted to send them to various regions to pacify and reassure the military governors.
The influential ministers of the Southern and Northern Bureaus, fearing this would be disadvantageous to them,
submitted memorials in succession to remonstrate.
The Emperor had no choice,
and in the summer,
in the fourth month,
issued an edict canceling all these plans.
17. The court, considering Dǒng Chāng's past diligence in presenting tribute,
and that his current actions
seemed like a mental illness,
issued an edict pardoning his crimes,
releasing him to return to his fields and village.
18. The Vice Minister of Revenue and concurrent Tongpingzhangshi Lù Xīshēng was dismissed and made Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent.
19. Yáng Xíngmì besieged Shòuzhōu
but could not capture it,
and was about to withdraw.
On Gēngyín,
his general Zhū Yánshòu requested to try attacking once more,
and captured it with the first drumbeat.
Because Yáng Xíngmì was about to withdraw, the defenders were lax in their precautions,
hence it was captured with the first drumbeat.
Gāo Yànwēn had surrendered Shòuzhōu to Zhū Quánzhōng,
and Zhū Quánzhōng appointed Jiāng Cóngxù as prefect.
Yáng Xíngmì captured him,
thus gaining both Háo and Shòu prefectures.
Not long after,
several tens of thousands of Biàn troops attacked Shòuzhōu.
The troops in the prefecture were few,
and officials and people were terrified.
Zhū Yánshòu's regulation
was for each banner in the army to have twenty-five cavalrymen.
He ordered the Black Cloud Company commander Lǐ Hòu to lead ten banners to attack the Biàn troops,
but he was unsuccessful.
Zhū Yánshòu was about to execute him,
but Lǐ Hòu pleaded that the disparity in numbers was too great,
and requested additional troops to try again,
vowing to die if unsuccessful.
The chief military inspector Chái Zàiyòng of Rǔyáng also pleaded for him.
Lù Zhèn's *Nine States Records* states: Chái Zàiyòng's original name was Cún.
He served Sūn Rú,
and formed a death pact with a minor officer.
Someone reported that the minor officer was rebelling,
and Sūn Rú executed him.
He seized Cún and brought him forward,
interrogating him on why he rebelled.
Cún did not answer.
Asked again,
he replied:
"I formed a death pact with him.
If he rebelled, then I rebelled.
You executed him,
what more is there to ask?"
Sūn Rú, finding this remarkable, said:
"If you truly did not rebel,
I will employ you again."
Hence he changed his name.
The term "for"
is pronounced yú wèi fān.
Lǐ Hòu fought a desperate battle,
and Chái Zàiyòng assisted him.
Zhū Yánshòu then committed all his troops to follow up,
and the Biàn troops were defeated and fled.
Lǐ Hòu
was from Càizhōu.
Lǐ Hòu
was a remnant soldier of Sūn Rú.
Yáng Xíngmì also sent troops to raid Liánshuǐ,
and captured it.
The historian remarks that Yáng Xíngmì's territory gradually expanded.
Liánshuǐ County in Sìzhōu:
Dù Yòu said it was the Hàn dynasty's Chóuyóu County.
Sòng Bái said: According to the Qiúyóu city,
it is present-day Sùyù County.
In the Wèi it was called Hǎi'ān County,
in the Jìn it was within the boundaries of Sùyù,
the Sòng established the Dōnghǎi Commandery,
the Later Wèi changed it to Hǎi'ān Commandery,
the Sui abolished the commandery
and established Liánshuǐ County.
20. Qián Liú submitted a memorial stating that Dǒng Chāng's usurpation and rebellion
could not be pardoned,
and requested to lead his own regional troops to attack him.
Qián Liú originally harbored intentions to annex Dǒng Chāng.
Taking advantage of his usurpation of the title,
he invoked great righteousness and requested to attack him.
21. The Grand Tutor, Vice Director of the Chancellery, and concurrent Tongpingzhangshi Wéi Zhāodù retired as Grand Guardian.
22. On Wùxū,
Liú Jiànfēng was appointed Military Governor of Wǔ'ān.
Liú Jiànfēng appointed Mǎ Yīn as Commander of the Inner and Outer Cavalry and Infantry Armies.
This sets the stage for Mǎ Yīn succeeding Liú Jiànfēng.
23. Yáng Xíngmì sent an envoy to Qián Liú,
stating that Dǒng Chāng had already reformed,
and should be pardoned.
Yáng Xíngmì wanted to preserve Dǒng Chāng to check Qián Liú later,
preventing him from contending with himself.
He urged him to present tribute to the court.
24. HéDōng sent its generals Shǐ Yǎn and Lǐ Chéngsì with ten thousand cavalry galloping into Yùn.
Lǐ Kèyòng sent Shǐ Yǎn and others again to rescue Yǎn and Yùn,
but they were unable to return.
Exhausting troops for distant objectives
has been cautioned against since ancient times.
25. In the fifth month,
an edict was issued stripping Dǒng Chāng of his offices and ranks,
and entrusting Qián Liú with attacking him.
26. Initially,
Wáng Xíngyú sought the position of Minister of Works but did not obtain it.
See the second year of Jǐngfú in the previous volume.
Within the capital region, there were eight garrison armies,
subordinate to the Left and Right Armies.
These were the Left and Right Divine Strategy Armies.
Hán Jiàn sought control of them;
Héyáng,
a county established in the Hàn dynasty,
belonged to Tóngzhōu in the Táng dynasty.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: the county is located 120 lǐ east of the prefecture.
Hé,
pronounced as "hé."
Jìn,
pronounced as qí jìn fān;
the same applies below.
Wáng Xíngyú sought control of them.
Liángyuán County,
belonged to Jīngzhōu.
"These are the emperor's forbidden armies,
how can they be obtained!"
Wáng Kē and Wáng Gǒng contended for Hézhōng,
Xíngyú, Jiàn, and Lǐ Màozhēn all petitioned on behalf of Gǒng,
but were unsuccessful,
which shamed them.
Gǒng sent someone to tell the three commanders:
"Kē refuses to yield his position and has formed a marriage alliance with Hédōng,
which will surely be disadvantageous to you all.
I request to attack him."
Xíngyú sent his younger brother, the Jiédùshǐ of Kuàngguó, Xíngyuē, to attack Hézhōng.
At that time, Tóngzhōu was designated as the Kuàngguó Army.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Tóngzhōu is 75 lǐ east of Hézhōng.
Xíngyú then joined Màozhēn and Jiàn, each leading several thousand elite troops to the court.
On the jiǎzǐ day,
they reached the capital,
and the residents of the wards and markets all fled into hiding.
The emperor ascended the Ānfú Gate to await them.
The three commanders displayed their armored troops in full array,
bowing and performing ceremonial dances below the gate.
The emperor stood at the palace balcony,
personally questioning them:
The end of the eaves is called the balcony.
Question,
pronounced qù jí fān.
"You did not memorialize and await a response,
but instead led troops into the capital city.
What are your intentions?
If you cannot serve me,
today I request to yield the path to the worthy!"
Xíngyú and Màozhēn were sweating and unable to speak,
only Hán Jiàn roughly explained the reason for coming to court.
The emperor feasted the three commanders.
The three commanders memorialized:
"The Southern and Northern Bureaus each have factions,
corrupting and disrupting court governance.
Wéi Zhāodù's campaign against Xīchuān was misguided.
The campaign against Xīchuān is recorded in volumes 257 and 258.
It did not align with public sentiment,
we request his execution."
The emperor did not grant this.
On that day,
Xíngyú and others killed Zhāodù and Xī at the Dūtíng Post Station.
The Dūtíng Post Station,
is located on the west street outside the Zhūquè Gate,
the second ward north of the Hánguāng Gate.
They further said:
"Wáng Kē and Wáng Gǒng are not distinguished by legitimate and illegitimate status.
We request to remove Wáng Gǒng from Hézhōng,
transfer Wáng Xíngyuē to Shǎn,
and Wáng Kē to Tóngzhōu."
The emperor granted all of this.
Initially,
the three commanders plotted to depose the emperor,
and install Prince Jí Bǎo;
by this time,
hearing that Lǐ Kèyòng had already raised troops in Hédōng,
Xíngyú and Màozhēn each left two thousand troops to guard the capital,
and together with Jiàn, took leave to return to their garrisons.
The Minister of Revenue, Yáng Kān, was demoted to Prefect of Yǎzhōu.
Kān,
was the son of Yúqīng,
Yáng Yúqīng appears in the annals of Emperor Wénzōng.
27. Initially,
Cuī Yìn was appointed as the Jiédùshǐ of Hézhōng.
The Hédōng memorial officer Xuē Zhìqín openly declared:
"Although Lord Cuī is of great virtue,
replacing Wáng Kē with him
is not as favorable as Lord Liú of Guāngdé is to our lord."
Lord Liú of Guāngdé refers to
the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, Liú Chóngwàng.
Guāngdé,
is the name of a ward,
within Cháng'ān city.
In the late Táng,
ministers who had contemporary prestige
were often referred to by the ward they resided in.
Guāngdé Ward,
is the sixth ward from the north on the third street west of Zhūquè Street,
where the Jīngzhào Prefecture is located.
Upon hearing Zhìqín's words,
Chóngwàng was demoted to Military Commander of Zhāozhōu.
Lǐ Kèyòng heard that the troops of the three garrisons had violated the palace gates.
That same day, he dispatched thirteen envoys to mobilize the northern troops.
The northern troops,
are the various tribal troops from Dàiběi.
28. In the sixth month,
on the gēngyín day,
Qián Liú was appointed as the Pacification Commissioner of Zhèdōng;
Liú again dispatched troops to attack Dǒng Chāng.
29. On the xīnmǎo day,
the former Prefect of Jūnzhōu, Kǒng Wěi, and the former Registrar of Xiùzhōu, Zhāng Jùn, were both appointed as Advisors to the Heir Apparent.
On the rénchén day,
Wěi was appointed as Minister of Personnel,
restoring his rank and nobility;
on the guǐsì day,
he was appointed as Minister of Works,
concurrently serving as Vice Director of the Chancellery and Tongpingzhangshi.
Zhāng Jùn was appointed as Minister of War and Commissioner of Taxes and Transport for All Circuits.
The demotions of Kǒng Wěi and Zhāng Jùn are recorded in the first year of Dàshùn in volume 258.
Now the emperor intended to reinstate them.
Jùn resided in Chángshuǐ.
The emperor, because Cuī Zhāowěi and others were colluding externally with the military governors,
and factions were contending with each other,
wished to obtain upright and outspoken individuals,
thus suddenly employed Wěi and Jùn.
Wěi, due to illness,
was carried in a sedan to the capital.
He met the emperor,
tearfully and firmly declined;
the emperor did not permit it.
30. Lǐ Kèyòng massively mobilized tribal and Hàn troops to march south.
He submitted a memorial stating that Wáng Xíngyú, Lǐ Màozhēn, and Hán Jiàn had led troops to violate the palace gates,
murdered ministers,
and requested to attack them.
Lǐ Kèyòng actually sided with Wáng Kē,
proclaiming the crimes of the three commanders and memorializing to request punitive action.
Xíngyú and others were greatly afraid.
Kèyòng's army reached Jiàngzhōu.
The Prefect, Wáng Yáo, closed the city and resisted them;
Kèyòng attacked,
and in ten days,
captured it,
beheading Yáo at the army gate,
and killing over a thousand people in the city who resisted.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the bǐngchén day, the first day of the month,
Kèyòng reached Hézhōng,
and Wáng Kē went to greet him on the road.
The Jiédùshǐ of Kuàngguó, Wáng Xíngyuē, was defeated at Cháoyì.
On the wùwǔ day,
Xíngyuē abandoned Tóngzhōu and fled.
On the jǐwèi day,
he reached the capital.
Xíngyuē's younger brother, Xíngshí, was then the Commander of the Left Army.
The Divine Strategy Left Army is not this.
West of Zhūquè Street,
is called the West Market.
The Shatuo troops were about to arrive.
He requested the imperial carriage to go to Bīnzhōu.
On the gēngshēn day,
the Privy Commissioner, Luò Quánguàn, memorialized requesting the imperial carriage to go to Fèngxiáng.
The emperor said:
"I have received Kèyòng's memorial,
and he is still stationed with his army in Hézhōng.
Even if the Shatuo reach here,
I have the means to resist them.
You all should each pacify your own armies,
and not let them be shaken."
The Right Army Commander-in-Chief Lǐ Jìpéng,
was an adopted son of Lǐ Màozhēn.
Chéng Dàchāng's Yōng Lù states: The Left and Right Armies of the Northern Army
were both located within the imperial park.
The Left Three Armies were east of the Inner Eastern Park,
which was east of the Dàmíng Palace park.
The Right Three Armies were west of the Jiǔxiān Gate,
with Jiǔxiān located at the northwest corner of the Inner Eastern Park.
The Left Three Armies
were the Left Shéncè, Left Lóngwǔ, and Left Yǔlín Armies.
The Right Three Armies
were the Right Shéncè, Right Lóngwǔ, and Right Yǔlín Armies.
I note that the Left and Right Six Armies mentioned in Yōng Lù
were the palace guards after the reigns of Emperor Dàizōng and Dézōng.
When Emperor Xīzōng fled to Shǔ during the Guāngmíng era,
these six armies scattered.
Tián Lìngzī recruited fifty-two new divisions in Chéngdū,
assigning them to the Left and Right Shéncè Armies;
from that time onward,
whenever the so-called Left and Right Armies are mentioned,
they refer to these armies,
which were garrisoned inside and outside the capital city,
and were not exclusively within the imperial park.
If at this time Wáng Xíngshí and Lǐ Jìpéng served as Left and Right Army Commanders-in-Chief,
it is likely that the troops left behind by the two commanders of Bīn and Qí for palace guard duty were themselves divided into left and right.
They plotted with Luò Quánguàn to seize the emperor and take him to Fèngxiáng;
the Palace Army Commander Liú Jǐngxuān and Wáng Xíngshí learned of this,
and wanted to seize the emperor and take him to Bīnzhōu;
Kǒng Wěi openly rebuked Jǐngxuān,
believing it unwise to lightly abandon the palace.
Toward evening,
Jìpéng repeatedly petitioned for the imperial carriage to depart,
whereupon Wáng Xíngyuē led the Left Army to attack the Right Army,
their clamor shaking the earth.
Hearing the disturbance,
the emperor ascended the Chéngtiān Tower,
intending to command them to stop,
while the Pěngrì Division Commander Lǐ Yún led his own troops
to guard before the tower.
Lǐ Jìpéng attacked Yún with Fèngxiáng troops,
while Wáng Xíngyuē, believing Lǐ Jìpéng intended to seize the imperial carriage first and take it to Qí,
attacked the Right Army.
Lǐ Jìpéng should have been fighting Xíngyuē,
but instead attacked Lǐ Yún
because Yún was guarding the emperor,
making it impossible to seize him and take him away.
An arrow struck the tower's rafters,
and the attendants helped the emperor descend the tower;
Jìpéng then set fire to the palace gates,
smoke and flames obscuring the sky.
At that time, six divisions of Yánzhōu troops were stationed in the capital,
whom both armies had long feared,
and the emperor urgently summoned them to enter and guard;
upon their arrival,
the two armies retreated,
each returning to Bīnzhōu and Fèngxiáng.
The city fell into great chaos,
with widespread looting,
and the emperor, along with the princes and close attendants, took refuge in Lǐ Yún's camp,
while the Hùbì Division Commander Lǐ Jūshí led his troops to arrive afterward.
The Hùbì Division was also one of the fifty-four Shéncè divisions,
also known as the Hùbì Division.
The character "shuài"
is read as "lǜ."
There were rumors that Wáng Xíngyú and Lǐ Màozhēn intended to come personally to welcome the imperial carriage,
and the emperor, fearing coercion,
on the Xīnyǒu day,
used the two divisions of Yún and Jūshí for self-defense,
exiting through the Qǐxià Gate.
The Qǐxià Gate
was the first gate on the eastern side of the southern wall of Cháng'ān.
They spent the night at Shāchéng Town.
Shāchéng Town
was south of Cháng'ān,
in the near suburbs.

It seems Kèyòng did not personally besiege Huázhōu,

At that time, the Grand Ancestor was north of the Wèi River,
and some petty entertainers advised the Grand Ancestor to enter the court and personally grasp military power.
The Grand Ancestor also believed that Quánzhōng was plotting against him,
and the court could not make a decision,

Cúnxìn and Gài Yǔ seized the opportunity to secretly advise: 'Your Highness's family has been loyal for generations,
and this campaign is to suppress rebellion.
Above, it is because Bīn and Fèng are disloyal,
but as long as your loyalty is known to the world,
then the three rebels can easily be pacified.
However, those frivolous individuals,
who do not understand the greater principle,
may use unconsulted plans to temporarily please the court's sentiments.
Even if they are entertainers' words,
they should not be allowed to act like this.
The capital is within reach,
and the Emperor's hearing is not far,
so this truly does not benefit your heroic virtue.
Now the three villains are in dire straits,
and we must quickly plan against them.
Delaying matters leads to changes,
and we should not hesitate.'
The Grand Ancestor said: 'Your words are correct.'
That same day, he sent out the army,

However, considering that Kèyòng was planning major affairs,
they certainly were not matters that entertainers could participate in.
Moreover, according to the Veritable Records,
on the Jǐchǒu day, Kèyòng advanced and camped at Wèiqiáo,

There were only four days in between,

Furthermore, if it is said that petty individuals advised entering the court,

not remained north of the Wèi River.
This is merely the followers of Lǐ Cúnxìn wanting to attribute merit to Cúnxìn.
