Kèyòng was by nature strict and impatient,
and even for minor faults, those around him were often executed,
with none daring to disobey or oppose him;
only Gài Yù was clever and perceptive,
able to discern his intentions,
and through tactful words supplemented and benefited him,
with none of his advice going unheeded.
If Kèyòng became angry with an officer or official without just cause,
Yù would always pretend to share his anger,
and Kèyòng would often then relent;
when he had remonstrances or admonitions,
he would always cite recent events as analogies;
because of this, Kèyòng loved and trusted him,
and within his domain, none did not rely on him,
and his authority equaled that of Kèyòng.
When the court or neighboring circuits sent envoys to Héxiān,
the rewards and gifts they brought,
first went to Kèyòng,
and second to Yù's household.
Zhū Quánzhōng repeatedly sent agents to sow discord,
and even spread rumors that Gài Yù had replaced Kèyòng,
but Kèyòng treated him even more generously.
Since ancient times, when heroes contended for the realm,
they necessarily relied on brave and wise men for their service;
but among those who attended them closely,
observing their moods and expressions,
there were also clever, perceptive, and ingratiating individuals,
such as Gài Yù was to Lǐ Kèyòng.
On the day Bǐngshēn,
Wáng Jiàn attacked Dōngchuān.
His subordinate general Wáng Zōngbì was captured by Dōngchuān troops.
Lù Zhèn's *Jiǔ Guó Zhì* states: Wáng Zōngbì was plundering territory at Fēiwū,
when he was captured by Gù Yànhuī.
On the day Wùxū,
Tōngzhōu Prefect Lǐ Yǎnzhāo led his two thousand troops to surrender to Jiàn.
Tōngzhōu
is present-day Dázhōu.
Lǐ Yǎnzhāo was also a Fèngxiáng general.
Lǐ Kèyòng sent his Administrative Secretary Lǐ Xíjí to the court to express gratitude for the imperial grace.
In the first year of the Jǐngfèng era,
the marching headquarters established the position of Administrative Secretary;
after the Kāiyuán era,
all military governors established it;
it was responsible for documents related to court audiences, diplomatic missions, recommendations, sacrifices, prayers, and blessings,
as well as matters of orders, promotions, and demotions.
"In recent years,
the Guānfǔ region has not been peaceful.
Guān
refers to the various passes such as Pú, Tóng, Lǒng, Shǔ, and Lántián.
Fǔ
refers to the Three Adjuncts.
Guānnèi
is the territory of the Han dynasty's Three Adjuncts.
We should then seize Fèngxiáng,
accomplishing a single effort for lasting peace,
the opportunity must not be lost.
Your subject has stationed troops north of the Wèi River,
specifically awaiting your command for advance or halt."
The Emperor consulted with his noble intimates.
Some said:
"If Màozhēn is again destroyed,
then the Shātuó will become greatly powerful,
and the court will be in danger!"
The Emperor then bestowed an edict upon Kèyòng,
praising his loyalty and sincerity.
Kuǎn
means sincerity.
"Among those disloyal,
Xíngyú was the worst.
Since We fled the capital,
Màozhēn and Hán Jiàn have recognized their crimes,
have not forgotten the grace of the state,
and have continuously fulfilled their tribute duties.
It is appropriate to cease military actions and let the people rest."
Kèyòng, having received the edict, desisted.
Afterwards, he privately told the edict-bearing envoy:
"Observing the court's intention,
it seems they suspect Kèyòng of harboring different ambitions.
However, if Màozhēn is not removed,
there will be no peaceful days in Guānzhōng."
Later, when Lǐ Màozhēn again encroached upon the capital,
Kèyòng was also unable to rescue it.
Some of his officers and aides said:
"Now we are close to the imperial court,
how can we not enter to see the Son of Heaven!"
Kèyòng hesitated and had not decided,
when Gài Yù said to Kèyòng:
"Previously, Wáng Xíngyú and his ilk allowed their troops to run wild and rebel,
causing the imperial carriage to flee,
and the people to scatter.
Now the Son of Heaven has just returned and is not yet settled,
people's hearts are still fearful.
If Your Highness leads troops across the Wèi River,
I fear it will again alarm the capital.
Gài Yù's words to Lǐ Kèyòng meant that he could not disband his troops and enter the court,
nor could he enter with his multitude,
as that would repeat the actions of the three commanders of Bīn, Qí, and Huá.
The duty lies in aiding the king,
not in entering for an audience.
I hope you will consider this carefully!"
Kèyòng laughed and said:
"Even Gài Yù does not wish for me to enter the court,
let alone the people of the realm!"
He then submitted a memorial stating:
"Your subject commands a large army,
and dares not directly enter the court for an audience,
and furthermore fears that the tribal soldiers might invade and harass the inhabitants north of the Wèi."
On the day Xīnhài,
he led his troops eastward back.
When the memorial reached the capital,
those above and below began to feel at ease.
An edict bestowed three hundred thousand strings of cash upon the Héxiān soldiers.
After Kèyòng left,
Lǐ Màozhēn remained as arrogant and overbearing as before.
Many of the prefectures and counties in Héxī were seized by Màozhēn.
Héxī
refers to the various prefectures such as Liáng, Guā, Shā, and Sù.
After Zhū Quánzhōng left Yǎnzhōu,
(Zhū Qióng died and Quánzhōng returned.) Zhū Jǐn closed the city gates and did not come out again.
When Cóngzhōu was about to return,
he spread the rumor
that "Tiānpíng and Héxiān relief troops have arrived,
I am leading troops northwest to intercept them."
At midnight,
he secretly returned to his original camp.
Jǐn, believing Cóngzhōu's elite troops had all gone out,
indeed sent troops to attack the camp.
Cóngzhōu suddenly charged out and fought fiercely,
killing over a thousand men,
and capturing their commander-in-chief Sūn Hànjūn before returning.
Zhènhǎi Military Governor Qián Liú was additionally appointed Concurrently Palace Attendant.
Zhāngyì Military Governor Zhāng Xuān died.
His son Zhāng Liǎn was appointed Acting Military Vice Commissioner.
Zhū Xuān and Zhū Jǐn were repeatedly attacked by Zhū Quánzhōng.
The people lost their farming,
and both financial resources and strength were exhausted.
They sent urgent pleas for help to Héxiān.
Lǐ Kèyòng sent his generals Shǐ Yǎn and Lǐ Chéngsì with several thousand cavalry, borrowing a route through Wèi to rescue them.
Shǐ Yǎn and Lǐ Chéngsì from this point subsequently entered Huáinán with Zhū Jǐn.
Ānzhōu Defense Commissioner Jiā Shèng
(Surname Compendium: The surname Jiā descends from the Zhou dynasty Grand Master Jiā Fù;
also, among the ducal clan of Lǔ was the lineage of Zǐjiā.) fearing he would be implicated in disaster,
together with Commanding Officer Liú Shìzhèng and Military Inspector Chén Kěfán, led three thousand troops to attack Guìzhōu,
killed Surveillance Commissioner Zhōu Yuánjìng and replaced him.
The reason they could attack Guìzhōu from distant Ānzhōu and capture it was that
the cities and towns along the Jiāng and Xiāng were desolate and ruined,
the defending troops were few and weak,
there was no danger of interception along the route,
and the people of Guì did not expect their arrival,
so they killed their commander and replaced him.
Fán,
pronounced fú yuán fān.
Kěfán personally killed him with a blade,
recommended Shìzhèng to administer the military headquarters affairs,
and Kěfán himself became Vice Commissioner.
An edict immediately appointed Shìzhèng as Surveillance
Commissioner.
Xuánhuī
was a man of Wú.
This sets the stage for their later being annexed by Liú and Chén, and then by Mǎ Yín.
Third Year
(Bǐngchén, 896)
Spring,
first month.
Xīchuān general Wáng Zōngkuí attacked and captured Lóngzhōu,
killing Prefect Tián Fǎng.
At this time, Lóngzhōu likely belonged to Lǐ Màozhēn.
Fǎng,
pronounced fāng wǎng fān.
2 On Dīngsì,
Liú Jiànfēng sent the capital commandant Mǎ Yīn to lead troops against Jiǎng Xūn,
attacking the Dìngshèng Fort,
and captured it.
Last year,
Jiǎng Xūn had sent troops to garrison Dìngshèng Fort.
3 On Xīnwèi,
Ān Rényì arrived at Húzhōu with a naval force,
intending to cross the river to support Dǒng Chāng.
Ān Rényì came from Rùnzhōu with a naval force to Húzhōu.
From where could he cross the river?
He likely intended to sail from Húzhōu into Liǔpǔ and cross at Xīlíng.
However, Qián Liú was in Hángzhōu,
and would not allow him to reach Xīlíng.
Rényì was unable to cross.
Chāng sent his general Tāng Jiù to defend Shíchéng.
The Huìjī Chronicles: Shíchéng Mountain is thirty lǐ northeast of Shānyīn County.
4 In the intercalary month,
Kèyòng sent the Fan and Han capital commandant Lǐ Cúnxìn.
This marks the beginning of another event;
"Kèyòng"
should have
"Lǐ"
above it.
Zhū Quánzhōng sent someone to tell Luó Hóngxìn:
"Kèyòng's ambition is to swallow Héběi.
When his army returns,
your esteemed region will be in peril."
Cúnxìn did not discipline his troops strictly,
and they encroached upon and harassed the people of Wèi.
Hóngxìn was angered,
and dispatched thirty thousand troops to launch a night attack against them.
Cúnxìn's army was routed,
retreating to defend Míngzhōu,
losing twenty to thirty percent of his soldiers.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì,
Shēn County is ninety lǐ west of Wèizhōu.
Luó Hóngxìn, wishing to attack Lǐ Cúnxìn,
must have set out his army in the morning to be able to arrive by night;
Lǐ Cúnxìn's defeat
was due to unclear reconnaissance.
Sàng,
read as sàng.
The armies of Shǐ Yǎn and Lǐ Chéngsì were cut off and unable to return.
From then on, Hóngxìn severed relations with Hédōng,
focusing entirely on Biàn.
Quánzhōng was then planning to take Yǎn and Yùn,
fearing Hóngxìn might challenge him from behind.
Whenever Hóngxìn sent gifts,
Quánzhōng would invariably face north and bow to receive them before the messenger,
saying:
"Sixth Elder Brother is to me,
twice my age in seniority,
certainly not comparable to the other neighboring commanders."
"Shòu"
should be
"shòu".
Luó Hóngxìn,
was the sixth.
The Book of Rites records: If someone is twice one's age,
one should serve them as a father.
How could Zhū Quánzhōng know the rites?
He was merely feigning respect to sever the alliance between Bìng and Wèi.
Zhǎng,
read as zhǎng.
Zhū lín,
refers to the various commanders of regions neighboring Xuānwǔ.
Because of this, Quánzhōng was able to concentrate fully on the east.
Meaning to focus on attacking Yǎn and Yùn.
5 On Dīnghài,
the Guǒzhōu Prefect Zhāng
Xióng surrendered to Wáng Jiàn.
Sòng Bái said: Guǒzhōu Nánchōng Commandery,
Liú Zhāng initially separated the area above Diànjiāng to establish Bā Commandery,
governing here.
In the sixth year of Jiàn'ān,
Zhāng changed the commandery to Bāxī,
moving the seat of government to Làngzhōng.
The present commandery is west of the Jiālíng River.
When Wèi pacified Shǔ,
it established Nán Dàngqú Commandery at Shígǒubà, thirty-seven lǐ north of the present prefecture,
and the county seat was also moved to the commandery seat.
Suí abolished the commandery,
merging it into Làngzhōng,
again becoming part of Bāxī County territory,
and still moved Bāxī County,
governing Ānhàn City.
In the eighteenth year of Kāihuáng,
it was changed to Nánchōng County.
In the fourth year of Táng Wǔdé,
Guǒzhōu was separately established,
named after Guǒ Mountain eight lǐ south of the commandery.
6 In the second month,
on Wùchén,
Gù Quánwǔ and Xǔ Zàisī defeated Tāng Jiù at Shíchéng.
The Emperor, acceding to Yáng Xíngmì's request,
pardoned Dǒng Chāng,
restoring his official titles and ranks;
Qián Liú did not comply.
7 He appointed Prince Tōng Zī to oversee the affairs of the various imperial guard generals.
Prince Tōng Zī,
was a son of Emperor Xuānzōng.
8 Zhū Quánzhōng recommended the Minister of War Zhāng Jùn,
and the Emperor wished to reappoint him as chancellor;
Lǐ Kèyòng submitted a memorial requesting to dispatch troops to attack Quánzhōng,
and stated
"If Jùn becomes chancellor in the morning,
I will arrive at the court by evening!"
Observing Lǐ Kèyòng's memorial,
to claim it was not coercing the sovereign,
I do not believe it.
The Emperor issued an edict to reconcile them.
9 In the third month,
he appointed Tiānxióng acting military governor Lǐ Jìhuī as military governor.
10 Bǎodà military governor Lǐ Sīxiào submitted a request to retire,
recommending his younger brother Lǐ Sījìng as his replacement.
An edict appointed Sīxiào as Grand Preceptor,
allowing him to retire,
and Sījìng as acting military governor of Bǎodà.
11 Zhū Quánzhōng sent Páng Shīgǔ to lead troops to attack Yùnzhōu,
defeating the Yùn troops at Mǎjiá.
Mǎjiá,
was one of the nine rivers dredged by Yǔ.
The Commentary on the Water Classic: The Jì River flows north from Xūchāng County past the east of Yú Mountain,
joining the Mǎjiá River on the left;
the river's head receives water from the Jì,
flowing northwest,
passing north of Ānmín Mountain,
then passing east of Táo City,
then flowing northeast past the south of Yú Mountain,
then flowing east into the Jì,
called the Mǎjiá Estuary.
Bǎi,
read as bài.
12 On Jǐyǒu,
Gù Quánwǔ and others attacked Yúyáo,
and the Míngzhōu Prefect Huáng Shèng sent troops to assist them;
Dǒng Chāng sent his general Xú Zhāng to rescue Yúyáo,
but Quánwǔ attacked and captured him.
13 In summer,
the fourth month,
on Xīnyǒu,
the river rose,
threatening to destroy the walls of Huázhōu.
Zhū Quánzhōng ordered it to be split into two channels,
flanking Huá City and flowing east,
causing even greater harm.
14 Lǐ Kèyòng attacked Luó Hóngxìn,
in retaliation for Lǐ Cúnxìn's defeat.
He killed over ten thousand Wèi soldiers,
and advanced to attack Wèizhōu.
15 The Wǔ'ān military governor Liú Jiànfēng, having achieved his ambitions,
(the vessels of petty men are easily filled;
Liú Jiànfēng had just obtained Chángshā,
and was already satisfied.)
did not attend to governmental affairs.
The wife of Chángzhí soldier Chén Shàn was beautiful,
and Jiànfēng had an affair with her.
Shàn hid an iron mace in his sleeve and struck Jiànfēng dead;
the other generals killed Shàn,
and welcomed the army supervisor Zhāng Jí as acting military governor.
As Jí was about to enter the headquarters,
his horse suddenly kicked and bit him,
injuring his left thigh.
At that time, Mǎ Yīn was attacking Shàozhōu and had not yet captured it.
In the first month of this year,
Liú Jiànfēng had sent Mǎ Yīn to attack Shàozhōu.
"Lord Mǎ is brave and strategic,
generous, kind, and delights in goodness,
qualities I do not possess.
He is truly the rightful lord."
Nǎi,
means you.
Lè,
read as lè.
Yīn hesitated and did not set out.
The Tīngzhí army general Yáo
Yànzhāng persuaded Yīn, saying:
"You, Sir, and Liú Lóngxiāng and Supervisor Zhāng
are men of the same standing.
Now Lóngxiāng has met with misfortune,
and Supervisor Zhāng has injured his thigh.
By Heaven's decree and the people's hopes,
who else but you, Sir, should it fall upon?"
Yīn then sent his personal attendant deputy commandant Lǐ Qióng to remain and attack Shàozhōu,
and went directly to Chángshā.
16. The Huáinán army fought with the Zhènhǎi army at Huángtiāndàng.
The Great River, passing through the boundary of Shēngzhōu,
becomes increasingly deep and wide.
From Lǎoguànzī to Báishā,
it spans over thirty lǐ in width,
commonly referred to as Huángtiāndàng.
At that time, after the Huáinán army had defeated the Zhè army at Huángtiāndàng,
they proceeded to besiege Sūzhōu,
which was not the same Huángtiāndàng mentioned earlier.
In the third year of the Xīníng era of the Sòng dynasty,
Jiá Dǎn, a native of Kūnshān, submitted a memorial on water conservancy,
stating that within the boundaries of Chángzhōu County, there were Chángdàng and Huángtiāndàng,
whose waters flowed from the lakes above
and connected to the sea below,
precisely where the Huáinán and Zhè armies fought.
Yáng Xíngmì then besieged Sūzhōu.
17. Qián Liú, Zhōng Chuán, and Dù Hóng, fearing the strength of Yáng Xíngmì,
all sought aid from Zhū Quánzhōng.
Later, Zhōng and Dù were unable to protect their territories,
while the Qián clan alone passed their land down to sons and grandsons.
From this, it is understood that whether a state or a family endures
depends on the people involved.
They were allowed to act according to circumstances.
18. Dǒng Chāng sent someone to spy on Qián Liú’s troops.
Anyone who reported their strength and prosperity would incur his anger,
and be executed;
those who said the troops were exhausted and provisions depleted
would be rewarded.
On the day Wùyín,
Yuán Bīn surrendered Yúyáo to Qián Liú;
Gù Quánwǔ and Xǔ Zàisī advanced their troops to the walls of Yuèzhōu.
In the fifth month,
Dǒng Chāng went out to battle and was defeated,
retreating behind the city walls to defend himself,
with Gù Quánwǔ and others besieging him.
Dǒng Chāng then grew fearful,
abandoned his imperial title,
and resumed calling himself Military Commissioner.
19. Mǎ Yīn arrived at Chángshā,
Zhāng Jí entered the government office in a sedan chair,
and sat to receive Mǎ Yīn’s bow and greeting.
Afterward,
he ordered Mǎ Yīn to ascend to the audience hall,
yielding the position of Acting Military Commissioner to him.
He then hurried down,
leading the generals and officials in offering congratulations.
Sitting to receive bows and greetings
was the ritual for an Acting Military Commissioner receiving the formal greetings of generals and officers;
leading the generals and officials in offering congratulations
was the ritual for the Army Supervisor congratulating the new Acting Military Commissioner.
The character "shuài"
is read as "lǜ."
He replaced Mǎ Yīn in leading troops to attack Shàozhōu.
20. On the day Guǐwèi,
Lù Yǐng, the garrison commander of Chángshú in Sūzhōu, surrendered the city to Yáng Xíngmì,
capturing the prefect Chéng Jí.
Yáng Xíngmì inspected the possessions in Chéng Jí’s home,
finding only books and medicines.
Impressed by his integrity,
he allowed him to return,
appointing him as Army Supervisor.
Chéng Jí bowed and wept, saying:
"My entire family of a hundred people are under Lord Qián’s control.
Having lost Sūzhōu, I cannot die;
how dare I seek wealth and honor!
I only wish to exchange my own life for the lives of my hundred family members!"
He drew his sword, intending to stab himself.
Yáng Xíngmì quickly seized his hand,
stopping him,
and housed him in a government residence.
Even though there were weapons in his room,
Yáng Xíngmì would often visit him wearing simple clothing,
dining and drinking with him,
without any suspicion.
If Yáng Xíngmì treated all captives like Chéng Jí,
would that not be excessive?
This must have been based on some insight.
When Qián Liú heard that Sūzhōu had fallen,
he urgently summoned Gù Quánwǔ,
ordering him to hasten to Xīlíng to prepare against Yáng Xíngmì.
Gù Quánwǔ said:
"Yuèzhōu is the rebel’s stronghold.
How can we abandon it
when it is on the verge of being captured!
I request to first capture Yuèzhōu,
and then recover Sūzhōu."
Qián Liú agreed.
History records that Gù Quánwǔ understood the proper sequence in military operations.
21. The Huáinán general Zhū Yánshòu suddenly arrived at Qízhōu,
besieging the city.
The general Jiǎ Gōngduó was out hunting
and could not return,
so he hid troops in the forest.
He ordered two brave soldiers to wear sheepskins and enter Zhū Yánshòu’s camp at night,
mingling among the sheep.
They secretly entered the city,
agreeing to open the gates and light a fire at midnight as a signal.
Then, wearing the sheepskins again, they returned to report.
Jiǎ Gōngduó led his troops to the south of the city as scheduled.
When a fire was lit within the gates,
they fought fiercely,
breaking through the siege and entering the city.
Zhū Yánshòu exclaimed in surprise:
"I often feared they would break out of the siege,
but instead they broke into it.
If this is the case,
how can the city be taken quickly!"
He then reported to Yáng Xíngmì,
requesting someone from the army who had old ties with Jiǎ Gōngduó to take a pledge letter, gold, and silk to persuade him,
promising a marriage alliance.
Chái Zàiyòng, the Deputy Training Commissioner of Shòuzhōu, volunteered to go.
Approaching the city walls, he spoke with Jiǎ Gōngduó,
explaining the advantages and disadvantages.
After several days,
Jiǎ Gōngduó and the prefect Féng Jìngzhāng requested to surrender.
Féng Jìngzhāng was appointed Left Chief Guard,
a position in Huáinán.
This was a command of the imperial guard.
In the third year of the Guāngqǐ era of Emperor Xīzōng,
Féng Jìngzhāng seized Qízhōu,
and now surrendered.
Lù Zhèn’s *Jiǔ Guó Zhì* states: Jiǎ Duó was born in Shàngcài,
rebelled against Qín Zōngquán,
crossed the Huái River,
and met his old acquaintance Féng Jìngzhāng.
Guided by him, they attacked and captured Qíchūn,
with Féng Jìngzhāng being made commander
and Jiǎ Duó becoming a general.
They fortified the city and sharpened their weapons to strengthen themselves.
They killed the prefect Liú Cún.
From then on, Yáng Xíngmì fully controlled the territory of Huáinán.
22. On the day Bǐngxū,
the Emperor sent a palace envoy to Zǐzhōu to mediate peace between the two Chuāns.
Although Wáng Jiàn obeyed the decree and returned to Chéngdū,
hostilities had not yet ceased.
23. Cuī Zhāowěi again sought help from Zhū Quánzhōng.
On the day Wùzǐ,
the Emperor sent a palace envoy to grant Cuī Zhāowěi death.
On the way to Jīngnán,
he caught up with him,
and executed him.
Both inside and outside the court, all rejoiced.
Cuī Zhāowěi colluded with Bīn and Qí to kill Dù Ràngnéng, Wéi Zhāodù, and Lǐ Xī,
and in the end, it also led to his own death.
Forming cliques for wicked purposes—
what benefit did it truly bring!
24. The Jīngnán Military Commissioner Chéng Ruì, along with his general Xǔ Cún, advanced up the river to seize territory,
capturing all the prefectures and counties along the river.
The Wǔtài Military Commissioner Wáng Jiànzhào abandoned Qiánzhōu,
gathering his remaining troops to defend Fēngdū.
Fēngdū
was located in the territory of Zhǐ County in the Bā Commandery of the Hàn dynasty.
In the Later Hàn, Píngdū County was established there,
named after the mountain.
The Liáng dynasty established the Línjiāng Commandery,
and the Suí dynasty abolished the commandery, making it a county.
In the second year of the Yìníng era,
Fēngdū County was separated from Línjiāng.
During the Táng, it belonged to Zhōngzhōu.
The *Jiǔ Yù Zhì* states: It is located ninety lǐ west of the prefecture.
Chéng Ruì appointed his general Zhào Wǔ as Acting Military Commissioner of Qiánzhōng,
and Xǔ Cún as Prefect of Wànzhōu.
Knowing that Xǔ Cún was discontent,
Chéng Rùi sent someone to spy on him,
reporting:
"Cún does not attend to the affairs of the prefecture;
every day he goes out to play kickball."
Chéng Rùi said:
"Cún is planning to flee;
he is first strengthening his legs."
He dispatched troops to attack him,
and Xǔ Cún abandoned the city and fled.
Chéng Rùi was not tolerated by Zhāng Wéi,
yet he himself could not tolerate Xǔ Cún;
jealousy of the worthy and envy of the capable
is the nature of ordinary men.
He encamped at Máobà.
Zhào Wǔ repeatedly attacked Fēngdū,
and Wáng Jiànzhào could not hold it.
In the first year of the Wéndé era,
Wáng Jiànzhào obtained the Jiéduìshǐ of Qiánzhōng,
but now he was defeated and fled.
Shù,
suǒ jiǎo fān.
Wáng Jiàn, wary of Xǔ Cún's courage and strategy,
wanted to kill him.
His secretary, Gāo Zhú, said:
"You are gathering heroes to plan for hegemony;
he, in dire straits, has come to submit to us—
why kill him!"
Wáng Jiàn made him garrison Shǔzhōu,
but secretly ordered the prefect of Shǔzhōu, Wáng Zōngwǎn, to observe him.
Zōngwǎn secretly reported that Cún was loyal, brave, humble, and cautious,
possessing the talent of a fine general.
Wáng Jiàn then spared him,
changing his name to Wáng Zōngbō.
Yet Zōngwǎn never let Zōngbō know that he had saved him.
Zōngbō's original clerk, Liǔ Xiūyè,
often urged Zōngbō to be cautious and calm to avoid disaster.
Later, when Zōngbō served as a general under Wáng Jiàn,
encountering strong enemies,
he would personally lead where other generals feared to go.
And when he achieved merit,
he would claim illness,
never boasting of his accomplishments.
Thus he was able to preserve his merit and reputation to the end.
On the 25th, jiǎwǔ,
at night,
Gù Quánwǔ urgently attacked Yuèzhōu.
At dawn on yǐwèi,
he captured its outer walls.
Dǒng Chāng still held the inner citadel and resisted.
On wùxū,
