Yáng Xíngmì submitted a memorial recommending that Shīyuè's son, the former Prefect of Mián Prefecture, Lǐ Yànhuī, administer the prefectural affairs.
(Textual analysis note: The Shílù states:
"In the second year of Qiánníng,
the fourth month,
Zhōngguó Jiedushi Lǐ Shīyuè died,
and his grandson Yànhuī was appointed as Liúhòu."
We now follow the New Annals and the Shíguó Jìnián.)
49. Ān Rényì, a general of Huáinán, attacked Wù Prefecture.
50. In the twelfth month,
troops from Dōngchuān burned and plundered the territories of Hàn, Méi, Zī, and Jiǎn prefectures.
(The four prefectures of Hàn, Méi, Zī, and Jiǎn
were all under the jurisdiction of Xīchuān.)
51. Xuē Wáng Zhīróu, the Qīnghǎi Jiedushi, was traveling to his post and had reached Húnán when
the Yájiàng of Guǎngzhōu, Lú Jū and Tán Hóng, occupied the territory and barred his entry.
Hóng was sent to defend Duān Prefecture.
Hóng formed an alliance with Liú Yǐn, the Prefect of Fēng Prefecture,
promising him his daughter in marriage.
Yǐn pretended to agree,
and under the pretext of personally meeting the bride,
concealed armed men in his boats.
At night, he entered Duān Prefecture,
and beheaded Hóng.
He then proceeded to attack Guǎngzhōu,
and beheaded Jū.
(According to the Jiǔyù Zhì,
from Fēng Prefecture one travels southeast, passing through the territory of Kāng Prefecture before reaching Duān Prefecture.
From Duān Prefecture, it is 240 lǐ east to Guǎngzhōu.)
He then arrayed his troops in full military regalia to welcome the new commander,
following the ceremonial protocols of peaceful times.
Punctuated by Wáng Chóngwǔ, proofread by Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí.
Compiled by Imperial Command
by Sīmǎ Guāng.
Later
student from Tiāntái.
Fourth year of Qiánníng
1 Spring,
first month,
Jiǎshēn day,
Hán Jiàn memorialized:
"The garrison commander Zhāng Xíngsī and others
(Zhāng Xíngsī,
was the garrison commander of Huázhōu.
Commander,
read as 'jiàng'.)
are all princes of the royal house.
Mù, Sháo, and Hán
are descendants of Emperor Dàizōng;
Péng,
is a descendant of Emperor Sùzōng;
Chén,
is a descendant of Emperor Wénzōng;
the histories have all omitted their names and lineages.
They plotted to abduct the imperial carriage and take it to Hézhōng."
Hán Jiàn disliked the princes commanding troops,
so he had Xíngsī and others accuse them.
The Emperor was greatly alarmed,
and summoned Jiàn to admonish him;
Jiàn claimed illness and did not enter.
He ordered the princes to go to Jiàn and explain themselves,
but Jiàn submitted a memorial stating:
"The princes suddenly came to my office,
with unpredictable intentions.
(Jiàn claimed the princes were plotting rebellion,
an unpredictable event.)
I should not meet with the princes."
He further stated:
"The princes should themselves avoid suspicion,
and must not act lightly.
If Your Majesty, out of fraternal affection, wishes to be tolerant,
I request that according to the old regulations,
they be ordered to return to the Sixteen Residences,
where excellent tutors be carefully selected,
to teach them the classics,
and they not be allowed to command troops or participate in government."
Citing the old regulations of the Kāiyuán and Tiānbǎo eras,
which did not allow the princes to leave their residences.
"I beg to disband their ragtag troops,
to glorify the transformative influence of the Línzhǐ."
(The preface to the Odes states: When the influence of the Guānjū prevails,
even the princes of a declining age
are as sincere and substantial as in the time of the Línzhǐ.)
He led his elite troops to surround the traveling palace,
using military force to coerce the sovereign.
The Emperor had no choice,
that evening,
issued an edict ordering all soldiers under the princes' command to be disbanded and sent back to their villages,
the princes were compelled to return to the Sixteen Residences,
and their armor and weapons were all entrusted to Hán Jiàn for custody.
Jiàn further memorialized:
"Your Majesty selects the worthy and appoints the capable,
which is sufficient to quell disorder.
Why must there be a separate establishment of the four imperial guard armies!
(The four armies,
namely Ānshèng, Pěngchén, Bǎoníng, and Xuānhuà.
Their establishment is seen in the previous year of this volume.)
This violates the principle of impartiality and non-partisanship.
(The Book of Documents says: Without partiality, without faction,
the Kingly Way is vast and open.
How would Hán Jiàn recognize words from the Documents?
Lǐ Jùchuān taught him,
which is why he could not avoid execution.)
One version
has the character
"hòu"
followed further by
"yǒu".
In peacetime they still contemplate causing trouble,
in times of crisis they certainly will not be of use,
yet they are allowed to carry bows and blades,
in close proximity to the imperial carriage.
I secretly tremble with fear,
and beg that they all be disbanded."
An edict
complied with this as well.
Thereupon, the more than twenty thousand troops of the four imperial guard armies were all disbanded,
and the Emperor's personal army was completely gone.
The Pěngrì commander Lǐ Jūn,
who had rendered the foremost service in escorting the Emperor at Shímén,
(the Shímén escorting incident is seen in the second year of the previous volume.)
Escort,
read as 'cóng'.)
Jiàn further memorialized:
"At the end of Emperor Xuánzōng's reign,
Prince Yǒng Lín briefly went to Jiāngnán,
and quickly plotted rebellion.
(The event is seen in the first and second years of the Zhìdé era of Emperor Sùzōng's annals.)
During the Guāngqǐ era, Zhū Méi disrupted the norm,
and both supported members of the imperial clan to win popular support.
(Referring to the Tibetans establishing Guǎngwǔ Prince Chénghóng and Zhū Méi establishing Xiāng Prince Yùn,
events each seen in previous annals.)
Support,
read as 'yuán'.)
I beg that they all be summoned back."
(Referring to Yán Prince Jièpī and others.)
"Various alchemists enter and leave the forbidden palace,
bewildering the imperial hearing.
They should all be prohibited,
and not allowed to enter the palace."
(Referring to Xǔ Yánshì and others.)
After Jiàn had confined the princes in separate residences,
knowing the Emperor was displeased,
he then petitioned to establish Prince Dé as Crown Prince,
hoping to resolve the situation.
Dīnghài day,
an edict was issued establishing Prince Dé Yòu as Crown Prince,
and he was further renamed Yù.
2 Pang Shígǔ and Gé Cóngzhōu combined their forces to attack Yùnzhōu.
Zhū Xuān had few troops and exhausted provisions,
so he no longer ventured out to fight,
but instead channeled water to create deep moats to fortify himself.
On Xīnmǎo,
Shígǔ and others encamped southwest of the water,
ordering the construction of a pontoon bridge.
On Guǐsì,
they secretly breached the moat's water.
On Bǐngshēn,
the pontoon bridge was completed,
and Shígǔ crossed first with his central army at night.
Upon hearing this,
Xuān abandoned the city and fled to Zhōngdū.
According to the Jiǔyùzhì,
Zhōngdū County is sixty lǐ southeast of Yùnzhōu.
Villagers captured Xuān along with his wife and children and presented them.
In the second year of Emperor Xīzōng's Zhōnghé era,
Zhū Xuān obtained Yùnzhōu,
and by this time it was lost.
Examination of discrepancies: The Liáng Tàizǔ Jì in Xuē Jūzhèng's History of the Five Dynasties states:
"On Xīnmǎo,
they encamped by the Jì River,
and Pang Shígǔ ordered the generals to dismantle wood to build a bridge.
On the night of Yǐwèi,
Shígǔ crossed first with his central army,
Zhū Xuān abandoned his fortifications and fled at night,
and Gé Cóngzhōu captured Xuān along with his wife and sons and presented them."
According to this, the Jì River had dried up greatly since the time of Wáng Mǎng,
and could no longer cross the Yellow River to the south,
so since then there has been no Jì River south of the Yellow River.
The Biān Yílù states:
"In the fifth month,
cavalry was dispatched to the Yùnzhōu army front to recall Cóngzhōu,
sending him directly to command troops at Huánshuǐ,
to replace Hóu Yán,
while Shígǔ remained to attack Yùn."
The Liáng Tàizǔ Shílù states:
"In the first month of the fourth year,
they again used the Huánshuǐ troops to launch a major campaign against Yùn.
On the fifteenth day, Xīnmǎo,
they encamped southwest of the river outside,
and Pang Shígǔ ordered the generals to dismantle wood to build a bridge for a night crossing.
On Guǐsì,
the vanguard used a hundred trusted men to secretly breach the river mouth.
On Jiǎwǔ,
the pontoon bridge was assembled at the water's edge.
On the night of Yǐwèi,
Shígǔ's central army crossed first,
the noise shaking within the fortifications.
Upon hearing this,
Zhū Xuān abandoned his fortifications and fled."
The Biān Yílù states:
"On Jǐmǎo of the first month in the fourth year,
Zhū Xuān had few troops and exhausted provisions,
not daring to venture out to fight,
but with deep trenches and high ramparts,
it was difficult to cross.
Cóngzhōu and Shígǔ then took small boats from within the Qīnghé,
gathered wild kudzu and thatch,
twisted them into giant cables,
and built a pontoon bridge south of the wall.
On Bǐngshēn,
the work was completed,
our troops crossed the bridge,
and Zhū Xuān fled."
None mention the Jì River.
Last year in the third month, Shígǔ had already defeated the Yùn troops at Mǎjiá,
pursued them to the west gate,
and occupied the old Luòtíngzi as a camp.
Crossing first on the night of Yǐwèi,
it was likely the Qīnghé water below Yùn City,
suspected to have been channeled by Zhū Xuān to encircle the city for solid defense,
so Shígǔ and others built a pontoon bridge for the troops to cross.
Since the river could be breached,
it clearly was not a natural watercourse.
The Old Annals state:
"On Guǐwèi,
Pang Shígǔ captured Yùnzhōu,
and Zhū Xuān with his wife, Madame Róng, broke through the encirclement and fled.
Xuān reached Zhōngdū,
where he was killed by villagers,
and Madame Róng was captured by the army."
The New Annals state:
"On Bǐngshēn,
Quánzhōng captured Yùnzhōu."
The Shílù states:
"In the second month,
on the first day, Bǐngwǔ,
Yùnzhōu was captured.
Xuān reached Zhōngdū,
where he was killed by disorderly troops,
and his wife, Madame Róng, went to Biàn and became a nun."
According to Xuē's History,
on Xīnmǎo they encamped by the Jì River,
so on Guǐwèi Yùn had not yet fallen.
The New Annals say Yùn fell on Bǐngshēn,
and the Shílù says the second month,
likely based on when the report arrived.
Now follow the Biān Yílù and the New Annals.
3 On Jǐhài,
Sūn Wò was dismissed as the Military Commissioner of the Fèngxiáng Four-Sides Campaign,
and Lǐ Màozhēn was pardoned,
hence the Fèngxiáng Four-Sides Campaign was dissolved.
According to the Fāngzhèn Biǎo,
in the first year of the Guānghuà era,
the Yánzhōu Bǎosài Military Commission was renamed the Níngsài Military Commission.
4 Qián Liú sent the Army Marshal Dù Léng to rescue Wùzhōu.
Ān Rényì shifted his troops to attack Mùzhōu,
but failed to capture it and withdrew.
Ān Rényì's attack on Wùzhōu is mentioned in the previous scroll last year.
Withdraw,
pronounced as "xuán" according to Xuān's annotation,
or also as the regular pronunciation.
5 Zhū Quánzhōng entered Yùnzhōu,
appointing Pang Shígǔ as the Interim Military Commissioner of Tiānpíng.

Examination of discrepancies: The Old Annals, the Liáng Tàizǔ Shílù, and Xuē Jūzhèng's History of the Five Dynasties biography of Shígǔ all state that Shígǔ was the Interim Military Commissioner of Yùnzhōu.
The Biān Yílù and Xuē's History Liáng Annals both state
"Yǒuyù."
According to the Biān Yílù,
"In the third month,
on Bǐngzǐ,
Yǒuyù was appointed Interim Military Commissioner of Yùnzhōu,
and Shígǔ as Interim Military Commissioner of Xúzhōu."
It seems initially Shígǔ was stationed in Yùnzhōu,
later replaced by Yǒuyù,
and Shígǔ was transferred to Xúzhōu.
Zhū Jǐn left his senior general Kāng Huáizhēn to guard Yǎnzhōu,
and together with the Hézhōng generals Shǐ Yǎn and Lǐ Chéngsì, plundered the territory of Xúzhōu to supply the army.
According to the Jiǔyùzhì: Yǎnzhōu is one hundred ten lǐ south,
which is the boundary of Xúzhōu.
Gé Cóngzhōu was sent with troops to raid Yǎnzhōu.
Hearing that Yùnzhōu had already fallen,
and the Biàn troops suddenly arrived,
Huáizhēn surrendered.
In the second month,
on Wùshēn,
Cóngzhōu entered Yǎnzhōu,
capturing Jǐn's wife and children.
When Zhū Jǐn returned,
he had nowhere to go,
leading his troops toward Yízhōu.
The prefect, Yǐn Chǔbīn, did not admit him,
so he fled to safeguard Hǎizhōu,
but pressed by Biàn troops,
together with Shǐ Yǎn and Lǐ Chéngsì, he led the prefectural people across the Huái River,
fleeing to Yáng Xíngmì.
In the second year of the Guāngqǐ era,
Zhū Jǐn took Yǎnzhōu,
and by this time he was defeated.
He was appointed as the Military Commissioner of Wǔníng.
Appointed,
meaning a remote appointment.
Quánzhōng took Jǐn's wife,
and led his troops back.
Madame Zhāng met him at Fēngqiū,
According to the Jiǔyùzhì: Fēngqiū County,
is sixty lǐ north of Biànzhōu.
Madame requested to see her,
Jǐn's wife bowed,
and Madame returned the bow,
and wept, saying:
"Yǎn and Yùn shared the same surname as the Minister of Works,
and swore to be brothers.
Over minor grievances and resentments,
they took up arms and attacked each other,
causing my sister-in-law to suffer humiliation here.
If one day Biànzhōu falls,
will I too be like my sister-in-law today!"
Quánzhōng then sent Jǐn's wife to a Buddhist temple to become a nun,
and executed Zhū Xuān at the Biàn Bridge.
Thus, Yùn, Qí, Cáo, Dì, Yǎn, Yí, Mì, Xú, Sù, Chén, Xǔ, Zhèng, Huá, and Pǔ all came under Quánzhōng's control.
Yùn, Qí, Cáo, Dì,
were under the Tiānpíng Army;
Yǎn, Yí, Mì,
under the Tàiníng Army;
Xú, Sù,
under the Gǎnhuà Army;
Chén, Xǔ,
under the Zhōngwǔ Army;
Zhèng, Huá, Pǔ,
under the Xuānyì Army.
These are the territories of the five military commands.
They also submitted to Quánzhōng.
Lǐ Cúnxìn was in Wèizhōu,
and upon hearing that Yǎn and Yùn had both fallen,
led his troops back.
Huáinán originally excelled at naval warfare,
but did not know cavalry archery.
After obtaining the Hézhōng, Yǎn, and Yùn troops,
the army's prestige greatly increased.
Shǐ Yǎn and Lǐ Chéngsì were both valiant generals of Hézhōng,
deeply regretted by Lǐ Kèyòng,
who sent an envoy via byways to Yáng Xíngmì to request their return;
Xíngmì agreed,
and also sent an envoy to Kèyòng to establish friendly relations.
6 On the Wùwǔ day,
Wáng Jiàn dispatched Huá Hóng, the prefect of Qióng Prefecture, and Wáng Zōngyòu, the prefect of Péng Prefecture, to lead fifty thousand troops to attack Dōngchuān.
He appointed Wáng Zōngjǐn, the prefect of Róng Prefecture, as the Vanguard Commander of the Western Campaign against Fèngxiáng.
They defeated Fèngxiáng generals Lǐ Jìhuī and others at Xuánwǔ.
Xuánwǔ,
was the Dīdào County of the Hàn dynasty,
renamed Xuánwǔ in the Jìn dynasty,
belonged to Yì Prefecture in the early Táng,
at that time belonged to Zǐ Prefecture,
renamed Zhōngjiāng in the Sòng dynasty,
located ninety lǐ west of Zǐ Prefecture.
Defeated,
bǔ mài fān.
His original name was Chóngběn,
an adopted son of Lǐ Màozhēn.
7 On the Jǐwèi day,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
8 The Emperor performed sacrifices at the temporary imperial ancestral temple.
At that time, the imperial cortege was stationed in Huá Prefecture,
and the Court of Imperial Sacrifices requested the temporary establishment of a traveling temple for sacrificial ceremonies.
9 On the Gēngshēn day,
Wáng Jiàn appointed Wáng Zōngkǎn, the Commander of the Juéyún Capital Army, as the Commander of the Yìngyuán Kāixiá Capital Army,
leading eight thousand troops towards Yú Prefecture;
and appointed Wáng Zōngruǎn, the Commander of the Juéshèng Capital Army, as the Kāijiāng Escort and Tribute Commissioner,
leading seven thousand troops towards Lú Prefecture.
On the Xīnyǒu day,
Zōngkǎn captured Yú Prefecture,
and accepted the surrender of Prefect Mù Chónghòu.
On the Guǐyǒu day,
Zōngruǎn captured Lú Prefecture,
executed Prefect Mǎ Jìngrú,
and the Xiá road was thus opened.
Yú and Lú
were both under the jurisdiction of Dōngchuān.
Wáng Jiàn's ambition was to expand his territory,
and he merely used opening the Xiá road for tribute transport as a pretext.
Towards,
qī yù fān.
The Fèngxiáng general Lǐ Jìzhāo came to rescue Zǐ Prefecture,
leaving a deputy general to guard Jiànmén.
The Xīchuān general Wáng Zōngbō attacked and captured him.
10 On the Yǐhài day,
Sūn Wò, the Vice Director of the Chancellery and Tongpingzhangshi, was dismissed and reverted to his original official post.
Zhū Pǔ, the Vice Director of the Secretariat and Tongpingzhangshi, was dismissed and made Director of the Palace Library.
After Zhū Pǔ took charge of governance,
none of his proposals proved effective,
(Zhū Pǔ had previously boasted that peace could be achieved within a little over a month; see the previous year in the previous scroll).
Mǎ Dàoyīn, the Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent, was favored by the Emperor due to his knowledge of astronomy,
and Xǔ Yánshì, the Director of the Palace Buildings, was favored due to his medical skills.
Hán Jiàn falsely accused these two of crimes and had them executed,
and further claimed that Wò and Pǔ had illicit connections with these two men,
hence they were dismissed from their ministerial posts.
Mǎ Dàoyīn and Xǔ Yánshì were close to the Emperor,
and the two ministers used them to report matters,
this certainly happened.
11 An edict appointed Yáng Xíngmì as the Commander-in-Chief of the Southern Campaign Armies,
to campaign against Dù Hóng, the Military Governor of Wǔchāng.
According to the New History's biography of Hóng,
Hóng attached himself to Zhū Quánzhōng,
cutting off the tribute route from the southeast,
and Yáng Xíngmì was ordered to campaign against him for this reason.
12 Zhāng Jí captured Shào Prefecture,
and captured Jiǎng Xūn.
(The attack by Tán troops on Jiǎng Xūn began in the first month of the third year of the previous scroll).
Jí,
jù yǐ fān.
13 In the third month,
on the Bǐngzǐ day,
Zhū Quánzhōng memorialized to appoint Gé Cóngzhōu, the prefect of Cáo Prefecture, as the Interim Military Governor of Tàiníng,
Zhū Yǒuyù as the Interim Military Governor of Tiānpíng,
and Páng Shīgǔ as the Interim Military Governor of Wǔníng.
Zhū Quánzhōng memorialized to grant these three military governorships to these three generals to build his faction.
At this time, it seems Gǎnhuà was changed back to Wǔníng.
14 Wáng Gǒng, the Military Governor of Bǎoyì, attacked Wáng Kē, the Military Governor of Hùguó.
Kē sought aid from Lǐ Kèyòng,
while Gǒng sought aid from Zhū Quánzhōng.
Xuānwǔ generals Zhāng Cùnjìng and Yáng Shīhòu defeated the Hézhōng troops south of Yīshì;
the Hézhōng general Lǐ Sìzhāo defeated the Shǎn troops at Yīshì,
and again defeated them at Zhāngdiàn,
thus lifting the siege of Hézhōng.
Shīhòu
was a man of Jīngōu.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì,
Wànshòu County in Yǐng Prefecture had the Jīngōu town.
Wànshòu,
was the Bǎichǐ town of Rǔyīn County in the Táng,
established as a county in the sixth year of the Kāibǎo era of the Sòng dynasty.
He was an adopted son of Lǐ Kèróu, the younger brother of Lǐ Kèyòng.
15 The Gǎnyì Army was renamed Zhāowǔ,
with its headquarters at Lì Prefecture.
The former Military Governor of Jìngnán, Sū Wénjiàn, was appointed as its Military Governor.
16 In summer,
the fourth month,
Lǐ Jìtáng, the Defense Commissioner of Tóng Prefecture, was appointed as the Military Governor of Kuāngguó.
Examination of discrepancies: According to the Veritable Records:
"Tóng Prefecture was granted the name Kuāngguó Army,
and Defense Commissioner Lǐ Jìtáng was appointed as the Military Governor of Kuāngguó."
According to the New History's Table of Military Governors,
in the second year of Qiánníng,
Tóng Prefecture was granted the name Kuāngguó Army.
Wáng Xíngyuē had already once served as Military Governor of Kuāngguó.
It seems that after Xíngyuē's death,
Jìtáng only served as Defense Commissioner,
and now the old name was restored.
He was an adopted son of Lǐ Màozhēn.
17 Lǐ Xún, the Senior Advisor of the Right, was appointed as the Pacification Commissioner to Liǎngchuān,
to mediate between Wáng Jiàn and Gù Yànhuī.
18 On the Xīnhài day,
Qián Liú dispatched Gù Quánwǔ and others to lead three thousand troops by sea to rescue Jiāxīng.
On the Jǐwèi day,
they arrived at the city walls,
attacked the Huáinán troops,
and inflicted a major defeat on them.
(The Huáinán siege of Jiāxīng began in the second year of the previous scroll).
19 Dù Hóng, being attacked by Yáng Xíngmì,
sought aid from Zhū Quánzhōng.
Quánzhōng dispatched his general Niè Jīn to raid Sì Prefecture,
and Zhū Yǒugōng to attack Huáng Prefecture.
Xíngmì dispatched Mǎ Xún, the Commander of the Right Black Cloud Army, and others to rescue Huáng Prefecture.
Qú Zhāng, the prefect of Huáng Prefecture, upon hearing of Yǒugōng's approach,
abandoned the city,
and gathered his forces to hold the Wǔchāng stockade to the south.
Wǔchāng,
an ancient county of the Hàn,
belonged to È Prefecture in the Táng.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: It is located 180 lǐ northeast of the prefectural seat,
and now the Shòuchāng Army is stationed there.
20 On the Guǐhài day,
the Liǎngzhè troops under Gù Quánwǔ and others destroyed eighteen Huáinán camps,
and captured over three thousand Huáinán officers and soldiers, including Wèi Yuē.
The Huáinán general Tián Yūn was stationed at Yìtíng Dài.
The Liǎngzhè troops took advantage of their victory to pursue him.
On the Jiǎxū day,
Yūn fled back from Hú Prefecture,
(withdrawing his army from Jiāxīng,
taking the route through Hú Prefecture,
to return to Xuān Prefecture).
Over a thousand of Yūn's troops perished.
21 Hán Jiàn detested several people including Zhāng Yī, the Minister of Justice,
and falsely accused them in memorials,
resulting in their demotion.
22 In the fifth month,
Cuī Hóng, the Military Governor of Fèngguó, was given the additional title of Tongpingzhangshi.
23 On the Xīnsì day,
Zhū Yǒugōng constructed a pontoon bridge at Fǎngǎng.
(Three lǐ west of Wǔchāng is Fán Mountain,
at the foot of which is Fán Stream,
which flows into the Yangtze,
called Fánkǒu.
It seems Zhū Yǒugōng built a pontoon bridge across the river,
reaching Fánkǒu,
to attack Wǔchāng).
On the Rénwǔ day,
he captured it,
seized Qú Zhāng,
and subsequently took Huáng Prefecture.
Examination of discrepancies: According to the Old History of the Five Dynasties, Liang Annals:
"On the Dīngchǒu day of the fifth month,
Zhū Yǒugōng sent an envoy to report,
saying he had inflicted a major defeat on the Huái rebels at Wǔchāng,
and recovered Huáng and È Prefectures."
According to the New History Annals:
"On the Rénwǔ day,
Quánzhōng captured Huáng Prefecture,
and its prefect Qú Zhāng died."
The biography of Zhū Yǒugōng writes it as Dí Zhāng,
while the Ten Kingdoms Chronicle writes it as Qú Zhāng.
According to the Wú Records: He captured Prefect Qú Zhāng,
which should be reliable.
24 On the Bǐngxū day,
Wáng Jiàn appointed Zhāng Lín, his Deputy Military Governor, to guard Chéngdū.
Zhāng Lín
was a trusted confidant of Wáng Jiàn.
When Jiàn attacked Chén Jìngxuǎn,
he also had him guard Qióng Prefecture.
He changed Huá Hóng's name to Wáng Zōngdí.
Huá Hóng had repeatedly achieved military merits,
and Wáng Jiàn thus adopted him as a son to secure his service and strength,
but his intention to kill Hóng likely began to sprout at this time.
Huá,
hù huà fān.
25 In the sixth month,
on the Jǐyǒu day,
Qián Liú went to Yuè Prefecture,
to receive the seal and tally of the Zhèndōng Military Governorship.
26. Lǐ Màozhēn submitted a memorial:
"Wáng Jiàn has been attacking Dōngchuān,
engaged in continuous warfare for years,
and does not heed imperial decrees."
Was Wáng Jiàn only attacking Dōngchuān?
The various prefectures under Lǐ Màozhēn's jurisdiction in Shānnán,
Wáng Jiàn had seized many of them as well;
lacking the strength to control him,
[Lǐ Màozhēn] wished to rely on the Son of Heaven's command to oversee him.
On the jiǎyín day
Wáng Jiàn was demoted to Prefect of Nánzhōu.
New Records: In the third year of Wǔdé,
the southern barbarians of Qián were pacified,
and Nánzhōu was established.
Sòng Bái said: Nánzhōu,
during the Warring States period was within the boundaries of the Bā state,
under Qín it was territory of Bā Commandery,
under Hàn it was within the jurisdiction of Jiāngzhōu.
In the third year of Táng Wǔdé,
the eastern boundary of Yúzhōu was divided off,
and Nánzhōu was established.
On the yǐmǎo day
Lǐ Màozhēn was appointed Military Commissioner of Xīchuān.
Tánwáng Sìzhōu was appointed Military Commissioner of Fèngxiáng.
27. On the guǐhài day,
Wáng Jiàn captured the southern stockade of Zǐzhōu,
capturing its general Lǐ Jìníng.
On the bǐngyín day,
the Imperial Envoy Lǐ Xún arrived at Zǐzhōu.
In the fourth month,
Lǐ Xún received his orders and set out,
only reaching [Zǐzhōu] in the sixth month.
On the jǐsì day
he met with Jiàn at Zhāngpá Stockade.
Jiàn pointed at the flag-bearers and said:
"The feelings of the warriors,
cannot be overruled."
28. Tánwáng proceeded to his garrison,
but Lǐ Màozhēn did not relinquish his post.
Given Lǐ Màozhēn's cunning and fierceness,
how could he be willing to hand over Fèngxiáng to another,
and risk danger to contend for Shǔ?
29. The Níngyuǎn Army was established in Róngzhōu,
with Lǐ Kèyòng's senior general Gài Yù appointed as Military Commissioner.
When Lǐ Kèyòng pacified Wáng Xíngyú,
Gài Yù, for his merit, was appointed Surveillance Commissioner of Róngguǎn,
and now was promoted to Military Commissioner.
30. In autumn,
the seventh month,
Jīngnán Military Commissioner Chéng Ruì was additionally appointed as Shìzhōng.
31. Hán Jiàn sent a letter to Lǐ Màozhēn;
Màozhēn lifted the siege of Fèngtiān,
and Tánwáng returned to Huàzhōu.
32. Tiānxióng Military Commissioner Lǐ Jìhuī was appointed Jìngnán Military Commissioner.
Lǐ Jìhuī moved from Qínzhōu to Bīnzhōu,
thus Bīnníng also came under Lǐ Màozhēn's control.
The character "nán" [in Jìngnán]
is pronounced nài.
33. On the gēngxū day,
Qián Liú returned to Hángzhōu,
returning from Yuè to Háng.
On the yǐwèi day,
he captured Sōngjiāng;
Sōngjiāng,
is located forty lǐ south of Sūzhōu,
where Huáinán had established a stockade to defend it.
On the wùxū day
he captured Wúxī;
Wúxī,
a Hàn dynasty county,
belonged to Chángzhōu under the Táng.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì,
it is ninety-one lǐ east of the prefectural seat.
On the xīnchǒu day
he captured Chángshú and Huátíng.
Sòng Bái said: Chángshú County,
from the Later Hàn to Wú was the seat of the Salt Superintendent,
under Jìn, Nánshā County was established,
under Liáng, Chángshú County was established.
The old city of Chángshú is located one hundred and thirty lǐ east of present-day Kūnshān County.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì,
it is seventy-five lǐ north of Sūzhōu.
In the tenth year of Tiānbǎo,
Huátíng County was established from part of Jiāxīng,
belonging to Sūzhōu,
located southwest of the prefectural seat;
now it belongs to Xiùzhōu.
34. Earlier,
when Lǐ Kèyòng seized Yōuzhōu,
see the 259th scroll, first year of Qiánníng.
he left garrison troops and ten trusted generals to manage its crucial affairs,
with all taxes and levies, beyond what supplied the army,
sent to Jìnyáng.
When the Emperor went to Huàzhōu,
Kèyòng levied troops from Rén'gōng,
and also sent letters to Chéngdé Military Commissioner Wáng Róng and Yìwǔ Military Commissioner Wáng Gào,
wishing to join with them to pacify Guānzhōng,
and escort the Son of Heaven back to Cháng'ān.
Rén'gōng declined, citing Qìdān incursions,
requiring troops for defense,
requesting to wait until the barbarians retreated,
before complying with the order.
Kèyòng repeatedly urged him,
with envoys following one after another,
but for months,
no troops were dispatched.
Kèyòng sent a letter reprimanding him,
Rén'gōng threw the letter on the ground,
cursed insolently,
imprisoned his envoy,
and intended to kill the Hé dōng garrison generals;
the garrison generals fled and escaped.
Kèyòng had left troops garrisoning Yōuzhōu,
see the previous scroll, second year of Qiánníng.
In the eighth month,
he personally led troops to attack Rén'gōng.
For those strategizing for Kèyòng,
the plan should have been to first raise Hé dōng's armies to aid the king,
after the situation was stabilized,
then move troops to Yān to demand accountability;
how could Liú Rén'gōng have escaped death then?
Not knowing to adopt this strategy,
he rashly raised an army out of anger,
his defeat was fitting.
35. The Emperor wished to go to Fèngtiān to personally campaign against Lǐ Màozhēn,
and ordered the chief ministers to deliberate;
the chief ministers earnestly remonstrated,
and he desisted.
Commentators generally say Emperor Zhāozōng acted on anger without considering the difficulties,
yet it is also lamentable.
36. Prince Yán, Jièpī, returned from Jìnyáng.
Jièpī's mission to Jìnyáng is described in the previous year's scroll.
"Since Your Majesty ascended the throne,
you have been at odds with the neighboring provinces,
the neighboring provinces being
Bīn, Qí, Tóng, and Huá.
The wicked delight in calamity,
causing the imperial carriage to be unsettled.
Recently, I memorialized to disband the military authority,
truly fearing unforeseen changes.
Now I hear that Prince Yán and Prince Tán are still harboring secret plots.
I hope Your Majesty will make a sagacious decision without hesitation,
to control matters before chaos arises.
The *Zhōushū* says: 'Control order before chaos arises.'
Jiàn's memorial quoted this,
which were the words of Lǐ Jùchuān.
Hán Jiàn had long wanted to kill the princes,
but he feared Lǐ Kèyòng,
so he did not dare act.
Now that Prince Yán has returned,
knowing that Kèyòng's troops cannot arrive,
he resolutely requested to kill them.
"How could it come to this!"
For several days, there was no reply.
Jiàn then, together with the Privy Councilor Liú Jìshù, forged an edict to dispatch troops and surround the Sixteen Mansions.
The princes, with disheveled hair,
some climbed over walls,
some ascended rooftops,
crying out
saying:
"The Emperor, save your children!"
Jiàn seized Princes Tōng, Yí, Mù, Jì, Sháo, Péng, Hán, Chén, Tán, Yán, and Dān—eleven princes in total—and took them to Shídī Valley,
where he killed them all.
Shídī Valley
is west of Huázhōu.
Ōuyáng Xiū's *Collection of Ancient Inscriptions* states: The Shrine of the Xiáokēng Lord,
now called the Temple of the Five Divisions,
has statues including Shídī Xīshùshùgǔ, Wǔlóu Xiānshēng, Dōngtái Yùshǐ, and General Wáng Jiǎn,
but their meanings are unclear.
The stele says:
"Shídī Shùgǔ,
connects south to Shāng and Luò."
It also says:
"In former times, for smooth governance,
officials and people prospered,
with Yùshǐ Dàfū, generals, and regional governors,
thus a shrine was established to repay their merits."
From this, we know the title "Five Divisions"
existed since the Hàn dynasty.
Thus,
Shídī refers to
the deity of Shídī Valley,
one of the Five Division deities.
Táng's Hán Jiàn killed the princes at Shídī Valley,
which is likely this valley.
The Xiáokēng Shrine
is in Zhèng County, Huázhōu.
*Textual Analysis* states: The *Old Annals*:
"On that day,
Princes Tōng, Tán, and the following eleven princes, along with their attendants, were all seized by Jiàn's troops,
taken to Shídī Valley,
and regardless of age,
all were killed."
The *Táng Bǔ Jì* states:
"The princes of the Six Mansions,
following previous discussions,
requested to establish a Rear Palace Guard.
Hán Jiàn, resentful and angry,
submitted a memorial arguing,
exchanging accusations with the princes.
The Emperor then bound ten people, including Prince Hán Kèliáng, and sent them to Hán Jiàn's residence.
Jiàn surrounded them with thorny branches in the main hall,
and for a whole night did not meet them.
Military officers remonstrated,
so he requested the princes return to the palace,
and disbanded the Rear Palace Guard."
The *New Annals*:
"In the eighth month,

Hán Jiàn killed Prince Tōng Zī, Prince Yí Yīn, Prince Sháo, Prince Péng, the succeeding Prince Hán, the succeeding Prince Chén, the succeeding Prince Tán Sìzhōu, the succeeding Prince Yán Jièpī, and the succeeding Prince Dān Yǔn."
According to Hán Jiàn's memorial in the *Old Annals*,
it lists eight people: Princes Mù, Jì, Sháo, Tōng, Péng, Hán, Yí, and Chén.
The *New Annals*' Imperial Clan Biographies,
initially the Emperor sent the succeeding Prince Yán Jièpī
and the succeeding Prince Dān Yǔn to see Lǐ Kèyòng,
and there was also the succeeding Prince Tán Sìzhōu,
making eleven people.
The *New Annals* and Biographies
have "Yí"
written as
"Yí."
According to this, Zhāozōng's son Yīn was enfeoffed as Prince Yí,
so another imperial clansman should not have been enfeoffed with the same title.
The *Old Annals*' Prince Yí
is likely reliable.
37. The Minister of Rites Sūn Wò was demoted to Military Advisor of Nánzhōu.
The Director of the Palace Library Zhū Pǔ was first demoted to Military Advisor of Kuízhōu,
then further demoted to Registrar of Chēnzhōu.
*Textual Analysis* states: The *Veritable Records*:
"Pǔ was demoted to Registrar of Chēnzhōu."
Xuē Tíngguī's *Fènggé Shūcí* contains the edict demoting Pǔ from Director of the Palace Library to Tutor of the Prince of Shǔ, with assignment to the Eastern Capital:
"He harbored no regard for court discipline,
and his audience was not arranged by the Chief Minister."
It further states:
"Still hoping for advisory meetings,
he came to disturb the clarifying governance."
Another edict demoting him to Military Assistant of Qúzhōu states:
"Remonstrating officials submitted memorials,
the Censorate spoke out strongly,
pointing out his schemes of stubborn reliance,
and resenting his plans of promoting treachery."
This differs slightly.
Now follow the *Veritable Records*.
Hé Yíng was rapidly promoted to Right Admonisher,
and by this time was also demoted to Military Advisor of Húzhōu.
Hé Yíng's recommendation of Zhū Pǔ is described in the previous year's scroll.
38. Zhōng Chuán wanted to attack Jízhōu Prefect Xiāngyáng Zhōu Bèi,
so Bèi led his followers and fled to Guǎnglíng.
Bèi,
pronunciation: [AS-FE4A] [AS-FBED] miǎn,
also pú mèi.
Shuài,
read as lǜ.
39. Wáng Jiàn fought over fifty battles with Gù Yànhuī.
In the ninth month,
on the first day, guǐyǒu,
he besieged Zǐzhōu.
Shǔzhōu Prefect Zhōu Déquán said to Jiàn:
"You have contended with Yànhuī for Dōngchuān for three years.
Soldiers are weary from arrows and stones,
and the people are exhausted from transporting supplies.
Many bandits in Dōngchuān occupy prefectures and counties.
Yànhuī is cowardly and lacking in strategy.
Wanting a plan for temporary ease,
he entices them with substantial profits,
relying on their rescue,
hence he stubbornly holds out and does not surrender.
Now if we send someone to explain fortune and misfortune to the bandit leaders,
rewarding those who come with official positions,
and intimidating those who do not submit with military force,
then what he relies on
will instead be used by us."
Jiàn followed this advice,
and Yànhuī's situation became increasingly isolated.
Déquán
was from Xǔzhōu.
40. On dīngchǒu,
Lǐ Kèyòng arrived at Ānsài Army.
Ānsài Army is east of Yùzhōu
and west of Guīzhōu.
The *New Treatise*: Southwest of Dīnglíng Chuān in Yōuzhōu is Ānsài Army.
On xīnsì
he attacked it.
Yōuzhōu general Shàn Kějí led cavalry to arrive.
Kèyòng was drinking at the time,
and the vanguard reported:
"The enemy has arrived!"
Kèyòng, drunk,
said:
"Where is Liú Réngōng?"
They replied:
"We only see Kějí and his like."
Kèyòng glared and said:
"Kějí and his like are hardly worthy opponents!"
He urgently ordered an attack.
That day there was heavy fog,
making people and objects indistinguishable.
Yōuzhōu general Yáng Shīkǎn had ambushed troops at Mùguā Jiàn.
According to the *New History*,
Mùguā Jiàn is also within Yùzhōu's borders.
He suffered over half his forces lost.
The historian says Lǐ Kèyòng underestimated the enemy,
and also did not have favorable conditions,
hence his defeat.
The Yōuzhōu troops then withdrew.
The historian says Kèyòng, though defeated, was spared also due to Heaven.
He reprimanded his senior general Lǐ Cúnxìn and others, saying:
"I neglected affairs due to drunkenness,
why did you not strenuously remonstrate!"
The rebellion at Xíngzhōu,
the defeat at Shēn County,
and the defeat at Mùguā Jiàn
were all Lǐ Cúnxìn's fault.
Yet Kèyòng remained close to and trusted him until the end,
which can be said to be a failure of punishment.
41. Húzhōu Prefect Lǐ Yànhuī wanted to attach the prefecture to Yáng Xíngmì.
Last year, Yáng Xíngmì memorialized to have Yànhuī administer Húzhōu,
hence he wanted to attach to him.
Yànhuī fled to Guǎnglíng,
and the Chief Commandant Shěn Yī surrendered the prefecture to Qián Liú.
From this, Qián Liú then possessed Húzhōu.
42. Zhāngyì Military Commissioner Zhāng Liǎn was appointed as Commander of the Western and Northern Fronts of the Fèngxiáng Campaign
to campaign against Lǐ Màozhēn.
43. Wang Jian was again appointed as the Military Commissioner of Xīchuān and concurrently as Tongpíngzhāngshì.
Wang Gao, the Military Commissioner of Yìwǔ, was additionally appointed as Tongpíngzhāngshì.
The official titles and ranks of Lǐ Màozhēn, the newly appointed Military Commissioner of Xīchuān, were stripped away,
and his original name, Sòng Wéntōng, was restored.
Initially, at Lǐ Màozhēn's request, the court launched a campaign against Wáng Jiàn.
Later, because Lǐ Màozhēn defied orders,
Wáng Jiàn was pardoned and a campaign was launched against Màozhēn.
The court's orders and decrees
were issued in the morning and changed by evening.
How could the feudal lords respect and trust such a government!
The imperial authority was not upheld,
a situation brought upon itself.
The bestowal of the surname Lǐ and given name Màozhēn is recorded in the second year of the Guāngqǐ era, in scroll 256.
44. After Zhū Quánzhōng gained control of Yǎnzhōu and Yùnzhōu,
his military forces grew even stronger.
He then launched a major attack against Yáng Xíngmì.
He sent Páng Shīgǔ with 70,000 troops from Xúzhōu, Sùzhōu, Sòngzhōu, and Huázhōu to encamp at Qīngkǒu.
Qīngkǒu
is present-day Qīnghékǒu.
Gé Cóngzhōu led troops from Yǎnzhōu, Yùnzhōu, Cáozhōu, and Púzhōu to encamp at Ānfēng,
intending to advance towards Shòuzhōu.
Ānfēng
was the Liù County of the Hàn dynasty,
with its old city located south of the county seat.
The Later Hàn established Ānfēng County.
By the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Shòuzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Ānfēng County
is located over sixty lǐ southeast of the prefectural seat.
The Shòuzhōu of the Táng dynasty
administered Shòuchūn County,
which was the Shòuyáng region of the Six Dynasties period.
At the end of the Five Dynasties,
Emperor Shìzōng of the Later Zhōu captured Shòuzhōu
and moved the administrative seat to Xiàcài.
Therefore, in the Sòng dynasty, Ānfēng was located southeast of Shòuzhōu.
Huáinán was shaken with fear.
45. Lǐ Jìtáng, the Military Commissioner of Kuāngguó, heard that the court was campaigning against Lǐ Màozhēn and became fearful.
Hán Jiàn further agitated him,
and Jìtáng fled to Fèngxiáng.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Jiàn was appointed as Military Commissioner of both the Zhènguó and Kuāngguó armies.
Hán Jiàn thus began to concurrently control Tóngzhōu and Huázhōu.
46. On the Rénzǐ day,
Hóu Shào, the administrator of Suízhōu, led 20,000 troops;
on the Yǐmǎo day,
Wáng Rénwēi, the administrator of Hézhōu, led 1,000 troops;
on the Wùwǔ day,
Lǐ Jìpǔ from Fèngxiáng brought 2,000 relief troops;
all surrendered to Wáng Jiàn.
Jiàn intensified his attack on Zǐzhōu.
On the Gēngshēn day,
Gù Yànhuī gathered his clan members and adopted sons for a final drink,
and sent Wáng Zōngbì to surrender to Jiàn.
The capture of Wáng Zōngbì by the Dōngchuān troops is recorded in the second year of the previous scroll.
He ordered his adopted son Yáo to kill him and the others drinking with him,
after which Yáo committed suicide.
In the third year of the Guāngqǐ era of Emperor Xīzōng,
Gù Yànlǎng gained control of Dōngchuān.
It passed to his younger brother Yànhuī,
and was destroyed at this point.
In the second year of the Qiánníng era,
Wáng Jiàn began his attack on Dōngchuān,
and it took approximately three years to conquer it.
Jiàn ordered Wáng Zōngwǎn to send troops separately to subdue Chāngzhōu, Pǔzhōu, and other prefectures,
and appointed Wáng Zōngdí as the Liúhòu of Dōngchuān.
47. Liú Réngōng memorialized, stating:
"Lǐ Kèyòng raised troops and attacked me without cause.
My commandery routed his faction at Mùguājiàn.
I request to serve as commander-in-chief to campaign against Kèyòng."
An edict denied the request.
He also sent a letter to Zhū Quánzhōng.
Quánzhōng memorialized to have Réngōng appointed as Tongpíngzhāngshì,
and the court complied.
Réngōng also sent an envoy to apologize to Kèyòng,
explaining his difficult position and feelings of insecurity.
Kèyòng's reply letter stated in summary:
"Now you, wielding the battle-axe and commanding troops,
governing the people and establishing laws,
when promoting scholars you desire their gratitude,
when selecting generals you hope for their repayment of kindness;
if you yourself do not act thus,
how can others be trusted!
Kèyòng was saying that since Réngōng had betrayed him,
others would also betray Réngōng.
The character "jiàng"
is pronounced with the "liàng" tone.
Suspicion and jealousy arise within the curtains,
you hold the Gānjiàng sword but dare not entrust it to others,
what words of oath can you inscribe while holding the alliance plate!"
48. On the Jiǎzǐ day,
the Emperor's son Mì was enfeoffed as the Prince of Jǐng,
Zuò as the Prince of Huī,
and Qí as the Prince of Qí.
49. Zhāng Liǎn, the Military Commissioner of Zhāngyì, was additionally appointed as Tongpíngzhāngshì.
50. Yáng Xíngmì and Zhū Jǐn led 30,000 troops to confront the Biàn army at Chǔzhōu.
A separate commander, Zhāng Xùn, led troops from Liánshuǐ to join them.
In the second year of the Qiánníng era,
Yáng Xíngmì first captured Liánshuǐ
and ordered Zhāng Xùn to defend it.
Páng Shīgǔ encamped at Qīngkǒu.
Someone said:
"The camp site is low-lying and wet,
it is not suitable for prolonged occupation."
He did not listen.
Shīgǔ, relying on his numerical superiority, underestimated the enemy,
and often spent his time playing chess.
Zhū Jǐn dammed the upper reaches of the Huái River,
intending to flood the camp.
Someone reported this to Shīgǔ,
but Shīgǔ considered it an attempt to confuse the troops,
and had the man executed.
In the eleventh month,
on the Guǐyǒu day,
Jǐn and the Huáinán general Hóu Zàn
secretly crossed the Huái River with 5,000 cavalry,
using the Biàn army's banners,
and advanced from the north towards the central army.
Zhāng Xùn breached the barricades and entered the camp;
the soldiers hurriedly resisted in confusion,
when the waters of the Huái River surged in,
throwing the Biàn army into panic and disorder.
Xíngmì led the main army across the Huái River,
and together with Jǐn and others attacked from both sides.
The Biàn army was utterly defeated,
with Shīgǔ and over 10,000 officers and soldiers beheaded,
and the remaining troops all scattered.
Gé Cóngzhōu was encamped northwest of Shòuzhōu.
Zhū Yánshòu, the Tuánliànshǐ of Shòuzhōu, attacked and defeated him,
forcing him to retreat and garrison at Háozhōu.
Hearing of Shīgǔ's defeat,
he fled back.
Xíngmì, Jǐn, and Yánshòu pursued him in victory,
catching up at the Pì River.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: The Pì River originates southwest of Qián County in Lújiāng,
northeast of Huòshān Mountain.
It flows northeast past the east of Liù County,
then northwest past the west of the old city of Ānfēng County,
and north into the Huái River.
The Lèipiān states: Pì,
pronounced bì zhì qiē,
is a river name,
located in Yìyáng.
According to records, the present-day Pì River is located ten lǐ west of Láiyuǎn Town,
Láiyuǎn Town is present-day Dōng Zhèngyáng,
two hundred lǐ east of Shòuzhōu.
The Huáinán troops attacked them,
killing or drowning almost all of them.
Cóngzhōu escaped alone.
Niú Cúnjié, the Commander of the Èhòu Capital, abandoned his horse and fought on foot.
Some of the various armies managed to cross the Huái River.
They went without food for four days.
There was heavy snowfall,
and the Biàn soldiers froze or starved to death along the road.
Fewer than a thousand returned.
Quánzhōng heard of the defeat,
and also fled back.
Xíngmì sent a letter to Quánzhōng, saying:
"Páng Shīgǔ and Gé Cóngzhōu
are no match.
You should come personally to the Huái River for a decisive battle."
Xíngmì held a grand assembly of his generals,
and said to his Deputy Military Commander Lǐ Chéngsì:
"Initially, I wanted to first advance towards Shòuzhōu,
but you, Deputy Commander, said it would be better to first head for Qīngkǒu.
Shīgǔ was defeated,
and Cóngzhōu fled on his own.
Now it has indeed turned out as you predicted."
He rewarded him with ten thousand strings of cash,
rewarding his prior strategic planning.
Xíngmì treated Chéngsì and Shǐ Yǎn very generously.
Residences and concubines
were all selected from the finest and bestowed upon them.
Therefore, these two served Xíngmì with utmost loyalty,
repeatedly achieving merit,
and eventually died in Huáinán.
From then on, Xíngmì secured and held the region between the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
and Quánzhōng could not contend with him.
51. On the Wùyín day,
the Virtuous Consort Hé was established as Empress.
The Empress,
was from Dōngchuān,
and gave birth to the Prince of Dé and the Prince of Huī.
52. Wáng Cháo, the Military Commissioner of Wēiwǔ, had a younger brother, Shěnzhī,
who served as Deputy Observation Commissioner.
When he made mistakes,
Cháo would still beat and flog him,
but Shěnzhī showed no resentment.
When Cháo fell seriously ill,
he passed over his own sons Yánxīng, Yánhóng, Yánfēng, and Yánxiū,
and ordered Shěnzhī to take charge of the military prefecture affairs.
In the twelfth month,
on the Dīngwèi day,
Cháo died.
Shěnzhī offered the position to his elder brother, the Cìshǐ of Quánzhōu, Shěnguī.
Shěnguī, considering that Shěnzhī had merit,
declined and would not accept.
Shěnzhī proclaimed himself Liúhòu of Fújiàn,
and submitted a memorial to the court.
53. On the Renxu day,
Wáng Jiàn returned from Zǐzhōu;
on the Wùchén day,
he arrived at Chéngdū.
That year,
the Nánzhào king Shùnhuà sent a letter addressed to the emperor and a wooden tablet from the Dūshuǎng office to the Central Secretariat,
using the reign title Zhōngxīng.
The imperial court intended to respond with an imperial edict.
Wáng Jiàn memorialized:
"Nánzhào is a minor barbarian state,
unworthy of an imperial edict.
As your servant is stationed in the southwest,
they certainly will not dare to violate our borders."
The court followed his advice.
Between Lízhōu and Yǎzhōu lived the shallow barbarians called King Liú, King Hǎo, and King Yáng,
each having their own tribes.
The great mountains and long valleys southwest of Lízhōu and Yǎzhōu
were all inhabited by barbarians,
their dwellings remote and deep.
However, the tribes of these three kings lived near the Hàn borders,
hence they were called shallow barbarians.
They were used to spy on Nánzhào,
but also accepted bribes from Nánzhào to gather intelligence on the actual situation in Chéngdū.
Whenever a new military governor took office,
the three kings would lead their chieftains to visit the governor's headquarters.
The military governor, believing this was due to his own prestige and virtue,
would report it to the court.
But secretly, the three kings collaborated with the senior generals,
and if the military governor lost the favor of his senior generals,
they would incite the various barbarians to cause disturbances.
Previously, most military governors were civil officials,
unwilling to stir up trouble,
so the senior generals often used this to seek appeasement,
and Nánzhào also relied on them to repeatedly create border troubles.
When Wáng Jiàn was appointed to guard Xīchuān,
he cut off their customary gifts,
and executed the Chief Yá officer Shān Xíngzhāng as a warning.
Shān Xíngzhāng
was a former general under Chén and Tián.
Wáng Jiàn executed him because of his collaboration with the shallow barbarians,
both to demonstrate authority to the various barbarians,
and to thoroughly eliminate old practices.
He did not set up border posts,
nor stationed a single soldier,
referring to the area south of the Qiónglái Pass.
Later, he sent Wáng Zōngbō to attack Nánzhào,
and when the three kings leaked military information,
he summoned and executed them.
History states that the method for securing the borders
lies solely in thoroughly understanding the true situation of the barbarian tribes near the border and thwarting their treachery,
then foreign barbarians will not dare to act disrespectfully or make moves.
54. The Right Reminder Zhāng Dàogǔ submitted a memorial,
stating:
"The state faces five perils and two disorders.
In the past, Emperor Wén of Hàn, not long after ascending the throne,
became well-versed in state affairs.
Now Your Majesty has been on the throne for ten years,
(the emperor ascended the throne in the first year of Wéndé;
it has been ten years until now;
if counting from the year after accession when the reign title was changed,
then it is nine years.)
Emperor Tàizōng internally pacified the Central Plains,
externally opened relations with the four barbarians;
states beyond the seas
all submitted as vassals.
Now the territories bequeathed by previous reigns are daily shrinking, nearly exhausted.
Although your servant is lowly and insignificant,
I secretly grieve that Your Majesty's court and altars of state, first manipulated by treacherous ministers,
will ultimately be possessed by rebel ministers!"
The fall of the Hàn and Táng dynasties
indeed matches Zhāng Dàogǔ's words.
Zhāng Dàogǔ was demoted to Registrar of Shīzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Shīzhōu
was the territory of Wū County in Hàn times;
the Great Emperor of Wú divided Wū County to establish Shāqú County;
in the third year of Jiàndé of Later Zhōu, Shīzhōu was established here;
Táng continued it.
Old records: Shīzhōu,
2,709 lǐ south of the capital.
(The emperor) announced this to the remonstrance officials.
Emperor Zhāozōng, amidst hardship and danger,
still punished those who spoke out,
so his downfall was fitting.
(Zhāng Dàogǔ) was from Qīngzhōu.
Zhāng Dàogǔ appears in the Comprehensive Mirror only in this incident;
recording his native place,
is likely out of sympathy for him.
First year of Guānghuà
(Wùwǔ, 898)
The court returned to the capital in the eighth month of this year,
then the reign title was changed.
1. In spring,
first month,
Liǎngzhè, Jiāngxī, Wǔchāng, and Zīqīng each sent envoys to the court,
requesting that Zhū Quánzhōng be made commander-in-chief,
to campaign against Yáng Xíngmì.
(Liǎngzhè's Qián Liú,
Jiāngxī's Zhōng Chuán,
Wǔchāng's Dù Hóng,
Zīqīng's Wáng Shīfàn,
all feared Yáng Xíngmì's strength,
and were partisans attached to Zhū Quánzhōng.)
2. Pínglú military governor Wáng Shīfàn was additionally appointed Tongpingzhangshi.
(Zīqīng
was the Pínglú Army.)
3. Minister of War Liú Chóngwàng was appointed Tongpingzhangshi,
and concurrently military governor of Dōngchuān;
Zhāoxìn defense commissioner Féng Xíngxí was appointed Zhāoxìn military governor.
(According to the Table of Regional Commands,
the Zhāoxìn defense commissioner was established in the first year of Guānghuà,
governing Jīnzhōu,
which differs from this.)
4. The emperor issued an edict blaming himself and ceasing military actions,
restored Lǐ Màozhēn's name and official titles,
and ordered all armies campaigning against Fèngxiáng to disband.
(This was Hán Jiàn's intention.)
5. On the Rénchén day,
Hézhōng military governor Wáng Kē went to Jìnyáng in person to fetch his bride;
Lǐ Kèyòng sent his general Lǐ Sìzhāo to guard Hézhōng.
6. Both Lǐ Màozhēn and Hán Jiàn sent letters to Lǐ Kèyòng,
stating that the imperial carriage had been traveling for years,
begging to repair friendly relations,
jointly support the royal house,
and also requesting craftsmen to assist in repairing the palace buildings;
Kèyòng agreed.
7. Earlier,
when Wáng Jiàn attacked Dōngchuān,
Gù Yànhuī sought help from Lǐ Màozhēn,
and Màozhēn ordered his generals to send troops to rescue him,
(the matter is seen above).
(Now Màozhēn) falsely claimed to have reformed,
and together with Hán Jiàn supported the Son of Heaven.
Upon hearing that Zhū Quánzhōng was constructing palaces in Luòyáng,
and had repeatedly memorialized to welcome the imperial carriage,
Màozhēn and Hán Jiàn grew fearful,
and requested to repair the palace buildings,
to escort the emperor back to Cháng'ān.
An edict appointed Hán Jiàn as Commissioner for Repairing Palaces.
Examination of discrepancies: The Veritable Records state:
"Jiàn, because the traveling palace was low and cramped,
with no place for viewing scenery,
memorialized offering his southern country estate.
Jiàn initially repaired the Southern Manor,
erected towers and pavilions,
dredged ponds,
intending to make it the Southern Palace,
to carry out the act of deposing and establishing.
His paternal uncle Fēng, seeing his overbearingness,
said to Jiàn: 'You are a commoner from between Chén and Xǔ,
who took advantage of the times of crisis and chaos,
to reach the position of regional commander.
Unable to feel gratitude for the sovereign's grace,
yet wishing to use the mere hundred lǐ of land of Tóng and Huà prefectures to carry out deposing and establishing,
the extermination of your clan is imminent.
I would rather end my own life first,
to avoid being implicated by you.'
From then on, Jiàn somewhat restrained his ambition.
When Lǐ Màozhēn memorialized requesting to assist in constructing palaces and gardens,
and hearing that Zhū Quánzhōng was repairing Luòyáng,
repeatedly memorializing to welcome the carriage,
Jiàn grew fearful,
hence urgently undertook repairs in Cháng'ān,
leading the various circuits in assisting the work,
and personally supervised the progress."
However, if Jiàn intended to depose and establish,
why would he need to first build a Southern Palace?
This is not adopted here.
Jiàn sent his commander-in-chief Cài Jìngsī to supervise the work.
After completion,
in the second month,
Jiàn went personally to inspect it.
8. Qián Liú requested to move the Zhènhǎi Army headquarters to Hángzhōu,
which was approved.
(The Zhènhǎi Army was originally based in Rùnzhōu;
now the army designation was moved to Hángzhōu.)
9. Lǐ Màozhēn was reappointed as military governor of Fèngxiáng.
10. In the third month,
on the Jǐchǒu day,
Wáng Shěnzhī was appointed acting military governor of Wēiwǔ.
11. Zhū Quánzhōng sent his deputy Wànnián Wěi Zhèn to present matters at court,
seeking to concurrently govern Tiānpíng.
The court had not yet granted this,
but Wěi Zhèn forcefully argued for it.
Since the reigns of Emperor Mùzōng and Emperor Jìngzōng,
the authority of imperial decrees had already weakened,
yet envoys sent by military governors to present matters at court did not dare to argue forcefully.
(The court) appointed Zhū Quánzhōng as military governor of the three commands of Xuānwǔ, Xuānyì, and Tiānpíng.
Zhū Quánzhōng appointed Wěi Zhèn as the acting military governor of Tiānpíng,
and appointed the former prefect of Táizhōu, Lǐ Zhèn, as deputy military governor of Tiānpíng.
According to the biography of Lǐ Zhèn in the Historical Records of the Five Dynasties,
Lǐ Zhèn was a general of the Imperial Guard,
and was appointed prefect of Táizhōu.
When bandits arose in eastern Zhèjiāng,
he did not proceed to his post,
but instead traveled west and passed through Biànzhōu,
where he presented strategies to Zhū Quánzhōng;
Zhū Quánzhōng retained him,
and thus he entered Zhū Quánzhōng's service.
He was the great-grandson of Lǐ Bàozhēn.
During the reigns of Emperor Dàizōng and Emperor Dézōng,
Lǐ Bàozhēn governed Zhāoyì,
achieving great merit.
12. The Huáinán general Zhōu Běn came to rescue Sūzhōu,
but was defeated by the Liǎngzhè general Gù Quánwǔ.
The Huáinán general Qín Péi captured Kūnshān with three thousand troops and garrisoned it.
Kūnshān,
was the territory of Lóu County in the Hàn dynasty;
the Liáng dynasty divided Lóu County to establish Xìnyì County,
and later divided Xìnyì County to establish Kūnshān County,
taking its name from Mount Kūn within the county boundaries;
during the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Sūzhōu.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì,
it was located seventy lǐ east of the prefectural seat.
13. Mǎ Yīn, the prefect of Tánzhōu and administrator of the Húnán military government, was appointed acting military governor of Wǔ'ān.
At that time, within the Húnán jurisdiction of seven prefectures,
the rebel leader Yáng Shīyuǎn occupied Héngzhōu,
Táng Shìmín occupied Yǒngzhōu,
Cài Jié occupied Dàozhōu,
Chén Yànqiān occupied Chēnzhōu,
and Lǔ Jǐngrén occupied Liánzhōu.
According to Lù Zhèn's Jiǔguó Zhì: Táng Mǐn and Cài Jié both gathered troops from their commanderies and occupied them.
Chén Yànqiān was from Guìyáng,
who killed the prefect Huáng Yuè,
and occupied Chēnzhōu.
Lǔ Jǐngrén originally followed Huáng Cháo,
but due to illness remained in Liánzhōu,
and subsequently occupied it.
The term "leader" (shuài)
is pronounced suǒ lèi fān.
Chēn (郴)
is pronounced chǒu lín fān.
This sets the stage for Mǎ Yīn to eventually seize all these prefectures.
14. Lú Yànwēi, the military governor of Yìchāng,
was cruel and brutal by nature,
and also disrespectful towards neighboring commands;
he contended with Liúlóng military governor Liú Réngōng over salt profits.
Liú Réngōng sent his son Liú Shǒuwén to lead troops and attack Cāngzhōu.
Lú Yànwēi abandoned the city,
and fled with his family to Wèizhōu;
Luó Hóngxìn did not accept him,
so he fled to Biànzhōu.
In the first year of the Guāngqǐ era (885),
Lú Yànwēi obtained Cāng and Jǐng,
and by this time was destroyed.
(The court) appointed Liú Shǒuwén as acting military governor of Yìchāng.
Liú Réngōng's military strength grew even stronger,
as he combined the forces of the Yōu and Cāng two commands,
hence his power increased.
He harbored ambitions to annex Héshuò,
and requested an imperial commission for Liú Shǒuwén,
but the court had not yet granted it.
When a palace eunuch envoy arrived at Fànyáng,
Liú Réngōng said to him:
"I already possess the authority (of a military governor),
I merely wish to obtain the genuine appointment from Cháng'ān,
why are repeated memorials rejected!
Convey this for me!"
His arrogance and insolence were such.
15. Zhū Quánzhōng established friendly relations with Liú Réngōng,
and joined forces with Wèibó troops to attack Lǐ Kèyòng.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Dīngwèi day,
Zhū Quánzhōng arrived at the walls of Jùlù,
defeated over ten thousand Hé dōng troops,
and pursued the fleeing enemy north to Qīngshān Pass.
According to the Wǔdài Zhì: In Lónggāng County of Xíngzhōu,
Emperor Wén of Suí established Qīngshān County in the 16th year of the Kāihuáng era (596),
which was abolished and merged into Lónggāng during the early Dàyè era of Emperor Yáng.
The term "defeat" (bài)
is pronounced bǔ mài fān.
16. The military governor of Hùguó, Wáng Kē, was concurrently appointed Zhōngshū Lìng.
17. On the Dīngmǎo day,
Zhū Quánzhōng sent Gě Cóngzhōu to divide his troops and attack Míngzhōu.
On the Wùchén day,
he captured it,
and beheaded the prefect Xíng Shànyì.
18. In the fifth month,
on the first day, Jǐsì,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the land.
19. Gě Cóngzhōu attacked Xíngzhōu,
and the prefect Mǎ Shīsù abandoned the city and fled.
On the Xīnwèi day,
the prefect of Cízhōu, Yuán Fèngtāo, slit his own throat.
Zhū Quánzhōng appointed Gě Cóngzhōu as acting military governor of Zhāoyì,
to guard Xíng, Míng, and Cí three prefectures and then return.
From this time, Bìng and Biàn contended annually over Xíng, Míng, and Cí three prefectures.
20. Lǐ Jìmì, the military governor of Wǔdìng, was appointed military governor of Shānnán Xīdào.
Lǐ Jìmì moved from Yángzhōu to Xīngyuán.
21. The court, hearing that Wáng Jiàn had already appointed Wáng Zōngdí as acting military governor of Dōngchuān,
recalled Liú Chóngwàng,
appointing him as Minister of War,
and still appointed Wáng Zōngdí as acting military governor.
22. The Húnán general Yáo Yànzhāng advised Mǎ Yīn,
requesting to seize Héng, Yǒng, Dào, Lián, and Chēn five prefectures,
and also recommended Lǐ Qióng as a general.
Mǎ Yīn appointed Lǐ Qióng and Qín Yànhuī as patrol commissioners of the seven prefectures north of the mountains,
with Zhāng Túyīng and Lǐ Táng as their deputies.
The five prefectures,
together with Tán and Shào, made seven.
They beheaded Yáng Shīyuǎn,
led troops towards Yǒngzhōu,
besieged it for over a month,
and Táng Shìmín fled and died.
Mǎ Yīn appointed Lǐ Táng as prefect of Yǒngzhōu.
23. In the sixth month,
Zhào Xǔ, the prefect of Háozhōu, was appointed military governor of Zhōngwǔ.
Zhào Xǔ
was the younger brother of Zhōu Chōu.
24. In autumn,
the seventh month,
Léi Mǎn, the military governor of Wǔzhēn, was given the additional title of Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
According to the Fāngzhèn Biǎo: In the first year of the Guānghuà era (898),
the Wǔzhēn command was established,
governing Lǐ, Lǎng, and Xù three prefectures,
with its seat at Lǐzhōu.
25. Zhào Kuāngníng, the military governor of Zhōngyì, heard that Zhū Quánzhōng had suffered a defeat at Qīngkǒu,
(Note: The Zhōngyì Army
was Shānnán Dōngdào.)
(The defeat at Qīngkǒu occurred in the eleventh month of the previous year.)
Zhū Quánzhōng sent the prefect of Sùzhōu, Wèishì Shì Shūcóng, to lead troops to attack him.
On the Bǐngshēn day,
he captured Tángzhōu,
captured the prefect of Suízhōu, Zhào Kuānglín,
and defeated Xiāngzhōu troops at Dèngchéng.
26. In the eighth month,
on the Gēngxū day,
Huázhōu was renamed Xīngdé Prefecture.
This was because the imperial carriage had temporarily resided there.
27. On the Wùwǔ day,
the Biàn general Kāng Huáizhēn attacked Dèngzhōu,
captured it,
and captured the prefect Guó Xiāng.
Zhào Kuāngníng grew fearful,
and sent an envoy to submit to Zhū Quánzhōng,
which Zhū Quánzhōng accepted.
This sets the stage for Zhū Quánzhōng to attack Zhào Kuāngníng again later.
28. On the Jǐwèi day,
the imperial carriage departed from Huázhōu;
on the Rénxū day,
it arrived at Cháng'ān;
on the Jiǎzǐ day,
a general amnesty was proclaimed,
and the era name was changed.
The era name was changed to Guānghuà.
The Emperor wished for the military governors to live in harmony,
so he appointed the Crown Prince's Advisor Zhāng Yǒufú as the Pacification Commissioner for Hé dōng and Biànzhōu,
bestowing edicts upon Lǐ Kèyòng and Zhū Quánzhōng,
and also ordering the chief ministers to write letters to them,
urging them to reconcile.
Lǐ Kèyòng wished to obey the edict,
but was ashamed to be the first to yield,
so he sent a letter to Wáng Róng,
asking him to communicate with Zhū Quánzhōng;
but Zhū Quánzhōng refused.
(Because) Zhū Quánzhōng's military strength was currently strong,
he therefore refused.
29. In the ninth month,
on the Yǐhài day,
Hán Jiàn was given the additional titles of Grand Tutor and Governor of Xīngdé Prefecture;
previously,
when the Emperor resided in Huázhōu,
he consequently made Huázhōu into Xīngdé Prefecture.
Luó Hóngxìn was given the additional title of Zhōngshū Lìng.
30. On the Jǐchǒu day,
Wáng Zōngdí, the acting military governor of Dōngchuān, advised Wáng Jiàn,
stating that the territory of Dōngchuān spanned five thousand lǐ,
and official correspondence back and forth
often took several months,
so he requested to separate Suì, Hé, Lú, Yú, and Chāng five prefectures to form a separate command;
Wáng Jiàn submitted a memorial reporting this.
Gu Quánwǔ attacked Sūzhōu;
the food in the city and for the relief troops was exhausted,
on the jiǎshēn day,
Tái Méng, the Sūzhōu prefect appointed by Huáinán, abandoned the city and fled.
Even with strong walls and deep moats,
they cannot be held without grain.
Although Tái Méng was a fine general of Huáinán,
what could he do about it!
Quánwǔ captured Sūzhōu.
In the third year of Qiánníng,
Huáinán had seized Sūzhōu,
and now indeed, as Gu Quánwǔ had said, it was recovered.
Jiǔyùzhì: Chángzhōu's Wúxī County had the Wàngtíng Town,
located forty-five lǐ north of Sūzhōu,
and another forty-five lǐ to Wúxī.
Defeated,
bǔ mài fān.
Quánwǔ led over ten thousand men to attack it;
Péi repeatedly came out to fight,
having the sick wear armor and hold spears,
and the strong draw bows and crossbows,
causing Quánwǔ to retreat each time.
Seeing that the bows and crossbows had long range,
he therefore retreated.
Gòu,
jū hòu fān.
Wèi,
yú wèi fān.
Quánwǔ had once been a monk,
Péi sealed a letter offering surrender,
Quánwǔ was pleased,
summoned the generals to open the letter,
but it was a volume of Buddhist scriptures.
Quánwǔ was greatly ashamed,
and said:
"Péi does not fear death,
how does he have leisure to mock me!"
He increased troops to attack the city,
diverted water to flood it,
the walls collapsed,
food was exhausted,
and Péi then surrendered.
Qián Liú prepared a feast for a thousand people to receive him,
and when he came out,
"nǎi",
should be
"jí".
[Chapter: B eleven-line edition correctly has
"jí".
Looking at the preceding text of Zīzhìtōngjiàn,
Qín Péi had taken three thousand men to capture Kūnshān and hold it,
and when he surrendered,
the weak troops numbered less than a hundred,
so his soldiers had nearly all died in battle and defense,
the survivors being only about one-thirtieth.
"So weak and few,
how dare they resist for long!"
Lǚ,
means multitude.
Relying on the multitude to resist,
is called lǚjù.
"Péi in righteousness does not betray Lord Yáng,
now he surrenders only because his strength is exhausted,
not because his heart surrenders."
Liú praised his words.
Gu Quánwǔ also urged Liú to pardon him,
and Liú agreed.
People of the time called Quánwǔ a gentleman.
Gu Quánwǔ was very perceptive and measured,
thus able to assist Qián Liú in holding a region.
Zhǎng,
zhī liǎng fān.
32 The Wèibó military governor Luó Hóngxìn died.
Kǎoyì says: Xuē Jūzhèng's Old History of the Five Dynasties, Liáng Annals, Hóngxìn's biography, and Tàizǔ's Chronicle all say Hóngxìn died in August.
According to August, Emperor Zhāozōng returned to the capital,
Hóngxìn was still given an official title.
Old Annals and Biography say he died in September,
now follow that.
Shílù says October,
probably when the report arrived.
33 Biàn general Zhū Yǒugōng led troops back from Jiāng, Huái,
passed Ānzhōu,
Zhū Yǒugōng had captured Huángzhōu,
and on the way back passed Ānzhōu.
Jiǔyùzhì: Huángzhōu is three hundred lǐ west to Ānzhōu.
He plotted to seize the Biàn army,
in winter,
October,
on the jǐhài day,
Yǒugōng attacked and killed him.
34 Lǐ Kèyòng sent his generals Lǐ Sìzhāo and Zhōu Déwēi with twenty thousand infantry and cavalry out of Qīngshān,
intending to recover the three prefectures east of the mountains.
The three prefectures east of the mountains,
are Xíng, Míng, and Cí;
in May of this year,
Gě Cóngzhōu had taken them.
On the rényín day
they attacked Xíngzhōu;
Gě Cóngzhōu came out to fight,
and greatly defeated them.
Sìzhāo and others led troops back into Qīngshān,
Cóngzhōu pursued them,
intending to block their retreat route;
the infantry collapsed on their own,
Sìzhāo could not control them.
Then Héngchōng commander Lǐ Sìyuán arrived with his troops,
Xuēshǐ Míngzōng Annals says: Luó Hóngxìn ambushed and defeated Lǐ Cúnxìn at Shēn County,
the emperor fought bravely covering the retreat and returned,
Wǔhuáng praised his achievement,
and immediately gave the five hundred cavalry under him the name Héngchōng command.
"If we also leave,
then the situation will be unsustainable,
let me try to attack them for you."
Sìzhāo said:
"Good!
I ask to follow behind you."
Sìyuán then removed saddles and sharpened arrows,
deployed formations on high ground,
pointing and gesturing left and right,
the Xíng people could not fathom it.
Sìyuán charged straight ahead and fought fiercely,
Sìzhāo followed,
and Cóngzhōu then retreated.
Déwēi,
was from Mǎyì.
Mǎyì,
is an old county name from Qín and Hàn times,
long abandoned;
in the fifth year of Kāiyuán,
Shàoyáng County of Shuòzhōu was divided,
and Mǎyì County was established at the old Dàtóng Army city,
belonging to Shuòzhōu.
35 On the guǐmǎo day,
Wáng Shěnzhī, acting military governor of Wēiwǔ, was appointed military governor.
36 Appointed Luó Shàowēi as acting military governor of Wèibó.
37 On the dīngsì day,
Wáng Zōngdí, acting military governor of Dōngchuān, was appointed military governor.
38 Added Shìzhōng to the concurrent titles of Zhāng Quányì, military governor of Yòuguó.
39 Wáng Gǒng led Biàn troops to invade Hézhōng,
Wáng Kē appealed for help to Lǐ Kèyòng;
Kèyòng sent Lǐ Sìzhāo to rescue him,
and defeated the Biàn troops at Húbì.
Jiǔyùzhì: Rónghé County of Hézhōng Prefecture has Húbì Town.
Rónghé,
was Táng's Bǎodǐng County,
renamed during Sòng's Xiángfú period.
Defeated,
bǔ mài fān.
Former Chángzhōu prefect Wáng Zhù,
was upright and principled by nature,
and had contemporary reputation;
an edict summoned him,
and people of the time thought he would become chancellor.
Passing through Shǎn,
Wáng Zhù responded to the summons,
passing through Shǎnzhōu on the way.
Shǎn,
shī rǎn fān.
Gǒng requested to pay respects according to the rites for nephews,
but Zhù firmly declined.
Gǒng was angry,
Gǒng, because Zhù shared the same surname,
was of an older generation,
and about to become chancellor,
requested to observe the rites for nephews,
to establish closeness with him,
but Zhù declined.
Gǒng thought Zhù looked down on his family's humble origins and rejected him,
hence the anger.
Kǎoyì says: Regarding Zhù becoming Jǐshìzhōng and meeting his death,
Old Annals and Shílù have no year or month,
now attach it here because of Gǒng's attack on Hézhōng.
He plundered his belongings,
and reported that his boat had capsized.
The court did not dare to investigate.
History shows that Táng's authority and orders were not obeyed,
the military governors were violent and overbearing,
Wáng Zhù suffered cruel murder but no one dared to inquire.
Jié,
qù jí fān.
40 In the intercalary month,
Qián Liú appointed his general Cáo Guī as military commissioner of Sūzhōu,
and sent Wáng Qiú to attack Wùzhōu.
41 In November,
on the jiǎyín day,
established the imperial son Zhēn as Prince Yǎ,
and Xiáng as Prince Qióng.
42 Appointed Luó Shàowēi, acting military governor of Wèibó, as military governor.
43 Qúzhōu prefect Chén Jí requested to surrender to Yáng Xíngmì,
Qián Liú sent Gu Quánwǔ to attack him.
44. Zhū Quánzhōng, because Fèngguó military commissioner Cuī Hóng had dealings with Yáng Xíngmì,
Huáixī and
Huáinán are neighboring circuits.
Cuī Hóng was afraid,
and requested to send his younger brother, the capital commandant Cuī Xián, as a hostage,
and said:
"The officers and soldiers are stubborn and fierce,
and do not accept control.
I request to send two thousand men to your command to follow in campaigns."
Zhū Quánzhōng agreed.
This is the basis for Zhū Quánzhōng sending Cuī Xián to conscript troops, and the Cài generals killing Cuī Xián, seizing Cuī Hóng, and fleeing to Huáinán.
Cún Jìng
was from Cáozhōu.
45. In the twelfth month,
the Zhāoyì military commissioner Xuē Zhìqín died.
When Lǐ Kèyòng pacified Wáng Xíngyú,
see the second year of Qiánníng in the previous scroll.
Lǐ Kèyòng said:
"Xíngyú relied on his merit to coerce the sovereign,
therefore I and you, sir, campaigned against and executed him.
The day we defeated the rebels,
I first memorialized urging Sū Wénjiàn to proceed to his garrison.
The matter is seen in the same place.
Urge,
read as 'prompt'.
If we now repeatedly change our minds,
the discussions at court and among the people
will certainly clamor, saying we are again acting like Xíngyú did.
My relationship with you, sir, is like one body,
so I certainly have no stinginess,
but wait until I return to my garrison,
and I will further discuss merits and rewards for you, sir."
Hǎn Zhī was displeased and withdrew,
and privately said to Gài Yù:
"Since Hǎn Zhī lost Héyáng,
I have relied on your great shelter,
and many years have passed.
Lately I have aged and declined,
and am weary of military campaigns.
If I could receive the pity of my king and the Grand Tutor,
King,
refers to Lǐ Kèyòng.
Grand Tutor,
refers to Gài Yù.
allowing me to rest troops and recuperate from illness for a few years,
and then retire to my hometown,
that would be fortunate."
Yù spoke for him,
but Kèyòng did not respond.
Whenever a military governorship was vacant,
discussions never reached Hǎn Zhī,
and Hǎn Zhī was very depressed.
Yù feared he had other intentions,
and urgently spoke for him.
Kèyòng said:
"As for Hǎn Zhī, do I begrudge him a single military governorship?
But Hǎn Zhī
is a hawk;
when hungry it is useful,
but when full it flies away!"
Drawing from Cáo Cāo's idea of controlling Lǚ Bù to express this.
Betray,
read as 'pèi'.
When Zhìqín died,
for ten days there was no commander.
Hǎn Zhī led Zézhōu troops and entered Lùzhōu at night,
occupying it.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Zézhōu is 165 li north to Lùzhōu.
Commander,
read as 'shuài'.
He said:
"Xuē Tiěshān has died."
Xuē Zhìqín followed Kèyòng from rising in Dàiběi,
his initial name was Tiěshān.
"I feared those with unfulfilled ambitions would cause trouble,
therefore Hǎn Zhī took command to pacify and control,
awaiting the king's decision."
Decision means
the king deciding whether it is permissible or not.
He sent someone to reprimand him.
Hǎn Zhī then sent his son
to request surrender to Zhū Quánzhōng,
and arrested the Hé dōng generals Mǎ Gài and others, and Qìnzhōu prefect Fù Yáo, sending them to Biànzhōu.
Kèyòng sent Lǐ Sìzhāo to lead troops against him.
From this,
Lǐ Kèyòng could no longer contend with Zhū Quánzhōng for Xíng, Míng, and Cí, but contended for Zé and Lù instead.
He seized Hǎn Zhī's family and sent them to Jìnyáng.
First taking Zézhōu,
he caught Lǐ Hǎnzhī unprepared,
and also captured his family.
History states Lǐ Sìzhāo used troops with strategy.
46. Yáng Xíngmì sent Chéng Jí
back to Liǎngzhè in exchange for Wèi Yuē and others.
Huáinán capturing Chéng Jí is seen in the third year of Qiánníng in the previous scroll.
Liǎngzhè capturing Wèi Yuē is seen in last year's fourth month.
Yáng and Qián contended for Sūzhōu.
Tái Méng, Zhōu Běn, and Qín Péi were all famous Huáinán generals,
but were trapped by the Zhè people,
and ultimately could not hold it.
Yáng Xíngmì knew Qián Liú was not easily to be taken lightly,
therefore he returned Chéng Jí to exchange for Wèi Yuē,
his intention being to seek reconciliation.
Qián Liú also knew himself to be not as strong as Yáng Xíngmì,
therefore he agreed to it quickly.
47. Shàozhōu prefect Zēng Gǔn raised troops to attack Guǎngzhōu.
The prefectural general Wáng Huái led warships to respond to him.
Qīnghǎi marching army commander Liú Yǐn defeated them in one battle.
Shàozhōu general Liú Tóng again occupied Zhēn and Hán.
Yǐn campaigned against and beheaded him.
1. Spring,
first month,
Dīngwèi day,
the Secretariat Vice Director and concurrently Minister of Personnel
Cuī Yìn was dismissed and retained his original office.
He appointed the Minister of War Lù Yǐ as Tongpingzhangshi.
Cuī Yìn and Lù Yǐ alternately were appointed and dismissed.
2. Zhū Quánzhōng memorialized to appoint Lǐ Hǎnzhī as Zhāoyì military commissioner.
He also memorialized to appoint acting Héyáng deputy commander Dīng Huì, Wǔníng deputy commander Wáng Jìngráo,
and Zhāngyì deputy commander Zhāng Kē all as military commissioners.
Héyáng and Wǔníng were both attached to Zhū Quánzhōng.
Only Zhāng Kē was in Jīngzhōu,
yet he requested the commissioner's insignia for him,
also to win him over.
3. Yáng Xíngmì and Zhū Jǐn led troops numbering tens of thousands to attack Xúzhōu,
camping at Lǚliáng.
Zhū Quánzhōng sent cavalry general Zhāng Guīhòu to rescue it.
4. Liú Réngōng mobilized troops from twelve prefectures including Yōu and Cāng, totaling one hundred thousand men.
The twelve prefectures: Yōu, Zhuō, Yíng, Mò, Píng, Yíng, Jì, Guī, Tán, Cāng, Jǐng, and Dé.
The Yōuzhōu circuit further included the three prefectures of Yù, Xīn, and Wǔ.
Liú Réngōng kept them to guard against Hédōng,
and did not mobilize their troops.
He attacked Bèizhōu,
captured it,
and of the over ten thousand households in the city,
slaughtered them all,
throwing the corpses into the Qīngshuǐ River.
Qīngshuǐ River,
is the water of the Qīnghé River.
Réngōng advanced to attack Wèizhōu,
camping north of the city.
Wèibó military commissioner Luó Shàowēi sought help from Zhū Quánzhōng.
5. Zhū Quánzhōng sent Cuī Xián back to Càizhōu.
Cuī Hóng sent his younger brother Xián as a hostage,
see last year.
Second month,
the Cài general Cuī Jǐngsī and others killed Xián,
seized Cuī Hóng,
and drove all the soldiers and people across the Huái River to flee to Yáng Xíngmì.
The soldiers and people gradually fled back.
Attachment to native land and reluctance to move
is the constant nature of human feelings.
Quánzhōng ordered Xǔzhōu prefect Zhū Yǒuyù to guard Càizhōu.
6. Zhū Quánzhōng personally led troops to rescue Xúzhōu.
Yáng Xíngmì heard of it,
and led his troops away.
The Biàn people caught up with them at Xiàpī.
Xiàpī,
an ancient county,
belonged to Xúzhōu in the Táng.
Jiǔyù Zhì:
It is 180 li east of Xúzhōu.
Quánzhōng traveled as far as Huīzhōu.
This year,
Zhū Quánzhōng memorialized to establish Huīzhōu from Dàngshān, Yúchéng, and Shànfù of Sòngzhōu,
and Chéngwǔ of Cáozhōu.
It was established as Huīzhōu,
which is the territory of Dānzhōu.
Then he returned.
7 In the third month,
Zhū Quánzhōng dispatched his generals Lǐ Sī'ān and Zhāng Cúnjìng to lead troops to rescue Wèi-Bó,
stationing them at Nèihuáng.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Nèihuáng County is located 214 li southwest of Wèi Prefecture.
On Guǐmǎo,
Quánzhōng stationed his central army at Huá Prefecture.
Liú Réngōng said to his son Shǒuwén:
"Your courage is ten times that of Sī'ān.
You should first capture that rabble,

He then sent Shǒuwén and his brother-in-law Shàn Kějí to lead 50,000 elite troops to attack Sī'ān at Nèihuáng.
On Dīngwèi,
Sī'ān had his general Yuán Xiàngxiān lay an ambush with troops on the right bank of the Qīngshuǐ.
The Qí River flows east past Nèihuáng,
where it is called the Báigōu River,
and also called the Qīng River.
Fányáng,
an ancient Hàn dynasty county,
was merged and abolished into Nèihuáng during the Táng.
Dù Yòu states: The old city of the Hàn dynasty Fányáng County was located northwest of Nèihuáng County.
Shǒuwén pursued them,
reaching north of Nèihuáng.
Sī'ān reined in his troops and turned to fight.
The ambushing troops sprang forth,
attacking from both sides.
The Yōuzhōu troops were utterly defeated.
Kějí was beheaded,
and thirty thousand men were killed or captured.
Shǒuwén barely escaped with his life.
Kějí
was a valiant general of Yōuzhōu,
nicknamed
"Shàn the Invincible".
The Yān army lost him and their morale plummeted.
Lǐ Kèyòng underestimated Shàn Kějí and suffered defeat at Mùguā Jiàn;
Liú Réngōng underestimated Lǐ Sī'ān and Shàn Kějí lost his head.
Therefore, those who employ troops must guard against underestimating the enemy.
Sàng (喪),
is pronounced sàng, with the tone falling then rising.
He was a man of Chénliú.
At that time, Gě Cóngzhōu, leading eight hundred elite cavalry from Xíng Prefecture, had already entered Wèi Prefecture.
On Wùshēn,
Réngōng attacked the Shàngshuǐ Pass and the Guàntáo Gate.
The Guàntáo Gate,
the northern gate of Wèi Prefecture's city wall,

one heads towards Guàntáo County,
hence it was named after the county.
[Cóngzhōu] said to the gatekeeper:
"There is a formidable enemy ahead,

He ordered the gate leaves closed.
Cóngzhōu and others fought desperately to the death.
Réngōng was again utterly defeated,

The next day,

Réngōng and his son burned their camp and fled.
The men of Biàn and Wèi pursued them in a long, unimpeded advance.
Reaching Línqīng,
they drove his masses into the Yǒngjì Canal,
