The Zhèn army also sent troops to intercept and attack them on the eastern border.
The Zhèn army,
refers to the troops of Wáng Róng.
Shēn and Jì
were the eastern border of Zhào.
Corpses lay piled upon each other.
From this point on, Réngōng never recovered his strength,

The military power of both Yōu and Bìng was thwarted,
therefore Quánzhōng became increasingly arrogant.
Hèng (橫),
is pronounced hèng, with the falling tone.
He was a man of the Héxī Hú tribe.

When Liú Réngōng attacked Wèi Prefecture,

Lǐ Kèyòng dispatched Lǐ Sìzhāo to lead troops to rescue him.

Ever since Lǐ Cúnxìn's defeat at Shēn County,

Before the Bìng troops arrived,
the Biàn men had achieved merit,

8 Gě Cóngzhōu, riding the momentum of defeating Yōuzhōu,
attacked Hédōng from Tǔmén,
capturing Chéngtiān Army.
A separate general, Shì Shūcóng, entered from Mǎlǐng.
Mǎlǐng
is located eighty li southeast of Tàigǔ County in Tàiyuán Prefecture.
Jìn divided the Hàn dynasty Zhān County to establish Lèpíng County,

Yúcì
is an ancient county,
which belonged to Tàiyuán Prefecture during the Táng.
Shūcóng had a valiant general named Chén Zhāng,
nicknamed
"Chén the Yaksha".
He served as the vanguard.
Common saying has it that in the underworld there are ghostly envoys called yakshas.
At the time, people considered Chén Zhāng to be as fierce, formidable, and fearsome as a yaksha,
hence they called him that.
"What Hédōng relies on is Zhōu Yángwǔ.
Zhōu Déwēi's childhood name was Yángwǔ.
I request a prefecture as my reward."
Kèyòng heard of this
and warned Déwēi.
Déwēi said:
"He is just boasting."
They fought at Dòngwō.
The Dòngwō River originates from the northern mountains of Zhān County,
flows east then bends south,
passes east of the old city of Shòuyáng County,
and flows west past the south of Yúcì County.
This is according to the Shuǐjīng Zhù.
The Wèi Shōu Dìxíng Zhì states: The Dòngwō River has sources: one at Mùguā Ridge,
one at Zhān Ridge,
one at Dàlián Mountain,
and one below Yuánguò Shrine.
The five waters converge,
therefore it was called Tóngguò.
Later, the pronunciation shifted to Dòngwō.
According to this, Gāo Huān established the Grand Chancellor's residence at Jìnyáng,
and Wèi Shōu had already inscribed his name at the hegemon's residence.
When Qí received the abdication from Wèi,
Jìnyáng was made the secondary capital.
Wèi Shōu often accompanied his lord back and forth to the Jìnyáng Palace,
so he should have known the exactness of place names.
[Déwēi] said to his subordinates:
"When you see Chén the Yaksha, immediately flee."
Zhāng indeed pursued them.
Déwēi, wielding an iron mace, struck him, knocking him from his horse,
and captured him alive to present as an offering.
Thereupon, he attacked Shūcóng,
utterly defeating him,
and beheading three thousand.
Shūcóng abandoned his camp and fled.
Déwēi pursued him,
driving him out past the Shíhuì Pass,
and beheading over a thousand more.
Cóngzhōu also withdrew and returned.
9 On Dīngsì,
Zhū Quánzhōng sent the Héyáng military governor Dīng Huì to attack Zé Prefecture,
and he captured it.
Last year in the twelfth month,
the Hédōng troops had taken Zé Prefecture.
Kǎoyì states: The Shílù records:
"On Dīngsì,
Gě Cóngzhōu recaptured Zé Prefecture."
According to the Biānyílù:
"On Dīngsì,
Héyáng's Dīng Huì recovered Zé Prefecture."
The Shílù says Cóngzhōu,
which is an error.
The Táng Tàizǔ Jìniánlù states:
"In the third month,
Zhōu Déwēi defeated Shì Shūcóng at the Dòngwō post station.
Previously, the rebel Wēn had ordered Dīng Huì to lead troops to assist Lǐ Hǎnzhī,
garrisoning Lù Prefecture.
By this time,
Gě Cóngzhōu re-entered Lù Prefecture to replace Dīng Huì,
and the rebels again captured our Zé Prefecture."
The Liáng Shílù and the Xuē Shǐ Liáng Jì both state that it was in the sixth month that Cóngzhōu was sent into Lù Prefecture.
The Jìniánlù here connects subsequent events.
10 Wù Prefecture Governor Wáng Tán was besieged by Liǎngzhè.
Last year in the intercalary month,
the Liǎngzhè troops attacked Wù Prefecture.
According to the Xuān-Shè observation circuit,
it had previously been elevated to Níngguó Army,
with Tián Yún appointed as military governor.
Shè (歙),
is pronounced shè, with the falling-rising tone.
In the fourth month,
Yún dispatched the Field Headquarters Commander-in-Chief Kāng Rú and others to rescue him.
11 In the fifth month,
on Jiǎwǔ,
the Wǔxìn Army was established at Suì Prefecture,
placing Suì, Hé, and five other prefectures under its jurisdiction.
This was Wáng Jiàn's ambition.
12. Lǐ Kèyòng dispatched the Fan and Han cavalry and infantry commander-in-chief Lǐ Jūnqìng to lead troops to attack Lǐ Hǎnzhī.
On Yǐhài,
they besieged Lùzhōu.
Zhū Quánzhōng advanced and stationed at Héyáng.
On Xīnchǒu,
he sent his general Zhāng Cúnjìng to rescue it.
On Rényín,
he further sent Dīng Huì to lead troops in succession;
they heavily defeated the Hé dōng troops,

Kèyòng executed Jūnqìng and his deputy generals Yī Shěn and Lǐ Hóngxí.
He appointed Lǐ Sìzhāo as the Fan and Han cavalry and infantry commander-in-chief,
replacing him to attack Lùzhōu.
13. On Gēngxū,
Kāng Rú and others defeated the Liǎngzhè troops at Lóngqiū.
Lóngqiū,
originally the Hàn dynasty's Tàimò County,
was renamed Lóngqiū in the eighth year of the Zhēnguàn era,
which is present-day Lóngyóu County.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It belongs to Qúzhōu,
located seventy-five lǐ east of the prefecture.
Defeated,
bǔ mài fān.
Wáng Qiú was the main general,
who attacked Wùzhōu but was captured at Lóngqiū.
This was likely because the Zhè troops engaged the Xuān troops in battle.
In the first year of Jǐngfú,
Wáng Tán obtained Wùzhōu,
and by now had lost it.
14. In the sixth month,
on Yǐchǒu,
Lǐ Hǎnzhī's illness became critical.
On Dīngmǎo,
Quánzhōng petitioned to appoint Hǎnzhī as the Héyáng military governor,
and appointed Dīng Huì as the Zhāoyì military governor.
Not long after,
he also had his general Zhāng Guībà guard Xíngzhōu,
and sent Gé Cóngzhōu to replace Huì in guarding Lùzhōu.
Examination of discrepancies: The Biān Yí Lù states:
"In the sixth month,
on Yǐchǒu,
Lǐ Hǎnzhī's illness was severe,
and he requested to return to Héyáng.
On Dīngmǎo,
His Majesty ordered the withdrawal of the main army,
appointing Dīng Huì to temporarily manage affairs,
to pacify and care for Shàngdǎng,
after which His Majesty returned east."
It does not mention sending Cóngzhōu into Lù.
Xuē Jūzhèng's Wǔdài Shǐ Liáng Jì states:
"In the sixth month,
the Emperor petitioned to appoint Dīng Huì as the Lùzhōu military governor,
due to Lǐ Hǎnzhī's critical illness.
He also sent Gé Cóngzhōu to enter Lùzhōu via the Gùzhèn route,
to reinforce Dīng Huì."
The Liáng Shílù and Hòutáng Jì both state that he replaced Huì.
From this point until the fall of Lùzhōu,
when Hè Délún fled,
Huì's name is no longer seen.
Perhaps after Lǐ Hǎnzhī died,
Huì was recalled to guard Héyáng,
and Cóngzhōu replaced him,
but this cannot be known for certain.
Now, regarding Huì's garrisoning of Lù,
we conclude the account here.
15. The Western Chuān general Wáng Zōngjí was appointed as the Wǔxìn military governor.
This was at the request of Wáng Jiàn.
His original surname was Gān,
and he was from Hóngzhōu.
16. On Dīngchǒu,
Lǐ Hǎnzhī died in Huáizhōu.
Lǐ Hǎnzhī traveled from Lùzhōu to Héyáng,
and died upon reaching Huáizhōu.
17. The Bǎoyì military governor Wáng Gǒng,
was suspicious and cruel by nature.
Even his wife, children, and close associates
often could not ensure their own safety.
At this time, a military mutiny occurred,
and he was killed by his subordinates.
In the early years of Emperor Xīzōng's Zhōnghé era,
Wáng Chóngyíng garrisoned Shǎn,
and it passed to his son Gǒng,
ending at this point.
18. In autumn,
the seventh month,
Zhū Quánzhōng's garrison commander at Hǎizhōu, Chén Hànbīn, requested to surrender to Yáng Xíngmì.
The Huáihǎi Yóuyì envoy Zhāng Xùn, suspecting Hànbīn's intentions were uncertain,
together with the Liánshuǐ Fáng'è envoy Lújiāng Wáng Wǎn, led two thousand troops straight to Hǎizhōu,
and subsequently occupied the city.
From then on, Yáng Xíngmì possessed Hǎizhōu.
Qù,
qī yù fān.
19. The Jīngnán military governor Chéng Ruì was additionally appointed as Zhōngshū Lìng.
20. Mǎ Yīn sent his general Lǐ Táng to attack Dàozhōu.
Cài Jié gathered the Zǐ Mán people,
and set an ambush in a narrow pass to attack them,
heavily defeating Táng's troops.
Táng said:
"What the Mán rely on are the mountains and forests.
If we fight on level ground,
how could they defeat us!"
He then ordered to set fire to the forest using the wind,
the flames illuminating heaven and earth.
The Zǐ Mán fled in panic,
and they subsequently captured Dàozhōu,
apprehended Jié,
and executed him.
21. Zhū Quánzhōng recalled Gé Cóngzhōu from Lùzhōu,
and had Hè Délún guard it.
In the eighth month,
on Bǐngyín,
Lǐ Sìzhāo led troops to the walls of Lùzhōu,
dividing his forces to attack Zézhōu.
On Jǐsì,
the Biàn general Liú abandoned Zézhōu and fled.
The Hé dōng troops advanced and captured Tiānjǐng Pass,
appointing Lǐ Xiàozhāng as the prefect of Zézhōu.
"Lǐ Xiàozhāng"
should be
"Lǐ Cúnzhāng".
Sìzhāo daily had his armored cavalry encircle the city,
capturing foragers and herders,
and harvesting all grain within thirty lǐ of the city walls.
On Yǐyǒu,
Délún and others abandoned the city and fled under cover of night,
heading toward Húguān.
Since Délún's troops could not leave the city to forage or herd,
and the grain outside the city was also depleted,
both provisions and reinforcements were cut off,
making their flight inevitable.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Húguān County is located twenty-five lǐ east of Lùzhōu.
Qù,
qī yù fān.
Lǐ Cúnshěn,
also known as Fú Cúnshěn.
They killed and captured many.
Gé Cóngzhōu arrived with reinforcements,
but upon hearing that Délún and others had already been defeated,
he withdrew.
22. In the ninth month,
on Guǐmǎo,
the Fèngxiáng military governor Lǐ Màozhēn was appointed as the Fèngxiáng and Zhāngyì military governor.
In this year,

Textual analysis: The Táng Lièzǔ Shílù, the Xīn Tángshū Basic Annals, Lù Zhèn's Jiǔguó Zhì, and the Chǔ Shìjiā all say that in the second year of Guānghuà (899), Mǎ Yīn captured Guìzhōu.

Only Cáo Yǎn's Húxiāng Mǎshì Gùshì states:
"In the jiǎzǐ year of Tiānfù (904), Xuān Shèng entered Guìzhōu from Ānzhōu.
In the dīngmǎo year of Tiānyòu (907),
the twelfth month,
he captured the seven prefectures north of the ridges;
the following tenth month,
he pacified Guìzhōu."
This is extremely erroneous.
The Xīn Tángshū Fāngzhèn Biǎo states:
"In the third year of Guānghuà (900),
the Guìguǎn military commissioner was promoted to Jìngjiāng military governor."
Yet the Basic Annals state:
"In the second year of Qiánníng (895),
the Ānzhōu defense commissioner Xuān Shèng captured Guìzhōu,
and the Jìngjiāng military governor Zhōu Yuánjìng's subordinate general Liú Shìzhèng died there."
The chronology is already reversed,
and furthermore, taking Shìzhèng as Yuánjìng's subordinate who died together is
particularly erroneous.
Now, according to the Wǔ'ān military governor's secretary Lín Chóngxǐ's inscription for the Wǔwēi Wáng Temple Stele, it states:
"Our king had been on the throne for five years when Guìlín submitted."
From the third year of Qiánníng (896) to the third year of Guānghuà (900) is five years,
which also matches the Shílù,
therefore I follow this.

inflicting many casualties and capturing prisoners;
Lǐ Cúnjìn defeated the Biàn army at Dòngwō.
As the Biàn army was large,
supplies of fodder and grain were insufficient,
and the prolonged rain
caused the soldiers to suffer from malaria and dysentery,
so Zhū Quánzhōng recalled his troops.
In the fifth month,
Shūcóng and others returned from the Shíhuì Pass.
Examination of Discrepancies: The Biān Yílù states:
"In the fourth month,
on the Rénxū day,
Lǐ Kèyòng sent Zhāng Tè with a letter requesting to renew friendly relations,
so orders were given for the various armies to halt and remain in place.
Special envoys were dispatched to Tàiyuán,
allowing the resumption of friendly relations.
Moreover, the Bīngzhōu region is cold,
and the seasons arrive late.
With many warhorses,
wild grasses were insufficient for grazing,
so orders were soon given for Shì Shūcóng to withdraw his troops."
The Later Táng Tàizǔ Jì states:
"In the fifth month,
Shì Shūcóng and the surrounding enemy armies all retreated."
The Xuēshǐ Liáng Jì
places the withdrawal in the fourth month.
The Later Táng Jì
places the Biàn army’s retreat in the fifth month.
It is likely that Quánzhōng ordered the withdrawal in the fourth month,
but Shūcóng and others left Jìnyáng in the fifth month,
hence the differing records in the state histories.
The HéDōng generals Zhōu Déwēi and Lǐ Sìzhāo pursued them with five thousand elite cavalry,
inflicting heavy casualties and capturing many.
Prior to this,
Fénzhōu Prefect Lǐ Tǎng surrendered the entire prefecture to the Biàn army.
Kèyòng sent his general Lǐ Cúnshěn to attack it,
capturing it in three days,
seizing Tǎng,
and executing him.
When Shì Shūcóng passed through Shàngdǎng,
Mèng Qiān took his clan and followed him south.
Zhū Quánzhōng sent Dīng Huì to replace him in defending Lùzhōu.
This sets the stage for Dīng Huì’s later defection to Lǐ Kèyòng.
14. Zhū Quánzhōng petitioned to be appointed Military Governor of Hézhōng,
while secretly urging officials and commoners to request him as their commander.
On the Guǐmǎo day,
Quánzhōng was appointed Military Governor of the four circuits: Xuānwǔ, Xuānyì, Tiānpíng, and Hùguó.
At that time,
from Pú and Shǎn eastward,
all the way to the sea,
south to the Huái River,
north to the Yellow River,
all military towns were under Zhū Quánzhōng’s control.
If Quánzhōng had expanded by annexing neighboring circuits,
he should have concurrently held Yòuguó, Héyáng, and Shǎnguó,
not bypassed these three to take Hézhōng;
Quánzhōng’s reason for holding Hézhōng
was to control the court from above,
and to contain Lǐ Kèyòng from below.
15. On the Jǐyǒu day,
the Zhènhǎi and Zhèndōng Military Governor Qián Liú was additionally appointed as Acting Palace Attendant.
16. When Cuī Yìn abolished the two armies’ yeast sales,
he also prohibited it in nearby military towns.
Lǐ Màozhēn valued the profits,
and submitted a memorial requesting to come to the court to argue his case.
Lǐ Màozhēn was in Fèngxiáng,
a nearby military town,
hence he contested the profits from yeast sales.
When Màozhēn arrived in the capital,
Hán Quánhuì formed a deep alliance with him.
Cuī Yìn began to fear,
and secretly cultivated even closer ties with Zhū Quánzhōng,
becoming enemies with Màozhēn.
17. The Yòuguó Military Governor Zhāng Quányì was concurrently appointed as Secretariat Director.
18. In the sixth month,
on the Guǐhài day,
Zhū Quánzhōng went to Hézhōng.
Examination of Discrepancies: Xuē Jūzhèng’s Historical Records of the Five Dynasties, Liáng Annals states:
"On the Gēngshēn day,
the Emperor departed from Dàliáng."
Here, the Biān Yílù is followed.
19. When the Emperor was restored to the throne,
the Secretariat Drafter Línghú Huàn and the Supervising Secretary Hán Wò both participated in the plot,
so they were promoted to Hanlin Academicians.
They were frequently summoned for audiences,
and consulted on confidential matters.
Huàn
was the son of Línghú Táo.
At that time, the Emperor entrusted all military and state affairs to Cuī Yìn.
Whenever Yìn presented matters,
the Emperor would converse with him leisurely,
sometimes until candles were lit.
The eunuchs watched him with fear and sidelong glances,
and all consulted Yìn before acting.
Yìn was determined to eradicate them completely.
Hán Wò repeatedly advised:
"Matters should not be handled too extremely.
These people cannot be entirely eliminated either.
I fear their faction, if pressed too hard,
may cause other changes."
Yìn did not listen.
On the Dīngmǎo day,
the Emperor summoned Wò alone,
and asked:
"Among the Palace Commissioners, the wicked are numerous.
How should they be dealt with?"
Wò replied:
"During the incident at the Eastern Palace,
which Palace Commissioner was not complicit in the evil?
Dealing with them should have been done at the New Year,
referring to the time when Liú Jìshù and others were executed.
The Emperor said:
"At that time,
why did you not speak to Cuī Yìn about this?"
Wò replied:
"I saw Your Majesty’s edict stating,
'Apart from the four families of Liú Jìshù and others,
the rest are not to be questioned at all.'
What a ruler values most
is nothing greater than trustworthiness.
Once such an edict was issued,
it should have been firmly upheld.
If even one more person were executed,
then everyone would fear for their lives.
However, many have since been removed,
which is why they are now agitated and uneasy.
Your Majesty might as well select a few of the most wicked,
clearly announce their crimes,
and punish them according to the law.
Then, comfort and instruct the rest, saying: 'I fear you all think I harbor hidden intentions.
From now on, you need not doubt.'
Then select the most loyal and honest among them to serve as their leaders.
Reward those among their followers who do good,
and punish those who commit crimes.
Then all will be at peace.
Now, these people, both in public and private service, number in the tens of thousands.
'Public'
refers to those holding official positions.
'Private'
refers to those adopted or supported by eunuchs in their private households, not yet registered with the state.
The way of an emperor
should be to stabilize with gravity and magnanimity,
and govern with fairness and justice.
As for petty cleverness and schemes,
when one scheme arises, another will respond.
In the end, no great achievement can be made.
This is like trying to sort silk but only tangling it further.
'To sort silk but tangle it'
is a saying of Zhòng Zhòng of Lǔ from the Zuǒzhuàn.
Dù Yù’s commentary states: When silk is seen tangled and matted,
it only becomes more disordered.
They are scattered across the four directions;
if one can first reclaim this authority,
then there is nothing that cannot be accomplished."
The Emperor deeply agreed,
and said:
"This matter will ultimately be entrusted to you."
Alas!
In the world, there are certainly those who can understand and speak of things but cannot carry them through to the end.
Hán Wò was such a man.
Entrust,
is pronounced as zhǔ.
20. Lǐ Kèyòng sent his generals Lǐ Sìzhāo and Zhōu Déwēi to lead troops out of Yīndì Pass,
attacking Xízhōu.
Prefect Táng Lǐ surrendered.
They then attacked Cízhōu,
and Prefect Zhāng Huái surrendered.
In the intercalary month,
Dīng Huì, Military Commissioner of Héyáng, was appointed Military Commissioner of Zhāoyì.
Textual analysis: In the Old History of the Five Dynasties, the biography of Dīng Huì states:
"Due to illness, he retired from his post in Héyáng and lived in Luòyáng.
In the later years of Liáng Zǔ, he grew suspicious and jealous,
so many generals with great achievements were exterminated along with their clans.
Huì secretly harbored the intention to avoid disaster,
and pleaded illness for several years.
In the first year of the Tiānfù era,
after Liáng Zǔ had taken possession of Hézhōng, Jìn, and Jiàng,
he then appointed Huì as Military Commissioner of Zhāoyì."
According to this, in the sixth month of the second year of the Guānghuà era,
Huì was appointed Military Commissioner of Zhāoyì from Héyáng.
In the ninth month,
Lǐ Kèyòng captured Lùzhōu,
and recommended Mèng Qiān as Military Commissioner.
At that time, Hǎn Zhī had already died,
so Huì must have resumed command of Héyáng.
Up to this point, it had only been two years,
so it was not a case of retiring due to illness and pleading illness for several years.
Moreover,
at that time, Zhū Quánzhōng had not yet begun to execute his senior generals;
it is suspected that after Huì surrendered to Hédōng,
the author of his biography mistakenly placed events from the Tiānyòu era earlier in the narrative.
This appointment followed the request of Zhū Quánzhōng.
A Daoist priest named Dù Cóngfǎ, using sorcery and deceit, incited the people of Chāng, Pǔ, and Hé prefectures to rebel.
Wáng Jiàn dispatched the Field Army Commander Wáng Zōng'àn to lead thirty thousand troops, joining forces with the armies of Dōngchuān and Wǔxìn to suppress them.
Zōng'àn
was originally named Jí Jiàn.
Cuī Yǐn requested the Emperor to exterminate all the eunuchs,
and to have palace women manage the affairs of the various internal offices instead;
at that time, eunuchs separately held the commissions for the various internal offices.
Upon hearing of this,
Hán Quánhuī and others tearfully pleaded for mercy before the Emperor.
The Emperor then ordered Cuī Yǐn,
"If you have matters to report, submit them in sealed memorials;
do not present them orally."
The eunuchs sought several beautiful women who were literate,
had them enter the palace,
and secretly ordered them to spy on and investigate the matter,
thereby uncovering all of Cuī Yǐn's secret plans.
The Emperor was unaware of this.
Quánhuī and others were greatly frightened.
Whenever they gathered for banquets,
they would weep and bid each other farewell,
day and night plotting ways to remove Cuī Yǐn.
At that time, Cuī Yǐn held the position of Commissioner of the Three Treasuries.
Quánhuī and others incited the Imperial Guard to clamor before the Emperor,
complaining that Cuī Yǐn had reduced their winter clothing allowances.
The Emperor had no choice
but to relieve Cuī Yǐn of his post as Salt and Iron Commissioner.
At that time, Zhū Quánzhōng and Lǐ Màozhēn each had the intention of controlling the Emperor to command the feudal lords.
Quánzhōng wanted the Emperor to move to the Eastern Capital,
while Màozhēn wanted him to move to Fèngxiáng.
Cuī Yǐn, knowing his plot had been exposed
and the situation was urgent,
sent a letter to Zhū Quánzhōng,
claiming to have received a secret edict
ordering Quánzhōng to send troops to escort the imperial carriage,
and further stating:
"The recent restoration of the throne,
was entirely due to your excellent planning."
Cuī Yǐn said that the plan for the restoration all came from Quánzhōng.
According to the Old Book's Imperial Annals,
after Quánzhōng annexed Hézhōng,
he was promoted to Grand Preceptor and concurrently Zhongshu Ling,
hence he was addressed as 'Lìnggōng'.
When Lǐ Màozhēn came to court,
see the first month of this year.
Chāo,
pronounced as Chǔ Jiāo fān.
You will surely become a criminal,
not only will your achievements be taken by others,
but you will also face punitive campaigns!"
Upon receiving the letter,
in autumn,
the seventh month,
on the jiǎyín day,
Quánzhōng hurriedly returned to Dàliáng to mobilize troops.
Textual analysis: The Tang Tàizǔ Jìnián Lù states:
"When the Biàn forces invaded Tónghuà,
the eunuchs learned of Cuī Yǐn's plot.
At that time, Yǐn exclusively controlled the Three Treasuries and currency,
Hán Quánhuī incited the Imperial Guard,
and when Yǐn went out,
they gathered and clamored,
complaining about the reduction of winter clothing;
the soldiers also went before the Emperor to lodge their complaints.
The Emperor, yielding to public sentiment,
dismissed Cuī Yǐn from his administrative post."
Cuī Yǐn, angered,
urgently summoned Zhū Wēn,
requesting him to lead troops into the court to assist."
The Táng Bǔ Jì states:
"At that time, Zhū Quánzhōng was in Hézhōng.
Yǐn secretly drafted an urgent edict ordering Quánzhōng to come to court,
and also wrote a letter saying such and such.
Upon receiving this edict and letter,
Quánzhōng immediately set out from Hézhōng,
returning to Biàn."
According to this, at that time Quánzhōng had not invaded Tónghuà,
and Yǐn had not yet been dismissed.
The Jìnián Lù is mistaken.
Now follow the Táng Bǔ Jì.
Wáng Zōngkǎn, the commander of Lóngtái Garrison in Xīchuān, and others suppressed Dù Cóngfǎ,
and pacified the rebellion.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Ānyuè County in Pǔ Prefecture had a Lóngtái Garrison.
In the eighth month,
on the jiǎshēn day,
the Emperor asked Hán Wò:
"I have heard that Lù Yǐ was displeased with my restoration to the throne.
On New Year's Day, he changed his clothes,
rode a small horse out of the Qǐxià Gate.
Is this true?"
Qǐxià Gate was
the first gate on the eastern side of the southern wall of the capital city.
Xià,
pronounced as hù yǎ fān.
"The plan for the restoration,
was known only to me, Cuī Yǐn, and a few others.
Yǐ did not know about it.
Suddenly hearing of a change in the palace one morning,
how could people not be shocked and alarmed!
Changing clothes and fleeing to escape,
such a thing is quite possible!
If Your Majesty blames him, as a chancellor, for lacking the resolve to die for the cause, that is acceptable.
But as for being displeased with the restoration,
I fear that comes from the mouths of slanderers.
I hope Your Majesty will investigate this!"
The Emperor then let the matter drop.
Hán Quánhuī and others, fearing execution,
plotted to use military force to control the Emperor.
They thus formed a close alliance with Lǐ Jìzhāo, Lǐ Jìhuì, Lǐ Yànbì, and Lǐ Jìyún;
only Jìzhāo refused to comply.
Another day,
the Emperor asked Hán Wò:
"What have you heard outside?"
He replied:
"I have only heard that the commissioners are anxious and fearful,
and are associating with the 'meritorious officials' and Jìyún.
'Meritorious officials'
refers to Lǐ Jìzhāo, Lǐ Jìhuì, and Lǐ Yànbì.
But I do not know if this is actually true or not."
The Emperor said:
"This is not unfounded.
Recently, Jìhuì, Yànbì, and their ilk have been speaking increasingly arrogantly,
making it hard to bear.
Líng Hú Huàn wants me to summon Cuī Yǐn and Quánhuī and others to the inner palace,
host a banquet to reconcile them.
What do you think?"
He replied:
"If you do that, their violence and perversity will only increase."
The Emperor asked:
"What should be done then?"
He replied:
"The only way is to clearly punish a few individuals,
swiftly banish them,
and allow the rest to reform themselves.
Then perhaps the situation can be calmed.
If no one is questioned at all,
they will surely know that Your Majesty has something in mind,
and will grow even more unsettled.
The matter will ultimately not be resolved."
The Emperor said:
"Good!"
However, the eunuchs, relying on their factional support being established,
gradually began to disobey imperial decrees.
Sometimes the Emperor would send them out,
appointing them as army supervisors or demoting them to guard the imperial mausoleums.
'Demoting them to guard the imperial mausoleums' means
stripping them of their official robes and assigning them to labor at the various mausoleums.
The Emperor could do nothing about it.
Someone reported to Yáng Xíngmì that
Qián Liú had been killed by bandits.
Xíngmì dispatched the Infantry Commander-in-Chief Lǐ Shénfú and others to lead troops to capture Hángzhōu.
The Liǎngzhè generals Gù Quánwǔ and others set up eight stockades to resist them.
On the 27th day of the ninth month,
Guǐchǒu,
the Emperor urgently summoned Hán Wò
and said to him:
"I have heard that Quánzhōng wishes to come to eliminate the wicked ones at the ruler's side.
This is indeed utmost loyalty,
but he must be made to share the merit with Màozhēn.
If the two commanders contend with each other,
then the situation will become perilous.
You, for my sake, tell Cuī Yìn
to swiftly send letters by fast horse to the two garrisons,
urging them to join in planning together.
That would be excellent."
On Rénxū,
the Emperor again said to Wò:
"Jìhuái, Yànbǐ and their ilk grow increasingly arrogant and domineering.
Several days ago, they entered together with Jìyún,
and right in the eastern part of the palace hall, they had young boys sing to accompany their drinking.
'Accompany'
means to assist.
Wò replied:
"Your servant certainly knows this is the case;
this matter was mishandled from the beginning.
At the time of their achievement on New Year's Day,
referring to the execution of Liú and Wáng,
and the welcoming of the Emperor's restoration.
they should not have been permitted to come and go within the palace precincts.
These men have always lacked understanding.
They repeatedly request audiences,
or presumptuously and casually recommend people.
If they meet with the slightest refusal,
then they harbor resentment.
Moreover, they only know to crave profit.
The eunuch commissioners hired them with substantial benefits,
meaning Hán Quánhuái and others used profit to entice Jìhuái and Yànbǐ,
so they follow their every direction and act for their use,
as if hired for wages.
Cuī Yìn originally kept the guard troops
intending to use them to control the eunuch commissioners.
Meaning he kept the Qí troops to control the eunuchs.
The event is recorded in the first month of this year.
What is to be done!
If the Biàn troops come,
they will certainly fight with the Qí troops beneath the palace gates.
Your servant privately trembles with fear."
The Emperor could only look distressed, worried, and dejected.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on Wùxū,
Zhū Quánzhōng launched a massive army from Dàliáng.
Textual analysis notes: Xuē Jūzhèng's History of the Five Dynasties states:
"In the tenth month,
on Wùxū,
he received a secret edict to proceed to Cháng'ān.
At that time, the court's military and state affairs
were solely entrusted to Cuī Yìn.
Cuī in every matter restricted and suppressed the eunuchs,
causing the eunuchs to view him with hostility.
One day, Cuī made a memorial in the informal palace hall,
wishing to completely remove them.
Quánhuái and others, leaning against the wall, overheard this.
The palace eunuchs glared at Cuī with eyes wide with rage.
Using heavy bribes and sweet words, they enticed the regional commanders,
making them their shields and supports.
At times during banquets and gatherings,
they would face each other and shed tears.
At that time, Cuī solely controlled the finances of the three revenue departments.
Quánhuái and others instructed the imperial guards to complain about him before Emperor Zhāozōng;
Emperor Zhāozōng had no choice but to dismiss Cuī from his administrative duties.
Cuī urgently summoned Tàizǔ (Zhū Quánzhōng),
requesting him to bring troops to assist the court.
Hence this march took place."
According to this, before the Emperor went to Fèngxiáng,
Cuī Yìn had not been dismissed from the chancellorship.
This account is roughly the same as the Tàizǔ Jìnián Lù,
and is also mistaken.
On the 28th, Lǐ Shénfú and Gù Quánwǔ had been locked in a stalemate for a long time.
Shénfú captured a Hángzhōu prisoner,
and allowed him to come and go within his private quarters.
Shénfú said to his generals:
"The Hángzhōu troops are still strong.
Our army should retreat tonight."
The Hángzhōu prisoner ran to report to Quánwǔ.
Shénfú ordered his men not to pursue,
deliberately letting the Hángzhōu prisoner escape to report to Quánwǔ in order to lure him.
Shénfú acted as the rear guard,
and had the Field Operations Commandant Lǚ Shīzào lay an ambush at the foot of Qīngshān.
Shěn Kuò states: Lín'ān County has a Qīngshān town.
Lù Zhèn's Jiǔguózhì records it as 'setting an ambush on the Qīngshān road'.
Quánwǔ sent troops in pursuit;
Shénfú and Shīzào attacked from both sides,
inflicting a major defeat,
beheading five thousand,
and capturing Quánwǔ alive.
When Qián Liú heard this,
he exclaimed in shock and wept:
"I have lost my fine general!"
Shénfú advanced to attack Lín'ān.
Lín'ān County
is the place where Qián Liú rose to power,
and where the Yìjǐn Army is stationed.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Lín'ān County is 120 lǐ west of Hángzhōu.
On the 29th, Hán Quánhuái heard that Zhū Quánzhōng was about to arrive.
On Dīngyǒu,
he ordered Lǐ Jìyún, Lǐ Yànbǐ and others to lead troops to seize the Emperor,
requesting him to proceed to Fèngxiáng.
Additional troops were deployed to guard all gates of the palace precincts.
Textual analysis notes: According to the Jīnluán Jì:
"On the 20th, I entered for duty.
The night before,
Lord Cuī sent word,
asking to see me tomorrow.
I arrived at his gate early in the morning,
and Cuī showed me the imperial rescript."
If so, then adding men to guard the gates and the issuing of the imperial rescript
both occurred on the 19th.
The Shílù states:
"On Jǐhài,
men were assigned to guard the gates."
Jǐhài
was the 21st.
The Shílù is mistaken.
The Emperor sent someone to secretly bestow an imperial rescript upon Cuī Yìn.
The words were all filled with grief and anguish.
It ended saying:
"For the great plan of the ancestral temples and the state,
the situation compels me to travel west.
You and the others should travel east.
'Travel west'
means he will proceed to Fèngxiáng.
He orders Yìn and the others to travel east,
to urge Zhū Quánzhōng to advance his troops.
How distressing!"
On Wùxū,
the Emperor sent Lady Zhàoguó out to speak to Hán Wò:
He ordered a palace woman to go to the Academy of Scholars to speak to him.
The New and Old Books of Tang, Imperial Annals state: Lady Zhàoguó, née Yán.
'Spoke'
is pronounced niù, according to Niú Jù's phonetic notation.
"This morning, Yànbǐ and his ilk were utterly disrespectful.
I wished to summon you for an audience,
but the situation made it impossible."
And she said:
"The Emperor and the Empress could only face each other weeping."
From then on,
the academicians no longer gained audiences.
On Guǐmǎo,
Hán Quánhuái and others had the Emperor enter the inner court to summon all officials.
When all officials entered through the inner court gate to see him in the inner hall,
it was called 'entering the inner court'.
On Bǐngwǔ,
the Bǐngwǔ edict followed the old regulations of the Dàzhōng era,
as seen above.
On this day,
the Yányīng Hall was opened for audience,
and Quánhuái and others immediately attended at the Emperor's side,
jointly discussing government affairs.
On Dīngwèi,
the Shéncè Army Commander-in-Chief Lǐ Jìyún dispatched his troops to plunder the treasures, curtains, and ritual objects from the inner treasury.
Hán Quánhuái sent people to secretly escort the various princes and palace women ahead to Fèngxiáng.
'To'
means to go.
On Wùshēn,
Zhū Quánzhōng reached Hézhōng,
and submitted a memorial requesting the imperial carriage to proceed to the Eastern Capital.
The capital was thrown into great alarm,
with officials and commoners fleeing and hiding in the mountains and valleys.
On this day,
all officials failed to attend court,
and before the palace gates it was silent and deserted.
In the eleventh month,
on Jǐyǒu, the first day of the month,
Lǐ Jìyún and others led troops before the palace gates,
prohibiting people from entering or exiting,
and the various armies engaged in widespread plundering.
Officials and commoners wearing paper or cloth jackets
filled the streets as far as the eye could see.
Hán Jiàn had his staff officer Sīmǎ Yè take charge as Acting Military Governor of Kuāngguó.
Zhū Quánzhōng led the armies of the four garrisons, seventy thousand strong, towards Tóngzhōu.
The armies of the four garrisons
were from Xuānwǔ, Xuānyì, Tiānpíng, and Hùguó.
'Towards'
is pronounced qū, according to the Qīyù phonetic notation.
Hán Quánhuí and others, because Lǐ Jìzhāo did not side with them,
blocked him and prevented him from seeing the emperor.
At that time, Cuī Yìn’s residence was in Kāihuà Fāng.
According to the Biography of Sūn Dézhāo in the History of the Five Dynasties,
Kāihuà Fāng was located on the eastern street of Cháng'ān.
"Sixty,"
should be
"six thousand."
[Chapter note: In the twelve-line edition,
"ten"
is correctly written as
"thousand."
] Shuài,
read as shuài.
The history states that the reason Cuī Yìn did not die at the hands of the eunuchs
was because they all went to rely on him.
They relied on Lǐ Jìzhāo’s troops to avoid the violent plundering by the imperial guards and Qí troops.
On Gēngxū,
the emperor sent the Attendant Official Zhāng Shàosūn to summon the officials,
but Cuī Yìn and others all submitted memorials declining and did not come.
On Rénzǐ,
Hán Quánhuí and others deployed troops in front of the palace hall,
and said to the emperor:
"Zhū Quánzhōng is pressing the capital with a large army,
intending to seize the Son of Heaven and move to Luòyáng,
seeking abdication and succession;
we, your subjects, request to escort Your Majesty to Fèngxiáng,
to gather troops and resist him."
The emperor did not consent,
and instead took up a sword and ascended the Qǐqiǎo Tower.
Hán Quánhuí and others forced the emperor to descend the tower.
The emperor had only just reached the Shòuchūn Hall
when Lǐ Yǎnbì had already set fire to the imperial quarters.
The imperial quarters
were the residence of the Son of Heaven and the empress.
The emperor sat alone in the Sīzhèng Hall,
with one foot raised,
and the other foot resting on the railing.
Tà
is the same as tà.
The railing
refers to the hall’s balustrade.
There were no attendants beside him.
After a short while,
having no alternative,
he, along with the empress, consorts, various princes, and over a hundred others, all mounted horses.
The sound of their wailing was unceasing.
As they left the palace gate,
they looked back at the imperial palace,
where the fire was already blazing fiercely.

Xiào,

Could Fū and Biàn have faced each other

Lǐ Jìqiú.

According to the Old Annals and the *Compilation of Omissions*, both state
"on Xīnwèi in the first month,
Kěfàn and others were executed."

However, the *Liáng Veritable Records*, *Supplementary Táng Annals*, *Continued Records of the Fortunes of the Realm*, *Jīnluán Jì*, *Supplementary Records of the Táng Era*, and Xuē Jūzhèng's *History of the Five Dynasties: Liáng Annals*, and the New Táng Annals,
either say the day after Jǐsì,
or the 28th.
The latter is followed here.
It seems that although Zhū Quánzhōng and Cuī Yìn memorialized about abolishing the eunuch commissions
and recalling the army supervisors to the capital,
in fact, they had already secretly executed them that same day.
It was not until the second month, on Guǐyǒu, that an edict was issued granting them death,
hence Emperor Zhāozōng mourned them and performed sacrifices.
They were eliminated both inside and outside the palace.
Those who were on missions outside
were ordered to be captured and executed wherever they were,
leaving only thirty young and weak eunuchs in yellow robes to perform cleaning duties.
Eunuchs of lower rank wore yellow.
The character "洒"
is pronounced as "suǒ mài fān,"
or as usual.
The character "掃"
is pronounced as "sū bào fān,"
or as usual.
They were chosen for their deep-rooted local customs
and cautious, simple nature.
The emperor pitied Kěfàn and others, some of whom were innocent,
and composed a text to sacrifice to them.
From then on, the proclamation of imperial decrees
was all done by palace women going in and out;
the troops of the two armies and the eight external garrisons were all placed under the Six Armies.
This refers to the troops of the eight internal and external garrisons commanded by the Left and Right Shéncè Armies.
Your subject, Guāng, remarks: The use of power by eunuchs,
as a calamity for the state,
has a long history.
Because they move in and out of the palace precincts,
the ruler, from childhood to adulthood,
becomes intimate and familiar with them,
unlike the Three Dukes and Six Ministers,
who have audiences only at set times
and can be strictly feared.
Among them, moreover, are those with clever and sharp minds,
eloquent and glib in speech,
who observe expressions,
cater to inclinations,
and when given orders, present no risk of disobedience,
while carrying out tasks yields satisfactory results.
Unless the ruler is of supreme wisdom,
discerning the nature of things,
considering dangers with deep foresight,
and aside from their service,
does not entrust them with affairs,
then the close ones grow daily more intimate,
while the distant ones grow daily more estranged.
Sweet words and humble requests are sometimes heeded,
and slanders that seep in like water or feel personal are sometimes listened to.
The *Analects*: Confucius said:
"If slanders that seep in like water
and accusations that feel personal
do not prevail with him,
he may indeed be called discerning."
Zhū Xī's commentary states: Seeping in,
like water soaking and irrigating,
moistening gradually and not abruptly.
Feeling personal,
refers to what is felt on the skin, where gain and loss are切身.
Unaware, one is imperceptibly influenced by those close at hand,
like drinking strong wine,
savoring its flavor but forgetting its intoxication.
If the power over promotions, demotions, punishments, and rewards shifts, yet the state does not face danger and chaos,
such a thing has never occurred.
In the decline of the Eastern Hàn,
eunuchs were most notorious for their arrogance and tyranny.
However, they all relied on the sovereign's authority,
leaning on the city walls and altars.
This means that eunuchs, being close to the sovereign, had something to rely on,
much like foxes in the city walls or rats at the altars,
unafraid of being smoked out or burned.
None were able to coerce the Son of Heaven as if controlling an infant,
with the power to depose and appoint at will,
moving east or west according to their whims,
making the Son of Heaven fear them as if riding a tiger or wolf while clutching a venomous snake,
as was the case in the Táng dynasty.
The reason for this is none other than
the fact that in Hàn, they did not hold military power,
whereas in Táng, they did.
The harm done to the people by pests and vermin
cannot be fully enumerated.
Removing
the office of palace eunuchs
dates from the time of the Three Kings,
and is fully recorded in the Book of Songs and the Rites.
The Book of Songs contains the poem "Xiàng Bó."
The Rites include the duties of palace eunuchs.
They facilitate communication between the inner and outer courts;
how can they be dispensed with?
Take Xiàng Bó's hatred of evil, for example.
During the reign of King Yōu of Zhōu,
a eunuch, wounded by slander, composed the poem "Xiàng Bó."
The Record says: "Loving the worthy as one loves the black robe,
hating the wicked as Xiàng Bó did."
The Zuǒzhuàn records: Duke Xiàn of Jìn believed slanders
and sent the eunuch Pī to attack Prince Chóng'ěr at Púchéng;
Chóng'ěr leaped over the wall and escaped,
but Pī cut off his sleeve.
When Chóng'ěr later returned to his state,
Pī requested an audience.
The duke sent someone to reproach him, saying:
"During the campaign at Púchéng,
the ruler's order was to arrive in one night,
yet you arrived immediately.
Later, when I was with the Dí ruler,
hunting by the Wèi River,
you came on behalf of Duke Huì to seek my death.
You were ordered to arrive in three nights,
yet you arrived by the second night.
Though you had the ruler's order,
why were you so swift!"
Pī replied:
"A ruler's orders admit no second thoughts;
this is an ancient rule.
To eliminate the ruler's enemies,
I exerted all my strength.
Whether they were men of Pú or men of Dí,
what did I care?
Now that you have ascended the throne,
will there be no enemies like those of Pú or Dí?"
The duke granted him an audience,
and Pī informed him of the plot by Lǚ and Xì,
enabling the duke to escape harm.
This event is recorded in the 48th volume, in the first year of the Yǒngyuán era of Emperor Hé of Hàn.
The event is recorded in the 57th volume, in the second year of the Guānghé era of Emperor Líng of Hàn,
and in the 58th volume, in the first year of the Zhōngpíng era.
Mǎ Cúnliàng's suppression of rebellion,
Yáng Fùguāng's campaign against rebels,
and Yán Zūnměi's avoidance of power
are all recorded in previous annals.
The event is recorded in the annals of Later Liáng.
However, the ruler should not consult them on political matters
or allow them to promote or dismiss scholar-officials,
lest they gain enough authority to sway others.
If they indeed commit crimes,
minor ones should be punished,
major ones executed,
with no leniency or pardon;
in this way,
even if they are allowed to act arbitrarily,
who would dare?
How can one fail to distinguish good from bad,
or choose between right and wrong,
and seek to exterminate them like weeds or wild beasts?
Would that not lead to chaos?
Thus, Yuán Shào acted first, and Dǒng Zhuó weakened the Hàn,
as recorded in the annals of Emperors Líng and Xiàn of Hàn.
Though it satisfied momentary anger, the state perished as a result.
This is like burning clothes because they are dirty
or cutting down a tree because it is infested with worms;
does that not cause even greater harm?
Confucius said:
"If a man is without humaneness,
and you hate him too intensely,
it will lead to disorder."
See the Analects.
4 Wáng Shīfàn sent an envoy to inform Lǐ Kèyòng of his uprising,
and Kèyòng sent a letter praising him.
The Hé dōng supervisor Zhāng Chéngyè also urged Kèyòng to send troops to rescue Fèngxiáng.
Kèyòng attacked Jìnzhōu,
but upon hearing that the imperial carriage had returned east,
he halted.
5 Yáng Xíngmì, acting under imperial authority, promoted Zhū Jǐn to deputy commander-in-chief of the eastern front armies and concurrent tóngpíngzhāngshì,
appointed Shēngzhōu prefect Lǐ Shénfú as Huáinán campaign marshal and È-Yuè campaign commander,
with Shūzhōu militia commander Liú Cún as his deputy,
and sent troops to attack Dù Hóng.
Hóng's general Luò Yīn, stationed at Yǒngxīng,
abandoned the city and fled,
and the county resident Fāng Zhào occupied the city and surrendered.
Shénfú said:
"Yǒngxīng is a major county,
crucial for supply transport;
we have already secured half of Èzhōu!"
Yǒngxīng
was the territory of È County in Hàn times;
Wú separated È to establish Xīnyáng County,
Suí renamed Xīnyáng as Yǒngxīng,
and Táng placed it under Èzhōu.
The Jiǔyùzhì states: it is 405 lǐ southeast of Èzhōu,
and present-day Shòuchāngjūn is located there.
Surrendered,
pronounced with the jiàng tone.
Wáng Chóngwǔ punctuated; Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí proofread.
Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial order.
Later Student Tiāntāi
Third Year of Tiānfù
(Guǐhài, 903)
1 In the second month,
on the first day, Rénshēn,
an edict was issued:
"All appointments made while in Fèngxiáng Prefecture
are hereby suspended."
At that time, all eunuchs had been executed,
except for Hé dōng supervisor Zhāng Chéngyè, Yōuzhōu supervisor Zhāng Jūhàn, Qīnghǎi supervisor Chéng Kuāngróu, Xīchuān supervisor Yú Quányīn, and retired official Yán Zūnměi,
who were hidden and protected by Lǐ Kèyòng, Liú Rén'gōng, Yáng Xíngmì, and Wáng Jiàn.
Other prisoners were executed to comply with the edict.
2 On Jiǎxū,
Ménxiàshìláng and concurrent tóngpíngzhāngshì Lù Yǐ was demoted to tutor of the Prince of Yí and assigned to a separate office.
The Prince of Yí, Lǐ,
was an imperial prince.
"Lǐ"
is also written as
"Yīn."
Edicts were issued to all circuits,
except Fèngxiáng.
Yǐ said:
"Though Lǐ Màozhēn's crimes are great,
the court has not yet severed ties with him;
now, to exclude him alone from the edicts
shows a lack of magnanimity."
Examination of discrepancies: The Old History records:
"After the emperor returned to the capital, he issued pardons to all circuits,
and edicts were sent to each,
except Fèngxiáng.
Yǐ memorialized"
and so on.
According to this, no pardon had been issued at that time;
it was likely only the issuance of edicts.
Perhaps Yǐ made this proposal before the pardon,
which angered Cuī Yìn.
Yìn memorialized to have him demoted.
Palace women Sòng Róu and ten others, all presented by Hán Quánhuī,
(the presentation of Sòng Róu and others is recorded in the first year of the previous volume.)
were sent to Jīngzhào to be beaten to death.
3 The emperor said to Hán Wò:
"Though Cuī Yìn is utterly loyal,
he employs more schemes than you."
Wò replied:
"A ruler of the world
has all states as his eyes and ears;
how can he deceive them with schemes?
It is better to be sincere and straightforward;
though daily calculations may fall short, yearly calculations will yield surplus."
Using a phrase from the Zhuāngzǐ.
4 On the Bǐngzǐ day,
the Vice Minister of Works and Concurrently Grand Councilor Sū Jiǎn,
and the Vice Minister of Personnel Lú Guāngqǐ,
were both ordered to commit suicide.
On the Dīngchǒu day,
the Vice Minister of the Secretariat and Concurrently Grand Councilor Wáng Pǔ was appointed as a Guest of the Crown Prince and assigned to a separate office,
all because they were disliked by Cuī Yìn.
(From
"Dīngchǒu"
to
"disliked by"
are twenty-six characters,
added according to Zhāng Yù's collation notes on the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn based on Song editions.
) Sū Jiǎn and Lú Guāngqǐ were both appointed as councilors by Fèngxiáng,
and Cuī Yìn disliked them for aligning themselves with Hán Quánhuí and Lǐ Màozhēn,
so he had them killed.
Textual analysis notes: According to the Veritable Records:
"Jiǎn and Guāngqǐ were both ordered to commit suicide.
Another account says
Jiǎn was exiled to Huánzhōu."
The Táng Tàizǔ Jìnián Lù states:
"Initially, when the emperor went to Fèngxiáng,
Lú Guāngqǐ and Wéi Yífàn were appointed as councilors,
and Sū Jiǎn was also appointed as a Grand Councilor.
After the emperor returned to the palace,
Yìn, harboring resentment over past events,
within a month,
demoted and exiled them all.
Lù Yǐ was demoted to Tutor to the Prince of Yí,
Wáng Pǔ to Guest of the Crown Prince,
and Sū Jiǎn was ordered to commit suicide."
The Xù Bǎoyùn Lù states:
"On the fifth day of the second month,
more than one hundred officials, including the councilors serving under the Prince of Qí, Lú Guāngqǐ and others,
were all ordered to commit suicide."
The New History Annals state:
"Zhū Quánzhōng killed Sū Jiǎn and Lú Guāngqǐ."
The Old History biography of Yìn states:
"When Emperor Zhāozōng first went to Fèngxiáng,
he appointed Lú Guāngqǐ, Wéi Yífàn, Sū Jiǎn, and others as councilors.
After returning to the capital,
Yìn demoted and dismissed them all."
The New History biography of Guāngqǐ states:
"Jiǎn was exiled to Huánzhōu,
and Guāngqǐ was ordered to commit suicide,"
which matches the annotation in the Bǎoyùn Lù.
"Jiǎn exiled to Huánzhōu"
does not appear to have a clear source.
5 On the Wùyín day,
Zhū Quánzhōng was granted the title "Meritorious Subject Who Reversed Heaven, Rebuilt the State, Exhausted Loyalty, and Maintained Uprightness."
His aides, such as Jìng Xiáng, were granted the title "Meritorious Subject Who Welcomed the Imperial Carriage and Assisted in Governance."
His generals, such as Zhū Yǒuníng, were granted the title "Meritorious Subject Who Welcomed the Imperial Carriage with Resolute Bravery."
Officers below the rank of Dūtóu were granted the title "Meritorious Subject Who Pacified the Four Garrisons and Quelled Difficulties."
The emperor discussed honoring Quánzhōng,
intending to appoint a prince as the Marshal of the Armies of All Circuits,
with Quánzhōng as his deputy.
Cuī Yìn requested that Prince Huī, Zuò, be appointed.
The emperor said:
"Prince Pú is the eldest."
Yìn, following Quánzhōng's secret instruction,
took advantage of Zuò's youth,
and insisted on his appointment.
On the Jǐmǎo day,
Zuò was appointed as the Marshal of the Armies of All Circuits.
Textual analysis notes: The Jīnluán Jì states:
"The emperor said: 'I consider Prince Pú to be the eldest,'"
and so on.
The New History biographies state:

"The emperor had seventeen sons: Déwáng Yù, Dìwáng Xǔ, Qiánwáng Xì, Yíwáng Yīn, Suìwáng Yī, Jǐngwáng Mì, Huīwáng Zuò, Qíwáng Qí, Yǎwáng Zhēn, Qióngwáng Xiáng, Duānwáng Zhēn, Fēngwáng Qí, Héwáng Fú, Dēngwáng Xǐ, Jiāwáng Hù, Yǐngwáng Tí, and Càiwáng Yòu.
Empress Hé gave birth to Yù and Zuò,
while the mothers of the others are unknown."
The Old History biographies state that Emperor Zhāozōng had ten sons,
excluding Duānwáng Zhēn and the six that follow.
According to the New and Old Histories,
none of Emperor Zhāozōng's sons held the title Prince Pú.
Sūn Guāngxiàn's Xù Tōnglì states:
"Prince Pú was named Xún,
a son of Emperor Zhāozōng,
and his mother was Empress Wáng.
After the death of Emperor Āi,
Zhū Quánzhōng enthroned Xún as emperor,
changing the era name to Tiānshòu.
The following year,
he abdicated in favor of the Liáng."
This is an erroneous account by Guāngxiàn.
Emperor Zhāozōng also had no Empress Wáng.
The Prince Pú mentioned in the Jīnluán Jì
likely refers to Déwáng after his title was changed.
On the Gēngchén day,
Quánzhōng was appointed as Grand Commandant,
acting as Deputy Marshal,
and promoted to Prince of Liáng.
Yìn was appointed as Minister over the Masses and concurrently Palace Attendant.
Yìn, relying on Quánzhōng's power,
monopolized authority and acted arbitrarily.
The emperor's every move had to be reported to him.
Among the court officials who had accompanied the emperor to Fèngxiáng,
more than thirty were demoted or exiled.
Rewards and punishments were based on his personal likes and dislikes.
Those he favored were rewarded,
and those he disliked were punished.
Everyone was terrified and walked in fear.
Jìng Xiáng was appointed as Grand Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury,
and Zhū Yǒuníng was appointed as Military Commissioner of Níngyuǎn.
The Níngyuǎn Army,
located in Róngzhōu,
was then controlled by Páng Jùzhāo.
Since the Five Dynasties, there have been nominal military commissioners,
and this is an example.
He was appointed as Military Commissioner of Tiānxióng,
and troops were sent to escort him to Qínzhōu.
"Zhī" means "to go."
The Qí troops blocked the road,
so he could not reach it.
"Huán" is pronounced as "xuān" or according to its usual reading.
6 Earlier,
when the Hanlin Academician Recipient of Edicts Hán Wò passed the imperial examination,
the Censor-in-Chief Zhào Chóng was the chief examiner.
After the emperor returned from Fèngxiáng,
he intended to appoint Wò as councilor.
Wò recommended Chóng and the Vice Minister of War Wáng Zàn in his place.
The emperor was about to agree,
but Cuī Yìn, disliking the division of his power,
had Zhū Quánzhōng intervene to oppose it.
Quánzhōng said to the emperor:
"Zhào Chóng is the epitome of frivolity,
and Wáng Zàn is incompetent.
How could Hán Wò recklessly recommend them as councilors?"
Seeing Quánzhōng's intense anger,
the emperor had no choice.
On the Guǐwèi day,
Wò was demoted to Military Advisor of Púzhōu.
The emperor secretly bid farewell to Wò in tears.
Wò said:
"This man is no longer what he used to be,"
referring to Zhū Quánzhōng.
"I cannot bear to witness the humiliation of usurpation and regicide!"
Alas!
How late Hán Wò was in realizing this!
Yet, when Emperor Zhāozōng heard these words,
how could he bear it?
He could only drown his sorrows in wine.
7 On the Jǐchǒu day,
the emperor ordered Zhū Quánzhōng to write to Lǐ Màozhēn,
demanding the return of Princess Píngyuán.
Màozhēn did not dare to refuse
and immediately sent her back.
Princess Píngyuán had been married to Màozhēn's son Sòng Kǎn,
as recorded in the previous year's scroll.
8 On the Rénchén day,
Zhū Yǒuyù was appointed as Military Commissioner of Zhènguó.
Textual analysis notes: According to the Veritable Records:
"On the Rénchén day,
Xīngdé Prefecture was renamed Huázhōu,
granted the name Gǎnhuà Army,
and Yǒuyù was appointed as its Military Commissioner."
According to the Biānyí Lù,
in the third year of Tiānyòu,
on the Yǐchǒu day of the intercalary twelfth month, an edict stated:
"The titles Zhènguó and Xīngdé
should both be discontinued."
Xuē Jūzhèng's Historical Records of the Five Dynasties, Geography Section states:
"Huázhōu
was the Gǎnhuà Army under the Liáng."
The Liáng Meritorious Officials Biographies state:
"In the third year of Tiānfù,
Yǒuyù was appointed as acting Military Commissioner of Zhènguó."
Here, the Veritable Records are followed.
9 On the Yǐwèi day,
Quánzhōng petitioned to leave ten thousand infantry and cavalry in the former two armies.
At that time, the Shéncè two armies had been disbanded,
but their camps and offices remained.
He also appointed the Biàn general Zhāng Tíngfàn as Palace Garden Commissioner,
Wáng Yīn as Imperial City Commissioner,
and Jiǎng Xuánhuī as Street Commissioner.
Thus, Quánzhōng's followers were spread throughout the imperial guards and the capital's auxiliary regions.
The northern gate imperial guards of the Táng
were all stationed in the palace gardens.
The various government offices and the southern administrative guards
were all located within the imperial city.
The private residences of officials and the common people in the wards and markets
were all situated on the left and right sides of the Zhūquè Street.
Now, Quánzhōng appointed his trusted followers as commissioners,
consolidating control over the capital's auxiliary regions.
Getting rid of a viper only to be met by a tiger—
this describes Emperor Zhāozōng's situation.
On the Wùxū day,
Quánzhōng bid farewell to return to his military command,
taking his leave to return to Dàliáng.
The emperor also held a farewell banquet for him at the Yánxǐ Tower.
The emperor stood by the palace railing, weeping as they parted,
and ordered Quánzhōng to mount his horse in front of the tower.
This was to show him exceptional favor.
(Regarding "mounted in front,"
Shízhǎng glosses it.)
Quánzhōng also harmonized and presented a poem;
he further presented
five "Willow Branch Lyrics."
The "Willow Branch Lyrics,"
are what are now called língqǔ (short song forms).
Present-day song forms such as Qīngpíng Diào, Shuǐ Diào Gē, Zhèzhī, Púsà Mán, and Bā Shēng Gānzhōu,
are all remnants of the late Táng melodies.
Also, many Táng people composed "Willow Branch" poems,
all being heptasyllabic quatrains.
Tradition holds they originated from the Líyuán musical repertoire of the Kāiyuán era,
hence Zhāng Hù has a "Breaking Willow" lyric that says:
"Do not break the willow branches before the palace,
Xuánzōng once blew them in his flute."
Cuī Yìn alone escorted him to Bà Bridge.
Examining it by the Táng postal system's distances,
Bà Bridge Station should be thirty lǐ east of Chánglè Station.
At the second watch of the night,
Yìn finally returned and entered the city;
the emperor again summoned him for an audience,
asking about Quánzhōng's well-being;
they set out wine and had music played,
continuing until the fourth watch before ending.
The historian remarks that the emperor summoned people at irregular times,
and feasted and drank without restraint.
10. Appointed Péi Shū, the Jīngdōng military governor, as Menxià Shìláng and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
11. Lǐ Kèyòng's envoy returned to Jìnyáng,
and spoke of Cuī Yìn's tyranny.
Kèyòng said:
"Yìn, as a subject,
externally relies on the bandit's power,
internally coerces his sovereign.
He already controls the court administration,
and also grasps military authority.
When authority is heavy, resentment is many;
when power is equal, conflict arises.
The destruction of his family and the fall of the state
are before his very eyes!"
The historian remarks that Lǐ Kèyòng had insight.
(Regarding "court,"
it is glossed Zhíyáo.)
12. Zhū Quánzhōng, about to depart,
memorialized:
"Between Kèyòng and me,
there is originally no great grievance.
I beg to generously bestow favor and grace upon him,
and send a high minister to console and reassure him,
so that he may know my intent."
The memorial-submitting clerk reported this to Kèyòng.
(This was the memorial-submitting clerk from Hédōng.)
"The bandit wants to deal with Zīqīng,
but fears I will attack his rear!"
(Dealing with Zīqīng
means attacking Wáng Shīfàn.)
The historian remarks that Zhū Quánzhōng was crafty and deceitful,
and Lǐ Kèyòng had already anticipated his true situation.
(Regarding "attack,"
it is glossed Jūyǐ.)
13. In the third month,
on the Wùwǔ day,
Zhū Quánzhōng reached Dàliáng.
Wáng Shīfàn's younger brother Shīlǔ besieged Qí Prefecture.
(Zhū Quánzhōng, having annexed Yǎn and Yùn,
thereby also possessed Qí Prefecture.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: From Yǎn Prefecture north to Qí Prefecture is 360 lǐ.)
Shīfàn sent troops to reinforce Liú Xún's army,
but Yǒuníng attacked and captured them.
Consequently, Yǎn Prefecture's aid was cut off,
and Gé Cóngzhōu led troops to besiege it.
(Liú Xún's capture of Yǎn Prefecture is recorded in the first month of this year in the previous scroll.)
On the Wùchén day,
Quánzhōng led an additional 100,000 troops from the Four Commands and the Wèibó army to follow up.
14. Huáinán general Lǐ Shénfú besieged È Prefecture.
(In the first month of this year,
Yáng Xíngmì sent Lǐ Shénfú to attack Dù Hóng,
the matter began in the previous scroll.)
He said to the supervising eunuch Yǐn Jiànfēng:
"Tonight I will burn it for you."
Jiànfēng did not believe him.
At the time, Dù Hóng sought aid from Zhū Quánzhōng.
Shénfú sent his subordinate general Qín Gāo in a light boat to Shèkǒu.
(Shèkǒu is above Wǔkǒu,
and Xiàpǔ is on the opposite bank.
Regarding "Shè,"
it is glossed Shūshè.)
Hóng, thinking rescue troops had arrived,
indeed burned reeds in response.
15. In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Jǐmǎo day,
Zhū Quánzhōng was appointed to administer the affairs of the Yuánshuài Fǔ.
(Huīwáng was young and immature;
appointing Zhū Quánzhōng to administer the Yuánshuài Fǔ
meant all military authority in the realm was henceforth vested in him.)
16. The administrator of Wēn Prefecture affairs, Dīng Zhāng, was killed by the carpenter Lǐ Yàn.
(Dīng Zhāng obtaining Wēn Prefecture is recorded in the second year in the previous scroll.
He had not received a court appointment as prefect,
and was only called administrator of prefecture affairs.)
17. Wáng Shīfàn sought aid from Huáinán.
On the Yǐwèi day,
Yáng Xíngmì sent his general Wáng Màozhāng with 7,000 infantry and cavalry to rescue him,

there was no need for the military designation there,
so its name was transferred to Jīngzhào.
In the second year of Tiānyòu,
Zhèng Zāng was still the deputy commander of the Western Capital.
Thus, although a military designation was established,
the capital name still remained.
Liú Zhījùn, the prefect of Zhèngzhōu, was appointed as the military governor of Kuāngguó.
On the Dīngsì day,
the Emperor again sent a secret envoy with a silk edict to urgently inform Wáng Jiàn, Yáng Xíngmì, Lǐ Kèyòng, and others,
ordering them to unite the feudal towns to plan for restoration,
saying:
"Once I reach Luòyáng,
I will be imprisoned and confined.
Edicts and decrees will all come from his hands,
and my intentions will no longer be communicated!"
Yáng Xíngmì sent Qián Chuánliáo and his wife, along with Gù Quánwǔ, back to Qiántáng.
Qián Chuánliáo had been a hostage with Yáng Xíngmì,
as seen in the second year of Tiānfù in the previous volume.
Lǐ Shénfú, the military commander of Huáinán, was appointed as the pacification commissioner of Èyuè,
and again led troops to attack Dù Hóng.
Tián Jūn had already been pacified,
so Lǐ Shénfú was again sent to attack Dù Hóng.
He requested to spare Èyuè
and restore the former good relations.
Xíngmì replied:
"Wait until the Son of Heaven returns to Cháng'ān,
then we will cease military operations and restore good relations."
Yáng Xíngmì's heart was set on expanding his territory,
while Zhū Quánzhōng's heart was set on usurping the Táng.
Quánzhōng lacked the strength to rescue Dù Hóng,
hence these words.
Xíngmì's reply
used the pretext of heavenly punishment to refute his argument,
but his true ambition was not in this.
Hǎo, pronounced as hū dào fān.
7 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the Xīnsì day,
Zhū Quánzhōng memorialized that the palaces and buildings in Luòyáng were now completed,
and requested the imperial carriage to depart early.
Memorials and petitions followed one after another.
The Emperor repeatedly sent palace attendants to convey that the Empress had just given birth,
and was not yet fit to travel,
requesting to wait until the tenth month to proceed east.
Zhū Quánzhōng suspected the Emperor was hesitating and waiting for a change in circumstances,
suspecting the Emperor was lingering to await armies from the various circuits coming to the aid of the sovereign.
He said to his subordinate general Kòu Yànqīng:
"You go quickly to Shǎn,
and urge the 'official family' to set out today!"
For a subject to summon his sovereign—
what kind of language is this!
Huá Dū had a mind that disregarded his sovereign before he proceeded to evil deeds;
the gentleman knew this at the time he attacked the Kǒng clan.
As for the mind of Zhū Quánzhōng,
manifested in his countenance,
expressed in his voice—
was it one that had a sovereign,
or one that had no sovereign!
Furthermore, note that during the Western Hàn, court ministers referred to the Son of Heaven as
"the county official";
since the Eastern Hàn, he was called
"the state family";
during the Táng period, within the palace they generally called the Son of Heaven
"the household master".
Also, the court ministers and lesser ones called him
"the official family".
Some say: the meaning likely derives from the Five Emperors who treated the world as public (official),
and the Three Kings who treated the world as family.
On the Dīngyǒu day,
the imperial carriage departed from Shǎn;
on the Rényín day,
Zhū Quánzhōng met it at Xīn'ān.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Xīn'ān County is seventy lǐ west of Luòyáng.
The Director of the Astrological Service reported:
"The stars and celestial signs show changes,
the critical period is this autumn,
it is unfavorable to travel east."
This was an omen of the regicide in the Pepper Palace.
Heaven's display of celestial phenomena to warn—
is it not abundantly clear!
At this point,

Zhū Quánzhōng ordered the medical official Xǔ Zhāoyuǎn to accuse the Medical Official Commissioner Yán Yòuzhī, the Director of the Astrological Service Wáng Chí, the Palace Intendant Wéi Zhōu, and the Lady of the State of Jìn, Kě Zhèng, among others, of plotting to harm the Marshal.
He had them all arrested and killed.
At the end of the Táng, the post of Medical Official Commissioner was established to oversee the medical officials.
Palace Intendant,
was a duty of the Palace Attendants Service during the High Táng.
By the Sòng,
following the Táng system,
there were Chief Palace Attendants of the Left and Right Bans, Palace Attendants of the Left and Right Bans, and Vice Palace Attendants.
The deaths of Yán Yòuzhī and Wáng Chí
were because they spoke of the stars and celestial signs;
the deaths of Wéi Zhōu and Kě Zhèng
were because they were close confidants who whispered.
The Marshal,
was Zhū Quánzhōng.
On the Guǐmǎo day,
the Emperor rested at Gǔshuǐ.
Gǔshuǐ,
is west of Luò City.
Rest,
pronunciation: qù lì fān.
The Six Armies had all scattered and vanished,
leaving only the polo-playing attendants and the young servants of the inner gardens, totaling over two hundred persons,
who followed the Emperor eastward.
Examination of discrepancies: The Hòu Táng Jìnián Lù says five hundred men;
the Veritable Records follow this.
Here we follow the Old Annals and the Old History of the Five Dynasties.
Food was set out for them in tents,
and they were all strangled to death.
Over two hundred others of similar size and age had been pre-selected,
dressed in their clothes,
to replace them as guards.
The Emperor did not notice at first,
and only realized after several days.
From then on, all the attendants in charge of duties and orders around the Emperor
were Zhū Quánzhōng's men.
On the Jiǎchén day,
the imperial carriage departed from Gǔshuǐ,
entered the palace,
ascended the main hall,
and received court congratulations.
At that time, the Zhēnguān Hall was used as the main hall,
and the Chóngxūn Hall was used for inner court audiences.
Court,
pronunciation: zhí yáo fān.
On the Yǐsì day,
the Emperor appeared at the Guāngzhèng Gate.
At that time, after moving the capital to Luò,
palace gate names were changed;
the Chánglè Gate was renamed the Guāngzhèng Gate.
The reign title was changed.
It was changed to Tiānyòu.
An edict was issued to campaign against Lǐ Màozhēn and Yáng Chóngběn.
On the Wùshēn day,
an imperial order decreed that within the various palace offices, only the nine commissioners including the Xuānhuī were to be retained.

At that time, only the two Xuānhuī bureaus, the Small Stables, the Fēngdé Storehouse, the Imperial Kitchen, the Guest Reception Bureau, the Palace Gate Bureau, the Flying Dragon Stables, and the Manors Bureau—nine commissioners—were retained.
All others were abolished,
and henceforth palace ladies were not to serve as commissioners.
Examination of discrepancies: The Biānyí Lù states:
"On the Wùshēn day,
the imperial carriage had just arrived in the eastern capital Luò,
expenses were vast;
moreover, state funds were not abundant,
all affairs were in initial stages,
therefore redundant offices and bureaus were eliminated.
Henceforth, apart from retaining the Xuānhuī and other nine commissioners,
all others are abolished,
and palace ladies are not to be appointed as commissioners."
It seems that after the initial purge of the eunuchs,
the various inner commissioners were all held by palace ladies;
at this point, outsiders began to be used.
However, the Veritable Records changed 'serve as commissioners' to 'announce affairs',
which is an error.
Note: After the eunuchs were executed,
palace ladies were used to announce imperial decrees and serve as the various inner commissioners.
Since they announced imperial decrees,
the Veritable Records saying 'announce affairs'
is not entirely wrong either.
But in the third year of Tiānyòu,
palace ladies were dismissed from announcing imperial decrees,
therefore the Veritable Records is considered in error.
Wáng Yīn was made Commissioner of the Northern Xuānhuī Bureau and concurrently Commissioner of the Imperial City.
Zhāng Tíngfàn was made General of the Golden Guards and concurrently Commissioner of the Streets.
Wéi Zhèn was made Governor of Hénán Prefecture and concurrently Vice Commissioner of the Six Armies and Various Guards.
Also, the Deputy Military Governor of Wǔníng, Zhū Yǒugōng, was summoned to be Commander of the Left Dragon Martial Army,
and the Military Governor of Bǎodà, Shì Shūcōng, to be Commander of the Right Dragon Martial Army,
to be in charge of the palace guard.
All were trusted confidants of Zhū Quánzhōng.
On the Guǐchǒu day,
Zhāng Quányì was appointed Military Governor of Tiānpíng.
On the Yǐmǎo day,
Zhū Quánzhōng was appointed Military Governor of four circuits: Hùguó, Xuānwǔ, Xuānyì, and Zhōngwǔ.
Zhū Quánzhōng was previously Military Governor of four circuits: Xuānwǔ, Tiānpíng, Xuānyì, and Hùguó;
because Zhāng Quányì had the merit of managing and repairing Luòyáng for many years,
and now Luòyáng was established as the capital,
it was no longer a military circuit,
therefore Tiānpíng was given to Quányì,
and he himself concurrently held Zhōngwǔ to make four circuits.
8 The Military Governor of Zhènhǎi and Zhèndōng, the Prince of Yuè, Qián Liú, requested to be enfeoffed as the Prince of Wúyuè;
the court did not permit it.
Zhū Quánzhōng spoke to the chief ministers on his behalf,
and he was instead enfeoffed as the Prince of Wú.
In the first year of Tiānfù,
Qián Liú was enfeoffed as the Prince of Yuè.
For,
pronunciation: yú wèi fān.
Instead,
pronunciation: gōng héng fān.
9 The name of Wèibó was changed to Tiānxióng Army.
Emperor Dàizōng made Wèibó the Tiānxióng Army to honor Tián Chéngsì;
by Emperor Dézong's time,
Tián Yuè rebelled,
later returned to allegiance,
and was appointed Military Governor of Wèibó.
Now the old title of Tiānxióng Army was restored.
On the Guǐhài day,
the Military Governor of Tiānxióng, the Prince of Chángshā Commandery, Luó Shàowēi, was advanced in rank to the Prince of Yè.

First Year of Tiānyòu

1 In the fifth month,
on the Bǐngyín day,
the Military Governor of Héyáng, Zhāng Hànyú, was given the additional title of Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì.
2 The Emperor feasted Zhū Quánzhōng and all the officials at the Chóngxūn Hall.
At that time, the front hall of the Luòyáng Palace was called the Zhēnguān Hall,
and the inner court hall was called the Chóngxūn Hall.
The Emperor again summoned Zhū Quánzhōng to a feast in the inner palace;
Zhū Quánzhōng was suspicious,
and did not enter.
The Emperor said:
"If Quánzhōng does not wish to come,
have Jìng Xiáng come."
Quánzhōng nudged Xiáng to make him leave,
saying:
"Xiáng is also drunk."
Quánzhōng suspected the Emperor wanted to plot against him;
Jìng Xiáng was his trusted confidant,
therefore he did not let him enter either.
Nudge,
pronunciation: tā dí fān.
On the Xīnwèi day,
Quánzhōng returned east;
on the Yǐhài day,
he reached Dàliáng.
3 Zhōngyì Jiédùshǐ Zhào Kuāngníng dispatched a naval force upstream through the gorges to attack Wáng Jiàn’s Kuízhōu.
Zhào Kuāngníng used the troops of Xiāngyáng to spy on Kuímén.
Kuízhōu lies at the upper reaches of the Three Gorges.
Attacking it by sailing upstream,
hence the term “upstream through the gorges.”
Upstream,
Shí Zhǎng fān.
Wànzhōu Cìshǐ Zhāng Wǔ made iron cables to block the middle of the river,
erecting barriers at both ends,
calling it
“Locking the Gorge.”
4 In the sixth month,
Lǐ Màozhēn, Wáng Jiàn, and Lǐ Jìhuī issued a joint proclamation to raise troops to attack Zhū Quánzhōng.
Zhū Quánzhōng appointed Zhènguó Jiédùshǐ Zhū Yǒuyù as the expeditionary commander-in-chief,
leading infantry and cavalry to attack
them.
At that time,
the Shǔ troops did not advance,
and Zhū Quánzhōng’s forces could not reach them,
so he ordered Zhū Yǒuyù to attack Qí and Bīn.
He led his troops to station at Tóngzhōu.
Liú Xún was in Fūzhōu,
close to Lǐ Màozhēn and Jìhuī,
but with no support connecting them,
so he was ordered to abandon Fūzhōu and return to station at Tóngzhōu,
joining forces with Zhū Yǒuyù.
Fū,
pronounced fū.
On Guǐchǒu,
Zhū Quánzhōng led his troops from Dàliáng westward to attack Màozhēn and others.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on Jiǎzǐ,
he passed through Dōngdū and entered for an audience.
On Rénshēn,
he reached Hézhōng.
5 The generals of Xīchuān urged Wáng Jiàn to take advantage of Lǐ Màozhēn’s decline
to attack and seize Fèngxiáng.
Jiàn consulted his Jiédù Pànguān Féng Juān,
and Juān said:
“Weapons are instruments of misfortune,
harming the people and exhausting resources,
and should not be used to the extreme.
This means one should not exhaust military force.
Using all one’s military strength,
loving war without cease,
is exhausting military force.
The situation is such that they cannot coexist.
Liáng,
Zhū Quánzhōng.
Jìn,
Lǐ Kèyòng.
If they raise troops against Shǔ,
even if Zhūgě Liàng were reborn,
he could not withstand them.
Fèngxiáng is
Shǔ’s protective barrier.
It would be better to establish friendly relations with them,
forming a marriage alliance.
In times of peace, focus on agriculture and training troops,
securing and strengthening the borders.
In times of trouble, observe their movements,
watch for opportunities,
and act accordingly—this ensures complete safety.”
Jiàn said:
“Excellent!
Although Màozhēn is mediocre,
he has a reputation for being fierce and tough,
feared far and wide.
He is insufficient to contend with Quánzhōng,
but more than enough to defend himself.
Making him our protective barrier
brings great benefits.”
So he established friendly relations with Màozhēn.
Wáng Jiàn, having annexed the various prefectures south of the mountains,
guarded by the passes,
relied on Lǐ Màozhēn as a protective barrier outside the passes,
hence he established friendly relations with him.
Friendly relations,
Hū dào fān.
On Bǐngzǐ,
Màozhēn sent Pànguān Zhào Huáng to Xīchuān,
to seek a marriage for his nephew, Tiānxióng Jiédùshǐ Jìxūn.
Jiàn gave his daughter to him in marriage.
Màozhēn repeatedly requested goods and armor from Jiàn,
and Jiàn gave them all to him.
Depleting military supplies to enrich an enemy—
was this Wáng Jiàn’s true intention?
Relying on him for protection,
he did not tire of the repeated requests.
Repeatedly,
Suǒ jiǎo fān.
Wáng Jiàn’s taxes were heavy,
and no one dared speak out.
Féng Juān took advantage of Jiàn’s birthday to present a eulogy,
first praising his achievements and virtues,
then speaking of the people’s suffering.
Jiàn, ashamed, thanked him:
“With your loyal admonitions,
why worry about achievements!”
He rewarded him with gold and silk.
From then on, taxes were slightly reduced.
History records that Féng Juān used the eulogy to offer advice,
so his admonitions were easily accepted.
Taxes,
Lì shàn fān.
6 Earlier,
when Zhū Quánzhōng escorted the imperial carriage back from Fèngxiáng,
see volume 263, third year of Tiānfù.
Escorted back,
Cóng Xuān fān,
also as the original character.
and seeing that the emperor was already mature in age,
he disliked it,
and privately said to Cuī Yìn:
“Prince Dé once usurped the imperial throne,
referring to his enthronement by Liú Jìshù.
See events in volume 262, third year of Guānghuà and first year of Tiānfù.
Why don’t you mention this!”
Yìn spoke to the emperor.
The emperor asked Quánzhōng,
and Quánzhōng said:
“Between father and son, Your Majesty,
how dare I privately discuss it?
This is Cuī Yìn betraying me.”
History records Zhū Quánzhōng’s cunning.
The emperor worried daily about unforeseen events,
drinking deeply all day with the empress,
or weeping together.
Quánzhōng sent Shūmìshǐ Jiǎng Xuánhuī to spy on the emperor,
so all his movements were known.
The emperor casually said to Xuánhuī:
“Prince Dé is my beloved son.
Why does Quánzhōng insist on killing him?”
He then wept,
biting his middle finger until it bled.
Xuánhuī reported all this to Quánzhōng.
History records Emperor Zhāozōng’s frivolity hastening disaster.
Casually,
Qiān róng fān.
Bite,
Wǔ jié fān.
Report,
Niú jù fān.
At that time, Lǐ Màozhēn, Yáng Chóngběn, Lǐ Kèyòng, Liú Rén’gōng, Wáng Jiàn, Yáng Xíngmì, and Zhào Kuāngníng exchanged proclamations,
all using the restoration of the dynasty as their pretext.
Quánzhōng was leading troops westward to attack,
attacking Qí and Bīn to the west.
Fearing internal changes,
he wanted to install a young ruler,
making it easier to plan abdication and succession.
So he sent Pànguān Lǐ Zhèn to Luòyáng,
to plot with Xuánhuī, Zuǒ Lóngwǔ Tǒngjūn Zhū Yǒugōng, and Yòu Lóngwǔ Tǒngjūn Shì Shūcóng.
In the eighth month,
on Rényín,
the emperor was in the Pepper Hall,
Pepper Hall,
the empress’s hall.

It was said there was an urgent report from the front,
the front,
referring to the expeditionary camp to the west.
Lady Péi Zhēnyī opened the door and saw soldiers,
saying:
“Why bring soldiers for an urgent report?”
Shǐ Tài killed her.
Xuánhuī asked:
“Where is His Majesty?”
Shǎoyí Lǐ Jiànróng, leaning against the railing, cried out:
“Rather kill us,

The emperor, drunk,
suddenly rose,

Shǐ Tài pursued and assassinated him.
He was thirty-eight.
Tài also killed her.
They also wanted to kill Empress Hé,
but she begged Xuánhuī for mercy,
and he released her.
Empress Hé begged Jiǎng Xuánhuī for her life but ultimately died because of Xuánhuī.
Compromising principles to prolong life—
how could it compare to sacrificing oneself for Emperor Zhāozōng without losing integrity!
On Guǐmǎo,
Jiǎng Xuánhuī forged an edict claiming Lǐ Jiànróng and Péi Zhēnyī had committed regicide,
and it was appropriate to install Prince Huī Zuò as crown prince,
renamed Chù,

He also forged an empress’s order,
for the crown prince to ascend before the coffin.
The palace was terrified,
not daring to cry aloud.
On Bǐngwǔ,
Emperor Zhāoxuān ascended the throne,
aged thirteen.
7 Lǐ Kèyòng reappointed Zhāng Chéngyè as Jiānjūn.
Lǐ Kèyòng hid Zhāng Chéngyè; see previous volume, third year of Tiānfù.
Jiānjūn,
Gǔ xián fān.
8. Lǐ Shénfú, a general of Huáinán, attacked Èzhōu but had not yet captured it.
In the third year of the Tiānfù era,
Lǐ Shénfú first attacked Èzhōu.
In the first year of the Tiānyòu era, he attacked Èzhōu again.
These events are both recorded in the previous volume.
Upon returning to Guǎnglíng,
Yáng Xíngmì appointed Liú Cún of Bìyáng, the Tuánliànshǐ of Shūzhōu, to replace him as the Zhāotǎoshǐ.
Bìyáng
