In the Later Wèi dynasty, Shímǎ County was established there.
Later, the name was corrupted to Shàngmǎ.
It was abolished in the first year of the Zhēnguàn era.
In the sixteenth year of the Kāiyuán era, part of Húyáng was again separated to establish Shàngmǎ County.
In the first year of the Tiānbǎo era, it was renamed Bìyáng,
and placed under Tángzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Bìyáng County was originally the territory of Wǔyīn County in the Hàn dynasty, etc.,
as above.
In the Táng dynasty, it was changed to Bìyáng,
because the place was located north of the Bì River.
Tángzhōu was administered from there.
Bì
is pronounced with the initial "b" and the rhyme "ì".
Tái Méng, the Guāncháshǐ of Xuānzhōu, died.
Yáng Xíngmì appointed his son, Yáng Wò, the commander of the Yánèi Zhūjūn, as the Guāncháshǐ of Xuānzhōu.
Xú Wēn, the commander of the Right Yá Dūzhǐhuīshǐ, said to Yáng Wò:

Jí

9. In the ninth month,
on the Jǐsì day,
the Empress was honored as Empress Dowager.

then south to Luògǔ.
Stationing at Yǒngshòu

On the Xīnwèi day,
he returned east.
11. In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Xīnmǎo day, the first day of the month,

Feigning shock,
he wailed,
threw himself to the ground,

he arrived at the Eastern Capital.

The Emperor
refers to Emperor Zhāoxuān.
The culprits
are those who assassinated the sovereign.
Some soldiers of the imperial escort force plundered rice in the market.
On the Jiǎwǔ day,
Zhū Quánzhōng memorialized that Zhū Yǒugōng and Shì Shūcóng failed to restrain their soldiers,
who encroached upon and disturbed the markets,
using this as the crime of the two men.
He still dared not openly charge them with the crime of regicide.
He restored their original names to Lǐ Yànwēi.
Lǐ Yànwēi
was from Shòuzhōu.
He was a guest in Biànzhōu,
accumulating wealth and practicing chivalry.
Zhū Quánzhōng loved him and treated him as a son.
For textual analysis, see the 259th volume, second year of the Jǐngfú era.
Soon, both were ordered to commit suicide.
Yànwēi, facing execution, shouted loudly:

On the Bǐngshēn day,
Zhāng Quányì, the Tiānpíng Jiédùshǐ, came to court.
On the Dīngyǒu day,
Zhū Quánzhōng was again appointed as Xuānwǔ, Hùguó, Xuānyì, and Tiānpíng Jiédùshǐ;
and Zhāng Quányì was appointed as Hénán Yǐn, concurrently Zhōngwǔ Jiédùshǐ, and put in charge of the affairs of the Six Armies and various guards.
Zhū Quánzhōng concurrently held Zhōngwǔ,
and Zhāng Quányì commanded Tiānpíng,
as seen in the previous volume, last year.
After Zhū Yǒugōng and Shì Shūcóng were executed,
Zhāng Quányì was put in charge of the palace guard.
On the Yǐsì day,
Zhū Quánzhōng took leave and went to his garrison.
On the Gēngxū day,
he arrived at Dàliáng.
13. Zhū Yǒuyù, the Zhènguó Jiédùshǐ, died at Líyuán.
He died at the Líyuán military camp.

and surrendered to Zhū Quánzhōng.
Yáng Xíngmì sent troops to besiege it,

On the Wùchén day,
Zhū Quánzhōng personally led fifty thousand troops from Yǐngzhōu across the Huái River.
From Yǐngshàng County in Yǐngzhōu, he took Zhèngyáng to cross the Huái River.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì,
Huòqiū County is 127 li east of Shòuzhōu.
Note: During the Yuánfēng period, Shòuzhōu was administered from Xiàcài.
The Huáinán troops lifted the siege of Guāngzhōu and returned to Guǎnglíng.

Examination of discrepancies: The "Veritable Records of Liáng Tàizǔ" and Xuē Jūzhèng's "History of the Five Dynasties, Liáng Annals" both state:

and also sent his younger brother to take control of Jīngnán,

He had already dispatched commander Yáng Shīhòu to campaign against him.
The next day,
Quánzhōng personally led the army to advance."
The "Compilation of Omitted Records" states:
"On the rénchén day of the eighth month,

He arrived that day,
and then a campaign against Xiāngzhōu commander Zhào Kuāngníng was discussed.

chariots and troops were massively mobilized,
and Yáng Shīhòu was entrusted with overall command of the military administration.
On the jǐhài day,
the Emperor led his personal infantry and cavalry to follow behind the main army,
and that night they lodged at Wèishì."
The present account follows this.
Xuē's History states:
"Tàizǔ, planning for the abdication and succession,
because the Kuāngníng brothers both held military governorships,
first sent an envoy to convey his intentions.
Níng, facing the envoy, shed tears,
replying, 'I have received deep favor from the state;
how dare I recklessly harbor other ambitions following the times!'
The envoy reported back,
and Tàizǔ was greatly angered.
In the autumn of the second year of Tiānyòu, seventh month,
he dispatched Yáng Shīhòu to lead troops to campaign against him.
On the xīnwèi day,
Quánzhōng launched a southern expedition,
presenting a memorial listing Kuāngníng's crimes,
requesting the stripping of his official titles and nobility."
Considering that Quánzhōng had forcibly moved Emperor Zhāozōng to Luòyáng,
and Kuāngníng, together with Xíngmì and others, had issued a joint proclamation to the various circuits to campaign against him,
how could Quánzhōng possibly have inquired about abdication with him!
This is not adopted here.

Xuānyì administered Rǔ, Zhèng, and Huá;
Tiānpíng administered Yùn, Cáo, Pú, and Jì;
Hùguó administered Hézhōng, Jìn, Jiàng, Cí, and Xí;
Tiānxióng administered Wèi, Bó, Bèi, Wèi, Chán, and Xiàng;
Wǔshùn administered Zhèn, Jì, Shēn, and Zhào;
Yòuguó administered Jīngzhào, Shāng, and Huá;
Héyáng administered Mèng and Huái;
Yìwǔ administered Dìng, Qí, and Yì;
Zhāoyì administered Lù and Zé;
Bǎoyì administered Xíng, Míng, and Cí;
Róngzhāo administered Jīn, Jūn, and Fáng;
Wǔdìng administered Yáng;

Huáinán and the Zhè forces had been contending for the three prefectures of Wù, Mù, and Qú;
by this time, they all returned to the control of the Qián clan.
Chén,
is read as zhèn (array).
Shuài,
is read as shuài (to lead).
"The Zhè troops are close to us yet do not move;
they are belittling us.
I request to attack them!"
Lǚ Shīzào, emboldened by his victory at Qīngshān,
looked down upon the Zhè forces.
Jìn,
is pronounced jìn.
"I received orders to welcome Administrator Chén.
Now that he is here,
why should we fight again?
They surely have preparations waiting for us."
He then led his troops back.
Zhōu Běn served as the rearguard.
The Zhè troops followed closely behind,
but Zhōu Běn set an ambush along the way
and inflicted a major defeat upon them.
24 In the ninth month,
on the Xīnhài day, the first day of the month,
Zhū Quánzhōng crossed the river from Báimǎ.
On the Dīngmǎo day,
he arrived at Cāngzhōu
and encamped at Chánglú.
Dù Yòu said: Chánglú County of Cāngzhōu,
in Hàn times was called Cānlú.
In Sòng times, the county was abolished and became Chánglú Town,
belonging to Qīngchí County.
The people of Cāng did not come out.
Luó Shàowēi supplied provisions,
transporting them from Wèi to Chánglú over five hundred lǐ,
with an unbroken line along the road.
He also built a Marshal's Residence in Wèi.
The relay stations and pavilions along the route provided wine, food, tents, and various utensils.
For the tens of thousands of people, high and low,
not a single thing was lacking.
Luó Shàowēi served Zhū Quánzhōng generously,
not only to repay his kindness,
but also fearing that while attacking Guó, he might take Yú as well.
25 Qín Péi captured Hóngzhōu,
taking captive Zhōng Kuāngshí and five thousand others, and returned.
In the second year of the Xīzōng era's Zhōnghé period,
Zhōng Chuán occupied Hóngzhōu.
It ended with Kuāngshí.
Péi was appointed as the Hóngzhōu Military Commissioner.
Thus, the Yáng clan of Huáinán came to possess the territory of Jiāngxī.
26 Jìngnán Military Governor Yáng Chóngběn led the armies of Fèngxiáng, Bǎosāi, Zhāngyì, and Bǎoyì to attack Xiàzhōu.
"Bǎoyì"
should be
"Bǎodà".
This is because the Bǎoyì Army administered Xíng, Míng, and Cí,
which are in Shāndōng;
while the Bǎodà Army administered Fū and Fāng,
and together with Bīn, Qí, and other garrisons, were all in Guānxī.
Nán,
is pronounced nàn.
Xià,
is pronounced xià.
They beheaded over three thousand,
and captured Fāngzhōu Prefect Liú Yànhuī.
Fāngzhōu
was under the jurisdiction of the Bǎodà Army.
Using this to verify the earlier mention of
"Bǎoyì",
the error is clear.
27 Liú Réngōng came to rescue Cāngzhōu
but suffered repeated defeats in battle.
He then issued an order within his territory:
"All males aged fifteen and above,
seventy and below,
must prepare their own weapons and provisions and proceed to the army camp.
After the army departs,
if there is even one man remaining in the villages,
punishment will be without pardon!"
Someone admonished him:
"Now the old and weak are all going,
and women cannot transport supplies.
If this order is enforced,
there will be widespread indiscriminate punishment."
He then ordered all those fit to bear arms to go.
They tattooed their faces with the words
"Dìngbà Corps".
Scholars tattooed their wrists or arms
with the words
"Wholeheartedly Serve the Lord".
Thus, within the territory, among the scholars and commoners,
except for infants and young children, none were without tattoos.
He obtained a force of one hundred thousand,
and encamped at Wǎqiáo.
At that time, the Biàn army had built fortifications surrounding Cāngzhōu,
so tight that not even birds or rodents could pass through.
Liú Réngōng, fearing their strength,
did not dare to engage in battle.
Within the city, food was exhausted.
They made pellets from earth to eat,
and some even captured and ate each other.
Zhū Quánzhōng sent someone to persuade Liú Shǒuwén, saying:
"Reinforcements cannot reach you in time.
Why not surrender early?"
Shǒuwén climbed the city wall and replied:
"I, in relation to Yōuzhōu,
am father and son.
The Prince of Liáng is using great righteousness to subdue the realm.
If a son betrays his father and comes to you,
how will you use him?"
Zhū Quánzhōng felt ashamed at the straightforwardness of his words,
and for his sake, eased the attack.
28 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Bǐngxū day,
Wáng Jiàn first established a mobile administration in Shǔ.
Examination of Discrepancies says: According to the Continued Record of Precious Fortunes,
on the sixth day of the tenth month of the sixth year of Tiānfù, this proclamation was issued.
Thus it was in this year's tenth month.
He wailed in grief,
declaring:
"Since the imperial carriage moved east,
referring to Emperor Zhāozōng's move to Luòyáng.
I request to temporarily establish a mobile administration,
following the precedents of Lǐ Shèng and Zhèng Tián,
to carry out imperial orders for appointments and enfeoffments."
According to the record: When Lǐ Shèng campaigned against Zhǔ Cǐ,
he stationed at Dōng Wèi Bridge,
and only requested to temporarily appoint his subordinates Zhào Guāngxiǎn, Táng Liángchén, and Zhāng Yù as prefects of Yáng, Lì, and Jiàn prefectures,
to secure the strategic passage between Shǔ and Hàn.
The emperor had no time to grant this.
Later, he temporarily appointed Zhāng Yù as Junior Governor of the Capital Region to manage fodder and grain within the capital region,
and petitioned for official positions for Mèng Shè and Duàn Wēiyǒng, surrendered generals of Lǐ Huáiguāng.
He never carried out imperial orders for appointments and enfeoffments.
Zhèng Tián's acting on his own authority is recorded in the 254th scroll, in the first year of Emperor Xīzōng's Guāngmíng era.
29 Liú Réngōng sought aid from Hédōng,
sending over a hundred missions.
Lǐ Kèyòng harbored resentment against Réngōng for his duplicity.
Liú Réngōng had rebelled against Lǐ Kèyòng with Yōuzhōu,
and also allied with Zhū Quánzhōng to attack him.
This was what Kèyòng deeply hated.
His son Lǐ Cúnxù admonished him:
"The current situation in the realm:
seven or eight out of ten submit to Zhū Wēn.
Even powerful regions like Wèibó, Zhèn, and Dìng have all attached themselves to him.
North of the river,
the only ones who can trouble Wēn are us and Yōu and Cāng.
Now Yōu and Cāng are besieged by Wēn.
If we do not join forces with them to resist him,
it is not to our advantage.
Those who aim for the realm do not dwell on minor grievances.
Moreover, he once brought us hardship, yet if we rescue him in his crisis,
and win him over with virtue,
then in one move, both name and substance will be attached to us.
This is the time for our revival.
We must not miss this opportunity."
The historian remarks that Lǐ Cúnxù's wisdom and insight could supplement what his father lacked.
He discussed with his generals and officers the plan to summon the Yōuzhōu troops and attack Lùzhōu together,
saying:
"For them, it can lift the siege;
for us, it can expand our territory."
He then agreed to make peace with Réngōng
and summoned his troops.
Réngōng dispatched Capital
Commander Lǐ Pǔ to lead thirty thousand troops to Jìnyáng.
Kèyòng sent his generals Zhōu Déwēi and Lǐ Sìzhāo to lead troops and together with them attack Lùzhōu.
30 Xiàzhōu sent an urgent plea for help to Zhū Quánzhōng.
On the Wùxū day,
Quánzhōng dispatched Liú Zhījùn and his general Kāng Huáiyīng to rescue them.
Yáng Chóngběn led the troops of six garrisons, fifty thousand strong,
and encamped at Měiyuán.
Based on the text above,
Yáng Chóngběn was leading the troops of five garrisons.
He probably combined the troops of Qín and Lǒng to make six garrisons.
Chóngběn was heavily defeated
and returned to Bīnzhōu.
31 Wǔzhēn Military Governor Léi Yànwēi
repeatedly raided Jīngnán.
Acting Military Governor Hè Huái shut the city gates and defended himself.
Last year in the ninth month,
the Biàn general Hè Huái defended Jīngnán.
He was replaced by Yǐngzhōu Defense Commissioner Gāo Jìchāng.
Gāo Jìchāng from this point on came to possess Jīngnán.
Ní Kěfú from this point on pledged his service to Gāo Jìchāng.
The Lǎng troops
were the troops of Léi Yànwēi.
32 In the eleventh month,
Liú Zhījùn and Kāng Huáizhēn
judging from this,
the text above mistakenly wrote
"Huáiyīng".
...below;
Zhījùn was additionally appointed Tóng Píngzhāng Shì,
and Huáizhēn was made Military Commissioner of Bǎoyì.
I fear it was likely that Kāng Huáizhēn was ordered to Fūzhì,
"Bǎoyì"
should be
"Bǎodà";
this is verified by the Comprehensive Mirror's record next year of Kāng Huáizhēn as Military Commissioner of Bǎopíng,
but I also fear it was indeed Bǎoyì from this point.
The Western Army,
refers to the armies of Bīn and Qí.
33 The Governor of Hú Prefecture, Gāo Yàn, died,
and his son Gāo Lǐ succeeded him.
34 In the twelfth month,
on the yǐyǒu day,
Qián Liú submitted a memorial recommending the Army Commander Wáng Jǐngrén;
an edict was issued appointing Jǐngrén as Military Commissioner of Níngguó.
Wáng Jǐngrén is Wáng Màozhāng,
who abandoned Xuān Prefecture and returned to Qián Liú in the first month of this year.
Textual Analysis states: According to Xuē Jūzhèng's Old History of the Five Dynasties:
"Liú recruited him as Army Commander for the two prefectures,
and fully reported the situation.
Emperor Tàizǔ again ordered him to hold the titles of Military Commissioner of Xuān Prefecture and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì from afar."
Ōuyáng Xiū's New History of the Five Dynasties says:
"Liú memorialized for Jǐngrén to be appointed Military Commissioner of Xuān Prefecture."
I now follow this.
35 Zhū Quánzhōng divided tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry,
and sent Army Commander Lǐ Zhōuyí to lead them,
marching from Héyáng to rescue Lù Prefecture.
36 In the intercalary month,
on the yǐchǒu day,
the Zhènguó Army and Xīngdé Prefecture were abolished and reverted to Huá Prefecture,
placed under the Kuāngguó Military Commissioner,
and Jīn and Shāng Prefectures were carved out and placed under the Yòuguó Army.
Combining Tóng and Huá into one military district,
and carving out Jīn and Shāng to place under Yòuguó,
were both intended to strengthen their resources and power to defend against Bīn and Qí.
37 Earlier,
when the mournful news of Emperor Zhāozōng's death reached Lù Prefecture,
the Military Commissioner of Zhāoyì, Dīng Huì, led his officers and soldiers in wearing plain white mourning clothes and weeping for a long time.
When Lǐ Sìzhāo attacked Lù Prefecture,
Huì surrendered his entire army to Hédōng.
Textual Analysis states: According to the Tang Tàizǔ Jìnián Lù:
"On the dīngyǒu day,
Dīng Huì opened the gates and welcomed them in surrender.
In the intercalary twelfth month,
Tàizǔ appointed Lǐ Sìzhāo as the commander of Lù."
Xuē Jūzhèng's Old History of the Five Dynasties, the Liáng Annals, places it in the intercalary month,
while the Later Táng Annals places it in the twelfth month.
I now follow the New and Old Tang Annals, the Old History Liáng Annals, and the Biān Yí Lù.
Huì met Lǐ Kèyòng,
and wept, saying:
"It was not that Huì lacked the strength to hold out.
The Prince of Liáng tyrannized and abused the Tang house.
Although Huì received his favor of promotion and selection,
I truly could not bear his actions,
and thus have come to submit to you."
To lack a sense of right and wrong is to not be human;
Dīng Huì was one who possessed a sense of right and wrong!
He was placed above the other generals.
On the jǐsì day,
Zhū Quánzhōng ordered the various armies to prepare siege equipment,
intending to attack Cāng Prefecture.
On the rénshēn day,
he learned that Lù Prefecture was lost;
on the jiǎxū day,
he led his troops back.
Prior to this,
fodder and grain had been requisitioned from north and south of the Yellow River,
transported by land and water to the front lines,
piled up like mountains in the various camps.
As Quánzhōng was about to return,
he ordered it all burned,
the smoke and flames stretching for several miles.
That which was on boats was holed and sunk.
Liú Shǒuwén sent a letter to Quánzhōng, saying:
"Your Majesty, for the sake of the common people,
has pardoned my offenses,
lifted the siege, and departed—
this is Your Majesty's kindness.
The several tens of thousands of mouths in the city
have gone without food for months.
Rather than burning it into smoke,
or sinking it into mud,
I beg to be given the remainder to save them."
Quánzhōng, for his sake, left several granaries to give to him.
Liú Shǒuwén's words were humble and his situation pitiable,
thus even Quánzhōng's cruel and violent nature was moved by it.
遺 (wèi),
read as wèi according to the Jì Fān.
乞 (qǐ),
pronounced qì.
為 (wèi),
read as wèi according to the Yú Wèi Fān.
The Hédōng troops attacked Zé Prefecture,
but failed to capture it and withdrew.
38 The Governor of Jí Prefecture, Péng Gān, sent an envoy to request surrender to Húnán.
Since the Zhōng clan had perished,
Péng Gān thus requested surrender to the Mǎ clan.
玕 (gān),
pronounced gān.
Lù Zhèn's Jiǔ Guó Zhì writes it as
Zhōng Chuán appointed him as Governor of Jí Prefecture.
